descs.en: Lin Xiaoran is dramatic, affectionate, and impossible to handle. Zhou Yichen is patient, gentle, and hopelessly weak against her tears. Somehow, they fit together perfectly.

chapters.desc: He knew she was trouble the moment she started crying—and he still loved her too much to stop spoiling her.
chapters.title: The Boy Who Always Smiled at Her
chapters.content:
The winter sunlight spilled across the school rooftop, pale gold against the chilly afternoon air.

“Zhou Yichen, move.”

The boy sitting lazily on the bench looked up with his usual smile already waiting.

“You’re the one who came late, Xiaoran.”

Lin Xiaoran huffed dramatically and squeezed herself beside him anyway, shoulder shoving him hard enough that he nearly lost balance.

“You did that on purpose.”

“You’re too weak.”

“You literally attacked me.”

“But you’re still smiling.”

Because he always did. Whenever Lin Xiaoran was around, Zhou Yichen smiled like he forgot how to stop. He was the kind of boy girls whispered about in hallways—tall, calm, unfairly handsome, top student, captain of the basketball team. Yet the moment his girlfriend appeared, all that composed coolness disappeared into helpless indulgence. Especially when she pouted, and even more when she cried. And Lin Xiaoran cried easily.

“You brought milk tea?” she asked, eyes brightening.

Yichen handed her the warm cup from his coat pocket.

“Half sugar. No pearls.”

“Good boyfriend.” She pinched his cheek with satisfaction.

“You say that like you’re reviewing customer service.”

“I am.”

He laughed while she drank happily beside him, kicking her legs against the bench. From the rooftop door, their friends watched with disgust.

“Every day,” Chen Yuhao sighed.

Beside him, Tang Meilin rolled her eyes.

“You’re just jealous because you don’t have a girlfriend.”

Yuhao instantly straightened.

“That’s rude.”

Meanwhile, Xiaoran noticed them and waved.

“Why are you both standing there like divorced parents?”

“Because watching you two gives me diabetes,” Yuhao replied.

Yichen only smiled again. Meilin crossed her arms.

“Actually, Xiaoran, you should appreciate him more. If my future boyfriend tolerated even half your nonsense, I’d build him a temple.”

“I’m perfectly appreciative,” Xiaoran declared.

Yichen raised a brow.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She was cute in a way that made people forgive her far too easily. Yichen most of all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The problem started a week later. Basketball practice had just ended when Xiaoran came to the gym carrying snacks for Yichen. The gym still smelled of floor polish and sweat, and the last few players were dragging the ball cart back to the storeroom. But the moment she entered, she saw a girl from Class 2 handing him a towel. Pretty. Tall. Elegant. Exactly Xiaoran’s least favorite type. The girl smiled.

“Your game today was amazing.”

“Thanks,” Yichen replied politely.

That should have been the end. But inside Lin Xiaoran’s head, jealousy was loud. She walked over with a sweet smile that already made Yuhao—watching from nearby—mutter:

“Oh no.”

Xiaoran wrapped herself around Yichen’s arm possessively.

“Yichen who’s this?” she said brightly.

The girl introduced herself politely. Xiaoran smiled even wider.

“Ohhh, you’re the girl who confessed to him last semester, right?”

Silence. The girl’s face stiffened. Yuhao covered his face with both hands. Even Yichen’s smile disappeared. Xiaoran continued casually:

“You’re still trying?”

“Xiaoran,” Yichen said.

That tone alone made her pause. The girl looked close to tears as she hurried away. And suddenly the gym felt cold. Yichen gently removed Xiaoran’s arms from his sleeve.

“You went too far.”

Her chest tightened.

“What? I was joking.”

“It wasn’t funny.”

“She likes you.”

“And? That doesn’t mean you get to humiliate her.” His voice stayed calm, which somehow felt worse.

Xiaoran’s eyes went red. Yichen sighed internally the second he saw it. Because there it was. The tears. Always so fast.

“I’m not scolding you,” he said, more gently.

“But you’re angry.”

“I don’t like what you did.”

“You care more about her feelings than mine?”

“That’s not what I said.”

But Xiaoran already looked devastated.

“I was jealous,” she whispered.

Yichen rubbed his forehead.

“I know. But jealousy isn’t an excuse to hurt someone.”

She bit her lip hard, eyes watery. And then the worst possible thing happened.

“You’re being mean to me…”

Yichen nearly lost the argument right there. Lin Xiaoran crying was the one thing he had no defense against. He made himself stay firm anyway.

“Xiaoran. Don’t avoid the point.”

The tears spilled over. Great. Now he felt like the villain in a tragic romance drama. She turned and ran out of the gym before he could stop her. Yuhao walked over slowly.

“…You survived longer than expected.”

“Shut up.”

“You made her cry.”

“I KNOW.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Xiaoran ignored him for two days. Which meant: no waiting outside his classroom. No stealing his drinks. No dramatic good morning voice messages. No random “Do you love me more today or yesterday?” questions. Half the school noticed how miserable Zhou Yichen looked.

“He looks like a ghost haunting his own desk,” Yuhao commented.

“Go apologize already,” Meilin said.

“I’m not apologizing for telling her she was wrong.”

“But you’re suffering,” Yuhao pointed out.

Yichen leaned back in frustration. The truth was, he missed her. He even missed being annoyed by her.

That evening, he finally found her sitting alone behind the library, hugging her knees, sleeves pulled down over her hands the way she always did when she was sulking. The moment she saw him, she looked away.

“I’m still angry.”

“I know. You said so in seventeen messages.”

Her lips twitched slightly before she hid it again. Yichen sat beside her. For a moment, neither spoke. Then he sighed.

“Xiaoran.”

Silence.

“I’m sorry I was harsh.”

She sniffed. Here we go again.

“But, you really hurt her feelings,” he said gently.

“I know…”

“And if someone treated you like that?”

“I’d cry for ten business days.”

Despite himself, Yichen laughed. Xiaoran finally looked at him, eyes still watery.

“I just hated seeing her near you.”

“I know.”

“She looked so pretty.”

“You’re prettier.”

“That answer was too fast.”

“Because it’s true.”

Her ears turned pink. Yichen reached over and pulled her closer by the sleeve.

“You can be jealous. But don’t become cruel because of it,” he murmured.

Xiaoran lowered her head guiltily.

“…Okay.”

“And no more embarrassing people publicly.”

“…Okay.”

“And no crying every time I correct you.”

“I can’t control that.”

“You absolutely can.”

“You said you wouldn’t scold me anymore.”

Yichen sighed with complete defeat before pulling her into his arms anyway. She melted against him like a satisfied cat.

“You spoil her too much,” Meilin called from somewhere nearby.

The two looked up to find Yuhao and Meilin holding convenience store snacks while spying openly. Yuhao pointed accusingly.

“See? THIS is why she acts like a menace.”

Yichen didn’t even deny it. Xiaoran looked extremely pleased with herself. Then she tilted her head up at Yichen sweetly.

“You still love me?”

He looked down at her. She knew exactly what she was doing to him.

“Unfortunately, way too much,” he said, kissing her forehead lightly.
chapters.epigraph: “Some people are impossible to handle—and impossible not to love.”

chapters.desc: A claw machine, a chance meeting, and one boy who smiled like he already knew she was meant to stay.
chapters.title: Strawberry Milk Confession
chapters.content:
It started with a claw machine. Lin Xiaoran stood in the arcade with her arms crossed, glaring at the stupid plush bunny trapped behind the glass like it had insulted her whole family. Around her, the machines flashed and jingled, and somewhere behind her a group of middle schoolers were screaming over a racing game.

“This machine is rigged.”

“It’s not,” said a calm voice beside her.

She turned. And for half a second, she forgot what she’d been about to say. The boy standing there was tall, clean-looking, dressed in their school uniform with his sleeves rolled up. Sharp brows. Pretty eyes. The kind of face that got talked about in group chats. Most annoyingly, he was smiling. Not smug, not teasing. Just warm. Lin Xiaoran recovered quickly.

“You work for the machine company or something?”

The boy laughed.

“No. You’re just grabbing the bunny wrong.”

“I’ve tried eleven times.”

“That explains the problem.”

“What does THAT mean?”

“You’re impatient.”

She narrowed her eyes. Who even was this guy? The boy stepped beside her.

“Move.”

“Excuse me?”

“You want the bunny or not?”

Xiaoran shuffled aside and watched him suspiciously. He fed in a coin, adjusted the claw once—and won the bunny on the first try. Xiaoran gasped in betrayal.

“That’s impossible.”

He picked up the bunny and handed it to her.

“There.”

She hugged the plush automatically before catching herself.

“…Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

Then he smiled again. And for some reason, her heart skipped. It was annoying.

“What’s your name?”

“Zhou Yichen.”

Oh. So this was THE Zhou Yichen. Top student. Basketball captain. Third-year legend. Girls from other schools literally waited outside games for him. Xiaoran’s guard went straight up.

“Hm. You’re overrated.”

Yichen blinked once. Then he laughed—properly, like she’d said something genuinely funny.

“You’re cute,” he said absentmindedly.

Lin Xiaoran nearly dropped the bunny.

“What?!”

“Nothing.”

His smile only deepened. And that was the first problem.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that, they somehow kept meeting everywhere. Library. Convenience store. Bus stop. School festival prep. It became suspicious enough that Tang Meilin accused fate of being too obvious.

“You like him,” Meilin declared.

“I absolutely do not.”

“You brushed your hair three times when he walked past.”

“That was wind maintenance.”

“That’s not a thing.”

Lin Xiaoran pretended not to hear. But secretly, she noticed things. Like how Zhou Yichen always looked relaxed around everyone else, but around her, he smiled more. How he remembered every tiny thing she said. How he once turned up with strawberry milk after hearing her complain that the cafeteria had been sold out for three days. How he never got annoyed even when she acted bratty on purpose. Which she did frequently.

“Move,” she’d say, shoving him aside in the hallway.

“You walked into me.”

“You exist in my path.”

“That sounds like a personal issue.”

“Hm.”

And somehow, he always looked amused instead of offended. It made her chest feel weird.

One rainy afternoon, Xiaoran forgot her umbrella after cram school.

By the time she reached the school gate, the rain was coming down in sheets, bouncing off the pavement.

“…Great.”

“You’ll get sick.”

She turned to find Zhou Yichen standing behind her holding a black umbrella. Again. Smiling, as usual.

“Were you waiting for someone?”

“You.”

Her heart stumbled so hard it was humiliating.

“…Why?”

“You texted the class group complaining about the rain.”

“That doesn’t mean come rescue me.”

“But you sounded pitiful.”

“I was NOT pitiful.”

“You used three crying emojis.”

“That’s expressive communication.”

Yichen laughed before opening the umbrella over her head.

“Come on.”

The walk home became dangerous for Lin Xiaoran’s emotional stability. Zhou Yichen was gentle in ways she wasn’t prepared for. He tilted the umbrella toward her side. Walked closer to the road so passing cars wouldn’t splash her. Listened carefully even when she rambled nonsense. And worst of all, he looked at her like she mattered.

By the time they reached her apartment building, Xiaoran already knew she was doomed. Yichen looked down at her.

“You should go inside before you catch a cold.”

“…Okay.”

But neither moved. Rain poured softly around them. Xiaoran clutched the plush bunny still attached to her bag. Then blurted—

“Do you like me?”

Silence. Yichen blinked, clearly surprised. Unfortunately for her pride, nerves only made Lin Xiaoran more reckless.

“Because if you DON’T, then you should stop acting so nice to me all the time because it’s confusing,” she rushed out.

Yichen stared at her for two seconds. Then, slowly, he smiled. The smile that always made her weak.

“What if I do like you?”

Xiaoran’s brain stopped working.

“Oh.”

Very intelligent response. Yichen stepped closer under the umbrella. Up close, she could see his knuckles had gone white around the handle.

“What if I’ve liked you since the arcade?”

“…That fast?”

“You called me overrated within thirty seconds.”

“And that made you fall in love?”

“I found it refreshing.”

She stared at him, ears turning pink. This was bad. Now she wanted to say it too. And Lin Xiaoran hated being vulnerable. But she also hated lying. So after a full minute of silent suffering, she mumbled—

“…I like you too.”

Yichen’s whole face softened.

“Yeah?”

“I think about you too much. It’s affecting my studies,” she confessed with deep annoyance.

He laughed. And suddenly Xiaoran realized something that scared her a little. Zhou Yichen looked happiest when he was with her.

“Lin Xiaoran,” he said gently.

“…What?”

“Do you want to go out with me?”

Her eyes widened.

“So suddenly?”

“You confessed first.”

“That’s true.”

“And I don’t want anyone else asking you before I do.”

Her heart did something alarming. She tried to act calm anyway.

“Hm. I’ll consider it.”

Yichen raised a brow.

“You confessed two minutes ago.”

“That was before. This is negotiation.”

He laughed again, lowering his head slightly closer to hers.

“Okay then. Please let me be your boyfriend,” he murmured.

Xiaoran lasted exactly three seconds before smiling shyly.

“…Fine.”

“Fine?”

“Don’t push your luck, Zhou Yichen.”

“Yes, girlfriend.”

And hearing him say it for the first time felt warmer than the umbrella over their heads.
chapters.epigraph: “He found her in chaos, and stayed like it was home.”

chapters.desc: The first strawberry milk of the day is finished before lunch. The second comes with a boy who is very bad at pretending he was just passing.
chapters.title: The Second Strawberry Milk
chapters.epigraph: “So you don’t have to drink two.”
chapters.content:
The first strawberry milk of the day had been finished before lunch. Zhou Yichen had left it on her desk before the morning bell, on his way back to his own classroom two doors down, and walked off before she could say anything about it.

Lin Xiaoran had kept the empty carton on her desk for longer than necessary, mostly because Tang Meilin had spent the entire morning making comments about it. The milk wasn’t special. It was an ordinary carton from the school convenience store, with a pink label and a little strawberry printed on the front. The person who had bought it was the problem, because he had been her boyfriend for exactly six days, and nothing he gave her could go in the bin yet.

And, unfortunately, Meilin had noticed.

“You’re still looking at it.”

Xiaoran looked away from the empty carton.

“I’m not.”

“You’ve looked at it four times.”

“I was looking at the clock.”

“The clock is above the blackboard.”

Xiaoran slowly turned toward her friend.

Meilin smiled.

“Would you like me to ask Zhou Yichen to buy you another one?”

“Don’t you dare.”

“Why? He seems quite good at it.”

Xiaoran reached for her pencil case and lightly hit Meilin’s arm with it.

Meilin laughed, entirely pleased with herself.

The conversation might have ended there if not for what happened after their next class.

Xiaoran had just returned to her desk when she noticed something sitting beside her notebook.

A carton of strawberry milk.

She stopped.

Then she looked around.

It was the same brand as the one Yichen had bought her.

She thought Yichen had come by during the break. But the corridor outside was full of the wrong people, and he never left things without making sure she saw him leave them.

She picked up the carton.

It was cold.

“What’s that?” Meilin asked.

Xiaoran turned toward her.

“I don’t know.”

Meilin leaned over to inspect it.

“Strawberry milk.”

“I can read.”

“Someone bought you one?”

“Apparently.”

Meilin looked at the carton, then at Xiaoran, and her expression changed.

“Oh.”

Xiaoran didn’t like that particular oh.

“Maybe your strawberry milk story has become famous,” Meilin said.

Before Xiaoran could ask what she meant, a boy from the next row approached their desks.

It was Rong Hao, one of their classmates. He was friendly enough, usually lending people notes when they missed a lesson and occasionally helping the class monitor carry things.

He stopped beside Xiaoran’s desk.

“Did you get it?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“The milk?”

“Yeah. I bought it.”

“You did?”

“I heard you liked it.”

Xiaoran glanced at Meilin.

Meilin was interested in arranging her stationery.

Rong Hao scratched the back of his neck.

“At lunch I heard you telling Tang Meilin about the strawberry milk Zhou Yichen bought you. You said it was the best one in the shop, right? I was going to the convenience store anyway, so I thought I’d get you one.”

Xiaoran looked down at the carton again.

“Oh.”

She hadn’t realized anyone else had been listening, although, to be fair, she had described the milk to Meilin at a volume meant for the whole cafeteria.

“Thank you. That’s really nice of you,” she said politely.

“No problem.”

Rong Hao smiled, then returned to his seat.

The moment he was gone, Meilin slowly turned toward her.

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face is saying something.”

Meilin glanced at the milk.

“Two strawberry milks.”

Xiaoran sighed.

“One is from Yichen. One is from Rong Hao.”

“Yes. I can count.”

“They’re just milk.”

“Of course.”

Meilin picked up her pen and tapped it against the desk.

“So, what are you going to do?”

“Drink it.”

“Which one?”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“Both, eventually.”

Meilin burst out laughing.

“That’s a very diplomatic answer.”

Xiaoran opened the carton and took a sip, determined to behave as if nothing unusual had happened.

It was sweet.

A little too sweet, actually.

She looked at the carton again.

Her eyes drifted toward the classroom door, and Zhou Yichen appeared in it.

He was talking to one of his teammates, a basketball tucked under one arm, completely relaxed, until his eyes moved across the room and stopped at Xiaoran’s desk. More precisely, at the strawberry milk in her hand.

He didn’t react right away. He handed the ball to his teammate, said something that sent the other boy off down the corridor, and walked in as if Class 3 were his own.

“Another one?”

Xiaoran nearly swallowed the wrong way.

Meilin lowered her head.

Yichen stopped beside their desks, his expression as composed as ever. “Did you like the first one that much?”

Xiaoran put the carton down.

“Someone else bought this.”

“I can see that.”

She looked at him carefully.

His expression wasn’t displeased. If anything, there was a faint trace of amusement in his eyes.

“Rong Hao bought it,” she explained.

Yichen glanced toward the boy’s seat.

“Did he?”

“He heard me at lunch.”

“About the milk?”

Xiaoran nodded. Yichen looked at her for another moment, and his mouth curved slightly.

“I see.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means Rong Hao has good hearing.” He was still smiling.

“You’re smiling.”

“Am I not allowed to?”

Meilin made a small choking sound beside her.

Xiaoran ignored her.

Yichen reached for the empty carton that was still sitting near the corner of Xiaoran’s desk. He picked it up, examined it, then placed it in the recycling bin beside the wall.

“You kept that?”

Xiaoran’s face warmed.

“I forgot to throw it away.”

“Of course.”

The bell went. On his way out he stopped at Rong Hao’s desk, and half the class held its breath, but all he said was, “Good choice. That’s the one she likes,” in the same voice he used to thank the dinner ladies. Rong Hao went red to the ears and said thanks for some reason. Yichen tapped the corner of Xiaoran’s desk once on his way past and left for his own classroom without any hurry, as if he had all the time in the world and a teacher wasn’t already walking up the corridor behind him.

Meilin waited until he was out of sight before leaning close to Xiaoran.

“He’s smiling.”

“I know.”

“You’re blushing.”

“I am not.”

“You’re holding the strawberry milk like it’s evidence.”

Xiaoran looked down.

She was, in fact, holding the carton with both hands.

She put it down immediately.

Meilin laughed.

Ten minutes into the next lesson, while the teacher was copying a diagram onto the board, Xiaoran’s phone buzzed against her thigh. She slid it halfway out of her pocket under the desk.

Yichen: Is the second one as good as the first?

Xiaoran: It’s sweeter.

Yichen: Then don’t drink too much. You’ll get a stomachache.

Xiaoran: Are you jealous of strawberry milk?

There was a long gap. Long enough for the teacher to finish the diagram and turn around, and for Xiaoran to put on the face of someone who had been listening.

Yichen: No.

Yichen: I’m considering buying you something else next time.

She covered her mouth with her hand and pretended to cough.

Meilin, who had been watching the whole thing from the side, leaned over just enough to whisper. “Well?”

Xiaoran put her phone away and copied the diagram neatly, which was answer enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the afternoon break she went down to the convenience store and bought a packet of sesame biscuits, the expensive kind in the gold wrapper. Meilin followed her back upstairs and watched her put the packet on Rong Hao’s desk.

“For the milk. Thank you,” Xiaoran said.

Rong Hao looked at the biscuits, then at her, and seemed to understand something, because he laughed a little and said, “Okay. We’re even.”

“We’re even,” Xiaoran agreed, relieved.

On the way back to their seats, Meilin bumped her shoulder. “That was the most polite rejection I’ve ever seen.”

“It wasn’t a rejection. It was biscuits.”

“It was a receipt,” Meilin said.

By the end of the school day, Xiaoran had finished the second carton. She didn’t know whether Yichen had heard about the biscuits, but he was waiting outside her classroom door when the last bell went, and he looked at the empty carton in her hand.

“Finished?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

They walked toward the stairs together, and somewhere between the second floor and the first he said, casually, “Next time, I’ll buy you one before anyone else gets the idea.”

Xiaoran looked up at him.

“Why?”

He glanced down.

A small, teasing smile appeared.

“So you don’t have to drink two.”

She laughed.

“That sounds like a terrible problem.”

“For you, perhaps.”

He walked ahead by half a step, leaving her to catch up, and she did, the empty carton swinging from two fingers until she remembered she was allowed to throw this one away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning there was a carton of strawberry milk on her desk before the first bell. A yellow sticky note was stuck to the front, in handwriting she was getting to know.

First.

Meilin read it over her shoulder and groaned so loudly that three people turned around.

Xiaoran peeled the note off and stuck it inside the cover of her maths notebook, where nobody would look, and took out her phone.

Xiaoran: First?

Yichen: First.

Xiaoran: What time did you get here?

Yichen: Early enough.

She drank it slowly, all the way through the morning reading, and didn’t share a single sip when Meilin asked.

chapters.desc: The first time he walked her home, it rained too hard to see the street. The second time the sun is out, and he takes the long way on purpose.
chapters.title: Walking Her Home
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll walk you home again.”
chapters.content:
The first time Zhou Yichen walked Lin Xiaoran home, it had rained so hard that neither of them had seen the street. He had seen her face under the umbrella, her building’s front door, and little in between.

The second time, a week later, the sun was out.

“I’m walking you home,” he said.

They were standing outside the school building. Most students had already left, and the afternoon light stretched across the empty courtyard. Xiaoran looked up from the book she was holding.

Xiaoran stared at him.

Then she smiled.

“Why?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Because it’s getting late.”

She glanced at the sky.

It wasn’t late. There was still plenty of sunlight.

But she didn’t argue.

Instead, she tilted her head. “You know where I live.”

“I know where your front door is. It was raining sideways. I didn’t see the street.”

“Then I’ll show you. That way,” she said, with a look he would only understand later, and pointed toward the main road.

For the first ten minutes nothing seemed unusual. They talked about a mathematics question that had ruined her afternoon and the teacher who had assigned an unreasonable amount of homework for a Friday. Xiaoran was halfway through something Meilin had said at lunch when Yichen slowed down in front of a fruit shop.

The shop had a striped awning and a crate of peaches by the door. An old man sat on a stool beside the crate, fanning himself with a folded newspaper.

“That shop sells really good peaches,” Xiaoran said.

“You said that already.”

“Did I?”

“About fifteen minutes ago. In front of this shop.” He looked at the awning, then at the bus stop on the corner, which also looked familiar.

“There are two fruit shops on this road.”

“With the same man?”

The old man lifted his newspaper at them in greeting. Xiaoran waved back, which didn’t help her case.

“Lin Xiaoran, do you know the way to your house?” Yichen said.

“Of course I know the way to my house.”

“Then why have we walked in a circle?”

She studied the peaches with great interest. “It’s a rectangle, technically.”

He closed his eyes for a second. When he opened them he was laughing, not loudly, a quiet, helpless laugh that made her look at the ground.

“On purpose?”

“You said you’d walk me home. You didn’t say how long it had to take.”

The old man had stopped fanning himself to listen. Yichen bought two peaches from him, mostly out of embarrassment, and the old man told him Xiaoran’s mother bought from him every Sunday and that he should take the left at the corner if he wanted to get anywhere today.

“Thank you,” Yichen said, politely.

Xiaoran stood beside him with her face in the collar of her uniform.

Once they were out of earshot, he turned to her. “Twenty minutes.”

She pressed her lips together. “I know.”

“Past the same peaches twice.”

“They’re very good peaches.”

He looked at her. She looked back, and he laughed again.

Xiaoran frowned.

“Stop laughing.”

“I’m sorry.”

“You don’t sound sorry.”

“I really am.”

She walked a little faster.

Yichen followed easily.

After a few steps he caught up and took her hand.

“Don’t be upset.”

“I’m not upset.”

“Then why are you walking so quickly?”

“Because now you know, and it’s embarrassing.”

He smiled. “All right.”

She met his eyes.

“You don’t have to walk me anymore.”

“I know.”

“You’re going to be late.”

“I’m not.”

“You’ve already spent twenty minutes.”

“That’s all right.”

She looked at him. He wasn’t teasing now. His expression was calm, and his hand was warm around hers.

“I said I’d walk you home. I haven’t done that yet.”

Xiaoran looked away.

For some reason, that made her feel a little shy.

She let him hold her hand.

The direct route took eight minutes. They took the left at the corner, crossed at the intersection, and turned into a quieter residential street, and Xiaoran pointed out the landmarks anyway, because she had decided he would see them.

“That’s where I fell off my bike when I was nine.”

Yichen looked at the stretch of pavement, which had no features at all. “Did you cry?”

“For a reasonable amount of time.”

A little farther ahead, she pointed toward a small bakery. “They have really good bread.”

Yichen looked at the storefront.

“Do you like it?”

“Yes. Their strawberry buns are especially good.”

He looked down at her.

“Another strawberry?”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re still thinking about the milk?”

“Apparently, it’s becoming a theme.”

She grinned.

“Maybe you should buy me a strawberry bun next time.”

“All right.”

She blinked.

“I was joking.”

“I wasn’t.”

She looked at him, then quickly turned her face toward the road.

Yichen noticed the small smile she was trying to hide and didn’t say anything. He just went into the bakery, which smelled of butter and hot sugar, and came out with a paper bag that was already going see-through at one corner.

“I was joking,” she said again.

“You said that. Sit.” He broke the bun in half and held out the bigger piece.

They sat on the low step outside the bakery, between a bicycle and a pot of dying geraniums, and ate it with their schoolbags on their knees. The filling was too sweet and still warm. Xiaoran got some on her thumb and licked it off without thinking, and Yichen looked hard at the traffic.

“Meilin and I usually take the 46. It goes the other way round, past the hospital. It’s faster,” she said.

“Then why walk?”

“The bus doesn’t go past the peaches. And on the bus you can’t talk properly. Somebody’s grandmother always listens.” She brushed crumbs off her skirt.

“Somebody’s grandfather listened today.”

“He doesn’t count. He’s on our side.”

Yichen finished his half of the bun and folded the paper bag into a small neat square, because he was the kind of person who did that, and she watched him do it and thought, with some alarm, that she liked watching him fold a paper bag.

When they finally reached the entrance to her residential compound, Xiaoran slowed down.

“Here.”

Yichen looked ahead.

The entrance was modest, with a small security booth and a row of trees along the pavement.

He glanced at her. “So this is what it looks like when it isn’t raining.”

She nodded. Last week he had seen a wet gate and a doorway; now there was the security booth with a radio playing opera, a row of plane trees, a bicycle chained to the railing with a basket full of leeks. It wasn’t much. She had wanted him to have it anyway, the whole route, and the rectangle had been the only way she could think of to make it longer.

He held up the paper bag. “One of these is for your mother.”

“She’ll ask who they’re from.”

“Tell her the old man insisted.”

Xiaoran laughed.

He looked at the entrance again.

“Do you usually come home alone?”

“Sometimes. Sometimes with Meilin.”

“All right.”

She tilted her head.

“Why?”

“Just asking.”

He looked back at her.

“Let me know when you get inside.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Okay.”

Neither of them moved.

The afternoon was getting quieter. A few people passed through the gate, and somewhere inside the compound, a bicycle bell rang.

Xiaoran adjusted the strap of her bag.

“Thank you for walking me home.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Even the rectangle?”

“I’ll walk the rectangle again if you want. Just tell me first.”

“That ruins it.”

He laughed, and she looked pleased with herself.

Then she took a small step backward.

“Go home.”

Yichen glanced at the road behind him.

“I will.”

She hesitated.

Then, before she could change her mind, she reached forward and lightly caught his sleeve.

“Yichen.”

He looked down at her hand, then at her face.

“Hm?”

“Next time, I’ll take you the short way.”

His expression softened.

“Next time?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yes.”

He met her eyes.

Then his familiar smile appeared.

“Then I’ll walk you home again.”

She smiled back.

“Okay.”

He released her sleeve gently.

“Go inside.”

She turned toward the gate, took a few steps, then looked back.

Yichen was still standing there.

She waved.

He lifted his hand in response.

Only after she disappeared through the entrance did he finally turn around.

Yichen was halfway down the street when his phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: I’m home! Mom says thank you for the peach and who is the old man.

Yichen: Good. Tell her it’s a long story.

Xiaoran: It’s a rectangle.

He put his phone away, then took it out again a few steps later.

Yichen: Why the long way?

The typing dots appeared and disappeared twice.

Xiaoran: I wanted to show you.

He read the message twice, standing on the corner by the bakery.

Yichen: I know. Thank you. I’ll remember the fruit shop and the bakery.

Xiaoran: Mostly the bakery.

Yichen: Noted.

The walk home took him twenty minutes longer than it should have, because he went back past the fruit shop to see if he could find the rectangle on his own. He could. It had been an inefficient way to spend an afternoon, and he was fairly sure she had planned that part too.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen noticed her long before she noticed him—loud, chaotic, impossible to forget—and quietly decided she would become his favorite coincidence.
chapters.title: All Our Coincidences Were Intentional
chapters.content:
Before Zhou Yichen ever spoke to Lin Xiaoran, he already knew three things about her. First, she was loud. Second, she was dramatic. Third, she could cry faster than anyone he had ever met.

The first time he noticed her was outside the teachers’ office. A girl in a slightly messy uniform stood there arguing with a teacher over confiscated snacks.

“But I need instant noodles,” she protested.

“You don’t.”

“What if I faint from heartbreak during math class?”

“You won’t.”

“How can you be so sure?”

At first, Yichen had only been walking past. Then the girl sighed and muttered under her breath—

“This school suppresses artistic souls.”

The teacher nearly laughed despite herself. Yichen did too. The girl was cute. Not just pretty—every single thing she felt showed on her face. That should’ve been the end of it. But after noticing someone once, somehow you kept seeing them everywhere. In the cafeteria complaining because her pudding was sold out. In the hallway fake-crying because her friend Tang Meilin refused to lend her lip gloss. In class presentations confidently speaking nonsense with full conviction.

“She’s ridiculous,” Chen Yuhao commented one afternoon while the basketball team walked past the courtyard.

Below them, Lin Xiaoran sat on a bench sulking while Meilin ignored her.

“What happened?” Yichen asked.

“She lost rock-paper-scissors.”

“…That’s why she looks heartbroken?”

“She takes competition seriously.”

Yichen watched as Xiaoran grabbed Meilin’s sleeve and whined something shameless enough to make Meilin shove her away. Instead of getting angry, Xiaoran just laughed, loud and careless, like she had never once worried what anyone thought of her. Yichen looked away after a second. For some reason, he was smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second time she truly caught his attention was during rain duty week. Students rushed through the corridors while teachers yelled about slippery floors. Yichen carried sports equipment back toward the gym when he noticed a familiar figure crouching beside the school garden. Lin Xiaoran was crouched in the rain with a tiny soaked kitten tucked inside her jacket, her own hair dripping.

“What are you doing?” Meilin asked beside her.

“It looked cold.”

“You’re also cold.”

“I’m tougher than him.”

The kitten meowed pitifully. Xiaoran looked devastated.

“Oh no. Don’t sound so pitiful,” she whispered, hugging it carefully.

Yichen laughed before he could stop himself. Xiaoran looked up. Their eyes met for the first time. Yichen saw her properly then. Soft features. Bright eyes. Pink lips slightly parted in surprise. For one second, Xiaoran simply stared. Then her eyes narrowed.

“…Why are you laughing?”

“Nothing.”

“You definitely laughed at me.”

“A little.”

“Hm. Rude.”

But she didn’t actually sound offended. Yichen walked away afterward. But he kept thinking about her. About how she held the kitten so gently. About how expressive her face was. About how alive she felt compared to everyone else around him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The arcade encounter one week later wasn’t exactly coincidence. Well. Not entirely. The basketball team had won a practice match nearby, and Yuhao suggested going to the shopping center arcade afterward. Yichen normally would’ve refused. But walking past the claw machines, he stopped. There she was again. Lin Xiaoran. Standing before a claw machine with absolute fury on her face.

“I’ve already spent twenty-seven yuan,” she told Meilin.

“Then stop.”

“No.”

“The bunny looks ugly anyway.”

“Don’t insult him.”

Yichen watched silently from several machines away. Xiaoran failed again. And again. Then she crouched in front of the machine and pointed accusingly.

“You and I are enemies now.”

Meilin looked exhausted.

“You’re talking to a machine.”

“It started first.”

Yichen laughed. Before he knew it, he was walking toward her.

“You’re grabbing the bunny wrong.”

Xiaoran spun around. Yichen almost smiled. It was exactly the face she’d made defending instant noodles to the teacher.

“You work for the machine company or something?” she demanded.

And just like that, they were talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the arcade, the “coincidences” started piling up. Except most of them were caused by Zhou Yichen himself. He simply never admitted it. Like the convenience store encounter. Xiaoran entered after school craving strawberry milk only to discover the shelf empty.

“This country has failed me,” she sighed.

A hand appeared beside her, holding the exact drink.

“You can have mine.”

She turned. Zhou Yichen stood there as if this were fate, and not because he’d bought the last bottle ten minutes earlier, knowing the store was almost out.

“…Why are you here?”

“Buying water.”

“You bought strawberry milk.”

“I wanted this earlier. But not anymore.”

She laughed despite herself. Right then, Yichen decided he wanted to make her laugh as often as possible.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then came the library coincidence. Which was definitely not coincidence. Yuhao had mentioned that Xiaoran studied there every Wednesday, because her home WiFi died every week for “mysterious reasons.” The mysterious reason turned out to be her neighbor, who had been stealing it to download pirated games. So, naturally, Yichen started studying there every Wednesday too.

The first time Xiaoran spotted him, she squinted at him.

“You’re everywhere.”

“That sounds romantic.”

“That sounds creepy.”

He smiled lazily.

“Then I’ll leave.”

“…I didn’t say leave.”

Yichen sat back down. Xiaoran looked horrified at herself for saying that out loud. He nearly laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then came the bus stop coincidence. The café coincidence. The hallway coincidence. The school festival coincidence.

At first, Xiaoran genuinely believed fate kept pushing them together.

Meanwhile, Yuhao watched Yichen deliberately take the long way between classes just to “accidentally” run into Xiaoran near Building C.

“You’re actually shameless,” Yuhao said.

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“You changed your entire lunch schedule because she eats earlier.”

“Coincidence.”

“You hate the cafeteria before noon.”

“People change.”

Yichen rubbed the back of his neck, which was what he always did when he was lying. Yuhao stared at him in disbelief. Zhou Yichen—calm, rational, untouchable Zhou Yichen—was staging run-ins like the lead in a romance drama. And he looked happy doing it. The moment she came into view, his whole expression changed. His smile went warm and easy, like she’d brought the sun in with her and didn’t know it.

One afternoon, Yuhao finally asked the obvious question.

“What exactly do you like about her so much?”

Yichen looked toward the courtyard below. Lin Xiaoran was down there again, complaining about something while Meilin ate her lunch in peace. Probably another crisis. Yichen watched her, smiling without realizing it.

“She makes everything feel less tiring.”

Yuhao blinked. Below them, Xiaoran happened to look up. Their eyes met across the courtyard. Her whole face lit up, like she was happy to see him and hadn’t noticed yet. Yichen smiled wider. And right then, he knew he was in serious trouble.
chapters.epigraph: “Before he ever spoke to her, he had already started choosing her.”

chapters.desc: Evening self-study seats are now assigned by exam rank, both classes together, and fourteen desks between her and Zhou Yichen is thirteen too many.
chapters.title: Seat Swap
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to rush.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had never considered academic rankings important.

She cared about passing her exams, getting decent grades, and not having to spend her weekends buried under revision notes. She liked learning things that interested her, but she had never been the sort of student who measured her happiness by the number beside her name on an examination list.

Until the seating arrangement changed.

Class 3 and Class 1 shared evening self-study. Every night from seven to nine, both classes sat in the big room on the fourth floor, the one with the broken clock and the fans that only worked on one side, and until that Monday everyone had sat wherever they liked. Which meant Xiaoran had sat one desk from Zhou Yichen for three weeks, and had begun to think of that as a law of nature.

On Monday the grade director walked in with a stack of papers and announced that, starting that night, self-study seats would be assigned by the results of the latest monthly examination, both classes ranked together. The highest-ranking student would choose first, then the second, then the third, all the way down.

There was a collective groan.

“Teacher, why?”

“Because some of you have been treating the back row like a holiday resort,” the director said.

Xiaoran was busy looking through her pencil case.

She didn’t mind where she sat, as long as it was where she already was. Then the director began reading the rankings.

“First, Zhou Yichen.”

Xiaoran looked up.

Yichen stood, collected his result sheet, and walked to the front.

He glanced at the room, chose a desk near the middle, and put his books down.

The director called the second name.

By the time the director reached the lower half of the list, Xiaoran had begun to wonder whether her name would be called before or after Meilin’s.

Then she heard it.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

She stood up.

She found an available seat and sat down.

Only after arranging her books did she realize something.

Yichen was sitting farther away than before.

Xiaoran stared.

She turned to Meilin, behind her.

“How many people are between us and Zhou Yichen?”

Meilin followed her gaze and counted the desks under her breath. “Fourteen. Fifteen if you count Chen Yuhao, who is basically two people.”

Xiaoran looked forward again.

She could see the back of Yichen’s head.

He was already taking out his textbook.

She turned back to Meilin.

“I don’t like this.”

Meilin slowly smiled.

“Interesting.”

“What?”

“You’ve never complained about your seat before.”

“I haven’t.”

“And now?”

Xiaoran lowered her voice.

“He’s too far away.”

Meilin stared at her for two seconds.

Then she put her hand over her mouth.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“Your shoulders are shaking.”

Meilin bent over her desk.

“I’m trying.”

The first night was manageable.

Xiaoran could still see Yichen if she looked past the students in front of her. At the eight o’clock break she could walk over to his desk. In the daytime they were in different classrooms anyway, so it wasn’t as if the new seats had taken anything away from the day. Only the evening, and the evening had been the best part.

But there were small inconveniences.

When Yichen sighed at a physics problem, she couldn’t hear it. When the teacher on duty walked out for ten minutes, she couldn’t slide a note onto his desk. And when she finished an exercise, she couldn’t casually lean over and compare answers with him.

On Tuesday, she tried to solve the problem herself. She waited until the eight o’clock break, then walked over to Yichen’s desk.

He was reading something when she arrived.

“Yichen.”

He looked up.

“Yes?”

“Do you like your new seat?”

He glanced around.

“It’s fine.”

“Isn’t it a little far from everyone?”

“Not particularly.”

Xiaoran pulled out the empty chair beside him.

“Can I sit here?”

“Of course.”

She sat down.

For the next ten minutes, they talked about homework, the upcoming quiz, and whether the cafeteria had changed its menu again.

Unfortunately, the bell rang.

Xiaoran returned to her seat, and the distance remained.

On Wednesday, Meilin discovered something. It was just after lunch, in their own classroom, and Xiaoran had opened her history textbook and was copying dates into a notebook in three colors.

Meilin watched her for a while.

Then she leaned forward.

“What are you doing?”

“Studying.”

“I can see that.”

“Then why are you asking?”

Meilin pointed at the textbook.

“Since when do you review history during lunch?”

Xiaoran continued writing.

“Since today.”

“Why?”

“Because there’s a test.”

“In four weeks.”

“I know.”

“You’re serious.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yes.”

Meilin sat back slowly.

A moment later, she asked, “Is this about Zhou Yichen?”

Xiaoran’s pen stopped.

“No.”

Meilin nodded thoughtfully.

“All right.”

She returned to her own lunch.

Xiaoran resumed writing.

Three seconds later, Meilin spoke again.

“Because if it is, I think you should just admit it.”

Xiaoran turned.

“Meilin!”

Meilin laughed.

“Fine, fine.”

She leaned closer.

“But seriously, what happened? You suddenly look like someone who’s preparing for an academic competition.”

Xiaoran lowered her voice.

“I just want to improve my ranking.”

“Why?”

Xiaoran looked down at her notes.

Then, she said, “I want to sit closer.”

Meilin went still.

A smile slowly spread across her face.

“Oh.”

“Don’t.”

“How close?”

Xiaoran hesitated.

Then she muttered, “Within two desks.”

Meilin stared at her.

And then she laughed until the student in front turned around.

By Thursday, Xiaoran had done the arithmetic, which was the only arithmetic she would willingly do. Mathematics was a lost cause; she could study it for a month and gain four points. But history, English, Chinese and politics were subjects where effort turned into marks, and there were four of them. She reviewed history at lunch, read English vocabulary before homeroom, and spent the self-study hour on the essay questions she normally left until the night before.

She still asked Yichen for help with mathematics, because there was no point in pretending, and because he could explain things without making her feel stupid for asking. At Thursday’s break she brought her exercise book to his desk.

“Can you look at this?”

Yichen put down his pen.

“Which question?”

“This one.”

He glanced at the page.

“You made a mistake here.”

Xiaoran leaned closer.

“Where?”

He pointed to the calculation.

“You changed the sign.”

She examined it, then sighed.

“Oh.”

“Try it again.”

She took her pencil and started working.

Yichen watched her.

“You’ve been working harder lately.”

Xiaoran looked up. “Have I?”

“You’ve been writing the whole time. Every time I turn round.”

“You turn round?”

“I want to see if you’re asleep. Try it again.” He tapped the question.

She nodded. “I want to improve.”

He smiled.

“That’s good.”

She looked at him, trying to gauge whether he suspected anything.

He didn’t seem to.

So she returned to the question.

After a moment, he reached for another piece of paper and wrote down a shorter method.

“Try this way. It’s easier to remember.”

She looked at his handwriting, then at him.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

She took the paper.

She was about to go back to her desk when he said, “You don’t have to rush.”

Xiaoran paused.

“Your grades. There’s time before the next examination,” he said.

Her mouth tipped up.

“I know.”

He nodded.

“Good.”

She returned to her seat with the paper tucked carefully inside her exercise book.

Meilin watched her arrive.

“Did he ask why you’re studying so hard?”

Xiaoran sat down.

“No.”

“Did he figure it out?”

“No.”

Meilin smiled.

“He’s clever. I don’t believe you.”

Xiaoran opened her book.

“Then don’t.”

The days passed.

Xiaoran’s study routine became a little more serious than she had intended.

She began finishing her homework earlier, checking answers twice, and asking questions whenever she encountered something she didn’t understand. She didn’t become the best student in the class. She still got distracted.

She still spent too much time choosing highlighters. Mathematics still treated her like a stranger.

And she still occasionally stared out of the window instead of listening to the teacher.

But she was trying.

Actually trying.

The night before the next monthly examination, Meilin called her.

“Are you studying?”

“Yes.”

“You’re not watching a drama?”

“No.”

“Are you sick?”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Meilin!”

“I’m worried. You’ve changed.”

“I haven’t changed.”

“You’ve been studying every day.”

“That’s normal.”

“Not for you.”

Xiaoran rolled onto her back and looked at the ceiling.

“Can you stop?”

Meilin laughed.

Then her voice softened.

“Seriously, don’t put too much pressure on yourself.”

“I’m not.”

“Good. You know you don’t have to get first place.”

“I know.”

“And you don’t have to get into the first few ranks just because of him.”

Xiaoran was quiet.

“I know. But I want to,” she said after a while.

Meilin didn’t tease her this time.

“All right. Then do your best.”

“I will.”

The results were released the following Monday.

Xiaoran was more nervous than she had expected.

She stood near the classroom noticeboard, looking for her name.

The rankings were listed from top to bottom.

Her eyes moved down the page.

She found Yichen first.

As expected, he was near the top.

Then she searched for herself.

She read the number beside her name.

Once.

Twice.

Then she smiled.

She had improved. Quite a bit, actually. Her mathematics mark had gone up by three points, which was a rounding error, but history had gone up by nineteen and English by eleven, and together they had moved her up the combined list by thirteen places.

Meilin appeared beside her.

“Well?”

Xiaoran pointed.

Meilin looked.

Then her eyebrows lifted.

“Oh! That’s a good improvement.”

Xiaoran nodded, trying not to look too pleased.

“I know.”

Meilin examined the ranking list again and started counting, using her finger.

“Your seat. Think about who’s choosing before you. If the people above you do what they always do, you’ll be within two desks,” she said.

For a moment, Xiaoran didn’t say anything. Then her smile grew. “Really?”

“Really.”

She looked back at the list.

Her ranking was still not close to Yichen’s.

But it was enough.

She had done it.

The new seats were chosen at seven that evening, while the director stood at the front with the list.

Yichen had already chosen his seat.

He was placing his textbooks on the desk when he heard someone stop beside him.

He looked up.

Xiaoran stood there, holding her books against her chest.

“Hi.”

Something in his face eased.

“Hi.”

She glanced at the seat behind him, then at the one beside it.

“Looks like we’re closer now.”

Yichen looked at the new arrangement, then back at her.

“Yes.”

“I improved.”

“I noticed.”

Her eyes widened slightly.

“You noticed?”

He nodded.

“Thirteen places. Nineteen points in history. I looked.” He said it the way other people read out football scores.

Xiaoran tried to look casual. “Yes. I studied.”

“I can tell. You seem quite happy about the new arrangement.” He glanced at the seat she was about to take, then back at her.

He was smiling, not enough to make it obvious to anyone else, just that quiet, knowing smile that made her suspect he understood more than he was saying.

She narrowed her eyes. “Are you making fun of me?”

“No. I’m proud of the history.”

“Only the history?”

“The mathematics went up three points. I’m proud of that too, in a different way.”

She shook her head at him. “You’re strange.”

Yichen laughed. “All right.”

She placed her books on her new desk.

It was close enough. Not directly beside him, but close enough that she could turn her head and catch his attention without having to look across half the room.

She sat down, then looked toward him.

“Yichen. Can you see me from there?”

He looked at her, then at the distance between their desks.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He went back to arranging his books.

“You could have just told me you wanted to sit closer,” he said, perfectly calm.

Xiaoran froze. Her cheeks began to warm. She stared at him for a second, then leaned forward and whispered, “How did you know?”

He met her eyes.

“You’re not particularly subtle.”

Xiaoran’s mouth fell open.

“Yichen!”

He laughed.

The teacher on duty came in before she could defend herself, and the room went quiet.

Xiaoran opened her textbook, still warm in the face. A few minutes later, a folded piece of paper landed on the corner of her desk, passed back by the girl between them, who didn’t even look up. Yichen was facing the blackboard.

She opened it.

Congratulations on your new seat.

She picked up her pen.

Thank you.

She hesitated, then added:

It was a lot of work.

The paper returned to him.

He read it.

Then wrote:

I know.

She waited.

Another line appeared beneath it.

I’ll try not to move too far away next time.

Xiaoran bit back a smile.

She wrote:

You’d better.

Yichen read her reply, folded the paper, and put it inside his book.

Xiaoran found it much easier to concentrate after that. Mathematics, unfortunately, didn’t.

chapters.desc: Meilin notices that Lin Xiaoran’s sevens have started to look exactly like someone else’s.
chapters.title: His Handwriting in Her Notebook
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to change your handwriting. I liked it before, too.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had never paid much attention to her handwriting.

It was readable. That was enough.

Her notes were usually a mixture of carefully written headings, hurried explanations, little doodles in the margins, and occasional stars drawn beside things she thought were important. Her numbers were sometimes too round, her letters occasionally leaned in different directions, and her sevens had a small horizontal stroke through the middle.

It was an ordinary handwriting style.

Until Tang Meilin noticed something.

“Did you change your handwriting?”

Xiaoran continued copying the notes from the blackboard.

“No.”

Meilin leaned closer.

“Then why does your seven look different?”

Xiaoran stopped writing.

She looked down at her notebook.

A perfectly ordinary number seven sat at the end of her calculation.

“What about it?”

Meilin pointed.

“You used to write them like this.”

She took Xiaoran’s spare paper and wrote a seven: a short horizontal line, followed by a diagonal stroke.

Then she wrote another one, this time adding a small line through the middle.

“And now you write them like this.”

Xiaoran looked at the two numbers, then casually took the paper away.

“What’s wrong with that?”

“Nothing. I’m just curious.”

“People’s handwriting changes.”

“Does it?”

“Yes.”

Meilin rested her chin on her hand.

“Interesting.”

Xiaoran turned back to her notes.

She had a feeling this conversation wasn’t going to end well.

The truth was that she hadn’t consciously decided to change her handwriting.

It had happened gradually.

A few days earlier, at the eight o’clock break in evening self-study, she had borrowed one of Yichen’s notebooks to check a solution. He had pulled his chair over to the end of her desk, two seats down from his own, and explained the question while she copied his method.

His handwriting was neat without looking overly deliberate. His notes were organized, his calculations aligned, and his numbers were consistently shaped.

His sevens had a distinct little line through the middle. So did his zeds, in the physics formulas, and his fours were closed at the top like little flags. He wrote fast without ever looking hurried, and when he crossed something out he drew one straight line through it instead of scribbling, so you could still read what he had got wrong. Xiaoran’s crossings-out looked like small storms. She had sat there with his notebook open, the fans turning on one side of the room, and found it oddly calming, the way some people found it calming to watch fish.

Xiaoran had noticed it while copying a formula.

Then, when she returned to her own notebook, she had written the same number.

It looked nice, so she did it again, and again, and by the end of the week it had become hers without asking permission.

She hadn’t thought much about it until Meilin pointed it out.

Unfortunately, Meilin wasn’t the sort of person who let interesting discoveries go.

“Is it Zhou Yichen’s handwriting?”

Xiaoran’s pen slipped.

“Your seven,” Meilin said, smiling.

“How would you know?”

“Because I’ve seen his notes.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

Meilin leaned closer.

“His sevens look exactly like that.”

“They don’t.”

“They do.”

“Lots of people write sevens like that.”

“True.”

Meilin nodded thoughtfully. “But you didn’t before.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

Meilin’s smile widened.

“Oh, my goodness.”

“Don’t.”

“You’ve started copying his handwriting.”

“I’m not copying it!”

“Then why does your seven look like his?”

“Because it’s a normal seven!”

Meilin laughed.

Xiaoran turned away, cheeks beginning to warm.

She decided that from now on, she would write her sevens normally.

It was a perfectly reasonable decision.

She lasted until the next mathematics lesson.

Yichen noticed nothing unusual at first.

He was finishing a physics exercise at the self-study break when Xiaoran came over with her notebook. “Can you check this?”

She placed her notebook in front of him.

He glanced at the question.

“You’ve got the answer right.”

“Really?”

He nodded.

“Your calculation here is correct.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Good.”

He turned the notebook slightly, looking at the working.

Then his eyes paused.

He looked at the number she had written.

A small line through the seven.

His gaze moved to the next calculation.

Another one, then another.

He didn’t say anything immediately.

Xiaoran watched him. “Why are you looking at it like that?”

He laughed under his breath.

“Your handwriting has changed.”

Xiaoran froze.

She hadn’t expected him to notice.

“Has it?”

“Mm.”

She tried to look unconcerned.

“Maybe.”

He looked down again.

Then, quite casually, he asked, “Did you start writing your sevens like mine?”

Xiaoran’s face warmed.

She immediately reached for her notebook.

“No!”

Yichen let her take it.

He didn’t laugh.

He looked at her with an expression that suggested he was enjoying himself.

“All right.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Don’t smile.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He leaned back slightly. “Is it a bad thing? Writing them like mine.”

Xiaoran looked down at the notebook in her hands. “No.”

“Okay.” He returned to his exercise.

The conversation was over.

Or so he seemed to think.

Xiaoran stood there for another moment. “You really noticed?”

“Of course.”

“Why?”

He looked at her notebook.

“Because I look at your notes sometimes.”

That was all.

He said it as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world.

Xiaoran found the cover of her notebook interesting.

“Anyway, thank you.”

She turned and walked back to her desk.

Yichen watched her go, a smile remaining on his face.

During the afternoon break the next day, Meilin finally received confirmation. Xiaoran was rewriting a few notes when Meilin glanced down.

“You’re still doing the sevens.”

Xiaoran examined the number she had just written and closed her notebook.

Meilin stared at her.

“You know, you could just admit it.”

“Admit what?”

“That you like his handwriting.”

Xiaoran looked away.

“I think it looks neat.”

Meilin nodded.

“Of course.”

“That’s all.”

“Of course.”

Xiaoran turned toward her.

“Why are you saying it like that?”

Meilin smiled.

“Because it’s cute.”

Xiaoran made a face.

“It’s just a number.”

“Then why are you blushing over it?”

“I’m not!”

Meilin laughed.

She took out her own notebook and wrote a seven with a line through it.

“Look. I’m doing it too.”

Xiaoran stared.

“Yours looks strange.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

Meilin looked at the number, then at Xiaoran.

“Maybe I need to practice.”

Xiaoran groaned.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next week, Chen Yuhao borrowed Yichen’s physics notes at the self-study break, because his own were mostly drawings of basketball shoes, and he got four pages in before he stopped.

“Why is there a star here?”

Yichen didn’t look up from his book. “It’s important.”

“You’ve never drawn a star in your life. There’s one on every page. Since Tuesday. Zhou Yichen. Are these her stars?” Yuhao flipped back a page, then another. He held the notebook up to the light, as if the stars might be a watermark.

Three desks away, Xiaoran had gone completely still, her pen hovering over a history date.

“They’re stars. Nobody owns stars,” Yichen said.

“She does. She puts them next to everything. She put one next to the lunch menu.”

“Then I’m borrowing them.” Yichen held out his hand for the notebook, and Yuhao gave it back, because there was nothing else to do with a person who said things like that in a calm voice in a room full of people.

Meilin leaned over the back of Xiaoran’s chair and whispered, “He’s copying you back.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer. She drew a small star beside the date she had been about to write, neatly, the best star she had ever drawn.

That Friday, Yichen was waiting outside the Class 3 door when Xiaoran finished packing her books.

She walked over, holding her notebook against her chest.

“Going home?”

“Yes.”

They walked out together.

After a few steps, he glanced at the notebook.

“Did you finish the mathematics exercise?”

“Almost. I got distracted by a star.”

He smiled and didn’t ask which one.

Just before they reached the stairs, he said, looking ahead, “You don’t have to change your handwriting. I liked it before, too.”

She blinked at him.

She didn’t understand what he meant.

Then she realized.

He had remembered.

He knew she had been embarrassed.

And now he was reassuring her about something that was, objectively, not important at all.

Xiaoran lowered her gaze.

“I wasn’t trying to change it.”

“I know.”

“I just thought your sevens looked neat.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Thank you.”

She looked up.

He was smiling again.

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re teasing me.”

“A little.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed.

He reached over and took her notebook from her hands, opened it to the page she had been writing on, and looked for a while at the calculations, the stars, and all those little sevens. Then he handed it back.

“Your handwriting is easier to recognize than mine,” he said a few steps later.

She met his eyes.

“Why?”

“Because it’s yours.”

She went quiet.

“Even if you borrow a few of my numbers,” he said, with the smallest smile.

Xiaoran laughed and lightly bumped her shoulder against his arm.

“You’re never going to let me forget this, are you?”

“Probably not.”

She shook her head. When she opened her notebook that evening to finish her homework, she didn’t change her sevens back.

chapters.desc: The rain starts at the last bell, there is one umbrella between them, and a great deal to negotiate about who holds it.
chapters.title: Umbrella Etiquette
chapters.epigraph: “I know. But let me.”
chapters.content:
The rain began just as the last bell rang.

At first, it was only a light drizzle against the classroom windows.

Students were still packing their bags when the sky darkened, and within minutes, the rain had become heavy enough to blur the buildings across the road.

Xiaoran stood near the classroom window, watching the water gather along the pavement.

“Oh.”

Meilin looked up from her bag.

“What?”

“It’s raining.”

Meilin glanced outside.

“Very observant.”

Xiaoran ignored her.

“Do you have an umbrella?”

“Yes.”

Xiaoran turned.

“Really?”

Meilin pulled a small folding umbrella from her bag.

“Of course.”

Xiaoran looked at it, then at Meilin.

“Can we share?”

Meilin considered her.

“Where’s yours?”

Xiaoran smiled.

“At home.”

Meilin stared.

“Why?”

“I forgot.”

“You forgot your umbrella?”

“It wasn’t raining this morning.”

Meilin looked outside again.

“That’s generally how weather works.”

Xiaoran sighed.

Meilin shook her head and pointed her umbrella at the door like a sword. “Go ask your boyfriend. Mine is for one person and I’m the person.”

Yichen was already waiting outside the Class 3 door. He had come straight down the corridor from his own classroom and was talking to Chen Yuhao when Xiaoran approached.

“Yichen.”

He turned.

“Finished?”

She nodded, then looked outside.

“Do you have an umbrella?”

He glanced toward the rain.

“Yes.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Can we share?”

He met her eyes.

Then reached into the side pocket of his schoolbag and took out a dark umbrella.

“Come on.”

She followed him downstairs.

The rain was heavier than it had looked from the classroom.

Yichen opened the umbrella just outside the school gate.

It was large enough for two people, although not so large that they could walk without paying attention to each other.

Xiaoran stepped beneath it.

Yichen adjusted the handle slightly, positioning the umbrella over both of them.

“Ready?”

She nodded.

They started walking.

For the first few minutes, everything was fine.

They talked about their homework, the next day’s schedule, and whether they should buy something from the convenience store before going home.

Then Xiaoran looked up.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Your shoulder is wet.”

He glanced down.

A small patch of his uniform had darkened where the rain had reached it.

“It’s fine.”

She looked at the umbrella, then at him.

“You’re holding it too far over me.”

He adjusted the umbrella slightly toward the middle.

“Better?”

She examined his shoulder.

“Not really.”

“Then what do you suggest?”

“Hold it in the middle.”

“It is in the middle.”

“No, it’s not.”

He turned to her.

She pointed at his hand.

“Your hand is over there.”

He looked down at the handle, then at her.

“Would you like to hold it?”

Xiaoran immediately took the handle.

“Yes.”

Yichen let go.

She adjusted the umbrella with great seriousness, moving it slightly toward him.

“There.”

He glanced up.

“Thank you.”

She nodded.

“You’re welcome.”

They continued walking for about thirty seconds.

Then Xiaoran noticed that her own shoulder was getting wet.

She looked up.

The umbrella had shifted.

“Yichen.”

He glanced down.

“Hm?”

“My shoulder is wet now.”

He looked at the patch of rainwater on her uniform, then at the umbrella.

“You moved it.”

“Because yours was wet.”

“And now yours is wet.”

She looked at him.

“Then move closer.”

“All right.”

He stepped closer.

Their shoulders touched.

Xiaoran adjusted the umbrella again.

“Better.”

Yichen looked down at the small space between them.

“Much better.”

The problem was that Xiaoran had a specific idea of how an umbrella should be shared.

Both people should remain dry.

Neither person should have to walk too close to the edge.

And the umbrella should be held exactly in the middle.

Yichen, on the other hand, seemed perfectly content to let one side of his shoulder get wet.

This became an issue when they reached a quieter stretch of pavement.

Xiaoran noticed another patch of water on his sleeve.

She stopped.

“You’re getting wet again.”

Yichen stopped with her.

“It’s only a little.”

“That’s not the point.”

He held her gaze.

“What is the point?”

“The umbrella is supposed to cover both people.”

“It does.”

“Then why are you wet?”

Something in his face eased.

“Because it’s raining.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“That’s not funny.”

“I didn’t say it was.”

She moved closer and tried to push the umbrella toward him.

Yichen caught the handle before it tilted too far.

“Careful.”

“Your shoulder!”

“It’s fine.”

“Mine would be fine too.”

He looked down at her.

“Is that what you want?”

She nodded firmly.

“Yes.”

He studied her face.

Then he shifted the umbrella toward her again.

Xiaoran frowned. “You’re doing it again.”

He smiled.

“I know.”

She looked exasperated.

“Why?”

He lowered his head slightly.

“Because I’d rather get wet than have you get cold.”

Xiaoran went quiet.

She looked at him for a second.

Then her expression changed.

“That’s not fair.”

Yichen raised his eyebrows.

“What isn’t?”

“You can’t say things like that when we’re arguing about an umbrella.”

He laughed.

“Why not?”

“Because then I can’t argue properly.”

His smile widened.

“Is that so?”

She nodded.

He took the umbrella handle from her, moved it over both of them, and put his free hand lightly on her shoulder, guiding her under the covered side until there was no gap left to argue about.

“Is it fair now?”

She examined the umbrella.

Their shoulders were touching, and the umbrella was finally positioned evenly.

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

They started walking again.

A few minutes later, Xiaoran noticed something else.

Yichen was holding the umbrella with his right hand, but his left hand was occupied holding her schoolbag.

She met his eyes.

“Why are you carrying my bag?”

“You gave it to me.”

“When?”

“Just now.”

She tried to remember.

She had handed it to him while adjusting the umbrella.

Apparently, she had forgotten to take it back.

“Oh.”

He glanced at her.

“Do you want it?”

She shook her head.

“No. You can hold it.”

“All right.”

They walked a little farther.

Then she looked at his shoulder again.

It was still slightly wet.

She sighed. “You’re a terrible umbrella partner.”

Yichen smiled. “You’re very concerned about my shoulder.”

“Of course I am.”

“Why?”

She looked at him as if the answer were obvious.

“Because you’re going to get cold.”

He was quiet, and his expression softened in a way that made her look at the pavement.

“Let’s keep walking,” he said.

They eventually reached the small convenience store near the residential road.

Xiaoran stopped outside.

“Do you want to go in?”

Yichen glanced at the rain.

“For what?”

“Something warm.”

He studied her.

“Are you cold?”

“A little.”

He folded the umbrella slightly as they stepped beneath the store’s awning.

“Then let’s get something.”

Xiaoran walked toward the drinks refrigerator.

She looked through the bottles and cartons.

Then she turned around.

“Hot milk?”

Yichen nodded.

“Sure.”

She picked up two cartons of warm milk from the heated display.

One for herself.

One for him.

At the counter, Yichen reached for his wallet.

Xiaoran immediately put one hand over the drinks.

“I’ll pay.”

He considered her.

“Why?”

“Because you’re already carrying my bag and holding the umbrella.”

He glanced at her.

“That’s not much.”

“I know. But let me.”

He considered her, then stepped aside.

“All right.”

Xiaoran paid and handed him his drink.

He accepted it.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

They stood beneath the awning for a few minutes, drinking their milk while the rain continued.

Xiaoran looked at the wet patch on his shoulder, then at her own completely dry uniform.

She frowned.

“See? You’re still wet.”

Yichen glanced down.

“Only a little.”

She held out her drink.

“Here.”

He glanced at her.

“What?”

“Hold this.”

He took it.

Xiaoran reached up and brushed a few raindrops from his shoulder with her hand.

Yichen looked down at her.

She was concentrating so seriously that he almost laughed.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“It’s all right.”

She finished brushing the water away, then stepped back.

“There.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Thank you.”

She nodded.

“Next time, we need a bigger umbrella.”

Yichen looked at the umbrella resting against the wall.

“This one is already quite big.”

“Not big enough.”

“All right.”

She looked satisfied.

By the time they resumed walking, the rain had softened.

Yichen opened the umbrella again.

Xiaoran stepped underneath.

This time, she didn’t argue about the position.

Instead, she moved closer and slipped her arm through his, which turned out to solve the whole problem, because there was no longer any space between them for the rain to get into. He glanced down at her arm and adjusted the umbrella slightly.

They walked for a while.

“Next time, if your shoulder gets wet, tell me,” Xiaoran said.

He looked down at her.

“All right.”

“And don’t pretend it’s fine.”

“I won’t.”

She nodded.

A few steps later, he asked, “And if your shoulder gets wet?”

“I’ll tell you.”

“Good.”

That made her grin.

“See? We have a system now.”

“Very efficient,” Yichen said.

She looked pleased with herself.

When they reached the turn where they usually separated, Xiaoran stopped.

“Thank you for the umbrella.”

Yichen nodded.

“You’re welcome.”

She looked at his shoulder one last time.

It was still a little damp.

She sighed.

“You’re going to get wet again tomorrow if it rains.”

“Then I’ll bring a bigger umbrella.”

“You said that last time.”

“Then I’ll bring two.”

She smiled.

Then she reached out and gently tugged the edge of his sleeve.

“Goodbye.”

“Goodbye.”

She turned to leave.

After a few steps, she looked back.

Yichen was still standing there, holding the umbrella.

She waved.

He raised his hand.

Then, just before she disappeared around the corner, she called out:

“Yichen!”

He looked up.

“Yes?”

“Next time, you can hold my hand too!”

He smiled.

“All right.”

She disappeared.

Yichen stood there for another moment, his left shoulder wet through, and shook his head with a quiet laugh.

He bought a bigger umbrella that weekend, navy, with a wooden handle. The first time it rained, she stood under it, looked up at all that extra space, and moved closer anyway.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran thought she understood Zhou Yichen completely… until she saw what his silence looked like when someone else tried to take his place.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Finally Got Jealous
chapters.content:
The first sign something was wrong was that Zhou Yichen stopped smiling. Not completely. Just… less. And for someone like Zhou Yichen, who usually looked at Lin Xiaoran like she personally invented happiness, the difference was obvious to everyone. Everyone except Lin Xiaoran.

“Yichen, someone confessed to me today,” she announced proudly during lunch.

Chen Yuhao choked on his drink. Tang Meilin slowly lowered her spoon. Across the table, Zhou Yichen looked up calmly.

“Oh?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“A first-year boy.”

“…Mm.”

“He said I’m cute.”

“…He’s right.”

Yuhao glanced at Yichen’s hand. He was holding his chopsticks a little too tightly. That answer was far too calm. Xiaoran carried on happily, with no idea what she was walking into.

“Then he asked if I wanted to watch a movie with him.”

“What did you say?” Meilin asked carefully.

“I told him I already have a boyfriend, obviously.”

Yichen nodded once.

“Good.”

“But then, he got sad so I comforted him a little,” Xiaoran said while opening her yogurt.

Silence. Yuhao became interested in his food. Yichen smiled faintly.

“What does ‘comforted him a little’ mean?”

“Oh, nothing serious. I just told him he’ll definitely find someone prettier and kinder than me someday.” Xiaoran waved casually.

Yichen stared at her.

“Prettier than you?”

“Yes.”

“You told another guy that?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…Should I not?”

Meilin closed her eyes briefly. Oh no. The problem with Zhou Yichen was that he almost never got jealous. Girls liked him, confessed to him, and texted him all the time. Xiaoran got jealous about it at least twice a month. Yichen stayed calm through all of it—secure, and endlessly patient with her. So when he finally did get jealous, nobody knew what to expect.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second sign something was wrong came after school. Zhou Yichen waited outside Xiaoran’s classroom every afternoon. Today, he wasn’t there. Confused, Xiaoran wandered around Building B looking for him. She finally found him near the basketball court, talking with his teammates.

“Yichen!”

He looked over. Same handsome face. Same small smile. But something about him felt cooler. Further away. Xiaoran didn’t like it at all. She walked over and grabbed his sleeve out of habit.

“Why didn’t you wait for me?”

“I was busy.”

That had literally never stopped him before. Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“…Are you angry?”

“No.”

That was a lie, even if he told it nicely. Before she could investigate further, another voice interrupted.

“Senior Xiaoran!”

Everyone turned. A younger boy jogged over with a can of coffee, looking nervous. The same first-year. He faltered when he saw Zhou Yichen standing beside her. But he worked up his courage and held the drink out to Xiaoran.

“Thank you for earlier. I bought your favorite flavor,” he said shyly.

Xiaoran looked surprised.

“How did you know my favorite?”

“You mentioned it.”

“Oh.”

She reached for it without thinking—only for another hand to take it first. Silence. Zhou Yichen held the can in one hand, smiling politely. It wasn’t a friendly smile.

“Thank you. But she doesn’t drink coffee after 5 p.m,” he said gently.

The younger boy froze completely. Xiaoran blinked.

“…I do sometimes.”

Yichen looked at her.

“You couldn’t sleep until two last time.”

“…Oh.”

The boy was starting to sweat.

“I-I just wanted to thank senior…”

“You already did. That’s enough.” Yichen’s voice stayed pleasant.

Even Yuhao, watching from nearby, nearly saluted. That was the most boyfriend move he had ever seen. The boy made his escape. As soon as he was gone, Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“…You scared him.”

“He’ll survive.”

“…You’re definitely angry.”

“I said I’m not.”

“You’re doing your fake customer-service smile.”

Yuhao walked off. He didn’t want to witness whatever happened next.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, Lin Xiaoran lay sprawled across her bed, video calling Meilin.

“I think Zhou Yichen is malfunctioning.”

“He’s jealous.”

“…Huh?”

Meilin stared at her through the screen.

“You really don’t notice things unless they hit you with a chair.”

“What’s there to notice?”

“He’s obsessed with you.”

“Well, yes. Obviously.”

“And another guy openly approached you.”

“But I rejected him!”

“You also comforted him.”

“He looked sad!”

Meilin sighed.

“Xiaoran. Imagine a pretty girl confessed to Yichen, then Yichen comforted her gently and accepted gifts from her.”

Xiaoran sat bolt upright.

“…Oh.”

“Exactly.”

Suddenly, everything replayed in her head. Yichen not waiting after class. The weird smile. Taking the coffee. The calm voice that somehow felt colder than usual. Oh no. Zhou Yichen was jealous. And for some reason, knowing that made her chest feel warm. Which was probably not the right reaction.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran arrived at school carrying two strawberry milks. One for herself. One peace offering. She found Zhou Yichen in the library before morning class, reading quietly near the windows. Sunlight fell across his face. He looked annoyingly good. Xiaoran crept over and set the drink down beside him.

“For you.”

Yichen glanced at it.

“Bribery?”

“Yes.”

He laughed quietly despite himself. Good. Progress. Xiaoran sat beside him, fidgeting slightly.

“…Are you still jealous?”

“I wasn’t jealous.”

He rubbed the back of his neck.

“Liar.”

“I was concerned.”

“You stole his coffee like a drama villain.”

“He bought it for my girlfriend.”

The way he said my girlfriend so naturally made her ears go warm. Yichen finally closed his book and looked at her properly.

“I trust you. I just don’t like other guys trying to take my place,” he said.

Xiaoran blinked slowly.

“…That’s kind of hot.”

For the first time, Yichen looked genuinely caught off guard. Then he laughed helplessly, covering his eyes briefly.

“You’re unbelievable.”

“No but seriously. You’re usually so calm. Seeing you jealous is kind of…” Xiaoran said, leaning closer.

“Kind of?”

“…Cute.”

Yichen stared at her.

“I was miserable yesterday.”
