He had arrived at school on time, completed his morning reading, and even helped a classmate with a question before the first bell.

Everything was perfectly normal.

Except that every time he thought about Xiaoran, his mind returned to yesterday: the way she had nodded too fast when he asked, the second of complete stillness, and then the chair tipping backward and his arm going round her before she hit the floor. She had said she hated having bones. He had laughed into her shoulder and kissed her hair, and then walked her home, and neither of them had said one coherent sentence the whole way.

He had wanted to kiss her again. He hadn’t.

Now, the next morning, he was beginning to understand that perhaps walking her home had been the easiest part.

Because he had no idea how he was supposed to greet her.

“Yichen.”

He turned.

Yuhao was standing beside his desk, holding a basketball.

“You’re coming to the court later?”

“Probably.”

Yuhao studied him.

“What’s wrong with you?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m usually quiet.”

“Not like this.”

Yichen looked at him.

Yuhao grinned.

“Did you lose a game?”

“No.”

“Did your mother scold you?”

“No.”

“Did you fight with Xiaoran?”

Yichen paused.

Only.

But Yuhao caught it.

His grin widened.

“Oh?”

Yichen picked up his pen.

“Go to class.”

“Wait. Did you actually fight?”

“We didn’t.”

“Then why do you look like you’re avoiding someone?”

Yichen didn’t answer.

Yuhao leaned closer.

“Is it Xiaoran?”

Yichen finally looked at him.

“Chen Yuhao.”

“Yes?”

“Don’t you have somewhere to be?”

Yuhao laughed.

That was enough of an answer for him.

The first encounter happened during the break between classes.

Xiaoran had been sent to the office to deliver some papers. She was walking down the corridor with Meilin when she saw Yichen approaching from the other end.

Her steps slowed.

Meilin noticed immediately.

“Oh.”

Xiaoran kept walking.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your ears have,” Meilin said, and smiled.

Yichen was walking with Yuhao. He noticed them at almost the same moment.

His gaze met Xiaoran’s.

She looked away.

He looked away too.

They passed each other.

Neither said hello. Neither smiled.

Neither did anything remotely resembling what they usually did.

Meilin stopped walking. Xiaoran took two more steps before realizing her friend wasn’t beside her, and turned. Meilin looked at her,

then at the boys disappearing round the corner, then back at her. “Interesting.”

Xiaoran’s face warmed.

“Nothing is interesting.”

“Of course.”

“Meilin.”

“Yes?”

“Please.”

Meilin laughed and continued walking.

By lunchtime, the situation had become unbearable.

Xiaoran had seen Yichen three times.

The first time, she had pretended to be occupied with her books. The second time, she had remembered something she needed to ask Meilin.

The third time, she had nearly walked into a pillar because she had been looking in the opposite direction.

She was beginning to suspect that avoiding someone required more energy than actually talking to them.

Meanwhile, Yichen had been equally unsuccessful.

He had considered going to her classroom. At the long break he had even walked down the corridor as far as the Class 3 back door, which stood open because the radiator in there was broken and always on. Through the gap he could see her at her desk by the window, talking to Meilin with her hands, the way she did when she was explaining something that had gone wrong. She was laughing. Then she glanced at the door, not at him, just at the door, and the laugh stopped as if someone had turned it off, and she put her face down on her arms.

He had walked back to his own classroom before she could lift her head. Rong Hao, coming the other way with a stack of exercise books, had said hello to him and got no answer, and later told everyone in Class 3 that Zhou Yichen had looked like a man who had forgotten his own name.

It was possible she needed time. It was also possible, and this thought arrived as he sat back down, that she was avoiding him because she regretted yesterday.

That thought had stayed with him longer than he liked.

He was still thinking about it when Yuhao dropped into the seat opposite him at lunch.

“All right.”

Yichen looked up.

“What?”

Yuhao pointed his chopsticks at him. “Are you two fighting?”

Yichen blinked. “Who?”

Yuhao stared.

“Don’t insult me.”

Yichen returned to his food.

“We’re not fighting.”

“Then why haven’t you talked to her today?”

“She’s in her class. I’m in mine.”

“Her class is forty meters away.”

“Excellent observation.”

Yuhao narrowed his eyes.

“Did something happen?”

Yichen didn’t answer.

Yuhao leaned back, looking delighted with himself.

“Oh, something definitely happened.”

“Eat your lunch.”

“Did you say something stupid?”

“No.”

“Did she say something stupid?”

“No.”

“Did you forget an anniversary?”

Yichen looked at him.

“What anniversary?”

Yuhao shrugged.

“How would I know? Maybe you have one.”

Yichen sighed.

Yuhao watched him for another moment, and his expression changed. Two days ago at this same table, Meilin had asked whether they had kissed yet, and Yichen had kept eating, and Xiaoran had choked on her drink.

Yuhao slowly lowered his chopsticks. “Did you kiss her?”

Yichen’s hand paused.

It was barely noticeable.

But Yuhao had known him long enough.

His eyes widened.

“No way.”

Yichen looked at him.

“Lower your voice.”

Yuhao’s mouth fell open.

Then he leaned forward, whispering loudly.

“You did!”

Yichen put down his chopsticks.

“Yuhao.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

“Quiet.”

Yuhao looked as if he had just discovered the most important secret in the history of their school.

He sat back, trying hard not to grin.

Then he nodded.

“Ah.”

Yichen said nothing.

Yuhao nodded again.

“That explains everything.”

“What does it explain?”

“Why you’re both acting like strangers.”

Yichen looked down.

“Congratulations, by the way,” Yuhao said, grinning.

Yichen gave him a flat look.

“Thank you.”

“Was it awkward?”

“No.”

“You’re lying.”

Yichen didn’t respond.

Yuhao laughed.

“Unbelievable. You can play basketball in front of an entire crowd without getting nervous, but one kiss and you can’t even say hello to your girlfriend.”

Yichen picked up his chopsticks again.

“You’re enjoying this too much.”

“Of course I am.”

After lunch, Yichen finally found her.

Xiaoran was standing near the staircase, waiting for Meilin, who had gone back to the classroom to retrieve her pencil case.

He approached.

“Xiaoran.”

She turned.

Her heart immediately began behaving terribly.

“Yichen.”

There was a pause, then both of them looked away.

Yichen almost smiled.

“Have you been avoiding me?”

“No.”

“All right.”

She met his eyes.

“Have you?”

“No.”

Another pause.

She looked down at her shoes.

He watched her. “Are you uncomfortable? About yesterday.”

Her cheeks turned pink.

He waited.

She opened her mouth, then closed it again.

Finally, she shook her head.

“No.”

“Good.”

He looked relieved, though only slightly.

Xiaoran noticed.

Her fingers tightened around the strap of her bag.

“I just... I don’t know how to act.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“Neither do I.”

She looked at him in surprise.

“You don’t?”

Something in his face eased.

“Do I look like I know what I’m doing?”

She considered him.

Unfortunately, he looked perfectly composed.

“Yes.”

He laughed.

“That’s misleading.”

She smiled.

It was small, but it was there.

He took a step closer.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Do you regret it?”

Her smile disappeared.

“No.”

The answer came quickly.

Yichen looked at her.

She lowered her eyes, embarrassed by how quickly she had answered. “I just keep thinking about it. And about the chair.”

His expression changed.

Not dramatically.

Just a small movement at the corner of his mouth, a warmth in his eyes.

“Me too. Not the chair.”

Xiaoran looked up.

He reached out and gently adjusted the strap of her bag where it had slipped from her shoulder.

“Then we don’t have to pretend nothing happened.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

“And you don’t have to avoid me.”

“I wasn’t avoiding you.”

He laughed under his breath.

“All right.”

She frowned.

“Why do you keep saying that?”

“Because I believe you.”

She squinted at him.

He looked far too amused.

He lowered his voice. “Although you did walk into a pillar this morning.”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened.

“You saw that?”

“I heard about it.”

“From who?”

He smiled.

“Meilin.”

“Traitor.”

He laughed.

She finally laughed too.

The awkwardness didn’t disappear completely, but it loosened.

Yichen looked at her for another moment. “Can I hold your hand?”

Her face warmed again.

She glanced toward the staircase.

There were students passing by.

“Here?”

“Only if you want.”

She hesitated, then slipped her hand into his.

His fingers closed around hers.

Nothing dramatic happened.

No one stopped walking.

The school didn’t fall silent.

But Xiaoran felt the familiar warmth of his hand, and for the first time that morning, she could breathe normally.

Yichen looked down at their joined hands, then at her.

“Better?”

She nodded, and didn’t let go.

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Good.”

Meilin returned a minute later.

She stopped when she saw them, then looked at their hands, then at Xiaoran’s face.

“Ah.”

Xiaoran immediately tried to pull her hand away.

Yichen didn’t hold on.

He let her go, his expression calm.

Meilin raised an eyebrow.

“Did you two make up?”

Xiaoran nearly choked.

“We weren’t fighting!”

Meilin looked at Yichen.

He gave her a small, polite smile.

“No.”

Meilin nodded slowly.

“Good. I was worried.”

Xiaoran glared at her.

“You weren’t worried.”

“You’re right. I was curious.”

Yichen laughed. Xiaoran covered her face. She was never going to survive this.

✦ ✦ ✦

She survived until seven o’clock, when evening self-study began, and she remembered that the seats were by rank and that his was two desks away from hers.

For the first forty minutes she managed well. She did her English reading. She underlined things. She didn’t look to her left at all, which took so much concentration that she read the same paragraph about the water cycle four times.

At twenty to eight, a folded note landed on her desk, passed along by the girl between them, who had started doing this without being asked and without looking up, like a postal service.

You’re allowed to look over here. We agreed.

She wrote underneath: I’m studying.

The note went back. It came back.

You’ve been on that page since seven.

She turned her head. He was facing his physics book with a perfectly straight face, but the tips of his ears had gone pink again, and she remembered that they had done that yesterday too, right after, when he had looked so calm and wasn’t. It was the most reassuring thing she had seen all day.

She looked at him for the whole of the next minute, on purpose, until he gave up and looked back.

Mr. Pan, at the front, cleared his throat at nobody in particular. Meilin, behind her, made a noise into her sleeve that could have been a sneeze.

Xiaoran went back to the water cycle and read the paragraph a fifth time, and this time it went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, when Yichen called at half past nine, Xiaoran answered almost immediately.

She sat on her bed, smiling at the sound of his voice.

There was a short silence, then she heard him laugh.

“What’s funny?”

“We spent the entire day trying not to look at each other. And then the whole of self-study looking.”

She covered her face with her free hand.

“Don’t remind me.”

“And Yuhao figured it out.”

“Don’t remind me about that either.”

Yichen laughed.

“All right.”

She lay down, holding the phone closer.

After a moment, she said, “Tomorrow, can we just act normal?”

He was silent for a second. “We can try.”

“Really try.”

“I’ll do my best.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“And no looking away.”

“That might be difficult.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re distracting.”

Her face warmed. She pulled the blanket up to her chin. “You’re making me embarrassed on purpose.”

He laughed.

“Good night, Xiaoran.”

She smiled into her pillow.

“Good night.”

The next morning, at the school gate, he said good morning and she said good morning, and they both looked straight at each other while they did it, and then Xiaoran walked into the gatepost. Behind them, Yuhao said “Normal” to nobody in particular, and kept walking.

chapters.desc: A grade trip, a shared bus, and a whole day of not holding hands in front of the teachers. He counts how many times she reaches for his.
chapters.title: Practicing Not Holding Hands
chapters.epigraph: “No. I had to practice all day. Not holding your hand.”
chapters.content:
The school trip was supposed to be educational.

That was what their teachers had said.

A day outside the classroom, visiting a historical site, learning about its architecture, and completing a worksheet in groups.

Class 1 and Class 3 would share a bus, as they shared evening self-study and most of the timetable’s misfortunes, and Lin Xiaoran had been looking forward to it for a week.

Not because she was interested in historical architecture.

But because it meant spending an entire day outside school.

And, more importantly, because Yichen would be there.

There was only one problem.

The teachers had made it clear that everyone was expected to stay with their assigned groups: no wandering off, no running ahead, no unnecessary noise. The grade director had added, looking at nobody, that the school’s rules on inappropriate closeness between students applied on trips as well. Xiaoran had noticed something else. There would be teachers everywhere: at the entrance, on the bus, in every exhibition hall, and probably in places where teachers had no reason to be.

She looked at Yichen as they gathered outside school.

He was standing with Yuhao, holding a folded itinerary.

She walked over. “Morning.”

“Morning,” he said.

Her hand moved instinctively toward his.

Then she remembered the teachers.

Her fingers stopped halfway.

Yichen noticed.

He looked down at her hand, then at her.

A small smile appeared.

Xiaoran immediately withdrew it and examined a button on her sleeve.

She narrowed her eyes.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

His smile widened.

The bus seating arrangement was announced before they boarded.

Students were to sit according to their assigned groups.

Xiaoran was placed with Meilin and two other girls.

Yichen was with Yuhao and two boys.

Xiaoran stared at the list, then at Meilin.

“Why?”

“Why are we in different groups?”

“Because we’re in different classes. Which you knew when you started dating him,” Meilin said.

Xiaoran gave her a look.

Meilin sighed.

“You’re going to survive.”

“I know.”

“Then stop looking like someone has cancelled your birthday.”

Xiaoran looked back toward Yichen.

He was speaking to Yuhao, completely unbothered.

She felt mildly betrayed.

The bus ride was the first test.

Xiaoran sat beside Meilin, with the aisle separating her from Yichen’s group.

It was only a short distance.

She could see him if she turned her head.

Which she did.

Several times.

On the third occasion, Meilin leaned closer.

“You’re going to get a neck injury.”

Xiaoran turned forward.

“I was looking outside.”

“Outside is on the other side.”

Xiaoran looked out of the window.

“There’s scenery.”

Meilin followed her gaze.

There was a parking lot.

“Beautiful.”

Xiaoran ignored her.

Across the aisle, Yichen glanced over.

Their eyes met.

Something in his face eased.

She smiled back.

Then, almost instinctively, she lifted her hand slightly.

He looked at it, then at the teacher sitting near the front.

He raised his eyebrows.

Xiaoran lowered her hand.

Meilin watched the entire exchange.

“Are you two communicating in secret?”

“No.”

“Because that looked like a very complicated conversation.”

Xiaoran looked out the window.

“Please sleep.”

At the historical site, the teachers divided everyone into smaller groups and handed out worksheets.

The students were instructed to move through the designated exhibition areas in order.

Xiaoran was reading the first information board when Yichen appeared beside her.

“How’s your worksheet?”

She looked up.

“Hard.”

He glanced at the question.

“What’s difficult?”

“Everything.”

He smiled.

“That’s a little dramatic.”

She pointed at the board.

“Look at all these words.”

He leaned closer to read.

Their shoulders nearly touched.

Xiaoran felt a smile tug at her lips, then a teacher’s voice came from behind them.

“Students, please keep moving. Don’t block the display.”

They immediately stepped apart.

Yichen looked at her.

Neither said anything.

Then he handed her the information sheet.

“Read the second paragraph.”

She took it.

“Okay.”

The teacher passed by.

Xiaoran waited until he was out of earshot.

Then whispered, “We’re being watched.”

Yichen smiled.

“Apparently.”

“Everywhere.”

“Seems that way.”

She sighed.

He met her eyes.

“Do you want to finish the worksheet first?”

“Yes.”

“Then we can walk around together.”

Her expression brightened.

“Really?”

“Within the designated area.”

That made her grin.

“Very responsible, Zhou Yichen.”

“I try.”

The second test was the outdoor courtyard.

It was large, with stone pathways and old trees providing shade. Students were scattered around, taking photographs and discussing the worksheet.

Xiaoran had finished her questions.

Yichen had finished his too.

They were finally free to walk around.

Together.

Without needing to pretend they had a reason to stand beside each other.

They walked along the stone path.

Xiaoran’s hand brushed against his.

Once.

Twice.

On the third time, Yichen looked down.

She looked away.

That got a smile out of him.

“Do you want to hold my hand?”

She whispered, “There’s a teacher.”

He glanced toward the other side of the courtyard.

Indeed, one of their teachers was standing near a group of students.

“Then we won’t.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“You’re not disappointed?”

He gave her a curious look.

“Why would I be?”

She shrugged.

“I don’t know.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“We can hold hands another time.”

She nodded.

Then, after a moment, she whispered, “But I want to.”

Yichen looked at her.

His expression softened.

He didn’t reach for her hand.

Instead, he let his fingers brush hers once more as they walked.

A tiny compromise.

Xiaoran smiled.

By lunchtime, the situation had become ridiculous.

They had managed to stand beside each other for almost twenty minutes without holding hands.

Xiaoran considered this a personal achievement.

Yichen considered it mildly amusing.

They were sitting at the picnic tables with their respective groups. Yuhao was talking animatedly about something that had happened on the bus, while Meilin was opening her lunch.

Xiaoran sat opposite Yichen.

She had placed her water bottle beside her lunch box.

Yichen noticed that she was struggling with the bottle cap.

He reached across the table.

“Give it to me.”

She handed it over.

He opened it and returned it.

Their fingers touched.

Xiaoran smiled.

Then Yuhao looked between them.

“What was that?”

Yichen looked at him.

“What?”

Yuhao pointed at the bottle.

“Why did you open it for her?”

“She couldn’t open it.”

Yuhao looked at Xiaoran.

“Your hands are broken?”

Xiaoran glared.

“No.”

“Then—”

“Eat your lunch, Yuhao.”

Yuhao laughed.

Meilin shook her head.

“You really have no survival instinct.”

Yuhao looked at her.

“What did I do?”

“Nothing. That’s the problem.”

Xiaoran took a bite of her lunch, trying not to smile.

Under the table, Yichen’s shoe lightly touched hers.

She looked up.

He was listening to Yuhao, his expression perfectly normal.

But when she glanced down, his foot remained beside hers.

She nudged him once.

He nudged back.

It was childish.

It was also, somehow, enough.

The third test came during the group photograph.

Their teacher gathered everyone in front of the main building.

“Girls in the front, boys behind. Please stand in your assigned groups.”

Xiaoran found herself beside Meilin.

Yichen stood one row behind her.

She glanced over her shoulder.

He was looking at her.

She smiled.

The teacher raised the camera.

“Everyone look here!”

Xiaoran turned forward.

Just before the photograph was taken, she felt something lightly brush the back of her hand.

She looked down.

Yichen’s fingers were resting against hers.

Not holding.

Just touching.

She fought the urge to smile too widely.

The camera flashed.

And when the teacher announced that they were done, Xiaoran turned around.

Yichen was already looking at her.

“Was that allowed?” she whispered.

He smiled.

“Technically, we weren’t holding hands.”

She laughed.

“You’re finding loopholes.”

“Learning from you.”

She gave him a delighted look.

Then their teacher called for everyone to line up again.

They stepped apart.

On the bus ride back, Xiaoran was exhausted.

She had spent the day walking, answering questions, taking photographs, and repeatedly reminding herself not to reach for Yichen’s hand.

She was sitting beside Meilin again.

This time, however, she was too tired to keep looking across the aisle.

Her head rested against the window.

Meilin glanced at her.

“Sleepy?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Very.”

“Then sleep.”

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

A few minutes later, she felt something touch her shoulder.

She opened one eye.

Yichen was standing in the aisle.

The bus had stopped because their teacher was checking the headcount.

He held out a small packet of biscuits.

“You didn’t eat much at lunch.”

Xiaoran took it.

“Thank you.”

“Rest.”

That made her grin.

Then, as he turned to return to his seat, she caught the edge of his sleeve.

He looked back.

She glanced at the teacher near the front.

Then whispered, “See you after we get off.”

His expression softened.

“All right.”

She released his sleeve.

He returned to his seat.

Meilin looked at the biscuits, then at Xiaoran. “You two are a public health risk.”

Xiaoran smiled, tucked the biscuits into her bag, and closed her eyes again.

When they finally returned to school, the teachers gathered everyone for a final announcement.

“Please remember to take all your belongings. Don’t leave anything on the bus. You may go home once your group leader has checked your attendance.”

Xiaoran waited with Meilin near the school gate.

Yichen was still with Yuhao, helping carry a box of leftover materials back to the classroom.

She watched him from a distance.

Meilin followed her gaze.

“Go.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“What?”

“Go say goodbye.”

“But—”

“There’s no teacher standing next to you anymore.”

Xiaoran smiled.

She didn’t need to be told twice.

She walked toward him.

Yichen saw her approaching and handed the box to Yuhao.

“Take this inside.”

Yuhao looked at Xiaoran, then at Yichen.

His smile became unbearable.

“Of course.”

He took the box and walked away.

Xiaoran stopped in front of Yichen.

They looked at each other.

Then Yichen held out his hand.

“Now?”

His mouth curved.

“Now.”

She placed her hand in his.

His fingers closed around hers.

Xiaoran let out a small, satisfied sigh.

Yichen glanced down.

“That difficult?”

She nodded seriously.

“Very.”

He laughed.

“You’re exaggerating.”

“No. I had to practice all day. Not holding your hand.”

His smile softened.

“How did you do?”

She considered it.

“Not very well.”

He laughed, then lifted their joined hands slightly.

“Neither did I.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Really?”

“Really. I counted. You reached for it twelve times.”

“And you?”

He considered lying. “Fourteen.”

She swung their joined hands, once and then twice, all the way to the gate, where the grade director was standing with a clipboard, and let go so fast that she nearly took his watch with her.

chapters.desc: Someone from Class 5 dedicates a song to her on the morning radio, and Zhou Yichen takes the news very calmly, for him.
chapters.title: The Radio Dedication
chapters.epigraph: “I hope you don’t feel embarrassed about the song. It was really thoughtful.”
chapters.content:
The first time Lin Xiaoran heard her name over the school radio, she nearly dropped her pencil.

It was Wednesday morning, just before the first lesson.

The school radio played every morning during the short break before classes officially began. Usually, it was a mixture of announcements, weather updates, birthday greetings, and song requests submitted by students.

Xiaoran rarely paid attention.

She preferred using those few minutes to finish homework she had forgotten the night before.

That morning, however, Tang Meilin was unusually interested in the broadcast.

“Turn it up.”

Xiaoran continued writing. “It’s already loud.”

“Listen.”

“I’m listening.”

“No, you’re not.”

Meilin reached over and tapped the volume button on the classroom radio.

A cheerful student announcer’s voice filled the room.

“Good morning, everyone! We have a special dedication today. This next song is requested for Lin Xiaoran in Class 3.”

Xiaoran’s pencil stopped.

Meilin slowly turned her head.

Xiaoran looked up. The announcer continued, sounding pleased with herself.

“To Lin Xiaoran in Class 3, someone would like you to hear this song. The message simply says, ‘Hope you have a good day.’ Signed, Z.”

For a moment, Xiaoran didn’t move.

Then Meilin’s eyes widened.

“Lin. Xiaoran.”

“Don’t.”

“Someone just dedicated a love song to you.”

“It’s probably a mistake.”

“To your exact name and class?”

Xiaoran looked toward the radio.

The opening notes of a familiar romantic song began playing.

Meilin leaned closer, practically vibrating with curiosity.

“And signed Z.”

Xiaoran’s face warmed.

She looked down at her notebook, pretending to be interested in the unfinished mathematics question.

“Maybe there are other people with the same name.”

“How many Lin Xiaorans in Class 3 do you know?”

“Meilin. Please stop talking.”

Meilin smiled.

“Oh, this is going to be a wonderful morning.”

The song lasted four minutes and twelve seconds.

Meilin spent every second of it watching Xiaoran.

Xiaoran spent every second pretending not to notice.

When the broadcast finally moved on to the morning announcements, Meilin put down her pen.

“So.”

Xiaoran turned a page.

“So what?”

“Who do you think Z is?”

“I don’t know.”

“Do you think it’s Zhou Yichen?”

Xiaoran’s fingers paused.

Meilin caught it immediately.

“Ah.”

“Don’t ah me.”

“You thought of him too.”

“I didn’t.”

“You did.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

It wasn’t an unreasonable guess. Yichen’s surname was Zhou. The dedication had been signed with a Z. And after yesterday’s school trip, after the entire day of trying not to hold hands, she had been thinking about him a lot.

Perhaps he had submitted the request.

Perhaps he had wanted to surprise her.

The thought made her stomach flutter.

She tried not to smile.

Meilin watched her expression change.

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m not.”

“Your mouth says otherwise.”

Xiaoran quickly picked up her pencil.

“Can we do our homework?”

Meilin leaned back in her chair, thoroughly entertained.

“Of course, Miss Lin. I’ll leave you to think about your mysterious admirer.”

In Class 1, Yichen had heard the broadcast perfectly well. He had been halfway through a mouthful of water when the announcer said Xiaoran’s name, and he had looked up at the speaker above the blackboard, and then the signature came. Z. His surname began with that letter. It was an understandable assumption. Unfortunately, he hadn’t sent it.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He looked at Yuhao, who had appeared beside his desk with an expression that suggested he was about to be annoying.

“Congratulations.”

“For what?”

Yuhao pulled out a chair and sat backward on it.

“Your romantic side.”

Yichen looked at him.

Yuhao grinned.

“That was quite something. A love song over the school radio? Very bold.”

“I didn’t send it.”

Yuhao blinked, then laughed.

“You’re joking.”

“I’m not.”

“Wait. You didn’t?”

Yichen shook his head.

Yuhao’s grin slowly faded into an expression of genuine surprise.

“Oh.”

Yichen returned to his book.

Yuhao studied him.

“Then someone else sent it?”

“Apparently.”

“For Xiaoran?”

“That’s what the announcement said.”

Yuhao leaned forward.

“Do you know who?”

“No.”

“You’re not curious?”

Yichen turned a page.

“A little.”

Yuhao stared at him.

“That’s it?”

Yichen looked up.

“What would you like me to do?”

“At least look mildly threatened. Someone just dedicated a love song to your girlfriend.”

Yichen gave him a quiet, amused look.

“Would that make you feel better?”

Yuhao laughed. “You’re no fun at all.”

Yichen didn’t answer.

But his attention had drifted back toward the corridor outside.

He wondered whether Xiaoran had heard it.

More importantly, he wondered whether she thought it was him.

She found him during the morning break.

Yichen was standing near the staircase, speaking to a classmate. When he noticed Xiaoran approaching, he excused himself and walked over.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

She stood in front of him, holding her books against her chest.

She seemed to be searching for something to say.

Yichen waited.

Finally, she asked, “Did you listen to the radio this morning?”

“I did.”

Her eyes lifted.

“Oh.”

He watched her expression. “You heard it too.”

She nodded.

A small pause followed.

Then she asked, trying hard to sound casual, “Did you send that song?”

Yichen looked at her. He couldn’t help the faint smile. “No.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Oh.”

“Did you think I did?”

She looked down at her books.

“Your surname starts with Z.”

“That’s true.”

“And it was for someone in Class 3.”

“Also true.”

“So I thought...”

She trailed off.

Yichen looked at her, his expression softening.

“Sorry to disappoint you.”

Her head lifted immediately.

“I’m not disappointed!”

That got a smile out of him.

“All right.”

She squinted at him.

“You’re teasing me.”

“A little.”

She shifted her books to the other arm.

“Then who do you think sent it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Are you curious?”

“Yes.”

She looked surprised.

Yichen said, “Someone knows your name and class. I’d like to know who.”

There was nothing sharp in his voice. No accusation, no demand. Just a quiet curiosity.

Xiaoran considered him.

Then she asked, “Are you upset?”

“Should I be?”

“I don’t know.”

He smiled slightly.

“Did you want me to be?”

“No!”

He laughed.

She looked at him, embarrassed.

Yichen reached out and gently straightened the corner of a paper sticking out from her book.

“Don’t worry about it. It’s just a song.”

Xiaoran nodded. “I did think it might be you,” she said.

His eyes met hers.

“Why?”

“Because...”

She hesitated, her cheeks warming.

“Because you might do something like that.”

He looked at her for a second.

Then his smile became warmer.

“I’ll remember that.”

By lunchtime, the dedication had become the most interesting topic in Class 3.

Meilin had apparently told two other girls.

Those two had told someone else.

And by the time Xiaoran returned from buying drinks, three people were already discussing the mysterious sender.

“Maybe it’s someone from another class.”

“Maybe it’s someone who has liked her for a long time.”

“Maybe Z is his actual initial.”

Xiaoran placed her drink on the desk.

“Can everyone please stop?”

Meilin looked up.

“You’re famous.”

“I don’t want to be famous.”

“You should have thought of that before you got a song.”

One of the girls smiled.

“Xiaoran, do you know who it is?”

“No.”

“Do you have any guesses?”

“No.”

Meilin rested her chin on her hand.

“She thought it was Zhou Yichen.”

Xiaoran turned sharply.

“Meilin!”

“Of course she did. Who else signs things with a Z and walks into our classroom like he pays rent?” said one of the girls.

“We’re not discussing this,” Xiaoran announced.

Meilin laughed.

“Fine, fine.”

But she was still smiling when the lunch bell rang.

The answer came unexpectedly after school.

Xiaoran was putting her books into her bag when a boy from Class 5 appeared at the classroom door. Zeng Bowen. She knew his name because he ran the school radio’s request box on Wednesdays, and for no other reason.

“Lin Xiaoran?”

She looked up.

“Yes?”

He seemed a little nervous.

“Can I talk to you for a moment?”

Meilin, who was packing beside her, immediately looked interested.

Xiaoran stood.

“Sure.”

The boy glanced at Meilin, then lowered his voice.

“Did you hear the radio dedication this morning?”

Xiaoran’s expression changed.

A moment passed.

Then she understood.

“Was that you?”

He rubbed the back of his neck.

“Yeah.”

“Oh.”

He gave her a slightly embarrassed smile.

“I wasn’t sure if you’d know who it was. I thought signing with just Z would be less awkward.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

They had spoken perhaps four times, all of them about the sports festival banner.

“Thank you for the song. It was nice,” she said politely.

He smiled.

“I’m glad you liked it.”

There was a short silence. “I was wondering if you’d like to go to the bookshop with me sometime. There’s a new one near the station.”

Xiaoran’s fingers tightened around her bag strap.

She didn’t want to embarrass him.

But she also didn’t want to give him the wrong idea.

“That’s kind of you. But I don’t think I should,” she said gently.

His smile faltered slightly.

“Oh.”

“I’m sorry.”

He nodded, looking a little disappointed but not angry.

“Is it because of Zhou Yichen?”

Xiaoran went quiet.

She could have avoided answering.

Instead, she nodded.

“Yes.”

The boy looked down, then gave a small laugh.

“I thought so.”

Xiaoran felt bad.

“I hope you don’t feel embarrassed about the song. It was really thoughtful.”

“Don’t worry. I knew it was a risk.”

He gave her one last smile before leaving.

Meilin waited until he was out of sight, then slowly turned toward Xiaoran.

“Well.”

Xiaoran sighed.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your eyebrows did.”

Meilin grinned.

“Should I tell Zhou Yichen?”

“No!”

“Why not? He might want to know.”

Xiaoran picked up her bag.

“He doesn’t need to.”

Meilin followed her out.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Not even a little?”

Xiaoran stopped walking.

Then she looked at Meilin.

“Fine. Maybe a little.”

Meilin burst out laughing.

Yichen was waiting near the school gate.

He was standing with Yuhao, who was talking about their basketball practice later. When Xiaoran approached, Yichen glanced up.

“Ready?”

“Yes.”

Yuhao looked between them.

“Am I walking with you two?”

Yichen looked at him.

“Do you want to?”

Yuhao considered it, then shook his head.

“Actually, I remembered something.”

He walked away with a laugh.

Xiaoran watched him leave.

“He’s strange.”

“He’s been strange since primary school. I’ve known him since primary school.”

They started walking.

For a while, they talked about ordinary things: the homework they had to finish, the school trip worksheet, and whether it would rain the next day.

Then Xiaoran glanced at him.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Someone told me who sent the song.”

He met her eyes.

“Did they?”

She nodded.

“His name starts with Z. Zeng Bowen, Class 5.”

Yichen smiled. “The radio boy.”

“He asked me to go to a bookshop with him.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“And?”

“I said no.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

She waited.

He continued walking.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“That’s all?”

He turned his head.

“What else?”

“I don’t know. Aren’t you going to ask why?”

Yichen smiled.

“Do I need to?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Then I don’t.”

She walked beside him for a few steps, then slipped her hand into his.

Yichen looked down, his fingers naturally closing around hers.

“Why are you holding my hand?”

She looked ahead.

“Because I want to.”

“All right.”

“I told him I already have someone,” she said after a moment.

Yichen’s gaze shifted toward her, and stayed there.

His expression softened.

“Who?”

Xiaoran stopped walking.

She stared at him.

He looked perfectly serious, although the slight curve at the corner of his mouth gave him away.

“Zhou Yichen,” she said.

His mouth curved.

“That sounds familiar.”

She gave his hand a little squeeze.

“Don’t be annoying.”

He laughed and resumed walking.

That evening, Xiaoran received a message from him.

Yichen: Did you like the song?

She stared at the screen.

Then typed:

Xiaoran: It was nice.

A moment later:

Yichen: Good.

She waited, then another message appeared.

Yichen: I might dedicate one to you someday.

Xiaoran sat up.

She read it again.

Then typed:

Xiaoran: Really?

Yichen: If I do, I’ll put your name on it.

Her mouth tipped up.

Xiaoran: Not just Lin Xiaoran in Class 3?

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Then what?

The reply took a little longer.

Yichen: Lin Xiaoran. My favorite person.

She pressed her phone against her chest.

A ridiculous smile spread across her face.

Then she typed:

Xiaoran: That’s not very anonymous.

Yichen: I don’t intend to be.

She laughed, lying back against her pillow, and took a screenshot, and then a second screenshot in case the first one went missing.

chapters.desc: One weekend of romance dramas, one very specific request, and an empty hallway after practice.
chapters.title: Better Than the Drama
chapters.epigraph: “Real life has no background music. It has something better.”
chapters.content:
The problem started with a drama. Specifically, a forty-episode romance drama Lin Xiaoran had promised herself she would watch exactly one episode of on Saturday night. By Sunday afternoon she was on episode thirty-one, wrapped in Yichen’s stolen hoodie, eating shrimp crackers in the dark like a raccoon. Then episode thirty-two happened. Rain on a rooftop. The male lead tilting the female lead’s chin up. A pause long enough for the piano to swell, and then a kiss so slow and certain that Xiaoran had to pause the video and lie face down on her bed for a while.

She watched it four times. Then she thought about her own first kiss. The empty classroom. The way Yichen had asked first. The way it had been soft and warm for one perfect second—right before she lost her balance and nearly toppled off the chair, and he had to catch her mid-kiss. It had been sweet. It had been theirs. It had also had no background music whatsoever. At 11:40 PM she texted Tang Meilin.

Xiaoran: is it normal to be jealous of a fictional couple

Meilin: go to sleep

Xiaoran: their kiss had BACKGROUND MUSIC

Meilin: yours had a chair. you told me. twice

Xiaoran: I HATE THAT YOU REMEMBER

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday, Xiaoran couldn’t look Zhou Yichen in the eye. Nothing had happened. That was the problem. Somewhere around episode thirty-four she had made a decision: she wanted a proper kiss. A drama kiss. Slow, deliberate, no furniture involved. She just had no idea how to ask for one. Every time Yichen glanced at her in class, her brain started playing the piano music.

“You’re red,” he observed at lunch.

“It’s warm.”

“It’s raining.”

“Warm rain.”

Across the table, Chen Yuhao narrowed his eyes. “She’s been weird since homeroom.”

“She watched a drama all weekend,” Meilin said, without looking up from her planner.

“MEILIN.”

Yichen looked at her with sudden interest. Xiaoran stuffed an entire dumpling into her mouth so she wouldn’t have to answer. By the last period, she had drafted the request eleven different ways in the margins of her notebook and crossed out every single one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Practice ran late, so the school was nearly empty by the time Yichen came upstairs for his bag. Evening sun lay across the third-floor hallway in long gold stripes. Somewhere downstairs, a few students were still laughing. Xiaoran was waiting outside the classroom, holding his water bottle like a hostage.

“You didn’t have to wait,” he said, pulling on his hoodie.

“I did.”

“Why?”

She took a deep breath. All eleven drafts vanished at once.

“Kiss me like episode thirty-two.”

Yichen stopped with one arm still in his sleeve.

“…What?”

“Nothing.”

“You said episode thirty-two.”

“I said nothing.”

He finished pulling the hoodie on, slowly, and looked at her the way he looked at a math problem he already knew the answer to.

“Is this the drama?”

“There is no drama.”

“Meilin said—”

“Meilin is a liar.”

The corner of his mouth moved. Then, before she could escape, he leaned down and kissed her—quick and light, over before she had even closed her eyes. Xiaoran blinked.

“…That’s it?”

“Hm.”

“That wasn’t episode thirty-two.”

“What was it?”

“A trailer.”

That made him laugh, low and surprised. He set his bag down against the wall.

“So what happens in episode thirty-two?”

She should have said nothing. She should have run. Instead she grabbed the front of his hoodie with both hands, cheeks burning, and said the bravest thing she had said all year.

“…Again. Properly this time.”

Yichen smiled, then leaned down slowly, patiently, giving her plenty of time to panic and run away. This time, Lin Xiaoran didn’t run—even though her heartbeat sounded medically dangerous, even though he was close enough now that she could feel his breath, close enough that her fingers tightened in the front of his hoodie without her permission. That tiny movement softened his whole expression, like he found her nervousness cute instead of embarrassing. Which made everything worse.

“Still scared?” he murmured.

“A little.”

“You wanted this.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you trembling?”

“Because YOU’RE handsome.”

Yichen laughed under his breath, and that sound, this close, made her knees weak. His hand settled at her waist—not forceful, just enough to steady her when she leaned in. Warm fingers resting lightly against her side, like he was still making sure she was okay. He always made sure first. That bit of gentleness melted what was left of her panic. He kissed her again—slower this time, not teasing, not quick. A real kiss. His thumb brushed her waist without him seeming to notice, and Xiaoran finally understood why romance dramas were so popular. Her brain stopped working entirely.

She held on to his hoodie and kissed him back—awkwardly at first, then a little better when Yichen smiled against her lips like he was quietly encouraging her. That tiny smile in the middle of the kiss got to her more than the kiss itself. It was so… Yichen. Patient. Warm. Even this became gentle because it was him. Then he tilted his head and kissed her again—still soft, still careful, but longer, until Xiaoran’s knees nearly gave up.

One of her hands slid up and caught lightly at the back of his neck. Yichen went still for a fraction of a second—then his other hand steadied her waist more firmly. Not intense. Just instinctive. Protective. When they finally pulled apart, Xiaoran looked completely dazed—eyes unfocused, breathing uneven—while Zhou Yichen somehow still looked calmer than her. Slightly flushed, maybe. But infinitely more composed. Unfair.

“…Oh my god,” Xiaoran whispered weakly.

Yichen’s lips twitched.

“What?”

“That drama ruined my life.”

He laughed quietly again before brushing hair away from her face carefully.

“You’re cute.”

“That’s not the issue.”

“The issue is—”

She stopped abruptly. Because Yichen leaned closer again. Not kissing her yet—just close enough that she forgot the sentence entirely.

“…You were saying?” he murmured.

Nothing. Lin Xiaoran no longer had thoughts.

“I forgot what I was saying,” she admitted honestly.

That finally broke Yichen completely. He laughed properly this time, lowering his forehead briefly against hers. Somehow that felt even more intimate than the kissing.

“You spent the entire day panicking over this?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“You’re unbelievable.”

“You kissed me like a drama lead.”

Yichen smiled helplessly and kissed her cheek instead—gentler, familiar—and that small kiss made her chest ache in a completely different way. Dramatic kisses were exciting. This felt affectionate. Real. Then after a moment, Yichen looked at her.

“…Disappointed?”

Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“What?”

“You watched those drama scenes all weekend. So?” A tiny teasing smile appeared again.

Silence. Xiaoran grabbed his sleeve.

“Zhou Yichen. You’re never allowed to ask questions like that after kissing someone.”

“So you WERE comparing.”

“I was… curious.”

“Results?”

She stared at him for two full seconds. Then honestly—

“…Better than the drama.”

Yichen froze. Just slightly. But Xiaoran noticed, and her confidence came roaring back.

“AHA.”

She had finally found a way to embarrass Zhou Yichen. His ears were faintly red. Victory. Beautiful victory.

“You’re blushing,” she whispered.

“No I’m not.”

“Oh my god you ARE.”

Before she could keep bullying him, Yichen pulled her closer by the waist—smoothly, effortlessly—and Xiaoran forgot how to speak for the second time.

“You’re getting brave now,” he murmured near her ear.

“That’s because I won.”

“There was a competition?”

“There’s always competition.”

Yichen laughed softly again.

“You know what your problem is? You say things confidently. Then you panic the second I respond.” His thumb brushed lightly against her waist again.

True. Painfully true. Xiaoran buried her face in his shoulder.

“I hate this relationship.”

“No you don’t.”

“…Okay maybe not.”

The hallway stayed quiet. Gold evening light stretched across the floor by the windows, and somewhere downstairs, a few students were still talking. Neither of them moved—mostly because Xiaoran refused to look him in the eye after that kiss, and Yichen looked suspiciously comfortable holding her there.

“Xiaoran, you know you can just kiss me whenever you want, right?”

Silence.

“WHAT KIND OF SENTENCE IS THAT.”

Yichen only smiled, completely unbothered, like he had said something perfectly reasonable. Xiaoran glared at him. Then, before she could lose her nerve, she rose onto her toes and kissed him—quick, clumsy, and entirely her own idea. This time, it was Zhou Yichen who forgot how to speak.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran wanted one proper date. She didn’t expect a street band to describe her relationship out loud.
chapters.title: The Song That Knew Too Much
chapters.epigraph: “Some songs sound like they were written about you. Some actually were.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen and Lin Xiaoran’s dates usually ended in chaos, not romance. Most weekends meant Chen Yuhao screaming at video games in somebody’s living room while Tang Meilin judged everyone from the couch. Yichen would sit beside Xiaoran. Xiaoran would steal his hoodie. And the whole afternoon would disappear without either of them noticing. So when Xiaoran announced—

“We’re going on a REAL date tomorrow.”

—everyone reacted differently. Yuhao nearly choked. Meilin looked suspicious. Zhou Yichen just looked amused.

On Saturday morning, sunlight filled Xiaoran’s bedroom while she tore through her wardrobe. Today mattered. Not that she would admit it. Okay, maybe a little. The problem was Douyin. All week, her feed had been full of ridiculously aesthetic couples walking down pretty streets, holding hands, soft music playing. Now Xiaoran wanted that too. Just once. A proper date. Just the two of them. No basketball, no friends, no Yuhao screaming “GET A ROOM” every ten minutes. And sometimes she missed him, even though she saw him almost every day. Which sounded insane. But it was true.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You look nervous,” Yichen said the second Xiaoran climbed into the car he’d borrowed from his dad.

“I’m not nervous.”

“You changed outfits three times.”

“How do YOU know that?”

“You posted mirror selfies accidentally.”

“…Oh.”

Yichen laughed and handed her a milk tea. Half sugar, no pearls. Of course he remembered. Xiaoran’s carefully prepared cool image cracked a little.

“You’re bribing me already,” she accused.

“It’s 10 a.m.”

“Exactly.”

Yichen smiled at the road. Zhou Yichen out of his school uniform was a problem. Gray sweater. A watch loose around his wrist. Hair a little messy from the wind. It was upsetting. Xiaoran stared too long. Yichen noticed.

“You’re doing it again.”

“I’m observing.”

“What’s your conclusion?”

Xiaoran turned to the window.

“…My boyfriend looks like a perfume ad.”

Yichen nearly laughed into the steering wheel.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first half of the date went surprisingly well. They wandered through shopping streets, shared snacks, and argued over claw machines. Xiaoran lost six tries at a plush rabbit before Yichen won it on his first—exactly like the day they met.

“Show-off,” she muttered, hugging it anyway.

“You spent twenty yuan.”

“It was a strategic investment.”

At one point they stopped at a tiny café Xiaoran had found on Douyin. The desserts were beautiful. The portions were microscopic.

“People online lied to me,” Xiaoran whispered while staring at her tiny cake.

“You wanted aesthetics.”

“I also wanted survival.”

Yichen pushed half of his toward her without a word. Zhou Yichen always remembered things. He noticed things, and quietly took care of her before she even asked: picking the cilantro out of her noodles, catching her wrist when she drifted toward the road, carrying her bag after she complained exactly once. Those tiny things softened her heart more than any grand gesture could.

✦ ✦ ✦

By evening, the streets had gone quiet. Golden light stretched across the sidewalks, and the little shops switched on their warm lights one by one. Xiaoran walked beside Yichen, swinging their joined hands.

“Tired?” he asked.

“No.”

“You walked slower.”

“I’m preserving the date.”

Yichen looked amused. “That’s not how time works.”

“You don’t know romance.”

Then music drifted down the street. A small student band was playing outside a café on the riverside corner. Nothing fancy—a guitarist, a keyboard player, and a singer laughing shyly at the little crowd that had gathered. Xiaoran stopped walking.

“Ooooh.”

She tugged Yichen to the back of the crowd. The singer adjusted the microphone and smiled.

“This next song is dedicated to people who accidentally fell in love with someone troublesome,” he said lightly.

The crowd laughed. Beside Yichen, Xiaoran gasped.

“Wow. That’s targeted harassment against you,” she whispered.

Yichen glanced down.

“Interesting. I thought it sounded like you.”

“Rude.”

Then the guitar started, soft and warm, the kind of melody that belonged to sunsets. The singer began—

“She talks too much when she gets excited,
Gets angry over things that don’t matter,
Cries when I tease her even a little—
But somehow the world gets quieter beside her.”

Xiaoran blinked once.

“…Wait.”

Yichen’s lips twitched. The singer continued.

“She steals my jackets like they belong to her,
Complains every day but still waits for me after class,
Everyone says she’s hard to handle—
So why do I keep smiling when I see her?”

That line was a little too accurate. Yichen laughed under his breath. Xiaoran turned slowly.

“…Why are you laughing.”

Yichen looked away, still smiling.

“This song is weird.”

“What does that mean?”

“It knows too much.”

Xiaoran squinted at him as the music softened into the chorus.

“Maybe love isn’t peaceful after all,
Maybe love is noisy and clingy and impossible,
But if she disappeared for even one day—
I think my whole life would feel empty.”

Silence. A breeze moved down the street. Cars passed. Somewhere behind them, people were laughing. But Zhou Yichen couldn’t really hear any of it anymore. Every lyric kept turning into Lin Xiaoran: her dramatic voice, the way she’d clung to him before his family trip, her tiny angry face when she was jealous, the way she filled every silence without trying, the way even the worst days got lighter once she showed up. And the chorus was painfully true. If Xiaoran disappeared from his life now, everything really would feel emptier.

Beside him, Xiaoran had stopped joking too. When she looked up, Yichen was already looking at her—like the song had just told everyone his secrets.

“…Stop looking at me like that,” she muttered.

“Like what?”

“Like YOU wrote the lyrics.”

Yichen smiled a little, then leaned in just enough that only she could hear—

“The chorus is true though.”

Xiaoran’s face went red.

“Zhou Yichen, you can’t suddenly say romantic things during public music events.”

Yichen laughed and laced his fingers through hers a little tighter. The singer moved into the last verse—

“She’ll probably never realize this,
But every ordinary day became brighter after meeting her,
So if loving her means losing my peace forever—
Then honestly… I don’t mind at all.”

And for the first time that whole day, Lin Xiaoran understood why people loved romance songs so much. Not because the lyrics were dramatic. Because when you were standing next to the right person, every line sounded true.

chapters.desc: Her cousin and her boyfriend are spending Saturday together. Lin Xiaoran has concerns.
chapters.title: Lin Jun Stole Her Boyfriend for a Day
chapters.epigraph: “The scariest meeting isn’t meeting the parents. It’s meeting the cousin who knows everything.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran knew something was wrong the moment Zhou Yichen smiled at his phone during lunch. Not a normal smile. A suspicious one. She narrowed her eyes.

“Who are you texting.”

Yichen glanced up. “Lin Jun.”

“My cousin?” Xiaoran repeated slowly.

“Hm.”

“…Why.”

“He asked if I wanted to hang out Saturday.”

A longer silence. Then Xiaoran pointed at him.

“Absolutely not.”

Across the table, Chen Yuhao looked delighted. “Oho.”

Tang Meilin didn’t even look up from her phone. Everyone had seen this coming. Ever since Lin Jun moved back from Shanghai for a new job, he and Zhou Yichen had gotten along disgustingly well. It made no sense. One was Xiaoran’s emotionally exhausted older cousin. The other was her emotionally exhausted boyfriend. Apparently shared suffering created male friendship. Traitors. Both of them.

“Why are YOU two hanging out?” Xiaoran demanded.

Yichen looked unbothered. “He wants to know me better.”

“That sounds like an interrogation.”

Yuhao nodded seriously. “It probably is.”

Meilin sipped her drink calmly. “Honestly fair.”

“WHOSE SIDE ARE YOU ON?”

Nobody answered, because Lin Jun investigating Zhou Yichen was extremely understandable. If Xiaoran dated some random guy, her family would absolutely run a background check. Still, Xiaoran hated it. Somehow, she felt left out. Which was ridiculous. But true.

“You’re stealing my boyfriend,” she told Jun on a video call that evening.

Lin Jun looked completely relaxed.

“He’ll survive.”

“That’s not the issue.”

“What is the issue?”

“You two are bonding without supervision.”

Jun laughed.

“Why do you sound like a worried mother?”

“Because you’re suspicious.”

From the corner of the screen, Yichen sipped his water and watched the argument unfold, thoroughly entertained. Traitor.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came, and Lin Xiaoran became the most restless person alive.

“This feels wrong,” she muttered, pacing Meilin’s bedroom.

Meilin, lying on her bed with a face mask on, already looked exhausted.

“It’s one afternoon.”

“My cousin and boyfriend are going on a date.”

“It’s not a date.”

“How do YOU know.”

“Because one of them basically raised you.”

“That doesn’t stop men from being weird.”

Across the city, Zhou Yichen was finding the whole thing interesting. He liked Lin Jun. Calm, sharp, easy to talk to. And dangerously observant. The two of them were walking through a riverside shopping district with iced coffees.

“You know. Xiaoran thinks I’m stealing you,” Jun said eventually.

Yichen laughed.

“She told me that too.”

Yichen smiled. Very Xiaoran. For a while, the conversation stayed easy—basketball, university, Jun’s years working in Shanghai. Then, naturally, it turned to Xiaoran.

“How long have you liked her?” Jun asked.

Yichen thought about it.

“…Longer than she realized.”

Jun nodded, like that made sense. After a moment—

“She’s difficult sometimes.”

Yichen laughed.

“That’s true.”

“But. She’s sincere.” Jun glanced sideways briefly.

“I know.”

“She gets attached deeply to people.”

Yichen knew that too, probably better than anyone now. Lin Xiaoran loved loudly, clingily, like she had never learned how to hold back. Maybe that was why he liked her so much.

“She talks about you constantly,” Jun said.

Yichen sighed. “Apparently everyone knows that.”

“Trust me. You have no idea.”

Jun stopped outside a small convenience store.

“You know what she used to do as a kid?”

Yichen sensed danger.

“What?”

“She cried because I went on a school trip for three days.”

“Oh my god,” said Xiaoran’s voice behind them.

Both men turned. There she was, three meters away with Meilin, looking deeply betrayed.

Jun blinked. “What are you doing here?”

“You shared your location accidentally.”

Then Yichen laughed until he nearly dropped his drink. Jun looked horrified.

“You TRACKED me?”

“I was worried!”

“You’re insane.”

“You STOLE MY BOYFRIEND.”

A woman walking her dog gave them a wide berth. Meilin covered her face.

“I told her not to come.”

“You participated willingly,” Xiaoran accused.

“I was kidnapped.”

Jun sighed and looked at Yichen.

“…You see what we dealt with growing up?”

Yichen smiled.

“Every day.”

Xiaoran marched over and grabbed Yichen’s sleeve.

“Are you done bonding?”

Jun looked offended.

“He likes me more than you now.”

“That’s fake.”

“You sure?”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“Yichen. Choose carefully.”

The threat would have been scarier if she weren’t holding his sleeve like an angry kitten. Yichen looked from one cousin to the other. Then he answered—

“He buys me coffee.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

Jun nearly collapsed laughing. Xiaoran looked devastated.

“Wow, my cousin and my boyfriend,” she whispered.

Yichen finally smiled and pulled her closer by the wrist. Then, near her ear—

“You know no one replaces you.”

Instant recovery. Meilin watched them over her face mask.

“Disgusting.”

Jun nodded solemnly. “Actually unbearable.”

But Xiaoran had already cheered up. Maybe Lin Jun and Zhou Yichen getting along wasn’t the worst thing. Especially since they both already looked equally exhausted from dealing with her. A true family connection, really.

chapters.desc: Two weeks at her grandparents’ house in the town, a television with four channels, and a phone that rings at exactly nine every night.
chapters.title: The Holiday Call Schedule
chapters.epigraph: “No. I miss seeing you.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran spent the last two weeks of the summer holiday at her grandparents’ house, in the small town four hours from the city where she had lived until she was twelve. There was a persimmon tree in the courtyard, a television that only got four channels, and a bedroom she shared with her grandmother because the other one was full of her grandfather’s fishing equipment.

On the first night, Zhou Yichen called at nine.

Exactly nine. Lin Xiaoran had been waiting since quarter to.

She was sitting cross-legged on her bed, wearing her favorite oversized T-shirt, with her phone placed beside her pillow. Every few minutes, she would pick it up, check the screen, and put it down again.

Her grandmother, who was folding clothes on the other bed, had been watching this for fifteen minutes.

“Are you waiting for someone?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“No.”

Her grandmother glanced at the phone.

“Then why do you keep looking at it?”

“I’m checking the time.”

“The clock is on the wall.”

Xiaoran went quiet.

Her grandmother smiled but didn’t say anything.

Then, at precisely nine, the phone began to ring.

Xiaoran’s eyes lit up.

She reached for it immediately.

Unfortunately, her grandmother was faster.

“Oh, someone’s calling.”

“Grandma!”

Her grandmother picked up the phone.

“Hello?”

Xiaoran froze.

There was a brief silence on the other end, then a polite male voice answered.

“Hello, Grandma. I’m Zhou Yichen.”

Her grandmother looked at Xiaoran.

Xiaoran looked horrified.

Her grandmother smiled.

“Ah! Yichen!”

Xiaoran’s mouth fell open.

She hadn’t even told her grandmother his full name. She had mentioned him, several times, perhaps more than several, possibly every day since she arrived, but that wasn’t the point.

“How are you, child?” her grandmother asked warmly.

“I’m well, thank you. How are you?”

“Good, good. I’m doing well.”

Xiaoran slowly reached for the phone.

“Grandma, give it to me.”

Her grandmother raised one finger, asking her to wait.

“Have you eaten dinner?”

“Yes, Grandma.”

“Good. Are you still studying?”

“Yes. We have some homework during the holiday.”

“Oh, that’s good. You must study hard.”

“I will.”

Xiaoran tried again.

“Grandma.”

Her grandmother ignored her.

“Are you calling because you want to speak to Xiaoran?”

“Yes.”

“Ah, then let me ask you something first.”

Xiaoran closed her eyes. She knew that tone. It was the tone her grandmother used on the man who sold eggs at the market, and the egg man had once taken forty minutes to get away.

Eight minutes in, Xiaoran was sitting on the edge of her bed, watching her grandmother conduct what appeared to be a formal interview. In the courtyard, her grandfather turned his radio up, which was what he did whenever an interview started.

“So, Yichen, how long have you known my granddaughter?”

“Since school.”

“Since school? That’s nice. Are you in the same class?”

“No, Grandma. We’re in different classes.”

“Ah. But you see each other every day?”

“Most days.”

“That’s good.”

Xiaoran mouthed, Grandma, please.

Her grandmother gave her a reassuring smile and carried on. “Do you like studying?”

“Yes, I do.”

“What subjects do you like?”

“Mathematics and physics.”

Her grandmother nodded approvingly.

“Good. Mathematics is important.”

Xiaoran covered her face with a pillow.

Four hours away, Yichen was sitting at his desk in his bedroom with his back straight. He had expected to hear Xiaoran’s voice. Instead he had been speaking to her grandmother for nearly ten minutes, and he had the feeling, which he recognized from oral exams, that the hard questions hadn’t started yet.

“Do you play sports?”

“Yes. Basketball.”

“Basketball! That’s good. Does Xiaoran watch you play?”

Yichen paused.

Then his voice softened a little.

“Sometimes.”

“Does she understand basketball?”

He smiled.

“She’s learning.”

Xiaoran lifted her head.

She heard that.

“Hey!”

“I understand basketball!”

Yichen laughed.

Her grandmother smiled.

“That’s good. You can teach her more.”

“I’d be happy to.”

Xiaoran stared at the phone.

He was enjoying this.

She could hear it in his voice.

By quarter past, the questions had become more personal.

“Yichen, what do your parents do?”

He answered politely.

“Does your mother cook?”

“Yes, sometimes.”

“Do you help her?”

“When I’m home, I do.”

“Good. Boys should know how to do things themselves.”

“Yes, Grandma.”

“Can you cook?”

“A little.”

Xiaoran’s head turned. She mouthed, A little? She had seen him make fried rice exactly once, and the kitchen had needed a day to recover.

“I can make a few simple dishes,” Yichen said.

Her grandmother sounded impressed.

“That’s very good. Xiaoran doesn’t know much about cooking.”

“Grandma!”

“It’s true,” her grandmother said.

Xiaoran folded her arms.

“I know how to cook.”

“Last time you made eggs, you forgot to turn off the stove.”

“That was one time!”

Yichen laughed.

Her grandmother continued speaking as if nothing had happened.

“She’s sometimes careless. You must remind her to be careful.”

“I will.”

Xiaoran looked at the phone.

“Don’t agree with everything she says!”

Yichen’s laughter became slightly more audible.

Her grandmother smiled.

“See? She’s always like this.”

“I know.”

Xiaoran stopped.

She slowly turned toward the phone.

I know?

Her grandmother looked delighted.

“You’re familiar with her temper, then.”

“Yes, Grandma.”

Xiaoran grabbed a pillow and pressed it against her face. She was going to remember this.

Twenty-five minutes in, she finally managed to interrupt.

“Grandma, can I talk to him now?”

Her grandmother looked at the phone.

“Wait a moment.”

She turned back toward the call.

“Yichen, do you have a girlfriend?”

Silence.

Xiaoran nearly dropped the pillow.

“GRANDMA!”

“Why would you ask that?”

Her grandmother calmly returned her attention to the phone.

Yichen was quiet for a brief moment.

Then he answered.

“Yes, Grandma.”

Xiaoran froze.

Her grandmother’s expression brightened.

“Ah! You do?”

“Yes.”

“Is she a good girl?”

Yichen glanced toward his bedroom window.

Something in his face eased.

“Very good.”

Xiaoran stared at the phone.

Her grandmother asked another question.

“Does she study hard?”

“She does.”

“Is she obedient?”

Yichen paused.

Xiaoran’s eyes widened.

She silently warned him not to answer carelessly.

He seemed to understand.

“She’s kind.”

Her grandmother laughed.

“That’s not what I asked.”

Yichen smiled.

“She’s also quite playful.”

Xiaoran pointed at the phone.

“Don’t!”

Her grandmother laughed harder.

“Ah, I see. You two must get along very well.”

“Yes, Grandma.”

His answer came without hesitation.

And, Xiaoran forgot to be embarrassed.

Half an hour in, her grandmother finally handed over the phone.

“Here. Talk to him.”

Xiaoran snatched it gently.

“Hello?”

There was a small pause.

Then Yichen’s familiar voice came through.

“Hello.”

She immediately lowered her voice.

“Why didn’t you tell her you wanted to speak to me?”

“I did.”

“When?”

“At the beginning.”

“And then?”

“She asked me a question.”

Xiaoran stared at the wall.

“One question?”

He laughed.

“Several.”

She lay back on her bed.

“How long has it been?”

Yichen glanced at the clock.

“About thirty-five minutes.”

“Thirty-five minutes?!”

“Mm.”

She covered her face.

“I’m so sorry.”

“Why?”

“My grandmother interviewed you.”

“She was very nice.”

“She asked whether you had a girlfriend!”

“I noticed.”

Xiaoran groaned. “She’s going to ask me about this tomorrow.”

“Is that bad?”

“Yes!”

“Why?”

“Because she’ll want to know everything.”

He was quiet. “Would that be a problem?”

Xiaoran turned onto her side.

“No.”

Her voice became smaller.

“Just embarrassing.”

Yichen smiled.

“I see.”

She picked at the edge of her blanket.

“Did you really not mind?”

“No.”

“She asked so many questions.”

“I know.”

“She even asked about your parents.”

“Yes.”

“And cooking.”

“Yes.”

“And whether you had a girlfriend.”

He laughed.

“You’re repeating the questions.”

“Because there were too many!”

“I liked talking to her,” he said.

Xiaoran went quiet.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because she’s important to you.”

She stared at the ceiling.

That was unfair.

He always seemed to find a way to say something that made her forget whatever she had been complaining about.

She smiled.

“You’re too good at answering questions.”

“Was I being tested?”

“Maybe.”

“Did I pass?”

She considered it.

“Not sure.”

He laughed.

They talked for another fifteen minutes.

Xiaoran told him about the dumplings her grandmother had made, the neighbor who had come over that afternoon to look at her and say she’d grown, and how she had fallen asleep in front of one of the four channels.

Yichen listened.

He told her about his day, his basketball practice, and the homework he still hadn’t finished.

Their conversation moved easily from one subject to another.

It was comfortable.

It felt like the usual conversations they had after school, except now there was no classroom bell waiting to interrupt them.

A little before ten, her grandmother began getting ready for bed. Xiaoran leaned closer to the phone and whispered, “Grandma is going to sleep.”

“All right.”

“Tomorrow, I’ll answer the phone myself.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Okay.”

She hesitated. “Unless she gets there first.”

He laughed.

“Then I’ll talk to her again.”

Xiaoran smiled despite herself.

“You’re not afraid of her?”

“Should I be?”

“She asks a lot of questions.”

“I noticed.”

“She might ask something even more embarrassing tomorrow.”

Yichen considered it.

“Then I’ll answer politely.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Good night, Yichen.”

“Good night, Xiaoran.”

She was about to end the call when he said, “Wait. Did you have a good day?”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Yes.”

“Good. Sleep early.”

“You too.”

She ended the call.

Then she lay still, looking at the phone in her hand.

From the other side of the room, her grandmother spoke.

“He’s a polite boy.”

“Grandma. You talked to him for forty minutes.”

Her grandmother smiled.

“He’s easy to talk to.”

Xiaoran buried her face in her pillow.

The next night, Xiaoran prepared in advance.

By five to nine she was sitting beside her phone with the volume checked, and her grandmother was in the kitchen. At exactly nine, the phone rang.

Xiaoran grabbed it.

“Hello!”

“Hello.”

Her face brightened.

“Yichen!”

He smiled on the other end.

“Did I call at a bad time?”

“No. I was waiting.”

“Did your grandmother go to bed?”

Xiaoran looked toward the kitchen.

“Not yet.”

“Should I prepare myself?”

She giggled.

“Yes. Be careful.”

“Understood.”

They talked for a few minutes.

Then Xiaoran heard footsteps.

She looked up.

Her grandmother appeared at the bedroom door.

She glanced at the phone, then at Xiaoran.

“Is that Yichen?”

Xiaoran slowly closed her eyes.

Yichen heard the question.

He smiled.

“Good evening, Grandma.”

Her grandmother smiled brightly.

“Ah, Yichen! Have you eaten?”

Xiaoran looked at the ceiling.

Not again.

By the fourth night, it had become a routine. Nine o’clock meant Yichen would call. Sometimes Xiaoran answered. Sometimes her grandmother answered first. Once her grandmother was already sitting beside the phone at ten to nine, with her reading glasses on, as if there might be something to read.

Yichen learned that her grandmother liked to ask whether he had eaten, whether he had studied, and whether basketball practice was tiring. He answered every question patiently. On the sixth night she asked him to say hello to her husband, and Yichen spent four minutes shouting pleasantries at a man who was holding the phone the wrong way up.

On the fifth night, Xiaoran finally protested.

“Grandma, you can’t keep interviewing him every night!”

Her grandmother looked up from her knitting.

“Why not?”

“Because he’s calling me!”

“Then you can talk after I’ve finished.”

“Finished what?”

“Talking.”

Xiaoran stared.

Her grandmother smiled.

“He’s a nice boy. What’s wrong with knowing him better?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth, then closed it.

There wasn’t really a good answer.

Her grandmother continued knitting.

“Besides, he always calls at nine. Very punctual.”

Xiaoran looked down at her phone.

She couldn’t help smiling.

On the ninth night, Yichen called at nine as usual.

This time, Xiaoran answered first.

“Hello!”

“Hello.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Grandma’s watching television.”

“That’s good.”

“I think we can talk properly tonight.”

He laughed.

“How was your day?”

“Good. I went shopping with Grandma.”

“What did you buy?”

She began telling him about a little hair clip she had found, a new notebook, and the snacks her grandmother had insisted on buying.

They were halfway through the conversation when her grandmother walked into the room.

Xiaoran glanced up.

Her grandmother looked at the phone.

Then she smiled.

“Yichen?”

Xiaoran immediately shook her head.

Her grandmother ignored her.

“Have you eaten?”

Yichen’s voice came through the speaker.

“Yes, Grandma.”

“Good. Don’t study too late.”

“I won’t.”

“And tell your parents I said hello.”

“I will.”

Her grandmother nodded, satisfied.

Then she turned to Xiaoran.

“All right. You can talk now.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

Her grandmother walked away.

Xiaoran blinked.

That was surprisingly quick.

She returned her attention to the phone.

“She’s finally letting us talk.”

Yichen smiled.

“That’s good.”

Xiaoran settled against her pillow.

“Your grandmother asked me something yesterday,” he said.

She sat up.

“What?”

“She asked whether I was planning to keep calling you after the holiday.”

Xiaoran went still.

“What did you say?”

Yichen was quiet.

Then he answered.

“That I’d like to.”

She looked down at her blanket.

Her smile appeared slowly.

“Oh.”

“Is that all?”

She shook her head, even though he couldn’t see her.

“No.”

“Then what?”

She pulled the blanket up to her chin.

“I’d like that too.”

On the last night of the holiday, Yichen called at nine.

Xiaoran answered immediately.

“Hello.”

“Hello.”

She was sitting beside her suitcase, which was already half-packed. Tomorrow her father would drive up to fetch her, and the day after that, school started.

“Are you ready to come back?” he asked.

“Yes. I miss school.”

He laughed.

“Really?”

“No. I miss seeing you.”

There was a brief silence.

Then he said, “I miss you too.”

She smiled.

They talked about the first day back, whether they would see each other before class, and what they wanted to eat once they were back in the city.

Then, just as Xiaoran was about to say goodnight, her grandmother appeared at the door.

She looked at the phone, then at Xiaoran.

“Is Yichen there?”

Xiaoran sighed.

“Yes, Grandma.”

Her grandmother stepped closer.

“Yichen, does your school start on Monday too?”

“Yes, Grandma.”

“Good. Make sure you eat breakfast.”

“I will.”

“And don’t forget your jacket. The weather might be cold.”

“All right.”

Her grandmother nodded.

Then she looked at Xiaoran.

“Tell him to come visit us sometime.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Grandma!”

Yichen answered before she could object.

“I’d be happy to, Grandma.”

Her grandmother smiled.

“Good. You’re always welcome.”

Then she left.

Xiaoran sat still.

Yichen was quiet on the other end.

Finally, she whispered, “You’re really going to visit?”

“If your grandmother invites me.”

She hid her face.

“She’s going to be so happy.”

“Then I’ll come.”

Xiaoran smiled into her blanket.

“Good night, Yichen.”

“Good night.”

She ended the call.

She looked at the phone before putting it down.

The next morning her father’s car came up the lane at ten. Her grandmother packed a bag of persimmons into the boot, then another bag of dried mushrooms, then a jar of chili oil wrapped in three layers of newspaper, and then she held Xiaoran’s face in both hands at the gate.

“Tell Yichen to eat breakfast.”

“Grandma, I don’t see him at breakfast.”

“Then tell him at lunch.”

Her grandmother let go of her face and turned to Xiaoran’s father, who had been loading the boot and listening to all this with a slowly changing expression.

“He calls at nine. Very punctual,” she said.

Her father shut the boot. He said nothing at all for the first hour of the drive. Somewhere past the second toll gate he said, “Who calls at nine?”

Xiaoran pretended to be asleep for the next three hours, and it was the most difficult performance of her life.

chapters.desc: One bad landing in a close game, and Lin Xiaoran learns what real fear feels like.
chapters.title: Don’t Scare Me Like That Again
chapters.epigraph: “Some people love quietly. She loved like a fire alarm.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran hated basketball injuries. Not normal hate. Personal hate. Basketball injuries meant blood, limping, bruises, and Zhou Yichen saying “I’m fine” while obviously not fine. And Zhou Yichen got hurt often enough that Xiaoran had developed a small trauma response to the word “injury.” Usually it wasn’t serious. A sprained wrist. A bruised shoulder. A sore ankle. Things athletes shrugged off, and things Xiaoran absolutely didn’t. Still, even she knew basketball was rough. So normally, she saved the drama for afterward.

Today was different.

✦ ✦ ✦

Final quarter of the city league semifinal, and the gym was deafening. The score was close. Everyone was screaming. Xiaoran sat beside Meilin in the bleachers, clutching Yichen’s jacket in both hands.

“He looks tired,” she muttered, for the tenth time.

“He’s played three quarters nonstop,” Meilin said.

“But he looks EXTRA tired.”

“He’s sweating because he’s a human being.”

Xiaoran ignored her. Something felt wrong today. The game had turned rough early. One player on the other team kept going after Yichen—nothing technically illegal, just too physical. And Yichen, competitive Yichen, only got colder each quarter. More intense. More reckless.

Eventually, Meilin noticed too.

“…He’s getting irritated.”

On the court, Yichen blocked a shot and drove forward again, fast and sharp. The crowd roared. Then it all happened too fast. One shove. One bad landing. The horrible screech of sneakers skidding across the floor—and Zhou Yichen went down. Hard. The gym went silent. Xiaoran froze—her whole brain froze—because Yichen wasn’t getting up. He stayed down, gripping his leg, while players crowded around him. Coach Wang ran onto the court. A whistle. Someone in the crowd gasped.

And somewhere nearby, someone whispered—

“That looked bad.”

That sentence alone broke something in Xiaoran.

“Yichen.”

Her voice came out small. Then louder—

“YICHEN.”

Meilin grabbed her wrist before she could run onto the court.

“Xiaoran wait—”

But Xiaoran couldn’t breathe properly. Yichen still wasn’t standing. Worse, he looked like he was in real pain—the kind he usually hid in a second. His face was pale, his jaw tight, his breathing uneven.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time Yichen had been helped to the bench, Xiaoran was crying. Not dramatic crying. Real tears. The medical staff examined his ankle while Coach Wang argued with the referees.

“It’s probably a bad sprain,” Meilin said gently.

Probably. Xiaoran hated that word. Probably still meant maybe not. Finally, Yichen looked up—straight at the bleachers, straight at her. The second he saw her crying, the pain on his face gave way to something else: worry. For her. Even now. Idiot. He mouthed something: I’m okay. Xiaoran nearly cried harder, because he was so obviously NOT okay.

✦ ✦ ✦

The game ended eventually. Xiaoran didn’t remember the score, or the crowd leaving, or anyone talking to her. She only remembered rushing to the medical room afterward with shaking hands and pushing the door open. Yichen was sitting on the examination bed while the doctor wrapped his ankle. He looked up when she came in.

“…Hey.”

That one word nearly undid her.

“You scared me,” she whispered.

Yichen paused. Then his expression softened. He could tell she’d been genuinely terrified. Xiaoran walked closer, trying hard not to cry again. She failed.

“Does it hurt badly?”

“A little.”

“That means yes.”

“A reasonable amount.”

“What does THAT mean?!”

Yichen managed a weak smile, which somehow made it worse. Why was he comforting her? He was the one who was hurt. The doctor finished and stood.

“No fractures. But severe sprain. He needs proper rest,” he explained calmly.

Rest. Thank god. Not surgery, not the hospital, not permanent damage. The second the doctor left, Xiaoran let out a shaky breath, maybe her first in an hour. Then she hit Yichen’s shoulder. Not hard.

“I hate you.”

Yichen blinked.

“That seems harsh.”

“You fell like you were dying.”

“I twisted my ankle.”

“You scared me to death.”

Her voice cracked on the last word, and Yichen’s face went soft. This wasn’t Xiaoran being dramatic. She had genuinely panicked—probably imagined the worst possible ending in the first three seconds.

“…Come here,” he said.

Xiaoran was beside him before he finished saying it. Yichen pulled her carefully against him, one hand at the back of her head. Only then did Xiaoran notice how cold her hands had gone.

“I’m okay,” he murmured into her hair.

“You weren’t moving.”

“I know.”

“You looked hurt.”

“I was hurt.”

“That’s worse.”

Yichen laughed under his breath—then hissed when he moved wrong. Xiaoran pulled back.

“SEE.”

“Relax.”

“DON’T RELAX.”
