He smiled helplessly. This was exactly why he hid injuries from her sometimes. When something happened to someone she loved, Lin Xiaoran didn’t do anything halfway. Sometimes he found that a little overwhelming. But never unwanted. Never that.

“You know, players get injured all the time,” he said after a while.

“I know.”

“Then why were you crying like someone announced my funeral?”

“Because it was YOU.”

She said it without even thinking, and it hit harder than he expected. Yichen looked at her for a second—her red eyes, the worry she still couldn’t hide—then gently brushed his thumb under her eye.

“You really got scared huh?”

Xiaoran tried to glare.

“You think?”

“I’m sorry.”

Zhou Yichen rarely apologized for getting hurt. It usually wasn’t his fault. But he meant this one, like he regretted scaring her more than the injury itself. Xiaoran sniffed.

“You better recover properly.”

“Hm.”

“And no pretending you’re okay just to practice again.”

“Hm.”

“And no acting cool.”

“That one’s difficult.”

She hit his shoulder again. Yichen laughed and caught her hand this time, lacing their fingers together. Comforting her again, without even thinking about it. Outside the medical room, the evening light was fading across the empty gym. The match was long over. The crowd was gone. Everything had finally gone quiet. Only then did Xiaoran realize something embarrassing: her heartbeat had only calmed down once she was holding Zhou Yichen’s hand again.

chapters.desc: A sprained ankle in the city semifinal, a week on crutches, and a girlfriend who carries everything until he asks her to ask first.
chapters.title: Crutches
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want you to get hurt.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen had played basketball for years. He knew how to fall and how to land, and he knew the difference between a bruise that would be gone in two days and an injury that needed proper attention. On Saturday, in the last quarter of the city league semifinal, a shove from a boy who had been leaning on him all game had taught him that knowing how to fall didn’t mean you got to choose when.

Severe sprain, the doctor had said. No fracture. Crutches for two days, no basketball for three weeks, and rest, which Yichen had heard as a suggestion and Xiaoran had heard as a law of physics.

On Monday morning his mother dropped him at the school gate. Xiaoran was already standing there. She had been standing there, Meilin told him later, since ten past seven, in a wind that had turned her ears red, holding a carton of milk that had gone warm in her hand.

She watched him get out of the car, crutches first, and her face did something complicated.

“Does it hurt?”

“Not much.”

“That means a lot.”

“It means not much. Good morning.” He got the crutches under his arms.

She crouched down right there by the gate, in front of everyone arriving for morning reading, and looked at the bandage with her brows drawn together, as if she could see through it. On Saturday night in the medical room she had cried, and hit his shoulder, and told him she hated him. This morning she didn’t do any of those things. She only looked, and that was worse.

“You’re going to be okay, right?”

“Yes.”

“Promise?”

He looked down at her. “Promise.”

Only then did her shoulders relax, and she stood up, and the first problem began, which was convincing Xiaoran that he could manage perfectly well with his crutches.

“I can carry my own bag,” Yichen said.

“No.”

He met her eyes.

“No?”

She had already taken his schoolbag off his mother’s back seat and slung it over her shoulder.

“I’ll carry it.”

“Xiaoran, it’s not heavy.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

“Then I can carry it.”

He watched her pick up the plastic bag his mother had packed, which contained an ice pack, his lunch, and a cushion for his ankle that he had specifically asked her not to pack. Xiaoran was now carrying his schoolbag, his books, the plastic bag, and her own bag.

Yichen reached for the last one.

She moved it out of reach.

“No.”

He sighed.

“You’re carrying too much.”

“I’m fine.”

“Give me your bag.”

“Absolutely not.”

He looked at her, then at Meilin.

Meilin shrugged.

“Don’t look at me. She’s already decided.”

Chen Yuhao, arriving at the gate on his bicycle, had stopped to enjoy the entire situation.

“Wow. Xiaoran, you’re very devoted.”

She turned toward him. “Where were you on Saturday when that boy was pushing him all game?”

Yuhao immediately stepped back. “On the bench. With a broken finger. As you know.”

“Then go and be useful with nine fingers somewhere else.”

He went, with Meilin, who was still laughing.

Yichen adjusted his grip on the crutches.

“Come on.”

Xiaoran walked beside him. She had decided that she would carry everything up to Class 1 on the third floor. Yichen had decided that he would try to convince her otherwise. Neither was making much progress.

By the second flight of stairs, Xiaoran was beginning to regret her confidence.

The schoolbag was heavier than she had expected.

The plastic bag kept slipping down her wrist, and her own bag was digging into her shoulder.

Yichen moved slowly beside her, carefully placing his crutches one step at a time.

“Give me something.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I’m fine.”

She shifted the bags again.

One of the books started slipping out of his schoolbag.

She tried to catch it without dropping anything else.

Her foot landed awkwardly on the edge of the next step.

For one alarming second, she lost her balance.

“Xiaoran!”

Yichen reacted immediately.

He caught her arm, pulling her back before she could fall.

The plastic bag dropped.

Two books slid across the floor.

She stood frozen, her heart racing.

Yichen’s expression had changed completely.

“Are you hurt?”

She shook her head.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He looked down at her feet.

“Your ankle?”

“It’s fine.”

He didn’t look convinced.

He steadied himself against the railing, then looked at her again.

“Give me the bags.”

“Yichen—”

“Now.”

His voice wasn’t loud, but it was firm enough to make her stop.

She slowly handed him the schoolbag.

He couldn’t carry it himself, so he leaned it against the wall while she collected the fallen books.

Then he looked at her.

“You nearly fell.”

“But I didn’t.”

“That’s not the point.”

She frowned.

“I was only trying to help.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you angry?”

He exhaled.

“I’m not angry because you wanted to help. I’m worried because you were carrying everything, and you nearly hurt yourself.”

Xiaoran looked down.

He softened his voice.

“You don’t have to do everything for me.”

She was quiet.

Then she said, “I wanted to.”

Yichen looked at her.

“I know. But wanting to help doesn’t mean you have to hurt yourself doing it,” he repeated.

She didn’t answer.

He reached out and brushed a loose strand of hair away from her face. “Let me ask someone else to carry the bags. You can walk beside me.”

She nodded, although her expression stayed a little unhappy.

Yuhao, who had heard his name shouted from two floors down, came back for the bags without saying anything clever, which was how Xiaoran knew she had frightened everybody. She walked the last flight beside Yichen with nothing in her hands at all, glancing at his crutches on every step.

Outside the Class 1 door, he stopped. “Are you upset?”

“No.”

He waited.

She looked away.

“Maybe a little.”

“Because I told you not to carry everything?”

“Because you keep telling me not to do things.”

Yichen studied her face.

“I don’t want you to get hurt.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

She pressed her lips together.

“I don’t know. Sometimes I feel like you don’t need me to do anything.”

His expression softened.

“Is that what you think?”

She shrugged.

He leaned slightly toward her, careful not to put too much weight on his injured ankle.

“Xiaoran, I need you to understand something.”

She met his eyes.

“I like that you take care of me. I like that you worry about me. I like that you want to carry my things even when they’re heavier than you expect.”

A tiny smile appeared on her face.

“But I don’t want you to think you have to prove that you care by doing everything.”

She lowered her eyes.

He continued gently, “You can just walk beside me. That’s enough.”

She was quiet for a few seconds. Then she looked at his hands, both of which were busy with crutches, and then she hooked one finger through the belt loop of his trousers instead, where nobody in the corridor could see.

“Can I at least hold this?”

He laughed. “Yes.”

“Even if I’m not carrying anything?”

“That’s what it’s for.”

She finally smiled properly, let go, and ran back down to Class 3, and was late for morning reading for the first time that year.

The next morning, Xiaoran arrived at the gate with two things: a small bag of snacks for Yichen, and a determined expression.

His mother’s car pulled up at twenty past seven. His ankle was still swollen and this was the last day of the crutches, and he looked inconvenienced but otherwise perfectly fine.

She walked up to him.

“Good morning.”

“Morning.”

She held out the snack bag.

“For you.”

He accepted it.

“What’s this?”

“Things you can eat during break.”

He looked inside.

There were biscuits, fruit, and a small carton of milk.

He looked back at her.

“Thank you.”

She nodded.

Then, without asking, she reached for his schoolbag.

Yichen raised an eyebrow.

Xiaoran stopped.

They stared at each other.

Then she sighed.

“Fine. I’ll ask first.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right.”

“Can I carry your bag?”

He considered it.

“Yes.”

Her expression brightened.

“Only the schoolbag.”

She pouted.

“You’re negotiating.”

“I’m being reasonable.”

“You’re very difficult to take care of.”

He laughed.

“Then you should reconsider.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

She seemed to consider the statement seriously.

Then she smiled.

“You’re stuck with me.”

She carried his schoolbag up all three flights, and it was too heavy for her, and he let her, because she had asked.

At lunch, Meilin found them on the second-floor landing, Yichen on the step with his crutches propped beside him and Xiaoran one step below, both eating biscuits out of the same bag.

“You carried it,” Meilin said.

“He let me,” said Xiaoran, with enormous dignity, and Meilin looked at Yichen, who didn’t deny anything, and went away again, shaking her head at both of them.

chapters.desc: Three weeks off the court. One girlfriend in full nurse mode. Zhou Yichen may not survive his own recovery.
chapters.title: Don’t Limp. I’ll Cry Again.
chapters.epigraph: “The injury healed in weeks. The worry took longer.”
chapters.content:
The aftermath of Zhou Yichen’s injury was unbearable for exactly one reason: Lin Xiaoran, treating him like a critically endangered patient.

“Walk slower.”

“I am walking.”

“You limped.”

“I didn’t.”

“It looked painful.”

Yichen was standing by his locker while Xiaoran hovered nearby like an anxious ghost. It had been three days since the injury, and somehow she had gotten worse instead of calmer. The sprain meant no basketball for at least three weeks, which annoyed Yichen enough already. Xiaoran was acting like he’d come back from a war. Yesterday she’d carried his bag, even though it was clearly too heavy for her. This morning she’d bought him breakfast, water, AND vitamins. At lunch she’d pulled out his chair for him.

“Xiaoran, I injured my ankle.”

“Yes.”

“Not my entire body.”

“You don’t know how interconnected health is.”

Across the classroom, Yuhao looked deeply entertained.

“She’s entered nurse mode.”

Meilin nodded. “It only gets worse from here.”

“I can hear both of you,” Xiaoran snapped.

Two seconds later—

“Yichen don’t stand too long.”

Yichen sighed into his hand. The worst part was that he couldn’t stop her. Every time he said he was fine, her eyes went watery. It wasn’t fair.

✦ ✦ ✦

Things got worse after school, because Zhou Yichen made one terrible mistake: he forgot Xiaoran was behind him on the stairs and walked a little faster than usual.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

The entire hallway turned. Yichen stopped. Behind him, Xiaoran looked genuinely horrified.

“Why are you moving like that?!”

“…Like a human?”

“You’re injured.”

“My legs still function.”

“Not correctly.”

Before he could argue, Xiaoran took his arm. Not dramatically, this time. Carefully, like she was afraid too much pressure might hurt him. Yichen felt guilty instead of amused. She still looked shaken from that day.

“You know,” he said more as they went down the stairs, “I’m recovering fine.”

“I know.”

“But?”

Xiaoran looked away. Then, quieter—

“When you fell… You really scared me.” She swallowed slightly.

Oh. Again, the fear she couldn’t hide. Yichen remembered it too: the crying, her shaking hands, the way she’d looked at him like the world had almost ended. Part of him still felt bad for putting that look on her face.

“You know I’d tell you if it was serious right?” he murmured.

Xiaoran nodded. Then, after a pause—

“But you also always say you’re fine even when you’re not.”

That was fair. Yichen sighed.

“I hate when you’re reasonable.”

“I learned from Meilin.”

“Of course you did.”

Finally, Xiaoran smiled a little, small and relieved, and somehow that smile made Yichen less annoyed about the whole injury.

✦ ✦ ✦

The peace lasted about twelve hours. The next morning, Xiaoran was back in full disaster mode.

“Why are you carrying THAT.”

Yichen blinked. He was holding a bag of basketballs outside the gym storeroom.

“…Because Coach asked?”

Yichen stared at her. Xiaoran stared back. Then she marched over and took the bag right out of his hands.

“Xiaoran.”

“You need rest.”

“It weighs five kilograms.”

“Exactly.”

“Then why are YOU carrying it?”

Silence. Xiaoran made it two steps before she started struggling. Nearby, Yuhao nearly collapsed laughing.

“This relationship is incredible.”

Meilin looked exhausted. “One of them has no survival instincts. The other has no logic.”

“WHICH ONE.”

“Both.”

Yichen took the bag back before Xiaoran hurt herself instead. Then, without thinking, he crouched and retied the shoelace she’d been stepping on all morning. It happened so casually that neither of them noticed. Yuhao did. Yuhao never missed a chance to be annoying.

“Oh my god. You two are disgusting,” he whispered.

Xiaoran went red.

“We literally did nothing.”

“He bent down like a husband in a drama.”

“SHUT UP.”

Yichen just smiled, stood up, and tapped her forehead.

“You’re worrying too much.”

“I’m not.”

“You almost cried because I carried basketballs.”

“That was a reasonable reaction.”

It was exhausting. It was also cute.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon, it started pouring after class. Most students waited by the entrance for parents or buses. Xiaoran sat beside Yichen and watched the rain hammer the courtyard. For once, she wasn’t talking. No complaining. Just quiet.

“Does it still hurt?”

Yichen glanced at his wrapped ankle.

“A little.”

“See.”

Yichen smiled helplessly. After a moment—

“Come here.”

Xiaoran shifted closer, and Yichen rested his chin on her hair, holding her hand loosely.

“I’m okay,” he murmured again.

This time, Xiaoran didn’t argue. She leaned into him and whispered—

“…You can’t get seriously hurt.”

“Hm?”

“I don’t like it.”

It sounded so simple. Almost childish. But Yichen knew what she meant. She couldn’t stand seeing him in pain, or not knowing, or the idea of something bad happening to him. That kind of love scared him sometimes. Nobody had ever worried about him that fiercely before. Not even himself.

“You fell for three seconds and I already imagined widowhood.”

Yichen choked on a laugh.

“WIDOWHOOD?”

“I panicked.”

“We’re in high school.”

“That doesn’t stop tragedy.”

Yichen laughed so much his ankle shifted wrong again.

“DON’T MOVE.”

“Okay okay.”

“See? SEE?”

He was still smiling while she scolded him. And for the first time since the injury, the fear they had both been carrying started to fade.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran overhears that she’s holding Zhou Yichen back—and starts to wonder if they’re right.
chapters.title: Should We Break Up?
chapters.epigraph: “The cruelest words are the ones we quietly agree with.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran usually ignored rumors. Not because she was emotionally strong. She just didn’t care enough. People talked all the time anyway—about grades, relationships, appearances. Half the school practically ran on gossip. So whenever Xiaoran overheard someone talking about her, she usually rolled her eyes and walked away. This time, they mentioned Zhou Yichen too. And that changed everything.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened on a Thursday after class. Xiaoran had stayed late helping Meilin decorate classroom boards for school festival week.

By the time she finished, the hallways were almost empty. She was heading for the back staircase, texting Yichen, when she heard it.

“…Honestly, Zhou Yichen could do way better.”

Xiaoran slowed down. Girls’ voices, somewhere around the corner by the storage room. Normally she would have kept walking. Then—

“I don’t even understand what he sees in Lin Xiaoran.”

Silence. Xiaoran stopped. She didn’t mean to. Her feet just stopped. The voices went on.

“I heard he rejected training invitations because she wanted attention.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“No seriously. My friend from Class 3 said he skipped extra practice before because Xiaoran was upset.”

“She’s honestly holding him back.”

“And he used to be way more focused before dating.”

The girls laughed—not loudly, not cruelly. Just casually, like they really believed it. Somehow that was worse. Xiaoran stayed frozen, because the worst part was that some of it was technically true. A few weeks ago, Yichen really had turned down an extra match. But not because of her. She knew that. His ankle hadn’t fully healed, and Coach Wang had told him not to overdo it. Still, hearing people say she was dragging him down lodged painfully in her chest. Especially because… what if other people thought so too?

✦ ✦ ✦

After that day, something changed. Not dramatically. Quietly enough that only the people closest to Xiaoran noticed. She still smiled, still joked, still clung to Yichen. But sometimes she went quiet afterward, especially when basketball came up.

Like now: Saturday afternoon at Meilin’s house, everyone eating snacks while Yuhao rambled excitedly about an upcoming invitational tournament. Apparently several schools had asked for Yichen by name.

“Coach says scouts might come too,” Yuhao said proudly.

Meilin nodded. “That’s huge.”

Normally Xiaoran would have bragged like she’d personally trained Zhou Yichen herself. Today, she only smiled and looked down at her drink. Yichen noticed, of course. Later that evening, walking her home, he finally asked—

“What’s wrong?”

Xiaoran blinked innocently.

“Hm?”

“You’ve been weird for two weeks.”

“I’m always weird.”

“Not like this.”

Silence. The evening wind moved through the quiet street. Then, more—

“You stop talking whenever basketball gets mentioned.”

Oh. So he had noticed that too. Of course he had. Zhou Yichen noticed everything about her, even the moods she worked hardest to hide.

“…Nothing’s wrong,” she said eventually.

“Liar.”

He said it so simply, so certainly, that Xiaoran nearly cried right there. He knew her too well now. Yichen slowed down and looked at her properly.

“Did someone say something?”

The question landed too close. Xiaoran’s fingers tightened around her sleeve, and Yichen understood. His expression cooled.

“Who?”

“No one.”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked away. She didn’t want him angry. That wasn’t the point. The point was that the words wouldn’t leave her head. Holding him back. Distracting him. Making him less focused. She knew how talented Yichen was, how seriously everyone talked about his future. Meanwhile she still got lost near school and cried over math. The comparison suddenly felt unbearable.

“So what if they’re right?”

Yichen stopped walking.

“…What?”

Xiaoran stared straight ahead.

“I mean… You were already doing so well before me.” She forced a small laugh.

“Xiaoran.”

“And everyone expects so much from you.”

His expression changed. Serious now. Actually serious. But Xiaoran kept going before she could lose her nerve.

“What if dating me really makes things harder for you?”

Silence. Then, very—

“Should we break up?”

The world went still. Even Xiaoran felt strange after saying it, like the sentence didn’t belong to her. Just thinking it already hurt. Zhou Yichen just looked at her. He wasn’t angry or shocked, only deeply focused, like he was trying to work out how she’d gotten there on her own.

“Who told you that?”

Xiaoran looked down.

“No one directly.”

“What exactly did they say?”

“…That I hold you back.”

Out loud, it sounded embarrassingly small. Yichen was quiet for two seconds. Then he laughed—not mocking, just disbelieving—and that confused Xiaoran even more.

“You’re laughing?”

“I’m trying very hard not to get angry.”

“Oh.”

Then he took her hand, lacing his fingers through hers.

“Look at me,” he said.

Slowly, Xiaoran did, and immediately regretted it. He was looking at her far too softly.

“You think I’d choose basketball over you?”

“That’s not what I mea—”

“If dating you affected me negatively. I would’ve ended things already,” he said calmly.

Xiaoran blinked. That was painfully logical.

“But instead, you’re the person I want beside me after every game. You’re the first person I look for in crowds,” he said more.

Another silence.

“And you think that makes my life worse?”

Xiaoran’s chest ached. Hearing him say it so directly was almost too much.

“But your future—”

“My future is my responsibility.”

He said it like he’d decided that a long time ago. Yichen sighed and stepped closer.

“You know why I skipped that extra match?”

Xiaoran nodded weakly. “Your ankle.”

“Exactly. Not because of you.” His thumb brushed lightly across her knuckles.

“I know.”

“Then why believe strangers over me?”

That question hurt the most, because she didn’t know. Maybe loving someone that talented made insecurity grow. Like one day he might realize he deserved someone better. More mature. Less troublesome. Maybe Yichen understood that already, because he pulled her into his arms.

“You know what actually distracts me? You crying over imaginary breakups,” he murmured into her hair.

“I hate you.”

“No you don’t.”

Unfortunately, he was right. Now Xiaoran just felt ridiculous—for overthinking alone this long, for almost believing strangers over Yichen. After a while, she muttered into his hoodie—

“…You really don’t want to break up?”

Yichen pulled back just enough to look at her properly. Then, flatly—

“Absolutely not.”

“Oh.”

“And honestly, you’re not escaping me that easily,” he said calmly.

Xiaoran laughed—her first real laugh in weeks.

“Finally,” Yichen murmured.

And just like that, Lin Xiaoran finally felt like herself again.

chapters.desc: The Monday after she asked whether they should break up, a folded note on her desk answers her in one word.
chapters.title: One Word
chapters.epigraph: “I know. But I’d like you not to say it unless you do.”
chapters.content:
The question hadn’t been planned. That was the first thing Lin Xiaoran wanted to make clear, if anyone ever asked, which she hoped nobody would.

She hadn’t gone to Meilin’s house on Saturday intending to ask her boyfriend whether they should break up. She had gone for the snacks. But two weeks of carrying around what the girls by the storage room had said, holding him back, he used to be more focused, had worn a groove in her, and on the walk home the question had come out of the groove before she could stop it.

He had laughed, and said he was trying hard not to get angry, and asked her why she believed strangers over him. And when she asked again, into his hoodie, whether he really didn’t want to, he had said absolutely not in a voice so flat and certain that she had laughed for the first time in weeks.

She had gone to bed happy.

At two in the morning she woke up and thought about the storage room again.

She picked up her phone and typed are you sure? and looked at it, and deleted it, because he had already answered twice and a third time would be embarrassing. Then she lay awake until four, being embarrassed anyway.

Sunday was fine. She did her homework. She ate dinner. She didn’t text him about it, and he didn’t text her about it, and they talked about a drama and a cat video and the invitational, and it was all normal, and underneath the normal the question sat there like a stone in a shoe.

On Monday morning she opened her locker, and there was a folded piece of paper on top of her chemistry textbook.

No name. No greeting. One word in the middle of the page, in handwriting she knew better than her own.

No.

And underneath it, much smaller, as if added after some thought:

(In case you ask again.)

She stood in front of her locker and read it four times. Then she folded it along its crease and put it in the pocket of her skirt, and kept her hand on it all the way to Class 3, as if it might get out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Meilin found her five minutes before morning reading, sitting at her desk and staring at nothing.

“You’re doing that thing again.”

“What thing?”

“Looking like you’ve lost something, or found something, and you can’t decide which.”

Xiaoran hesitated, then took the paper out of her pocket and handed it over. Meilin unfolded it, read the word, read the small line, and looked up.

“No to what?”

So Xiaoran told her. The storage room, the girls, the friend from Class 3 who apparently reported on everyone, the walk home, the question.

Meilin’s face went through several stages. By the end it had settled on something Xiaoran had only seen once before, when a boy in primary school had thrown Xiaoran’s lunchbox in the pond.

“You asked Zhou Yichen if you should break up. Because of three girls by a mop cupboard,” Meilin said slowly.

“It was a storage room.”

“Which three?”

“Meilin.”

“I’m only asking for their names. For research. He wrote you a note so you’d have it in writing.” Meilin looked at the note again, and her face changed back.

“I know.”

“So you’d stop asking.”

“I know.”

“He knows you. Go and find him at break. And don’t cry in the corridor, it’s festival week and people will talk,” Meilin said, not entirely as a compliment, and handed it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was outside the teachers’ office at the long break, talking to Coach Wang about the invitational, his ankle strapped but steady now, no limp unless he forgot. When the coach went back inside, Yichen turned and saw Xiaoran waiting a few steps away with something in her hand.

He looked at the note. Then at her.

“Morning.”

“Morning. You already answered. On Saturday.” She unfolded it, even though they both knew what it said.

“I know.”

“Twice.”

“I know. You asked twice. So I thought you’d ask a third time. Probably late at night, when I wasn’t there to say it. So I wrote it down.” He leaned his shoulder against the wall.

She looked at him. She thought about two in the morning and are you sure? and the delete key, and didn’t say anything, and he watched her not say anything, and understood all of it anyway.

“Two o’clock?” he said.

“Ten past.”

He nodded, as if that were about what he’d expected.

“Xiaoran. On Saturday I laughed because you were standing right there, and you were fine, and I could see you were fine. Then I got home. It wasn’t funny at home.” His voice was quieter now. He looked down at the note in her hand.

She hadn’t thought about that. Not once, in two days of thinking. She had thought about the girls and about herself, about whether she was too much and whether she held him back. She hadn’t thought about him walking back to his house on Saturday night with that sentence in his ears.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“I know you didn’t mean it.”

“I didn’t.”

“I know. But I’d like you not to say it unless you do. If you ever mean it, say it, and we’ll talk properly. If you don’t, ask me something else. Ask me whether I’m sure. Ask me a hundred times. I’ll write it on every page of your notebook.” He said it without any heat at all, the way he told her to eat breakfast, and somehow that made it land harder.

Her eyes had started to sting. Meilin had specifically said not to cry in the corridor.

“I’m not crying.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were thinking it.”

He laughed, and pushed off the wall, and stepped close enough that she could put her forehead against his shoulder, which she did, in the corridor, in festival week, where people would talk.

“Those girls,” he said into her hair.

“Don’t.”

“I wasn’t going to do anything. I was going to tell Coach Wang to put the real reason for my rest days on the team noticeboard. In large print.”

She laughed into his shirt. “That’s doing something.”

“It’s a noticeboard. Noticeboards are neutral.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When the bell went, she put the note back in her pocket.

“Keep it,” he said.

“I was going to.”

“I know. I’m saying it anyway.”

She walked back toward Class 3, then turned round at the corner.

“Yichen. If I ask you something silly again, will you still answer?”

“Depends how silly.”

“Is the invitational on a Saturday?”

He looked at her, and the smile started slowly at one corner.

“Yes. Sit behind the bench. Coach already said.”

She went back to class and was useless all through mathematics, which was normal, and happy all through mathematics, which wasn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday morning there was a new sheet of paper on the basketball noticeboard outside the gym, in large print, pinned at eye level between the training schedule and a poster about dental hygiene.

TEAM NOTICE. Z. Yichen: rest days 4, 6, 11 and 13 (right ankle, doctor’s instructions). Not optional. — Coach Wang

It was the most boring notice anyone had ever pinned to that board, and by lunchtime half the grade had read it, because the other half had told them to.

Meilin took a photograph of it and sent it to Xiaoran with no caption at all.

Xiaoran stood in front of it at the afternoon break for longer than necessary. Two girls she half recognized from the storage room came down the corridor, slowed, read it, and looked at each other, and one of them said, “Oh,” in a small voice, and they walked on a little faster than before.

Xiaoran didn’t say anything. She didn’t need to. The noticeboard was neutral.

When she got back to Class 3, there was a second folded note on her desk. She didn’t know how he had got it there; he was in physics on the other side of the building. Possibly Rong Hao. Possibly a pigeon.

Still no.

That night she put the note inside the clear back cover of her phone case, where it stayed for the rest of high school, a small white square with one word on it, gradually going soft at the folds. She didn’t need to take it out and read it often. Knowing it was there turned out to be enough.

Once, much later, at two in the morning, she did take it out. She read it, put it back, and went to sleep.

The rest days, for the record, were the fourth, the sixth, the eleventh and the thirteenth. He rested on all of them. On each one he sat at the side of the gym with his ankle up on a chair, doing physics homework, in full view of anyone who cared to look.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen eats chili oil like water. Lin Xiaoran decides to build a tolerance. It goes about as well as expected.
chapters.title: You’re Crying Over Chili Oil?
chapters.epigraph: “Love is wanting to share someone’s world, even when it burns.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen had one frightening talent: he could eat spicy food like his tongue had signed a legal immunity contract. Not normal spicy. Unhinged spicy. The kind that made other people reconsider their life choices after one bite. And Zhou Yichen stayed calm, unbothered, completely fine. Lin Xiaoran absolutely hated it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It’s literally red.”

“That’s usually what chili oil looks like.”

“No. That’s not food. That’s lava,” Xiaoran whispered, staring at his noodles in horror.

The four of them were at a noodle shop near school after basketball practice. Rain was pouring outside. Yuhao was happily demolishing a plate of fried rice, Meilin looked spiritually exhausted as always, and Zhou Yichen was calmly adding MORE chili oil to an already dangerous bowl of noodles.

“You’re trying to impress someone.”

“I’m eating dinner.”

“That cannot taste good.”

Yichen glanced at her lazily. “Want to try?”

“Absolutely not.”

Three minutes later, Xiaoran stole a bite anyway, because curiosity always won. Instant regret.

“WATER.”

Yuhao choked laughing.

“She’s dying.”

“IT BURNS.”

“You took half the spoon,” Meilin pointed out.

“I THOUGHT HE WAS EXAGGERATING.”

Yichen pushed his drink toward her before she could combust.

“Slow down.”

“YOU EAT THIS WILLINGLY?”

“It’s not that spicy.”

Meilin stared at him blankly. “You’ve lost human sensation.”

The noodle shop owner wandered over and set a glass of milk in front of Xiaoran without a word, like he’d seen this before. Accurate. Zhou Yichen kept eating peacefully while Xiaoran sat there blinking back tears from one bite. One. His bowl looked like lava.

“This relationship won’t survive long-term,” Xiaoran whispered afterward, clutching her iced tea.

“Because of chili oil?” Yichen asked.

“Yes.”

“That feels unreasonable.”

“No, actually dietary incompatibility destroys marriages,” Yuhao interrupted seriously.

“Why are you talking like a divorced uncle?” Meilin asked tiredly.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that, the spicy food situation got personal, because Zhou Yichen started teasing her about it. Subtly. Constantly. Very annoyingly. At lunch the next day—

“Want some?”

“No.”

“It’s mild.”

“You’re a liar.”

Yichen smiled a little and ate the noodles himself. No reaction. No suffering. No weakness. That annoyed Xiaoran most of all. How was he so handsome while casually eating lava? It felt biologically unfair.

One afternoon after school, Xiaoran finally snapped.

“I’m building spice tolerance.”

Yichen looked up from his homework.

“…Why.”

“So I can understand your world.”

Meilin looked concerned.

“Please don’t.”

“Too late.”

Yuhao grinned. “This’ll be funny.”

It wasn’t funny. Not even slightly.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first attempt was a disaster. Xiaoran bought “mild” skewers from a street stall after school. “Mild,” the vendor promised. Lies. Cruel lies.

Halfway through the second skewer, Xiaoran’s eyes were already streaming. Yichen sighed and handed her tissues.

“You don’t need to force yourself.”

“I can do this.”

“You’re crying.”

“That’s temporary weakness.”

She took another bite out of pure stubbornness and coughed so hard she had to sit down on the curb. Yuhao had to lean against a wall to laugh.

“She’s crying over a skewer.”

Meilin rubbed her forehead. “I knew this would happen.”

Yichen watched her—the stubborn face, the watery eyes, the way she kept going anyway. Hopelessly cute.

“Okay, enough,” he said, taking the skewer from her.

“No.”

“You stopped breathing earlier.”

“I’m adapting.”

“You’re dying.”

Xiaoran glared at him over her carton of milk. Then, after a moment—

“…How are you eating this normally?”

Yichen shrugged. “I grew up with it.”

“That explains a lot.”

He laughed under his breath, then wiped a bit of sauce from the corner of her mouth with his thumb. Small. Automatic. Xiaoran’s heartbeat betrayed her anyway. Stupid handsome boyfriend.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later, Xiaoran tried again. And again. And slowly, her tolerance actually improved. Not much, but enough that she could eat medium-spicy noodles without crying in public, which she considered a historic achievement.

“Wow, love really changes people,” Yuhao said one lunch break.

“Exactly,” Xiaoran said proudly over her spicy hotpot.

Then her expression changed. Meilin narrowed her eyes.

“…Too spicy?”

Xiaoran’s eyes went watery.

“No.”

“Liar.”

“I’m fine.”

Then tears started rolling silently down her face. Yuhao lost it.

“She’s crying again.”

“I HATE ALL OF YOU.”

Yichen looked helpless as he pushed her drink closer.

“You pushed too hard again.”

“But I almost survived.”

Yichen laughed and handed her more tissues. Then, more—

“You know you don’t actually need to like spicy food because of me.”

Xiaoran sniffed.

“But you love it.”

“Hm.”

“And I wanted to experience things you like too.”

Oh. That one caught him off guard. Yichen looked at her for a second—flushed cheeks, watery eyes, all that stubborn sincerity she never bothered hiding. Then he smiled.

“You already do,” he said.

Xiaoran blinked.

“Hm?”

“You already understand my world enough.”

Silence.

Yuhao gagged. “Oh my god.”

Meilin nodded tiredly. “Actually unbearable.”

But Xiaoran was too busy staring at Yichen to care, her heart melting embarrassingly fast. Then, after a pause—

“…I’m still learning spicy food.”

“Why?”

“So one day we can eat extra spicy hotpot together romantically.”

Yichen laughed and squeezed her hand under the table.

“Okay. But we’re bringing milk,” he said.

chapters.desc: A double date with the rival captain and the girl Xiaoran once fought on the café street. What could go wrong?
chapters.title: Should We Even Be Sitting Together?
chapters.epigraph: “Peace treaties are usually signed over food.”
chapters.content:
A double date with Zhou Yichen and Song Kai was already a terrible idea. Adding their girlfriends? Disaster. Especially because, technically, Lin Xiaoran and Xu Hani still hated each other after the Hair-Pulling Incident. Not publicly, just spiritually. Which was somehow worse. So when Song Kai suggested—

“Why don’t the four of us eat together once so things stop being awkward?”

—nobody was thrilled. Xu Hani looked offended. Xiaoran looked ready to commit crimes again. And Zhou Yichen immediately got a headache.

✦ ✦ ✦

“This is stupid,” Xiaoran hissed, fixing her hair outside the restaurant.

“It’s just dinner.”

“It’s diplomatic negotiations.”

Beside her, Yichen sighed. She wasn’t entirely wrong. Song Kai had picked a barbecue place by the river. Neutral territory, apparently. Very strategic. Yichen watched her mentally prepare for war.

“Remember, you promised not to fight,” he said calmly.

“I only fight when provoked.”

“That sentence inspires zero confidence.”

Xiaoran crossed her arms.

“Why are YOU calm? Your rival is literally inside.”

“Basketball rival,” Yichen corrected.

“That’s still testosterone tension.”

Inside, Song Kai already looked exhausted.

“Hani, please don’t provoke Xiaoran,” he warned carefully.

“I don’t care about her enough to provoke her.”

Song Kai sighed. This dinner was going to kill him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five minutes later, all four of them were sitting together. Painfully awkwardly. The restaurant was warm and noisy, meat sizzling on the grill in the middle of the table. Their table, though, was pure tension. Xu Hani drank water elegantly. Lin Xiaoran stabbed her grilled mushrooms like they’d wronged her. The two boys exchanged an exhausted look.

“Great atmosphere,” Song Kai muttered.

“No one’s bleeding yet,” Yichen answered.

“Amazing progress.”

Across the table, Hani suddenly spoke.

“So. Still fighting people over your boyfriend?” She looked at Xiaoran lazily.

Silence. Yichen closed his eyes. Here we go. Xiaoran smiled sweetly.

“Still talking too much?”

Song Kai grabbed his drink. Oh no. Yichen calmly put more meat in Xiaoran’s bowl before she could escalate. A distraction tactic. Very experienced boyfriend behavior. It only worked for a while.

“You know, people at my school still talk about that fight,” Hani said casually.

“Good, at least someone found meaning in your hair loss,” Xiaoran answered.

Song Kai choked on his water. Yichen lowered his head, trying hard not to laugh.

“Hani,” Song Kai warned tiredly.

“What?” Hani replied innocently.

“You too,” Yichen said quietly toward Xiaoran.

“I’m literally peaceful.”

“You threatened her hairstyle.”

It should have exploded already. Somehow it didn’t—mostly because the boys had gotten weirdly good at crisis management since dating these two. At one point, Hani complained about university applications and Xiaoran accidentally agreed with her. Both girls paused, like neither had expected common ground. The boys watched in silence, afraid to break the spell. Then a waiter set a plate of extremely spicy meat in front of Hani instead of Xiaoran. Hani took a casual bite. Instant regret.

“…Why is this so spicy?!”

Xiaoran blinked—then burst out laughing. Not mocking. Genuinely helpless laughter.

“OH MY GOD.”

Hani glared with watery eyes.

“Why are you happy.”

“You look exactly like me last month.”

Yichen sighed. The spicy food incident. Traumatic memories. Song Kai looked more and more entertained as Xiaoran pushed a glass of milk toward Hani without thinking.

“Drink this before you pass away.”

“…Thanks.”

“You’re still annoying though.”

“Same to you.”

Progress. Questionable, but still progress. Later, the conversation drifted back to basketball. Unfortunately. Song Kai smirked at Yichen.

“You still owe me a proper rematch.”

“You sound obsessed,” Yichen answered calmly.

“Because you got lucky.”

Xiaoran sat up straighter. Danger. Hani noticed too.

“Oh my god. Look at her face,” Hani muttered.

“What face?” Song Kai asked.

“The ‘don’t insult my boyfriend’ face.”

“I DON’T HAVE A FACE.”

“You absolutely do.”

Under the table, Yichen took Xiaoran’s wrist and gave it a gentle squeeze. Calm down. Song Kai laughed openly.

“She really gets angry over you instantly.”

“That’s because he’s talented,” Xiaoran said stubbornly.

Yichen looked tired.

“Xiaoran.”

“No. I’m serious.”

Hani looked at her strangely. Not mocking this time. Thoughtful.

“…You really like him huh?”

The whole table paused. The question sounded unexpectedly sincere, and even Xiaoran blinked, like the obviousness of the answer had surprised her for a second.

“Of course I do.”

No embarrassment, no joke. Just honest. The mood at the table shifted after that—softer, less hostile. Even Hani looked calmer, like she’d understood something. Beside her, Yichen had gone quiet. Hearing her answer like that, so naturally, still got to him every time. Then Song Kai ruined it.

“Disgusting,” he muttered.

Hani rolled her eyes.

“Your relationship is honestly exhausting to watch.”

“Thank you,” Xiaoran answered proudly.

“That wasn’t a compliment.”

“I accepted it anyway.”

Yichen finally laughed and put more meat on her plate, the way he always did without thinking. Watching that made Hani glance at Song Kai beside her. Song Kai looked horrified.

“…Don’t start.”

Too late. Across the table, Xiaoran noticed. A slow, dangerous smile spread across her face.

“Oh, nOW who’s on a weird double date?” she whispered delightedly.

chapters.desc: Fourteen days to find the perfect gift for a boy who already has everything—and remembers everything.
chapters.title: The Birthday Gift Problem
chapters.epigraph: “The best gifts aren’t bought. They’re remembered.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had exactly fourteen days before Zhou Yichen’s birthday. Which should’ve been enough time. Unfortunately, she was Lin Xiaoran, which meant a simple birthday present turned into a national crisis.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I don’t know what to buy him.”

Xiaoran lay face-down across Tang Meilin’s bed, suffering. Meilin kept doing her homework.

“You’ve been repeating that sentence for forty minutes.”

“Because LOVE is difficult.”

“Buying gifts isn’t love. It’s shopping.”

“Not for soulmates.”

Zhou Yichen was incredibly easy to please. Too easy. That was the problem. Basketball shoes? He’d smile. A hoodie? He’d smile. A handwritten note? He’d probably smile like an idiot. Which made choosing harder. Xiaoran wanted it to feel special. Not expensive. Just… important. Something that would make him think, Ah. This is so Xiaoran. Every idea felt stupid after five minutes.

“He already has shoes.”

“Then buy something else.”

“He has everything.”

“He doesn’t own a spaceship.”

“That’s because I’m poor.”

Meilin’s phone buzzed. She glanced at it.

“Oh. Yichen asked if you’re alive.” Meilin looked up.

Xiaoran groaned into the blankets.

“No one understands my suffering.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen, meanwhile, supposedly had no idea. Which was impressive, because Xiaoran was terrible at hiding things, especially excitement. Three days before his birthday, she followed him around school like a suspicious little criminal, disappeared at lunch, and came back looking stressed. Yuhao noticed.

“She’s planning something.”

“Obviously,” Yichen answered calmly.

“She looked at your wrist for thirty seconds earlier.”

Yichen paused. Interesting.

Later, at basketball practice, Yichen was sitting courtside with a water bottle when Xiaoran appeared out of nowhere. Too cheerful. Suspiciously cheerful.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Hypothetically.”

“Bad start already.”

“If someone gave you a birthday gift… What would mean the most to you?” She sat down beside him casually.

Yichen looked at her, then smiled a little.

“You’re asking for yourself?”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Okay maybe.”

He laughed and wiped the sweat from his neck with a towel, which distracted Xiaoran for three full seconds. Ridiculously handsome athlete boyfriend. Very inconvenient. Then he answered honestly—

“Anything from you.”

“That’s NOT HELPFUL.”

Yuhao, who had overheard everything, called over—

“Buy him matching underwear.”

“GET OUT.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem was that Zhou Yichen remembered everything. Her milk tea order. Her exam schedule. The exact bakery she liked. Random things she’d said months ago. Meanwhile, Xiaoran regularly lost her own phone. How was she supposed to compete with someone that thoughtful? Then one evening, sorting through old photos, Xiaoran froze. Inside a storage box was something she’d almost forgotten: the claw machine bunny. A little faded now. A tiny white rabbit. And she remembered.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first thing Zhou Yichen ever won for her, back before they were even dating. She had failed eleven times in a row; he’d stepped in and won it on the first try. Later, after they got together, she’d waved it at him and joked—

“If we ever break up in the future, I’m keeping this.”

And Yichen had said, completely calmly—

“We’re not breaking up.”

At the time, she’d laughed. Now, remembering it made her chest ache, because he had meant it, even back then. And suddenly Xiaoran knew exactly what to give him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen’s birthday arrived. No big party. Just close friends having dinner at Yuhao’s house. Very normal. Very warm. Yuhao gave him basketball accessories. Meilin gave him practical stationery, because she valued function over romance. Then everyone looked at Xiaoran, who had suddenly become nervous.

“Oh? Special girlfriend gift.” Yuhao grinned.

“Shut up.”

Yichen watched as she pulled out a medium-sized paper bag, her sleeves tugged down over her hands.

“…It’s not expensive,” she muttered.

“No one asked.”

“I’m managing expectations.”

Then she handed it to him. Yichen expected something cute. Maybe handmade. Maybe dramatic. Instead, he went still when he opened the box. Inside was the old white rabbit, carefully cleaned, with a simple silver bracelet around its neck. Small. Minimal. Exactly the kind he would actually wear every day. For a second, he said nothing, which made Xiaoran panic.

“Oh no.”

Yichen looked up.

“…You kept this?”

“Of course I kept it.”

Silence.

“You remembered?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…The claw machine?”

“No. What you said afterward.” His voice went soft.

Oh. That. Xiaoran’s face went hot. He remembered that too? The others looked lost.

“What are you two talking about?” Yuhao asked.

“History,” Meilin answered wisely.

Then Xiaoran looked at Yichen again.

“You said we wouldn’t break up. So I thought… maybe the rabbit should stay with the original owner for your birthday.” She tried laughing lightly.

The room was quiet for exactly two seconds. Then Yuhao grabbed Meilin’s sleeve.

“WHY ARE THEY LIKE THIS.”

“Quiet.”

Zhou Yichen was still looking at the bracelet, the rabbit, Xiaoran sitting there pretending not to panic. No expensive gift could have hit him harder. Lin Xiaoran always managed to give him things that felt frighteningly sincere. He reached over and took her hand.

“You know, this might be my favorite gift ever,” he murmured.

Xiaoran went red.

“Don’t say things like that publicly.”

“It’s my birthday.”

“That’s not how birthdays work.”

Yichen laughed, then put the bracelet on right there. Somehow that hit Xiaoran embarrassingly hard. It looked right on him, like it had always belonged there. Yuhao stared at them.

“I’m single because the universe hates me.”

Meilin nodded sympathetically.

“Correct.”

chapters.desc: Their first anniversary lands a week after his birthday, and Lin Xiaoran has three coins to her name. So they make a rule: nobody spends anything.
chapters.title: One Year, Exactly
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll pay it back next year.”
chapters.content:
The problem with celebrating an anniversary one week after a birthday was that, apparently, love was expensive.

At least, that was Lin Xiaoran’s conclusion.

She had discovered this while sitting at her desk on a Monday evening, staring at the contents of her wallet.

Three coins, a receipt from the stationery shop, and a discount coupon for a drink she didn’t even like.

She turned the wallet upside down, as if a forgotten banknote might fall out if she shook it hard enough.

Nothing.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Then she looked at the calendar beside her desk, where December 6 had a red heart drawn round it.

Their anniversary was tomorrow.

She closed her eyes.

A week ago, she had been perfectly happy with her financial decisions. Zhou Yichen’s birthday had been a success. She had spent fourteen days panicking about his gift and every yuan she had saved on the silver bracelet round the rabbit’s neck.

And he had loved it.

That was the important part.

He had looked at her with that rare, unguarded expression that always made her feel as if she’d managed to give him something far more meaningful than the actual present.

But the bracelet had taken everything.

Yichen, on the other hand, had never been broke in his life, and his idea of a small present came in a box inside another box. Whatever he had planned for tomorrow, she couldn’t match it.

She hadn’t thought about that when she bought the bracelet. She’d been busy being in love.

Xiaoran picked up her phone.

Xiaoran: Yichen.

Yichen: Hm?

Xiaoran: What are you doing tomorrow?

Yichen: School.

Xiaoran: After school.

Yichen: Nothing planned.

She narrowed her eyes.

Xiaoran: Nothing?

Yichen: Should there be something?

Xiaoran: No.

A pause.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: What?

Yichen: What happened?

She looked at her wallet again, then typed.

Xiaoran: Hypothetically, if someone had no money, would you still love them?

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: Depends.

Her eyes widened.

Xiaoran: Depends on WHAT?

Yichen: Whether they’ve been spending it on something unnecessary.

She stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: You’re a terrible boyfriend.

Yichen: I’m joking.

Yichen: I love you even when you’re broke.

Xiaoran smiled despite herself, then another message arrived.

Yichen: Is this about tomorrow?

She hesitated.

Xiaoran: Maybe.

Yichen: Go to sleep. We’ll talk tomorrow.

She put her phone down, still feeling vaguely unsettled.

He knew. Of course he knew, and that made her more nervous.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran arrived at school with a plan.

It wasn’t an impressive plan.

In fact, it consisted of three steps:

1. Don’t mention the anniversary.
2. Don’t look disappointed.
3. Hope Yichen hasn’t prepared a surprise.

The third step was the most difficult.

Because Zhou Yichen was the sort of person who could make arrangements and somehow produce something she hadn’t expected.

He might have reserved a restaurant. He might have bought her something. He might have planned a date.

And she had absolutely nothing.

She was standing near the classroom entrance when he arrived.

He was carrying his schoolbag over one shoulder, his uniform neat as usual. His eyes found her almost immediately.

“Morning.”

“Morning.”

He leaned down slightly and pressed a kiss into her hair.

She smiled.

Then he looked at her face.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re thinking too loudly.”

“I’m not.”

“All right.”

He reached for her hand.

She took it, but her expression remained suspiciously serious.

Yichen studied her for another moment.

“Did you sleep?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

“Yes.”

“Then why do you look like you’re about to negotiate a business contract?”

She met his eyes.

“Maybe I am.”

His mouth curved.

“With whom?”

“You.”

“What’s the proposal?”

She hesitated.

Then she said, “We shouldn’t spend money today. Either of us.”

Yichen looked at her.

He said nothing.

Then he smiled.

“That’s the proposal?”

“Yes.”

“Accepted.”

She blinked.

“Just like that?”

“Would you like me to negotiate?”

“No.”

“Then we’re done.”

She stared at him, searching his face for signs that he was hiding something.

He squeezed her hand.

“Happy anniversary, Xiaoran.”

Her heart gave a small, unexpected flutter.

She looked down at their joined hands.

“Happy anniversary.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The school day was almost unbearable.

Not because of the lessons.

Well, partly because of the lessons.

But mostly because Xiaoran kept remembering that today was their anniversary.

She had been dating Zhou Yichen for exactly one year.

Three hundred and sixty-five days.

She had counted.

Not that she would admit it.

She remembered the first time he had walked her home. The first time he had held her hand. The first time he had called her his girlfriend, and how she had spent the rest of that evening smiling at absolutely nothing.

She remembered their first disagreement, their first proper date, the first time she had fallen asleep on his shoulder, and the first time she had realized that being with him wasn’t just exciting.

It was comfortable.

He had become part of her ordinary days.

And she liked that more than she knew how to explain.

During lunch, she found herself staring at him across the table.

Yichen was listening to Chen Yuhao talk about something, occasionally responding with a few words. His expression was relaxed, his attention divided between the conversation and the food in front of him.

Then, as if sensing her gaze, he turned.

Their eyes met.

He raised an eyebrow.

She looked away.

A moment later, her phone vibrated.

Yichen: What?

He was still listening to Yuhao, but his phone was in his hand beneath the table.

Xiaoran: Nothing.

Yichen: You’ve been staring.

Xiaoran: Can’t I look at my boyfriend?

Yichen: You can.

Yichen: You’re making me nervous.

She smiled.

Xiaoran: Good.

This time, he smiled too.

Across the table, Tang Meilin noticed the exchange and rolled her eyes.

“Can you two communicate normally for five minutes?”

Xiaoran put her phone away.

“We are communicating normally.”

“You’re texting each other while sitting across the table.”

“That’s normal.”

Chen Yuhao leaned forward.

“Actually, I think they’re celebrating their anniversary by pretending the rest of us don’t exist.”

Yichen calmly took a sip of water.

“You’re welcome to leave.”

Yuhao stared at him.

“On their anniversary? You can’t even pretend to be polite?”

“Why would I?”

Meilin laughed.

Xiaoran kicked Yichen lightly beneath the table.

He glanced at her, looking entirely innocent.

She mouthed, Be nice.

He mouthed back, I am.

She shook her head.

He smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

After school, they didn’t go anywhere immediately.

Yichen walked her to the small convenience store near the school gate.

Xiaoran stopped in front of the entrance.

“Why are we here?”

“Are you thirsty?”

“A little.”

He opened the door for her.

“Then choose something.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Didn’t we agree not to spend money?”

“We did.”

“Then—”

“We’re not buying anything.”

He walked inside.

She followed him, increasingly confused.

Yichen went straight to the refrigerated section, took out two bottles of water, then walked toward the cashier.

Xiaoran watched him.

“Yichen.”

He met her eyes.

“What?”

“Those cost money.”

“I know.”

She folded her arms.

He placed the bottles on the counter.

“Two, please.”

She looked at him in disbelief.

When they stepped outside, she immediately confronted him.

“You said we wouldn’t spend money.”

“We won’t.”

“You just bought water.”

“Three yuan.”

“That’s still money.”

He handed her one bottle.

“Then I’ll pay it back next year.”

She stared at him.

He unscrewed his own bottle and took a drink.

“Besides, you said you were thirsty.”

Xiaoran looked at the water in her hand, then at him.

“You’re impossible.”

“Happy anniversary.”

She laughed, unable to remain annoyed.

They started walking.

Their route was familiar. Past the school gate, down the street lined with small shops, across the pedestrian crossing, and toward the little neighborhood park where they had spent time together before.

It wasn’t a special place.

There was a playground, a few benches, a small pond, and a path that circled the trees.

But it was one of the first places where they had spent time together without needing an excuse.

They had come here after school during the early months of dating, sometimes with snacks, sometimes with homework, sometimes because neither wanted to go home yet.

Yichen led her toward their usual bench.

Xiaoran stopped.

“Wait.”

He turned.

“What?”

“Are we going to sit here?”

“Unless you have somewhere else in mind.”

She looked around.

The park was quiet. A few children were playing near the swings, and an elderly man was walking his dog.

Then she smiled.

“I like here.”

“I know.”

They sat down.

For a while, neither said anything.

Xiaoran placed her schoolbag beside her and opened her water bottle.

Yichen sat close enough that their shoulders touched.

She looked at him.

“Did you really not prepare anything?”

He turned toward her.

“What do you mean?”

“Anything.”

He considered her expression.

Then he reached into his schoolbag and took out a folded piece of paper.

Her eyes widened.

“Yichen!”

He turned to her.

“What?”

“You said—”

“I didn’t buy anything.”

He handed it to her.

She accepted it carefully.

The paper was folded into a neat rectangle. Her name was written on the outside in his familiar handwriting.

She unfolded it.

Inside was a short letter in his slanted handwriting, with a few words crossed out and rewritten.

Xiaoran,

One year ago, you agreed to be my girlfriend.

I remember being nervous that day. I didn’t think you noticed, but you probably did.

This year has been good. Better than I expected, actually.

I like that you tell me about things I don’t understand. I like that you ask me questions even when you already know the answer. I like that you get excited over small things and that you sometimes talk so much you forget what you were saying.

I like walking you home. I like saving you a seat. I like knowing you’ll look for me when you enter a room.

I don’t know what next year will be like. We have exams, university applications, and a lot of things ahead of us. But I hope I get to spend it with you.

Thank you for this year.

I love you.

—Yichen

Xiaoran read it once, then again.

Her lips pressed together.

She looked down at the paper, trying hard not to let her expression give her away.

Yichen watched her.

“Too much?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Then?”

She looked up.

“You’re so unfair.”

He frowned slightly.

“How?”

“You can’t just write things like this.”

A small smile appeared on his face.

“Why not?”

“Because I don’t have anything.”

He held her gaze.

Then he reached over and gently took the letter from her hands, folded it along its original creases, and placed it back in her palm.

“You don’t need to.”

“But—”

“Xiaoran. I wanted to write it. That’s all.” He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

She looked at the letter again.

“You were nervous. That night. Your knuckles were white on the umbrella,” she said.

“You noticed.”

“I notice things too, Zhou Yichen.”

Then she leaned over and rested her head against his shoulder.

Yichen shifted slightly, making it easier for her to settle there.

“Thank you,” she whispered.

He kissed her hair.

“You’re welcome.”

A few minutes passed before Xiaoran sat up again.

“Wait.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“What?”

“I have something.”

He looked at her with mild surprise.

“You said you didn’t have anything.”

“I don’t.”

“Then what is it?”

She took out her phone.

He watched as she opened the photo gallery.

She scrolled for a while, then turned the screen toward him.

It was the first photograph she had taken after he asked her out: the plush bunny on her bag, dripping wet, photographed in the lift because she hadn’t known what else to do with her hands.

The next one was the two of them outside the bakery a week later. Meilin had taken it. Yichen was looking at her, and Xiaoran was smiling at the camera.

Yichen studied it.

“I remember.”

“Of course you do.”

She swiped to the next picture.

Another one, then another.

There were pictures from their first few months together. A blurry photo of their hands. A picture of him carrying her books. A photograph of them sitting together after school, with her head resting on his shoulder.

Some were poorly framed. Some were blurry.

Some were so ordinary that she had almost forgotten taking them.

But she had kept all of them.

“I made an album,” she said.

Yichen looked at her.

“When?”

“Over the past few days.”

She continued scrolling.

“I wanted to give you something, but then I remembered I’d spent everything on your birthday. So I thought maybe I could just put together the pictures I already had.”

She looked slightly embarrassed.

“It’s not very good.”

He didn’t answer immediately.

He was looking at the screen.

At their first picture.

At all the little moments she had collected without making a big deal of them.

Then he looked at her.

“Can I have it?”

She blinked.

“You want it?”

“Of course.”

“It’s just pictures.”

“I know.”

She hesitated, then sent him the album.

His phone vibrated.

He opened it.

She had called it One Year.

Beneath it were dozens of photographs, arranged in chronological order.

The first picture was the wet bunny.

The last one was from his birthday, taken only a week ago.

He was holding the rabbit, the bracelet already on his wrist, looking at her with an expression she had caught without realizing how much it gave away.

Yichen stared at that picture for a while.

Then he looked at her.

“You kept all of these?”

“Mhm.”

“Even the blurry ones?”

“The blurry ones most of all.”

“Why?”

“Because they’re memories.”

He smiled.

She watched him scroll.

“Do you like it?”

He locked his phone and put it away.

Then he turned toward her fully.

“I love it.”

Her smile appeared.

He reached for her hand.

“Thank you.”

She leaned forward and hugged him.

He wrapped both arms around her, holding her close.

They stayed like that.

There was no music and no dinner reservation, only a park bench after an ordinary school day, and Xiaoran thought it was exactly right.

The sun was beginning to set when they finally stood up.

Yichen picked up both schoolbags.

Xiaoran reached for hers.

“I can carry it.”

“I know.”

“Then give it to me.”

He looked at her.

“Do you want it?”

She paused, then smiled.

“No.”

“Thought so.”

They walked toward the park entrance, their hands joined.

A few steps later, Xiaoran slowed down.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you think our first year was good?”

He studied her.

“Yes.”

“Even when we argued?”

“Yes.”

“Even when I got upset over silly things?”

“Sometimes.”

She stopped walking.

“Sometimes?”

He turned toward her, his expression perfectly composed.

“Some things weren’t silly.”

She studied his face.

“You’re supposed to say all of them were understandable.”

“That would be dishonest.”

She gasped.

He laughed and tugged gently at her hand, bringing her closer.

“But I liked this year. All of it. Even the difficult parts,” he said.

Her expression softened.

“Why?”

“Because it was with you.”

She was quiet.

Then she pulled him down by the collar and kissed his cheek.

“You’re getting better at saying things.”

“Was I bad before?”

“A little.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

She laughed.

They continued walking.

After a while, Yichen glanced at her.

“Do you know what I think?”

“What?”

“Next year, we should save some money.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“For what?”

“Our second anniversary.”

She considered it, then shook her head.

“No.”

“No?”

“We’ll save money for other things.”

“Like what?”

“Food.”

He considered her.

“Food?”

“And dates.”

“Those are the same thing.”

“Not necessarily. We can save for a trip. Or go somewhere we’ve never been. Or buy something together. Maybe we’ll have more money next year.” She was getting animated now.

“Maybe.”

“And we should save for your birthday too.”

He looked at her.

“You’re already planning my next birthday?”

“Of course.”

“That’s a long way away.”

“It’s never too early.”

He laughed.

Then, after a moment, he said, “I don’t need anything expensive.”

She turned to him.

“I know.”

“Just so you remember.”

“I know, Yichen.”

He squeezed her hand.

“Then we’re fine.”

At the crossing, they had to stop for the red light.

Xiaoran stood beside him, rocking slightly on her heels.

She looked down at their hands.

Then at the date on her phone. December 6. One year, exactly.

She felt the urge to say something, though she wasn’t quite sure how to put it into words.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I’m glad you asked me out.”

He turned toward her.

She looked ahead, a little embarrassed.

“I mean... I’m glad we started dating.”

His expression softened.

“So am I.”

“I didn’t know what it would be like, you know? Having a boyfriend.”

“Was it disappointing?”

She turned to him immediately.

“No!”

“Good.”

“You’re teasing me.”

“A little.”

She leaned against his arm.

“I just mean... I didn’t know that it would feel like this.”

“Like what?”

She thought about it.

“Like having someone I can tell everything to. Someone I want to see even when I’ve already seen him all day. Someone who makes boring days better. And someone who steals my food.”

“I don’t steal your food.”

“You do.”

“You offer it.”

“That’s different.”

He smiled.

She held his gaze.

“And I didn’t know I’d like ordinary things this much.”

He was quiet.

Then he lifted their joined hands and kissed her fingers.

“I think ordinary things are the best part.”

The traffic light turned green.

But neither moved immediately.

Xiaoran smiled.

“Happy first anniversary, Zhou Yichen.”

He looked at her with that quiet, familiar warmth.

“Happy first anniversary, Lin Xiaoran.”

Then he bent his head and kissed her, slow and warm, while the traffic went round them and the last of the sun lay across the pavement. Her stomach did something ridiculous. She held on to his sleeve so she wouldn’t float off the curb.

When he pulled away, Xiaoran’s cheeks were pink.

She looked at him.

“One year.”

“One year.”

“Exactly.”

He smiled.

“Would you like another?”

She blinked.

“Another what?”

“Year.”

Her expression changed.

Then she smiled so brightly that he couldn’t help laughing.

“Yes.”

“All right.”

He took her hand again.

“Then let’s go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, Xiaoran lay on her bed with Yichen’s letter beside her pillow.

She had read it so many times that she could almost remember every sentence.

Her phone buzzed.

Yichen: Did you get home safely?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: Good.

Xiaoran: I read your letter again.

Yichen: And?

Xiaoran: I like it.

Yichen: That’s good.

Xiaoran: I love you.

A short pause.

Yichen: I love you too.

She smiled at the screen, then another message appeared.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Hm?

Yichen: Next year, let’s not worry so much about buying each other things.

She looked at the message.

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: Because I think we already have enough.

She read it twice.

Then she typed.

Xiaoran: What do we have?

His reply came a moment later.

Yichen: Each other.

Xiaoran pressed her phone against her chest.

It was such a simple answer.

She liked it anyway. He had written her a letter because he wanted to, she had given him a folder of blurry photographs because she wanted to remember, and they had walked home along the same streets as always. Nothing had felt missing.

A week ago she had spent everything she had on his birthday. Today the whole anniversary had cost three yuan, and he had promised to pay it back.

She fell asleep with the letter under her pillow.

chapters.desc: The first cold morning of the year, a navy scarf, and a grandmother who is asked, at some length, how to embroider letters.
chapters.title: Winter Uniform
chapters.epigraph: “Tell your mother I like her scarf.”
chapters.content:
The first genuinely cold morning of the year arrived without warning.

One day, Xiaoran had been complaining that the classroom windows were too warm; the next, she was standing outside the school gates with her hands tucked into her sleeves, wondering why the weather had decided to become so unpleasant.

She had underestimated winter.

Her coat was buttoned all the way up, but the wind still found its way through the gaps. She rubbed her hands together, blowing warm air into her palms while waiting for Yichen.

He arrived a few minutes later, carrying his schoolbag over one shoulder. His uniform was neat as usual, and a navy-blue scarf was wrapped around his neck.

Xiaoran noticed it immediately.

She looked at the scarf, then at him.

“You’re wearing a scarf.”

Yichen glanced down. “Observant.”

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.”

She stepped closer, studying it. The scarf was a deep navy, simple and soft-looking, with a small set of initials embroidered near one end.

Z.Y.C.

She tilted her head.

“Is that yours?”

“No. I borrowed it from someone.”

Xiaoran gave him a flat look. “Your initials are literally on it.”

“Then you have your answer.”

She reached for the end of the scarf, carefully turning it over to examine the stitching. The letters were small and neat, worked in a slightly lighter shade of blue.

“Who made it?”

“My mother.”

Xiaoran looked up.

Yichen adjusted the strap of his schoolbag. “She stitched the initials herself.”

“Your mother made this?”

“Mm.”

“By hand?”

“Would you like me to arrange an interview with her?”

She ignored his teasing, still looking at the scarf.

“That’s so nice.”

He watched her expression soften.

“She made it last winter. She thought I wouldn’t remember which scarf was mine if I left it somewhere,” he explained.

“And was she right?”

“Twice a winter, on average.”

Xiaoran laughed.

She touched the embroidered initials again, her thumb brushing over the thread.

It was a small detail, but somehow it made the scarf feel more personal. Not something bought because it was fashionable or expensive, but something someone had taken the time to make for him.

“Does she make things for you often?”

“Not often. She used to make more when I was younger.”

“That’s lovely.”

Yichen looked at her hands. Her fingers had gone pink from the cold.

“You’re freezing.”

“I’m fine.”

“Your hands disagree.”

Before she could protest, he unwound the scarf.

Xiaoran watched him with suspicion. “What are you doing?”

“Giving you something to keep your hands warm.”

“You’ll be cold.”

“I have a coat.”

“So do I.”

“Your coat isn’t doing a very good job.”

He wrapped the scarf around her neck, adjusting it so it sat comfortably. It was still warm from being around his neck, and the fabric smelled of his laundry detergent.

Xiaoran went quiet.

The scarf was a little long on her. One end rested against her chest, the other fell almost to her waist.

She looked down at the embroidered initials.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Your initials are on it.”

“I noticed.”

“People will know it’s yours.”

“That’s generally what initials are for.”

She looked up at him, trying to decide whether he was deliberately being difficult.

He only smiled.

“Besides, I don’t think anyone will mistake you for me,” he said, tucking the loose end neatly beneath her coat.

“Why not?”

“You’re considerably shorter.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed, and she pushed his arm.

They started walking toward the school building. Xiaoran kept touching the scarf, occasionally pulling it closer around her neck.

After a while, she asked, “Does your mother know you’re giving it away?”

“I’m not giving it away.”

“You just put it on me.”

“Temporarily.”

“Then what if I don’t return it?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Are you planning to steal it?”

She considered the question with exaggerated seriousness.

“Maybe.”

“Then I’ll have to tell my mother.”

Xiaoran gasped. “You wouldn’t.” She had met his mother exactly twice, at an airport and in a car, and both times Mrs. Zhou had been so kind that Xiaoran had gone home and lain on her bed for an hour.

“She’ll probably be pleased. She made it for me to keep warm, and apparently I’ve found someone who needs it more.”

She looked away, smiling.

It was difficult to tell whether he was teasing her or being sincere. With Yichen, it was often both.

At the classroom corridor, she finally stopped him.

“Wait.”

He turned.

Xiaoran carefully removed the scarf, folded it once, then held it out to him.

“Here.”

Yichen looked at it, then at her.

“You’re returning it already?”

“You’ll need it.”

“I’m fine.”

“Your mother made it for you. You should wear it.”

He accepted the scarf, but instead of putting it back on, he draped it over his arm.

“Then let’s make an arrangement.”

“What arrangement?”

“You can borrow it whenever you’re cold.”

She blinked. “Really?”

“Provided you return it.”

“That’s a very strict borrowing policy.”

“I’ll consider making exceptions for reliable borrowers.”

“How do I become a reliable borrower?”

“Start by not stealing it.”

She laughed, and he reached out to straighten the collar of her coat.

“Keep your hands in your pockets. And don’t stand outside waiting for me in the cold tomorrow,” he reminded her.

“How will you know I’m there?”

“I’ll look for you.”

He said it so casually that she almost missed the tenderness in it.

Almost.

She smiled and nodded.

“Okay.”

Yichen turned toward his classroom, but before he could leave, she called after him.

“Yichen?”

He looked back.

“Tell your mother I like her scarf.”

His expression softened.

“I will.”

“And tell her she has good taste.”

“She’ll be happy to hear that.”

“Tell her I’ll give it back.”

He gave her a slow, amused smile. “I’ll leave that part out.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re laughing at me.”

“Not at all.”

“You are.”

“Go to class, Xiaoran.”

She walked away, still smiling.

That afternoon, when the temperature dropped again, Yichen found her waiting near the school gate. She had both hands tucked into her sleeves, her nose slightly pink.

He approached without saying anything and unwound his navy scarf.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Again?”

“Apparently, you haven’t learned how to dress for winter.”

“I dressed perfectly well.”

“You’re shivering.”

He wrapped the scarf around her neck.

She looked down at the embroidered initials, then up at him.

“Your mother is going to think you don’t know how to take care of yourself.”

Yichen adjusted the scarf beneath her chin.

“Then I’ll tell her I’ve been taking care of someone else.”

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

She tugged the scarf closer and followed him through the school gates.

✦ ✦ ✦

In Class 3, at morning reading, she forgot to take it off. Rong Hao, passing her desk with the homework register, read the stitching at the end and said “Z.Y.C.” out loud, like a man reading a car number plate, and half the row turned round.

Meilin didn’t even look up from her English. “You’re wearing his name.”

“I’m wearing a scarf.”

“With his name on it.”

Xiaoran took it off and folded it in her lap under the desk, and kept her hand on it through two periods, and on the way home she had an idea.

That night she rang her grandmother.

“Grandma. How do you embroider letters?”

There was a pause on the line of a woman putting down her knitting. “Which letters?”

“Just letters. Initials.”

“Whose initials?”

“Mine.”

“On what?”

Xiaoran looked at the navy scarf, which she hadn’t returned, which was folded on her pillow. “On something.”

“Is this the boy who calls at nine?”

It took forty minutes. Her grandmother explained backstitch, then satin stitch, then told her to forget satin stitch because she would only make a mess, then asked whether the boy was still eating breakfast, then explained backstitch again. Xiaoran found a needle in her mother’s sewing tin and a reel of white thread, and at one in the morning, on the end of the scarf without his initials, inside the fold where nobody would see, she had stitched three crooked letters.

L.X.R.

The R had a tail that went somewhere it shouldn’t. She had pricked her finger twice. She looked at it under her desk lamp and thought it was the worst embroidery she had ever seen and also the best thing she had ever made.

She gave the scarf back at the gate the next morning, folded so the inside end was hidden.

He found it at the eight o’clock break, in self-study, when he unwound it to put on the back of his chair. She watched him find it, from two desks away, without turning her head. He turned the end over in his fingers. He looked at it. Then he folded it back so the letters were on the inside, the way she had left them, and put it on again, and didn’t take it off for the rest of the evening, although the radiators in that room were the only ones in the school that worked.

The note came back to her desk at quarter to nine.

Your R is drunk.

She wrote underneath: Give it back then.

No.

✦ ✦ ✦

For the rest of winter, the navy scarf became a familiar sight. Sometimes Yichen wore it. Sometimes Xiaoran did. In February, when she finally went to his house properly for the first time and sat at his family’s table in a state of controlled terror, it was hanging by the front door, and Mrs. Zhou took it down to put round Xiaoran’s neck when she left, and turned the end over, and saw the crooked white letters inside the fold.

She didn’t say anything. She only smiled, and tucked the end in.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran has never cooked. Zhou Yichen’s parents are out on Saturday. She’s going to cook anyway.
chapters.title: This Tastes Suspiciously Edible
chapters.epigraph: “The secret ingredient is stubbornness.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran decided to cook for Zhou Yichen because of one dangerous thought: How hard could it be? Historically, that thought had ruined many lives.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’ve never cooked before.”

Tang Meilin said it in the tone of someone watching a preventable tragedy. They were in the supermarket, Xiaoran pushing the cart with terrifying confidence.

“I can learn.”

“You almost burned instant noodles last year.”

“That was a microwave issue.”

“You put METAL inside.”

“Technicality.”

Xiaoran kept tossing things into the cart: eggs, tomatoes, beef, green onions. Whatever she’d seen in cooking videos.

“…Do you even know what you’re making?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

Silence.

“Love.”

“Okay we’re doomed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It had started innocently. Yesterday at lunch, Yichen had mentioned—

“My parents won’t be home Saturday.”

Xiaoran’s drama-poisoned brain immediately translated that into: perfect romantic cooking opportunity. Realistically, she should have ordered takeout and lied. But Lin Xiaoran had too much pride. If she was going to cook for her boyfriend, she was going to actually cook, even if civilization collapsed.
