So Friday night was preparation night: three hours of cooking tutorials, two breakdowns, and one nearly catastrophic knife incident.

“Your fingers are more important than romance,” Meilin warned over video call.

“I know.”

“Why are you holding the knife like that.”

“…Like a warrior?”

“Like a threat to society.”

Xiaoran kept chopping, badly. Cooking looked so much easier in videos. Why did onions require suffering? Why was the oil attacking her? Why did garlic burn in three seconds?!

“This is impossible.”

“It’s fried rice, not nuclear engineering.”

“You don’t understand pressure.”

Meilin understood perfectly. The pressure was Lin Xiaoran desperately wanting Zhou Yichen to like something she’d made herself. Which made the whole thing kind of cute. Dangerous. But cute.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came too fast, and now Xiaoran was standing in Yichen’s kitchen in an apron, questioning every decision she had ever made. Yichen sat at the counter, watching. Too.

“Why are you staring at me.”

“You invited me here.”

“To EAT. Not observe.”

“Hm.”

That calm little hm irritated her, mostly because he looked far too good sitting there in a gray hoodie, chin propped on one hand, watching her cook. Very distracting.

“You’re nervous,” he said after a while.

“I’m NOT nervous.”

“You added salt twice.”

Silence. Xiaoran looked down at the bowl. Oh no. OH NO. Yichen laughed under his breath while Xiaoran panicked.

“This is a disaster.”

“It’s fixable.”

“How.”

“We start over.”

No annoyance, no disappointment. Just calm. And somehow that made Xiaoran feel less stressed right away. Then Yichen got up and came over, close enough that Xiaoran forgot how to breathe normally. Stupid handsome boyfriend.

“You missed some eggshell too,” he murmured.

“…Where.”

Instead of answering, Yichen reached past her shoulder and carefully picked the tiny piece of shell out of the bowl. Warmth flooded Xiaoran’s face. Domestic Zhou Yichen was a problem. Then he glanced down at her.

“…Cute apron.”

“Don’t mock me.”

“I’m serious.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Because it’s pink.”

“It was the only one Meilin had.”

Unfortunately, the pink apron had tiny strawberries on it, and Zhou Yichen was visibly fighting a laugh every five minutes. Unbearable man.

✦ ✦ ✦

The cooking actually improved after that, mostly because Yichen stopped sitting there and helped. Not taking over. Just helping—washing vegetables beside her, passing things, stopping her from committing seasoning crimes. At one point, Xiaoran frowned at the pan.

“Does this look cooked?”

Yichen leaned in to check. Way too close. Xiaoran could smell his shampoo again. Disaster.

“Hm, almost,” he murmured thoughtfully.

Then he reached around her to turn the heat down—one arm beside her, his chest almost touching her shoulder—and Lin Xiaoran forgot about cooking entirely.

“…You’re distracting.”

“I’m fixing your fire hazard.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

Yichen smiled a little, then looked down at her in that quiet, soft way. The one that ruined her every time.

“What are you saying, then?” he asked.

Nothing. Her brain had stopped working again. Meanwhile, the rice was burning.

“OH MY GOD.”

Romance, interrupted. Tragic.

✦ ✦ ✦

An hour later, the food was done. And it looked… surprisingly normal. Actual edible-looking food. Xiaoran stared at the table.

“…Why does this look successful.”

Yichen sat across from her calmly.

“You worked hard.”

“That doesn’t guarantee quality.”

Then came the most terrifying moment of Xiaoran’s life: Yichen picking up the spoon. She watched him like a criminal awaiting sentencing.

“Be honest. If it’s bad, just say it,” she warned.

“Hm.”

“No boyfriend lies.”

“Hm.”

“And don’t force yourself.”

“I understand.”

Then he took a bite. Silence. One second. Two seconds. Three—

“…Wait.”

Xiaoran stopped breathing.

“It’s bad?”

“No.”

He looked genuinely surprised. He looked at the food, then at her.

“…This is actually really good.”

“…What.”

“The beef’s seasoned properly. The rice texture’s good too.”

Then Lin Xiaoran screamed.

“OH MY GOD.”

Yichen started laughing as Xiaoran grabbed his sleeve.

“YOU’RE NOT LYING?”

“I’m not.”

Xiaoran dropped into her chair and covered her face.

“I’m talented.”

“You almost poisoned the kitchen earlier.”

“BUT NOT THE FOOD.”

The pride all over her face was adorable, and Yichen couldn’t stop smiling as she celebrated over fried rice like she’d won a national award.

“You know, I thought this would taste terrible,” he said, taking another bite.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

“I still came prepared to eat everything.”

“That’s NOT ROMANTIC.”

“It is from my perspective.”

Xiaoran glared at him. Yichen laughed again. After a moment, casually, he reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear. Xiaoran forgot the entire conversation. Yichen looked at her flushed face and smiled.

“…You should cook for me again sometime.”

Somehow, that meant more to her than the food turning out well.

chapters.desc: A sudden downpour, a useless umbrella, and one sentence Lin Xiaoran really didn’t mean to say out loud.
chapters.title: Holding Hands Is Warm, But Hugging in the Rain Is Dangerous
chapters.epigraph: “Some storms are worth getting caught in.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran hated rain. Not emotionally. Physically. Rain ruined hair, shoes, makeup, moods, dignity, and occasionally public transport. Zhou Yichen, strangely, loved it. Not in a poetic way. He just liked the quiet, the cooler air, the way the basketball court smelled afterward. Today, though, the rain was dangerous for a completely different reason.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Run faster!”

“I AM RUNNING.”

“You’re WALKING. Your legs are just long.”

They were sprinting through a sudden evening downpour after leaving the arcade downtown. Ten minutes ago, the weather had been perfect. Now? Total betrayal from the sky. Xiaoran held her bag over her head while Yichen tried to angle their one umbrella against a wind that seemed to have a personal grudge.

“This umbrella is decorative,” Xiaoran complained loudly.

“It’s trying its best.”

“WE’RE STILL DYING.”

Yichen laughed and pulled her closer by the wrist so she wouldn’t slip on the wet sidewalk. Even drenched, that small thing made her heart go soft. Very annoying. Finally they ducked under the awning of a closed bookstore, both breathing hard. Rain came down in silver sheets around them, headlights smeared across the wet street. And suddenly the whole thing felt unfairly romantic. Xiaoran noticed. Unfortunately. Rain still clung to Yichen’s hair. His sleeves were pushed halfway up, his shoulders soaked from shielding her. He looked like a scene from one of her dramas.

Zhou Yichen looked down at her.

“…Why are you staring.”

“Nothing.”

“You’ve been quiet for thirty seconds.”

“That’s because rain lowers my IQ.”

“Hm.”

His thumb brushed across her knuckles absentmindedly. A small, automatic thing. But suddenly Xiaoran was hyperaware of everything: the sound of the rain, how close he was, how warm his hand was. Maybe because the weather felt softer, her chest did too.

“Holding hands is warm,” she mumbled.

Yichen glanced at her.

“What?”

Oops. Accidental thought leak. Xiaoran looked away.

“Nothing.”

But Zhou Yichen always got curious at the worst possible times.

“What did you say?”

Silence. Then, defiantly—

“I said holding hands is warm.”

“And?”

She hesitated. Why did this suddenly feel embarrassing? Then—

“…But hugging feels warmer.”

Silence. When Xiaoran finally looked up, Yichen was watching her. He wasn’t teasing or laughing, just looking at her with that soft expression that always made her weak. Then, slowly, he let go of her hand. Xiaoran blinked.

“Hm?”

Instead of answering, Yichen stepped closer and, without a word, pulled her into his arms. Warmth wrapped around her. Not sudden. Just steady. His hoodie smelled faintly like rain and laundry detergent, and one hand settled at the back of her head. Xiaoran understood something then. Holding hands was warm. But this was dangerous. Hugging Zhou Yichen in the cold rain made the whole world quietly disappear—the noisy street, the weather, the passing cars—until there was only the steady beat of his heart under her cheek.

Above her head, Yichen murmured—

“Better?”

His voice was lower like this. Closer. Xiaoran tightened her arms around him.

“…A little.”

“A little?”

“Okay maybe a lot.”

He laughed under his breath, and she felt it against her forehead. Outside their little shelter, the rain kept pouring. Neither of them moved. After a while, very—

“You’re cold,” he murmured.

“That’s because SOMEONE gave me fake umbrella protection.”

“Hm.”

“That hm means guilt.”

Yichen smiled and rubbed her arm through her damp cardigan, trying to warm her up. That small thing got to her more than any grand gesture could. Then thunder cracked overhead. Xiaoran flinched, and Yichen’s arms tightened around her before he even thought about it. The realization hit her embarrassingly hard. Being loved by Zhou Yichen was genuinely unfair sometimes. Then—

“Yichen, I think rain might actually be romantic.”

“Only now?”

“I’m growing as a person.”

He laughed softly again. After a moment, Yichen looked down at her. Close. Way too close. The rain blurred behind him and the yellow streetlights caught in his eyes, and Xiaoran’s heartbeat went ridiculous again. This was exactly like the drama scenes she screamed over. Except better, because it was real.

“You say things like that way too easily,” Yichen murmured.

“I do not.”

“Hugging is warmer?”

Silence. Okay. Maybe she did. Xiaoran buried her face deeper in his chest.

“I take it back.”

“Too late.”

“Delete the memory.”

“Impossible.”

After a second, he kissed the top of her damp hair. Soft and quick. And that tiny kiss destroyed whatever dignity she had left.

“This relationship, is making me too happy,” she whispered weakly.

chapters.desc: A teacher’s wedding, one cream-colored dress, and the evening Zhou Yichen forgot how to talk.
chapters.title: Xiaoran Looks Beautiful Today
chapters.epigraph: “He had seen her every day. He had never seen her like this.”
chapters.content:
At exactly 5:42 p.m., Zhou Yichen realized Lin Xiaoran looked too beautiful today. Not everyday cute. Dangerous. The kind that made him briefly forget how conversations worked. Which irritated him a little, because he prided himself on composure. That composure disappeared the second Xiaoran stepped out of Tang Meilin’s room.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You can breathe now.”

Yuhao’s voice snapped him back to reality. He looked deeply entertained, because Zhou Yichen had frozen. For three full seconds. They were waiting downstairs at Meilin’s apartment before heading to Teacher Su’s wedding banquet. Teacher Su taught literature and had somehow become everyone’s emotional support teacher, so a few of her closest students had been invited—including some unfairly attractive teenagers. Specifically, Lin Xiaoran. She came down the stairs slowly, fiddling with one small earring, and Yichen’s brain stopped working again.

Xiaoran almost never dressed up. Usually it was oversized sweaters, school uniform, hoodies—his, often. Tonight she wore a soft cream dress that fell just below her knees. Simple. Elegant. Not trying to look older. Just pretty. Her hair was curled at the ends, framing her face. Tiny pearl earrings. Light makeup. She still looked completely like herself, just prettier, in a way that felt unfair to society. Xiaoran looked nervous the second she noticed everyone staring.

“…Why are you all acting weird.”

Meilin crossed her arms proudly.

“Because I worked hard.”

“Meilin spent forty minutes fixing your hair,” Yuhao said.

“I almost lost my life,” Meilin corrected.

Then she looked at Yichen, and paused. Her boyfriend was staring. Openly. Completely focused on her.

“…Why are YOU acting weird?”

Yichen blinked. Twice. Still staring. Yuhao nearly collapsed laughing beside him.

“Oh my god.”

Then, Yichen said—

“You look beautiful.”

Zhou Yichen almost never gave compliments that directly. His were usually smaller, softer, private. This one came out on instinct, before he could think, and it hit Xiaoran harder than any dramatic flirting could. Her whole face went red.

“…Oh.”

Brilliant response. Yichen seemed a little calmer now that he’d said it. His eyes kept moving over her face anyway, still taking her in, and Xiaoran noticed, which only made it worse.

“Stop looking at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like… Like THIS.” She gestured helplessly.

Yuhao cut in—

“He looks like he just discovered women.”

“Shut up.”

Meilin sighed.

“Can we leave before these two combust.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The banquet was warm and lively: golden lights, soft music, round tables full of chatting relatives and teachers. The students sat together off to one side, trying to behave. Keyword: trying. Teacher Su looked so happy that it made everyone emotional, especially when she nearly cried at the sight of her former students all dressed up.

“You all grew up so fast,” she sniffed.

Xiaoran hugged her carefully, then ruined the moment immediately—

“Teacher, you look like a movie star today.”

Teacher Su laughed through tears.

“Still talking nonsense.”

Yichen stood nearby holding the gift bag. And once again, he looked at Xiaoran and lost his train of thought. It kept happening all evening—the way she smiled politely at older relatives, the way she laughed, the way the warm light caught her earrings.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He blinked. Teacher Su smiled knowingly.

“You’ve been staring at Xiaoran all evening.”

Xiaoran nearly dropped her tea. The other students choked trying not to laugh. Even Meilin looked delighted. Outwardly, Yichen stayed calm. Inwardly, not at all. The tips of his ears gave him away. Teacher Su continued smiling warmly.

“You two are very cute together.”

Xiaoran buried her face in her hands.

“This wedding is attacking me personally.”

Yichen looked away, the corner of his mouth lifting, which only made everything worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night, as the guests began to leave, a light rain started outside the hotel entrance—soft enough not to matter. The others waited for their rides while Xiaoran and Yichen stood a little apart under the decorative lights by the garden path. A quiet moment. Warm night air. Everything felt softer. Xiaoran looked down at her shoes.

Yichen glanced at her, then didn’t look away.

“You look beautiful tonight.”

Xiaoran looked away fast. Why did simple compliments from him feel so dangerous? Yichen stepped closer, close enough that his suit jacket brushed her sleeve. He looked unfair tonight too. Black formalwear should be banned for teenage boys. Especially Zhou Yichen.

“I think everyone noticed,” Xiaoran mumbled.

“What?”

“That you kept looking at me.”

“It’s hard not to.”

Silence. Was he trying to kill her tonight? Yichen looked thoughtful, like he wanted to say something else. Then, very—

“You know what scared me earlier? When you came downstairs.”

“…Why?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“Because for one second. I genuinely forgot how to talk,” he admitted.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

chapters.desc: One secondhand poetry book. One very dramatic girlfriend. One week nobody at school will ever forget.
chapters.title: Xiaoran Became a Poetry Menace
chapters.epigraph: “Even ordinary afternoons become literature.”
chapters.content:
It started because Lin Xiaoran bought one old poetry book at a secondhand bookstore. One book. That was all it took to destroy the peace.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It smells intellectual.”

Tang Meilin stared at the dusty hardcover in horror. The four of them were at a café on Saturday while Xiaoran proudly showed off her purchase: an old, faded hardcover of translated classical poetry and romantic prose. She already looked like a changed woman.

“It’s vintage,” she corrected seriously.

“It smells like someone’s grandfather.”

“That’s called history.”

Yichen glanced at it, stirring his iced coffee.

“Do you even like poetry?”

“I’m evolving.”

Yuhao looked suspicious.

“Last month you said philosophy was fake.”

“That was before literature entered my soul.”

Meilin sighed.

“We’re doomed.”

Unfortunately, she was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Monday morning, Lin Xiaoran was unbearable. Not normal unbearable. Poetic unbearable, which was worse. She leaned against her desk in the morning sun.

“Some people, are like moonlight reflected across water,” she sighed.

Silence. Meilin looked up from her homework.

“…What.”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“Beautiful but impossible to hold.”

Yuhao stared. Zhou Yichen stopped writing and slowly looked at her. Where was this coming from? Then, calmly—

“Good morning to you too.”

Xiaoran nodded wisely.

“The moon also rises gently.”

“I hate this already,” Meilin muttered.

It got worse. Much worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch, Yuhao stole a dumpling off Xiaoran’s plate. Instead of yelling like a normal person, she narrowed her eyes and whispered:

“Greed is a fire that consumes friendship.”

Yuhao froze.

“…What.”

“Ancient wisdom.”

“That was a threat.”

“That dumpling had meaning.”

Yichen nearly smiled into his drink. Watching Xiaoran weaponize poetry all day was getting more entertaining by the hour, especially because she so clearly felt intelligent now. Then she turned to him. Danger.

“What,” Yichen said.

Xiaoran pointed her chopsticks at him.

“You know, there’s a phrase here that reminds me of you,” she murmured.

Silence. Yichen leaned back.

“Hm?”

“‘The pine tree does not bend easily before winter winds.’”

Meilin gagged. Yuhao looked horrified. Xiaoran went on proudly—

“It means someone calm and steadfast.”

“I know what pine trees symbolize,” Yichen answered calmly.

“Oh.”

“But thank you.”

He said it simply, gently, and it got to Xiaoran embarrassingly hard. Zhou Yichen always took her nonsense seriously. Even poetic nonsense.

“You’re not making fun of me?”

“Should I?”

“No.”

“Then no.”

Meilin watched the interaction with dead eyes.

“I’m dropping out of school.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem started on Wednesday, because Xiaoran had memorized too many lines. Way too many. Now she ambushed people with them all day. At PE class—

“The wind today feels lonely.”

During math—

“Numbers are humanity’s attempt to organize chaos.”

While eating crackers—

“Crisp sounds remind us life is fragile.”

Yuhao finally snapped.

“WHO GAVE HER THIS BOOK.”

In afternoon study hall, Yichen sat beside Xiaoran while she copied poetry into a notebook—concentrating hard, a tiny frown on her face, completely serious. Dangerously cute. Then, without looking up—

“Yichen, if I died young, would you compare me to flowers?”

Silence. Yichen slowly turned toward her.

“…What kind of sentence is that.”

“It’s literary.”

“It’s creepy.”

Xiaoran finally looked up.

“In poetry, beautiful people always die tragically.”

“You’re not dying.”

Xiaoran smiled—small and soft, like that answer pleased her far too much. Yichen noticed, and that tiny expression got to him too.

“What would you compare me to then?” she asked.

Yichen thought about it for a second, while nearby Meilin and Yuhao braced for emotional damage.

“You remind me of sunlight.”

No teasing, no hesitation. Just honest. Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“…That was way too romantic.”

“You asked.”

“But you answered TOO well.”

Yuhao grabbed Meilin’s arm.

“I can’t survive this.”

Yichen went back to his notes like he hadn’t just destroyed everyone. After a moment, he said—

“Sunlight’s noisy too.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

“And she’s back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By Friday, the poetry phase should have been over. Instead, it evolved. Xiaoran started leaving tiny folded notes in Yichen’s notebooks. Not love letters, exactly. Just random lines—some romantic, some threatening, some completely incomprehensible. For example:

“The stars tonight resemble your emotional unavailability.”

“Even mountains erode eventually, unlike your stubbornness.”

And:

“If abandoned, I will haunt you artistically.”

In chemistry, Yichen opened his notebook and found another one. He unfolded it calmly.

“When I look at you, even ordinary afternoons become literature.”

Slowly, the corner of his mouth lifted. Across the room, Xiaoran saw it and hid behind her textbook. Writing the lines had been fine. Watching him read them was embarrassing. Beside her, Meilin looked spiritually exhausted.

“You’re both becoming worse.”

“No we’re becoming cultured.”

“You’re becoming insane.”

Fair criticism. Then a folded note landed on Xiaoran’s desk. She opened it. Inside, in Zhou Yichen’s neat, slightly slanted handwriting:

“You should keep reading poetry.”

And below that, one more line:

“Because you sound cute when you talk like this.”

Xiaoran put her forehead down on the desk with a thunk. Across the room, Zhou Yichen smiled a little and went back to work, completely unaffected. On the outside. Terrible man.

chapters.desc: Mock exams are coming, and Xiaoran makes a rule for library study that turns out to be mostly a rule against herself.
chapters.title: Mock Exam Season
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not going to tell me I should study harder?”
chapters.content:
The rule was Xiaoran’s idea.

Which, in retrospect, was probably why it had been such a terrible idea.

It began on a Tuesday afternoon, after she had spent nearly an hour trying to revise mathematics while Yichen sat beside her in the library.

The mock examinations were approaching, and the entire school seemed to have become a place where people spoke in whispers, carried extra stationery, and looked vaguely distressed whenever someone mentioned the word revision.

Xiaoran was no exception.

She had spread her notes across the table, opened her textbook, arranged her pens by color, and written a small list of topics she needed to review.

She had also spent the last fifteen minutes looking at Yichen.

Not deliberately, she would insist.

It was just that he was sitting beside her.

And whenever she looked up from her notes, he happened to be there.

He was reading through a practice paper, one hand holding the page while the other wrote something in the margin. His expression was focused, his handwriting neat, and he had the irritating habit of looking completely unbothered by subjects that made her want to lie face-down on the table.

Xiaoran glanced at him again.

Yichen didn’t look up.

She looked back at her notes.

A minute passed.

She met his eyes.

This time, he caught her. “You’ve been staring.”

“I haven’t.”

He put down his pen.

“All right.”

The way he said it made her feel as if he was politely allowing her to lie.

Xiaoran frowned at him. “You’re distracting.”

“How?”

She hesitated.

It was difficult to say, Because I like looking at you, and I keep forgetting what I’m supposed to be doing.

So she said, “You keep moving.”

Yichen looked at his own hands.

“I was writing.”

“Exactly.”

He looked at her for another moment before the corner of his mouth lifted.

Xiaoran immediately regretted speaking.

“Fine, new rule,” she announced, sitting straighter.

“Should I be concerned?”

“We’re not allowed to look at each other.”

He blinked.

“For how long?”

She glanced at the clock.

“For the next nine minutes.”

“Nine?”

“Ten sounds like a punishment. Nine sounds like a challenge.”

Yichen considered this.

“That makes perfect sense.”

“Don’t sound so sarcastic.”

“I’m not.”

He looked at the clock, then back at her.

“All right. Nine minutes.”

Xiaoran extended her hand across the table.

“Promise?”

He shook it.

“Promise.”

They turned back to their respective notes.

For the first thirty seconds, everything went remarkably well.

Xiaoran read the first question on her practice paper. She wrote down the formula, checked her notes, and began working through the calculation.

She was doing perfectly fine.

Until she remembered that Yichen was sitting beside her.

She could see the edge of his sleeve in her peripheral vision. She could hear the faint movement of his pen against the paper. She knew exactly where he was without looking.

Which was the problem.

She pressed her lips together and continued writing.

One minute.

Two minutes.

At the third minute, Yichen shifted in his chair.

Xiaoran’s eyes instinctively moved toward him.

She caught herself just in time and snapped her attention back to the page.

A small smile appeared on Yichen’s face.

He didn’t say anything.

That was worse.

She could feel him being amused.

At the fourth minute, she reached for her eraser. It rolled toward the edge of the table, and Yichen caught it before it fell.

He placed it beside her notebook.

“Thank you,” she whispered.

“You’re welcome.”

She stared at the eraser.

Technically, he had spoken to her.

But he hadn’t looked at her.

That was allowed.

Probably.

At the fifth minute, Xiaoran began to wonder whether he was deliberately making it difficult.

She heard the faintest sound from beside her.

A page turning, then another.

Then his pen tapping once against the table.

She refused to look.

At the sixth minute, she made a mistake in her calculation.

She erased it.

Made the same mistake again.

Erased it once more.

Yichen’s voice came from beside her. “You’ve dropped a two.”

Xiaoran froze.

“We’re not supposed to look at each other.”

“I didn’t.”

“You’re not supposed to help me either.”

“That’s a different rule.”

She looked at the clock.

“You’re changing the rules.”

“I’m pointing out an error.”

“Without looking at me.”

“Would you prefer I look?”

“No!”

His quiet laughter made her grip her pen more tightly.

At the seventh minute, she was certain he was enjoying this far too much. At the eighth, she had stopped understanding the question.

At the ninth, she caught herself watching his reflection in the dark window.

She immediately looked away.

Yichen noticed.

Of course he noticed.

But he was kind enough not to mention it.

At the eighth minute, Xiaoran began counting down. She could absolutely survive one more minute without looking at her boyfriend. Forty seconds: she turned a page. Twenty: Yichen shifted slightly closer to reach for his water bottle, and she stared at her notebook so hard that her eyes began to dry out. Ten, nine, eight, all the way down, under her breath.

“Done.”

Xiaoran immediately turned toward him.

Yichen was already looking at her.

He had been waiting.

Neither of them spoke.

Then he smiled.

A small smile, not even a mischievous one.

Just that slow, familiar smile that began at the corner of his mouth and gradually made his eyes soften.

Xiaoran felt her face warm. “Why are you looking at me like that?”

“You told me I wasn’t allowed to.”

“And now it’s over.”

“I know.”

He leaned back slightly, studying her expression.

“Nine minutes. That was difficult.”

Xiaoran nodded with great seriousness.

“Very.”

Yichen glanced at her notebook.

“How much work did you finish?”

She looked down.

There was one completed question, half a calculation, and a small doodle of a cat in the corner of the page.

He took it in, then looked back at her.

“Productive.”

“Don’t.”

“I only said one word.”

“It was a mean word.”

His smile deepened.

Xiaoran folded her arms.

“You’re not allowed to tease me.”

“Is that another rule?”

“Yes.”

“How long does it last?”

“Until the mock exams are over.”

“That’s a long time.”

“Then you should be careful.”

He nodded as if taking the matter seriously.

“Understood.”

She returned to her notes, determined to recover some dignity.

A few seconds later, Yichen pushed a small piece of paper toward her.

She looked at it.

It was a short calculation, written neatly in his handwriting, with a small correction beneath it.

You made a mistake here. Try again.

Xiaoran glanced at him.

He was already looking at his own paper.

She picked up her pen and worked through the question again.

This time, she got it right.

She turned the paper toward him pleased.

Yichen looked at the answer and nodded.

“Correct.”

A smile spread across her face.

“See?”

“Very good.”

She sat a little straighter.

“Perhaps we should make another rule,” he said.

“What rule?”

“No looking at me until you’ve finished the next five questions.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“That’s not fair.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re making the rules now.”

“You started it.”

She eyed him.

Yichen smiled and returned to his paper.

For a while, they actually studied.

And when the library clock moved toward closing time, Xiaoran had finished four questions, corrected two mistakes, and written a full page of notes.

She packed her things with a satisfied little hum.

Yichen glanced at her notebook.

“One more question.”

“Tomorrow.”

“You said you wanted to finish this chapter today.”

“I’ve changed my mind.”

He closed his book.

“All right.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You’re not going to make me stay?”

“No.”

“You’re not going to tell me I should study harder?”

“No.”

“You’re not going to say that mock exams are important?”

Yichen stood and picked up his bag.

“They are important.”

Xiaoran groaned.

“But you’ve been studying for two hours. We can continue tomorrow.”

She smiled, pleased that he had said it without making her feel guilty.

They walked out of the library together.

At the corridor, Xiaoran slipped her hand into his.

Yichen glanced down at their joined hands, then at her.

“Is this allowed?”

“What?”

“Looking at each other.”

She turned to him.

“The nine minutes are over.”

“Good.”

He squeezed her hand gently.

They walked toward the school gates, their shoulders occasionally brushing.

After a few steps, Xiaoran spoke again.

“Actually, I think I could’ve lasted longer.”

“Could you?”

“Of course.”

“How long?”

She thought about it.

“Maybe twenty minutes.”

Yichen nodded.

“Let’s test that tomorrow.”

Her expression changed immediately.

“No.”

He laughed.

“I thought you were confident.”

“I was. But I’ve reconsidered.”

“Already?”

“Yes. I think nine minutes is a very reasonable limit.”

Yichen looked down at her, smiling. “Then nine minutes it is.”

She got her mock results three weeks later: mathematics up six points, history the highest in the grade. On the top of the mathematics paper, beside the mark, the teacher had written Better. Stop drawing cats. She showed it to Yichen at the gate, and he looked at it, and said she had probably drawn the cat in the ninth minute.

chapters.desc: His first game back after the injury. Scouts in the stands. Lin Xiaoran, holding nothing.
chapters.title: The Game the Scouts Came to See
chapters.epigraph: “Some people worry with their whole body.”
chapters.content:
The invitational was on a Saturday, and Lin Xiaoran hadn’t slept properly since Wednesday. It wasn’t the scouts. Everyone at school had been talking about the scouts for two weeks—how many were coming, which universities, whether one of them was from Beijing. Yuhao had a theory that one of them was secretly a former national team player. Nobody knew where he’d heard it. Xiaoran didn’t care about any of that.

She cared about his ankle.

“It’s fine,” Yichen said on Friday, for what had to be the fortieth time.

“Show me.”

“We’re in a convenience store.”

“Show me anyway.”

He sighed, put down the onigiri, and rolled his ankle slowly in a full circle, right there between the drinks fridge and the instant noodles. The cashier watched them over the counter with open interest.

“See?”

“It made a noise.”

“That was my shoe.”

“Shoes don’t make noises.”

“These are basketball shoes. They squeak. Coach Wang cleared me. The physio cleared me. I’ve practiced for ten days.” He picked the onigiri back up.

Xiaoran tugged her sleeves down over her hands and said nothing.

Yichen studied her. Then he bought her a strawberry milk she hadn’t asked for, stuck the straw in for her, and said more, “I won’t do anything stupid.”

“You said that last time.”

“Last time someone pushed me.”

“What if someone pushes you again?”

“Then I’ll fall better.”

That wasn’t the reassurance he thought it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

The gym on Saturday was louder than the semifinal had been. Students from four schools packed the bleachers, and someone had hung a hand-painted banner for their team that spelled “invitational” with two Ls. Near the scorer’s table, three adults in plain jackets sat with clipboards, not cheering for anyone. Everyone kept looking at them. Xiaoran sat between Meilin and Yuhao, gripping nothing this time. She’d decided that on the way in. No jacket to strangle, no water bottle to wring. If she held something, she would only hold it harder.

“You’re very calm,” Meilin said.

“I am extremely calm.”

“Your knee is bouncing.”

Xiaoran put a hand on her knee to stop it. Down on the court, the teams were warming up. Yichen moved through the layup line like he always did—easy, unhurried, a little bored-looking, which Xiaoran had learned meant he was concentrating. Then, on his way back to the end of the line, he glanced up at the bleachers, found her, and tapped the tape on his left ankle twice with two fingers.

It took her a second to understand. See? Fine.

“Oh my god. Did he just send you a signal?” Yuhao said.

“No.”

“He did. He sent a signal.”

“It was a cramp.”

“In his fingers?”

Two rows behind them, a pair of girls had gone quiet. Xiaoran recognized one of their voices before she recognized the face—the storage-room voice. She’s honestly holding him back. The girl looked away the second their eyes met. Xiaoran turned back to the court and found, to her own surprise, that she didn’t care what the girl thought anymore. She had a much more important job today, which wasn’t passing out.

✦ ✦ ✦

For the first quarter, Yichen played carefully. Too carefully. He passed when he could have driven. He landed on both feet every time, like someone stepping off a curb. Xiaoran noticed, and so did the other team, and by the end of the quarter they were down by six. At the break, Coach Wang said something to him that nobody in the stands could hear. Yichen nodded once, wiped his face on his shirt, and walked back on.

Then he stopped being careful. It wasn’t reckless—Xiaoran knew reckless now; reckless was the semifinal, cold and angry and going straight through people. This was different. He looked like himself again. He read a pass before it happened and took it the length of the floor. He pulled up for a jumper with a defender in his face and didn’t even watch it go in. When a player from the other team bumped him on a drive, he stumbled, caught himself, and kept going, and Xiaoran forgot to breathe for that entire second and remembered all at once when he scored.

“He’s okay,” Meilin said, like she knew.

“I know,” Xiaoran said, and her voice came out wobbly.

By the fourth quarter, the three adults by the scorer’s table had stopped writing and started just watching. They won by eleven. Yichen played the whole second half and didn’t limp once.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterward, the gym emptied slowly. Xiaoran waited by the side door with Meilin and Yuhao, which was where she always waited, except today it took much longer than usual, because Yichen was talking to one of the men in plain jackets. Then to a second one. Coach Wang stood beside him the whole time with his arms folded and the expression of a man trying hard not to look proud.

“That’s Beijing, I’m almost sure that one’s Beijing,” Yuhao whispered.

“You don’t know that.”

“I have a feeling.”

When Yichen finally came over, he had two business cards in his hand and his hair was still damp from the showers.

“Well? Were they impressed? Did they cry?” Yuhao demanded.

“Nobody cried.”

“Did they say ‘generational talent’?”

“No.”

“Did they say anything?”

Yichen thought about it. “One of them asked about my grades.”

Yuhao looked personally betrayed by higher education. Meilin dragged him off to buy drinks, which was the most obvious exit Xiaoran had ever seen, and suddenly it was just the two of them by the side door, the evening coming in cool around them. Xiaoran looked at his ankle. Yichen looked at her looking at his ankle.

“Still fine,” he said.

“I didn’t ask.”

“You were going to.”

She was. She bit her lip instead. Then, because there was no point pretending, she said, “You were really good today.”

“Hm.”

“Not normal good. Scary good.”

“You noticed the first quarter.”

“You were scared. I saw,” she said.

He didn’t deny it. That surprised her more than anything else. Zhou Yichen, who said “I’m fine” about everything, turned the business cards over in his fingers and said, “A little.”

“What changed?”

He watched her, like he was deciding how much to say.

“Coach told me to stop playing like I was afraid of getting hurt. And I looked up, and you weren’t holding anything,” he said.

Xiaoran blinked. “What?”

“Last time you held my jacket so hard you stretched the sleeve. Today your hands were empty. So I figured you weren’t that worried.” The corner of his mouth lifted.

“I was VERY worried.”

“I know that now.”

“I was worried with my whole body. I just didn’t hold anything.”

He laughed, and took her hand—the empty one—and laced his fingers through hers.

“Then thank you for worrying without strangling anything,” he said.

She leaned her forehead against his arm and let out a breath she felt like she’d been holding since Wednesday. A few weeks later, the first recruitment letter arrived. By the end of the month there were four, spread across his desk in a neat, terrifying row, and Xiaoran started to understand that the future everyone kept talking about had an address now. But that came later.

That evening, they just walked home slowly, at his pace for once, while she told him in great detail every moment of the game she had almost died during. He listened to all of it.

chapters.desc: Walking her home after the game the scouts came to see, he gives her one of the two cards that were pressed into his hand.
chapters.title: The Scout’s Card
chapters.epigraph: “When you become a really good basketball player, can I still keep it?”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran told him every moment of the game on the walk home, the first quarter when he had looked afraid, the second when he hadn’t, the steal in the third that had made Yuhao stand on his seat, and by the time they turned into her street she had run out of game and started on the scouts.

Would he have to travel? Would he need to attend trials?

Would it interfere with school?

Did Yichen think he would do it?

He answered what he could, which wasn’t much. One of the men had asked about his grades, and the other had asked whether his parents would come to a meeting, and neither had promised him anything. He would need to speak with his parents and find out more before deciding anything.

Xiaoran nodded along.

She was trying to be sensible.

But she was also terribly excited.

At her building’s gate, under the plane trees, Yichen reached into his jacket and took out one of the two business cards. The one Yuhao had sworn was Beijing.

“Here.”

Xiaoran looked at it.

“What?”

“Keep it.”

She blinked at him.

“Why?”

“You seem more interested in it than I am.”

“That’s not true.”

“Isn’t it?”

She accepted the card carefully.

It was white, a little bent at one corner from his pocket, with a name, a youth development program in Beijing, and a phone number printed neatly across the front. Yuhao had been right.

Xiaoran turned it over.

“You’re really giving this to me?”

“Yes.”

“But it’s yours.”

“I have the other one. And the number’s in my phone.”

She looked up.

“Then why don’t you keep it?”

Yichen shrugged.

“You can keep the card.”

She looked down at it again.

It was such an ordinary thing. A small piece of paper that could easily be misplaced between the pages of a textbook or forgotten in the bottom of a schoolbag.

Yet it represented something.

Someone had watched him play and seen something worth approaching. Someone who didn’t know him as Zhou Yichen of Class 1, who had friends who teased him and sometimes forgot his physics homework.

Someone had seen him as a basketball player.

And Xiaoran wanted to keep that moment.

“Don’t lose it,” Yichen said.

She immediately looked up.

“I won’t.”

“I know.”

“I mean it.”

“I know, Xiaoran.”

She slipped the card carefully into the small compartment of her bag, then zipped it closed.

Yichen watched her.

“You’re treating it like something valuable.”

“It is valuable.”

“It’s a business card.”

“It’s your business card.”

“Technically, it’s his.”

She ignored him.

He laughed under his breath.

“All right. Keep it safe.”

“I will.”

She stood at the gate, one hand holding the strap of her bag.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you think you’ll do it?”

He knew what she meant.

“I’ll find out more first.”

“You’re interested?”

“Of course.”

She nodded.

“I think you should.”

He studied her face.

“You don’t think it’ll be too much?”

“With school?”

“With everything.”

Xiaoran thought about it before answering.

“I think you can decide after you know what it involves. But if it’s something you want, you shouldn’t turn it down just because you’re worried it might be difficult.”

He met her eyes.

Then he smiled.

“That’s sensible.”

“I can be sensible.”

“Sometimes.”

She frowned.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He reached out and squeezed her hand.

“I’ll think about it.”

She nodded, satisfied.

“Good.”

He waited until she had gone inside before turning away.

That night, Xiaoran sat at her desk long after dinner.

Her schoolbooks were open. Her mathematics exercises were unfinished. A pen rested between her fingers.

And beside her notebook was the scout’s card.

She had taken it out of her bag as soon as she returned home.

At first, she had only wanted to look at it properly. Then she had read the printed details again. Then she had turned it over, although there was nothing on the back.

She picked it up once more.

The scout’s name. The organization.

The contact number.

She imagined Yichen receiving another call. She imagined him attending a trial, playing against people he had never met, and discovering new things about the sport he loved.

She imagined him getting better.

Not that she thought he needed to be better.

She already thought he was wonderful.

But she knew how much he cared about basketball. She had seen him stay behind after practice, repeating the same movement until he was satisfied. She had watched him review matches and listen carefully when his coach corrected him.

Sometimes, he worked so hard that she wondered whether he ever allowed himself to enjoy being good at something.

She placed the card beside her pencil case, then picked it up again.

It was silly.

She knew it was silly.

But she was happy.

Very, happy for him.

A little later, her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Have you finished studying?

Xiaoran: Almost.

Yichen: That’s not an answer.

Xiaoran: I am thinking.

Yichen: About mathematics?

She glanced at the card.

Xiaoran: Yes.

A moment passed.

Yichen: You’re lying.

She laughed.

Xiaoran: Maybe.

Yichen: What are you thinking about?

Xiaoran: Your card.

Yichen: I thought you were keeping it safe.

Xiaoran: I am.

Yichen: Then why are you thinking about it?

Xiaoran: Because I’m happy.

His reply came a little later.

Yichen: I’m glad.

She smiled at the screen.

Xiaoran: You should be proud of yourself too.

Yichen: I am.

Xiaoran: Really?

Yichen: Yes. But I haven’t done anything yet.

She read the message twice.

Then typed:

Xiaoran: Someone noticed you. That’s already something.

This time, his reply came quickly.

Yichen: Good night, Xiaoran.

She frowned.

Xiaoran: That’s all?

Yichen: You should sleep. You have school tomorrow.

Xiaoran: You’re avoiding my compliment.

Yichen: I’m accepting it.

Xiaoran: You don’t sound like it.

Yichen: Then I’ll say it properly tomorrow.

She grinned.

Xiaoran: Okay. Good night.

Yichen: Good night. Don’t stay up too late.

She put her phone down, then looked at the card again.

At bedtime, Xiaoran placed the card inside a small notebook she kept beside her bed.

She opened it once more, checked that it was still there, and closed the cover.

Then she paused.

After a moment, she took it out again.

The notebook was too bulky to put under her pillow. She didn’t want to crease the card, either.

She considered putting it in her drawer.

But that felt too far away.

Finally, she slipped the card into a small paper sleeve and placed it beneath the edge of her pillow, where it would stay flat and safe.

She lay down, pulled the blanket over herself, and turned off the bedside lamp.

For several minutes, she stared at the ceiling.

She was thinking about the match.

About the scout.

About Yichen’s face when he had told her someone wanted to speak with him.

And about how he had handed her the card without hesitation, as if it was perfectly natural for her to keep something that mattered to him.

She smiled into her pillow.

It wasn’t her achievement.

She hadn’t played the match. She hadn’t made the shots. She hadn’t spent all those afternoons practicing.

But she had been there.

She had seen him work for it, even before anyone else had noticed.

And now she had something small to remember the beginning by.

The next morning, Yichen was waiting near the school gate when Xiaoran arrived.

She looked unusually cheerful.

He noticed immediately.

“Good morning.”

“Good morning.”

“Did you sleep well?”

“Very well.”

He studied her for a second.

“Why do you look so pleased with yourself?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

She nodded.

Then, after a brief hesitation, she leaned closer and whispered, “I put your card under my pillow.”

Yichen went still.

He seemed unsure whether he had heard her correctly.

“Under your pillow?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“To keep it safe.”

He turned to her.

“Your bag has a compartment.”

“I know.”

“And your desk has a drawer.”

“I know.”

“But you put it under your pillow.”

Xiaoran nodded, entirely unembarrassed.

“It’s important.”

Yichen lowered his gaze, and a smile began to form.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“It’s a business card.”

She frowned.

“Why does everyone keep saying that?”

“Because it is.”

“Well, it’s an important business card.”

He laughed.

She watched his expression, waiting for him to tease her further.

Instead, he reached out and gently tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“Then I’m glad you’re keeping it.”

Her expression softened.

He glanced at her bag.

“Just don’t bring it to school loose. You’ll lose it.”

“I won’t.”

“You’re sure?”

She nodded.

Something in his face eased.

“All right. I trust you.”

They began walking toward the school building.

After a few steps, Xiaoran slipped her hand into his.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“When you become a really good basketball player, can I still keep it?”

He looked down at her.

“When. Not if,” he repeated.

She nodded, as if that had been obvious.

His smile grew.

“Then you can keep it.”

“Even if you get more important cards?”

“Even then.”

“Even if you become famous?”

He considered that. “Then you’ll need a safe.”

Xiaoran smiled, satisfied.

Three weeks later the first recruitment letter came to his house, and she was there when he opened it, and she didn’t say anything about the card. But that night, after he had walked her home, she took the card out from under her pillow and put it in the back of the notebook where she kept things that were going to matter, behind a pressed leaf from the day he asked her out and a strawberry milk label she wouldn’t have admitted to keeping.

chapters.desc: University offers are arriving for Zhou Yichen. Lin Xiaoran is quietly terrified of where they might take him.
chapters.title: Which Future Includes You?
chapters.epigraph: “Plans change. People stay.”
chapters.content:
Choosing universities should have been exciting. Lin Xiaoran treated it like impending doom.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re staring at the same page.”

Tang Meilin looked up from her laptop. Xiaoran hadn’t moved in a while. University brochures covered the whole café table—prestigious schools, scholarship pamphlets, department rankings. And in the middle of it all, Zhou Yichen’s basketball recruitment letters. Apparently being tall, smart, and athletic wasn’t enough. Universities wanted him too. Annoying, honestly.

“I hate higher education,” Xiaoran muttered.

“That’s because applications started.”

“No. It’s because adulthood is scary.” She slumped across the table.

Meilin sighed. Fair. Lately everyone talked about the future constantly—majors, dorms, career plans, cities. It scared Xiaoran more than exams did. Not because she didn’t have dreams. Because for the first time, she realized dreams could pull people in different directions. And Zhou Yichen had so many options, while she still changed her mind about careers every three weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem had started yesterday, when Xiaoran overheard teachers talking about Yichen after basketball practice.

“He could definitely enter Beijing.”

“Or Shanghai.”

“His coach said sports universities are contacting him too.”

“He has a strong future.”

Strong future. The words lodged in her chest. Suddenly the future wasn’t abstract anymore. It was real, and terrifyingly far away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen noticed the change right away, because Lin Xiaoran physically couldn’t hide her feelings. At lunch she sat beside him, poking at her rice. Quiet. Too quiet.

“You failed a test?” Yichen asked.

“No.”

“You lost something?”

“Yes.”

Yichen paused.

“What.”

“My peace.”

“You’ve been weird since yesterday.”

“I’m reflecting on life.”

Across from them, Yuhao was eating noodles peacefully. Then he decided to get involved.

“She’s probably thinking about universities.”

Silence. Traitor. Xiaoran glared.

“How do YOU know?”

“You’ve been reposting sad quotes.”

Meilin nodded from beside him.

“One literally said ‘distance turns even stars into strangers.’”

Yichen blinked, then slowly turned to Xiaoran. Now he understood. Xiaoran immediately regretted existing. Out loud, it sounded dramatically pathetic.

“Forget I ever spoke,” she muttered.

But Zhou Yichen looked thoughtful now, which only made her more nervous.

“Come with me after school.”

“Where.”

“You’ll see.”

“Every time someone says that in a drama, something terrible happens.”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After school, Yichen took her to the old outdoor court behind campus, the quiet one that was usually empty in the evenings. The sky was cloudy, the wind cool. Peaceful. Xiaoran sat beside him on the bench, bracing for devastation. What if he really wanted a university far away? What if he left? What if—

“What university do YOU want?”

His question cut her spiral short.

“Hm?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“What do you want?”

Silence. Nobody had asked her that yet. Everyone asked about scores, options, being practical. Not what she wanted.

“I don’t know yet.”

“That’s okay.”

“But you do. You already have plans.”

Yichen leaned back against the bench.

“Not really.”

“You literally have recruitment offers.”

“That’s basketball.”

“That’s your future.”

He glanced at her, then said calmly—

“You’re part of my future too.”

He said it so naturally, like it was obvious, like there had never been another possibility. Xiaoran’s chest ached.

“But what if your best opportunity is somewhere far?”

Yichen didn’t answer right away. He looked out at the empty court for a moment.

“Do you know why I haven’t accepted anything yet?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…Why?”

“Because I’m waiting for your applications first.”

Silence.

“WHAT.”

He said it so calmly, like it wasn’t a completely insane boyfriend thing to say. Xiaoran stared at him in horror.

“You can’t make life decisions around me!”

“I can.”

“That’s unhealthy.”

Finally, Yichen laughed—warm and quiet—while Xiaoran kept short-circuiting beside him. Then he looked at her again.

“I’m serious. I’ll choose the place that makes the most sense for both of us.”

That scared Xiaoran more than distance did. Because suddenly she understood that Zhou Yichen loved her in frighteningly serious ways. Quietly and steadily. Real. Shaped like a future.

“What if I don’t get into good schools?”

“You will.”

“But WHAT IF.”

“Then we’ll figure it out.”

Simple again. It always was with him, like nothing was frightening if they faced it together.

“I don’t need everything perfectly planned right now, Xiaoran.”

The wind moved through his hair as the evening light faded behind the court, and somehow he looked older. Not in age. Just steadier.

“I just know I don’t want a future without you in it.”

Silence. Then the tears came, because Lin Xiaoran always cried when she was overwhelmed.

“Why are you crying?” Yichen sighed.

“You said things.”

Even crying, she shifted closer until her shoulder pressed against his arm. After a moment, very—

“What if we fight more in university?”

“We will.”

“What if we get busy?”

“We will.”

“What if you meet prettier girls?”

Yichen looked deeply unimpressed.

“Seriously?”

“I’m planning ahead.”

“You’ll still be annoying there too.”

“Oh.”

“And I’ll still love you there too.”

Xiaoran covered her face.

“This conversation is a personal attack.”

Yichen smiled and gently pulled her hands away from her face. Then—

“Stop being scared alone.”

Somehow, that comforted her most of all. Maybe the future really was uncertain. Maybe university would change things. Maybe growing up would be messy. But sitting beside Zhou Yichen, his hand warm around hers under the evening sky, the future didn’t feel quite so frightening anymore.

chapters.desc: One internet question. One very serious girlfriend. Zhou Yichen was not prepared.
chapters.title: Would You Still Love Me If I Was a Capybara?
chapters.epigraph: “Real love answers ridiculous questions sincerely.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen should have known peace never lasted long around Lin Xiaoran, especially when she went quiet. Quiet usually meant one of three things: she wanted something, she had done something, or she had discovered internet nonsense. Today, it was the third one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen was doing homework at Xiaoran’s house while she lay upside down across the bed beside him, scrolling through videos. A normal, safe afternoon. Or so he thought.

“Yichen, would you still love me if I was a capybara?”

Yichen’s pencil slowed to a stop. What kind of question was that? Xiaoran was watching him from upside down, waiting. Completely serious.

“…A capybara.”

“Yes.”

Yichen blinked. Twice.

“…The giant rodent?”

“Don’t call me that.”

“I’m asking for clarification.”

Xiaoran sat up.

“You’re stalling. That means hesitation.”

“There SHOULD be hesitation.”

Across the room, Tang Meilin looked up from her phone with dead eyes.

“Oh no.”

Yichen set his pencil down. Experience had taught him that this kind of conversation could get dangerous. Then, calmly—

“Why specifically a capybara?”

“They’re calm.”

“You’re not calm.”

“They’re cute.”

“Hm.”

“And they sit in hot springs with oranges.”

“Important trait.”

“Exactly.”

Yichen considered her. Then—

“Yes.”

Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“…Really?”

“You asked.”

Meilin groaned.

“You people are impossible.”

But Xiaoran wasn’t finished.

“What if I was an ugly capybara?”

Yichen sighed.

“There’s no such thing.”

“Wrong answer. Some capybaras definitely look unemployed.”

“That’s oddly judgmental.”

“I’m asking seriously.”

Yichen leaned back in his chair. Then, calmly—

“You’d still be Xiaoran.”

Simple and warm, and Xiaoran’s whole face softened. Disaster. Zhou Yichen always answered ridiculous questions sincerely.

“What if I couldn’t talk anymore because I was a capybara?”

“You already say nonsense half the time.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

Meilin nearly collapsed laughing. Yichen finally smiled a little.

“You’d still follow me around.”

“That’s true.”

“And steal my food.”

“ALSO TRUE.”

“See?”

Xiaoran stared at him suspiciously now.

“…You’ve thought about this too comfortably.”

“I adapted quickly.”

Meilin cut in tiredly—

“Can I ask why this conversation exists.”

Xiaoran grabbed her phone and shoved a video at them. On screen, a capybara sat peacefully while tiny ducklings climbed onto its head. Yichen watched.

“…Okay.”

“LOOK AT THEM.”

“Hm.”

“They look so calm.”

Fair. Even Yichen had to admit the capybara looked weirdly at peace. Then Xiaoran pointed accusingly.

“See? If I became one, you’d live a calmer life.”

“No.”

“No?”

“You’d still create problems somehow.”

Silence.

“…That’s true.”

Meilin nodded.

“You’d become the first capybara banned from libraries.”

“Why specifically libraries.”

“You’d chew the books.”

“That’s species discrimination.”

Yichen went back to his homework. Conversation over, probably. Unfortunately, Lin Xiaoran still had thoughts. Too many thoughts.

“Would you pet me?”

The pencil stopped again.

Meilin got up and headed for the kitchen. “I need water.” Coward.

Yichen looked back at Xiaoran, who was now sitting cross-legged, hugging a pillow, waiting seriously. Then, calmly—

“Yes.”

“…Really?”

“Hm.”

“How.”

Yichen considered it. Then he reached over and patted her hair. Once. Twice.

“Like that,” he answered.

Silence. Xiaoran completely malfunctioned. Why did the simplest affection from him always hit harder than expected? Yichen looked suspiciously amused.

Xiaoran crawled over until her head was resting on his shoulder. Very capybara behavior, somehow. Yichen glanced down.

“What now.”

“I’m testing if you’d still cuddle me.”

“You’re already doing that.”

“Oh.”

“Would you still date me publicly?”

“Yes.”

“What if society judged you.”

“I already date you now.”

“ZHOU YICHEN?!”

Meanwhile Meilin shouted from the kitchen—

“HE GOT YOU THERE.”

chapters.desc: Lunch at Zhou Yichen’s house, with both his parents home. Lin Xiaoran is not emotionally prepared.
chapters.title: I’m Invited to Zhou Yichen’s House?
chapters.epigraph: “You learn the most about someone from the people who raised them.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran knew something was wrong the moment Zhou Yichen casually said—

“Come over tomorrow.”

Silence.

“…Where.”

“My house.”

A longer silence. Excuse her? His house? While his parents were HOME?

✦ ✦ ✦

That Friday night, Xiaoran sat frozen on her bed while Tang Meilin watched her spiral.

“He invited me casually.”

“Hm.”

“CASUALLY.”

Meilin looked up from her phone.

“You’ve already met his parents before.”

“That was different.”

Technically true. The first time Xiaoran met the Zhou family was the airport goodbye before their trip. The second was the ride home when Yichen came back. Both times were short, sweet, and polite. Mrs. Zhou smiled warmly. Mr. Zhou seemed calm and gentle. Nobody asked serious relationship questions. It had almost felt like they saw her as just a cute high school girlfriend. Young. Temporary, maybe. Which had actually made her less nervous.

But now he had invited her over on a Saturday, with both his parents home. Then Xiaoran sat bolt upright.

“Oh my god.”

“What now.”

“What if this is evaluation day.”

“…Evaluation day.”

“What if his mother secretly observes whether I can become a daughter-in-law.”

Meilin stared at her.

“You’ve watched too many dramas.”

“YOU DON’T KNOW RICH FAMILY CULTURE.”

“The Zhou family is literally normal.”

“That’s what makes them scarier.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came too fast, and Lin Xiaoran spent TWO HOURS choosing clothes. Not too pretty—suspicious. Not too casual—lazy. Not too cute—impossible.

Meanwhile Zhou Yichen received seventeen messages during basketball practice.

Xiaoran: Does your mother prefer elegant girls or cheerful girls

Yichen: Normal girls.

Xiaoran: That didn’t help.

Then later—

Xiaoran: What if your father hates me

Yichen: He won’t.

Xiaoran: How do you know

Yichen: Because you’re cute.

Xiaoran lost focus for the next fifteen minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time Yichen met her at his front gate that afternoon, Lin Xiaoran looked one small inconvenience away from collapse. She was holding a cake box awkwardly—hair carefully done, white top, soft pink skirt. Yichen almost smiled. She had clearly tried hard.

“You’re nervous.”

“No I’m not.”

“You nearly walked into the mailbox.”

“…It came out of nowhere.”

Before Yichen could answer, the front door swung open and Mrs. Zhou appeared.

“Oh, Xiaoran’s here!”

Warm smile, gentle voice, no scary mother-in-law aura whatsoever. Which somehow made Xiaoran MORE nervous.

“Hello, Auntie, I brought cake,” she said quickly, with a small bow.

“You’re so polite. Come inside quickly,” Mrs. Zhou laughed.

In the living room, Mr. Zhou looked up from his newspaper.

“Yichen finally stopped hiding his girlfriend from us.”

Xiaoran froze. Yichen sighed.

“Dad.”

Mrs. Zhou laughed, and the air softened a little.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Zhou house felt exactly like Yichen. Clean, comfortable, quiet but warm. Neatly organized bookshelves. Basketball photos along the hallway, including one of a gap-toothed little Yichen holding a ball almost as big as he was. Soft music coming from the kitchen. Seeing him in his own home got to Xiaoran more than she expected. This was his real space. The place he grew up. The place he became himself.

“Xiaoran, sit beside me,” Mrs. Zhou said warmly from the sofa.

“Oh.”

Yichen looked suspiciously amused. Traitor boyfriend. So Xiaoran sat down carefully beside Mrs. Zhou while Yichen disappeared into the kitchen. Abandoned.

“He talks about you a lot.”

Silence. Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“…He does?”

Mrs. Zhou smiled knowingly.

“Hm.”

“Oh.”

Her ears went pink. Zhou Yichen talked about her at home? What did he say? Had he mentioned the time she cried over math homework?

“You don’t need to be nervous around us.”

Her voice was soft, like she really meant it.

“We already met you before. You’re exactly what I expected,” she said.

Silence. Somehow that made Xiaoran even more nervous.

“…Good expected?”

Mrs. Zhou laughed lightly.

“Very cute expected.”

Yichen came back from the kitchen with drinks just in time to see Xiaoran quietly malfunctioning beside his mother. It almost made him laugh. Lin Xiaoran, who talked nonstop around everyone else, was sitting perfectly upright with both hands in her lap, trying desperately to behave. Then Mr. Zhou spoke from across the room.

“So.”

Oh no. Xiaoran sat up straighter.

“Does Yichen bully you at school?”

“Yes.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“He judges my math.”

“You failed two quizzes.”

“See? Bullying.”

Unexpectedly, Mr. Zhou laughed. Actually laughed. And the whole room relaxed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was easier after that. Not because Xiaoran stopped being nervous, but because the Zhou family was surprisingly normal. Mrs. Zhou kept putting food in her bowl. Mr. Zhou calmly asked about university plans. Nobody interrogated her. Nobody acted weird. At one point, Mrs. Zhou sighed fondly, watching Yichen peel shrimp for Xiaoran without even thinking about it.

“He really likes you.”

Yichen paused. Xiaoran nearly dropped her chopsticks. Adults really just SAID things.

“He spoils her too much,” Mr. Zhou added.

“That’s true,” Mrs. Zhou agreed.

Yichen finally looked a little helpless.

“You’re both making her nervous.”

“We’re telling the truth,” his mother replied calmly.

Then she turned toward Xiaoran again.

“He’s been calmer since dating you.”

Xiaoran blinked, holding her bowl.

“…Calmer?”

Mrs. Zhou smiled.

“Hm. Yichen used to stay in his room a lot more.”

Across the table, Yichen paused—a tiny pause, almost invisible. But Xiaoran noticed. Mrs. Zhou went on—

“He was always a good child. Responsible. Quiet. Never caused trouble.”

“That sounds accurate,” Xiaoran nodded automatically.

“But sometimes,” Mrs. Zhou added, “he carried things by himself too much.”

The table went quiet, and Xiaoran was curious. She knew Zhou Yichen at school—basketball captain Zhou Yichen, calm boyfriend Zhou Yichen, the boy who spoiled her endlessly while staying perfectly composed. But what had he been like here, before her? Before she could stop herself—

“What was Yichen like at home?”

Yichen looked up slowly.

“…Xiaoran.”

Too late. Mrs. Zhou was already smiling.

“Oh, he was very serious.”

“Mom.”

“He’d come home, finish homework, practice basketball, study again.”

“That still sounds like him.”

“Hm, but now he laughs more.”

Yichen actually looked a little embarrassed. A rare sight. Xiaoran stared at him.

“…You didn’t laugh before?”

“I laughed.”

Both his parents looked unconvinced.

“Not often,” Mr. Zhou corrected calmly.

“Oh my god.”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“You were a robot.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“It’s TRUE.”

Yichen sighed while Mrs. Zhou laughed.

“He laughs a lot when he talks to you at home.”

Xiaoran froze.

“…At home?”

“Hm. Sometimes we hear him on calls with you.” Mrs. Zhou nodded casually.

Across the table, Yichen closed his eyes. Complete defeat. Xiaoran’s ears went pink.

“WAIT.”

“He’d be sitting there looking normal,” Mrs. Zhou continued gently, “then suddenly smiling at his phone.”

“Mom.”

“And once, he laughed so hard because of you that his father thought something happened,” she said thoughtfully.

Mr. Zhou nodded once.

“I was concerned.”

Xiaoran turned slowly to Yichen, who looked deeply resigned.

“…You laugh like that because of me?”

“You say stupid things constantly.”

“That’s not the important part.”

Xiaoran’s chest went painfully soft. Picturing Zhou Yichen alone at home, smiling at her messages, got to her more than she expected—especially because at school he always looked so composed. Apparently he carried little pieces of her into his private world too.

“What else does he do?”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“No, I want to know.”

Mrs. Zhou nearly laughed again. Mr. Zhou added calmly—

“He checks his phone more now.”

“Oh my god,” Xiaoran whispered.

Yichen looked exhausted.

“You’re all enjoying this too much.”

It felt unfair. At school, Zhou Yichen had dignity. Respect. Control. Meanwhile his parents were casually revealing that yes, he smiled at her texts alone. Yes, he waited for her calls. Yes, he was happier now. Mrs. Zhou looked at Xiaoran warmly.

“Thank you for taking care of him.”

That made Xiaoran go still. Nobody had ever put it that way. People always talked about how much Yichen took care of HER—protected her, spoiled her, loved her patiently. But his mother was thanking her, like she mattered just as much in his life.

“I don’t think I do much,” Xiaoran admitted honestly.

Across the table, Yichen looked at her, and before anyone else could speak—

“You do.”

Xiaoran’s heart stumbled. Then, holding her gaze—

“You make things lighter.”

Mrs. Zhou smiled. Mr. Zhou looked unsurprised. Xiaoran forgot how to breathe. He’d said it in front of his parents, so naturally. No teasing. No joking. Just honest. Under the table, her fingers found his hand. And this time, Yichen held on first.

chapters.desc: One Friday in March, while his son is in a meeting about his future, Mr. Zhou drives her home and asks about hers.
chapters.title: His Father’s Question
chapters.epigraph: “I hope you get to do what you want.”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had always thought that being driven home by someone else’s parent was a slightly different experience from being driven home by her own.

There was a particular kind of politeness involved. She sat a little straighter, kept her schoolbag on her lap, and made sure she didn’t accidentally touch anything in the car. Even if the parent was perfectly kind, she couldn’t quite relax the way she did when she was with Yichen.

Mr. Zhou, however, seemed determined to make her comfortable.

“Have you eaten anything?” he asked as he turned out of the school entrance.

Xiaoran looked up from her seat. “I had something at the break.”

“Something?”

“A bun.”

“That doesn’t sound like much.”

She smiled apologetically. “I wasn’t very hungry.”

Mr. Zhou glanced at her through the rear-view mirror. “You should eat properly. You’ve been studying hard lately, haven’t you?”

Xiaoran hesitated.

She wasn’t sure whether Yichen had told his parents about her studying habits, or whether this was the sort of thing adults asked students.

“A little,” she answered.

“The first mock?”

“Yes. It’s in two weeks.”

“Then don’t stay up too late. Studying is important, but you need to look after yourself too.”

“I will. Thank you, Uncle.”

He nodded, apparently satisfied.

Yichen wasn’t in the car. He was still upstairs in Coach Wang’s office with a man from the Beijing youth program, the one on the card under her pillow, and the meeting had already run an hour over. Mr. Zhou had come to join it, been told it would be another hour, and found Xiaoran on the bench outside the gym where she had been waiting since five.

She had refused the lift twice. Then Yichen had come down the stairs for thirty seconds between one question and the next, looked at her, looked at the dark outside, and said quite calmly, “Let my father take you. It’s getting late.”

Which had left her little room to argue. Mr. Zhou would drive her and come back. He said it as if it were nothing, and it was across the city.

The car was quiet for a while. Xiaoran watched the familiar streets pass through the window, occasionally recognizing a shop or a turn.

Mr. Zhou broke the silence again.

“Xiaoran, have you thought about what you want to study in the future?”

She turned toward him.

It was an ordinary question. One that teachers had begun asking more frequently as they approached the next stage of school.

Still, she found herself thinking before answering.

“I have a few ideas.”

“Such as?”

“I’m interested in media. Maybe communications, or something related to creative work.”

Mr. Zhou nodded slowly.

“Media?”

“Yes. I like the process of making things. Writing, putting ideas together, telling stories. I enjoy thinking about how people understand something when they see or hear it.”

She paused. “I’m not completely sure which direction yet.”

“That’s all right. You don’t have to decide everything now.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I know. But I want to have a clearer idea before I choose.”

“That’s sensible.”

He stopped at a red light.

“Do you enjoy your subjects at school?”

“Some of them.”

“Which ones?”

“Literature, mostly. And I like the subjects where we get to make presentations or work on projects.”

“What about mathematics?”

Xiaoran went quiet.

Mr. Zhou glanced at her reflection in the mirror.

“That bad?”

She let out a small laugh. “I’m trying.”

“Trying is good.”

“I’ve been practicing more recently.”

“Because of the mock exams?”

“Yes.”

He nodded, then said with a faint smile, “Yichen has been studying quite a bit too.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“Really?”

“Don’t tell him I said that. He’ll think I’m reporting on him.”

She laughed.

“He’s quite good at studying.”

“He’s capable. But he sometimes spends so much time on basketball that I have to remind him there are other things in the world.”

Xiaoran smiled at the window.

“He’s been working hard.”

“I know.”

There was a quiet understanding in Mr. Zhou’s voice. He wasn’t dismissing his son’s dedication to basketball, but neither was he pretending that school could be ignored.

He said, “We’ll talk about the program properly tonight. It’s an interesting opportunity, but there are many things to consider. He tells me you’re keeping one of the cards.” He glanced at the mirror.

Xiaoran went red in the back seat. “He told you that?”

“He told his mother. His mother tells me everything. It’s how our family works.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“He’s excited, I think.”

“Is he?”

She considered the question.

“He’s trying not to show it.”

Mr. Zhou laughed.

“That sounds like him.”

The light turned green.

For a few moments, neither spoke. Then Mr. Zhou asked, “And what do your parents think about your interest in media?”

“They’re supportive. They want me to do well in school first, of course.”

“Naturally.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“My mother asks me about my grades quite often.”

“That’s because she cares.”

“I know. Sometimes I think she worries more than I do.” She looked down at her hands.

“Parents are rather good at that.”

His tone was so matter-of-fact that Xiaoran laughed.

Mr. Zhou glanced at her again. “What does your mother do?”

“She’s an accountant.”

“Then she’ll understand why I asked about mathematics. I think it’s good that you have something you’re interested in. Not everyone knows what they want at this age, and even if your plans change later, having an interest gives you somewhere to start,” he said, and she laughed, and he seemed pleased with himself.

Xiaoran listened carefully.

“Take your time exploring it. Look at different courses, understand what the work involves, and think about what kind of life you want. Don’t choose something simply because someone tells you it’s a good choice.”

She nodded.

“I’ll remember that.”

“Good.”

They approached her neighborhood.

Xiaoran recognized the next turn and sat forward a little.

“Uncle, you can stop near the entrance. I’ll walk from there.”

“Are you sure? I can take you all the way.”

“It’s okay. It’s just a short walk.”

Mr. Zhou pulled over safely.

She unfastened her seatbelt and gathered her schoolbag.

“Thank you for driving me home.”

“You’re welcome. Be careful on your way.”

She opened the door, then hesitated.

“Uncle?”

“Yes?”

“Thank you for asking about my plans.”

He looked at her, slightly surprised.

“Why are you thanking me?”

“Because sometimes adults ask what we want to study, but it feels like there’s already a correct answer.”

Mr. Zhou smiled.

“I see.”

“I liked what you said.”

“I’m glad.”

She bowed her head politely before stepping out.

“Goodbye, Uncle.”

“Goodbye, Xiaoran. And tell your mother not to let you study too late.”

She laughed. “I’ll try.”

He waited until she had reached the entrance before driving away.

Yichen called her at half past ten, from his own bedroom, sounding tired.

“Did you get home safely?”

“Yes.”

“My father said you did. He also said you were polite and that you’re afraid of mathematics.”

“That’s both true.”

Xiaoran was lying on her bed, her mathematics notebook open beside her.

“Your father asked me what I wanted to study.”

There was a brief pause.

“He did?”

“Yes.”

“What did you tell him?”

“Media. Communications. Something creative.”

“And?”

“He said I should explore different courses and think about what kind of life I want.”

Yichen was quiet.

“That’s good advice.”

“I thought so too.”

She heard him turn a page.

“Did he say anything else?”

“He told me you’re studying quite a bit.”

Yichen exhaled.

“Of course he did.”

Xiaoran giggled.

“He said I shouldn’t tell you he was reporting on you.”

“Then you shouldn’t have told me.”

“You asked!”

“Fair.”

She rolled onto her stomach, smiling at the phone.

“Your father is very nice.”

“He’s fond of you.”

Her smile softened.

“Really?”

“Mm.”

“How do you know?”

“Because he doesn’t usually drive people home and interview them about their future.”

“That wasn’t an interview!”

“Wasn’t it?”

“No. He was just asking.”

Yichen laughed. “Did you feel uncomfortable?”

Xiaoran thought about it.

“At first, a little. But he was easy to talk to.”

“Good.”

She twirled the corner of her notebook.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you know what you want to do?”

“After school?”

“Yes. Besides basketball.”

He didn’t answer immediately.

“I’m still thinking about it. The man tonight wants an answer by summer. My father wants me to finish school first and choose a university, and do the program after, if they’ll wait. I don’t want to decide before I understand what I’m getting into,” he admitted.

She couldn’t help smiling.

“That’s sensible.”

“Sometimes.”

“Sometimes?”

“Apparently, I’m not allowed to be sensible all the time.”

She laughed.

Then she said, more, “I hope you get to do what you want.”

Yichen’s voice softened.

“I hope you do too.”

They stayed on the phone a little longer, talking about school and the next day’s homework. When they finally said good night, Xiaoran went back to her mathematics exercises and did two whole questions, and then, because it was nearly midnight and nobody was watching, she opened a browser and typed media and communication degree and read for an hour about a future she hadn’t chosen yet, in a city she hadn’t chosen either.

chapters.desc: A photograph from the New Year gala, hidden badly in a mathematics textbook, and an accountant mother who finds it.
chapters.title: Her Mother Finds the Photo
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not going to tell me I shouldn’t date him?”
chapters.content:
The photograph wasn’t well hidden.

That was the first mistake.

The second was leaving it inside a mathematics textbook.

Xiaoran had taken it out the previous evening to look at it again. It was a small printed photograph from the New Year gala in January, taken by Meilin on her phone and printed at the shop by the school gate for two yuan.

Yichen stood beside her, one hand resting lightly behind her shoulder. Xiaoran was smiling at the camera, her head tilted slightly toward him. He wasn’t looking directly at the camera, though. His eyes were on her.

It was an ordinary photograph.

Nothing dramatic. Nothing that would make someone gasp.

But Xiaoran liked it.

She liked the way she looked happy. She liked the way Yichen looked at her. And she liked that, even though they had known the camera was there, neither of them had seemed concerned about posing.

She had slipped it between the pages of her textbook, intending to put it back into her notebook later.

Then she forgot.

The following afternoon, her mother found it.

Xiaoran had just returned home and was washing her hands when her mother called from the kitchen.

“Xiaoran?”

“Yes?”

“Can you come in here a moment?”

There was nothing unusual about the request.

Still, something in her mother’s voice made her suspicious.

She dried her hands and walked into the kitchen.

Her mother was sitting at the table with a glass of water beside her. On the table, next to a stack of school papers, lay the photograph.

Xiaoran stopped.

Oh.

Her mother looked up.

“Is this yours?”

Xiaoran stared at the photograph.

“Yes.”

“Who took it?”

“One of my friends.”

Her mother picked it up, examining it.

“And who’s this?”

Xiaoran knew perfectly well that her mother knew.

She had mentioned Yichen before, in passing, usually when she was talking about school or basketball. And her father had been asking since last summer, at intervals, who it was that called at nine.

But there was a difference between hearing about a boy and finding a photograph of one’s daughter standing beside him.

“Zhou Yichen,” Xiaoran answered.

Her mother looked at her.

“The boy you’ve mentioned before?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yes.”

Her mother glanced down at the photograph again.

“He’s handsome.”

Xiaoran nearly choked on her own breath.

“Mom!”

“What? He is.”

“That’s not the point.”

Her mother smiled. “Then what is the point?”

Xiaoran pulled out the chair opposite her and sat down interested in the edge of the table.

Her mother placed the photograph down.

“Are you two close?”

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

“Yes.”

“How close?”

She looked up.

“Mom.”

Her mother laughed.

“I’m asking a question.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

She could have avoided answering. She could have said they were friends, which was technically true.

But she had never wanted to hide Yichen from her mother.

And there was something about seeing the photograph on the kitchen table that made her feel she ought to be honest.

“He’s my boyfriend.”

Her mother didn’t immediately respond.

She looked at Xiaoran, then glanced at the photograph again.

“Ah.”

Xiaoran waited.

Her mother took a sip of water.

“How long?”

Xiaoran gave her a small, uncertain smile.

“A while.”

“How long is a while?”

She told her.

Her mother’s eyebrows lifted slightly. “Fifteen months?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Since before the summer. Since before Grandma’s. The boy who calls at nine.” Her mother put the pieces together with the speed of a woman who did other people’s tax returns for a living.

“Yes.”
