“Your father has asked me four times who calls at nine. I told him it was a study group. Why didn’t you tell me properly?” She took a sip of water.

“I thought you knew.”

“I knew you had a close friend named Zhou Yichen. I didn’t know he was your boyfriend.”

Xiaoran lowered her eyes.

“Sorry.”

Her mother reached across the table and touched her hand.

“You don’t have to apologize. I’m not angry.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“You’re not?”

“Why would I be?”

She hesitated.

“I don’t know. I thought you might be upset that I didn’t tell you.”

Her mother gave her hand a gentle squeeze.

“I’m a little surprised. That’s all.”

Xiaoran relaxed slightly.

Her mother looked at the photograph again.

“Does he treat you well?”

The question came.

And Xiaoran answered just as.

“Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes, Mom.”

“What is he like?”

Xiaoran thought about it.

There were so many things she could say that choosing one felt impossible.

“He’s kind. He’s very patient. He listens to me, even when I’m talking about something silly. And he’s really hardworking,” she began.

Her mother smiled.

“You sound very fond of him.”

Xiaoran looked down. “I am.”

“Does he make you happy?”

The answer came without hesitation.

“Yes.”

Her mother watched her.

Then she picked up the photograph again.

“He’s looking at you.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“What?”

“In the photograph. You’re looking at the camera, but he’s looking at you.”

Xiaoran leaned forward, examining it.

She hadn’t noticed that before.

Her face warmed all over again.

“Maybe he didn’t hear the photographer.”

Her mother gave her an amused look.

“Perhaps.”

“Mom.”

“I’m not saying anything.”

“You are.”

Her mother laughed.

The conversation felt almost too easy. Xiaoran had expected a lecture, perhaps a long list of questions about boys and relationships.

Instead, her mother seemed more interested in understanding what this relationship meant to her.

Then she glanced at the school papers. “How are your grades?”

Xiaoran’s shoulders lowered. She had known it was coming.

“They’re fine.”

“Fine?”

“Mostly.”

“Your first mock is in two weeks.”

“I know.”

“Have you been keeping up with your revision?”

“Yes.”

Her mother looked at her.

Xiaoran corrected herself.

“Mostly.”

Her mother shook her head, smiling.

“Xiaoran.”

“I’ve been studying.”

“I know you have. I’m not asking you to stop seeing your friends or enjoying yourself. But you need to keep your priorities straight.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“I understand.”

“Having a boyfriend isn’t a problem. But I don’t want you to become so distracted that you forget about your own future.”

“I won’t.”

Her mother studied her face.

“Do you understand what I mean?”

“Yes. I still have my own things to do. School, exams, and deciding what I want to study.”

“Exactly.”

Xiaoran looked at the photograph.

“I don’t think he’s the kind of person who would want me to give those things up.”

Her mother followed her gaze.

“No?”

She shook her head.

“He studies too. And he has basketball. We both have things we’re working toward.”

Her mother nodded slowly.

“That’s good.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“You’re not going to tell me I shouldn’t date him?”

Her mother smiled.

“Would you listen if I did?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth, then closed it.

Her mother laughed.

“That’s what I thought.”

“Mom!”

“I’m not giving you permission to neglect your studies. But I don’t think having feelings for someone is something you need to be ashamed of,” she said, still smiling.

Xiaoran went quiet.

Her mother reached for the photograph and slid it across the table.

“Just remember that you are still growing up. You have your own plans, your own interests, and your own life. Don’t make every decision around another person, no matter how much you like him.”

Xiaoran looked at her mother.

“I won’t.”

“And if something ever makes you uncomfortable, you can tell me. You don’t have to hide things because you’re afraid I’ll be upset.”

That made Xiaoran’s expression soften.

“Okay.”

Her mother reached over and brushed a strand of hair away from her forehead.

“Good.”

The conversation might have ended there, except her mother picked up the photograph once more.

“Can I ask you something?”

Xiaoran immediately became wary.

“What?”

“Does he know you’re keeping this?”

“Of course.”

“Does he have a copy?”

Xiaoran nodded.

Her mother smiled.

“Then I suppose it’s a nice photograph.”

Xiaoran reached across the table.

“Can I have it back?”

Her mother held it just out of reach.

“Why?”

“Because it’s mine!”

“I’m only looking.”

“You’ve been looking for ten minutes.”

“All right, all right.”

She handed it over.

Xiaoran held the photograph carefully, checking that it hadn’t been bent.

Her mother watched her.

“You really like him.”

Xiaoran’s fingers stilled.

Then she nodded.

“Yes.”

Her mother smiled.

“That’s nice, sweetheart.”

Later that evening, Xiaoran was sitting at the kitchen table again, this time with her mathematics workbook open.

Her mother placed a plate of cut fruit beside her.

“Take a break after you finish that page.”

“Okay.”

Her mother glanced at the photograph, now safely tucked inside Xiaoran’s notebook.

“Is that where you’re keeping it?”

Xiaoran looked down.

“Yes.”

“Not inside your mathematics textbook this time?”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened.

“You knew?”

Her mother laughed.

“Of course. I found it there.”

Xiaoran covered her face with one hand.

“That’s embarrassing.”

“Why? It’s just a photograph.”

“It’s embarrassing because you found it.”

Her mother sat opposite her.

“Do you know what I was thinking earlier?”

Xiaoran shook her head.

“I was thinking that you’re getting older. Soon you’ll have to make decisions about university, about what you want to do, and about the kind of person you want to become.”

Xiaoran listened.

“And somewhere in all of that, there’s this boy.”

Her mother smiled.

“I suppose that’s part of growing up too.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“Are you really okay with it?”

Her mother reached for a piece of fruit.

“I’m okay with you being happy. I’m also going to keep asking about your grades.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“I expected that.”

“Good. Then we understand each other.”

Her mother stood, gathering the empty glass from the counter.

“And Xiaoran?”

“Yes?”

“Next time you take a photograph with him, ask someone to take one where you’re both looking at the camera.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to see his face properly. And because your father will want to see it, once I’ve told him it isn’t a study group. I’ll tell him after the gaokao. He cries.” She paused at the door.

“Mom!”

Her mother laughed as she walked away.

Xiaoran sat at the table, cheeks warm, staring at the page in front of her.

A few minutes later, she took out her phone.

Xiaoran: My mother found our photograph.

Yichen replied a little later.

Yichen: The one from the school event?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: What did she say?

Xiaoran smiled as she typed.

Xiaoran: She said you’re handsome.

There was a pause.

Yichen: Your mother has good judgment.

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

Xiaoran: You’re so shameless.

Yichen: Did she say anything else?

She looked toward the kitchen, where her mother was putting away the dishes.

Xiaoran: She asked if you treat me well.

Yichen: What did you say?

Xiaoran: That you do.

Yichen: Good.

Then another message appeared.

Yichen: Did she ask about your grades?

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: Why are you like this?

Yichen: Because I know your mother.

She laughed again.

Xiaoran: She told me not to neglect my studies.

Yichen: She’s right.

Xiaoran: You’re supposed to be on my side.

Yichen: I am. That’s why I’m telling you to finish your mathematics.

Xiaoran made a face at her phone.

Then she looked at the photograph inside her notebook, the one where he was looking at her and not the camera, and found that it looked different now that her mother had seen it. Not less private. Just less hidden.

She finished the page of mathematics. It took forty minutes and she got two wrong, and when she brought it to the living room to be checked, as she had every evening since primary school, her mother marked it in red pen at the coffee table and said, without looking up, “Tell the boy who calls at nine that his girlfriend can’t add.”

chapters.desc: For her first birthday as his girlfriend, Zhou Yichen plans everything—and remembers something she forgot.
chapters.title: The Birthday Where Zhou Yichen Lost Financial Control
chapters.epigraph: “He remembered the things she forgot she wanted.”
chapters.content:
Three days before Lin Xiaoran’s birthday, Chen Yuhao noticed something suspicious.

“…Why are there shopping bags in your locker.”

Zhou Yichen closed the locker calmly.

“Nothing.”

“Those are luxury brand bags.”

“Basketball-related.”

“Are basketballs sold in jewelry stores now?”

Nearby, Tang Meilin looked exhausted.

“He’s gone.”

“What.”

“He entered rich devoted boyfriend territory.”

Zhou Yichen had been acting strange all week—checking his phone constantly, leaving practice early, ignoring his teammates. At one point he’d turned down basketball plans because he had “important things to prepare.” Terrifying. Finally, Yuhao cornered him at break.

“What did you buy her.”

“Nothing excessive.”

Silence.

“…That answer means it’s excessive.”

Yichen looked away. A tiny pause. A bad sign.

“She mentioned wanting it once.”

“Oh no.”

“And forgot about it afterward.”

“Oh NO.”

Yuhao clutched his chest.

“This man is too far gone.”

“Stop being weird.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Xiaoran had no idea, mostly because she’d spent the whole week invested in one question: would Zhou Yichen do something romantic? Not expensive. Not huge. Just… romantic. It was their first birthday together. Then, on Friday night, she got a message.

Yichen: Tomorrow morning. Wear something comfortable.

Xiaoran screamed into her pillow.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday arrived with suspiciously perfect weather—warm sun, a soft breeze, a bright blue sky. Romantic conditions. Xiaoran spent ninety minutes choosing an outfit. Something cute but effortless, which took tremendous effort. She settled on a pale blue dress with tiny ribbons at the sleeves. Soft. Pretty. Very girlfriend. Then the doorbell rang, and the second Xiaoran opened the door, her heartbeat betrayed her. Zhou Yichen looked unfair today. Black long-sleeve shirt. Relaxed jeans. Hair a little messy from the wind, one hand in his pocket. And the way his eyes went soft the second he saw her.

Yichen blinked.

“…You dressed up.”

“You noticed too fast.”

“You’re pretty.”

Xiaoran turned around.

“No. Restart the greeting.”

Yichen laughed softly near the doorway.

“Okay. Take two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first half of the date was surprisingly normal: lunch, wandering downtown, holding hands, stealing each other’s drinks. At one point Xiaoran dragged him into a stationery shop and judged notebooks for twenty minutes.

“This one looks smart.”

“It’s paper.”

“You don’t understand aesthetics.”

Later, they wandered through crowded shopping streets, sunlight bouncing off the shop windows, a comfortable quiet between them. Until Yichen stopped walking.

“Hm?”

“Wait here.”

Before she could investigate, he disappeared into a nearby store and came back a few minutes later with another shopping bag.

“…What’s that.”

“Nothing.”

“That’s a boyfriend lie.”

“It’s your birthday.”

“That doesn’t answer the question.”

Yichen just smiled and kept walking, which only made her more curious.

✦ ✦ ✦

As evening came, Yichen took her to the riverside—golden sunset on the water, street musicians playing, warm lights coming on along the walkway. Beautiful. Dangerously romantic. Then Xiaoran noticed a small cake box on a reserved table by the river. Beside it, her favorite flowers.

“…You planned this?”

“Hm.”

“By yourself?”

“I had help.”

“From who.”

“Unfortunately Yuhao.”

Xiaoran sat down, staring at it all. Nothing extravagant. Warm lights, a pretty view, a small cake, the exact desserts she liked. Somehow that made it feel even more sincere.

“This is really pretty.”

Yichen relaxed a little. He’d spent two weeks planning this—not because Xiaoran demanded grand gestures, but because she deserved the effort.

“Oh wait.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes suspiciously.

“…What’s inside the shopping bag.”

Silence. Yichen looked away. Another bad sign.

“Open it later.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“NOW.”

With visible resignation, Zhou Yichen handed over the bag, and Xiaoran froze. Inside was the necklace she’d pointed at MONTHS ago while window shopping—a delicate silver chain with a tiny star charm. She’d looked at it and said—

“Way too expensive.”

And then she’d forgotten all about it. Apparently, Zhou Yichen hadn’t.

“You remembered?”

Yichen looked oddly calm, which usually meant he was nervous.

“You liked it.”

“That was months ago.”

He shrugged. But his heart was already racing. He’d worried about this gift too much—too romantic, maybe, too serious. The moment Xiaoran touched the necklace and her eyes went soft, relief hit him all at once.

“I wanted your first birthday gift from me to be something you’d keep for a long time.”

Silence. Xiaoran’s eyes went suspiciously watery.

“Oh no. Don’t cry,” Yichen sighed immediately.

“I’m NOT crying.”

“You literally are.”

“It’s because you’re acting too much like a husband.”

“…That’s your complaint?”

“Yes.”

Yichen laughed despite himself, and that familiar laugh made the evening warmer.

He held out his hand.

Xiaoran leaned closer. Carefully, Yichen lifted the necklace and fastened it around her neck himself—warm fingers brushing her skin, close enough that she could smell his cologne, close enough to hear him breathe. Her heart started racing too. Then, near her ear—

“Pretty.”

That one word was too much. The necklace mattered less than the way he looked at her wearing it, like she was precious long before the gift was.

“Do you like it?”

Xiaoran looked at him for a long second—the boy who remembered things she forgot herself, who planned, who spoiled her endlessly without ever making it feel heavy. Her chest felt too full. Before Yichen could say anything else, Xiaoran stood up and hugged him tight. No warning. No speech. Just her arms around him and her face pressed against his shoulder. Yichen froze for a second. Then his arms closed around her waist, holding her steady. The riverside lights shimmered around them while music drifted through the evening air.

“I really like it,” Xiaoran mumbled against his shoulder.

Yichen smiled softly near her hair.

“Hm.”

“You’re too good at this boyfriend thing. My heart can’t take it.”

He laughed—the soft laugh only she ever heard this close. Xiaoran pulled back a little, hands still loosely gripping his sleeves, eyes suspiciously emotional. Then she tugged him down and kissed his cheek. Soft. Quick. Enough to make Zhou Yichen go completely still. Lin Xiaoran almost never started things this directly. Usually she got shy halfway through. But maybe it was the lights, or her birthday, or just loving him too much—she kissed him first anyway. Then her face went red.

“…Oh no.”

Yichen looked at her, very. Something in his eyes had changed—softer, darker, more focused. And Xiaoran realized that kissing her boyfriend out of nowhere beside a romantic river might have been a tactical error.

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“How am I looking at you.”

“Like you’re planning crimes.”

Yichen laughed under his breath before pulling her back closer lightly by the waist again.

“Too late.”

“Zhou Yichen, this is MY birthday. You’re supposed to behave.”

“No one told me that rule.”

Xiaoran hid her burning face against his chest again while Yichen held her there. With the necklace resting against her skin and his heartbeat steady under her ear, Lin Xiaoran felt dangerously happy. Too happy. Which usually meant Zhou Yichen was about to make things worse. She was right. After a few quiet seconds, Yichen tilted her chin up, slow and careful.

“…What?” she whispered.

Yichen just looked at her. The riverside lights caught in his eyes, the night breeze moved around them, and he looked unbearably handsome again.

“You kissed me first.”

“That was a mistake.”

“You should forget it happened.”

“I don’t think I will.”

Xiaoran’s ears went even redder. The way he was looking at her felt unfair—focused, warm, like she was the only thing worth paying attention to tonight.

“Can I kiss you back?”

He usually just kissed her by now—her forehead, quick kisses, small affections. Asking like this felt much more dangerous. Much more intimate. Xiaoran forgot how speaking worked.

“…You’re asking?”

“I’m being polite.”

“That’s somehow worse.”

Yichen laughed under his breath.

“Hm?”

That stupid calm hm, the one that always made her surrender. So, weakly—

“…Okay.”

Yichen’s whole face softened. Then he leaned down slowly—enough time for Xiaoran to panic, for her fingers to tighten on his sleeves, for her heartbeat to become completely ridiculous. His lips met hers—warm, gentle, unhurried, like he wanted the moment to last. That made it worse. Zhou Yichen kissed exactly the way he loved her. Patiently. Carefully. Completely. Xiaoran melted, eyes closing, his hand resting light and steady at her waist. The city lights blurred behind them, music drifted from somewhere by the river, and for a few quiet seconds nothing else existed but him.

Then he kissed her again, a little deeper. Still gentle. Still controlled. But enough to make Xiaoran’s knees feel unreliable. He pulled back slowly, their foreheads almost touching, both of them breathing quieter now. Xiaoran immediately hid her face against his chest again. Total failure.

“…I can’t survive this birthday,” she mumbled.

Yichen laughed while holding her closer.

“You started it.”

“I was being affectionate.”

He smiled against her hair.

“Happy birthday, Xiaoran.”

Hearing him say it like that, still holding her by the glowing river, felt more special than every gift combined.

chapters.desc: Xiaoran wants to follow him to university. Yichen says no. Their first real fight about the future.
chapters.title: Somewhere Between Your Dream and Mine
chapters.epigraph: “Love isn’t following someone. It’s finding the place where both of you can grow.”
chapters.content:
The fight started because they both loved each other too much, which felt deeply unfair.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I said I can follow you.”

“And I said no.”

Lin Xiaoran stood in the empty classroom after school, glaring at Zhou Yichen. Outside, the evening sun stretched across the desks. Inside, it was war. University applications were real now. Painfully real. And the closer the deadlines got, the more careful Zhou Yichen became around her. Too careful. The kind of careful that got on Xiaoran’s nerves.

“I don’t understand why you’re acting difficult,” she complained.

“I’m not.”

“You literally ARE.”

“No, I’m thinking realistically.”

“And realistically. I can just apply wherever you go,” Xiaoran crossed her arms stubbornly.

Silence.

“No.”

Too fast. Too firm. Xiaoran’s chest tightened. That hurt more than she expected.

“…Why not.”

Yichen sighed and pressed his fingers to his temple. This conversation scared him too—more than basketball, more than entrance exams—because their future suddenly felt fragile in ways neither of them understood yet.

“Because I don’t want you choosing your future around me.”

“But you literally said you were considering MY applications.”

“That’s different.”

“How is that different?!”

Good question. Terrible question. The real answer was simple: Zhou Yichen trusted himself to give things up for her. He didn’t want her giving things up for him. Not this young, and not before she’d even figured herself out. Xiaoran looked upset now. Not dramatic upset. Hurt. Yichen immediately regretted his tone.

“I’m not saying I don’t want us together.”

“But that’s what it sounds like.”

“It’s not.”

“Then explain properly.”

For a moment, neither of them spoke. Somewhere outside, a basketball thudded against the court. Then Yichen sat down in one of the chairs by the window, tired and thoughtful. After a second, Xiaoran sat beside him. Still upset. But closer anyway. Always closer anyway.

“When I think about university. I get scared too,” Yichen admitted.

Xiaoran blinked. Zhou Yichen almost never admitted to being afraid. Especially not this calmly. Then he said—

“What if basketball stops working out. What if classes become too hard. What if we fight more. What if we grow differently.”

His voice was steady, but she could hear the uncertainty underneath. Her anger softened. He wasn’t pushing her away. He was scared of failing both their futures somehow.

“I don’t even know what dream I want yet,” she admitted.

It was embarrassing to admit. Everyone else seemed so sure—medicine, business, law, engineering. Xiaoran changed interests depending on her mood and whatever drama she was watching. Last month it was interior design. Before that, psychology. Before THAT, she’d nearly decided to open a café because the aesthetic felt healing.

“I just know I want you there.”

It made Yichen’s chest ache, because he wanted the same thing. More than anything. After a moment, he took her hand carefully between both of his.

“Okay. Then let’s think about this differently,” he murmured.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“How.”

“We stop choosing FOR each other.”

Silence.

“And instead?”

“We choose somewhere both of us can grow.”

Something gentler than sacrifice or compromise. Something shared. Then Yichen pulled a folded brochure from his bag. Xiaoran blinked in confusion.

“…What’s this.”

“A university halfway between our options.”

She looked down at it. A strong school. Good academics. A decent basketball program. Not the farthest, not the closest. Balanced. Then Xiaoran looked back up.

“You researched this already?”

“Hm.”

“When?”

“Last week.”

He really had been thinking about it seriously. Not avoiding it. Trying to solve it on his own.

“You idiot,” she whispered.

“Hm.”

“You made me think we were breaking up.”

“We were discussing universities.”

“Same thing.”

Yichen laughed under his breath.

“It doesn’t have to be this exact place.”

“But…”

“I just wanted us to find a middle ground together,” Yichen said.

That sentence fixed something in Xiaoran. Suddenly the future didn’t feel like losing or following. It felt shared—something they’d build slowly, together.

“What if we both get rejected.”

“We’ll cry. Then we apply somewhere else.”

“What if we become long distance anyway?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“Then we try.”

He said it so simply. Not because life was simple, but because loving her wasn’t something he ever questioned first.

“I don’t care if we end up in different cities temporarily. I just don’t want either of us regretting our choices later,” he admitted.

Silence. Xiaoran leaned against his shoulder. Warm evening light filled the classroom, and for the first time in weeks, the future stopped feeling like something trying to pull them apart.

“You know what’s annoying?”

“Hm?”

“You sound mature today. It’s annoying.”

Yichen smiled slightly.

Meanwhile Xiaoran looked down at the brochure again before mumbling—

“…I like this school.”

Yichen’s fingers tightened gently around hers.

“Me too.”

Then after a second—casually—

“If we go there together, you’ll still buy me snacks, right?” Xiaoran said thoughtfully.

Yichen looked deeply unimpressed.

“This is your priority?”

“Yes.”

“…Then yes.”

Immediate satisfaction.

“Okay. Now I feel ready for adulthood.” Xiaoran nodded seriously.

chapters.desc: Forty days before the gaokao, a sticky note appears under her pencil case. Every morning after that, the number changes.
chapters.title: Forty Days Left
chapters.epigraph: “It’s never not been there.”
chapters.content:
The countdown began with a sticky note.

Xiaoran found it on her desk one Monday morning, tucked beneath the corner of her pencil case.

She had arrived early, as usual, and was still taking her books out when she noticed the small square of yellow paper.

There was a number written in the middle, 40, and beneath it, in familiar handwriting: Forty days. Don’t panic.

She stared at it.

Then she turned toward the classroom door.

Yichen was standing there, one hand holding his schoolbag strap. He had come from the other corridor, probably on his way to his own classroom.

When he noticed her looking at him, he raised his eyebrows. Xiaoran held up the note. “What’s this?”

“A note.”

“I can see that.”

“Then I don’t think there’s a problem.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Did you put this here?”

“Maybe.”

“Why?”

He glanced at the number.

“Because there are forty days left.”

“I know that.”

“Good. Then the note is working.”

She tried not to smile.

“You’re making a countdown?”

“You’re making one too, aren’t you?”

Xiaoran glanced at the small calendar she had pinned beside her desk. She had been crossing off days since the beginning of the month, although she hadn’t told him.

Yichen noticed the calendar.

His mouth curved slightly.

“Looks like we’re doing the same thing.”

“Mine is more organized.”

“I can see that.”

“Yours is just a number on a piece of paper.”

“And yet you picked it up.”

She folded the note carefully and placed it inside her pencil case.

Yichen watched her do it.

“Don’t lose it.”

“I won’t.”

“All right. Study well.”

He left before she could think of another reply.

It became a routine after that. Every morning, Xiaoran found a note beneath her pencil case, and the number changed. On Sundays, when school was shut, the number came by text at seven, with nothing else, and she would reply with a thumbs-up and go back to sleep.

39. One day closer. One chapter at a time.

38. Remember to eat breakfast.

37. You know more than you think you do.

36. Don’t spend twenty minutes worrying about one question.

That one made her laugh because it was painfully accurate.

She started keeping every note in a small envelope inside her desk drawer.

On the thirty-fifth day, she decided to reply.

She wrote a note of her own and slipped it into the pocket of Yichen’s schoolbag when he wasn’t looking.

35. You should also remember to eat breakfast.

He found it during the break.

When he appeared outside her classroom, holding the note between two fingers, Xiaoran looked entirely innocent.

“What’s this?”

“A note.”

“I can see that.”

“Then I don’t think there’s a problem.”

He met her eyes.

Then he smiled.

“Very funny.”

She beamed.

“Thank you.”

He folded the note and put it into his pocket.

The following morning, her note was waiting as usual.

34. I had breakfast. Did you?

Xiaoran wrote back:

Yes. Mom checked. Mom also asked who leaves you notes.

His reply:

Good. Keep listening to her.

She rolled her eyes, but she kept that note too.

On the thirtieth morning, the note wasn’t under her pencil case. It was in Mr. Pan’s hand.

The self-study supervisor had been patrolling the corridor before homeroom, as he did every day, with a thermos and an expression of permanent suspicion, and had seen a boy from Class 1 slip into Class 3 with nothing in his hands and come out again with nothing in his hands, and had drawn his own conclusions.

He held the note up at the front of the room. Xiaoran felt the blood leave her face.

“Thirty. Sleep is also revision,” Mr. Pan read aloud.

He looked at the class over the top of his glasses. Thirty-eight students looked back.

“Correct,” he said. He put the note down on Xiaoran’s desk on his way out, and didn’t mention it again, then or ever.

Meilin had to put her head down on her arms and stay there until the bell. Xiaoran kept that note in a separate pocket of the envelope.

As the days passed, the notes became less about the countdown and more about the small things they wanted the other person to remember.

29. You don’t have to get every question right.

26. Your handwriting gets worse when you’re tired. Go to bed earlier.

21. I’ve watched you work harder this month than I’ve worked all year.

That one made her stop.

She read it once, then again.

She folded it carefully and placed it inside the envelope.

At school, they were both busier than before. Their teachers had increased the revision sessions, practice papers filled their afternoons, and even their conversations sometimes became brief exchanges about homework.

They still walked together whenever they could.

Sometimes they sat in the library, studying at the same table without speaking for nearly an hour. Sometimes Yichen walked her to the school gate and reminded her to rest. Sometimes Xiaoran brought him a snack because she knew he would forget to buy one after basketball practice.

They didn’t need to spend every moment together. They only made sure they didn’t disappear from each other’s days.

On the fifteenth morning, Xiaoran found a note with no countdown number.

Just a sentence.

When this is over, we’ll have time to do something other than study.

She smiled to herself.

At the end of the school day, she found him near the stairs.

“What’s the plan?” she asked.

Yichen looked at her.

“What plan?”

“After the exam.”

“We haven’t discussed it.”

“Then we should.”

“What would you like to do?”

She considered it.

“Sleep.”

“Reasonable.”

“Eat something nice.”

“Also reasonable.”

“Go somewhere without bringing textbooks.”

“That might be difficult.”

“Yichen.”

He smiled.

“All right. No textbooks.”

“And you can’t talk about basketball training.”

“That’s becoming quite restrictive.”

She laughed.

“Just one day.”

“One day, then.”

She looked pleased.

“Good.”

He reached for her hand.

“Let’s get through these fifteen days first.”

She squeezed his hand.

“Together.”

On the twelfth morning there was no note.

Xiaoran lifted her pencil case, then her textbooks, then her whole bag, and checked under the desk, and under Meilin’s desk, and was halfway to checking the bin when Meilin caught her wrist.

“It’s one note.”

“It’s never not been there.”

“Maybe he overslept.”

“He doesn’t oversleep. He’s never overslept in his life.”

He hadn’t overslept. At the first break he came to the Class 3 door with a mask on and a voice like gravel, and held up his left hand. Written across the back of it, in blue pen, was 12, and under that, smaller, fever, clinic, sorry. He had come in for the morning anyway, because there were twelve days left and he refused to miss one.

“Go home,” she said, horrified.

“After lunch. My mother’s coming. I’ll write it properly tomorrow.” He looked at her pencil case on the desk behind her.

The next morning there were two notes. 12 and 11. The 12 said Don’t come to school with a fever. (Do as I say, not as I do.)

On the seventh morning, the note was slightly different.

7. One week. Trust yourself.

Xiaoran read it at her desk, then took out a pen and wrote beneath it.

I do. Mostly.

She left the note in the envelope that evening.

The next morning:

6. Mostly is enough.

She laughed so loudly that Meilin, sitting beside her, looked over, and then glanced at the note, then at Xiaoran.

“Is this the daily boyfriend correspondence?”

Xiaoran covered the paper with her hand.

“Don’t read it.”

“I didn’t. I have eyes, though.”

“Meilin.”

Her friend leaned back in her chair, grinning.

“You’re lucky. If someone left me motivational notes every morning, I’d probably marry him.”

Xiaoran nearly dropped her pen.

“Don’t say things like that!”

Meilin laughed.

“Then stop looking so happy.”

Xiaoran folded the note and tucked it away.

She didn’t tell Meilin that she had kept every single one.

On the third morning, Yichen’s note read:

3. Three days. Don’t let the last stretch scare you.

She wrote back:

It isn’t the last stretch that’s scary. It’s the actual exam.

He replied the following morning:

2. Then focus on the question in front of you. Not the whole exam.

And on the final morning, she found one last note.

1. Tomorrow, just do your best. I’ll see you after.

Xiaoran held it.

Then she folded it and put it inside the envelope with the others.

There were thirty-five notes in the envelope, and five text messages she had screenshotted and printed at the shop by the gate for one yuan each, so that the set was complete. She had counted. Then she put the envelope in the drawer, under her pajamas, where her mother would never look, and laid out four pens on top of her admission card for the morning, in case three stopped working.

chapters.desc: The gaokao: two exam venues across the city, one fraction question, and a taxi that took thirty-one minutes.
chapters.title: Two Days in June
chapters.epigraph: “You always know the first step. Write that.”
chapters.content:
The night before the gaokao, Lin Xiaoran packed her exam bag four times. Admission ticket. ID card. Two black pens, two spare black pens, two pencils, an eraser shaped like a strawberry that she had been told wasn’t technically allowed and was bringing anyway for morale. A clear plastic pencil case, because the rules said clear. A watch without a screen, because the rules said no screens. She unpacked it all, checked it, and packed it again.

At 9:30 her phone lit up.

Yichen: Stop repacking your bag.

Xiaoran: how do you know

Yichen: Because it’s 9:30.

Xiaoran: that’s not evidence

Yichen: Call me.

She called. He picked up on the first ring, sitting at his desk with his study glasses pushed up into his hair, a single lamp on behind him. He didn’t look nervous. He never looked nervous. It was one of the most irritating things about him.

“What if I forget how fractions work,” she said, instead of hello.

“You won’t.”

“They’re arrogant. I told you. They think they’re better than whole numbers.”

“You scored a hundred on the final.”

“That was a different me. That me had you sitting beside her for three weeks.”

He was quiet for a second.

“That me is still you. I didn’t do the test,” he said.

She pulled her knees up to her chest and didn’t answer, because there was a lump in her throat that had appeared out of nowhere. They weren’t even going to be in the same building tomorrow. The exam venues were assigned by student number: Xiaoran at the middle school on the east side, Yichen across the city near the river. She had looked it up on the map three times. Forty minutes by car.

“You’ll be fine,” he said.

“You can’t know that.”

“I know you. Go to sleep. Don’t look at notes.”

“I already put the notes away.”

“Where?”

“…Under my pillow.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

She moved them to her desk while he watched, then lay down with the phone on the pillow beside her. Neither of them hung up. At some point she fell asleep listening to him turn pages, and when she woke at six the call had ended at 11:52 and there was one message.

Yichen: Eat breakfast. I’ll see you after math.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother drove her to the exam site herself. Mrs. Lin wasn’t a soft woman. She was an accountant, and she approached the gaokao the way she approached the end of the tax year: with a checklist, a thermos, and no patience for nonsense. On the way she quizzed Xiaoran on the contents of her bag without once looking away from the road.

“Admission ticket.”

“Yes.”

“ID.”

“Yes.”

“Pens.”

“Four.”

“Why four?”

“In case three stop working.”

Her mother sighed through her nose, which in Mrs. Lin meant she was trying not to laugh. Xiaoran’s father hadn’t come, because her father cried at things like this, and her mother had decided that crying outside an exam gate was bad for morale. Instead he had sent fourteen messages since six a.m., most of them stickers of cartoon rabbits holding banners. The street outside the school was already full. Parents three deep along the barrier. Police directing traffic. A row of mothers in red qipao for luck, a few fathers holding sunflowers. Someone had set up a tent handing out free water. When the gates opened, the students went in one by one past the ID check, and the parents stayed outside, holding thermoses, not talking much.

Before Xiaoran got out of the car, her mother reached over and straightened the collar of her shirt. It was the only soft thing she did all morning.

“Don’t leave anything blank. Even if you don’t know. Write something,” Mrs. Lin said.

“I know.”

“And don’t look at the clock every two minutes. You do that.”

“I don’t do that.”

Her mother just looked at her. Xiaoran got out of the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chinese in the morning was fine. Better than fine—the essay prompt was about a small thing that had changed how you saw someone, and Xiaoran wrote eight hundred words about a boy at an arcade who won a stuffed bunny out of a claw machine on the first try and then pretended it had been luck. She changed his name and the setting. She didn’t change the bunny. Math in the afternoon was a war.

She hit the first fraction question twenty minutes in and froze completely. Her mind went blank and white like a fresh page. The girl at the next desk was writing fast. The clock on the wall said 3:21. Don’t look at the clock every two minutes. She put her pen down. Closed her eyes for one breath. Then she heard it, absurdly clearly—a calm voice across a study table, three weeks before the final, pushing a sheet of paper back toward her: Slow down. You always know the first step. Write that.

She wrote the first step. Then the second. She didn’t finish every question. There was one near the end she only half understood, and she wrote everything she knew about it anyway, because her mother had said to, and because leaving it blank felt like giving up out loud. When the bell rang at five, her hand ached and her shirt was stuck to her back and she had no idea how it had gone.

She walked out into the sunlight with two hundred other students, and the crowd of parents outside surged against the barrier, and somewhere in the middle of all of it—Zhou Yichen was standing by the tent with the free water, holding a strawberry milk. Xiaoran stopped dead. He wasn’t supposed to be here. His exam had ended at the same time as hers, forty minutes away, across the river.

“How,” she said, when she reached him.

“Taxi.”

“You can’t have—it’s forty minutes—”

“Thirty-one. The driver was motivated. How was it?” He put the strawberry milk in her hands and studied her face.

She opened her mouth to say terrible, and what came out instead was:

“I didn’t leave anything blank.”

Something in his expression went soft.

“Good,” he said.

Behind him, Mrs. Lin was getting out of the car. She looked at Yichen. She looked at the strawberry milk. She looked at her daughter, who was obviously about to cry in public. Then she got back in the car and waited, and for once didn’t honk.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second day passed in a blur of English and science, and by the time the last bell rang on the evening of the eighth, Xiaoran didn’t feel happy or sad or relieved. She just felt empty, like someone had carefully poured everything out of her and set her down.

That night the four of them met at the noodle shop near school, because none of them could think of anywhere better. Yuhao ate three bowls and announced he would never read a book again. Meilin, who had already worked out her expected score to within five points, refused to tell anyone the number. Xiaoran fell asleep against Yichen’s shoulder halfway through her noodles and woke up to Yuhao filming her.

Afterward, Yichen walked her home. The streets smelled like rain that hadn’t come yet.

“It’s done,” she said, at her building’s gate.

“Hm.”

“Whatever happens, it’s done.”

“It is.”

She looked up at him. He had come straight from his own exam, crossed a city in a taxi, and stood outside a school gate in June heat with a strawberry milk going warm in his hand. He had never once told her he was nervous for himself.

“Were you scared? Today?” she asked.

He thought about it honestly, which was one of the things she loved about him.

“During my exam, no. Waiting outside your gate, a little,” he said.

“Why?”

“Because if it went badly, you’d have walked out alone.”

Xiaoran stared at him. Then she hugged him, hard, right there at the gate, where her father could absolutely see from the fourth-floor window and was absolutely watching.

“Thank you for the taxi,” she mumbled into his shirt.

“Thank the driver.”

“I’m thanking you.”

He rested his chin on her hair.

“Then you’re welcome. Now go inside. Your dad is waving,” he said.

chapters.desc: Neither father goes to the gaokao. On the second evening, one of them takes out the rubbish.
chapters.title: Two Fathers
chapters.epigraph: “He brought her a strawberry milk.”
chapters.content:
Lin Hongwei didn’t go to the gaokao.

He had wanted to. He had told his wife so, in the kitchen, three weeks before, and his wife had looked at him over the top of her reading glasses and said, “You cried at her primary school graduation. You cried when she got her ears pierced.”

“That was different.”

“You cried at the dentist. Her dentist. Not yours.”

So on the seventh of June, at half past six in the morning, he stood at the fourth-floor window in his vest and watched his wife’s car turn out of the compound with his daughter in the passenger seat, and then he went into the kitchen and made braised fish for a family of nine.

He wasn’t a man who said much. He worked in the city water bureau and had done for twenty-three years, and he liked things that ran where they were supposed to. He didn’t know what to do with a day in which his only child was sitting in a room he couldn’t see, answering questions he couldn’t help with, and so he did what he knew. He cooked. He cleaned the kitchen. He cooked again. At eleven he rang his wife, who said, “She’s inside. She’s fine. Stop ringing me,” and hung up. At twelve he rang her again.

On the second evening, when the last bell had gone at the venue across the city, his daughter rang to say she was going to the noodle shop with Meilin and Yuhao and the boy.

He had known about the boy since March. His wife had told him, in the end, in bed, in the dark, so that he couldn’t see her face and she couldn’t see his: The one who calls at nine. It isn’t a study group. He had lain awake afterward, thinking about the summer before, the long drive back from his mother-in-law’s with a persimmon tree’s worth of fruit in the boot and his daughter pretending to be asleep for three hours.

He had decided, eventually, that a boy who rang at exactly the same time every night for two weeks, and was polite to his mother-in-law for forty minutes, was probably not the worst thing that could happen. He hadn’t said this to anyone. He hadn’t met the boy. He had seen him once, from this window, at a distance of four floors, carrying an umbrella.

At half past nine he went to the window again.

They were at the building gate under the streetlight, the two of them, his daughter and the boy, and she was talking with her hands the way she did when she was too tired to make sense, and the boy was listening, the way Lin Hongwei hadn’t expected a boy to listen. Then she put her arms round him, hard, right there, and the boy put his chin down on her hair as if he had done it many times and still thought about it each time.

Lin Hongwei waved, because his daughter would want to know he was there. The boy saw him first. He said something, and she let go and looked up and waved back, embarrassed, and came inside.

He heard her on the stairs, four flights, slower than usual. He heard the door, and his wife say “Shoes,” and his daughter say “I know,” and the bathroom door, and the water.

Then he went back to the window, because he had seen something else and wanted to be sure. At the compound gate, under the plane trees, a dark car had pulled in and stopped with its headlights off. The boy hadn’t walked away. The boy had got into it.

Lin Hongwei looked at the car. Then he went into the kitchen, where the rubbish bag under the sink was perhaps a third full, and looked at that too.

“Where are you going?” his wife said, when he came through with it.

“Rubbish.”

She looked at the bag. She looked at him, in his vest and slippers. She looked, at the window.

“Take your time,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Mingyuan hadn’t gone to the gaokao either.

His son had asked him not to. Not unkindly, at breakfast a week before: If you’re outside, I’ll think about you being outside. So Zhou Mingyuan had gone to his office instead, and closed the door, and spent two days not reading the same quarterly report.

At five past nine on the second evening, his phone lit up.

Yichen: Can you pick me up from Xiaoran’s building? I don’t think I can walk home.

He had driven across the city faster than he would have admitted to, and parked at the compound gate under the plane trees, and his son had come out of the dark and got into the passenger seat and said “Thank you” and was asleep before the seatbelt clicked. Two days of exams. A taxi across the city in the June heat between the last paper and her gate, with a strawberry milk. Noodles. Whatever had happened by the building door. He had his head against the window and his mouth slightly open, and he looked twelve years old.

Zhou Mingyuan didn’t start the engine at once. He sat in the dark with his hands on the wheel and looked at his son. Then he got out of the car, because it was a warm night and his back hurt, and stood beside it.

A man came out of the building with a bag of rubbish.

He was in his fifties, in a vest and slippers, and he walked to the bins by the gate slowly, the way people walk when the rubbish isn’t the reason. He put the bag in the bin. He looked at the car. He looked at the boy asleep in the passenger seat, and then at the man standing beside it, and Zhou Mingyuan understood who he was in the same moment the other man understood who he was.

There was a pause in which neither of them knew what to do with his hands.

“Zhou. Yichen’s father,” said Zhou Mingyuan.

“Lin. Xiaoran’s.”

They shook hands over the bonnet. Lin Hongwei’s hand was damp; he had been washing a great many dishes.

“Long two days,” said Zhou Mingyuan.

“Long two days,” said Lin Hongwei.

They both looked through the car window. Yichen didn’t wake up. Somewhere in the compound a television was playing the evening news, and a woman on a balcony was calling a child in.

“The exams. Did he say how they went?” said Lin Hongwei.

“He said they were fine. He says everything is fine.”

“So does she.”

They considered this, two men who had each, separately, been told for two days that everything was fine, and who had each, separately, not believed a word of it.

“He’s asleep,” Zhou Mingyuan said, unnecessarily.

“Yes.”

“He came by taxi. From his own venue. To meet her at the gate.”

“I know. She told us. Twice. He brought her a strawberry milk,” Lin Hongwei said. He looked at the boy longer.

“That’s what he does,” said Zhou Mingyuan, as if it were a family failing.

That was all. Lin Hongwei nodded once, and said, “Drive carefully,” and Zhou Mingyuan said, “Good night,” and the other man went back across the dark courtyard in his slippers and up the stairs, and didn’t look back, although on the fourth floor a curtain moved.

Zhou Mingyuan got into the car and started the engine as gently as he could, so as not to wake his son.

Yichen woke at the second red light, all at once, the way he always had as a child.

“Was I asleep long?”

“Nine minutes.”

His son looked out at the road, and then at him. “Did anything happen?”

Zhou Mingyuan considered the question. “A man took out his rubbish,” he said, and the light changed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, Mrs. Lin was sitting on the sofa with her feet up for the first time in two days. Xiaoran was in the shower, singing badly.

“Well?” Mrs. Lin said.

Her husband sat down beside her.

“His father, drives a very clean car,” he said, after some thought.

Mrs. Lin waited.

“And the boy was asleep. He was so tired he couldn’t keep his eyes open. And he still walked her to the door first,” he said.

She looked at him. His eyes were wet. She handed him a tissue from the box on the coffee table without comment, because she had brought it out of the bedroom at eight o’clock for exactly this reason, and he took it, and they sat there together listening to their daughter sing in the shower, which she hadn’t done since February.

Neither of them told Xiaoran. Mrs. Lin, who had been told about the car, kept it to herself on principle, and across the city Mrs. Zhou was told nothing at all, because her husband had decided it didn’t count.

chapters.desc: Eight days until the scores come out, a girl who refreshes the page every four minutes, and a capybara café.
chapters.title: Waiting for Scores
chapters.epigraph: “Do you think we’ll be okay?”
chapters.content:
By the sixteenth day after the gaokao, with eight still to go before the scores came out, Xiaoran had developed a habit that was beginning to concern everyone around her.

She checked her phone.

Then refreshed the page. Then checked the official announcement schedule.

Then checked the page again, even though nothing had changed.

Yichen had noticed it on their first phone call that morning.

He had listened to her explain that the scores might come out earlier this year, that half of Class 3 was posting estimated marks in the group chat, and that Rong Hao had found a website that claimed to predict the release time to the minute.

He let her finish.

Then he asked, “Have you eaten?”

Xiaoran paused.

“That’s unrelated.”

“Have you?”

“Yes.”

“What did you eat?”

“Breakfast.”

“What?”

She sighed. “A sandwich.”

“Good.”

A few seconds passed.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you think the results might come out today?”

“I don’t know.”

“What if they do?”

“Then we’ll check them.”

“What if the website crashes?”

“Then we’ll wait.”

“What if—”

“Xiaoran.”

She stopped.

His voice was calm, almost amused.

“You’re going to exhaust yourself before the results even come out.”

She looked at her phone.

“I’m not doing anything.”

“You’ve checked the announcement page six times since I called.”

“How do you know?”

“Because you’ve told me six times.”

She went quiet.

Then he said, “Come out with me tomorrow.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere.”

“That’s not a location.”

“A café.”

“What kind?”

“You’ll see.”

She narrowed her eyes, although he couldn’t see her through the phone.

“Is it a surprise?”

“Something like that.”

“Is it far?”

“Two metro lines and a short walk. You’re going to sit down and look at animals. I’ll be at your gate at ten.”

He ended the call before she could interrogate him further.

At ten the next morning, Yichen was standing at her compound gate under the plane trees, at a careful distance from her building’s door, because her mother was home and he hadn’t yet been introduced to her mother in any way that counted.

Xiaoran came out wearing a light cardigan, a comfortable skirt, and the small shoulder bag she usually carried. Her phone was already in her hand.

Yichen looked at it, then at her. “Good morning.”

“Good morning. Where are we going?”

“Metro.”

“You’re being suspicious.”

“Thank you.”

They changed lines once, and walked ten minutes down a street of shuttered bicycle shops, and stopped outside a small café tucked away from the busier roads. The entrance had a simple wooden sign, and through the windows Xiaoran could see people sitting around low tables.

She read the sign, then looked at Yichen, then read it again.

“Capybara?”

He nodded.

She turned toward him. Months ago she had asked him whether he would still love her if she were a capybara, and he had thought about it for an unreasonable length of time before saying yes. “You’re taking me to see capybaras?”

“That’s what the sign says.”

Her face brightened so quickly that he smiled.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I wanted to see that expression.”

She met his eyes.

Then she hurried toward the entrance.

Yichen followed, laughing.

Inside, the café was warm and pleasantly quiet. A few capybaras rested in a designated area, occasionally wandering around or approaching visitors who had been given permission to feed them.

Xiaoran stopped just inside.

“Oh.”

Yichen watched her expression change from curiosity to complete delight.

One of the capybaras was sitting near a wooden platform, looking thoroughly unbothered by the world.

Xiaoran lowered her voice.

“Look at it.”

“I see it.”

“It’s so round.”

“Yes.”

“It looks like it has no worries.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“That’s probably why I brought you here.”

She turned toward him.

He gave her an innocent expression.

“Go on. You can say hello.”

She spent the next several minutes reading the instructions, washing her hands, and carefully offering food to one of the capybaras. She was so absorbed that she barely noticed Yichen taking a photograph.

Until he showed it to her.

“Look.”

She leaned closer.

The photograph showed her crouching beside the capybara, smiling at it with an expression of unrestrained happiness.

“Look at it! It’s leaning on me!”

He looked at the picture again. “I was looking at you.”

She took his phone and examined it more closely.

“Send it to me.”

“I will.”

She returned his phone, then reached for her own.

Yichen held out his hand.

She turned to him.

“What?”

“Your phone.”

“Why?”

“Because we’re here.”

She glanced at the capybaras, then at him.

“Are you confiscating it?”

“Temporarily.”

“Yichen.”

“You’ve been checking the results page every few minutes. I thought we agreed to spend today doing something else.”

She looked down at her phone.

It was true.

But handing it over felt strangely difficult.

“What if the results come out?”

“Then you’ll find out.”

“What if someone messages me?”

“They can wait.”

“What if—”

He held his hand out patiently.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Then she sighed dramatically and placed her phone in his palm.

“Fine.”

“Thank you.”

“But don’t look at my messages.”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t turn it off.”

“I won’t.”

“And if the results come out, tell me immediately.”

“I will.”

She watched him put the phone into the inner pocket of his jacket.

Then she pointed at him.

“You’re responsible for it.”

“Understood.”

“Very responsible.”

“I’ll do my best.”

She eyed him.

That got a smile out of him.

“Now, go look at your new friend.”

The next hour passed more quickly than Xiaoran expected.

She fed the capybaras, watched one of them settle down near a warm spot, and spent a surprisingly long time discussing whether they looked more like oversized guinea pigs or small, unusually calm bears.

Yichen listened to every opinion.

He even took another photograph when she tried to imitate the capybara’s expression, and showed it to her, and said, “Peaceful. It’s frightening.”

She smiled proudly. “Then I should be a capybara.”

“I think you’d get bored.”

“Why?”

“You’d have to sit still all day.”

She considered this.

“Maybe.”

He leaned back in his chair.

“You’re not very good at doing nothing.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Neither are you.”

“That’s fair.”

They ordered drinks and something small to eat. For once, Xiaoran didn’t keep glancing at the clock or reaching for her phone.

She was still thinking about the results, of course.

But it wasn’t consuming every thought.

At one point, she watched a capybara slowly wander across the enclosure.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you think we’ll be okay?”

He looked at her.

She wasn’t asking about the capybaras.

He set down his drink.

“Whatever the results are?”

“Yes.”

He considered his answer rather than rushing to reassure her.

“I think we’ll have choices to make. Some of them might be difficult. But we’ve both worked hard, and we’ll deal with whatever comes.”

Xiaoran looked down at her hands.

“What if I don’t get the course I want?”

“Then we’ll look at the other options.”

“What if I have to go somewhere far away?”

“Then we’ll figure out how to manage it.”

She looked up.

“You’re not worried?”

“Of course I am.”

She blinked.

Yichen smiled.

“I’m not made of stone, Xiaoran.”

She laughed.

“I know.”

“But worrying now won’t change the results.”

He reached across the table and touched her fingers.

“And I don’t want you to spend every day until then being afraid of something that hasn’t happened.”

She looked at their hands, then nodded.

“Okay.”

He squeezed her fingers once.

“Besides, you have a very important responsibility today.”

“What?”

“Keeping the capybara company.”

She laughed.

“That’s a very serious job.”

“I can tell.”

When they finally left, the afternoon sun was warm.

Yichen retrieved her phone from his jacket and handed it back.

Xiaoran looked at the screen.

There were several messages in the class group, two missed calls from Meilin, and a notification from the official results website.

Her heart jumped. She opened it immediately.

Yichen watched her.

“Anything?”

She read the notification, then exhaled.

“It’s just a reminder about the release schedule. Nothing yet.”

“All right.”

She put her phone away.

He raised an eyebrow.

“You’re not checking again?”

She held his gaze, then smiled.

“No.”

“Good.”

At the corner, Xiaoran stopped and looked back at the café.

“I want to come again.”

“We can.”

“With Meilin too.”

“All right.”

“And maybe we can feed the round one again.”

“Of course.”

Her legs were tired, and he waved down a taxi instead of the metro without asking whether she minded, and she got in and looked at him as he slid in beside her. “Thank you.”

“For what?”

“For bringing me here.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“You’re welcome.”

She buckled her seatbelt. “I didn’t check my phone for almost two hours.”

“An impressive achievement.”

“Don’t make fun of me.”

“I’ll put it on your CV.”

She smiled, satisfied. On the drive back her phone stayed in her bag, and for the first time in sixteen days she fell asleep before they reached her street, with her head against his shoulder and a smear of capybara pellet dust on her skirt. Yichen asked the driver, to turn the radio down.

chapters.desc: Applications are in, results are coming, and four friends are refreshing their portals in the same hour.
chapters.title: The Day Our Futures Arrived
chapters.epigraph: “Some futures arrive all at once.”
chapters.content:
Application season turned their whole class a little unhinged. Some students got motivational. Some got religious. Some got frighteningly competitive. Lin Xiaoran got dramatic. Naturally.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I think I’m going to faint.”

“You said that yesterday too.”

“This is a CONTINUOUS faint.”

Xiaoran was lying across the cafeteria table while Tang Meilin calmly worked through practice questions beside her. All around them, people were talking about applications—interviews, scholarships, majors, cities. The future was everywhere now, and it exhausted Xiaoran. She still couldn’t believe they were old enough for this. Then Zhou Yichen walked over with drinks—tall, calm, unfairly reliable-looking—and Xiaoran sat up a little, like a flower turning toward the sun. Embarrassing, honestly.

Yichen handed over her usual drink without a word and sat down beside her.

“You ate lunch?”

“Yes.”

“She ate fries,” Meilin corrected.

“Fries are a vegetable.”

“They are not,” Meilin said.

Yichen sighed, opened the lunchbox beside her, and put the chopsticks in her hand.

“Eat properly.”

Watching him do that without thinking made Xiaoran’s chest ache a little these days. University meant that one day, this wouldn’t happen every afternoon anymore. Yuhao dropped into the seat across from them.

“I’ve decided.”

“Hm?”

“If university life doesn’t give me romance, I’m suing society.”

Meilin didn’t even look up.

“You’d lose the case.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After weeks of discussions, tears, arguments, and spiraling, Xiaoran and Yichen had finally chosen their universities. Together, without either of them giving something up. Zhou Yichen applied mostly to universities with strong business programs and good basketball teams. Basketball mattered to him, but he thought realistically about the future too—something Xiaoran admired, even if she teased him for being “too mature.” Xiaoran chose media and communication studies, which surprised nobody. Lin Xiaoran physically couldn’t stop talking. But more than that, she loved stories, people, ideas. Even her random obsessions somehow fit.

When she told Yichen, he didn’t look surprised at all.

“You were always going to choose something people-related.”

“What does THAT mean.”

“You make strangers tell you their life stories in cafés.”

“That’s charisma.”

“That’s weird.”

Still, he smiled afterward—soft and proud—and that meant more than any compliment. In the end, they both applied to Huaining University in Shanghai: a respected school with strong programs and a competitive basketball team. Yichen could have chased a higher-ranked school and she could have picked an easier one, but this was the place that felt right. The middle ground they’d found together. They both applied to backup schools too, because unlike romance dramas, real life required common sense.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then results day arrived, and peace died immediately.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I can’t open it.”

“You literally have to.”

“I’d rather disappear.”

Xiaoran sat frozen in Yichen’s bedroom, staring at her laptop like it might bite. Yichen sat beside her, much too calm.

“How are you not nervous?” she demanded.

“I am nervous.”

“No you’re not. Your face looks normal.”

“My heart rate is elevated.”

“That’s not normal.”

Across the room, Yuhao was pacing and Meilin had gone pale, because somehow all four of them were getting results within the same hour. Terrible planning by the universe. Yuhao screamed.

“I GOT IN.”

Immediate chaos. Meilin grabbed his laptop.

“YOU ACTUALLY DID.”

“I’M EDUCATED.”

Xiaoran’s anxiety went up about five hundred percent.

“Oh my god.”

Yichen reached over and squeezed her hand.

“Open it with me.”

It made breathing a little easier. Slowly, Xiaoran clicked into the portal. Loading. Loading. Loading—silence. Dead silence. Yichen leaned closer.

“What.”

Xiaoran blinked. Twice. Then she covered her mouth, because there it was. Admission confirmed. Huaining University. Media and Communication Studies. For a full second, she couldn’t process it.

“OH MY GOD.”

Screaming. Tears. Total collapse. Yichen caught her when she launched herself at him.

“I GOT IN.”

“I know.”

“YICHEN I GOT IN.”

His arms tightened around her while she nearly cried into his shoulder from relief. Then she froze. Wait.

“…Your results.”

“Hm.”

“You didn’t check yours yet.”

Silence.

“Oh no.”

Now they were both nervous. Yuhao and Meilin watched like sports commentators.

“This relationship controls my blood pressure,” Yuhao whispered.

Then Yichen opened his own portal. Quiet room. One second. Two. Three— Accepted. Business Administration. Huaining University. Xiaoran started crying again.

“Why are you crying more than me?” Yichen laughed.

“BECAUSE THIS IS CINEMATIC.”

Xiaoran grabbed his face with both hands.

“We’re going together.”

“Hm.”

“ZHOU YICHEN WE’RE GOING TO UNIVERSITY TOGETHER.”

His eyes went soft at the happiness all over her face. And—

“So we are.”

It felt bigger than anything. Suddenly the future wasn’t blurry anymore. Dorms. Classes. A new city. Adult life. Together. Xiaoran looked at him again.

“We survived.”

“Application season, yes.”

“No. The future.” She smiled shakily through tears.

And for the first time, Zhou Yichen let himself believe that maybe they really would make it there together.

chapters.desc: Two dining tables across the city, a spreadsheet with weightings, a slideshow with transitions, and one first choice.
chapters.title: The Application Form
chapters.epigraph: “Is she good? At her subject.”
chapters.content:
On the last Sunday of June, two dining tables on opposite sides of the city looked exactly as serious as each other.

At the Lins’, there was a laptop, a printer that had been carried in from the bedroom, three highlighters, and a spreadsheet. Mrs. Lin had built the spreadsheet herself over four evenings, after work, with the study door shut. It had a column for each university on Xiaoran’s list, a row for everything that mattered, and a final row labeled WEIGHTED SCORE, which nobody was allowed to look at until the end.

At the Zhous’, there was a folder for each option, a second folder for the youth program in Beijing, and a laptop on which Mr. Zhou had prepared, Yichen would later tell her in a tone of real distress, a slideshow.

Xiaoran sat opposite her parents with her hands folded on the table, as if she had been summoned. Her phone was in her lap, under the table. It buzzed once.

Yichen: My father has made slides.

She turned the phone over under the edge of the table.

Xiaoran: My mother has made a spreadsheet. With weightings.

Yichen: Slides beat weightings.

Xiaoran: Weightings have formulas.

Yichen: Slides have transitions.

“Xiaoran, phone,” said her mother, without looking up from the laptop.

She put it back in her lap.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Media and communication. Four options. Two in Shanghai, one in Hangzhou, one here,” Mrs. Lin said, running her highlighter down the first column.

“Huaining first,” Xiaoran said.

“I know Huaining is first. You’ve said Huaining is first eleven times since April. We’re not discussing which is first. We’re discussing why. If you can tell me why, I’ll put it first. If you can’t, the spreadsheet will.” Her mother looked at her over the reading glasses.

Xiaoran had been preparing for this, in a sense, since she was nine, when her mother had made her explain the reasoning behind a request for a hamster. She took a breath and explained. The practical modules. The second-year production project, the one where you made a real film for a real client. The teacher whose documentary she had watched three times. The internship placements in the final year. The fact that, of the four, it was the only one where she had read the course list and wanted to start that afternoon.

Her father, who had said nothing so far, wrote something on the corner of the printout.

“And the boy,” her mother said, in exactly the same voice.

Xiaoran went still.

“He’s applying there too. Business. I’m not stupid. Is that the reason?” her mother went on, highlighting.

“No,” Xiaoran said. And then, because her mother would know if it wasn’t the whole truth, “It’s not the first reason. It’s not in the top three.”

“Where is it?”

Xiaoran thought about it honestly. “Fifth.”

Her mother looked at her, then typed something into the spreadsheet. Xiaoran couldn’t see what.

Her father spoke for the first time. “How far is it from the station?”

“Forty minutes by metro. Then a bus.”

“How often is the bus?”

“Dad.”

“It’s a reasonable question.”

It was, she supposed. She looked it up for him on her phone, since the phone was now evidently allowed. Every twelve minutes, until eleven at night. He wrote that down too, under whatever he had already written in the corner, and underlined eleven twice, and she knew without asking that he was already working out what she would do if she ever missed the last one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the city, Mr. Zhou had reached slide nine.

He said, “The program will wait one year. Possibly two. I asked. Their man was very clear that they would rather have you at nineteen with a university behind you than at eighteen with nothing.”

Yichen nodded. He had known this since March; he had stood on the stairs outside Coach Wang’s office and heard most of it. But it was different on a slide.

“So the question isn’t basketball or university. The question is which university lets you keep basketball properly. Your father and I would like you to have both,” his mother said, from the end of the table, where she was peeling a pear in one long spiral.

“I’d like that too.”

“Then,” said Mr. Zhou, and clicked, and slide ten came up with four logos and a comparison of their basketball programs, their business schools, and their distance from home in hours by train.

Huaining was in the middle. Not the highest-ranked business school on the slide; not the strongest team. The only one where both columns were green.

His father had colored them himself, with a green highlighter he had bought specially, which was still on the table beside the laptop with its cap off.

Yichen looked at the slide for a while. Under the table, his phone buzzed.

Xiaoran: My mother asked if you’re the reason.

Yichen: What did you say?

Xiaoran: Fifth.

He laughed out loud, and both his parents looked at him, and he said “Sorry” and put the phone in his pocket.

“Is something funny?” his father asked.

“No. Huaining. First,” Yichen said.

“Why?”

He gave the reasons. The coach. The business school’s internship scheme. The fact that the team trained in the mornings, so lectures weren’t sacrificed. He gave them clearly and in order, the way his father liked, and his father nodded at each one.

“And Xiaoran,” his mother said, setting down the pear.

He had known it was coming. His mother always got there eventually, by a more direct road than his father.

“She’s applying there too.”

“We know.”

Yichen said, “It’s not the reason. We agreed. Neither of us chooses for the other. If she’d wanted Hangzhou, I’d have said go. It’s on the list. It’s not near the top.”

“Where?”

“Fifth,” he said, and his mother looked at him for a second, and then laughed, without explaining why, and started on another pear.

“There is one more slide,” Mr. Zhou said.

Slide eleven was white, with a single word in the middle: Questions?

Yichen looked at it. “Do you have any?”

“One. Is she good? At her subject.” His father folded his hands on the table, the way he did in meetings he intended to win.

Yichen thought of the short films she made on her phone and showed nobody but him, and the documentary she had watched three times, and the way she went quiet and certain behind a camera, like someone else entirely.

“Yes, better than I am at mine,” he said.

His father looked at him. Then he nodded, as if a column of figures had finally balanced, and closed the laptop.

“Then she’ll be all right anywhere. And so will you,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past nine, Mrs. Lin turned the laptop round.

WEIGHTED SCORE. Huaining: 8.7. Next highest: 7.1.

“Well. There we are. It’s first because it’s first. Not because of the boy,” she said.

Xiaoran looked at the spreadsheet. Near the bottom, in the row her mother had added while she was talking, in small gray type, was a line she hadn’t been meant to see.

Someone sensible nearby: +0.2.

She looked up. Her mother had already taken her glasses off and was cleaning them on her sleeve, with great concentration.

Her father cleared his throat. “Your mother’s very thorough,” he said, and got up, and went into the kitchen, and ran the tap for longer than washing one cup required.

While he was gone, Xiaoran picked up the printout. In the corner, in her father’s small, square handwriting, the kind he used for meter readings at the bureau, he had written three words while she was talking.

She wants to start.

Underneath, in her mother’s pen, there was a tick.

✦ ✦ ✦

They filled in the forms online at ten, both families, within twenty minutes of each other. First choices: Huaining, Huaining. Backups chosen by the spreadsheet and the slideshow respectively, because unlike in dramas, real life required common sense.

At eleven, Xiaoran sat on her bed with the confirmation screenshot open.

Xiaoran: Submitted.

Yichen: Submitted.

Xiaoran: My mother gave you 0.2 points.

Yichen: Out of what?

Xiaoran: I don’t know. I think it’s a lot.

Yichen: My father colored your university green.

Xiaoran: It’s your university too.

Yichen: He colored it before he knew which one you’d picked. He did it in April.

Xiaoran: What did your mother laugh at?

Yichen: I told her you were fifth.

Xiaoran: I told mine the same.

Yichen: I know. I think that’s what she was laughing at.

She read that twice, and then a third time, in case it changed. Then she turned the light off and lay in the dark with the phone on her chest, and thought about two dining tables, and a spreadsheet, and a slideshow, and four adults who had never sat at the same table and possibly never would, all of them working toward the same small, green, sensible outcome.

chapters.desc: One summer gap, one campus in Shanghai, and a café they’ve already decided is theirs.
chapters.title: Practicing Our Future
chapters.epigraph: “Practice makes the future less frightening.”
chapters.content:
After results came out, something strange happened. Everyone suddenly had nothing to do. School was technically over, but graduation hadn’t happened yet, and university hadn’t started. They were stuck in a weird one-month gap where life felt paused. No uniforms. No exams. No schedules. Just waiting. Lin Xiaoran loved it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“This feels wrong.”

They had taken the train into Shanghai for the day, and Xiaoran was walking beside Zhou Yichen near Huaining University’s main gate, iced coffee in hand. The summer air was warm and breezy, sunlight glinting off glass buildings and tree-lined paths. Students wandered past with laptops, skateboards, books. Adult-looking people. Terrifying, honestly.

Yichen glanced down at her. “What feels wrong?”

“We’re here without homework.”

“That’s called freedom.”

“I don’t trust it.”

It was their third unofficial “future practice date”: visiting the campus, exploring nearby streets, pretending they already belonged here. Xiaoran was enjoying it far more than she’d expected. The more familiar the campus became, the less frightening adulthood felt. Then she stopped walking.

“Oh.”

“What.”

Xiaoran pointed at a café across the road: floor-to-ceiling windows, warm lighting, bookshelves along the walls, soft music drifting outside. And, most importantly, cute desserts.

“That’s OUR café.”

Silence. Yichen followed her gaze.

“…You decided that in three seconds.”

“Yes.”

“Based on what criteria.”

“The vibe.”

“That’s not a system.”

Ten minutes later, they went in anyway, because Zhou Yichen indulged her too much.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside smelled like coffee and vanilla—warm, comfortable, university. Students typed on laptops while couples shared desserts by the windows. Xiaoran was immediately moved.

“Oh my god.”

“What now.”

“We’re becoming adults aesthetically.”

She grabbed a menu and sat down across from him.

“No matter what happens, this is our meeting spot,” she announced seriously.

“Hm.”

“After classes.”

“Hm.”

“If we fight, you still have to come here.”

“You’re planning future arguments already?”

“I’m realistic.”

Yichen watched her over the menu. Hearing her talk so easily about their future got to him more than he expected. Months ago, she’d cried over applications. Now she was casually planning which café they’d go to after lectures. Growth. Very cute growth.

“What if the drinks are bad?” Yichen asked.

Xiaoran froze. Oh. Good point.

“This relationship depends entirely on beverage quality.”

“Thought so.”

So, naturally, they ordered far too much: two drinks, three desserts, and a sandwich neither of them planned to share and both of them did. About fifteen minutes later, Xiaoran put both hands flat on the table.

“It’s perfect. The strawberry cake is perfect.”

Yichen looked around the café—sunlight through the windows, Xiaoran across from him talking happily about nothing—and the future suddenly felt close. Real, not abstract anymore.

“You’re excited,” he observed.

Xiaoran blinked, then smiled a little.

“…I think I am.”

It made Yichen smile too. For weeks he’d worried that all the university talk only stressed her out. Now she looked genuinely happy imagining what came next. Xiaoran leaned forward.

“We should choose more places.”

“What places.”

“Important relationship infrastructure.”

“…Infrastructure.”

“Yes.”

So that was the rest of the afternoon: future practice.

✦ ✦ ✦

They started with a bookstore, where Xiaoran found the communication shelves and immediately started judging textbook covers.

“This one looks arrogant.”

“It’s a grammar book.”

“Exactly.”

Then Yichen dragged her to the sports center—huge courts, training rooms, bright indoor gyms. Watching him there made Xiaoran pause. He already fit here somehow. Tall under the university banners, confident, comfortable, like the future had been waiting for him. Then he turned around.

“What.”

Oops. Caught staring again.

“…Nothing.”

“You’re staring again.”

Then he reached over and fixed the twisted strap of her bag. A small, automatic thing. Xiaoran’s chest went painfully soft. Adulthood might change a lot of things, but she couldn’t imagine him ever stopping these tiny ways of caring.

“You know what’s weird? I used to think university would feel super romantic.”

“And now?”

“It mostly feels expensive.”

Yichen laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, the sky turned orange above the campus while they sat by the lake behind the library, drinks half-finished beside them, a warm summer wind moving through the trees. Xiaoran rested her head on Yichen’s shoulder. Not dramatically, this time. Just comfortably. And after a moment—

“Do you think we’ll change a lot?”

Silence. Yichen looked out at the water.

“…Probably.”

“Oh.”

“But I don’t think that’s bad.”

Somewhere nearby, students were laughing.

“My mom said people change after university.”

“They do.”

“What if you become too cool for me.”

Yichen looked unimpressed.

“You ask strange questions.”

“I’m serious.”

“No matter what university does to me, you’ll still be the first person I call when something happens,” he said.

Xiaoran groaned into his shoulder.

“Why are you suddenly romantic again.”

“You started it.”

She looked around slowly—at the paths they’d walk, the café they’d chosen, the buildings waiting for them—and instead of scared, she felt warm. Like this future already held little pieces of them.

“We’re really growing up.”

“Hm.”

“Still, we should try every dessert here before the semester starts,” Xiaoran said thoughtfully.

“Obviously.”

chapters.desc: On graduation day, Lin Xiaoran accidentally asks Zhou Yichen to marry her. His answer is worse.
chapters.title: Yichen, Will You Marry Me?
chapters.epigraph: “Some questions are asked too early. Some answers are not.”
chapters.content:
Graduation day felt strange. Too loud. Too emotional. Too bright, somehow. The school grounds were full of students taking pictures while teachers pretended not to cry. Uniforms for the last time. Classrooms for the last time. High school ending under the summer sun. Lin Xiaoran didn’t handle emotional transitions well.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Don’t cry before photos.”

“I’m NOT crying.”

“Your eyes say otherwise.”

Tang Meilin was fixing Xiaoran’s graduation ribbon while Xiaoran blinked through suspiciously shiny eyes. Nearby, Yuhao took about fifty group selfies nobody had asked for. Across the courtyard, Zhou Yichen was talking with a few teachers outside the basketball building. Tall in the afternoon sun. Calm. Steady. Still exactly Zhou Yichen, even today. And Xiaoran got emotional all over again. They had really survived high school. Meilin noticed her staring.

“…She’s doing it again.”

“What.”

“You’re doing the boyfriend-staring thing.”

Yuhao zoomed in with his phone camera.

“Look at her face.”

“DELETE THAT.”

“You look like a wife seeing her husband return from war.”

“That’s literally just graduation.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The ceremony was emotional chaos: teachers giving speeches, students crying, parents taking far too many photos, and one boy confessing publicly and getting rejected on the spot. A historic disaster. Xiaoran spent most of it leaning sleepily against Yichen, because it was too warm. At some point, without thinking, she found his hand under the sleeve of her gown, and his fingers closed around hers right away. Everything softened—the noise, the crowd, the fear of growing up—because Zhou Yichen still felt exactly the same beside her.
