“My mom used to say sick people become troublesome. So I just… got used to handling it myself,” she admitted eventually.

Something in Zhou Yichen’s chest tightened. This girl carried strange habits so quietly. He stepped closer. Xiaoran blinked.

“…What.”

Yichen touched her forehead. Still warm.

“You know what’s annoying? You act clingy every normal day.”

“…That sounds rude.”

“But the second you actually need someone, you suddenly try doing everything alone,” he said.

Xiaoran stayed quiet.

“I don’t want to trouble you.”

That sentence genuinely upset him. Not angry-upset. Heart-hurting upset.

“Lin Xiaoran, you know what troubles me more?”

She looked up slowly.

“You being sick and pretending you don’t need me.”

Yichen sighed and brushed the messy hair away from her forehead.

“You let me spoil you every other day. So why can’t you let me take care of you too?”

Xiaoran’s throat tightened. The way he said it—calmly, naturally, as if caring for her wasn’t an obligation or a burden or a sacrifice, just something obvious—was too much.

“…I don’t know.”

Yichen looked at her for a second. Without asking, he pulled her into his arms, and her stubbornness gave way all at once. She was tired. Very tired. Then softly near her hair—

“You don’t have to act strong around me all the time.”

Very weakly—

“…Can I be clingy now.”

Yichen laughed.

“Always.”

Lin Xiaoran wrapped her arms around his waist properly and buried her burning face against his chest. Like herself again.

chapters.desc: The lift in her building is stuck on four, she has two bottles of water for the dispenser, and he made an educated guess.
chapters.title: The Broken Lift
chapters.epigraph: “Besides, I wanted to see you.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that something was wrong was the silence.

Xiaoran stood in the lobby of her apartment building, staring at the elevator display.

It had been stuck on the number four for the past six minutes.

She pressed the button again.

Nothing.

She pressed it a second time.

Still nothing.

Then she looked down at the two large bottles of water beside her feet.

“You’re joking.”

She had just returned from the convenience store. Her apartment was on the fourth floor, and she had bought two replacement water bottles for the dispenser because the old one had run out that morning.

She looked at the staircase, then at the bottles, then back at the staircase.

“All right.”

She bent down and tried to lift one.

It moved approximately three centimeters.

She straightened.

“No.”

A man passing through the lobby glanced at her.

Xiaoran smiled politely, as if she hadn’t just lost an argument with a water bottle.

She checked her phone.

There was a message from Yichen.

Finished your class?

She replied. Yes. Home now. Then, after considering the situation: The lift is broken.

His reply came quickly. Where are you?

Lobby. With two water bottles. We’re not friends anymore.

Wait there. I’m on campus. Twenty minutes.

Xiaoran looked at the message, then at the bottles.

She smiled.

He lived across the road, but he was on campus, and he was probably going to tell her to ask the building staff for help.

That would be sensible.

Unfortunately, Zhou Yichen had a habit of being more helpful than she expected.

Twenty minutes later, he arrived.

Xiaoran was sitting on one of the lobby benches, scrolling through her phone. The two water bottles were still beside her.

She looked up when the entrance doors opened.

Yichen walked in wearing a dark T-shirt and his usual backpack, slightly out of breath, as if he had run the last part from the bus stop.

“You came,” she said.

He glanced at the bottles. “Helping. With your water.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“I was just going to ask the building staff.”

“And did you ask them?”

“No.”

“Then let’s go.”

He bent down, picked up one of the bottles, and examined it.

“Two?”

“Yes.”

“Why did you buy two?”

“Because we need two.”

He met her eyes.

“Of course.”

She watched him pick up the second bottle.

“Wait.”

He looked over his shoulder.

“You’re carrying both?”

“Yes.”

“Yichen, they’re heavy.”

“I noticed.”

“Then let’s take one each.”

He turned to her.

“Can you carry one?”

She hesitated.

“...Probably.”

“Then we’ll see.”

He shifted one bottle into a more secure position.

Xiaoran reached for it.

He moved it slightly out of her reach.

“Not this one.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s heavier.”

“They’re the same.”

“This one feels heavier.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re making that up.”

“Possibly.”

He started toward the staircase.

She hurried after him.

The first floor was easy.

The second was manageable.

By the third, Xiaoran had begun to appreciate the fact that she wasn’t carrying anything.

Yichen, meanwhile, had one bottle held securely against his side and the other gripped by its handle. He was climbing steadily, without complaint.

She followed behind him.

“Are you okay?”

“Yes.”

“Is it heavy?”

“A little.”

“Should we rest?”

He looked back at her.

“Do you want to rest?”

“No.”

“Then keep walking.”

She laughed.

At the landing between the third and fourth floors, he finally stopped to adjust his grip.

Xiaoran immediately stepped closer.

“Give me one.”

“No.”

“Yichen.”

“Almost there.”

“You’re going to hurt your arm.”

He looked at her.

“I’m fine.”

She frowned.

His mouth curved.

“You’re very concerned for someone who was prepared to leave both bottles downstairs.”

“I was going to ask for help!”

“From whom?”

“The building staff.”

“They weren’t here.”

“I would have found someone.”

He gave her a look.

She sighed.

“Fine. But you’re not allowed to complain later.”

“I’ll try to remember.”

When they reached the fourth floor, Xiaoran hurried ahead and opened the apartment door.

Yichen carried the bottles inside and placed them beside the dispenser.

He straightened, rolling one shoulder slightly.

Xiaoran noticed immediately.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

She stepped closer and examined his arm as if she were conducting a medical assessment.

He watched her with quiet amusement, then reached out and lightly touched her cheek. “You’re worrying.”

“Because you carried two enormous bottles up four floors!”

“Four floors isn’t enormous.”

“You’re not allowed to say that. You didn’t have to do it.”

That got a smile out of him.

“You’re welcome.”

She stared at him.

Then she laughed, pushing his arm lightly.

“You’re so annoying.”

She immediately went to the kitchen to get him water.

Yichen followed, setting his backpack on the dining chair.

“Sit down,” she instructed.

“I’m not injured.”

“Sit.”

He held her gaze.

She pointed at the chair.

He sat.

Xiaoran placed a glass of water in front of him, then stood with her hands on her hips.

“Drink.”

He picked up the glass.

“Yes, boss.”

She smiled, satisfied.

Then she crouched beside the water dispenser and began preparing the replacement bottle.

Yichen watched her struggle with the plastic wrapping.

“Need help?”

“No.”

She pulled at the wrapping.

It didn’t move.

She tried again.

Still nothing.

Yichen waited.

She met his eyes.

“Don’t.”

He raised both hands.

“I’m not doing anything.”

She finally tore the wrapping open and stood up, looking pleased with herself.

“See?”

“Very impressive.”

“Thank you.”

She lifted the bottle slightly, trying to position it above the dispenser.

Yichen stood.

“Let me.”

“I can do it.”

“I know.”

He took the bottle from her hands and placed it securely into position.

Xiaoran watched him.

Then she looked at the dispenser, then at him.

“...You came all the way here just to carry water?”

“Yes.”

“You could have stayed on campus.”

“I could have.”

She folded her arms.

“Why didn’t you?”

He turned toward her.

His expression was almost puzzled, as if the answer was too obvious to require an explanation.

“Because you needed help.”

She looked at him.

He reached over and brushed a loose strand of hair away from her face.

“Besides, I wanted to see you.”

Her expression softened.

Then she smiled. “You’re very good at making excuses.”

He pressed a kiss to her temple.

“Then I should probably make another one.”

“What?”

“I’m thirsty.”

She laughed.

“You just drank a whole glass.”

“That was before I carried the water.”

She shook her head and reached for his hand.

They ended up sitting on the sofa together.

Yichen had taken off his backpack, and Xiaoran had brought out some fruit. She was peeling an orange while he checked the building maintenance notice on her phone.

“The notice says the lift will be fixed tomorrow,” he said.

“That’s good.”

“Until then, don’t buy anything heavy.”

She turned to him.

“What if I need something?”

“Ask me.”

That made her grin.

“What if you’re busy?”

“Then ask the building staff.”

“What if they’re not there?”

“Call me.”

“What if you’re in class?”

“I’ll call you back.”

She considered this.

Then she held out a piece of orange.

He took it.

“You’re very confident that I’ll always be available.”

He studied her.

“Not always. But I’ll help when I can.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“That’s a better answer.”

He ate the orange.

After a moment, she leaned against his shoulder.

“Thank you for coming.”

He rested his cheek against her hair.

“You’re welcome.”

A comfortable silence settled between them.

Then Xiaoran lifted her head.

“Actually, I have a question.”

“Hm?”

“How did you know which water bottle was heavier?”

Yichen looked at her.

She narrowed her eyes.

“You said one was heavier.”

“I didn’t know.”

She stared.

“You lied?”

“I made an educated guess.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed as she hit his arm.

When he eventually prepared to leave, Xiaoran followed him to the door.

“Message me when you get home.”

“I will.”

“And don’t carry anything heavy.”

He looked at her.

“That’s usually your responsibility.”

She gasped.

“You’re making fun of me again.”

“A little.”

She hooked a hand behind his neck and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you, my personal delivery service.”

“You’re welcome.”

Then he glanced toward the water dispenser.

“Don’t forget to drink enough water.”

“Yes.”

“And don’t try carrying another bottle upstairs.”

“I won’t.”

He considered her.

She looked back innocently.

He sighed, amused.

“Xiaoran.”

“Fine. I won’t.”

Satisfied, he kissed her hair and left.

The following morning, the elevator was still broken.

Xiaoran discovered this on her way out.

She stared at the maintenance notice.

Then she took a photograph and sent it to Yichen.

Still broken.

He replied:

Don’t buy water today.

She smiled.

I wasn’t planning to.

A moment later:

Good.

She was about to put her phone away when another message arrived.

I’ll bring some when I come over tonight.

Xiaoran looked at the screen.

Then she laughed.

She typed:

Are you my boyfriend or the building’s water supplier?

His reply came almost immediately.

Depends. Which one gets to see you more often?

She shook her head, smiling all the way down the stairs.

The lift wasn’t fixed the next day, or the day after. A second notice went up over the first, and then a third, each one promising a date that came and went. By spring someone had drawn a small flower on the button. By the summer nobody in the building pressed it anymore, and Yichen had carried, by his own count, which he kept in his phone, thirty-one bottles of water up four floors.

It stayed broken. She stopped minding. It turned out she lived in a building where, every week or so, someone came up the stairs for her.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen joins the university basketball team. Lin Xiaoran discovers he has fans.
chapters.title: Too Many Girls Know Zhou Yichen
chapters.epigraph: “Because when I play seriously, I want you there.”
chapters.content:
University life settled down slowly after the first few chaotic months. Classes became routine. Assignments became suffering. And somehow, Zhou Yichen and Lin Xiaoran adapted surprisingly well: different majors, different schedules, different buildings, but still eating together, still walking each other home, still disgustingly in love. At least until Zhou Yichen made one important decision.

“I’m joining the university basketball team.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The café table went quiet. Xiaoran blinked slowly over her drink.

“…Seriously?”

Yichen nodded once.

“Hm.”

Across from them, Luo Jiayi gasped.

“Oh my god.”

Meanwhile Sun Ning looked unsurprised. Everyone had seen it coming. Zhou Yichen loved basketball too much to stay away, and after months of adjusting to university and business faculty pressure, he finally had time again. Xiaoran leaned across the table.

“You’ll become busier.”

“Yes.”

“You’ll have practice every day.”

“Probably.”

“…There’ll be female fans.”

Dead silence. That, Yichen knew, was the real concern.

“There are already female students.”

“That’s different.”

She was right. The second Zhou Yichen joined the team, campus life became deeply irritating—for her specifically.

✦ ✦ ✦

First practice day, university indoor court, and the atmosphere already looked dangerous. The team was competitive, fast, aggressive—serious basketball. And Zhou Yichen fit in too well. Too naturally. Too attractively. He stood by the court in black practice gear, taping his wrist, hair already damp, expression focused. Basketball Zhou Yichen felt different from everyday Zhou Yichen—more intense, more confident, more… boyfriend-threatening. Courtside, Xiaoran sat beside Luo Jiayi, suffering.

“…Why does he suddenly look like a drama poster?”

Jiayi stared openly.

“I understand women now.”

“Stop looking at him.”

“I physically can’t.”

A girl nearby whispered loudly:

“That’s Zhou Yichen from business faculty right?”

“He’s so handsome.”

“I heard he’s rich too.”

Xiaoran’s eye twitched. Then practice started, and Zhou Yichen became terrifyingly competitive. Sharp passes. Fast footwork. Completely focused. The kind of player people couldn’t stop watching. Even the coach looked impressed. One clean three-pointer dropped through the net, and the gym cheered—including several random girls. Unacceptable. Xiaoran sat there frozen.

“…Too many women know him.”

Jiayi nearly choked laughing.

“You sound like an emperor losing territory.”

“He belongs to ME.”

Across the court, Yichen glanced up and found Xiaoran pouting in the stands. The corner of his mouth curved—just for her. Unfortunately, that made the girls nearby scream harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Practice ended nearly two hours later. While the team stayed behind to talk through drills, Xiaoran waited outside, nursing her wounds. Finally Yichen came out, bag over one shoulder, hair damp, shirt clinging to him from practice. This was horrible. Several girls in the hallway turned to look. One whispered,

“He looks even better after practice.”

Xiaoran almost started a war. Yichen walked straight past them, stopped in front of her, and squeezed her cheek.

“There you are.”

Dead silence. The girls froze.

“…You did that on purpose.”

“Hm?”

“The cheek thing.”

“You were glaring at strangers.”

“I was protecting what’s mine.”

Yichen laughed. Then he took her bag off her shoulder without thinking, the way he always did, and that small, familiar thing soothed her jealousy a little. However much attention he got, he still treated her like she was special without even trying.

“…Are girls always this obsessed with basketball players.”

“Yes.”

“Oh.”

“Jealous?”

“Extremely.”

Yichen looked amused.

“You knew I played basketball already.”

“Not university-athlete basketball.”

“Difference?”

“You look better now. It’s annoying.”

Xiaoran grabbed his sleeve.

“…You won’t forget me because of basketball right?”

Yichen looked at her calmly. And understood the real feeling underneath all that jealousy. Not insecurity, exactly. Just the fear of being left behind while he kept getting brighter.

“Come to practice tomorrow too.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…Why.”

Yichen adjusted her grip on his sleeve.

“Because when I play seriously. I want you there,” he admitted.

Silence.

“You’re my girlfriend.”

He said it like it settled everything. All the irritation drained out of Xiaoran at once.

“…Fine.”

“Hm.”

“But if too many girls scream again. I’m starting a war,” she warned.

Yichen laughed under his breath. “Please don’t.”

He touched the back of her head briefly.

“Just support me normally.”

That alone made Lin Xiaoran feel embarrassingly proud.

chapters.desc: Three months, one passed exam season, and the first trip that’s just the two of them.
chapters.title: The Chengdu Promise Finally Happened
chapters.epigraph: “Giant pandas were only the second-best thing in Chengdu.”
chapters.content:
The problem with making promises to Lin Xiaoran—was that she remembered them forever. So from the moment Zhou Yichen casually said:

“If you pass all your finals, I’ll take you to Chengdu.”

She had been preparing for the trip ever since—including mentally greeting the pandas.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months later, they were standing in Chengdu Tianfu Airport together. Alone. No friends, no classmates, no accidental third wheels. Just the two of them. It felt strange, because despite how long they had been together, most of their outings somehow involved other people. This was an actual couple trip. Xiaoran stood by the luggage carousel, practically vibrating.

“Yichen. We’re in panda territory.”

“You’ve said that six times.”

“This is the best place on earth.”

Yichen laughed while pulling their suitcase down easily. Then he fixed her crooked scarf, the same way he used to fix her crooked hair ribbon.

“Cold?” he asked.

“A little.”

“Your hands?”

“Frozen.”

Yichen took them in his without another word, warm fingers wrapping around hers as easily as breathing, and somehow Chengdu already felt softer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first disaster happened thirty minutes later. Lin Xiaoran got distracted by street food immediately.

“Yichen LOOK.”

“Hm?”

“Bunny-shaped buns.”

“You already ate on the plane.”

“That was airplane food. It doesn’t count.”

Ten minutes later she was happily eating spicy noodles at a tiny restaurant while Yichen watched from across the table. At least—until Xiaoran stopped moving. Silence.

“…Yichen. My mouth hurts.”

The consequences. Lin Xiaoran loved spicy food in theory and handled it like a weak Victorian noblewoman. Whatever tolerance she had built during her chili-oil training had clearly expired. Chengdu showed no mercy. Then Yichen sighed.

“How much chili did you add.”

“…The auntie said ‘medium.’”

“You trusted local standards?”

“I was arrogant.”

Her eyes were already watering. Yichen pushed an iced soy milk toward her.

“Drink.”

Xiaoran grabbed it with both hands. The restaurant aunties were openly watching them. One said something in Sichuan dialect, smiling. Yichen understood enough to catch:

“Your girlfriend is cute.”

Xiaoran understood enough to be embarrassed.

“She’s making fun of me.”

“No.”

“What did she say.”

“That you’re cute.”

“…Oh.”

“She’s correct.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran kicked his shoe under the table.

“You can’t flirt while I’m dying from spice.”

“I’m multitasking.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second disaster happened at the panda base. Lin Xiaoran forgot humans required rest. The moment she saw the first giant panda rolling down a hill, she lost all composure.

“YICHEN.”

“Hm.”

“LOOK AT HIM.”

“He’s eating bamboo.”

“HE’S PERFECT.”

She grabbed Yichen’s sleeve.

“Take photo.”

Five minutes later:

“Another one.”

Ten minutes later:

“Wait, this one is looking at me.”

Twenty minutes later:

“Yichen crouch lower the angle matters.”

Meanwhile Zhou Yichen—business student, basketball player, future corporate elite—spent the morning as a full-time panda photographer, without a single complaint, mostly because watching Xiaoran this happy was worth it. After roughly four hundred panda photos, Xiaoran turned around.

“Yichen, I understand life now.”

“Since when?”

“We should retire here.”

“To the panda base?”

“Yes.”

“You can’t survive without food delivery.”

“…The pandas will provide.”

While laughing at her nonsense—Yichen noticed how relaxed she looked here. No assignments. No stress. Just bright eyes and soft excitement every few minutes. He liked seeing this version of her too much.

“Yichen. Take a picture with me.”

Xiaoran usually hated asking strangers for couple photos. Today she looked determined. Of course Yichen agreed. A nearby tourist helped take the photo. And in the picture—Xiaoran smiled brightly while hugging his arm. Zhou Yichen was looking down at her instead of the camera—soft-eyed, completely gone. The tourist who took it laughed.

“Young man, you’re looking at your girlfriend too lovingly,” she teased.

Dead silence. Xiaoran nearly exploded. Yichen didn’t deny it at all—just took the phone back and said,

“Thank you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night it started to rain while they were walking near Jinli Ancient Street. Warm lights reflected off the wet stone, the shops glowing, and Lin Xiaoran had, of course, forgotten that umbrellas existed.

“…We’re going to die.”

“We’re getting wet.”

“Same thing.”

Yichen pulled her under a shop awning—just like a closed bookstore, years ago, in another city—and suddenly they were close. Xiaoran looked up at him. His hair was already damp. Dark coat. His hand still holding hers. Suddenly the whole trip felt different. At home, their relationship lived between class schedules and everyday routines. Out here, far from campus, it was obvious: they belonged in each other’s lives now.

“…Thank you for bringing me.”

Yichen looked down.

“For pandas?”

“For remembering.”

“You studied hard for them.”

“And?”

“I keep my promises.”

Hearing it here, in Chengdu, with the rain all around them, made Xiaoran’s heart ache a little. She leaned forward and rested against his chest, and Yichen wrapped an arm around her like instinct. Then softly above her head—

“Cold?”

“A little.”

She tipped her head back. He was already looking at her. He kissed her under the shared umbrella, the rain loud on the nylon, his hand flat and warm between her shoulder blades.

He pulled her closer without a word. At that moment—Lin Xiaoran decided giant pandas were only the second-best thing in Chengdu.

chapters.desc: His first university tournament is four days away. Lin Xiaoran has discovered potassium.
chapters.title: The Week Lin Xiaoran Became a Sports Nutrition Expert
chapters.epigraph: “Your body belongs to university basketball now.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen’s first university basketball tournament was approaching. Lin Xiaoran took this development extremely seriously. Concerningly seriously.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started after one casual conversation.

“Coach said we need to stay in good condition this week,” Yichen mentioned while packing his bag after practice.

Xiaoran nodded absentmindedly.

“What kind of condition.”

“Physical.”

“What does that include.”

“Sleep. Food. Training.”

Silence. Lin Xiaoran opened her phone, and Yichen immediately sensed future problems.

“…What are you searching.”

“Nutritional support for athletes.”

“…Here we go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning—Yichen received twelve messages before 8 AM.

Xiaoran: athletes need protein

Xiaoran: also potassium

Xiaoran: why do bananas sound medically important

Xiaoran: DO NOT EAT INSTANT NOODLES THIS WEEK

Yichen sat in business statistics, staring at his phone with exhausted amusement. Then another message arrived.

Xiaoran: i made meal schedule

Yichen: Why.

Xiaoran: because your body belongs to university basketball now

Yichen: That sounds concerning.

Xiaoran: and to me emotionally

✦ ✦ ✦

Things escalated quickly. By Wednesday, Lin Xiaoran had become a full-time sports mom. She brought homemade fruit containers to practice. She sent hydration reminders every hour. She downloaded articles with titles like Foods That Improve Athletic Performance. The basketball team watched it all in disbelief. At the practice break, Xiaoran stood courtside holding a thermal lunch bag.

“Yichen.”

One teammate blinked slowly.

“…Did your girlfriend pack your lunch.”

Yichen took the bag calmly.

“Hm.”

Another player looked devastated.

“My girlfriend forgot my birthday.”

Xiaoran ignored everyone and opened the containers.

“Eat this first.”

Yichen looked down: chicken, vegetables, rice. Actually balanced. Suspiciously balanced.

“…You made this?”

“Hm.”

“Without burning the kitchen?”

“Rude.”

In fairness, the last time she had cooked for him, she’d nearly set his kitchen on fire first. Then another teammate whispered:

“She’s actually taking this seriously.”

No one understood how seriously. The night before, Lin Xiaoran had spent three hours researching whether walnuts improved concentration in sports. Three hours.

“Also, you cannot drink iced coffee this week,” Xiaoran said seriously.

Dead silence. Yichen blinked.

“…Excuse me.”

“It affects your body.”

“My body survived finals week.”

“This is DIFFERENT.”

Then she narrowed her eyes suspiciously.

“How many coffees today.”

Silence.

“…Yichen.”

“One.”

“You’re lying.”

“…Two.”

The basketball team nearly collapsed laughing. Xiaoran looked genuinely disappointed.

“Your tournament is in four days.”

“It’s just coffee.”

“Michael Jordan probably drank water.”

“Michael Jordan absolutely drank coffee.”

“That’s not the point.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The funniest part was that Zhou Yichen actually listened. Mostly. Enough to shock everyone around him. One teammate stared in disbelief during lunch.

“You stopped drinking energy drinks?”

Yichen looked calm.

“She’ll lecture me.”

“…You’re scared of your girlfriend?”

“No.”

Pause.

“…A little.”

Lin Xiaoran’s disappointed face was a terrifying weapon.

That evening, Yichen arrived at Xiaoran’s apartment to find another disaster: the kitchen, covered in ingredients, and in the middle of it, Lin Xiaoran in an apron, watching a recipe video with deadly focus. Yichen stopped in the doorway.

“…What’s happening.”

“Recovery soup.”

“Is that safe?”

“I researched.”

That made it worse. Xiaoran held up a spoon.

“Taste.”

Yichen tasted it carefully. It was good. Shockingly good. He blinked once.

“…This is edible.”

“EXCUSE ME.”

“I meant good.”

“Hm.”

Then proudly—

“It has nutrients.”

“Everything has nutrients.”

“This one has athlete nutrients.”

While she went back to stirring, Yichen leaned against the counter and watched her—hair tied up messily, sleeves rolled, muttering nutritional facts to herself—and it felt strangely warm. This girl, who regularly forgot her own umbrella, was trying this hard for him.

“You don’t actually need to do all this.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“I know.”

“Then why.”

“Because you care about basketball a lot.”

She looked away and pretended to focus on the soup. But Yichen understood. This was how she supported him—not loudly, not dramatically, just by trying hard in small ways. He came up behind her, wrapped one arm loosely around her waist, and rested his chin on her shoulder. The kitchen went quiet. Then softly near her ear—

“Thank you.”

Xiaoran froze.

“…For soup?”

“For caring this much.”

“…You better win now.”

Yichen laughed against her hair.

“No pressure.”

“I researched potassium for you. Also, I packed bananas for tomorrow.”

“Of course you did.”

chapters.desc: Number eleven, a stadium full of fans, and a final minute Lin Xiaoran will scream through.
chapters.title: The First Tournament Was Very Bad for Lin Xiaoran’s Heart
chapters.epigraph: “You know what I kept thinking during the game? That you were watching.”
chapters.content:
By the time Zhou Yichen’s first university tournament arrived—Lin Xiaoran had become half girlfriend, half team manager. She monitored his sleep. She threatened teammates who gave him iced drinks. She packed fruit containers like it was war. She even made him eat walnuts because, apparently,

“Your brain also plays basketball.”

The team found the whole thing hilarious. They had also started calling Yichen “Captain Zhou” within a week of him joining—half a joke about his high school title, half because the seniors had already started listening to him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday morning. Tournament day. The university stadium was already packed, the atmosphere loud and competitive and, unfortunately, full of women.

“Why are there THIS many girls.”

Luo Jiayi looked around calmly.

“Basketball tournament.”

“No. This feels hormonal.”

The moment the team walked out for warm-ups, the noise doubled. And at the center of the problem, of course, was Zhou Yichen. Black warm-up jacket, tall frame, focused expression, a basketball spinning lazily in one hand. Tournament Zhou Yichen looked even more dangerous than practice Zhou Yichen—colder, sharper, his usual softness replaced by pure competition. Lin Xiaoran stared.

“…Oh no.”

Jiayi looked amused already.

“What.”

“He became 100 times more handsome.”

“Correct.”

“This is horrible.”

Things became worse once the game actually started. Zhou Yichen played terrifyingly well—fast, precise, every motion clean and confident. And unlike in everyday life, he barely smiled on court, which somehow made him even more attractive. Unfair. One clean steal. Fast break. Score. The stadium exploded, very much including the female students. Behind Xiaoran, a row of girls was whispering.

“Number eleven is INSANE.”

“He’s so handsome.”

“Who is he?”

“He’s from business faculty.”

“Does he have a girlfriend?”

Dead silence. Xiaoran turned around. Very slowly.

“…Yes.”

The girls froze immediately. Then awkwardly—

“Oh.”

“Very much yes,” Xiaoran said calmly.

During a timeout, Yichen glanced up at the stands and found her right away—still pouting, still clutching his water bottle like it was hers. His expression softened. A tiny change, barely noticeable, except Xiaoran noticed. Competitive Zhou Yichen looking only at her in a stadium full of people was deeply dangerous.

✦ ✦ ✦

By halftime, the university team led comfortably and looked ready to collapse. Xiaoran stood by the bench with snacks and drinks like a one-woman support staff. One teammate blinked slowly.

“…Did she prepare all this herself.”

Another grabbed banana slices immediately.

“Captain Zhou’s girlfriend is basically our nutrition department.”

Yichen sat drinking water, his hair dark with sweat. Xiaoran approached carefully.

“…You okay?”

“Hm.”

“Tired?”

“A little.”

“Do you need sugar.”

“You sound like a worried auntie.”

“Because you’re sweating like crazy.”

One teammate nearby whispered:

“He listens to her differently.”

Another nodded seriously.

“Scary honestly.”

It was true. However focused he was on the game, the second Xiaoran spoke to him, his whole expression relaxed. Xiaoran noticed a small red scrape on his arm. Immediate panic.

“What happened there.”

Yichen glanced down casually.

“Nothing.”

“YOU’RE BLEEDING.”

“It’s tiny.”

“That’s still your BODY.”

The whole bench watched in silence while Xiaoran inspected his arm like he had come back from a war.

“Does it hurt?”

Yichen looked at her for one second.

“Not really.”

The way she was looking at him—worried, protective, trying so hard to take care of him—made every exhausting minute worth it. Then before the second half started—Xiaoran caught his sleeve. Yichen looked down.

“…Hm?”

“Win properly.”

Just two words, but her eyes were so sincere—so trusting, so proud already—that something in Zhou Yichen tightened. He really wanted to win now. Not just for the team. For her, too.

“I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Final quarter. Close score. The other team caught up and pressed hard, the noise became overwhelming, and on court, Zhou Yichen became terrifying—focused eyes, quick decisions, sharp, aggressive plays. Even his teammates started relying on him without thinking. Last minute. Tie score. A fast break—and Yichen scored. The stadium exploded. The university team had won, and his teammates mobbed him. In the stands, Lin Xiaoran stood frozen. Seeing Zhou Yichen like this felt unreal: breathing hard, hair a mess, a victory smile finally breaking through after a whole game of serious focus. He looked brightest exactly here, on court, doing what he loved. Through the whole crowd, Yichen looked up and searched for her first. Before his teammates, before the coach.

When their eyes met, he smiled properly—warm, real, nothing like the competitive face from earlier—and it hit harder than the win itself. Jiayi grabbed her by both shoulders.

“GO DOWN THERE.”

“Huh?”

“YOUR BOYFRIEND LOOKS LIKE A SPORTS DRAMA MALE LEAD.”

✦ ✦ ✦

A few minutes later, Xiaoran finally reached him by the sideline. The team was still celebrating nearby; Yichen had stepped slightly apart to drink water, still flushed from the game, still unfairly handsome.

“You won.”

“Hm.”

Xiaoran looked up at him and said, sincerely—

“…You looked really cool.”

Dead silence. Compliments from Lin Xiaoran usually sounded chaotic. This one sounded honest. Soft. Almost shy. Yichen laughed under his breath.

“Only cool?”

“Hm?”

“You screamed my name three times during fourth quarter.”

“…YOU HEARD THAT?”

“The whole stadium heard that.”

His teammates started laughing. Xiaoran covered her face in horror.

“No one told you to become that handsome while playing.”

Yichen stepped closer, close enough that only she could hear.

“You know what I kept thinking during the game?”

“…What.”

“That you were watching. So I wanted to play well.”

Lin Xiaoran almost forgot how breathing worked after that.

chapters.desc: The team wants to celebrate. Lin Xiaoran plans to slip away. Zhou Yichen has other plans.
chapters.title: “You’re Coming With Me.”
chapters.epigraph: “So why are you acting like you don’t belong beside me?”
chapters.content:
After winning their first university tournament—the basketball team became completely unbearable. Loud. Overexcited. Sweaty. Half the team was crowded around Zhou Yichen, shouting about where to celebrate.

“Hotpot.”

“No, barbecue.”

“Private room karaoke.”

“Captain Zhou decides.”

Lin Xiaoran stood a little behind the group, holding Yichen’s jacket and water bottle like temporary storage staff. She was already planning to leave. The tournament was over. He’d won. Mission complete. This was team territory now, not girlfriend territory. One teammate threw an arm around Yichen.

“Captain Zhou, bring your girlfriend tonight.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran waved both hands.

“Oh no no no.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“She’s coming.”

“…Excuse me?”

Another teammate grinned.

“YES bring her.”

“Our team nutritionist deserves celebration too.”

“That was ONE banana container,” Xiaoran protested.

“It changed my life,” someone said.

Everyone agreed, which somehow made Xiaoran more uncomfortable, not less. She was dating Yichen, but she still felt a little awkward around his basketball world. The team knew her. Liked her, even. She still felt like an outsider standing next to something important to him.

“You go. I’ll head home,” she whispered to Yichen.

Yichen looked at her once.

“No.”

Xiaoran frowned.

“You should celebrate with your teammates.”

“I am.”

“…Without me.”

Yichen looked genuinely confused.

“Why without you.”

To him, the question made no sense. Xiaoran lowered her voice.

“Because I’m not part of the team.”

Dead silence. Yichen’s expression sharpened.

“Who said that.”

“No one.”

“Then why are you thinking it.”

Xiaoran looked away. Said out loud, it sounded childish. But still—this win belonged to them. The players. The coach. Not her. She didn’t want anyone thinking, Why is the captain’s clingy girlfriend here?

“I don’t want to bother everyone.”

That sentence always bothered Zhou Yichen more than anything. Without another word, he took his jacket out of her hands and put it around her shoulders instead, still warm from him.

“Come with me.”

“…Yichen.”

“Xiaoran.”

“That’s your team celebration.”

“And you supported me this entire month.”

Silence.

“You think I don’t know how much effort you put in?”

Suddenly she remembered all of it—the nutrition schedules, waiting through practices, researching athlete meals at 2 AM, packing snacks, cheering louder than anyone. Then Yichen said—

“You stayed up helping me review game footage before qualifiers.”

“…You were stressed.”

“You came to every practice.”

“That’s normal.”

“You worried more about my sleep schedule than I did.”

A few teammates had overheard, and immediately looked emotional. One whispered,

“Captain Zhou’s girlfriend is actually amazing.”

Another nodded seriously.

“She takes this more seriously than Coach.”

Xiaoran grew more embarrassed by the second.

“That’s because I’m your girlfriend.”

Yichen looked down at her calmly.

“Yes.”

One word, but the way he said it made it heavier, like it already explained everything that mattered.

“So why are you acting like you don’t belong beside me?”

“I just… didn’t want people to think I was forcing myself into your space,” Xiaoran admitted.

For one second—Yichen looked stunned. Then he laughed—not mocking, just helpless, hopelessly fond—and reached up to fix her messy hair.

“Lin Xiaoran, you know what the team calls you?”

“…What.”

“Our unofficial manager.”

“…WHAT?”

“You boss everyone around. You scolded Zhang Rui for buying iced cola before practice.”

The teammates nearby burst out laughing.

“She scolded us like a disappointed mother.”

“She told Fang Ze sleep matters more than male ego.”

“Honestly she’s terrifying.”

Xiaoran covered her face. Yichen looked more and more amused.

“No one thinks you’re bothering us. They’re happy you’re here.”

Hearing that from him mattered more than hearing it from anyone else.

“…Really?”

Yichen looked at her like the answer was obvious.

“Hm.”

He laced their fingers together—warm, steady, certain—and her nervousness eased. Then one teammate shouted,

“CAPTAIN ZHOU STOP FLIRTING AND COME EAT.”

Another pointed accusingly.

“He goes soft around her!”

Yichen ignored them completely. Then calmly to Xiaoran—

“You’re coming.”

“…Do I have a choice.”

“No.”

A small smile finally appeared.

“Besides, I want you there,” he said.

That alone would have made Lin Xiaoran follow him anywhere.

chapters.desc: Hotpot, three victory speeches, and a quiet walk home under the streetlights.
chapters.title: After the Celebration, Zhou Yichen Became Too Gentle
chapters.epigraph: “When we won, I searched for you first.”
chapters.content:
The basketball team celebration lasted way too long. Hotpot. Shouting. Three separate victory speeches nobody asked for. Somehow every teammate got more emotional the more he ate—especially Zhang Rui.

“I LOVE THIS TEAM.”

“You cried because the beef finished.”

“THAT WAS SYMBOLIC.”

Lin Xiaoran sat beside Zhou Yichen watching the team spiral into post-victory chaos, and it felt strangely nice. Earlier she had worried she wouldn’t belong. Now everyone included her without thinking—they were even calling her “team manager,” unironically. Terrifying. Fang Ze pointed across the table.

“Captain Zhou.”

Yichen looked up calmly.

“You smiled seventy percent more tonight because your girlfriend came.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran choked on her drink. Yichen stayed completely calm.

“…Only seventy?”

The entire table exploded screaming.

“OH MY GOD.”

“THAT’S DISGUSTING.”

“WHY IS HE FLIRTING NATURALLY.”

Xiaoran stared at him in horror.

“You can’t say things like that publicly.”

“You survived.”

“No, I did not.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time dinner ended, the city had gone quiet—late-night lights along the campus streets, a cold wind, the warmth of the celebration still lingering. Now it was only Yichen and Xiaoran, walking slowly toward her apartment. Alone for the first time all day.

“…Your teammates are fun.”

“Hm.”

“They’re also very noisy.”

“Correct.”

Xiaoran kicked a pebble along the sidewalk.

“…I’m glad I went.”

Yichen glanced at her. That sentence mattered more than she realized.

“I told you. You belong there.”

Xiaoran looked away.

“…I still felt nervous.”

“Why.”

“Because you looked so… different today.”

Yichen blinked.

“Different?”

“You looked really cool.”

Dead silence. That compliment again—soft, sincere, dangerous for his heart.

“Everyone likes you there.”

“That worries you?”

“A little.”

A very Lin Xiaoran answer.

“You shine a lot when you play basketball.”

Silence.

“And?”

“And I don’t know. It just suddenly feels like a lot of people can see how good you are now.” She frowned lightly.

Ah. It was that strange fear of falling too far behind someone you love.

“Xiaoran, you know what I wanted after the game?”

“…What?”

Yichen kept his eyes on the road ahead.

“You, beside me at the celebration. When we won, I looked for you first.”

She remembered. She remembered that moment exactly—the crowd screaming, his teammates all around him, and him still looking for her first.

“You really like me a lot huh.”

Yichen laughed.

“Again with that.”

“What.”

“You acting surprised every time.”

“Well you hide it calmly.”

Xiaoran stopped walking. Yichen turned.

“…What happened.”

But instead of answering—she just looked at him under the streetlights. He looked unfair tonight—relaxed after the win, hair still messy from the game, hands in his jacket pockets, tired eyes on nobody but her.

“…You’re too handsome lately.”

Yichen actually smiled this time—a real one, the dangerous kind.

Xiaoran stepped in and hugged him tightly. Warm hoodie, familiar comfort, all at once. And against his chest—

“…I’m proud of you.”

That hit harder than the entire tournament. Yichen wrapped both arms around her properly and held her close, carefully, like something precious. Then softly above her head—

“Say that again.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“You’ll become arrogant.”

Too late. Zhou Yichen’s heart was already beating embarrassingly fast. He lowered his head and pressed one slow kiss to her hair—gentle, lingering, more affectionate than teasing.

“Thank you for supporting me.”

Xiaoran’s fingers tightened in his hoodie. Hearing him say it so was unfair.

“…You’re suddenly too gentle.”

Yichen laughed under his breath.

“No.”

“No?”

“You just finally stopped running away every time I say something honest.”

Xiaoran buried her face deeper in his chest.

“Stop talking.”

“Running away again.”

She lifted her head to argue and he kissed her instead, gently, once on the mouth and once on the forehead, which was worse, because now she had nothing left to argue with.

chapters.desc: Team photo day, a photographer who wants the players only, and a boyfriend with other ideas about who belongs in the picture.
chapters.title: Team Photo Day
chapters.epigraph: “I think it’s better with you in it.”
chapters.content:
The problem with dating a university basketball player, Xiaoran had discovered, was that his schedule occasionally became her schedule.

Not officially, of course.

She wasn’t on the team. She didn’t attend their training sessions unless invited, didn’t know all the players’ statistics, and couldn’t tell the difference between some of the more complicated plays Yichen occasionally explained to her.

But she knew when his matches were, which days he had training, and approximately how long he would take to shower afterward.

She also knew that if she happened to be nearby when his practice ended, he would usually find her before leaving.

That was how she ended up at the university sports center on a Friday afternoon.

She had come to return a book to Yichen.

Nothing more.

At least, that was what she had told him.

“You’re here?”

Yichen’s voice came from behind her.

Xiaoran turned.

He was still wearing his basketball uniform, a towel hanging around his neck. His hair was damp with sweat, and there was a faint flush across his face from training.

She lifted the book.

“Delivery.”

He glanced at it.

“You walked all the way here to return one book?”

“Yes.”

“You could have given it to me tomorrow.”

“But then it wouldn’t be returned today.”

His mouth curved.

“Very responsible.”

“I know.”

He took the book from her and tucked it into his bag.

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

She hesitated.

He met her eyes.

“Xiaoran.”

“A sandwich.”

“When?”

She considered the question.

“...Lunch.”

“It’s nearly five.”

“Time is a social construct.”

Yichen laughed under his breath.

“Come on. I’ll get changed.”

She nodded, then noticed several players gathering near the court.

A photographer was setting up a camera at the far end.

“What’s happening?”

“Team photo.”

“Oh.”

Yichen glanced toward the photographer.

“They’re taking the official university team picture today. Apparently the schedule was changed.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Okay. I’ll wait outside.”

“All right. Give me ten minutes.”

He disappeared toward the changing rooms.

Xiaoran found a seat near the court and took out her phone.

She was halfway through replying to Ning when someone called her.

“Xiaoran!”

She looked up.

Fang Ze was walking toward her, holding a basketball.

“You’re here to watch?”

“No, I just came to return something.”

“Yichen?”

She nodded.

Fang Ze grinned.

“He’s changing. The photographer’s already here. We’re taking the picture in a bit.”

“Good luck.”

He looked at her phone.

“You’re not going to take one?”

“Of what?”

“The team.”

“Oh, no. I’m not part of the team.”

Fang Ze laughed.

“Obviously.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“Why did you say that?”

“Nothing. Stay there. I’ll be back.”

He walked away before she could ask.

Xiaoran returned to her phone.

The photographer wanted several versions.

One standing arrangement, one with the players seated, and another with everyone holding their basketballs.

The players were called into position.

Yichen emerged from the changing room just as the photographer was asking them to adjust their spacing.

He spotted Xiaoran near the sideline.

She waved.

He lifted his hand in return.

Then Coach called him over. “Zhou. Middle.”

He joined the others.

Xiaoran watched, amused by how seriously everyone was taking the arrangement.

The photographer stepped back.

“Move closer. You’re leaving a gap.”

Two players shuffled inward.

“Good. Keep your shoulders straight.”

A student assistant approached Xiaoran carrying a small stack of equipment.

“Excuse me, could you hold these for a moment?”

Xiaoran stood.

“Sure.”

She took the clipboard and two basketballs from him.

“Thanks. We’re short on hands today.”

“No problem.”

The assistant hurried away.

Xiaoran was left holding the equipment, standing just beside the group.

The photographer looked up.

“Could you move a little closer?”

She looked behind her, then at him.

“Me?”

“Yes, please. You’re blocking the banner.”

“Oh! Sorry.”

She stepped sideways.

“Actually, could you stand there for a second? Just until we finish adjusting the front row. You’re already in the frame,” the photographer called.

Xiaoran looked at the players, then at the camera.

“Should I?”

“Just there. Thank you.”

She glanced toward Yichen.

He was watching her.

His expression was already beginning to change.

A small smile appeared at the corner of his mouth.

Xiaoran mouthed, What?

He shook his head.

Nothing.

She turned toward the photographer again.

“All right.”

The photographer raised his camera.

“Everyone, look here.”

Xiaoran stood at the end of the second row, still holding one basketball.

She wasn’t sure what she was supposed to do with it.

Fang Ze, at the end of the row beside her, leaned over. “Just hold it. Team manager. Of course you’re in it.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

“Ready?”

The players straightened.

Yichen stood near the center, his expression composed.

He looked at the camera.

Then, just before the shutter clicked, his eyes moved toward Xiaoran.

She noticed.

He was smiling.

Not the polite smile he used for official photographs.

The other one.

The one that usually meant he was about to tease her.

She immediately looked away. The camera flashed.

“Good. One more.”

Another flash.

“Perfect.”

The photographer lowered the camera.

“Thank you, everyone.”

Xiaoran quickly handed the basketball back to the assistant.

“Thank you,” he said.

“You’re welcome.”

She turned toward Yichen.

He was walking over.

She looked suspiciously at his face.

“What?”

He stopped in front of her. “Why are you smiling?” she demanded.

“You’re in the photo.”

She blinked.

“...What?”

“The team photo.”

She looked toward the photographer, then toward the camera, then back at Yichen.

“Oh.”

“Yes.”

“I was only helping.”

“I know.”

“They asked me to stand there.”

“I saw.”

She squinted at him.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

His smile grew.

“You’re standing in the official university basketball team photograph holding a basketball.”

“Because someone gave it to me!”

“Of course.”

She covered her face.

Yichen laughed.

The team gathered around the photographer to check the pictures.

Xiaoran stayed a little behind, intending to leave before anyone made a bigger deal out of it.

Unfortunately, Fang Ze noticed her.

“Hey! Come here.”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“You’re in the picture.”

“I know!”

“Come and see!”

Yichen looked at her.

“Come on.”

She walked over reluctantly.

The photographer scrolled through the images on his camera.

The first photograph appeared.

There they were.

The university basketball team, arranged neatly in their official uniforms, looking serious and professional.

And at the end of the second row was Xiaoran.

Holding a basketball.

Looking slightly confused.

She stared at the screen.

Then she slowly turned toward Yichen.

He was looking at the photograph with an expression of complete satisfaction.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I thought you knew.”

“How would I know?”

“You were standing there.”

“Because they told me to!”

Fang Ze started laughing.

Coach leaned closer to the screen. “Actually, it looks pretty good.”

Xiaoran looked horrified.

“Please don’t say that.”

The photographer smiled.

“It’s a nice picture. Everyone looks natural.”

“That’s because I didn’t know I was in it,” Xiaoran muttered.

Yichen glanced down at her.

“That’s probably why.”

She elbowed him gently.

He caught her hand before she could pull away. “You look like you belong in it,” he said, and he wasn’t teasing now.

She felt her cheeks warm. “Stop it.”

“You need a uniform next time.”

She let go of his hand.

“Absolutely not.”

He laughed.

The photograph was uploaded to the university’s sports department page the following week.

Xiaoran discovered it because Ning sent her a screenshot.

IS THAT YOU???

Xiaoran stared at the image, then at the message.

Then she typed:

Unfortunately.

Ning replied immediately.

WHY ARE YOU IN THE TEAM PHOTO?

Long story.

YOU LOOK LIKE YOU BELONG THERE.

Xiaoran laughed and opened the photograph again.

The image had already been shared several times by students from the university.

The caption read:

University Basketball Team — Official Team Photograph

She zoomed in.

She was in it.

At the end of the second row.

Holding a basketball.

Looking as if she had accidentally wandered into the wrong event.

She saved the photograph.

Then she sent it to Yichen.

Look what you’ve done.

He replied:

What did I do?

I’m famous now.

Congratulations.

I’m not even a basketball player.

I know.

She waited, then another message appeared.

But you look good beside us.

Her mouth tipped up.

That evening, Yichen came over to her apartment.

Xiaoran was sitting on the sofa when he arrived, scrolling through the photograph again.

He sat beside her.

“Still looking at it?”

She turned the phone toward him.

“Look at my face.”

He examined the picture.

“You look surprised.”

“I was surprised.”

“You look cute.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re biased.”

“Probably.”

She zoomed in on the players around her.

“Everyone else looks so serious.”

“That’s because it’s an official photograph.”

“And then there’s me.”

“You’re part of the photograph,” he said.

“Not the team.”

“That’s a technical distinction.”

She laughed.

Then she looked at the image again.

“Do you think they’ll remove me?”

“Why would they?”

“Because I’m not on the team.”

Yichen took her phone gently and zoomed out.

The whole team appeared on the screen.

He looked at it.

Then he handed the phone back.

“I think it’s better with you in it.”

She blinked.

“Why?”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“Because it’s the picture I’ll remember.”

Her expression softened.

She didn’t know what to say.

Then she leaned against his shoulder.

“You’re being sweet again.”

“I can stop.”

“Don’t.”

He pressed his mouth to her hair.

She looked down at the photograph one last time.

“Can you send me the original?”

“Of course.”

“And don’t tell anyone I was embarrassed.”

“I won’t.”

She nodded.

“But if they make another one next year. I want to stand beside you properly,” she said after a few seconds.

Yichen turned his head.

“Beside me?”

“Yes. Not at the end.”

He smiled.

“I’ll see what I can arrange.”

She looked up at him.

“You’re not allowed to arrange anything.”

“All right.”

He kissed her, briefly.

“Next time, I’ll make sure you know when the photographer is coming.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Good.”

Then she paused.

“Actually, no. Don’t.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“Because then I might have to dress properly.”

He laughed. The next year they did make another one, and the photographer, the same man, looked along the second row before he raised the camera and said, “Where’s the girl with the ball?”

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran’s first field assignment. Zhou Yichen moves his schedule to hold her iced tea.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Was Completely Useless During the Assignment
chapters.epigraph: “If you got nervous, I wanted to be there already.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran’s first major media faculty assignment sounded serious academically. A campus documentary project. Students had to go off campus, interview small local business owners, record footage and atmosphere shots, and edit it all into a short visual story. Very professional. Very independent. Very “real university student.” Xiaoran was handling it surprisingly well, which should have been the end of the story. Unfortunately, Zhou Yichen decided he needed to come anyway, despite being completely irrelevant to media production.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You do realize I can survive outside alone.”

Yichen nodded calmly while walking beside her.

“Hm.”

“Then why are you here.”

“You said the filming location is far.”

“It’s literally two subway stations away.”

“And?”

“And you have business faculty group discussion later.”

“I moved it.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran stopped walking.

“…You moved your schedule?”

“Hm.”

“FOR THIS?”

Yichen looked genuinely confused by her reaction.

“You sounded nervous yesterday.”

Because yes, she had been nervous yesterday—not because she couldn’t do the assignment, but because it was her first time doing field interviews alone. New place, new people, equipment she was responsible for. And somehow Yichen had noticed without her saying a word.

“…I didn’t ask you to come.”

“You didn’t need to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The funniest part was that Zhou Yichen contributed absolutely nothing academically. Nothing. Xiaoran interviewed a bakery owner, holding the camera carefully, while Yichen sat in the corner with her spare tote bag and iced tea like emotionally supportive furniture. The bakery auntie kept glancing at him curiously.

“That’s your boyfriend right?”

Dead silence. Xiaoran nearly dropped the microphone.

“…Yes.”

“He’s been staring at you the entire time.”

Across the shop, Yichen looked up, not even embarrassed. The auntie laughed.

“He looks more nervous than you.”

She was right. Despite acting calm, Yichen had spent the last hour silently monitoring everything. Was the road crowded? Had she eaten lunch? Was the equipment too heavy? Would strangers bother her? Entirely unnecessary concerns. Still there. Afterward, reviewing footage outside the café, Xiaoran finally turned to him.

“…You’re weird today.”

“Hm?”

“You keep following me.”

“I’m walking normally.”

“No, you are not.”

Every time she moved locations, Yichen followed—holding umbrellas, carrying equipment, opening doors, standing nearby during interviews while contributing zero information. A male student came over.

“Excuse me, are you filming for media faculty?” he asked Xiaoran.

“Ah, yes.”

“I’m from journalism. If you need help with editing software—”

“No need.”

Dead silence. The poor student blinked. Zhou Yichen had answered before Xiaoran could even open her mouth—calmly, naturally, possessively. Xiaoran stared at him.

“…Why did YOU answer.”

Yichen looked calm.

“You already know editing.”

“That’s not the point.”

The journalism student escaped. Smart man. Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“…Were you jealous?”

“No.”

“You interrupted him.”

“He was staring at you too long.”

“HA. Jealous.”

Yichen said nothing, which was confirmation. Xiaoran grinned.

“You followed me around all day because of jealousy?”

“I followed you because you get lost.”

“That’s also true.”

By sunset, the assignment was done. Xiaoran was tired and hungry, and genuinely happy. She had done well today. The interviews went smoothly, the footage looked good, and for the first time since starting university she felt capable at this.

“…I think I’m getting better at this. I wasn’t even that nervous by the end.”

Yichen looked at her.

“You did well.”

Calm, simple praise—but compliments from him always felt more serious.

“Thank you for coming with me.”

“You really didn’t need to.”

“I know,” he said.

Xiaoran blinked. Then Yichen continued calmly—

“You’re capable of handling things yourself.”

“Then why come?”

For one second—he looked thoughtful, like he was trying to explain something difficult simply.

“Because I wanted to see you doing what you like. And if you got nervous. I wanted to be there already,” he admitted.

The evening suddenly felt warmer, and Lin Xiaoran’s heart went soft. He really did treat her like someone precious, all the time.

“…You know you didn’t help at all, right? You contributed nothing.”

Yichen laughed.

“I carried bags.”

“You held iced tea.”

“Important support role.”

Xiaoran stepped closer, smiling, and hooked both arms around his waist. Then against his chest—

“…Still liked having you there though.”

That small, honest confession hit Zhou Yichen harder than he expected. Then softly above her head—

“Good.”

Then he kissed her cheek, like he’d been wanting to all day.

chapters.desc: The library lights flicker at closing time while she reads the same paragraph for the fourth time. Someone is waiting outside.
chapters.title: Library Closing Time
chapters.epigraph: “I liked seeing you outside.”
chapters.content:
By the time Xiaoran noticed the lights flickering, she had already read the same paragraph four times.

The material wasn’t difficult. Her brain had decided that understanding the relationship between media representation and audience perception could wait until tomorrow.

She rubbed her eyes and looked at the clock in the corner of her laptop. It was a quarter to ten.

She glanced around.

The university library was unusually quiet. Most of the students had already left, and the few remaining people were packing their things. Outside the tall windows, the campus had settled into the darkness of a late evening.

Xiaoran checked her phone.

There were two messages from Yichen, half an hour apart.

Yichen: Still studying?

Yichen: Have you eaten?

She had replied to neither.

Not because she was ignoring him, but because she had put her phone on silent and tucked it beneath her notebook.

She quickly typed.

Still studying. Sorry, didn’t see your messages.

His reply arrived almost immediately.

Library?

Yes.

What time are you leaving?

She looked at the unfinished notes on her screen.

Soon.

Then she said:

Probably.

A few seconds passed.

I’ll wait outside.

Xiaoran smiled.

You don’t have to. I can go home myself.

I know.

Then another message:

I’ll wait anyway.

She put her phone down, smiling to herself.

Just a little longer, she decided.

Twenty minutes, at most.

A few minutes after ten, the first announcement came through the library speakers.

“Dear students, the library will be closing in ten minutes. Please begin preparing to leave.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“Ten minutes?”

She stared at her notes.

There was no way she could finish everything in ten minutes.

She saved her document, packed her notebook, and began gathering her things. She was just reaching for her charger when the lights above her flickered.

Once.

Twice, then the entire floor went dark.

Xiaoran froze.

There was only the faint emergency lighting near the exit signs and the distant sound of someone talking in the corridor.

Then she heard a click.

The automatic lights had switched off.

“Oh.”

She looked toward the nearest exit.

It was farther away than she remembered.

She picked up her phone and turned on the flashlight.

The beam illuminated her desk, her bag, and the notebook she had nearly forgotten.

She sighed.

“Wonderful.”

Her phone vibrated.

Yichen: I’m outside. Take your time.

Xiaoran stared at the message.

Then she typed:

The lights went off.

His reply came quickly.

Are you out?

No.

Where are you?

Second floor. Near the windows.

Stay there. I’ll come to the entrance.

She blinked.

You can’t come inside. They’re closing.

I’ll see what I can do.

She was about to reply when the lights near the staircase flickered on.

A security guard appeared at the far end of the floor.

“Anyone still here?”

Xiaoran raised her hand.

“Here!”

He walked over, looking mildly surprised.

“Still studying?”

“Sorry. I didn’t realize it was this late.”

“Come on. I’ll walk you out.”

She quickly picked up her bag.

As she followed him toward the staircase, she sent Yichen one more message.

Coming down now.

Yichen was standing outside the library entrance.

He had two milk teas in one hand and his phone in the other, its flashlight switched on.

When Xiaoran finally emerged with the security guard, she found him looking toward the doorway.

His expression changed the moment he saw her.

Not dramatically.

Just enough for the slight tension around his eyes to disappear.

“Xiaoran.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Hi.”

He looked at her face, then at her bag.

“Everything okay?”

“Yes. The lights went off while I was packing.”

He nodded.

“Did you get scared?”

She considered lying.

Then she looked at his phone torch.

And the two milk teas.

And the way he had apparently been waiting outside in the dark.

“A little.”

His expression softened.

He handed her one of the milk teas.

“Here.”

She accepted it.

“What’s this?”

“Milk tea.”

“I can see that.”

“You said you were studying late.”

She looked at the cup, then at him. It said half sugar, no pearls on the lid in marker. “You bought me milk tea?”

“Yes.”

“And yourself?”

He lifted the other cup.

“Also milk tea.”

“That’s very thoughtful.”

“I thought you’d need it.”

She took a sip.

It was still warm.

Yichen glanced at the library behind her.

“How long were you inside after the lights went off?”

“Not long. The security guard came to get me.”

“Good.”

He met her eyes.

“Next time, don’t stay until the building has to turn the lights off to remind you to leave.”

She smiled sheepishly.

“I was almost finished.”

“That usually means another hour.”

“Not always.”

He gave her a look.

She laughed.

They began walking toward the main campus road.

Yichen kept his phone flashlight on, pointing it toward the pavement whenever they passed a darker stretch of the walkway.

Xiaoran looked at the light, then at him.

“Why did you bring your phone torch?”

He glanced down.

“Because you said the lights went off.”

“But I was inside.”

“I thought the entrance might be dark.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“You prepared for everything.”

“Not everything.”

“What’s missing?”

He turned to her.

“A better plan for getting you out of the library before closing.”

She laughed.

“That’s not your responsibility.”

“I know.”

He took a sip of his milk tea.

“But I don’t mind.”

They walked for a little while.

The campus was peaceful at this hour. A few students were crossing the courtyard, and the trees along the path moved gently in the evening breeze.

Xiaoran slipped her free hand into his.

“How long have you been waiting?”

“Not long.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“How long?”

He glanced at his watch.

“About twenty minutes.”

“Yichen!”

“What?”

“You said not long.”

“Twenty minutes isn’t very long.”

She stopped walking.

He stopped too.

She looked at him, her expression caught somewhere between fondness and mild disapproval.

“You could have gone home.”

“I could have.”

“Why didn’t you?”

He looked down at their joined hands, then back at her.

“You were still studying.”

She blinked at him.

He continued, perfectly calm.

“And I wanted to see you.”

Her expression softened.

She looked away interested in the milk tea cup.

“You’re unfair.”

“How?”

“You say things like that so casually.”

Something in his face eased.

“Would you prefer I made a formal announcement?”

She laughed and leaned against his arm.

“No.”

“Good.”

When they reached the campus gate, Xiaoran checked her phone.

There was a message from Ning.

Are you still at the library?

She replied.

Just left. The lights went off.

Ning sent three shocked emojis, then another message appeared.

Did you get locked inside?

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen.

He was walking beside her, his phone torch still illuminating the pavement.

She took a photograph of his hand holding the phone and sent it to Ning.

No. I have a personal lighting service.

Ning replied almost immediately.

HAHAHAHA. Is that Yichen?

Xiaoran smiled.

Who else?

She put her phone away. “Ning thinks you’re my personal lighting service.”

He looked at the phone in his hand, then at her.

“Is that what I am?”

“Apparently.”

He nodded thoughtfully.

“Then I should charge you.”

She gasped.

“You’re charging your girlfriend?”

“Professional services.”

“What do you accept?”

He looked at her.

“A proper dinner next time you study late.”

That made her grin.

“That’s not payment. That’s just dinner.”

“Then I’ll consider it a benefit.”

She laughed.

At her apartment building, Yichen walked her to the entrance.

She finished her milk tea and held the empty cup in one hand.

“Thank you for waiting.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And for the milk tea.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And the torch.”

He looked at his phone.

“You’re welcome.”

She smiled.

Then she stepped closer and wrapped her arms around him.

Yichen returned the hug, one hand resting against her back.

“Good night,” she murmured.

“Good night. Message me when you’re upstairs.”

She pulled away.

“You’re not going to walk me to my door?”

“Would you like me to?”

That made her grin.

“No. I can manage four flights of stairs in the dark. I’ve had practice.”

“All right.”

She pulled him down by the collar and kissed his cheek.

Then she turned toward the entrance.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked back.

He lifted his phone slightly.

“Don’t forget your bag.”

She glanced down.

Her bag was still hanging from her shoulder.

She looked at him.

He laughed under his breath.

“I thought I’d check.”

She laughed.

“Good night, Yichen!”

“Good night.”

Later, after she had showered and changed into her pajamas, Xiaoran found a message waiting on her phone.

Yichen: Home?

Xiaoran: Yes. Just finished showering.

Yichen: Good. Sleep early.

She typed:

Thank you for the milk tea and the torch.

He replied:

You’re welcome.

Then, after a moment:

Next time, I’ll bring a portable lamp.

Xiaoran laughed.

Next time, I’ll leave before the lights go off.

I’ll believe that when I see it.

She smiled and sent him a heart.

A few seconds later, her phone rang.

She answered.

“Hello?”

“Have you finished your notes?”

She groaned.

“Why are you asking?”

“Because I know you.”

“I finished most of them.”

“Most?”

“I’ll do the rest tomorrow.”

“Good.”

There was a comfortable pause.

Then she said, “I liked seeing you outside.”

Yichen was quiet.

“Even with the terrible lighting?”

She laughed. “The lighting was the best part.”

He laughed.

“I’ll remember that.”

She settled deeper into her pillow.

“Good night.”

“Good night, Xiaoran.”

After they hung up, she glanced at the photograph she had sent Ning.

His hand.

His phone.

The small circle of light on the pavement.

It wasn’t a romantic photograph. There were no flowers, no beautiful scenery, and certainly no carefully planned date.

Just his hand, and a phone, and a small circle of light on the pavement. She made it her lock screen, and the next time she studied late, she left the library twenty minutes before closing, and he was outside anyway, with the same milk tea, because he had guessed.

chapters.desc: A national media strategy competition, a month of 2 AM study sessions, and something Lin Xiaoran wants to prove.
chapters.title: Lin Xiaoran’s First Win
chapters.epigraph: “I want to know I can be good at something difficult too.”
chapters.content:
Nobody expected Lin Xiaoran to voluntarily join an academic competition. Including Lin Xiaoran herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It’s not academic-academic,” she defended weakly while waving the registration poster at Zhou Yichen.

He looked down calmly. National University Creative Media Strategy Competition. Project-based, presentation-based, research-based. Very brain-based. Yichen looked back up slowly.

“…This looks deeply academic.”

“It’s media.”

“There are charts.”

“Creative charts.”

The competition involved far more than creativity. Students had to build a full media campaign proposal—research, audience analysis, branding strategy, content planning—and then defend it in front of judges. Weeks of thinking. Tragic news for Lin Xiaoran, who was creative but hated structured intellectual suffering. So why join? Because at university, for the first time, she wanted to prove something—not to teachers or classmates, just to herself. That she wasn’t only “cute.” Wasn’t only “Yichen’s girlfriend.” Wasn’t only emotional chaos in human form. That maybe she could actually make something good.

✦ ✦ ✦

The month of preparation was horrifying, because Lin Xiaoran briefly turned into a serious person. Very briefly. 2 AM, the business faculty study room, and Xiaoran sat buried in papers, muttering at her laptop.

“…Why are statistics shaped like this.”

Across from her, Yichen was reviewing her slides.

“You wrote this chart wrong.”

“I hate graphs.”

“You labeled the age demographic backwards.”

“Oh my god.”

A few business students at the next table were watching with fascination: the famous basketball player Zhou Yichen, spending his nights patiently helping his girlfriend organize competition data. Without complaint. Xiaoran collapsed across the table.

“Yichen. My brain feels boiled.”

“You’ve said that every night this week.”

“Because it’s true.”

But for all the complaining, she worked hard. Harder than Yichen had ever seen. She watched research videos during meals, practiced her presentation alone, and redid entire sections because “it doesn’t feel smart enough.” She even woke up early voluntarily, which genuinely scared him. One night, while fixing her presentation notes, Yichen asked,

“Why are you pushing yourself this hard.”

Then Xiaoran answered softly without looking up—

“…Because I want to win something myself.”

Dead silence. Something in him softened. She sounded sincere. Not bratty, not dramatic. Just honest.

“You already do a lot well.”

Xiaoran frowned.

“That sounds like comfort.”

“It’s true.”

“No. I want proof. I want to know I can actually be good at something difficult too.”

The room went quiet. Yichen reached over and squeezed the back of her neck gently.

“You are.”

Like he had never once doubted it. Somehow, that made her work even harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Competition day came too fast. A university auditorium. Several schools. Formal clothes. Actual judges. Lin Xiaoran wanted to disappear.

“This was a terrible decision.”

Beside her, Yichen straightened the sleeve of her blazer.

“You practiced enough.”

“What if my voice dies.”

“Then I’ll answer questions.”

“You’re not allowed to.”

“I’ll do it anyway.”

Yichen wasn’t technically part of the competition. Not even remotely. He had come simply because “you’ll be nervous.” Correct. Right before they went into the hall, Xiaoran grabbed his wrist.

“…Do I look stupid.”

Dead silence. That question alone showed how nervous she was. Yichen looked at her carefully. Professional outfit. Hair tied neatly. Presentation folder clutched tight. Trying so hard not to panic. She looked beautiful—but more than that, she looked serious. Determined. Like someone slowly growing into herself.

“You look cool.”

Silence.

“And smart.”

That one hit harder. Much harder. People complimented her looks all the time. But Zhou Yichen—someone genuinely brilliant—calling her smart?

“…Don’t say things that affect my heart before presentations.”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The presentation itself felt surreal. At first her hands shook, her voice was nervous, her breathing uneven. Then, somewhere in the middle, she relaxed—because she realized she actually understood her project, deeply. Every late night, every revision, every practice run was inside her now. Slowly, her confidence showed: clear explanations, sharp ideas, unexpectedly strong answers when the judges questioned her. Even the audience looked impressed. From the back row, Zhou Yichen couldn’t stop staring. Not because she looked cute, or because she was his girlfriend, but because she looked capable. Bright. Passionate. Like someone standing properly in her own world. It made his chest tighten. Lin Xiaoran had grown so much without even noticing.

Results. Third place. Second place. And then—

“First place…”

“…Lin Xiaoran’s team from the Media Faculty.”

Xiaoran froze.

“…What.”

Her teammates screamed first. Someone grabbed her. The auditorium broke into applause, and Lin Xiaoran stood on stage holding her certificate, completely stunned. She genuinely hadn’t expected to win. Not really. Her eyes went straight to the audience. There—Yichen, standing near the back, smiling. Not surprised. Like he had known all along. Somehow that nearly made her cry harder than the award.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside the auditorium, Xiaoran ran straight to him, still clutching the trophy awkwardly, eyes bright, cheeks pink. And before Yichen could even speak—

“I WON.”

“Hm.”

“I ACTUALLY WON.”

“I know.”

“You knew?!”

Yichen laughed and steadied her before she tripped.

“You worked hard enough.”

“No but—”

Xiaoran stopped talking, because looking at him, she realized something embarrassing: the person who had believed in her first was always Zhou Yichen. Even before she believed in herself.

“…I think I’m really happy.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“I know.”

He reached over and fixed her messy hair.

“You looked really cool up there.”

Somehow, hearing that from him felt even better than winning first place.

On the steps outside the hall he kissed her with the certificate crushed between them, and she laughed into it, and didn’t care which of her classmates walked past.

chapters.desc: A livestream assignment, thirty identical bottles, and eyeliner—the destroyer of relationships.
chapters.title: Can My Boyfriend Do My Makeup?
chapters.epigraph: “Why is this harder than free throws?”
chapters.content:
The assignment sounded simple. Too simple. Which should have been the first warning sign. As part of her media production course, Lin Xiaoran had to run a livestream: audience interaction, an engagement challenge, real-time content, something entertaining. Then her professor added one more requirement.

“It has to be authentic.”

The moment Xiaoran heard that word—she knew exactly who her victim would be.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three days later, Zhou Yichen received a message.

Xiaoran: Need your help.

Yichen: Okay.

Xiaoran: For an assignment.

Yichen: Okay.

Xiaoran: You have to do my makeup live on camera.

Yichen: …

Yichen: What?

✦ ✦ ✦

The livestream was titled Can My Boyfriend Do My Makeup? A terrible idea. An excellent idea. A successful idea, mostly because Zhou Yichen looked like he wanted to flee the country.

✦ ✦ ✦

The livestream started at 7 PM. Within ten minutes, several hundred viewers had joined: mostly university students, some of Xiaoran’s classmates, a suspicious number of basketball team members, and, unfortunately, Chen Yuhao. The comments exploded right away.

“IS THIS THE BASKETBALL GUY?”

“WHY DOES HE LOOK SO NERVOUS”

“HE LOOKS LIKE HE’S ABOUT TO TAKE AN EXAM”

“HE LOOKS TOO HANDSOME FOR THIS”

Zhou Yichen stared at the products spread across the table—foundation, concealer, primer, powder, blush, contour, bronzer, highlighter—and went still.

“Why are there so many.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“That’s your problem.”

“This is unreasonable.”

“You survived business school.”

“Business school never gave me thirty identical bottles.”

The chat lost it.

“HE’S RIGHT”

“THIRTY IDENTICAL BOTTLES”

“I’M CRYING”

Yichen picked up a tube.

“What is this.”

“Primer.”

“What does it do.”

“I don’t know.”

“You don’t know?”

“I just use it.”

Dead silence. Yichen looked genuinely betrayed.

“YOU DON’T KNOW?”

“NO.”

The audience couldn’t stop laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually, the challenge began, and Xiaoran fully expected disaster. Zhou Yichen’s hands weren’t exactly made for makeup. Basketball, weight training—his hands were large, rough, strong. Not the kind anyone associated with delicate beauty routines. But the moment he actually started, something changed. Zhou Yichen took the task seriously. Far too seriously, like everything else. He leaned in, studying her face, wearing the same focused expression he had before tournaments. The comments changed.

“WAIT”

“WHY IS HE TRYING SO HARD”

“THIS IS CUTE”

“HE LOOKS MORE NERVOUS THAN SHE DOES”

He was. Terrified—not of embarrassing himself, but of hurting her. The makeup sponge hovered uncertainly near her face.

“Am I pressing too hard?”

“No.”

“This?”

“No.”

“This?”

“No.”

“Yichen.”

“What.”

“You’ve blended the same spot for a full minute.”

“I want consistency.”

The comments exploded again. Yichen kept concentrating. The closer he got, the more nervous he became. Makeup apparently required precision, and Xiaoran’s skin looked so soft. The opposite of basketball. One wrong move and he’d ruin everything.

Then came eyeliner. The final boss. The destroyer of relationships. The chat noticed immediately.

“OH NO”

“GOOD LUCK BRO”

“HE’S FINISHED”

Even Xiaoran got nervous. Eyeliner. Yichen stared at the tiny brush. Then at her eye. Then at the brush again.

“Why is this harder than free throws.”

“Because if you miss, it’s my face.”

Very gently, he lifted her chin—one hand supporting her face, the other holding the eyeliner—and the room went quiet. Even the comments slowed down. Everything felt softer. Closer. His concentration was absolute. His thumb rested lightly against her cheek.

“Don’t move.”

“I’m not moving.”

“Good.”

For several seconds, neither of them spoke. He was just trying his best—not to mess up, not to poke her eye, not to ruin her assignment.

“Your eyelashes are really long.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran blinked. The chat exploded.

“HE’S GONE”

“IT’S OVER”

“THAT WAS NOT NECESSARY”

“WHY WAS THAT SO SWEET”

Yichen looked confused.

“What.”

“You just complimented my eyelashes.”

“…I was making an observation.”

The audience refused to believe him. Correctly.

✦ ✦ ✦

After nearly an hour, it was finished. Xiaoran looked in the mirror and blinked. Then blinked again.

“…Wait.”

Yichen looked worried.

“What happened.”

“It’s good.”

“What.”

“It’s actually good.”

Dead silence. Nobody had expected that. Not even him. The blush placement worked. The foundation matched. The eyeliner had survived. Not professional—but pretty. Very pretty. Then the comments poured in.

“HE COOKED”

“HOW DID HE WIN”

“BEGINNER’S LUCK”

“I’M SHOWING THIS TO MY BOYFRIEND”
