Yichen looked like he had just finished a final exam.

“Good.”

Xiaoran looked at him—really looked. The tired eyes. The careful attention he’d put into every tiny detail. And suddenly she understood: the makeup wasn’t the important part. The important part was that he had cared about every brush stroke, because it was her face. Before the stream ended, she leaned over and kissed his cheek. Quick. Unexpected. The comments descended into chaos. Zhou Yichen froze. After surviving foundation, blush, eyeliner, and public humiliation, the hardest part of the evening was still Lin Xiaoran. Very on brand.

chapters.desc: Four hours of silence, one genuinely angry boyfriend, and a stuffed panda deployed as a weapon.
chapters.title: The Selfie That Made Zhou Yichen Forget Why He Was Angry
chapters.epigraph: “You cannot send selfies during arguments.”
chapters.content:
There was a important rule in Zhou Yichen and Lin Xiaoran’s relationship. If Zhou Yichen became genuinely angry, Lin Xiaoran usually went quiet right away, because for all her spoiled behavior, she hated disappointing him. Today was different. Today she decided to fight back with selfies.

✦ ✦ ✦

The argument itself wasn’t even dramatic. It started because Xiaoran forgot something important. Again. She forgot to tell Yichen she’d be staying late with her media project group. Normally not a big deal—except she disappeared for almost four hours with her phone nearly dead. No messages. No updates. Zhou Yichen spent those four hours getting irritated, then worried, then irritated again because he was worried. A terrible combination—especially since this wasn’t the first time. Orientation day had gone almost exactly like this, minus the media senior.

By the time she finally called him, his mood was terrible.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Hello?”

“Yichen.”

Nothing on the other end. Just silence.

“Oh no.”

Zhou Yichen almost never gave the silent treatment. This was serious.

“Where are you.”

“…Media building.”

“You remembered your phone exists.”

“That’s a little aggressive.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

Uh oh. Boyfriend genuinely angry.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thirty minutes later, they met outside her apartment building, and Yichen was still angry. Calm angry, which was much worse. The terrifying version. They sat on a bench, Yichen talking and Xiaoran listening like a student being disciplined.

“You couldn’t send one message?”

“I forgot.”

“You couldn’t borrow a phone? You couldn’t tell me beforehand?”

Xiaoran had no answer.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked down guiltily, because he was right. Completely right.

“I was busy.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you angry?”

Dead silence. Wrong question. Very wrong question. Yichen finally looked at her, and that made her feel worse—not because he looked angry, but because he looked worried. Actually worried.

“I thought something happened.”

Silence.

“I called twelve times.”

Silence.

“You weren’t answering.”

The argument stopped feeling funny. This wasn’t about control, or checking up on her, or being possessive. He had been scared.

“…Sorry.”

Yichen sighed, long and tired, and stood up.

“I’m going back.”

“…Still angry?”

“Hm.”

“…How angry.”

Yichen looked at her once.

“…Very.” Then he walked away.

Uh oh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three hours later, Zhou Yichen was still angry. Not furious. Just stubbornly annoyed, which honestly lasted longer. He sat in his apartment reviewing notes, trying to focus, mostly failing, because his phone kept lighting up.

Xiaoran: Are you still angry

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: How much

Yichen: Enough.

Xiaoran: That doesn’t explain anything

Yichen: Good.

Xiaoran: You’re being mean.

No response. Two minutes later—another message.

Xiaoran: :(

Ignored. Thirty seconds later—

Xiaoran: I apologized already

Ignored. Five minutes of silence. Finally. Peace. Then his phone vibrated again. Yichen opened it without thinking—and froze. Lin Xiaoran had sent a selfie.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t even a special selfie. That was the worst part. Just her, sitting on her bed in oversized pajamas, hair messy from the shower, holding a stuffed panda against her cheek and pouting. Caption: still angry? This girl. This absolutely shameless girl.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen stared at the picture. Then stared longer. Then rubbed his forehead, because his anger was suddenly much harder to hold on to. Unfortunately, Xiaoran knew him too well. Another photo arrived. Different angle. Same pout. Caption: i think this face deserves forgiveness

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Liar.

Yichen: Not lying.

Xiaoran: Then why did you save the photo

She had somehow noticed. Terrifying woman.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across campus, Xiaoran grinned victoriously from her bed. She knew exactly what she was doing. Then another message.

Xiaoran: Look

Attached: another selfie. This time hugging the panda. Caption: this girl misses her boyfriend

Yichen: That girl is irresponsible.

Xiaoran: But cute.

Yichen: That’s not relevant.

Xiaoran: It feels relevant.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: You’re smiling.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: You are.

Yichen: Go to sleep.

Xiaoran: HAHA

Caught. Completely.

✦ ✦ ✦

The worst part was that she wasn’t even apologizing properly anymore. Now she was teasing him. Deliberately. Weaponizing cuteness. Another photo arrived. Yichen groaned, because somehow she looked even cuter in this one. Caption: boyfriend still angry :( Then another. Caption: he doesn’t love me anymore :( Then another. Caption: single woman era begins. Yichen called her. Immediately, before she could send any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second she answered, Xiaoran started laughing.

“You’re unbelievable.”

“Oh, NOW he calls.”

“Lin Xiaoran, you cannot send selfies during arguments.”

“Why.”

“Because it’s cheating.”

“I learned from experts.”

“You are the expert.”

Then a short silence. A comfortable one. The anger was finally fading.

“…Are you still angry?”

This time it sounded sincere. Not teasing. Just soft. Yichen sighed. He wasn’t angry anymore. Not really. Annoyed? A little. Worried? Still. But angry? Impossible—not after hearing her voice, not after those stupid photos, not after knowing she was safe.

“A little.”

“Liar.”

“Hm.”

“You forgave me already.”

Then Yichen admitted—

“…Mostly.”

Victory. Xiaoran smiled brightly.

“I’ll message next time.”

“You said that at orientation.”

“I mean it this time.”

“I know.”

“…Send me the third photo.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing so hard she nearly dropped her phone.

“YOU SAVED THEM.”

“No.”

“YOU DID.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

The silence confirmed everything. Somewhere in his apartment, Zhou Yichen realized he had lost the argument completely. Again. Lin Xiaoran could beat him with nothing but a messy selfie and a stuffed panda—a strategy he considered deeply unfair.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran posts three photos for the first time in months. Zhou Yichen makes the mistake of scrolling down.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Read the Comments
chapters.epigraph: “I just didn’t like everyone else liking them too.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran rarely posted on social media. Mostly because she forgot it existed. Her entire account was one photo of a cake, two photos of a panda, one blurry sunset, and a picture of Zhou Yichen’s sleeve from two years ago. That was it. So when she posted after almost three months of silence, the whole friend group noticed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The cause was stupid, as most important Xiaoran events were. Earlier that week, her faculty had finished a photography workshop—portraits, lighting, composition, editing, all the artsy things media students loved. Xiaoran hadn’t cared much, until her classmates showed her the final photos. She looked amazing. Not because the photos were revealing—they weren’t—but because for the first time she looked mature. Elegant. Confident. Different from her usual cute, chaotic self. Even she was surprised.

“That’s me?”

Her classmate laughed.

“Who else would it be?”

“No, seriously.”

She stared at the photo again: a long black dress, soft lighting, hair falling over one shoulder, looking straight into the camera. For once she didn’t look like someone about to ask a capybara-related question. She looked pretty. Very pretty. Her classmates encouraged her.

“Post it.”

“No.”

“Post it.”

“No.”

“POST IT.”

Peer pressure won.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Xiaoran uploaded three photos. Caption: Media assignment finally finished ✨ Nothing dramatic. Nothing suggestive. Just beautiful photos. Unfortunately, the internet remembered she existed.

✦ ✦ ✦

By midnight the post had exploded, far beyond her usual engagement. Classmates. Seniors. Friends. People she barely knew. Pretty. Gorgeous. Stunning. Beautiful.

Then came the problem: male comments. Lots of male comments.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran woke up to dozens of notifications. Elsewhere on campus, Zhou Yichen discovered the post.

✦ ✦ ✦

At first he just smiled. The photos looked incredible. He stared for several seconds. Then longer. Then saved one, for completely reasonable boyfriend reasons. Then he opened the comments. Mistake. Huge mistake.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Senior, you’re beautiful.”

“Can I get to know you?”

“Media faculty goddess.”

“Whoever dates her is lucky.”

“Marry me.”

Dead silence. Zhou Yichen stared. Then stared harder. Then kept scrolling, which made everything worse, because the comments kept going. And going.

✦ ✦ ✦

By lunchtime, Chen Yuhao had already received a message.

Yichen: People are annoying.

Yuhao: What happened?

Yichen: Read Xiaoran’s comments.

Five minutes later—

Yuhao: HAHAHAHAHAHA

Yuhao: You’re jealous.

Yichen: No.

Yuhao: You’re definitely jealous.

Yichen: No.

Yuhao: You sent me fourteen screenshots.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran remained completely unaware, sitting outside the media building eating snacks in peace—until Yichen appeared and sat down beside her. Very calmly. Too calmly. Xiaoran became suspicious.

“…Why do you look like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re plotting.”

“I’m not.”

Liar. Very obvious liar. Yichen held out his phone. Her post.

“…Oh.”

Silence.

“Oh.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“You read the comments.”

“Hm.”

“And?”

Another silence.

“A lot of people seem interested.”

Zhou Yichen only sounded this calm when he was actively trying not to be unreasonable. Xiaoran blinked.

“…Are you jealous?”

“No.”

Too fast. She grinned.

“Oh my god.”

Yichen looked away, which confirmed everything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The funny part was that Xiaoran didn’t feel annoyed. She felt delighted. Zhou Yichen was usually ridiculously secure—calm, confident, unbothered. So every time this tiny bit of jealousy showed up—at orientation, with the journalism student, and now here—it delighted her all over again. She scooted closer.

“…Do you know why I posted them?”

Yichen looked at her.

“No.”

“Because I liked how I looked. I thought maybe I’d gotten a little prettier.”

Silence. Yichen laughed—one quiet, helpless laugh. After all this, that was her reason? Not attention. Not validation. Just simple happiness.

“You did.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Hm?”

“You looked beautiful.”

That compliment mattered more than every comment combined.

“I liked the photos.”

“…Really?”

“Hm.”

Another pause.

“I just didn’t like everyone else liking them too.”

Actual honesty. Xiaoran burst out laughing—hard—until Yichen caught her wrist.

“Stop laughing.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“This is adorable.”

She leaned in, eyes sparkling.

“Too bad.”

“…What.”

“I’m posting more photos eventually.”

Yichen sighed deeply, like a man accepting fate. He wasn’t upset that she’d posted, or that she looked beautiful. If anything, he liked seeing her confident. The problem was simply that everyone else noticed too. A deeply inconvenient development. Xiaoran tucked herself against his shoulder, still smiling.

“Don’t worry. No matter how many comments I get…”

She squeezed his hand lightly.

“…I’m still your girlfriend.”

The last trace of jealousy disappeared, because that was the only thing he actually cared about.

chapters.desc: Finals week, a stress habit nobody noticed, and Zhou Yichen at the campus pharmacy with enough supplies for a minor apocalypse.
chapters.title: Stop Biting Your Lip
chapters.epigraph: “Because you take care of everyone except yourself.”
chapters.content:
There was something important everyone knew about Lin Xiaoran. She looked delicate. Soft voice, pretty face, cute habits—the kind of girl who looked like she belonged in a romance drama. Reality was different. Lin Xiaoran had the pain tolerance of a construction worker. The problem started during finals month. Specifically, the week from hell: a media project deadline, two presentations, three exams, one group assignment, and approximately zero remaining brain cells.

For seven straight days, Xiaoran survived almost entirely on coffee, snacks, and academic suffering, and Zhou Yichen grew more and more concerned. Something felt off.

“Eat properly.”

“I am.”

“Cookies don’t count.”

“They count.”

“No.”

Then later—

“Sleep.”

“I’m editing.”

“It’s two in the morning.”

“I’m almost done.”

“You said that yesterday.”

And the day before. And the day before that. The worst part was that Xiaoran didn’t notice anything wrong herself. Until one afternoon. Media building. Group project meeting. Everyone exhausted, everyone academically dying. Xiaoran sat reviewing footage, absentmindedly chewing her lower lip—a bad habit when she was stressed. She had been doing it all week without realizing. One teammate froze.

“…Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Your mouth.”

“My mouth what?”

“You are literally bleeding.”

Dead silence. Xiaoran blinked. She touched her lower lip. Red. Actual blood.

“…Oh.”

“Oh?!”

Between dehydration, stress, and constant lip-biting, the skin had finally cracked badly. Xiaoran looked completely unconcerned.

“It doesn’t hurt.”

“THAT IS NOT THE POINT.”

Someone made the mistake of telling Luo Jiayi, and Luo Jiayi made the mistake of texting Zhou Yichen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes later, the meeting room door opened and Zhou Yichen walked in. The whole group recognized him, mostly because he was impossible not to recognize: university basketball team, business faculty, and—unfortunately for Xiaoran—her boyfriend. One teammate whispered,

“Oh no.”

Another nodded.

“She’s getting parented.”

Yichen walked straight to her, stopped, looked down, and frowned. It looked worse than he had expected—a visible crack in her lower lip, slightly swollen, still red. Xiaoran smiled innocently.

“Hi.”

No response.

“How long.”

“…What?”

“How long has this been happening.”

“…Today?”

A lie. A terrible one. One teammate betrayed her immediately.

“Three days.”

“QIN LU.”

Yichen closed his eyes briefly, like a man asking heaven for patience.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five minutes later, Xiaoran was sitting in the campus pharmacy against her will while Yichen bought medicine.

“It doesn’t even hurt.”

“Hm.”

“You’re overreacting.”

“Hm.”

“Yichen.”

“Hm.”

The one-syllable answers meant danger. Finally he sat down beside her with lip balm, healing ointment, water, and enough supplies to survive a minor apocalypse.

“This is ridiculous.”

Yichen looked at her. He tilted her chin up, gently, to look, and his mood got worse. She kept saying it wasn’t serious, but it looked painful.

“Stop biting them.”

“I don’t do it on purpose.”

“I know. But you still do it.”

Silence. Because he was right. Again. Annoyingly right.

Then came the embarrassing part: Yichen decided to apply the medicine himself. In public. At the pharmacy. While people watched.

“Open your mouth.”

“What.”

“Medicine.”

“I can do it.”

“No.”

“Yichen.”

“No.”

Dead silence. He was stubborn today. Eventually, Xiaoran surrendered, for survival purposes. Behind the counter, the pharmacist watched the whole thing with open amusement while Yichen applied the medicine extremely carefully, like she was made of glass.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

A lie. It did hurt a little now, but admitting that felt inconvenient. Yichen narrowed his eyes.

“You just flinched.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

Caught. Again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterward, they walked back toward campus on a quiet afternoon, students everywhere, until Yichen finally spoke.

“You’ve been stressed.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“A little.”

The truth.

“I’m okay.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you worried?”

Yichen stopped walking and looked at her—really looked. Tired eyes. Messy hair. An exhausted expression she thought nobody noticed.

“Because you take care of everyone except yourself. You’ll spend three hours helping teammates. You’ll remember my practice schedule. You’ll remind other people to sleep. But you won’t take care of yourself.”

For once, Lin Xiaoran had no argument, because he was completely right. Again.

“…Sorry.”

Yichen sighed—long, helpless, fond. The sigh of a man who had been dating Lin Xiaoran for years. He reached over and pinched her cheek.

“Stop apologizing.”

“What then?”

“Take care of yourself.”

“I’ll try.”

“You will.”

“I said I’ll try.”

“You will.”

The Zhou Yichen certainty, absolutely impossible to argue with.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, she got a message.

Yichen: Did you apply the medicine?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: Photo.

Xiaoran: WHAT

Yichen: Evidence.

Xiaoran: You’re insane.

Yichen: Photo.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five minutes later, she sent a selfie: lip balm visible, pouting. Caption: medical patient suffering A minute later, his reply came.

Yichen: Cute.

This man had spent the whole afternoon worrying himself sick, and still found her cute. Absolutely hopeless boyfriend.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning he was outside her building with a new tube of lip balm and two coffees. He checked her lip first, with his thumb, carefully, like a doctor with no qualifications at all. Then he kissed her, even more carefully.

“Better?”

“Medically, yes.”

chapters.desc: The first summer home from university, a city-league game with Meilin and Yuhao in the stands, and a father who arrives in the third quarter and leaves with one sentence.
chapters.title: Home for Summer
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t watch the ball. I watch you.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Lin Xiaoran noticed about coming home for the summer was that the neighborhood hadn’t changed. The old convenience store still had the same faded blue sign. The bakery near the intersection still sold sesame cakes that were slightly too sweet. The playground near the primary school still had a broken swing, and the old men who gathered outside the chess shop still seemed to know everybody’s business.

The second thing she noticed was that Tang Meilin and Chen Yuhao hadn’t become any less annoying.

“Shanghai has changed you,” Yuhao declared.

Xiaoran, who was sitting on the low wall outside the convenience store with a cold drink in her hand, looked at him.

“How?”

“You’ve become more expensive.”

Meilin snorted.

“She was always expensive. You just couldn’t afford her standards.”

“Exactly! Thank you.” Xiaoran pointed at Meilin.

Yuhao looked between them. “I see. Two against one. This is why I don’t come home.”

“You came home yesterday,” Meilin reminded him.

“That was before I knew you two were here.”

Xiaoran laughed.

It felt strange, in a good way, to be back in the same place with the same people after a year of university. They had spent months exchanging messages, sending pictures of campus life, complaining about assignments, and arranging video calls whenever their schedules aligned.

But sitting together like this, with Meilin stealing her drink and Yuhao talking nonsense, was different.

There was no need to explain anything.

They could pick up where they had left off.

Yichen arrived a little later.

He was wearing a plain white T-shirt and dark trousers, his hair slightly damp from the summer heat. His basketball bag hung over one shoulder.

Yuhao spotted him first.

“Look who finally decided to visit us.”

Yichen glanced at him. “I live here.”

“Temporarily.”

“Still longer than you.”

Meilin laughed.

Xiaoran had already stood up.

“You’re late.”

“By five minutes.”

“Seven.”

He looked at her, then at the drink in her hand.

“Have you eaten?”

She blinked.

“Lovely to see you too.”

“Hello. Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Something.”

He gave her a look.

She sighed. “A sandwich.”

“When?”

“At lunchtime.”

“It’s almost four.”

“I know how clocks work, Yichen.”

He reached for her hand, taking her empty drink bottle with the other.

“Come on. I’ll get you something.”

Yuhao watched them walk toward the shop.

“One year of university. And they’re still like this,” he said thoughtfully.

Meilin crossed her arms.

“Some things never improve.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The city-league game was on Saturday evening.

Yichen had been invited to play for a local team during the summer break. It wasn’t a professional competition, but it was a proper city-league tournament, with teams from different districts, regular spectators, referees, and enough local pride to make every match competitive.

He hadn’t planned to play at first.

He had university training to consider, and the summer was supposed to be a break. But the invitation came through an old coach who knew his playing history, and Yichen had agreed after checking the schedule.

Xiaoran found out about the game when he mentioned it casually over dinner.

“You’re playing on Saturday?”

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I just did.”

She stared at him.

He looked back, entirely composed.

“That’s not what I meant.”

“I know.”

“Yichen.”

He smiled slightly.

She pointed her chopsticks at him. “I’m coming.”

“I assumed you would.”

“Good.”

Across the table, Yuhao leaned forward.

“Can we come too?”

Yichen nodded. “Of course.”

Meilin looked at Xiaoran.

“Are you going to become one of those basketball girlfriends who scream every time their boyfriend touches the ball?”

Xiaoran considered this.

“Probably.”

Yichen continued eating.

“Please don’t.”

She turned to him.

“Why?”

“I’d like to hear the coach.”

Yuhao burst out laughing.

“He’s already regretting inviting us.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday arrived with an oppressive summer heat.

The outdoor court had been set up for the tournament, though the main playing area was covered by a roof. There were rows of plastic seats along the sidelines, small stalls selling drinks and snacks, and a crowd that had begun gathering well before the first game.

Xiaoran arrived with Meilin and Yuhao.

She was wearing a loose summer dress, sneakers, and a cap to keep the sun off her face. In her bag were tissues, a bottle of water, sunscreen, and a small towel.

Meilin looked inside.

“Are you preparing for a basketball game or a three-day expedition?”

“Yichen sweats a lot.”

“He’s playing, Xiaoran. That’s generally what happens.”

“I know.”

Yuhao leaned over.

“Did you bring a first-aid kit too?”

She met his eyes.

“No.”

“Disappointing.”

“Would you like me to bring one for you?”

“Why? Are you planning to get injured?”

“Your mouth is going to get you injured.”

Meilin laughed as they found their seats.

Yichen was already warming up.

Xiaoran spotted him almost immediately.

He was moving through a shooting drill with his teammates, his attention fixed on the basket. His posture was relaxed but focused, the ball leaving his hands with a familiar rhythm.

She watched him make a shot, then another, then another.

Yuhao followed her gaze.

“He’s gotten better.”

Meilin nodded. “He looks stronger too.”

Xiaoran smiled, pleased by their observation.

“He trains a lot.”

“We know. You’ve told us,” Yuhao said.

“I have not.”

Meilin gave her a flat look.

“You sent us a video of him practicing at eleven at night.”

“Because he made a really good shot!”

“And then you sent another one.”

“That was a different shot.”

Yuhao shook his head.

“Love is a disease.”

Xiaoran ignored him.

On the court, Yichen finished his warm-up and glanced toward the seats.

His eyes found her.

She lifted both hands and waved.

He smiled, a small one, then raised his hand in acknowledgment.

Meilin leaned toward Xiaoran.

“That smile.”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Meilin.”

“He’s looking at you like he has a whole separate game happening over there.”

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

“Stop.”

Yuhao nodded solemnly.

“Very serious competition. One opponent. One girl. One hand wave.”

“Both of you are unbearable.”

The game started at six.

Yichen’s team had a difficult opponent.

The first quarter was fast and physical, with both sides trading baskets. Yichen played as a guard, helping organize the offense and moving between the perimeter and the paint depending on the defensive setup.

Xiaoran didn’t understand every tactical decision, but she had watched enough of his games to recognize when something was going well.

She knew the difference between his relaxed expression and the one he wore when he was fully locked in.

Tonight, he was serious.

He communicated constantly with his teammates, calling out screens, directing movement, and adjusting when the opposing team changed its defense.

He wasn’t the loudest player on the court.

But his teammates listened.

In the second quarter, he intercepted a pass and drove toward the basket. A defender stepped across his path. Yichen changed direction, slipped past him, and finished with a layup.

Xiaoran stood up.

“Yes!”

Yuhao clapped.

Meilin laughed. “There she goes.”

Xiaoran didn’t sit down immediately.

Yichen jogged back on defense, expression unchanged.

Then he glanced toward the stands.

She was still standing.

He shook his head, almost smiling.

“He’s looking at you,” Meilin whispered.

“He’s not.”

“He is.”

Xiaoran sat down, trying to look composed.

A few minutes later, Yichen made a three-pointer.

She stood up again.

This time, Yuhao joined her.

“THAT’S MY GUY!”

Yichen turned his head toward the stands.

His expression suggested he was reconsidering his friendship with all three of them.

Meilin laughed until she had to cover her mouth.

Mr. Zhou arrived midway through the third quarter.

Xiaoran noticed him before Yichen did.

A tall man in a light shirt stepped into the seating area, accompanied by another older man. He spoke to someone near the entrance, then looked toward the court.

He didn’t appear rushed. He didn’t appear interested in finding a seat, either.

He went straight to a chair in the back row without looking for a better one.

Xiaoran recognized him immediately.

She had met Yichen’s father several times. He was always polite, measured, and difficult to read. Unlike Yichen’s mother, who was warm and openly affectionate, Mr. Zhou rarely expressed much through his face.

Xiaoran nudged Meilin.

“Yichen’s father is here.”

Meilin turned.

“Oh.”

Yuhao glanced over.

“Didn’t know he was coming.”

“Neither did I.”

On the court, Yichen was preparing to receive a pass when his eyes moved toward the stands.

He saw his father.

There was no obvious reaction.

No smile, no wave, no change in posture.

He looked away and continued playing.

Xiaoran watched him carefully.

She wondered whether he had known his father might come.

The game continued.

Yichen’s team was trailing by four points. Their opponents had become more aggressive defensively, forcing several turnovers.

Yichen adjusted.

He slowed the pace, called for a screen, and moved the ball around rather than forcing a difficult shot. On the next possession, he found a teammate cutting toward the basket.

The pass was clean.

The teammate scored.

Xiaoran clapped.

Then, a little later, Yichen drove toward the baseline and passed to the opposite corner.

Another basket.

The gap narrowed. The final minutes became increasingly tense.

The opposing team called a timeout.

Players gathered around their coach.

Yichen stood with his hands on his hips, listening.

From the stands, Xiaoran noticed his father checking his watch.

She didn’t think much of it.

When play resumed, Yichen received the ball near the top of the key. His defender pressed close, leaving little room to move.

A teammate cut toward the basket.

Yichen passed.

But the pass came a fraction too early.

The teammate hadn’t completed his movement. The ball traveled behind him, and the opposing team intercepted it.

A fast break followed.

The crowd groaned.

Yichen immediately turned and sprinted back, but the opponent scored before his team could recover.

Xiaoran’s fingers tightened around her water bottle.

He didn’t look frustrated.

Not outwardly.

He took his position again.

The game ended with Yichen’s team losing by three points.

A respectable loss, which was still a loss.

The players shook hands, exchanged a few words, and gathered near their bench.

Xiaoran was already making her way down the steps.

“Yichen!”

He turned when he heard her.

His expression changed slightly when he saw her approaching, the tension in his shoulders easing.

“Hey.”

She stopped in front of him.

“You’re sweaty.”

He met her eyes.

“I just played a game.”

“I know.”

She held out the towel.

He accepted it, wiping his face.

“How was it?”

“Good.”

She tilted her head.

“Good?”

“We lost.”

“I saw.”

He glanced at her.

“You don’t have to pretend.”

“I’m not pretending. You played well.”

“Not perfectly.”

“No one plays perfectly.”

He smiled.

“That’s a very generous assessment.”

“It’s an accurate one.”

He looked at her, then reached out and touched the brim of her cap.

“Did you enjoy watching?”

“Very much.”

He laughed.

Before he could say anything else, Yuhao appeared behind her.

“That was a good game, man.”

Yichen nodded. “Thanks.”

“That pass in the fourth quarter, though.”

Meilin elbowed Yuhao.

“Can you let him breathe first?”

“What? I’m discussing basketball.”

“You’re discussing his mistake.”

Yichen shook his head.

“It’s fine.”

Yuhao raised both hands.

“See? He’s fine.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

“Have you eaten?”

He sighed.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Can I change first?”

She blinked.

“Oh. Yes.”

He smiled and brushed his fingers against hers.

“I’ll be back.”

By the time Yichen returned, the crowd had begun to disperse.

Xiaoran was standing beside the small refreshment stall with Meilin and Yuhao. They had bought cold drinks and were arguing about where to eat.

Yichen joined them, carrying his basketball bag.

“Hotpot,” Yuhao declared.

“It’s too hot for hotpot,” Meilin said.

“Hotpot is never too hot.”

“You’re the reason people lose their appetite.”

Xiaoran turned toward Yichen.

“What do you want?”

He looked at the three of them.

“Anything.”

Yuhao groaned.

“Why are you all so difficult?”

“Because you ask questions without accepting answers,” Yichen replied.

Xiaoran laughed.

They eventually agreed on a small noodle restaurant near the old commercial street.

But before they left, Xiaoran noticed Mr. Zhou standing near the edge of the court.

He was speaking to the older man who had arrived with him.

Yichen noticed him too.

His steps slowed.

“Yichen,” Xiaoran said.

He turned to her.

“Your father.”

“I see.”

Mr. Zhou turned toward them.

His gaze settled on his son.

“Yichen.”

“Dad.”

The greeting was brief.

Mr. Zhou looked at the basketball bag over his shoulder.

“Finished?”

“Yes.”

“How did it go?”

“We lost by three.”

His father nodded once.

Then his eyes moved toward the court.

“Your fourth-quarter possession. You passed too early.” He waited, and when Yichen said nothing, he finished it.

There was no anger in his voice, only a short, precise observation.

Yichen’s expression remained composed.

“The cut wasn’t finished.”

“Then you should have waited.”

“I know.”

His father looked at him for another moment.

Then he checked his watch.

“I have to go.”

Xiaoran looked at the man.

He had arrived late.

He was leaving before the players had even finished packing up.

Mr. Zhou nodded to her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Good evening, Uncle Zhou.”

“Good evening.”

He turned back to Yichen.

“Keep training.”

Then he left.

He hadn’t said well played, or asked how university was going. One observation, a reminder to keep training, and then his back going out through the gate.

None of them spoke.

Yuhao was the first to break the silence.

“Well.”

Meilin gave him a warning look.

He closed his mouth.

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

His face was unreadable.

She wasn’t sure whether he was disappointed, irritated, or used to it.

“Yichen?”

He adjusted the strap of his bag.

“Hm?”

“Do you want to go?”

He nodded.

“Let’s go.”

She reached for his hand.

He took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was noisy.

Yuhao complained about the restaurant’s portion sizes. Meilin accused him of ordering too much. Xiaoran tried to steal a piece of food from Yichen’s bowl, and he moved it away just far enough to make her protest.

For a while, everything returned to normal.

But Xiaoran noticed that Yichen was quieter than usual, even for him.

But there were moments when she caught him looking at his phone without actually doing anything, or staring at the table while Yuhao told a story.

Eventually, Meilin and Yuhao started arguing about an old high-school incident.

Xiaoran leaned closer to Yichen.

“Are you okay?”

He held her gaze.

“Yes.”

She studied his face.

“Really?”

He smiled slightly.

“Really.”

She didn’t push.

Instead, she slipped her hand beneath the table and found his.

He looked down.

Then his fingers closed around hers.

After a moment, he leaned toward her.

“Don’t worry.”

She looked at him.

“I’m not.”

His expression suggested he didn’t believe her.

She gave his hand a small squeeze.

“I just wanted to hold your hand.”

His gaze softened.

“All right.”

He brought her hand to his lips and kissed her knuckles beneath the table.

Across from them, Yuhao was still talking.

Meilin noticed.

She smiled to herself and returned to her food.

They walked home together after dinner.

The summer evening was warm, the streets illuminated by shop signs and the occasional passing motorcycle. Yuhao had gone in the opposite direction, while Meilin had been picked up by her parents.

Xiaoran and Yichen took the longer route.

They passed the old primary school, the small park, and the bakery street where she had once got hopelessly lost trying to buy him pastries.

Yichen carried both their bags.

Xiaoran walked beside him, occasionally brushing her shoulder against his.

After a while, she asked, “Did you know your father was coming?”

“No.”

She nodded.

“Did you want him to?”

Yichen was quiet.

Then he said, “It doesn’t matter.”

Xiaoran looked up at him.

It wasn’t quite an answer.

But she understood that he wasn’t ready to give her a different one.

She looked ahead.

“Your pass wasn’t bad.”

He studied her.

“What?”

“The pass. In the fourth quarter.”

He gave her a faint smile.

“You don’t have to defend me.”

“I’m not defending you.”

“Then?”

“I’m telling you what I saw. You saw the opening. You made the pass. Your teammate wasn’t ready. It happens.”

Yichen’s gaze returned to the road.

“That’s why it’s a mistake.”

“Yes.”

She said it so plainly that he looked at her again.

She smiled.

“You’re allowed to make mistakes, you know.”

He laughed.

“Thank you for the permission.”

“You’re welcome.”

They walked a little further.

Then he said, “He was right.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“About the pass?”

“Yes.”

She nodded.

“Then you can work on it.”

He considered her.

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“Nothing.”

She smiled.

“You’re very good at basketball, Yichen. That doesn’t mean you can’t improve.”

He was quiet.

Then he reached down and took her hand.

“I know.”

She leaned against his arm.

After a moment, she asked, “Are you disappointed?”

He considered the question.

“Not about the game.”

She waited.

He didn’t elaborate.

She didn’t ask him to.

Instead, she lifted their joined hands and swung them gently between them.

“Come on.”

“Where?”

“Home.”

He looked down at her.

Then he smiled.

“All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night, Yichen returned to his room after showering.

His basketball bag sat beside his desk.

He took out his shoes, towel, and water bottle, placing each item where it belonged. Then he checked his phone.

There was a message from his father.

Dad: Review the fourth-quarter footage if you can get it.

Yichen looked at the message.

A few seconds later, another one arrived.

Dad: Your footwork is better than at the invitational.

He read it twice. His father hadn’t been at the invitational. He must have found the footage.

He typed a short reply.

Yichen: I’ll review it.

He put the phone down.

Across the room, an old drawer stood slightly open. Inside were school certificates, photographs, a few medals, and things he hadn’t looked at in years.

He pushed it shut.

Then he returned to his desk, opened his laptop, and searched for the game footage.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next afternoon, Xiaoran found him at the small basketball court behind the community center.

She had expected him to be there.

He was alone, wearing a dark training shirt, shooting from the perimeter.

The ball hit the rim.

He retrieved it.

Took another shot.

This time, it went in.

Xiaoran stood by the fence, watching him for a while before calling out.

“Excuse me.”

He turned.

His expression softened when he saw her.

“You’re here.”

“Am I interrupting?”

“No.”

She walked over, holding a plastic bag.

“I brought something.”

He glanced at it.

“What?”

“Food.”

“For me?”

“For you. I ate mine on the way.”

He laughed.

She placed the bag on the bench.

“Your mother said you might be here.”

“She told you?”

“She asked me to bring you something.”

He shook his head, smiling.

Xiaoran took out a small container.

“Fruit.”

“Thank you.”

“And a sandwich.”

“Thank you.”

“And—”

“Xiaoran.”

She stopped.

He looked at her, amused.

“What else?”

She took out a small packet of tissues.

“You’re welcome.”

He laughed and accepted it.

She sat on the bench while he finished a few more shots.

After a while, he came over, drinking water.

“How long have you been here?”

“Long enough.”

“Watching?”

“Yes.”

“Did I play well?”

She tilted her head.

“Do you want an honest answer?”

“Always.”

“You do a little bounce on your toes before you shoot when you’re annoyed. You did it four times.”

He stared at her.

Then his mouth curved.

“Who taught you that?”

“Me. I don’t watch the ball. I watch you.”

“Impressive.”

She smiled proudly.

He sat beside her.

For a while, they ate in comfortable silence.

Then Xiaoran looked at him.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Last night you told me it doesn’t matter.”

He didn’t answer.

“You don’t have to tell me everything straight away. Just don’t say it doesn’t matter and then come out here on your own the next day.”

He looked at the hoop, and then at her. Then he lifted her hand and pressed a kiss against her fingers.

“I’ll remember.”

She nodded.

“Good.”

He leaned back against the bench.

The court was quiet, with only the occasional sound of a ball bouncing from the far end.

After a while, Xiaoran let her head drop onto his shoulder.

“By the way.”

“Hm?”

“You’re playing again next week?”

“Probably.”

“Then I’ll come.”

“All right.”

“And Meilin and Yuhao.”

He closed his eyes.

“Do we have to invite Yuhao?”

She laughed.

“Yes.”

“Unfortunate.”

“He cheered for you.”

“He shouted at the wrong time.”

“That’s because he’s enthusiastic.”

“He’s loud.”

“Same thing.”

Yichen smiled and kissed her temple.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, when Yichen returned home, he found his father in the study.

Mr. Zhou was reading through some documents.

Yichen stood at the door.

“Dad.”

His father looked up.

“Yes?”

“About yesterday.”

Mr. Zhou put down his pen.

Yichen entered and stood across from the desk.

“The pass was early.”

His father nodded.

“I know.”

“I saw the cut, but I didn’t wait for him to finish.”

Mr. Zhou watched him.

“Then you know what to correct.”

“Yes.”

A brief silence followed.

Yichen looked at his father.

“Did you watch the whole game?”

Mr. Zhou’s expression remained neutral.

“Most of it.”

“You arrived during the third quarter.”

“I had something to attend to.”

Yichen nodded.

His father returned his gaze to the documents.

“Your mother said you’re staying here for the summer.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t neglect your training.”

“I won’t.”

“Good.”

That was the end of the conversation.

Yichen left the study.

He didn’t expect anything more.

But as he walked down the corridor, he heard his father’s voice again.

“Yichen.”

He stopped and turned.

Mr. Zhou was still seated behind the desk.

“Your defense has improved.”

Yichen looked at him.

A small pause.

“Thank you.”

His father nodded once.

Yichen returned to his room.

✦ ✦ ✦

A few days later, Xiaoran found herself in Yichen’s room while he was downstairs.

She had come over to return a book, and his mother had told her she could leave it on his desk.

The room looked much the same as she remembered. Neat, quiet, with everything in its place.

She put the book down.

Then she noticed an old metal box on the shelf, a little dusty, with a faded basketball sticker on the lid. The lid wasn’t quite shut. When she reached up to push it closed, a photograph slid out onto the shelf.

A boy of about twelve in a jersey far too big for him, holding a small trophy in a school gym. In the front row of the stands behind him, Mrs. Zhou was waving with both hands.

Xiaoran smiled and laid the photograph back on top of the medals inside.

When Yichen came upstairs, he found her sitting on the edge of his bed.

“Your book’s on the desk.”

“Thank you.”

He glanced at the shelf, then at her.

“Did you find something?”

“You at twelve. In a jersey like a dress. Your mom was in the front row.”

“She came to everything.”

“And your dad?”

He took the box down and closed the lid properly.

“He never had time.”

He said it the way people mention the weather, and she didn’t ask again.

Instead, she smiled and held out her hand.

She held out her hand.

He walked over, taking her hand.

She pulled him down beside her.

“You’re very handsome.”

“That’s unrelated.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you telling me?”

“Because I want to.”

He smiled and leaned down to kiss her forehead.

“All right.”

She rested against him.

Downstairs, his mother called them for dinner. Neither of them moved until she called twice.

chapters.desc: A typhoon comes up the coast on the night of his first dinner inside her family’s home, and her mother makes up the spare room.
chapters.title: Summer Dinner, Her House
chapters.epigraph: “Thank you for inviting me.”
chapters.content:
The rain had started at four, sideways, the way it did in July when a typhoon was coming up the coast, and by the time Yichen climbed the stairs to the fourth floor his umbrella had turned inside out twice. The first thing he noticed when Xiaoran opened the front door was the pair of slippers waiting neatly beside the entrance. The second thing was the extra pair beside them.

The third was the fact that her mother was standing directly behind her, smiling as if she’d been waiting for this moment all afternoon.

“Yichen! You’re here.”

He smiled politely, holding the paper bags in his hands.

“Good evening, Auntie. Sorry to bother you.”

“Bother me? Come in, come in. Why are you standing outside like a delivery man?”

Xiaoran turned around.

“Mom, let him take his shoes off first.”

Her mother looked at her.

“I know how people take their shoes off, Xiaoran.”

“Then why are you rushing him?”

“Because dinner is getting cold.”

Yichen stepped inside.

“Thank you for having me, Auntie.”

Her mother accepted the bags.

“Oh, you brought things. You shouldn’t have.”

“It’s just some fruit and pastries.”

“Very thoughtful. Come in. Your father is in the living room.”

Xiaoran watched the exchange with a growing sense of unease.

Something was wrong.

Her mother was being much too pleasant.

Her mother had met him exactly twice before: forty seconds outside a gaokao gate, and one whole moving day in Shanghai, during which she had inspected his posture, his handwriting on a box label, and the way he carried a rice cooker up four flights of stairs. Afterward, in the car, she had said only, “He labels things properly,” which from Mrs. Lin was high praise.

But this was the first time he had come through their front door. For two years he had been the boy at the gate, the boy who called at nine, the boy her father had once watched from the window. Now he was in the hallway in her father’s spare slippers, holding a bag of fruit, as her boyfriend.

And her mother had apparently decided to make that obvious.

“Come on,” Xiaoran muttered, taking Yichen’s hand.

He glanced down at their joined hands, then at her. His expression was perfectly composed, but the slight curve at the corner of his mouth told her he had noticed her nervousness. He leaned closer.

“Should I let go?”

She immediately tightened her fingers around his.

“No.”

His smile grew.

“All right.”

Her father was sitting in the living room, watching the typhoon warning on the news, a red map with a white spiral crawling up toward their city.

When he saw Yichen, he switched it off, which Xiaoran had never seen him do during a weather forecast in her life.

“You’re here.”

“Good evening, Uncle.”

“Come, sit down.”

Xiaoran’s father gestured toward the sofa. Yichen placed his hands together politely before sitting beside him.

Xiaoran remained standing, watching them.

She had expected some awkwardness. Perhaps a few questions about university, basketball, or his family. Maybe her father would make a joke about how much time they spent together.

Instead, her father started talking about the weather, which tonight was at least relevant, then the traffic, which tonight was hopeless, then the university basketball team.

Yichen answered naturally, never appearing uncomfortable. He was good at this. He knew how to speak to adults without sounding overly formal, and he never tried too hard to impress anyone.

Xiaoran eventually sat beside him.

Her mother came out of the kitchen carrying a plate of fruit.

“Yichen, would you like some?”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Eat more. You’ve been training, haven’t you?”

“Yes, a few times a week.”

“Then you need to eat properly.”

“Mom, he’s not starving,” Xiaoran interrupted.

Her mother looked at her.

“I didn’t say he was.”

“You’re feeding him like he’s been lost in the mountains.”

Her father laughed.

Yichen lowered his head slightly, hiding a smile.

Xiaoran turned to him.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He reached for a piece of fruit.

“Would you like some?”

“You’re changing the subject.”

“Would you?”

She took one.

Her mother watched them, visibly pleased.

It was going to be a long evening.

Dinner was even worse.

Not because the food was bad. Quite the opposite. Her mother had prepared far too much, and Xiaoran was beginning to suspect that she had been planning the meal for several days.

There were dishes Yichen liked, dishes Xiaoran liked, and at least two dishes that her mother insisted were especially good for someone who played basketball.

Yichen thanked her every time she served him.

Xiaoran, meanwhile, was being ignored.

“Yichen, have some more.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Do you like this?”

“Very much.”

“As much as the dumplings on moving day?”

“Those were the best thing I ate that week, Auntie.”

“They were frozen,” said her mother, pleased.

Her mother smiled.

Xiaoran put down her chopsticks.

“Hello? I’m also sitting here.”

“We can see you,” said her father.

“Then why is nobody asking whether I want more?”

“You have hands,” her mother said.

Yichen moved a dish closer to her.

“Here.”

She met his eyes.

“Thank you.”

He smiled.

Her mother noticed.

“See? Yichen is more attentive than you.”

Xiaoran’s mouth fell open.

“Mom!”

Her father laughed into his tea, then had to put the cup down and wipe his eyes, because he was a man who found it hard to laugh without also, slightly, crying.

Yichen, to his credit, didn’t look pleased with himself. He continued eating, although the amusement in his eyes was unmistakable.

A little later, her father asked him about his studies.

“Business, right?”

“Yes, Uncle.”

“How are you finding it?”

“It’s interesting. There are quite a few group projects this semester.”

“Do you enjoy it?”

“I do. Though basketball takes up quite a bit of time.”

Her father nodded.

“You must manage your schedule carefully.”

“I try to.”

“And Xiaoran?”

“What about her?” Yichen said.

“Does she study properly?”

Xiaoran stopped chewing.

“Dad.”

Her father ignored her.

“She tends to leave things until the last minute.”

“Dad!”

Yichen considered the question.

“She’s actually quite diligent.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

He continued calmly.

“She works hard when she has something she wants to accomplish. Sometimes she gets distracted, but she usually manages her deadlines.”

Her father looked satisfied.

“That’s true.”

Xiaoran stared at Yichen.

He had managed to defend her without lying.

She nudged his leg beneath the table. He glanced at her, his expression innocent. He was being far too good at this.

After dinner, her mother asked Yichen to help bring some things upstairs.

Xiaoran immediately stood.

“I’ll do it.”

“You can help clear the table,” her mother replied.

“I can carry things.”

“I know. That’s why I’m asking you to clear the table.”

Yichen stood up.

“It’s all right, Auntie. I can help.”

Her mother smiled.

“Thank you. Come with me.”

Xiaoran watched them disappear toward the staircase.

Something was definitely wrong.

She quickly finished clearing the table and followed.

She found them in the hallway outside the spare bedroom.

Her mother was standing beside the open door.

Yichen was holding a folded blanket.

And the room—

Xiaoran stopped.

The spare room had been made up.

Not tidied.

Made up.

There were fresh bedsheets, two pillows, a neatly folded blanket, a small bedside lamp, and a bottle of water on the table. Her mother had even put a clean towel on the bed.

It looked like a hotel room.

An obvious hotel room.

For one particular guest.

Xiaoran stared.

“Mom.”

Her mother turned.

“What?”

“What is this?”

“A room.”

“I can see that.”

“Then why are you asking?”

Xiaoran pointed toward the bed.

“Why does it look like someone is checking into a hotel?”

Her mother looked at the room, then at Yichen. “The metro stops at nine during a typhoon warning. It’s twenty to. The buses stopped at seven. Your mother can’t drive in this, and I’m not letting a taxi drive you across a river in it either.”

Xiaoran’s face changed. Yichen went still.

“I’ve been watching that storm since Tuesday. I made the bed on Wednesday,” her mother said, completely unbothered.

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

He was holding the blanket with both hands, looking as if he had just been handed a unexpected responsibility.

Then he turned toward her mother.

“Thank you, Auntie. That’s very kind of you.”

Her mother nodded.

“Of course. You can use this room. If you need anything, just tell me.”

Xiaoran looked between them. “You made it on Wednesday? Before asking him?”

Her mother looked genuinely confused. “Would you prefer I made him sleep on the sofa?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth.

Closed it.

Opened it again.

“No, but—”

“Then what’s the problem?”

“Thank you, Auntie. I’ll message my mother,” Yichen said.

“I already did. On Wednesday. She sent a thumbs-up. Xiaoran, show him where the bathroom is. I’ll bring a toothbrush,” said Mrs. Lin. She turned away.

And she walked away.

Leaving the two of them standing in the hallway.

In front of a clearly prepared spare bedroom.

Xiaoran slowly turned toward Yichen.

He was looking at the room, then at her.

His mouth was beginning to curve.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face is saying something.”

He looked down at the blanket in his hands.

“Your mother is very thoughtful.”

“Yichen.”

“She even prepared two pillows.”

“Stop.”

He looked at her, his expression now unmistakably amused.

“Would you like to inspect the room?”

She covered her face.

“I hate this.”

He laughed.

“No, you don’t.”

She peeked at him through her fingers.

He was still smiling.

And that was somehow worse.

Later, when her mother had finished showing him where everything was, Xiaoran dragged him by the sleeve to the end of the hallway, and he followed without protest.

She stopped beside the window and lowered her voice.

“You’re not actually staying, are you?”

He met her eyes.

“Would you like me to leave?”

“No!”

His eyebrows lifted.

She realized what she’d said.

“I mean—no, you don’t have to. I just didn’t know my mother had a whole plan.”

“Your mother had the forecast. She sent my mother a screenshot of it.”

“And you just accepted?”

He tilted his head.

“Would refusing have been more polite?”

Xiaoran stared at him.

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Besides, I don’t mind staying.”

She glanced toward the spare bedroom.

“She made the bed.”

“I noticed.”

“She put two pillows.”

“I noticed that too.”

“There’s a towel.”

“Very observant.”

She gave him a helpless look.

He finally laughed.

Then he reached for her hand.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Your parents know we’re together.”

She nodded.

“I know.”

“They invited me into their home.”

“I know.”

“They prepared a room for me.”

“I know!”

He smiled, gently squeezing her fingers.

“Then I don’t think there’s anything to worry about.”

She looked down.

It wasn’t that she was embarrassed to have him there. She wanted him there. She liked the idea of him having dinner with her family, sitting in the living room with her father, and being treated as someone who belonged.

It was just strange.

For two years he had been the boy outside. Tonight he was standing in her hallway holding one of her mother’s towels, and the rain was hitting the window like gravel, and her parents knew exactly who he was.

She looked up.

“Are you nervous?”

He considered it.

“A little.”

“Really?”

“Your father has been looking at me quite carefully.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“He likes you.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you nervous?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Because I want him to keep liking me.”

Her expression softened.

He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“And your mother.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“She already likes you more than me.”

“That might be true.”

She gasped.

“You’re supposed to deny it!”

He laughed. “Come on. Back to the living room before your mother comes looking for us.”

The evening continued with tea and fruit in the living room.

Her father asked Yichen about his basketball matches, and her mother brought out an old photo album.

Xiaoran recognized it immediately.

“Mom. No.”

Her mother sat down with it.

“What?”

“Put it away.”

“Why?”

“Because I know what’s inside.”

Yichen glanced at the album.

“What is it?”

“Nothing,” Xiaoran said quickly.

Her mother opened it.

“Here. Look at Xiaoran when she was little.”

Yichen leaned forward.

Xiaoran tried to close the album.

Her mother moved it away.

“Don’t disturb me.”

Yichen looked at the photograph. A little girl with short hair, a round face, and a serious expression was standing in front of a birthday cake under a persimmon tree, in a courtyard he wouldn’t see for another seven months. Her cheeks were puffed out, and she appeared to be arguing with someone outside the frame.

Something in his face eased.

“That’s you?”

Xiaoran covered her face.

“Unfortunately.”

“You were cute.”

“Don’t encourage her. She was very stubborn,” her mother said.

“Was?”

Her father laughed.

Xiaoran turned toward Yichen.

“You’re enjoying this too much.”

He looked at another photograph.

“What’s this one?”

Her mother brightened.

“Oh, that’s her first day of primary school.”

Yichen studied the picture.

Xiaoran was wearing a little backpack and holding her mother’s hand outside a school gate he didn’t recognize. Her expression was deeply unhappy.

“Her first day in the city. Twelve years old. New school, new everything. She said she wanted to go back to her grandmother’s and keep chickens,” her mother explained.

Yichen smiled.

“That sounds familiar.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“Excuse me?”

He looked at her, amused, and said nothing at all, and her mother laughed.

“She’s still like that sometimes.”

“Mom!”

Yichen gently turned another page.

He wasn’t laughing loudly or making a big deal out of the photographs. He looked at each one with genuine interest, occasionally asking her mother questions.

Xiaoran watched him.

There was something intimate about seeing him here.

He knew her in ways her parents didn’t. He knew what she was like when she was tired, when she was excited, when she was trying not to cry over something small. He knew the version of her that existed outside this house.

And now he was learning about the little girl who had lived here long before he met her.

At some point, her father got up to answer a phone call, and her mother went back into the kitchen.

Yichen closed the album.

“Your childhood photographs are very cute.”

She groaned.

“Please forget them.”

“Why?”

“Because I have an image to maintain.”

He looked at her.

“What image?”

She narrowed her eyes. “A sophisticated university student.”

He smiled. “I see.”

“Don’t look at me like you know me.”

His expression softened.

“I do know you.”

She fell quiet.

He reached for her hand beneath the table.

And somehow, the familiar warmth of his fingers made the unfamiliar feeling of having him in her family home seem a little less overwhelming.

By the time the night grew late, Xiaoran’s mother had prepared a small plate of fruit for Yichen to take upstairs.

“Don’t stay up too late,” she told them.

Xiaoran nodded.

“Okay.”

“Yichen, if you need anything, just call me.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“And make sure you get enough rest.”

“I will.”

Her mother looked at Xiaoran.

“You too.”

“Yes, Mom.”

Her mother paused at the door. “And don’t keep him awake talking all night.”

Xiaoran nearly choked.

“Mom!”

Her mother smiled.

“Good night.”

She walked away.

Yichen waited until she was out of sight before looking at Xiaoran.

She pointed a warning finger at him.

“Don’t.”

He pressed his lips together.

His shoulders moved slightly.

“You’re laughing.”

“I’m not.”

“You are!”

He finally let out a quiet laugh.

She hit his arm. “You’re enjoying my suffering.”

“A little.”

“You’re terrible.”

He took her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Good night, Xiaoran.”

She looked at him, then at the spare bedroom.

“Good night.”

He started toward the room.

She watched him before calling.

“Yichen?”

He turned.

“Yes?”

She hesitated. “Thank you for coming.”

His expression changed, and the teasing went out of it. He walked back and moved her hair off her cheek.

“Thank you for inviting me.”

Her mouth tipped up.

Then he kissed her.

“Go to sleep. I’ll see you tomorrow.”

She nodded, and watched him go into the room her mother had made up on Wednesday, and heard the door close.

At some point after midnight the wind turned, and something on a balcony across the courtyard came loose and banged for an hour. In the morning her mother said she hadn’t heard a thing. Her father said he hadn’t either, but at breakfast he put the last fried egg on Yichen’s plate without asking, and that was how Xiaoran knew he had been awake too, listening to the house with one more person in it.

chapters.desc: The next evening she takes him to the Friday market by the river, the one her family went to every week the year they moved to the city.
chapters.title: The Hometown Night Market
chapters.epigraph: “I like seeing where you grew up. The second half of it.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had lived in this city his whole life, and he had never once been to the Friday night market by the river.

His family didn’t do night markets. Xiaoran’s family had done almost nothing else for the first year after they moved here from the town, when she was twelve and knew nobody, and her father had taken her every Friday to make the city feel smaller. The typhoon had gone through in the night and out to sea by noon, and the air had that washed, flattened feeling it got afterward, and the stalls were back up by six.

She held his hand and led him through the crowd as if she were showing him a place that belonged to both of them.

“Come on,” she said, tugging him forward.

“Where are we going?”

“Night market.”

“Is it far?”

“Two streets. Why are you walking so slowly?”

He looked at their joined hands.

“You’re pulling me in three different directions.”

“Because there are three different things I want to show you.”

“Which one first?”

She thought about it, then pointed toward a row of stalls.

“Food.”

He nodded.

“Good choice.”

The night market was already crowded.

Warm lights hung above the stalls, illuminating rows of food, handmade accessories, clothes, and little household items. The air smelled of grilled meat, fried snacks, sweet desserts, and something spicy that made Xiaoran immediately turn her head.

Yichen followed her gaze.

“That one?”

“I used to eat it when I was younger.”

“Do you want some?”

“Yes.”

He stepped forward to order.

Xiaoran watched him speak to the vendor, then looked around while they waited.

She was clearly in her element.

She pointed out familiar stalls, told him which vendors had been there for years, and complained about the ones that had changed their recipes.

“That one used to be better,” she said, pointing at a dessert stall.

“How long ago?”

“Years.”

“Then maybe the owner changed.”

“Maybe. But the taste changed too.”

He nodded solemnly.

“I see.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re not taking me seriously.”

“I am.”

“You’re just agreeing with everything.”

“Would you prefer I argue?”

She considered it.

“No.”

“Then I’m doing well.”

She laughed.

They bought more food than either of them had intended.

Xiaoran insisted on trying several things, claiming she hadn’t eaten them in a long time. Yichen carried most of the bags while she walked beside him, occasionally stealing something from whichever bag was easiest to reach.

At one stall, she stopped in front of a tray of small pastries.

“These.”

Yichen looked at the tray.

“Do you want one?”

“Two.”

He ordered two.

The vendor placed them in a small paper bag, and Xiaoran immediately took one.

She bit into it.

Then her expression changed.

Yichen noticed.

“Too hot?”

She nodded, cheeks slightly puffed as she tried not to burn her tongue.

He reached for the water bottle in his bag and handed it to her.

She took it gratefully.

“Thank you.”

“Careful.”

She swallowed and looked at the pastry.

“It’s still good.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Of course.”

She held out the remaining piece toward him.

“Try.”

He leaned down and took a bite.

“Good?”

She nodded, mouth full. He looked at the pastry.

“Then we should get another bag.”

Her eyes brightened.

“Really?”

“You’re going to eat it anyway.”

She smiled.

“You’re learning.”

They eventually reached a quieter section of the market, where a few small stalls sold handmade jewelry and hair clips. Xiaoran stopped at one.

She leaned forward to look.

Yichen stood beside her, still holding their food.

“Do you like something?”

“Just looking.”

She picked up a small hair clip, examined it, then put it back.

A moment later, she moved to another tray.

Yichen watched her.

“That one?”

She held up a little silver-colored charm.

“It’s cute.”

“Do you want it?”

“No. I’m just looking.”

He didn’t say anything.

She went on browsing, and eventually settled on a hair clip shaped like a small silver persimmon, with one leaf.

The vendor told her the price.

Xiaoran reached for her wallet.

Yichen watched her pay.

Then, as they walked away, he asked, “Why didn’t you let me buy it?”

She turned to him.

“Because I wanted to buy it.”

“All right.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Besides, I have money.”

“I know.”

“And I don’t need you to buy everything.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She clipped it into her hair above her left ear without a mirror, slightly crooked. He looked at it, then reached over and moved it a centimeter, so the leaf sat straight.

“There’s a persimmon tree at my grandmother’s. In the courtyard. In the photo you saw last night,” she said.

“The birthday cake.”

“I was nine. I’d just fallen out of it.”

A little later, they found a small game stall.

Xiaoran stopped immediately.

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Games?”

“Look.”

She pointed toward a row of prizes hanging behind the counter.

There was a small plush rabbit among them.

Yichen looked at it.

“Do you want that?”

She nodded.

“It’s cute.”

He examined the game.

The rules were simple enough: toss a ring around one of the bottles to win a prize.

Xiaoran tried first.

Her ring landed beside the bottle.

She frowned.

Again.

Missed.

Again.

Missed.

She turned toward Yichen.

“This game is unfair.”

He looked at the bottles.

“How?”

“The rings are too small.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Would you like me to try?”

She immediately stepped aside.

“Yes.”

He took the rings. He looked at the bottles the way he looked at a free throw. His first ring hit the neck of a bottle and bounced off. His second landed beside the first one of hers. His third went somewhere behind the stall, and the vendor said “Ah,” sympathetically.

Xiaoran stared at him. “You play basketball.”

“Basketball has a bigger ring.”

“Yichen!”

“I’m aware,” he said, with dignity.

She bought three more rings, out of pity, and took them herself, determined. The first missed. The second missed. The third dropped round the neck of a green bottle with a small, perfect clink.

Her face lit up. “I did it!”

The vendor took the plush rabbit down from its hook and gave it to her, and she turned and held it up to Yichen like a trophy, and he leaned down and kissed her cheek in the middle of the market, in front of the vendor and a family of four.

“Well done.”

The vendor smiled at them.

Xiaoran’s face warmed.

She looked away interested in the plush toys.

They eventually found a small bench near the edge of the market.

Xiaoran sat down, placing the rabbit beside her.

Yichen handed her the last of their drinks and sat beside her.

For a while, they watched the crowd.

The night market was familiar to her in a way university never could be. She knew which streets connected to which, which stalls had the best food, and where the crowds would become difficult to navigate.

She had done the second half of her growing up here.

Yichen looked around.

“Do you come here often?”

“Not anymore. When I was younger, almost every week.”

“With your parents?”

“Sometimes. Sometimes with friends.”

She pointed toward a small alley.

“We used to go through there to get home faster. But my mom never let me walk it alone after dark.”

“Did you listen?”

“Of course.”

He raised an eyebrow.

She corrected herself.

“Most of the time.”

He laughed.

She leaned into his shoulder.

“I used to think this place was so big.”

“And now?”

“Now it feels smaller.”

He looked at the streets.

“Because you’ve grown up?”

“Maybe.”

She was quiet.

Then she turned her face slightly toward him.

“I’m glad you came.”

He looked down.

“Me too.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I wanted to show you this place properly.”

He brushed his thumb over her hand. “I like seeing where you grew up. The second half of it.”

She held his gaze.

“Why?”

“Because it tells me a little more about you.”

She lowered her eyes.

“I know the Xiaoran who goes to university, who studies too late, who takes photographs, who complains about group projects.”

She laughed.

“But I didn’t know the Xiaoran who used to come here every week and argue about which food stall was better.”

“I still argue about that.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She nudged him.

His mouth curved.

“And I like knowing.”

Her expression softened.

Then she tucked herself against his shoulder again.

They walked back to her building at half past nine, Xiaoran carrying the plush rabbit, Yichen carrying the remaining food. Her mother was on the fourth-floor balcony, taking in the washing that had survived the typhoon, and she leaned over the railing when she saw them at the gate.

“You’re back!”

“We went to the night market!”

“Did you eat properly?”

“Yes.”

“How much did you eat?”

“Quite a bit, Auntie,” Yichen called up.

“What’s that?”

Xiaoran held up the rabbit. “I won it! He lost three rings!”

Her mother looked at Yichen over the railing. “Basketball player,” she said, to nobody, and went inside with the washing.

He didn’t come up. His own house was twenty minutes away and the metro was running again, and the spare room had been for the storm. They sat instead on the low wall by the gate, where she had sat with Meilin and Yuhao at sixteen, and the security guard in the booth turned his radio down a little, out of either tact or curiosity.

“Are you planning to bring all of this back to campus?” he said, looking at the paper bags.

She looked up.

“Of course.”

“Even the rabbit?”

“The rabbit’s the main thing.” She sat it on the wall between them, facing the street, like a chaperone.

“Do you like the night market?”

“Yes.”

“Would you come again?”

He didn’t hesitate.

“Of course.”

“Even if I make you walk around for two hours?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I keep buying food?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I make you play those games again?”

He met her eyes.

“That depends.”

“On what?”

“Whether you’re going to let me win.”

She laughed and leaned against his shoulder, and he moved the rabbit out of the way and put his arm around her.

For a while, they stayed like that.

Then Xiaoran said, “I think I like having you here.”

He looked down at her.

“Here?”

“In this city. At my house. With my parents.”

His expression softened.

She continued, a little shy now.

“It feels nice. Like I don’t have to keep separating everything. My university life, my family, you...”

He understood what she meant.

He rested his cheek against her hair.

“You don’t have to.”

She looked up.

That got a smile out of him.

“I’m happy to be part of all of it.”

Her eyes softened.

Then she leaned forward and kissed him.

It was a small, slow kiss, followed by another against the corner of his mouth.

When she pulled away, he was smiling.

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re doing that smile again.”

“What smile?”

“The one that makes me feel like you’re thinking something.”

He brushed his thumb against her cheek. “I was thinking that your half of the city is quite nice.”

She looked suspicious.

“That’s all?”

“And that I wouldn’t mind coming back.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Good.”

He stood up and gave her the rabbit back. “Now go to sleep. I’m coming back at eight.”

“Why?”

“Your mother wants to take us to breakfast.”

Xiaoran lifted her head.

“She told you?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“While you were buying the rabbit.”

She blinked at him.

“Why does my mother tell you things before me?”

“Maybe she trusts me more.”

Xiaoran picked up the plush rabbit and gently hit his arm with it. Yichen laughed, caught the rabbit before it fell, and gave it back to her a second time.

From the fourth floor, a voice said, “Eight o’clock. Not five past,” and the balcony door slid shut.

chapters.desc: That summer he is in and out of her family’s home so often that one evening her mother says hello to the door.
chapters.title: The Door Says Hello
chapters.epigraph: “My mother said hello to a door.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had been to Xiaoran’s family home a handful of times that summer, since the night of the typhoon. He knew where the slippers were kept, which cupboard held the cups, and that her mother would always offer him more food even when he insisted he was full.

He was comfortable there.

Perhaps a little too comfortable.

Which was why he had never expected to find himself hiding behind a door.

It happened on a Saturday afternoon.

Xiaoran had invited him over to work on their respective assignments. Her mother was supposed to be out for most of the afternoon, and Xiaoran had confidently told him that they would have the living room to themselves.

She had been wrong.

Wrong.

“You’re sure she’s not coming back?”

Yichen sat at the dining table, looking at the laptop open in front of him.

Xiaoran was lying on the sofa with her feet tucked beneath her.

“She said she was going to visit Auntie Hui.”

“All right.”

“She won’t be back until dinner.”

“Okay.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Why are you asking so many questions?”

“Because of the rule.”

She laughed. Since the spring of the gaokao year, Mrs. Lin had had exactly one rule about Zhou Yichen, delivered at the kitchen table with a red pen in her hand: not in this flat when there’s no adult home.

“That rule was for high school.”

“It was never formally repealed.”

“I’m nineteen.”

“The rule doesn’t have an age on it. I checked,” Yichen said.

She laughed.

“My mother likes you.”

“I know.”

She lifted her head.

“You’re very confident.”

“She’s told me.”

Xiaoran smiled, remembering the last time her mother had sent him home with a container of food and instructions to remind Xiaoran to eat properly.

“She does like you.”

“Good,” he said, and returned his attention to his laptop.

They worked for a while.

Xiaoran was editing a presentation, while Yichen was reading through a document. Every so often, she would turn her screen toward him to ask a question. He would give her an answer, sometimes suggesting a different structure or pointing out something she had overlooked.

It was a comfortable afternoon.

Until the front door opened.

Xiaoran heard the sound first.

She froze.

Yichen looked up.

They both stared toward the entrance.

Then her mother’s voice came from the hallway.

“Xiaoran? I’m home!”

Xiaoran sat upright.

Her eyes widened.

Yichen closed his laptop.

“Didn’t you say—”

“I know!”

Her mother continued calling from the entrance.

“Xiaoran?”

“Coming!”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

For one brief second, neither moved.

“Hide,” she whispered. A year of that rule did things to a person.

Yichen blinked. “What?”

“Hide!”

“Xiaoran—”

“Please!”

She grabbed his wrist and pulled him away from the dining table.

The nearest door was the small storage room beside the living room.

She opened it.

Yichen looked inside.

It was full of cleaning supplies, spare household items, and several boxes that had clearly been there for years.

He looked back at her.

She clasped her hands together.

“Just for a minute.”

He stared at her.

Then, with the composure of a man who had apparently accepted that this was his afternoon now, he stepped inside.

Xiaoran closed the door.

Her mother came into the living room, still in her outdoor shoes, carrying a shopping bag. “Why is your laptop on the table?”

Xiaoran stood beside the sofa, trying to look natural.

“I’m studying.”

“Alone?”

“Yes.”

Her mother glanced at the two cups on the table.

Xiaoran followed her gaze.

One cup was hers.

The other was Yichen’s.

She looked at the cup, then at her mother, then at the cup again.

Her mother raised an eyebrow.

“Did you have someone over?”

Xiaoran smiled.

“No.”

A pause.

Her mother looked at the second cup.

“Then who drank this?”

Xiaoran looked at it.

“...Me.”

“Twice?”

She opened her mouth.

Closed it.

Then said, “I was thirsty.”

Her mother stared at her.

Xiaoran smiled harder.

It wasn’t working.

“All right. I’m going to put my things away,” her mother said slowly.

“Okay!”

Her mother walked down the hallway.

Xiaoran exhaled.

She turned toward the storage room.

And then she heard it.

A small sound.

A soft rustle.

She looked toward the door.

Her heart nearly stopped.

Her mother returned to the living room carrying a shopping bag.

She stopped.

Looked at Xiaoran, then looked at the storage room door.

“Why is that door closed?”

Xiaoran’s entire body went rigid.

“Because...”

Her mother waited.

“...I closed it.”

Her mother tilted her head.

“Why?”

Xiaoran looked at the door, then at her mother, then at the door again.

“Because it’s a door?”

Her mother blinked.

The room was completely silent.

Then her mother smiled.

“All right.”

She walked toward the storage room, and on the way she glanced, back at the hall, at the shoe rack beside the front door, where a pair of size forty-four trainers sat neatly beside Xiaoran’s slippers, laces tucked in, the way only one person in the world tucked in his laces.

Xiaoran moved immediately.

“Mom! Do you want tea?”

Her mother stopped.

“Tea?”

“Yes! I’ll make you tea.”

“That’s nice.”

Xiaoran rushed toward the kitchen.

Her mother continued toward the storage room.

And before Xiaoran could turn around, she heard her mother’s voice.

“Hello, door.”

Silence.

Then:

“Hello, Yichen.”

Xiaoran stopped in the kitchen doorway.

She closed her eyes.

There was no saving this.

Her mother opened the storage room door.

Yichen stood inside.

He was holding a folded umbrella in one hand.

He looked at her mother.

Then, with the same polite expression he used when greeting university professors and elderly relatives, he bowed his head slightly.

“Hello, Auntie.”

Her mother looked at him, then at the umbrella, then back at him.

“Yichen.”

“Yes, Auntie.”

“What are you doing in there?”

Yichen paused.

A perfectly reasonable man might have explained that he had been invited over, that Xiaoran had panicked, or that the situation had developed quickly.

Instead, he looked at the umbrella in his hand.

Then said:

“I was... looking for something.”

Her mother glanced at the shelves.

“An umbrella?”

“Yes.”

“Inside the storage room?”

“Yes.”

Her mother nodded slowly.

“Did you find it?”

Yichen looked down at the umbrella.

“Yes.”

Her mother smiled.

“Good.”

Xiaoran wanted the floor to open.

Her mother turned toward the kitchen.

“Xiaoran, why didn’t you tell me Yichen was here?”

Xiaoran appeared in the doorway.

She was blushing so hard that she could feel her ears burning.

“I was going to.”

“When?”

She looked at Yichen.

He was standing beside the storage room door, still holding the umbrella.

His expression was calm.

Too calm.

“Later,” Xiaoran muttered.

Her mother laughed.

“Later?”

“Yes.”

“Is he a secret?”

“No!”

“Then why was he hiding behind the door?”

Xiaoran covered her face.

Yichen, to his credit, didn’t laugh.

At least not openly.

He stepped forward.

“I’m sorry, Auntie. I should have greeted you properly when you came in.”

Her mother waved her hand.

“Don’t worry. I was just surprised.”

Then she looked at Xiaoran.

“Next time, don’t make your guest hide in the storage room.”

“Mom!”

Her mother laughed again.

The three of them ended up sitting in the living room.

Yichen had put the umbrella back where it belonged. Xiaoran had made tea. Her mother had brought out fruit and a plate of biscuits.

The atmosphere was perfectly normal.

Which somehow made Xiaoran feel even more embarrassed.

Her mother asked Yichen about his studies, his basketball schedule, and whether he had eaten lunch.

He answered each question politely.

Xiaoran sat beside him, occasionally giving her mother a warning look whenever she seemed about to mention the storage room.

Her mother ignored every single one.

“So, you two were studying together?” she said, pouring more tea.

“Yes, Auntie.”

“That’s good. Xiaoran has been busy with her projects lately.”

Yichen nodded.

“She’s been working hard.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

He glanced back at her.

There was a faint smile at the corner of his mouth.

She squinted at him.

Don’t you dare.

He looked away.

Her mother continued, “You should both remember to take breaks. Studying all day isn’t good.”

“Yes, Auntie.”

“And Yichen, you can come over whenever you like. You don’t have to hide.”

Xiaoran made a strangled sound.

Yichen lowered his head politely.

“Thank you, Auntie.”

Her mother smiled.

“Next time, take your shoes in with you,” she said, as casually as if she were commenting on the weather.

Xiaoran put both hands over her face.

Yichen finally laughed.

After her mother went into the kitchen, Xiaoran turned toward him.

“You laughed.”

He met her eyes.

“I did.”

“You weren’t supposed to.”

“I’m sorry.”

“No, you’re not.”
