She leaned closer and whispered, “You could have just come out.”

“You told me to hide.”

“Because I panicked!”

“I noticed.”

She looked at him.

He reached over and gently moved her hands away from her face.

“Don’t be embarrassed.”

“My mother said hello to a door.”

“She was being polite.”

Xiaoran made a helpless sound.

He laughed and pressed a kiss into her hair.

“At least she knows I’m here now.”

“She knew you were here before she opened the door. She saw your shoes.”

“I tuck my laces in. She knows that,” he said, with real regret.

“And she knows you were hiding.”

“Also true.”

“And she’ll probably remember this forever.”

He considered it.

“Probably.”

Xiaoran groaned and leaned against his shoulder.

Yichen wrapped an arm around her.

After a moment, he said, “For what it’s worth, your storage room has a very good umbrella.”

She lifted her head.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed again.

And from the kitchen, her mother’s voice called:

“Yichen, would you like some more fruit?”

He looked toward the kitchen.

“Yes, thank you, Auntie.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

He smiled down at her.

“What?”

“You’re too comfortable here.”

“Your mother invited me.”

“She invited you after finding you in a cupboard.”

“Storage room.”

She hit his arm.

He caught her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Next time, I’ll stay in the living room.”

“Next time?”

“Unless you tell me to hide again.”

She buried her face against his shoulder.

He was never going to let her forget this.

chapters.desc: Three years together, and Lin Xiaoran has never once seen Zhou Yichen watch basketball. Until 8 AM on a Saturday.
chapters.title: The Terrifying Discovery That Zhou Yichen Was a Nerd
chapters.epigraph: “It’s not nerd things. It’s an organized binder.”
chapters.content:
For almost three years, Lin Xiaoran believed she understood Zhou Yichen completely. Basketball. Business major. Good grades. Annoyingly handsome. Secret softie. Simple. Reasonable. Normal. Then one Saturday morning, she discovered a side of him that genuinely frightened her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It began because Xiaoran was bored. She had claimed one corner of Yichen’s sofa at eight in the morning, supposedly to study, and was mostly drawing pandas in the margins of her media theory notes. Yichen sat at the other end with his laptop. Peaceful. Normal. Then the laptop let out a roar—a full arena of people screaming at once. Xiaoran looked up.

“…What was that?”

“Hm?”

“That.”

Yichen glanced at the screen. “Oh. The game started.”

“What game? It’s eight in the morning.”

“It’s eight in the evening in New York.”

She stared at him. “You get up at eight on a Saturday to watch basketball?”

“Sometimes seven.”

“You never told me.”

“You never asked.”

Fair. Annoyingly fair. She already knew he loved basketball. Everyone knew. She had watched him play for three years, held his jacket through tournaments, researched potassium for him. But she had never once seen him watch it. So she climbed across the sofa and sat beside him, curious. That was her first mistake.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the screen, players ran up and down a court under blinding lights while two commentators talked fast. Xiaoran understood the basics: ball, hoop, tall men. Then she noticed something horrifying. Yichen was paying attention. Not casual attention, not background-noise attention. The kind of focus he usually reserved for his own games, elbows on his knees, eyes moving across the whole court instead of following the ball. One play ended in a missed shot. Immediately—

“He should have switched.”

Xiaoran turned slowly. “…What?”

“The big man stayed in drop coverage. That gave the guard the whole pull-up.”

“What.”

“And the weak-side help was late, so the corner was open anyway.”

“What.”

“They’ve been doing it all quarter. His shooting numbers off the dribble are the best in the league this month.”

“WHAT.”

Yichen finally looked at her, and paused, because she was staring at him like he had grown a second head.

“…You know what all of that means?” she asked.

“Hm.”

“ALL of it?”

“Hm.”

She grabbed both his shoulders. “WHO ARE YOU?”

✦ ✦ ✦

It got worse, because once she started asking questions, he answered them.

“How do you know they’ll lose?”

“They’re losing the possession battle. Too many turnovers.”

“The what battle?”

“And their spacing is terrible. Look—four guys on one side of the floor.”

“Yichen, you’re speaking wizard.”

“It’s basketball.”

“It is NOT the basketball I know. The basketball I know is you running around looking handsome and me screaming.”

“That’s also basketball.”

The terrifying part was that he wasn’t even trying. It just came out of him, the way math did, the way finding her in a crowd did. Then, during a commercial break, Xiaoran discovered the bookshelf. Huge mistake. Behind the business textbooks, filling an entire shelf, was a row of thick notebooks with years written on the spines in his neat handwriting, starting from when he was thirteen. She pulled one out. Inside were hand-drawn diagrams—circles and arrows and dotted lines—with notes in the margins. Backdoor cut works if the wing over-helps. Try in practice. Dad says I always pass too early.

Under the notebooks was a shoebox full of ticket stubs from city league games, a dog-eared book called Spacing, Tempo and the Modern Offense, and a binder of printed shot charts with colored highlighter on every page. She held up the binder like evidence in a courtroom.

“What is THIS.”

Yichen glanced over. “Shot charts.”

“You PRINTED them. And HIGHLIGHTED them.”

“It’s easier to see on paper.”

“You did this for FUN?”

“Hm.”

Silence. Her boyfriend was a nerd. An actual nerd. Not a basketball player who happened to be smart—a basketball nerd, with a filing system. Yichen looked confused by her reaction. To him this was obviously normal.

“My dad used to watch games with me. He’d pause the replay and ask what I would’ve done,” he said, by way of explanation.

“THAT DOESN’T EXPLAIN THE HIGHLIGHTER.”

He looked at the binder, then at her, then back at the binder, genuinely puzzled about where the problem was.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the game came back, the calm, composed Zhou Yichen disappeared entirely.

“Why would you take that shot? No. NO. There’s twenty seconds on the clock.”

“They just threw the game away.”

Xiaoran stared at him. This man was emotionally invested. Deeply, aggressively invested in a team on the other side of the planet that didn’t know he existed. Then, in the last minute, one player made a cut so clean the defense didn’t even turn around in time, caught the pass in stride, and laid it in. Yichen sat bolt upright.

“THAT was beautiful.”

Xiaoran had never heard him call anything beautiful except a basketball play of his own, and her. Apparently, now there were three things.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rest of the morning became educational suffering, because every time she asked one question, he answered with a lecture.

“What’s a pick-and-roll?”

Twenty minutes.

“What’s drop coverage?”

Fifteen minutes, with diagrams on the back of her media theory notes.

“Why does everyone keep yelling about spacing?”

Thirty minutes. She regretted that one deeply. When the game finally ended, Xiaoran sat slumped against the cushions, mentally exhausted. Yichen looked perfectly happy.

“…You really love this,” she said.

“Hm.”

Simple answer. But it landed differently, because she rarely saw him like this. No competing, no looking after everyone around him: just excited, the way a kid gets excited. A little nerdy.

“I didn’t know,” she said.

“Know what?”

“That you could talk this much.”

He laughed—properly laughed.

“You asked questions.”

“YOU HAD ANSWERS READY. You had DIAGRAMS.”

She leaned against his shoulder anyway, warm and comfortable.

“It’s cute,” she said.

“What is?”

“You. Getting this excited about nerd things.”

“It’s not nerd things.”

“You have a binder.”

“It’s an organized binder.”

“SEE.”

He laughed again, helplessly, and put an arm around her waist. Xiaoran smiled into his shoulder. Three years, and she was still finding new parts of him—especially the parts nobody else got to see.

“Want to watch the game tomorrow?” he asked.

She looked up, suspicious. “Are you trying to convert me?”

“Maybe.”

“Will there be another lecture?”

“Probably.”

“Then no.”

“Understandable.”

But for the rest of the week, Lin Xiaoran kept asking—completely out of nowhere, in the middle of lunch, in the library, once during a movie—“What’s drop coverage again?”

Just to watch Zhou Yichen accidentally turn into a basketball nerd all over again.

chapters.desc: She mutes a girl who posted about Yichen. He mutes an account that posted about her. Fang Ze finds out about both.
chapters.title: Blocked
chapters.epigraph: “Because they don’t know you.”
chapters.content:
The first account Xiaoran muted was a girl from the university’s neighboring faculty.

She didn’t even know the girl personally.

She only knew her name because it appeared beneath a photograph of Yichen, accompanied by a caption that made Xiaoran pause halfway through eating her breakfast.

Zhou Yichen is actually unfairly handsome. How does someone look this good after basketball practice?

I saw him at the sports center yesterday. He’s even taller in person.

Does anyone know if he’s single?

I heard he’s not.

That doesn’t mean we can’t admire him.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

Then she put down her spoon.

She wasn’t angry. Not exactly.

The girl hadn’t done anything wrong. Yichen was handsome. Xiaoran was aware of this fact long before the rest of the university had apparently reached a collective agreement about it.

It was just that she didn’t want to read about it while eating her breakfast.

She tapped the three dots.

Mute.

The post disappeared from her feed.

Xiaoran returned to her cereal.

Problem solved.

At least, that was what she thought.

Yichen discovered the situation that afternoon.

They were sitting together at the usual vending machine between their faculties, their twelve-minute meeting squeezed between Xiaoran’s media lecture and his next business class.

Xiaoran was drinking iced tea. Yichen had a bottle of water.

He was scrolling through his phone when he noticed her looking over his shoulder. “You’ve been staring at my screen.”

“I wasn’t.”

He turned the phone slightly toward her.

She immediately looked away.

Yichen’s mouth curved.

“All right.”

She took another sip.

A few seconds later, he said, “Did you see the post?”

“What post?”

“The one about the basketball team.”

“No.”

“The one with my photograph.”

“No.”

He looked at her. She looked back with an expression of complete innocence.

“Interesting,” he said.

She narrowed her eyes. “Why are you asking?”

“Someone sent it to me.”

“Who?”

“A friend.”

“What did they say?”

“That apparently I’m becoming popular.”

Xiaoran nearly choked on her drink.

Yichen reached over and took the bottle from her before she spilled it.

“Careful.”

She coughed once, then glared at him.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little.”

“You’re not popular.”

“Thank you.”

“I mean, you were already popular.”

“That’s better.”

She pressed her lips together, trying not to smile.

Yichen watched her for another moment before returning to his phone.

He didn’t ask whether she’d seen the post again.

He didn’t need to.

The second account she muted belonged to someone who had uploaded a video of Yichen playing basketball.

It was a perfectly ordinary university sports clip. The camera followed him during a match, capturing a few passes, a jump shot, and the moment he turned toward his teammates after scoring.

Xiaoran watched it twice.

Then she read the caption.

The Business faculty’s number one reason to attend university basketball games.

She stared.

Then she read the comments.

I came for the game but stayed for him.

His girlfriend must be so lucky.

Wait, he has a girlfriend?

Apparently, but I’ve never seen her.

Xiaoran paused.

She had never considered herself secretive.

She attended his matches when she could. His friends knew her. Some of his teammates knew her. Their university friends certainly knew they were together.

But they didn’t post each other constantly.

Still, she found herself staring at the last comment.

I’ve never seen her.

She muted the account.

Yichen’s discovery happened a day later.

He was waiting outside Xiaoran’s faculty building when his phone showed a notification from a university confession account.

Someone had posted a photograph of Xiaoran.

It was taken during a student media event. She was standing beside a display board, holding a camera, her hair tied back and her expression focused on something outside the frame.

The caption read:

Who is this girl from Media? Saw her at the exhibition. She’s really pretty.

Yichen looked at the photograph.

He recognized the event immediately.

He’d been there that afternoon, although Xiaoran hadn’t noticed him until he’d appeared beside her with a drink.

He read the comments, which he had promised himself after last spring he would never do again.

I think she’s in second year.

Does anyone know her name?

She’s always around the media building.

I heard she has a boyfriend.

Lucky guy.

Yichen stared at the screen.

Then he tapped the account.

Mute.

He returned to his messages.

A notification appeared.

Xiaoran: Where are you?

Yichen: Outside your building.

Xiaoran: Coming!

He slipped his phone into his pocket just as she appeared through the entrance.

“Yichen!”

He took her bag.

“Slow down.”

“I thought you were going to leave.”

“I said I’d wait.”

She smiled and reached for his hand.

They started walking.

After a moment, she looked up at him.

“Did you see the post?”

Yichen glanced down.

“What post?”

She stopped.

He stopped too.

For two seconds, they stared at each other.

Then Xiaoran’s eyes narrowed.

“...You muted it.”

Yichen smiled.

“Did you?”

She opened her mouth.

Closed it, then looked away.

He laughed.

It took another week for them to realize what was happening.

They were in the library, sitting opposite each other at a table near the windows.

Xiaoran was supposed to be working on a presentation. Yichen was reviewing lecture notes.

Her phone vibrated.

She glanced at it.

Nothing important.

She returned to her laptop.

A few minutes later, Yichen’s phone vibrated.

He checked it, then put it down.

Xiaoran noticed the notification.

“Who was that?”

“Fang Ze.”

“What did he want?”

“He sent me a post.”

“About what?”

“Someone.”

She looked up.

“Who?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Apparently, someone has been asking about you.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Me?”

“Yes.”

She sat a little straighter.

“Who?”

“I don’t know.”

“What did they say?”

“Fang Ze said the comments were getting ridiculous.”

She frowned.

“Why?”

Yichen tilted his phone toward her.

It was a screenshot.

The university confession account had uploaded another photograph of her, this time taken from behind while she was walking across campus with her camera bag.

The caption was harmless enough.

Does anyone know the girl who takes photographs around the Media faculty?

But the comments had become increasingly familiar.

She’s pretty.

I think she’s dating someone from Business.

Isn’t that Zhou Yichen’s girlfriend?

Wait, really?

Xiaoran looked at him, then at the screenshot, then back at him.

“How did Fang Ze even find this?”

“He follows the account.”

“Why?”

“Entertainment, apparently.”

She stared at the screen.

“That’s ridiculous.”

Yichen nodded.

“Agreed.”

She put her phone beside his.

“Did you mute it?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

Which was answer enough.

Xiaoran leaned back.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Did you mute the account?”

“Yes.”

She looked at him for another moment, then a smile appeared.

“You did.”

“You did too.”

“How do you know?”

He pointed at her phone.

“Because you haven’t received a single notification from that account in two weeks, and you’ve been suspiciously calm whenever someone mentions it.”

She looked offended.

“I am naturally calm.”

“Of course.”

“And I don’t care about those things.”

“Naturally.”

She eyed him.

“Stop agreeing with me like that.”

He laughed under his breath.

“All right.”

They went back to work for four minutes.

Then Xiaoran whispered, “Wait.”

Yichen looked up.

“What?”

“Are we both muting people who talk about each other?”

He considered it.

“Seems that way.”

She covered her mouth.

Her shoulders began to shake.

Yichen watched her, amused, until she finally laughed.

“We’re ridiculous.”

His mouth curved.

“A little.”

The actual confrontation happened over dinner.

An ordinary dinner with Fang Ze, who had somehow acquired information that neither of them had intended to share.

They were sitting at a small restaurant near campus. Fang Ze had been talking about a basketball match when he looked at Yichen.

“By the way, I sent you that post last week.”

Yichen nodded.

“I saw it.”

“You muted the account, didn’t you?”

“Yes.”

Fang Ze grinned.

“I knew it.”

Xiaoran looked up from her food.

“How did you know?”

“Because I sent him another post yesterday, and he didn’t react. Usually, he’d at least tell me the photograph was terrible.”

Yichen took a sip of water.

“Most of the photographs are terrible.”

“See? That’s what I’m talking about.”

Fang Ze turned to Xiaoran.

“And you. What about me?”

“You muted the confession account too, didn’t you?”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

Yichen looked at her.

Neither answered.

Fang Ze’s expression slowly changed.

“Oh, my God.”

“Don’t,” Yichen said.

Fang Ze leaned forward.

“You two are doing this?”

“We’re eating,” Yichen replied.

“You’re both muting accounts that post about the other person?”

Xiaoran put down her chopsticks.

“It’s not like that.”

“Then what is it like?”

She hesitated.

“Sometimes I don’t want to see people talking about him.”

Fang Ze grinned.

“And you?” he asked Yichen.

Yichen calmly picked up another piece of food.

“Same.”

Fang Ze stared at him, then looked between them, then burst out laughing.

“That’s actually insane.”

Xiaoran frowned.

“Why?”

“Because you two are behaving like a pair of jealous old people.”

“We’re not jealous,” Xiaoran protested.

Fang Ze nodded enthusiastically.

“Of course not.”

Yichen looked at him.

“Finish your dinner.”

“I’m just saying. The university has thousands of students, and you two have personally decided to protect each other from the existence of the internet.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

Fang Ze pointed at them.

“Look at you! You’re not even denying it!”

Later that evening, Xiaoran and Yichen walked back to campus together.

“Do you think we’re strange?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Compared to Fang Ze?”

“Generally.”

He thought.

“No.”

That made her grin.

“Good.”

They walked a little farther.

Then she asked, “Do you ever feel uncomfortable when people talk about me?”

“Sometimes.”

She looked up.

“Why?”

“Because they don’t know you.”

She was quiet.

He said, “They see a photograph, or a few seconds of a video, and decide they know something about you.”

Xiaoran looked down at the pavement.

“That’s true.”

“And I don’t particularly enjoy strangers discussing you as though you’re someone they know.”

She smiled.

“That’s a little possessive.”

“I’ve been called worse. Does it bother you?”

She considered the question, then shook her head.

“No.”

He squeezed her hand.

“What about you? Do you mind when people talk about me?” she asked.

“Not if they’re being respectful.”

She nodded.

“Me too.”

A pause.

“Although. I don’t like the comments asking if you’re single,” she said.

Yichen glanced at her.

“Why?”

“Because you’re not.”

His smile appeared slowly. “How do you know?”

She looked at him as if he had asked the most ridiculous question in the world.

“Because you’re dating me.”

He laughed.

“Right.”

She squeezed his hand.

“And I don’t like people asking whether you have a girlfriend when they could simply ask you.”

“That would require them to speak to me.”

“Exactly.”

He looked down at her, amused.

“Would you prefer I put a sign on my forehead?”

She considered it.

“Maybe.”

“What would it say?”

That made her grin.

“Taken. Please admire from a distance.”

Yichen laughed properly this time.

“I don’t think that’s necessary.”

“Why?”

He stopped walking.

Then gently drew her closer by their joined hands.

“Because the person I want to know I’m taken is already holding my hand.”

Xiaoran’s smile softened.

She looked at him for a second before leaning forward to kiss his cheek.

“That’s a good answer.”

“I thought so.”

She laughed and continued walking.

That night, Xiaoran was lying on her bed when she received a message from Yichen.

Yichen: Have you muted Fang Ze?

She blinked.

Xiaoran: What?

Yichen: He just sent me another post.

Xiaoran: About you?

Yichen: About us.

She sat up.

Xiaoran: What did he send?

A screenshot appeared.

It was a photograph of them walking across campus earlier that evening. Xiaoran was holding Yichen’s hand, looking up at him while he smiled down at her.

The caption read:

University’s most obvious couple. Seen together again.

She stared at it, then laughed.

Xiaoran: I’m muting Fang Ze.

Yichen: He’s not an account.

Xiaoran: He should be.

Yichen: Good night, Xiaoran.

She smiled at the screen.

Xiaoran: Good night.

A moment later, she sent another message.

Xiaoran: Actually, don’t mute him. I want to see what else he posts about us.

Yichen: I thought you didn’t like people talking about us.

Xiaoran: I don’t.

Yichen: Then?

Xiaoran: But I like seeing pictures of us.

He opened the photograph again.

He liked it too.

Not because anyone had posted it, or because people thought they looked good together.

But because Xiaoran was looking at him in that particular way she did when she forgot anyone else was around.

He saved the picture, then sent her one final message.

Yichen: I’ll keep this one.

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: I like the way you’re looking at me.

She stared at the screen, then buried her face in her pillow.

A few seconds later, she typed:

Xiaoran: You’re so annoying.

Yichen: I know.

She smiled into the pillow.

And, for the first time in two weeks, she opened the university confession account again.

Just to find the photograph.

She saved it, then muted the account again.

chapters.desc: Fang Ze unlocks Yichen’s phone with her birthday on the first try, and a Saturday in October turns into a conversation about passcodes.
chapters.title: The Passcode Swap
chapters.epigraph: “Because I made you tell me your passcode.”
chapters.content:
The argument started over a phone, and the phone wasn’t even hers.

It was a Saturday afternoon in October of their second year. Xiaoran was sitting cross-legged on Yichen’s sofa, across the road from her own building, waiting for him to finish getting ready for dinner, and she had just heard something deeply offensive from Fang Ze.

“He did what?”

“He unlocked it. At practice. I left it on the bench, Coach wanted the schedule, and Fang Ze picked it up and got in on the first try,” Yichen said from the bedroom.

“How?”

Yichen came out with his wallet, and looked at her the way he did when the answer was standing in front of him in socks.

“Your birthday.”

She stared at him. “Your passcode is still my birthday?”

“It’s been your birthday since I was seventeen.”

“And Fang Ze knows my birthday?”

“The whole team knows your birthday. You brought a cake to training.”

She had. She had forgotten that this made her birthday public information.

“Change it,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because if Fang Ze can get into your phone, so can anyone. That’s basic security. My mother would be horrified.”

He considered this. “Your mother would be horrified,” he agreed, and picked up his phone, and turned slightly away from her, and did something with his thumb.

“What did you change it to?”

“Something else.”

“What?”

“If I tell you. Fang Ze could get it out of you,” he said reasonably.

Her mouth fell open. “I would never tell Fang Ze.”

“You told him your birthday.”

“With a cake!”

He slipped the phone into his pocket, unbothered. Xiaoran looked at her own phone, then at him, and unlocked it with his birthday, and then, because she wasn’t going to be the only person in this relationship who could be bribed with cake, she changed it too.

“What’s yours now?” he asked.

“Something else.”

He smiled. “Fair.”

The actual problem appeared that evening.

They were sitting across from each other at a small restaurant near campus. Xiaoran had ordered noodles, while Yichen had chosen rice with grilled chicken. They were sharing a side dish, and she was halfway through telling him about an absurd conversation she’d had with a classmate when his phone lit up.

He glanced at it, then put it in his pocket.

Xiaoran noticed.

“Who was that?”

“Fang Ze.”

“What does he want?”

“He’s asking whether I’m coming to training tomorrow.”

“Then reply.”

“In a minute.”

He reached for his drink.

Xiaoran looked at him.

Then she said, casually, “You can use my phone if you want.”

He looked up.

“For what?”

“To check the time.”

He glanced at the clock on the wall.

“It’s right there.”

“Just offering.”

Yichen looked at her for another second.

Then his mouth curved.

“Thank you.”

She took another bite of her noodles.

A few minutes passed.

Then she reached across the table.

“Can I use your phone?”

He met her eyes.

“For what?”

“To check something.”

“What?”

“Something.”

He slid the phone toward her.

“Go ahead.”

Xiaoran picked it up.

The screen was locked.

She stared at it, then looked at him.

He stared back, perfectly calm.

“What’s the passcode?” she asked.

He took a sip of water.

“You told me to change it.”

“I didn’t mean from me!”

“You didn’t specify. I’m being thorough. Your mother would approve,” he said.

She put his phone down. “You’re unbelievable.”

She crossed her arms.

“Fine. What’s the new one?”

“That’s rather defeating the purpose.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed.

And that was how it began.

The next morning, Xiaoran discovered that her own phone had become an inconvenience.

She was running late for her first lecture and couldn’t remember the password she’d set the previous night. She had changed it, in a temper, to a combination she had been sure she would remember.

She hadn’t.

After three attempts, she stopped and stared at the screen.

Then she called Yichen.

He answered on the second ring.

“Good morning.”

“What’s your birthday?”

There was a pause.

“My birthday?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I forgot my new passcode.”

He was quiet.

Then she heard him laugh.

Not loudly. Just that low, amused laugh that made her immediately regret calling him.

“You’re laughing?”

“I’m sorry.”

“No, you’re not.”

“Not particularly.”

She groaned.

“Yichen.”

“Try the date we first met.”

She froze, then frowned.

“That’s not what I used.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

A pause.

“Try it anyway.”

She did.

The phone unlocked.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

Then she slowly pulled it away from her ear.

“You’re kidding.”

“I thought it might work.”

“You guessed?”

“Educated guess.”

She narrowed her eyes, even though he couldn’t see her.

“That’s cheating.”

“How?”

“You know me.”

“That is generally how relationships work.”

She hung up on him.

A second later, he sent her a message.

Yichen: Have a good lecture.

Xiaoran: I don’t like you.

Yichen: You remembered the passcode.

She stared at the message.

Then, against her better judgment, smiled.

For the first week, the arrangement was mostly amusing.

They had never been secretive with each other. They knew each other’s friends, routines, schedules, and general habits. They had no reason to inspect each other’s phones.

But they had developed a habit of casually using whichever phone was closest.

Yichen would sometimes ask Xiaoran to take a picture with his phone. Xiaoran would occasionally use his phone to check a restaurant address. She would send herself a photograph from his camera roll if he had taken one of her that she liked.

Now, every little thing required asking.

“Can you send me that?”

“Which one?”

“The photo you took yesterday.”

“From my phone?”

“Obviously.”

“All right.”

He sent it.

She looked at the picture, then at him.

“You could have just let me use your phone.”

“You could have just asked me to send it.”

“You’re so annoying.”

He kissed her temple.

“Thank you.”

It became a running joke.

At the library, Xiaoran once asked him to check the time on his phone.

He told her the time.

She asked to see the screen.

He turned it toward her.

She stared at the lock screen.

He stared at her.

Neither said anything.

Then he put the phone away.

She went back to her notes, looking deeply offended.

By the second week, their friends had noticed.

It happened during lunch with Fang Ze.

Fang Ze was sitting opposite them, watching Xiaoran lean across the table to ask Yichen something.

“Can you check the message I sent you?”

Yichen unlocked his phone, opened the chat, and read it aloud.

Xiaoran frowned.

“I wanted to see the picture.”

He forwarded it to her.

She opened it on her own phone.

Fang Ze watched the exchange.

Then he looked at Yichen.

“Why don’t you just let her use your phone?”

Yichen took a bite of his food.

“She doesn’t know the passcode.”

Fang Ze looked at Xiaoran.

“Why?”

“Because he changed it.”

“Why?”

“Because I changed mine.”

Fang Ze blinked.

“Why?”

Xiaoran sat back.

“Because he—”

Yichen calmly interrupted.

“Because she—”

They both stopped.

Fang Ze looked between them.

Then he slowly put down his chopsticks.

“Did you two have a fight?”

“No,” Xiaoran said.

“Yes,” Yichen said at the same time.

She turned to him.

“Excuse me?”

He turned to her.

“Didn’t we?”

“No!”

Fang Ze stared, then a grin spread across his face.

“Oh, this is excellent.”

“Don’t start,” Xiaoran warned.

“How long?”

“How long what?”

“How long have you two been refusing to share phone passcodes?”

Yichen checked his watch. “Nineteen days.”

Fang Ze looked delighted.

“You’re counting?”

“No.”

“You just answered very quickly.”

“I have a good memory.”

Xiaoran groaned.

Fang Ze leaned forward.

“Listen. I need to understand something. You two have been together for years, but you’re fighting over phone passwords?”

“We’re not fighting,” Xiaoran insisted.

Yichen nodded.

“Of course not.”

Fang Ze looked at him.

“Then why do you sound like you’re enjoying this?”

Yichen smiled.

“Because I am.”

Xiaoran kicked him lightly under the table.

He didn’t even flinch.

The third week was when the inconvenience became genuinely ridiculous.

Xiaoran had a group presentation coming up and needed to send Yichen a document she’d downloaded onto her phone. She was carrying several books, a coffee, and her laptop, so she handed him her phone without thinking.

“Can you send this to yourself?”

He took it.

Then both of them looked at the locked screen.

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

Yichen looked down at her.

“Would you like me to guess?”

“No.”

“All right.”

She put everything down on the nearest bench, unlocked her phone, and handed it back.

He sent the document.

Then, just as he was returning it, she caught his sleeve.

“Actually, wait.”

“Hm?”

She looked at him.

“What’s your passcode?”

He looked back.

There was a pause.

Then he said, “You really want to know?”

She hesitated.

“Maybe.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s annoying.”

“That’s not a particularly compelling reason.”

“Yichen.”

He leaned down slightly.

“Are you asking because you want to know, or because you want to win?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth, then closed it.

He nodded, as if she’d answered.

“Thought so.”

She stared at him.

“You are enjoying this far too much.”

“Perhaps.”

He kissed her hair and picked up her books.

“Come on. You’re going to be late.”

She followed him, muttering under her breath.

By the fourth week, they had become so accustomed to the arrangement that neither of them mentioned it.

They still used each other’s phones when necessary, but they asked first. They sent pictures instead of passing devices across the table. They remembered to forward documents. They had learned to live without the convenience.

And, perhaps most importantly, they had discovered that neither of them actually cared about knowing the other’s passcode.

The problem was that neither wanted to admit it first.

It was a Thursday evening when the opportunity finally appeared.

They were sitting in the university library, working at the same table. Xiaoran was editing a presentation, while Yichen was reading through a case study for his Business class.

Her phone battery was nearly dead.

She plugged it into the power bank in her bag, only to discover that the cable wasn’t working.

She sighed.

Yichen looked up.

“What happened?”

“Battery.”

He glanced at her phone.

“Use mine.”

She met his eyes.

He slid his phone across the table.

“There’s a charger in my bag. You can use the cable.”

She picked up the phone, then looked at the lock screen, then at him.

He was already reading again.

She turned the phone over in her hands.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You’re giving me your phone?”

“Yes.”

“Without changing the passcode?”

He looked up.

“Do you need to unlock it?”

She paused, then shook her head.

“No.”

“Then there’s no problem.”

She blinked at him.

He returned to his case study.

Xiaoran slowly put the phone down.

That was it?

After almost a month of this ridiculous competition, he was going to let her use his phone?

She leaned closer.

“You’re not going to ask for mine?”

He held her gaze.

“Do you want me to?”

“No.”

“Then I won’t.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re being very mature.”

“Thank you.”

“I don’t like it.”

Something in his face eased.

“That’s unfortunate.”

She returned to her presentation, but she couldn’t concentrate.

A few minutes later, she reached for his hand under the table.

He turned his palm upward, letting her fingers slip between his.

Neither said anything.

The month ended on a Sunday.

They were at Xiaoran’s apartment, spending the afternoon doing absolutely nothing productive. She was lying on the sofa with her head in Yichen’s lap, scrolling through her phone while he read.

At some point, she reached for his phone on the coffee table.

He glanced down.

“What do you need?”

“Nothing.”

She picked it up.

The screen lit up.

She looked at the lock screen.

Then she looked at him.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Are we still doing this?”

He closed his book.

“Doing what?”

She lifted his phone.

“The passcode thing.”

He looked at her.

Then he smiled.

“Are you tired of it?”

“Yes.”

“Then we can stop.”

She turned onto her back to look at him properly.

“Just like that?”

“Would you like a formal announcement?”

She laughed.

“Maybe.”

He put his book aside and held out his hand.

“Give me your phone.”

She handed it to him.

He unlocked it with the passcode she’d used since the beginning of the month.

She stared.

“You still remember it?”

“Of course.”

“But I changed it.”

“To our first meeting date.”

She blinked.

“How do you remember that?”

He gave her a look.

“Xiaoran.”

She smiled, slightly embarrassed.

He returned her phone.

Then she took his.

“What’s yours?”

He told her.

One, two, zero, six.

She entered the numbers, and the phone unlocked, and she sat looking at it. The sixth of December. The night of the umbrella and the bunny and please let me be your boyfriend.

“I tried your birthday. And mine again. And your student number, and four zeros, and the date of your first match,” she said.

“I know. You tried in the library. I watched.”

“I never tried this.”

“No, I noticed that too,” he agreed.

She handed it back, and didn’t say anything for a while.

He placed both phones on the coffee table.

Then he looked down at her.

“Are we finished?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He brushed her hair back.

“Good.”

She smiled up at him.

“Actually, I think I won.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“How?”

“Because I made you tell me your passcode.”

“You asked.”

“And you answered.”

“Would you like a medal?”

She considered it.

“Yes.”

He bent and kissed her hairline.

“There.”

She laughed.

“That’s not a medal.”

“It’s what I have.”

She reached up, hooked her arms around his neck, and pulled him down for another kiss.

When he lifted his head, his smile was still there.

“Anything else?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Don’t change it again.”

He studied her.

“Why would I?”

She shrugged.

“Just checking.”

He kissed her cheek.

“All right.”

“But if you do. I’m changing mine too,” she said after a few seconds.

He laughed.

“I assumed as much.”

She settled back against him, satisfied.

Their phones stayed on the coffee table, unlocked and forgotten. On Monday at practice, Fang Ze picked up Yichen’s phone from the bench, tried her birthday, tried it again, and put it down, wounded, and nobody on the team ever found out what the new number meant.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen says he doesn’t need anything for his birthday. Lin Xiaoran remembers one sentence from three months ago.
chapters.title: Two Tickets to the Garden
chapters.epigraph: “Of course I remembered.”
chapters.content:
For most people, buying Zhou Yichen a birthday gift was difficult, because he already had everything. A family with money. Good grades. Basketball. Expensive watches, expensive shoes, expensive everything. Whenever his birthday came around, he said the same thing.

“I don’t need anything.”

Annoying answer. Especially for Lin Xiaoran, because this year she wanted the gift to matter.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months before his birthday, she found out what it should be. It was another early weekend morning on his sofa. Since discovering that her boyfriend was secretly a basketball nerd, Xiaoran had become slightly interested in watching games—not much, just enough to understand when he started speaking wizard. She was eating crackers. He was explaining things nobody had asked about. Normal relationship activities. Then the broadcast cut to a wide shot of the arena: an enormous round ceiling, a sea of people, the court glowing in the middle like a stage.

“That’s the Garden,” Yichen said.

“Hm?”

“Madison Square Garden. New York. One day I want to watch a game there.” He was quiet for a second.

Xiaoran looked over, because Zhou Yichen almost never said things like that. He was still watching the screen, completely casual, as if he hadn’t just told her a dream.

“Really?”

“Hm.”

“Why that one?”

“It’s the Garden.”

“That explains nothing.”

He laughed. “The history. The building. The way the crowd sounds. Dad and I used to say we’d go. When I was a kid. He never had the time.” By the end his voice had gone quieter.

“Why not now?”

He shrugged. “Season’s during school. Tickets. Flights. Planning. Maybe someday.” He said it lightly.

Then he went back to explaining spacing, like the conversation had never happened. Lin Xiaoran remembered every word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months later, his birthday arrived. Yichen expected something small. A handmade gift, maybe. Clothes. One of Xiaoran’s chaotic, sincere little presents with a card covered in stickers. Instead she handed him an envelope.

“What is this?”

“Open it.”

He was immediately suspicious, because she looked far too excited. Inside were two tickets. For several seconds, Zhou Yichen’s brain stopped working. He read them, then read them again, then a third time, as if they might rearrange themselves into something more reasonable. New York. Madison Square Garden. A Saturday night in January, during winter break. Two seats, high up, in a section number that began with a two.

“…Yichen?”

Nothing. He was staring at the tickets like they might disappear.

“What is this,” he finally said, very.

Xiaoran blinked. “…Your birthday gift?”

“No.”

“What do you mean, no?”

“No. Xiaoran. These are tickets to the Garden.” He sounded genuinely stunned. A rare event.

“I know.”

“I can read.”

“Good.”

“LIN XIAORAN.”

She started laughing, because he looked so shocked, and the famous calm Zhou Yichen had apparently stopped functioning entirely.

“How,” he said.

So she explained. The prize money from the competition. The freelance video jobs she’d taken on weekends, editing a bakery’s promotional clips and a classmate’s cousin’s wedding. Three months of birthday budget. Learning far more about game schedules and seat maps than she had ever wanted to. Waking up at four in the morning to buy them the minute they went on sale. All because of one sentence on a Saturday morning.

“I wanted to surprise you,” she said.

He didn’t say anything. Suddenly Xiaoran felt nervous. Maybe it was too much. Maybe the seats were too high, or January was a bad time, or he’d rather go with his father, or—Yichen stood up. He walked around the table, pulled her to her feet, and hugged her. Hard. So suddenly that she almost squeaked.

“Yichen?”

He didn’t answer. He didn’t let go, either.

“…Are you okay?”

Then he laughed—soft, disbelieving, almost helpless—against her hair.

“You’re insane.”

“I know.”

“You’re actually insane.”

But he still wasn’t letting go, and that told her everything. Zhou Yichen wasn’t a dramatic person. He didn’t get emotional easily or react loudly. Right now, he looked completely overwhelmed.

“You remembered,” he said.

“Hm?”

“The Garden thing.”

And suddenly she understood. The tickets, New York, even basketball mattered less than this: she had listened. One random morning, one casual sentence, one small dream he’d said out loud and then put away—and she had remembered.

“Of course I remembered,” she said.

He looked down at her, and for once his calm expression was nowhere to be found. The girl he loved had spent three months working and saving for this, just to make him happy. How was anyone supposed to stay calm after that?

“If someone asked me what the best birthday gift I’ve ever gotten was—” he said.

His hand found hers.

“It would be this.”

Xiaoran looked extremely pleased.

“Better than your car?”

“Yes.”

“Better than your watch?”

“Yes.”

“Better than—”

“Stop comparing yourself to objects.”

She laughed. Then a thought hit her.

“Wait. You’re taking me, right? I bought two.”

He finally smiled—the real one, the one that only showed up for her.

“Obviously.”

He laced his fingers through hers.

“You bought the tickets. The least I can do is take the girl I love to New York to use them.”

She kissed him for that, on the mouth, on his sofa, with the game still paused behind them and both his arms round her before she’d finished.

For the next three days, Chen Yuhao became extremely tired of hearing Zhou Yichen talk about Madison Square Garden over the phone. This was impressive, because normally talking too much was Xiaoran’s job.

chapters.desc: Her first paid job earns her two thousand yuan, and she spends every cent of it on a lens.
chapters.title: Her First Paid Gig
chapters.epigraph: “Because I worked for it.”
chapters.content:
The first time Xiaoran earned money from something she had made herself, she received exactly two thousand yuan.

She spent every cent of it on a camera lens.

Yichen thought this was exactly like her.

He just hadn’t expected her to be quite so pleased about it.

It started with a message from one of her seniors in the Media faculty.

A small independent fashion label was looking for someone to photograph its new collection. Nothing extravagant: a half-day shoot, a handful of models, some outdoor and indoor setups, and enough photographs for its social media campaign.

The senior had recommended Xiaoran after seeing a series of photographs she’d taken for a university club event.

At first, Xiaoran assumed there had been a mistake.

She read the message three times, checked the account, and even searched the brand’s name to make sure it was real.

Then she called Meilin.

“Meilin.”

“What?”

“I think someone wants to pay me to take pictures.”

A pause.

“Congratulations?”

“No, listen. They actually want to pay me.”

“Yes, Xiaoran. That’s generally what paid work means.”

“They said two thousand yuan.”

“That’s good.”

“For one shoot.”

“Still good.”

Xiaoran sat upright on her bed, on the fourth floor, in the studio with the broken lift.

“Meilin, I could buy a lens.”

Meilin laughed.

“You haven’t even done the job yet.”

“I know. But I could.”

“Maybe wait until you’ve earned the money before spending it in your head.”

Xiaoran ignored that advice completely.

The shoot took place on a Saturday.

Xiaoran spent the previous evening checking her equipment, charging batteries, cleaning her camera, and writing a small list of shots she wanted to capture.

She was nervous, although she tried not to show it.

It wasn’t the first time she’d photographed people. She had taken pictures for university events and friends, and she was comfortable behind the camera. But this was different. Someone had hired her. Someone was trusting her to deliver something they intended to use professionally.

There was a responsibility attached to that.

She arrived early, introduced herself to the small team, and spent the first twenty minutes observing the location.

The creative director was friendly but busy. The models were young, the styling was simple, and the atmosphere was more relaxed than Xiaoran had expected.

Once she started shooting, her nervousness gradually disappeared.

She moved around the space, adjusted her angles, asked the models to turn slightly toward the light, and occasionally stopped to rearrange a sleeve or move a stray strand of hair.

“Could you look over there for a second?”

“Chin slightly down.”

“Perfect. Hold that.”

She was focused, occasionally biting her lower lip while checking the screen.

At one point, the creative director came over to look at the photographs.

“These are really nice.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“Really?”

“Yes. I like how you’re using the natural light. It feels quite effortless.”

The praise made her smile, but she didn’t let herself get distracted.

“Thank you. I think we can get another set near the window before we finish.”

By the time the shoot ended, she was tired, hungry, and more confident than when she’d arrived.

She had done it.

Not perfectly, perhaps. There were things she’d already noted that she wanted to improve next time. But she had delivered the photographs, received positive feedback, and earned money from something she genuinely enjoyed.

It felt different from receiving an allowance or having someone buy her something.

This money had come from her own work.

And she was absurdly happy about it.

Yichen found out that evening.

They were sitting together at a small café near campus. He had just finished basketball practice, his hair still slightly damp from his shower, while Xiaoran had arrived with her laptop and an expression that suggested she was holding back some important news.

He noticed almost immediately.

“Something happened.”

She smiled. “How do you know?”

“You walked in like you’d won something.”

She laughed and pulled her phone from her bag.

“I got paid today.”

His expression changed.

“Your shoot?”

She nodded enthusiastically. “Two thousand yuan.”

“That’s great.”

“I know!”

He smiled at her excitement.

“How did it go?”

“Really well. They liked the pictures, and the creative director said she liked the natural lighting. I was a little nervous at first, but after a while it was fine. I think I could’ve done some things better, though.”

“You’ll have another chance to improve them next time.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re assuming there’ll be a next time?”

“Did they say they wouldn’t hire you again?”

“No.”

“Then why wouldn’t there be?”

She stared at him before breaking into a smile.

“You’re right.”

He reached across the table and touched her hand. “Two thousand yuan. For your own pictures,” he said, as if he were reading out a final score.

It was such a simple thing to say, and Xiaoran felt her cheeks warm anyway.

She looked down at their hands.

“Thank you.”

“What are you going to do with the money?”

Her smile became suspiciously bright.

“Buy something.”

“Something?”

“A lens.”

Yichen nodded.

“Which one?”

She named it: a secondhand portrait lens from a shop near the station, two thousand and forty yuan, which she had visited three times in October to hold.

He recognized it from the photographs she had sent him from the shop.

“That’s the one you’ve been looking at?”

“Yes.”

“For how long?”

“Quite a while.”

“Then you should get it.”

She eyed him.

“You’re not even going to ask whether I should save the money?”

“Do you want to save it?”

She thought about it.

“Not really.”

“Then buy the lens.”

She laughed.

“You’re very supportive of my financial decisions.”

“I’m supportive of you buying something you’ve been wanting with money you earned yourself.”

That made her quiet.

She looked at him, her expression softening.

“That’s exactly why I want to buy it.”

“Because I earned it,” she said.

His gaze stayed on her.

“I know.”

“I don’t want you to buy it for me.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“I know, but—”

“Xiaoran.”

She stopped.

He rubbed his thumb gently over the back of her hand.

“You don’t have to explain that to me.”

She looked at him, then nodded.

“Okay.”

“Now show me the lens again. I want to make sure you aren’t buying something ridiculous.”

She gasped.

“Excuse me?”

“I’m asking a reasonable question.”

“You don’t even know anything about photography.”

“I know enough to recognize an expensive purchase.”

“That’s not the same thing!”

He laughed.

The next afternoon, Xiaoran went to the camera store.

She had researched the lens thoroughly, compared prices, watched reviews, and read enough photography forums to develop strong opinions about things she hadn’t even known existed a week earlier.

Yichen accompanied her.

Not because she needed him to make the decision, but because he had offered to come along after basketball practice.

He stood beside her while she examined the display model.

“Is this it?” he asked.

“Yes.”

She carefully lifted the lens, checking its weight and looking through it.

The salesperson explained a few details, and Xiaoran listened attentively, asking questions about compatibility, autofocus, and the difference between the display model and the boxed one.

Yichen watched her.

He liked seeing her like this.

She was usually expressive, often distracted by whatever caught her attention, but when she cared about something, she could become remarkably focused. Her questions were precise, her attention thorough, and her excitement barely contained.

When the salesperson finally asked whether she’d like to purchase it, Xiaoran looked at the price tag one more time.

Then she nodded.

“Yes, please.”

She paid with the money from her first gig, every yuan of it and forty of her own.

Yichen didn’t comment when she checked the receipt twice.

He only smiled when she held the box against her chest.

They stopped at a small bakery on the way back.

Xiaoran had been unusually quiet for the past few minutes, looking at the box on her lap.

Yichen glanced over.

“Regretting it?”

She looked up immediately.

“No!”

“Then?”

She turned the box slightly, as if admiring it from another angle.

“I just can’t believe I bought it.”

He smiled.

“You’ve been talking about it for months.”

“I know, but now it’s actually mine.”

“Yes.”

“Because I worked for it.”

“Yes.”

She turned to him.

“Do you think that’s silly?”

“What?”

“Being this happy about a lens.”

He gave her a mildly puzzled look.

“Why would it be silly?”

“I don’t know. It’s just a lens.”

“Then why did you want it?”

“Because it’ll help me take better pictures.”

“And you like taking pictures.”

She nodded.

“So?”

“Then it’s not just a lens.”

“It’s something you wanted, something you worked for, and something that will help you do what you enjoy. I think you’re allowed to be happy about it.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

Then she leaned across the small space between them and kissed his cheek.

“You’re so nice.”

He turned his face slightly toward her.

“Only now?”

She laughed.

“No. Always.”

“Good.”

That evening, Xiaoran tested her new lens.

She photographed the sunlight coming through her bedroom curtains, the little ceramic cup on her desk, the flowers in the kitchen, and the view from her window.

Then she turned toward Yichen.

He was sitting on the floor beside her desk, looking through a basketball schedule on his phone.

She lifted her camera.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Look here.”

He raised his eyes.

Click.

She checked the photograph.

He looked like himself, which was what made her smile.

The light had fallen across his face beautifully, catching the slight curve of his smile and the relaxed expression he wore when he wasn’t paying attention to anyone else.

She took another.

He looked at her over the top of his phone.

“Am I your test subject?”

“Yes.”

“Should I charge you?”

She lowered the camera.

“Why? You’re getting free photographs.”

“Then I should be compensated in another way.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“What do you want?”

He put his phone down.

“A kiss.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“That’s your payment?”

“For now.”

She rolled her eyes, but walked over anyway.

Yichen reached for her waist and pulled her gently between his knees. She leaned down and kissed him, smiling when he kept one hand at her waist after she tried to pull away.

“One more,” he murmured.

“You said one.”

“I’ve changed my mind.”

She laughed and kissed his forehead instead.

“That’s all you’re getting.”

He looked up at her, amused.

“Very strict.”

“Professional photographer. I have boundaries.”

“Understood.”

She returned to her camera, but not before he caught her hand and pressed a kiss to her knuckles.

Later that night, she sent Meilin a photograph of the lens sitting neatly on her desk.

Xiaoran: Bought it.

Meilin: Congratulations. How much did you spend?

Xiaoran: All of it.

Meilin: Of course you did.

Xiaoran: I don’t regret it.

Meilin: You better use it properly.

Xiaoran: I will.

A moment later, Meilin sent another message.

Meilin: Did your boyfriend pay for any of it?

Xiaoran glanced toward Yichen, who was sitting on her bed, reading something for class.

Xiaoran: He bought dinner. I bought my own lens.

Meilin: Good. At least someone has financial sense.

Xiaoran laughed.

Yichen looked up.

“What?”

“Meilin.”

“Should I be concerned?”

“Probably.”

He smiled and returned to his reading.

Xiaoran looked at her camera again.

Two hundred dollars.

A half-day of work.

A box on her desk that she couldn’t stop looking at.

It wasn’t a large achievement, in the scheme of things. She knew that. But it was the first.

Yichen watched her from across the room. She was smiling at the lens again. He shook his head, amused, and didn’t say anything, which she noticed, and liked.

She lifted the camera once more.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“One more picture.”

He closed his book and gave her his attention.

This time, he smiled directly at the camera.

Click.

And Xiaoran knew exactly which photograph she would keep.

chapters.desc: A week after the Garden tickets, Lin Xiaoran turns up to their third anniversary with two packets of instant noodles. Zhou Yichen notices more than she thinks.
chapters.title: Three Years, Quietly
chapters.epigraph: “We’re together. We had dinner. You’re sitting on my sofa. I don’t see the problem.”
chapters.content:
By the time their third anniversary arrived, Lin Xiaoran had become exceptionally skilled at pretending she wasn’t broke.

It was a skill she had been building since a Tuesday morning in October, when she woke up at four to buy two tickets the minute they went on sale.

She had learned to walk past cafés without looking at the menus. She had become good at saying she wasn’t hungry when her friends suggested ordering dessert. She had discovered that the university cafeteria’s cheapest meal was actually quite acceptable if she added enough chilli oil.

And she had become an expert at refusing Zhou Yichen’s offers to buy her things without making it sound like she was refusing him.

The problem was that Zhou Yichen knew her well.

He noticed things. He noticed that she had stopped ordering her usual milk tea after class. He noticed that she had begun checking prices before choosing what to eat. He noticed that she had once taken a considerable amount of time deciding whether she really needed a new notebook. He also noticed that, whenever he suggested going somewhere, she became interested in staying home.

He hadn’t said anything.

Not yet.

But he was beginning to suspect something.

And today, of all days, she had arrived at his apartment carrying a plastic bag containing two packets of instant noodles.

Yichen opened the door.

He looked at the bag, then at her.

“Happy anniversary.”

Xiaoran smiled brightly.

“Happy anniversary!”

He stepped aside to let her in.

She walked past him, took off her shoes, and headed straight for the kitchen.

Yichen closed the door.

“What’s in the bag?”

“Dinner.”

He looked at the plastic bag again.

“That’s dinner?”

“Yes.”

“Interesting.”

She turned around.

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re judging my culinary choices.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He followed her into the kitchen.

Xiaoran placed the two packets on the counter with the seriousness of someone presenting a carefully prepared menu.

“Tonight’s special.”

Yichen looked at the packaging.

“Instant noodles.”

“Correct.”

“Two servings.”

“Very good.”

“With what?”

She paused, then lifted a finger.

“Eggs.”

He nodded.

“Anything else?”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

“Just asking.”

“Green onions.”

“Anything else?”

“You’re asking too many questions for someone who hasn’t offered to cook.”

He smiled.

“All right. I’ll cook.”

She immediately handed him the packets.

“Thank you.”

He looked at her, amused.

It wasn’t that he disliked instant noodles. He had eaten them plenty of times, especially during busy periods at university.

But their third anniversary dinner was apparently going to be prepared in his kitchen with two packets of noodles and whatever ingredients they could find in his refrigerator.

He looked at Xiaoran.

She was already opening the refrigerator, examining its contents.

“Do you have eggs?”

“Yes.”

“Green onions?”

“Top drawer.”

“Vegetables?”

“Some.”

She glanced over her shoulder.

“You’re surprisingly well-stocked.”

“I live here.”

“That’s not a guarantee.”

He leaned against the counter, watching her.

She took out two eggs, a small bunch of green onions, and a container of vegetables.

Then she looked at him.

“Don’t just stand there.”

“What would you like me to do?”

“Wash these.”

He accepted the vegetables.

“Yes, chef.”

“Good assistant.”

The noodles were Xiaoran’s idea.

The decision to eat at his apartment had been hers too. She had told him she wanted something simple, that she didn’t feel like dressing up, and that they had both been busy enough lately without making a big occasion of it.

All of that was true.

What she hadn’t told him was what the tickets had really cost.

He knew about the prize money and the weekend editing jobs. She’d told him at his birthday dinner a week ago, while he was still holding the envelope. She hadn’t told him that the seats had gone up in price on the morning of the sale, or that the difference had come out of everything else: her milk tea, her phone top-up, the new tote bag she’d been going to buy in November, and most of December.

She didn’t regret a single yuan. She just hadn’t expected their third anniversary to arrive one week later.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“Hm?”

“Your noodles are boiling over.”

Her eyes widened.

“Oh!”

She hurried toward the stove.

Yichen moved aside, letting her take over.

“You’re supposed to watch them.”

“I was watching.”

“You were thinking.”

“That’s the same thing.”

“Not when the water is escaping.”

She looked at the pot, then at him.

“You’re very talkative today.”

He smiled and handed her the chopsticks.

She stirred the noodles, muttering something about how difficult it was to cook with an audience.

Yichen didn’t tell her that he had already noticed the way she had been calculating expenses in her head whenever they went out.

He didn’t tell her that he had seen her hesitate before buying a drink last week.

And he certainly didn’t tell her that, when she had arrived earlier, he had noticed she was carrying the same old tote bag she had been using for months, even though its strap was beginning to fray.

He had considered asking.

But he had also noticed something else.

She was happy, the plain kind, nothing like the bright show she put on when she wanted to distract him from something.

She had been smiling since she arrived.

And he didn’t want to turn their anniversary into an interrogation.

So he let her stir the noodles.

They ate on his sofa.

The coffee table had been cleared, leaving enough space for two bowls, two pairs of chopsticks, and a small plate of sliced fruit.

Xiaoran had insisted on arranging everything herself.

She had even found two matching glasses for their drinks.

Yichen looked at the table.

“Very elaborate.”

She sat down beside him.

“Don’t underestimate my preparation.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

She handed him his bowl.

“Happy anniversary.”

He accepted it.

“Happy anniversary.”

They touched their glasses together.

Then Xiaoran took her first bite.

She closed her eyes.

“Mmm.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Good?”

“Very.”

He tasted his own.

“It’s good.”

She smiled proudly.

“See?”

“Although I suspect the chef had something to do with it.”

“Obviously.”

He leaned back against the sofa.

She settled beside him, her legs folded beneath her, and began eating as if it were a banquet.

Yichen watched her.

“You’re hungry.”

She met his eyes.

“Of course. It’s dinner.”

“You could have told me earlier.”

“Why?”

“I could have prepared something.”

She waved her chopsticks.

“This is prepared.”

“All right.”

She continued eating.

After a while, she looked at him.

“You’re looking at me.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“You’re making me nervous.”

He tilted his head slightly.

“Why?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re doing that thing.”

“What thing?”

“Looking at me like you’re trying to figure something out.”

He smiled.

“Maybe I am.”

She looked down at her bowl.

“Don’t.”

“All right.”

He returned to his noodles.

She watched him for a second, then moved a piece of egg from her bowl into his.

He looked down.

“What’s this?”

“Your share.”

“You gave me the bigger piece.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s our anniversary.”

He met her eyes.

“Does that mean I get the bigger piece every anniversary?”

“Of course.”

“That’s a generous tradition.”

“I’m a generous girlfriend.”

“I know.”

She smiled, pleased.

He picked up the egg and ate it.

After dinner, Xiaoran insisted on washing the dishes.

Yichen told her he could do it.

She told him that he had cooked.

He reminded her that she had brought the ingredients.

She said that was hardly a contribution.

Eventually, they compromised.

She washed.

He dried.

It was a familiar arrangement.

Their shoulders occasionally brushed as they worked. Sometimes she passed him a plate without looking, and he took it without needing to ask. When she reached for the dish towel, he handed it to her before she could.

At one point, she turned around too quickly and almost bumped into him.

He caught her by the waist.

“Careful.”

“You’re standing too close.”

“This is my kitchen.”

“That’s not an excuse.”

He smiled.

She remained where she was, his hand still resting at her waist.

Then she lifted her wet hands.

“Don’t.”

He looked at them.

“What?”

“I know what you’re thinking.”

“I’m not thinking anything.”

“You’re going to wipe your hands on me.”

He looked at her.

Then his smile grew.

“That’s a good idea.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed and released her.

She pointed a wet finger at him.

“Don’t you dare.”

He stepped away, still smiling.

She shook her head, returning to the sink.

A few minutes later, he came up behind her and rested his chin on her shoulder.

She leaned back against him.

“Done?”

“Almost.”

He wrapped his arms around her waist.

She rinsed the last bowl and placed it on the rack.

Then she turned within his arms.

She smiled.

He lowered his head and kissed her.

It was a soft kiss at first, familiar and affectionate. She rested her hands against his chest, then slid them around his neck when he kissed her again.

When they separated, she stayed close.

“Three years,” she whispered.

“Three years.”

“That’s quite a long time.”

“Is it?”

She nodded.

“We’ve known each other for so long.”

“Not long enough.”

She turned to him.

His expression was calm, but there was something warm in his eyes.

She smiled.

“That’s a good answer.”

“I thought so.”

She laughed and kissed his cheek.

They returned to the sofa.

Xiaoran curled up beside him, her head resting on his shoulder. Yichen picked up the remote and opened a streaming service.

“What do you want to watch?”

“Something.”

“That’s helpful.”

“Something romantic.”

He turned to her.

“Do you want to watch a romance?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s our anniversary.”

He nodded.

“Reasonable.”

He scrolled through the options.

She watched him for a while before speaking.

“Actually, I don’t mind what we watch.”

He looked over.

“Then why did you say romance?”

“Because I wanted to.”

He smiled and selected a film.

The opening scene began.

Xiaoran settled more comfortably against him, pulling a cushion into her lap.

Yichen put one arm around her shoulders.

For the first twenty minutes, she watched attentively.

Then she started commenting on the characters.

“Why would she believe him?”

Yichen glanced at the screen.

“Maybe she likes him.”

“That’s not a reason to be stupid.”

He laughed.

A little later, she complained about the male lead’s inability to communicate.

“See? This is why people should talk.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Do you think we communicate well?”

She considered it.

“Most of the time.”

“Most?”

“Sometimes you just look at me.”

“That’s because you usually know what I’m thinking.”

She smiled.

“Not always.”

“Then ask.”

She looked at him.

“All right. What are you thinking now?”

He held her gaze.

“That you’re comfortable.”

“That’s all?”

“And that I like having you here.”

Her expression softened.

She shifted closer, resting her cheek against his chest.

“Me too.”

He kissed her hair.

Halfway through the film, Yichen noticed that Xiaoran was scrolling through her phone.

She wasn’t really reading anything.

She opened an app, closed it, checked the time, then returned to the home screen.

He didn’t ask.

A few minutes later, she put the phone down, then picked it up again.

He glanced at the screen.

She was looking at a banking app.

Her thumb hovered over something before she locked the phone.

Yichen looked back at the television.

He had seen enough.

She was worrying about money.

He remembered the way she had declined his offer to take her shopping last weekend. The way she had insisted on splitting a meal when he offered to pay. The way she had become interested in cooking at home.

He had a fair idea why. A week ago she had handed him two tickets to the Garden and told him, glowing, about the prize money and the bakery videos. She hadn’t said a word about what came after. He didn’t want to embarrass her by asking.

So he did something else.

He reached for the fruit on the table and offered her a slice.

She held his gaze.

“Thank you.”

He nodded.

A moment later, he asked casually, “Have you been busy lately?”

She blinked.

“With what?”

“Everything.”

“University?”

“Among other things.”

She considered the question.

“Not especially.”

“All right.”

She looked at him.

“Why?”

“Just asking.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re suspicious.”

He smiled.

“Am I?”

“Yes.”

“Then I should be careful.”

She laughed and took another piece of fruit.

He didn’t ask about the banking app again.

A little later, Xiaoran sat up.

“Wait.”

Yichen paused the film.

“What?”

She looked around the living room.

“Did you prepare anything?”

He studied her.

“What kind of thing?”

“For our anniversary.”

He considered her.

“Does dinner count?”

“Yes.”

“Then I prepared dinner.”

“That’s cheating. I brought dinner.”

“I cooked it.”

“With my ingredients.”

“Which I cooked.”

She laughed.

“Honestly.”

He leaned back.

“Would you like something else?”

She shook her head quickly.

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He watched her face.

She smiled.

“Really. I don’t need anything.”

He believed that she meant it.

At least, he believed that she didn’t need something expensive.

But he wondered whether there was something she wanted and was deliberately avoiding.

He didn’t know how to ask without making it sound like he was questioning her financial situation.

So he reached for her hand.

“Then stay here.”

She tilted her head.

“That’s the plan.”

“Good.”

He pulled her gently closer.

She laughed as she settled against him.

At around ten, Xiaoran’s phone rang.

It was Tang Meilin.

Xiaoran answered.

“Hello?”

Meilin’s voice came through immediately.

“Happy anniversary!”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you!”

“Where are you?”

“At Yichen’s.”

“What did you do?”

“Nothing much.”

“Nothing much?”

“We ate.”

“What did you eat?”

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen.

He was looking at the paused film, listening without appearing to listen.

“Instant noodles.”

There was a silence.

Then Meilin said, “You’re joking.”

“No.”

“On your third anniversary?”

“Yes.”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Did he forget?”

Yichen looked over.

Xiaoran immediately shook her head.

“No! He didn’t forget.”

“Then why are you eating instant noodles?”

“Because we wanted to.”

Meilin sounded unconvinced.

“Are you sure?”

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen again.

He was still looking at her, his expression unreadable.

She smiled.

“Of course.”

Meilin sighed.

“Fine. Enjoy your romantic noodles.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Goodnight.”

“Goodnight. Tell him I said happy anniversary too.”

“I will.”

She ended the call.

Yichen looked at her.

“Meilin?”

“Mhm.”

“What did she say?”

“She thinks we’re strange.”

He smiled.

“She’s not wrong.”

Xiaoran leaned against him.

“She asked why we ate instant noodles.”

“And what did you say?”

“That we wanted to.”

He looked down at her.

“Good answer.”

She smiled.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “Do you think it’s strange?”

“What?”

“Our anniversary.”

He considered the question.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“Why would it be?”

She shrugged.

“I don’t know. Three years is a long time. People usually do something special.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Is this not special?”

She blinked.

He gestured vaguely toward the room.

“We’re together. We had dinner. You’re sitting on my sofa. I don’t see the problem.”

“You’re making it sound very simple.”

“It is simple.”

He reached over and tucked her hair behind her ear.

“I want to spend today with you. I am.”

She looked at him.

Then she leaned forward and kissed him.

“All right.”

Later, they moved to his bedroom.

Xiaoran wanted to lie down and finish the film on his tablet.

Yichen sat against the headboard, and she settled beside him with her legs across his lap.

He played with her fingers while the film continued.

After a while, she spoke.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“What’s your favorite memory from the past three years?”

He looked down at her.

“That’s difficult.”

“Why?”

“There are too many.”

She smiled.

“Choose one.”

He thought.

“Probably the day we started dating.”

She blinked.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I was waiting for you to say yes.”

She laughed.

“You made me say it first.”

“You said it first all by yourself. I was just holding the umbrella.”

She looked at him with a soft expression.

“I remember.”

He brushed his thumb across her knuckles.

“What about you?”

She thought about it.

There were so many.

The first time he had held her hand. The first time he had kissed her. Their first anniversary, when they had spent almost nothing and somehow ended up with a day she remembered more fondly than many expensive dates.

His birthday a week ago, and the look on his face when he opened the envelope.

“I think... I like the ordinary days.” She smiled.

He considered her.

“Why?”

“Because there are so many of them. Special days are nice. Birthdays, anniversaries, holidays. But most of our time isn’t spent doing something special. It’s just... this.”

She gestured toward the room.

“Watching something. Eating. Talking. Sometimes studying. Sometimes doing nothing.”

“And you like that?”

“Very much.”

He leaned down and kissed her temple.

“Then we’ll have more.”

She studied his face.

It was nearly midnight when Yichen walked her to the door.

Xiaoran had put on her shoes and found her keys, and left her tote bag on his sofa without noticing.

She turned toward him.

“Today was nice.”

“Yes.”

“Even though we didn’t do anything.”

“We did plenty.”

“Like what?”

“Eating.”

She laughed.

“That’s not enough.”

“Watching a film.”

“Still not enough.”

“Talking.”

She smiled.

“Better.”

He reached for her waist and pulled her closer.

“Being with you.”

She looked up at him.

“That’s enough.”

He kissed her.

Then her forehead.

Then her cheek.

She rested her hands against his chest.

“Happy anniversary.”

“Happy anniversary.”

She hesitated.

Then said, “I love you.”

His expression softened.

“I love you too.”

She smiled and finally left.

Yichen watched until she disappeared into the elevator.

Then he closed the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found the notebook the next morning.

It had slid out of the tote bag she’d left on his sofa and fallen open at a page headed GARDEN in her round handwriting. He hadn’t meant to read it. He read it anyway.

Competition prize. Bakery clips, four weekends. Wedding edit. Birthday budget. Every line had a number beside it, and the numbers added up to the price of two seats in a section that began with a two.

Under that, in smaller writing, was a second list.

Milk tea: no.
Phone top-up: next month.
New tote: after New York.
New York food: 300 (pretzel??)

He sat down on the sofa with it.

So that was the instant noodles. And the frayed strap, and the milk tea, and the way she checked prices in the canteen as if they might bite. She’d given him the best birthday present of his life and was planning to eat on three hundred yuan for five days in New York.

He felt surprised first, then something warmer, then an ache in his chest he didn’t have a name for.

He closed the notebook, slid it back into the tote bag exactly where it had been, and picked up his phone. The Garden’s website took a while to load. He read about the seats closest to the court, and then about something called a pregame tour. Then he opened his banking app and typed in the amount she had paid, copied from the top of her page.

✦ ✦ ✦

When Xiaoran arrived that evening, Yichen was in the kitchen.

She walked in, placed her bag down, and immediately looked at him.

“Why are you smiling?”

He glanced over.

“Maybe I’m happy.”

“Why?”

He turned off the stove.

“Can’t I be happy?”

“You’re suspicious again.”

He laughed.

She walked toward him.

“What are you cooking?”

“Dinner.”

“What kind?”

“Something better than instant noodles.”

She gasped.

“Are you insulting yesterday’s dinner?”

“Never.”

He handed her a plate.

She looked at it, then at him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Why are you being so nice?”

He smiled.

“Because it’s Saturday.”

“That makes no sense.”

“Does it need to?”

She studied him.

He looked perfectly normal.

Too normal, perhaps.

But she couldn’t work out what was different.

He placed another plate on the counter and came closer, brushing a strand of hair behind her ear.

“Eat first.”

She glanced up at him, then smiled.

“Okay.”

He kissed her hair.

She didn’t notice his eyes staying on her a second longer than usual, or know that he’d read a page of her notebook that morning. He served her dinner, listened to her talk about her week, and let her believe he hadn’t noticed anything at all.

She had been perfectly happy with the trade. He could see that, and he wasn’t going to take it from her.

Yichen looked at her across the table.

She was telling him a story, her hands flying, about something that had happened in class that week.

He listened.

Smiling.

When she finished, he reached across the table and took her hand.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me again.”

“I like looking at you.”

Her cheeks warmed.

“That’s not fair.”

He smiled.

“Why?”

“Because I can’t concentrate when you say things like that.”

He laughed.

Then he lifted her hand and kissed her fingers.

“Happy third anniversary, Xiaoran.”

She blinked.

“That was yesterday.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“Then happy third anniversary, Yichen.”

He held her hand a little longer. He couldn’t wait to see her face in New York. Until then he let her keep her secret, and kept his.

He pretended not to notice, and she pretended instant noodles were all she had wanted. They were both excellent at it.

chapters.desc: Snow, a pretzel the size of her head, and an envelope that makes Lin Xiaoran shout in a Chinatown noodle shop.
chapters.title: New York Before Tip-Off
chapters.epigraph: “The gift was never the money.”
chapters.content:
The day before the game, Lin Xiaoran discovered two things. First, New York was absurdly big. Second, Zhou Yichen was richer than she remembered.

✦ ✦ ✦

The moment they stepped out of the hotel, Xiaoran stopped walking. Completely. It had snowed overnight. The street was a canyon of buildings so tall she had to tip her head all the way back to see where they ended. Yellow taxis honked at nothing. Steam rose out of a grate in the road like the city was breathing. A man walked past carrying a Christmas tree, three weeks after Christmas, as if that were normal.

“…Xiaoran?”

She pointed at everything at once.

“It looks fake.”

“It’s a city.”

“No. It looks like someone built a movie set and forgot to take it down.” She pointed again, at a building with a gold roof.

Yichen smiled. Watching her see New York, he decided, was better than seeing it himself. Every five minutes she discovered something new. Every ten minutes she took another photo. Every fifteen minutes she stopped dead in the middle of the sidewalk to stare up at something and got gently steered aside by a New Yorker who didn’t have time for this. They walked until their faces went numb. They watched skaters go around the rink under a giant gold statue. They shared a hot pretzel the size of Xiaoran’s head, which she declared “a little disappointing but still important.” They got lost twice—once in Central Park, once inside a single department store.

By evening they were sitting in a tiny noodle place in Chinatown, because a long flight and one hotel breakfast had already made Xiaoran homesick for broth, and the conversation finally turned to tomorrow. The game. The reason they had flown halfway around the world.

“I’m excited. Even though I still only understand half of what’s happening,” Xiaoran said.

“Hm.”

“You’ll explain.”

“Hm.”

“No lectures longer than ten minutes.”

“…Hm.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Why are you so happy?”

Yichen looked away. Which was already suspicious.

“There’s something I need to tell you.”

Uh oh.

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

“That sounds like something happened.”

“Not really.”

Then he slid an envelope across the table.

“…What is this.”

“Open it.”

Now it was her turn to be suspicious. Inside were documents. New tickets. Not their tickets—their tickets were safely in her bag, in a plastic sleeve, because she had checked them every hour since Shanghai. These had different section numbers. A lot lower. The row said A. Xiaoran read them twice.

“…Yichen.”

“Hm.”

“These are not our tickets.”

“Hm.”
