“These say courtside.”

“Hm.”

She looked up, slowly.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

The tone that meant I know exactly what you’ve done. He stayed calm, mostly because he had known this was coming.

“You upgraded them.”

“Hm.”

“You upgraded EVERYTHING. Yichen, I know how much these cost.” She flipped through the rest. Courtside seats. A pregame arena tour. Access to watch the teams warm up from the tunnel.

“Hm.”

“I WORKED FOR MONTHS.”

“I know.”

“I SAVED FOR MONTHS.”

“I know.”

The noodle shop owner glanced over from behind the counter. Two tables away, an elderly couple had stopped eating to watch. Then Xiaoran found the actual crime, tucked at the very back: a bank transfer receipt for exactly the amount she had paid for the original tickets. Silence.

“…No.”

Yichen sighed. Yes. This part. Always this part.

“No?”

“No. Absolutely not.” She folded her arms.

“Xiaoran.”

“No.”

“Listen first.”

“No.”

He took her hand across the table.

He said, “You gave me the best birthday gift I’ve ever had. You worked weekends for it. You saved your competition money. You got up at four in the morning to buy those tickets.”

She stayed quiet.

“And because I know how hard you worked, the last thing I want is for you to spend everything you saved on me,” he went on, thumb moving over her knuckles.

That made the argument harder. Much harder.

“The gift was never the money. It was that you remembered. That you wanted me here,” he said.

It was exactly the kind of answer Xiaoran couldn’t fight, because he wasn’t brushing her effort aside or replacing it. He understood what it had meant.

“You don’t get it,” she said, quieter.

“Then explain.”

She looked away. “…I wanted to give you something myself.”

Not the money. The feeling. Yichen lifted her hand and pressed a kiss to her fingers, right there in the noodle shop, in front of the elderly couple, who looked thrilled.

“You did. The moment you bought those first tickets, you already did,” he said.

Xiaoran felt her heart give way a little. Then she pointed at him across the noodles.

“You still upgraded everything.”

“Hm.”

“You didn’t have to.”

“I wanted to.”

“Show-off.”

“Hm.”

At least he admitted it. She kept the original tickets anyway. She wasn’t going to use them, but she folded them carefully back into their plastic sleeve and put them in the inside pocket of her coat, where they stayed for the rest of the trip.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, on the arena tour, they walked out of the tunnel onto the empty court. The ceiling rose above them, enormous and round, rows and rows of empty seats climbing toward it in every direction. A lone janitor was polishing the floor. Their guide was saying something about history and famous nights. Xiaoran forgot she was annoyed. Beside her, Zhou Yichen stood at the edge of the court with his hands in his coat pockets, still, looking like the happiest man on Earth.

Actually—no. The happiest man on Earth wasn’t looking at the court. He wasn’t looking at the ceiling or the banners or the famous floor. He was looking at her. Because somehow, the best part of the whole trip wasn’t the Garden. It was watching Lin Xiaoran see it with him.

chapters.desc: Back from New York, she is wide awake at seventeen minutes past three. Across the road, so is he.
chapters.title: Jet Lag
chapters.epigraph: “If it’s dark, I go back to sleep.”
chapters.content:
The problem with returning from New York was that Xiaoran’s body had apparently decided Shanghai was no longer in the correct time zone.

It was seventeen minutes past three in the morning, and she was wide awake.

Not pleasantly awake, either, or the kind of awake that came with a burst of inspiration or the urge to reorganize her desk. She was lying in bed in her fourth-floor studio, staring at the ceiling, feeling as if she ought to be having breakfast somewhere in Manhattan.

Across the road and eleven floors up, Yichen was presumably asleep. He had adjusted to the time difference the way he adjusted to everything, by deciding to.

She picked up her phone.

Xiaoran: Are you awake?

She watched the screen. A minute passed. Then:

Yichen: I am now.

Xiaoran: Sorry.

Yichen: Jet lag?

Xiaoran: I think my body is still at the Garden.

Yichen: Are you hungry?

She considered it honestly.

Xiaoran: A little.

Yichen: What do you want?

Xiaoran: Noodles?

There was a pause long enough for her to imagine him looking at the clock.

Yichen: Instant?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: Ten minutes.

He was at her door in eight, in a hoodie and the shoes he wore to take out the bins, with his hair flattened on one side.

“You came,” she said.

“You said noodles. I brought fish balls. You never have any.” He held up a plastic bag.

The kitchen lights were too bright for three in the morning.

Xiaoran stood in front of the cupboard, wearing an oversized T-shirt and a pair of soft shorts, her hair tied into a loose, messy ponytail.

Yichen was beside the stove, filling a pot with water.

She watched him. “You’re really making noodles. At three in the morning.”

“You asked for them.”

“I thought you’d tell me to go back to sleep.”

“I considered it.”

He turned on the stove.

“Would you have listened?”

“No.”

“Exactly.”

She laughed.

They had returned from New York two days earlier.

The trip had been wonderful, although exhausting. They had walked until their feet hurt, visited places Xiaoran had only seen in photographs, taken too many pictures, and eaten more than either of them had planned.

Yichen had been better at adjusting to the time difference.

Xiaoran, on the other hand, seemed to have brought New York back with her.

She was sleepy during the afternoon, wide awake at midnight, and increasingly convinced that the best time to eat was somewhere between two and four in the morning.

Yichen opened her small refrigerator, which contained a bottle of soy sauce, two eggs and a lemon, and looked at it in silence.

“Egg?”

“Yes.”

“Vegetables?”

“Yes.”

“Anything else?”

She thought. “The fish balls.”

“We’re making instant noodles, not hotpot.”

“You brought them.”

“I brought them because you’d ask,” he said, and tipped them in.

The first bowl was ready at half past three.

Yichen placed it on the kitchen counter, then set a second bowl beside it.

Xiaoran climbed onto one of the kitchen stools.

He handed her a pair of chopsticks.

She took a bite, then closed her eyes.

“Oh.”

He sat opposite her.

“Well?”

“Perfect.”

He tasted his own.

“It’s instant noodles.”

“Don’t ruin the moment.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

She continued eating, occasionally picking fish balls out of his bowl.

After the third time, Yichen looked down at his noodles.

“Are you planning to eat mine too?”

She looked at him innocently.

“You have more.”

“We have the same amount.”

“Your bowl looks fuller.”

“Because you keep taking from it.”

She laughed.

He pushed the bowl slightly toward her.

“Here.”

“Really?”

“Apparently, I’m not going to win this argument.”

She took another fish ball.

“Thank you.”

He watched her eat.

Then he said, “You know, this is becoming a habit.”

“What is?”

“Being awake at three in the morning.”

She shrugged.

“It’s not my fault.”

“Whose fault is it?”

“New York.”

He nodded thoughtfully.

“I see.”

“It’s the time difference.”

“Of course.”

“And the flight.”

“Naturally.”

“And the fact that I slept for four hours this afternoon.”

He met her eyes.

“That last one might be relevant.”

She pointed her chopsticks at him.

“Don’t.”

Something in his face eased.

The next night, Xiaoran woke up at five to three. She stared at the ceiling. She tried to close her eyes. After ten minutes she reached for her phone.

Xiaoran: Are you awake?

Yichen: No.

She bit her lip to stop herself from laughing.

Xiaoran: Then who replied?

Yichen: A very tired person.

Xiaoran: Noodles?

There was a pause.

Yichen: Give me five minutes.

He knocked in six.

By the fourth night, they had developed a routine. At three, Xiaoran would wake up. By five past, she would be staring at the ceiling. At ten past, she would decide whether she was hungry. At a quarter past, Yichen would receive a message from a person one road and eleven floors away, and by twenty past, they would both be standing in her kitchen, which was one meter wide.

The first night had been spontaneous.

The second night had been an exception.

By the fourth, Yichen had started stocking her kitchen cupboard. Xiaoran discovered this when she opened it and found a small stack of her favorite flavor, and a bag of fish balls in her freezer compartment that she hadn’t bought.

She turned around slowly.

“Yichen.”

He was pouring water into the kettle. “Why are there so many?”

He looked at the packets.

“Because we keep eating them.”

“You bought them?”

“Yes.”

“For us?”

“Who else?”

She walked over and wrapped her arms around his waist and pressed her cheek against his chest.

“You’re cute.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I’m buying groceries.”

“Exactly.”

He laughed and rested his hand on the back of her head.

“Go wash your hands.”

She tightened her arms.

“One more minute.”

He let her stay.

On the sixth night, Yichen had training at seven the next morning. He had gone to bed at ten, hoping to get back to a normal schedule, and she had told him not to answer if she texted.

At six minutes past three, Xiaoran woke up. She looked at her phone. She didn’t text him.

She got up, as if he could hear her from across the road, turned on only the small light above the counter, and opened the cupboard. There were two packets left. She took one. She was just filling the pot when someone knocked at the door, twice.

He was standing in the corridor with his hair sticking up and his eyes still heavy with sleep.

“Why are you awake?” she said.

“Why are you making noodles?”

She glanced at the packet in her hand. “...Because I’m hungry?”

He rubbed his face. “You could have texted.”

“You have training.”

“I know. Move.” He walked past her into the kitchen and took the pot from her hand and adjusted the water.

“You need sleep.”

“So do you.”

“I’m not the one with training.”

“Then you can keep me company,” he said, and she sat on the counter, swinging her legs, while he made the noodles.

After a while she said, “How did you know?”

He turned off the stove. “Your light.”

She met his eyes.

“I can see your window from mine. It’s the only one on this side of the street that’s ever on at three. Usually I don’t wake up. Tonight I did,” he said, as if he were admitting to something.

“You looked?”

“I always look. If it’s dark, I go back to sleep.” He put the noodles into two bowls and set hers beside her on the counter.

She was quiet. “And if it’s on?”

“Then you’re up. And I’d rather be up too,” he said.

He sat on the step by the door, because there was nowhere else to sit, and picked up his chopsticks. “Now eat. I have training in four hours.”

She leaned down from the counter and put her chin on his hair.

“Eat your noodles,” he said, into his bowl.

The seventh night was different. At three, Xiaoran woke up and reached for her phone, and there was already a message waiting.

Yichen: Your light’s off. Are you awake?

She stared at it, then at the dark window, then typed.

Xiaoran: Yes. I’m trying not to be.

Yichen: Me too.

Xiaoran: Are you hungry?

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Me neither.

Yichen: Then go back to sleep.

Xiaoran: Okay.

Thirty seconds passed.

Xiaoran: But what if we make noodles?

There was a long pause. Then her phone rang, and when she answered, he was laughing, the low, helpless laugh he only did when nobody else could hear.

“Two small bowls,” he said.

“Two!”

“Small.”

“Deal,” she said, already out of bed, and switched the light on so he would see it.

The following morning, Xiaoran opened her refrigerator and found a small note stuck to the door with a magnet shaped like a dumpling.

It was written in Yichen’s handwriting.

3 A.M. Noodle Club.

Below it, in smaller letters:

Members: 2.

She stared at it, then laughed.

When Yichen came over that evening, she held up the note.

“What’s this?”

“An official club,” he said.

Her mouth tipped up.

“Do we have rules?”

“Yes.”

“What rules?”

He looked at her.

“Rule number one: no noodles if we’re not hungry.”

She nodded seriously.

“Reasonable.”

“Rule number two: no waking each other up if the other person has an early morning.”

She hesitated.

“That’s a difficult one.”

“I know.”

“Any other rules?”

He considered.

“Rule number three: whoever finishes the last packet has to buy more.”

She laughed.

“Agreed.”

She took the note and stuck it on the refrigerator properly.

Underneath his handwriting, she wrote one more line.

Rule number four: Yichen must always add fish balls.

He read it.

“That’s not a rule.”

“It is now.”

He shook his head, smiling.

Their sleep schedules eventually returned to normal.

The 3 a.m. wake-ups became less frequent, then stopped altogether.

But the little note stayed on the refrigerator.

And sometimes, when Xiaoran had a late study night or Yichen returned from basketball practice hungry, one of them would open the cupboard, find the familiar packets, and glance at the note.

A few weeks later, on an ordinary Friday night, Xiaoran was at her desk finishing an assignment when Yichen, who had come over to study and had given up, looked up from her bed.

“Are you hungry?”

She looked up.

“A little.”

He nodded toward the kitchen.

“Noodles?”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“What time is it?”

“Eleven.”

She considered it.

“That’s too early.”

He turned to her.

“Too early?”

“For the club.”

He laughed.

“Then we’ll wait.”

She closed her laptop and stood up.

“Actually, let’s make them now.”

“Why?”

She slipped her hand into his.

“Because we don’t need jet lag to have noodles together.”

Yichen looked at her.

Then he smiled and squeezed her hand. “All right.”

When he walked home that night, at midnight, he looked up from the road the way he always did. Her light was on. He waited until it went off.

chapters.desc: Game day at Madison Square Garden. But first, a fashion crisis on Fifth Avenue.
chapters.title: The Day Lin Xiaoran Wanted to Look Grown-Up
chapters.epigraph: “Not cute. Not pretty. Beautiful.”
chapters.content:
Game day. Saturday. The day the whole trip had been building toward. The day Lin Xiaoran discovered a completely unexpected crisis. The crisis wasn’t basketball. It wasn’t New York, or the fact that she still understood about forty-seven percent of what Yichen said about defensive schemes. The crisis was fashion.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started at breakfast, in a café on Fifth Avenue, where Xiaoran made the mistake of looking out of the window. Every woman who walked past looked effortless. Long wool coats. Leather gloves. Scarves wrapped like they’d been styled for a magazine. Sleek hair, good boots, the kind of confidence that made a gray sidewalk look like a runway. Then Xiaoran looked down at herself. Puffy white jacket. Comfortable jeans. Sneakers. A small panda keychain hanging from her bag.

She looked like a university student. Because she was a university student. But today, for some reason, she suddenly felt young. Across the table, Yichen looked up from his coffee and noticed her face immediately.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran pointed at a woman outside the window. “Look.”

He looked. “…Okay.”

“She looks like an adult.”

He looked at the woman, then at Xiaoran, then at the woman again.

“I don’t understand the problem.”

“I look like someone’s daughter.”

Yichen nearly laughed. “Xiaoran.”

“No, seriously. Look at her. She looks sophisticated. I look like I got lost on a school trip.” Another woman passed—camel coat, red lipstick, coffee in one gloved hand.

That was when he did laugh—a real one—which only made her more offended.

“THIS IS SERIOUS.”

“It isn’t.”

“YICHEN.”

His smile widened. The idea of Lin Xiaoran having an identity crisis on Fifth Avenue was, to him, extremely funny.

Unfortunately, once she decided something, she was impossible. Thirty minutes later they were shopping—not because Yichen suggested it, but because Xiaoran had announced, “I am becoming elegant today,” and apparently this was non-negotiable.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next three hours were chaos. The first dress was too mature. The second was too fancy. The third made her look, in her own words, like she was attending someone’s divorce. The fourth almost worked, except for the sleeves, which had opinions. Yichen followed behind, carrying more and more shopping bags. Patient. Hopelessly supportive.

At one point, a saleswoman smiled at Xiaoran and said, “Your husband is very patient.”

Xiaoran nearly choked. Yichen looked suspiciously pleased. Neither of them corrected her. Then Xiaoran found it: a soft burgundy knit dress with a simple neckline and long sleeves, warm enough for January, and a long camel coat to wear over it. Feminine without trying too hard. When she looked in the mirror, she paused.

“…Oh.”

The saleswoman smiled. “That’s the one.”

Even Xiaoran couldn’t argue. She looked older, somehow. Softer. More sure of herself. Still herself—just slightly different. Then she looked over at Yichen. Big mistake. He had gone completely silent.

“…Yichen?”

Nothing.

“Yichen?”

The saleswoman smiled knowingly. “Oh.”

Finally he cleared his throat. “…It looks good.”

Short answer. Too short. Which told Xiaoran everything, because Zhou Yichen only got this brief when he was completely compromised. She smiled in triumph. Success. Unfortunately, the next problem appeared at the register. Yichen paying. Again.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“Yichen.”

“Xiaoran. You bought me the Garden. Let me buy you a dress. You got up at four in the morning for those tickets. Let me win one argument this trip.” Then he made his winning argument.

Deeply annoying. But sensible. So the dress became Yichen’s purchase, a fact he looked suspiciously happy about for the rest of the afternoon.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, they took a yellow cab to the arena, and the city outside the window was all lights. Inside, the Garden was nothing like the empty building from the tour. It was full and loud and alive, twenty thousand people under that enormous round ceiling, music thumping, the court shining like it was lit from underneath. Their seats were so close to the floor that Xiaoran could hear the players’ sneakers squeak during warm-ups and see the sweat on the referees’ foreheads.

She stood by her seat in the burgundy dress and the new coat, holding her phone, not even taking photos, just looking. Then she caught her reflection in the glass of the scorer’s table. The dress. The coat. Her hair, which she had spent forty minutes on in the hotel bathroom. For once, she didn’t see a girl who had gotten lost on a school trip. She saw a woman.

It felt nice. Then she noticed Yichen looking at her. Again.

“…What.”

Nothing.

“Yichen. What.”

He looked away. Then—

“You look beautiful.”

Somehow, after years together, it still worked on her every single time. And this time, the way he said it felt different. Not cute. Not pretty. Beautiful. The word stayed with her. Then the lights went down, the crowd roared, and the game began, and the atmosphere changed completely. Even Xiaoran felt it—the pressure, the speed, how much every possession seemed to matter. And beside her, Yichen changed too. He leaned forward, elbows on his knees, eyes moving across the whole floor at once, tracking every screen and rotation the way he did on the sofa at eight in the morning, except now it was right in front of him. Every time a play worked exactly the way he had explained it on the back of her notes, he made a small sound under his breath, like a man watching a magic trick he already knew the secret to and loved anyway.

He looked ridiculously handsome. Xiaoran decided basketball was dangerous. Not playing it—watching someone you love fall in love with it all over again, three feet from the court. Late in the fourth quarter, a player went flying out of bounds after a loose ball and landed in the second row, two seats down. The whole crowd gasped. Yichen shot to his feet with everyone else. Xiaoran wasn’t watching the player.

She was watching him. He looked happier than she had seen him all year. Without thinking, she slipped her hand into his. He glanced down, surprised for half a second. Then he laced their fingers together and turned back to the game, and didn’t let go. The final minutes went by in a roar. The buzzer sounded. Confetti didn’t fall, because it was a regular season game in January, but it felt like it should have.

And standing there together, in the loudest building Xiaoran had ever been in, both of them realized the same thing. Years from now, when they remembered New York, they probably wouldn’t remember the final score. Or who made which shot, or the defensive schemes, or the forty-seven percent. They would remember this. Her first grown-up dress. His inability to stop looking at her. The noise, the lights, the snow waiting outside.

And the hand he didn’t let go of the whole way home.

chapters.desc: A few comments read at 2 AM, two weeks of skipped meals, and a date that ends in a quiet café.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Found Out Lin Xiaoran Was Dieting
chapters.epigraph: “Who told you that you needed to change?”
chapters.content:
There were many things Zhou Yichen worried about. Basketball injuries. Exams. Career plans. Whether Xiaoran remembered her student card. Normal, reasonable concerns. One concern had never crossed his mind, because it sounded impossible: Lin Xiaoran dieting. The girl who once ate three desserts on a single date. The girl who considered bubble tea a personality trait. The girl who treated snacks as emotional support. Dieting? Impossible. Which was exactly why he didn’t notice at first.

It started with social media. Again. Always social media.

✦ ✦ ✦

A month earlier, Xiaoran had posted photos from New York: the burgundy dress, the city lights, a version of herself that looked a little more woman than girl. The response was overwhelmingly positive. Some of it wasn’t. Nothing cruel. Nothing dramatic. Just enough.

“She’s pretty but she’d look even better if she lost a little weight.”

“Her face is beautiful.”

“A slimmer figure would be perfect.”

Stupid, unimportant comments—the kind most people would ignore. Except Xiaoran read them at 2 AM, scientifically the worst time to read anything. And somehow they stayed with her. Not because she hated herself. She didn’t. But for the first time, she started wondering: what if? So Lin Xiaoran made a terrible decision. She started dieting, secretly. The bad kind: skipping breakfast, tiny lunches, coffee instead of food, water whenever she was hungry—the kind of diet guaranteed to make everyone miserable, especially her.

The strange part was that nobody noticed right away. Xiaoran acted mostly normal, and university was busy—deadlines, projects, practices, exams, life. Even Zhou Yichen missed it, for almost two weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then came Saturday. Date day. The plan was simple: lunch, shopping, walking around the city, dinner. Xiaoran woke up feeling awful. Her stomach had spent two weeks surviving on disappointment and caffeine, and it was finally protesting. Violently. She still said nothing, because she didn’t want Yichen to worry. Terrible decision.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon the stomachache was worse. Walking hurt. Standing hurt. Existing hurt. Somehow she kept smiling—until Yichen stopped walking.

“Xiaoran, what’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

A terrible lie. She looked pale—pale—and Zhou Yichen knew her too well.

“No.”

“What?”

“Something hurts.”

Dead silence. Caught. Again.

“…My stomach.”

Everything changed, because Zhou Yichen’s expression changed. Worry. Always worry first.

“When did it start?”

“A little while ago.”

“How long.”

She hesitated.

“Xiaoran.”

“…This morning.”

The truth, finally. She’d been hiding it all morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ten minutes later they were sitting in a quiet café. A warm drink in front of her. Food in front of her. Food she wasn’t touching. And finally, Yichen actually noticed.

“…Why aren’t you eating.”

Silence. Then more silence.

“…I’m not hungry.”

Wrong answer. Very wrong answer. Suddenly the pieces connected: the smaller meals, the constant coffee, the weight she’d lost, how tired she’d been. Everything. Dead silence.

“Have you been dieting?”

Uh oh. Xiaoran looked away. The universal sign of guilt. Zhou Yichen became angry. The worst kind: quiet angry.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

She winced. He had used her full name. Maximum danger.

“Answer me.”

“…A little.”

“A little.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

“You’ve barely been eating for two weeks.”

Oops. Of course he knew. Nothing stayed hidden from him forever.

“Why.”

Suddenly Xiaoran felt stupid. The comments sounded ridiculous now. Embarrassing. Small.

“…I wanted to look prettier.”

The anger disappeared. Completely. That answer hurt worse. Much worse.

“Xiaoran.”

She didn’t look up. Couldn’t. A hand touched her forehead, warm. Then a kiss—right on her forehead, soft and lingering. Xiaoran blinked, confused. She had expected a lecture. Not that.

“Look at me.”

She did. Big mistake. His eyes looked sad. Actually sad. Somehow that was worse than anger.

“Who told you that you needed to change?”

Xiaoran shook her head.

“Don’t do that.”

Another kiss to her temple, gentle and patient.

“Who.”

“…Nobody.”

A lie. But he let it go. That wasn’t the point. Then another kiss against her hair. And another. Each one impossibly gentle.

“What am I supposed to do with you?”

His voice sounded helpless.

“Yichen—”

Another kiss.

“You skip meals.”

Kiss.

“You drink coffee instead.”

Kiss.

“You get sick.”

Kiss.

“And somehow you’re surprised your stomach hurts.”

By now, Xiaoran’s ears were red. Being scolded while being repeatedly kissed was confusing.

“I just wanted to look prettier.”

Then Yichen laughed. His hand moved to hold her cheek, gently.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“You took me to New York. You worked for months to buy those tickets. You won competitions. You make everyone around you happier. And somehow the thing you’re worried about is losing weight?”

She looked down, because it sounded ridiculous when he said it.

“I just…”

Nothing came out. She didn’t even know anymore. Yichen sighed—the sigh he saved for her alone—and pushed the food toward her.

“Eat.”

Xiaoran didn’t move.

“Eat. Or I’m carrying you home.”

He sounded completely serious, which made it believable.

“You won’t think I’m ugly?”

Yichen leaned forward and kissed her cheek again, longer this time, then whispered,

“You’re beautiful when you’re eating. You’re beautiful when you’re studying. You’re beautiful when you’re talking too much. You’re beautiful when you’re annoying.”

“That’s rude.”

“Accurate.”

Then, more seriously: “If comments like that get in your head again, tell me. Don’t fix it by not eating.”

A tiny smile appeared. There she was—the real Xiaoran. Watching her finally pick up her fork made Zhou Yichen more relieved than winning a basketball game. He still spent the rest of the date kissing her forehead every twenty minutes, just to make sure she remembered. And every single time, he said:

“Eat your food.”

Which was considerably less romantic.

chapters.desc: A month after the dieting weeks, a photograph of his lunch arrives every day at noon. He never asks about hers.
chapters.title: Lunch, Every Day
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want you to feel like you have to prove anything to me.”
chapters.content:
The first photograph arrived at 11:48 a.m.

Xiaoran was sitting in the lecture hall, half-listening to her professor explain the relationship between visual language and audience interpretation, when her phone vibrated against the desk.

She glanced down. A photograph from Yichen, of a cafeteria tray: rice, grilled chicken, vegetables, and a bowl of soup. The composition was surprisingly neat, with the cutlery placed parallel to the edge of the tray.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Then she typed.

Xiaoran: ?

His reply came a minute later.

Yichen: Lunch.

She almost laughed.

Xiaoran: I can see that.

Yichen: Good.

She shook her head, smiling, and put her phone away.

She didn’t know it yet, but it was going to become a daily occurrence.

It had started a few days earlier, after what Yichen privately considered one of the more frustrating conversations they’d had since January. Not an argument, quite. But a month after the dieting weeks, the ones he had found out about in the worst possible way, he had noticed that Xiaoran was skipping meals again.

She had been busy with assignments, group discussions, and a university media competition she was preparing for. Her schedule had become a mess, and she’d developed the habit of drinking coffee in the morning, eating a few bites of something in the afternoon, and convincing herself that she wasn’t hungry when evening came.

The first time he’d noticed, he’d asked whether she’d eaten.

She’d said yes.

The second time, he’d found her eating a packet of biscuits for dinner.

The third time, she’d casually mentioned that she was trying to be more disciplined about her eating habits.

He hadn’t liked the way she’d said it.

Not because he thought she shouldn’t care about her health or appearance, but because she’d begun treating food like something she had to earn.

He’d asked her about it.

She’d brushed him off.

He hadn’t pushed.

Instead, he’d told her that he wanted her to eat properly, even when she was busy, and that he wasn’t going to turn every meal into a discussion.

She had promised she would try.

He knew her well enough not to expect that promise to solve everything overnight.

So he started with something else.

A photograph.

The second photograph arrived just after twelve the following day.

A bowl of noodles with sliced beef, greens, and a boiled egg.

Yichen: Lunch.

Xiaoran replied while walking between faculties.

Xiaoran: You eat noodles a lot.

Yichen: It’s convenient.

Xiaoran: You should eat more vegetables.

Yichen: There are vegetables.

She zoomed in.

There were, technically, three pieces of green vegetable.

She laughed.

Xiaoran: Three leaves don’t count.

Yichen: I’ll inform the cafeteria.

She put her phone away, still smiling.

He didn’t ask what she was eating.

He didn’t ask whether she’d eaten.

Just a photograph.

By the end of the first week, she had started recognizing the pattern. Some time between half past eleven and half past twelve, depending on his classes and training, a photograph would arrive.

Rice and chicken.

Noodles.

A sandwich.

Something from the university cafeteria.

Once, a unappealing-looking bowl of porridge that made Xiaoran question his food choices.

Xiaoran: What happened to your lunch?

Yichen: It’s porridge.

Xiaoran: It looks like cement.

Yichen: It’s good.

Xiaoran: Are you sure you’re not eating construction materials?

He sent a photograph of his spoon.

Yichen: Would you like evidence?

She laughed so loudly in the library that the girl beside her turned around.

And Yichen never asked about her lunch.

Not once.

On Monday of the second week, Xiaoran decided to investigate.

She was sitting in the university cafeteria with Ning and Jiayi when her phone vibrated: a photograph of a chicken rice bowl. She looked at it, then at the food in front of her. She had a sandwich, a small cup of yogurt, and an iced coffee.

She took a photograph of her own lunch.

Then she sent it to him.

Xiaoran: Mine.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: Looks good.

She waited.

Nothing else.

She frowned.

Xiaoran: That’s all?

Yichen: What else?

Xiaoran: You’re not asking if I ate?

Yichen: You just sent me a photograph of your lunch.

She stared at the screen, then laughed.

Ning leaned over. “You’re smiling at your phone.”

“Yichen sent me lunch.”

Ning blinked.

“Your boyfriend sent you food?”

“No. A photograph of his food.”

Jiayi looked up. “Why?”

Xiaoran considered the question, and found, uncomfortably, that she did know. “I’m not sure.”

She looked back at her phone, then another message arrived.

Yichen: Enjoy your lunch.

She smiled.

The photographs continued.

By the third week, she had started looking forward to them.

Sometimes they arrived while she was in class. Sometimes while she was working on an assignment. Once, during a chaotic group meeting, she received a photograph of an ordinary plate of fried rice.

She stared at it for a few seconds before replying.

Xiaoran: Your lunch looks happier than my group members.

Yichen: That’s because it doesn’t have a deadline.

She laughed.

On another day, she sent him a photograph of her lunch before he could send his.

It was a proper meal this time: rice, fish, vegetables, and soup.

Xiaoran: I ate.

Yichen: I can see that.

Xiaoran: A proper meal.

Yichen: Good.

She waited.

Then:

Yichen: Looks nice.

She smiled at the screen.

One afternoon, she decided to ask him directly.

They were sitting beneath a tree near the business faculty. Yichen had finished his morning lectures, while Xiaoran had a gap before her next class.

She was eating a small dessert he’d bought on the way over.

He was reading something on his tablet.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Why do you send me photographs of your lunch every day?”

He looked up.

“Do you not like them?”

She shook her head.

“No, I like them.”

“Then what’s the problem?”

“There’s no problem.”

He put his tablet down.

“All right.”

She studied his face.

“You’re not curious about what I eat?”

He looked at her. “Do you want me to be?”

She blinked.

“That’s not what I mean.”

“Then what do you mean?”

She took another bite of dessert, thinking.

“You never ask whether I’ve eaten.”

He was quiet.

Then he said, “I know.”

She met his eyes.

He reached for the tissue beside her and gently wiped a little cream from the corner of her mouth.

“I don’t want you to feel like I’m checking up on you.”

Her expression softened.

“I know you don’t like being reminded about food all the time. And I know you’ve been trying to make your own decisions about it.”

She looked down at her dessert.

“So you just send me your lunch?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He leaned back against the tree.

“Because I thought I’d tell you what I’m doing without asking you to report what you’re doing.”

She turned to him.

He met her eyes.

“If you want to tell me about your lunch, you can. If you don’t, that’s fine too.”

She didn’t say anything.

Then she smiled a little.

“You’re sneaky.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“How?”

“You made me curious about your lunch so I’d think about mine.”

He considered that.

“Did it work?”

“Don’t look so pleased with yourself.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

He laughed.

Then he reached over and took her empty dessert cup.

“Finish your class. I’ll see you later.”

She watched him stand.

“Yichen.”

He turned.

“Yes?”

“What’s for dinner?”

“You’re asking me?”

She smiled. “I’m curious.”

He shook his head, amused.

“Let’s decide later.”

The photographs became part of their everyday routine.

It wasn’t a grand gesture, and neither of them announced that it had become a habit.

But Xiaoran began to notice little things.

When he had basketball practice during lunch, the photograph arrived later. When he had a match, he sometimes sent a picture of whatever he’d managed to eat between classes and training.

When he tried something new, he’d send her a photograph before taking the first bite.

Once, he sent a picture of a unattractive cafeteria dish.

Xiaoran: Yichen, what is that?

Yichen: Lunch.

Xiaoran: You keep saying that like it explains everything.

Yichen: It does.

Xiaoran: I refuse to believe you’re eating that voluntarily.

Yichen: I was hungry.

She sent him a laughing sticker.

Then, without thinking, she sent a photograph of her own meal.

He replied:

Yichen: Looks good.

And that was it.

He never made a big deal of it.

One Thursday, Xiaoran had a difficult morning.

Her group project had become a mess, her professor had given them additional revisions, and she’d spent most of her lunch break trying to fix a section that wasn’t even hers.

By the time she finally sat down, it was almost two.

Her phone vibrated.

A photograph.

Yichen’s lunch was a simple rice bowl with grilled fish and vegetables.

Yichen: Lunch.

She looked at the photograph.

Then she looked at the time.

She hadn’t eaten.

Her stomach was beginning to ache, but she was so irritated that she didn’t feel like getting up.

She put her phone down.

A few minutes later, it vibrated again.

Yichen: This one’s better than yesterday.

She couldn’t help smiling.

Then she typed.

Xiaoran: I haven’t eaten yet.

She stared at the message before sending it.

It felt strange to admit.

His reply came quickly.

Yichen: Busy?

Xiaoran: Very.

Yichen: Have you got time now?

Xiaoran: I suppose.

Yichen: Go eat something, then.

She looked at the screen, then another message arrived.

Yichen: I’ll wait.

That made her grin.

Xiaoran: You don’t have to.

Yichen: I know.

The familiar words made her laugh.

She put her laptop away and went to the cafeteria.

When she arrived at the table where Yichen was waiting, he had already finished his lunch.

He was looking through his notes, a bottle of water beside him.

She placed her tray down.

“You’re here.”

He looked up.

“Yes.”

“You said you’d wait.”

“I did.”

She sat opposite him.

He didn’t say anything about the food. He moved his notes aside to make room for her tray.

She looked at him.

“You really don’t ask.”

“Ask what?”

“Whether I’ve eaten.”

He smiled slightly.

“You’ve already told me.”

She laughed.

Then she began eating.

He returned to his notes, occasionally glancing up when she spoke.

She told him about the group project, the revisions, and how one of her teammates had apparently developed the ability to disappear whenever work needed to be done.

Yichen listened, asking a few questions but never taking over the conversation.

When she finished her meal, she pushed the empty tray aside.

He looked at it.

“Good?”

She nodded, with her mouth full, which was the point.

That got a smile out of him.

“Good.”

She leaned forward and rested her chin on her hand.

“You’re really good at this.”

“At what?”

“Taking care of me without making me feel like I’m being taken care of.”

He met her eyes.

Then he reached across the table and moved her hair off her cheek.

“I don’t want you to feel like you have to prove anything to me.”

She smiled.

“I know.”

He returned to his notes.

A moment later, she picked up her phone and took a photograph of his empty lunch tray.

He looked up.

“What are you doing?”

She showed him the picture.

“Sending you mine.”

He glanced at the screen.

“That’s my tray.”

“Exactly.”

He shook his head, laughing.

By the end of the semester, the photographs had become so ordinary that Xiaoran almost forgot they hadn’t always been part of her day.

She had a small collection of them in their chat.

Some were beautifully arranged meals. Some were blurry pictures taken in a hurry. One was mostly his basketball bag with a sandwich barely visible in the corner.

She had started saving the funny ones.

One afternoon, while scrolling through their messages, she noticed something.

There were dozens of photographs of his lunch.

And almost as many photographs of hers.

That made her grin.

Then she sent him a message.

Xiaoran: Do you know how many lunch pictures you’ve sent me?

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: A lot.

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: You should start a food account.

Yichen: Would you follow it?

Xiaoran: Obviously.

Yichen: Then I suppose I should continue.

She laughed.

A few seconds later, another photograph arrived.

A bowl of noodles.

Yichen: Today’s lunch.

She zoomed in.

There were fish balls.

She smiled and typed.

Xiaoran: You put fish balls in it.

Yichen: The Noodle Club has standards.

She looked at the photograph for another moment.

Then she sent one of her own.

A simple lunch she’d bought between classes.

Xiaoran: Today’s lunch.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: Looks good.

Then:

Yichen: Enjoy it.

Xiaoran smiled at her phone.

He had never asked her to send a photograph. He had never asked what she’d eaten, or whether. He had only let her into an ordinary part of his day, every day, until she began to let him into hers.

She didn’t tell him that she had started eating lunch partly so she would have something to send back. She suspected he knew.

chapters.desc: A thirteen-day family vacation. Lin Xiaoran is a mature adult. Day Three is concerning.
chapters.title: Two Weeks Was Apparently Too Long
chapters.epigraph: “I hate family vacations.”
chapters.content:
When Zhou Yichen announced he was leaving on a thirteen-day family vacation, Lin Xiaoran laughed. Actually laughed.

“That’s fine.”

“Hm.”

“I’m a mature adult.”

“Hm.”

“I can survive two weeks.”

“Hm.”

Tang Meilin, who had been there for the One-Week Clingy Disaster of high school, looked deeply suspicious. Whenever Xiaoran claimed she was emotionally stable, disaster usually followed. Day One wasn’t bad at all. Yichen left in the morning. Xiaoran went to class, worked on assignments, had dinner with friends. Perfectly normal. At 10 PM she called him, for three hours. Still normal. Probably. Day Two was manageable. She sent him pictures of lunch, of campus, of a cat near the media building. Then another cat. Then another. Then a cloud that vaguely resembled a cat. Yichen replied: You sent me six cats today.

Xiaoran: You’re welcome.

Day Three was concerning, because after class she walked toward the business building out of habit—then remembered Yichen wasn’t there. He was several countries away. It hit surprisingly hard.

“…Oh.”

For the first time, campus felt a little bigger. A little emptier. Which was ridiculous, because she had survived sixteen whole years before meeting him. Yet somehow the place felt wrong without him. Day Four, things escalated.

“You’re staring at your phone.”

One of her classmates pointed it out.

“I’m not.”

“You checked it six times.”

“I received messages.”

“Not from him.”

Xiaoran had no answer.

Caught. Yichen, meanwhile, appeared to be having the time of his life. At least, that’s what his photos suggested: beaches, resorts, family dinners, mountain views. Every picture looked amazing, which only made Xiaoran more annoyed. How dare he enjoy himself while she suffered? A completely unreasonable thought. But still. Day Five, she stole one of his hoodies. Again. Not because she missed him. Obviously. It just happened to smell faintly like his cologne, which was entirely unrelated.

Day Six, the video calls got longer. Day Seven, even longer. At one point, Mrs. Zhou wandered into the background and laughed.

“Still talking?”

Dead silence. They had been talking for two hours.

“Mom.”

“What?”

Mrs. Zhou looked delighted. She waved at Xiaoran.

“He’s been carrying his phone around all day waiting for your messages.”

Dead silence. Yichen looked horrified.

“Mom. Please leave.”

Xiaoran was trying hard not to smile. That information was valuable. Very valuable. Day Eight, the suffering peaked. Not dramatically. Quietly.

That afternoon, Xiaoran won a small media competition. Normally Yichen was the first person she’d tell—not because she had to, but because she wanted to. But it was the middle of the night where he was. Suddenly the win felt slightly incomplete, which surprised her. Later that night, his reply arrived. Three words. Proud of you. She stared at them for five minutes. Day Nine, Chen Yuhao called.

“Are you alive?”

“Barely.”

“It’s been nine days.”

“Feels like nine years.”

“You’re ridiculous.”

“Correct.”

Day Ten, she started counting. Three days left. Then two. Then one. Every conversation somehow included, “When are you coming back?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually, even Yichen noticed.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You asked me that six times.”

“I’m just checking.”

“Xiaoran.”

“…Fine. I miss you.”

Silence.

“I know.”

Simple and soft, the kind of answer that made missing him worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final day arrived. Thirteen days. Long enough for Xiaoran to decide she hated extended vacations. The airport felt familiar now—she had done this once before, in high school, for one single week. This time she wasn’t dramatic. Not visibly. No clinging, no pouting, no speeches. Just waiting. Patiently. Okay—not patiently. She checked the arrival board twelve times. Finally the doors opened, and there he was. Black shirt. Travel backpack. Slightly messy hair. The same Zhou Yichen—and somehow not, because after almost two weeks, seeing him in person felt strangely unreal.

Then he spotted her and smiled, and just like that, everything felt normal again. Yichen walked toward her.

“Hi.”

Xiaoran threw herself at him. Without any grace at all, hard enough that Yichen took a step back catching her. Her arms tightened, and for a while neither of them said anything. Thirteen days wasn’t forever. But it had been long enough for Xiaoran to realize something: she didn’t just like spending time with Zhou Yichen. He had quietly become part of what made ordinary days feel complete. Finally she muttered into his shoulder,

“I hate family vacations.”

Yichen laughed—the familiar laugh, the one she had missed most.

“I noticed.”

His arms tightened around her. Warm. Safe. Home. After a pause, near her ear, he whispered,

“You know… I missed you too.”

She leaned back just far enough to kiss him, in the middle of arrivals, while her suitcase fell over beside them and neither of them picked it up.

Xiaoran hugged him even tighter, which made Zhou Yichen laugh again. Apparently two weeks apart had only made his girlfriend clingier—an outcome that surprised absolutely nobody.

chapters.desc: A lost French couple, a café near campus, and a language Lin Xiaoran forgot to mention.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Discovered His Girlfriend Secretly Spoke French
chapters.epigraph: “The same thing she’d been telling him all along—just in a different language.”
chapters.content:
There were many surprising things about Lin Xiaoran. Some were expected: her ability to get lost in places she’d visited twenty times, her talent for creating problems out of nothing, her habit of asking questions like:

“Would you still love me if I became a refrigerator?”

A follow-up, apparently, to the capybara question. Normal Xiaoran behavior. What Zhou Yichen didn’t expect—was discovering she spoke French. Not badly, either. Fluently enough to make people stare. And she had apparently been practicing for months without telling him. The betrayal was unbelievable. It started on a random Saturday. They were having lunch at a café near campus. Nothing unusual. Just a quiet date—until Xiaoran froze.

“Hm?”

Yichen looked up.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened, and she sat up straighter. Very suspicious. Across the café, a middle-aged French couple stood looking lost—the man holding a map, the woman holding a phone. Xiaoran stood up.

“I’m back in a minute.”

And walked toward them. Yichen blinked. Okay. Probably helping with directions. Then Xiaoran opened her mouth. French came out. Perfect French. Not textbook French, not app French—real, conversational French. Dead silence. Because WHAT. The French couple immediately brightened. A full conversation followed—questions, answers, directions, recommendations, laughing. Zhou Yichen sat there, staring. Who was this woman? That was his girlfriend. Supposedly. Yet somehow she had unlocked an entire language pack without informing him.

The conversation continued for several minutes. Then Xiaoran smiled, said goodbye, came back, sat down, and went straight back to her juice. Like nothing had happened. Dead silence.

Finally Yichen spoke.

“What.”

“What?”

“You speak French.”

“Oh.”

OH? That was the response?

“Since when?”

“Recently.”

“Recently enough to have a whole conversation?”

Xiaoran went quiet.

Caught. A guilty smile appeared.

“A few months.”

Dead silence.

“A FEW MONTHS?”

She had hidden an entire language. Like a criminal.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

Xiaoran looked genuinely confused.

“I wanted to surprise you.”

Mission accomplished. Yichen was absolutely surprised. Then suspicious.

“When did you learn?”

“Every night.”

“Every night.”

“Mhm.”

“You already have assignments. And competitions.”

“Mhm.”

“You already watch random documentaries about things nobody cares about.”

“Mhm.”

“So when exactly did you have time?”

Xiaoran proudly pointed at herself.

“I am gifted.”

“No.”

“Okay maybe I sacrificed sleep.”

“Thought so.”

The truth. It was always sleep deprivation.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually the story came out. Months ago, Xiaoran had watched a French film for one of her media courses. Then another. Then another. Then she had become obsessed, which was on-brand: when Xiaoran liked something, she liked it aggressively. Normal people watched movies. Xiaoran accidentally learned a language. Then Yichen had an idea. His eyes narrowed.

“Say something.”

“What.”

“In French.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“Embarrassing.”

“You were just speaking confidently.”

“That was practical French.”

“This is boyfriend French.”

Yichen refused to let it go. For twenty whole minutes. Until Xiaoran surrendered.

“Fine.”

Very, she said something in French—soft, fast, beautiful, and completely incomprehensible to him.

“What did you say?”

Xiaoran looked away. Very suspicious.

“Nothing.”

“That’s a lie.”

“It’s not important.”

“Xiaoran.”

“No.”

Now he was definitely curious. If she refused to translate, it meant something. After several more minutes of interrogation, she gave up.

“…I said you’re handsome.”

Yichen smiled. Not a big smile. The dangerous one—the one that always caused problems.

“Oh. That’s all?”

“Yes.”

“Only handsome?”

“YICHEN.”

His smile widened. Xiaoran secretly learning French and then using it to compliment him was absurdly adorable. Then he leaned closer.

“Teach me.”

“What?”

“French.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“Because you’ll immediately use it against me.”

Correct. His face confirmed it immediately.

Three weeks later, he had learned enough French to recognize one specific phrase—one Xiaoran muttered while studying, thinking he wasn’t paying attention. Thinking he couldn’t understand. A terrible mistake. He heard it perfectly, and this time he understood.

“Je t’aime.”

I love you. Simple. Soft. Unconscious. The kind of thing she probably didn’t realize she’d said out loud. Then Yichen closed his textbook.

“What.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“What?”

“You love me?”

Xiaoran froze. No. NO. He wasn’t supposed to understand that yet. Yichen looked unbearably pleased. From that day on, whenever Xiaoran forgot herself and slipped into French, Yichen paid close attention. His girlfriend had spent months on French, and the first important thing she had learned to say was the same thing she had been telling him all along. Just in a different language.

chapters.desc: A peaceful Saturday at the Zhou house, until Mrs. Zhou’s best friend’s daughter walks in calling him “ge.”
chapters.title: The Worst Visitor in Zhou Family History
chapters.epigraph: “The real problem had always been Xiaoran’s own imagination.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran wasn’t nervous. She had visited the Zhou family house several times already. Mrs. Zhou liked her. Mr. Zhou liked her. Even the neighbors’ cat that slept on the Zhou family wall liked her. Everything was fine. Then Jiang Meimei arrived, and nothing was fine anymore. The disaster started on a Saturday afternoon. Xiaoran was curled up beside Zhou Yichen on the living room sofa, stealing his snacks. Mrs. Zhou was chatting happily, Mr. Zhou was reading, and Yichen was pretending to study. Life was peaceful.

Then the front door opened. Mrs. Zhou brightened at once.

“Oh! Meimei is here!”

Dead silence. Who? The answer appeared five seconds later. A girl walked into the living room—beautiful, elegant, perfect posture, perfect makeup, perfect smile. The kind of woman who had clearly never tripped over her own feet. Unlike Xiaoran, who had once gotten lost inside a shopping mall. Twice.

“Hello Auntie.”

The girl smiled sweetly. Mrs. Zhou immediately hugged her.

“Meimei!”

Uh oh. Xiaoran’s instincts went off like an alarm, then came the fatal sentence.

“Xiaoran, this is Jiang Meimei. She’s my best friend’s daughter,” Mrs. Zhou said with a smile.

Dead silence. BEST FRIEND’S DAUGHTER? That phrase alone carried terrifying power.

“Meimei practically grew up with Yichen.”

Dead silence. WHAT. Xiaoran slowly turned toward her boyfriend. Yichen looked completely normal, which made it worse. He clearly wasn’t surprised. Meaning he already knew her. Meaning they had history. Meaning—

“Yichen ge.”

Jiang Meimei smiled. Ge. The dreaded honorific.

Meanwhile Yichen simply nodded.

“Meimei.”

HE KNEW HER NAME. Xiaoran sat up straighter. This was serious. Then the conversation started, and somehow everything got worse.

“Oh, Yichen ge, are you still playing basketball?”

“Yes.”

“I saw your tournament photos.”

“Mm.”

“I showed them to my parents.”

“Mm.”

Their families were connected. Xiaoran hated everything. Jiang Meimei sat elegantly across from them, perfect in every way. The killing blow. Mrs. Zhou laughed.

“You know, when they were children, everyone thought Meimei and Yichen would become a couple.”

Xiaoran nearly inhaled a potato chip wrong. Jiang Meimei laughed politely. Mrs. Zhou laughed. Mr. Zhou laughed. Even the cat on the wall looked suspicious. Only Yichen looked exhausted—he had clearly heard this story a thousand times. Xiaoran hadn’t, and now she was suffering. Greatly.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next hour was torture—not because Jiang Meimei did anything wrong. That was the problem. She was nice. Kind, polite, friendly, impossible to dislike. Which made Xiaoran dislike the situation even more. Then, over tea, Jiang Meimei casually mentioned—

“I still have the birthday gift Yichen gave me years ago.”

A birthday gift. HE BOUGHT HER GIFTS. Xiaoran was spiraling. Internally. Externally she was smiling—a normal smile. Definitely not dying. A hand landed on her knee—warm, steady. Yichen. Without even looking at her, he squeezed once. A warning. He could apparently feel the jealousy radiating off her. Traitor. The real disaster happened later. Mrs. Zhou asked Yichen to help carry something upstairs, and Xiaoran was left alone with Jiang Meimei.

The moment he was gone, panic set in. Now they would have to talk. Woman to woman. Nightmare. Jiang Meimei smiled. Xiaoran prepared for battle. Then, unexpectedly, Meimei laughed.

“You look terrified.”

“…What?”

“You’ve been staring at me for two hours.”

Caught. Immediately. Meimei smiled again, genuinely amused.

“You’re much cuter than I expected.”

“…Expected?”

“Mrs. Zhou talks about you constantly.”

“She does?”

“All the time.”

Then Meimei leaned closer.

“And honestly, I understand now.”

Xiaoran blinked. What was happening? Meimei laughed again.

“You know, Yichen ge never liked any girls growing up. Never.”

Then she pointed upstairs.

“The fact he looks at you the way he does is honestly shocking.”

Now Xiaoran wanted details. Many details.

“What way?”

Meimei stared at her, then burst out laughing.

“Oh my God.”

“What?”

“You don’t know.”

Know what? Before Xiaoran could ask, footsteps sounded on the stairs. Yichen was back, and both girls immediately looked at him—one amused, one confused. Yichen looked instantly suspicious.

“…What happened?”

“Nothing,” Jiang Meimei said.

“Nothing,” Xiaoran said, in exactly the same tone. Very dangerous.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, after Jiang Meimei finally left, Xiaoran cornered her boyfriend.

“What way?”

Yichen blinked.

“What.”

“Jiang Meimei said you look at me differently.”

Realization, followed immediately by annoyance. Meimei had started problems on her way out. Wonderful. Yichen sighed.

“Forget it.”

“No.”

“Please.”

“NO.”

Several minutes of relentless pestering later, he finally surrendered.

“The way someone looks at the person they love.”

Direct hit. Xiaoran froze completely. Yichen looked away, slightly embarrassed. Xiaoran scooted closer. Then closer. Then leaned into his shoulder, smiling.

“Okay.”

“Okay?”

“I’ve decided.”

“What.”

“I don’t hate Jiang Meimei anymore.”

“…You hated her?”

“Briefly.”

“Why.”

“She was too pretty.”

Yichen laughed. And just like that—the greatest threat in Lin Xiaoran’s imagination was over—mostly because Jiang Meimei had never been a rival at all. The real problem had always been Xiaoran’s imagination, which, unfortunately for everyone involved, was far more dangerous.

chapters.desc: Lunar New Year at her grandparents’ house, and one uncle with opinions about why she’s dating Zhou Yichen.
chapters.title: The One Thing Lin Xiaoran Could Never Tolerate
chapters.epigraph: “I chose him because he’s Zhou Yichen.”
chapters.content:
There were many things Lin Xiaoran disliked. Early classes. Group projects. Spicy food stronger than her tolerance, which was most spicy food. People who walked slowly in crowded places. But there was one thing she genuinely hated: gold diggers. Not because she was rich. She wasn’t. Her family lived comfortably—her mother an accountant, her father an engineer—not wealthy, not poor. Enough for food, for school, to get through a month without worrying. Nothing more, nothing less.

So it always made Xiaoran uncomfortable when people assumed she was dating Zhou Yichen for his money—especially since she had liked him long before she knew how wealthy his family actually was. Not everyone understood that. Including Uncle Deng: a distant relative from another city, the kind who appeared once every few years and somehow had opinions about everyone’s lives. It happened at Lunar New Year, at her grandparents’ house. Lots of relatives, lots of food, lots of noise, lots of gossip. A normal family gathering—until someone mentioned Zhou Yichen.

Everyone became interested.

“That’s the boyfriend in the business program at Huaining University, right?”

“Very handsome.”

“Excellent grades.”

“Good family.”

It was harmless—until Uncle Deng laughed and said, casually,

“Well, Xiaoran certainly found herself a rich boyfriend.”

The room quieted slightly. Xiaoran paused.

“Smart girl. Nowadays girls know how to choose,” Uncle Deng went on.

Dead silence. No. Not that. Not that. Across the table, her mother frowned and set down her cup with a small, sharp click. Uncle Deng didn’t notice. Or didn’t care.

“Honestly, if I were young again, I’d choose someone wealthy too.”

A few relatives looked uncomfortable. The implication was obvious. Xiaoran hated it. Not because it embarrassed her—because it insulted everything she felt for Yichen. Every late-night study session, every tournament, every argument, every moment, reduced to money. Xiaoran put down her chopsticks. Quietly.

“Uncle, if Yichen wasn’t rich, I’d still date him.”

The room went silent. Everyone knew that tone. The dangerous Xiaoran tone. Uncle Deng laughed.

“Of course you’d say that.”

Xiaoran smiled. It wasn’t a friendly smile.

“Actually, when we started dating, I didn’t know his family was wealthy.”

Silence.

“He was just annoying.”

Several cousins burst out laughing. Accurate.

“He studied with me. He helped me. He listened to me complain. He stayed beside me when I failed things. He celebrated when I succeeded.”

Then she looked directly at Uncle Deng.

“So no. I didn’t choose him because he’s rich.”

The room got quieter. Nobody was joking anymore.

“I chose him because he’s Zhou Yichen.”

Dead silence. Even her grandmother looked moved. Uncle Deng looked a little embarrassed, but still tried to defend himself.

“I wasn’t criticizing you.”

“Maybe not. But it sounded like you were criticizing him,” Xiaoran replied.

That surprised everyone. Most people would have defended themselves first. Xiaoran defended Yichen first. Always. Without thinking.

“You know what bothers me?”

Nobody answered.

“People think money is why someone stays.”

Her fingers tightened slightly around her teacup.

“But I’ve seen people with money treat others terribly. And I’ve seen people with nothing give everything.”

Then she smiled. A small smile. The real one this time.

“Yichen just happens to have both.”

Her grandmother laughed first.

“That’s a good answer.”

The tension broke. Conversation resumed, food returned, and the family gossip moved on.

Later that evening, as Xiaoran walked home, her phone rang. Yichen.

“Hm?”

“Lin Jun told me what happened.”

Family networks were terrifying.

“What part?”

“The part where you defended my honor.”

Then she heard him laughing.

“No, tell me.”

“I just think it’s nice.”

Xiaoran rolled her eyes.

“It wasn’t nice.”

“It was.”

“He was being annoying.”

“And?”

“And nobody gets to talk about you like that.”

A softer silence, the kind Yichen only ever had around her.

“So if I lost everything tomorrow…”

“No.”

“What?”

“No hypothetical questions.”

“Answer.”

She sighed. Then finally said:

“If you lost everything tomorrow, I’d still be there. Unfortunately.”

Yichen laughed—a real laugh, the kind she loved most. Somehow it felt worth more than all the money in the world.

chapters.desc: Grandma Lin wants to see the boy up close. Uncle Deng will be there. So will the dumplings.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Meets the Relatives
chapters.epigraph: “That one’s acceptable.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came from her grandmother, which meant nobody could refuse it.

Three days after Uncle Deng’s comment at New Year dinner, Grandma Lin called Xiaoran’s mother, and Xiaoran’s mother called Xiaoran into the kitchen, and said, without turning around from the sink, “Your grandmother wants the boy at dinner on the fifth.”

Xiaoran froze with a mandarin halfway to her mouth.

“…The boy?”

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Why?”

“She says if you’re going to defend someone in front of the whole family like that, she wants to see what he looks like up close. Your uncle will be there.” Her mother turned off the tap.

“Uncle Deng?”

“He’s staying until the seventh.”

Xiaoran put the mandarin down. “Mom. That’s a trap.”

“It’s dinner,” said Mrs. Lin, which in her language meant yes, and you’re both walking into it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen arrived at five, exactly on time, which Xiaoran had known he would. What she hadn’t expected was how he arrived. No black car. He came up the lane from the bus stop on foot, in a plain dark coat, carrying a fruit basket in one hand and a paper bag in the other. Inside the bag were a tin of good tea for her grandfather, a box of pastries from the old bakery near their high school, and a small pot of narcissus for her grandmother, because Xiaoran had once mentioned, months ago and only once, that her grandmother liked them.

She met him at the gate.

“You took the bus.”

“Hm.”

“You never take the bus.”

He looked at the house—the red couplets on the door, the paper lanterns, the sound of a dozen relatives talking over a television—and then back at her.

“Your uncle thinks I’m a rich boyfriend. I didn’t want to give him a parking space to prove it,” he said.

Xiaoran stared at him. Then she reached up and fixed the collar of his coat, which didn’t need fixing, mostly so she’d have something to do with her hands.

“You’re nervous,” she said.

“Very.”

That surprised her so much she forgot to be nervous herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside, it was exactly as bad as she’d feared and also completely different. Her grandmother took one look at the narcissus and said “Hm,” in a tone Xiaoran had only ever heard her use for good melons. Her father shook Yichen’s hand for too long and then had to go stand in the kitchen for a minute. Lin Jun, lounging on the sofa with a beer, raised it in Yichen’s direction like they were old war buddies, which, after the day he’d “stolen” him, they sort of were.

Then the questions started. The aunties wanted to know his height, his major, his grades, and whether he could cook. The uncles wanted to know what business he planned to go into and whether he’d thought about the civil service. Two small cousins wanted to know if he could dunk, and when he said yes, they wanted proof, immediately, in the courtyard, and had to be held back by the hoods of their jackets.

Yichen answered all of it. Calmly. Politely. Without once mentioning his family’s company, or his car, or anything he owned. When one auntie asked what his parents did, he said “My father runs a business, and my mother keeps him from working too much,” and the auntie laughed and moved on. Across the room, Uncle Deng watched all of this over his teacup and didn’t say anything. Xiaoran watched Uncle Deng.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened at the dumpling table. Every year on the fifth, the whole family folded dumplings together, and every year it was a competition nobody admitted was a competition. Grandma Lin sat at the head of the table, folding perfect pleated dumplings at terrifying speed. Xiaoran’s were lopsided but sealed. Lin Jun’s were somehow perfect, which was annoying. Yichen’s were a disaster. He held the wrapper like it was an exam question. He put in too much filling. He pinched the edges with enormous concentration, and the dumpling burst at the seam and lay there on the board, looking injured.

One of the little cousins burst out laughing. So did Grandma Lin.

“Again,” she said, and pushed another wrapper toward him.

He tried again. It was worse.

“You’re better at basketball,” Xiaoran told him.

“I’m better at everything than this.”

Uncle Deng put down his teacup.

“Must be strange, doing things with your own hands for once,” he said.

The table didn’t go silent, exactly. But it got quieter. Xiaoran felt her mother go still beside her. She opened her mouth.

Under the table, Yichen’s knee touched hers. Wait. He picked up a third wrapper.

He said, “It is. My dad says money is the easiest thing to have and the easiest thing to lose. He made me work in one of his warehouses the summer I was fifteen so I’d understand that. I was bad at that too. For the first week.” He spooned in less filling this time.

Uncle Deng raised his eyebrows.

“And. Xiaoran told me what she said to you at New Year,” Yichen said, still looking at the dumpling.

Now the table really did go quiet.

“I’m not sure I’ve earned all of it yet. But I’m trying to,” he said.

He pinched the edges closed. It held. Grandma Lin picked it up, turned it over, and put it on the tray with her own.

“That one’s acceptable,” she announced.

Across the table, Uncle Deng looked at Yichen. Then he picked up his teacup again, and said, gruffly, to nobody in particular, “Too much filling’s a common mistake.”

It was the closest thing to an apology anyone in the family had ever heard from him.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, the cousins dragged everyone out into the courtyard for sparklers. The air smelled like gunpowder and cold. Somewhere down the lane, someone was setting off firecrackers, and the little cousins screamed and ran in circles, writing their names in light. Xiaoran stood by the door with Yichen, holding a sparkler she’d forgotten to light.

“You didn’t have to say that. About earning it,” she said.

“I meant it.”

“I know. That’s why you didn’t have to say it.”

He didn’t answer. He just took her sparkler, lit it from his own, and handed it back. Behind them, the door opened. Xiaoran’s mother came out, wrapped in her coat, holding something red. She walked straight up to Yichen and held out an envelope. He looked at it. Then at Xiaoran. Then back at the envelope, completely lost.

“Auntie, I can’t—”

“Take it. It’s New Year,” said Mrs. Lin.

He took it with both hands, the way you were supposed to, and bowed. Mrs. Lin nodded once, brisk as always, and went back inside without another word. Yichen stared at the red envelope in his hands.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm.”

“What does it mean? When the parents give it to—” He stopped.

Xiaoran looked at the door her mother had just closed, at the warm light behind the paper lanterns, at the shape of her grandmother at the window pretending not to watch. She knew exactly what it meant. In her family, the first red envelope from her mother didn’t go to friends, or classmates, or a boy someone was dating for now. It went to someone they expected to see at this table next year. And the year after that.

“It means, you have to come back next year and fold better dumplings,” she said, and her voice wobbled.

He looked at her for a long time in the flickering light. Then he tucked the envelope carefully into the inside pocket of his coat, over his heart, and didn’t say anything at all. He didn’t have to.

chapters.desc: A weekly viewing report, eleven hours of dramas, and the most dangerous thing Zhou Yichen has ever done: change a password.
chapters.title: Netflix vs Zhou Yichen
chapters.epigraph: “You violated my human rights.”
chapters.content:
There were many ways to start a relationship conflict. Jealousy. Miscommunication. Trust issues. Different life goals. Lin Xiaoran and Zhou Yichen managed to have one over Netflix—specifically, because Zhou Yichen accidentally found out how much Netflix Xiaoran watched in a single day. The discovery happened on a Tuesday. Yichen paid for the subscription. Not because Xiaoran couldn’t—because he’d insisted.

“Just use mine.”

At the time, Xiaoran thought that was sweet. A mistake.

One afternoon, Yichen got a notification: weekly viewing activity. Normally he ignored those. This time, he opened it—and froze.

“…What?”

The watch history went on. And on. Episodes one through seven of one show. Then another show. Then another. Dead silence. According to Netflix, Lin Xiaoran had spent almost eleven hours watching dramas on Sunday. Eleven. Hours. Yichen messaged her.

Yichen: How many hours were you on Netflix Sunday?

Seen. Typing. Stopped typing. Typing again.

Xiaoran: Why.

Yichen: Answer the question.

Xiaoran: Approximately.

Yichen: How many.

Xiaoran: The number isn’t important.

The number was important.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: …

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Maybe.

Yichen: Maybe?

Xiaoran: Nine?

Yichen: The report says eleven.

Dead silence. She had forgotten Netflix tracked things. Traitors, all of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen showed up at her apartment holding groceries, concern, and judgment.

“Eleven hours?”

“It was a weekend.”

“Eleven hours.”

“It sounds worse when you say it.”

“Because it is worse.”

Xiaoran crossed her arms.

“It was educational.”

“What was educational?”

“The romance.”

“No.”

“The character development.”

“No.”

“The cinematography.”

“No.”

Dead silence. Then Yichen opened her refrigerator and discovered she had skipped lunch. The atmosphere got much worse. After the diet incident, skipped meals were the one thing he never joked about.

“Xiaoran. You skipped meals.”

“I forgot.”

“You remembered fourteen episodes.”

Xiaoran had nothing to say to that.

Then came the betrayal. The greatest betrayal.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Netflix logged her out. Because what? WHAT? She tried again. Nothing. Again. Nothing. Then her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Temporary restriction.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: You did WHAT?

Yichen: One week.

Xiaoran: ONE WEEK?

Yichen: You need sunlight.

Xiaoran: I HAVE SUNLIGHT.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: I SAW SUNLIGHT THROUGH THE WINDOW.

Yichen: That’s not the same thing.

The war began. For the first time in months, Lin Xiaoran ignored Zhou Yichen completely. No messages. No calls. No random photos. No good morning, no good night. Nothing. Yichen lasted exactly six hours before he got uncomfortable. Normally his phone held three cat photos, two random observations, one complaint, five unrelated thoughts, and at least one look at this cloud. Today: nothing. The silence was deeply unsettling. Evening came. Still nothing. The next day, nothing. Day three, nothing. By then, even Chen Yuhao had noticed.

“What did you do?”

“I blocked Netflix.”

“You idiot.”

“She watched eleven hours.”

“That’s not the point.”

“Then what’s the point?”

“You touched her freedom.”

Yuhao shook his head.

“She’s going to hold this grudge forever.”

A terrifying possibility.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen found Xiaoran in the media building working on an assignment. She looked up, saw him, and looked straight back down. The audacity.

“Xiaoran.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

Nothing. Finally Yichen sat down beside her, close enough that their shoulders touched. Still ignored. Five minutes passed. Then ten. Finally, Yichen sighed.

“Are you done?”

“No.”

Her first words in three days. Progress.

“You’re really angry.”

“Correct.”

“It was for your health.”

“You violated my rights.”

Her rights. Netflix had apparently become a legal issue. Then Xiaoran turned—actually turned—and pointed at him.

“I was three episodes away from the confession.”

“The confession?”

“Three episodes.”

The heartbreak in her voice almost made him laugh. Almost. Yichen rubbed his forehead. The whole argument was ridiculous.

“I was worried.”

Her anger wavered. That tone was unfair—the genuine one, the honest one.

“You skipped meals. You slept at three.”

More silence.

“You watched until your eyes hurt.”

Xiaoran looked away. Caught. Again.

“I know.”

The fight lost all momentum. The truth was, she knew. And Yichen knew she knew. After a moment, he took out his phone, opened Netflix, changed the password, and handed it over.

Her anger vanished. Completely. Like magic. Traitorous woman. She grabbed his sleeve—the universal sign of peace.

“Thank you.”

“Conditions.”

“What.”

“No eleven-hour marathons.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

“Xiaoran.”

“Ten?”

“No.”

“Nine?”

“No.”

“Eight?”

“No.”

She tucked herself against his shoulder. The ultimate negotiating strategy, and unfortunately the most effective one, because Zhou Yichen immediately knew he had already lost. Just like every other argument with Lin Xiaoran.

“Six hours maximum,” he said.

Xiaoran gasped.

“Victory.”

“That’s not a victory.”

“It is to me.”

Then she smiled—the bright one, the one that made Yichen forgive things far too easily. As she happily logged back into Netflix, Yichen realized blocking her had been a mistake. Not because she was angry—because a drama-deprived Lin Xiaoran was much harder to handle than a drama-addicted one. A lesson he never repeated.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran is “extremely busy.” Her lie lasts approximately three minutes.
chapters.title: The World’s Worst Liar
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody who was actually busy sent updates about how busy they were.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran was many things. Cute. Dramatic. Smart. Chaotic. A good liar wasn’t one of them. The problem wasn’t that she couldn’t make up stories. She absolutely could. The problem was that Zhou Yichen knew her far too well, which was why her latest lie lasted approximately three minutes. A personal record. The disaster started on a Wednesday afternoon. Yichen had practice. Normally Xiaoran waited for him afterward. Today she wasn’t there. Instead, he got a message.

Xiaoran: I’m busy.

Dead silence. The message already looked suspicious. Not busy with what. Not talk later. Just: I’m busy. Then another message arrived.

Xiaoran: Extremely busy.

Yichen smiled. Nobody who was actually busy sent updates about how busy they were.

An hour later, he found her at the campus café, looking guilty. The moment she saw him, she sat up straight. Too quickly. Like a criminal.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

Silence. Yichen sat down across from her—calm, patient—and waited. Eventually, Lin Xiaoran always confessed. She simply couldn’t help herself. And right on schedule, she started talking.

“Today was productive.”

“Oh?”

“Very productive.”

“Hm.”

“I was studying.”

The first lie. Tiny, harmless. But Yichen noticed—not because of the words, but because she tugged her sleeves down over her hands, the way she had for years whenever she was nervous.

“Very serious studying.”

“Hm.”

“Educational.”

“Hm.”

“Academic.”

“Hm.”

Yichen’s mouth twitched. Now she was overexplaining. Another sign. Xiaoran kept talking, and the more she talked, the worse it got.

“I definitely wasn’t doing anything strange.”

The self-report. Nobody had accused her of anything, and she was already defending herself. Yichen was enjoying himself enormously. Watching Xiaoran lie was one of life’s simplest pleasures—not because she was convincing, but because she wasn’t. At all.

“I spent the entire afternoon being responsible.”

“Responsible.”

“Very.”

“Hm.”

“I would never waste time.”

Now Yichen had to look away, because his smile was becoming noticeable. Xiaoran noticed anyway. Uh oh. She knew that smile—the one that appeared whenever he caught her doing something ridiculous. And suddenly she was flustered. Not because she’d been caught. Because he looked unfairly handsome. There was something deeply dangerous about Zhou Yichen when he knew something she didn’t know he knew. Relaxed, confident, amused—the slight smile, the calm eyes, the feeling that he was letting her dig her own grave and enjoying every second. A disaster.

Yichen leaned back, comfortable, watching.

“So. What exactly were you studying?”

Dead silence. Details. The enemy of every liar. Xiaoran panicked.

“Media.”

“What part?”

“…Media media.”

Yichen’s smile widened, just slightly, and somehow that made her heart beat faster. Not because of the interrogation. Because he looked ridiculously attractive. This was terrible.

“Which assignment?”

“The assignment.”

“Which one?”

“The… important one.”

“Hm.”

The smile grew, slowly, until Xiaoran wanted to hide under the table. Not from embarrassment. From him. Why was he looking at her like that? Yichen folded his arms, still smiling, still patient, obviously entertained.

“Xiaoran.”

“What.”

“Look at me.”

“No.”

Yichen laughed, which made things worse. He leaned forward, close enough that she could see the amusement in his eyes.

“Why not?”

“Reasons.”

“What reasons?”

“Personal reasons.”

“Such as?”

He was enjoying this far too much. Xiaoran pointed at him.

“Stop smiling.”

“What smile?”

THAT smile. The teasing one, the one that showed up whenever he felt completely in control. Which was unfortunately right now. Yichen tilted his head, still smiling, still impossible, and asked,

“How long were you watching dramas?”

Direct hit. The truth. And the worst part? He had known from the very first sentence. The entire conversation had been a trap. A cruel, cruel trap. Xiaoran covered her face, defeated.

“Four hours.”

“Hm.”

“Maybe five.”

“Hm.”

“…Six.”

Exactly the six-hour limit from the Netflix treaty. Technically she hadn’t even broken the rule. She had just lied about getting close to it, which was somehow more embarrassing. The confession. As always. Yichen laughed—victorious, annoyingly handsome—and Xiaoran peeked through her fingers, only to regret it immediately. He was still smiling at her like that. Still far too attractive for someone who had just interrogated her.

He reached over and gently moved her hands away from her face.

“Hi.”

Xiaoran groaned.

“I don’t like you.”

“Liar.”

The worst part was that he was right about that, too.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran has discovered a new research topic. It has categories, lists, and ratings. Zhou Yichen would like it to stop.
chapters.title: The Internet Was a Mistake
chapters.epigraph: “Do you know how dangerous you are?”
chapters.content:
There were many things Zhou Yichen feared. Basketball injuries. Losing important tournaments. Lin Xiaoran attempting to cook without supervision. But one thing caused problems more consistently than all of them: the internet. Every time Xiaoran discovered a new interest online, everyone suffered. This week’s victim was Zhou Yichen. It started on a Thursday evening. Yichen was studying. Peacefully. Productively. A rare event. Then his phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: Question.
