Every message that started with “Question” was dangerous.

Yichen: What.

Xiaoran: Did you know there are different types of kisses?

Dead silence.

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: There are SO MANY.

Yichen: Why are you researching this.

Seen. No reply. Which was somehow more alarming.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next day, Yichen found out why. Xiaoran showed up outside his lecture hall carrying a notebook. Not suspicious normally. Extremely suspicious when carried by Lin Xiaoran.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I have information.”

“About?”

“Kisses.”

Dead silence. Several students nearby walked away. Smart people. Xiaoran opened the notebook. It had notes. NOTES.

“Look.”

Yichen looked, and immediately regretted it. She had clearly spent hours on this. There were categories. Lists. Observations. Ratings.

“Why.”

“Educational purposes.”

“No.”

“Fine. Curiosity.”

At least that was honest. Xiaoran pointed at the page.

“Apparently there are forehead kisses.”

“You know that.”

“You do those.”

“Correct.”

“Cheek kisses.”

“You know that too.”

“Hand kisses.”

Yichen didn’t answer.

“Eskimo kisses.”

Then she flipped another page.

“And French kisses.”

Dead silence. The real reason. Yichen understood everything. He closed the notebook, slowly.

“No.”

“What.”

“No.”

“You haven’t even heard my proposal.”

“I don’t need to. I know exactly where this conversation is going.”

He was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three hours later, in a quiet corner of the campus garden, Xiaoran was still talking about it. Relentlessly.

“Why does it have that name?”

“I don’t know.”

“Who invented it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Why is it famous?”

“Xiaoran. Please stop interviewing me.”

She pouted. It had absolutely no effect. Mostly. She rested her chin on his shoulder, thinking. Dangerous.

“I think couples probably try different things naturally.”

Yichen sensed disaster approaching. Rapidly. Xiaoran looked up—curious, innocent, hopelessly unaware.

“…Do you?”

Sometimes Yichen wondered how one person could be so smart and so clueless at the same time. She could analyze media campaigns, win competitions, research anything—and still completely fail to understand the effect she had on him. Very, Yichen sighed.

“Xiaoran, do you have any idea what you do to me?”

“What does that mean?”

Exactly. She didn’t know. Not even slightly. He reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear—a familiar gesture that made her smile right away.

“There.”

“There what?”

“That smile.”

“…What about it?”

“You do things like that. You ask questions. You get curious. Then you look at me like everything is simple.”

Xiaoran blinked, completely confused. Yichen laughed. Of course she was. Then he leaned in and pressed a kiss into her hair—gentle, warm, familiar. The kiss he always gave her, the one that calmed her down every time.

“There.”

“What was that for?”

“Because I like that one.”

Xiaoran smiled again.

“So that’s a no?”

“Absolutely.”

“This relationship has no freedom.”

Yichen actually laughed—a real laugh, the kind she loved hearing. Xiaoran leaned against him, happy. The internet might have introduced her to dozens of kinds of kisses, but her favorite was still the simplest: Zhou Yichen looking at her like she was the best thing that had ever happened to him, and kissing her forehead like he was quietly reminding himself she was real. Even if she occasionally came up with terrifying research topics.

chapters.desc: In his dream, Lin Xiaoran is a famous idol who has never met him. He does not take it well.
chapters.title: The Dream That Made Zhou Yichen Hug Xiaoran at 3 AM
chapters.epigraph: “The one who knew exactly who Zhou Yichen was.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen rarely remembered his dreams. Most disappeared the moment he woke up. This one didn’t. Unfortunately. The dream started normally. At least—normal by dream standards. He was on campus. Walking toward the media building. Looking for Xiaoran. People started screaming. Not scared screaming. Excited screaming. The kind of screaming usually reserved for celebrities. Yichen stopped. Confused. Then he heard it.

“XIAORAN!”

“LIN XIAORAN!”

“SHE’S HERE!”

Dead silence. Because what? A black van pulled up. Security appeared. Cameras. Hundreds of fans. And out stepped—Lin Xiaoran. Except not his Xiaoran. Well—still his Xiaoran. Different. Much different. Her hair was longer and perfectly styled, her makeup flawless, her clothes designer. Beautiful. Actually breathtaking—the kind of beautiful that made entire crowds stop moving. And apparently—In this dream—she was a famous idol. Dead silence. Dream Yichen was just as confused as real Yichen.

Then Xiaoran smiled. The crowd lost their minds. People screamed louder. Phones everywhere. Security closed in around her. A terrifying realization appeared. Nobody was acting strange. Meaning this was normal. For her. Then Xiaoran walked past him. Completely past him—without stopping, without smiling, without even looking. Like he didn’t exist. Dead silence. That felt awful. Then Yichen followed. Because apparently dream logic said that was acceptable. The next several days became increasingly horrifying.

Because Dream Xiaoran genuinely didn’t know him. Not as a boyfriend, not as a friend, not at all. Meanwhile, Yichen was still himself—still a university student, still a basketball player, still hopelessly in love with her. Only now his girlfriend was an international celebrity who had never met him. Worst dream ever.

Then came the truly evil part. The fan meeting. Because somehow—dream Yichen ended up there. Standing in line like everyone else. Holding merchandise like everyone else. Waiting his turn like everyone else. The humiliation was unbelievable. He reached the table. And there she was. Beautiful, smiling, perfect—and completely unfamiliar.

“Hello.”

Her idol smile appeared—professional, warm, practiced. The one she gave thousands of people. Not the real one, not his, and somehow that hurt. Then she looked up.

“What’s your name?”

What kind of nightmare was this?

“My…”

His voice actually failed. Dream Xiaoran waited politely. Completely unaware she was destroying him.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Nice to meet you.”

And that was somehow worse. Much worse. Because no. No it wasn’t. She was supposed to know him. She was supposed to steal his hoodies, send him forty messages a day, hug him out of nowhere while he studied. Not this. Never this. Then Dream Xiaoran signed his album.

“Thank you for supporting me.”

Support. Not boyfriend. Not Yichen. Not idiot. Not mine. Support. The dream became increasingly absurd afterward. Yichen somehow went to her concerts. Watched her interviews. Watched her get more famous, watched millions of people love her—and every single time, she looked right through him like a stranger. Then one day in the dream—things became unbearable. Because an interviewer asked:

“What kind of man is your ideal type?”

Dream Yichen paid close attention. Obviously. And Xiaoran thought carefully. Then smiled.

“I think someone gentle.”

Good.

“Someone patient.”

Good.

“Someone who makes me feel safe.”

Excellent. Then she laughed.

“I don’t know though. I’ve never met someone like that.”

Dream Yichen almost had a breakdown. WHAT DO YOU MEAN. HE WAS RIGHT THERE. The dream jumped again. Now he stood backstage after a concert. Watching her from a distance. Dream Xiaoran turned. Actually turned. Their eyes met, for the first time. She walked toward him. Closer. Closer. Until she was standing right in front of him. Finally.

“Do I know you?”

The world exploded. Zhou Yichen woke up immediately. 3:17 AM. Dark room. Heart pounding. Genuine irritation. That dream had been cruel. Then he felt something warm and heavy against his side. Lin Xiaoran. They had both fallen asleep on his sofa halfway through a movie, under the same blanket, and she was still there—completely real. No idol, no fame, nothing out of reach. Just Xiaoran. His Xiaoran, drooling slightly on his shoulder. Very glamorous. It was the first time she’d ever still been at his place after midnight. Her own studio was across the road, and somewhere around the second film neither of them had wanted to walk her there.

Yichen stared at her for several seconds. He wrapped both arms around her, tight enough that she made a confused, sleepy noise.

“Hm?”

Half asleep. Barely conscious.

“What happened?”

Nothing. How was he supposed to explain? Sorry, I had a dream where you were a celebrity and didn’t know me, so now I’m emotionally damaged. Impossible. Then Xiaoran opened one eye.

“…Yichen?”

He was still hugging her. Not letting go.

“You okay?”

“…Bad dream.”

Her sleepy expression softened.

“Oh.”

Without even waking up properly, she wrapped her arms around him too.

“There.”

“What.”

“Better.”

Half asleep, and completely unaware she had just fixed everything. Then she yawned.

“You’re my favorite person.”

Sleepy Xiaoran was dangerous. Two seconds later, she was asleep again. Zhou Yichen lay staring at the ceiling, his heart finally calming down. The dream version had been beautiful. World-famous. Perfect. But he preferred this one—the clingy one, the dramatic one, the one who stole his hoodies and never stopped talking. The one who knew exactly who Zhou Yichen was. Before falling asleep again, he tightened his arms around her, just to make sure. In case Dream Xiaoran got any more ideas.

In the morning she woke up under his blanket with a crease from his shirt on her cheek and a cup of warm milk on the floor beside the sofa. He kissed her good morning before she could be embarrassed about the drooling. It worked, mostly.

After that it stopped being an accident. By spring there was a toothbrush in his bathroom, a drawer that was hers, and a spare key on her ring. She slept at his apartment on Fridays and most Saturdays and went back across the road on Sunday nights, because her studio, she said, still needed her. It mostly needed her laundry.

chapters.desc: Jiayi and Ning want a night out by the river. Lin Xiaoran has never been to a club. Zhou Yichen has, exactly twice.
chapters.title: The First Night Out
chapters.epigraph: “Since we were seventeen.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had never been to a club. Not once. Not in high school, when some of her classmates had started sneaking into places with fake confidence and borrowed jackets, and not in her first year at Huaining either, because clubs had always sounded to her like somewhere you went to shout at people you could already text.

Then on Friday afternoon her phone lit up.

Jiayi: We’re going out tonight. The place by the river. Ning’s coming. You’re coming.

Ning: You are actually coming this time.

Xiaoran: What do people even DO there

Jiayi: Dance. Drink. Exist loudly.

Xiaoran: That’s suspiciously vague

Ning: PLEASE

She stared at the screen. She was curious. A little intimidated. Mostly curious. Meilin and Yuhao were at universities hours away now, and Jiayi and Ning were the first friends she’d made here on her own, the two who’d lost her in the festival crowd in her first month and then spent ten frantic minutes looking for her. She wanted to do things with them.

She just didn’t know what to expect. So naturally she rang the person who knew almost everything.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Have you ever been to a club?”

A short pause. “Yes.”

She sat up on her bed. “When?”

“The one by the river? Twice. Once after the spring league final, and once for Fang Ze’s twentieth birthday.”

“You never told me that.”

“I told you both times. The first time you were asleep by ten and sent me a sticker of a sleeping panda at eleven. The second time you were up finishing your competition slides and sent me nine stickers and a photo of your face mask.” She could hear him smiling.

She remembered the face mask. She didn’t remember the club.

“You said the team’s going out.”

“The team went out. To a club. I drove three of them home at half past eleven, because I don’t drink when I’m driving, and I was in bed by midnight. Why?”

“…I’m going tonight. With Jiayi and Ning.”

“Your first time.”

“How do you know?”

“Because you just asked me what people do there.”

“That’s not evidence.”

“It’s fairly convincing evidence.”

She ignored that. “Would you come?”

“Of course.”

She smiled at the ceiling. “Really?”

“Did you think I’d say no?”

“I thought you might have training.”

“Not on a Friday. And not tonight,” said Zhou Yichen.

At half past seven he knocked on the door of her studio. Black shirt, dark trousers, the plain watch he always wore. Nothing special. Unfortunately he had the kind of face that made nothing special look expensive.

She’d chosen a fitted top, a short skirt, boots, a small bag, a little more eyeliner than usual, and an hour on her hair.

He looked at her for a second longer than he needed to. “Beautiful.”

Then his eyes went to the bag. “What’s in there?”

“Important things.”

He looked when she opened it. Phone, wallet, lip gloss, powder, a hair tie, a tiny perfume, two packets of tissues, a stuffed panda keyring, and an amount of miscellaneous items that defied classification.

“Are you going to a club or moving house?”

“Don’t judge me.”

He took out the perfume, handed it to her to use now, and put the panda keyring on her desk. “Less in the bag. You’ll put something down somewhere.”

“I’m not that careless.”

He looked at her. She looked back. A few seconds passed.

“…Sometimes.”

He checked that her phone was charged, did up the strap of her bag where it had twisted, and didn’t say one word about the skirt.

“If you feel uncomfortable, tell me. We’ll leave whenever you want. And you don’t have to drink because everyone else does.”

“I know.”

“I know you know,” he said, and held out his hand.

The club was much louder than she’d imagined. The bass came up through the floor into her boots. Lights swung across the ceiling and the dance floor was a single moving animal made of people.

She stopped in the doorway, and he stopped with her.

“Too much?”

“No. Just— Wow.” She looked round.

“First impression?”

“Very loud.”

“That’s generally the point.”

Jiayi saw them first and screamed her name across the room, then saw who she’d brought, and her mouth fell open. “You brought the basketball one?”

“My personal guide,” said Xiaoran proudly.

At the bar she spent five minutes reading the menu as if it were an exam paper. “What’s this one?”

“A cocktail.”

“And this?”

“Also a cocktail.”

“What’s the difference?”

“The ingredients.”

“Very helpful,” she said, and he laughed, and then explained properly: which were sweet, which were strong, which tasted like juice and weren’t. He ordered himself water with lemon, because the car was outside. When she chose something pink he put a glass of water beside it without comment.

She took a sip and her eyes went wide. “It tastes like juice.”

“Be careful with those.”

“Why?”

“Some drinks are much stronger than they taste.”

She looked at the glass with deep suspicion. “That’s dishonest.”

“Very,” he agreed.

When the music changed, Jiayi grabbed her hand. “Come and dance.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

“Go. I’ll watch your things,” he said.

At first she was awful. She didn’t know what to do with her hands, wasn’t sure whether she was on the beat, and laughed every time she bumped into someone, which was often. Ning showed her a step. Jiayi showed her another. Somewhere around the third song she stopped thinking about it, and started having fun.

From the edge of the floor, Yichen watched. He wasn’t interested in the dancing. He was interested in the way her face changed every time she got a step right, and the way she looked over her shoulder every minute or two to check he was still there, and lit up every time she found him.

She came back breathless. “I danced.”

“I saw.”

“Was I good?”

“Very.”

“You’re biased.”

“Completely.”

She took his hand. “Come with me.”

He put the water down.

He wasn’t an enthusiastic dancer. He was, unfairly, a good one: one hand at her waist, the other holding hers, moving as if the music were something he’d been told about once and filed away. She stared up at him.

“You can dance.”

“Can I?”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“You never asked. Stop watching your feet. Follow the music,” he said, and bent his head so that she could hear him over the bass.

She did. It was much less frightening with him.

Later, sitting in the quiet corner he’d found without seeming to look for it, she studied him over her water.

“How do you know all this? Where the quiet seats are. Which drinks. Where the bathroom is. How to get the bartender’s attention without waving.”

“I’ve been here twice.”

“Twice is not enough to know where the bathroom is.”

“It’s exactly enough to know where the bathroom is.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Did girls come up to you? Those two times?”

The real question.

“A few.”

“And?”

“And I said I had a girlfriend, and showed them the photo of you in the face mask.”

She gasped. “You did not.”

“Fang Ze has it on his phone. The team manager is quite famous on the team.”

She hid her face in his shoulder, which was where she’d been going to put it anyway. Then she lifted it. “Have you ever brought a girl here?”

He smiled slowly. “I’ve only ever had one girlfriend, Xiaoran. Since we were seventeen. She’s never been to a club before tonight.”

Her cheeks went pink. “…I’m here now.”

“Exactly,” he said, and kissed her temple, and she forgot her next question.

By midnight she was pleasantly exhausted. Jiayi hugged her at the door and made her promise to come again. Ning took a photograph of the two of them under the sign that Xiaoran made her delete and then made her send.

In the car she leaned back against the seat and turned her head towards him. “I had fun.”

“I know. You’ve been smiling for three hours.”

A few streets later she said, “Did you? Have fun? Even though you were looking after me the whole time?”

He kept his eyes on the road. “I didn’t spend the evening looking after you instead of having fun. I spent it having fun with you.”

She went quiet. Then she reached across the console and took his free hand.

“Next time I want to go with your team.”

“All right.”

“And dance more.”

“All right.”

“And try a different drink.”

“We’ll see.”

“You’re not going to stop me?”

“I’m going to make sure you know what’s in it.”

“Deal. Wait. Those two times. How long did you stay?” She thought for a moment.

“About two hours each.”

“And you drove everyone home.”

“Somebody had to.”

“So you’ve been to a club twice, drunk water both times, and gone to bed before midnight.”

“Yes.”

“Zhou Yichen, you’re the most boring man in Shanghai,” she said, delighted.

“Probably. But tonight I wasn’t bored at all,” he said.

She kissed his cheek at a red light. He drove the rest of the way home with one hand on the wheel and the other holding hers, already certain that tomorrow would bring a detailed review of everything she’d seen, and at least forty more questions.

He wasn’t complaining. Not even slightly.

chapters.desc: Her father’s fiftieth birthday lunch, and an aunt from the town who would like to know exactly what a media degree pays.
chapters.title: The Aunt Who Asks About Salaries
chapters.epigraph: “No. It means I know you’ll take it seriously.”
chapters.content:
The trouble began with a question about university.

It was supposed to be a pleasant family lunch: her father’s fiftieth birthday, on the second Saturday of March, for which Xiaoran and Yichen had taken the early train back from Shanghai. Her mother’s younger sister had come in from the town on the bus, with a bag of dried mushrooms and the confidence of a woman who had missed New Year with flu and was determined to catch up on everything she’d missed, including the boy.

Everyone at New Year had seen him. Uncle Deng had made his comment, and Grandma had summoned him to dinner on the fifth, and the whole family had decided he would do. Auntie Hui had seen none of it. She had been in bed with a hot water bottle, hearing about it on the phone.

Yichen had arrived with a box of pastries from the old bakery near their high school, greeted everyone properly, and settled into the living room with her father, who was wearing a new shirt and pretending not to know it was his birthday.

Everything had been perfectly normal.

Until lunch.

“So, Yichen, you’re studying Business, aren’t you?” Auntie Hui began, placing a piece of fish on her plate.

“Yes, Auntie.”

“That’s good. Business has a lot of opportunities. Finance, management, investment. Very practical.”

Yichen smiled politely.

“There’s quite a range of career paths, yes.”

“And you’re playing basketball too?”

“Yes. For the university team.”

“That’s impressive. You must be very busy.”

“It’s manageable.”

Auntie Hui nodded approvingly.

Then she turned toward Xiaoran.

“And you, Xiaoran? Media, right?”

Xiaoran swallowed her food.

“Yes.”

“What are you planning to do after graduation?”

“I’m still exploring. I’m interested in creative production, advertising, and maybe content strategy.”

“Ah.”

The particular tone of that single syllable made Xiaoran look up.

Auntie Hui smiled.

“That’s interesting. But is it stable?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“I think it can be.”

“Can be?”

Her mother, sitting beside her, continued eating.

Xiaoran gave a smile.

“There’s quite a lot you can do with a Media degree.”

“Of course, of course. But you know, these days, it’s difficult. Everyone wants to work in media. Everyone wants to be a content creator.”

Her aunt turned back to Yichen.

“Business is different. At least you have a clearer future.”

Yichen put down his chopsticks.

He didn’t say anything yet.

Xiaoran, meanwhile, was beginning to recognize the direction of the conversation.

She had been here before.

It was never a question about what she wanted to do. It always became a comparison between what she studied and what someone else studied, between what was practical and what was supposedly uncertain.

“It’s still early. I have time to figure things out,” Xiaoran said.

“That’s true. You’re young.”

Her aunt nodded, then added casually:

“Although, when you’re choosing a career, you should think about your future family too. It’s not easy if both people have unstable jobs.”

Xiaoran’s chopsticks paused.

Her father looked up.

Yichen remained quiet.

Auntie Hui continued, apparently encouraged by the lack of immediate resistance.

“Of course, it’s good to have your own career. But a girl should also think practically. If your boyfriend has a good career, you don’t need to put so much pressure on yourself to earn a lot.”

Xiaoran’s expression tightened, and she looked at her mother. “Mom—”

Her aunt waved a hand.

“I’m only giving advice. Yichen is studying Business. His prospects are probably better. You should think about these things.”

Xiaoran was about to answer.

But Yichen spoke first.

“Auntie, I think Xiaoran’s career should be based on what she wants to build, not on what I might earn.”

His voice was calm.

Not loud.

But the table went quiet.

Auntie Hui turned toward him.

“Oh, of course. I didn’t mean—”

“I understand.”

He gave her a polite smile.

“But I don’t think her future should be treated as something that depends on mine.”

Xiaoran turned her head.

She hadn’t expected him to say anything.

Yichen continued, still perfectly composed.

“She’s good at what she does. She’s hardworking, and she’s already gaining experience outside her coursework. I think she should have the opportunity to pursue that properly.”

Her aunt nodded, although her expression had changed slightly.

“Yes, yes. I’m sure she’s capable. But I’m asking about practical matters. You two are together, so naturally you’ll have to consider money eventually.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Eventually, perhaps. But we’re still university students.”

A faint smile touched his lips.

“I haven’t even graduated. It would be rather ambitious of me to start discussing my future salary as though it’s already in my bank account.”

His father would probably have laughed at that.

Xiaoran nearly did.

Her aunt gave an awkward chuckle.

“Well, that’s true.”

Then she looked at Xiaoran again.

“But you should still think about it. How much do you expect to earn after graduation?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth.

Yichen answered before she could.

“She doesn’t have to decide that today, Auntie.”

There was no irritation in his voice.

No sharpness.

Just a quiet, unmistakable refusal to let the conversation continue in that direction.

He picked up his glass of water.

“And I don’t think it’s fair to ask her to justify her future income when nobody is asking me to justify mine.”

For the first time, Auntie Hui seemed unsure of what to say.

Xiaoran looked at him.

Then, slowly, she lowered her eyes to her plate, hiding the smile threatening to appear.

Her mother finally intervened.

“Exactly. They’re studying. Let them enjoy university first.”

Her father nodded.

“There’s plenty of time to worry about salaries.”

The conversation moved on.

But Xiaoran didn’t miss the way Yichen moved the dish of vegetables closer to her, as if nothing unusual had happened.

She waited until they were in the kitchen.

Yichen had volunteered to carry some plates, and Xiaoran had followed him on the pretext of getting more water.

The moment they were alone, she leaned against the counter.

“Yichen.”

He placed the plates beside the sink.

“Hm?”

“You answered for me.”

He turned.

“Yes.”

She studied his expression.

He didn’t look pleased with himself. If anything, he seemed to be considering whether he’d said too much.

“Was that okay?” he asked.

She blinked, then smiled.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She crossed her arms.

“You didn’t even hesitate.”

“Would you have preferred I waited?”

“No. I just didn’t expect it.”

He leaned back against the counter beside her.

“She was putting you in a position where you had to defend your choices.”

Xiaoran looked down.

“She does that sometimes.”

“I noticed.”

She let out a small breath.

“I could have answered her.”

“I know.”

He said it immediately.

Not you didn’t need to answer or I had to protect you.

Just that he knew she could.

He met her eyes.

“I wasn’t answering because I thought you couldn’t handle it.”

Her expression softened.

“I know.”

“I just didn’t think you should have to explain yourself to everyone at the table.”

She was quiet.

Then she reached over and lightly tugged at the sleeve of his shirt.

“Thank you.”

He looked down at her hand.

“You’re welcome.”

She tilted her head. “Also, that thing you said about your future salary being in your bank account was funny.”

“Good. I was hoping someone would appreciate it. Your father did. He coughed.”

She laughed.

Then she looked at him more carefully.

“Do you really think my career will work out?”

Yichen’s expression changed.

He turned fully toward her.

“Yes.”

She blinked.

“You’re very confident.”

“I’ve seen you work.”

“That doesn’t mean I’ll succeed.”

“No. It means I know you’ll take it seriously.”

He brushed his thumb over the back of her hand.

“You don’t have to know exactly where you’ll end up. You just have to keep choosing what you want to do.”

“And if I don’t earn much?”

He turned to her.

“Then you’ll earn what you earn.”

She waited.

“And we’ll both figure out our own lives. But I don’t want you choosing something because you’re worried about being financially dependent on me, or because someone thinks your degree isn’t practical enough.”

Her eyes softened.

“Okay.”

He leaned closer and kissed her, briefly.

“Now, are you getting water or did you bring me here to have a private meeting?”

She laughed.

“Both.”

“Very efficient.”

When they returned to the dining room, Auntie Hui was asking Yichen’s opinion about the university basketball league.

He answered politely, explaining a little about their upcoming matches.

Xiaoran sat beside him and began eating again.

A few minutes later, her aunt turned to her.

“Xiaoran, have you thought about doing an internship during the summer?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yes. I’m looking at a few creative studios.”

“That’s good. You should get experience early.”

“I’ve already done a small photography project for a local brand.”

“Oh? Paid?”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Yes.”

“That’s nice.”

Her aunt seemed to consider that.

Then she asked, “How much did they pay?”

Xiaoran nearly choked on her water.

Yichen, beside her, calmly reached for the teapot.

Her mother gave her sister a warning look. “Enough about money, Hui.”

“What? I’m just curious!”

Yichen placed the teapot down.

“She was happy with the project, Auntie. I think that’s more important for her first paid assignment.”

Xiaoran turned to him.

He didn’t look at her.

He was serving her tea.

She pressed her lips together.

This time, she was definitely going to laugh.

The gathering ended in the late afternoon.

Yichen helped her father move a few things back into the storage room before saying goodbye to everyone.

Her mother packed some fruit for him to take back.

Auntie Hui, perhaps sensing that she had been a little too persistent, came over before he left, and pressed half the dried mushrooms on him for his mother.

“Yichen, it was nice seeing you.”

“Likewise, Auntie.”

“Come again when you have time.”

“Thank you.”

She glanced at Xiaoran.

“Both of you should visit more often.”

Xiaoran smiled politely.

“We will.”

And that was that.

No dramatic confrontation.

No argument.

Just a family lunch that had been slightly more exhausting than expected.

Xiaoran walked him to the bus stop at the end of her road; he was going to his own parents’ house for the night. Their hands were linked.

She had been quiet for several minutes. He glanced at her. “What are you thinking about?”

She swung their joined hands gently.

“You know, that was the first time you answered for me in front of everyone.”

“I know.”

“Usually, you let me handle things myself.”

“I still do.”

“I know.”

She looked at him.

“But today you just... stepped in.”

He was quiet.

Then he said, “I didn’t want you to feel like you had to sit there and listen to someone reduce your future to a comparison with mine.”

She looked down at their hands.

“I didn’t like that either.”

“I know.”

She walked a little closer to him.

“Do you think she’ll ask again?”

“Probably.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re not even pretending otherwise.”

“Would you like me to lie?”

“No.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

They reached the pedestrian crossing. Yichen stopped, keeping her hand in his as they waited for the light to change.

Then Xiaoran said, “Next time, I might answer her myself.”

He looked down at her.

“All right.”

“But if she starts comparing our salaries again...”

He waited.

She smiled sweetly.

“You can answer.”

His mouth curved.

“Understood.”

The crossing light changed.

He led her forward.

After a few steps, she looked up at him again.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you think we’ll earn a lot of money in the future?”

He considered it.

“I hope so.”

She laughed.

“That’s not very romantic.”

He glanced at her, amused.

“What would you prefer?”

She pretended to think.

“Something like, ‘Don’t worry, I’ll take care of everything.’”

He looked at her, and his smile widened. “Would that make you happy?”

She nodded, playing along.

“Maybe.”

He leaned closer as they walked.

“Then I’ll tell you this instead. I hope we both earn enough to do the things we want, go where we want, and never have to make our decisions out of fear.”

She met his eyes.

“And?”

“And I hope we still like having lunch together when we’re old.”

She laughed.

“That’s your big romantic promise?”

“It’s a very important one.”

She slipped her arm through his.

“Okay. I like that.”

He held her gaze.

“Good.”

That evening, Xiaoran received a message while she was preparing her university notes.

Yichen: Did you get home?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: Good.

She stared at their chat before typing.

Xiaoran: I was thinking.

Yichen: Dangerous.

She laughed.

Xiaoran: If I become a very successful creative director one day, I’ll buy you a car.

Yichen: I have a car.

Xiaoran: A better one.

Yichen: What kind?

Xiaoran: You can’t ask. It’s a surprise.

Yichen: Then I look forward to it.

She smiled.

Xiaoran: And if I don’t become successful?

His reply took a little longer.

Yichen: Then you can buy me dinner.

She laughed.

Xiaoran: Only dinner?

Yichen: A good dinner.

Xiaoran: Greedy.

Yichen: I’m not asking about your salary.

She stared at the message.

Then was laughing too much and had to put her phone down.

A moment later, another message appeared.

Yichen: For the record, I’m looking forward to seeing what you become. Not what you earn.

Xiaoran read it twice.

Then she typed:

Xiaoran: I hope you know I’m looking forward to seeing what you become too.

His reply came quickly.

Yichen: I know. Good night, Xiaoran.

She lay on her childhood bed with the phone on her chest. In the next room, her father was telling her mother, at great length, that the boy had said what I might earn and not what I will earn, and that this showed modesty, and her mother was telling him to go to sleep, it was his birthday and he was fifty.

chapters.desc: Three rejections in one week, deleted before anyone can ask. She stops saying “guess what” at dinner. He notices.
chapters.title: The Emails She Didn’t Forward
chapters.epigraph: “I made an exception.”
chapters.content:
The first rejection arrived on a Tuesday, at 11:04 in the morning, in the middle of a lecture on audience segmentation.

Dear Ms. Lin, thank you for your interest in our Summer Associate Program. After careful consideration…

Lin Xiaoran read it under the desk. Then she read the first line again, as if it might have changed its mind.

It hadn’t.

She deleted it.

She looked at the empty space where it had been. Then she looked at the back of the head of the boy in front of her, who was asleep, and at the lecturer, who was explaining the difference between a demographic and a persona as if it might save someone’s life.

Then she went to the deleted folder and deleted it from there too, which felt better, and wrote audience segmentation neatly at the top of a fresh page, and underlined it twice, and didn’t hear another word for forty minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had applied to nine places.

This had been a sensible number in January. In January she had still been the girl who’d won a national media strategy competition the year before. There had been a trophy shaped like a speech bubble on her shelf and a photograph of her holding it on the faculty noticeboard, and Zhou Yichen had looked at that photograph for so long, every time they walked past it, that Jiayi had started calling it the shrine.

In January, nine applications had felt like nine doors that were already a little bit open.

By the end of March, four of them had said nothing at all.

On the Tuesday, one said no.

On the Thursday, two more did.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Guess what,” said Xiaoran every evening at dinner, normally.

It was how she started. She had started every dinner that way since high school. Guess what, the professor wore odd socks. Guess what, a pigeon walked into the lecture hall and nobody did anything. Guess what, Ning said something so mean to a boy in our group that he apologized to her.

Yichen never guessed. That wasn’t the point. The point was that she said it, and he put his chopsticks down, and she told him.

On Thursday night, at the noodle place behind the sports hall, she didn’t say it.

She told him about the lecture. She told him about Jiayi’s new earrings. She ate all her noodles. She stole two of his dumplings, which was normal, and didn’t make a speech about it, which wasn’t.

He noticed. He didn’t say anything. He moved the dumplings closer to her side of the table.

On Friday she didn’t say it either.

On Saturday he put his chopsticks down before she’d started.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Nothing’s wrong. I’m tired. Assignments.” She smiled at him. It was a good smile. She’d practiced it in the lift.

He looked at her. Then he nodded, and picked his chopsticks up again, and let her have it.

That was the worst part. He believed her, or he let her think he did, and she sat there being believed and felt terrible.

✦ ✦ ✦

The thing was, she couldn’t tell him.

Not because he’d be unkind. He would be the opposite of unkind. He would be so kind it would be unbearable.

He would say their loss. He would say you won a national competition. And then, because he was Zhou Yichen and because his family owned a great many warehouses and knew a great many people, he would say, carefully, I could ask someone.

And she would have to say no.

She had sat at her grandparents’ table at New Year and listened to Uncle Deng explain, in front of everyone, why a girl from an ordinary family dated a boy like that. She had heard the word he hadn’t quite used. She had held Yichen’s hand under the table so hard her knuckles hurt.

She wasn’t going to get her first internship because somebody knew somebody who knew Mr. Zhou.

So she didn’t tell him. She just stopped saying guess what, because there wasn’t anything to guess.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday night, after the second and third emails, she sat on the stairs outside her studio at midnight, on the fourth floor, because her room felt too small to be disappointed in. She rang Meilin.

Meilin answered on the second ring from a dormitory four hundred kilometers away, sounding exactly as she had at sixteen.

“You only ring at midnight when something’s wrong.”

“Nothing’s wrong.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

So she told her. The nine applications. The three noes. The four silences. The trophy shaped like a speech bubble, which she now couldn’t look at.

Meilin listened to all of it, which was rare, because Meilin usually interrupted by the second sentence.

“Does Yichen know?”

“No.”

“You’re sitting on a staircase at midnight so your boyfriend who lives across the road won’t see your face.”

“…Maybe.”

“Xiaoran. You’re not scared he’ll fix it. You’re scared he’ll see you lose,” said Meilin, in the voice she’d used in the noodle shop the winter before, the one that had made the four of them promise not to drift.

Xiaoran didn’t answer. A moth knocked against the stair light.

“He’s seen you lose before. He watched you get forty-three in maths. He stayed,” said Meilin.

Xiaoran laughed, which hurt, and went back inside, and didn’t tell him the next day either.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ning found out first, because Ning found out everything.

“You’ve been refreshing your email like it owes you money,” she said on Monday, in the library, without looking up from her own laptop.

“I’m checking for a group assignment.”

“We don’t have a group assignment.”

“Then I’m checking for nothing.”

Ning turned her screen round. On it was the Summer Associate Program page of a large agency in the financial district, with a large red banner across the top that said APPLICATIONS CLOSED.

“They rejected me too. On Tuesday. I laughed for ten minutes. Did they reject you?” said Ning.

Xiaoran looked at her.

“And two others. And four haven’t answered,” she said, very.

Ning considered this.

“Does Captain Zhou know?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because he’d fix it.”

Ning was quiet for longer than usual. Then she said, “He can’t fix it. He’s a business student. They don’t even know what a content calendar is.”

Xiaoran laughed, a little wetly, into her sleeve, and Ning pushed a packet of tissues across the desk without comment, which was the kindest thing Sun Ning had ever done in public.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found out on Wednesday.

Not from Ning. Ning would have died first.

He found out because Xiaoran came out of a one-to-one with her portfolio tutor and walked straight into the campus café, and straight through it, and into the bathroom at the back, and stayed there for nineteen minutes.

He knew it was nineteen minutes because he was sitting at their table by the window waiting for her, the way he did every Wednesday at four, with her milk tea already bought and going warm.

When she came out her eyes were red and she had powdered over it, badly, and she sat down and picked up the milk tea and said, “Sorry. Long queue.”

There was no queue. There was never a queue. There was one bathroom and he had watched the door the entire time.

He didn’t say that.

He said, “Okay.”

She drank half her milk tea through the straw without breathing.

He waited.

He was good at waiting. He had waited for her outside exam halls and dressing rooms and once, memorably, outside a bookshop for an hour and ten minutes while she read the first chapter of nine different novels to decide which one she deserved.

“My tutor says my portfolio’s too safe. She says I win competitions because I’m good at telling a panel what it wants to hear, and agencies can smell that. She says I should send them something I’m scared of,” she said, to the milk tea.

“Is that why you were in the bathroom?”

“No. I was in the bathroom because three companies have said no and four haven’t bothered and I haven’t told you, and I didn’t want you to find out from my face.” She put the cup down.

Silence.

Then he said, “Which three?”

She told him.

He nodded slowly, as if she’d given him a list of patients and he was deciding which to see first. He didn’t say their loss. He didn’t say you won a national competition.

He said, “And you didn’t tell me because you thought I’d ask someone.”

She looked up.

“How do you know that?”

Yichen said, “Because I thought about it on Saturday. When you didn’t say guess what. I thought, if it’s what I think it is, I know three people I could call. And then I thought, she’d never forgive me.”

Her mouth opened.

“You knew on Saturday?”

“I guessed on Saturday.”

“You never guess! That’s the whole point! You never guess!”

“I made an exception,” he said.

She stared at him across the table with her ruined powder and her half a milk tea, and then she started laughing, and then the laugh turned into something else halfway through, and she put her face down on her folded arms on the table and cried properly, in the middle of the campus café, at four in the afternoon.

He didn’t come round the table. He reached across it and put his hand on the back of her head and kept it there, warm and still, until she’d finished.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I’m not calling anyone. I want you to know that first,” he said later, walking her home.

“Good.”

“Not my father. Not my father’s friends. Not my father’s friends’ daughters, who all work in marketing, apparently, and all went to the same famous university.”

“How do you know that?”

“My mother tells me. Every holiday.”

She snorted.

“But I’ll do one thing. If you let me,” he said.

“What?”

“Your tutor said send something you’re scared of. What are you scared of?” He stopped at the bottom of her stairs.

She thought about it.

Then she told him.

There was a campaign she had never shown anyone. Not the competition one, all neat charts and audience personas. A real one. For the old noodle shop near their high school, the one with the soft menu and the owner who still gave her milk instead of chili. She’d made it last winter, after she’d sat in that shop with Meilin and Yuhao and been afraid for the first time that the four of them would drift apart. Photographs. A short video. Copy written in the owner’s own words. It was messy and sentimental and it wasn’t strategic at all.

“It’s embarrassing,” she said.

“Is it good?”

She hesitated.

“…It’s the best thing I’ve made.”

“Then send that,” said Yichen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kept his word. He didn’t call anyone.

What he did was worse.

He became, for nine days, the most unpleasant mock interviewer in the history of Huaining University.

“Why should we hire you instead of the other two hundred applicants?”

“Because I’m—”

“Don’t say passionate.”

“I wasn’t going to say passionate.”

“You were going to say passionate.”

“…I was going to say passionate.”

“Everyone says passionate. Again.”

He sat at his desk in a shirt with the sleeves rolled up, looking at her over his laptop as if she were a quarterly forecast that didn’t add up, and asked her the worst questions he could find. What’s your biggest weakness. Tell me about a time you failed. Why do you want to work in a city where you don’t know anyone. Why should we believe a competition win wasn’t luck.

On the fourth evening she said “passionate” by accident and he simply looked at her over the laptop until she threw a cushion at him. On the sixth she cried halfway through tell me about a time you failed, because the honest answer was this week, and he waited, and when she’d finished he said, “That. Say that. But without the crying,” and she laughed so much she couldn’t breathe.

The last one made her so angry she answered it perfectly.

He wrote something down.

“What did you write?”

“Nothing.”

She leaned over the desk and looked. He had written that one and underlined it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth day she rewrote the noodle shop campaign for the fourth time and sent it, with a new cover letter, to a media company in Beijing that she had found at one in the morning and not mentioned to anyone, not even Ning or Jiayi.

Not to Yichen.

It wasn’t a secret, exactly.

It was just that if it said no, she wanted to be the only one who knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three weeks later she was sitting cross-legged on his bed on a Thursday evening with her laptop on her knees, pretending to edit a group presentation, when the email came in.

She saw the company name.

Her stomach did something complicated.

Yichen was at his desk with a textbook open, reading the same page he’d been reading for twenty minutes because she’d been humming.

She opened the email.

She read the first line.

She read it again, slowly, as if it were in a language she’d only just learned.

Then she read the whole thing three times, and opened two more tabs to check the company was real, and that the program was real, and that she was real, and looked at the address at the bottom, which was in Beijing, more than a thousand kilometers from this bed and this boy and this terrible, wonderful, too-quiet room.

She looked up at him.

He was still reading the same page.

She took a breath.

“Yichen.”

chapters.desc: She has told Yichen about the internship in Beijing. Now she has to tell her mother, who will tell her father, who will cry.
chapters.title: Telling Her Parents About Beijing
chapters.epigraph: “You’re my daughter. How could I not worry?”
chapters.content:
She had told Yichen the night the email came, sitting cross-legged on his bed with her laptop on her knees, in a voice that came out much higher than she meant it to. He had put down his textbook and said her name, and then congratulations, and then nothing at all for a while, because he was holding her.

Eight weeks. A media company in Beijing, more than a thousand kilometers from his bed and his books and his too-quiet room. An internship program she had found at one in the morning and applied to without telling anyone.

Telling him had been the easy part.

“Tell your mother the same way you told me. Start with the part you want,” he said the next morning, at the door.

She called her mother the following evening.

Yichen wasn’t in the room.

Not because Xiaoran had asked him to leave, but because he knew this was a conversation she needed to have herself.

He was in the kitchen, preparing tea.

She sat at the dining table with her phone against her ear.

“Hello, Mom.”

“Xiaoran? Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What did you eat?”

“Rice.”

“With what?”

“Mom.”

Her mother laughed.

“All right, all right. What is it? You sound serious.”

Xiaoran looked down at the notes she had written.

She had prepared everything.

The program dates. The university partnership. The accommodation arrangements. The travel details. The contact information.

She had even prepared answers to questions her mother hadn’t asked yet.

“Actually, Mom, I wanted to tell you something.”

“Hm?”

“I applied for a summer internship.”

“Oh?”

“It’s at a media company. Production, campaigns, real clients. They emailed me on Thursday.”

Her mother was quiet, listening.

Xiaoran continued.

“I got accepted.”

There was a small pause.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“That’s good! Congratulations.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you.”

“Which company?”

“It’s in Beijing.”

And then—

Silence.

Not the comfortable silence of someone listening.

Not the pause before another question.

Just silence.

Xiaoran’s smile slowly faded.

She looked at the phone.

“Mom?”

There was a faint sound on the other end.

Her mother hadn’t hung up.

But she wasn’t speaking.

Xiaoran swallowed.

“It’s only for eight weeks.”

Still nothing.

“They arrange accommodation for the interns. The company has sent the details, and I’ve already checked the schedule. I’ll send you everything.”

Her mother finally spoke.

“Beijing?”

“Yes.”

“Why Beijing?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Because the company is there.”

“I know that. I mean, why did you choose something so far away?”

Xiaoran looked at the table.

“It’s a good opportunity.”

“Couldn’t you find something here?”

She had expected the question.

She had even written down an answer.

But hearing it from her mother made her feel strangely small.

“There are opportunities in Shanghai too. I applied to three of them. They said no. This one said yes,” she said carefully. She hadn’t told her mother that either.

Her mother didn’t respond immediately.

Then she asked, “When did you apply?”

“A few weeks ago.”

“And you only tell me now?”

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

“I didn’t know if I would get accepted.”

“So you applied without discussing it with us?”

She looked down at her hands.

“I wanted to try first.”

Another silence.

This time, Xiaoran knew her mother was upset.

Not necessarily angry.

But something had shifted in her voice.

Her mother asked, “Have you already decided to go?”

Xiaoran hesitated, then answered honestly.

“I want to.”

The silence that followed was longer.

She could hear something moving in the background. Perhaps her mother was putting something down, perhaps she had walked into another room.

Xiaoran waited.

“Mom?”

“Hm?”

“Are you angry?”

“No.”

But her mother’s answer came too quickly.

Xiaoran’s throat tightened.

“Then why aren’t you saying anything?”

Her mother exhaled.

“I’m thinking.”

Xiaoran nodded, although she couldn’t see her.

“Okay.”

“You’re still young, Xiaoran.”

“I’m in university, Mom.”

“I know you’re in university.”

“I’m not going without knowing anything. I’ve checked everything.”

“Beijing is not next door.”

“I know.”

“And eight weeks is a long time.”

“I know.”

Her mother went quiet again.

Xiaoran stared at the edge of the table.

She had imagined this conversation going differently. Perhaps her mother would be excited. Perhaps she would ask what she would learn, whether she would meet interesting people, what she would bring back.

Instead, Xiaoran was explaining why she wanted to leave.

She felt the familiar urge to make the conversation easier by saying she could decline. She could say it wasn’t important. She could say there were other programs.

She could say she hadn’t decided.

But she didn’t want to.

For once, she didn’t want to make her excitement smaller just because someone else was frightened by it.

“Mom,” she said.

Her mother answered.

“What?”

“I really want to go.”

There was another pause.

“I know.”

“I’ve been wanting to do something like this for a while. I want to see how people work in a different place. I want to learn more about production, and I think it’ll help me understand what I want to do after university.”

Her voice became softer.

“I’m not going because I want to leave home. I just want to try something.”

Her mother didn’t answer.

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

Then, finally, she heard her mother’s voice.

“Let me think about it.”

Xiaoran’s chest tightened.

“Okay.”

“Send me the details.”

“I will.”

“And don’t book anything yet.”

“I won’t.”

Her mother paused. “Have you eaten properly today?”

Xiaoran let out a small, almost helpless laugh.

“Yes, Mom.”

“All right.”

“Okay.”

“Good night.”

“Good night.”

The call ended.

Xiaoran kept the phone against her ear for a few seconds after the line had gone silent.

Then she lowered it.

She stared at the screen.

She didn’t cry.

Not immediately.

She just sat there, feeling as if she had spent the last fifteen minutes holding something heavy without realizing how much it weighed.

Yichen found her still sitting at the table when he came out of the kitchen.

He placed a cup of tea in front of her.

“How did it go?”

“She said she’ll think about it.”

He pulled out the chair beside her.

“All right.”

“She didn’t say yes.”

“She didn’t say no either.”

Xiaoran looked down at her tea.

“She went quiet.”

He waited.

“After I said Beijing, she just... stopped talking.”

Yichen sat beside her.

She rubbed her thumb against the side of the cup.

“I knew she might be worried, but I didn’t think she’d go completely silent.”

He didn’t immediately tell her that everything would be fine.

He knew better than to offer reassurance he couldn’t guarantee.

Instead, he asked, “What did you tell her?”

“Everything. The program, the schedule, the accommodation. I told her why I wanted to go.”

“Good.”

“But she kept asking why I couldn’t find something here.”

He nodded slowly.

“Did you tell her why this one mattered to you?”

“Yes.”

“Then you’ve done your part for today.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“That’s it?”

“For today.”

She leaned back in her chair.

“I feel like I should have prepared better.”

“You prepared.”

“Maybe I should have told her before applying.”

“Maybe.”

She turned toward him.

“You’re not helping.”

He smiled slightly.

“I’m not going to tell you that every decision you’ve made was perfect. But applying for a program because you wanted the opportunity isn’t something you need to apologize for.”

She looked down.

“I don’t want her to think I’m being careless.”

“Then show her you’re not.”

He reached for her hand.

“Send her the details. Let her read everything. Answer her questions. You don’t have to convince her in one phone call.”

Xiaoran was quiet.

Then she asked, “What if she still doesn’t want me to go?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Then you’ll have another conversation.”

“What if she says no?”

“We’ll think about what to do when that happens.”

She studied his face.

He was calm, as always.

Not dismissing her worries, not promising to solve them.

Just sitting there with her.

“You’re not going to tell me to go anyway?”

He tilted his head.

“Do you want me to?”

She thought about it.

“No.”

“Then I won’t.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“But I do want you to go if this is something you genuinely want.”

Her eyes softened.

“Even though it’s far?”

“Because it’s something you’ve worked for.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You’re going to miss me.”

“Yes.”

“Very much?”

“Probably.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“Probably?”

He gave her a smile.

“Do you need me to exaggerate?”

“Yes.”

“Terribly. I’ll be miserable. I’ll forget how to eat. I’ll stare out of windows.”

She laughed.

“You’re so dramatic.”

“You asked.”

She leaned against his shoulder.

He kissed her temple.

After a while, he said, “When is the program?”

“Summer.”

“That gives you time to sort everything out.”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“And you can call me.”

“Obviously.”

“Video call?”

“Obviously.”

“Every day?”

She looked up.

“Are you going to miss me that much?”

“Would you like an honest answer?”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Yes.”

“Yes.”

Her expression softened.

He brushed a strand of hair behind her ear.

“But I don’t want you spending your time in Beijing worrying about whether I’m lonely here.”

She laughed.

“I wouldn’t.”

“Good.”

“I might worry about whether you’re eating.”

“That’s reasonable.”

“And whether you’re sleeping.”

“Less reasonable.”

“And whether you’re training too much.”

He smiled.

“You’re going to be very busy.”

She nodded seriously.

“Yes. I have a lot of responsibilities.”

He kissed her hair.

“Then perhaps we should start preparing.”

The next morning, Xiaoran sent her mother the program information.

A long message.

A PDF.

The official schedule. The accommodation details. The university contact.

The dates.

She added a final sentence.

Xiaoran: I really hope I can go, Mom. I think it’ll be good for me. I’ll answer anything you’re worried about.

Her mother didn’t reply immediately.

Xiaoran put her phone down and went to class.

When she checked again during the afternoon break, there was a message.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): I have read the information.

Xiaoran’s heart lifted.

Another message followed.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): The accommodation details are clear. I want to know who will be responsible for you while you’re there.

Xiaoran smiled.

It wasn’t approval.

But it was a question.

A real one.

She replied with the intern coordinator’s information and explained how the interns would be supervised.

Her mother responded with a simple:

Mom (Accounts Dept.): All right. I’ll look at it properly.

Xiaoran stared at the message for a while.

Then she sent a screenshot to Yichen.

Xiaoran: She replied.

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: She asked about the coordinator.

Yichen: That’s good.

Xiaoran: You think so?

Yichen: She’s asking about the arrangements now. That’s a conversation.

Xiaoran smiled.

Xiaoran: I think you’re right.

Yichen: I’m usually right.

Xiaoran: Don’t ruin the moment.

A few days later, her mother called again.

This time, Xiaoran was sitting outside the faculty building, waiting for Yichen to finish his lecture.

She answered immediately.

“Hello, Mom.”

“Are you busy?”

“No. I’m waiting for someone.”

Her mother asked a few more questions about the internship.

Who would be going with her?

Would she have classmates there?

How would she travel from the airport?

What would she do if she became ill?

Xiaoran answered each one patiently.

She had already looked into most of it. For the rest, she promised to check and send the information.

Then her mother went quiet again.

Xiaoran’s fingers tightened around her phone.

“Mom?”

“Hm?”

“Are you still worried?”

“Of course I’m worried.”

Xiaoran looked toward the university gate.

Her mother sighed.

“You’re my daughter. How could I not worry?”

Something in Xiaoran’s chest softened.

“I know.”

“You’ve never stayed away for that long.”

“I know.”

“And Beijing is far.”

“I know, Mom.”

There was a pause.

Then her mother said, “But you seem to have thought about it properly.”

Xiaoran stopped moving.

Her eyes widened slightly.

“Mom?”

“I’m not saying I’m not worried.”

“I know.”

“And I still want to check some things.”

“Okay.”

“But if everything is arranged properly...”

Her mother paused.

Xiaoran barely breathed.

“...then I suppose you can go.”

For a moment, Xiaoran didn’t say anything.

She had expected questions.

More hesitation.

Perhaps another request to wait.

She hadn’t expected those words.

“Mom?”

“What?”

“Are you saying yes?”

Her mother gave a small laugh.

“I’m saying you can go if everything is settled properly. Don’t make me repeat myself.”

Xiaoran’s smile appeared so quickly it almost hurt.

“Okay.”

“And call me when you arrive.”

“I will.”

“And when you get to the accommodation.”

“I will.”

“And don’t go wandering around by yourself late at night.”

“Mom.”

“I’m serious.”

“I know.”

“Keep your phone charged.”

“I will.”

“Eat properly.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Yes.”

“And send me pictures.”

She blinked.

“Pictures?”

“Of the places you visit. I want to see.”

Xiaoran looked down at her shoes.

Her eyes had started to sting.

“Okay, Mom.”

Her mother softened her voice.

“Have you told Yichen?”

Xiaoran laughed through the sudden tightness in her throat.

“Not yet.”

“Tell him. He’ll probably be happy.”

“Probably?”

“He’s been encouraging you, hasn’t he?”

Xiaoran looked up.

Across the courtyard, Yichen had just emerged from his faculty building. He was walking toward her, phone in hand, looking for her.

She smiled.

“Yes.”

“Then tell him.”

“I will.”

Her mother paused.

Then, more: “Your father is going to cry. I’m telling you now so you can be ready.”

Xiaoran’s expression crumpled a little.

She looked away.

“Mom...”

“Don’t cry.”

“I’m not crying.”

“Your voice sounds strange.”

“I’m fine.”

Her mother laughed.

“All right. Go and do your things.”

“Okay.”

“Take care of yourself.”

“I will. Love you.”

“Love you too.”

The call ended.

Xiaoran lowered her phone.

She remained seated.

Then she looked up and saw Yichen standing in front of her.

He had noticed her expression.

“What happened?”

She met his eyes.

Then her smile broke through.

“She said yes.”

His face changed immediately.

“Really?”

“She said I can go.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I can go to Beijing.”

He crouched slightly in front of her, taking her hands.

“Congratulations.”

She laughed.

He pulled her into a hug.

She wrapped both arms around his shoulders, pressing her face into his neck.

For a few seconds, she didn’t say anything.

Then, muffled against his shirt, she whispered, “I thought she was going to say no.”

Yichen held her a little closer.

“I know.”

“She went quiet, and I thought...”

She stopped.

He rubbed her back.

“She needed time.”

Xiaoran nodded.

Then she pulled away enough to look at him.

“She wants pictures.”

“Of Beijing?”

“Yes.”

“Then you’ll have to take plenty.”

“I’ll send them to you too.”

“I’d expect that.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“And you have to answer my calls.”

“I will.”

“Even if you’re training?”

“After training.”

“What if I call because I miss you?”

He met her eyes.

“Then I’ll answer as soon as I can.”

That made her grin.

“Good.”

He brushed his thumb beneath her eye, catching the little trace of moisture there.

“Are you happy?”

She nodded.

“Very.”

He leaned forward and kissed her temple.

“Then I’m happy too.”

She looked at him.

Then, with a mischievous little smile, she asked, “Are you going to miss me?”

He gave her a look.

“We’ve discussed this.”

“I want to hear it again.”

“Terribly.”

She laughed.

“Good.”

He stood and offered her his hand.

“Come on. Let’s celebrate.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere you like.”

She took his hand and stood.

Then she thought.

“I want noodles.”

“All right.”

“And dessert.”

“All right.”

“And I want you to listen to me talk about Beijing for the entire dinner.”

That got a smile out of him.

“That sounds manageable.”

“Without complaining.”

“That might be more difficult.”

She hit his arm lightly.

He caught her hand and brought it to his lips.

“Come on, future Beijing intern.”

She turned to him.

The words made her smile all over again.

She ate her noodles and talked about Beijing for the entire dinner, and he complained exactly once, about the subway map, which she had already memorized, and which she then explained to him in full.

chapters.desc: A summer internship in Beijing. A training camp outside the city. Eight weeks and more than a thousand kilometres.
chapters.title: The Internship in Another City
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want you to go tomorrow.”
chapters.content:
The first time Lin Xiaoran mentioned Beijing, Zhou Yichen thought she was talking about a drama.

She was sitting cross-legged on his bed, laptop balanced on her thighs, hair tied into a messy ponytail. There were three open tabs on her screen, a half-finished cup of milk tea beside her, and an expression he had learned to recognize.

Excitement.

The kind that made her forget to blink.

“Yichen.”

He looked up from his textbook. “Hm?”

“I got an offer.”

His eyes moved to her face. “For what?”

She turned the laptop around.

A media company in Beijing. A summer internship program. Eight weeks. A competitive placement, with opportunities to work on real campaigns, assist with production, and contribute to editorial projects.

He read the page carefully.

Then he looked at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“I know.”

“You got it?”

“I got it.”

He closed his textbook.

For a moment, she thought he might say something practical. Ask about accommodation, the company, the schedule, whether she had checked the transportation arrangements.

Instead, he smiled.

A proper smile.

“Congratulations.”

Her face brightened. “Really?”

“Why would I not congratulate you?”

“I don’t know. Maybe because it’s in Beijing.”

He glanced at the laptop again. “It’s a good opportunity.”

“It’s very far.”

“I know.”

“Eight weeks.”

“I can read.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re not helping.”

He reached over and gently tugged the end of her ponytail.

“I’m trying to understand why you’re looking at me like I’ve personally arranged for Beijing to be on the other side of the country.”

“You could have arranged for it to be closer.”

“Unfortunately, my influence has limits.”

She laughed, and he pulled her closer by the waist, pressing a kiss against her temple.

He was genuinely happy for her.

He knew how much work she had put into building her portfolio, from last year’s competition to the two campaign samples she had rewritten four times since. He remembered the nights she had stayed up revising projects, the frustration when her first applications went unanswered, and the way she had pretended not to care when a company rejected her.

This was something she had earned.

He wasn’t going to make her feel guilty for receiving it.

But later that night, when Xiaoran had fallen asleep beside him, he found himself looking at the internship page again.

Eight weeks.

Beijing.

He calculated the distance without meaning to.

Then he locked his phone and turned toward her.

She was sleeping with one hand curled near her cheek, her hair scattered across his pillow. He gently moved a strand away from her face.

“Eight weeks,” he whispered.

She didn’t hear him.

He kissed her cheek anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

The training camp call came three days later.

Yichen was in the university gym when his coach asked him to stay behind after practice.

The invitation was for a summer training camp outside the city. A chance to train with a more competitive group, work with experienced coaches, and potentially secure a place in a larger university-level tournament roster. Coaches from other programmes usually came to watch the final week.

It was the kind of opportunity he had been working toward since joining the basketball team.

He listened, asked a few questions, and accepted.

When he told Xiaoran, she was sitting across from him in a café, enthusiastically explaining the internship’s orientation schedule.

She stopped mid-sentence.

“Wait.”

“Training camp?”

“Mm.”

“When?”

“Same period as your internship.”

She stared at him.

He nodded.

For a few seconds, neither of them spoke.

Then Xiaoran slowly lowered her straw.

“So we’re both leaving.”

“Looks like it.”

“Different cities.”

“Yes.”

“For almost two months.”

“Eight weeks.”

She gave him a wounded look. “Why are you repeating the number?”

“Because you keep asking.”

“Maybe I’m hoping you’ll say something different.”

He reached across the table and touched her fingers.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked down at their hands.

“It’s a good opportunity for you. And the training camp is important to me,” he said.

“I know.”

“Then we should go.”

She nodded.

It was the reasonable answer.

The correct answer.

The answer they would both have given if they were discussing anyone else’s relationship.

But she didn’t smile.

And he noticed.

✦ ✦ ✦

They spent the next two weeks preparing for their separate departures.

Xiaoran researched accommodation, transportation, nearby convenience stores, and the safest routes between her apartment and the company. She made a spreadsheet with far too many tabs. Yichen checked the details with her, pointed out two things she had overlooked, and helped her compare the available options.

He even accompanied her to buy luggage.

She chose a pale blue suitcase.

He thought it was too small.

She thought he was being dramatic.

They compromised by buying a slightly larger one.

At the training camp, Yichen would be staying in shared accommodation with the other players. He packed his sportswear, shoes, recovery equipment, and a few personal belongings.

Xiaoran watched him fold his clothes.

“You’re very efficient.”

“Someone has to be.”

“I packed my suitcase yesterday.”

“You packed it three times.”

“Because I kept remembering things.”

“You brought four pairs of shoes.”

“They’re different.”

“They’re all white.”

She looked offended. “They are not.”

He glanced at the suitcase.

She followed his gaze.

“Fine. Three are white.”

He smiled.

She threw a T-shirt at him.

He caught it easily.

For all their teasing, the packing days were strangely difficult.

They had always been together in the small, ordinary ways that made a relationship feel effortless. A quick visit after class. Dinner after practice. A message asking whether the other had eaten. A hand reaching across a table without needing to ask.

Now, every small thing seemed to have an ending attached to it.

The last time they would shop together before leaving.

The last dinner at their usual place.

The last evening studying in the same room.

The last night she could fall asleep with her head against his shoulder.

Neither of them said it aloud.

✦ ✦ ✦

The night before Xiaoran’s flight, she went to Yichen’s apartment.

She arrived with a small paper bag.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“Something for you.”

He took it.

Inside was a compact photo album.

Not an expensive one. Just a simple little book with photographs she had printed over the past few months.

Their first university basketball game. A picture of him looking away while she took a photograph. A café receipt with a ridiculous doodle she had drawn. A photo of them in Chengdu, standing in front of the panda enclosure. A blurry picture of his hand holding hers inside a car.

There were captions written in her handwriting.

Some were silly.

Some were embarrassingly sentimental.

He turned each page slowly.

At the end, there was a small note.

For when you miss me. Which will probably be often, because I’m lovable.

He looked at her.

She was suddenly interested in the sleeve of her sweater.

“It’s not a big gift.”

“Xiaoran.”

“You don’t have to say anything. It’s just something I thought—”

He closed the album and set it carefully on the table.

Then he pulled her into his arms.

She went willingly, pressing her cheek against his chest.

“Thank you,” he murmured.

“You like it?”

“I love it.”

“Really?”

He leaned back just enough to look at her.

“I’ll take it with me.”

She smiled.

Then, after a moment, her expression softened.

“Don’t lose it.”

“I won’t.”

“Don’t let your teammates borrow it.”

“Why would they borrow my photo album?”

“I don’t know. Maybe they’ll want to see how pretty your girlfriend is.”

He laughed.

“Very confident.”

“It’s a fact.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair.

She closed her eyes.

For a while, they stayed like that, holding each other in the quiet apartment.

Eventually, she whispered, “I’m going to miss you.”

His arms tightened slightly.

“I know.”

“That’s all?”

He lowered his head, his cheek brushing her hair.

“I’m going to miss you too.”

She pulled away to look at him.

“That’s still not enough.”

He studied her face for a second.

Then he cupped her cheek.

“I don’t want you to go tomorrow.”

Her expression changed.

He rarely said things like that.

Not because he didn’t feel them, but because he usually preferred to make her feel secure rather than burden her with everything he was thinking.

But tonight, he was tired of pretending the distance was something he could simply calculate and manage.

“I know you should go. I know it’s important. And I want you to have it,” he said.

She swallowed.

“But I don’t want you to go.”

Her eyes became glossy.

“Yichen…”

He brushed his thumb beneath her eye before a tear could fall.

“I’m not asking you to stay.”

“I know.”

“I just want you to know that wanting you here and wanting you to succeed aren’t mutually exclusive.”

That was when she finally cried.

A few tears she couldn’t quite stop.

Yichen pulled her back against him.

“Hey.”

“I’m fine.”

“You’re crying on my shirt.”

“Then don’t wear such a nice shirt.”

He let out a small breath of laughter, kissing her hair.

“That’s my solution?”

“It’s a very practical one.”

He held her until she stopped trying to hide her tears.

✦ ✦ ✦

The airport was worse than either of them expected.

Xiaoran had insisted she was going to be fine.

She had said it while brushing her teeth, while checking her ID card, while eating breakfast, and again in the car.

By the time they reached the departure hall, she had become unusually quiet.

Yichen pulled her suitcase beside him.

“Have you checked everything?”

“ID card, phone, wallet, charger.”

“Laptop?”

“Yes.”

“Internship documents?”

“Yes.”

“Medicine?”

She nodded.

“Good.”

She looked up at him.

“You sound like my father.”

“Your father probably has excellent judgment.”

“Don’t agree with me.”

He smiled faintly.

They stood near the entrance to the security area.

People moved around them, dragging suitcases and talking on their phones. Announcements echoed overhead.

Xiaoran looked at the entrance, then at him, then back at the entrance.

“Can you come with me?”

“I can accompany you to the security line.”

“I mean…”

She stopped.

He understood.

He stepped closer and wrapped his arms around her.

She buried her face against his chest.

“I don’t want to leave you.”

His hand moved slowly over her back.

“I know.”

“What if I get lonely?”

“Call me.”

“What if you’re training?”

“I’ll call you back.”

“What if I’m busy?”

“Then I’ll wait.”

“What if—”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

He touched her cheek.

“We’ll figure it out.”

She nodded, but her lips trembled.

He kissed her temple.

Then her left cheek.

Then her right.

Finally, he kissed her lips, gently and without rushing, as if he were trying to give her something to carry with her.

When he pulled away, she held onto his jacket.

“Don’t forget me.”

His expression changed.

For the first time that morning, he looked almost offended.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You think eight weeks is enough to make me forget you?”

She tried to smile.

He lowered his forehead to hers.

“I’ve spent years getting used to having you around. I’m not going to suddenly become unfamiliar with you because you’re in another city.”

“Okay.”

“Go make something of this opportunity.”

She sniffed.

“Okay.”

“And eat properly.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t skip meals because you’re busy.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t walk around with your phone out in unfamiliar places.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t—”

She pressed a finger against his lips.

“I’m going to miss you even more if you keep giving me homework.”

He kissed her fingertip.

“Then go.”

She hugged him one last time.

And when she finally walked toward security, she turned around twice.

He was still there both times.

The third time, he raised his hand.

She waved.

Then she disappeared into the crowd.

Yichen remained where he was for a little longer than necessary.

His phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: Don’t look so handsome when I leave. It’s unfair.

He looked at the message.

A small smile appeared.

Yichen: I’ll try to look worse next time.

Xiaoran: You can’t. It’s genetic.

He laughed under his breath.

Then he put his phone away and went home.

The apartment was quiet.

Her cup was still on the table.

A hair tie was on the sofa.

One of her slippers had somehow ended up beneath his desk.

He picked it up and placed it beside the other one.

Then he opened the little photo album.

He looked at the first photograph for a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week was easy.

Or at least, they tried to make it easy.

Xiaoran sent him photographs of Beijing.

The office building.

The view from her apartment.

A bowl of noodles she claimed was the best thing she had ever eaten.

A photograph of herself wearing her internship identification card, looking pleased with her own reflection.

Xiaoran: Do I look professional?

Yichen: Very.

Xiaoran: Really?

Yichen: You look like someone who knows what she’s doing.

Xiaoran: I don’t.

Yichen: They don’t need to know that.

She laughed at her phone in the middle of the office.

He sent her pictures of the training camp in return.

The court.

His teammates.

A photograph of his shoes after practice.

She complained that he was terrible at taking pictures.

He told her that he was documenting his surroundings, not producing a magazine.

Their video calls were frequent.

Sometimes they spoke for an hour.

Sometimes only ten minutes.

Sometimes Xiaoran would call him while walking home, and he would stay on the line until she reached her apartment.

She would tell him about the people she met, the projects she was assigned, the things she learned.

He would tell her about practice, his teammates, the training schedule, and the coach who seemed to believe that sleep was a privilege rather than a biological necessity.

They were busy.

But they were happy.

Until the second week.

It happened on a Thursday.

Xiaoran had been working on a campaign proposal for most of the day. Her supervisor had asked her to revise several sections, and she had stayed late to finish the changes.

By the time she got back to her apartment, it was nearly ten.

She showered, ate something small, and called Yichen.

No answer.

She assumed he was still training.

She sent a message.

Xiaoran: Are you done?

No reply.

She changed into her pajamas and sat on the bed.

Then she opened their chat again.

Still nothing.

She knew he was busy.

She knew the training camp was demanding.

She knew he couldn’t always answer.

But she missed him.

That was all.

She wanted to hear him say her name.

She wanted to complain about her supervisor, tell him about the ridiculous coffee machine at work, and ask whether he had eaten.

She wanted to hear his voice.

At 10:47 p.m., her phone finally rang.

She answered immediately.

“Yichen?”

“Sorry.”

His voice sounded tired.

She sat up. “It’s okay. Are you done?”

“Just finished.”

“Did you eat?”

“Mm.”

“What did you eat?”

“Dinner.”

She frowned. “That’s not an answer.”

He gave a quiet laugh.

“Rice, chicken, vegetables. Happy?”

“Very.”

There was a pause.

Then he asked, “How was your day?”

She opened her mouth.

And, she didn’t know where to start.

She had been waiting all evening to tell him everything. But now that he was finally there, she could hear the exhaustion in his voice.

“Fine,” she said.

“Just fine?”

“Mm.”

“Anything interesting?”

She looked down at her blanket.

“Not really.”

He was quiet.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then sleep early.”

She nodded, although he couldn’t see her.

“Okay.”

“I’ll call you tomorrow.”

“Okay.”

“Goodnight.”

“Goodnight.”

The call ended.

She stared at the screen.

It had been less than four minutes.

She knew he was tired.

She knew he had done nothing wrong.

Still, the disappointment settled in her chest.

She put her phone down and turned off the light.

For the first time since arriving in Beijing, she cried herself to sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next few days were worse.

Not because anything terrible happened.

That was the problem.

Nothing terrible happened.

Xiaoran continued going to work. She completed her assignments, attended meetings, learned how to navigate the city, and gradually became more comfortable with her colleagues.

Yichen continued training.

His schedule became more intense as the camp approached its final evaluation. There were additional sessions, recovery work, and team meetings.

Their calls became shorter.

Their messages became less frequent.

They still said good morning.

They still said goodnight.

They still told each other to eat.

But something had changed.
