Xiaoran stopped sending him every little thing.

She stopped taking photographs of her lunch just to show him.

She stopped calling him when she walked home.

When something funny happened, she sometimes opened their chat, typed a message, and deleted it.

She didn’t want to become another responsibility in his day.

Yichen noticed.

Of course he noticed.

He knew her habits too well.

He knew that when Xiaoran was excited, she sent messages in clusters. When she was annoyed, she sent voice notes. When she was sleepy, she used fewer punctuation marks.

And when she was trying not to bother him, she became excessively considerate.

It was the last one that worried him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday night, he called her after practice.

She answered after several rings.

“Hello?”

“Busy?”

“No. I was just washing my hair.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Rice.”

“With?”

She paused.

“Food.”

He closed his eyes briefly.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I’m asking because I care, not because I’m conducting an investigation.”

She laughed.

“I had beef noodles.”

“Good.”

There was a silence.

He sat on the edge of his bed, phone against his ear.

“How was your week?”

“Good.”

“Work?”

“Good.”

“Your supervisor?”

“Good.”

He leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees.

“You’ve become very fond of that word.”

She smiled faintly.

“It’s a useful word.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I’m really okay.”

“I didn’t say you weren’t.”

She looked out of the window.

The city lights blurred slightly.

“I just don’t want you to worry.”

His jaw tightened.

“Why would I not worry?”

“Because you’re busy.”

“I’m aware of my schedule.”

“And the training camp is important.”

“So is your internship.”

She didn’t answer.

He waited.

Then, he asked, “Are you lonely?”

Her eyes stung.

She wanted to say no.

She wanted to be mature about it. She wanted to be the girlfriend who supported him without needing anything in return.

But she was tired of being mature.

“A little,” she admitted.

His expression softened.

“How little?”

She laughed weakly.

“Quite a lot.”

He leaned back against the wall.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I know you’re tired.”

“I’m tired, Xiaoran. I’m not unavailable.”

She pressed her lips together.

“I don’t want you to feel like you have to call me.”

“I don’t.”

“Or like you have to make time for me.”

“I want to make time for you.”

“Yichen…”

“Listen to me.”

His voice was gentle, but firm enough to make her stop.

“You’re not asking me to abandon training. You’re asking your boyfriend to spend time with you.”

She looked down.

“That’s different?”

“Very.”

A tear slipped down her cheek.

He exhaled slowly.

“Are you crying?”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Maybe.”

He closed his eyes.

He hated being unable to reach her.

He hated that there were more than a thousand kilometers between them, that he couldn’t take her face in his hands, couldn’t wipe the tears away, couldn’t pull her against his chest and let her complain until she felt better.

“Show me your face,” he said.

She turned on her camera.

Her eyes were red.

He stared at her.

Then he smiled gently.

“Hello, pretty girl.”

She sniffed.

“Don’t.”

“Why?”

“I’m crying.”

“I can see that.”

“Then don’t call me pretty.”

“Would you prefer I call you a disaster?”

She laughed despite herself.

“Better,” he murmured.

Her smile faded again.

“I miss you.”

His gaze softened.

“I miss you too.”

“I miss you so much.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

He was quiet.

Then he said, “You’re right. I probably don’t know exactly how much.”

She looked at him.

“But I know that when I finish training, the first thing I do is check my phone to see whether you’ve messaged me. I know that I keep looking at the time because I want to know whether you’re awake. And I know that I have been sleeping with your ridiculous photo album beside my bed.”

Her lips parted.

He glanced away for a moment, almost embarrassed by his own confession.

“Is that enough evidence?”

She covered her mouth.

“Yichen…”

“I’m not asking you to pretend this is easy.”

He looked directly into the camera.

“It’s not easy for me either.”

chapters.desc: Shorter calls, one missed night that matters, and a station where this time she’s the one waiting.
chapters.title: The Internship in Another City (Part 2)
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t make yourself smaller just because I’m far away.”
chapters.content:
The next week, they tried something different.

They stopped treating their calls like appointments that had to be squeezed into the end of the day.

Instead, they began sharing their ordinary lives again.

Yichen would send her a photograph of his breakfast before practice.

Xiaoran would send him a voice note while walking to work.

He would call her for five minutes during his lunch break, even if all he had to say was that the training session had been exhausting.

She would send him a photograph of the sky outside her office.

Sometimes they didn’t even have anything to say.

They simply stayed on the phone while doing their own things.

One evening, Xiaoran was working on a presentation when Yichen called.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

“What are you doing?”

“Working.”

“Still?”

“Almost done.”

He heard the sound of her keyboard.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

She told him.

He was quiet.

Then he said, “I miss you.”

Her fingers stopped.

She looked at the phone.

“Why are you saying that suddenly?”

“Because I do.”

She smiled at the screen.

“I miss you too.”

He opened his arms.

She blinked.

“What?”

He reached for her.

She looked at the phone again.

“Yichen, we’re on a video call.”

“I know.”

She laughed.

“Then how?”

“Use your imagination.”

She leaned toward the camera and pressed a kiss against the screen.

He watched her.

Then he smiled.

“That’s not very convincing.”

“It’s all you get.”

“Unfortunate.”

She laughed again.

And for the first time in days, the distance felt a little less cruel.

✦ ✦ ✦

But the hardest moment came during the sixth week.

Xiaoran had been selected to assist with a presentation for a major client.

It was a small role, but a meaningful one. She had worked hard on the research and was excited about the opportunity.

She wanted to tell Yichen.

She wanted him to be proud of her.

She wanted to hear him say that he had known she could do it.

But the presentation was scheduled on the same day as the training camp’s final evaluation.

They had discussed it beforehand.

He had promised to call her afterward.

She had promised to send him a message once the presentation ended.

The day went well.

Better than well.

Her supervisor praised her work in front of the team. One of the senior staff members even asked whether she would be interested in assisting with another project.

Xiaoran walked out of the office feeling almost weightless.

She took out her phone.

There was a message from Yichen.

Yichen: Finished. Going into evaluation soon. I’ll call you when I’m done.

She smiled and typed.

Xiaoran: Good luck! Don’t injure yourself. I’ll tell you something later.

She waited.

Then she decided to send a photograph of herself outside the building.

She was smiling so brightly that her cheeks hurt.

Xiaoran: I did well today :)

He reacted with a heart.

Then he went into evaluation.

Hours passed.

She went back to her apartment, showered, ate dinner, and waited.

At 9:30 p.m., there was still no call.

At 10:15 p.m., she sent a message.

Xiaoran: How did it go?

No reply.

At 11:00 p.m., she finally called.

His phone rang.

And rang.

And rang.

No answer.

She told herself he was probably with the team.

She told herself he might be celebrating.

She told herself there was no reason to be upset.

At midnight, she fell asleep with her phone beside her.

The next morning, she woke to a message.

Yichen: Sorry. The evaluation ran late, then we had a team meeting. I just got back. Are you awake?

She read it.

Then she read it again.

She knew it was reasonable.

She knew he had a demanding day.

But she couldn’t stop the small, ugly thought that had appeared in her mind.

I had something important to tell you.

She typed.

Deleted.

Typed again.

Xiaoran: It’s okay. Hope everything went well.

She put the phone down.

A few minutes later, it rang.

She stared at his name, then answered.

“Morning.”

“Morning.”

His voice was tired.

“Did you sleep?”

“Mm.”

“I’m sorry I missed your call.”

“It’s okay.”

He was quiet.

“Xiaoran, how was your presentation?”

She swallowed.

“Good.”

“Just good?”

She smiled faintly.

“It went well. My supervisor liked it.”

“That’s great.”

“Mm.”

“What did they say?”

She told him.

She explained the praise, the possible next project, the way she had managed to answer a difficult question without freezing.

Yichen listened carefully.

He asked questions.

He remembered the names of the people she mentioned.

He told her that he was proud of her.

And she believed him.

But she still felt sad.

When she finished, he said, “I wish I could have heard about it last night.”

She looked down.

“It’s okay.”

“I wanted to.”

“I know.”

“Xiaoran.”

She closed her eyes.

“I’m not angry with you.”

“I know.”

“Then what is it?”

She was silent.

Finally, she whispered, “I just wanted you there.”

The words were small.

But they carried everything.

“I wanted to call you after the presentation. I wanted to tell you while I was still excited. I wanted to hear you say you were proud of me before I went to sleep.”

Her voice trembled.

“I know you had your evaluation. I know it was important. I know you didn’t do anything wrong. But I still wanted you.”

Yichen didn’t speak.

She continued, trying to hold herself together.

“And I hate that sometimes I feel like I’m waiting for the little pieces of your day that are left over. I know that’s not fair, because you’re probably feeling the same way. But I miss being part of your ordinary day.”

He sat still.

Then he looked down at his hands.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

“I think I’ve been trying too hard to make sure you don’t feel like you’re sacrificing anything for me.”

She listened.

“I keep telling myself that if I work hard enough, if I finish training properly, if I don’t complain, then these eight weeks will pass quickly. And I thought that was what you needed from me.”

He paused.

“But I might have forgotten that you don’t need me to be impressive from another city.”

Her eyes filled.

“You need me to be your boyfriend.”

He looked at the camera.

“I’m sorry.”

She shook her head.

“Don’t.”

“I should have called.”

“You were busy.”

“I could have sent a message before the meeting.”

She didn’t answer.

“I can’t always be available. But I can do better at making sure you don’t feel like you’re waiting for me to remember you,” he said.

She pressed her lips together.

“And you don’t have to be considerate every time you miss me. You can be selfish sometimes,” he said.

She laughed through her tears.

“I’m already quite selfish.”

“I know.”

“Excuse me?”

“Very.”

She wiped her cheek.

He smiled faintly.

“That’s one of the things I like about you.”

She looked at him.

“I like that you want me. I like that you tell me when you miss me. I like that you still want to tell me every little thing, even when you think it’s unimportant.”

His voice softened.

“Don’t make yourself smaller just because I’m far away.”

That broke her.

She covered her face and cried.

Yichen watched her, wishing desperately that the screen would disappear and leave him with the real girl instead.

“Come here,” he murmured.

She lowered her hands.

He held his palm against the camera.

She placed hers against it.

It was ridiculous.

It was insufficient.

But they stayed that way for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final two weeks passed more gently.

Not because they missed each other less.

They simply became better at admitting it.

Xiaoran began calling him whenever she wanted, without apologizing for it.

Yichen started sending her voice messages when he knew he wouldn’t be able to answer immediately.

He told her when he was going into practice.

She told him when she had a deadline.

They made plans for the day they would see each other again.

She wanted to eat hotpot.

He wanted to sleep.

She wanted to go shopping.

He wanted to hold her hand and do absolutely nothing.

They compromised.

Hotpot first, then shopping, then nothing.

One night, Yichen called her after a particularly difficult practice.

He was lying on his bed, hair still damp from his shower.

Xiaoran was sitting at her desk, wearing an oversized T-shirt.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Do you think we’ll be different when we come back?”

He looked at her.

“Different how?”

“I don’t know. Maybe we’ll get used to being alone.”

He was quiet.

Then he said, “I hope we get used to being apart when we have to.”

She blinked.

“But not because we prefer it.”

Her expression softened.

He said, “I don’t want us to become people who need to be together every second to feel secure. But I also don’t want us to pretend we don’t miss each other.”

She nodded slowly.

“I think that’s fair.”

He studied her.

“Are you worried?”

“A little.”

“About what?”

She hesitated.

“About going back to normal and realizing how much we missed.”

He smiled gently.

“Then we’ll make up for it.”

“How?”

“Start with dinner.”

She laughed.

“That’s your plan?”

“It’s a good plan.”

“What about kissing?”

“Also included.”

“Cuddling?”

“Obviously.”

“Will you hold my hand?”

He looked at her as if the question were absurd.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I’ve been waiting eight weeks.”

She smiled.

Then, she said, “Me too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her internship finished three days before his camp did, so this time she was the one waiting.

The day Yichen returned, Xiaoran arrived at the station nearly forty minutes early.

She checked the arrival board three times.

She checked her phone.

She bought a bottle of water.

She didn’t drink it.

When the train finally arrived, she stood near the exit with her hands clasped together.

People began coming out.

One after another.

Then she saw him.

A black duffel bag over one shoulder. A backpack in one hand. His hair slightly longer than when he left. His expression tired, but his eyes searching.

He saw her almost immediately.

And smiled.

Xiaoran didn’t walk.

She ran.

He barely had time to put his bag down before she threw her arms around him.

“Yichen!”

He caught her, laughing as he wrapped both arms around her.

“Careful.”

“I missed you.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

He pressed his cheek against her hair.

“I missed you too.”

She tightened her arms around his waist.

For a moment, neither moved.

The station was noisy.

People were passing them.

His bag was on the floor.

None of it mattered.

She drew back to look at him.

Then she frowned.

“You’re thinner.”

“You’re imagining things.”

“You have been training too much.”

He smiled.

“You’ve been worrying too much.”

“That’s because you don’t take care of yourself.”

“I do.”

“Not enough.”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“Hello.”

“What?”

“I’m home.”

Her face crumpled.

He saw it immediately and pulled her back into his arms.

She buried her face against his neck.

“Don’t say things like that.”

“Why?”

“I’ll cry.”

He kissed her temple.

“Then cry.”

And she did.

Not because she was sad.

Not because the distance had broken anything.

Because she had spent eight weeks missing the weight of his arms, the warmth of his body, the sound of his voice without a speaker between them.

She had missed him in ways she hadn’t known how to explain.

Now he was here.

And she could finally stop imagining what it would feel like to hug him again.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went to dinner that evening.

As promised, hotpot.

Xiaoran sat opposite him, watching him eat.

He noticed after the third time.

“You’re staring.”

“I’m observing.”

“Anything interesting?”

She nodded solemnly.

“Your face.”

He laughed.

She smiled.

Then she reached across the table and touched his hand.

He turned his palm upward, letting her fingers slide into his.

They ate slowly.

They talked about the internship, the training camp, the people they had met, the things they had learned, and all the small details they had saved for each other.

At some point, Xiaoran told him about the presentation again.

This time, he was sitting right across from her.

He listened without looking at his phone.

He asked questions.

He laughed at the parts she found funny.

When she finished, he said, “I’m proud of you.”

She looked down at their joined hands.

“You already said that.”

“I know.”

“Then why say it again?”

“Because I wanted to say it while I was here.”

She looked up.

He smiled.

She squeezed his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, they went back to his apartment.

Xiaoran took off her shoes and walked straight to the sofa.

Then she turned around and opened her arms.

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

She opened her arms.

He put his keys down.

“I’m coming.”

She held her arms out wider.

He walked over, bent down, and let her wrap herself around him.

She kissed his cheek, then the other.

Then his jaw.

He laughed.

“What’s this?”

“Eight weeks of missed affection.”

“That’s quite a lot.”

“I haven’t finished.”

“I can tell.”

She pulled back, looked at him, and kissed his lips.

This time, he didn’t tease her.

He held her face gently and kissed her properly, slowly, with the kind of affection that had been difficult to fit into a phone call.

When they separated, she rested her forehead against his.

“Can we stay like this?”

He brushed her hair behind her ear.

“As long as you want.”

“Even if I don’t let you move?”

“Then I’ll have to negotiate.”

She smiled.

“I’m a difficult negotiator.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She rested her head against his chest.

His arms settled around her.

For a while, they said nothing.

Then Xiaoran murmured, “I thought the distance would make everything feel different.”

He looked down at her.

“Does it?”

She thought about it.

“Not really.”

“Good.”

She traced a small circle on his shirt.

“I think I understand something now.”

“What?”

“I don’t need you to be beside me all the time.”

He listened.

“But I really, really like it when you are.”

He smiled.

“That’s convenient.”

“Why?”

“Because I really, really like being beside you.”

She grinned.

Then she leaned up and kissed him again.

He held her a little closer.

Eight weeks ago, they had stood at an airport entrance, both pretending that the distance would be manageable.

It had been difficult.

There had been lonely evenings, missed calls, quiet disappointments, and moments when loving each other from far away felt like trying to hold water in their hands.

But they had learned something.

They could be ambitious without abandoning each other.

They could be lonely without being ashamed of it.

They could miss each other without making the other person feel guilty.

And most importantly, they could keep choosing each other even when their lives were moving in different directions.

Xiaoran eventually fell asleep against his chest.

Yichen looked down at her.

Her hand was still curled into his shirt, as if she had no intention of letting him go again.

He gently kissed her hair.

“Eight weeks,” he whispered.

She stirred.

“Don’t count anymore.”

He smiled.

“Okay.”

“I’m home now.”

He watched her.

Then he kissed her hair.

“Me too.”

chapters.desc: A point guard from Hangzhou posts one photograph from camp. The whole team sees it. Captain Zhou may never recover.
chapters.title: The Photograph in His Training Bag
chapters.epigraph: “I held it anyway.”
chapters.content:
The photograph had been posted at 1:12 a.m. on the last night of the summer training camp, by a point guard from a university in Hangzhou whom Zhou Yichen had shared a room with for eight weeks and would now never forgive.

It showed Yichen asleep on a narrow dormitory bed, one arm thrown over his eyes, still in his training shirt.

On his chest, held flat under his other hand as if someone might try to take it, was a small photo album.

The caption said: every night for eight weeks. every single night. we have suffered.

By the first university practice of the autumn semester, the entire Huaining basketball team had seen it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen knew something was wrong the moment he walked into the changing room, because it went quiet.

The Huaining changing room was never quiet. It was twelve men, a speaker playing three songs at once, and Fang Ze explaining something about his own calves.

Now it was silent.

Twelve faces turned towards him with expressions of enormous, innocent interest.

“Afternoon, Captain Zhou,” said Fang Ze.

“Afternoon.”

“How was camp?”

“Fine.”

“Fine, did you sleep well?” said Fang Ze, nodding slowly.

Yichen put his bag down on the bench.

“Who sent it to you.”

“Sent what?”

“Fang Ze.”

Fang Ze held up his phone. On it was the photograph, enlarged so that the album filled the screen. Someone had circled it in red.

“Every night. Every single night,” said Fang Ze, in a voice of great tenderness.

The room collapsed. Somebody fell off the bench. Somebody else started reading the caption aloud in a high, trembling voice, like a poem at a funeral, and had to stop halfway because he was crying with laughter.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran heard about it forty minutes later, when she arrived at the gym with two drinks, which had become her habit since first year, and found the entire team doing a warm-up lap with the clear intention of passing as close to her as possible.

“Afternoon, team manager!”

“Hello?”

“Team manager, quick question.”

“Yes?”

“Is it true you made Captain Zhou a book?”

She stopped walking.

At the far end of the court, Yichen, who had been stretching his hamstrings with tremendous concentration, closed his eyes.

“What book?”

Fang Ze jogged past backwards. “The one he slept with. For eight weeks. Every night.”

Xiaoran turned slowly and looked across the court at her boyfriend.

Her boyfriend didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Every night?” she said in the corridor afterwards.

“He’s exaggerating.”

“There’s a photograph.”

“It was one night.”

“The caption says every night.”

“The caption was written by a man from Hangzhou who snores, and has no credibility,” said Yichen.

She looked at him. He looked at the vending machine as if it had personally wronged him.

She had been home from Beijing for five days. She had been told, by him, at the station, with his arms round her, that he had missed her. She had been told, on the phone, at the worst point of the internship, that he’d been sleeping with her ridiculous photo album beside his bed.

Beside. Not on.

“You held it. While you were asleep. Like a teddy bear,” she said.

“I fell asleep reading it.”

“Every night?”

“Xiaoran.”

“Did you read the captions?”

He didn’t answer.

“The one on the Chengdu page? This panda eats more than me but don’t tell him?” She stepped closer.

The corner of his mouth went.

“I read the captions,” he said.

“Every night?”

He looked at her then, properly, the way he did when he’d decided there was no point lying.

“Most nights. The other nights I was too tired to open it. I held it anyway,” said Zhou Yichen.

She hadn’t expected that.

For a moment she couldn’t say anything at all. She stood in the corridor outside the Huaining gym with two cups of iced tea sweating in her hands and her face doing something she couldn’t control.

Then she said, “Show me where it is now.”

“No.”

“Yichen.”

“It’s in my bag.”

“You brought it to practice?”

“It was in my bag at camp. I haven’t unpacked,” he said, with dignity.

“You’ve been home two days.”

“I’ve been busy.”

She put both drinks down on top of the vending machine, the old one by the gym door that had once eaten a whole week of Fang Ze’s change, unzipped the front pocket of the sports bag on his shoulder before he could stop her, and there it was: her little album, the corners a bit soft now, one page loose. A café receipt was tucked inside the back cover that hadn’t been there when she’d given it to him.

She took it out.

It was from the camp canteen, dated the second week, the night she’d cried herself to sleep in Beijing. On the back, in his neat handwriting, it said: Call her at lunch tomorrow, not after. She says fine when she means not fine.

She looked up at him.

He held out his hand for it, and she didn’t give it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The team saw them come back into the gym. She was holding his hand. He was holding both drinks. Neither of them was saying anything.

“Oh no. She’s crying. Captain, you made the team manager cry,” said Fang Ze, delighted.

“She’s not crying,” said Yichen.

“I’m a little bit crying,” said Xiaoran.

The whole team went “Ohhhh” at once, like a single enormous embarrassing animal.

Coach blew his whistle so hard a ball rolled off the rack.

“Zhou! Lin! Out of my gym if you’re going to do that. Everyone else, line. Now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out of practice at seven. She was sitting on the low wall outside the gym with the album on her knees, turning the pages slowly, the way he must have done in a narrow bed in a dormitory two hours outside the city.

He sat down next to her.

“Coach wants to see me tomorrow,” he said.

“Because of the crying?”

“Because the man who ran the camp rang him. Somebody watched the last week. Asked for my name.” He was quiet for a second.

She turned her head.

“Somebody who?”

“He didn’t say.”

He was looking straight ahead at the car park, but she knew that face. It was the face he’d worn at seventeen, the night before the game the scouts came to see.

“Probably nobody,” he said.

“Probably somebody.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Probably somebody,” she said again, and let her head drop onto his shoulder, and held his hand on top of the album, and he didn’t argue.

A minute later his phone buzzed in his pocket. He took it out and looked at it and laughed under his breath.

Fang Ze: team group chat has voted. the album is now an official team mascot. it travels to away games. this is not a democracy

“Absolutely not,” said Yichen, and typed it.

Fang Ze: too late captain. we’ve ordered it a jersey

✦ ✦ ✦

The jersey arrived the following Tuesday.

It was navy blue, the size of a postcard, with HUAINING across the front and a number eleven on the back, and Fang Ze presented it in the changing room before practice with the solemnity of a man handing over a medal.

“For the album. Since it’s clearly a member of this team,” he said.

“It isn’t coming to away games.”

“It’s already on the travel list. Coach signed it.”

“Coach did not sign it.”

Fang Ze unfolded a sheet of paper. At the bottom, under twelve names and one that said Album (Lin), in Coach’s terrible handwriting, was the word Fine.

Yichen looked at it.

Then he took the tiny jersey, without a word, and went to his locker.

When Xiaoran came in at the end of practice with two drinks, the locker door was open. On the top shelf, between his spare shoes and a roll of tape, sat her photo album, its soft corners propped against the metal wall, wearing a navy blue jersey with a number eleven on the back.

She stopped in the doorway with both hands over her mouth.

“Don’t,” said Yichen, from the bench.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face said something.”

“My face, is saying that you are the most embarrassing boyfriend in the history of this university, and that I’m going to tell everyone, and that I love you,” said Xiaoran, coming over and sitting down beside him with the drinks.

The changing room, which had gone quiet, made the noise again: one enormous, embarrassing ohhhh.

Yichen closed his eyes.

But he didn’t take the jersey off the album. Not that day, and not when the team traveled to its first away game of the season, and not three weeks later, when a man in a dark jacket sat at the back of the gym and wrote something down.

chapters.desc: A man in a dark jacket at the back of the university gym, a message from a professional club, and a very small basketball keychain.
chapters.title: The Scout at the Back of the Gym
chapters.epigraph: “Then you’ll still be Zhou Yichen.”
chapters.content:
The first person to notice Zhou Yichen wasn’t his coach.

It wasn’t his teammates, either.

It was a man sitting at the back of the university gym, wearing a dark jacket and holding a tablet on his lap.

Yichen didn’t know who he was.

He didn’t even notice him.

At that moment, he was too busy trying to win a practice game, three weeks into the autumn semester.

The score was 78–76.

There were twenty seconds left.

His teammate called for the ball, but Yichen had already seen the opening. He moved past the defender, changed direction, and drove toward the basket. Another player stepped in to block him.

Yichen didn’t hesitate.

He jumped.

The ball left his fingertips just before the defender’s hand reached it.

Two points.

The gym erupted.

His teammates shouted. Someone slapped his back. The coach blew his whistle, looking thoroughly pleased with himself.

Yichen merely jogged back, expression composed, as if he hadn’t just made the winning shot.

From the back of the gym, the man in the dark jacket looked down at his tablet.

Then he wrote something.

Xiaoran was waiting outside the gym with two drinks.

She had originally planned to watch the entire practice, but after nearly an hour, her attention had wandered to her phone, then to the vending machine, then to a conversation with one of Yichen’s teammates who had come out to refill his water bottle.

Still, she had watched the final game.

And she was proud of herself for not shouting when Yichen made the winning shot.

She had only clapped.

Quite loudly.

When Yichen finally emerged, his hair was damp, his training shirt clinging slightly to his shoulders, and his sports bag hanging from one hand.

Xiaoran immediately held out a drink.

“Congratulations.”

He took it.

“For what?”

“For winning.”

“It was practice.”

“You still won.”

He glanced at her. “You were watching?”

“Of course.”

“From the beginning?”

She hesitated.

He smiled.

“Xiaoran.”

“I watched the important parts.”

“What happened in the first quarter?”

“Basketball.”

He laughed.

She followed him toward the benches, talking about how one of his teammates had nearly fallen over during a particularly dramatic attempt at defending him.

Yichen listened, occasionally correcting her interpretation of what had happened.

Then he stopped.

“Wait here a moment.”

“Why?”

“I need to speak to Coach.”

She nodded and sat down.

Yichen walked back into the gym.

Xiaoran watched him approach the coach, who was standing near the scorer’s table with another man.

The man in the dark jacket.

She noticed him because he looked strangely out of place among the students. He wasn’t wearing sportswear, wasn’t carrying a gym bag, and didn’t seem particularly interested in the rest of the team.

He was speaking to the coach.

Then he looked at Yichen.

Xiaoran tilted her head.

Something about the way the man shook Yichen’s hand made her curious.

When Yichen returned, she immediately asked, “Who was that?”

“Someone Coach knows.”

“Someone important?”

“Maybe.”

“Yichen.”

He looked at her.

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re hiding something.”

He smiled slightly.

“Am I?”

She stared at him.

He took a sip of his drink.

“Let’s go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The message arrived two days later.

Yichen was in the middle of a lecture when his phone vibrated.

An unfamiliar number.

He almost ignored it.

Then he saw the message.

Hello, Zhou Yichen. This is Lou Wei from the player recruitment department of the Shanghai Herons Basketball Club. We met briefly at your university gym on Tuesday. I would like to discuss a potential trial opportunity with you.

He read it twice.

Then he put his phone down.

For the next twenty minutes, he tried to pay attention to his professor.

He failed.

After class, he called the number.

The conversation lasted nearly fifteen minutes.

The club had been observing university-level competitions and had received recommendations from several coaches, including the one who had run his summer camp. They were interested in inviting him for a trial session.

It wasn’t an offer.

It wasn’t a contract.

It was an opportunity to be evaluated by a professional club.

A serious one.

Yichen asked about the schedule, the training expectations, and what would happen after the trial.

He listened carefully.

When the call ended, he stood outside the lecture hall for a while.

Then he opened Xiaoran’s chat.

Yichen: Are you free tonight?

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: I have something to tell you.

Xiaoran: Are you injured?

He stared at the message.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Did you fail an exam?

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Did you buy another car?

He laughed.

Yichen: Come have dinner with me.

Xiaoran: You’re making me nervous.

Yichen: Good. You’ll be more curious when you see me.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran arrived at the restaurant ten minutes early.

Yichen was already there.

He had changed into a simple dark shirt, his hair neatly styled, and his expression was unusually thoughtful.

She sat down immediately.

“Tell me.”

He pushed the menu toward her.

“Order first.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I’m not eating until you tell me.”

He considered her, then gave a quiet laugh.

“Someone from the Herons contacted me.”

“The basketball club?”

“They want me to attend a trial.”

For a moment, she didn’t respond.

Then her eyes widened.

“Wait. A professional club?”

“It’s a trial.”

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“A professional club.”

“I heard you the first time.”

“They want you?”

“They want to evaluate me.”

She placed both hands on the table.

“That’s amazing.”

He smiled.

She was already leaning forward, her excitement practically spilling across the table.

“When?”

“Next month.”

“How long?”

“A few days initially. Depending on the evaluation, there may be further opportunities.”

“Are you going?”

He looked at her.

“Yes.”

She nodded immediately.

“Of course you’re going.”

He watched her.

“You’re not surprised?”

“I am surprised.”

“You look very calm.”

“I’m trying to behave like a supportive girlfriend.”

He laughed.

“That’s a new development.”

She ignored him.

“I’m serious. You should go. You worked so hard to get here.”

He reached across the table and touched her hand.

“Thank you.”

She squeezed his fingers.

Then, as if remembering something, she suddenly sat straighter.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Does this mean you’ll become a professional basketball player?”

“Not necessarily.”

“But you could?”

“It’s possible.”

Her eyes shone.

“Yichen…”

He smiled at her expression.

She looked so happy that he almost forgot how carefully he had been considering the invitation.

Almost.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next few weeks were different.

Yichen’s training schedule became more demanding.

He spoke with his university coach about the opportunity, adjusted his routine, and began preparing specifically for the trial.

His shooting drills became more precise.

His conditioning sessions became longer.

He studied footage of the club’s previous games and familiarized himself with their style of play.

He was serious about it.

Very serious.

Xiaoran noticed.

She noticed the way he sometimes stayed behind after practice to repeat a drill. She noticed how carefully he managed his meals and sleep. She noticed that his usual relaxed evenings were increasingly occupied by recovery sessions and reviewing game footage.

She tried to be supportive.

She really did.

She even learned how to prepare a few simple meals that suited his training schedule.

Unfortunately, she was still not particularly good at cooking.

The first time she made chicken breast, it was so dry that Yichen needed two glasses of water to finish it.

She watched him chew.

“Is it bad?”

He swallowed.

“No.”

“Really?”

“It’s edible.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s not a compliment.”

He smiled and reached for her hand.

“It’s good that you tried.”

She looked at the plate.

“I wanted to make something useful.”

“You already do.”

“Don’t say that just because you don’t want to hurt my feelings.”

“I’m not.”

He leaned over and kissed her cheek.

“Besides, I like having you around.”

She smiled.

Then she pushed the plate toward him.

“Finish it.”

He looked at the chicken, then at her.

“Yes, ma’am.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The night before the trial, Xiaoran came over.

Yichen was reviewing footage on his laptop when she arrived.

She had brought food, a small paper bag, and an expression that suggested she had been planning something.

He glanced at the bag.

“What did you buy?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“It’s a surprise.”

She placed the bag on the table and sat beside him.

“Have you finished reviewing?”

“Almost.”

“Then stop.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“Because your brain needs rest.”

He looked at the screen.

“Five more minutes.”

She stared at him.

He stared back.

She reached over and gently closed the laptop.

“Your five minutes are over.”

He laughed.

“Very authoritative.”

“I’m serious.”

“I know.”

She took his hand and examined his fingers.

His palms were rough from training. There was a small patch of redness near one knuckle.

She brushed her thumb over it.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

“Are you nervous?”

He looked at her.

“A little.”

It was an honest answer.

She seemed surprised.

“Really?”

“It’s a professional trial. I’d be more concerned if I weren’t nervous.”

She nodded thoughtfully.

Then she opened the paper bag.

Inside was a small keychain.

A miniature basketball, with his initials engraved on the back.

He looked at it.

“What’s this?”

“Good luck charm.”

He turned it over in his hand.

“You made this?”

“I ordered it. But I chose the design.”

He smiled.

“Very thoughtful.”

“Don’t lose it.”

“I won’t.”

She hesitated.

Then she said, “I know it’s just a trial. And I know there are lots of things that can happen. But I hope you get what you want.”

He looked at her.

She said, “I hope they see how good you are. Not just because you’re tall or handsome or because you can jump very high.”

He laughed.

“Thank you for including my height and appearance.”

“I’m being serious.”

“I know.”

She looked down at their hands.

“I’ve watched you work so hard. Sometimes I think you don’t even realize how much you’ve improved.”

His expression softened.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

She reached for him.

He pulled her closer until she was sitting against him.

She leaned into his shoulder.

For a while, neither spoke.

Then he said, “Do you know what I’m thinking?”

“What?”

“That I should have asked you to come with me.”

She lifted her head.

“To the trial?”

“Mm.”

“Can I?”

“Of course.”

Her eyes widened.

“Really?”

He smiled.

“If you want to.”

She tried not to look too excited.

Failed.

“Then I’ll come.”

He laughed and kissed her cheek.

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The trial took place at the club’s training facility.

It was much larger than the university gym.

The court was polished, the equipment was professional, and the atmosphere was noticeably different. There were no casual conversations between drills, no students wandering in and out, no teammates joking around while waiting for their turn.

Everyone seemed focused.

Xiaoran sat in the spectator area with her hands clasped around a bottle of water.

She had dressed comfortably, but she had spent an unreasonable amount of time deciding what to wear.

She wanted to look presentable.

She also wanted to avoid looking like someone who had come merely to watch her boyfriend.

Although, technically, that was exactly what she had come to do.

Yichen had told her not to worry.

She had worried anyway.

When he walked onto the court, she immediately sat straighter.

He was wearing the trial uniform.

A simple training jersey with his assigned number.

His hair was neatly arranged, his expression composed, and his posture confident.

She had seen him play countless times.

At university.

During tournaments.

During casual games with friends.

But this felt different.

He wasn’t playing in front of people who already knew him.

He was being evaluated.

And he knew it.

The first session focused on physical assessment and individual drills.

Speed.

Footwork.

Shooting accuracy.

Defensive positioning.

Yichen moved with a level of intensity Xiaoran rarely saw outside important games.

He didn’t waste movement.

He didn’t complain.

When he missed a shot, he retrieved the ball and repeated the attempt.

When the coach corrected his footwork, he listened and adjusted.

When another player challenged him during a defensive drill, he responded immediately.

He was competitive.

Quietly, relentlessly competitive.

Xiaoran watched him and felt her chest swell with pride, then came the scrimmage.

The players were divided into teams.

Yichen was assigned to a group with several athletes who had already played at a higher level.

At first, he seemed to be observing.

Learning their rhythm.

Understanding how they moved.

Then he began to adapt.

He found passing lanes.

Anticipated defensive movements.

Created space.

And when the opportunity came, he drove toward the basket and scored.

The coach called out something.

Yichen nodded.

He was sweating heavily now.

His breathing had become more pronounced, but his focus never wavered.

Xiaoran found herself gripping the edge of her seat.

A player from the opposing team made a sharp move, trying to get past him.

Yichen intercepted.

The ball changed possession.

He passed it forward.

His teammate scored.

Xiaoran almost stood up.

She caught herself at the last second.

Then she whispered, “That’s my boyfriend.”

A woman sitting two seats away glanced at her and smiled.

Xiaoran immediately looked down.

The trial ended late in the afternoon.

Yichen walked toward the changing rooms with the other players.

Xiaoran waited.

She had sent him a message earlier, but he hadn’t checked his phone.

When he finally came out, his hair was damp, his shoulders slightly slumped from exhaustion, and his expression unreadable.

She stood immediately.

“How was it?”

He took the bag she was holding.

“Long.”

“That’s all?”

“Very long.”

She looked at his face.

“Are you okay?”

“I’m fine.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

He considered the question.

“Yes.”

Her smile returned.

“Really?”

“It’s different.”

“Different good or different bad?”

“Different challenging.”

She nodded.

He took her hand.

“Let’s get something to eat.”

She walked beside him, but she couldn’t help looking at him.

He seemed quieter than usual.

Not upset.

Just thoughtful.

After a few minutes, she asked, “Do you think you did well?”

He glanced at her.

“I think I did what I could.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He smiled faintly.

“Then yes. I think I did well.”

She squeezed his hand.

“Good.”

“You’re very quiet.”

“I’m trying not to ask a hundred questions.”

“That’s considerate.”

“I have at least two hundred.”

He laughed.

“Save them for dinner.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The call came three days later.

Yichen was at home when his phone rang.

He listened carefully.

Xiaoran was sitting on the sofa, pretending to read.

She had been pretending for the past fifteen minutes.

When he ended the call, she immediately looked up.

“What happened?”

He sat down beside her.

“The club wants me to come back for another evaluation.”

Her face lit up.

“Really?”

“There’s a second stage. They’ll assess how I perform with the main training group.”

She put her book down.

“Yichen!”

He smiled.

She grabbed his arm.

“That’s good, isn’t it?”

“It is.”

“That’s really good!”

He laughed as she threw her arms around him.

She hugged him so tightly that he had to lean back against the sofa.

“Congratulations!”

“Thank you.”

“I’m so proud of you.”

He rested his chin against her head.

“Thank you.”

She pulled away.

“Are you happy?”

He looked at her.

“Yes. A little nervous about the next stage.”

“That’s normal.”

“Mm.”

She studied his face.

“You’ll do well.”

“You’re very confident.”

“Of course. I’ve seen you play.”

He reached up and tucked a strand of hair behind her ear.

“And if I don’t?”

She frowned.

“Then you’ll still be Zhou Yichen.”

He looked at her.

She continued, as if explaining something obvious.

“You’ll still be the person who studies business, makes fun of my cooking, steals my drinks, and pretends he doesn’t like being hugged.”

“I don’t pretend.”

“You do.”

“Never.”

She smiled.

“And you’ll still be my boyfriend.”

His expression softened.

She touched his cheek.

“Getting selected would be wonderful. But it doesn’t decide whether I’m proud of you.”

For a moment, he said nothing.

Then he leaned forward and pressed a kiss into her hair.

He crooked a finger at her.

She went willingly.

He held her against him, one hand resting at the back of her head.

“Do you know something?” he murmured.

“What?”

“When I first started playing basketball seriously, I thought the best part would be getting better.”

She looked up.

“And now?”

He smiled.

“Now I think the best part is having someone to tell when something good happens.”

Her expression softened.

“Then tell me everything.”

“I will.”

“Even the boring parts.”

“Especially the boring parts.”

She nodded, satisfied.

Then she remembered something.

“Wait.”

He looked down.

“What?”

“Does this mean I have to learn how professional basketball works?”

He laughed.

“You don’t have to.”

“But I want to understand.”

“You already understand more than you think.”

“Really?”

“Mm.”

She looked pleased.

“Then next time, I’ll sit with the serious expression.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You already do that.”

“Because I’m naturally intelligent.”

“Of course.”

“And the girlfriend of a very handsome boyfriend.”

He laughed, pulling her closer.

“That’s a very important qualification.”

She grinned.

Then she kissed his cheek.

He turned his head slightly and caught her lips instead.

When he pulled away, she blinked.

“That’s cheating.”

He smiled, looking entirely unrepentant.

“Then I suppose I’ll do it again.”

And he kissed her once more.

Outside, the evening settled over the campus.

Somewhere across the city, a professional club was reviewing footage of a university player they had noticed at the back of a gym.

They had seen his speed, his discipline, his court awareness, and his competitive instincts.

They had seen a young athlete with potential.

But they hadn’t seen the boy who carefully saved a miniature basketball keychain because his girlfriend had given it to him.

They hadn’t seen the way he checked his phone after every session, hoping to find a message from her.

They hadn’t seen how, after years of working toward something, he had finally begun to imagine what his future might look like.

And, for the first time, that future was beginning to look a little bigger than the university gym.

Yichen didn’t know yet where it would lead.

But when Xiaoran tucked herself against his shoulder and asked whether he wanted her to come to the next evaluation, he answered without hesitation.

“Of course.”

She smiled.

“Then I’ll be there.”

He kissed her hair.

“I know.”

chapters.desc: While he talks to his coach, a recruiter sits down beside Lin Xiaoran and asks a few questions. She answers every single one.
chapters.title: The Girlfriend Who Didn’t Know She Was Being Interviewed
chapters.epigraph: “That’s why they should ask me.”
chapters.content:
By the time the second evaluation ended, Xiaoran had developed a specific understanding of professional basketball.

It involved a lot of running, a lot of shouting, an unreasonable number of whistles, and Zhou Yichen looking so handsome that she sometimes forgot what she was supposed to be watching.

She was beginning to suspect that the last part was a personal problem.

The evaluation had lasted nearly three hours. Unlike the first session, this one had included practice with the club’s main training group. The pace was faster, the players were stronger, and the coaches seemed considerably less interested in offering encouragement.

Yichen had been focused from beginning to end.

He wasn’t the loudest player on the court. He didn’t celebrate every successful play or complain when a teammate made a mistake. He simply adjusted, observed, and played.

And Xiaoran had noticed something else.

When he was challenged, he became even more composed.

It was almost annoying.

She had watched him lose possession once, recover immediately, and make a defensive play that earned an approving nod from one of the coaches. Later, when he missed a difficult shot, he didn’t look frustrated. He simply retrieved the ball and tried again.

By the time the session ended, Xiaoran was practically glowing with pride.

She waited near the entrance with his water bottle and a small towel.

When Yichen finally walked over, she handed them to him.

“Here.”

“Thank you.”

“You were good.”

He wiped his face. “Just good?”

She tilted her head.

“Very good.”

“Better.”

She smiled.

He took the water bottle from her and drank half of it before asking, “How long have you been waiting?”

“Not long.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Twenty minutes.”

He glanced at the clock.

“Practice ended ten minutes ago.”

“I know.”

“So?”

She smiled innocently.

“I was enjoying the atmosphere.”

He looked at the empty corridor, then back at her.

“Of course.”

She took the towel from his hand and folded it over her arm.

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Hungry?”

“Very.”

“Good. I found a restaurant nearby.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You found it?”

“I researched.”

“Should I be concerned?”

“Why?”

“Your research sometimes involves choosing restaurants based on how pretty the desserts look.”

“That’s a perfectly valid research method.”

He laughed and gently touched her hair.

“Give me ten minutes. I need to speak with Coach.”

“Okay.”

“Stay here.”

She nodded.

He walked back toward the training area.

Xiaoran found a seat near the hallway and began looking through her phone, completely unaware that someone had been observing her for the past few minutes.

“Excuse me.”

She looked up.

A man in his late thirties stood a short distance away. He wore a dark polo shirt with the club’s logo embroidered on the chest and held a tablet.

“Are you waiting for Zhou Yichen?”

“Yes.”

“I’m with the club’s recruitment department. My name is Jiao Rui.”

Xiaoran immediately stood.

“Oh, hello.”

He smiled politely.

“You’re his girlfriend, right?”

She blinked, then nodded.

“Yes.”

“I’m sorry to interrupt. I wanted to ask you something, if you don’t mind.”

“Of course.”

He gestured toward the empty seat beside her.

“May I?”

She nodded again.

Jiao Rui sat down.

“I’ve seen you at both evaluation sessions.”

Xiaoran looked slightly surprised.

“Really?”

“You’re quite attentive.”

She laughed awkwardly.

“I’m just watching my boyfriend.”

“That’s precisely why I’d like to ask you a few questions.”

She didn’t think much of it.

After all, he worked for the club. Perhaps he wanted to know more about Yichen’s university background, or whether Yichen had any particular preferences regarding training schedules.

She straightened a little.

“Sure.”

Jiao Rui glanced at his tablet.

“What do you think of Zhou Yichen as a player?”

Xiaoran paused.

Then she smiled.

“Oh.”

She seemed relieved.

“That’s easy.”

Jiao Rui smiled back.

She thought for a moment.

“Very good.”

He waited.

She looked at him.

“What?”

“Could you tell me a little more?”

Xiaoran nodded seriously.

“Of course.”

She turned slightly toward the court, where a few players were still practicing.

“First, I think he’s very observant. He doesn’t always immediately react to what’s happening. Sometimes he watches for a moment before deciding what to do. I think that’s one of his strengths.”

Jiao Rui began typing.

“And?”

“He adapts quickly. I noticed it today. The first time he played with the group, he was still figuring out everyone’s rhythm. But today, he seemed much more comfortable.”

“Interesting.”

“And he’s very disciplined.”

“How so?”

“He doesn’t like wasting time.”

She smiled.

“Actually, sometimes I think he’s a little too disciplined.”

Jiao Rui looked up.

“Too disciplined?”

“Mm. If he has something he wants to improve, he’ll keep doing it until he’s satisfied. Even when he’s already tired.”

She hesitated.

“Although I’m not sure whether that’s a bad thing for a player.”

Jiao Rui shook his head.

“Not necessarily.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“I think it’s good. But he also needs to know when to rest.”

Jiao Rui typed something else.

“Do you think he’s competitive?”

She almost laughed.

“Very.”

“Can you elaborate?”

Xiaoran looked at him with an expression of absolute sincerity.

“Have you seen him play?”

Jiao Rui laughed.

“I have.”

“Then you probably already know.”

He smiled.

“Still, I’d like to hear your perspective.”

She considered it.

“He doesn’t necessarily show it in the way people expect. He doesn’t need to talk about winning all the time. But once he’s playing, he really wants to win.”

She paused.

“Sometimes he gets this expression…”

“What expression?”

She tried to imitate Yichen’s focused face, narrowing her eyes and pressing her lips together.

Jiao Rui laughed.

“Like that?”

“Yes!”

She nodded enthusiastically.

“That’s the expression. When he looks like that, I usually know I shouldn’t disturb him.”

“Does he get frustrated when things don’t go his way?”

“He does, but he doesn’t take it out on other people.”

Her answer came quickly.

“He might be unhappy with himself, but he doesn’t blame his teammates. At least, I’ve never seen him do that.”

Jiao Rui looked at her.

“And what would you say is his biggest weakness?”

Xiaoran fell silent.

This question required more thought.

She looked down at her hands.

“Maybe…”

She frowned.

“He can be a little too hard on himself.”

Jiao Rui waited.

“Sometimes, when he makes a mistake, he doesn’t seem satisfied even after correcting it. He’ll keep thinking about it.”

She looked up.

“I don’t think he’s afraid of failing. I think he just has very high expectations of himself.”

Jiao Rui nodded slowly.

“And outside the court?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Outside?”

“Yes. What is he like?”

She smiled almost immediately.

“Very different.”

“How so?”

“He’s quiet. He’s actually quite patient, although he pretends he’s not.”

Jiao Rui looked amused.

“Pretends?”

“Yes.”

She seemed increasingly comfortable now.

“He’s also very attentive. He remembers things people tell him, even when they don’t think he’s listening. He’s good at noticing small changes.”

“Does that translate into his relationships with teammates?”

“I think so.”

She nodded.

“He doesn’t always say much, but he pays attention. I think he’s the kind of person who notices when someone isn’t doing well.”

Jiao Rui made another note.

“Would you say he’s a leader?”

Xiaoran thought carefully.

“Not because he wants everyone to listen to him.”

She smiled.

“I think he leads more through what he does. He takes responsibility. He doesn’t expect other people to work harder than he does.”

Jiao Rui looked up.

“That’s a strong endorsement.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“I’m his girlfriend. I’m supposed to say nice things.”

“Would you say these things if you weren’t?”

She paused.

Then her expression became a little more serious.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because they’re true.”

There was no hesitation.

She said, “I don’t think you should select him just because I’m saying he’s wonderful. You should watch him play. Watch how he responds when he’s tired, when he’s behind, when someone makes a mistake, or when he doesn’t get the ball.”

She glanced toward the court.

“Those things tell you more about a person.”

Jiao Rui stopped typing.

For the first time, he looked at her with something more than polite interest.

“That’s a good point.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you.”

He studied her for another moment.

“Do you think he wants to become a professional player?”

Her smile softened.

“Yes.”

“Are you certain?”

“Very.”

“How do you know?”

She looked down briefly.

“Because I’ve seen how he works for it.”

Then she looked back at Jiao Rui.

“He doesn’t talk about it all the time. But I know it’s important to him.”

She paused.

“And I think he’d regret not trying.”

Jiao Rui nodded.

“Would you support him if it meant a significant change in his life?”

“Of course.”

“Even if it meant moving to another city one day?”

“Yes.”

“Even if his schedule became more demanding?”

She smiled.

“I’d probably complain about how little time I get with him.”

Jiao Rui laughed.

“But you’d support him?”

“Absolutely.”

She said it so naturally that Jiao Rui didn’t need to ask again.

“His career belongs to him. I want him to have the chance to find out how far he can go,” she said.

She looked at the man.

“I don’t want him to look back one day and wonder what would have happened if he’d tried.”

Jiao Rui’s expression became thoughtful.

Then he closed his tablet.

“Thank you, Miss Lin.”

She nodded.

“Of course.”

He stood.

“And I hope you continue supporting him.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I will.”

He took a few steps away before turning back.

“One more thing.”

“Yes?”

“Has Zhou Yichen ever told you about his expectations for this opportunity?”

She considered it.

“He wants to do well. But I don’t think he’s assuming anything will happen.”

Jiao Rui smiled.

“That’s good.”

Then he walked away.

Xiaoran watched him disappear down the corridor.

She sat back down.

Then she opened her phone.

Xiaoran: Yichen.

Xiaoran: I just spoke to someone from your club.

Xiaoran: I think he was asking about you.

Xiaoran: I said you’re very good.

She considered that, then sent another message.

Xiaoran: And handsome.

Yichen returned about five minutes later.

He found her sitting in the same place, looking rather pleased with herself.

“Who were you talking to?”

“Someone from the recruitment department.”

He stopped.

“Jiao Rui?”

“Yes! You know him?”

Yichen placed his sports bag beside the seat.

“He’s one of the people overseeing the evaluation.”

“Oh.”

He looked at her.

“What did he want?”

“To ask me some questions.”

Yichen’s expression remained neutral.

“What questions?”

She began counting on her fingers.

“What I think of you as a player. Your strengths. Your weaknesses. Whether you’re competitive. What you’re like outside the court. Whether you want to become a professional player.”

Yichen stared at her.

She smiled.

“He asked quite a lot.”

A pause.

Then Yichen asked, “And what did you say?”

She looked offended.

“Obviously, I said good things.”

“Obviously?”

“Do you think I’d tell him you’re annoying?”

He tilted his head.

He laughed.

She reached for her bag.

“Come on. I’m hungry.”

But Yichen hadn’t moved.

He was looking at her with a slightly different expression now.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Did you know he was evaluating you?”

She stopped.

Her brows drew together.

“What?”

“He was interviewing you.”

She blinked, then blinked again.

“Interviewing me?”

“Mm.”

“For what?”

“To see what kind of person you are.”

She stared at him.

Then slowly looked in the direction Jiao Rui had disappeared.

“Wait.”

Yichen watched her.

“Wait, wait, wait.”

She turned back.

“He was interviewing me?”

“That’s what it sounds like.”

“About you?”

“Yes.”

She opened her mouth.

Closed it, then opened it again.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

Yichen smiled.

“You didn’t ask.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed.

She covered her face with both hands.

“Oh my god.”

He reached over and gently pulled one hand away.

“What?”

“I was talking so much.”

“I noticed.”

“I told him you were too disciplined.”

“You weren’t wrong.”

“I said you had a scary face when you’re competitive.”

“Also not wrong.”

“I told him you were patient.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Were you lying?”

“Don’t make this worse.”

He laughed again.

She remembered something.

“And I told him you’re handsome.”

His smile became more pronounced.

“Did you?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She looked at him in disbelief.

“That’s all you have to say?”

“What else should I say?”

“You should be embarrassed!”

“Why?”

“Because I said it to someone from your workplace!”

He leaned closer.

“Would you prefer I tell him you’re beautiful?”

She froze.

He smiled.

“Would that be embarrassing?”

Her cheeks warmed.

“That’s different.”

“How?”

“Because…”

She struggled to find an answer.

Yichen watched her with quiet amusement.

Then he reached over, gently brushed a loose strand of hair away from her face, and kissed her temple.

“Thank you.”

She looked up.

“For what?”

“For saying those things.”

Her expression softened.

“I meant them.”

“I know.”

He took her hand.

“And for what it’s worth, I think you gave him a better answer than I would have.”

She looked surprised.

“Really?”

“Mm.”

“What would you have said?”

He considered it.

“I’m hardworking. I want to improve. I’m competitive. I can adapt.”

She nodded.

“That’s very you.”

“And I would have probably forgotten to mention that I don’t blame my teammates.”

She smiled.

“See? That’s why they should ask me.”

He laughed.

“Apparently.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They were halfway to the restaurant when Yichen’s phone rang.

It was Jiao Rui.

Yichen answered.

“Hello.”

“Zhou Yichen. Sorry to call you after the session.”

“It’s fine.”

“I wanted to let you know that the recruitment team has completed its initial discussion.”

Yichen slowed his pace.

Xiaoran glanced at him.

“We’d like to invite you to the next stage of the process. There are still several assessments ahead, but your performance today was encouraging,” Jiao Rui said.

Yichen listened carefully.

“Thank you. I appreciate the opportunity.”

“We’ll send the schedule and details tomorrow.”

“Understood.”

The call ended.

Xiaoran immediately looked at him.

“Well?”

He turned toward her.

“They want me to proceed to the next stage.”

Her face lit up.

“Yichen!”

He smiled.

She grabbed his arm.

“That’s amazing!”

“It’s good news.”

“It’s very good news!”

He laughed as she bounced slightly on her heels.

Then she stopped.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Does that mean my interview helped?”

He looked at her.

“Maybe.”

Her eyes widened.

“Really?”

“Perhaps they liked your answers.”

She looked extremely pleased with herself.

“I knew it.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You knew what?”

“That I was a good candidate.”

He laughed.

“You weren’t the one being evaluated.”

“Apparently, I was.”

He took her hand and started walking again.

“Then congratulations.”

“Thank you.”

“Should I buy you dinner to celebrate?”

She looked at him.

“Obviously.”

“Anything you want.”

She thought for a moment.

“Crayfish. The spicy kind.”

“Fine.”

“And dessert.”

“Fine.”

“And you have to tell me what the next stage involves.”

“I’ll tell you when I know.”

“And I want to know what they thought of my answers.”

He smiled.

“Very curious.”

“Of course. I’ve invested in this recruitment process.”

“Have you?”

“Emotionally.”

He laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that evening, after dropping Xiaoran home, Yichen received another message from Jiao Rui.

Your girlfriend gave us a interesting perspective today.

Yichen read it, then another message appeared.

She was thoughtful, objective, and clearly understands your motivations. She didn’t exaggerate your strengths, and she was willing to acknowledge areas where you could improve.

Yichen leaned back in his car.

He smiled.

Then he typed.

That sounds like her.

Jiao Rui replied almost immediately.

She also seems supportive of your career.

Yichen looked through the windshield.

For a moment, he thought about Xiaoran sitting in the corridor, speaking earnestly about his work ethic, his competitiveness, and his ambitions.

He imagined her explaining that she wanted him to have the chance to discover how far he could go.

He had known she supported him.

He had never doubted it.

But hearing that she had said it so naturally, without knowing anyone was evaluating her, made something warm settle in his chest.

He typed one final message.

I’m lucky to have her.

Then he put his phone away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran received a message.

Yichen: Good morning.

Xiaoran: Good morning!

Yichen: I have something to tell you.

She immediately sat up in bed.

Xiaoran: WHAT

Yichen: Jiao Rui said you did well yesterday.

She stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: HE SAID THAT?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: WHAT DID HE SAY EXACTLY

Yichen: That you were thoughtful and objective.

Xiaoran: Objective???

Yichen: Apparently.

Xiaoran: I told him you’re annoying.

Yichen: He didn’t mention that part.

Xiaoran: Good.

A few seconds passed.

Xiaoran: Wait.

Xiaoran: Did you tell him I’m beautiful?

Yichen smiled at his phone.

Yichen: No.

She frowned at the screen.

Xiaoran: Why not?

Yichen: I thought that was obvious.

She stared at the message.

Then her phone rang.

She answered.

“What?”

“Hi.”

She tried to sound stern.

“You should have told him.”

“Told him what?”

“That I’m beautiful.”

He laughed.

“Would you like me to call him now?”

“No!”

“Why not?”

“It’s embarrassing!”

He smiled, imagining her expression.

“Yesterday you were happy to tell him I was handsome.”

“That’s different.”

“So everyone’s allowed to hear that I’m handsome, and nobody’s allowed to hear that you’re beautiful?”

“Yes! Because you already know you’re handsome!”

He laughed.

Then his voice softened.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

“Thank you for supporting me.”

She went quiet.

He said, “I know you always do. But hearing you talk about it yesterday meant a lot.”

She smiled, suddenly feeling shy.

“I didn’t say anything special.”

“You did.”

“I just told him what I thought.”

“Exactly.”

There was a pause.

Then she said, “I really do want you to succeed.”

“I know.”

“Even if you get really busy.”

“I know.”

“Even if you have to travel.”

“I know.”

“Even if you become famous and forget your girlfriend.”

He laughed.

“That’s the one I can’t promise.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

“I’m joking.”

“You’re not funny.”

“I’m a little funny.”

“No.”

He let her complain for another moment before speaking again.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“If I ever become a professional player, I think you’ll be the first person I’ll want to tell.”

She went quiet.

Then she smiled.

“Then I’ll make sure my phone is always on.”

He leaned back in his chair.

“Good.”

“And I’ll come to your games.”

“I’d like that.”

“And I’ll cheer loudly.”

“I know.”

“And I’ll bring your water bottle.”

He laughed.

“Very important.”

“And if you lose, I’ll still say you’re handsome.”

He smiled.

“That’s reassuring.”

She grinned.

“See? I’m an excellent candidate.”

He shook his head, amused.

“You are.”

She didn’t know whether he meant it as a girlfriend, a supporter, or the accidental interviewee of the year.

But she liked the sound of it anyway.

And Yichen, who had spent years learning to perform under pressure, compete without losing composure, and take every opportunity seriously, found himself thinking that there was something particularly wonderful about having someone who could see all of that and still remember to call him handsome.

Especially when she had no idea she was being interviewed.

chapters.desc: Her production group is filming the university team, and the captain is excellent at basketball and very bad at being filmed.
chapters.title: Her Team Films His Team
chapters.epigraph: “Winning matters. But I think how you get there matters too.”
chapters.content:
The problem began with a camera.

More specifically, with Xiaoran’s camera, a university media project, and Zhou Yichen making the mistake of agreeing to be helpful.

It was supposed to be a straightforward assignment.

Her production group had been asked to create a short promotional feature for the university’s sports department, highlighting the basketball team’s preparation for its upcoming inter-university tournament. They needed practice footage, player interviews, behind-the-scenes moments, and a short sequence introducing the team’s captain.

Xiaoran had volunteered to coordinate the shoot.

She had also made the mistake of telling her teammates that she knew the captain personally.

“Personally?” Jiayi had repeated when she first mentioned it.

Xiaoran nodded.

“You have been dating him for nearly four years.”

“That’s what personally means.”

“Can you get us access to training?”

“Probably.”

“Can you get us an interview?”

“Of course.”

“Can you get him to look at the camera?”

Xiaoran had paused.

Then she’d said, with complete confidence, “That’s easy.”

She would later regret those words.

The sports center was already busy when Xiaoran arrived with her team.

She had her camera strapped across her shoulder, a small equipment bag in one hand, and a clipboard tucked beneath her arm.

Yichen was on the court, warming up with the rest of the team.

He noticed her almost immediately.

His expression changed slightly when he saw her. Not enough for anyone else to notice, perhaps, but enough for Xiaoran to catch the familiar softening around his eyes.

He finished his conversation with Fang Ze before walking over.

“You’re early.”

“Professional people are early.”

“You’re usually late.”

“Professional people are occasionally late.”

He glanced at the camera.

“You’re filming today?”

“Yes. Your team is the subject.”

“Should I be concerned?”

She smiled.

“Not unless you have something to hide.”

He met her eyes.

Then his mouth curved.

“Nothing you don’t already know.”

Xiaoran blinked.

He had said it so casually that she almost missed the teasing implication.

“Go warm up. You’re interfering with my production,” she said, lifting her clipboard between them.

“All right, producer.”

He leaned down and kissed her cheek before returning to the court.

Behind Xiaoran, Jiayi made a small noise.

She turned.

“Why are you looking at me like that?”

“Nothing, Producer.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

The first twenty minutes went smoothly.

The team was cooperative. Fang Ze was comfortable in front of the camera, answering questions with enough energy that Jiayi immediately decided he should be the opening interview.

Xu Bo, the second-string guard, was even more enthusiastic.

He volunteered to demonstrate a shooting drill, missed his first attempt, and insisted the camera had distracted him.

“It was a warm-up shot,” he explained.

Xiaoran lowered the camera.

“You weren’t even on the team.”

“Exactly. I was warming up emotionally.”

Jiayi laughed.

Yichen, meanwhile, was doing his best to avoid being interviewed.

He had no problem playing basketball in front of a crowd. He could handle a packed gym, an opponent shouting in his face, or a last-second shot with the entire university watching.

But apparently, being asked to stand in front of a camera and talk about himself was a different matter.

The first time Xiaoran pointed the camera at him, he looked directly into the lens.

“Zhou Yichen, captain of the university basketball team. Final year. What does this tournament mean to you? It means we have to win.”

Xiaoran waited.

Jiayi waited.

The camera kept recording.

Yichen looked at them.

“What?”

Xiaoran lowered the camera.

“That’s it?”

“That’s the answer.”

“Can you elaborate?”

He considered it.

“We have trained for it.”

“Yes.”

“We want to win.”

“Yes.”

“And we will try our best.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

Fang Ze, standing behind him, started laughing.

Yichen glanced over his shoulder.

“What’s funny?”

“Nothing, Captain.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

“Okay. Let’s try again.”

Yichen nodded.

She raised the camera.

“What makes your team different from the other teams competing this year?”

He looked into the lens.

“We’re good.”

A beat of silence followed.

Xu Bo, from the bench, nearly choked on his water.

Xiaoran slowly lowered the camera.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You can’t just say you’re good.”

“Why not?”

“Because this is a promotional feature. You have to give people something to work with.”

He looked genuinely thoughtful.

“Then what should I say?”

She looked at him.

It was an unfair question. He was looking at her with such calm sincerity that she couldn’t even tell whether he was teasing her.

“Talk about teamwork.”

He nodded.

“Teamwork is important.”

“Your preparation.”

“We prepare.”

“Your coach.”

“Our coach is good.”

Xu Bo bent forward, laughing.

Fang Ze turned away.

Jiayi covered her mouth.

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

“You’re doing this on purpose.”

Yichen’s expression remained perfectly composed.

“I’m answering your questions.”

“You’re answering them like you’re being interrogated.”

He smiled.

“Is there a difference?”

She pointed at him with the camera.

“Don’t smile. I’m trying to be serious.”

That only made his smile more obvious.

The next attempt was worse.

Xiaoran decided to change tactics.

Instead of conducting a formal interview, she asked him to walk through the training facility while she filmed him. She wanted natural footage: him checking the equipment, speaking to teammates, reviewing plays with the coach.

It sounded simple.

Until she realized that Yichen became unnaturally aware of the camera whenever he noticed it pointing in his direction.

He would stop talking.

Or look away.

Or become interested in something outside the frame.

At one point, Xiaoran was filming him discussing a play with Fang Ze. The moment Yichen noticed the camera, his expression became so neutral that he looked like he was attending a disciplinary meeting.

“Keep talking,” Xiaoran called.

He continued.

Fang Ze said something.

Yichen nodded.

Then he glanced toward the camera again.

Xiaoran lowered it.

“Why did you stop?”

“I didn’t.”

“You did.”

“I was listening.”

“You looked at me.”

“I can listen and look at you.”

Jiayi, standing beside Xiaoran, murmured, “That’s actually quite romantic.”

Xiaoran elbowed her.

Yichen heard it.

His mouth twitched.

Xiaoran immediately lifted the camera again.

“Don’t laugh. Just keep going.”

He looked at the lens.

The smile disappeared.

She sighed.

By the time they took a short break, Xiaoran had accumulated nearly forty minutes of footage and little of it was usable.

She sat on the bench beside the court, reviewing the clips.

Yichen approached with a bottle of water.

“How’s the shoot?”

She met his eyes.

“Terrible.”

He handed her the bottle.

“Why?”

“Because someone is terrible on camera.”

He sat beside her.

“Who?”

She turned the screen toward him.

He watched a clip of himself answering the interview question.

We’re good.

Then another.

We prepare.

Then a third, in which he had looked directly into the camera and said nothing for almost six seconds before asking whether she was finished.

He watched the footage without changing expression.

Xiaoran studied his face.

“Well?”

He handed the camera back.

“Seems fine.”

“Fine?”

“Yes.”

“You look like you’re being held hostage.”

He laughed.

“That’s exaggerated.”

“Look at your face.”

“You’re smiling in real life right now. Why can’t you do that when the camera is on?”

“Because you’re behind it.”

She blinked.

“What does that mean?”

He took a drink of water.

“When you’re talking to me, I’m looking at you. When you point that thing at me, I’m looking at the camera.”

“Yes. That’s the point.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

He looked at her.

“Then I don’t know where to look.”

She stared at him for a second.

Then she laughed.

It was such an unexpected answer.

“You’re a university basketball captain. You’ve played in front of hundreds of people.”

“That’s different.”

“How?”

“They’re watching the game.”

“And we’re filming you playing basketball.”

“That’s also different.”

She squinted at him.

“You’re hopeless.”

He laughed under his breath.

“You’re the one who said it would be easy.”

Xiaoran groaned and let her head drop onto his shoulder.

He rested his cheek against her hair.

“Do you want me to try again?”

She lifted her head.

“Yes.”

“All right.”

“Seriously?”

“Of course.”

He touched her chin lightly, turning her face toward him.

“You’re welcome, Producer.”

The next interview took place near the court.

Xiaoran positioned him in front of the university’s basketball banner. The lighting was good, the background was clean, and the rest of the team had been instructed to stay out of the shot.

She checked the framing.

“Okay. Look at me first.”

Yichen did.

“Not the camera?”

“Not yet. Just me.”

He nodded.

She stood just beside the lens.

“Tell me about your team.”

He turned to her.

It seemed as if he had forgotten the camera was there.

“We’ve been together for a long time. Most of us have played with each other for several seasons. We know each other’s habits, strengths, and weaknesses. We know when someone needs to be pushed and when someone needs a little room,” he began.

“We’ve had a difficult season. Some of us have been injured, some have had to balance training with internships, and we’ve had to adjust our play more than once. But everyone has stayed committed.”

“That’s what I’m proud of. Not just the results, but the way everyone has kept showing up.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Good.”

He nodded, then looked toward the camera.

His expression immediately changed.

Xiaoran nearly laughed.

“Don’t look at it yet!”

He looked back at her.

“Sorry.”

“One more time. This time, imagine you’re talking to someone who doesn’t know anything about basketball.”

“All right.”

“Explain why they should come watch your team.”

Yichen thought.

Then he looked at her.

“Because it’s more interesting when you watch it in person.”

She waited.

He continued.

“You can hear the communication on the court. You can see how quickly things change. And you can tell how much work goes into every possession.”

“That’s good.”

He held her gaze.

“Would you come?”

“To the match?”

“Yes.”

“I’m already coming.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you asking?”

His mouth curved.

“Just checking.”

She looked down at her clipboard, trying not to smile too much.

Behind the camera, Jiayi whispered, “That one is usable.”

Xiaoran pretended not to hear.

The rest of the filming went better once Xiaoran stopped trying to make Yichen perform for the camera.

She filmed him during drills, caught him laughing with Fang Ze, recorded him explaining a defensive rotation to a younger teammate, and got a few good shots of him walking off the court with a towel around his neck.

Those were the moments he looked most natural.

Xiaoran filmed him during a shooting drill.

He made five consecutive shots.

On the sixth, the ball bounced off the rim.

He caught the rebound and looked toward her.

She lowered the camera.

“What?”

He shook his head.

“Nothing.”

“You looked at me.”

“I missed.”

“You’re allowed to miss.”

“Not when you’re filming.”

She laughed.

“Don’t worry. I’ll edit it out.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You’re going to remove my mistakes?”

“Of course.”

“That’s dishonest.”

“That’s filmmaking.”

He laughed and passed the ball to Fang Ze.

A few minutes later, when Xiaoran was checking the footage, she noticed that he had made every shot while she was filming.

Except the sixth.

She kept that one.

The most difficult part of the afternoon was the closing interview.

Xiaoran wanted a short statement from the captain to finish the feature.

She set up the camera one last time.

Yichen stood in front of the lens, still wearing his training shirt. His hair was slightly damp, and there was a faint flush across his cheeks from practice.

She adjusted the focus.

“Okay. Last one.”

He nodded.

“At the end of the tournament, what do you hope people will remember about this team?”

Yichen looked at her.

Then he glanced at the camera, then back at her.

Xiaoran smiled encouragingly.

He took a breath.

“I hope they remember that we played together.”

She waited.

“That we trusted each other, even when things weren’t going well. And that we didn’t stop working when the result wasn’t what we wanted. Winning matters. But I think how you get there matters too.”

Xiaoran held his gaze.

For once, he hadn’t looked away.

“Good,” she said.

He nodded.
