Then, just as she was about to stop recording, he said, “Are you finished?”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Yes!”

He relaxed immediately.

“Good.”

She lowered the camera.

“You’re so bad at this.”

“But you got what you needed.”

She looked at the screen.

He was right.

She had.

The editing session took place two days later.

Xiaoran sat at the desk in her studio, headphones on, surrounded by footage and notes. Yichen was on her sofa, reviewing a case study for one of his third-year business modules.

Every so often, he looked over.

She had been quiet for nearly an hour.

Then she made a small noise.

He glanced up.

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

He waited.

She replayed something.

Then she started laughing.

Yichen closed his book.

“What?”

She patted the space beside her.

He got up and walked behind her chair.

She turned the laptop toward him.

It was a clip from the beginning of the shoot.

On the screen, Yichen stood in front of the camera, shoulders squared, hands loosely clasped in front of him.

He looked straight into the lens.

Then he said, in a completely serious voice:

“We’re good.”

Xiaoran burst into laughter again.

Yichen watched the clip, then looked at her.

“Why are you watching that?”

“Because it’s funny.”

“It’s a normal answer.”

“It’s not.”

He leaned one hand on the back of her chair.

She clicked to another clip.

We prepare.

Then another.

Our coach is good.

Yichen closed his eyes.

“Xiaoran.”

She was laughing too hard to answer.

He looked at the screen again.

“You’re keeping these?”

“Absolutely.”

“For what?”

“Personal archives.”

“Delete them.”

“No.”

He looked down at her.

“Producer.”

“Captain.”

“Delete them.”

She turned in her chair, grinning.

“Are you embarrassed?”

“No.”

“Then why should I delete them?”

He looked at her.

Then his familiar, slow smile appeared.

“Because I know you.”

She blinked.

“What does that mean?”

“It means you’ll show Meilin.”

Xiaoran’s smile widened.

He was right.

She had already sent one clip to Meilin.

Yichen sighed.

“Of course.”

The feature was submitted the following afternoon.

The final video was just over four minutes long. It included the team’s warm-up routine, a few practice sequences, interviews with several players, and a closing statement from Yichen.

Jiayi messaged the group chat to congratulate everyone.

The sports department approved the video and asked whether they could use it for the university’s official social media account.

Then Meilin sent her a message.

Meilin: I saw the video.

Xiaoran: Good, right?

Meilin: Very professional.

Xiaoran: Thank you.

Meilin: Your boyfriend looks handsome.

Xiaoran smiled.

Xiaoran: Obviously.

Meilin: But why does he look like he’s attending a job interview?

Xiaoran laughed.

Xiaoran: Don’t start.

Meilin: The part where he says “We’re good” is my favorite.

Xiaoran: That’s not in the final version.

Meilin: Tragic. It’s his best work.

Xiaoran put her phone down, still smiling.

That evening, Yichen was sitting on the sofa when Xiaoran brought her laptop over.

“Look.”

He moved his book aside.

She opened the project folder and showed him the final video.

He watched it from beginning to end.

This time, he didn’t complain about the camera.

He watched Fang Ze’s interview, the training sequences, the younger players laughing between drills, and the closing statement.

When it ended, he nodded.

“Good work.”

She sat beside him, tucking her legs beneath herself.

Then she closed the laptop.

“You’re actually quite good at being filmed when you’re not trying.”

He studied her.

“Is that a compliment?”

“Yes.”

“Thank you.”

She leaned into his shoulder.

After a moment, she said, “I think I know why you’re so bad at it.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re always aware that someone’s watching you.”

He was quiet.

She said, “When you’re playing, you don’t care. You’re focused on the game. When you’re talking to your teammates, you’re just talking to them. But when you know the camera is there, you start thinking about how you look.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“That’s quite an analysis.”

“I’m a Media student.”

“Of course.”

That made her grin.

“And maybe you’re not used to being the subject.”

He considered that.

Then he said, “Maybe.”

She lifted her head.

“Do you know what I liked most?”

“What?”

“When you forgot I was filming.”

He considered her.

Her mouth tipped up.

“That’s when you looked the most like yourself.”

His expression softened.

He watched her.

Then he reached over and brushed her hair back.

“You’re good at this.”

“At filming?”

“At noticing things.”

She smiled, pleased.

“I know.”

He laughed.

She leaned in and kissed him.

When she pulled away, he caught her hand before she could return to her laptop.

“One condition.”

She looked at him.

“What?”

“Next time you film me, no interviews.”

“Why?”

“Just record the game.”

She considered it.

“That’s not a bad idea.”

“Good.”

“But I might still ask you questions.”

He sighed.

“Xiaoran.”

She grinned.

“Just one.”

He looked at her, already suspicious.

“What question?”

She leaned closer, smiling sweetly.

“Zhou Yichen, why are you so handsome?”

He stared at her, then that slow, teasing smile appeared.

“Is that part of your assignment?”

She felt her cheeks warm.

“No.”

“Then you don’t need a camera.”

He leaned down and kissed her.

chapters.desc: His first professional scrimmage, and his name isn’t called. Somebody’s father made a phone call.
chapters.title: The First Time He Doesn’t Play
chapters.epigraph: “Then keep trying.”
chapters.content:
The first time Zhou Yichen sat on the sidelines of a professional basketball court, he wasn’t injured.

He wasn’t resting.

And he hadn’t been told to conserve his energy.

He simply hadn’t been selected.

It was a strange feeling.

For the past several weeks, he had been working toward this opportunity. He had passed the initial evaluation, impressed the coaching staff enough to be invited back, and earned a place in the extended training group.

He knew he wasn’t the strongest player there. He wasn’t naive enough to believe that one good evaluation would make him indispensable.

He was prepared to compete.

He was prepared to be challenged.

What he hadn’t expected was to be excluded before the competition even began.

The morning started normally.

He arrived early, changed into his training uniform, and joined the other players for warm-ups. He greeted the coaching staff, exchanged a few words with the players he had met during the previous evaluation, and began stretching.

Then the head coach announced the scrimmage lineup.

Names were called.

One by one, players moved toward the court.

Yichen waited.

His name never came.

At first, he assumed there would be another rotation, then the assistant coach approached him.

“Zhou Yichen?”

“Yes.”

“You’ll observe this session from the sidelines.”

Yichen glanced toward the court.

“Am I injured?”

“No. The coaching staff has made the selection for today’s scrimmage.”

He nodded once.

“Understood.”

The assistant coach seemed ready to leave, but Yichen asked one more question.

“Is there anything specific you’d like me to observe?”

The man paused.

“Just watch the session.”

Yichen nodded.

“Okay.”

And that was it.

No explanation.

No criticism.

No feedback.

He picked up his water bottle and moved toward the bench.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran noticed something was wrong almost immediately.

She had arrived a little later than usual because Yichen had told her the session would start with a warm-up and that she didn’t need to rush.

She entered the spectator area carrying two drinks and scanned the court.

She found him.

But he wasn’t playing.

He was sitting on the bench, elbows resting on his knees, watching the scrimmage.

For a moment, she thought he might be waiting for his turn.

She sat down and placed his drink beside him.

“Yichen.”

“Hey.”

She smiled.

“Why are you sitting here?”

“Not selected for the scrimmage.”

Her smile faded slightly.

“Oh.”

He reached for the bottle.

“It’s fine.”

She watched him open it.

“Are you injured?”

“No.”

“Did something happen?”

“No.”

He took a drink.

“They selected a different group.”

She looked toward the court.

Several players were moving through a fast-paced drill. One of them was a young man she vaguely recognized from the previous evaluation.

“Are you going to play later?”

“Not sure.”

She nodded slowly.

Then she looked at him again.

He seemed perfectly calm.

His posture was relaxed. His expression was neutral. He wasn’t visibly upset or embarrassed.

But Xiaoran knew him well enough to recognize when his quietness meant something.

She sat beside him.

“Do you want me to stay?”

“You came all this way. Of course you can stay.”

She smiled faintly.

“That’s not what I asked.”

He looked at her for a second.

Then he reached over and touched her hand.

“Stay if you want to.”

So she stayed.

For the next three hours, Yichen didn’t play a single minute.

He watched the scrimmage from beginning to end.

At first, Xiaoran tried to watch with him.

She followed the ball, paid attention to the players, and occasionally glanced at Yichen to see whether he was taking notes.

He was.

Not on paper, but mentally.

He watched how the guards communicated. He observed the defensive rotations, the pace of transitions, and the way certain players created space.

He wasn’t simply sitting there waiting to be called.

He was studying.

But after a while, Xiaoran began noticing something that bothered her.

A player on the court was making repeated mistakes.

He missed an open pass. He lost possession twice. He failed to rotate during a defensive play, leaving another player to cover his position.

Yet he remained in the scrimmage.

The coaches didn’t remove him.

Instead, they seemed unusually patient with him.

During a break, the player walked toward the coaching staff. One of the men approached him, placed a hand on his shoulder, and spoke to him with a familiarity that didn’t resemble the way the other players were being treated.

Xiaoran leaned slightly toward Yichen.

“Who’s that?”

“Which one?”

“The one wearing number seventeen.”

Yichen glanced over.

“Not sure. I think his family knows someone in management.”

She frowned.

“Does he play well?”

Yichen looked back at the court.

“He has potential.”

It was a careful answer.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“That’s not what I asked.”

He smiled faintly.

“Then no. Not particularly well today.”

She looked back at the player.

“Then why is he still playing?”

Yichen didn’t answer immediately.

He watched the player receive the ball, attempt a difficult shot, and miss.

A teammate retrieved the rebound.

The scrimmage continued.

“Maybe the coaches see something I don’t,” he said.

Xiaoran didn’t look convinced.

✦ ✦ ✦

The explanation came during lunch.

Yichen had stepped away to speak with one of the assistant coaches. Xiaoran was sitting alone near the cafeteria entrance when she overheard two staff members talking.

They weren’t speaking particularly.

“Wasn’t that the director’s nephew?”

“That’s what I heard.”

“His father called this morning. Apparently, they want him included in the development group.”

“And Zhou?”

“Which one?”

“The university player. Yichen.”

“Oh. He’s good, but the decision has already been made for today’s session.”

“That’s unfortunate. His evaluation numbers were better.”

One of them gave a small laugh.

“Numbers aren’t everything.”

The conversation moved on.

Xiaoran sat still.

She looked through the glass toward the training court.

Yichen was standing beside the assistant coach, listening to something being explained.

His expression was attentive.

He nodded.

Asked a question, then thanked the coach.

He looked completely unaware of what she had just heard.

Or perhaps he already knew.

She wasn’t sure which possibility made her feel worse.

She waited until they were alone.

They were walking toward the parking area when she finally spoke.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“I heard something.”

He looked at her.

“What?”

She hesitated.

“About number seventeen.”

His expression changed slightly.

Then he looked ahead again.

“What about him?”

“Apparently, he’s related to someone in management.”

Yichen didn’t respond.

She continued.

“Someone said he was included because his family asked for it.”

He adjusted the strap of his bag.

“That’s possible.”

“Possible?”

He nodded.

“I don’t know the full situation.”

She stopped walking.

He took another step before noticing.

When he turned, she was looking at him with a deeply unhappy expression.

“What’s wrong?”

“You knew?”

He considered the question.

“I suspected.”

“Since when?”

“After the lineup was announced.”

She stared at him.

“Then why didn’t you tell me?”

He walked back toward her.

“Because I didn’t have anything confirmed.”

“But you knew something was wrong.”

“I knew I hadn’t been selected. That’s all.”

“Yichen.”

He looked at her.

She seemed to be struggling with something.

It wasn’t quite anger.

It was more complicated than that.

“Did they even give you a chance?”

He was quiet.

Then he answered honestly.

“Not today.”

Her eyes became glossy.

He noticed immediately.

“Hey.”

She looked away.

“I’m fine.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I’m not the one who sat on a bench for three hours.”

He let out a small breath.

He held out his hand.

She didn’t move.

He reached for her hand and gently pulled her closer.

She looked up at him.

“I hate it.”

“I know.”

“I hate that you worked so hard, and then someone can just decide that another person should get your place.”

He listened.

“I know you’re not supposed to be selected every time. I know you still have to prove yourself. But you should at least be given the chance to play.”

Her voice grew quieter.

“You went there to compete.”

He looked at her.

Then he lifted his hand and brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“I know.”

“Doesn’t it make you angry?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

Then he said, “Yes.”

She looked at him.

It was the first time he had admitted it.

“I am angry. But I’m not going to let that become the only thing I take away from today,” he said.

She lowered her eyes.

He gently tilted her chin back toward him.

“I watched the entire scrimmage. I learned how they rotate, how they defend, and what kind of pace they expect. I also saw what I need to improve.”

“But you should have been playing.”

“Maybe.”

“Yichen…”

He smiled faintly.

“I’m not saying it doesn’t matter.”

He took her hand.

“I’m saying I don’t want to spend the rest of the day thinking about someone else’s connections.”

She looked at him.

He said, “I came here because I want to become a better player. I still want that.”

Her expression softened.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen was unusually quiet.

He finished dinner, showered, and sat at his desk reviewing the footage he had managed to obtain from the session.

Xiaoran was on his bed, lying on her stomach and watching him.

She had been quiet for nearly twenty minutes.

Eventually, she couldn’t take it anymore.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

She held out her hand.

He turned his chair.

“What?”

“Come here first.”

He looked at her, then closed his laptop.

She moved toward the edge of the bed.

He stood and walked over.

“What is it?”

She held out both hands.

He took them.

Then she pulled him down until he was sitting beside her.

“Are you disappointed?”

He looked at her.

She looked back.

He knew she wasn’t asking whether he was angry.

She wanted to know whether he was hurt.

And perhaps he was.

A little more than he had allowed himself to acknowledge.

“I am,” he admitted.

Her fingers tightened around his.

“I thought I would get to play today. I prepared for it.”

She nodded.

“I know.”

“I wanted to see how I performed against them. I wanted to know where I stood.”

He looked down at their hands.

“Instead, I spent the afternoon watching.”

Xiaoran moved closer.

“I’m sorry.”

“Why are you apologizing?”

“Because I don’t know what else to say.”

He smiled slightly.

“You don’t have to say anything.”

She shook her head.

“I want to.”

Then she leaned forward and wrapped her arms around him.

He accepted the hug, one hand settling against her back.

She pressed her cheek against his shoulder.

“You know what I think?”

“What?”

“I think they made a mistake.”

He laughed.

“That’s a little biased.”

“I’m allowed to be biased.”

“Of course.”

She pulled back.

“But I also think you’re going to prove yourself. Not because you need to prove anything to that person. Just because I know how much you love playing.”

He looked at her.

She touched his cheek.

“I like watching you play, Yichen.”

His expression softened.

“Even when I don’t win?”

“Even then.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Meaning?”

“Because you look very serious when you’re trying to fix them.”

He laughed.

She smiled.

Then her expression became gentle again.

“I don’t want you to think that today means you’re not good enough.”

He was quiet.

She said, “You were invited there for a reason. They saw something in you. One person’s decision doesn’t erase that.”

He looked at her.

Then he leaned forward and kissed her hair.

“Thank you.”

She smiled.

“Welcome.”

He kissed her cheek, then the other.

She narrowed her eyes.

“Why are you kissing me?”

“Am I not allowed?”

“You’re distracting me.”

“Good.”

She laughed and leaned into him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The following morning, Yichen arrived at the training facility earlier than usual.

He greeted the staff, changed, and began his warm-up.

He didn’t know whether he would be selected for the next scrimmage.

He didn’t know whether the same situation would happen again.

But he came prepared.

During the individual drills, he performed well.

His footwork was sharper. His passes were more deliberate. His defensive positioning had improved.

He listened to the coaches.

He corrected mistakes.

He worked.

At the end of the session, the assistant coach approached him.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He turned.

“Yes?”

“Good work today.”

“Thank you.”

“The head coach would like to see you tomorrow. There may be another opportunity for you to join the scrimmage.”

Yichen nodded.

“Understood.”

The assistant coach paused.

“Don’t be discouraged by yesterday.”

Yichen looked at him.

The man continued, “There are decisions happening here that aren’t always related to performance. You should know that.”

For the first time, Yichen’s expression became slightly colder.

“I understand.”

“Keep doing what you’re doing.”

“I will.”

The assistant coach left.

Yichen stood there.

Then he picked up his bag.

He didn’t feel triumphant.

He wasn’t reassured.

But he felt something settle inside him.

At least someone had acknowledged it.

Xiaoran was waiting outside when he came out.

She was holding two drinks again.

He smiled when he saw her.

“Again?”

“It’s becoming my job.”

“Should I pay you?”

She considered it.

“Maybe.”

He took the drink.

“How was today?”

“Good.”

“Really?”

“Mm.”

She looked at his face, trying to read it.

Then he told her about the assistant coach’s conversation.

She listened carefully.

When he finished, she nodded.

“Good.”

“That’s all?”

She looked at him.

“What else should I say?”

“Perhaps something about how handsome I was during practice.”

She stared at him, then burst out laughing.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He smiled.

“Was I not?”

She shook her head, still laughing.

“Unbelievable.”

He reached for her hand.

“Let’s go.”

She walked beside him, swinging their joined hands lightly.

After a moment, she looked up.

“Yichen?”

“Hmm?”

“Next time you play, I’ll cheer louder.”

He glanced at her.

“Were you holding back?”

“Very.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

She smiled.

“I’m saving it.”

He squeezed her hand.

“Then I’ll look forward to it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next day, Yichen was selected for the development group’s scrimmage.

Not because someone had decided to be generous.

Not because the club had changed its mind about nepotism.

He was selected because the coaching staff wanted to evaluate him properly.

And this time, he played.

He didn’t dominate every possession. He made mistakes, missed a shot, and had to adjust to the pace of players who were more experienced than he was.

But he competed.

He defended.

He communicated.

He made a difficult pass that created an opening for his teammate, and later scored from a position he had been studying since the previous session.

From the spectator area, Xiaoran finally stood up.

“YES!”

Several people turned.

She immediately sat down.

Yichen heard her anyway.

He glanced toward the seats.

She gave him an enthusiastic thumbs-up.

He smiled briefly before returning his attention to the game.

After the session, he walked toward her.

She was already waiting.

“How was I?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“That’s your question?”

“Yes.”

He pretended to think.

“Not bad.”

She gasped.

“Not bad?”

“Pretty good.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed and pulled her into a hug.

She wrapped her arms around his waist.

“I saw everything.”

“Did you?”

“Yes. Your pass was amazing.”

“Thank you.”

“And your defense.”

“Mm.”

“And that shot.”

He smiled.

“You watched carefully.”

“Of course.”

She looked up at him.

“I’m glad you got to play.”

His expression softened.

“Me too.”

She reached up and gently wiped a small drop of sweat near his temple.

Then she said, “You know, the day you sat on the bench, I was very angry.”

“I noticed.”

“Today I’m happy.”

“I’m glad.”

“But I’m still angry.”

He laughed.

“That’s fair.”

She smiled.

He bent and kissed her hairline.

Then he whispered, “I think I’ll remember that day for a long time.”

She looked at him.

“Because you didn’t play?”

“Because I learned something.”

“What?”

He glanced toward the court.

“That getting an opportunity doesn’t always mean getting a fair chance.”

She listened.

“But it also doesn’t mean I should stop trying.”

He looked back at her.

“And I think I needed to learn that.”

She smiled.

Then she tugged him down and kissed his cheek.

“Then keep trying.”

He held her hand.

“I will.”

And they left the training facility together.

His phone buzzed on the way to the car. The schedule for Friday: the third evaluation, a full scrimmage, groups to be confirmed on the day.

He showed her the screen. She read it twice and looked up at him with her eyes bright.

“Friday,” she said.

“Friday.”

“I’m coming.”

He had known that before she said it.

chapters.desc: The third evaluation, the main group at last, and a folder of letters from people who never told him they’d written.
chapters.title: The Player They Almost Overlooked
chapters.epigraph: “I liked that you didn’t let them make you feel small.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen had never been particularly interested in being underestimated.

He didn’t enjoy proving people wrong for the sake of it. He didn’t need an audience to work hard, and he certainly wasn’t the type to turn every disagreement into a competition.

But he did believe in one thing.

If someone wanted to judge his ability, they should at least give him the chance to play.

He had spent three hours on a bench while another player’s family connections bought a place in the scrimmage. He had played two days later, and played well, but one good afternoon with the development group hadn’t answered the question the bench had left him with: whether the club was genuinely interested in his ability at all.

Fortunately, he wasn’t the only person who had noticed.

The third evaluation was scheduled for Friday morning.

Xiaoran accompanied him, as usual.

She had become familiar with the training facility by now. She knew which entrance led to the spectator area, which vending machine occasionally swallowed coins, and which staff member always greeted Yichen by name.

She also knew that Yichen had been training harder than usual.

He hadn’t complained.

He hadn’t mentioned the previous incident again.

But she had seen him reviewing footage late at night, practicing his footwork after university training, and adjusting his schedule to accommodate the additional sessions.

She had also noticed that he was quieter whenever the club contacted him.

That morning, she found him adjusting the straps of his sports bag.

“Ready?”

“Almost.”

She looked at him.

“Nervous?”

“A little.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Good?”

“Means you care.”

He laughed.

Then he pressed a kiss to her temple.

“Stay hydrated.”

“I’m not the one playing.”

“You forget to drink water when you’re watching.”

She gasped.

“That’s not true.”

He gave her a look.

She took the water bottle from him.

“Fine.”

“Good girl.”

She immediately looked away.

“Don’t say that in public.”

He laughed and took her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

The atmosphere inside the training facility was noticeably different.

There were more people present than during the previous sessions.

Two senior coaches stood near the court, speaking with a man Xiaoran recognized from the first evaluation. A few staff members were carrying tablets and clipboards. Near the entrance, a woman in a dark blazer was reviewing a printed document with the club’s general manager.

Yichen greeted the staff he knew.

One of the assistant coaches approached him.

“Zhou. Good to see you.”

“Good morning.”

“Ready for today?”

“Yes.”

The coach smiled.

“Good. We’ll be running a full scrimmage.”

Yichen nodded.

Then the coach added, “You’ll be playing with the main group.”

For a brief moment, Yichen’s expression changed.

Not dramatically.

Just enough for Xiaoran to notice.

“Understood. Thank you.”

The assistant coach patted his shoulder before walking away.

Xiaoran waited until they were alone.

“Main group?”

“That’s what he said.”

She smiled.

“Finally.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Don’t get too excited.”

“I’m already excited.”

“Try not to shout.”

“No promises.”

He laughed and went to change.

✦ ✦ ✦

The scrimmage began twenty minutes later.

Yichen was assigned to the second unit, playing alongside several experienced players.

It wasn’t an easy position.

He was the newest member of the group, and the others had already developed an understanding of one another. Their movements were instinctive. They knew when to cut, when to pass, and when to switch defensive assignments without needing to communicate.

Yichen had to read them quickly.

The first few minutes were cautious.

He focused on positioning, made simple passes, and avoided forcing opportunities that weren’t there, then the pace increased.

An opposing guard attempted to drive through the middle.

Yichen anticipated the movement and shifted across, forcing him toward the sideline. The player passed the ball away, but Yichen had already moved to cover the next passing lane.

The ball changed possession.

His teammate looked toward him.

Yichen received the pass, assessed the court, and immediately sent it to the opposite wing.

A clean shot.

Three points.

The head coach looked up from his notes.

A few possessions later, Yichen was tested again.

This time, his defender was taller and more physically experienced. He attempted to use his strength to push Yichen away from the basket.

Yichen held his position.

He didn’t try to overpower him.

Instead, he adjusted his angle, anticipated the next movement, and forced a difficult shot.

Miss.

Rebound.

His team recovered the ball.

The scrimmage continued.

From the spectator area, Xiaoran had stopped looking at her phone entirely.

She was leaning forward, both hands wrapped around her drink.

She wasn’t familiar with every technical detail, but she understood enough to recognize the difference between Yichen playing well and Yichen being challenged.

Today, he was being challenged.

And he was responding.

Halfway through the session, something happened.

One of the senior players made a mistake during a defensive rotation. The opposing team immediately exploited the opening, creating a clear scoring opportunity.

Yichen saw it.

He moved across the court, covered the gap, and prevented the shot.

But the recovery left his own position exposed.

The ball moved again.

A teammate shouted for help.

Yichen turned, sprinted back, and managed to contest the shot just before it was released.

The ball bounced off the rim.

His teammate collected it.

The coach blew his whistle.

“Good recovery!”

Yichen nodded and returned to position.

He didn’t celebrate.

He simply continued playing.

At the sideline, one of the evaluators leaned toward the head coach.

“That’s the university player?”

“Yes. Zhou Yichen.”

“He reads the court well.”

“Very well. His defensive awareness has improved considerably since the initial recommendation.”

The evaluator watched another possession.

“He’s not forcing his way into the game.”

“No. That’s one of his better qualities.”

The head coach glanced at his notes.

“He’s adaptable. We received his university performance reports before the first evaluation. His coaches have been quite consistent in their assessment.”

The evaluator looked down at the document.

“Three separate recommendations?”

“Three.”

He nodded.

“Interesting.”

The first half ended.

Yichen walked toward the bench, breathing heavily.

A teammate passed him a towel.

“Good defense.”

“Thanks.”

“You’re from the university team?”

“Yeah.”

“Which university?”

Yichen told him.

The player nodded.

“Your coach is quite well known. I think our assistant coach trained with him years ago.”

Yichen smiled politely.

“Possibly.”

Before the conversation could continue, the assistant coach approached.

“Zhou, take a few minutes. We’ll rotate the lineup.”

Yichen nodded.

He sat down and drank water.

Then his phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: You’re doing so well.

He glanced toward the spectator area.

She was already smiling at him.

Yichen: Watch the game.

Xiaoran: I am watching.

Yichen: Then stop texting.

Xiaoran: You’re very bossy.

He smiled and put his phone away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second half was more demanding.

The coaches changed the matchups, placing Yichen against one of the strongest guards in the group.

It was a deliberate challenge.

The player was fast, physically strong, and experienced enough to recognize defensive patterns.

For the first few possessions, Yichen struggled.

His opponent got past him once and scored.

Then he drew a foul.

Yichen didn’t react.

He adjusted his stance and watched more carefully.

The next time, he forced the player toward the left side.

The possession became uncomfortable.

The opponent tried to create space, but Yichen stayed close enough to contest the shot without committing a foul.

The shot missed.

On the next possession, Yichen intercepted a pass.

He moved forward, but instead of attempting to score himself, he passed to a teammate who had a better angle.

The teammate scored.

The head coach nodded.

A few minutes later, Yichen made his own shot, then another.

He wasn’t suddenly the best player on the court.

He wasn’t dominating the scrimmage.

But he was making himself useful in ways that mattered.

He was learning the rhythm of the team.

He was communicating.

He was defending.

He was making decisions under pressure.

And most importantly, he wasn’t trying to prove that he deserved to be there by doing everything himself.

He was playing basketball.

By the final whistle, the sweat had soaked through his training shirt.

He bent forward with his hands on his knees, catching his breath.

The assistant coach approached.

“Good session.”

“Thank you.”

“Get some water. We’ll speak afterward.”

Yichen nodded.

Across the court, the head coach was already speaking with the evaluators.

One of them was smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran was waiting outside the changing area when Yichen came out.

He had showered and changed into a clean shirt, his sports bag hanging over one shoulder.

She immediately approached him.

“Yichen!”

He smiled.

“Hello.”

“You were amazing.”

She reached for his hand.

“I saw everything.”

“Everything?”

“Almost everything.”

He raised an eyebrow.

She corrected herself.

“Most of everything.”

He laughed.

Then she looked at him more carefully.

“Are you happy?”

He considered it.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“Let’s wait a little. Coach said he wanted to speak with me.”

They sat near the corridor.

Xiaoran leaned against his shoulder, occasionally glancing toward the meeting room.

A few minutes later, the door opened.

The head coach came out with two senior staff members.

“Zhou Yichen?”

Yichen stood.

“Yes.”

“Come with us for a moment.”

He nodded, then the head coach glanced at Xiaoran.

“Your girlfriend can join us if she’d like. We won’t be discussing anything confidential.”

Xiaoran looked surprised.

Yichen turned toward her.

“Come.”

She stood immediately.

The meeting room was smaller than she expected.

There was a long table, several chairs, and a screen displaying footage from the scrimmage.

Lou Wei, the scout from the back of the university gym, was there, along with the head coach and another senior evaluator.

A woman introduced herself as the club’s recruitment director.

“Zhou, please sit.”

Yichen took the seat nearest the screen.

Xiaoran sat beside him.

The recruitment director opened a folder.

“First, I want to say that today’s performance was very encouraging.”

Yichen nodded.

“Thank you.”

“We’ve reviewed your initial evaluation, your second assessment, and today’s scrimmage. There are several areas we’d like you to continue developing, but your overall progress has been quite consistent.”

She turned toward the screen.

“This is one of the plays from the second half.”

The footage showed Yichen defending against the senior guard.

“Your opponent had a physical advantage. You didn’t attempt to match his strength directly. Instead, you changed your positioning and restricted his options.”

She paused the video.

“That was a good decision.”

Yichen watched the screen.

“I thought he would try to drive toward the middle again.”

“And you anticipated it correctly.”

The head coach leaned back.

“Your university coach mentioned that you tend to learn quickly from repeated situations. We saw that today.”

Yichen nodded.

“I’m glad.”

The recruitment director looked through her notes.

“We’ve also received additional information from your university.”

Yichen looked up.

“Additional information?”

“Yes.”

She placed several documents on the table.

“Your head coach submitted a formal recommendation after your first evaluation. We also received an endorsement from the university’s Director of Athletics.”

Yichen glanced at the documents.

The university’s official letterhead was visible.

The recruitment director continued.

“Your department’s faculty advisor also provided confirmation of your academic standing and your ability to manage your university responsibilities alongside competitive training.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

He seemed genuinely surprised.

The director smiled.

“Apparently, you have quite a few people supporting you.”

Yichen looked down at the documents again.

“May I ask who submitted the recommendation?”

“Certainly.”

She opened the folder.

“Your university head coach, naturally. The Director of Athletics, who oversees the university’s competitive sports programs. The university’s Sports Development Office also provided your competition records and training history.”

She paused.

“And Professor Xie, your faculty’s academic advisor, sent a separate letter confirming that you’ve maintained good academic performance while participating in the basketball program.”

Yichen blinked.

Professor Xie?

He knew the professor.

He had never discussed the professional trial with him in detail.

The recruitment director continued.

“Your university’s Deputy Director of Student Affairs also contacted our club through an official university channel. He didn’t ask us to select you. He simply wanted to ensure that your application was considered properly and that your academic and athletic commitments were understood.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Why would he do that?”

The head coach answered.

“Because your university takes its athletes seriously.”

He smiled.

“Your university coach has been recommending you for some time. He believes you have the discipline and potential to progress beyond university-level competition. The Director of Athletics agreed.”

The recruitment director added, “They were particularly clear about one thing. They wanted you evaluated on your own performance.”

Yichen was quiet.

He hadn’t expected this.

He knew his university coach thought highly of him. He knew the basketball department had been supportive.

But he hadn’t realized that several people had taken the time to formally advocate for him.

The head coach leaned forward.

“There’s something else you should know.”

Yichen looked at him.

“The first scrimmage.”

The room became a little quieter.

The recruitment director exchanged a glance with the head coach.

“We’re aware that you weren’t selected.”

Yichen nodded.

“Yes.”

“We also know that the selection process for that particular session was influenced by an external recommendation.”

Xiaoran’s expression changed.

The head coach continued.

“One of the players included in that lineup had a family connection to a senior figure associated with the club. His participation was requested.”

Yichen remained still.

The recruitment director spoke more directly.

“To be clear, that decision was not made by the technical evaluation team. It was an administrative request that affected the initial lineup.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

He didn’t appear surprised.

But his jaw had tightened slightly.

The head coach continued.

“We reviewed the situation internally. The player in question has his own development pathway, and we don’t object to giving young athletes opportunities. But opportunities in a professional environment must still be supported by performance.”

He looked directly at Yichen.

“You were invited because our scouts saw potential in you. You should have been given a proper opportunity to demonstrate it from the beginning.”

Yichen nodded once.

“Thank you for clarifying.”

The recruitment director closed the folder.

“We don’t want you to think that today’s session was arranged to compensate for what happened previously.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Today’s evaluation was conducted because we wanted to assess you properly. The technical staff were satisfied with your performance, and the results were consistent with the recommendations we received.”

“Your university has been very supportive, but the final decision will still depend on our own assessment.”

Yichen nodded.

“I understand.”

“Good.”

The head coach looked at him.

“We’d like to invite you to the next stage.”

For the first time during the meeting, Yichen’s expression visibly changed.

“The next stage?”

“Yes. A longer training period with the development group. You’ll train with us on selected days, and we’ll continue assessing your performance, physical condition, and compatibility with the team.”

The recruitment director added, “It’s not a contract offer yet. But it’s a meaningful step.”

Yichen sat a little straighter.

“Thank you. I’d be very interested.”

The head coach smiled.

“We thought you might be.”

Xiaoran had been quiet throughout the meeting.

She was trying to behave.

She really was.

But when the meeting ended and they stepped into the corridor, she immediately turned toward Yichen.

“Yichen.”

He looked down.

“Hmm?”

“Your university.”

He smiled.

“What about it?”

“They did all that?”

“Apparently.”

She looked almost overwhelmed.

“Your head coach, the athletic director, your professor…”

“And the student affairs office.”

She stared at him.

“That’s so many people.”

He laughed.

“I didn’t know either.”

She looked at him for another moment.

Then her expression changed.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Your professor actually wrote a letter?”

“Looks like it.”

“Professor Xie?”

“Mm.”

“The one who always asks you why you’re leaving class early for training?”

He laughed.

“Yes.”

She covered her mouth.

“He likes you!”

“He’s my professor.”

“He likes you as a student!”

“That’s generally how it works.”

She ignored him.

Then she looked at the meeting room again.

“Yichen, they really believe in you.”

He followed her gaze.

For a moment, he didn’t say anything.

Then he nodded.

“Yes.”

Her smile became softer.

“That’s nice.”

He looked down at her.

“Very.”

She reached for his hand.

He took it.

And they continued walking.

✦ ✦ ✦

The confrontation happened unexpectedly.

They were passing the reception area when a familiar voice called out.

“Zhou Yichen.”

Yichen turned.

It was the man from the club’s administration office who had handled the initial lineup arrangements.

Beside him stood the young player from the first scrimmage.

Number seventeen.

He looked uncomfortable.

The staff member approached.

“I heard you’ve been invited to the next stage.”

“Yes.”

“Congratulations.”

“Thank you.”

There was an awkward pause.

Then the staff member said, “About the first session…”

Yichen waited.

“I understand that the situation may have been frustrating.”

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen.

The staff member continued, “The club sometimes receives requests from people who have supported the organization for a long time. It’s not always easy to manage those expectations.”

Yichen’s expression remained calm.

“I understand that.”

The man seemed relieved.

“Good. I hope there are no hard feelings.”

Yichen looked at him.

Then he answered, politely but clearly.

“I don’t have a problem with someone being given an opportunity.”

The staff member nodded.

“But I do think everyone should understand what that opportunity means.”

The man’s expression changed slightly.

Yichen continued.

“If a player is selected for a scrimmage, I assume it’s because the technical staff want to evaluate his ability. If the selection is made for another reason, that’s fine too. But it shouldn’t be confused with a professional assessment.”

The corridor became quiet.

The young player looked down.

Yichen didn’t raise his voice.

He didn’t sound angry.

If anything, his composure made his words more difficult to dismiss.

“I came here because I was invited to compete. I prepared for the sessions, and I expected to be evaluated on the court. That’s all.”

The staff member cleared his throat.

“Of course.”

Yichen nodded.

“I appreciate the opportunity to continue. I hope the next stages will be decided by the coaching staff.”

The man looked at him.

Then he nodded.

“That’s fair.”

The young player finally spoke.

“Congratulations.”

Yichen turned toward him.

“Thank you.”

There was no hostility in his expression.

He didn’t blame the young man for having connections.

He simply didn’t pretend the situation had been fair.

Then Yichen gave a polite nod and continued walking with Xiaoran.

They didn’t speak until they reached the parking area.

Xiaoran was holding his hand.

Her fingers were wrapped around his, and she seemed to be thinking hard.

Eventually, she looked up.

“You were so cool.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“I’m glad.”

“Very cool.”

He smiled.

“Thank you.”

She walked a little farther before speaking again.

“But I was also a little scared.”

He looked down.

“Why?”

“Because you sounded so serious.”

He laughed.

“Was I frightening?”

“A little.”

“I’m sorry.”

She shook her head.

“No. I liked it.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You liked being frightened?”

“I liked that you didn’t let them make you feel small.”

He stopped walking.

She stopped with him.

He studied her.

Then he gently moved a strand of hair away from her face.

“I wasn’t going to argue with them.”

“I know.”

“I just wanted to make my position clear.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“And you did.”

He looked at her, then kissed her cheek.

“Thank you for coming today.”

“Why are you thanking me?”

“Because you’ve been here for every evaluation.”

She smiled.

“Of course.”

“You’ve watched me play.”

“Mm.”

“And you’ve watched me not play.”

She laughed.

“Unfortunately.”

“Still came back.”

She looked at him as if the answer were obvious.

“Yichen.”

“What?”

“I’m your girlfriend.”

He nodded.

“I know.”

“So?”

He laughed.

“Nothing.”

She stepped closer and wrapped her arms around his waist.

He held her.

Then she whispered, “Look at you.”

His expression softened.

“Thank you.”

“Not because they invited you to the next stage.”

He looked down.

“Why, then?”

“Because you didn’t let one unfair day change the way you approached the next one.”

He was quiet.

She said, “You still worked hard. You still played properly. You didn’t become arrogant just because they finally gave you a chance.”

She looked up at him.

“And you didn’t become bitter just because someone else had an easier way in.”

Yichen smiled faintly.

“That’s a very generous assessment.”

“It’s true.”

He bent down and kissed her.

A gentle kiss, then another, just above her cheek.

She smiled against him.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen received a message from his university coach.

Coach: Heard about today’s evaluation. Well done.

Yichen replied.

Yichen: Thank you, Coach. I appreciate your recommendation.

A few minutes later, his phone rang.

He answered.

“Coach.”

“Zhou. How did it go?”

“They’ve invited me to the next development stage.”

There was a brief silence, then the coach laughed.

“Good. I knew they’d see it.”

Yichen smiled.

“Thank you for helping me.”

“Don’t thank me too much. I only gave them your records and told them what I’ve seen.”

“You also contacted the athletic director.”

“Of course. You’re one of our players. If there’s an opportunity for you to develop, the university should support you.”

Yichen looked down.

The coach continued.

“Listen. I want you to remember something.”

“Yes?”

“Don’t let the professional club become the only place where you measure your value. You have a good future in basketball, but you still have to develop. Keep your academics in order. Keep your training consistent. Don’t let the attention distract you.”

“I understand.”

“Good. And don’t become too proud.”

Yichen laughed.

“I won’t.”

“Your teammates will become unbearable if they hear you’re getting special attention.”

“I’ll keep it quiet.”

The coach chuckled.

“Too late. The sports office already knows.”

Yichen closed his eyes briefly.

“Already?”

“Of course. The Director of Athletics has been asking about you since the first evaluation.”

Yichen laughed.

“Understood.”

“Good. Keep working.”

The call ended.

Yichen sat.

Then he opened his messages and sent Xiaoran a screenshot.

Yichen: Coach called.

Xiaoran: WHAT DID HE SAY

Yichen: Told me not to become arrogant.

Xiaoran: That’s because he knows your girlfriend is already very proud of you.

Yichen: Is that so?

Xiaoran: Extremely.

Yichen: Then I should be careful.

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: I might become arrogant.

She sent him a series of angry stickers.

He laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night, Xiaoran called him.

She was already in bed, her hair tied loosely, and her face looking slightly sleepy.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“I was thinking.”

“About?”

“Your university.”

He smiled.

“What about it?”

“I didn’t know they would support you like that.”

He leaned back against his pillows.

“Neither did I.”

“Do you think they really believe you’ll become a professional player?”

He thought for a moment.

“I think they believe I deserve the chance to find out.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“That’s even better.”

He looked at her through the screen.

“Why?”

“Because they’re not promising you anything. They’re just making sure you aren’t overlooked.”

He was quiet.

She said, “Your coach saw your potential. The athletic director supported the recommendation. Your professor wanted to make sure your studies wouldn’t be a problem. And the sports office helped organize everything.”

She paused.

“That’s a lot of people believing in you.”

Yichen smiled faintly.

“Apparently.”

She rested her chin on her pillow.

“You know what I think?”

“What?”

“I think you should invite all of them to your first professional game.”

He laughed.

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

“That’s quite a large audience.”

“Good. They should see you play.”

He watched her.

Then he said, “You’ll be there too.”

She smiled.

“Obviously.”

“Front row?”

“Of course.”

“Will you shout?”

She nodded seriously.

“Very loudly.”

He smiled.

“Then I’ll have to make sure I play well.”

She laughed.

“No pressure.”

He reached toward his phone, adjusting the angle slightly.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

He opened his arms.

She leaned closer to the screen.

He kissed his fingertips and touched them lightly against the camera.

She giggled.

“That’s not a real kiss.”

“It’s all I can give you right now.”

“Then you owe me one.”

“I owe you several.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, a formal email arrived from the club.

The subject line read:

Invitation to Development Training Program – Zhou Yichen

It outlined the next stage, including training dates, fitness assessments, performance reviews, and a possible longer-term development arrangement.

It wasn’t a contract.

It wasn’t a guarantee.

But it was real progress.

Yichen read the email carefully.

Then he forwarded it to his university coach.

A few minutes later, his coach replied.

Good. Now earn the next one.

Yichen smiled.

He saved the email.

Then he opened Xiaoran’s chat.

Yichen: It came.

Xiaoran: THE EMAIL?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: SEND ME A SCREENSHOT.

He sent it.

She replied almost immediately.

Xiaoran: I’M SO PROUD OF YOU.

Then another message.

Xiaoran: Wait.

Xiaoran: Does this mean I should start learning how to be a professional basketball player’s girlfriend?

Yichen laughed.

Yichen: What does that involve?

Xiaoran: Looking pretty. Supporting you. Bringing water. Not embarrassing you.

Yichen: You’re already doing three out of four.

Xiaoran: WHICH ONE AM I NOT DOING?

He smiled.

Yichen: The last one.

She sent him an angry sticker.

Then:

Xiaoran: Fine. I’ll embarrass you even more when you become famous.

Yichen looked at the message.

He could almost picture her saying it, cheeks puffed out, eyes bright, entirely convinced that she had the right to tease him regardless of how far his career went.

He typed back.

Yichen: I’ll look forward to it.

And he meant it.

Because the club had finally given him a proper chance.

His university had stood behind him.

The evaluators had recognized his performance.

But the part he would remember most wasn’t the meeting, the recommendation letters, or the invitation to the next stage.

It was the girl who had watched him sit on the sidelines, who had stayed when he didn’t get to play, and who had been just as proud of him on the difficult day as she was on the day he finally proved himself.

He hadn’t needed her to defend him.

He hadn’t needed her to fight his battles.

He only needed to look toward the spectator seats and know she was there.

And she always was.

chapters.desc: A new sponsor’s logo on his sleeve, and Zhou Yichen is ready to walk away. Lin Xiaoran goes to dinner with his father instead.
chapters.title: Not Number Seventeen
chapters.epigraph: “I’m going to earn it.”
chapters.content:
The new training kit arrived on the Monday of Zhou Yichen’s second week with the development group, in a stack of plastic bags on the bench outside the Herons’ changing room.

Navy, like the old one. Same heron on the chest.

And on the left sleeve, a new patch. A small square logo in gray and white that he had seen every day of his childhood: on the side of trucks, on the gates of warehouses, on the corner of the letterhead his father used for everything, including birthday cards.

He stood there with the shirt in his hands.

“New sponsor. Logistics company. Big one. Signed on Friday. You’ll see their people at the game on Saturday,” said the kit man cheerfully.

Behind him, somebody laughed.

Yichen turned.

Number seventeen was sitting on the bench, lacing his shoes. The director’s nephew. The boy who’d played a full scrimmage on his first day while Yichen sat and watched. He’d been polite since. Careful. He looked at the patch on the sleeve, and at the name on the shirt in Yichen’s hands, and at Yichen’s face, and he worked it out a second after Yichen did.

“Zhou. Oh,” he said slowly.

Then he smiled. It was almost relieved.

“So you’re one of us now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran knew something had happened the moment he got into the car.

He didn’t say anything. That wasn’t unusual. He drove her back from the training facility most Mondays without saying much, because he was tired and she was talking.

But he didn’t put his hand on her knee at the first red light.

He always put his hand on her knee at the first red light.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“What happened?”

He told her at the second red light, in about forty words, in a voice so flat that she didn’t understand at first how bad it was.

Then she did.

“Your father’s company is sponsoring the Herons.”

“Yes.”

“Did he know you were there?”

“I don’t know.”

“Did you tell him?”

The light changed. He drove.

“I didn’t tell my parents about the trial. Any of it. The scout. The evaluations. The development group,” he said at last.

She stared at him.

“Why?”

Yichen said, “Because my father knows half the people on that club’s board, and I wanted to find out if I was good enough without him knowing any of them. And now everyone in that changing room thinks the same thing about me that I thought about number seventeen.” His hands were still on the wheel.

She opened her mouth.

He said, “I’m going to turn it down.”

“What?”

“The development program. I’ll write to them tomorrow.”

“Yichen—”

“I won’t be that, Xiaoran. I sat on that bench for three hours. I watched him play because somebody’s father rang somebody. I am not going to walk into that gym on Saturday with my father’s name on my arm.” He still hadn’t raised his voice. He never did.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang his father that night. She sat on the end of his bed and listened to one side of it, which was enough.

“…No. I’m not angry. I’m asking you to cancel it.”

A long silence.

“Then don’t cancel it. Move it to another club.”

Another silence.

“Forty jobs. Yes. I heard you. Then I’ll leave the club.” He was standing at the window with his back to her, one hand flat on the glass, the way he stood at the free-throw line when he was counting.

A shorter silence.

“Because it’s mine, Dad. It was the only thing that was.”

He ended the call. He stood at the window for a while. Then he came and sat down beside her on the bed, and she put her arms round him from the side, and he let her, and didn’t say anything else that night at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t, technically, plan to have dinner with Mr. Zhou.

What she planned was to find out which hotel he was staying at for the signing week, which took one message to Mrs. Zhou, who adored her and asked no questions. Then she meant to leave him a polite note.

The note turned into a phone call.

The phone call turned into “Come and eat with me, Xiaoran. I’m on my own and the hotel restaurant is very sad.”

So at seven on Wednesday she was sitting in a hotel dining room with white tablecloths and a view of the river, across from a calm, gray-haired man in a cardigan who had once told his son he always passed too early. He poured her tea himself.

“He doesn’t know you’re here,” said Mr. Zhou. It wasn’t a question.

“No.”

“He’ll be angry.”

“He’s already angry.”

“With me.”

“With himself, and with you, a bit,” said Xiaoran, and then, because she’d decided in the taxi that she wasn’t going to be polite for the whole of dinner.

Mr. Zhou smiled. It was the first time she’d ever seen where Yichen got it from: the smile that happened only at one corner, as if the rest of the face hadn’t been told.

He said, “I didn’t know he was there. I want you to know that, even if he doesn’t believe it. The board’s chairman mentioned it at the signing dinner. Your son’s in our development group, you must be very proud. I said yes. I didn’t know what he was talking about. My son has a whole life I find out about from other men at dinners.” He turned his teacup a quarter turn.

She didn’t know what to say to that.

So she said the thing she’d come to say.

“Uncle. Can I tell you about the first day?”

He looked at her.

She told him. All of it. The lineup announced, and Yichen’s name not in it. The assistant coach saying just watch. Three hours on a bench. Number seventeen missing pass after pass and staying on the court. The two staff members by the cafeteria, his father called this morning. Yichen in the car park afterwards saying I’m not going to let that be the only thing I take from today, and then going home and watching the footage until two in the morning.

“He sat on a bench for three hours, because of somebody’s father,” said Xiaoran.

Her voice wobbled. She ignored it.

“Please don’t make him the next one.”

The restaurant was quiet. Somewhere a waiter put down a tray.

Mr. Zhou looked at her. She made herself look back. She was five years old in a kindergarten playground, planted in front of a boy twice her size. She was nineteen at her grandparents’ table holding Yichen’s hand so hard it hurt. She was twenty in a hotel dining room with her tea going cold. She didn’t look away.

“My wife said you’d do this,” said Mr. Zhou finally.

“Auntie said—?”

“She said, that girl will go and stand in front of you, and you had better listen. I’m not canceling the contract, Xiaoran. There are forty people in that warehouse in Pudong whose jobs depend on it. My son is right about almost everything, and he is wrong about that.” He put his cup down.

Her heart sank.

“But,” said Mr. Zhou.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday afternoon the Herons’ general manager called Yichen into his office and closed the door.

He came out twenty minutes later with a sheet of paper in his hand and drove straight to the media building, where Xiaoran was in a seminar, and waited outside it for fifty minutes, which he hadn’t done since first year.

When she came out he held it up.

It was a copy of a letter, on his father’s letterhead, to the club’s board. Two paragraphs. The second one said that the sponsorship agreement was conditional on one thing: that every selection decision concerning Zhou Yichen would be made by the technical staff alone, recorded in writing with the reasons, and that the sponsor would never be told any of them. If that was ever broken, the money stopped.

At the bottom, in his father’s small square handwriting: He’s yours to judge. Not mine. Please judge him properly.

“He sent it on Wednesday night. At eleven. After a dinner. With you,” said Yichen. He looked at her.

“Ah,” said Xiaoran.

“You went to dinner with my father.”

“It was a very sad hotel restaurant. He was on his own.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I didn’t ask him to do that! I just told him about the bench. That’s all. I told him about the first day, and I told him not to make you the next one, and then I ate a very small fish and went home.” She held up both hands.

He looked at her. He looked at the letter. He looked at her again.

“You stood in front of him,” he said.

“…A bit.”

He didn’t say anything else. He folded the letter in half and put it inside his jacket, against his chest, the way he’d held a photo album in a dormitory bed for eight weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

The development scrimmage on Saturday was open to staff and families, which in practice meant eleven people in a stand built for four hundred.

Xiaoran sat in the third row with two drinks.

Yichen played. He started. He didn’t do anything spectacular. He did a hundred small correct things, and once, late in the second half, he made a pass to number seventeen that was so clean the boy scored without having to think, and looked at him afterwards with an expression Xiaoran couldn’t read from the stand.

In the corridor at half-time she heard number seventeen say to him, “Your dad’s the sponsor?”

“Yes.”

“Mine’s on the board. He sits in the front row. Every time.”

Yichen looked at him. Something passed between them that Xiaoran couldn’t name and wasn’t meant to.

“Then play like he isn’t there,” said Yichen, and went back out.

It was only at the final whistle that she saw him look up past her, to the very back of the stand, and stop.

She turned round.

In the last row, on his own, in a gray cardigan, sat Mr. Zhou. He hadn’t told anyone he was coming. He was holding a paper cup of tea from the vending machine that was famous for swallowing coins.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was waiting outside the changing room afterwards. Xiaoran hung back by the vending machine, badly pretending to choose something.

“Dad.”

“You started.”

“I did.”

“You passed too early, twice.”

Yichen almost laughed. “I know.”

Mr. Zhou took an envelope out of his cardigan pocket. It was thick and soft at the corners, the kind that had been carried around for years.

He said, “Your mother found these when she was turning out my desk. I thought you should have them. I’ve been meaning to say something about them since you were fifteen, and I never found the right dinner.”

Yichen opened it.

Ticket stubs. Dozens of them. Cheap paper, faded ink, school-gym tickets and city-league tickets and the invitational tournament the scouts had come to. Every game Yichen had played from the age of twelve to eighteen. On the back of each, in the same small square hand, a seat number. Always the back row.

“You said you never had time,” said Yichen. His voice had gone strange.

“I didn’t. I left early and went back to the office after. I sat at the back so you wouldn’t play for me. I thought if you knew I was there you’d play to impress me, instead of playing. I was wrong about that. I’d like to stop being wrong about it.” Mr. Zhou looked at the court.

Yichen didn’t say anything.

Mr. Zhou put a hand on his shoulder, briefly, the way men in that family did everything.

“You took her to the Garden. Good. I’d have talked through the whole game,” he said.

Then he nodded across the corridor at Xiaoran, who was now holding a can of something she hadn’t meant to buy, and said, “Thank you for dinner. Next time I’ll choose the restaurant. That fish was an insult,” and walked away towards the car park with his hands in his cardigan pockets.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car park was nearly empty. Yichen put his bag in the boot. Then he turned round, took the can out of her hand and put it on the roof of the car, and backed her up against the passenger door.

“You went to dinner with my father,” he said.

“You said that already.”

“I’m still processing it.”

“You’ll have to process faster. I’m cold.”

He kissed her.

Properly this time, with both hands on her face and three days of not saying anything in it, until she had to hold on to his jacket. When he finally pulled back he rested his forehead on hers, and for the first time since a plastic bag on a bench on Monday, he laughed.

“What?”

“You ate a very small fish.”

“It was a very small fish!”

He laughed again, helplessly, into her hair, and she wrapped her arms round him in the empty car park outside the Herons’ training facility, with the letter folded inside his jacket and an envelope of ticket stubs on the back seat. She thought that she’d stand in front of anyone, any time, if it meant hearing that again.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“Are you still turning it down?”

He lifted his head and looked at her, and at the facility behind her with its lights going off one by one, and at the stand where his father had sat in the back row.

“No, I’m going to earn it,” said Zhou Yichen.

chapters.desc: Her parents visit without telling her. Her mother inspects his fridge. Her father takes him fishing. Nobody invites her.
chapters.title: Her Parents Come to Shanghai
chapters.epigraph: “You can be their favourite child.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had always believed that introducing Zhou Yichen to her parents would be a relatively straightforward process.

Her mother liked him.

Her father liked him.

In fact, sometimes she suspected they liked him more than they liked her.

Still, she hadn’t expected them to become so comfortable with her boyfriend that they would eventually start making independent arrangements with him.

Without telling her.

Especially not when those arrangements involved her mother’s sudden inspection of his apartment and her father’s fishing trip.

And especially not when she was the last person to find out.

It started on a Thursday afternoon.

Xiaoran was sitting in the university library, struggling with a media project, when her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Are you finished with class?

Xiaoran: Not yet. Why?

Yichen: Nothing. Just checking.

Xiaoran: Suspicious.

Yichen: What did I do?

Xiaoran: You said nothing. That’s suspicious.

He sent her a laughing emoji.

She put her phone down and returned to her work.

Meanwhile, across the road from her university, Zhou Yichen was standing inside his apartment, opening the door for two unexpected visitors.

“Uncle. Auntie.”

Lin Xiaoran’s mother stepped inside first.

She was carrying a handbag and a small shopping bag. Her father followed, holding a paper bag of fruit.

“Yichen, we didn’t disturb you, did we?”

“No, not at all. Please come in.”

He took the bags from them.

Xiaoran’s mother looked around.

Then she stopped.

“Oh.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Is something wrong?”

“No, no.”

She walked farther into the living room.

“It’s very clean.”

Yichen smiled politely.

“Thank you.”

Her father put the fruit on the kitchen counter.

“Where’s Xiaoran?”

“She has class. I think she’ll finish around five.”

“Oh, good. Then we can take our time.”

Yichen looked at him.

“Take our time?”

Her father smiled.

“Your auntie wanted to see where you live.”

Yichen turned toward Xiaoran’s mother.

She was already examining the kitchen.

“It’s quite spacious. And the kitchen is clean,” she commented.

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Do you cook?”

“Sometimes.”

“What do you usually eat?”

“Mostly simple meals.”

She opened one of the cabinets.

“Do you have enough bowls?”

Yichen blinked.

“Yes.”

“Plates?”

“Yes.”

“Rice cooker?”

He pointed toward the counter.

“Over there.”

She nodded approvingly.

Then she opened the refrigerator.

Yichen watched her.

He was beginning to understand why Xiaoran occasionally complained that her mother could inspect an entire household in less than ten minutes.

“Yichen.”

“Yes, Auntie?”

“Why is there so little fruit?”

He paused.

“I haven’t gone grocery shopping recently.”

Her mother looked at him, then at the refrigerator, then back at him.

“Do you know Xiaoran likes fruit?”

“I know.”

“Especially strawberries.”

“I know.”

“Then you should keep some.”

He smiled.

“I’ll remember.”

Her father laughed from the living room.

“Don’t worry about him. He’s probably better organized than our daughter.”

Xiaoran’s mother turned.

“That is exactly why I’m checking.”

Yichen lowered his head slightly, hiding a smile.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time Xiaoran finished class, her parents had been at Yichen’s apartment for most of the afternoon, and her mother had taken him to the supermarket downstairs and supervised the fruit aisle personally.

She was completely unaware.

She sent him a message.

Xiaoran: I’m done!

Yichen: Good. Are you hungry?

Xiaoran: A little.

Yichen: Come over later. I’ll make dinner.

Xiaoran: What are you making?

Yichen: Something you’ll eat.

Xiaoran: That’s not an answer.

Yichen: You’ll find out.

She smiled at her phone.

Then she packed her things and crossed the road.

She didn’t bother calling him because she knew the door code.

When she entered the apartment, she was already speaking.

“Yichen! I’m here!”

A familiar voice answered from the living room.

“Xiaoran?”

She froze.

That wasn’t Yichen’s voice.

It was her father’s.

She slowly turned her head.

Her mother was sitting on the sofa.

Her father was beside her, holding a cup of tea.

Yichen was standing near the dining table.

All three looked at her.

Xiaoran stared.

Her father smiled.

“Hello.”

She blinked.

Then she looked at her mother, then at Yichen, then back at her father.

“...What are you doing here?”

Her mother frowned.

“Visiting.”

“Visiting whom?”

Her father pointed toward Yichen.

“Your boyfriend.”

Xiaoran’s mouth opened.

Closed.

Opened again.

“Why didn’t anyone tell me?”

Her mother looked genuinely puzzled.

“Why? We wanted to surprise you.”

“Surprise me?”

She turned toward Yichen.

He was trying hard not to smile.

“You knew?”

He nodded.

“Since this afternoon.”

Her eyes widened.

“You knew since this afternoon?”

“Your parents came over while you were in class.”

“And you didn’t tell me?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“Your mother asked me not to.”

Xiaoran turned toward her mother.

“Mom!”

Her mother picked up her tea.

“What?”

“You told him not to tell me?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“So we could surprise you.”

Xiaoran looked around the room.

Then she pointed at Yichen.

“Why is my boyfriend cooperating with you?”

Her father laughed.

“Because he’s a sensible young man.”

Xiaoran looked betrayed.

“Dad!”

Yichen finally laughed.

He walked over and gently took her bag.

“Have you eaten?”

“Don’t change the subject.”

“I’m asking because you said you were hungry.”

“I’m angry.”

“Can you be angry while eating?”

Her father burst out laughing.

Her mother shook her head.

“See? He knows how to handle you.”

Xiaoran was beginning to regret introducing them.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was, unfortunately, pleasant.

Yichen prepared a few dishes while Xiaoran’s mother helped him in the kitchen despite his insistence that she could sit down.

Her father sat at the dining table, asking Yichen about basketball.

“How’s the professional club?”

“I’m currently training with their development group.”

“That’s good. Are they treating you well?”

“It’s going well so far.”

“Don’t overwork yourself.”

“I’ll be careful.”

Her father nodded.

Then he asked, “Do you still play university basketball?”

“Yes. When the schedule allows.”

“Good. Don’t abandon your university studies.”

“I won’t.”

Xiaoran sat beside him, quietly eating.

She occasionally glanced at Yichen.

He was answering her father’s questions patiently, occasionally smiling, occasionally explaining something about the training schedule.

Her father seemed pleased.

Her mother placed another serving of vegetables on Yichen’s plate.

“Eat more.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Don’t be so polite. You’re practically family.”

Xiaoran nearly choked on her rice.

Her father laughed.

Her mother continued eating as if she hadn’t said anything unusual.

Yichen, meanwhile, simply smiled.

“Thank you.”

Xiaoran leaned closer to him.

“Practically family?”

“Is there a problem?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Don’t look so happy.”

His lips curved.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He leaned closer, lowering his voice.

“Would you prefer I looked unhappy?”

She immediately turned back to her food.

Yichen smiled and placed a piece of fish into her bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran woke up to find a message from her father.

Dad: Yichen and I are going out today.

She stared at the screen, then sat up.

Xiaoran: Where?

Dad: Fishing.

She blinked.

Xiaoran: Fishing?

Dad: Yes.

Xiaoran: With Yichen?

Dad: Correct.

Xiaoran: What about me?

Her father replied several seconds later.

Dad: You have class, don’t you?

She stared at the message, then another arrived.

Dad: Don’t worry. We’ll bring you something.

Xiaoran put down her phone.

She stared at the ceiling.

Her parents had arrived in Shanghai.

Her mother had inspected her boyfriend’s apartment.

Her father had apparently arranged a fishing trip with him.

And nobody had invited her.

She immediately called Yichen.

He answered after two rings.

“Good morning.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

His voice sounded amused.

“And good morning.”

“Are you going fishing?”

“Yes.”

“With my father?”

“Yes.”

“Without me?”

He laughed.

“You have class.”

“I can skip class.”

“No.”

She frowned.

“Why not?”

“Because you have a presentation.”

She went quiet.

Then she remembered.

“Oh.”

He chuckled.

“Did you forget?”

“No.”

A pause.

“Maybe.”

He laughed again.

She heard movement in the background.

“Are you already with him?”

“I’m picking him up in a few minutes.”

She sighed dramatically.

“Have fun with my father.”

“I will.”

“Don’t have too much fun.”

“Why?”

“Because he’s my father.”

Yichen laughed.

“I’m aware.”

“Don’t become closer to him than I am.”

There was a brief silence.

Then he said, calmly, “I think it’s too late.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed.

“Go prepare for your presentation.”

She grumbled something unintelligible.

Before hanging up, he said, “I’ll send you pictures.”

She brightened slightly.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

“Okay. Then you can go.”

“Thank you for granting permission.”

She smiled despite herself.

“Bye.”

“Bye, Xiaoran.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fishing trip turned out to be more successful than either man expected.

Yichen had driven her father to a quiet fishing spot outside the city. It was a place her father had visited several times during his business trips to Shanghai.

He had brought his own rods, in the boot of the car he’d driven up from home.

Yichen had brought a small camera.

“You take pictures?” her father asked.

“Sometimes.”

“Of what?”

“Mostly scenery. Basketball games. Xiaoran.”

Her father looked at him, then smiled.

“Ah.”

Yichen realized what he had said.

He smiled faintly.

“She’s usually the most interesting subject.”

Her father laughed.

“Good answer.”

They settled beside the water.

For a while, they talked about fishing.

Her father explained the equipment, the bait, and how to recognize when a fish was biting.

Yichen listened attentively.

He wasn’t particularly experienced, but he was patient.

Her father seemed to enjoy teaching him.

Eventually, Yichen managed to catch a fish.

It wasn’t particularly large.

But her father looked pleased.

“Not bad!”

Yichen lifted the fishing rod slightly.

“Is this the correct size?”

Her father laughed.

“It’s your first one. You should be proud.”

Yichen took a picture of the fish.

Then he took another of the water, the fishing rods, and her father sitting beside him.

“Take one of me,” her father said.

Yichen turned the camera toward him.

Her father posed with the fish.

Yichen took several pictures.

Then he looked at the screen.

“Uncle, this one is good.”

“Let me see.”

He showed him.

Her father nodded.

“Send it to me.”

“Of course.”

After a moment, Yichen looked at him.

“Would you like a picture together?”

Her father smiled.

“Sure.”

Yichen placed the camera on a small stand, set the timer, and sat beside him.

The first picture was slightly awkward.

The second was better.

In the third, her father was laughing while Yichen looked toward him.

It was probably the best one.

Her father examined it.

“Good. Send me that one too.”

Yichen nodded.

Then he sent the pictures to Xiaoran.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran was in the university cafeteria when the pictures arrived.

She opened the first one.

A fish.

The second one.

Her father holding the fish.

The third.

Her father and Yichen sitting beside each other, smiling.

She stared, then another picture arrived.

Yichen standing behind her father, holding the fishing rod while her father demonstrated something.

She stared even harder.

Then she called him.

He answered almost immediately.

“Hello?”

“Why do you look so happy?”

He laughed.

“Good afternoon.”

“I’m serious.”

“We’re having a good time.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Where am I in these pictures?”

“Not there.”

“Exactly!”

He laughed.

She heard her father in the background.

“Is that Xiaoran?”

Yichen turned slightly.

“Yes.”

“Tell her we’re having fun!”

Xiaoran heard him.

Her mouth fell open.

“DAD!”

Her father laughed loudly.

Yichen was laughing too.

She looked betrayed.

“Why are you both laughing?”

Her father came closer to the phone.

“Xiaoran, we’re fishing.”

“I know!”

“Your boyfriend caught a fish.”

“I saw!”

“Not bad for his first time.”

She sighed.

“Dad, why did you take him fishing without me?”

Her father answered naturally.

“Because you don’t know how to fish.”

Xiaoran froze.

“Excuse me?”

Her father continued.

“And you have class.”

“I can learn!”

“Next time.”

“Next time?”

“Of course.”

She looked at Yichen.

He was smiling.

“Don’t encourage him,” she warned.

Yichen nodded solemnly.

“I won’t.”

Her father spoke again.

“Yichen is very patient. He listens carefully. You should learn from him.”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened.

“Dad! I’m your daughter!”

Her father laughed.

“That’s why I’m telling you.”

She ended the call.

Not because she was genuinely angry.

But because she couldn’t stand hearing the two men laugh together anymore.

✦ ✦ ✦

About twenty minutes later, her mother called.

Xiaoran answered immediately.

“Mom!”

“Yes?”

“Why didn’t you tell me you were going to Yichen’s apartment?”

Her mother sounded completely unbothered.

“I told you last week we might come up.”

“You said might!”

“And then we came.”

“You didn’t tell me you were inspecting his apartment!”

“Inspecting?”

“Yes! You opened his cabinets!”

Her mother laughed.

“Of course. I wanted to see how he lived.”

“Mom!”

“What?”

“That’s my boyfriend’s house!”

“Exactly. I wanted to make sure he was taking care of himself.”

Xiaoran rubbed her forehead.

“Why?”

“Because he takes care of you.”

She stopped.

Her mother continued, “You spend so much time at his apartment. I wanted to see whether he had everything he needed.”

Xiaoran went quiet.

Then her mother added, “I made him buy strawberries. Don’t eat them all in one day.”

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

“Mom, please.”

“And vegetables. His refrigerator was almost empty before I got there.”

“He has vegetables!”

“He does now.”

“Mom.”

“And you should eat properly when you’re there.”

Xiaoran looked up at the ceiling.

“Why are you both treating him like your son?”

Her mother laughed.

“Would that be a problem?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth, then closed it.

She couldn’t find a suitable answer.

Her mother continued, “He’s a good boy. We like him.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened despite herself.

Then her mother added, “Much more organized than you.”

The softness disappeared.

“Mom!”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen returned to his apartment.

He had a small bag of fish her father had insisted on bringing back.

He placed it in the kitchen and called Xiaoran.

“Are you home?”

“Almost.”

“Come over.”

“Why?”

“I have something for you.”

She arrived fifteen minutes later.

The moment he opened the door, she walked inside with a suspicious expression.

“What?”

He held up the bag.

“Your father caught more fish than I did. He asked me to bring some back.”

She looked inside, then looked at him.

“Are you trying to bribe me?”

“Is it working?”

“No.”

He placed the bag in the kitchen.

Then he turned back toward her.

“How was your presentation?”

She blinked.

“You remembered?”

“Of course.”

“It went well.”

“Good.”

He bent and kissed her hairline.

She looked up at him.

Then she glanced toward the living room.

“Did you really have fun with my father?”

“Yes.”

“More fun than with me?”

He smiled.

“Different kind of fun.”

She crossed her arms.

“Explain.”

“He taught me how to fish.”

“I can teach you.”

“You don’t know how.”

“I can learn.”

He laughed.

She stepped closer.

“And did you talk about me?”

“A little.”

Her eyes widened.

“What did you say?”

“Nothing much.”

“Yichen.”

He looked at her, amused.

“I said you’re usually the most interesting subject to photograph.”

She blinked.

Then her cheeks turned pink.

“You said that?”

“Mm.”

“To my father?”

“Yes.”

She looked away.

“That’s embarrassing.”

He smiled and reached for her hand.

“Why?”

“Because.”

He gently pulled her closer.

“Your father seemed pleased.”

“Really?”
