“He was. He also told me to take care of you.”

Her expression softened.

“What did you say?”

Yichen brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“I told him I would.”

She studied him.

Then leaned forward and wrapped her arms around his waist.

He held her naturally, one hand resting against her back.

After a while, she mumbled into his shirt.

“I still think you betrayed me.”

He laughed.

“By going fishing?”

“By becoming friends with my father without me.”

“Would you like me to stop?”

She pulled back immediately.

“No!”

He smiled.

“Then what’s the problem?”

She thought about it, then sighed.

“Nothing.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair.

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The following morning, Xiaoran discovered something even worse.

Her father had posted a picture on his social media.

It was the picture Yichen had taken of them together by the water.

The caption read:

Good company, good weather, and a successful fishing day.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Then she noticed a comment from her mother.

Yichen is considerate. Next time, bring him to dinner again.

And another comment from her aunt.

Is that Yichen? Even more handsome than at New Year.

Her father replied:

Yes. Very good young man.

Xiaoran slowly put down her phone.

Then she opened Yichen’s chat.

Xiaoran: Your reputation in my family is getting out of control.

Yichen: What happened?

She sent him the screenshot.

Yichen: Your father posted the picture.

Xiaoran: YOU KNEW?

Yichen: He asked me to send it to him.

Xiaoran: AND YOU DIDN’T TELL ME?

Yichen: I thought you’d see it.

Xiaoran: I AM SEEING IT NOW.

A few seconds passed.

Then he sent another message.

Yichen: Your father said we should go fishing again next month.

She stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: WE?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: What about me?

Yichen: He said you can come next time.

She narrowed her eyes.

Xiaoran: He said I CAN COME?

Yichen: His exact words.

She buried her face in her pillow.

Her phone vibrated again.

Yichen: I’ll teach you how to fish.

She lifted her head.

Xiaoran: You barely know how.

Yichen: Then we’ll learn together.

She smiled, then another message arrived.

Yichen: Your mother also asked whether you have enough clothes for the changing weather.

Xiaoran froze.

Xiaoran: Why is my mother messaging you?

Yichen: She asked me to remind you to bring a jacket.

She stared at the screen.

Then typed:

Xiaoran: Zhou Yichen.

Yichen: Yes?

Xiaoran: I think you’re my parents’ favorite child now.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: I don’t think so.

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: Your father said I’m his favorite fishing partner.

She screamed into her pillow.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, when Yichen picked her up from the library, she was still pretending to be upset.

He opened the passenger door for her.

She got in without looking at him.

He closed the door, walked around, and settled into the driver’s seat.

“Still angry?”

“Very.”

He started the car.

“Should I apologize?”

“For what?”

“I’m not sure yet.”

She tried not to smile.

He noticed.

Of course he noticed.

At the next red light, he turned toward her.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Your father asked me to take care of you.”

She looked at him.

“And?”

“And your mother asked me to make sure you eat properly.”

She nodded.

“That’s true.”

“So I have quite a few responsibilities.”

She looked suspicious.

“What responsibilities?”

He reached over and gently squeezed her hand.

“Taking you to class when you oversleep. Making sure you eat lunch. Keeping fruit in the refrigerator. Reminding you to bring a jacket.”

She stared at him.

“That’s a lot.”

“Apparently.”

She smiled.

Then she leaned over and kissed his cheek.

“Fine.”

He glanced at her.

“Fine?”

“You can be their favorite child.”

He laughed.

“Thank you.”

“But I’m still their actual daughter.”

“Of course.”

“And I’m your girlfriend.”

He raised her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“That’s the most important part.”

She smiled, satisfied.

Then, after a moment, she said:

“Next time you go fishing, I’m coming.”

He nodded.

“Of course.”

“And you’re teaching me.”

“I will.”

“And if I catch a bigger fish than you, you have to take my picture.”

He smiled.

“Several pictures.”

“Good.”

The traffic light turned green.

Yichen drove forward, still holding her hand.

And Xiaoran, who had spent the past two days feeling as though her parents had adopted her boyfriend, finally decided that perhaps it wasn’t such a terrible thing.

As long as she was invited next time.

And as long as nobody opened her boyfriend’s refrigerator without telling her first.

chapters.desc: Her father comes to watch Yichen play and sends her a photograph from his seat. It is in the wrong stand.
chapters.title: Her Father in the Wrong Stand
chapters.epigraph: “Even if I have to travel?”
chapters.content:
The first sign that something had gone wrong was the message Xiaoran received twenty minutes before tip-off.

Dad (Water Bureau): I’m here.

She smiled and typed back.

Xiaoran: Where are you?

Dad (Water Bureau): The stands.

Xiaoran: Which section?

There was a pause, then a photograph arrived.

It showed her father sitting comfortably among a group of people wearing the opposing university’s colors.

Xiaoran stared at it.

She enlarged the photograph.

Then she looked at the ticket she’d sent him earlier.

Then she looked at the photograph again.

“Oh, no.”

Yichen was beside her, tightening the laces of his basketball shoes. He glanced up.

“What happened?”

“My dad.”

“What about him?”

“He’s in the wrong stand.”

Yichen looked at the photograph.

A faint smile appeared.

“He’s made friends.”

“Yichen!”

“What?”

“Those are the home fans. He’s on their side of the gym.”

“I can see that.”

“He’s sitting with them!”

Yichen looked at the photograph again. Xiaoran’s father was seated between two older men, one of whom appeared to be explaining something to him while pointing toward the court.

He looked perfectly comfortable.

Yichen’s smile grew.

“Your father seems to be enjoying himself.”

Xiaoran immediately called him.

Her father answered on the third ring.

“Hello?”

“Dad! Where are you?”

“In the stands.”

“Which stands?”

“Why are you asking me that? I’m watching your boyfriend’s game.”

“You’re in the home section!”

There was a pause.

Her father looked around.

Then he looked at the people sitting beside him.

“Oh.”

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

“Oh?”

“They were very helpful. They showed me where to sit.”

“Dad, you’re in the wrong stand!”

“I followed the signs.”

“Those are their fans!”

Another pause.

“Well, the seats are quite good.”

Yichen was now openly smiling.

Xiaoran covered the phone’s microphone.

“He’s not moving.”

Yichen leaned closer.

“Tell him to enjoy the game.”

She glared at him, then returned to the call.

“Just stay there. Don’t argue with anyone, okay?”

Her father sounded mildly offended.

“Why would I argue?”

She glanced at the opposing university supporters waving their flags.

“Because you’re wearing our university’s jacket.”

“I’ve noticed.”

“Dad.”

“Xiaoran, I’m here to watch basketball. Not start a fight.”

She sighed.

“Fine. I’ll see you after the game.”

“All right. Tell Yichen I said good luck.”

She hung up.

Yichen was still smiling.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your shoulders are saying plenty.”

He stood and picked up his warm-up jacket.

“Should I be worried?”

“About what?”

“Your father changing sides.”

She blinked at him.

Then he laughed, kissed her hair, and headed toward the court.

The game was close.

It was one of the final university fixtures of the season, and the atmosphere was louder than usual. The opposing team had a strong home crowd, and the away section was packed with students who had traveled to support their university.

Xiaoran spent most of the first half trying to locate her father.

She eventually found him.

He was still sitting in the same place.

And, inexplicably, he was talking to the man beside him.

She sent him a message.

Xiaoran: Are you cheering for our team?

Dad (Water Bureau): Of course.

A moment later, another message arrived.

Dad (Water Bureau): The man beside me says your boyfriend is very good.

Xiaoran smiled.

Xiaoran: He is.

Dad (Water Bureau): I know.

She looked toward the court.

Yichen was moving into position, listening to his coach. He looked focused, composed, and entirely unaware that his girlfriend’s father was currently representing their university from enemy territory.

When he scored, Xiaoran stood with the rest of the away supporters.

Her father stood too.

She saw him clap.

Then, a moment later, she saw him exchange a few words with the man beside him.

She wondered what they were discussing.

Probably Yichen.

Her father had always been interested in his basketball, but he rarely asked questions that were about the game. He tended to ask about the things behind it: training schedules, recovery, injuries, university commitments, and what came after.

Xiaoran knew he was proud of Yichen.

She also knew her father wasn’t the sort of person who showed that pride by saying it directly.

He showed it by remembering details.

By asking whether Yichen had eaten. By noticing when he was limping.

By watching the entire match even when he had accidentally bought a ticket for the wrong section.

The final quarter began.

Yichen’s team was leading by three points.

With less than two minutes remaining, the opposing team called a timeout.

Xiaoran stood near the railing, her fingers clasped together.

Her father sent another message.

Dad (Water Bureau): He’s playing well.

She smiled.

Xiaoran: I know.

Dad (Water Bureau): His ankle looks fine today.

Her smile faded slightly.

She looked toward the court.

Yichen was standing near his teammates, one hand on his hip. He had taken a hard landing earlier, but he was moving normally now.

She typed back.

Xiaoran: It’s fine. He’s been careful.

Her father didn’t reply.

The game resumed.

Yichen made a crucial defensive play, then assisted the final basket that put his team ahead by five.

The whistle sounded.

The away section erupted.

Xiaoran cheered, laughing as Jiayi, who had come with her, grabbed her shoulders.

They had won.

And from the opposite side of the court, Yichen looked up toward the stands.

He found Xiaoran almost immediately.

She waved.

Something in his face eased.

Then, beside her, he noticed her father.

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted slightly.

Her father raised one hand in greeting.

Yichen nodded respectfully.

Even from that distance, Xiaoran could see the amusement in his expression.

After the game, Xiaoran found her father near the exit.

He was still wearing the university jacket and carrying a paper cup of tea.

“Did you enjoy yourself?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Did you make friends?”

Her father looked toward the two men who had been sitting beside him.

“They were nice.”

She shook her head.

“You really stayed there the whole time.”

“Why would I move? I could see the court perfectly.”

Yichen approached before she could respond.

He was carrying his sports bag, his hair damp from the game, and there was a faint flush across his cheeks.

“Uncle.”

Her father turned.

“Yichen. Good game.”

“Thank you for coming.”

“Of course.”

Yichen glanced toward the stands.

“How was the view?”

“Very good. Although I think I was the only person cheering for your university.”

Yichen smiled.

“I noticed.”

Xiaoran looked between them.

“Can we please stop discussing the wrong stand?”

Her father laughed.

Yichen’s smile remained.

“Uncle, did you come alone?”

“Yes. Your auntie stayed at the hotel. Migraine. She’ll meet us for dinner, she says, if we win.”

“Thank you for coming all this way.”

Her father nodded.

Then his expression changed slightly.

“How’s the ankle?”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

Yichen answered without hesitation.

“Fine. No pain.”

“Any swelling after the last game?”

“No.”

“Have you been seeing the physiotherapist?”

“Yes, as scheduled.”

Her father nodded.

The conversation sounded ordinary.

But Xiaoran knew that particular tone.

Her father wasn’t asking out of casual curiosity.

He was checking.

And Yichen understood that too.

They ended up sitting in a quieter area near the sports center café.

Xiaoran went to get drinks, leaving her father and Yichen at a small table.

When she returned, she noticed that the conversation had become more serious.

Her father was leaning back slightly, his hands around his tea.

Yichen sat opposite him, listening.

She slowed down.

“...and if the club offers you a contract after graduation what happens if your ankle goes?” her father was saying.

Xiaoran stopped.

She knew Yichen had been speaking with representatives about possible professional opportunities after university. Nothing had been finalised, and there were still decisions to be made after graduation. But it was becoming real enough that people had started asking questions.

Her father continued.

“I’m not asking because I think something will happen. I’m asking because injuries are part of the sport.”

Yichen nodded.

“I understand.”

“Have you looked at the terms?”

“Some of them. I haven’t received the final contract yet.”

“And if you get injured before the contract is secured?”

“That depends on the club’s offer and the medical assessment.”

Her father listened.

Yichen continued, speaking calmly.

“I know what I’m risking. I’m also aware that playing professionally isn’t something I can guarantee forever. Even without an injury, there are no guarantees.”

Her father nodded slowly.

“What happens if you can’t play?”

Yichen didn’t answer immediately.

He looked down at his hands.

Then he said, “I’ll have to find something else to do.”

“Such as?”

“Coaching, sports management, maybe something related to the business side of the sport. I’ve studied business for a reason.”

Her father smiled.

“Good answer.”

Yichen smiled too.

“But I don’t want to pretend that I have everything figured out. I want to play. I’ve worked toward it for years, and I’d like to see how far I can go.”

“That’s understandable.”

“I’ll make sure I understand the contract before signing anything. The medical provisions, insurance, injury clauses, guaranteed payments, rehabilitation support. All of it.”

Her father nodded.

Then he asked, “And if the contract isn’t as good as you hoped?”

“I won’t sign it just because I’m afraid another opportunity won’t come.”

Her father studied him.

Yichen met his gaze.

“I know I have to think beyond the excitement of being offered a professional position.”

Neither spoke.

Then her father took a sip of tea.

“That’s what I wanted to hear.”

Xiaoran stood a few steps away, holding three drinks.

She hadn’t intended to listen.

But she hadn’t expected to hear her father ask a question that serious, either.

Yichen noticed her first.

His eyes moved toward her.

She walked over and placed the drinks on the table.

“What are you two discussing?”

Her father looked at her.

“Basketball.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That sounds suspicious.”

Yichen reached for his drink.

“Your father was asking about my future.”

She looked at him, then at her father.

“Oh.”

Her father smiled.

“Someone has to ask.”

Xiaoran sat beside Yichen.

“Why does everyone keep asking about graduation?”

Her father looked amused.

“Because you’re graduating.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

“It’s a very good answer.”

Yichen laughed.

He rested his hand on her ankle beneath the table.

She looked down at it, then back at him.

His thumb moved once, reassuringly.

She didn’t ask anything else.

But later, when her father had gone to speak to another family he knew, she turned toward Yichen.

“Are you okay?”

He nodded.

“Yes.”

“That was a lot of questions.”

“Your father is thorough.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“He’s worried.”

“I know.”

“About your ankle.”

“I know.”

She looked down at his leg.

Yichen followed her gaze.

Then he gently caught her chin, turning her face back toward him.

“It’s fine.”

She nodded.

“I know.”

He kissed her temple.

“And I’m being careful.”

“I’ve noticed.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

She tucked herself against his shoulder.

“Because I love you.”

His expression softened.

He kissed her hair.

“I love you too.”

On the way home, Xiaoran sat in the back seat beside her father while Yichen drove.

Her father had insisted they all have dinner together.

Xiaoran was quiet for a while, watching the streetlights pass.

Then she leaned forward slightly.

“Dad?”

“Hm?”

“Why did you ask him about the contract?”

Her father glanced at her through the rear-view mirror.

“Because he’s at that stage of his life.”

“But he’s still in university.”

“Exactly.”

She frowned.

Her father continued, “It’s easy to think about the exciting parts. The offer, the team, the salary, the games. But a career is also about what happens when things don’t go as planned.”

Xiaoran looked toward Yichen.

He was listening, though he kept his eyes on the road.

Her father went on.

“He’s worked hard. I don’t want him to make a decision without understanding what he’s agreeing to.”

She nodded.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “Do you think he’ll be okay?”

Her father smiled.

“Your boyfriend?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

Her father looked toward the road.

“I think he’ll be all right.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Because he’s smart?”

“Because he knows that being good at something doesn’t mean he’s invincible.”

She looked at Yichen.

He glanced at her in the mirror.

Their eyes met.

He smiled.

She smiled back.

Her father noticed.

But he didn’t say anything.

At dinner, her father told her mother about the match.

He left out the part about sitting in the wrong stand.

Xiaoran didn’t.

Her mother laughed until she had to put down her chopsticks.

“You sat with the opposing supporters?”

“They were very friendly.”

“Did you cheer for the other team?”

“Of course not.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

“He stood up when Yichen scored.”

Her father looked at her.

“That was because everyone else stood up.”

Yichen lowered his head, smiling into his rice.

Her mother shook her head.

“Next time, check your ticket properly.”

“I will.”

Then her father looked at Yichen.

“Next time, tell me which section to book.”

Yichen nodded.

“Of course, Uncle.”

Xiaoran smiled.

The next time.

It was a small thing to say.

But she liked hearing it.

Later that night, after Yichen had taken her home, she found herself thinking about the conversation in the café.

She was standing beside his car, holding the strap of her bag.

“Yichen?”

He turned off the engine.

“Hm?”

“About what my dad asked.”

He met her eyes.

“The contract?”

“Does it scare you?”

He considered the question.

“Sometimes.”

She hadn’t expected him to say that.

He said, “Not the possibility of getting injured itself. I know that’s part of the sport. It’s more the uncertainty. You can prepare as much as possible, but you can’t control everything.”

She nodded slowly.

“And you still want to do it?”

“Yes.”

There was no hesitation in his answer.

Xiaoran smiled.

“Then I hope you get it.”

He turned to her.

“Even if it means I’ll be busy?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I have to travel?”

“Yes.”

“Even if you complain that I don’t have enough time for you?”

She squinted at him.

“I don’t complain that much.”

“Of course.”

She reached for his hand.

“I want you to do something you love. I don’t want you to look back and wonder whether you could have done it.”

He squeezed her fingers.

“And you?”

“What about me?”

“What do you want after graduation?”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I want to work somewhere that lets me make things I’m proud of.”

“Then I hope you get that too.”

She looked at him.

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“We’ll work out the rest.”

She nodded.

She leaned against him, her cheek resting near his shoulder.

Then she lifted her head.

“Next time, I’m checking my dad’s ticket.”

Yichen laughed.

“Good idea.”

“And if he ends up in the wrong stand again, I’m leaving him there.”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Your father made friends.”

She laughed.

“You’re taking his side?”

“I’m simply acknowledging that he had a good afternoon.”

She shook her head.

Then she kissed him goodnight.

And when she walked toward her building, Yichen waited until the light on the fourth floor went on before driving away.

He had a lot to think about.

The final year. The contract. The medical terms.

The uncertain future.

But he also remembered something her father had said before Xiaoran returned with the drinks.

I don’t need you to promise nothing will happen. I just want you to understand what you’re choosing.

Yichen thought that was fair.

And he intended to do exactly that.

chapters.desc: Five hours of silence from an away game, and Lin Xiaoran finally learns what twenty-three unread messages feel like from the other side.
chapters.title: The Night His Phone Died
chapters.epigraph: “Once was all I could manage.”
chapters.content:
The first hour, Xiaoran was patient.

The second hour, she was understanding.

By the fifth hour, she was beginning to understand something she had never quite understood before.

How it felt to be Zhou Yichen.

It started with a perfectly ordinary message.

Yichen, 5:42 PM: Game finished. We’re heading back to the hotel. I’ll call you after dinner.

Xiaoran had been waiting for his message all afternoon. The away game was in another city, and although he had told her not to stay up waiting, she had promised she would only call if he wasn’t too tired. He’d be back on the team bus the next afternoon.

She sent him a sticker of a tiny rabbit saluting.

Xiaoran, 5:44 PM: Okay! Don’t forget to eat properly.

Yichen, 5:45 PM: I won’t.

Xiaoran, 5:45 PM: And drink water.

Yichen, 5:46 PM: Yes, coach.

She smiled at her phone.

Then she put it down and went back to editing her university assignment.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 6:30, she checked her phone.

Nothing.

That was fine. They were probably having dinner.

At 7:00, she checked again.

Still nothing.

She opened their chat, reread his last message, and typed:

Did you eat yet?

She deleted it.

He was with his teammates. She didn’t want to become the girlfriend who kept asking questions every ten minutes.

At 7:18, she sent a photograph of the dinner she had ordered.

Xiaoran, 7:18 PM: My dinner. Yours better look more nutritious than this.

No reply.

She ate while watching a variety show, occasionally glancing at the screen.

At 8:00, she checked again.

At 8:15, she sent a sticker.

At 8:40, she finally called.

The phone rang.

And rang.

And eventually went to voicemail.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

“He’s probably showering.”

She said it aloud, as if hearing herself say it would make the explanation more convincing.

She put her phone down.

Five minutes later, she picked it up again.

She checked the team group photos posted by the university’s basketball account. There was one from the court, one of the players celebrating, and another showing the team getting onto their bus.

She zoomed in on the last photograph.

There he was.

Zhou Yichen, wearing his team jacket, standing near the back of the group. His hair was slightly damp, and he was looking down at something in his hand.

His phone, presumably.

Xiaoran frowned.

He had his phone.

She knew that was an unreasonable conclusion to draw from a photograph taken God knew when, but it didn’t stop her from looking at it again.

At 9:03, she called him a second time.

No answer.

At 9:17, she sent another message.

Xiaoran, 9:17 PM: Are you busy?

Then, after staring at the message for several seconds:

Call me when you’re free.

She put the phone beside her pillow.

She tried to concentrate on her assignment.

She really did.

But every few minutes, her eyes drifted toward the phone. She began to notice how quiet her room was. How long the evening was becoming. How she had so many small things she wanted to tell him.

Her lecturer had praised her presentation.

She had seen a funny dog on the way home.

She had bought a new hair clip and wanted him to tell her whether it suited her.

Nothing important.

But she wanted to tell him anyway.

At 9:45, she opened their chat again.

The last thing he had said was Yes, coach.

She pressed her lips together.

“Zhou Yichen.”

There was no one to hear her complaint.

She sent him a sticker of a little rabbit sitting alone in the rain.

Then she immediately regretted it.

It looked too pitiful.

She deleted it.

The message remained marked as deleted.

“Ah!”

She dropped her phone onto the bed and covered her face with both hands.

This was ridiculous.

He was at an away game. He was probably tired. He had a team dinner, teammates, coaches, and a bus journey. He was allowed to have a life outside their relationship.

She knew all of that.

She also knew that five hours wasn’t an unreasonable amount of time to be unavailable.

But knowing something logically and feeling it were two entirely different things.

✦ ✦ ✦

And then, unexpectedly, she remembered orientation day.

The first week of university. He had walked her all the way to the Media building first, because his own orientation started later and her sense of direction was a known disaster. He had told her to text him if she got lost.

She hadn’t got lost.

She had got bored, wandered downstairs at the break, and stood talking to a senior called Gu Ming while her phone sat on silent at the bottom of her bag.

Twenty-three unread messages.

She remembered the moment she heard her name behind her, much too calm. She remembered his face: not angry the way other people were angry. Worse. Quiet. He had already been to the orientation hall to look for her, and she hadn’t been there.

At the time, she had mostly felt guilty, and then relieved when he finally smiled.

She had never really thought about the two hours before that.

The two hours in which he had sent twenty-three messages and heard nothing back.

Xiaoran looked at their chat.

Then she looked at the time.

10:21 PM.

“Oh.”

For the first time, she understood exactly what he had felt that day.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 10:46 PM, Xiaoran finally decided to stop waiting.

She brushed her teeth, changed into her pajamas, and climbed into bed.

Her phone was on the bedside table.

She turned it face down, then turned it back up, then face down again.

She lasted approximately four minutes.

At 10:53, she opened their chat and typed:

I’m going to sleep. Hope you got back safely.

She hesitated.

Then added:

Good night.

She pressed send.

For a moment, she stared at the two gray message bubbles.

Then she put her phone back on the bedside table and settled beneath the blanket.

She was almost asleep when it happened.

A vibration, then another.

Then the familiar ringtone she had assigned exclusively to one person.

Xiaoran sat up so quickly that her blanket slipped to her waist.

Zhou Yichen calling…

She answered immediately.

“Hello?”

“Xiaoran?”

His voice was slightly rough, tired, and unmistakably familiar.

She closed her eyes.

“You’re alive.”

There was a pause, then a quiet laugh.

“Yes. I’m alive.”

“Your phone?”

“Dead.”

She blinked.

“What?”

“My phone died on the way back. I didn’t realize until we sat down to dinner.”

Xiaoran stared at the screen as though it might provide further explanation.

“Your phone died?”

“Completely. Dinner, then recovery, then two hours of footage with Coach. I borrowed my roommate’s charger, but his cable wasn’t compatible. Fang Ze had the right one, and he didn’t get back to the room until half past ten.”

“Then why didn’t you borrow someone else’s phone?”

“Your number’s in mine. I don’t know it by heart. I do now. Fang Ze tested me twice. Then mine turned on and I called you.” He sounded deeply ashamed of this.

She went quiet.

Yichen noticed immediately.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

She pulled the blanket closer.

“Nothing. I was just waiting.”

There was a small silence.

“How long?”

“Not that long.”

“How long, Xiaoran?”

She glanced at the clock.

“Five hours.”

He didn’t respond immediately.

Then, “I’m sorry.”

She had expected him to laugh at her, perhaps tease her for being impatient.

Instead, his apology made something in her chest loosen.

She said, “I thought you were busy. Then I thought you were eating. Then I thought you were showering. Then I thought maybe you were talking to your teammates.”

“Mhm.”

“And then I thought maybe you saw my messages but didn’t have time to answer.”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I wasn’t ignoring you.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

She pressed her lips together.

“...I know now.”

He exhaled, the sound coming through the speaker.

“Did you worry?”

She considered lying.

But she had spent the last five hours imagining all sorts of explanations. There was no point pretending she hadn’t.

“A little.”

“Only a little?”

“Don’t push it.”

He laughed.

She could almost picture him sitting on the edge of the hotel bed, one hand holding his phone, his hair still damp after a shower.

“Did you eat?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Food.”

“That’s a very informative answer.”

“Rice. Chicken. Vegetables. Happy?”

“Very.”

“And you?”

“I ate with the team.”

“Properly?”

“Yes.”

“Don’t lie.”

“I’m not.”

She hummed, still not entirely satisfied.

Yichen was quiet.

Then he asked, “Did you finish your assignment?”

“Almost.”

“Don’t stay up too late.”

“I was already going to sleep.”

“Good.”

Another pause.

This time, Xiaoran was the one who didn’t want to end the call.

“Yichen?”

“I’m here.”

“Do you remember orientation day?”

A pause.

“Twenty-three messages,” he said.

She closed her eyes.

“You counted.”

“I sent them.”

She played with the corner of her blanket.

“Was it like this?”

“What?”

“Waiting for someone to answer. Checking your phone. Wondering what they’re doing.”

Yichen didn’t answer immediately.

When he did, his voice was gentle.

“Worse. At least tonight you knew I was with twelve other people and a coach.”

“And that day you didn’t know I was downstairs.”

“I didn’t know you were downstairs talking to Gu Ming.”

“You remember his name?”

“I remember everything about that day.”

She laughed into her pillow, a small, guilty laugh.

“You only said it once. That I scared you.”

“Once was all I could manage.”

Xiaoran stared at the ceiling.

“Oh.”

“Why?”

“Because I think I understand now.”

“Understand what?”

“Why you always ask me to message you when I arrive.”

He smiled on the other end.

“That wasn’t a particularly complicated mystery.”

“Don’t ruin my moment.”

“Sorry.”

“And why you ask whether I’ve eaten, even when I tell you I’m going out for only an hour.”

“That’s a different matter. You forget to eat.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed.

She rolled onto her side, hugging her pillow.

“I thought you were just being fussy.”

“I am.”

“At least you admit it.”

“But I’m also allowed to worry about my girlfriend.”

She went quiet again.

Then, in a much smaller voice, “I missed you.”

His teasing disappeared.

“I missed you too.”

“You were only gone for one night.”

“I know.”

“That’s not very long.”

“No.”

“But it felt long.”

He was silent.

Then she heard the faint rustle of fabric.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Next time, if my phone dies, I’ll find a way to let you know. I’ll ask Fang Ze to message you, or borrow someone else’s phone.”

She smiled.

“You don’t have to make a whole emergency communication plan.”

“I’d rather you know I’m safe.”

Her smile grew.

“Okay.”

“And you?”

“Me?”

“If you can’t reach me, don’t spend five hours imagining every possible explanation.”

She frowned.

“I didn’t imagine every possible explanation.”

“Only a few?”

“...Quite a few.”

He chuckled.

“Just send me one message. If I can answer, I will. If I can’t, I’ll get back to you when I can.”

She nodded, even though he couldn’t see her.

“Okay.”

“And don’t be afraid to tell me you’re worried.”

“I wasn’t afraid.”

“You deleted a message.”

Xiaoran froze.

“...How do you know that?”

“Because I saw the notification that you had deleted one.”

She buried her face in her pillow.

“Oh my God.”

“What did it say?”

“Nothing.”

“Was it important?”

“No.”

“Was it a picture?”

“No!”

“Then what was it?”

“Good night, Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed, a low, unhurried sound.

“All right. I’ll let you keep your secrets.”

She lifted her head.

“You’re not going to ask again?”

“I could.”

“But?”

“But I know you’ll get embarrassed.”

She narrowed her eyes at the phone.

He was smiling. She could hear it.

“You’re so annoying.”

“Mhm.”

“Very annoying.”

“All right.”

“Don’t just agree with me!”

“What would you like me to say?”

She thought for a moment.

“That you missed me.”

“I already said that.”

“Say it again.”

His answer came without hesitation.

“I missed you, Xiaoran.”

Her cheeks warmed.

“Okay.”

“Anything else?”

She hesitated.

Then she whispered, “I wish you were here.”

The silence that followed was different.

It was the kind of quiet that came when both people were thinking the same thing.

“I’ll be back tomorrow afternoon,” he said.

“I know.”

“I’ll come straight to see you.”

“You don’t have to. You should rest.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

“Because I want to.”

She smiled into her pillow.

“Okay.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next afternoon, Xiaoran was waiting outside the university’s main entrance.

She had told herself she was only there because she happened to finish class early.

It was a lie.

She had checked the time of his arrival three times, changed her outfit once, and bought two drinks from the café near the entrance because she remembered he liked the iced Americano from there.

When the team bus finally turned in at the gate, she straightened.

It stopped in front of her with a long sigh of brakes.

Yichen stepped out, wearing a dark jacket and carrying his duffel bag over one shoulder.

He looked tired.

Not terribly so, but there were faint shadows beneath his eyes, and his hair was slightly disheveled from the journey.

Xiaoran walked toward him.

He barely had time to put his bag down before she wrapped both arms around his waist.

Yichen’s expression softened.

He held her close, one hand settling between her shoulder blades, the other gently cradling the back of her head.

“Hello,” he murmured.

She pressed her cheek against his chest.

“Hello.”

“Waiting long?”

“No.”

He glanced at the two drinks in her hand.

“How long?”

“Not long.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Twenty minutes.”

He smiled and pressed his mouth to her hair.

“Thank you for waiting.”

She leaned back to see him.

“You’re welcome.”

His eyes moved over her face, taking in the little pout she hadn’t quite managed to hide.

“Still upset?”

“No.”

“Really?”

“Maybe a little.”

He nodded seriously.

“Then I should apologize properly.”

She blinked.

“How?”

He pressed a kiss to her hair.

Then her left cheek.

Then her right.

Xiaoran’s pout weakened.

“That’s not enough.”

“Not enough?”

She nodded with great seriousness.

Yichen’s mouth curved.

“What else does the offended party require?”

She looked at his lips, then quickly looked away.

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

“You’re tired.”

He studied her for a second, then gently touched her chin.

“I’m tired. I’m not too tired to kiss my girlfriend.”

Her face turned pink.

“Who said anything about kissing?”

“You’ve been looking at my mouth for the past ten seconds.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed and kissed her properly.

It was unhurried, warm, and familiar. His hand rested lightly against her cheek, his thumb brushing once beneath her eye before he pulled away.

Xiaoran looked at him, a little dazed.

He smiled.

“Better?”

“Much.”

“Good.”

She handed him the iced Americano.

“I bought this for you.”

He accepted it, looking at the cup before turning back to her.

“You remembered.”

“Of course I remembered.”

“Thank you.”

She watched him take a sip.

Then, as they walked toward the car park, she slipped her hand into his.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I think I understand something now.”

He glanced at her.

“What?”

“You’re always so calm when I get lost or don’t answer quickly. But I think you’re not actually calm.”

His fingers tightened gently around hers.

He considered that.

“Sometimes.”

She looked up at him.

“Then I’ll try to be more considerate.”

He smiled.

“You don’t have to change everything because of one evening.”

“I know. But I want to.”

She swung their joined hands lightly.

“And you should also be more considerate.”

“How?”

“Don’t let your phone die.”

He laughed.

“I’ll do my best.”

“Bring a power bank.”

“All right.”

“And a spare cable.”

“Anything else?”

She pretended to think.

“Maybe a satellite phone.”

“That’s a little excessive.”

“You have a girlfriend who worries.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She nudged his arm.

He looked down at her, his expression quietly affectionate.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Next time, if you’re worried, just tell me. You don’t have to pretend you’re fine.”

She looked at him.

For once, she didn’t have a playful answer ready.

Instead, she squeezed his hand.

“Okay.”

He lifted their joined hands and kissed her knuckles.

“And I’ll do the same.”

“Good.”

They reached the car park, where his car had been sitting for two days under a layer of leaves. Yichen opened the passenger door for her, then placed his bag in the back.

Before getting in, Xiaoran caught his sleeve.

He turned.

“What is it?”

She watched him, then caught his face in both hands and kissed his cheek.

“Welcome back.”

His expression softened in a way that made her heart flutter.

He leaned down, returning a kiss to her temple.

“I’m home.”

And somehow, that was the part that made her happiest.

Those two words.

Because she had spent the previous evening learning what it felt like to wait for someone she loved.

And now she understood why, every time she walked away from him, Zhou Yichen always watched until she was safely out of sight.

chapters.desc: She wins four concert tickets for six friends who have waited weeks, and she would rather not be the one who chooses.
chapters.title: Ticket Allocation
chapters.epigraph: “Besides, I got the ticket.”
chapters.content:
The problem began with four tickets.

Not five.

Xiaoran counted them twice to make sure.

Four glossy debut tickets sat on the dining table, arranged neatly beside her laptop. Each had a different seat number, and each was worth more than she had expected when she first entered the ticket lottery.

She stared at them.

“There’s a problem.”

Yichen, who was sitting on the sofa with his business textbook open, turned a page.

“What problem?”

“Four tickets.”

He glanced at the table.

“Yes.”

“Six people.”

He looked up properly.

Xiaoran turned her laptop toward him. On the screen was a group chat with Tang Meilin, Chen Yuhao, Jiayi, and Ning.

The five of them in the chat, and Yichen, who wasn’t in the chat because he refused to be in any chat with the word besties in its name, had been talking about the concert for weeks. Meilin and Yuhao had already booked trains into Shanghai for the weekend; it was going to be the first time all six of them had been in one city since the summer. It was an artist Xiaoran had followed since high school, and the announcement of the first major concert had sent her into a small frenzy. She’d entered the ticket lottery with the others, expecting nothing.

Somehow, she had won four tickets.

Four, the most one account could buy.

For six people.

Yichen closed his textbook. “Who are the six?”

Xiaoran looked at him as if he had asked her to recite the alphabet. “Me, you, Meilin, Yuhao, Jiayi and Ning.”

“Jiayi said her cousin’s getting married that Saturday.”

“She did. So five. Five people. Four tickets.” Xiaoran counted on her fingers again, which didn’t change anything.

“And one of the four is yours. You won them,” Yichen said.

“I’m not taking one just because I won them.”

“You are. So three tickets. Four people.” He looked at her.

She picked up one ticket and examined it as if the answer might be printed on the back. “Three tickets, and four people who matter.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“You’re counting me as one of the people who matter?”

She met his eyes.

“Don’t start.”

Something in his face eased.

“I’m just clarifying.”

“You’re obviously one of them.”

“Obviously.”

She put the ticket down.

“Anyway, I don’t know what to do.”

“Have you asked everyone?”

“Not yet.”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t want anyone to feel like they’re being left out.”

Yichen leaned back against the sofa.

“Then don’t make it a decision for them.”

She frowned.

“What does that mean?”

“Tell them what happened. Let everyone decide whether they want to go.”

“But someone still won’t get a ticket.”

“That’s true.”

He said it so calmly that she almost glared at him.

“You’re not helping.”

“I’m trying to.”

“You’re being too reasonable.”

“Would you prefer I panic with you?”

She considered it.

“...A little.”

Yichen laughed.

He reached for her hand as she passed the sofa, drawing her down beside him.

“Let’s ask them first.”

The group chat became a disaster within three minutes.

Xiaoran: Important announcement. I won the ticket lottery.

Meilin: WHAT.

Yuhao: OUR GIRL.

Ning: XIAORAN!!!

Meilin: Four tickets, right?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yuhao: Perfect. Four of us.

Xiaoran: There are five of us.

Yuhao: ...

Meilin: Oh.

Ning: Wait.

Yuhao: I suddenly remember I have a very important appointment.

Meilin: You are not sacrificing yourself. Don’t be dramatic.

Yuhao: I was being noble.

Meilin: You were being annoying.

Xiaoran stared at the conversation.

Then she typed.

Xiaoran: I don’t want anyone to feel forced to give up their ticket. We can discuss it properly.

Meilin: Xiaoran, breathe.

Ning: Exactly. Nobody’s going to fight over this.

Yuhao: I might.

Meilin: You can fight me.

Yuhao: I withdraw.

She looked at Yichen.

“They’re already fighting.”

“Yuhao and Meilin?”

“Yes.”

“That’s normal.”

She let her head drop onto his shoulder.

“I don’t want to choose.”

“Then don’t.”

“But someone has to.”

“Not necessarily.”

“Wait until you see them.”

They met at a café near campus on Friday evening, two hours after Meilin and Yuhao’s train got in. Meilin arrived first, followed by Ning. Yuhao appeared ten minutes late, still carrying his weekend bag and a drink, looking entirely too pleased with himself.

Meilin dropped into the chair opposite them.

“All right. Show me the tickets.”

Xiaoran took out her phone and opened the confirmation.

“Good seats.”

“Really?”

“Yes. You did well.”

“I didn’t do anything. I just got lucky.”

“Luck is a skill.”

Yuhao leaned over the table.

“Can I see?”

Meilin moved the phone away.

“Don’t breathe on it.”

“Why?”

“Because you have bad luck.”

Yuhao looked offended.

Ning laughed.

Xiaoran watched them, then took a breath.

“Okay. So, about the tickets.”

Meilin waved a hand.

“Let’s establish something first. Nobody is going to be upset with you. You won them. One of them is yours, and that is not up for a vote. You don’t owe us anything.”

“I know, but—”

“No, listen. We’ve all been excited about this, but it’s not worth making you miserable over.” Meilin’s voice softened.

Ning nodded.

“She’s right. We can figure it out.”

Yuhao lifted his drink.

“I volunteer to give up my ticket.”

Everyone looked at him.

He shrugged.

“What? I’m generous.”

Meilin narrowed her eyes.

“Why?”

“Because I can.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

“I have excellent character.”

“You have a suspicious expression.”

Yuhao laughed.

Xiaoran looked between them.

“Are you sure?”

Yuhao nodded.

“Honestly, I don’t mind. I like the artist, but I was mostly going because all of us were going.”

Ning looked thoughtful.

“I actually feel the same way. I really want to go, but if someone else wants it more, I’m happy to sit this one out.”

Meilin glanced at her.

“Don’t say that just to be nice.”

“I’m not.”

Yichen had been quiet throughout the conversation. He was sitting beside Xiaoran, one hand resting near hers on the table.

Meilin finally turned to him.

“What about you?”

Xiaoran looked at him too.

Yichen raised his eyebrows slightly.

“What about me?”

“You’re one of the four tickets.”

He glanced at Xiaoran.

She was already looking at him with a small crease between her brows.

She wanted him there.

But she didn’t want to take a ticket away from someone else just because she wanted him beside her.

Yichen reached for her hand beneath the table.

“I don’t mind sitting this one out.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“But you said you wanted to hear them live.”

“I do. I’ll hear them down the phone at the end of every song, because you’ll call me.”

“That’s not the same.”

“No. It isn’t.”

She studied his face.

He gave her a smile.

“Go with your friends. Enjoy yourself.”

Then she leaned back.

“Actually, I have a proposal.”

Yuhao groaned.

“That sounds dangerous.”

“Shut up.”

She took out her phone.

“Let’s put the four names in a random draw. Three tickets. Whoever isn’t picked gets first claim on the next concert.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“That’s fair.”

“Exactly.”

Yuhao nodded.

“Finally, democracy.”

Meilin looked at him.

“You’re not allowed to speak.”

They wrote the four names on separate pieces of paper.

Ning folded them.

Yuhao insisted on mixing them.

Meilin accused him of trying to manipulate the outcome.

Xiaoran, meanwhile, was visibly nervous.

“Why are you so tense?” he murmured.

“Because.”

“Because?”

“Because I don’t want to see anyone disappointed.”

He rubbed his thumb over her knuckles.

“Whatever happens, we’ll be fine.”

She turned to him.

“You’re really okay not going?”

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“I’d rather you enjoy the concert than spend the whole evening worrying about me.”

She smiled a little.

Then Ning placed the folded papers in the middle of the table.

“Ready?”

Nobody answered.

Yuhao raised his hand.

“Wait. Should we have dramatic music?”

Meilin kicked him under the table.

“Pick one.”

The first name was Meilin.

She grinned.

“Excellent.”

The second was Ning.

She smiled, looking relieved.

The third paper remained, and the fourth.

Yuhao reached for it.

“Allow me.”

Meilin caught his wrist.

“Don’t make it theatrical.”

He pulled his hand away.

“You’re ruining the moment.”

He unfolded the paper.

His expression changed.

Then he burst out laughing.

“What?”

Meilin leaned forward.

Yuhao turned the paper around.

ZHOU YICHEN.

Nobody said anything.

Then Xiaoran stared at the paper. Then at Yichen, then back at the paper.

“Wait.”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“You got it.”

“So it seems.”

“You got the ticket.”

“Yes.”

She looked genuinely surprised.

He smiled.

“Are you disappointed?”

“No! I’m happy.” She immediately shook her head.

“Good.”

“But—”

He tilted his head.

“But?”

She looked at the last folded paper.

Yuhao opened it.

His own name.

He stared at it, then looked up.

“Well.”

Meilin covered her mouth.

Ning started laughing.

Yuhao placed the paper on the table with exaggerated dignity.

“I have been betrayed by probability.”

Meilin laughed.

“You volunteered to give up your ticket!”

“That was before probability personally attacked me.”

Xiaoran reached across the table.

“Yuhao, are you really okay?”

He waved her off.

“Of course. I’m going to spend that evening doing something much more meaningful.”

“Like what?”

“Watching you all post concert videos and regretting my generosity.”

Meilin shook her head. “You’re a tragedy.”

Yuhao grinned.

“But seriously, I’m fine. You four go. Send me videos.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Of course.”

On the way back to campus, Xiaoran was unusually quiet.

Yichen noticed.

He had her bag over one shoulder, and their hands were linked between them.

“What are you thinking about?”

“Yuhao.”

“He’s fine.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

She looked up.

“I was thinking... if you hadn’t gotten the ticket, I would’ve wanted to give mine to you.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Would you?”

“Yes.”

“Even though you’ve been waiting for this concert for months?”

She hesitated.

“Maybe.”

He stopped walking.

She turned toward him.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why did you stop?”

He looked at her, his expression quiet.

“Because I want you to know something.”

She waited.

“I like going places with you. I like watching things with you. I like being included in the things you’re excited about.”

Her fingers tightened around his.

“But I don’t need to be included in everything.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Sometimes, you should go with your friends. Sometimes, you should have an experience that’s yours.”

She nodded slowly.

“And I’ll still be here when you come back.”

Her expression softened.

Yichen lifted their joined hands and kissed her knuckles.

“Besides, I got the ticket.”

She laughed.

“You’re right.”

“Very lucky.”

“Extremely.”

“Almost suspicious.”

She nudged his arm.

“Don’t ruin it.”

That got a smile out of him.

The night of the concert, Xiaoran sent him a photograph of the four tickets.

They were standing outside the venue: Xiaoran, Meilin, Ning, and Yichen.

Yuhao had taken the photograph before leaving them, loudly reminding everyone to enjoy themselves on his behalf.

Xiaoran: We’re here!

Yichen: I can see that.

Xiaoran: Yuhao says he hates us.

Yichen: He’ll recover.

Xiaoran: Meilin says she’s going to buy him something so he’ll stop complaining.

Yichen: That might work.

A few minutes later, she sent another picture.

This time, it was of the stage.

Xiaoran: It’s starting soon.

Yichen: Enjoy it.

Xiaoran: Wish you were here.

He smiled at his phone.

Yichen: I’m right beside you.

She looked up.

He was standing next to her, one hand holding their drinks, the other reaching for hers.

She smiled and slipped her fingers between his.

“Right.”

He leaned down.

“Don’t spend the concert messaging me.”

“I wasn’t.”

“You were.”

“I was just updating you.”

“Very considerate.”

She laughed, then the lights dimmed.

The crowd erupted.

Xiaoran turned toward the stage, her face bright with excitement. Yichen watched her before looking forward too.

The next morning, Yuhao received four photographs.

One of the stage. One of Meilin singing with her eyes closed.

One of Ning laughing.

And one of Xiaoran and Yichen, taken during the encore.

Xiaoran was looking at the stage, smiling so brightly that her cheeks were raised. Yichen stood beside her, his arm around her shoulders, looking at her instead of the performers.

Yuhao stared at the photograph, then sent a message to the group.

Yuhao: I see how it is.

Meilin: What now?

Yuhao: I gave up my ticket and still got excluded from the romantic photography.

Xiaoran: It’s a nice picture!

Yuhao: It’s disgusting.

Yichen: I’ll send you the stage photos.

Yuhao: Thank you. At least one person respects me.

Meilin: You literally volunteered to give up your ticket.

Yuhao: I WAS YOUNG AND NAIVE.

Xiaoran laughed so much she had to put her phone down.

Yichen, sitting beside her in the university café, glanced over.

“Yuhao?”

She nodded.

“He’s still grieving.”

“Understandable.”

She leaned against his shoulder.

She opened the photograph again, then looked at him.

“Next time, we’ll get five tickets.”

Yichen turned his head.

“Next time?”

“Obviously.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right.”

She rested her cheek against his shoulder.

“Five tickets.”

“Five.”

“And nobody gets sacrificed.”

“Agreed.”

A beat passed. “Unless Yuhao volunteers again,” he said.

She burst out laughing.

“Yichen!”

He kissed her, entirely unrepentant.

chapters.desc: A schedule planned to the minute, a cup and a fruit bowl, and a sunset that refuses to cooperate.
chapters.title: Four Years, Planned Badly
chapters.epigraph: “That one’s flexible.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had a schedule.

Not a vague schedule.

Not a general idea of what she and Zhou Yichen might do on their anniversary.

A schedule.

Down to the minute.

She had spent three evenings preparing it, one afternoon revising it, and approximately forty minutes arguing with herself about whether the sunset was better at 4:52 or 4:55.

At the top of her notebook, written in pink ink with three little hearts, was the title:

OUR FOURTH ANNIVERSARY — A PERFECT DAY.

Below it:

08:00 — Wake up.

08:05 — Send anniversary greeting.

08:10 — Receive anniversary greeting.

08:15 — Get ready.

09:00 — Breakfast.

09:45 — First surprise.

10:30 — Activity chosen by Xiaoran.

12:00 — Lunch.

13:30 — Second surprise.

15:00 — Free time (romantic interaction encouraged).

16:50 — Sunset.

18:30 — Dinner.

20:00 — Final surprise.

21:00 — End of anniversary.

She stared at the last line, then crossed it out.

21:00 — No end.

Much better.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was admiring her work when her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Are you awake?

Xiaoran glanced at the clock.

7:56 AM.

She immediately sat up.

Four minutes early.

He was ruining the schedule already.

Xiaoran: No.

Yichen: Then who’s replying?

Xiaoran: My assistant.

Yichen: Good morning to your assistant, then.

She giggled.

Before she could reply, another message arrived.

Yichen: Happy fourth anniversary, Xiaoran.

Her smile softened.

Four years.

Four years since they had started dating. Four years of knowing how he took his coffee, which side of the bed he preferred, how he looked when he was concentrating, and the exact expression he made when she was about to do something ridiculous.

Four years of being loved by Zhou Yichen.

She typed carefully.

Xiaoran: Happy anniversary, boyfriend.

Then she added a heart, then three more, then a sticker of two little bears hugging.

Her phone rang.

She answered immediately.

“Hello!”

“Good morning.”

“Good morning!”

“Did you sleep well?”

“Perfectly.”

“You’re unusually energetic.”

“Because today is a very important day.”

“I know.”

There was a smile in his voice.

“Are you ready?”

Xiaoran looked at her notebook.

“More than ready.”

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

A pause.

“That’s not reassuring.”

She laughed.

“Come pick me up at nine!”

“I’ll be there.”

“And don’t be late.”

“I won’t.”

“And wear something nice.”

“What counts as nice?”

“Something that makes me want to kiss you.”

Yichen laughed.

“That’s a rather broad requirement.”

“Then you shouldn’t have asked.”

“All right. I’ll see you soon.”

She hung up, looked at the notebook, and made her first adjustment.

08:10 — Receive anniversary greeting.

Completed.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:02, Zhou Yichen arrived.

Xiaoran was waiting downstairs, dressed in a pretty cream-colored dress with a small ribbon in her hair. She had a little bag over her shoulder and a notebook tucked inside it.

Yichen stepped out of the car.

He wore a dark shirt with the sleeves casually folded to his forearms, tailored trousers, and a watch she had once told him looked particularly good on him.

He looked at her, then smiled.

He reached for her.

Xiaoran approached with a bright smile, expecting a greeting.

Instead, he took her hand, pulled her gently closer, and kissed her hair.

“Happy anniversary.”

She beamed.

“Happy anniversary!”

His gaze lingered on her face.

“You look beautiful.”

“I know.”

He raised an eyebrow.

She quickly corrected herself.

“I mean, thank you. You’re also very handsome.”

“Only also?”

“Extremely handsome.”

“Better.”

He opened the passenger door for her.

Xiaoran got in, carefully arranging her dress. As he walked around to the driver’s side, she took out her notebook.

Yichen noticed.

“What are you reading?”

“Nothing.”

“Your notebook?”

“It’s a private document.”

“Should I be concerned?”

“No.”

He started the car.

She turned toward him.

“Before we go, I have something to say.”

“I’m listening.”

“Today, you must follow my instructions.”

“All right.”

“No complaining.”

“Understood.”

“No asking too many questions.”

“That’s going to be difficult.”

“And you have to pretend to be surprised when I surprise you.”

He glanced at her.

“How do you pretend to be surprised?”

“Like this.”

She opened her mouth, widened her eyes, and raised both hands.

Yichen considered her.

Then he laughed.

“Very convincing.”

“Don’t laugh! I’m demonstrating!”

“Sorry.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re already making this difficult.”

He reached over and squeezed her hand.

“All right, director. I’ll cooperate.”

✦ ✦ ✦

09:00 — Breakfast.

The first destination was the little café near campus that they had claimed as theirs the week they moved to Shanghai, the summer before first year.

Xiaoran had chosen it deliberately.

The place hadn’t changed much. The wooden tables were still slightly uneven, the window seats still caught the morning light, and the owner still remembered them.

“Ah, you two! It’s been a while.” the woman greeted them warmly.

Xiaoran smiled.

“Hello, Auntie!”

The woman looked between them.

“Still together?”

Xiaoran nearly choked.

“Auntie!”

Yichen, meanwhile, looked perfectly comfortable.

“Four years today.”

“Four years! That’s wonderful. You must take good care of her.” The woman clapped her hands.

“I will.”

Xiaoran turned to him.

“Why did you answer so seriously?”

“Was I supposed to lie?”

She nudged his knee under the table.

He smiled.

They ordered the same breakfast they had ordered the first morning they found the place: pancakes, eggs, and two drinks.

Xiaoran had remembered the details.

Yichen had remembered too.

When the food arrived, he cut a piece of pancake and placed it on her plate.

She looked at it, then at him.

“You’re supposed to let me do that today.”

“Why?”

“Because I’m the planner.”

“Does that mean I can’t take care of you?”

She considered this.

“No. You can take care of me. But I should also take care of you.”

“Then we’re both doing our jobs.”

She liked that answer.

After breakfast, she took out her phone.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Photograph.”

He leaned toward her.

She raised the phone, positioning them carefully. Yichen looked at the camera, but just before she pressed the shutter, he turned and kissed her cheek.

The photograph captured her surprised expression and his smile.

Xiaoran stared at it.

“You’re cheating.”

“How?”

“I wasn’t ready.”

“You look happy.”

She zoomed in.

Unfortunately, he was right.

She looked happy.

She saved it.

✦ ✦ ✦

09:45 — First surprise.

Xiaoran led him to a small photography studio.

Yichen looked at the sign, then at her.

“What’s this?”

“Surprise number one.”

Inside, a photographer greeted them. Xiaoran had booked a short couple’s portrait session.

Yichen looked at her.

“You arranged this?”

“Yes.”

“How long ago?”

“Two weeks.”

He glanced at the photographer, then back at her.

“Did you choose the clothes?”

“Obviously.”

She pulled a small envelope from her bag.

“Here.”

Inside were two printed photographs.

The first was from their high-school days, taken when they were still young and slightly awkward about being photographed together. Yichen had one arm around her shoulders, while Xiaoran was smiling so widely that her eyes were almost closed.

The second was more recent, taken during their university years.

They stood side by side, a little more grown up, but with the same comfortable closeness.

Yichen studied them.

“You kept these?”

“Of course.”

She pointed at the first photograph.

“Look at your hair.”

He looked down.

“My hair?”

“It was so flat.”

“It was raining.”

“Your expression was also so serious.”

“I was trying to take a good photograph.”

“You looked like you were attending a business meeting.”

He gave her a sidelong glance.

“Perhaps I was already practicing.”

She laughed.

The photographer called them over.

They took several photographs: one formal, one playful, one with Xiaoran standing on her toes to kiss his cheek, then the photographer suggested a final pose.

“Could you stand closer? Perhaps the gentleman can hold her waist.”

Yichen’s hand settled naturally at Xiaoran’s waist.

“And look at each other.”

They did.

Xiaoran was prepared to smile.

But Yichen was looking at her with an expression she knew very well.

Quiet. Warm. A little amused.

“What?” she whispered.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“It’s a photograph.”

“You’re supposed to look at the camera.”

“Then look at the camera.”

She tried.

He leaned closer and murmured, “You’re very pretty.”

Her cheeks warmed.

The camera clicked.

The photographer laughed.

“That one is lovely.”

Xiaoran didn’t need to see the result to know she would like it.

✦ ✦ ✦

10:30 — Activity chosen by Xiaoran.

This was where things began to go wrong.

She had booked a pottery class.

A romantic pottery class.

She had imagined them sitting side by side, making matching cups, laughing, and perhaps getting a little clay on each other’s noses.

The reality was that Xiaoran’s cup began collapsing after seven minutes.

“Why is it leaning?”

Yichen glanced at it.

“You’re pressing too hard on one side.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“Don’t criticize my cup.”

“I’m helping.”

“You’re making it worse.”

He looked at her clay, then at his own.

His was perfectly symmetrical.

Xiaoran stared at it.

“Why is yours so good?”

“I followed the instructor’s directions.”

“I followed the instructor’s directions!”

“You were looking at me.”

She paused.

“...That’s irrelevant.”

He smiled.

The instructor came over and helped her reshape the clay.

“Don’t worry. It takes practice.”

Xiaoran nodded solemnly.

“I’ll try again.”

Ten minutes later, she accidentally pressed too hard.

The cup collapsed.

She stared at the clay.

Yichen pressed his lips together.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

He finally laughed.

She turned toward him, scandalized.

“You’re laughing at me!”

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not sorry.”

He leaned over and gently wiped a small streak of clay from her cheek.

“No, I’m not.”

She looked at him.

His smile was so attractive that she forgot her complaint for a second.

Then she remembered.

“Stop being handsome. It’s distracting.”

He laughed again.

By the end of the class, Yichen had made a neat little cup.

Xiaoran had made something that resembled a bowl with an uncertain identity.

The instructor placed their creations side by side.

“Very nice! A matching set.”

Xiaoran looked at the two pieces.

“His is a cup.”

She pointed at hers.

“Mine is a fruit bowl.”

Yichen considered it.

“Then we have a complete household.”

She gasped.

“You’re going to use it?”

“Of course.”

He looked at her.

Her expression softened.

Then she quickly looked away.

“That’s a very good answer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

12:00 — Lunch.

Xiaoran had chosen a restaurant with a view of the city.

She had also arranged a small dessert plate with a handwritten message:

Four years with you. Still my favorite person.

Yichen read it, then looked at her.

“Did you write this?”

“Yes.”

“It’s nice.”

“Just nice?”

He set the card down.

“It’s very nice.”

She waited.

He didn’t elaborate.

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re supposed to say something more romantic.”

He leaned back.

“What would you like me to say?”

“Something like, ‘You’re the best thing that ever happened to me.’”

He looked at her.

Then said, “You’re the best thing that ever happened to me.”

She blinked.

He continued calmly.

“Was that what you wanted?”

“Don’t say it like you’re reading from a script!”

His mouth curved.

“Would you prefer a spontaneous version?”

“Yes.”

He found her hand on the table.

“Four years ago, I thought I was a fairly patient person.”

“Then I met you.”

“Excuse me?”

He smiled.

“I learned that I could spend an entire afternoon waiting for someone to decide what to eat, change her mind three times, and still be happy about it.”

Xiaoran tried not to smile.

“That’s not romantic.”

“I also learned that I like being the person you tell everything to. Even things that don’t matter.”

She went still.

“That I look forward to seeing your name on my phone. That I remember the smallest things you say. That when something good happens, you’re the first person I want to tell.”

His thumb brushed over her knuckles.

“And that after four years, I still look at you and feel very lucky that you chose me.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

Her lips parted slightly.

Then she looked down at their hands.

“You’re cheating.”

He smiled.

“How?”

“You didn’t tell me you were going to say something like that.”

“I didn’t know I was going to.”

She pressed her lips together, trying to hide her smile.

It didn’t work.

“Eat your lunch,” she mumbled.

He laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

13:30 — Second surprise.

This was supposed to be the most organized part of the day.

Xiaoran had booked a private room in a small gallery that hosted a rotating exhibition.

But when they arrived, the staff informed them that the room was unavailable for another thirty minutes due to a scheduling mistake.

Xiaoran stared.

“Thirty minutes?”

The staff apologized.

She checked her notebook.

13:30.

The exact time.

She checked again, as if the numbers might change out of sympathy.

Yichen stood beside her, watching.

“It’s fine.”

“But we have a schedule.”

“I noticed.”

“Everything is supposed to happen at the correct time.”

He glanced at his watch.

“We’re still together. I think we’re doing all right.”

She sighed.

“You don’t understand. I planned this.”

“I know.”

“And now we’re waiting.”

“We can wait.”

She looked at him.

He was completely unbothered.

It was almost offensive.

“How are you so calm?”

He looked down at her.

“Because I’m with you.”

She stared, then looked away.

“You’re doing that on purpose.”

“Doing what?”

“Saying things.”

He smiled.

They spent the next thirty minutes wandering around the gallery. Xiaoran stopped at every painting, reading the descriptions aloud and occasionally inventing stories about the people depicted.

Yichen followed her, listening.

At one painting, she stood.

It showed two people sitting together on a balcony, their shoulders touching, looking out at the sea.

“It’s nice,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because they’re not doing anything special. They’re just sitting together.”

Yichen looked at the painting, then at her.

“That sounds familiar.”

She smiled.

“Maybe that’s what I want when we’re old.”

“What?”

“To sit together. Somewhere with a nice view. You can read your newspaper, and I’ll bother you.”

“You don’t need to wait until we’re old to do that.”

She turned to him.

“Really?”

“You can bother me now.”

She laughed and slipped her hand into his.

When the gallery room finally opened, Xiaoran led him inside.

There were photographs displayed along the walls.

Their photographs.

Some were printed from old pictures she had collected. Others were candid shots from their university years: Yichen holding her bag while she tied her shoelaces, Xiaoran falling asleep on his shoulder, their hands intertwined on a café table, a blurry photograph of them laughing.

At the center was a small table with a scrapbook.

Yichen picked it up.

The first page read:

FOUR YEARS OF US.

He turned the pages slowly.

There were little notes beside the photographs.

The first time you walked me home.

The day you waited outside my classroom because I forgot my umbrella.

The first time you watched my presentation.

The day you joined the basketball team.

The day I realized I wanted to keep choosing you.

He paused at the last one.

Xiaoran was watching him.

“I wanted to make something you could keep. Not just photographs on your phone. Something physical,” she said.

He turned another page.

There was a photograph of them sitting on a bench, taken from behind.

Underneath, she had written:

I don’t remember what we were talking about. I just remember thinking that I could sit beside you for a long time.

Yichen closed the scrapbook gently.

For a moment, he said nothing.

Then he looked at her.

“You made all of this?”

She nodded.

“Some of the photographs were from your phone. I stole them.”

“I noticed some were missing.”

She winced.

“Sorry.”

He smiled faintly.

“That’s all right.”

He set the scrapbook down and drew her into his arms.

Xiaoran wrapped hers around his waist.

He kissed her hair.

“Thank you.”

She smiled against his chest.

“You’re welcome.”

He held her for a little longer than she expected.

When he finally pulled away, his eyes were warm.

“Can I have one more photograph?”

“Of what?”

“Us.”

She immediately reached for her phone.

“Of course!”

But he shook his head.

“Not with the phone.”

He took the scrapbook, opened it to the final page, and placed it back on the table.

Then he took her hand.

“Let’s make another memory.”

✦ ✦ ✦

15:00 — Free time (romantic interaction encouraged).

Xiaoran had written that part as a joke.

Unfortunately, Yichen had taken it seriously.

They went to a quiet park nearby. The afternoon was cold and bright, and the plane trees had dropped nearly all their leaves on the paths.

They bought ice cream anyway, because Xiaoran said anniversaries didn’t have weather.

Xiaoran chose strawberry.

Yichen chose coffee.

She took one bite of his, then another, then a third.

He watched her.

“Is yours not good?”

“It’s good.”

“Then why are you eating mine?”

“Because yours is also good.”

He gave her the cup.

She smiled triumphantly.

They found a bench and sat together.

Xiaoran leaned against his shoulder, holding the ice cream with both hands.

For a while, they simply watched people passing by.

Then she remembered something.

“Oh!”

Yichen looked down.

“What?”

“I forgot something.”

He glanced at his watch.

“What’s next?”

“Nothing. I just forgot to tell you something.”

“All right.”

She sat up.

“I want to say thank you.”

He turned toward her.

“For what?”

“For these four years.”

He didn’t interrupt.

She looked at her ice cream.

“I know I’m sometimes difficult.”

“Sometimes?”

She turned sharply.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Continue.”

She laughed and lightly hit his arm.

“I’m serious.”

“I know.”

She took a breath.

“Thank you for being patient with me. For listening to me even when I talk too much. For remembering things I forget. For not making me feel silly when I’m excited about something small.”

Her voice softened.

“And for letting me be myself.”

Yichen watched her.

She looked up.

“I know you have your own dreams and things you want to do. I don’t want you to feel like you have to make everything about me.”

“I don’t.”

“I know. But I still want you to know that I’m proud of you. And I want to be someone who makes your life happier, too.”

He was quiet.

Then he set his ice cream aside and turned fully toward her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“You don’t have to earn your place in my life by making it easier.”

She blinked.

He reached for her hand.

“I love you when you’re organized. I love you when you forget where you put your phone. I love you when you make a schedule and get upset because the gallery is thirty minutes late.”

She laughed.

“I wasn’t upset.”

“You checked your notebook four times.”

“Because it was late!”

He smiled.

“I know.”

His fingers threaded through hers.

“And I love that you think about these things. That you remember our first dates. That you wanted to make today special.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“But you don’t have to plan every minute for me to enjoy being with you.”

She looked at him.

He leaned closer.

“Some of my favorite moments with you weren’t planned at all.”

“Like what?”

“The time you got lost and called me from the wrong building.”

She groaned.

“That’s not romantic.”

“The time you fell asleep during a movie and insisted you were still watching.”

“I was listening.”

“The time you tried to teach me a dance and nearly kicked my knee.”

She covered her face.

“Why are all your memories embarrassing?”

“Because they’re memorable.”

He gently pulled her hands away from her face.

“And because I love them.”

She smiled.

Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“You’re my favorite person.”

He looked at her.

“You’re mine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

16:50 — Sunset.

This was the part Xiaoran had been most excited about.

She had chosen a quiet riverside spot where the city skyline looked particularly beautiful in the evening light.

She had checked the sunset time three days in advance.

She had checked it again yesterday.

She had even checked it that morning.

Everything was supposed to be perfect.

Except the weather had other plans.

Clouds gathered over the horizon, and the sunset was less golden than she had imagined.

Xiaoran stood with her hands on her hips.

“Unbelievable.”

Yichen stood beside her.

“What happened?”

“The sky.”

He looked up.

“It looks fine.”

“It was supposed to be prettier.”

He studied the clouds.

“Should I call someone?”

She turned to him.

“Don’t be ridiculous.”

He smiled.

They stood by the railing, watching the city lights slowly appear.

Xiaoran took out her phone.

“Let’s take a photograph.”

Yichen stepped behind her and wrapped his arms around her waist.

She held the phone up.

“Smile.”

He looked at the camera.

She pressed the shutter.

Then she looked at the photograph.

It was lovely.

The sky was cloudy, the river reflected the lights, and Yichen’s chin rested lightly against her shoulder.

She looked at it, then smiled.

“Actually, I like it.”

He kissed her cheek.

“Good.”

She turned in his arms.

“Even though the sunset wasn’t perfect?”

He looked at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I didn’t come here for the sunset.”

Her expression softened.

He brushed a strand of hair away from her face.

“I came here with you.”

She smiled.

Then she pulled his head down and kissed him.

It was a gentle kiss, warm and familiar.

When she pulled away, he studied her.

Then he kissed her cheek.

“Ready for dinner?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

18:30 — Dinner.

The restaurant was small, intimate, and beautifully lit.

Xiaoran had chosen a private table near the window.

She had also prepared a small gift.

It was a watch strap in a color she knew he liked, with a tiny engraving on the underside.

Yichen opened the box.

His eyes moved over the strap, then to the engraving.

For all the time we’ve spent, and all the time still waiting.

He looked at her.

“Xiaoran.”

She smiled nervously.

“Do you like it?”

He ran his thumb over the engraving.

“I love it.”

She exhaled.

“Good. I was worried you wouldn’t.”

He closed the box and set it down carefully.

Then he reached for the bag beside his chair.

“I have something for you too.”

Her eyes widened.

“You do?”

He handed her a small box.

Inside was a thin silver bracelet with a tiny panda charm, no bigger than her fingernail.

She already had a star. He’d given it to her on her first birthday as his girlfriend, and she was wearing it now. He’d remembered that too.

She touched it gently.

“It’s beautiful.”

“Turn it over.”

She did.

There was a small engraving on the back.

My favorite place is beside you.

Her eyes lifted.

Yichen was watching her.

She smiled, but her eyes were already beginning to shine.

“You wrote this?”

“I chose it.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s true.”

She looked down again.

Then she leaned across the table and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you.”

He smiled.

“You’re welcome.”

She touched the charm again.

“I’ll wear it every day.”

“Don’t. You’ll damage it.”

She frowned.

“Then when?”

“On days you want to.”

“But I want to every day.”

He laughed.

“Then we’ll see.”

Dinner continued with conversation, laughter, and a few photographs.

At one point, Xiaoran checked her notebook under the table.

Yichen noticed.

“What’s next?”

“Final surprise.”

“At eight?”

She nodded.

He glanced at his watch.

“It’s 7:56.”

She stared, then looked at her notebook, then at him.

“You’re not supposed to know the time.”

“I have a watch.”

She sighed.

“Fine. Close your eyes.”

He leaned back.

“Here?”

“Yes.”

He closed his eyes.

Xiaoran stood and walked around the table.

“Don’t peek.”

“I’m not.”

She took his hand.

“Come with me.”

He followed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

20:00 — Final surprise.

The final surprise wasn’t a restaurant, an activity, or another carefully arranged event.

It was the little private room upstairs, which she had rented for the evening and planned down to the last string of lights.

There were photographs hanging on strings, warm lights around the walls, and a table in the center with a cake.

Four candles stood on top.

A small card sat beside it.

Yichen opened his eyes.

For a moment, he simply looked around.

Xiaoran stood beside him, nervous.

“Surprise.”

He looked at the photographs.

Some were funny. Some were sweet. Some were so ordinary that he wondered when she had taken them.

There was one of him asleep on a sofa, his hand still holding hers.

Another of her laughing with her mouth full.

One of them walking through the rain.

One of their hands intertwined over the gear shift of his car.

And one from that morning at the café, which Ning had printed at a shop round the corner an hour before.

He turned toward her.

“You did all this?”

“I planned it. Jiayi and Ning hung the lights while we were at the gallery.”

He smiled.

“Did you ask them to keep it secret?”

“Yes. Ning said I was being dramatic. Jiayi cried.”

“Ning knows you well.”

Xiaoran glared.

“Don’t agree with her.”

He laughed.

Then he walked toward the table.

The cake had a simple message written on it:

FOUR YEARS. STILL NOT TIRED OF YOU.

Yichen read it, then looked at her.

“Not tired of me?”

“Not even a little.”

“That’s fortunate.”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t intend to go anywhere.”

She smiled.

He looked at the candles.

“Should I make a wish?”

“Yes.”

He closed his eyes.

Xiaoran watched him.

She wondered what he would wish for.

More basketball victories? A successful future? A life where everything went according to plan?

He opened his eyes and blew out the candles.

She clapped.

“Did you make a wish?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Can’t tell you.”

“Why?”

“Then it won’t come true.”

She pouted.

“That’s inconvenient.”

He laughed.

She cut the cake, giving him the first slice.

Then she took a breath.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I have one last thing.”

He set down his fork.

“All right.”

She reached into her bag and took out a folded piece of paper.

It was the schedule.

He accepted it.

At the bottom, under 21:00 — No end, she had squeezed in one more line in a different pen.

Tell Zhou Yichen why I love him.

He looked at her.

She took the paper back and unfolded it.

“Okay. So. I made this schedule because I wanted today to be perfect. I wanted you to have a really good anniversary, and I wanted you to know how much I love you.”

She looked down at the paper.

“But I think I made a mistake.”

He watched her.

“I spent so much time planning what we would do that I forgot the most important part.”

“You.”

His expression softened.

She continued, a little shy now.

“I love you because you’re you. Because you’re patient with me, because you’re thoughtful, because you make me feel safe without making me feel small. Because you always listen, even when I talk about something that happened three hours ago and somehow need to explain it from the beginning.”

“I love you because you make ordinary things feel important. And because even after four years, I still get excited when I know I’m going to see you.”

Her voice grew quieter.

“I don’t know what the next four years will look like. Maybe we’ll be busy. Maybe we’ll have difficult days. Maybe some things won’t go according to plan.”

She glanced at the schedule.

“Probably a lot of things.”

He laughed.

“But I want all of it. The good days, the difficult days, the ordinary days. I want to keep choosing you.”

She folded the paper.

“Happy anniversary, Zhou Yichen.”

For a moment, he didn’t move.

Then he stood.

Xiaoran looked up at him.

“What’s wrong?”

He came around the table and stopped in front of her.

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

He took the paper from her hand and placed it carefully on the table.

Then he reached for her waist.

“Because I’ve been listening.”

She smiled.

“Good.”
