“And because I have something to say too.”

She tilted her head.

“Okay.”

He looked at her.

“Four years ago, I started dating a girl who had a habit of making everything more complicated than it needed to be.”

Xiaoran gasped.

“Excuse me?”

“She was stubborn. She talked too much when she was excited. She got embarrassed easily, but tried very hard to hide it.”

“You’re describing me.”

“I am.”

“That’s not a very flattering anniversary speech.”

He laughed.

“But she also made me look forward to things I hadn’t thought about before. She made me want to share every ordinary part of my day. She made me understand that happiness doesn’t always have to be something extraordinary.”

His hand settled more securely at her waist.

“Sometimes it’s just having someone beside you while you eat breakfast. Someone who steals your ice cream. Someone who makes a terrible pottery bowl and insists it’s a fruit dish.”

She burst into laughter.

“You’re never going to let that go!”

“No.”

He brushed his thumb against her waist.

“And somewhere along the way, I stopped thinking about what it would be like to have a future with you.”

His eyes held hers.

“I started thinking about what I could do to make that future happen.”

Her laughter faded.

He leaned closer.

“I don’t need every day to be perfect, Xiaoran. I don’t need you to plan every minute. I just want to be there when the minutes happen.”

Her eyes grew warm.

“Yichen...”

He smiled faintly.

“Four years, and you’re still the person I want to come home to. The person I want to tell everything to. The person I want beside me when something good happens, and the person I want to hold when things aren’t so good.”

He lifted a hand to her cheek.

“And if I get to choose again, I’ll choose you again.”

She looked at him, her lips trembling into a smile.

“Even if I make you do pottery?”

“Even then.”

“Even if I make a schedule?”

He glanced at the paper on the table.

“That one requires further negotiation.”

She laughed.

And then he kissed her.

It began gently, his palm warm against her cheek, his other arm drawing her closer.

Xiaoran hooked a hand behind his neck, her hands finding his shoulders.

He kissed her again, slower this time, lingering as though he had nowhere else to be.

She smiled against his lips.

He felt it.

“What?” he murmured.

“Nothing.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Because I’m happy.”

His expression softened.

He brushed his nose lightly against hers.

“Good.”

Then he kissed her again.

This time, there was no teasing smile, no playful interruption, no carefully timed moment.

He kissed her with all the affection he had been holding back throughout the day. His arm tightened around her waist, bringing her close, while his hand slid gently to the back of her head.

Xiaoran’s fingers curled into his shirt.

She had kissed him thousands of times by now.

But there was something about the way he kissed her tonight that made her heart stumble.

It was warm and unhurried, but there was a depth to it that made her forget the room, the photographs, the cake, and the carefully planned schedule.

When he finally pulled away, she was still holding on to him.

Her cheeks were flushed.

Yichen looked at her.

“Happy?”

“Very.”

He kissed the corner of her mouth.

“Good.”

She looked at him, then at the schedule lying on the table.

“Wait.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“What?”

“I didn’t plan anything after that.”

He looked at the clock.

It was already 9:17.

“No end. And nothing written under it,” he read off the paper.

“That was the romantic part!”

He watched her.

Then calmly picked up the paper, turned it over, and wrote something on the back.

She watched him.

“What are you doing?”

He handed it to her.

At the bottom, in his neat handwriting, was a new line:

21:18 — Kiss Xiaoran again.

She looked up.

He smiled.

“That one’s flexible.”

She laughed, her cheeks turning pink all over again.

“You’re changing my schedule!”

“Just one item.”

“That’s not how planning works.”

“Then I apologize.”

He leaned closer.

“May I?”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

He kissed her again.

And when the kiss ended, Xiaoran decided that perhaps there was one thing she hadn’t planned badly at all.

Four years ago, she had chosen Zhou Yichen.

And she was still choosing him.

Tomorrow, she would probably make another schedule.

But tonight, she let him hold her for as long as he wanted, with the candles burned out, the cake half-finished, and the clock entirely forgotten.

For once, she didn’t need to know what time it was.

chapters.desc: A third-year group project, one teammate who never answers messages, and a boyfriend who offers to talk to him politely.
chapters.title: Group Project From Hell
chapters.epigraph: “And I checked yours. Two of the page numbers were wrong.”
chapters.content:
By the third year of university, Xiaoran had learned several important things about group projects.

One: the person who suggested creating a group chat was rarely the person who did the most work.

Two: the person who said I’ll handle the research might disappear for three days.

And three: there was always, without fail, one person who never answered messages until the night before the deadline.

Unfortunately, this semester, she had found that person.

His name was Dou Kai.

He had joined their group meeting once, nodded through the entire discussion, volunteered to find references, and then vanished.

For four days.

Xiaoran had sent him three messages.

Ning had sent him two.

Their other group member had tried calling.

Nothing.

On Thursday evening, Xiaoran was sitting at the library with her laptop open, staring at the group chat as if her sheer disappointment might make someone reply.

Yichen sat opposite her, working through a case study for one of his Business courses.

He had been listening to her complain for fourteen minutes.

“Maybe he’s busy,” he said.

Xiaoran slowly turned her head.

“Don’t defend him.”

“I’m not.”

“You said maybe he’s busy.”

“That’s an observation.”

“He’s been busy for four days. Is he conducting research in another country? Has he lost access to electricity? Is his phone in the ocean?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Those are possibilities.”

She stared.

He smiled slightly.

She dropped her forehead onto her folded arms.

“I hate group projects.”

He reached over and moved her coffee away from the edge of the table.

“What exactly has he agreed to do?”

“Research and references. We divided the sections on Monday. He’s supposed to find academic sources for our topic and send them to us.”

“And he hasn’t?”

“He hasn’t even read the messages.”

Yichen glanced at her screen.

The group chat was open. The last message was from Xiaoran, sent that afternoon.

Hi, Kai. Just checking whether you’ve made progress on the references. We need to consolidate everything by tomorrow.

No response.

Yichen leaned back.

“Would you like me to talk to him?”

Xiaoran lifted her head and narrowed her eyes. “About what?”

“His responsibilities.”

She studied his expression.

It was perfectly calm.

Too calm.

“How?”

“Politely.”

She blinked.

Then she laughed.

“You’re going to talk politely to him?”

“Yes.”

“Zhou Yichen, you look like you’re about to negotiate a corporate acquisition.”

“That would probably be easier.”

She laughed harder.

He waited until she had finished.

“Do you want me to?”

Xiaoran looked at him.

She knew Yichen. He wasn’t the sort of person who enjoyed unnecessary confrontation. He rarely raised his voice, and he had a particular way of making people feel that they ought to reconsider their decisions without him having to say much.

Which was precisely why the offer was so tempting.

But she shook her head.

“No. I can handle it.”

“I know.”

“Really.”

“I know, Xiaoran.”

He reached across the table and gently tapped the corner of her laptop.

“But you don’t have to spend your entire evening being angry at someone who isn’t answering.”

She looked down at the group chat, then back at him.

“...Can you help me write one more message?”

“Of course.”

She pushed her laptop toward him.

Yichen read the previous messages, considered them, and began typing.

His version was concise.

Hi, Kai. We need your section and references by 6 p.m. tomorrow so we can complete the final report. If you’re unable to finish it, please let us know tonight so we can redistribute the work. Thank you.

Xiaoran read it, then looked at him.

“That’s very polite.”

“Yes.”

“Very professional.”

“Yes.”

“Very scary.”

He smiled.

“Good.”

She burst out laughing.

The next morning, Dou Kai finally replied.

He sent a single message.

Sorry, guys. Been busy. I’ll do it tonight.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

She was sitting beside Ning outside their faculty building.

Ning read the message over her shoulder.

“That’s it?”

“Apparently.”

“Did he even say what he was busy with?”

“No.”

Ning sighed.

“At least he replied.”

Xiaoran looked at the message again.

Then she forwarded it to Yichen.

He lives.

Yichen replied almost immediately.

Good news.

She sent another message.

He says he’ll do it tonight.

Then let’s see if he does.

She smiled at her phone.

Ning watched her.

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re texting your boyfriend.”

“I’m checking something.”

“Your boyfriend.”

Xiaoran put her phone away.

“Can we please finish the presentation?”

By midnight, Dou Kai had sent nothing. Xiaoran sent one final message, Kai, we’re waiting for your section, please send whatever you have, and then Ning rang her, and by quarter past they had agreed to split the missing section between them and write it themselves. Xiaoran sent Yichen a message.

I think I need you to talk politely to him now.

Yichen was still awake, reading.

His reply came a moment later.

Tomorrow?

Tomorrow.

All right.

Then:

Go to sleep.

She sent him a photograph of her laptop.

I’m suffering.

I can see that.

Do you feel sorry for me?

Very much.

How much?

Enough to buy you breakfast tomorrow.

She smiled.

Accepted.

The following afternoon, Yichen accompanied her to the building where Dou Kai’s next lecture was scheduled to finish.

Xiaoran hadn’t originally intended to bring him.

She had mentioned that she needed to speak to Kai after class, and Yichen had offered to walk with her.

He was carrying his backpack over one shoulder, looking entirely unbothered.

Xiaoran, on the other hand, was nervous.

“Don’t be too harsh.”

“I won’t.”

“Really.”

“I said I’d talk politely.”

“Your definition of polite might be different from mine.”

He glanced down at her.

“Would you prefer I smile?”

She considered it.

“...Maybe.”

His mouth curved.

She immediately looked away.

“Not like that.”

He laughed.

They waited near the corridor.

When Dou Kai finally emerged, Xiaoran stepped forward.

“Kai.”

He turned.

“Oh, Xiaoran.”

“Hi. Do you have a minute?”

“Sure.”

His eyes shifted to Yichen.

“And...?”

“Zhou Yichen,” Yichen introduced himself, offering a polite nod.

Dou Kai nodded back, slightly confused.

Xiaoran explained the situation.

“We’ve finished the rest of the report, but your section is still missing. We had to redistribute the work last night because we couldn’t reach you.”

Kai scratched the back of his neck.

“Yeah, sorry. I’ve been really busy.”

Yichen spoke for the first time.

“That’s understandable. But when you accept a section in a group project, the others plan their work around your contribution.”

His voice was even. Neither unfriendly nor aggressive.

Just clear.

Kai nodded.

“Yeah, I know.”

“Then if you can’t finish it, you should tell them early. It gives everyone a chance to adjust.”

“Right.”

Yichen smiled politely.

“Xiaoran and Ning stayed up late finishing the section you were responsible for. They didn’t have to do that.”

Kai looked at Xiaoran.

“Sorry.”

She nodded.

“Thank you. We just need you to be more responsive next time.”

“Yeah. I understand.”

“Good. Then I think that’s settled,” said Yichen, with another small nod.

It was over in less than three minutes.

No raised voices. No confrontation.

No dramatic speech.

Just a polite conversation.

Dou Kai walked away looking more thoughtful than when he had arrived.

Xiaoran stood beside Yichen.

Then she looked in the direction Kai had disappeared, then back at Yichen.

“...That was it?”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t threaten him?”

“No.”

“You didn’t tell him he was irresponsible?”

“I implied it.”

She stared.

Yichen adjusted the strap of his backpack.

“Politely.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

“You’re unbelievable.”

“Did it help?”

“Yes.”

“Then you’re welcome.”

She slipped her hand into his.

“Thank you.”

He squeezed it.

“Now, about that breakfast.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re still buying?”

“I believe I promised.”

“Then I want something nice.”

“Of course.”

“And dessert.”

“That’s not breakfast.”

“It can be.”

He smiled. “Let’s negotiate.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the next group meeting, Dou Kai arrived first. He had four cups of milk tea in a cardboard tray, one of them half sugar with no pearls, which meant he had asked someone, and a printed version of his section, which was late and also, to everyone’s surprise, good.

“I redid the references. And I checked yours. Two of the page numbers were wrong,” he said, to the table rather than to anyone.

Ning took her milk tea and looked at Xiaoran over the top of it.

They presented on Friday. Dou Kai did the first five minutes and didn’t look at his notes once. Afterward, in the corridor, while the others were arguing about where to eat, he fell into step beside Xiaoran and said, “Is your boyfriend in Business?”

“Yes.”

“He’s terrifying.”

“He was being polite,” Xiaoran said.

“I know. That’s what was terrifying,” said Dou Kai, with feeling.

They got an A minus. She sent Yichen a photograph of the mark, and he replied with a photograph of a breakfast menu, with the desserts circled.

She laughed as they walked away.

And, as far as Xiaoran was concerned, Zhou Yichen’s ability to sound perfectly pleasant while making someone reconsider their entire attitude toward teamwork was one of his most useful talents.

chapters.desc: One street interview, a million views, and a boyfriend who hasn’t posted anything in months.
chapters.title: The Girl on Everyone’s Feed
chapters.epigraph: “Please be kind to her.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Lin Xiaoran did wrong was answer a stranger’s question.

The second thing she did wrong was answer it so sweetly that half the internet fell in love with her.

And the third thing—though she wouldn’t discover this until much later—was forgetting that her boyfriend was also on the internet.

It happened on an ordinary Thursday afternoon.

Xiaoran had just finished a group meeting at the university and was walking toward a nearby shopping street. She had her earphones in, a canvas tote bag hanging from one shoulder, and was thinking about whether she should buy milk tea before going home.

She was halfway through checking the menu on her phone when someone approached her.

“Excuse me, miss?”

She looked up.

A young man stood in front of her, holding a microphone and smiling at a camera operator behind him.

“Would you mind answering a quick question for a video?”

Xiaoran pulled out one earphone.

“Me?”

“Yes. It’ll only take a minute.”

She glanced at the camera.

“Oh. Is this for a university project?”

The interviewer laughed.

“Something like that. I’m making street interview videos. Are you comfortable being filmed?”

Xiaoran hesitated, then nodded.

“Sure.”

“Great. I’m Mai Lang.”

He didn’t introduce his channel name, and Xiaoran didn’t recognize him anyway. She wasn’t particularly active on social media anymore. She used it to message friends, look at things she liked, and occasionally post photographs. She rarely watched interview videos or followed online personalities.

Mai Lang was, in fact, one of the most popular creators in the country in the category of social commentary and public knowledge. His channel had several million subscribers, and his street interviews often went viral because he asked ordinary people questions about complicated social issues.

Today, the topic was financial literacy.

“Let’s start with something simple. Do you think young people should be financially responsible for their parents once they start earning money?” he said.

Xiaoran blinked.

“Oh. That’s not simple.”

The interviewer laughed.

“Why not?”

She thought about it.

“I think they should care about their parents, but I don’t think responsibility should automatically mean paying for everything.”

Mai Lang nodded.

“Can you explain?”

Xiaoran shifted her tote bag higher on her shoulder.

“Well, parents and children are family, so naturally we should help each other. But I think it depends on the situation. Some parents are financially stable, some aren’t. Some children can afford to help, some are still struggling themselves.”

She paused, then added earnestly,

“I think it’s important to help without making either person feel like a burden.”

The interviewer looked interested.

“That’s a thoughtful answer. What if the parents sacrificed a lot to raise their children?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Then I think we should appreciate that. But I don’t think love should become a debt that has to be repaid with a fixed amount of money.”

Mai Lang’s eyebrows lifted slightly.

“Interesting. So you disagree with the idea that children owe their parents?”

“Not exactly.”

She frowned, searching for the right words.

“I think we owe them love and respect, but not necessarily a lifetime of financial repayment. Otherwise, it might make the relationship feel like a transaction.”

There was a brief pause.

Then Mai Lang smiled.

“That’s actually a very good distinction.”

Xiaoran smiled back, a little shy.

“Thank you.”

He moved to the next question.

“Second question. If your partner earns significantly more than you, should they pay for more things in the relationship?”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re asking me difficult questions today.”

“That’s the point.”

She thought about it.

“I think it depends on what both people are comfortable with. If one person earns more, it makes sense that they might contribute more sometimes. But I wouldn’t want someone to feel that they have to pay for everything just because they can.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to be with someone, not become their financial responsibility.”

The camera operator made a small sound of amusement.

Mai Lang smiled.

“And what if your partner insists?”

Xiaoran’s expression turned thoughtful.

“Then I’d probably tell him I appreciate it, but I still want to contribute in ways I can. Maybe I can’t pay for the same things, but I can still plan something, cook, remember what he likes, or do something meaningful.”

She smiled a little.

“I think being generous should be something you do because you love someone, not because you want to prove that you can afford them.”

Mai Lang nodded slowly.

“That’s a lovely answer.”

Xiaoran ducked her head.

“Thank you.”

He asked two more questions, one about online misinformation and another about whether universities should teach practical financial skills.

Xiaoran answered with the same thoughtful sincerity. She wasn’t trying to sound clever. She occasionally stumbled over her words, laughed at herself, and asked the interviewer to repeat one question because she wanted to make sure she understood it correctly.

At the end, Mai Lang lowered the microphone.

“Thank you for your time. Can I ask your name?”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“Are you a student?”

“Yes. I study Media.”

“That’s fitting.”

She laughed.

“Thank you. I was actually quite nervous.”

“You didn’t look nervous.”

“I was trying not to.”

He laughed.

“Well, thank you, Xiaoran. Have a nice day.”

“You too!”

She gave a small wave to the camera and continued walking.

She didn’t think much of it.

By the time she reached the milk tea shop, she had already forgotten most of the conversation.

✦ ✦ ✦

The video was uploaded that evening.

Its title was:

“Do Young People Owe Their Parents Everything? I Asked Strangers on the Street.”

Xiaoran appeared around the middle.

The first few minutes showed different people giving their opinions. Some were confident, some were uncertain, and a few gave answers that sparked immediate debate, then the video reached her.

The camera showed a girl in a cream cardigan, her hair falling loosely around her shoulders. She was holding a canvas tote bag, looking slightly surprised when the microphone was offered.

The interviewer asked his first question.

She blinked.

“Oh. That’s not simple.”

The comments started there.

And then she answered.

She didn’t make a speech. She simply explained her thoughts, occasionally smiling, her expression changing as she tried to find the right words.

By the time the video reached the second question, the comment section had begun to fill.

Top comments:

- “Wait, who is this girl? She’s so pretty.”
- “Her face is so unique. Not the usual influencer pretty. I can’t explain it.”
- “She’s cute but her answers are actually so mature.”
- “The way she pauses to think before answering. I love her.”
- “Her voice is so sweet???”
- “She looks like she doesn’t even know she’s being filmed.”
- “I came for the social commentary and stayed for the girl in the cream cardigan.”
- “Can we get her full interview?”
- “The boyfriend who gets to hear her talk every day must be winning at life.”

One comment received thousands of likes:

“She has the kind of pretty that makes you want to listen to whatever she’s saying.”

Another:

“She’s not trying to sound intelligent. She’s just genuinely thoughtful. That’s even more attractive.”

The video gained traction overnight.

By morning, it had been reposted across several platforms.

And Lin Xiaoran had absolutely no idea.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:17 AM, her phone began vibrating.

She was in bed, still half asleep.

The first message was from Chen Yuhao.

Yuhao: XIAORAN.

Then another.

Yuhao: WAKE UP.

Then a video.

She opened it.

The thumbnail showed a familiar face.

Her own.

Xiaoran sat upright.

“...Huh?”

She watched the video, then watched it again, then opened the comment section.

Her eyes widened.

“WHAT?”

She immediately called Yuhao.

He answered on the first ring.

“Good morning, celebrity!”

“YUHAO!”

He burst out laughing.

“Yes, yes, I know. I know. I watched the whole thing.”

“Why am I on the internet?”

“Because you went outside.”

“That’s not funny!”

“It is a little funny.”

She scrolled through the comments.

“Why are there so many comments?”

“Because the internet has discovered you.”

She looked at the view count, then looked again.

It had already crossed a million.

“Yuhao.”

“Hm?”

“Is this normal?”

“For you? No. For a viral video? Yes.”

She groaned.

“Why didn’t I know he was famous?”

Yuhao laughed until she had to move the phone away from her ear.

“Wait. You didn’t know who Mai Lang was?”

“No!”

“Xiaoran, he’s huge.”

“How was I supposed to know?”

“You’re literally a Media student!”

“That doesn’t mean I know every person on the internet!”

Yuhao was still laughing.

“Meilin is going to call you. Prepare yourself.”

As if summoned, another call appeared.

Tang Meilin calling…

Xiaoran answered.

“Meilin!”

“I’ve seen it.”

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not laughing.”

She sounded suspiciously amused.

“Meilin.”

“Okay, I’m laughing a little.”

Xiaoran flopped backward onto her pillow.

“I didn’t do anything!”

“That’s why it’s funny. You went out to buy milk tea and accidentally became a public figure.”

“I just answered questions!”

“Yes. And apparently you answered them beautifully.”

Meilin paused.

Then her voice became a little more serious.

“Actually, I liked your answers. Especially the part about love not being a debt.”

Xiaoran smiled faintly.

“Really?”

“Yes. You sounded like yourself.”

That made her feel a little better.

Until Meilin added:

“Also, you’re very pretty.”

Xiaoran covered her face.

“Please stop.”

“No. I’m going to enjoy this.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By lunchtime, her tagged account had become a small disaster.

Xiaoran had never been particularly active online. Her account was public, but most of her posts were ordinary photographs: campus, food, friends, trips, the occasional selfie, and a few pictures of Yichen.

She had around a thousand followers.

Now the number was climbing so quickly that she stopped checking.

People had found her account through the video.

They were liking old posts, commenting on photographs from months ago, and following her.

Some were polite.

Some were enthusiastic.

Some were strange.

Her direct messages were worse.

“Hi, I saw you in Mai Lang’s video. You’re really beautiful.”

“Are you single?”

“I’d love to get to know you.”

“You’re my ideal type.”

“Can I take you out for coffee?”

“I think we would get along. You seem very sweet.”

She stared at the screen, then closed the app.

Then opened it again because she wanted to see whether it had stopped.

It hadn’t.

She sent a screenshot to Meilin.

Xiaoran: Why are strangers asking me out?

Meilin: Because they have eyes.

Xiaoran: I don’t know them.

Meilin: They don’t know you either. That’s usually how strangers work.

Xiaoran: I’m blocking everyone.

Meilin: Good idea.

A few minutes later, another message arrived.

Meilin: By the way, don’t forget to tell your boyfriend.

Xiaoran paused.

Oh.

Her boyfriend.

She hadn’t told Yichen yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen found out at 12:36 PM.

Not from Xiaoran.

From Chen Yuhao.

Yichen was in the university sports facility. He had just finished a workout and was sitting on a bench, drinking water, when Yuhao sent him the video from his own campus two provinces away.

Yuhao: Your girlfriend is famous.

Yichen opened the link.

He watched the video from beginning to end.

At first, he was simply amused.

There was Xiaoran, standing on a busy street, looking slightly bewildered as someone held a microphone toward her.

He recognized the cardigan.

He recognized the canvas bag.

He recognized the expression she made when she was thinking hard about something.

Then he heard her answer the question about financial responsibility.

His mouth curved.

“That’s Xiaoran.”

His teammate glanced over.

He continued watching, then came the question about relationships and money.

Yichen leaned back against the bench.

He listened to her talk about wanting to contribute, about generosity, about being with someone rather than becoming their financial responsibility.

His expression softened.

He knew those things about her already.

He knew she disliked feeling indebted. He knew she wanted to be independent, even when he offered to help. He knew she appreciated thoughtful gestures more than expensive ones.

He watched the interviewer compliment her.

Then he opened the comments.

The first few made him smile.

The next few made him pause.

And then he reached the comment section.

He scrolled.

“She’s so pretty.”

“Her boyfriend must be the luckiest man alive.”

“I want to marry her.”

“Please tell me she’s single.”

“Someone find her account.”

Yichen’s thumb stopped.

He looked at the screen, then at the video again, then back at the comments.

Fang Ze, on the next bench, glanced over.

“What’s up?”

Yichen locked his phone.

“Nothing.”

Fang Ze narrowed his eyes.

“You don’t look like nothing.”

Yichen took another sip of water.

“My girlfriend went viral.”

Fang Ze immediately leaned over.

“Your girlfriend?”

Yichen handed him the phone.

Fang Ze watched a few seconds, then whistled.

“Oh. She’s pretty.”

Yichen looked at him.

Fang Ze raised both hands.

“Respectfully.”

Yichen took his phone back.

“Good.”

He stood, picked up his bag, and walked away.

Fang Ze watched him go, then looked at the phone.

“...He’s jealous.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 1:05 PM, Xiaoran finally sent him a message.

Xiaoran: Yichen.

He was already looking at his phone.

Yichen: Hm?

Xiaoran: Have you seen something strange today?

Yichen: Define strange.

Xiaoran: I think I accidentally became famous.

He smiled.

Yichen: I noticed.

Xiaoran: YOU SAW IT?

Yichen: Yuhao sent it to me.

Xiaoran: I didn’t know that man was famous!

Yichen: I gathered that.

Xiaoran: I was just buying milk tea.

Yichen: An eventful milk tea trip.

She sent him a crying sticker, then another message.

Xiaoran: People are sending me messages.

Yichen: I saw.

Xiaoran: It’s weird.

Yichen: You can ignore them. Block anyone who makes you uncomfortable.

Xiaoran: I know. I just didn’t expect it.

Yichen: Are you all right?

She looked at the question.

Xiaoran: Yes. Just a little overwhelmed.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: I’ll come see you after practice.

She smiled.

Xiaoran: Okay.

Then, because she was curious:

Xiaoran: Are you embarrassed that your girlfriend is famous?

Yichen looked at the message.

He smiled slowly.

Yichen: No.

A few seconds passed.

Yichen: I’m more concerned that so many people seem to think they have a chance.

Xiaoran stared, then burst out laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

He arrived at her apartment that evening.

Xiaoran opened the door wearing comfortable home clothes, her hair loosely tied up. She looked relieved when she saw him.

“Yichen!”

He stepped inside and set his bag down.

“Hello.”

She immediately wrapped her arms around his waist.

He held her, kissing her hair.

“How’s the celebrity?”

“Don’t call me that.”

“All right.”

He pulled back slightly.

“How’s my girlfriend?”

She smiled.

“Better.”

He touched her cheek.

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She took his hand and led him to the sofa.

“Look.”

She showed him her account.

Her follower count had increased dramatically. There were hundreds of new comments, and her inbox was still full.

Yichen scrolled through a few messages.

His expression remained composed.

Until he reached one.

“You’re so beautiful. I wish I could be your boyfriend.”

He read it, then another.

“If you’re single, I’d love to take you on a date.”

Then another.

“Your smile is addictive. Please reply.”

He handed the phone back.

“Quite enthusiastic.”

Then, more carefully: “Are you reading the comments at night?”

She knew exactly which night he meant. Two in the morning, a screen in the dark, two weeks of skipped meals afterwards.

“No, I read them at lunch, with Ning, and Ning says something rude about each one,” she said.

His shoulders went down a fraction. “Good.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Right?”

“Very.”

She studied his face.

“Are you upset?”

“No.”

“Really?”

He looked at her.

“Why would I be upset?”

“Because people are sending me messages.”

“They’re allowed to find you pretty.”

She blinked.

“You’re not jealous?”

Yichen considered that.

“I’m not particularly happy about strangers asking my girlfriend out.”

Her eyes brightened.

“So you are jealous!”

He smiled faintly.

“Did you want me to be?”

“No!”

“Then I won’t.”

She laughed.

He leaned back against the sofa.

“Although I do have a question.”

“What?”

“Why haven’t you told people you’re taken?”

She looked at him.

“I haven’t even had time to understand what’s happening!”

“I know.”

“And I don’t usually post relationship things.”

“I know that too.”

She tilted her head.

“Would you like me to?”

“Only if you want to.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I don’t mind.”

He nodded.

She hesitated. “But I don’t want to make a big announcement. That would be embarrassing.”

“Then don’t.”

She considered him.

“You’re being very reasonable.”

“Should I not be?”

“No, but...”

She leaned closer.

“Are you sure you’re not jealous?”

He looked at her.

Then he reached up and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“I’ve been your boyfriend for four years. I don’t think a few strangers in your inbox are going to change that.”

Her heart softened.

He continued, quieter:

“But I’d be lying if I said I enjoyed reading those messages.”

She giggled.

“You liked hearing that.”

He gave her a small, knowing smile.

“Are you happy now?”

“Very.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair.

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first post came at 9:42 PM.

It wasn’t a dramatic announcement.

It wasn’t a long caption.

It wasn’t even a photograph of their faces.

Yichen posted a story.

A photograph taken that evening.

Xiaoran was sitting beside him on the sofa, holding a cup of tea. Her face was turned toward him, and she was laughing at something outside the frame.

The photograph was slightly candid, the lighting warm.

His hand was visible in the corner, resting on her knee.

The caption was simple.

“My favorite person. Four years and counting.”

He tagged her.

Xiaoran saw it a few seconds later.

She looked up from her phone.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You posted me.”

“Yes.”

“On your story.”

“That’s generally where stories go.”

She laughed.

“You’re so annoying.”

He glanced at her.

“Do you want me to delete it?”

She looked at the photograph again.

Her smile softened.

“No.”

“Good.”

She reposted it.

With a small heart.

She thought that would be the end of it.

It wasn’t.

Within minutes, people began replying to his story.

Some were mutual friends congratulating them.

Some were surprised to learn she had a boyfriend.

Others were simply curious.

But a surprising number of people continued to send Xiaoran messages.

One person even replied to her repost:

“Oh, so that’s your friend? He’s handsome.”

Xiaoran stared at it, then turned toward Yichen.

“Yichen.”

“What?”

“People aren’t getting it.”

He glanced at her phone.

He read the reply.

Then his eyebrows lifted slightly.

“Apparently not.”

She showed him another message.

“You two look cute together! Is he your brother?”

Yichen looked at her.

For a moment, neither of them spoke.

Then he laughed.

Xiaoran covered her face.

“Why would they think you’re my brother?”

He shrugged.

“Perhaps I look responsible.”

“That’s not the point!”

He took her phone gently.

“May I?”

She watched him.

“What are you doing?”

“Clarifying something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 10:16 PM, Zhou Yichen posted on his feed for the first time in several months.

The photograph was simple.

It showed the two of them standing together at the riverside during their anniversary. Xiaoran was smiling at the camera, while Yichen was looking at her instead.

His arm was around her waist.

Her hand rested against his chest.

The little panda bracelet he had given her that day was on the wrist against his chest.

The caption read:

Four years with Lin Xiaoran.

She’s not just the girl in the interview. She’s the person I come home to, the person I want beside me, and the person I keep choosing.

Please be kind to her.

He tagged her account, then posted it.

Xiaoran stared at his screen, then at him, then back at his screen.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He placed his phone down.

“Yes?”

“You posted on your feed.”

“I did.”

“You haven’t posted anything in months.”

“I know.”

“And now you posted me.”

“Yes.”

She stared at him.

Then her mouth slowly curved.

“You’re claiming me.”

He looked at her.

His expression was calm, but there was a small smile at the corner of his mouth.

“Is that a problem?”

She shook her head, cheeks growing warm.

“No.”

“Good.”

She leaned closer.

“You’re a little jealous.”

“A little.”

She laughed.

“Only a little?”

He considered her.

Then reached for her waist and drew her closer.

“Would you like a more honest answer?”

Her smile widened.

“Yes.”

He lowered his voice.

“I don’t mind people knowing you’re beautiful. I don’t mind them appreciating your answers or finding you interesting.”

His thumb brushed lightly against her waist.

“But I don’t particularly enjoy watching strangers line up to ask whether you’re available.”

Xiaoran giggled.

“Why?”

“Because you’re not.”

Her heart gave a small, ridiculous flutter.

He continued, his voice still gentle.

“And because I happen to be very happy being the man you chose.”

She looked at him.

Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“You’re the only one I want.”

His expression softened.

“I know.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re supposed to say you want me too.”

“I want you too.”

She beamed, then glanced at his post again.

“Wait. You wrote ‘the person I come home to.’”

“Mhm.”

“That’s very romantic.”

She read it again, smiling to herself.

Then she looked at him.

“Can I comment?”

“Of course.”

She opened the comment section and typed.

Xiaoran: The person who steals your food and your ice cream.

Yichen laughed.

He replied:

Yichen: And somehow still the person I love most.

Xiaoran’s face turned pink.

She immediately locked her phone.

“Okay. Enough.”

He laughed.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re blushing.”

“I’m not.”

He leaned closer.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

He crooked a finger at her.

She moved toward him willingly.

He kissed her temple, then her cheek.

She smiled.

Then, because she was feeling particularly affectionate, she wrapped her arms around his neck and kissed him.

Yichen returned it, one hand settling at her waist.

When she pulled away, she was smiling.

“Happy?”

He looked at her.

“Very.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, the internet had found the post.

The comment section was full of congratulations, surprise, and people realizing that the handsome man in the photograph wasn’t merely a friend.

“WAIT SHE HAS A BOYFRIEND?”

“FOUR YEARS????”

“He’s so handsome too. They’re actually such a beautiful couple.”

“The way he’s looking at her in the photo. Oh, he’s gone.”

“He posted because people weren’t getting the hint, I’m crying.”

“The caption is so boyfriend-coded.”

“She answered a street interview and accidentally gave us a love story.”

Yuhao sent the post to their group chat.

Yuhao: HAHAHAHAHAHA.

Meilin: Finally, the public has been informed.

Yuhao: Yichen really went from one story to a whole feed announcement.

Meilin: Four years of being her boyfriend. He was probably waiting for a reason.

Xiaoran: YOU TWO ARE SO ANNOYING.

Yuhao: Celebrity, please don’t forget your old friends.

Xiaoran: I’m blocking both of you.

Meilin: You won’t.

Xiaoran: I might.

Yuhao: Tell your famous boyfriend we approve.

Xiaoran laughed so much she had to put her phone down.

Yichen, sitting beside her, looked over.

“What happened?”

“Yuhao and Meilin.”

“That explains it.”

She showed him the messages.

He read them, then shook his head.

“They haven’t changed.”

“Never.”

She leaned against his shoulder.

After a moment, she asked, “Do you think this will last long?”

“The attention?”

She nodded.

“Probably not forever.”

“Will people keep recognizing me?”

“Some might.”

She made a small face.

“I hope they don’t ask me difficult questions again.”

“You answered them well.”

“I was nervous.”

“I know.”

She looked up.

“Did you like my answers?”

He looked at her.

“I liked listening to you.”

Her expression softened.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

He brushed his fingers through her hair.

“You weren’t trying to impress anyone. You were just explaining what you believed.”

“That’s because I didn’t know who he was.”

Yichen laughed.

“Perhaps that’s why you were so comfortable.”

She thought about it, then sighed.

“I should have asked for his channel name.”

“Why?”

“So I could have known I was being filmed by someone famous.”

He looked at her, amused.

“Would you have answered differently?”

She considered it.

“No.”

“Then it wouldn’t have made much difference.”

She smiled.

“True.”

A moment passed.

Then she suddenly sat up.

“Wait.”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“Your post.”

“Hm?”

“You said I’m the person you come home to.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him with a suspicious little smile.

“Does that mean I can come over whenever I want?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Xiaoran, you already do.”

“Does that mean I can keep my things at your apartment?”

“You already have things there.”

She brightened.

“More things?”

He looked at her, then smiled.

“How many things are we talking about?”

She giggled.

“Maybe a little drawer.”

“A drawer?”

“Just one.”

He nodded thoughtfully.

“All right.”

Her eyes widened.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She immediately hugged his arm.

“You’re the best!”

He kissed her temple.

“Although I suspect one drawer will eventually become three.”

She looked up innocently.

“Why would you think that?”

“Experience.”

She laughed.

Then she settled against him again, perfectly content.

Her phone vibrated once more.

Another notification.

Another stranger.

Another comment.

She glanced at it, then turned the screen off and put it aside.

Yichen noticed.

“Not checking?”

“No.”

“Why?”

She tucked herself closer to him.

“Because I’m already sitting next to the person I want to talk to.”

He looked down at her.

His expression softened into that slow, familiar smile that always made her feel a little flustered.

“That’s a good decision.”

She smiled.

Then, after a few seconds, added:

“Also, can you buy me milk tea?”

He laughed.

“Ah. Back to normal.”

“What?”

“My famous girlfriend.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He kissed her hair before she could complain.

And somewhere online, people were still discovering Lin Xiaoran.

But the girl herself was much more interested in stealing her boyfriend’s drink.

chapters.desc: Winter break at her parents’ house. Her mother has photographs, stories, and absolutely no mercy.
chapters.title: The Little Warrior
chapters.epigraph: “Good night, little warrior.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had always known that Lin Xiaoran was brave.

He knew it from the way she never hesitated to speak up when someone was treated unfairly. From the way she could be stubborn about the smallest things, yet surprisingly firm when something genuinely mattered. From the way she would defend her friends even when she was clearly outnumbered.

He had seen her argue with people twice her size, stand up for strangers, and get herself into trouble because she couldn’t stand watching someone being bullied.

He sometimes teased her about having a little temper.

She would insist she didn’t.

But he had never really known where that part of her came from.

Until one afternoon in her hometown, while Xiaoran was upstairs looking for an old photo album, her mother told him stories about the little girl she used to be.

And Yichen discovered that his girlfriend had been a warrior long before he ever met her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened on their second day in Xiaoran’s hometown, the small town four hours from the city where she had lived until she was twelve, and where her grandparents’ house still stood at the end of a lane. Her parents had driven them down a week before New Year, before the relatives arrived, and Yichen had been given the guest room at the top of the stairs.

Her mother had been preparing fruit in the kitchen while her father was outside talking to a neighbor. Xiaoran had gone upstairs to find an old album her mother wanted to show him.

Yichen was sitting at the dining table, helping her mother arrange some fruit.

“Yichen, you can leave those there,” her mother said.

“It’s alright, Auntie. I can help.”

Her mother smiled.

“You’re always so considerate.”

He smiled politely.

She sat opposite him, looking at the neatly arranged fruit.

“Actually, I wanted to show you something.”

She reached for her phone.

“Wait a moment.”

Yichen looked up.

“What is it?”

“Some pictures of Xiaoran when she was little. I had all the old albums scanned last spring, so now I can embarrass her anywhere.”

He laughed.

“I’d like to see them.”

Her mother smiled in satisfaction.

“I thought you would.”

She opened her photo gallery and began scrolling.

The first picture showed a little girl with short hair, wearing a yellow dress. She was standing in front of a birthday cake, her cheeks covered in cream.

Yichen immediately recognized her eyes.

“That’s Xiaoran?”

Her mother laughed.

“Yes. She was four.”

“She looks very happy.”

“She was. And very naughty.”

Yichen smiled.

Her mother swiped to the next picture.

A little Xiaoran stood in a park, holding a plastic sword with both hands. Her expression was extremely serious.

Yichen laughed.

“What happened here?”

“Ah. She was pretending to be a hero.” Her mother shook her head affectionately.

“Really?”

“She used to play that game all the time. She would say she was protecting everyone.”

Yichen looked at the picture again.

The little girl had one hand on her waist, her chin lifted, and an expression that looked strangely familiar.

He smiled.

“She’s still like that.”

Her mother laughed.

“Exactly.”

Then she continued scrolling.

And the stories began.

“Xiaoran was always very protective of other children,” her mother said.

She showed him a picture of Xiaoran standing beside another little girl.

“She was in kindergarten here. This little girl was her friend.”

Yichen looked at the picture.

“What happened?”

“Her friend was being bullied by some older children.”

Her mother sighed, though there was affection in her expression.

“Xiaoran was only five or six. She saw them taking her friend’s toys and making her cry.”

Yichen listened.

“She went over and demanded that they return everything. Of course, the older children didn’t listen. They laughed at her.”

Her mother smiled.

“And then she stood in front of her friend and told them they weren’t allowed to bully her anymore.”

Yichen chuckled.

“That sounds like her.”

“She was so small. One of the boys was nearly twice her size.”

Her mother shook her head.

“I was watching from a distance. I thought she would get frightened and come back.”

Instead, Xiaoran had planted herself in front of the boy and refused to move.

“When I finally went over, she was holding her friend’s hand and telling the boys that she would call their teacher.”

Yichen smiled.

“Did she?”

“Of course. She dragged the teacher over herself.”

Her mother laughed.

“She didn’t even wait for me.”

Yichen looked at the picture again.

A little girl with round cheeks and short hair.

He could almost imagine her tiny voice, probably trembling with anger, demanding that someone behave properly.

“She was very brave,” he said.

Her mother nodded.

“Yes. But sometimes she was too brave for her own good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother scrolled again.

Then she stopped at a photograph.

It showed Xiaoran sitting on a low wall outside a small building. Her hair was messy, her knees were dusty, and she was holding a small ice cream.

Yichen looked at the picture.

“Did she fall?”

Her mother smiled.

“She had just fought with some boys.”

Yichen raised his eyebrows.

“Fought?”

“Not exactly a fight. Well…”

She paused, reconsidering.

“Actually, it was quite a fight.”

Yichen laughed.

“What happened?”

Her mother put the phone down for a moment.

“There was a boy in the neighborhood who liked bullying younger children. He would take their snacks, push them around, and sometimes make them cry. Xiaoran had complained about him several times.”

Yichen listened.

“One afternoon, she saw him pushing a younger boy near the playground. The little boy fell, and the boy laughed at him.”

Her mother’s expression became more serious.

“Xiaoran told him to stop. He ignored her. Then he pushed her too.”

Yichen’s smile disappeared.

“She fell?”

“Yes. She scraped her palms and knees.”

Her mother sighed.

“But she got up immediately.”

She shook her head.

“I remember it very clearly. She was crying, but she was trying so hard not to show it.”

Yichen looked at the photograph.

“What happened next?”

“She stood in front of him again. She told him that if he wanted to bully someone, he should bully someone his own size.”

Her mother laughed.

“Imagine that. A little girl with scraped knees telling a boy to find someone his own size.”

Yichen couldn’t help smiling.

Then her mother continued.

“The boy laughed at her. He told her she was already hurt and should go home.”

She paused.

“But Xiaoran didn’t move.”

Yichen looked at her.

“She stayed?”

“Until the boy left.”

Her mother shook her head.

“Afterward, she took the younger boy to his home. She even told his mother what happened.”

Yichen was quiet.

He could picture it too clearly.

A small girl, hurt and frightened, refusing to leave until she knew someone else was safe.

“Did you scold her?” he asked.

Her mother smiled.

“Of course. I was worried sick.”

She looked at the photograph again.

“But she didn’t understand why I was upset. She kept saying, ‘Mom, if I left, he would bully him again.’”

Yichen lowered his eyes.

Something warm and unfamiliar settled in his chest.

He wasn’t surprised that Xiaoran had been like this.

But hearing it from someone who had watched her grow up made the image feel different.

He was beginning to understand that her courage wasn’t something she had developed as she grew older.

It had always been there.

Even when she was too small to understand what courage meant.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then her mother found another picture.

This one was different.

Xiaoran was standing outside a clinic, wearing a pink shirt and holding a small bandage.

Her mother laughed as soon as she saw it.

“Oh, this one.”

Yichen looked at the picture.

“What happened?”

Her mother shook her head.

“This girl…”

She looked at him.

“Do you know that she once tried to scare a bully while her own foot was bleeding?”

Yichen blinked.

“Her foot?”

“Yes.”

She leaned back.

“This happened when she was about eight.”

Yichen put down the fruit knife he had been holding.

Her mother continued.

“There was a group of children who liked bullying a younger boy near the old playground. They would chase him away whenever he tried to play with them. Sometimes they would deliberately kick his things away.”

She shook her head.

“Xiaoran had already warned them several times. One day, she saw them surrounding him again.”

Yichen listened carefully.

“She ran over. There was a broken piece of tile near the playground, and she stepped on it while trying to get between them.”

Yichen’s eyebrows drew together.

“Did it cut her?”

“Quite badly. The sole of her foot was bleeding.”

He looked at the photograph again.

“But she didn’t tell anyone?”

Her mother laughed, although there was a hint of exasperation in it.

“No. That’s the ridiculous part.”

She explained that Xiaoran had noticed the blood almost immediately.

But the boy she was confronting had already begun laughing at her.

He told her she couldn’t even stand properly, so how could she stop him?

“And what did she do?” Yichen asked.

Her mother shook her head.

“She lifted her foot slightly, hid the injured part behind her other leg, and stood there with the most frightening expression she could manage.”

Yichen stared at her.

“While her foot was bleeding?”

“Yes!”

Her mother laughed.

“She told him, ‘You’d better leave before I get angry.’”

Yichen lowered his head.

A quiet laugh escaped him.

He could almost see Xiaoran doing exactly that.

Her mother continued, “The boy hesitated because she looked so serious. She was pale, and her eyes were full of tears, but she wouldn’t let him see that she was hurt.”

“Did he leave?”

“He did. Eventually, another child ran to get an adult, and the boys scattered.”

Her mother sighed.

“When I arrived, she was still standing there. Her foot had blood on it, and she was trying to pretend nothing had happened.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“What did you do?”

“I carried her to the clinic.”

Her mother looked at him.

“And do you know what she said?”

He shook his head.

“She asked me not to tell the younger boy she was hurt.”

Yichen looked up.

“Why?”

“Because she didn’t want him to feel guilty. She told me he had already been frightened enough.”

For a moment, neither of them spoke.

Her mother smiled sadly.

“She was so little. She didn’t know how to protect herself properly, but she was always thinking about how to protect someone else.”

Yichen looked down at the photograph.

A small pink-shirted girl, holding a bandage, smiling at the camera.

He wondered whether she had been smiling because the pain was gone, or because she had finally convinced everyone she was fine.

“Did she always hide her injuries?”

The question came out before Yichen realized he had asked it.

Her mother looked at him.

“Quite often.”

She scrolled through more pictures.

“Once, she fell off her bicycle while trying to help another child. She scraped her elbow and didn’t tell us until we noticed blood on her sleeve.”

Another picture.

“She got bitten by a dog when she was trying to pull a smaller child away from it. Thankfully, it was a very small dog, and the injury wasn’t serious. But she was more concerned about whether the little boy had been frightened.”

Another.

“She once came home with a swollen finger because she had tried to stop two children from pulling at each other’s schoolbags.”

Yichen listened.

He wasn’t smiling anymore.

Her mother noticed.

“Don’t look so worried. These things happened when she was young.”

“I know.”

“She grew up. She’s much more sensible now.”

Yichen nodded.

But he knew Xiaoran.

He knew how she sometimes brushed off a small injury.

How she would say she was fine before anyone had even asked.

How she could be more concerned about someone else’s discomfort than her own.

He had once watched her scrape her knee and immediately stand up, insisting that it didn’t hurt.

He remembered gently cleaning the wound while she complained that he was making a big deal out of nothing.

He had thought she was simply stubborn.

Her mother had told him so herself, at the top of four flights of stairs on moving day: she’ll tell you she’s fine when she isn’t. He’d thought it was a mother worrying. Then he’d watched it happen the week she got sick and tidied her studio instead of lying down, and again the fortnight she skipped meals and told him she wasn’t hungry.

Now he wondered how many times that little girl had learned to hide pain because she believed she needed to stay standing.

Her mother laughed.

“Actually, there’s another story.”

Yichen looked up.

“Another one?”

“Yes. This one is funny.”

She showed him a picture of Xiaoran wearing a red cape.

He smiled.

“Another hero?”

Her mother nodded.

“She organized the children in our neighborhood.”

“Organized them?”

“She made them form a group.”

Yichen laughed.

“What kind of group?”

“She called it the Neighborhood Protection Team.”

He laughed harder.

Her mother continued, clearly enjoying herself.

“She assigned everyone roles. One person was responsible for watching the playground. Another was supposed to report anyone bullying younger children. She even made them promise not to leave their friends behind.”

Yichen shook his head, smiling.

“How old was she?”

“Maybe seven.”

He laughed again.

“And did they listen?”

“Some did. Others just wanted to play.”

Her mother smiled.

“But she took it very seriously. She made everyone line up and gave them instructions.”

She turned to Yichen.

“Your girlfriend was a very strict little leader,” she said.

Yichen looked at the picture.

The little Xiaoran was standing in front of several children, her hands on her hips.

He could almost hear her.

You have to listen to me. Otherwise, how can we protect everyone?

He smiled.

“She’s still a leader sometimes.”

Her mother laughed.

“Yes. I can imagine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At that moment, footsteps came down the stairs.

“Mom? Where’s the photo album?”

Xiaoran appeared in the doorway.

She stopped when she saw the two of them.

Her mother was holding her phone.

Yichen was smiling.

A particular kind of smile.

She narrowed her eyes.

“What are you doing?”

Her mother looked up innocently.

“Showing Yichen your childhood pictures.”

Xiaoran froze.

“Which pictures?”

“Your childhood pictures.”

“Mom.”

Her mother smiled.

“What?”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

He looked back at her.

His expression was calm, but his eyes were full of amusement.

She immediately became suspicious.

“What did she tell you?”

“Nothing much.”

Her mother laughed.

“Nothing much? I told him everything!”

Xiaoran’s face changed.

“Mom!”

Her mother started counting on her fingers.

“I told him about the kindergarten incident, the playground, the Neighborhood Protection Team—”

“Mom!”

“And the time you cut your foot—”

“STOP!”

Yichen laughed.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“You heard that?”

“All of it.”

She covered her face.

“Oh my God.”

Her mother continued, completely unbothered.

“What’s wrong? Those were good stories.”

Xiaoran dropped her hands.

“They’re embarrassing!”

“Why? You were very brave.”

“Mom!”

Her mother laughed.

Then she looked at Yichen.

“She was a little warrior.”

Yichen smiled.

“Yes. I can see that.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“Don’t encourage her!”

He raised both hands slightly.

“I’m not.”

“You are!”

Her mother laughed until she had to put her phone down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when her mother went to prepare dinner, Xiaoran dragged Yichen upstairs to her old bedroom, which still had glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling.

She shut the door most of the way, because her grandmother was downstairs, and her grandmother was her grandmother.

Then she turned around.

“Tell me exactly what she said.”

He sat on the end of the bed.

“Everything.”

“Yichen.”

He looked up at her.

“She told me you used to protect other children.”

Xiaoran’s expression shifted.

“That’s all?”

“She also told me you once stood in front of a boy twice your size.”

She looked away.

“And?”

“You scraped your knees and palms. But you refused to leave until the other boy stopped bullying your friend.”

She sat beside him.

“Mom remembers everything.”

He smiled.

“Apparently.”

She was quiet.

Then she muttered, “It wasn’t a big deal.”

Yichen turned toward her.

“Wasn’t it?”

“No.”

“You were five or six.”

She shrugged.

“Children fight.”

He looked at her.

Then he said, “You also had a bleeding foot once.”

Her face immediately turned red.

“Mom told you that too?”

“Yes.”

“That’s so embarrassing.”

He smiled.

“You hid it because you wanted to scare the bully.”

She covered her face.

“Please don’t repeat that.”

He laughed.

Then he reached for her hand.

“Xiaoran.”

She peeked through her fingers.

“What?”

“Why didn’t you tell anyone you were hurt?”

She lowered her hands.

For a moment, she seemed to think about it.

Then she shrugged.

“I don’t know. I just wanted them to leave the other children alone.”

He looked at her.

“You were hurt too.”

“I know.”

“You could have asked an adult for help.”

“I know.”

He didn’t scold her.

He simply held her hand.

She looked at their joined fingers.

Then she smiled a little.

“It’s not like I did it because I wanted to be a hero.”

“What did you want?”

She thought about it.

“I didn’t like seeing people get picked on.”

“I know.”

“That’s all.”

He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“That’s not a small thing.”

She blinked.

He said, “You were little. You didn’t have to be responsible for everyone.”

She looked at him.

“But someone had to stop them.”

He was quiet.

Then he smiled faintly.

“You really haven’t changed much.”

She immediately protested.

“I have!”

“Have you?”

“Yes!”

He raised an eyebrow.

She thought for a second.

Then said, “I’m much more mature now.”

He smiled.

“Of course.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Why do you sound unconvinced?”

“I’m very convinced.”

“Liar.”

He laughed and pulled her closer.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen found himself looking at Xiaoran differently.

Not because he had discovered some extraordinary secret.

He already knew she was kind.

He already knew she was brave.

But now, when she raised her voice at her father for stealing food from her plate, when she complained that her mother was embarrassing her, when she laughed too loudly at a joke, he found himself imagining the little girl she had once been.

The little girl who had planted her feet in front of someone bigger.

The little girl who had stood on an injured foot because she didn’t want a bully to see her weakness.

The little girl who had organized an entire neighborhood protection team.

He wondered how many of those children still remembered her.

He wondered how many people had gone home safely because a small girl had decided she wasn’t going to walk away.

And he wondered how often she had come home, hiding her injuries until someone noticed.

He looked across the dining table.

Xiaoran was laughing at something her father had said.

Her mother placed another piece of food in her bowl.

She complained, but ate it anyway.

She looked happy.

Yichen smiled.

Then her mother glanced at him.

“Yichen, what are you thinking?”

He looked up.

“Nothing, Auntie.”

Her mother smiled.

“Were you surprised by her childhood stories?”

“A little.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Why are you still talking about that?”

Her father laughed.

“Because you were very famous on this lane.”

“Dad!”

Her mother added, “Everyone knew Xiaoran would come running if someone was being bullied.”

Xiaoran lowered her head.

“Can we talk about something else?”

Yichen smiled.

Her mother looked at him.

“She was always like that. Even when she was hurt, she wouldn’t tell us immediately.”

He glanced at Xiaoran.

She was concentrating hard on her rice.

Her father chuckled.

“That’s why her mother used to check her hands and knees whenever she came home.”

Yichen smiled faintly.

“I see. I’ll remember that.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“Remember what?”

He met her eyes.

“To check whether you’re hurt when you say you’re fine.”

She froze.

Her mother laughed.

“Good! You should.”

Xiaoran stared at both of them.

“Why are you forming an alliance?”

Yichen calmly picked up his chopsticks.

“I’m just learning.”

She kicked his foot lightly under the table.

He smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, after everyone else had gone to bed, Xiaoran was sitting cross-legged on the guest-room bed in her pajamas, scrolling through her phone, with the door left open the exact width her grandmother would consider respectable.

Yichen came back from brushing his teeth and found her looking at an old photograph.

He sat beside her.

“What are you looking at?”

She showed him.

It was the picture of her in the red cape.

Yichen smiled.

“Neighborhood Protection Team leader.”

She groaned.

“Please forget that name.”

“Why? I think it’s impressive.”

“I was seven.”

“Very young for a leadership position.”

She laughed and pushed his shoulder.

He took the phone gently.

Then he looked at the photograph again.

“Can I have this?”

She blinked.

“Why?”

“I like it.”

She studied his expression.

“You really like it?”

“Very much.”

“Fine. I’ll send it to you.”

He returned the phone.

Then he took her hand and examined her palm.

She looked at him.

“What are you doing?”

“Checking.”

“Checking what?”

“Whether you have any injuries.”

She laughed.

“Yichen, that was years ago.”

“I know.”

He turned her hand over, then gently kissed her palm.

She became quiet.

He looked at her.

“What?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing.”

He kissed the other palm too.

Then he said, “You don’t have to hide it when you’re hurt now.”

She looked at him.

He said, “You don’t have to pretend you’re not in pain just because you want to protect someone.”

Her expression softened.

“I know.”

“If something happens, tell me.”

She smiled.

“Okay.”

He watched her.

Then she leaned forward and wrapped her arms around his neck.

“Are you worried about me?”

“A little.”

“Why?”

He smiled faintly.

“Because I found out my girlfriend used to challenge boys twice her size while bleeding.”

She laughed against his shoulder.

“That makes me sound ridiculous.”

“It makes you sound brave.”

She lifted her head.

He brushed her hair away from her face.

“But you were still a little girl. You deserved someone looking after you too.”

For a moment, Xiaoran didn’t answer.

Then she hugged him again, a little tighter.

Yichen held her.

He didn’t tell her that he wished he could have known her back then.

That he wished he could have been the person who carried her to the clinic, cleaned her scraped knees, and told her she didn’t need to stand on an injured foot to prove she was brave.

He knew that was impossible.

He couldn’t go back and take care of the little girl she had been.

But he could take care of the woman who was still, in so many ways, that same little warrior.

And he intended to.

Much later, lying beside him on top of the covers with her head on his chest and her eyes nearly closed, Xiaoran suddenly spoke.

“Yichen?”

“Hmm?”

“Did my mother tell you anything else?”

He thought about it.

“She told me you once organized children into a protection team.”

Xiaoran groaned.

“Anything else?”

“She said you were very strict.”

She buried her face in his chest.

“I’m never speaking to her again.”

He laughed.

Then, after a pause, he said, “She also told me you were the kind of child who would share your snacks with anyone who forgot theirs.”

Xiaoran lifted her head.

“Oh.”

“And that you would always save the smallest piece for yourself.”

She smiled.

“That’s because I liked the bigger pieces.”

He laughed.

“I know.”

She settled against him again.

After a moment, she murmured, “I wasn’t always brave, you know.”

He looked down at her.

“What do you mean?”

“I got scared too. Sometimes I cried after everything was over.”

He brushed his fingers through her hair.

“That’s alright.”

“I just didn’t want them to see me cry.”

He smiled gently.

“You know, being brave doesn’t mean you never get scared.”

She looked up.

He kissed her cheek.

“It just means you did what you thought was right, even when you were scared.”

She stared at him, then smiled.

“That’s a very nice thing to say.”

“It’s true.”

She tucked herself closer.

“Yichen?”

“Hmm?”

“Don’t tell anyone about the Neighborhood Protection Team.”

He laughed.

“I won’t.”

“And don’t call me a little warrior.”

He paused.

“Alright.”

She closed her eyes, satisfied.

A few seconds passed.

Then he whispered, “Good night, little warrior.”

She immediately opened her eyes.

“ZHOU YICHEN!”

He burst out laughing, and from the bottom of the stairs her grandmother called up that some people in this house were trying to sleep, and Xiaoran fled back to her own room with her face burning.

And somewhere between her indignant complaints and his quiet laughter, Yichen decided that he rather liked knowing this part of her.

The brave little girl who had grown up into the woman he loved.

The girl who had always tried to protect everyone.

Even when she was the one who needed protecting.

And perhaps, for once, she could let someone else stand beside her.

chapters.desc: The Herons send a development contract on an ordinary Tuesday, and the first person Zhou Yichen calls is the girl choosing between two steamed buns.
chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.epigraph: “Because I wanted to tell you first.”
chapters.content:
The email arrived on a Tuesday morning, in the first week of the spring semester.

Zhou Yichen almost missed it.

He was sitting at his desk, reviewing a case study for his Business course, with a half-finished cup of coffee beside his laptop. His phone vibrated once. He glanced at it, expecting a message from his university basketball group.

Instead, he saw an unfamiliar notification.

Shanghai Herons — Player Development

His hand stopped on the trackpad.

He looked at the sender’s name.

Then he opened it.

The subject line was brief.

Development Contract Offer — Zhou Yichen

He read the email once, then again.

The message was formal, carefully worded, and accompanied by an official document outlining the club’s offer. It confirmed that, following his previous evaluations and subsequent development sessions, the Herons were prepared to offer him a place under their development contract program.

There were details about the development squad, training commitments, performance reviews, availability, and the club’s expectations for the rest of this season and the next.

It wasn’t a first-team contract, and it didn’t promise he would ever be named for a real game. It was a formal offer to keep going, from a club that had once almost overlooked him.

Yichen leaned back in his chair.

He read the document carefully, paying attention to every clause. He didn’t allow himself to become carried away by the subject line. He checked the obligations, the review process, the expected schedule, and the conditions surrounding his university commitments.

He reached the final page.

Then he returned to the first.

His phone was beside his laptop.

There were three people he would have to tell: his university coach, his father and Lin Xiaoran.

He picked up his phone.

For a few seconds, his thumb hovered over her contact.

Then he pressed call.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran was in the canteen, choosing between two kinds of steamed bun, when her phone rang.

She saw his name and answered immediately.

“Hello?”

“Are you busy?”

She glanced at the buns.

“Not really. I’m deciding what to eat.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Not yet.”

“Then don’t take too long.”

She smiled.

“Why? Are you hungry?”

“No.”

“Then why are you rushing me?”

“I’m not.”

She laughed, but something about his voice made her pause.

It wasn’t his usual tone.

He sounded composed, as always, but there was a particular stillness to him. As if he had something on his mind and was trying to decide how to say it.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“What’s wrong?”

A brief silence.

Then he said, “I received an email this morning.”

“From whom?”

“The Herons.”

Her expression changed.

She straightened in her chair.

“The Herons?”

“Yes.”

“What happened?”

“They’ve sent me an offer.”

For a second, Xiaoran didn’t respond.

She was afraid she had misunderstood.

“What kind of offer?”

“A development contract.”

She stared at the table.

Then her eyes widened.

“Wait.”

He heard the movement on her end, followed by the faint sound of her chair scraping against the floor.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“An actual contract?”

“A development contract. They’ve offered me a place in their program,” he clarified gently.

Her hand flew to her mouth.

“Oh my God.”

He laughed.

She stood up.

“Yichen!”

“I can hear you.”

“They offered you a contract?”

“Yes.”

“After the evaluations?”

“Yes.”

“After the scrimmage?”

“Yes, Xiaoran.”

She let out a breath that sounded almost like a laugh.

Then she covered her face with her free hand.

“Oh my God.”

Yichen leaned back in his chair, listening to her.

He had expected her to be happy.

He hadn’t expected her to sound quite so overwhelmed.

“Are you smiling?” he asked.

She pulled her hand away.

“Of course I’m smiling!”

“I thought so.”

“Are you smiling?”

He looked down at the document.

A small smile appeared.

“Yes.”

She made a tiny, excited sound.

Then, almost immediately, she asked, “Have you read everything?”

“Yes.”

“All the terms?”

“Yes.”

“Did you check the commitments? The schedule? What happens with university?”

“I did.”

“Are you sure?”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I read the whole document.”

She went quiet.

Then she laughed at herself.

“Sorry.”

“It’s fine.”

She sat down again, still holding the phone tightly.

“Yichen, I’m so happy for you.”

He didn’t answer immediately.

He looked at the email on his laptop, then at the phone in his hand.

“Thank you.”

She heard something in his voice.

Something quieter than excitement.

“Are you happy?”

He considered the question.

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“Then why do you sound so calm?”

“Because I’m talking to you.”

She blinked.

“What does that mean?”

“If I sound excited, you’ll become even more excited.”

She gasped.

“What’s wrong with that?”

“Nothing.”

“You should be excited!”

“I am.”

“Then act like it!”

He laughed.

And this time, the sound was unmistakable.

She smiled so hard her cheeks began to hurt.

For a few minutes, they talked about the offer.

He explained that the club had reviewed his development sessions and the latest performance reports. The coaching staff had agreed to move him forward, and the development department was now prepared to offer him a formal place.

Xiaoran listened carefully.

She asked about the next steps, whether he had to sign immediately, and whether the club expected him at training this week.

Yichen answered what he knew and admitted what he still needed to clarify.

He wasn’t going to pretend he had all the answers.

“Does it mean you’re going to play for them now?” she asked.

“Not exactly. It’s a development contract. I’ll be part of their program, with scheduled training and evaluations. It gives me a proper pathway, but I’ll still have to earn my place.”

She nodded, even though he couldn’t see her.

“Right.”

“I don’t want to treat it as if I’ve already made it.”

“I know.”

“There’s still a lot to prove.”

“Mm.”

He heard her take a breath.

Then she said, “But you got the offer.”

He smiled.

“Yes.”

“You got it, Yichen.”

“Yes.”

She laughed.

“I think I need to say that a few more times.”

“Go ahead.”

“You got the offer.”

He closed his eyes.

“I did.”

“I’m so proud of you.”

That made him quiet.

He knew she was proud. She’d said it after games and evaluations and bad training days. This sounded different, as if she were holding something precious and was afraid of dropping it.

He looked at the document again.

Then he said, “You’re the first person I’ve called.”

There was a pause.

“I know.”

“I haven’t called my coach.”

“Okay.”

“Or my father.”

She didn’t speak immediately.

Then she asked, “You called me first?”

“Yes.”

A smile slowly spread across her face.

“Why?”

He glanced toward the window.

Outside, the morning traffic continued as usual. Cars moved through the intersection, people crossed the pavement, and somewhere in the building, someone was talking loudly on the phone.

An ordinary Tuesday.

And yet something in his life had just changed.

“Because I wanted to tell you first.”

Xiaoran lowered her eyes.

She remembered the walk to dinner after his second evaluation, when she’d made him promise to tell her what the next stage involved. I’ll tell you when I know, he’d said.

He had known for ten minutes, and he’d called her before anyone.

“Yichen,” she said.

“Hm?”

“I’m really glad you called me.”

“I wanted to.”

She smiled.

“Then I’m glad.”

They didn’t rush to end the call.

Xiaoran eventually found a quiet corner outside the canteen, away from the noise of students moving between classes.

Yichen remained at his desk.

She asked him to send her the document.

He told her he would send the relevant parts once he had reviewed the personal information and confirmed what he could share.

She agreed, then immediately began asking questions again.

“How long is the development period?”

“We need to clarify that.”

“Will you have to travel?”

“Probably, depending on the training schedule.”

“Will it interfere with your classes?”

“That’s one of the things I need to discuss with the university.”

“Will you still be able to play for the university team?”

“Possibly, but there may be scheduling conflicts.”

She went quiet.

He noticed.

“Xiaoran.”

She sighed.

“I’m thinking.”

“About?”

“Fourth year.”

He leaned back.

So was he.

Fourth year had always seemed far away. It was the final year of their undergraduate degrees, the year of graduation projects, internships, final examinations, and decisions about what came next.

Now, it had become something more complicated.

“Let’s talk about it,” he said.

She nodded.

“Okay.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They met that evening at his apartment.

Xiaoran arrived with her laptop, a notebook, and two drinks.

Yichen opened the door.

He looked at the notebook.

“Are we having a meeting?”

She walked past him.

“Yes.”

“Should I prepare an agenda?”

“I already have one.”

He laughed.

She placed everything on the coffee table and sat down.

Yichen brought over his laptop, the contract document, and a glass of water.

Xiaoran looked at the screen.

“All right. Show me.”

He sat beside her.

For the next twenty minutes, they went through the offer together.

Yichen explained the structure of the development program, the club’s expectations, the evaluation process, and the commitments he would have to meet.

Xiaoran listened carefully.

She didn’t treat it like a fantasy.

She didn’t start planning his professional career on the assumption that everything would go perfectly.

Instead, she asked practical questions.

“What happens if your training schedule overlaps with a compulsory university class?”

“We’ll need to discuss that with the faculty.”

“Would you have to travel to another city for extended periods?”

“Possibly. The club hasn’t confirmed the full schedule yet.”

“What about your final-year project?”

“I’ll have to plan it properly.”

She nodded and wrote something down.

Yichen glanced at her notebook.

“You’re taking notes.”

“Of course.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to understand.”

He watched her.

Then he smiled.

She looked up.

“You’re doing that again.”

“What?”

“Looking at me like that.”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“I like watching you take things seriously.”

She tried not to smile.

“Well, someone has to.”

He laughed.

She returned to the document.

The biggest question wasn’t whether he wanted the opportunity.

He did.

That much was clear.

The question was how to make it work.

Fourth year would already be demanding. Yichen had a Business degree to complete, final-year coursework, and a capstone project. The development contract would require regular training, performance reviews, and potentially travel.

He couldn’t assume the club would arrange everything around his university schedule.

And he didn’t want to treat his education as something he could abandon if basketball became more promising.

Xiaoran understood that.

She also knew how much he wanted this.

She put down her pen.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“If the schedule becomes difficult, what are you most worried about?”

He considered the question.

“Not having enough time to do everything properly.”

“Meaning?”

“Training, university, recovery. I don’t want to do any of them halfway.”

She nodded.

“And what about us? I’m not asking because I’m worried you’ll forget about me.”

“I know.”

“I just want to understand what our fourth year might look like.”

He was quiet.

Then he said, “We’ll have to be more deliberate.”

She nodded.

“About time?”

“Time. Travel. Plans. Everything.”

He rested his forearms on his knees.

“I might have to spend some weekends away. There may be periods when training takes priority because of the program. I don’t know how much flexibility they’ll give me yet.”

Xiaoran listened.

“I don’t want to promise you that nothing will change.”

She met his eyes.

“Yichen, things are going to change anyway.”

“That’s true.”

“Your basketball is becoming more serious. My final year is coming. I’ll probably have my own projects, internships, and things to deal with. We can’t expect everything to stay exactly the same.”

He turned toward her.

“But I don’t want you to feel like you have to fit yourself around my schedule.”

She turned to him.

“I don’t.”

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

He held her gaze.

“I want you to have your own year too. Your own opportunities. I don’t want you to postpone something because you think you have to be available whenever I’m free.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“That’s good.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Good?”

“Because I don’t intend to.”

He laughed.

She leaned closer.

“But I also don’t want you to think that having a busy schedule means you have to handle everything alone. If you have a difficult week, tell me. If you’re tired, tell me. If you need to focus on training, tell me. I can understand that. What I don’t want is for you to decide on my behalf that I won’t understand.”

His expression softened.

“All right.”

“And I don’t want you to feel guilty every time you can’t see me.”

He was quiet.

“That’s going to be difficult.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“We’ll figure it out.”

He reached for her hand.

They began making a rough plan.

Not a rigid timetable.

Just a framework.
