First, Yichen would speak with the club to clarify the training schedule, travel expectations, and how the program would operate during the university term.

Then he would meet with his university coach and faculty advisor to understand what academic flexibility might be available, especially for compulsory sessions and his final-year project.

He would have the university’s legal office read the contract before he signed anything.

Xiaoran would have her own final-year commitments. She was likely to be occupied with a major Media project, and she wanted to explore internship opportunities without assuming that her schedule would always align with his.

They agreed that they would keep certain things for themselves.

Not as obligations, but as priorities.

One evening a week, if possible, would be theirs.

If he had to travel, they would make time for proper calls rather than relying entirely on short messages between activities.

If she had an important presentation, he would make an effort to be there whenever the schedule allowed.

And if either of them became overwhelmed, they would say so before resentment had time to build.

Xiaoran wrote everything down.

Then she looked at the page.

“That’s a lot.”

Yichen glanced at it.

He leaned closer.

“You’re the one who made the list.”

“I know. I’m just surprised.”

He smiled.

She looked at him.

“Do you think we can do it?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

Then he said, “I think we’ll have to learn.”

She smiled.

“That’s not very romantic.”

“Would you prefer I promise everything will be easy?”

“No.”

He took her hand.

“I’d rather promise I’ll keep talking to you. Even when things get difficult.”

She held his gaze.

“That’s better.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair.

Later, they moved to the kitchen.

Xiaoran was making tea while Yichen stood beside the counter, reading through the email again.

She tilted her head.

“Are you nervous?”

“A little.”

She looked surprised.

“Really?”

“Why wouldn’t I be?”

She placed the cups on the counter.

“I thought you’d be excited.”

“I am.”

“Then?”

He put the laptop aside.

“An offer is one thing. Accepting it means committing to what comes next. I’ve spent a long time trying to get here. I know what I want, but I also know what I’ll be responsible for if I say yes.”

She looked at him thoughtfully.

“You’re allowed to be nervous.”

“Thank you.”

“You’re also allowed to be excited.”

“I know.”

She stepped closer.

“Then be both.”

He looked down at her.

She reached up and adjusted the collar of his shirt.

“I know how hard you’ve worked. I know there were times when you weren’t sure the club would even give you a fair chance. And now they’ve offered you a place. I’m proud of you.”

He reached for her waist.

“Thank you.”

She smiled.

“You’re welcome. But don’t become too handsome and famous.”

He laughed.

“Is that your biggest concern?”

“Yes. I have to protect my position.”

“Your position?”

“Girlfriend. The only one.”

He looked at her with an amused expression.

“There’s no competition.”

“Good.”

He bent down and kissed her.

That night, Yichen finally called his university coach.

The conversation was practical. His coach congratulated him, asked about the offer, and advised him not to rush into signing before all the academic and training arrangements were clear.

Yichen agreed.

He then called his father.

Mr. Zhou answered after the second ring.

“Yichen.”

“Dad. The Herons sent me an offer.”

There was a pause.

“What kind?”

“A development contract.”

His father asked several questions about the program, the club’s expectations, and the terms. Yichen answered them as clearly as he could.

“Have the university’s legal office read it. Not me.”

“Because of the sponsorship.”

“Our name is on their sleeves. I won’t have anyone say I was in the room when they made you an offer.”

“I know.”

Another brief pause.

“Congratulations.”

Yichen looked toward the living room.

Xiaoran was sitting on the sofa, reading something on her tablet. She glanced up when she heard his father’s voice.

“Thank you,” Yichen said.

His father continued, “This is a good opportunity. But understand what it requires. A development contract is not the same as a guaranteed first-team position.”

“I know.”

“You’ll have to earn the next step.”

“I know.”

“Good. Call your mother. She’ll want to hear it from you, not from me.”

The call ended.

Yichen put his phone down.

Xiaoran looked up.

“How was it?”

“Fine.”

“Your father?”

“Yes.”

“What did he say?”

“He wants the legal office to read it. Not him.”

She nodded.

“That’s sensible.”

Yichen walked toward her and sat down.

She put her tablet aside.

“Have you told him you called me first?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Do you want me to?”

She smiled.

“No.”

He met her eyes.

Then he reached over and tucked her hair behind her ear.

“I wanted to tell you before everyone else.”

She leaned into his hand.

“I know.”

It was late when Xiaoran finally prepared to leave.

Yichen walked her to the door.

She put on her shoes, then turned back toward him.

“You’re really going to have a busy fourth year.”

“Probably.”

“Business final year, basketball development program, training, travel...”

“And you.”

She smiled.

“And me.”

He took her hand.

“Especially you.”

She laughed.

“Don’t say that just to make me happy.”

“I’m not. I don’t want you to become another item on my schedule. I want you to remain part of my life.”

Her expression softened.

“Then let me be part of it.”

“I will.”

She caught his collar and kissed him.

When she pulled away, he kept one hand at her waist.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I’m happy you called me first. Not because I needed to be first. Because I want to be someone you call when something important happens. Good or bad.”

His expression changed slightly.

He understood what she meant.

“I know,” he said.

Then he kissed her temple.

“And I will.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He opened the door for her.

She stepped into the corridor, then turned around one last time.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Congratulations.”

He smiled.

“Thank you.”

She lifted both hands and made a little celebratory gesture.

He laughed.

Then she disappeared down the corridor.

After she left, Yichen returned to his desk.

The email was still open.

The offer document was still waiting for his decision.

He sat down and read it once more.

There would be a lot to arrange.

He would need to understand how the program fitted around his final year, how much travel it meant, and what the next evaluation stage looked like.

There was no guarantee that he would make it to the first team.

There was no guarantee that the road ahead would be smooth.

But there was an opportunity.

A real one.

He opened his calendar and began marking the dates that needed attention.

Then his phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: I just remembered something.

Yichen: What?

Xiaoran: You haven’t celebrated properly.

He smiled.

Yichen: I thought we did.

Xiaoran: No. I mean your offer.

Yichen: We can celebrate after I understand the terms.

Xiaoran: That’s not an answer.

Yichen: What would you like to do?

A few seconds passed.

Xiaoran: Something nice.

Yichen: Define nice.

Xiaoran: Food. You. No laptops. No contract documents.

He smiled.

Yichen: Sounds good.

Xiaoran: And I get to say I’m proud of you again.

Yichen: You can say that whenever you want.

Xiaoran: I know. I just want to.

He looked at her message, then typed.

Yichen: Then I’ll listen whenever you do.

Her reply came quickly.

Xiaoran: Goodnight, future basketball star.

He laughed.

Yichen: Goodnight, future media professional.

Xiaoran: That’s not as cool.

Yichen: I disagree.

Xiaoran: You’re biased.

Yichen: Very.

He put the phone down.

Then he looked once more at the email.

The Herons had offered him a place in their development program.

It was the beginning of something he had worked toward.

But the first person he had wanted to tell wasn’t the coach who had trained him, or the father who had spent six years in the back row of his games.

It was the girl who had sat beside him through every uncertain stage, who had never mistaken his setbacks for a lack of ability, and who had always understood that his ambition was something he wanted to share—not something he needed to pursue alone.

He opened a new message to the club and began arranging a time to discuss the terms.

chapters.desc: His debut for the Herons, number eleven, with everyone who helped him get there in the stands, and his father in the front row for the first time.
chapters.title: First Real Game
chapters.epigraph: “She promised.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Xiaoran noticed when she walked into the arena was how big it was.

She had spent a lot of her life in basketball halls by now. University games, his tournaments, practice scrimmages, enough afternoons to know the smell of polished wood and rubber soles and the warm, metallic air under the lights.

But today felt different.

Today, Zhou Yichen wasn’t playing another game.

Today was his debut, his first official game for the Herons. Three weeks after he signed the development contract, his name had gone up on the game-day roster, and he had read it out to her over the phone twice.

She stood near the entrance, holding her ticket in one hand and her phone in the other. Row 1, it said. He’d remembered. Her eyes moved across the court, then toward the seating area. She had promised him she would cheer loudly.

She intended to keep that promise.

“Xiaoran!”

She turned.

Luo Jiayi was waving at her from the front row. Sun Ning stood beside her, holding a paper cup and looking as if she had already eaten something she wasn’t supposed to.

“You came early!” Jiayi called.

“I didn’t want to miss anything.”

Ning looked at the court. “You say that as if the game starts in five minutes. We still have nearly an hour.”

“That’s not the point.”

“What’s the point?”

“Today is important.”

Jiayi nodded solemnly. “Of course. The historic day when Zhou Yichen becomes a professional basketball player.”

“He’s not officially a first-team player,” Xiaoran corrected immediately.

Ning gave her a look.

“You’re very well informed.”

“Of course I am.”

Jiayi leaned toward Ning. “She’s been studying the club’s development structure again.”

“I heard that.”

“Good. I wanted you to.”

Xiaoran ignored him and walked toward their seats.

She had barely sat down when her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Have you arrived?

Xiaoran: Yes!

Yichen: Where are you sitting?

She sent him a photograph of the court from her seat.

Xiaoran: Here. You can find me.

Yichen: I can see you.

She looked up immediately.

Across the court, near the players’ entrance, Yichen stood with his teammates. He wore the Herons’ uniform, his number printed clearly across the front.

He was talking to one of the assistant coaches when his gaze lifted.

Their eyes met.

Xiaoran waved.

He gave her a smile and raised his hand.

Then he returned to the conversation.

She looked down at her phone.

Xiaoran: Don’t look too long. Focus on your game.

Yichen: I wasn’t looking for long.

Xiaoran: I saw you.

Yichen: Then you should focus on your seat.

She pressed her lips together, smiling.

Jiayi glanced over.

“He’s texting you?”

“No.”

“Your face says otherwise.”

Xiaoran put her phone away.

“Watch the court.”

Jiayi leaned forward.

“She’s already behaving like a player’s wife.”

“Luo Jiayi.”

“What? I didn’t say anything.”

Ning laughed.

The first surprise came when Xiaoran noticed Professor Xie.

He was seated a few rows behind the court, speaking with the university’s athletic director.

She recognized him immediately.

“Ning.”

“Hm?”

“Look behind us.”

Ning turned.

“Professor Xie?”

“And the athletic director.”

Jiayi followed their gaze.

“Oh. They’re here.”

Xiaoran looked back toward the court.

Yichen’s university coach was also present, standing near the Herons’ coaching staff.

She felt a strange warmth in her chest.

They had all come.

The people who had seen him during university practice, who had watched him work through the early evaluations, who had supported his request for a fair opportunity when the club’s initial selection process had been less than fair.

They were here to see him play.

And then she noticed someone else.

Four seats along her own row, a man in a dark jacket sat straight, his face unreadable.

Mr. Zhou.

“That’s Yichen’s dad,” Xiaoran whispered.

Jiayi leaned forward to look past her. “In the front row?”

Xiaoran didn’t say anything.

From the time Yichen was twelve, his father had sat in the back row of every game he played, so that his son wouldn’t play for him. Xiaoran knew about the ticket stubs. The last time she’d seen Mr. Zhou at one of Yichen’s games, the summer after first year, he had come in during the third quarter and left before the players had packed up.

Tonight the Herons’ sponsor had a box upstairs with his company’s name on the door, and he wasn’t in it. He was in the front row, where he could see the whole court.

Xiaoran looked toward the players’ entrance.

Yichen was speaking to a teammate, unaware of the small discovery she had just made.

She wondered whether he knew.

The warm-up began.

Yichen moved onto the court with the rest of the team.

Xiaoran sat forward immediately.

He looked different in the Herons’ uniform, as if something he’d been working toward for years had finally turned solid.

She watched him stretch, jog, and exchange passes with his teammates. His movements were familiar: controlled, efficient, without unnecessary gestures.

He received a pass near the wing and took a shot.

The ball went in.

Ning nodded.

“Good.”

Jiayi glanced at her.

“You sound like a commentator.”

“I am appreciating the game.”

Xiaoran was already clapping.

Yichen received another pass.

This time, he drove toward the basket, changed direction, and finished with a clean layup.

She clapped again.

“That’s my—”

She stopped.

Jiayi turned slowly.

“Your what?”

“Nothing.”

Ning grinned.

“Go on. Finish the sentence.”

“Shut up.”

On the court, Yichen moved toward the baseline to retrieve the ball.

He glanced toward the stands.

Xiaoran was still watching him.

He smiled.

She smiled back.

Then he looked away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before the game began, the teams gathered for their final instructions.

Yichen stood among his teammates, listening to the coach.

His expression was focused.

He had studied the opponent’s footage. He knew their defensive tendencies, their preferred rotations, and which players were likely to force a fast transition. He knew what his role was. He also knew that a debut wasn’t the time to prove everything in one possession.

He needed to play within the system.

Make the right decisions.

Earn his minutes.

The coach finished speaking and looked directly at him.

“Zhou.”

“Yes, Coach.”

“Don’t try to make the game bigger than it is.”

Yichen nodded.

“Understood.”

“Play the way you’ve been playing.”

“Yes, Coach.”

Kou Ran bumped his shoulder.

“Ready?”

Yichen looked toward the court.

“Ready.”

The game started quickly.

The Herons opened with a strong defensive possession, forcing the opposition to take a difficult shot. The rebound was secured, and the ball moved up the court.

Yichen began on the bench.

Xiaoran watched the game with both hands clasped around her drink.

She knew he wouldn’t necessarily start. The development contract didn’t guarantee him a place in the starting lineup, and she had never expected it to.

Still, she wanted to see him play.

She wanted to see what he would do when the game became real.

Number seventeen was at the far end of the bench. He stayed there all night.

The first quarter passed with the Herons maintaining a narrow lead.

Then, midway through the second quarter, the coach turned toward the bench.

“Zhou. Get ready.”

Yichen stood immediately.

Xiaoran’s fingers tightened around the edge of her seat.

Jiayi noticed.

“He’s going in.”

“I know.”

“You’re holding your breath.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

Yichen removed his warm-up top.

The navy jersey had a heron on the chest and an eleven on the back, the same number he’d worn for the university.

He listened to the assistant coach’s instructions, nodded once, and stepped toward the scorer’s table.

The announcer called his name.

“Making his debut for the Herons, number eleven, Zhou Yichen!”

Xiaoran forgot how to breathe.

Then she stood.

And clapped.

Loudly.

“YICHEN!”

Jiayi jumped up beside her, cupping her hands around her mouth.

“ZHOU YICHEN!”

Several people around them turned.

Xiaoran didn’t care.

She clapped harder.

On the court, Yichen glanced toward the stands.

He found her immediately.

She was standing, smiling so brightly that he could see it even from across the arena.

He gave her a small nod.

Then he stepped onto the court.

His first possession was simple.

He received the ball near the perimeter, looked at the defense, and passed it to the point guard before moving into position.

No unnecessary shot.

No attempt to force an impressive debut.

He followed the play, set a screen, and moved toward the corner.

The ball returned to him.

He took one dribble, drew the defender closer, then passed to his teammate cutting toward the basket.

A clean assist.

Xiaoran clapped.

“Good pass!”

Ning nodded.

“Very good.”

Jiayi smiled.

“He’s settling in.”

On the next possession, Yichen defended tightly, forcing the opposing guard to pass backward. He stayed disciplined, didn’t reach unnecessarily, and helped close the space.

The opponent missed.

The Herons recovered the rebound.

Yichen moved into transition.

A teammate passed him the ball near the wing.

He took a quick look at the basket.

The defender stepped forward.

Yichen changed direction, drove past him, and finished with a layup.

The ball dropped through the net.

The arena reacted.

Xiaoran practically jumped.

“YES!”

Jiayi caught her arm, laughing.

“Xiaoran!”

“HE SCORED!”

“I saw!”

“HE SCORED!”

Ning stood up and clapped.

“Good debut!”

Yichen jogged back on defense.

His face remained composed, but the corner of his mouth lifted.

He had heard her.

Of course he had.

The third quarter was more difficult.

The opposition adjusted their defense and began pressuring the Herons’ ball handlers.

Yichen was tested.

A pass was intercepted when he tried to force a narrow opening. The opponent converted it into a fast-break score.

He didn’t argue with the referee or look toward the bench.

He turned and ran back.

The next possession, he made a better decision.

He held the ball, waited for the defender to commit, then passed to the open teammate on the opposite side.

The Herons scored.

Xiaoran clapped again.

She had promised to cheer loudly.

She wasn’t going to reserve her enthusiasm only for his good moments.

When he made a mistake, she cheered for the next possession. When he defended well, she cheered.

When he made a pass that didn’t become an assist, she cheered.

And when he was substituted out for a brief rest, she clapped as he walked toward the bench.

Yichen sat down, accepted a towel, and took a drink of water.

Kou Ran leaned toward him.

“Your girlfriend is loud.”

Yichen looked toward the stands.

Xiaoran was talking animatedly to Ning, apparently explaining why one of his defensive rotations had been correct.

He smiled.

“She promised.”

Kou Ran laughed.

“She’s keeping it.”

During the break, the camera moved across the audience.

It passed Professor Xie, who was watching with a thoughtful expression, then the athletic director, who was speaking with the university coach.

Then it moved along the front row. Mr. Zhou was watching the court. He wasn’t smiling, and he wasn’t clapping, but he was there.

Xiaoran wondered whether he was still counting mistakes, the way he had at the city-league game. Or whether, for once, he was just watching his son play.

She turned back to the court.

Yichen was standing near the bench, listening to the coach.

She decided she wouldn’t spend his debut wondering what his father thought.

Today belonged to Yichen.

The fourth quarter began with the score close. The Herons were ahead by two points.

The coach sent Yichen back onto the court.

Xiaoran stood before she even realized she had moved.

Jiayi laughed.

“You’re going to stand for the entire quarter?”

“Maybe.”

“Your legs will hurt.”

“I don’t care.”

Ning looked toward the scoreboard.

“Three minutes left. This is getting interesting.”

The game became faster. The opposition scored.

The Herons responded.

Yichen defended a drive, recovered the loose ball, and moved it quickly to his teammate.

Another score.

The crowd grew louder.

With less than a minute remaining, the Herons were ahead by one.

The opposing team called a timeout.

The players gathered around their coach.

Yichen listened, breathing steadily.

He wiped his face with a towel and looked toward the stands.

Xiaoran was already standing.

She raised both hands around her mouth.

“YICHEN! YOU’VE GOT THIS!”

He smiled.

A small one.

But enough.

The timeout ended.

The opposing team took possession.

Yichen defended the wing, forcing the player toward the sideline. His teammate closed in, and the ball was passed back toward the middle.

A shot went up.

It missed.

The Herons secured the rebound.

The ball moved quickly down the court.

Yichen ran into position.

A teammate passed to him.

He caught it at the perimeter.

The defender approached.

For a fraction of a second, he considered taking the shot.

Then he saw the opening.

He drove, drew two defenders, and passed to the teammate cutting through the lane.

The ball went in.

The arena erupted.

Xiaoran screamed, with no dignity at all.

“YICHEN!”

Jiayi was laughing beside her. Ning was clapping so hard her paper cup nearly went over the advertising boards.

The Herons’ lead widened.

There were seconds left.

The opposition tried one final shot.

It missed.

The buzzer sounded.

The Herons won.

Yichen stood near the free-throw line as his teammates gathered around him.

A teammate grabbed his shoulders.

“Good game!”

Another bumped his chest.

“Welcome to the team!”

He smiled, breathing heavily. He had scored, assisted, defended, made mistakes, and recovered from them. He hadn’t dominated the game. He hadn’t needed to.

He had played his role.

And he had helped his team win.

The coach approached him and gave him a firm pat on the shoulder.

“Good work.”

“Thank you, Coach.”

“Good decisions in the final minute.”

Yichen nodded.

“I saw the cut.”

“Exactly. Keep doing that.”

Then the coach moved on.

Yichen looked toward the stands.

Xiaoran was still standing.

She was clapping with both hands raised, her cheeks flushed, her eyes bright.

He couldn’t help smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the game, the players gathered near the court for a team photograph and media duties.

Xiaoran waited with Jiayi and Ning near the meeting area.

She had sent him three messages already.

Xiaoran: YOU WERE SO GOOD.

Xiaoran: THE PASS IN THE LAST MINUTE!!!

Xiaoran: I AM STILL SO EXCITED.

Yichen glanced at his phone while waiting for the next interview.

He smiled.

Yichen: I noticed.

Xiaoran: You noticed what?

Yichen: You shouting.

Xiaoran: Good. That was the plan.

Yichen: I don’t think the people in the next section needed to know my name.

Xiaoran: They should know.

He laughed under his breath, then the media coordinator called him.

Professor Xie approached first.

“Yichen.”

Yichen turned.

“Professor.”

Professor Xie shook his hand.

“Congratulations. Your university coach has been telling us about your progress. It was good to see you finally make your debut.”

“Thank you for coming, Professor.”

“How did it feel?”

Yichen thought.

“Different from the scrimmages. The pace was higher, and the decisions had to be quicker.”

Professor Xie nodded.

“And?”

“I enjoyed it.”

The athletic director joined them.

“Well done, Zhou. Your university is proud to see you taking this opportunity forward.”

Yichen thanked him.

His university coach came over as well, smiling.

“You looked comfortable out there.”

“Thank you, Coach.”

“Don’t get too comfortable. There’s plenty more to learn.”

“I know.”

Professor Xie laughed.

“Let him enjoy his debut first.”

Yichen smiled.

The group talked about the game, his development, and how he would balance the next phase with his academic commitments.

It was a brief conversation, but it meant something to him.

They had seen him before the club contract.

They had seen him when the opportunity was uncertain.

And they were here now.

Then he saw his father.

Mr. Zhou stood a short distance away, waiting.

Yichen’s expression changed almost imperceptibly.

He excused himself from the group and walked over.

“Dad.”

Mr. Zhou looked at him.

“You played.”

Yichen almost smiled at the obvious statement.

“Yes.”

His father glanced toward the court.

“Your positioning is better than in the city league.”

Yichen nodded.

“I’ve worked on it.”

“I noticed.”

A pause.

Then Mr. Zhou said, “You didn’t force the final shot.”

“There was a better option.”

“Yes.”

Yichen looked at him.

His father held his gaze.

“Good decision.”

It wasn’t much of a compliment. But Yichen knew his father.

He knew what it meant for Mr. Zhou to come and sit in the front row. He knew what it meant for him to stay until the final buzzer, to watch the entire game, and to speak about something other than the one mistake he could have made.

“Thank you for coming,” Yichen said.

Mr. Zhou nodded.

“I wanted to see your debut.”

Yichen looked at him for a second longer.

Then he said, “I’m glad you did.”

His father gave a small nod.

They stood together for another moment before Mr. Zhou asked about the next development evaluation.

The conversation moved naturally toward practical matters.

But something small had shifted, and for now that was enough.

“YICHEN!”

He turned.

Xiaoran was waving from the meeting area.

She had clearly been waiting for him to finish speaking with his father.

Mr. Zhou glanced toward her.

“Your girlfriend is waiting.”

Yichen smiled.

“Yes.”

“Go.”

He nodded and walked over.

Xiaoran barely waited for him to reach her before she stepped forward.

“Congratulations!”

She wrapped her arms around him.

He caught her easily, one hand settling against her back.

“Thank you.”

“You were so good!”

He lowered his head slightly.

“Even the turnover?”

She drew back to look at him.

“That was one mistake.”

“One?”

“One mistake that happened. Then you made better decisions.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“Very analytical.”

“I watched carefully.”

“I can tell.”

She smiled, then looked at his face.

“Are you happy?”

He nodded.

“Very.”

She reached up and brushed a small damp strand of hair away from his forehead.

“You did it.”

He met her eyes.

She said it again, more.

“You made your debut.”

“Yes.”

“And I got to watch.”

His hand moved gently over her back.

“You were hard to miss.”

She laughed.

“Good.”

He glanced toward Jiayi and Ning, who were standing nearby.

“Did they survive?”

Jiayi raised her hand.

“Unfortunately, yes. Your girlfriend nearly destroyed my hearing.”

Xiaoran turned.

“You’re exaggerating.”

“Everyone around us knows your name now.”

“That’s a good thing.”

Ning laughed.

“She did keep her promise.”

Yichen looked down at Xiaoran.

“What promise?”

She lifted her chin.

“I told you I would cheer loudly.”

“I remember.”

“And?”

He leaned closer.

“You did.”

She smiled triumphantly.

“Exactly.”

They eventually left the arena together.

The evening air was cool, and the area outside the venue was crowded with people leaving the game.

Yichen carried his sports bag over one shoulder. Xiaoran walked beside him, still talking about the final quarter.

She described his assist in great detail, including the way the defender had shifted his weight and how Yichen had noticed the open lane.

He listened patiently.

When she finished, he asked, “Anything else?”

She thought.

“Your layup.”

“Anything else?”

“Your defense.”

“Anything else?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Why? Are you testing me?”

“Just checking whether you watched the game.”

“I watched every second!”

He smiled.

“I know.”

She met his eyes.

Then she asked, “Did you see your father?”

“Yes.”

“What did he say?”

“That my positioning was better.”

She nodded.

“That’s good.”

“He said the final decision was good too.”

Her smile softened.

“That’s really good.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“You’re happy?”

“Of course.”

He looked ahead.

“Me too.”

They walked a little farther before Xiaoran slipped her hand into his.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I think today was important.”

He looked at her.

“Because of the debut?”

“Yes. And that.”

She squeezed his hand.

“But because all the people who helped you get here were there. Your coach, Professor Xie, the athletic director... And your father.”

Yichen nodded.

“I noticed.”

“I’m glad.”

He turned toward her.

“And you.”

“What about me?”

“You were there too.”

She smiled.

“Of course I was.”

He stopped walking.

She turned back toward him.

“What?”

He lifted their joined hands and kissed the back of hers.

“Thank you for coming.”

She looked at him with a smile.

“Yichen, I wouldn’t miss it.”

“I know.”

“And next time, I’ll be even louder.”

He laughed.

“Should I warn the club?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

She leaned against his arm as they continued walking.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, after he had showered and finished his recovery routine, Yichen sat on the edge of his bed with his phone.

A message appeared.

Xiaoran: Are you still awake?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: I watched the recording again.

He smiled.

Yichen: Already?

Xiaoran: I wanted to see your debut again.

Yichen: Which part?

Xiaoran: All of it.

A moment later, another message arrived.

Xiaoran: Your father stayed until the end.

Yichen looked at the screen.

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: I think he was proud.

He considered that, then typed.

Yichen: Maybe.

Xiaoran: I think so.

He didn’t argue.

Another message appeared.

Xiaoran: I’m proud too.

He smiled.

Yichen: You told me already.

Xiaoran: I’m telling you again.

Yichen: Then I’ll listen again.

She sent a heart.

He looked at it before replying.

Yichen: I heard you from the court.

Xiaoran: Really?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: Even with everyone shouting?

Yichen: Especially you.

She didn’t reply immediately.

Then:

Xiaoran: I love you.

He leaned back against the headboard.

Yichen: I love you too.

He put the phone down.

For years, basketball had been something he had pursued through practice courts, university competitions, uncertain evaluations, and opportunities that hadn’t always come easily.

Today, he had stepped onto a different court wearing a different uniform.

He had made his debut.

There would be more games, harder opponents, and more difficult decisions ahead. He knew better than to mistake one good night for the end of a journey.

But he would remember this one: the announcer saying his name, his coach and Professor Xie and the athletic director sitting together, his father in the front row until the buzzer, and Lin Xiaoran on her feet in the same row, as loud as she’d promised.

He picked up his phone one last time and opened the photograph she had sent him earlier.

It showed the court from her seat.

A little blurry.

A little crooked.

At the edge of the frame, by the players’ entrance, he could see himself.

He saved it.

Then he turned off the light.

chapters.desc: Tang Meilin and Chen Yuhao come to Shanghai for two nights. Meilin meets Jiayi and Ning, and Yuhao and Zhou Yichen get along far too well.
chapters.title: Visitors from Home
chapters.epigraph: “You know I still like you best.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that Tang Meilin and Chen Yuhao had arrived in Shanghai was a photograph.

On a Thursday afternoon in April, Xiaoran was sitting in the university library, trying to finish a presentation slide, when her phone vibrated.

Meilin: Guess who’s here.

Attached was a photograph of Meilin standing in front of a train station sign, smiling with one hand raised. Yuhao stood behind her, holding two suitcases and looking thoroughly unimpressed.

Xiaoran: MEILIN!!!

Xiaoran: YOU’RE HERE?!

Meilin: Unfortunately, yes. Your friend has dragged me to Shanghai.

Yuhao: I changed trains in her city so I could carry the luggage. Show some gratitude.

Meilin: You packed three pairs of shoes for a weekend.

Yuhao: They serve different purposes.

Xiaoran: DON’T MOVE. I’M COMING.

Meilin: Finish your slides first. We’re not dying.

Xiaoran: I don’t care.

Yuhao: We know.

Xiaoran was already packing her things.

A message arrived from Yichen.

Yichen: Leaving the library?

Xiaoran: MEILIN AND YUHAO ARE HERE.

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: I’M GOING TO GET THEM.

Yichen: I’ll meet you there.

She stopped.

Xiaoran: You don’t have to. I can go by myself.

Yichen: I know.

Yichen: I want to see them too.

She smiled at the screen.

Xiaoran: Okay. Hurry.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen arrived at the station before Xiaoran did.

He was standing near the exit, holding his phone in one hand, when a familiar voice called out.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He looked up.

Yuhao was approaching with one suitcase in each hand.

Meilin walked beside him, looking around the station.

“You’re early,” Yuhao said.

“You’re late.”

“We’re exactly on time.”

Yichen glanced at the suitcases.

“How long are you staying?”

“Two nights.”

“Then why do you have enough luggage for a week?”

Yuhao looked offended.

“Some people understand the importance of preparation.”

Meilin walked up and greeted Yichen.

“Long time no see.”

“Welcome to Shanghai.”

She smiled.

“Thank you. Where’s Xiaoran?”

“On her way.”

Yuhao looked around.

“She’s probably running.”

“She is.”

“Good. I want to see her nearly trip over her own feet.”

Yichen glanced at him.

“Don’t encourage her.”

Yuhao laughed.

Then, as if remembering something, he leaned closer.

“By the way, how’s your basketball?”

“Fine.”

“Fine?”

“Training’s going well.”

“Your debut was pretty impressive.”

Yichen looked at him.

“You watched?”

“On the stream. Xiaoran sent the group chat approximately seventeen messages during the game.”

Meilin corrected him.

“Forty-one.”

Yuhao nodded.

“Forty-one messages. I was kept informed of every possession.”

Yichen smiled.

“That sounds like her.”

“She also sent me a photograph of your face.”

“Which one?”

“The one where you were looking toward the stands.”

Yichen didn’t need to ask who had taken it.

“YICHEN!”

He turned just in time.

Xiaoran came running toward them, her bag bouncing against her side.

Meilin opened her arms.

“Slow down!”

Xiaoran ignored her and threw herself into the hug.

“You’re here!”

Meilin hugged her tightly.

“Yes, I’m here.”

“I missed you!”

“I missed you too.”

Xiaoran pulled back and looked at her face.

“You look the same.”

“Thank you?”

“Pretty.”

“That’s better.”

Then Xiaoran turned toward Yuhao.

He opened his arms.

She narrowed her eyes.

“Why are you standing like that?”

“Waiting for my welcome.”

“You don’t deserve one.”

“After I traveled all this way?”

“You complained about carrying the luggage.”

“Because I carried the luggage.”

She laughed and hugged him anyway.

Yuhao patted her head.

“Still short.”

Xiaoran immediately stepped on his shoe.

“Ow!”

Yichen watched them with a faint smile.

Some things really hadn’t changed.

Their first stop was a restaurant near the university.

Xiaoran had already made a reservation, and she had insisted on choosing somewhere with enough dishes for everyone to share.

Yuhao looked at the menu.

“Why is everything here so expensive?”

Xiaoran glanced at him.

“You’re the one who said you wanted to eat somewhere nice.”

“I said somewhere nice, not somewhere that requires financial planning.”

Meilin took the menu from him.

“Stop complaining.”

Yichen sat beside Xiaoran pouring tea into her cup.

“Order what you like,” he told the others.

Yuhao looked at him.

“That’s dangerous.”

“Why?”

“Because I’ll remember this.”

Yichen smiled.

“Then remember to order reasonably.”

Meilin laughed.

Xiaoran leaned toward Yichen.

“You’re being too nice to him.”

“I know.”

“He’s going to take advantage.”

“I know.”

Yuhao heard them.

“I can hear you.”

“Good,” Xiaoran replied.

The conversation quickly became noisy.

Meilin asked about Xiaoran’s Media projects and university life. Yuhao wanted to know more about Yichen’s training schedule, especially whether he had been traveling frequently for the development program.

Yichen answered without making it sound more impressive than it was.

“Some weeks are busier than others. It depends on the club’s schedule.”

Yuhao nodded.

“Still balancing university?”

“Yes.”

“That’s difficult.”

“It takes planning.”

Xiaoran reached for a piece of food.

“And he has a very strict calendar.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Who made me a strict calendar?”

“…I did.”

“Exactly.”

She smiled.

Meilin watched them.

“You two are still the same.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“What do you mean?”

“Nothing. Just that it’s nice.”

Yichen smiled.

Yuhao, meanwhile, was busy asking whether Yichen could teach him a few basketball moves.

“No,” Meilin said immediately.

Yuhao looked at her.

“Why?”

“Because you’ll hurt yourself.”

“I played basketball in school.”

“That was years ago.”

“I still remember.”

Yichen considered him.

“We can see.”

Yuhao looked delighted.

“Excellent.”

Meilin sighed.

“I already regret coming.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran brought Meilin to campus.

Yuhao had gone with Yichen to see the Herons’ training facility, which Xiaoran considered an unfair arrangement.

“Why does he get to go with Yichen?”

Meilin looked at her.

“Because he asked.”

“I could have asked.”

“You have classes.”

“I can skip one.”

“No.”

Xiaoran pouted.

Meilin laughed and linked their arms.

“Come on. Show me your university.”

They walked through the campus, stopping at the library, the student center, and the Media building.

Xiaoran introduced Meilin to a few classmates, then took her to the café where she often studied.

Meilin listened as Xiaoran described her projects, her professors, and the people she’d become friends with.

“You seem settled,” Meilin observed.

“I am.”

“Really?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“I was a little lost at first. But it’s nice now. I know where everything is.”

Meilin looked around.

“That’s good.”

“And I have friends here.”

“I can tell.”

Xiaoran smiled.

She was happy to have Meilin here, but she also wanted her to see the life she had built in Shanghai.

They stopped outside a café where two girls were waiting.

“Xiaoran!”

Jiayi waved.

Ning stood beside her, smiling.

Xiaoran waved back.

“Meilin, this is Luo Jiayi, and this is Sun Ning.”

Meilin greeted them.

“Hi. I’m Tang Meilin.”

Jiayi smiled.

“We’ve heard about you.”

Meilin glanced at Xiaoran.

“Have you?”

Xiaoran immediately looked suspicious.

“What did she say?”

Ning laughed.

“Nothing bad.”

“That’s not reassuring.”

Jiayi grinned.

“She said you were her best friend from high school.”

Meilin looked at Xiaoran.

“That’s all?”

Xiaoran nodded quickly.

“Yes.”

Ning added, “She also said you were very good at knowing when she’s being unreasonable.”

Meilin smiled.

“That’s accurate.”

Xiaoran stared at her.

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am. That’s why I know.”

The four of them sat together for coffee.

Meilin found herself liking Xiaoran’s university friends almost immediately. Jiayi was loud and outspoken, while Ning had a quieter sense of humor that made her comments unexpectedly sharp.

They asked about high school, and Meilin shared a few harmless stories.

“She used to get lost even when we were going somewhere familiar,” Meilin said.

Xiaoran looked betrayed.

“That happened once.”

“Three times.”

“One of those was your fault.”

“How?”

“You walked too fast.”

Jiayi laughed.

Ning leaned forward.

“Does Yichen still have to find you?”

Xiaoran hesitated.

Meilin answered for her.

“Yes.”

“Meilin!”

Everyone laughed.

Meilin looked at her with fondness.

“Don’t worry. She’s improved.”

Xiaoran folded her arms.

“Thank you.”

“She now gets lost with confidence.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Meanwhile, Yichen and Yuhao were getting along far too well.

It began innocently enough.

Yuhao had asked about the training facility, and Yichen had offered to show him around.

Then they started talking about basketball. Then professional sports, then training methods.

Then, somehow, they were standing near the practice court discussing the differences between offensive systems.

Yuhao, it turned out, still followed the sport much more closely than he let anyone know.

“You see that?” Yichen asked, pointing toward the court.

“The spacing?”

“Yes. If the weak-side defender moves too early, the corner opens.”

Yuhao nodded.

“Unless the ball handler hesitates.”

“Exactly.”

Yuhao looked at him.

“You’re annoyingly good at explaining things.”

Yichen smiled.

“Thank you.”

“That wasn’t a compliment.”

“I’ll take it.”

They continued talking.

By the time they reached the café near the facility, Yuhao had somehow convinced Yichen to join him for a game later that afternoon.

Yichen agreed.

Yuhao looked pleased with himself.

“Good. I want to see whether you’re actually as good as Xiaoran says.”

Yichen glanced at him.

“What does she say?”

Yuhao thought.

“That you’re handsome.”

Yichen waited.

“And?”

“Good at basketball.”

“Anything else?”

Yuhao grinned.

“That you’re very annoying when you know you’re right.”

Yichen laughed.

“That’s fair.”

Xiaoran found out about their new friendship through a photograph.

It was taken by Yuhao.

Yichen stood beside him, holding two drinks, while Yuhao pointed toward the camera with a grin.

The caption read:

Yuhao: Unexpected friendship of the year.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Then she sent a message to Meilin.

Xiaoran: Why are they together?

Meilin: Because they went out together.

Xiaoran: I know that. Why are they smiling like that?

Meilin: Maybe they like each other.

Xiaoran: MEILIN.

Meilin: What?

Xiaoran: They’re getting along too well.

Meilin laughed at her phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon, the four of them met at a basketball court.

Yichen and Yuhao had already been playing for nearly half an hour when Xiaoran and Meilin arrived.

Xiaoran stopped near the entrance.

Yuhao had the ball.

He attempted a shot.

It hit the rim.

Yichen caught the rebound.

“Your elbow.”

“What about it?”

“You’re bringing it out too far.”

Yuhao frowned.

“That’s how I shoot.”

“That’s why you missed.”

Xiaoran looked at Meilin.

“See?”

Meilin smiled.

“What?”

“They’re already arguing.”

“That’s how friendships work.”

Yuhao noticed them.

“Xiaoran! Come here.”

She pointed at herself.

“Me?”

“No, the other Lin Xiaoran.”

She walked closer.

“What?”

“Tell him I’m good.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Do you want an honest answer?”

Yuhao groaned.

Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re both terrible.”

Yichen retrieved the ball and passed it to her.

“Try.”

She caught it awkwardly.

“Why?”

“Let’s see.”

“I don’t know how.”

“I’ll show you.”

Yuhao immediately stepped aside.

“Good idea. I’m tired.”

Meilin gave him a look.

“You were playing for thirty minutes.”

“Exactly.”

Yichen stood beside Xiaoran and adjusted her hand position on the ball.

“Don’t hold it too tightly.”

She looked down.

“Like this?”

“Yes. Now bend your knees slightly.”

She did.

“Look at the basket.”

She raised her eyes.

Then she shot.

The ball hit the backboard and bounced away.

She stared at it.

Yichen smiled.

“Not bad.”

“That was terrible.”

“First try.”

Yuhao retrieved the ball.

“Let me show you.”

Meilin caught his arm.

“Don’t.”

He met her eyes.

“Why?”

“Because you’ll teach her the wrong way.”

Yichen laughed.

Xiaoran turned toward Meilin.

“Thank you.”

Yuhao looked deeply offended.

Later, they went to a nearby restaurant for dinner.

Yuhao and Yichen sat opposite each other, still discussing basketball.

Meilin and Xiaoran sat side by side.

Meilin watched the two men.

“Are they going to talk about this all night?”

Xiaoran sighed.

“I think so.”

“Did you know Yuhao was this interested?”

“Not this interested.”

Meilin took a sip of water.

“Yichen seems to enjoy it.”

Xiaoran looked across the table.

Yichen was listening to Yuhao explain something, occasionally correcting a detail. He looked relaxed.

She smiled.

“He’s having fun.”

Meilin noticed her expression.

“You like seeing him like this.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“He’s usually quite serious about basketball. It’s nice when he can just talk about it without worrying about anything.”

Meilin smiled.

Then she leaned closer.

“You’re happy here.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“What?”

“Shanghai. Your university. Your friends. Yichen.”

She looked down at her glass.

“Yes.”

Meilin reached over and squeezed her hand.

“Good.”

Xiaoran smiled.

For a while, they talked about home.

Their old neighborhood.

The school they had attended. The food they missed. The teachers they remembered.

The small things that seemed unimportant until they were far away from them.

At one point, Yuhao interrupted.

“Do you remember when Xiaoran got locked outside the classroom?”

Xiaoran’s head snapped up.

“No.”

Meilin looked delighted.

“Yes.”

“Don’t.”

Yuhao continued.

“She was supposed to lock up and take the class key to the teacher’s office, but she left it inside.”

“I was fifteen!”

“You were sixteen.”

“That doesn’t make it better!”

Yichen looked at her.

“What happened?”

Meilin smiled.

“She waited outside for twenty minutes before someone found her.”

Yichen looked amused.

“Why didn’t you call someone?”

“My phone was inside too.”

Yuhao nodded.

“She was very resourceful. She sat outside and waited.”

Xiaoran pointed at him.

“You were the one who shut the door!”

“That is not relevant.”

Yichen laughed.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He reached over and squeezed her hand under the table.

She tried to maintain her offended expression.

It didn’t last.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, because it was their last evening, they all went back to Yichen’s apartment.

Meilin and Yuhao were staying at a hotel, but Xiaoran had insisted that they come over before leaving the next morning.

There were snacks on the coffee table, a film playing in the background, and four people occupying the living room.

Yuhao had somehow ended up sitting beside Yichen, showing him a video on his phone.

Meilin was beside Xiaoran, scrolling through photographs from the weekend.

Xiaoran looked at one picture.

It showed Meilin laughing with Jiayi and Ning at the café.

“Look at this one.”

Meilin leaned closer.

“Oh, that’s nice.”

“I’ll send it to you.”

“Please do.”

Then Xiaoran swiped to another photograph.

It showed Yuhao and Yichen standing beside the basketball court, both looking serious while holding drinks.

She stared.

“Why do you have so many pictures together?”

Yuhao looked up.

“Because we’re friends.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“Since when?”

“Since this morning.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Is that a problem?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“No.”

“You’re sure?”

“Yes.”

Yuhao leaned toward Yichen.

“She’s jealous.”

Xiaoran threw a cushion at him.

Yuhao caught it, laughing.

Meilin shook her head.

“You’re all children.”

Yichen put the cushion back beside Xiaoran.

Then he leaned toward her and said, “You know I still like you best.”

She met his eyes.

“Obviously.”

“Obviously?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He kissed her temple.

Yuhao made a loud gagging noise.

“Please. We’re in the room.”

Xiaoran turned.

“You’re the one who came to our apartment.”

“Your apartment?”

“His apartment.”

“Then I’m leaving.”

Nobody moved.

Yuhao waited.

Then he sighed.

“Nobody appreciates me.”

Meilin laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran and Yichen went with them to the station.

Meilin hugged Xiaoran first.

“Come home when you can.”

“I will.”

“And don’t forget to rest.”

“I won’t.”

Meilin gave her a look.

“That’s what you always say.”

Xiaoran smiled.

Then Meilin hugged Yichen.

“Take care of her.”

He nodded.

“I will.”

Xiaoran immediately pulled back.

“Why are you telling him that? I can take care of myself.”

Meilin smiled.

“I know.”

Yuhao stepped forward and shook Yichen’s hand.

“Good game yesterday.”

“Thanks.”

“Next time, I’ll win.”

Yichen smiled.

“Next time, work on your shooting.”

Yuhao stared at him.

“You’re still thinking about that?”

“Yes.”

“Unbelievable.”

Xiaoran laughed.

Yuhao turned to her.

“And you. Don’t get too spoiled.”

She hugged him.

“Travel safely.”

He patted her back.

“Take care, little troublemaker.”

“Bye.”

They watched Meilin and Yuhao disappear into the crowd.

Xiaoran stood still.

Yichen slipped his hand into hers.

“Miss them already?”

“A little.”

He squeezed her hand.

“They’ll come again.”

She looked up.

“Really?”

“Why not?”

She smiled.

“Next time, I’ll make them stay longer.”

“Then we’ll need a bigger table.”

“And more food.”

“And perhaps another basketball court.”

She laughed.

“Yuhao will demand a rematch.”

“I know.”

They began walking toward the exit.

After a few steps, Xiaoran leaned against his arm.

“It was nice, wasn’t it?”

“Very.”

“Meilin liked Jiayi and Ning.”

“I noticed.”

“And Yuhao likes you.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Is that a problem?”

She sighed dramatically.

“I don’t know. You two are becoming too close.”

“Should I stop talking to him?”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because you seemed happy.”

He looked at her.

Then he lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“You’re very generous.”

She smiled.

“I know.”

They continued walking through the station, their hands joined.

Shanghai had become home in its own way: her classes, her friends, her favorite cafés, the life she had built since she left. It had still been good to have two people here who had known her before all of it, and to find out that Yuhao and Yichen could be friends, even if they were already far too pleased with themselves.

chapters.desc: The Media faculty makes a film that makes everyone cry. The Business faculty bankrupts a company. They’re both on the same stage.
chapters.title: The Last Scene Before the Credits
chapters.epigraph: “It only needed another day.”
chapters.content:
The university’s Annual Faculty Showcase was supposed to be a celebration of student talent.

Every faculty had been given a stage, a time slot, and a little freedom to show everyone what their students had been working on throughout the academic year.

Some faculties chose exhibitions. Some prepared musical performances. Others had interactive booths, demonstrations, and presentations.

The Media Faculty, naturally, decided to make a film.

And not just any film.

A twenty-minute short movie, written, directed, filmed, edited, and produced entirely by students.

The title was Before the Morning Comes.

Xiaoran had been involved from the beginning.

She was part of the creative team, helped develop the screenplay, participated in production planning, and eventually became the female lead after their original actress had to withdraw due to an unexpected schedule conflict.

She hadn’t planned on acting.

In fact, when the director first suggested it, she had stared at him as though he’d asked her to jump off the faculty building.

“Me?”

“Yes, you.”

“But I’m behind the camera.”

“You understand the character.”

“That doesn’t mean I can act.”

“We’ve seen you cry over fictional characters during editing.”

“That’s different!”

The director had simply smiled.

And somehow, two weeks later, Xiaoran was standing in front of a camera, wearing a pale blue cardigan and pretending that the person she loved was dying.

She hadn’t expected the role to affect her as much as it did.

The story was about two university students who fell in love while dealing with serious illnesses.

The male lead, played by a Media student named Chi Yuan, was diagnosed with a progressive heart condition. He knew his health was deteriorating, but he kept it from the female lead, afraid that she would spend the rest of their relationship worrying about him.

The female lead, played by Xiaoran, had her own diagnosis: a serious illness that required prolonged treatment and eventually threatened her ability to continue living the life she had imagined.

They met during a difficult period in their lives.

They fell in love in the middle of hospital appointments, late-night conversations, and small promises.

The tragedy wasn’t simply that they were sick.

It was that they had so many ordinary things they wanted to do together.

They wanted to graduate.

They wanted to travel.

They wanted to argue about what to eat.

They wanted to grow old.

And they knew they might not get all of it.

The film ended with the female lead sitting beside an empty hospital bed, holding a small notebook.

The final page contained a list of things they had wanted to do together.

At the bottom, she wrote:

If we had more time, I think I would still choose you.

Then the screen faded to black.

No music.

Just silence.

It was heartbreaking.

And Xiaoran had cried during the final recording.

Not because she was particularly good at acting, but because by then she had spent so much time with the character that the final scene felt strangely personal.

When the director called cut, she had remained sitting on the hospital bed, quietly wiping her eyes.

Chi Yuan, who played the male lead, had leaned over.

“Xiaoran, are you okay?”

She nodded.

“Yes. Just give me a minute.”

The director had looked at the footage and whispered to the cinematographer:

“Keep that take.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen knew about the film.

He had heard about it for weeks.

He had watched Xiaoran memorize her lines, listened to her complain about filming schedules, and occasionally received photographs of the production set.

He had even helped her rehearse a few scenes.

One evening, she had stood in front of him, holding her script.

“Okay. You’re the patient. I’m your girlfriend.”

Yichen had looked up from his laptop.

“All right.”

“You’re supposed to look sick.”

He stared at her.

She frowned.

“Not like that.”

“How should I look?”

“Like you’re hiding something.”

He gave her a calm look.

“I’m always hiding something.”

“Don’t make jokes. This is serious.”

He put his laptop aside.

“All right. Continue.”

She began reading her lines.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He answered with the line from the script.

“Because I didn’t want you to spend every day being afraid of losing me.”

Xiaoran paused, then looked at him.

“That was good.”

“Thank you.”

“Do it again, but sadder.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Are you directing me now?”

“Yes.”

He smiled.

She tried to continue, but his expression was too familiar. Too much like the real Yichen, sitting in front of her, listening patiently.

She suddenly felt embarrassed.

“Never mind.”

He reached for her hand.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. I just can’t act when you’re looking at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you love me.”

He smiled.

“That’s going to be difficult to change.”

She had thrown her script at him.

He caught it easily.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Business Faculty, meanwhile, had chosen something entirely different.

Their showcase team had initially proposed a traditional business case competition.

A panel of judges.

A simulated company.

A presentation.

A few financial charts.

It was sensible.

It was also terribly boring.

Their faculty advisor had listened to the proposal, looked at the students, and asked:

“Do you want the audience to remember your presentation tomorrow?”

Nobody answered.

“Then don’t give them another presentation.”

That was how they came up with The Last Company Standing, an interactive business simulation.

The Business students created a fictional company called Northstar, a once-successful consumer technology brand facing a sudden crisis.

The audience would become the company’s shareholders and board members.

They would be given a limited budget, incomplete information, and a series of decisions to make.

A product defect had been discovered.

A competitor was launching a cheaper alternative.

A supplier had suddenly withdrawn.

The company had to decide whether to recall its products, protect its reputation, cut costs, or invest in a new direction.

Every decision would affect the company’s simulated finances, public trust, employee morale, and long-term survival.

There would be live voting, a projected dashboard, and a final reveal showing the consequences of the audience’s choices.

Yichen was part of the Business Faculty’s organizing and strategy team.

He had helped design the financial model and the decision-making structure, making sure the simulation was realistic enough to be challenging but understandable to people outside Business.

He also ended up as one of the presenters.

His role was to act as the company’s Chief Strategy Officer.

The contrast between the two faculties couldn’t have been more obvious.

Media was preparing to make an entire auditorium cry.

Business was preparing to make the same auditorium argue about whether to fire a CEO.

Xiaoran found the concept hilarious.

“So you’re going to stand on stage and tell people their company is going bankrupt?”

“Not exactly.”

“What’s the difference?”

“I’ll explain why it’s going bankrupt.”

She laughed.

“That’s worse.”

He smiled.

“Would you like to join the board?”

“I don’t know anything about business.”

“That’s all right. Neither does the audience.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed and kissed her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

The day of the showcase arrived.

The university auditorium was packed.

Every faculty had decorated its section, and students were moving around in matching shirts, carrying equipment, checking microphones, and running through last-minute rehearsals.

The Media team had a small backstage room filled with laptops, costume bags, spare props, and a suspicious amount of snacks.

Xiaoran was wearing the costume for the film’s final scene: a simple white blouse, a pale blue cardigan, and a delicate necklace.

She was sitting in front of a mirror while Luo Jiayi, who had appointed herself the film’s hair, makeup and morale department, fixed a loose strand of hair.

“You look so pretty,” Jiayi said.

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you.”

“Are you nervous?”

“A little.”

“You’re not even presenting.”

“I’m acting in front of everyone.”

“You’re going to be fine.”

Xiaoran nodded.

She checked her phone.

A message from Yichen.

Yichen: Already there?

Xiaoran: Yes. Are you ready?

Yichen: Almost.

Xiaoran: Don’t forget to eat.

Yichen: You too.

Xiaoran: I did.

Yichen: What?

She sent him a photograph of a half-eaten sandwich.

Yichen: That’s not a meal.

Xiaoran: It’s a sandwich!

Yichen: Eat the rest.

She smiled and put her phone away.

Jiayi stepped back and examined her work.

“Ning’s saving us seats for the Business slot. Middle row. She says if we’re late she’s giving them to strangers.”

“She won’t.”

“She will. She enjoys it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Media Faculty’s slot was scheduled for 4:00 PM.

Before that, the Business Faculty had their performance.

Xiaoran managed to slip into the auditorium just before it began.

She found Ning in the middle row with her headphones round her neck and two coats on the seats beside her. Jiayi waved enthusiastically from the far end.

“Here! Your boyfriend is about to become a CEO!”

Xiaoran giggled and sat beside them.

The lights dimmed.

The Business Faculty’s presentation began with a short video showing the fictional company Northstar’s impressive growth, followed by the sudden announcement of a product safety crisis.

A projected headline appeared:

NORTHSTAR FACES MAJOR RECALL AFTER PRODUCT DEFECT DISCOVERED.

The audience immediately began whispering, then the presenters entered.

Yichen walked onto the stage wearing a dark suit, a white shirt, and a discreet name badge identifying him as the Chief Strategy Officer.

Xiaoran straightened.

Oh.

He looked handsome.

She had seen him in formal clothes many times, but seeing him under the stage lights, speaking confidently to a full auditorium, was different.

He looked entirely at ease.

“Good afternoon, shareholders.”

His voice carried clearly.

“Three days ago, Northstar discovered a defect in one of its flagship products. We have already received complaints from customers, and the media is beginning to investigate.”

The screen behind him displayed three options.

Option A: Immediate full recall.

Option B: Limited recall while investigating.

Option C: Continue sales while quietly resolving the issue.

Yichen looked across the audience.

“You have thirty seconds to decide.”

The voting began.

The room became lively almost immediately.

Students debated loudly. Some argued that a full recall would destroy the company’s finances. Others insisted that public safety had to come first.

Yichen listened to the arguments and occasionally responded to questions.

One student asked:

“What if the company doesn’t have enough cash to recall everything?”

Yichen answered without hesitation.

“Then we negotiate with suppliers, secure emergency financing, and prioritize the highest-risk products. Financial difficulty doesn’t make the underlying safety issue disappear.”

Xiaoran looked at Ning.

“He’s good.”

Ning smiled.

“Very good.”

On stage, the simulation progressed.

The audience chose a limited recall.

The dashboard updated.

Then came another problem: a major supplier had withdrawn, a competitor had announced a cheaper product, and a leaked internal email suggested the company had known about the defect earlier.

The room became even louder.

Yichen stood at the center of it all, calmly guiding the audience through each decision.

At the final reveal, the company’s simulated valuation had fallen, but its customer trust had recovered.

The Business team concluded that the company had survived, not because it avoided losses, but because it made a difficult decision early enough to protect its long-term credibility.

The audience applauded.

Ning leaned toward Xiaoran.

“Your boyfriend just made bankruptcy sound attractive.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Stop.”

Jiayi looked at the stage, chin in her hand.

“He’s really good at explaining things.”

Xiaoran nodded, smiling proudly.

Yichen looked toward the audience.

His eyes found her.

He gave her the smallest smile.

She waved discreetly.

He returned his attention to the stage.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 4:00 PM, the Media Faculty’s turn arrived.

The host introduced the film.

“Next, we have a short film produced by the Media Faculty’s student production team. Written, directed, filmed, and edited by our students, Before the Morning Comes explores love, illness, and the things we wish we had more time to do.”

The auditorium lights dimmed.

Xiaoran sat backstage, listening to the opening music through a monitor.

She had watched the film countless times during editing.

But hearing it play in the auditorium, with a full audience, made her nervous.

The opening scene appeared on the screen.

Two university students met in a small campus library.

The male lead was sitting alone, looking tired. The female lead approached him with a cup of coffee.

“You’re always here.”

“Maybe I like the library.”

“Or maybe you don’t have a life.”

He smiled.

“Maybe.”

The audience laughed.

The story unfolded.

Their first conversation.

Their growing friendship.

Their first date.

The quiet discovery of their illnesses.

The hospital corridors.

The doctor’s appointments.

The way they tried to pretend that everything was normal.

Then came the scene where the male lead finally told her the truth.

Xiaoran’s voice filled the auditorium.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I didn’t want you to look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re already saying goodbye.”

The auditorium became silent.

Xiaoran remembered filming that scene.

She remembered how she had held her breath after the line, how Chi Yuan had looked at her with such exhausted tenderness, and how the director had let the camera keep rolling.

The story continued.

The female lead’s own condition worsened.

They sat together on a hospital rooftop, sharing a packet of biscuits.

“You know what I wanted to do?” she asked.

“What?”

“Travel.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere. Somewhere with the sea.”

He smiled.

“We can still go.”

“You always say that.”

“Because I mean it.”

She smiled, but her eyes were wet.

The next scene showed them making a list.

Things they wanted to do together.

See the sea.

Eat at a restaurant without checking the time.

Watch the sunrise.

Graduate.

Take a photograph every year.

The final scene arrived.

The male lead’s hospital bed was empty.

The female lead sat beside it, holding the notebook.

She turned the pages.

One by one.

Then wrote:

If we had more time, I think I would still choose you.

The screen faded to black.

Silence.

For several seconds, nobody moved, then the ending music began.

The credits appeared.

And the auditorium erupted into applause.

Xiaoran remained backstage.

She was smiling, but her eyes were wet.

Her director hugged her.

“We did it.”

She nodded.

“We did.”

One of her classmates was crying.

Another was wiping her face with a tissue.

The director laughed.

“Look at us. We made everyone miserable.”

Xiaoran laughed through her tears.

“That’s not what we were trying to do!”

“Apparently, we succeeded.”

When the lights came back on, the host invited the Media team onto the stage.

Xiaoran walked out with the others.

The applause continued.

She felt a little overwhelmed by the number of people looking at her.

The host introduced the production team and asked a few questions.

“Xiaoran, you played the female lead. How was the experience?”

She took the microphone.

“Honestly, it was quite difficult. I’m more comfortable working behind the camera, so acting was a little outside my comfort zone.”

The audience laughed.

“But I think the story was very meaningful. We wanted to show that illness doesn’t only affect the person who is sick. It also affects the people who love them, and sometimes the hardest part is not knowing how to help each other.”

She paused.

“And I think we wanted to remind people not to postpone the small things they want to do with the people they love.”

The host nodded.

“That’s beautiful. Thank you.”

Xiaoran returned the microphone.

The applause came again.

She looked toward the audience.

And found Yichen.

He was standing near the aisle with his Business teammates, clapping.

He was looking directly at her.

His expression was proud.

Not exaggerated.

Not performative.

Just unmistakably proud.

She smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the showcase ended, the auditorium turned into a chaotic celebration.

Students were taking photographs, congratulating one another, and visiting the different faculty booths.

Xiaoran was surrounded by her classmates.

“Your acting was so good!”

“That final scene!”

“I cried!”

“Everyone cried!”

She laughed, thanking them.

Then Ning appeared from the sound booth.

She held out a tissue.

“For the actress.”

Xiaoran took it.

“Thank you.”

Ning looked at her.

“That was really good.”

She smiled.

“Really?”

“Yes. I was trying not to cry.”

Jiayi appeared beside her, mascara everywhere.

“I wasn’t trying.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

Jiayi hugged her.

“You did well.”

“Thank you.”

Then, from behind them, a familiar voice said:

“Congratulations.”

Xiaoran turned.

Yichen was standing there, his suit jacket folded over one arm.

She immediately smiled.

“Yichen!”

He opened his arms slightly.

She stepped into them.

He wrapped one arm around her waist and kissed her cheek.

“You did very well.”

She looked up.

“Did you watch the whole thing?”

“Of course.”

“Did you like it?”

“I did.”

She smiled.

Then she asked, “Did you cry?”

He looked at her.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

He considered it.

“I was distracted.”

“By what?”

He brushed his thumb against her cheek.

“Watching you.”

Her expression softened.

Then she noticed something.

“Wait. You were watching me instead of the film?”

“I watched both.”

She laughed.

“I can’t win with you.”

He smiled.

Jiayi and Ning exchanged a look.

Jiayi leaned toward Ning.

“I’ve known them almost three years, and he still looks at her like that.”

Ning nodded.

“Unfortunately.”

Xiaoran heard them.

“NING!”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, the two faculties ended up sharing a table at the refreshments area.

The Media team was discussing their film.

The Business team was debating the audience’s decisions during the simulation.

Yichen sat beside Xiaoran, one hand resting lightly on the back of her chair.

At some point, one of the Media students asked him:

“Yichen, what did you think of our film?”

He answered honestly.

“The story was well structured. The pacing was good, and the final scene was effective.”

The director nodded.

“Thank you.”

“Although I think the female lead could have been a little happier,” Yichen said.

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“Excuse me?”

“She spent the entire film crying.”

“Because her character was sick!”

“I know.”

“Then why are you complaining?”

He smiled.

“Personal preference.”

The table burst into laughter.

The director pointed at him.

“That’s not a valid film critique.”

Yichen nodded.

“Fair enough.”

Xiaoran leaned closer.

“You’re just biased.”

“Probably.”

She smiled.

Then one of Yichen’s Business teammates joined the conversation.

“Actually, we should collaborate next year.”

The Media director looked interested.

“How?”

“Business students create the crisis. Media students turn it into a documentary.”

Jiayi laughed.

“Imagine that. Northstar: The Documentary.”

Ning added, “Featuring Zhou Yichen as the CEO who refuses to admit the company is bankrupt.”

Yichen looked at her.

“I wasn’t the CEO.”

“Yet.”

Everyone laughed.

Xiaoran leaned against his shoulder.

For a moment, she watched the people around the table.

Her classmates, his teammates, Jiayi, Ning.

Two different faculties.

Two different worlds.

And somehow, both of them had found a way to stand on the same stage that day.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the event finally ended, the university campus was glowing with evening lights.

Xiaoran and Yichen walked toward the parking area together.

She was carrying a small bouquet her classmates had given her, while he held her bag.

“Are you tired?” he asked.

“A little.”

“Do you want to go home?”

She nodded.

They walked for a while.

Then Xiaoran spoke.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Did you really like the film?”

“Yes.”

“Which part?”

He thought about it.

“The list.”

“The list?”

“Things they wanted to do together.”

She looked up at him.

“Why?”

“Because it felt real.”

She nodded.

“I liked that part too.”

He glanced at her.

“Did it make you think about anything?”

She considered the question.

“Maybe.”

“What?”

She looked ahead.

“I don’t want to wait until something bad happens to do the things I want with you.”

He slowed slightly.

She continued.

“I want to travel with you. I want to graduate with you. I want to take more photographs, eat at more restaurants, see more places. I want to do ordinary things with you for a long time.”

He looked at her.

Then gently took the bouquet from her hands so he could hold her hand properly.

“Then let’s do them.”

She smiled.

“All of them?”

“As many as we can.”

“What if we can’t?”

“Then we’ll find something else.”

She looked at him.

He squeezed her hand.

“We don’t have to make a list of things we might lose. We can make one of things we want to experience.”

“That’s a very Business student answer.”

He laughed.

“Would you like me to make a spreadsheet?”

She gasped.

“Don’t you dare.”

He smiled.

Then, after a moment, he stopped walking.

Xiaoran turned.

“What?”

He set her bag down beside him, took her hand in both of his, and looked at her.

“You know what I was thinking during the final scene?”

She shook her head.

“I was thinking that I don’t want you to ever feel like you have to make every moment with me count.”

Her expression softened.

“I want you to have ordinary days with me. Boring days. Days when we don’t do anything special. Days when you complain about assignments and I complain about basketball practice.”

She smiled.

“Your complaints are much less interesting than mine.”

“Probably.”

He continued.

“I want to have enough ordinary days with you that we stop counting them.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

The words settled somewhere deep in her chest.

She stepped closer.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Can I kiss you?”

His mouth curved.

“You don’t need to ask.”

She leaned up and kissed him.

It was soft at first.

Then his hand moved to her waist, drawing her closer, and he returned the kiss with more feeling.

When she pulled away, he rested his forehead against hers.

“Congratulations, actress.”

She laughed.

“Congratulations, Chief Strategy Officer.”

“Which performance was better?”

She pretended to think.

“Mine.”

“Naturally.”

“Your company nearly went bankrupt.”

“Because the shareholders made poor decisions.”

“Excuses.”

He laughed and kissed her cheek.

Then her forehead.

Then, when she turned her face toward him with a small smile, he kissed her lips again.

They finally reached the car.

Before getting in, Xiaoran glanced at the university building behind them.

“Today was really nice.”

Yichen opened her door.

“It was.”

“Even though my film made everyone cry?”

“Even then.”

She got into the passenger seat.

He leaned down slightly before closing the door.

“Although I prefer the version of you that doesn’t have a tragic ending.”

She smiled.

“Me too.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair one last time, then closed the door.

As he walked around to the driver’s side, Xiaoran took out her phone and opened her notes.

She created a new list.

Things I Want to Do With Yichen.

1. See the sea together.
2. Travel somewhere neither of us has been.
3. Take photographs every year.
4. Watch the sunrise.
5. Eat at a restaurant without checking the time.
6. Graduate.
7. Have more ordinary days.
8. Keep choosing each other.

She looked at the list, then added one more.

9. Make sure Zhou Yichen never gets a tragic ending.

She smiled to herself.

When Yichen got into the car, he noticed.

“What are you smiling at?”

“Nothing.”

He glanced at her phone.

“Making another list?”

She hugged it to her chest.

“It’s private.”

He smiled and started the engine.

“All right.”

She reached over and took his hand before he shifted gears.

He looked at her.

She smiled.

“Let’s go home.”

And he did.

Because unlike the film they had shown that afternoon, their story didn’t need a final scene.

It only needed another day.

chapters.desc: A cracked wooden bench by the halfway vending machine becomes the place they meet between classes for most of a year.
chapters.title: Bench Days
chapters.epigraph: “Do you remember the first sign?”
chapters.content:
The bench wasn’t attractive.

It was a long wooden bench beneath a row of old trees, beside the halfway vending machine on the long walkway, at the exact point where the path to the library split off from the path to the sports center. One of its wooden slats had a small crack, the paint on its metal legs was peeling, and whenever it rained, the seat remained damp long after the rest of the campus had dried.

There were plenty of nicer places to sit.

Xiaoran had nevertheless decided it was her favorite place on campus.

Not because of the view.

Not because it was quiet.

But because, in their first autumn, Yichen had told her it was the most inconvenient bench on campus, too far from everything, damp, and right next to a machine that was always out of the green tea, and she had taken that as a challenge.

It had started during their first year.

Yichen had been walking back from basketball training when he found Xiaoran sitting on the bench, looking thoroughly annoyed with a piece of paper in her hand.

“What happened?”

“Someone stole my seat.”

He glanced at the empty space beside her.

“There’s an empty seat.”

“That’s not the point.”

He sat down anyway.

She showed him the paper.

It was a printed notice from the university facilities department. The bench was apparently scheduled for maintenance, and students had been asked not to use it for a few days.

“They put a sign here,” she complained.

Yichen looked around.

There was no sign.

“Where?”

“It fell down.”

“Then how do you know?”

“I saw it this morning.”

He looked at the bench, then at her.

“You’re sitting on it now.”

“Because there’s no sign.”

“Convenient.”

She turned to him.

“Are you saying I’m unreasonable?”

“I’m saying you’re very committed to sitting here.”

She huffed.

He smiled and rested his arm along the back of the bench.

“All right. We’ll find you another seat.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I like this one.”

He met her eyes.

Then he said, “You should put up a sign.”

She blinked.

“What sign?”

“Something that says it’s reserved.”

“For whom?”

He turned to her.

“For you.”

That made her grin.

“That’s a good idea.”

He had meant it as a joke.

Unfortunately, Xiaoran was good at taking jokes seriously.

Three days later, Yichen found a piece of white paper taped to the backrest.

It was neatly cut, with the words written in black marker.

RESERVED.

Nothing else.

He stopped walking.

Then he looked around.

Xiaoran was sitting at the far end of the bench, pretending to read a book.

He approached her.

“What’s this?”

She didn’t look up.

“A sign.”

“I can see that.”

“Then why are you asking?”

He picked up the edge of the paper.

“Reserved for whom?”

She turned a page.

“That’s confidential.”

He looked at her.

She kept reading.

Yichen slowly smiled.

“Should I be concerned?”

“Maybe.”

He sat beside her.

Neither said anything.

Then he pointed at the sign.

“You know, the university might remove this.”

“Let them try.”

“You’re prepared to defend it?”

“Absolutely.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

She finally looked at him.

“You’re not going to ask me to take it down?”

“No.”

“Why?”

He leaned back.

“Because I want to see how long it lasts.”

Xiaoran smiled triumphantly.

It lasted nine days. On the tenth, the paper was gone.

She discovered it during lunch and stood in front of the bench with her hands on her hips.

“Unbelievable.”

Yichen, who had been waiting for her, looked up from his phone.

“What?”

“They removed it.”

He glanced at the empty backrest.

“Tragic.”

“Don’t sound so pleased.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He slipped his phone into his pocket.

“Do you want me to make another one?”

She considered it, then shook her head.

“No. This time, I’ll write something better.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Better?”

“More mysterious.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Looking forward to it.”

The second sign appeared a week later.

It was smaller.

Neater.

And, rather than being taped to the backrest, it was placed inside a transparent plastic sleeve and secured with a little clip.

Yichen found it before Xiaoran did.

He stopped in front of the bench.

Read it, then laughed under his breath.

PLEASE DO NOT DISTURB.

He took a photograph.

A moment later, he sent it to her.

Yichen: Your reservation has become rather serious.

Xiaoran: Thank you for noticing.

Yichen: Who are we protecting from disturbance?

Xiaoran: The people sitting here.

Yichen: People?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: Plural?

Xiaoran: Don’t be difficult.

He looked at the sign again.

Then typed:

Yichen: Understood.

When Xiaoran arrived twenty minutes later, she found him sitting beneath the sign with his backpack beside him.

She looked at the paper, then at him.

“You’re disturbing the reservation.”

He looked up. “Then I’m in the right place. Should I leave?”

She pretended to consider it.

“Depends.”

“On?”
