“Whether you brought me something.”

He reached into his bag and produced a milk tea from the stall by the library, half sugar, no pearls.

Her eyes brightened.

“You’re forgiven.”

He handed it to her.

“Generous.”

She sat beside him.

Their shoulders touched.

For the next twelve minutes, they talked about nothing important. Her lecturer had assigned an unreasonable amount of reading. His teammate had forgotten his shoes for training. She had seen a ridiculous advertisement on her way to class and wanted to show him.

It was ordinary.

Comfortable.

A small pocket of time between their separate schedules.

Eventually, Yichen checked his watch.

“I have to go.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Training?”

“Yes.”

She held up her drink.

“Thank you.”

He leaned over and kissed her temple.

“See you later.”

He had taken only a few steps when she called after him.

“Yichen.”

He turned.

She pointed at the sign.

“Don’t forget. Please do not disturb.”

He looked at her, then at the bench, then back at her.

His smile appeared slowly.

“Wouldn’t dream of it.”

By their second year, the bench had become a habit.

Neither of them had officially declared it their meeting place.

They kept returning.

Some days, Xiaoran arrived first and left her bag on the seat beside her. Some days, Yichen came directly from the sports center, his hair still damp and his training shirt sticking slightly to his back.

Sometimes they had time for a proper conversation.

Sometimes they had only enough time for a drink and a quick kiss.

The signs changed.

PLEASE DO NOT DISTURB.

PRIVATE PROPERTY.

MEETING IN PROGRESS.

CURRENTLY OCCUPIED.

Yichen had never written one himself.

But he had started keeping spare paper and a marker in his backpack.

Xiaoran discovered this one afternoon when she was searching for a pen.

She pulled out a black marker, then a small stack of white paper, then another plastic sleeve.

She stared at the items.

“What’s this?”

Yichen looked up from his phone.

“Supplies.”

“For what?”

He glanced at the marker in her hand.

“Your project.”

She met his eyes, then slowly smiled.

“You’ve been carrying these around?”

“Not all the time.”

“Since when?”

“A while.”

Her smile widened.

“You’re participating.”

He put his phone down.

“Someone has to make sure the signs are legible.”

She laughed.

“You’re so annoying.”

He took the marker from her and uncapped it.

“Do you have a preference?”

“For what?”

“The next sign.”

She leaned closer, considering the blank paper.

Then she said, “Something simple.”

He waited.

She pointed at the top.

“Write ‘Do Not Move’.”

He wrote it.

She watched him.

Then added, “And underneath, write ‘We’re Coming Back’.”

His hand paused.

She was smiling, seemingly pleased with her own idea.

He lowered his eyes and finished the sentence.

DO NOT MOVE.

WE’RE COMING BACK.

He clipped it to the backrest.

Xiaoran leaned back to admire it.

“Perfect.”

Yichen looked at the sign, then at her.

“Very reassuring.”

“Exactly.”

The following week, Yichen had a match.

Xiaoran had planned to watch, but her group project had fallen behind schedule. She spent most of the afternoon in the Media faculty building, trying to finish an edit before the submission deadline.

She messaged him around four.

Xiaoran: I might not make it.

Yichen: Don’t worry. Finish your work.

Xiaoran: Are you sure?

Yichen: Yes. I’ll see you afterwards.

Xiaoran: Good luck.

Yichen: Thank you.

She sent him a small rabbit sticker.

He sent one back.

The match ended with a win.

By the time Yichen left the sports center, it was nearly seven. He was tired, hungry, and still had a little soreness in his shoulder.

He could have gone straight back to his dormitory.

Instead, he walked toward the bench.

There was a new sign.

He stopped.

It was written in Xiaoran’s handwriting.

HE WON.

Underneath, in smaller letters:

HE SHOULD BE PROUD OF HIMSELF.

Yichen stood there.

Then he took out his phone and photographed it.

Yichen: I see someone has been updating the sign.

Her reply came almost immediately.

Xiaoran: It’s important information.

Yichen: How did you know we won?

Xiaoran: I checked the university sports account.

Yichen: You were working.

Xiaoran: I can do two things.

He smiled.

Yichen: Thank you.

Xiaoran: You’re welcome.

A few seconds later:

Xiaoran: Did you eat?

Yichen: Not yet.

Xiaoran: Wait for me. I’m coming.

He looked toward the path, then sat down beneath the sign.

When Xiaoran arrived fifteen minutes later, she was carrying her laptop bag and two takeaway boxes.

She stopped in front of him.

“Hello.”

He looked up.

“Hello.”

She pointed at the sign.

“Did you see it?”

“I did.”

“Do you like it?”

He nodded.

“Very much.”

She sat beside him and handed him one of the boxes.

“I bought dinner.”

He accepted it.

“Thank you.”

She opened hers.

Then, after a moment, she looked at him.

“You should be proud.”

He held her gaze.

“Of the match?”

“Yes.”

“We played well.”

“I know.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Thank you for checking.”

She shrugged.

“Obviously.”

He looked at her for a little longer.

Then he leaned over and kissed her temple.

“You’re very sweet.”

She smiled down at her food.

“Eat before it gets cold.”

In their third year, the signs became less frequent.

Not because they had stopped visiting the bench.

But because they no longer needed them as often.

Their schedules had become more complicated. Xiaoran had group assignments, production work, and occasional photography jobs. Yichen had basketball training, matches, coursework, and team commitments.

Sometimes they went several days without sitting there together.

But whenever one of them passed the bench, they looked.

It became an unconscious habit.

One afternoon, Xiaoran arrived to find the bench empty.

No sign.

No Yichen.

She checked her phone.

There was a message from him.

Yichen: Where are you?

Xiaoran: Bench.

Yichen: I’ll be there in five minutes.

She sat down.

The bench was dry from the afternoon sun, and a few leaves had gathered beneath it. She placed her bag beside her and looked at the empty backrest.

Something about it made her smile.

When Yichen arrived, he was carrying two drinks.

He handed one to her.

“Here.”

She accepted it.

“Thank you.”

He sat down beside her.

For a while, they talked about their days. Xiaoran told him about a lecturer who had given her a difficult assignment. Yichen told her about an upcoming match and a teammate who had been making everyone stay late at training.

Then Xiaoran glanced at the empty backrest.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you remember the first sign?”

“Reserved.”

She smiled.

“You remember.”

“Of course.”

“What about the second?”

“Please do not disturb.”

“And the third?”

He looked at her.

“Meeting in progress.”

“Good memory.”

He took a sip of his drink.

“Why?”

She looked at the bench again.

“I was thinking we should make one more.”

“What should it say?”

She didn’t answer immediately.

Instead, she reached into her bag and pulled out a small folded piece of paper.

Yichen watched as she unfolded it.

It was blank.

She held it out to him.

“Your turn.”

He took it.

“Mine?”

“Yes. You’ve never made one.”

“I’ve made several.”

“You’ve written what I told you to write.”

“An important distinction.”

She laughed.

“Now you can write whatever you want.”

He looked at the paper, then at her.

He uncapped the marker she’d brought.

He seemed to consider it seriously.

Then he began writing.

When he finished, he handed it back.

Xiaoran looked down.

The handwriting was neat, slightly slanted.

SAME TIME TOMORROW?

She blinked, then looked at him.

“Four words?”

“Three and a question mark.”

That made her grin.

“You’re asking me out?”

“I’m asking whether you’ll be here tomorrow.”

“At the same time?”

“If possible.”

She looked at the sign again.

Then she reached for the marker.

“Wait.”

She added something underneath.

Yichen watched her write.

When she turned the paper around, it read:

SAME TIME TOMORROW?

OBVIOUSLY.

He laughed.

“Very confident.”

She clipped the sign to the backrest.

Then she leaned against him, pleased.

“Now it’s complete.”

He looked at the paper.

“Why?”

She lifted her head.

“Because you’ve finally written one.”

He turned toward her.

“And what does that mean?”

“It means you’re officially part of the project.”

He gave her a knowing look.

“After three years?”

“You’re a slow learner.”

He laughed, then reached for her hand.

Their fingers intertwined.

They sat there until the sun began to lower behind the buildings, talking about ordinary things and occasionally falling quiet.

The next day, the sign was gone.

Neither knew who had removed it.

Xiaoran was disappointed for thirty seconds before deciding that the university probably had a serious problem with their artistic expression.

Yichen suggested they make another.

She said no.

There was no need.

Because the following afternoon, when she reached the bench, he was already sitting there with two drinks.

She stopped in front of him.

He looked up.

“You’re late.”

She checked her watch.

“Three minutes.”

“Still late.”

She eyed him.

“Where’s the sign?”

He glanced at the empty backrest.

“Didn’t need one.”

She smiled.

Then she sat beside him, taking the drink he had brought.

“Same time tomorrow?”

He studied her.

“Obviously.”

And that became the last sign they ever needed.

chapters.desc: His first fan-signing as a Herons player. Someone asks him to sign her arm. Then someone familiar joins the queue.
chapters.title: The Girl at the End of the Queue
chapters.epigraph: “There’s a difference.”
chapters.content:
The first time Zhou Yichen attended a fan-signing event as a Herons player, he discovered that being recognized by strangers was a rather unusual experience.

Not unpleasant. Just unusual.

He was used to people watching him on the court. He was used to the noise of the crowd, the camera flashes, the occasional chant of his name after a particularly good play.

But this was different.

There were no basketballs, no opponents, no scoreboard. Just a long table, a neat row of signed jerseys, a stack of photographs, and several hundred fans waiting for their turn to speak to him.

“Smile a little,” his teammate, Kou Ran, murmured beside him.

Yichen glanced at him.

“I am smiling.”

“You look like you’re reviewing a business proposal.”

“I might be.”

Kou Ran laughed, nearly knocking over his water bottle.

The event had been organized at the end of the season to celebrate the club’s year and introduce its development players to the fans. Yichen was one of four invited to the signing session, and although he’d attended media events before, this was his first proper fan-signing.

He was dressed in the club’s navy jersey with the heron on the chest, sleeves fitted around his arms. His hair had been styled neatly, though a few strands had already fallen over his forehead.

He looked composed, as usual.

Unfortunately for him, that seemed to be precisely what the fans liked.

The first few fans asked for signatures on jerseys and basketballs. Some were nervous, some excited, and some had prepared entire speeches.

Yichen listened to each of them patiently.

“Thank you for supporting us.”

“I’ll keep working hard.”

“Hope to see you next season.”

He was polite, occasionally smiling, and never rushed anyone unnecessarily.

Then a girl in the queue approached him holding out her arm.

“Could you sign here?”

Yichen looked at the spot she’d pointed to.

“Your arm?”

She nodded enthusiastically. “Yes! If that’s okay.”

“Sure.”

He took the marker and carefully signed her forearm, making sure the ink wouldn’t smudge against her sleeve.

The girl looked down at his signature, practically glowing.

“Thank you! I’ll never wash this off.”

Yichen smiled faintly. “You should probably wash your hands, though.”

She laughed, thanked him again, and moved along.

Kou Ran leaned toward him.

“Popular.”

Yichen capped the marker. “It’s a signature.”

“On someone’s arm.”

“Would you prefer I sign yours?”

“Absolutely not. I have standards.”

Yichen gave him a look and continued.

He didn’t notice the familiar face several people behind the next fan.

Not immediately, anyway.

Because Lin Xiaoran was standing in the queue.

And she was trying hard not to laugh.

She had arrived a little earlier with Jiayi, who had been considerably more excited about the event than Xiaoran initially admitted to being, and who had brought a sign.

She’d told herself she was only there to support him.

She’d already watched his games, attended his university tournaments, listened to him explain basketball strategies at dinner, and endured his occasional complaints about training schedules.

She knew him.

She knew the way he looked when he was concentrating, the way his jaw tightened when he was frustrated, the way he rubbed the back of his neck when he was tired.

She also knew that he had absolutely no idea she was here.

She’d deliberately avoided telling him.

Because she wanted to surprise him.

And, perhaps more importantly, because she wanted to see what he would do when his girlfriend approached him like an ordinary fan.

The queue moved forward.

Xiaoran glanced at the girl who had just received his signature.

Then she looked down at her own arm.

A small smile appeared.

“Oh, I have an idea,” she murmured to herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen was signing a photograph when the next fan stepped forward.

“Hello.”

He looked up.

“Hello.”

The girl smiled brightly.

He looked back down at the photograph, then stopped.

The marker hovered over the paper.

For a moment, he simply stared at the person standing across from him.

Lin Xiaoran.

She was wearing a simple cream cardigan over a white top, her hair falling loosely around her shoulders. She had a small handbag hanging from one shoulder and a innocent expression on her face.

Far too innocent.

Yichen’s eyes moved from her face to the queue behind her, then back again.

His expression didn’t change much.

But the corners of his mouth began to lift.

“Hello,” he said again.

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

“Hello, Mr. Zhou.”

His smile deepened.

“Mr. Zhou?”

“I’m here for an autograph.”

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

He put the photograph down.

“Where would you like it?”

She held out her arm.

“Here, please.”

Yichen looked at her arm, then at her.

A quiet pause.

“You want me to sign your arm?”

“Yes.”

“Like the girl before you?”

Xiaoran blinked.

She hadn’t expected him to mention that.

“...You noticed?”

“I was sitting here.”

“Oh.”

He leaned back slightly, looking at her with an expression that was becoming increasingly difficult for her to ignore.

“Is that why you joined the queue?”

“Yes.”

“Just for my autograph?”

“Of course.”

“Nothing else?”

Xiaoran nodded with great conviction.

Yichen picked up the marker again.

“What’s your name?”

She stared at him.

He looked perfectly serious.

“Lin Xiaoran,” she answered.

He nodded slowly, as though committing this important information to memory.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“Yes.”

“Have we met before?”

Her mouth fell open.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed.

Not loudly, but enough that the staff member beside him glanced over.

It was the kind of laugh Xiaoran rarely got to see in public. His shoulders relaxed, his eyes curved, and the carefully composed expression he’d maintained throughout the event finally broke.

She immediately regretted coming.

Not because he had recognized her.

Because he was enjoying this far too much.

“Don’t laugh,” she whispered.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’m trying to be professional.”

“Then be professional.”

“All right.”

He straightened, picked up her arm gently, and uncapped the marker.

“Where exactly?”

Xiaoran pointed to the inside of her forearm.

“Here.”

He steadied her wrist with one hand and began writing.

She watched him.

His handwriting was neat, slightly slanted. He wrote her name first, then added a small basketball beside it.

When he finished, he didn’t immediately let go.

Instead, he turned her arm slightly to inspect his work.

“Anything else?”

Xiaoran considered it.

“Can you write something?”

“What?”

“Something special.”

His eyes lifted to hers.

“What would you like?”

She smiled.

“Write, ‘To my favorite fan.’”

Yichen stared at her.

Then his lips curved.

“That’s a difficult request.”

“Why?”

“Because I have to be fair to the other fans.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“Are you saying I’m not your favorite fan?”

“I’m saying I shouldn’t announce favoritism at a public event.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He lowered his voice slightly.

“Then ask me somewhere private.”

Her cheeks warmed.

She glanced at the staff member, who was politely pretending not to hear them.

“Just write it.”

Yichen looked at her for another second before adding a small line beneath her name.

To my favorite girl.

Xiaoran stared.

It was worse than what she’d asked for.

Much worse.

Because he hadn’t written fan.

He’d written girl.

And the way he looked at her while doing it made her suddenly forget the entire reason she’d planned this little performance.

“Done,” he said.

She looked down at her arm, then back at him.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Can I have a photo?”

“Of course.”

She stepped to the side of the table, and a staff member took her phone.

Yichen stood up slightly, leaning closer so they could fit into the frame.

Xiaoran smiled brightly at the camera.

Yichen looked at it too, but just before the photo was taken, he glanced down at her.

The camera caught it.

His eyes were on her, not the lens.

And his smile was unmistakably fond.

✦ ✦ ✦

When Xiaoran finally stepped away from the table, she could hear Kou Ran laughing.

“Was that your girlfriend?”

Yichen sat back down.

“Next.”

“Come on. Was that her?”

“Next.”

Kou Ran leaned closer, grinning.

“You wrote something different for her, didn’t you?”

Yichen picked up another photograph.

“Do you want me to sign your forehead?”

Kou Ran laughed.

“That’s a yes.”

The next fan approached, and Yichen returned to his usual polite manner.

But every now and then, his gaze drifted toward the side of the room.

Xiaoran was standing near the exit with Jiayi, looking down at her arm.

She was smiling at the signature.

Then she took a picture of it, then another.

Then she sent him something on her phone.

His own phone, placed face down beside his water bottle, vibrated.

He couldn’t check it yet.

He had a queue to finish.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was almost forty minutes before the signing ended.

By then, Yichen’s hand was slightly tired, his throat dry, and Kou Ran had already announced that he was never signing another basketball in his life.

Yichen thanked the staff, changed out of his jersey, and checked his phone.

There were three messages from Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: I got my autograph!!

Xiaoran: Very handsome handwriting. 10/10.

Xiaoran: And “favorite girl” is better than what I asked for.

He smiled.

He typed back.

Yichen: You weren’t a fan.

Yichen: You were distracting the player.

Her reply came almost immediately.

Xiaoran: Excuse me. I was very respectful.

Xiaoran: I even waited in the queue like everyone else.

Xiaoran: You should appreciate my professionalism.

Yichen shook his head, smiling to himself.

He found her near the lobby, sitting on a bench with her legs swinging slightly. Jiayi had apparently gone to buy a drink, leaving Xiaoran alone.

The moment she saw him, she stood up.

“Congratulations, Mr. Zhou. Your first fan-signing event is over.”

“Thank you.”

“How was it?”

“Good.”

“Were you nervous?”

“Not particularly.”

“Did you enjoy meeting your fans?”

“I did.”

She nodded thoughtfully.

“Did you enjoy meeting me?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Most.”

“Most?”

“By far.”

Her smile grew.

He stepped closer, reaching for her hand. His gaze dropped to the signature on her arm.

“You’ve been looking at that for forty minutes.”

“It’s precious.”

“It’s my handwriting.”

“Exactly.”

He turned her arm gently, examining the ink.

“Don’t rub it too much. It’ll smudge.”

“I know.”

“And don’t use alcohol wipes.”

“I know.”

“Don’t—”

“Zhou Yichen.”

He looked up.

“I’m not going to preserve my arm in a museum.”

His mouth curved.

“Good. I was beginning to worry.”

She leaned closer, lowering her voice.

“Actually, I have a complaint.”

“Already?”

“Yes. The girl before me got a signature on her arm, and you were very gentle with her.”

Yichen raised an eyebrow.

“Was I not gentle with you?”

“You were.”

“Then?”

“You didn’t smile at her like that.”

He studied her face.

“Like what?”

“Like you were trying to make me forget what I came here to say.”

A faint smile appeared.

“Did it work?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth.

Closed it, then looked away.

Yichen laughed.

He lifted her signed arm and pressed a kiss just above the ink, careful not to touch the fresh writing.

“There. A special edition,” he murmured.

Her cheeks turned pink.

“That’s cheating.”

“Why?”

“Because you can’t give the other fans that.”

“No.”

He said it so naturally that she looked back at him.

Yichen’s fingers slipped between hers.

“That’s the point.”

For a moment, Xiaoran forgot about the crowded lobby, the event staff, and the fact that his teammates were probably still nearby.

She looked down at their joined hands.

Then she tilted her head.

“Do you think people will recognize me now?”

“Why?”

“Because I’m the girl who got your special signature.”

He considered that.

“Possibly.”

“Should I post it?”

“If you want.”

She opened her camera and took another picture of her arm, making sure the words were clear.

Then she looked up at him.

“Can you take one with me?”

“Of course.”

She handed him her phone and stood beside him, lifting her signed arm.

Yichen took one photo, then another.

“Wait. This one looks like we’re just friends,” she said.

He glanced at the screen.

“What should I do?”

“Look like you love me.”

He looked at her.

A slow, amused smile spread across his face.

“Is this not how I usually look at you?”

Xiaoran stared at him.

Then she reached for her phone.

“Never mind. That’s enough.”

He laughed and handed it back.

She posted the picture with a caption:

Finally met my favorite player. He was professional. Would recommend.

Yichen glanced at it.

“Very professional?”

“Extremely.”

“Is that all?”

She thought for a moment, then added another line.

Also, I think he has a favorite fan.

Yichen took her phone, read the caption, and handed it back.

“That’s inaccurate.”

Xiaoran looked offended.

“What?”

“You’re not my favorite fan.”

She gasped.

He leaned down, pressing a kiss to her hair.

“You’re my girlfriend.”

And then, just as she was about to smile, he said:

“There’s a difference.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, after they returned to his apartment, Xiaoran was still talking about the event.

She had already shown him the pictures twice, recounted the moment Kou Ran had laughed, and explained that she thought the staff member had definitely recognized her.

Yichen listened while changing out of his clothes.

At one point, she held up her arm again.

“Look. It’s still there.”

He glanced over.

“Good.”

“I wonder how long it’ll last.”

“Probably a day or two.”

She looked disappointed.

“Only that long?”

“You can take a picture.”

“But it’s not the same.”

He walked over and sat beside her on the sofa.

“Then I’ll sign something else.”

She brightened.

“Really?”

“Your notebook. Your phone case. A basketball. Whatever you want.”

Xiaoran considered it.

“Can you sign my forehead?”

Yichen looked at her.

Then he smiled.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Permanent marker?”

Her eyes widened.

“Obviously not!”

He laughed, pulling her into his arms.

She settled against his chest, still holding out her arm for him to inspect.

“Actually, I think I understand why fans do that now,” she said.

“Why?”

“It’s nice to have something that reminds you of someone you admire.”

Yichen lowered his gaze to her.

“And who do you admire?”

She looked up at him, pretending to think.

“Hmm. A basketball player. Quite handsome. A little arrogant.”

“A little?”

“Very calm. Sometimes annoying.”

“Sounds unfortunate.”

“Terrible, really.”

He brushed her hair back.

“Should I be concerned?”

“Not really. He’s also my boyfriend.”

“That’s convenient.”

“Very.”

Yichen leaned down and kissed her.

It was brief at first, then lingered when she slipped her arms around his neck.

When he pulled away, she was smiling.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Mm?”

“When that girl asked you to sign her arm, did you think I would do the same?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I know you.”

She frowned slightly.

“What does that mean?”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“You’d find some way to make it more complicated.”

Xiaoran gasped.

“I did not!”

“You asked for a special message.”

“Because I’m special.”

“I know.”

“And you wrote something different for me.”

“I did.”

She smiled, satisfied.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “What if I hadn’t joined the queue? Would you have looked for me?”

Yichen’s expression softened.

He tucked her hair behind her ear.

“I was already looking for you before you came to the table.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“You saw me?”

“Not at first. But I knew you were somewhere in the room.”

“How?”

“Because Jiayi was in the queue holding a sign with my name on it in letters a foot high, and Jiayi doesn’t go anywhere without you.”

She burst into laughter.

“So you knew?”

“I suspected.”

“Then why did you ask if we’d met before?”

“You were enjoying yourself.”

He kissed her temple.

“And I wanted to see what you’d do.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“You knew I was planning something?”

“I know you.”

She buried her face against his chest, laughing.

Yichen wrapped both arms around her, resting his cheek lightly against her hair.

His first fan-signing had been a success, according to the club.

There had been a long queue, plenty of photographs, hundreds of signatures, and a considerable amount of attention.

But when he thought about the day later, the moment he remembered most clearly wasn’t the applause or the cameras.

It was a familiar girl standing at the end of the queue, holding out her arm with the most innocent expression he’d ever seen.

And the fact that, despite having spent the afternoon signing his name for hundreds of people, the only signature he wanted to give again was hers.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran wants to learn to drive. Zhou Yichen hands her the keys to the car he bought because of one joke.
chapters.title: The Most Expensive Driving Lesson
chapters.epigraph: “It’s a car. Not a family heirloom.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had recently developed an interest in driving.

It began rather innocently.

One afternoon, while she and Yichen were having lunch, she watched a woman effortlessly reverse her car into a narrow parking space outside the restaurant.

Xiaoran followed the car with her eyes until it disappeared.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Do you know how to drive?”

He looked up from his food.

“Do you think I don’t?”

“I know you do. I’m just asking.”

“Then yes.”

She nodded thoughtfully.

“Can you teach me?”

Yichen put down his chopsticks.

“Drive?”

“No, fly.”

He gave her a look.

She smiled, completely unbothered.

“I want to learn. I’ve been thinking about getting a driving licence.”

“That’s good.”

“Really?”

“Why wouldn’t it be?”

“I thought you might tell me it’s dangerous.”

“Driving is dangerous if you don’t learn properly. That’s why you need lessons.”

She leaned forward.

“Will you teach me?”

Yichen considered her.

“Do you want me to teach you, or do you want to learn at a driving school?”

“Both, maybe. I think learning from someone I know would be less scary.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Really?”

“I’ll teach you.”

She returned to her lunch, apparently satisfied.

Yichen, however, was already considering which car he should let her practice in.

There was his own car, the one he’d bought in first year because of one joke, which he drove to university and training every day. There were the cars at his family home, which he wouldn’t have considered for a beginner even if they hadn’t been in another city.

He decided his own would do. It was comfortable, easy to handle, and safe.

He didn’t anticipate that the biggest obstacle to Xiaoran’s first driving lesson would be the car itself.

✦ ✦ ✦

The following Saturday morning, Xiaoran arrived at his apartment wearing a loose white shirt, jeans, and sneakers.

She had brought a small notebook.

Yichen noticed it immediately.

“What’s that?”

“My driving notes.”

“You’ve already made notes?”

“Of course. I did some research.”

He looked at her notebook.

The first page had a title written in pink:

Things I Need to Remember Before Driving.

Underneath were several bullet points.

- Adjust seat.
- Adjust mirrors.
- Seatbelt.
- Check surroundings.
- Don’t panic.
- Don’t confuse brake and accelerator.
- Don’t hit anything.

Yichen read the last line twice.

“That’s a good objective.”

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m pleased you’re taking this seriously.”

He took his car keys from the counter.

“Let’s go.”

Xiaoran followed him downstairs, chatting about how she had watched several beginner driving videos the night before.

She was halfway through explaining the difference between parallel parking and reverse parking when they reached the underground garage.

Then she stopped.

Yichen pressed the key.

His car blinked its headlights at the far end of the empty bottom level.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Then she turned to him.

“...You want me to drive that?”

“Yes.”

“Your car?”

He glanced at it.

“That’s generally what it means when I hand you the keys.”

She ignored his teasing and looked back at the vehicle.

She had sat in its passenger seat a hundred times. She had eaten crisps in it, cried in it, fallen asleep in it on the way home from the airport after Chengdu. She had never once looked at it from the driver’s side.

It was beautiful. Low, polished, with an elegant dark exterior and a leather interior that looked as though it belonged in a luxury showroom rather than a university student’s garage.

She knew Yichen had money. She had known for a long time.

But knowing and being reminded of it were two different things.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Are you teaching me in this?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the car again, then at him.

“Can we borrow a different car?”

“Whose?”

“Anyone’s. Fang Ze’s.”

“Fang Ze’s car has a dent in every door.”

“Exactly. One more wouldn’t matter.”

“Why are you so worried about this one?”

She hesitated.

“Because this one looks expensive.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted slightly.

“It is.”

“Then why are you letting me drive it?”

“Because you want to learn.”

“But what if I scratch it?”

“Then we’ll deal with it.”

“What if I hit the wall?”

“Hopefully, you won’t.”

“What if—”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked at him.

He held the passenger-side door open.

“It’s a car. Not a family heirloom.”

“It’s an extremely expensive car.”

“And?”

“And I don’t want to be responsible for damaging it!”

Yichen smiled faintly.

“Then let’s make sure you don’t.”

He waited until she finally climbed into the driver’s seat.

She sat down carefully, almost as if she were afraid of leaving fingerprints on the leather.

Yichen walked around and got into the passenger seat.

He glanced at her.

“Why are you sitting like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re visiting a museum.”

“I am respecting the vehicle.”

He laughed.

“Adjust your seat first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

For the first fifteen minutes, they didn’t even start the engine.

Yichen explained the basic controls, helped her adjust the seat and mirrors, and showed her where the indicators, headlights, and wipers were.

Xiaoran listened attentively.

Sometimes she asked questions.

Sometimes she repeated what he said under her breath.

At one point, she turned toward him.

“Why are there so many buttons?”

“Most of them are straightforward.”

“That’s easy for you to say. You’ve been driving for years.”

“Fair enough.”

He patiently explained the controls again.

Then he showed her the gear selector.

“This is for changing gears. For now, just focus on the basic controls. Don’t worry about everything at once.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

“Seatbelt.”

She fastened it.

“Mirrors?”

She checked them.

“Good.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Ready?”

Xiaoran took a deep breath.

“Yes.”

He nodded toward the empty bays of the bottom level, where nobody parked on a Saturday morning.

“Start the engine.”

She pressed the button.

The engine came alive.

Her eyes widened slightly.

“It’s so loud.”

“It’s normal.”

“It sounds very powerful.”

“It is.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Are you sure this is a beginner-friendly car?”

Yichen laughed.

“It’s fine.”

“Your definition of fine is questionable.”

He settled back into his seat.

“Foot on the brake. We’ll move slowly.”

Xiaoran followed his instructions.

The car began rolling forward.

Very slowly.

Almost comically slowly.

Yichen watched the space ahead, then glanced at her.

“Good. Keep your hands steady.”

She looked intensely focused.

“I’m doing it.”

“You are.”

“I’m actually driving.”

“Yes.”

“Yichen, I’m driving your car.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She turned her head toward him, delighted.

“I’m driving!”

“Eyes on the road, Xiaoran.”

She immediately faced forward.

“Right. Sorry.”

He smiled.

It was a small thing, but he enjoyed watching her discover something new. She had a tendency to become completely absorbed in whatever interested her, and right now she was taking every instruction seriously.

She drove in a straight line, then made a gentle turn, then stopped.

Yichen nodded.

“Good.”

She exhaled.

“How was that?”

“Very good for your first attempt.”

Her smile was enormous.

Then she looked at the car.

“Nothing happened.”

“That’s usually the goal.”

She laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble began when Yichen asked her to practice turning into a parking space.

He explained the angle, the mirrors, and how to judge the distance.

Xiaoran listened.

She really did.

But when she started turning, she became convinced that the car was getting too close to the painted line.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Am I too close?”

“Not yet. Turn a little more.”

She turned the steering wheel.

“More?”

“A little.”

“Like this?”

“Good.”

Then she stopped.

“Wait.”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“I think I’m too close.”

“You’re fine.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

She glanced at the mirror, then the front, then the mirror again.

“Yichen, I don’t think I can do this.”

He looked at her face.

Her brows were drawn together, and her hands had tightened around the steering wheel.

He spoke calmly.

“Look at me for a second.”

She turned.

“Take a breath.”

She did.

“Nothing is happening. You’re moving slowly. I can see the distance, and I’ll tell you if you need to stop.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

“Trust your eyes, not your imagination.”

Xiaoran gave him a small, embarrassed smile.

“That’s difficult.”

“I know.”

He guided her through the rest of the turn.

She parked successfully.

Not perfectly centred, but safely within the lines.

When she stopped the car, she looked at him as if she had just completed an international driving competition.

“Did I do it?”

“You did.”

She let go of the steering wheel.

Then she turned toward him.

“I’m amazing.”

Yichen laughed.

“You are.”

She looked at the car again.

“Your car is still alive.”

“Thankfully.”

She reached over and lightly hit his arm.

“Don’t make fun of me!”

He caught her hand, bringing it to his lips for a brief kiss.

“I knew you could.”

That made her smile again.

✦ ✦ ✦

After nearly an hour, they decided to take a break.

Yichen drove the car out of the garage and parked at a quiet café nearby. Xiaoran was still talking about her first successful parking attempt.

“I think I understand the steering now.”

“Good.”

“And the mirrors.”

“Good.”

“And I didn’t panic.”

“You panicked a little.”

“I did not.”

He glanced at her.

“You asked me six times whether you were too close.”

“That’s not panic. That’s checking.”

“Of course.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Are you going to be a difficult driving instructor?”

“I thought I was being patient.”

“You are. But you have a very annoying face when you’re right.”

He smiled.

“I’m afraid that’s not something I can change.”

She took a sip of her drink.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “Can I drive again next week?”

“Whenever you want.”

“Really?”

“Of course.”

She hesitated.

“Even with this car?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Would you prefer I buy another car for your lessons?”

Her eyes widened.

“No!”

He laughed.

“I was joking.”

“Don’t joke about things like that.”

“Why?”

“Because you might actually do it.”

He didn’t answer immediately.

Which was, in itself, suspicious.

Xiaoran put down her drink.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“You’re not going to buy me a car just because I want to learn, are you?”

“Not today.”

“That’s not reassuring!”

He laughed, then reached across the table to brush a little foam from the corner of her mouth.

“Listen. You don’t need to worry about the price of the car every time you make a mistake. That’s why I’m here. We’ll start slowly, and when you’re ready, you’ll take lessons with a proper instructor too.”

“Why both?”

“Because I want you to learn properly. I’m your boyfriend, not a certified driving instructor.”

“Then why did you volunteer?”

“Because you asked me.”

His answer was so simple that she fell quiet.

He said, “And because I like spending time with you. Even if you spend half of it worrying about my car.”

She smiled.

“I wasn’t worrying about the car. I was worrying about your wallet.”

“That’s very considerate.”

“I’m serious!”

“I know.”

He turned her hand over and traced his thumb over her palm.

“But you don’t have to protect my wallet from yourself.”

Xiaoran looked at him for a while.

Then she smiled mischievously.

“So if I accidentally scratch your car, you’ll still love me?”

“Sadly.”

“Unfortunately?”

“It’s a serious inconvenience.”

She laughed, kicking his shoe lightly under the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

The following Saturday, Xiaoran arrived with her notebook again.

This time, she had added a new page.

Things I Must Not Do While Driving Yichen’s Car.

1. Panic.
2. Hit the accelerator too hard.
3. Hit the brake too hard.
4. Scratch the car.
5. Make Yichen regret teaching me.
6. Cry if I make a mistake.

Yichen read the list while standing beside her.

He looked at the last item, then at her.

“Why would you cry?”

“Because I might feel bad.”

He closed the notebook.

“Let’s add something.”

“What?”

He took her pen and wrote beneath the list.

7. Remember that learning is more important than being perfect.

Xiaoran read it, then looked up at him.

“That’s a very teacher-like thing to say.”

“I’m a good teacher.”

“You’re a very handsome teacher.”

He paused.

“Is that relevant to driving?”

“Very. It helps me stay motivated.”

He laughed, opening the passenger door for her.

“Get in, student.”

She climbed into the driver’s seat, looking considerably less intimidated than the week before.

Yichen settled beside her.

She adjusted the seat, checked the mirrors, and fastened her seatbelt without being reminded.

He watched her with quiet approval.

“Ready?”

She nodded.

Then she turned to him.

“Yichen?”

“Hmm?”

“If I become a really good driver, can I drive you somewhere?”

His expression softened.

“Where?”

“Anywhere you want.”

He considered it.

“Then take me home.”

She blinked.

“Your apartment?”

“Or somewhere else. I don’t mind.”

She smiled, placing both hands on the steering wheel.

“Okay. I’ll drive you home one day.”

Yichen leaned back, watching her start the engine.

“I’ll look forward to it.”

And he meant it.

Not because he particularly needed someone else to drive him around.

But because he could already imagine it: Xiaoran sitting proudly behind the wheel, insisting she knew the way, occasionally asking him to check the navigation, and getting offended whenever he suggested a different route.

He would probably end up driving anyway.

But he would let her have the keys.

After all, it was only a car.

And he had never been particularly good at saying no to her.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran passes her driving test first time and keeps a promise from the car park: she drives Zhou Yichen home, at twenty kilometres an hour.
chapters.title: She Passed
chapters.epigraph: “Goodnight, driver.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Lin Xiaoran did after passing her driving test was call Zhou Yichen.

The second thing she did was scream, which seemed like the correct response to passing.

“YICHEN!”

Yichen, who was in the middle of reviewing a document at his desk, immediately lifted his phone away from his ear.

He waited for the sound to settle.

Then he smiled.

“Nice to see you as well.”

“I passed!”

His hand stopped moving.

He looked at the document in front of him.

Then he leaned back in his chair.

“You passed?”

“YES!”

A laugh escaped him.

“Congratulations.”

“I passed, Yichen!”

“I heard you.”

“I really passed!”

“I know.”

She sounded breathless, as if she’d just finished running rather than completing a driving test.

He could almost picture her: eyes wide, cheeks flushed, probably holding her phone with both hands while trying hard not to jump around in public.

“How did it go?” he asked.

“At first, I was nervous.”

“Understandable.”

“But then I remembered everything my instructor taught me. I checked the mirrors, adjusted the seat, checked the blind spots, and did the parking.”

“Good.”

“And I didn’t hit anything.”

He smiled.

“That’s an important achievement.”

“Yichen!”

“I’m kidding.”

She went quiet for a second.

Then, in a much smaller voice, she said, “I passed on my first attempt.”

His expression softened.

“I know. You did well.”

There was a little pause.

Then she asked, “Are you free today?”

“Why?”

“Because...”

He waited.

She lowered her voice as if she were about to reveal a carefully guarded secret.

“I want to drive.”

“Where?”

“Home. Yours. You told me to take you home, and I said I would,” she said.

Yichen looked at his phone.

He remembered.

Seven weeks ago, on the bottom level of his building’s car park, she had sat behind his steering wheel looking at the dashboard as if it might explode if she pressed the wrong button. She had been afraid of scratching his car, afraid of the accelerator, afraid of everything. And at the end of that afternoon she had asked whether, if she ever got good, she could drive him somewhere.

Then take me home, he’d said.

He hadn’t forgotten.

“All right,” he said.

Her voice immediately brightened.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Come and get me.”

He glanced at the clock.

“With what?”

“Your car.”

“So I drive to the test center, so that you can drive me home.”

“Yes.”

“Good plan.”

“Don’t laugh!”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He was smiling too much to deny it.

✦ ✦ ✦

When Yichen pulled up outside the test center that afternoon, Xiaoran was waiting by the gate. She walked up to the car with a different face from the one she’d worn in his car park seven weeks ago. Today she looked proud of herself.

She held up her new licence.

“Look.”

Yichen took it.

He glanced at the details, then looked back at her.

“Congratulations, licensed driver.”

“Thank you.”

He gave it back.

“How does it feel?”

“Very good.”

“Confident?”

“Extremely.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Extremely?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He looked at the car.

“Should I be worried?”

She immediately frowned.

“Why would you be worried?”

“Just checking.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed and opened the passenger door.

“Get in, then.”

She didn’t move.

He met her eyes.

“What?”

“You’re supposed to let me drive.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you opening that door?”

He closed it again.

“Sorry, Madam Driver.”

She smiled with satisfaction.

“Better.”

He got into the passenger seat himself.

Xiaoran opened the driver’s door.

And then she stopped.

The familiar interior looked much more intimidating than it had when she was sitting beside him.

She had driven during her lessons. She had practiced parking, turning, braking, and changing lanes. She had passed the test.

But this was different.

This was Yichen’s car.

His expensive, beautiful, spotless car.

And he was going to sit beside her.

She took a breath.

Yichen watched her.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re staring at the steering wheel.”

“I’m checking it.”

“It’s the same steering wheel.”

“I know.”

He waited.

She finally sat down and adjusted the seat, then the mirrors, then the seat again.

Yichen watched her make three small adjustments.

“Comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She put her hands on the steering wheel.

He glanced at them.

“Ten and two?”

She met his eyes.

“Don’t test me.”

“Wouldn’t dare.”

The first few minutes went well.

She checked her mirrors, adjusted her position, fastened her seat belt, and started the engine.

Yichen remained quiet.

He didn’t reach for anything or offer unnecessary instructions.

He had learned during their first lesson that she became more nervous when he spoke too much.

She looked toward him.

“Ready?”

“Whenever you are.”

She slowly released the brake.

The car began moving.

At approximately twenty kilometers per hour.

Yichen looked at the speedometer, then at her, then back at the road.

He said nothing.

Xiaoran was concentrating so hard that her lips had pressed into a thin line.

The car rolled forward.

A little too slowly.

A car behind them maintained a respectful distance.

She glanced at the speedometer, then at the road, then at the speedometer again.

Yichen finally spoke.

“You’re allowed to go a little faster.”

“I know.”

“All right.”

She increased the speed.

To twenty-one kilometers per hour.

He turned his head slightly toward the window.

A smile appeared.

She noticed.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Am I not allowed to be happy?”

“Not like that.”

He looked at her.

“How should I smile?”

“Normally.”

“This is my normal smile.”

She gave him a suspicious look, then returned her attention to the road.

At the first intersection, Xiaoran slowed down.

She checked the traffic.

Waited.

Checked again.

Yichen watched her carefully.

She finally turned the steering wheel and completed the turn.

It was smooth.

He nodded.

“Good.”

She smiled without looking at him.

“Thank you.”

A little farther down the road, she asked, “Was that okay?”

“Yes.”

“Did I turn too early?”

“No.”

“Too late?”

“No.”

“Then it was perfect?”

He considered.

“Very good.”

She turned to him.

“Why can’t you say perfect?”

“Because I don’t want you to become arrogant.”

She gasped.

“I’m already a licensed driver!”

“Congratulations again.”

She smiled.

He reached over and gently touched her shoulder.

“You’re doing well. Keep your eyes on the road.”

She nodded.

And, for the next few minutes, they drove in comfortable silence.

At a red light, Xiaoran looked at him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Are you nervous?”

He turned toward her.

“About what?”

“My driving.”

He considered the question.

“Not particularly.”

“Really?”

“You’re driving safely.”

She looked pleased.

“Then you trust me?”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“Even with your car?”

He looked at the dashboard, then back at her.

“Even with my car.”

She seemed satisfied.

The light turned green.

She started moving again.

A moment later, she said, “I remember the first time you taught me.”

“I remember.”

“I was so scared.”

“You were.”

“I thought I would scratch your car.”

“You were more worried about that than your own safety.”

She frowned.

“That’s because your car is expensive.”

“And now?”

She looked ahead.

“Now I’m only a little worried.”

“About the car?”

“About you judging me.”

He turned his head.

“Why would I judge you?”

“Because you’re good at driving.”

“That doesn’t mean I expect you to drive like me. You just passed your test. You’re allowed to be inexperienced.”

She nodded slowly.

“Okay.”

“And you don’t need to prove anything to me.”

Her fingers relaxed slightly on the steering wheel.

“I know.”

He smiled.

“Good.”

The journey home took longer than usual.

Normally, Yichen could make the drive in a fraction of the time.

Today, they encountered every red light, every cautious turn, and every opportunity for Xiaoran to reduce her speed as if the road ahead might disappear.

At one point, they passed the café near campus, theirs since the week they’d moved to Shanghai.

“Should I turn here?”

“That’s not our route.”

“I know. I was just asking.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to see if you remembered.”

He turned to her.

“Remember what?”

“That it’s ours.”

“I remember.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

A few minutes later, she asked, “Do you think I’m a good driver?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

She looked at him.

“Yichen?”

“You’ve passed your test.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He smiled.

“You’re a good beginner.”

She looked offended.

“A beginner?”

“An inexperienced driver.”

“That’s worse!”

He laughed.

“Would you prefer I lie?”

She thought about it.

“No.”

“Then there you go.”

She huffed.

He reached over and squeezed her hand, careful not to distract her.

“You’ll get better with practice.”

She smiled again.

“I know.”

When they finally reached his residential complex, Xiaoran looked relieved. She had brought them home without hitting anything.

She slowed down as they approached the car park entrance.

Yichen gave her a few directions. She followed them, turned carefully, and took the ramp down to the bottom level, where she’d had her first lesson, then came the final challenge.

Parking.

She looked at the space, then at the mirrors, then at the space again.

Yichen waited.

“Take your time.”

She nodded.

The first attempt was slightly crooked.

She stopped.

Looked at the car, then looked at him.

He said nothing.

She reversed slowly, adjusted the angle, and tried again.

This time, the car settled neatly between the lines.

She put the car in park.

Turned off the engine.

And sat completely still.

Yichen looked at her.

“Done.”

She blinked.

Then she turned toward him.

“I did it.”

“You did.”

“I drove your car.”

“You did.”

“All the way home.”

He smiled.

“At twenty kilometers per hour.”

She stared at him.

Then her mouth fell open.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed.

She hit his arm lightly.

“Don’t make fun of me!”

“I’m not making fun of you.”

“You are!”

He reached over and took her hand.

“Xiaoran.”

She stopped.

He looked at her properly.

“You drove me home.”

Her expression softened.

She forgot to be offended.

Then she smiled.

“Yes.”

“Just like you said you would.”

She looked down at their joined hands.

“Yes.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Thank you.”

She turned toward him.

“You’re welcome.”

They didn’t get out immediately.

Xiaoran remained in the driver’s seat, looking at the dashboard.

Yichen watched her.

“What’s wrong now?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re staring again.”

She smiled.

“I just feel strange.”

“Why?”

“Because I finally did it.”

He nodded.

She turned toward him.

“Do you remember what I said during the first lesson?”

“That you wanted to drive me somewhere?”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“I wanted to take you home.”

He held her gaze.

“And you did.”

She nodded.

Then she leaned across the center console and wrapped her arms around him.

Yichen laughed at the sudden embrace, but his arms came around her immediately.

She rested her cheek against his shoulder.

“Next time, I’ll drive faster.”

“How much faster?”

“Maybe thirty.”

He looked down at her.

“Ambitious.”

“Forty, if I’m feeling brave.”

“Let’s not get ahead of ourselves.”

She laughed against his shoulder.

He kissed her temple.

“You’re doing well. There’s no need to rush.”

She pulled back.

“I know.”

He moved her hair off her cheek.

“And I like being your passenger.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She laughed.

“You’re so annoying.”

“You’re welcome.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, they ordered dinner and stayed in.

Xiaoran was still talking about the drive.

She described the turns she had made, the traffic light that had made her nervous, and how she had almost forgotten to check one of her mirrors before correcting herself.

Yichen listened, occasionally asking questions.

At some point, she took his phone and opened the map.

“Look.”

He glanced at the screen.

“What?”

“This was our route.”

He looked at the blue line.

“Yes.”

“It took us thirty-eight minutes.”

“Usually it takes fifteen.”

She nodded.

“Because I drove.”

“That’s right.”

She looked pleased.

Then she noticed something.

“Wait.”

“Hm?”

“Why did you save the route?”

He studied her.

“Maybe I didn’t.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Then why is it starred?”

“Because I wanted to remember the route.”

“Why?”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“Because you drove me home.”

She looked at him.

Then her cheeks warmed.

“That’s so unnecessary.”

He reached for her hand.

“I disagree.”

She smiled and leaned against his shoulder.

A few minutes later, her phone vibrated.

A message from Meilin.

Meilin: Heard you passed your driving test. Congratulations!

Xiaoran: THANK YOU!

Meilin: Have you driven yet?

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen.

Then she typed.

Xiaoran: I drove Yichen home today.

Meilin: Oh?

Xiaoran: Yes!

Meilin: How did it go?

Xiaoran smiled.

Xiaoran: Very well.

Yichen glanced at the screen.

“How fast?”

She held his gaze.

“Don’t.”

He laughed.

She continued typing.

Xiaoran: I drove safely.

Meilin replied almost immediately.

Meilin: How fast?

Xiaoran stared at the message.

Then, slowly, she turned toward Yichen.

He was already smiling.

“Don’t you dare.”

He laughed.

Later that night, when Xiaoran was ready to leave, Yichen walked her to the door.

She slipped on her shoes and turned toward him.

“Next time, I’ll drive you somewhere else.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere you want.”

He considered.

“Can I choose?”

“Yes.”

“Then take me somewhere you like.”

She blinked.

“That’s not fair.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted you to choose.”

He smiled.

“Then I’ll choose somewhere you like.”

She shook her head, laughing.

“You’re unbelievable.”

He kissed her hair.

“Goodnight, driver.”

She smiled.

“Goodnight, passenger.”

Then she stepped into the corridor.

Before the door closed, she turned around.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Next time, I’ll try to drive at thirty.”

He nodded solemnly.

“I look forward to it.”

She grinned.

“Don’t be scared.”

“I won’t.”

The door closed.

He had been driven home in his own car at twenty kilometers an hour, in more than twice the usual time, and he was still smiling when he locked the door.

chapters.desc: Her father’s car, the compound gate, and Yichen in the passenger seat trying very hard to look relaxed.
chapters.title: Her First Solo Drive
chapters.epigraph: “You were driving well. I knew that.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had never been nervous about Xiaoran driving.

He had, however, underestimated how difficult it would be to sit in the passenger seat while she did it.

“All right.”

Xiaoran adjusted the rear-view mirror, then the side mirror, then the rear-view mirror again.

Yichen sat beside her, fastening his seat belt. His expression was calm, his posture relaxed, and his hands rested neatly on his thighs.

“Ready?” he asked.

“Yes.”

She turned the key.

The engine started.

He looked back.

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re making me nervous.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face is saying something.”

Yichen smiled.

“Then I’ll stop using my face.”

She gave him a suspicious look before turning forward.

This was supposed to be a simple drive.

Her father’s car was a twelve-year-old silver Buick that he washed every Sunday and had never once let anyone else drive. He had agreed to let her take it out that afternoon, the first week of the summer holiday, provided she had someone experienced beside her. Xiaoran had immediately volunteered Yichen, partly because he was the most suitable person and partly because she wanted him to see that she could drive perfectly well.

She had passed her test in Shanghai six weeks ago. She had driven exactly two cars in her life, and both of them were Yichen’s: once on the bottom level of his car park, and once home from the test center. She knew the rules. She was prepared. And Yichen had promised not to interfere unless necessary.

“Okay. Let’s go,” she said, gripping the steering wheel.

The car moved forward.

Slowly.

Yichen looked through the windshield, then at the speedometer, then at Xiaoran.

“You’re doing well.”

“I know.”

“Just checking.”

She gave him a smile.

The car reached the compound gate. The security guard in the booth put down his newspaper to watch. She stopped, checked both directions twice, and carefully turned onto the road.

Yichen nodded.

“Good.”

Xiaoran’s smile grew.

“See?”

“See what?”

“I’m driving.”

“I noticed.”

“Without you doing anything.”

“Very impressive.”

She met his eyes.

He was smiling.

She felt a little more confident.

Then they approached their first intersection.

Xiaoran slowed down.

A car appeared from the right.

She stopped.

The other car passed.

She waited a moment longer than necessary.

Yichen glanced at her.

“Clear.”

“I can see.”

“Of course.”

She turned.

A little too sharply.

Yichen’s right hand moved instinctively toward the door handle.

He caught himself halfway, then placed it there anyway.

Xiaoran noticed.

Her eyes flicked toward his hand.

“What’s that?”

“What?”

“Your hand.”

He looked down.

It was resting on the passenger-side door handle.

“Nothing.”

“Why are you holding it?”

“Comfortable position.”

She looked at him.

“You’re holding the door handle.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He looked ahead.

“Just in case.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

“Yichen!”

He turned toward her, still perfectly composed.

“Eyes on the road.”

She laughed harder.

By the time they reached the main road, Xiaoran had regained her confidence.

She drove at a reasonable speed, kept a safe distance from the car ahead, and remembered to check her mirrors.

Yichen had stopped giving verbal instructions.

He was also still holding the door handle.

Not tightly.

Not dramatically.

Just firmly enough that Xiaoran could see the slight tension in his fingers.

She tried not to laugh.

She really did.

But after another few minutes, she couldn’t resist.

“Are you scared?”

“No.”

“Then why are you holding on?”

“Habit.”

“What habit?”

“Passenger habit.”

She turned to him.

“You weren’t like this when I drove you home from the test.”

“That was a straight road. And my car.”

She gasped. “So you trust me less in my dad’s car?”

“I trust you completely. I don’t trust your father’s opinion of me if we come back with a scratch,” he said.

“That’s not the same thing.”

His mouth curved.

“All right.”

“You’re laughing at me.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He looked out of the window.

His mouth was still curved.

Xiaoran made a small offended noise.

“Fine. I’ll show you.”

“Please don’t.”

She immediately laughed.

“You’re so annoying.”

The second incident happened when a motorcycle changed lanes ahead of them.

Xiaoran reacted correctly.

She eased off the accelerator, maintained her distance, and waited for the motorcycle to move ahead.

Nothing dangerous happened.

But Yichen’s fingers tightened around the handle.

Xiaoran noticed.

She glanced at him, then at the road, then back at him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Are you all right?”

“Perfectly.”

“Your hand.”

He looked down.

Still gripping.

He slowly loosened his fingers.

“Sorry.”

“You’re nervous.”

“A little.”

She blinked.

That was unexpected.

Yichen wasn’t someone who admitted to being nervous often, especially over something so ordinary.

“Really?”

He looked at her.

“Would you prefer I lie?”

“No.”

She considered him.

“Why?”

He glanced toward the road.

“Because I know how careful you are. But I also know you’re still getting used to driving on your own.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“So you’re worried about me?”

“I’m sitting beside you.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

He met her eyes.

“Yes. I’m worried about you.”

Her expression softened.

Then she turned her attention back to the road.

“Don’t worry. I’ll take good care of you.”

Yichen laughed.

“Thank you.”

Their destination was a small café about twenty minutes away.

Xiaoran had chosen it specifically because the route was relatively straightforward, the parking lot was spacious, and she had been there before with Meilin.

She had planned everything.

She had even checked the parking entrance on a map the night before.

What she hadn’t planned for was the fact that the parking lot was busier than usual.

She drove slowly between the parked cars, looking for an empty space.

“There’s one,” Yichen said.

“I see it.”

She turned on the indicator, then stopped.

The space was between two cars.

Not narrow.

But narrow enough.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Yichen waited.

She moved forward slightly.

Stopped.

Adjusted the steering wheel, then looked at him.

“Do you think I can fit?”

He looked at the space, then at her.

“Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the car on her left, then the car on her right, then the space again.

Yichen’s hand returned to the door handle.

Xiaoran noticed.

She slowly turned toward him.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“You’re doing it again.”

He looked down.

A pause.

Then he released the handle.

“Sorry.”

She smiled triumphantly.

“Good.”

She reversed carefully, checking her mirrors.

Yichen remained silent.

She adjusted once, then again.

Finally, the car settled neatly between the two vehicles.

She put it in park.

Silence.

Xiaoran looked at the parking lines, then at Yichen, then back at the parking lines.

A smile slowly spread across her face.

“I did it.”

Yichen looked at the car’s position.

“Perfectly.”

She turned toward him.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She unfastened her seat belt, looking thoroughly pleased with herself.

“See? You were worried for nothing.”

“You’re right.”

She leaned across the center console and kissed his cheek.

“Good boy.”

Yichen turned his head.

His eyebrows lifted.

“Good boy?”

She was already reaching for her bag.

“Yes.”

He caught her wrist gently before she could move away, leaned over, and kissed her cheek.

“Well done, driver.”

Her smile softened.

Then he said, “I’ll be submitting my passenger feedback later.”

She immediately pulled back.

“Don’t you dare.”

The drive back was easier.

Xiaoran was more relaxed now. She had become comfortable with the steering, and Yichen had finally stopped holding the door handle.

Mostly.

They were approaching a traffic light when it turned yellow.

Xiaoran slowed down and stopped safely before the line.

She held his gaze.

“Did you see that?”

“What?”

“I stopped.”

“I saw.”

“Correctly.”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“You’re supposed to praise me.”

“Excellent braking.”

She laughed.

“That’s not romantic.”

“Would you prefer something else?”

“Maybe.”

He thought.

“Very attractive braking technique.”

She burst into laughter.

“That’s worse!”

Yichen smiled, looking ahead.

The light turned green.

She drove on.

A few minutes later, she asked, “Were you really holding the door handle the entire time?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

She turned her head slightly.

“Yichen?”

“Most of the time.”

She laughed.

“Why didn’t you just tell me?”

“Because you were enjoying yourself.”

She tilted her head.

He said, “I didn’t want you to think you were doing badly.”

Her expression changed.

“Oh.”

He turned to her.

“You were driving well. I knew that.”

“Then why were you so nervous?”

He smiled a little.

“Knowing you’re capable and being comfortable with the fact that you’re in control of a moving vehicle are two different things.”

She laughed.

“You’re ridiculous.”

“Probably.”

She reached over and rested her hand on his forearm.

“Next time, I’ll drive again.”

“All right.”

“And you’ll stop holding the door handle.”

“I’ll try.”

“Yichen.”

“I’ll try very hard.”

She shook her head, smiling.

When they got back to the compound, her father was waiting at the gate beside the security booth, with his hands behind his back, as if he had happened to be passing.

He looked at the car, then at Xiaoran.

“How was it?”

“Good!”

Her father smiled.

“Any problems?”

“None.”

Yichen stepped out of the passenger seat.

Her father glanced at him.

“How was she?”

Yichen closed the door carefully.

“Very good.”

Xiaoran beamed.

“See?”

Her father nodded approvingly.

“Good. You can take it out again next time.”

“Really?”

“Yes. Just be careful.”

She nodded enthusiastically.

Her father turned toward Yichen.

“And you? Was the ride comfortable?”

Yichen paused.

Xiaoran looked at him.

Her eyes widened slightly.

He glanced at her, then back at her father.

“Very comfortable, Uncle.”

“Good.”

Her father walked once round the car, slowly, looked at the front bumper, and went inside.

Xiaoran waited until the door closed.

Then she turned toward Yichen.

“Very comfortable?”

He looked down at her.

“Yes.”

“You held the door handle like your life depended on it.”

“I was being polite.”

She stared.

“Polite?”

“I didn’t want to frighten the driver.”

She burst out laughing.

Yichen smiled and reached for her hand.

“Besides, you did well.”

She looked up at him.

Her expression softened.

Then she leaned against his chest, wrapping her arms around his waist.

“Next time, I’ll drive you somewhere farther.”

“All right.”

“And you won’t be scared.”

“I’ll see what I can do.”

She looked up.

“Promise?”

He brushed a loose strand of hair away from her cheek.

“I promise to be a very polite passenger.”

She laughed and kissed him.

Yichen kissed her cheek afterward, then glanced toward the car.

“Although, Xiaoran?”

“Hm?”

“Next time, perhaps we should practice parking somewhere with fewer witnesses.”

Her mouth fell open.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed as she swatted his arm.

And when she walked away, still complaining about his lack of faith in her driving, he followed with the same calm expression he’d worn throughout the afternoon.

His right hand, however, was still remembering the shape of the passenger door handle.

chapters.desc: He arrives with a printed packing list of thirty-two items. Hers has three, and the third is him.
chapters.title: Packing List
chapters.epigraph: “Your hairbrush was under a pillow.”
chapters.content:
The trouble began when Yichen showed her his packing list.

They were sitting on the floor of her bedroom, surrounded by an open suitcase, folded clothes, and several small piles of things that Xiaoran hadn’t yet decided whether she needed.

She was supposed to be packing for five days at her grandparents’ house in the town, where they were both going on Friday, because at New Year her grandfather had said in front of everyone, bring the boy in summer, I’ll teach him to fish properly, and in her family that counted as a summons.

Yichen, who had apparently decided that packing was a task requiring careful preparation, had arrived with a printed list.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Then she looked at him, then back at the paper.

“Thirty-two items?”

“Yes.”

“Thirty-two?”

“That’s the current list.”

She picked it up.

“Why does it say current?”

“Because I might add something.”

She slowly lowered the paper.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Are we moving?”

“No.”

“Are you going somewhere for six months?”

“No.”

“Then why do you have thirty-two items?”

He met her eyes.

“Because I don’t want to forget anything.”

Xiaoran glanced at the list again.

It was organized into categories.

Clothing.

Toiletries.

Documents.

Electronics.

Study materials.

Miscellaneous.

She began reading.

“One, shirts. Two, trousers. Three, shorts. Four, socks. Five, underwear...”

“Those are necessary.”

“I know they’re necessary! Six, sleepwear. Seven, jacket. Eight, basketball shoes. Nine, casual shoes. Ten, sandals...”

She looked up.

“How many shoes are you bringing?”

“Three pairs.”

“For a short journey?”

“I might need them.”

She continued reading.

At item sixteen, she stopped.

“Portable charger.”

“Yes.”

“Charging cable.”

“Yes.”

“Backup charging cable.”

“Yes.”

She met his eyes.

“Why?”

“In case the first one stops working.”

She stared at him.

Then she put the list down. “You’re a menace.”

Yichen smiled.

“Have you made yours?”

“Of course.”

“Can I see?”

She reached for her phone.

He waited.

She opened her notes app and turned the screen toward him.

There were three lines.

Xiaoran’s Packing List

1. Clothes.
2. Toiletries.
3. Yichen.

He read it once, then again.

His eyes lifted to hers.

“Three items?”

“Yes.”

“That’s your complete list?”

“Yes.”

He looked at the third item.

“Yichen?”

She nodded.

“You’re important.”

A small smile appeared on his face.

“Am I being packed?”

“Obviously.”

“Where?”

She pointed at the empty space beside her suitcase.

“Here.”

He laughed.

“That’s not how packing works.”

“Then you should be grateful I’m making an exception.”

He leaned back against the bed.

“Should I bring my own list?”

“You’re already bringing thirty-two things. I think you’ve covered it.”

Yichen asked whether she had packed everything.

This was his third mistake.

The first was showing her his list. The second was allowing her to compare it with hers.

The third was asking whether she had packed everything.

She hadn’t.

He discovered this when he opened the suitcase and found three tops, one pair of trousers, two dresses, a small toiletry bag, and a book.

“Where are your other clothes?”

“Those are my clothes.”

“For how long?”

She thought about it.

“Until we get back.”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You’re going to be away for several days.”

“I know.”

“You need more than this.”

She frowned.

“I have enough.”

He looked at the suitcase, then at her.

“How many days?”

“Five.”

“Five days, and you’ve packed this?”

“Yes.”

He picked up one of the folded tops.

“You’re planning to wear this more than once?”

“Probably.”

“All right.”

She smiled triumphantly.

He put the top back.

Then he noticed something else.

“Where’s your phone charger?”

“In my bag.”

“Toothbrush?”

“Toiletry bag.”

“Hairbrush?”

She blinked.

A pause.

“Somewhere.”

Yichen looked at her.

She sighed.

“Fine. I’ll add it.”

“Your identification?”

“In my wallet.”

“Wallet?”

“Yes.”

“Where?”

She pointed vaguely toward her desk.

He looked in that direction.

Her wallet was beside a stack of papers, a hair clip, and a half-empty packet of biscuits.

Yichen closed his eyes.

Xiaoran watched him.

“Don’t.”

“I’m not saying anything.”

“You’re thinking something.”

“I’m thinking we should check your bag together.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“See? You’re useful.”

“Only the third item?”

She laughed.

Her mother put her head round the door at that point, holding a basket of laundry, and stopped.

“What is that?”

“His packing list. Thirty-two items,” Xiaoran said.

Mrs. Lin put the basket down. She took the printed list from her daughter, read it from top to bottom, twice, without expression, the way she read the electricity bill, and handed it back to Yichen.

“Backup charging cable,” she said.

“In case the first one stops working, Auntie.”

“Good.”

She turned to Xiaoran.

“And yours?” she said.

Xiaoran showed her the phone. Her mother read all three lines. She looked at the third for slightly longer than the other two.

“Well, at least you’ve listed the important thing,” she said.

Then she took the pen from the floor, wrote Grandma’s tea (in the hall, DO NOT FORGET) at the bottom of Yichen’s list, because Yichen was clearly the one who would read it, picked up her laundry, and left.

They spent the next twenty minutes packing.

Yichen folded her clothes more neatly than she had. Xiaoran kept interrupting to tell him that she didn’t need everything arranged by size.

He disagreed.

She moved his toiletries to a different compartment.

He moved them back.

She added a small stuffed keychain to the side pocket.

He asked whether it needed to be on the list.

She told him it was emotionally important.

He accepted that without further argument.

At some point, she noticed that he had added three more items to his list.

“What’s number thirty-three?”

“An extra notebook.”

“Why?”

“In case I need one.”

“Number thirty-four?”

“Spare pen.”

“Number thirty-five?”

“Small first-aid kit.”

She blinked at him.

“Are you planning an expedition?”

He looked at the list.

“That’s probably enough.”

“Probably?”

He smiled.

She shook her head.

Then she took his printed list and added something at the bottom.

33. Xiaoran’s patience.

Yichen read it.

“That’s not an item.”

“It is. You need it. Mostly when you travel with me.”

He took the pen from her hand and wrote beneath it.

34. Xiaoran’s hairbrush.

She gasped.

“Why are you adding things to my list?”

“Because you forgot it.”

“I didn’t forget it. I was going to pack it.”

“Where is it?”

She looked around, then pointed toward the bed.

Yichen followed her finger.

The hairbrush was under a pillow.

He picked it up and placed it inside her toiletry bag.

“Of course you were.”

She laughed.

When they finally finished, Yichen’s suitcase was neatly arranged, his thirty-five-item list folded and placed in the front pocket.

Xiaoran’s suitcase was also ready.

She stood beside it with her hands on her hips.

“See? Three items.”

“Your list has grown.”

“Only because you interfered.”

“Your hairbrush was under a pillow.”

“That’s irrelevant.”

Something in his face eased.

She took her phone and opened the list again.

Then she showed him.

Xiaoran’s Packing List

1. Clothes.
2. Toiletries.
3. Yichen.

He looked at it.

“You’re keeping it?”

“Of course.”

“Even though you’ve packed more than three things?”

“Those are details.”

He nodded thoughtfully.

“Then I should revise mine.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

He took her phone gently, tapped the screen, and added a small note beneath the third item.

Already included.

She stared, then looked up at him.

“What’s that supposed to mean?”

He put the phone down.

“It means you don’t need to pack me separately.”

She tilted her head.

“Why not?”

He reached for her hand.

“Because wherever you go, I’m already planning to be there when you need me.”

Her expression softened.

She forgot about the suitcases, the lists, and the fact that he had somehow managed to turn packing into a thirty-five-item project.

Then she smiled.

“That’s a very long way of saying you’re coming with me.”

He didn’t deny it. He squeezed her hand.

“Then I’ll keep it simple next time.”

She looked at his printed list.

“Please do.”

He leaned over and kissed her, briefly.

“All right.”

A moment passed.

Then he glanced at the suitcase.

“Did you pack your charger?”

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed.

She threw a folded pair of socks at him.

On Friday morning, at the door, Yichen took out the list and went down it with a pencil, ticking. He ticked the shirts and all three pairs of his shoes and both charging cables and the first-aid kit, and at the bottom he ticked the tea, which was in the hall, and which Xiaoran had walked past twice.

She ticked her own list on her phone in the car. It took her four seconds. She showed him the third tick, and he looked out of the window, and her father, driving, pretended hard not to have heard any of it. Her mother, in the passenger seat, had the tea on her lap. She hadn’t trusted anyone else in the family with it.

chapters.desc: The last summer before their final year, at her grandparents’ house, where her grandfather has promised to teach him to fish properly.
chapters.title: Last Summer in the Hometown
chapters.epigraph: “Besides, I think your grandfather likes me.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had been to her grandparents’ house twice before, both times at New Year, when the house was full of relatives and her grandfather had been too busy pouring drinks for Uncle Deng to do more than look at him across the table. This was the first time in summer, the last summer before their final year. It was also the first time her grandfather had been holding a bamboo fishing rod when Yichen came up the lane from the bus stop, which, Xiaoran said later, should have been the warning.

“So, the fisherman,” her grandfather said. He was a lean man with a deeply tanned face and the sort of expression that made Xiaoran instinctively stand up straighter.

“Hello, Grandpa.”

“Her father says you can fish.”

“Her father took me once, in Shanghai. I caught nothing,” Yichen said carefully.

“He said you caught nothing very politely. Have you eaten?” Her grandfather took the gift bag, glanced inside, and nodded at the tea.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Good.” Behind him, in the doorway, her grandmother was drying her hands and beaming, and she called out, “Have you been eating breakfast?” the way she had every night at nine one summer, years ago, down a phone line.

“Every day, Grandma.”

Her grandfather looked at Xiaoran.

“Your grandmother made too much food again. Go help her.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“I just got here.”

“And now you’re going to help.”

She turned toward Yichen with an expression of betrayal.

He looked perfectly composed.

“Go ahead. I’ll be fine,” he said gently.

She narrowed her eyes at him.

It was the expression of someone who knew she was being dismissed from an important conversation and had no intention of forgiving anyone.

But she went inside.

Her grandfather watched her disappear through the kitchen door.

Then he turned back to Yichen.

“Today you’ll fish properly. Come with me.”

Xiaoran discovered the situation twenty minutes later.

She had been helping her grandmother arrange lunch when she noticed two figures walking toward the small pond behind the house.

One was her grandfather.

The other was Yichen.

Her grandfather was carrying two fishing rods.

Yichen was carrying a small bucket.

She stared.

Then she put down the plate in her hands.

“Grandma.”

“Hm?”

“Where are they going?”

“Fishing.”

Xiaoran turned toward the window.

“Oh no.”

Her grandmother followed her gaze and smiled.

“Grandpa is testing him,” Xiaoran said.

Her grandmother laughed.

“Your grandfather just wants someone to fish with.”

“Grandma.”

“Go and finish arranging the food.”

Xiaoran looked outside again.

Yichen was listening attentively while her grandfather explained something about the fishing equipment.

He nodded once.

Then her grandfather handed him a rod.

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

“He’s going to fail.”

He failed within twelve minutes.

Xiaoran knew because she had gone outside under the excuse of bringing them water.

She found Yichen sitting on a low wooden stool beside the pond, holding the fishing rod with a concentration usually reserved for difficult examination questions.

Her grandfather was beside him, looking thoroughly unimpressed.

“Too much movement,” the older man said.

Yichen adjusted his grip.

“Like this?”

“Don’t ask me. Watch the water.”

Yichen looked at the water.

Xiaoran approached.

“Grandpa.”

Her grandfather turned.

“Why are you here?”

“Bringing water.”

She placed the bottles beside them, then glanced at Yichen.

There was a faint crease between his eyebrows.

She almost laughed.

“How’s it going?”

“Fine.”

Her grandfather snorted.

“He’s been sitting there for ten minutes and hasn’t caught anything.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

Yichen glanced at her.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

She put a hand over her mouth.

Her grandfather pointed at the pond.

“Look. The fish can see you.”

Yichen looked down.

“Can they?”

“Of course they can. You’re moving like you’re trying to catch a thief.”

Xiaoran lost the battle and laughed.

Yichen looked at her with a quiet, pleading expression.

She immediately tried to compose herself.

“Sorry.”
