Her grandfather took a sip of water. “Basketball. He’s used to chasing things,” he said to Xiaoran, as if it explained the fish.

Yichen gave a polite smile.

“Something like that.”

“Fishing isn’t like basketball. You can’t run after the fish.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?”

Xiaoran turned away, shoulders shaking.

By the time lunch was ready, Yichen had caught nothing.

Not one fish.

Her grandfather, on the other hand, had caught two.

The difference was apparently important enough that he mentioned it three times while walking back.

“Two fish,” he said, holding up the bucket.

Yichen nodded.

“That’s impressive.”

“Not difficult if you know what you’re doing.”

“You’re very good at it, Grandpa.”

“Of course.”

Xiaoran walked between them, trying not to laugh.

When they reached the courtyard, she leaned closer to Yichen.

“How was your first fishing lesson?”

He looked down at her.

“Educational.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

“Did you catch anything?”

He gave her a look.

She smiled sweetly.

“I was just asking.”

“Your grandfather caught two.”

“I know. He told me.”

“Twice.”

She laughed.

Then, noticing the damp patch on his sleeve, she reached out and brushed at it.

“Did you get wet?”

“A little.”

“You’re terrible at fishing.”

“I’ve gathered that.”

She smiled up at him.

“Don’t worry. You’re good at other things.”

“Such as?”

She considered it.

“Basketball.”

“Thank you.”

“And studying.”

“Mm.”

“And...”

She looked at him, amused.

“Being my boyfriend.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“That one I intend to keep being good at.”

Before she could answer, her grandfather called from the courtyard.

“Yichen! Come help me with these fish.”

Yichen straightened.

“Coming, Grandpa.”

Xiaoran watched him walk away.

Then she hurried after him.

The real test came after dinner.

Her grandfather sat on the veranda with a cup of tea, while Yichen helped him put away the fishing equipment.

Xiaoran was sitting on the steps, peeling an orange.

Her grandfather glanced at Yichen.

“You’re not very good at fishing.”

Yichen smiled.

“Not yet.”

“Not yet?”

“I can learn.”

Her grandfather looked at him.

Then he nodded.

“That’s better.”

Xiaoran looked up.

Her grandfather continued, “A lot of young people don’t like being bad at something. They give up as soon as they fail.”

Yichen listened.

“Fishing takes patience. You have to sit there even when nothing happens.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?”

Yichen smiled slightly.

“I think I’m beginning to.”

Her grandfather looked toward Xiaoran.

“She’s not patient either.”

“Grandpa!”

Her grandfather ignored her.

“She gets bored easily. When she was little, she couldn’t sit still long enough to finish a meal.”

Yichen glanced at Xiaoran.

She was already looking offended.

“That’s not true.”

“Your grandmother used to chase you around the courtyard with a spoon.”

“Grandpa!”

Yichen lowered his head, hiding a smile.

Her grandfather looked back at him.

“Don’t let her get away with everything.”

Yichen’s smile softened.

“I’ll try.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“You’re supposed to defend me.”

“I think your grandfather has a point.”

She gasped.

Her grandfather laughed.

It was the first time that day he had laughed quite so openly.

Later, when Xiaoran walked Yichen to the guest room, she was still complaining.

“You betrayed me.”

“I didn’t.”

“You agreed with Grandpa.”

“He wasn’t wrong.”

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

Yichen stopped in the corridor and looked at her.

“I am.”

“Then why did you agree?”

He reached out, gently brushing her hair away from her cheek.

“Because I know you.”

She tried to remain annoyed.

It was difficult.

He laughed under his breath.

“Besides, I think your grandfather likes me.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“He made you sit beside a pond for an hour and watched you fail.”

“Perhaps that’s how he shows affection.”

She laughed.

Then she reached for his hand.

“Don’t worry. I’ll teach you how to fish next time.”

Yichen looked down at their joined hands.

“Will you?”

“Yes.”

“Are you good at it?”

She hesitated.

“...No.”

He laughed.

“Then perhaps we should find another teacher.”

She hit his arm.

And from the veranda, her grandfather’s voice carried through the evening air.

“Yichen! Next time, I’ll teach you properly!”

Yichen turned toward the veranda.

“Thank you, Grandpa!”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“Next time?”

He looked at her, entirely untroubled.

“Your grandfather invited me.”

She eyed him.

“You’ve been here one day.”

“He’s a very welcoming man.”

She shook her head, laughing.

But later that night, when she went to the kitchen for water, she found her grandfather sitting with her grandmother.

“He’s a good boy,” he said.

Xiaoran stopped.

Her grandmother smiled.

“Yes, he is.”

Her grandfather took another sip of tea.

“Not very good at fishing, though.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Grandpa!”

“What? It’s true.”

“Bring him again next summer,” he said after a moment.

Xiaoran smiled.

“I will.”

She went back to bed with the glass of water and didn’t drink any of it. Through the thin wall she could hear the two of them still talking, low, about the persimmon tree and the price of bait and the boy, and once her grandmother laughed, and once her grandfather said “Hopeless” with enormous affection, and she knew exactly who he meant.

chapters.desc: Mai Lang invites them onto his channel for a how-well-do-you-know-your-partner quiz. Somebody is going to be exposed.
chapters.title: The Couple Quiz Went Live
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t need a reason to want something.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came on a Tuesday evening.

Xiaoran was lying on Yichen’s sofa, scrolling through her phone while he sat beside her reviewing some documents from his Business faculty.

She suddenly made a small noise.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Do you remember Mai Lang?”

Yichen didn’t look up immediately.

“The man who made you famous on a milk tea run.”

“Yes. He does celebrities and athletes now. Those challenge videos.”

“I’ve seen a few videos.”

Xiaoran sat up.

“He invited us.”

That made Yichen look at her.

“Us?”

She turned her phone toward him.

On the screen was a message from Mai Lang’s production team.

They were preparing a couples’ special for his channel, featuring a How Well Do You Know Your Partner? challenge. The concept was simple: each couple would answer a series of preference questions separately, then compare their answers to see how well they knew each other.

They wanted Yichen and Xiaoran to participate.

Yichen read the message.

Then he looked at her.

“Do you want to go?”

Xiaoran’s eyes were already sparkling.

“Of course!”

“All right.”

She blinked.

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“You didn’t even ask what the questions would be.”

“It’s a preference quiz. I know your preferences.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s a very confident statement.”

He returned to his documents.

“Should I be worried?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I’m going to expose you.”

Yichen smiled without looking up.

“I look forward to it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The filming took place on Saturday afternoon at Mai Lang’s studio.

It was a bright, comfortable set with a large sofa, two individual answer boards, and a small table displaying several props. There were cameras positioned around the room, and a production assistant was checking the microphones.

Mai Lang greeted them enthusiastically.

“Finally! The couple everyone’s been asking me to invite.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Really?”

“Of course. I’ve seen your clips. Especially the basketball ones.”

Yichen shook his hand.

“Thank you for having us.”

Mai Lang looked between them.

“Four years together, right?”

“Four and a half,” Xiaoran corrected him.

“And you’re both confident you know each other well?”

Xiaoran immediately nodded.

“Very.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“She’s confident.”

She turned toward him.

“Why did you say it like that?”

Mai Lang burst out laughing.

“Interesting. We’re not even filming properly yet, and there’s already tension.”

Yichen smiled politely.

“She’s competitive.”

“I’m not!”

“You’re already arguing.”

“Because you’re provoking me!”

Mai Lang clapped his hands.

“Excellent. This is going to be fun.”

The rules were straightforward.

For every question, Xiaoran and Yichen would write down their own answers on separate boards. Then, before revealing them, they would each guess what the other person had written.

The goal wasn’t to answer correctly according to some official standard. It was to match their partner’s actual preference.

There were ten questions.

Mai Lang explained that the questions would cover everyday preferences, habits, food, dates, and little things people might or might not notice about their partners.

“Remember, you are not answering what you think your partner should like. You’re answering what they actually like,” he said, looking directly into the camera.

Xiaoran nodded seriously.

Yichen picked up his marker.

Mai Lang grinned.

“Let’s see whether four and a half years of dating has made you two experts.”

Round 1: Favorite Drink

Mai Lang held up the first card.

“What’s your partner’s favorite drink?”

Xiaoran immediately started writing.

Yichen wrote just as quickly.

“Okay! First, what does Xiaoran think Yichen’s favorite drink is?”

She revealed her board.

Black coffee.

Yichen nodded.

“Correct.”

Xiaoran looked pleased.

“See?”

Mai Lang turned to Yichen.

“What does Yichen think Xiaoran’s favorite drink is?”

He revealed his answer.

Milk tea. Half sugar. No pearls.

Xiaoran stared at him.

“Why did you write the whole order?”

“Because you have a very specific order.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“That’s not just knowing her favorite drink. That’s knowing her entire milk tea personality.”

Xiaoran pointed at Yichen’s board.

“Actually, sometimes I want less ice.”

“I know.”

“And sometimes I want pudding in it.”

“Mm.”

Mai Lang raised an eyebrow.

“Should we give him extra points?”

“No. Don’t encourage him,” Xiaoran said immediately.

Yichen looked amused.

Score: 1–1.

Round 2: Ideal Weekend

“What is your partner’s ideal way to spend a free weekend?”

Xiaoran thought for a moment.

Then she wrote her guess for him.

Stay home, watch something, eat good food, and do absolutely nothing.

Yichen turned over his own answer.

It was almost identical.

A quiet day at home. Good food, a movie or a series, and no schedule.

Xiaoran pointed at it.

“See? He’s the lazy one.”

“I’m very enthusiastic about doing nothing.”

“That’s called being lazy.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Yichen, what’s Xiaoran’s ideal weekend?”

Yichen revealed his guess.

Going somewhere new, preferably with me. Exploring, taking pictures, trying food, and having no strict itinerary.

Xiaoran’s mouth opened.

Then she turned over her own answer.

A little trip somewhere. Cute cafés, shopping, taking photos, and spending the whole day together.

She pointed at him.

“That’s basically the same!”

“Basically.”

Mai Lang leaned toward the camera.

“Notice how both of them included spending time together without explicitly saying it.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“She likes having somewhere to go, but she doesn’t like feeling rushed,” Yichen said.

She looked at him.

It was such a small detail.

But he was right.

Score: 2–2.

Round 3: Favorite Food

Mai Lang looked excited.

“This one can be dangerous. What is your partner’s favorite food?”

Xiaoran wrote quickly.

Yichen took a little longer.

Mai Lang turned to Xiaoran.

“What do you think Yichen wrote?”

She revealed:

Japanese food. Especially a good sushi or sashimi restaurant.

Yichen turned his board around.

Japanese food. Sushi, sashimi, and good grilled dishes.

“Correct!” Mai Lang announced.

Xiaoran smiled triumphantly.

“I know his taste.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“You do.”

“Okay, your turn.”

Yichen revealed his guess.

Hotpot.

Xiaoran blinked.

“That’s not my favorite food!”

“It’s one of your favorites.”

“Yes, but not the favorite.”

He looked at her.

“Then what is?”

She considered it.

“Maybe pasta?”

Yichen nodded slowly.

“Then I should have written pasta.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Wait, you don’t know her favorite food?”

Yichen looked at Xiaoran.

“I know what she likes to eat. I’m not sure she has one fixed favorite.”

Xiaoran paused.

That was actually true.

She liked pasta, hotpot, Japanese food, noodles, desserts, and a long list of other things.

Mai Lang looked at her.

“Is that acceptable?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“He’s right. I change my mind all the time.”

“That’s a very diplomatic way to avoid losing points,” Mai Lang teased.

Score: 3–2.

Round 4: Preferred Date

“What kind of date does your partner enjoy most?”

Xiaoran wrote first.

Yichen looked at her board, then at his own.

Mai Lang turned to Yichen.

“Your guess?”

He revealed:

Something thoughtful. Doesn’t have to be expensive. She likes when there’s something new to experience, but she also loves ordinary dates with me.

Xiaoran stared at the answer.

She smiled, a little softer.

“That’s right.”

Mai Lang nodded.

“Very detailed. Xiaoran?”

She revealed her guess for Yichen.

An activity he genuinely enjoys. Basketball, exploring a new place, or something he can get interested in. He likes sharing his interests with me.

Yichen looked at her board, then nodded.

“That’s right.”

Mai Lang looked between them.

“So both of you understand that the other person doesn’t necessarily need an elaborate date.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yichen doesn’t really care whether we’re going somewhere expensive. He just likes doing things properly.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“And she likes it when I plan something, but she also likes deciding things spontaneously.”

“Because sometimes your plans are too detailed.”

“I thought you liked that.”

“I do. But sometimes I want to wander around!”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Four years together, and they’re still negotiating their itinerary.”

Score: 4–3.

Round 5: Favorite Type of Weather

Mai Lang held up the next card.

“This sounds simple, but let’s see. What is your partner’s favorite weather?”

Xiaoran wrote.

Yichen wrote.

They revealed their guesses.

Xiaoran guessed Yichen preferred cool, sunny weather, the kind that made it comfortable to go outside without being too cold.

Yichen guessed Xiaoran preferred rainy weather when she could stay indoors, curled up with a blanket, a warm drink, and something to watch.

Both were correct.

Xiaoran pointed at him.

“Because I love rainy days.”

“You love rainy days when you don’t have to go anywhere.”

“Exactly.”

“If you have a morning class, suddenly you don’t like the rain.”

She gasped.

“That’s irrelevant!”

Mai Lang was laughing.

“Yichen, you know the conditions attached to her preferences.”

“Yes.”

Xiaoran hit his arm lightly.

He caught her hand and held it before letting go.

The cameras caught it.

Mai Lang noticed.

“Very casual. Very natural. The cameras are right here, by the way.”

Yichen smiled.

“Sorry.”

He didn’t look particularly sorry.

Score: 5–4.

Round 6: Shopping Preference

“Does your partner prefer shopping online or in person?”

Xiaoran wrote online for Yichen.

Yichen wrote in person for Xiaoran.

They revealed their answers.

Both correct.

Mai Lang looked at Xiaoran.

“Why online for Yichen?”

“He doesn’t like wasting time going through shops. If he knows what he wants, he’ll research it, compare things, and order it.”

Yichen nodded.

“Efficient.”

Mai Lang turned to him.

“Why in person for Xiaoran?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Because she likes seeing things properly before deciding. Especially clothes. She’ll say she’s just looking, then try on six things.”

Xiaoran frowned.

“That’s not true.”

“Seven, last time.”

She paused.

“Those were different styles.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“I’m learning so much about this relationship.”

Score: 6–5.

Round 7: What Makes Your Partner Happiest?

The next question appeared.

What small thing makes your partner happiest?

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

She thought for a little longer before writing.

Yichen also took his time.

Mai Lang turned to Xiaoran.

“What did you write for Yichen?”

She revealed:

When someone remembers the little things he mentions and makes an effort without him asking.

Yichen looked at her.

He didn’t speak immediately.

Then he nodded.

“That’s true.”

Mai Lang smiled.

“That’s a very thoughtful answer.”

Xiaoran shrugged a little.

“He doesn’t always say what he wants, but he notices when people pay attention.”

Yichen looked down at his board before revealing his answer for her.

When I give her my full attention. Especially when she’s telling me something she’s excited about.

Xiaoran stared.

Then she looked at him.

“That’s...”

Mai Lang waited.

“That’s very accurate,” she admitted.

Yichen smiled.

“She doesn’t always need me to solve something. Sometimes she just wants to tell me about it.”

Xiaoran lowered her eyes, smiling.

Mai Lang looked directly at the camera.

“Ladies and gentlemen, this is what happens when a couple actually listens to each other.”

Score: 7–6.

Round 8: Favorite Gift

“What kind of gift does your partner appreciate most?”

Xiaoran wrote something quickly.

Yichen looked at his board, then wrote.

Mai Lang turned to Yichen first.

“What do you think Xiaoran likes?”

He revealed:

Something personal. Something that shows the person remembers what she likes or something she mentioned wanting.

Xiaoran nodded.

“Correct.”

“Not necessarily expensive,” he said.

“Correct.”

“Although she does appreciate pretty things.”

She turned toward him.

“Of course I do.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Now, Xiaoran. What kind of gift does Yichen appreciate?”

She revealed:

Something related to his interests, but with thought behind it. Something he wouldn’t necessarily buy for himself.

Yichen nodded.

“That’s right.”

Mai Lang raised a finger.

“Can you give us an example?”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I once got him two tickets to a game at the Garden in New York for his birthday.”

Mai Lang’s eyes widened.

“Madison Square Garden?”

Yichen nodded.

“It was the one place I’d always wanted to go.”

Xiaoran said, “He only said it once, one weekend morning, watching a game on his sofa. I remembered. He was very happy.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“I was.”

Mai Lang leaned back.

“Okay, that’s a difficult standard for the rest of us.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You don’t have to buy someone a trip. It can be anything.”

Yichen said, “She once bought me a small thing related to something I’d mentioned casually. I liked that just as much.”

He didn’t elaborate, but Xiaoran knew exactly what he meant.

The miniature basketball keychain she’d given him before his first club trial.

She smiled at him.

Score: 8–7.

Round 9: Biggest Pet Peeve

Mai Lang looked delighted.

“Now we’re getting dangerous. What is your partner’s biggest pet peeve?”

Xiaoran immediately started writing.

Yichen looked at her and smiled.

“Already?”

“I know this one.”

She revealed:

People being inconsiderate. Especially when they waste other people’s time or don’t respect boundaries.

Yichen nodded.

“Correct.”

Mai Lang turned to him.

“What about Xiaoran?”

Yichen revealed:

People being dismissive when she’s explaining something she’s genuinely interested in. Also, being rushed when she’s making a decision.

Xiaoran’s eyebrows lifted.

“That’s right.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Interesting. So Yichen dislikes inconsideration, and Xiaoran dislikes being dismissed.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“I don’t mind if someone disagrees with me. But I don’t like when people make me feel silly for caring about something.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“That’s fair. And she doesn’t like when someone makes a decision for her because they think it’s easier.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

He had remembered that too.

Score: 9–8.

Round 10: The Little Luxury

Mai Lang picked up the final card.

“Last question. What is your partner’s favorite little luxury?”

Xiaoran immediately looked at Yichen.

He looked back at her.

Both started writing.

Mai Lang grinned.

“Final question. This could decide everything.”

He turned to Xiaoran.

“What does Yichen consider a little luxury?”

She revealed:

A really good meal, a comfortable hotel, and a quiet place where he doesn’t have to think about anything.

Yichen laughed.

“That’s accurate.”

Mai Lang nodded.

“Very reasonable.”

Then Yichen revealed his guess for Xiaoran.

Milk tea, pretty little things, and buying something she has been thinking about for a while.

Xiaoran stared.

“That’s not wrong.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Not wrong?”

She laughed.

“It’s correct!”

Mai Lang looked between them.

“So, final score...”

He checked the boards.

“Ten to nine! Xiaoran wins by one!”

Xiaoran jumped slightly.

“Really?”

“The only miss of the day: her favorite food!”

Yichen smiled.

Xiaoran turned toward him triumphantly.

“See? I told you I’d expose you.”

“You did.”

“On camera!”

“On camera,” he agreed.

Mai Lang clapped.

“Congratulations! Four years together and only one secret, and it’s pasta.”

Xiaoran immediately shook her head.

“No, no. We have secrets.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Do we?”

“Yes. You don’t know everything about me.”

“Like what?”

She looked thoughtful, then smiled mischievously.

“I’m not telling you.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“That’s a terrible way to end a nearly perfect score!”

✦ ✦ ✦

The official filming ended, but Mai Lang asked them to stay for a few extra minutes to record a short closing segment.

He sat opposite them.

“Before we finish, I want to ask one final question. Not part of the quiz.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Okay.”

Mai Lang looked at Yichen.

“After four years together, do you think knowing someone’s preferences becomes easier?”

Yichen considered the question.

“Some things become easier because you spend enough time together. You start noticing patterns. You know what they like, what they avoid, what makes them comfortable.”

He glanced at Xiaoran.

“But I don’t think you should assume you know everything just because you’ve been together for a long time.”

Mai Lang nodded.

“Why?”

“People change. Their preferences change. Sometimes they don’t even realize it themselves until they try something new.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

Yichen said, “I think it’s important to keep asking.”

Mai Lang turned to Xiaoran.

“What do you think?”

She looked down at her hands briefly.

“I think knowing someone’s preferences is nice, but I don’t think that’s the most important part.”

“What is?”

“Remembering that they’re still a person outside the relationship. They have their own interests, their own things they want to try, and their own opinions. I like that Yichen doesn’t always assume I’ll like something just because I liked it before.”

She smiled.

“He still asks me.”

Yichen looked at her.

“And she still surprises me.”

Mai Lang smiled.

“That’s a good answer. But I have to ask. Who do you think knows the other person better?”

Xiaoran pointed at herself.

“Me.”

Yichen didn’t even hesitate.

“Her.”

She turned toward him.

“Wait. You agree?”

“Yes.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Yichen surrendered very quickly!”

Yichen looked at Xiaoran.

“She pays attention to details I don’t even notice about myself.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

Then she smiled proudly.

“That’s because I’m observant.”

“I know.”

Mai Lang looked into the camera.

“That’s it for today’s episode. Apparently, these two know each other a little too well. Ten to nine, four years together, and still looking at each other like they’re on a first date.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

Yichen simply smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The video went live the following week.

Xiaoran watched it with Yichen at his apartment.

She had already watched the first few minutes twice, mostly because she thought her own expressions were funny.

“Look at your face here,” she said, pointing at the screen.

Yichen glanced over.

“What about it?”

“You looked so confident.”

“I was confident.”

“Too confident.”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“Did I get anything wrong?”

“That’s not the point.”

“What is the point?”

She paused.

“Your attitude.”

He smiled.

“My attitude?”

“Yes. You acted like you knew everything.”

“I knew most things.”

She turned toward him.

“Don’t be arrogant.”

He laughed.

She continued watching, then reached the part where he’d answered the question about what made her happiest.

When he said that she liked having his full attention, she went quiet.

Yichen noticed.

He looked at her.

“You’ve been staring at the screen without blinking.”

She turned away.

“I just think it’s sweet.”

He reached over and tucked a strand of hair behind her ear.

“It’s true.”

She smiled.

Then the video reached the final question, where she’d guessed his favorite little luxury.

Xiaoran suddenly sat upright.

“Wait!”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“I forgot something.”

“What?”

She picked up her phone and opened the comments.

There were already thousands.

People were praising their chemistry, laughing at the little exchanges, and pointing out how naturally Yichen watched Xiaoran whenever she spoke.

One comment caught her attention:

The way he doesn’t just know her favorite things, but understands WHY she likes them. That’s the real green flag.

She read it aloud.

Yichen glanced at the screen.

“That’s nice.”

Xiaoran scrolled further.

Another comment said:

Four years together and he still looks at her like he’s learning something new about her.

She stopped.

Then she turned toward him.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Do you really think you still have things to learn about me?”

He studied her.

“Of course.”

“Like what?”

He put his phone aside.

“What’s something you’ve wanted to try recently but haven’t told me?”

Xiaoran blinked.

She hadn’t expected him to turn the question around.

“That’s not fair.”

“Why?”

“Because now I have to think.”

He waited.

She looked up at the ceiling, thinking.

Then her eyes brightened.

“I want to learn ice skating.”

Yichen nodded.

“Ice skating?”

“Yes. I saw a video of a couple skating backwards holding hands. I want to try.”

“Then we can go.”

She smiled.

“Really?”

“Find a place you like.”

She leaned against his shoulder.

“And I want to try making pasta from scratch.”

“All right.”

“And maybe learn how to play tennis.”

He glanced down at her.

“Anything else?”

She thought for a moment.

“Actually, I want to go somewhere we’ve never been. Not a big trip. Just somewhere neither of us knows.”

Yichen nodded.

“Then we’ll do that too.”

She looked up at him.

“You’re making a list now?”

“I’m listening.”

Xiaoran smiled and wrapped her arms around his waist.

“You know, I think that’s my favorite thing about you.”

“What?”

“You never make me feel silly for wanting to try something.”

His expression softened.

He lowered his head and pressed a kiss into her hair.

“You don’t need a reason to want something.”

She looked at him.

She laughed and settled against him again.

On the television, the video continued playing, the credits rolling beneath a final shot of them laughing together.

Mai Lang’s title card appeared:

HOW WELL DO YOU KNOW YOUR PARTNER? — ZHOU YICHEN & LIN XIAORAN

They had scored ten to nine, and she was never going to let him forget the pasta.

But as Xiaoran rested her head against his chest, she thought that perhaps the best part wasn’t knowing each other’s favorite drinks, ideal weekends, or preferred gifts.

It was knowing that even after four years, there were still new things to discover.

And Yichen, who had quietly begun searching for ice rinks on his phone, seemed to agree.

chapters.desc: A full contract arrives on a Tuesday in his final year, and his father asks a question he has never asked before: what does Zhou Yichen want?
chapters.title: The Herons Want an Answer
chapters.epigraph: “Who did you want to tell first?”
chapters.content:
The email arrived at 9:17 on a Tuesday morning, in the second week of his final year.

Zhou Yichen was halfway through reviewing a case study when his phone vibrated beside his laptop. He glanced at the screen, expecting a message from Xiaoran or perhaps a reminder from his coach.

Instead, he saw Jiao Rui’s name, from the Herons’ recruitment department.

He opened it.

The first paragraph was formal. The second was familiar. By the third, he had stopped reading the words as words and started understanding what they meant.

The Herons were offering him a full professional contract.

It wasn’t another evaluation, or another year in the development program.

A contract.

His eyes moved down the page: a place on the first-team roster from November, his university timetable to be arranged between the club and the sports office, and an answer by Friday.

He read it once, then again.

A quiet breath left him.

His phone vibrated a second time.

Xiaoran: Are you busy?

He looked at the email again, then typed.

Yichen: Just received something.

Xiaoran: Is it bad?

Yichen: I haven’t decided.

Three dots appeared almost immediately.

Xiaoran: That sounds suspicious.

Xiaoran: What happened?

He considered telling her over text. Then he closed the email and picked up his phone.

Yichen: Can you come over tonight?

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: I want to tell you in person.

A pause.

Xiaoran: Okay.

Then, a few seconds later:

Xiaoran: Should I bring food?

That got a smile out of him.

Yichen: You can.

Xiaoran: That’s not an answer. Should I bring food because you’re upset or because you’re hungry?

Yichen: Both are possible.

Xiaoran: Zhou Yichen.

Yichen: Something good happened. I think.

Her reply came quickly.

Xiaoran: I’M COMING.

He put his phone down.

For a while, he didn’t return to his case study.

He had spent years imagining what this moment might feel like. When the scout first approached him, when he entered the development program, when he played his first game for the Herons, he had told himself not to think too far ahead.

One step at a time.

He had repeated it so often that it had become instinct.

Now the next step was sitting in front of him, written in a formal email with a deadline.

And it was bigger than the last one.

Xiaoran arrived at his apartment with a paper bag in one hand and her handbag slipping off her shoulder.

She had bought two portions of food from a place near campus, along with a small dessert she insisted was an emergency provision.

Yichen opened the door before she could knock a second time.

She looked at his face immediately.

“Okay. First, are you happy?”

He stepped aside to let her in.

“Lovely to see you too.”

“Hello. Are you happy?” She walked past him, then turned around.

He closed the door.

“I think so.”

“That’s not very convincing.”

“I’m still processing it.”

She put the food on the kitchen counter and turned to face him properly.

“Tell me.”

Yichen took his phone out, opened the email, and handed it to her.

She read the subject line.

Then she read it again.

Her eyes widened.

“Wait.”

He watched her.

“Wait, wait.”

“Take your time.”

“Is this—”

“Yes.”

She met his eyes.

“They’re offering you a full contract?”

“That’s what it says.”

“Not a development contract?”

“No.”

“Not another evaluation?”

“No.”

“A full contract?”

He nodded.

For one second, she stared at him. Then she made a small sound that was somewhere between a laugh and a gasp.

“Yichen!”

She threw her arms around him.

He caught her easily, one hand at her back, the other keeping his phone from being crushed between them.

She hugged him tightly, her cheek pressed against his chest.

“You did it.”

His expression softened.

“We’re not celebrating yet.”

“Why not?”

“Because I haven’t signed anything.”

“That’s a technicality.”

“It’s a fairly important technicality.”

She leaned back just enough to look at him.

“Don’t ruin my excitement with technicalities.”

“All right.”

She looked at him for another moment, then hugged him again.

This time, he held her longer.

There was something about hearing her say it that made the news feel more real. He had been careful with his expectations for so long that he hadn’t allowed himself to fully enjoy the possibility.

But Xiaoran was already enjoying it for both of them.

She pulled away eventually, though her hands remained around his waist.

“Are you happy?” she asked again, more.

Yichen looked down at her.

“Yes.”

Her smile softened.

“Good.”

Then she pointed toward the phone.

“Now show me the details.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You want to inspect the contract?”

“Obviously. I need to know what they’re offering my boyfriend.”

“Your boyfriend?”

“Yes. He’s quite promising.”

“Quite?”

“Don’t get arrogant.”

He laughed under his breath and brought her to the sofa.

They read through the email together.

Xiaoran was attentive, asking questions about the reporting date, training commitments, the duration of the contract, and what it would mean for his university schedule. She didn’t pretend to understand every technical detail, but she was interested in all of it.

When she reached the section about the club’s expectations, she stopped.

“They’re serious about you.”

“They wouldn’t offer it otherwise.”

“I know. But look at this. They’re not just asking you to play. They want you to be part of the team properly.” She pointed to the paragraph.

“That’s usually the point of a contract.”

She gave him a look.

“Can you let me be sentimental for five minutes?”

“Of course.”

She continued reading, but he noticed her smile returning.

A little later, she put the phone down.

“Have you told your father?”

“No.”

“Your coach?”

“Not yet.”

“Your university?”

“The club will coordinate with them once I respond.”

She nodded.

Then, after a pause, she asked, “Who did you want to tell first?”

Yichen looked at her.

“You.”

Her expression changed.

It wasn’t a dramatic change. Her lips parted a little, and the smile she had been wearing became something quieter.

“Oh.”

He reached over and brushed a loose strand of hair away from her cheek.

“Why?”

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked down at the phone.

“I just like being the first person you tell.”

“I know.”

“And you didn’t even tell me over text.”

“I wanted to see your face.”

She looked up again.

“Was it worth it?”

“Very.”

She tried to suppress her smile and failed.

Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“Congratulations, Zhou Yichen.”

He turned his face slightly.

“That’s all?”

“What?”

“That’s all I’m getting?”

She stared at him, then laughed.

“You’re so shameless.”

“Only asking.”

She leaned in and kissed him properly.

He let her pull away first, though his hand remained at her waist.

“Better?” she asked.

“Considerably.”

She rolled her eyes and settled against his shoulder.

For the rest of the evening, they talked about the contract in between eating dinner and arguing over which film to watch. Xiaoran tried to make him celebrate with a proper dessert, and he pointed out that she had already brought one.

“That one was emergency dessert.”

“And what is this?”

“Congratulations dessert.”

“How is it different?”

“Emotionally.”

He accepted this explanation without comment.

But when she was choosing a film, his gaze drifted back to the email on his phone.

The offer was real.

And so was the decision waiting behind it.

His father called the following afternoon.

Yichen was leaving the training facility when the call came in. He answered while walking toward the car park.

“Hello.”

“Are you free tonight?”

His father’s voice was as measured as ever.

“After training, yes.”

“Come home for dinner.”

Yichen paused.

“Is something happening?”

“No. I want to talk.”

“All right.”

The call ended shortly after.

Yichen stood with his phone in his hand.

His father had always been capable of making a simple sentence sound like an appointment with a board of directors.

He wasn’t surprised by the invitation. The club would have contacted the university, and there was little chance the news hadn’t reached his father through one channel or another.

Still, he wondered what exactly his father wanted to discuss.

He drove to the family home that evening.

Dinner was already on the table when he arrived. His mother greeted him warmly, asked whether the club fed him properly, and complained that he looked thinner.

Yichen assured her that he was fine.

His father was in the dining room, reading something on his tablet.

He looked up.

“You’re here.”

“Yes.”

They ate first.

His mother asked about Xiaoran, and Yichen told her that she was busy with her final-year preparations. She asked when Xiaoran was coming for dinner again, and he promised a date before the month was out.

His father listened without interrupting.

After dinner, his mother went to the living room to take a call. The two men remained at the dining table.

His father set his tablet aside.

“The Herons sent an offer.”

Yichen nodded.

“Yes.”

“A full contract.”

“That’s right.”

His father looked at him.

“Congratulations.”

The word was simple.

Yichen inclined his head.

“Thank you.”

His father poured himself a little tea. He didn’t immediately continue, and Yichen waited.

Then his father asked, “Have you decided?”

“Not yet.”

“Why?”

Yichen considered the question.

“Because I want to understand what I’m agreeing to.”

His father nodded once.

“That’s reasonable.”

He took a sip of tea.

“How long do they expect an answer?”

“By the end of the week.”

“And what do you think?”

Yichen leaned back slightly.

“I think it’s a good offer.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

His eyes lifted.

His father was looking directly at him now.

For years, their conversations about basketball had been built around performance. His training, his studies, his prospects, his decisions. Even when his father attended a game, he tended to speak about what had happened on the court rather than what it had meant to him.

The one sentence after the city-league game had stayed with Yichen.

You passed too early.

He remembered it.

He also remembered the words after his debut.

You didn’t force the final shot.

Neither had been a warm expression of affection, but both had meant something.

Now his father was asking him a different question.

“What do you want?” his father asked.

Yichen didn’t answer immediately.

His father waited.

“Not what the club wants. Not what your university thinks is best. Not what I think. What do you want?” he said.

For a moment, Yichen found himself looking at the tea in front of him.

It was a question he had asked himself many times.

He wanted to play.

That part was simple.

He wanted to know how far he could go if he gave basketball the seriousness it deserved. He wanted to test himself against players who were better, faster, more experienced. He wanted to find out whether the work he had put in over the last few years could become something more than a promising university career.

But he also wanted to finish his degree.

He wanted the knowledge he had worked for. He wanted the business world to remain a possibility, not a path he had abandoned because he was afraid of choosing.

And he wanted to make the decision without having to spend the rest of his life wondering whether he had been allowed to make it for himself.

“I want to play,” he said at last.

His father didn’t move.

“I want to know how far I can go. I don’t want to stop now just because there’s another option waiting for me.”

“And business?”

“I don’t intend to abandon it.”

“Basketball will take time.”

“I know.”

“Your studies will be affected.”

“I’ve considered that.”

“Your schedule will become more difficult.”

“Mm.”

His father studied him.

“You seem very certain about the difficulties.”

“I’ve been dealing with them already.”

A small silence followed.

Then his father asked, “And if it doesn’t work out?”

Yichen met his gaze.

“Then I’ll know I tried.”

His father looked down at his tea.

It wasn’t the answer he might have expected from a son who had grown up surrounded by the security of a family business. It wasn’t a promise of success, or a declaration that he would become the best player in the league.

It was an answer.

“I see,” his father said.

Yichen waited.

His father leaned back in his chair.

“When you were younger, I thought you were choosing basketball because you disliked the direction I had planned for you.”

Yichen’s expression remained calm, though something in his eyes sharpened.

“I never said that.”

“No. You didn’t.”

His father paused.

“I may have assumed too much.”

It was a small admission.

From him, it wasn’t small at all.

Yichen looked at his father.

“I don’t dislike the company.”

“I know.”

“I’ve always understood why you wanted me to learn the business.”

His father nodded.

“But I don’t want to enter it simply because it’s there.”

His father looked at him again.

“Then don’t.”

Yichen was quiet.

His father continued, “If you join the company one day, I want you to know why you’re there. I don’t want you sitting in a meeting wondering whether you could have been somewhere else.”

There was no dramatic shift in his voice. No sudden warmth, no attempt to turn the conversation into something it had never been.

But Yichen heard him.

For the first time, his father wasn’t asking him to prove that basketball could become a career.

He was asking him to choose a life he could accept.

“Thank you,” Yichen said.

His father gave a small nod.

“Don’t thank me yet. You still have to make a decision.”

Yichen almost smiled.

“Of course.”

“And don’t sign anything before you’ve read every clause.”

“I’ve read it.”

“Read it again.”

“I will.”

His father picked up his tablet, but before Yichen stood, he spoke once more.

“Your first game with the Herons was good.”

Yichen looked at him.

His father kept his eyes on the tablet.

“You played with discipline. You didn’t rush to prove anything.”

“Thank you.”

“Keep doing that.”

It wasn’t a long conversation.

But when Yichen left the dining room, he felt as if something that had been left unfinished for years had finally been given a place to rest.

Xiaoran was waiting for him when he returned to his apartment.

She was sitting on the sofa with her legs tucked underneath her, laptop open and a half-finished drink beside her. She had apparently been working, though the film paused on her screen suggested she had become distracted.

She looked up when he entered.

“You’re back.”

“Mm.”

“How was dinner?”

“Fine.”

She squinted at him.

“That was suspiciously short.”

He put his keys down.

“My father wanted to talk about the contract.”

She closed her laptop.

“Oh.”

Yichen took off his jacket and hung it up.

“He asked what I wanted.”

Xiaoran watched him.

“And?”

“I told him.”

She didn’t immediately ask what he had said. Instead, she waited until he came over and sat beside her.

“What did you tell him?”

“That I want to play.”

Her face softened.

“And what did he say?”

“He asked me to read the contract again.”

She blinked.

“That’s it?”

“He also said I shouldn’t join the company just because it’s there.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

Then she smiled.

“That’s actually quite a lot.”

“Yes.”

She moved closer, resting her head against his shoulder.

“How did it feel?”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Strange.”

“Strange?”

“I’m not used to him asking.”

She understood.

There were things about Yichen’s relationship with his father that she had learned gradually. Not through dramatic stories or long confessions, but through the small pauses in his conversations, the way he sometimes chose his words carefully, and the things he remembered even when he claimed they didn’t matter.

She knew that he respected his father.

She also knew that being respected and being understood weren’t always the same thing.

“Did you feel better after talking to him?” she asked.

“Yes.”

She nodded.

“Good.”

He met her eyes.

“You’re not going to ask what I’m going to choose?”

“I think I know what you want.”

“Do you?”

She lifted her head.

“You want to play.”

“That’s one part.”

“And you don’t want to give up business completely.”

“That’s another.”

She thought about it.

“Then I think you should find a way to have both, if that’s what you really want.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Very straightforward.”

“Well, I didn’t say it would be easy.”

“No?”

“No. I think you’ll be extremely busy. I think you’ll complain about having to study after training. I think you’ll come home tired and fall asleep before dinner sometimes.”

“That sounds unpleasant.”

“It does.”

She touched his arm.

“But I also think you’ll regret it if you don’t try.”

Yichen watched her.

She wasn’t telling him to choose basketball because she wanted to watch him play. She wasn’t telling him to choose business because it would be safer. She wasn’t treating his future like a decision that had to be made around her.

She was looking at him as if she trusted him to know himself.

“Would it bother you?” he asked.

“What?”

“If I had to spend more time away.”

Her expression changed slightly.

She knew what he meant.

A full contract would mean a different schedule. More training, more travel, more pressure. The comfortable routine they had built around university life would change.

She would have her own final-year projects, and he would have a professional season to navigate.

There would be days when they couldn’t meet.

There would be weekends when one of them had to leave before the other woke up.

It wasn’t an imaginary concern.

Xiaoran considered her answer carefully.

“Of course I’d miss you.”

“But that doesn’t mean I want you to give it up.”

He glanced at her.

“I don’t want you to say that just because you think it’s what I need to hear.”

She straightened.

“I’m not.”

She placed both hands on his shoulders, making sure he was looking at her.

“Yichen, I want you to have things that belong to you. I want you to have your basketball career. I want you to have your business degree. I want you to be proud of what you do.”

He turned to her.

“And I want you to come back to me when you’re done. Preferably with enough energy to eat dinner,” she said.

A quiet laugh escaped him.

“That’s your condition?”

“Yes. I’m very reasonable.”

“Very.”

“And you have to call me.”

“I can do that.”

“And send me pictures.”

“Of what?”

“Anything. The training facility. The hotel. Your food. Your shoes. Your face.”

“My face?”

“Your face, yes.”

He smiled.

“Understood.”

She seemed satisfied, then leaned forward and wrapped her arms around his neck.

Yichen drew her closer.

For a while, neither of them spoke.

He rested his cheek against her hair, one hand moving slowly along her back. She held him with the quiet certainty of someone who didn’t need to convince him to stay.

Eventually, she murmured, “You did it.”

He closed his eyes.

“Thank you.”

“Even if you haven’t signed yet.”

“I’ll remember that.”

“And when you do sign, I’m going to be even more annoying.”

“That sounds inevitable.”

“I’ll wear your jersey everywhere.”

He leaned back to look at her.

“Please don’t.”

She gasped.

“Why?”

“You’ll distract everyone.”

“Good. They should know.”

“Know what?”

“That I’m dating a professional basketball player.”

He gave her a slow, amused smile.

“Not yet.”

She looked at him, then pointed a finger at his chest.

“Don’t you dare become modest now. It’s too late.”

He caught her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“All right.”

She watched him, then her expression turned thoughtful.

“Do you know what I think?”

“What?”

“I think your father was waiting for you to say it.”

Yichen’s thumb brushed over her knuckles.

“Maybe.”

“Maybe?”

“He might have wanted to hear it for a long time.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Then I’m glad you told him.”

He held her gaze.

“So am I.”

Three days later, Yichen sat at his desk with the contract open in front of him.

He had read it twice.

Then a third time with the university’s sports office reviewing the academic arrangements. He had spoken with the Herons’ recruitment director, clarified the training schedule, and asked about the club’s expectations for his first season.

There were still details to consider.

But the question had changed.

It was no longer whether he wanted the opportunity.

He did.

The question was how to take it without losing sight of the rest of his life.

His phone lit up.

Xiaoran: Have you decided?

He looked at the message.

Yichen: Almost.

Xiaoran: That’s not a real answer.

Yichen: It is.

Xiaoran: Are you being difficult on purpose?

Yichen: A little.

Xiaoran: Zhou Yichen!

His mouth curved.

Yichen: I’ll call you tonight.

Xiaoran: Okay.

A moment later:

Xiaoran: Whatever you choose, I’m proud of you.

He read it twice.

Then he looked back at the contract.

Outside, the afternoon light was beginning to fade. His basketball shoes sat beside the door, still carrying the faint smell of the training court. His Business textbooks were stacked neatly on the other side of the desk.

Those two things had seemed like separate versions of his future.

Now, for the first time, he could imagine building a life in which neither had to disappear.

He picked up his pen.

Not to sign yet.

Just to mark the final page, where the acceptance instructions waited.

Then he took out his phone and called Xiaoran.

She answered on the second ring.

“Hello?”

“Are you busy?”

“Not anymore.”

He heard the soft rustle of paper on her end.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you calling?”

He leaned back in his chair, looking at the contract.

“I wanted to tell you something.”

There was a small pause.

“Okay.”

“I’m going to accept.”

Silence.

Then, “Really?”

“Yes.”

A delighted laugh came through the phone.

“Yichen!”

That got a smile out of him.

“I’ll still finish my degree. We’ll work out the schedule with the university and the club. I’ll have to travel more, and there’ll be a lot of things to adjust.”

“I know.”

“But I want to do it.”

She was quiet for a second.

Then she said, “I’m happy for you.”

He heard the smile in her voice.

“Thank you.”

“Are you nervous?”

“A little.”

“That’s okay.”

He looked down at the page.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“When I sign it, will you come with me?”

There was no hesitation.

“Of course.”

He smiled.

“Good.”

She made a small pleased sound.

“Wait. Does this mean I get to see you sign a real professional contract?”

“Yes.”

“Can I take pictures?”

“Within reason.”

“Can I bring flowers?”

“You’re not required to.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He laughed.

“Bring flowers if you want.”

“I do.”

He could picture her already: choosing something bright, probably asking the florist too many questions, then arriving with a bouquet almost as large as her enthusiasm.

“Then I’ll bring flowers,” she declared.

“All right.”

“And after that, dinner.”

“Of course.”

“My treat.”

He raised an eyebrow, though she couldn’t see him.

“Your treat?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because my boyfriend got a full contract.”

He laughed under his breath.

“That’s a good reason.”

“And I’m paying.”

“All right.”

She sounded pleased with herself.

“See? I’m supporting your career.”

“Very generously.”

“Don’t tease me.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He let her hear the smile in his voice.

“Maybe.”

She laughed.

For the first time since the email arrived, the future no longer felt like a list of conditions and deadlines. It felt like something he was choosing.

When he imagined the difficult days ahead—the long training sessions, the away games, the exams, the uncertainty—he could still picture the end of them.

A familiar apartment.

Two portions of dinner.

A girl who would ask him whether he had eaten, complain when he forgot to send pictures, and fall asleep against his shoulder while insisting she wasn’t tired.

He wanted the court. He wanted the degree.

He wanted the life he would build after both.

And he wanted her in it.

“Xiaoran?”

“Yes?”

“I’ll see you tonight.”

“You’re coming over?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll order food.”

He glanced at the clock.

“Don’t order too much.”

“Why?”

“Because you always order too much.”

“That’s because you eat half of mine.”

His mouth curved.

“Then order enough for two.”

“Obviously.”

The call ended a few minutes later.

Yichen looked once more at the contract.

Then he closed the laptop, put the printed copy in the drawer with the bundle of ticket stubs his father had given him the year before, and went to find his car keys.

chapters.desc: Her media module wants a documentary about ordinary intimacy. Lin Xiaoran chooses her subject in thirty seconds, then moves in with him for two weeks to observe it.
chapters.title: The Assignment Was to Study Love
chapters.epigraph: “Maybe that’s the problem with studying someone you love.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that something was wrong was Xiaoran’s expression when she let herself into his apartment on a Wednesday night.

She didn’t look tired, or annoyed, or even hungry. She looked suspicious.

Yichen, who was sitting on the sofa with his laptop open, glanced up from the business report he was reading. He had been home for nearly an hour, showered after training, and was halfway through reviewing a presentation for the following morning.

Xiaoran stood in the entrance, holding her tote bag against her chest.

He met her eyes.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s convincing.”

She narrowed her eyes at him. “Why do you always assume something is wrong?”

“Because you’ve been standing there for thirty seconds, staring at me like I’ve committed a crime.”

“I haven’t decided whether you have.”

Yichen closed his laptop.

“All right. What happened?”

Xiaoran walked over, dropped her bag beside the sofa, and sat down next to him. She looked at the coffee table, then at him, then back at the coffee table.

“I have a weird assignment.”

“How weird?”

“Very.”

“Is it illegal?”

“Zhou Yichen!”

“I’m asking.”

She slapped his arm lightly. He smiled, then waited.

Xiaoran took out her laptop and opened the university portal.

“Our lecturer gave us a project. It’s for this module about media, human behavior, and storytelling. We’re supposed to document something ordinary that people usually overlook, then turn it into a short-form documentary.”

“That doesn’t sound particularly weird.”

“Wait.”

She scrolled down.

“The assignment is called An Unusual Study of Ordinary Intimacy.”

Yichen read the title.

His expression remained neutral.

Xiaoran watched him carefully.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face.”

“My face is normal.”

“You’re already thinking something.”

He looked at the screen again. “What exactly are you supposed to do?”

She sighed dramatically.

“We have to observe a person in their natural environment. Study their habits, routines, small behaviours, and interactions. Then create a documentary about something that reveals their personality without relying on interviews or direct explanations.”

“Interesting.”

“That’s not the weird part.”

“All right.”

“We have to choose someone we know well.”

Yichen nodded.

“And the subject has to be someone whose ordinary behavior we might have stopped noticing because we’re too familiar with them.”

He turned to her.

She looked back.

There was a pause.

Then Yichen asked, calmly, “You’ve chosen me?”

Xiaoran’s mouth fell open.

“How did you know?”

“Because you’ve been staring at me for thirty seconds.”

“That’s not fair. I haven’t even told you the most embarrassing part.”

“Go on.”

She turned her laptop toward him.

There was a list of possible observation categories.

1. Repeated habits and unconscious gestures.
2. Behaviour around a familiar person.
3. Unspoken communication.
4. Emotional responses to ordinary situations.
5. The difference between what a person says and what they actually do.

Yichen read through them.

Then he leaned back.

“So I’m your research subject.”

“Temporarily.”

“How long?”

“Two weeks.”

“Two weeks?”

“Yes.”

“You’re at your own place from Sunday to Thursday.”

“Not for the next two weeks. The subject has to be observed in his natural environment.”

“My natural environment is the training court.”

“Your other one.”

He considered this.

“Do I get paid?”

“You’re my boyfriend.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

She hit his shoulder with the back of her hand.

Yichen laughed.

“Fine. I’ll cooperate.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Really?”

“Would you prefer I refuse?”

“No, but I thought you’d make fun of me.”

“I can do both.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

He reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“What’s the first thing you need to observe?”

Xiaoran hesitated.

Then she looked at him with the seriousness of a researcher preparing to conduct an important experiment.

“Your morning routine.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted.

“My morning routine?”

“Yes.”

“What about it?”

“I need to know what you do when you wake up.”

“I get up.”

“That’s not detailed enough.”

“I brush my teeth.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

Something in his face eased.

“All right, researcher. Ask your questions.”

The following morning, Xiaoran woke up earlier than usual.

She had no early class and no deadline. She had decided that the best way to conduct her research was to observe Yichen before he knew he was being observed.

Unfortunately, Yichen woke up before she could begin.

He opened his eyes and found her staring at him.

He blinked once.

“Good morning.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer.

Instead, she reached for her phone.

Yichen watched her unlock it.

“What are you doing?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re recording?”

“No.”

“Then why is your camera open?”

She quickly turned the screen off.

“You’re too observant.”

He smiled sleepily and reached for her waist, drawing her closer.

“You’re not very good at being inconspicuous.”

“Don’t interfere with my research.”

“I’m not.”

“You are. You’re changing your natural behavior because you know I’m watching.”

Yichen looked at her.

Then he deliberately closed his eyes again.

“Is this better?”

“No.”

He opened one eye.

“Then what would you like me to do?”

“Act normal.”

“I was sleeping.”

“Exactly. Continue.”

He stared at her.

Then, without another word, he pulled the blanket over both of them and rested his chin against her head.

Xiaoran tried to remain serious.

She really did.

But after a few seconds, she began laughing.

Yichen opened his eyes.

“What’s funny?”

“Nothing.”

“Your research is going well.”

“Shut up.”

He kissed her hair.

“Go back to sleep, researcher.”

She wrote in her notes later:

Subject appears to be unusually affectionate in the morning. Frequently initiates physical contact. Doesn’t seem to distinguish between being awake and being asleep when maintaining physical proximity.

She stared at the sentence.

Then added:

Possibly a habit rather than a conscious decision.

By the third day, Xiaoran had become a little too enthusiastic.

She had a small notebook now.

Yichen had discovered it beside her laptop, and although he hadn’t read the contents, he had noticed the increasingly serious way she observed him.

At breakfast, she watched him make coffee. At lunch, she watched him arrange the groceries.

At night, she watched him review his training schedule.

Sometimes he would catch her staring.

Sometimes he would deliberately do something unusual just to see whether she would write it down.

On Thursday evening, he was sitting at the dining table with his laptop when Xiaoran appeared from the kitchen carrying two cups of tea.

She placed one beside him.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

She sat opposite him.

Yichen took a sip.

Xiaoran watched.

He took another.

She watched again.

Finally, he put the cup down.

“Is there something on my face?”

“No.”

“Do I have something in my teeth?”

“No.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

She opened her notebook.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Why do you always put my cup on the right side?”

He glanced at the cup, then at her.

“Because you’re right-handed. How do you know?”

“You hold your spoon with your right hand. You use your right hand to pick up your phone. When you’re carrying things, you usually leave your right hand free.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

Yichen returned to his laptop.

She slowly wrote something down.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

“Read it.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s private research.”

He leaned back in his chair.

“You’re studying me, but I don’t get to see the results?”

“Correct.”

“Sounds unfair.”

“Research ethics.”

He laughed.

She looked at him again.

“Wait. Another question.”

“Hm?”

“Why do you always move my things when I’m not looking?”

“I don’t.”

“You do.”

“Give me an example.”

“My phone. When I leave it somewhere, you always put it beside me.”

“Because you forget where you put it.”

“My hair clip?”

“You leave it on the dining table.”

“My water bottle?”

“You forget to drink water.”

“My bag?”

“You once left it outside the bathroom.”

“That was one time.”

“Twice.”

She blinked at him.

Yichen smiled.

“Do you want me to stop?”

Xiaoran was quiet.

“No.”

He nodded, as if that settled the matter.

Then he returned to work.

Xiaoran looked down at her notebook.

Subject displays an unusual tendency to notice and correct small inconveniences in another person’s environment. He doesn’t seem to regard these actions as acts of care.

She paused.

Then wrote:

He appears to consider them ordinary.

The strangest part of the assignment came on Saturday.

Xiaoran had arranged a short observation session in the living room.

She placed her camera on a small tripod, adjusted the angle, and checked the lighting.

Yichen came out of the bedroom wearing a black T-shirt and gray sweatpants.

He stopped when he saw the equipment.

“What is this?”

“Filming.”

“Of me?”

“Yes.”

“What am I supposed to do?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at the camera, then at her.

“That’s a difficult instruction.”

“Just behave naturally.”

“You’re making that sound like a test.”

“It is.”

He sat on the sofa.

Xiaoran pressed record, then went to sit beside him with her laptop.

For the first few minutes, nothing happened.

Yichen read an article on his phone.

Xiaoran edited some footage.

He occasionally shifted his position, crossed his legs, or rubbed the back of his neck.

Then Xiaoran got up to retrieve something from the bedroom.

Yichen didn’t look up.

A minute later, she returned.

She had forgotten her water bottle.

She picked it up from the table and sat down again.

Yichen moved his phone slightly to make space for her bottle.

She noticed.

She said nothing.

A few minutes later, she leaned forward to look at something on his screen.

He tilted the phone toward her without being asked.

Then, when she sat back, he placed his hand on the back of the sofa behind her.

Not quite touching.

Just there.

Xiaoran continued reading.

Eventually, she leaned against his arm.

Yichen adjusted his position to make her more comfortable, then continued reading.

The camera kept recording.

Neither of them paid attention to it.

After twenty minutes, Xiaoran looked at the footage.

She watched the whole thing twice.

There was no dramatic moment.

No interesting action.

Just Yichen making space for her, tilting his phone, moving her water bottle, and adjusting his arm when she leaned against him.

She frowned.

This was supposed to be a documentary.

How could something so ordinary be interesting?

She rewound the footage, then watched it again.

Yichen noticed her expression.

“What’s wrong?”

“I think my footage is boring.”

He glanced at the screen.

“What were you expecting?”

“I don’t know. Something more obvious.”

“Like what?”

“Like you doing something.”

“I was doing something.”

“Reading.”

“And?”

“Moving my phone.”

He held her gaze.

“Would you prefer I juggle?”

She laughed despite herself.

“Honestly.”

Yichen closed his phone.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Maybe you’re looking for something that isn’t supposed to be obvious.”

She met his eyes.

He nodded toward the camera.

“You said the assignment was about things people stop noticing because they’re familiar with them.”

She went quiet.

“Maybe that’s why you think it’s boring.”

She looked at the footage again.

Yichen didn’t add anything.

He reached for her hand and began absentmindedly rubbing his thumb over her knuckles.

On Sunday, Xiaoran decided to interview him.

Not formally.

She sat opposite him at the dining table, with her phone recording audio.

Yichen had just finished lunch.

“Okay. Question one.”

“Go ahead.”

“What’s something you do every day without thinking about it?”

He considered the question.

“Check my training schedule.”

“That’s boring.”

“You asked.”

She frowned.

“Something else.”

“Check whether you’ve eaten.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“That’s not something you do.”

“It is.”

“Why?”

“Because you forget.”

“I do not.”

He gave her a look.

She lowered her eyes.

“Okay, sometimes. Sometimes I check whether you’ve got your keys before we leave.”

She looked at him.

“And whether your laptop is charged if you have a presentation.”

“How do you know that?”

“Because you complain when it isn’t.”

She looked down at her notes.

“Next question. What’s something you notice about me that I don’t realize you notice?”

Yichen didn’t answer immediately.

He looked at her, seemingly considering how to phrase it.

“You press your lips together when you’re concentrating.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“You do it when you’re editing something, too. And when you’re reading instructions.”

She instinctively pressed her lips together.

Yichen smiled.

“Like that.”

She immediately relaxed her mouth.

He continued.

“You also move your feet when you’re excited. Not very much. Just a little.”

Xiaoran looked down at her feet.

“Really?”

“And when you’re nervous, you start asking questions you already know the answers to.”

She looked up.

“That’s not true.”

“You’re doing it now.”

She closed her mouth.

He laughed.

She was beginning to suspect that the assignment was becoming dangerous.

“One more question,” she said.

“All right.”

“What’s something you do for me that you don’t think counts as affection?”

Yichen’s expression softened slightly.

He looked at her.

“Probably a lot of things.”

“Like?”

“Making sure your side of the bed isn’t too cold when you get in. Keeping the snacks you like in the kitchen. Remembering which food you don’t like. Waiting for you to finish talking even when I’m in a hurry.”

She stopped writing.

He noticed.

“Why?”

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

She turned to him.

“You’re making my assignment difficult.”

“How?”

“Because I don’t know how to write all that without making it sound like I’m writing a love letter.”

Yichen smiled.

“Maybe you are.”

She gave him a look.

He reached across the table and gently tapped the end of her pen.

“Don’t make it complicated.”

“Easy for you to say.”

“Just write what happened.”

She held his gaze.

Then she slowly nodded.

The night before the submission, Xiaoran sat on the floor in front of the television, surrounded by footage, photographs, notes, and an increasingly concerning number of sticky notes.

Yichen had finished training and showered. He came out of the bedroom to find her staring at her laptop with a deeply troubled expression.

He sat beside her.

“Still editing?”

“Yes.”

“How much is left?”

“Everything.”

He looked at the screen.

The documentary was currently titled The Ordinary Behaviour of Zhou Yichen.

He raised an eyebrow.

“Very flattering.”

“Don’t start.”

He watched her scroll through the footage.

There were clips of him making coffee, checking her laptop charger, moving her water bottle, holding the door, waiting for her to finish tying her shoelaces, and putting a blanket over her when she fell asleep on the sofa.

There was also a clip of him standing in the kitchen watching her explain a new recipe. He had been listening with an expression of such patient concentration that Xiaoran had included the entire thirty-second clip.

Yichen watched it.

Then he looked at her.

“Why did you record that?”

“Because you looked like you were attending a very important business meeting.”

“I was learning how to make your pasta.”

“Exactly.”

He laughed.

She leaned back against the sofa.

“I think I know what the documentary is about now.”

“What?”

She looked at the screen.

“It’s about how people show affection without actually saying anything.”

Yichen nodded.

“That sounds reasonable.”

“But I don’t want it to be too romantic. It’s an academic assignment.”

“Then don’t make it romantic.”

She looked at him.

“How?”

“Just be honest.”

She considered that.

Then she turned back to her laptop.

The final documentary was six minutes and forty seconds long.

She titled it Things We Stop Noticing.

The opening showed Yichen making two cups of coffee in the morning.

One black.

One with milk.

Then a shot of him moving her water bottle closer to her laptop.

Then a clip of his hand reaching back to find hers while they walked.

The narration was Xiaoran’s voice.

When we become familiar with someone, we stop noticing the small things they do. They become part of the background of our daily lives. We stop asking why someone remembers our preferences, why they make room for us, or why they seem to know what we need before we ask.

The footage continued.

Yichen opening the car door. Yichen waiting while she took photographs of a dessert. Yichen looking up from his laptop when she called his name.

Yichen placing a cushion behind her back.

These actions aren’t necessarily extraordinary. They are often too small to be remembered individually. But perhaps that is what makes them meaningful. They are repeated without expectation. They happen so naturally that the person doing them may not even consider them worth mentioning.

The final clip was from the living room.

Xiaoran had been sitting beside Yichen, editing something on her laptop. He was reading an article. Without looking away from the screen, he had reached over and tucked her hair behind her ear.

Then he had continued reading.

She had continued working.

Nothing else happened.

The narration ended.

I thought this assignment would require me to discover something unusual about someone I knew well. Instead, I realized that I had been surrounded by things I had stopped noticing.

The screen faded to black.

A single line came up in white: Sometimes the closeness isn’t in the moments we remember. It’s in the ones we stop recording.

Yichen watched the finished video in silence.

When it ended, Xiaoran turned toward him.

“Well?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

She began to worry.

“Is it bad?”

“No.”

“Then?”

He looked at the black screen.

“It’s good.”

“Just good?”

He turned toward her.

“It’s very good.”

She eyed him.

“You’re only saying that because I’m your girlfriend.”

“I’m saying that because it’s good.”

“You’re biased.”

“Probably.”

She groaned and let her head drop onto his shoulder.

Yichen smiled and kissed her hair.

After a moment, he said, “You know what I found interesting?”

“What?”

“You filmed me for two weeks, but most of the footage was actually about you.”

She lifted her head.

“What?”

“Look at it again.”

He pointed at the screen.

“You filmed me moving your things closer. You filmed me waiting for you. You filmed me making room for you. But the interesting part is how naturally you fit into all those moments.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

He said, “You didn’t have to ask me to make space. You didn’t have to ask me to wait. You just assumed I would.”

Her expression softened.

Yichen brushed his thumb across her cheek.

“That’s probably what familiarity looks like.”

She didn’t say anything.

Then she asked, “Does it bother you?”

“What?”

“That I take all those things for granted?”

Yichen considered her question.

“No.”

“Really?”

“I don’t do them so you’ll notice every time.”

He leaned forward and kissed her temple.

“But I like that you notice them eventually.”

Xiaoran smiled.

Then, as if remembering something, she quickly reached for her notebook.

Yichen watched her.

“What are you writing?”

“An additional observation.”

“About?”

She wrote something, then turned the notebook toward him.

Subject claims that his actions aren’t intended to be noticed. However, he appears pleased when they are.

Yichen read it.

Then he looked at her.

“That’s your conclusion?”

“Yes.”

“Interesting.”

“Thank you.”

He took the notebook from her hand and placed it on the coffee table.

Then he drew her into his arms.

“You’re welcome.”

She settled against his chest, smiling.

After a few seconds, she looked up.

“Wait. I have another question.”

“Of course you do.”

“If you could give my documentary a title, what would you call it?”

Yichen looked at her.

Then his lips curved.

“Living With Lin Xiaoran.”

She blinked.

“That’s not the assignment.”

“I know.”

“Why that?”

“Because you’ve been living here for two weeks, and most of the things you filmed only happen when you’re around.”

She stared at him, then slowly began to smile.

“That’s cheating.”

“How?”

“You’re supposed to be the subject.”

“I was.”

“But you made it about me.”

Yichen lowered his head and kissed her cheek.

“Maybe that’s the problem with studying someone you love.”

Xiaoran tilted her head.

“What problem?”

“You eventually realize you aren’t observing them from the outside anymore.”

He kissed her other cheek.

“You’re part of the footage.”

She looked at him, her expression growing soft.

Then she wrapped her arms around his neck and kissed him.

Yichen smiled against her lips, one hand settling at her waist.

When she pulled back, she looked pleased with herself.

“Good answer.”

“Will that be included in your report?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I need to maintain academic objectivity.”

He laughed.

She tucked herself against his chest again.

A few seconds passed.

Then she mombled, “Actually, I think I need to do a follow-up assignment.”

Yichen closed his eyes.

“What’s the topic this time?”

“How living together changes people’s behavior.”

He opened his eyes.

“How long?”

“Maybe a month.”

“Do I get paid this time?”

She looked up innocently.

“I’ll give you kisses.”

Yichen considered that.

“That’s not a particularly competitive offer.”

Xiaoran gasped.

“Excuse me?”

He smiled, slow and entirely too pleased with himself.

“Perhaps I should negotiate.”

She immediately understood the expression on his face.

Her cheeks warmed.

“You’re not allowed to flirt with the researcher.”

“I’m not flirting.”

“You are.”

“Then perhaps you should document it.”

Xiaoran stared at him before burying her face in his chest.

Yichen laughed, wrapped both arms around her, and pressed his mouth to her hair.

chapters.desc: She follows him to Saturday training in secret. He knows by the first drill, and has water and crackers left at her end of the corridor.
chapters.title: The Girl Who Couldn’t Keep Up
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not very good at surprising me.”
chapters.content:
Yichen’s training schedule wasn’t a secret.

At least, not from Xiaoran.

She knew his usual routine almost as well as he did. On training days, he left the apartment early, arrived at the facility before the team briefing, completed his individual warm-up, and then spent several hours on court. Depending on the day’s program, he would finish with conditioning, strength training, or recovery work.

He was disciplined about it.

Almost annoyingly so.

And Xiaoran had recently developed a particular interest in seeing him train.

Matches didn’t count, and neither did the open practices when he knew she was coming. She wanted to see him during his ordinary training.

The unremarkable parts.

The moments when he wasn’t performing for anyone.

She wanted to watch him run, shoot, practice footwork, listen to his coach, and concentrate on something he loved.

But there was one problem.

She didn’t want to disturb him.

Yichen had his routine. She knew how much he valued it, and she didn’t want him to feel obligated to entertain her or adjust his training just because she had decided to appear.

So, naturally, Xiaoran came up with a brilliant plan.

She would follow him.

Secretly.

And observe him from a distance.

It was a good plan.

In theory.

On Saturday morning, Yichen left the apartment at his usual time. The Herons trained on Saturdays, and she slept at his on Fridays. The plan practically wrote itself.

Xiaoran was still in bed when he kissed her hair.

“Going now.”

She made a sleepy noise.

“Mm.”

“Sleep a little longer.”

“Okay.”

He pulled the blanket up over her shoulder and left.

Five minutes later, Xiaoran opened one eye.

Ten minutes later, she was out of bed.

She had already prepared her clothes the night before: comfortable leggings, a loose athletic top, a light jacket, and a pair of trainers she hadn’t worn in a while.

She tied her hair into a ponytail, packed a small bag with her phone, water bottle, and some snacks, then checked the time.

Perfect.

She wasn’t going to interfere. She wasn’t even going to speak to him.

She would go to the facility, find somewhere to sit, and watch.

Easy.

Xiaoran looked at herself in the mirror.

“Operation: Observe Zhou Yichen.”

She nodded.

“Very professional.”

Yichen was already on court when she arrived.

The training facility was familiar to her. She had visited enough times to know the entrance, the reception area, and the route to the viewing section. She also knew which side of the court offered a clear view without being too close to the players.

She found a seat near the upper side of the court.

Then she spotted him.

He was wearing his training kit, basketball in hand, listening to one of the assistant coaches. His hair was slightly damp already, and his expression was focused.

Xiaoran’s eyes followed him as he stepped onto the court.

She had seen him play countless times.

But there was something different about watching him train.

There were no crowds cheering. No scoreboard to distract her. No dramatic moment that made everyone stand up.

Just the repeated sound of basketballs hitting the floor.

The squeak of shoes.

The coach’s instructions.

And Yichen.

He moved through the warm-up with practiced efficiency, his body seemingly familiar with every movement. He listened carefully, asked a question, then demonstrated the footwork again.

Xiaoran leaned forward.

He was handsome.

That was her first observation.

Her second observation was that he looked even more attractive when he was concentrating.

She quickly took out her phone and opened her notes.

Observation 1: Zhou Yichen looks serious during training.

She paused.

Then added:

Unfortunately, this makes him more handsome.

She smiled to herself.

The training began in earnest.

Yichen moved between shooting drills, defensive footwork, and short bursts of sprinting. His movements were controlled, economical, and precise. Even when he missed a shot, he didn’t react dramatically. He retrieved the ball, adjusted his position, and tried again.

Xiaoran watched him for nearly twenty minutes.

Then she began to feel slightly restless.

Not because she was bored.

Because sitting still seemed insufficient.

She wanted to see the court from another angle.

And perhaps, if she was being honest, she wanted to feel a little closer to what he was doing.

She stood up.

There was a quieter corridor along the side of the facility, with a glass partition overlooking part of the training area. She walked over and found a place where she could watch without getting in anyone’s way.

From there, she could see him even better.

She couldn’t help smiling.

Perfect.

Yichen was halfway through a conditioning drill when he noticed her.

It wasn’t that he had become distracted.

His focus remained on the court. He completed the sprint, changed direction, received the ball, and finished the sequence.

But between repetitions, his eyes moved toward the glass partition.

A familiar figure. A ponytail.

A light-colored jacket.

And a girl who was trying hard to look as if she wasn’t watching him.

Yichen’s mouth curved.

Just slightly.
