He turned back toward the court.

The next repetition began.

He didn’t call her name.

Didn’t wave.

Didn’t approach.

Instead, he continued his drill.

He knew Xiaoran well enough to understand what she was doing.

She hadn’t come to interrupt him. She was trying to give him space while satisfying her curiosity.

And, judging by the way she was standing with her phone held against her chest, she probably thought she was being discreet.

Yichen found that amusing.

He also noticed something else.

She was standing a little too close to the glass, shifting her weight from one foot to the other.

He glanced at the clock, then at the water station.

He made a mental note.

A few minutes later, during a break, he approached his teammate.

“Can you pass me the spare bottle?”

His teammate handed it over.

Yichen took a drink, then casually asked one of the facility staff to leave a bottle of water at the small table near the viewing corridor.

He didn’t explain why.

He returned to the court.

Xiaoran was beginning to realize that watching someone train was much more physically demanding than she had expected.

Not because she was exercising.

But because she had been standing.

She shifted her feet, then leaned against the wall, then straightened again when someone walked past.

She looked at the court.

Yichen was now practicing a series of movements involving quick changes of direction. His shoes squeaked against the floor as he moved between markers.

Xiaoran watched, fascinated.

He made it look so easy.

She knew it wasn’t.

She had seen the bruises he sometimes came home with, the tiredness after demanding training sessions, and the way he occasionally sat after a game, letting his body recover.

But seeing the repetition made her understand it differently.

He did the same movement again.

And again.

And again.

Not because he hadn’t done it correctly.

Because he wanted to do it better.

She looked down at her own trainers.

A thought occurred to her.

Perhaps she should try some of the movements.

Not now, obviously.

But maybe later.

She could ask him to teach her.

Just a little.

She smiled at the idea.

Then her eyes caught sight of something on the small table nearby.

A bottle of water.

Beside it was a packet of her favorite crackers.

Xiaoran blinked.

She looked around.

Nobody seemed to be paying attention.

She approached the table and examined the items.

There was no note.

But she recognized the water bottle.

It was the brand Yichen usually bought for her.

Her eyes slowly narrowed.

She looked back toward the court.

Yichen was facing the other direction, listening to his coach.

Xiaoran stared at him.

Then she smiled.

He knows.

She was almost certain.

The next thirty minutes were where Xiaoran’s plan began to fall apart.

She had originally intended to watch the entire training session.

But she had underestimated two things.

First, how long a professional athlete could train without seeming to lose his energy.

Second, how little stamina she herself possessed when required to stand around in an unfamiliar environment for an extended period.

She drank the water.

Ate the crackers, then found a nearby bench and sat down.

From there, she could still see the court.

Yichen was now doing repeated sprint drills.

Xiaoran watched the first few, then the next few.

Then she checked the time.

He was still going.

He was running as if he had somewhere urgent to be.

She frowned.

“How does he do that?”

A staff member passing by smiled.

“Long training history.”

Xiaoran nodded politely.

“Right.”

She looked down at her legs.

She had been sitting for approximately seven minutes.

And she was already considering whether she should take a nap.

She wasn’t proud of this.

But she was beginning to suspect that her boyfriend had been built differently.

Yichen noticed her sitting down.

He was in the middle of a shooting drill when his eyes moved toward the bench.

Xiaoran had her legs stretched out slightly, one hand resting on her knee.

She was watching him.

Then she caught him looking.

Her eyes widened.

She immediately pretended to be interested in the wall.

Yichen nearly laughed.

He turned back to the basket, received the ball, and made the shot.

His teammate caught the rebound.

“You’re in a good mood today.”

Yichen wiped his forehead with a towel.

“Am I not allowed to?”

His teammate gave him a knowing look.

Yichen took another drink.

“Focus on your own shooting.”

“Right.”

The teammate glanced toward the viewing area, then back at him.

“Oh.”

Yichen didn’t respond.

His teammate grinned.

“Understood.”

The final straw came during the conditioning session.

Xiaoran had decided to stand again.

She wanted to get a better view of the court, and the bench was slightly obstructed by a pillar.

She moved to the side, stood near the wall, and watched Yichen complete another series of sprints.

One.

Two.

Three.

Four.

She was impressed.

Then she became concerned. Then impressed again, then concerned.

By the time he finished, she was already feeling tired on his behalf.

She leaned her shoulder against the wall.

And, without thinking, she copied his stance.

Feet apart.

Knees slightly bent.

Arms relaxed.

She tried to imitate the way he positioned himself before a sprint.

It looked easy.

She bent her knees a little more, then straightened, then tried again.

Unfortunately, she had forgotten that she was wearing shoes with little grip.

Her foot slipped slightly.

She caught herself against the wall.

A soft gasp escaped her.

On court, Yichen turned his head.

He saw it.

His expression changed immediately.

Not alarmed exactly, but attentive.

He watched her straighten herself, check her shoe, and look around to make sure nobody had noticed.

Then she glanced toward him.

Their eyes met.

Neither moved.

Yichen’s lips curved.

A slow, knowing smile.

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

She looked away.

He shook his head slightly, amused, and turned back to his coach.

He still didn’t approach her.

But a few minutes later, when the coach called for a short recovery break, Yichen walked toward the water station.

He didn’t go directly to Xiaoran.

Instead, he stopped near the side entrance and spoke with a staff member.

Then he took a towel, wiped his face, and returned to the court.

Xiaoran watched him.

Her eyes narrowed.

He was definitely doing that on purpose.

The session ended almost twenty minutes later.

Yichen completed his final shooting drill, exchanged a few words with his coach, and gathered his belongings.

Only then did he walk toward the viewing corridor.

Xiaoran immediately sat up straighter.

She had been pretending to look at her phone.

Convincingly.

Yichen stopped in front of her.

“Good morning.”

“Good morning.”

He glanced at the water bottle beside her.

“Did you drink?”

“Yes.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He looked at her for another moment.

Then his mouth curved.

“Enjoying the training?”

Xiaoran tried to maintain a neutral expression.

“Yes.”

“Really?”

“Very much.”

“How long have you been here?”

She hesitated.

“Not long.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Xiaoran.”

“Okay, a while.”

“How long?”

“Since you started.”

He met her eyes.

She looked back.

Then she smiled sheepishly.

“Surprise.”

Yichen laughed.

“You’re not very good at surprising me.”

“I was trying!”

“I noticed.”

Her eyes widened.

“You knew?”

“From the beginning.”

“How?”

He leaned slightly toward her.

“Because I know what you look like when you’re trying not to be noticed.”

She frowned.

“What’s that supposed to mean?”

“You keep looking at me, then pretending to look somewhere else whenever I turn around.”

She gasped.

“You’re making that up.”

“All right.”

She studied his face.

“Wait. When did you first notice?”

“During the conditioning drill.”

“That’s so early!”

“Not really.”

“Then why didn’t you come over?”

Yichen took a moment to answer.

“Because you came here to watch me train, not to make me stop training.”

She blinked.

He said, “I figured you wanted to see my usual routine. So I let you.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

She looked down at her hands.

“I didn’t want to disturb you.”

“I know.”

“And I didn’t want you to change your schedule just because I came.”

“I didn’t.”

He reached over and gently straightened the strap of her bag.

“But I did make sure you had water.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“And crackers.”

“And crackers.”

That made her grin.

“You’re very considerate.”

“Someone has to be.”

She pinched his arm.

He laughed.

Then his gaze moved down toward her legs.

“How are you feeling?”

“I’m fine.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

He waited.

She sighed.

“My legs are a little tired.”

Yichen’s smile widened.

“A little?”

She gave him a warning look.

“Don’t.”

“Did you do some training yourself?”

“No.”

He glanced at her trainers.

“Then why are you tired?”

“I stood for a long time.”

He nodded solemnly.

“Very demanding.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed and reached for her hand.

“Come on. Let’s go.”

Where the glass ended and nobody from the team could see, he bent and kissed her, quickly, still warm from the court.

They were halfway down the corridor when Xiaoran stopped.

“Wait.”

Yichen turned.

“What?”

She looked at the court through the glass.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“How long were you training today?”

He told her.

She blinked.

“That’s so long.”

“It’s normal.”

“For you.”

He smiled.

“Yes.”

She looked at his legs, then at her own, then back at him.

“Can you teach me?”

Yichen studied her.

“Teach you what?”

“Some of the things you did today.”

“Basketball?”

“Not necessarily. The footwork. The running. Maybe the warm-up.”

He turned to her.

Then asked, “Why?”

She shrugged.

“I want to try.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right.”

Her face brightened.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

“But not during your usual training. I don’t want to interrupt.”

“We can do it on a day when I’m not training.”

She nodded enthusiastically.

“And you have to teach me properly.”

“I will.”

“And don’t laugh if I’m bad.”

Yichen looked at her.

“I won’t.”

“You’re thinking about laughing.”

“I’m thinking about how to keep you from falling over.”

She gasped.

“I can run!”

“I know.”

“I can!”

Something in his face eased.

“Then show me.”

She looked at him, then looked toward the exit.

“...Not today.”

Yichen laughed.

On the way home, Xiaoran was unusually quiet.

Yichen glanced at her from the driver’s seat.

“Tired?”

“A little.”

“Want to sleep?”

“No.”

A few seconds passed.

Then she turned toward him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you mind if I come again?”

He held her gaze.

“Why would I mind?”

“Because I don’t want you to feel like you’re being watched all the time.”

He smiled.

“I play in front of a few thousand people most weeks. I think I can handle one girl watching me.”

She pouted.

“That’s different.”

“How?”

“Because those people don’t know you.”

He studied her.

She was looking out the window now, her fingers playing with the strap of her bag.

“I like seeing you when you’re doing your own things. I don’t always get to see this side of you,” she said.

His expression softened.

“What side?”

“The serious one.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I’m serious with you.”

She laughed.

“No, you’re not. You’re always teasing me.”

“That’s also a side of me.”

“Unfortunately.”

He reached over and squeezed her hand.

“You can come whenever you want, Xiaoran. You don’t have to sneak around.”

“I know.”

“And if you want to watch, just tell me.”

“I don’t want you to feel like you need to pay attention to me.”

“I won’t.”

She looked at him.

He continued, calm and certain.

“I’ll train. You can watch. If I have a break, I’ll come find you. That’s all.”

She smiled more brightly.

“Okay.”

A moment later, she said, “But I think I should improve my stamina.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Why?”

“So I can stay longer.”

That got a smile out of him.

“You can sit down whenever you want.”

“No. I want to be able to walk around with you.”

He considered that, then nodded.

“All right. We’ll start slowly.”

She looked pleased.

She leaned back against the seat.

Then, after a moment, she turned toward him again.

“By the way.”

“Hm?”

“Your training outfit today was very nice.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“What did you like about it?”

She looked at him innocently.

“Everything.”

His lips curved.

“Is that part of your observation?”

“Yes.”

“What did you observe?”

That made her grin.

“That my boyfriend is very handsome.”

He laughed.

“That’s a biased conclusion.”

“I don’t care.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles at a red light.

“Noted.”

The following week, Xiaoran returned to the training facility.

This time, she didn’t sneak in.

She told Yichen beforehand.

She arrived a little after his warm-up had started, carrying her own water bottle and a small bag of snacks. She found her usual seat and settled down.

Yichen noticed her almost immediately.

He didn’t stop. He didn’t wave.

He glanced toward her, and when their eyes met, his lips curved into that familiar, teasing smile.

Xiaoran smiled back.

Then she opened her notebook.

Observation 2: Subject has become aware of the researcher’s presence and appears mildly pleased.

She watched him return to his drill.

A few minutes later, Yichen glanced over again.

She lifted her water bottle.

He nodded and went back to the drill.

Xiaoran sat down on the end of the bench, still breathing hard, and drank half his water.

chapters.desc: His first-team Herons jersey arrives, number eleven, with an extra O in his name.
chapters.title: Eleven, Misspelled
chapters.epigraph: “Actually, I liked the first one.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Xiaoran noticed was that Yichen’s name was wrong.

The second thing she noticed was that he hadn’t noticed.

He was standing in front of his new locker at the Herons training center, the first-team one with his name on a brass plate, halfway through changing into his training kit, when she appeared at the doorway with two drinks and a paper bag. Partners were allowed in the corridor on Thursdays. She had checked.

“Yichen.”

He looked over.

“You’re early.”

“I finished my presentation meeting sooner. I brought you something.” She held up the drinks.

He accepted the bottle she offered him, then leaned down to kiss her forehead.

“Thank you.”

She smiled, pleased with herself, before her eyes wandered to the open locker.

His first-team kit was hanging neatly inside, still creased from the packet: the navy jersey, number eleven, with his surname printed above it.

Except it wasn’t quite his surname.

Xiaoran stopped smiling.

She leaned closer, then closer again.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Your name.”

He glanced at his jersey.

“What about it?”

She pointed.

“That’s not your name.”

He looked.

There was a brief silence.

The jersey read:

ZHOOU

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

Yichen stared at it.

Then he looked at her.

“That’s unfortunate.”

She made a strangled sound.

“Unfortunate?”

“An extra letter.”

“An extra letter?”

“Yes.”

“Your name has grown.”

He looked at the jersey again, apparently considering the matter with the seriousness of a man reading the small print of a contract.

“Apparently.”

Xiaoran finally burst out laughing.

She put the drinks down on the bench and covered her mouth, shoulders shaking.

Yichen watched her.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not.”

“No, I’m not.”

He took the jersey off the hanger and examined the print.

“How did they manage this?”

“Maybe they thought you were special.”

“Special?”

“An upgraded Zhou.”

He gave her a look.

She laughed harder.

“Zhoou Yichen. Sounds very prestigious.”

“Does it?”

“Very. Like someone who owns several companies.”

He folded the jersey over his arm.

“Perhaps I should keep it.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“You’re not going to wear it?”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s wrong!”

“It’s still my number.”

“Yichen!”

He smiled.

She pointed at the extra O.

“That letter is not invited.”

He leaned closer, lowering his voice.

“Are you jealous?”

She looked at him.

“Of what?”

“There’s another O between us.”

For a moment, Xiaoran didn’t react.

Then she slowly looked at the jersey again.

“That’s terrible.”

“I thought so.”

“Don’t ever say that again.”

He laughed and kissed her cheek.

She picked up her phone.

“Give me that.”

“What?”

“The jersey.”

He handed it over.

She took a photograph, then another, making sure the misspelling was perfectly visible.

“What are you doing?”

“Documenting a historical event.”

“Naturally.”

“I’m sending this to Meilin.”

“Please don’t.”

She was already typing.

Xiaoran: URGENT. HIS NAME HAS BEEN REPLACED.

A second later, Meilin replied.

Meilin: HAHAHAHAHAHA.

Then:

Meilin: ZHOOU.

Then:

Meilin: Congratulations to the new member of the Zhou family.

Xiaoran showed him the screen.

Yichen looked at it.

“Your friends are very supportive.”

“She’s my friend.”

“That explains it.”

He put the jersey back in his locker.

Xiaoran was still smiling when she noticed him reaching for his training shirt.

“Wait.”

He turned.

“Yes?”

“Are you actually going to tell the kit manager?”

“I’ll tell him.”

“Good.”

He nodded. “I wouldn’t want the wrong person taking credit for my performance,” he said, with a completely straight face.

She stared at him, then laughed all over again.

The correction took three days.

Three days during which Xiaoran refused to call him anything other than Zhoou.

She did it over text. She did it when they met between lectures.

She did it once in front of Fang Ze, who still played for the university and came to watch Herons training whenever he could get in, and who immediately adopted the nickname with enthusiasm.

Yichen endured it with remarkable patience.

He endured it on the first evening, when her phone lit up on the café table between them while she was in the queue for napkins, and he looked down and saw that she had changed his name in her contacts.

Zhoou (Deluxe Edition): You forgot your straw.

He had sent that message himself, from across the café, to see what would happen. Now he knew.

“You renamed me,” he said, when she came back.

“I updated you. You’re the new model. More letters. Same great taste.” She took her phone and admired it.

“Change it back.”

“After the correction arrives.”

He endured it on the second morning, when Fang Ze sent him a photograph from the university changing room of a paper cup on which someone, in thick black marker, had written ZHOOU and drawn a small crown. The caption said only the people have spoken. Underneath it, eleven of his old teammates had reacted with the crown emoji.

He endured it, mostly, until lunch on the second day, when he opened his own contacts and made a change of his own.

That evening, from the other end of his sofa, she sent him a message asking whether he wanted noodles, because she was too comfortable to say it out loud. His phone lit up on the cushion between them, and she glanced down without meaning to, and stopped.

Linn Xiaoran: Noodles?

She looked at the screen. She looked at him.

“What is that.”

“An update.”

“I am spelled correctly.”

“So was I, until Thursday.”

“Yichen, that’s two Ns. Nobody has two Ns.”

“You’re the new model. More letters,” he said, without looking up from his laptop.

She stared at him, then picked up her own phone, opened his contact, typed, and held the screen up so he could see. Zhoou (Deluxe Edition, Do Not Return).

He laughed so that he had to put the laptop down.

On the third day, the kit manager, a small, gray, apologetic man everyone called Old Gu, found Yichen in the corridor and apologized for nearly a minute. It had been the printer, he said. A new printer. The printer had been spoken to. He was sorry, and he would like, if Zhou didn’t mind, to keep the wrong one for the wall of the kit room, where there was already a ZHANGG from 2019 and a jersey with the number printed upside down.

Yichen said he would think about it.

He didn’t tell Xiaoran about the wall until much later. If she had known it existed, she would have wanted to visit it.

On the fourth day, the corrected jersey arrived.

Xiaoran was there when he opened the package.

He held it up.

ZHOU

Perfectly spelled.

She nodded approvingly.

“Much better.”

“Thank you for your approval.”

“You’re welcome.”

He turned the jersey around, checking the number.

Then he looked at her.

“Disappointed?”

She blinked.

“About what?”

“No extra O.”

She rolled her eyes.

“Very funny.”

He folded the jersey and placed it inside his bag.

Xiaoran leaned against the locker beside him.

“Actually, I liked the first one.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“Because it was funny.”

“Only because it wasn’t your name.”

She considered that, then smiled.

“Maybe.”

Yichen closed his locker and kissed her.

“Thank you for bringing me my drinks.”

“You’re welcome, Zhoou.”

He sighed.

She grinned.

That Saturday was a home game. She sat in row F with Fang Ze, who had come straight from his own university training with his hair still wet, and when the announcer read out the starting five and said, “Number eleven, Zhou Yichen,” in the correct number of letters, Fang Ze leaned over and said “Zhoou” under his breath, and she elbowed him, and then said it herself.

Yichen played twenty-two minutes. He scored nine, which she knew because she counted, and made one bad pass, which she knew because the man behind her said so loudly, and which she then defended, to the man, at some length, until Fang Ze bought him a drink to make him stop. Afterward, in the corridor where partners were allowed on match days too, he came out with his bag over his shoulder and his hair damp and found her waiting.

“Nine,” she said.

“Eight. I missed a free throw.”

“Nine,” she said firmly, and held up her phone. She had changed his contact again.

Zhou Yichen (Original).

He looked at it for a while. Then he took out his own phone, and changed hers back to the correct number of Ns, and showed her, and she laughed and took his hand all the way to the car park, past the kit room and its wall.

And when he walked away toward the court, she followed him, still laughing to herself.

The misspelled jersey disappeared into the back of his wardrobe. He never wore it again, and he never threw it away, and when they moved in together a year later, it came with them in the box marked KEEP, folded so the extra O was on top.

chapters.desc: For one Sunday, the clingy one is Zhou Yichen.
chapters.title: Not Letting You Go Today
chapters.epigraph: “Today I don’t want to let you go.”
chapters.content:
There was something wrong with Zhou Yichen.

Xiaoran realized this at 9:23 on a Sunday morning, when she tried to get out of bed for the third time and he pulled her back without saying a word.

The first time, she had only wanted to get her phone from the bedside table. The second time, she had remembered that she hadn’t brushed her teeth.

The third time, she had announced that she was getting breakfast.

And every single time, Yichen had found a reason to keep her where she was.

Now she was lying on her back, staring at the ceiling, while he rested his cheek against her shoulder and held her around the waist.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I need to get up.”

“Why?”

She turned her head.

“Because it’s morning?”

“That isn’t a reason.”

She blinked.

“Since when?”

He didn’t answer. Instead, his arm tightened slightly around her waist, and he pressed a lazy kiss against her shoulder.

Xiaoran stared at him.

Usually, she was the one who did this.

She was the one who followed him from the bedroom to the kitchen, who leaned against him while he made coffee, who appeared beside his desk with absolutely no purpose except to occupy his attention. Yichen had always indulged her, sometimes teasing her about being unable to stay away for more than ten minutes.

But this?

This was different.

He had been following her around since she woke up.

And now he was actively preventing her from leaving the bed.

“Are you sleepy?” she asked.

“No.”

“Then why are you holding me?”

“Because I want to.”

She considered that answer.

“Okay...”

She tried to sit up.

His hand settled against her stomach.

“Where are you going?”

“Bathroom.”

“All right.”

He didn’t move.

She looked down at his arm.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You’re coming with me?”

He finally lifted his head.

A faint smile appeared.

“Would you like me to?”

“NO.”

He laughed, released her, and let her get out of bed.

Xiaoran walked toward the bathroom, glancing over her shoulder once.

He was still lying there.

Good.

She had won.

Except when she came out five minutes later, he was standing outside the bathroom door, waiting.

She stopped.

“...What?”

“Nothing.”

“Why are you standing here?”

“Waiting.”

“For what?”

He met her eyes.

“For you.”

She stared at him.

Then she narrowed her eyes.

“You’re being weird.”

His smile widened.

He reached out, gently tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear, and kissed her, briefly.

“Come on. Breakfast.”

By ten, Xiaoran had identified the problem.

Yichen wanted her attention.

Not in his usual quiet way, where he would occasionally pull her closer while reading or place a hand on her knee under the table.

No.

Today, he wanted her attention with an almost unreasonable level of determination.

When she sat on the kitchen counter while he prepared breakfast, he stood between her knees. When she reached for her phone, he asked what she was looking at. When she got down to help him, he moved the cutting board away from her and told her to sit.

When she finally finished eating and opened her laptop, he came over and stood behind her chair.

She looked up.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you standing there?”

He rested his hands on the back of her chair.

“Can’t I?”

“You can. But you’re blocking the light.”

He moved half a step.

She returned to her laptop.

A few seconds passed.

Then she felt his hand brush over her hair.

Another few seconds.

His fingers touched her shoulder.

Then he leaned down and kissed her temple.

Xiaoran slowly stopped typing.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“Are you bored?”

“No.”

“Are you lonely?”

He thought about it.

“A little.”

She turned around.

“But I’m right here.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

He looked at her, his expression calm.

“That’s why.”

She stared.

It took her a second to understand what he meant.

Then her cheeks warmed.

“...You want to be with me?”

“I am with you.”

“No, I mean—”

“I know what you mean.”

He smiled, and she immediately looked away.

That smile again: the one that made her forget what she had been trying to say.

She cleared her throat.

“Well, you can sit down.”

He pulled out the chair beside hers.

Then, instead of sitting normally, he dragged it closer until their knees touched.

Xiaoran looked at the gap between the chairs, then at him.

“You’re ridiculous.”

He opened his laptop.

“Get back to work.”

At eleven-thirty, Xiaoran received a message from Jiayi.

They had planned to meet at a café that afternoon to discuss a Media project. Xiaoran had already told her she would be there.

She glanced at the message and began typing.

Jiayi: Are we still meeting at two?

Xiaoran: Yes! I’ll be there.

Before she could send it, Yichen’s voice came from beside her.

“Where are you going?”

She looked up.

“To meet Jiayi.”

“When?”

“Two.”

He glanced at the time.

“Today?”

She laughed.

“Yes, today.”

He nodded.

Then he looked back at his laptop.

Xiaoran waited.

That was it?

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

“Nothing.”

“Yichen.”

He turned his head.

“What?”

“Do you have something planned?”

“No.”

“Then why are you asking?”

“I was checking.”

She studied his expression.

It was perfectly normal.

Too normal.

She sent the message.

Then she put her phone down.

Yichen’s hand found hers beneath the table.

He began rubbing his thumb over her knuckles.

Xiaoran looked at their joined hands.

“You’re doing it again. Being clingy.”

He turned to her.

“Does it bother you?”

She hesitated.

“No...”

His thumb continued moving gently over her hand.

“Then it’s fine.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

He was impossible.

At twelve-fifteen, she decided to test something.

She stood up.

“I’m going to get my bag.”

Yichen looked up immediately.

“Why?”

“Because I need to check something.”

He stood too.

“I’ll get it.”

“No. I can get it.”

He paused.

Then he sat back down.

Xiaoran walked toward the bedroom.

She reached the wardrobe, took out her bag, and checked its contents.

When she turned around, Yichen was standing in the doorway.

She froze.

She looked at him.

“...What?”

“Nothing.”

“Why are you here?”

He leaned against the doorframe.

“You were taking a while.”

“I was checking my bag.”

“I see.”

She eyed him.

“Did you follow me?”

“Yes.”

He said it so casually that she almost laughed.

“Why?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

Instead, he walked toward her, stopped close, and looked down at the bag in her hands.

“Do you have everything?”

“Yes.”

“Your charger?”

“Yes.”

“Notebook?”

“Yes.”

“Keys?”

She lifted them.

He nodded.

“Good.”

She blinked at him.

Then she put the bag down.

She opened her arms.

He raised an eyebrow but stepped closer.

She reached up and cupped his face.

“What’s going on with you today?”

He looked at her, his expression softening.

“Nothing’s going on.”

“Then why are you following me everywhere?”

He was quiet.

Then he lowered his head slightly, resting his forehead against hers.

“Because I like having you around.”

Her expression softened.

“You always have me around.”

“Not always.”

She blinked.

He continued, his voice low and unhurried.

“Sometimes you’re busy. Sometimes I’m busy. Sometimes we spend the whole day together and still barely get a chance to sit down.”

Xiaoran listened.

“And today?”

“Today I don’t want to let you go.”

She looked at him.

Then she laughed.

“You’re saying that as if I’m moving to another country.”

“I know you’re not.”

“Then?”

He gave her that small, almost helpless smile.

“I just want you here.”

Something warm spread through her chest.

She pulled him down by the collar and kissed his cheek.

“Okay.”

He held her gaze.

“Okay?”

“Yes. You can be clingy today.”

His eyes softened.

“Thank you.”

She laughed.

“But don’t follow me into the bathroom.”

He laughed.

“I’ll try.”

At one-thirty, Xiaoran was getting ready to leave.

Yichen sat down on the bed, watching her put on her earrings.

She glanced at him through the mirror.

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Can’t I?”

“You can. But you’re making me nervous.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Why?”

“Because you’re staring.”

“You’re pretty.”

Her fingers stopped.

She looked at him through the mirror.

Then she quickly returned to adjusting her earrings.

“That’s not relevant.”

“Isn’t it?”

“No.”

He stood and walked over.

She expected him to kiss her cheek.

Instead, he stood behind her and rested his chin lightly on her shoulder, his arms slipping around her waist.

Xiaoran looked at their reflection.

He was taller, his face relaxed, his eyes fixed on hers in the mirror.

She placed her hands over his.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I’m really going.”

“I know.”

“You’re not going to stop me?”

He was quiet.

Then he pressed a kiss against her cheek.

“No.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Good.”

She turned around and kissed him properly.

It was supposed to be a quick goodbye kiss.

But when she tried to pull away, he followed her, stealing another.

Then another, softer one near the corner of her mouth.

She laughed against his lips.

“You’re doing it again.”

“One more.”

“That’s what you said last time.”

“Then this is the last one.”

She let him kiss her.

When he finally released her, she picked up her bag.

“Bye.”

He walked her to the door.

She put on her shoes.

He handed her the keys she had forgotten on the counter.

“Thank you.”

Then he kissed her hair.

“Text me when you arrive.”

“I will.”

She opened the door.

And just before she stepped out, she turned back.

He was still standing there.

She smiled.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

She reached for him.

He walked over.

She held his face and kissed him once more.

“Don’t miss me too much.”

He looked at her with a faint smile.

“Too late.”

She laughed all the way down the corridor.

The café meeting lasted longer than expected.

Jiayi and Ning were discussing the project’s visual direction, and Xiaoran had become so involved in the conversation that she barely checked her phone.

When she finally looked down, she found four messages.

Yichen: Arrived?

Yichen: Lunch?

Yichen: What are you doing?

Yichen: Are you busy?

Her mouth tipped up.

Xiaoran: Yes, I arrived.

Xiaoran: I ate.

Xiaoran: We’re discussing the project.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: All right.

A few seconds later:

Yichen: Miss you.

Xiaoran stared at the message.

Then she covered her mouth.

Jiayi noticed.

Ning glanced over.

“Yichen?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“How did you know?”

Jiayi laughed.

“Your face.”

Xiaoran looked down again.

She typed.

Xiaoran: We only separated an hour ago.

Yichen: I know.

Xiaoran: You’re very clingy today.

Yichen: Yes.

She blinked.

He wasn’t even denying it.

Xiaoran: Are you okay?

Yichen: Perfectly fine.

Xiaoran: Then why?

Yichen: No particular reason.

A moment later, another message appeared.

Yichen: I want to see you.

She pressed her lips together.

This was unfair.

She had spent years being the one who said things like that.

Now he was doing it with such calm sincerity that she didn’t know how to respond.

Xiaoran: I’ll come back after we’re done.

Yichen: I’ll be here.

She smiled at the screen.

Jiayi leaned forward.

“You’re smiling again.”

Xiaoran put her phone away.

“Can we work?”

Ning laughed.

“Sure.”

When Xiaoran returned, it was nearly five.

She unlocked the apartment door and stepped inside.

“Yichen?”

“I’m here.”

His voice came from the living room.

She put down her bag and walked over.

He was sitting on the sofa with his laptop open.

The moment he saw her, he closed it.

Xiaoran stopped.

“...Were you waiting for me?”

“Yes.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What did you have?”

“Something.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“That’s not an answer.”

He held out his hand.

He held out his hand.

She walked toward him.

He caught her hand and gently pulled her down onto the sofa beside him.

Then he wrapped both arms around her and drew her against his chest.

Xiaoran laughed.

“Yichen!”

He buried his face against her shoulder.

She blinked.

He wasn’t even teasing.

He was holding her.

She slowly relaxed against him.

“Did you miss me?”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“How much?”

He lifted his head.

“Do you want an accurate answer?”

She nodded.

He considered it.

“Enough that I checked the time several times.”

She laughed.

“That’s not a measurement.”

“Then I don’t have one.”

She reached up and touched his cheek.

“You’re really clingy today.”

He caught her hand and kissed her palm.

“You’ve mentioned that.”

“Because it’s true.”

“Does it bother you?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

He studied her.

“Good.”

She leaned closer.

“Actually, I think it’s cute.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“Cute?”

“Yes.”

He gave her a look.

She grinned.

“Very cute.”

“Careful.”

“Why?”

“You might encourage me.”

She laughed.

“Maybe I want to.”

He looked at her.

Then he leaned forward and kissed her.

It was warm and unhurried, his hand resting against her cheek. When he pulled away, he stayed close enough that their noses almost touched.

“Then I’ll take advantage of that.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“You’re already taking advantage.”

“Of what?”

“My kindness.”

He laughed.

Later, they ordered dinner.

Xiaoran sat cross-legged on the sofa, leaning against Yichen while they waited for the delivery.

He had one arm around her and was absentmindedly playing with her fingers.

She looked down at their hands.

Then she looked at him.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Why today?”

He stopped moving his thumb.

“What do you mean?”

“You’re usually affectionate. You like being around me. But today you’re... Extra.” She searched for the right word.

His mouth curved.

“Extra?”

“Unbearably extra.”

He laughed.

She waited.

He looked toward the window.

“Maybe because I’ve been thinking about the next few months.”

“The Herons?”

“Partly. Training, university, everything.”

She nodded.

His schedule had become more demanding since he’d signed the full contract. There were more sessions, more expectations, and more decisions to make about his future.

“Have you been stressed?”

“Not particularly.”

“Then?”

He considered his answer.

“Sometimes I get so focused on what I need to do next that I forget to enjoy what’s already here.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

He said, “Today I had the time. So I wanted to spend it with you.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Then why didn’t you just say that?”

“I did.”

“You said you didn’t want to let me go.”

“That’s what I meant.”

She laughed and leaned into his shoulder.

“You’re so strange.”

“I know.”

She lifted her head.

“Are you secretly enjoying this?”

“Very much.”

She gasped.

“So you know how it feels!”

That got a smile out of him.

“Of course.”

“Then you understand how difficult it is when you keep walking away to do your own things.”

He turned toward her.

“Do you?”

“Sometimes.”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“Then I’ll make sure you don’t have to wonder whether I want you around.”

Her expression softened.

She leaned forward and kissed him.

The food arrived.

They ate on the sofa, sharing dishes and occasionally arguing over who had taken the last piece.

After dinner, Xiaoran tried to get up to wash the dishes.

Yichen caught her hand.

“I’ll do it.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re going to do everything today?”

“Would you like to?”

She thought about it.

“No.”

“Then sit.”

She laughed.

“You’re spoiling me.”

He stood, gathered the plates, and carried them to the kitchen.

Xiaoran followed him.

He glanced over his shoulder.

“Where are you going?”

“Nowhere.”

He smiled.

She leaned against the kitchen counter while he washed the dishes.

After a moment, she walked over and wrapped her arms around his waist from behind.

Yichen paused.

Then his smile appeared.

“What’s this?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re following me.”

“Yes.”

He laughed.

She rested her cheek against his back.

“How does it feel?”

“Good.”

She tightened her arms.

“Really?”

“Very.”

That made her grin.

“Then maybe I’ll be clingy today too.”

He turned off the tap, dried his hands, and turned around inside her embrace.

“Is that so?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He bent down and kissed her temple.

“Then I won’t complain.”

She turned to him.

“Even if I follow you everywhere?”

“Even then.”

“Even if I keep asking what you’re doing?”

“Yes.”

He laughed under his breath.

Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re unbelievable.”

He wrapped his arms around her.

“And you’re not?”

She considered it.

Then she nodded.

“Fair.”

By the time they went to bed, Yichen had returned to his usual level of composure.

Mostly.

Xiaoran was lying on her side, scrolling through her phone, when she felt his arm settle around her waist.

She smiled without looking up.

“Again?”

“Hm?”

“You’re holding me.”

“Is that a problem?”

She put her phone down and turned toward him.

“No.”

He drew her closer.

She tucked herself against his chest, resting one hand over his shirt.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Tomorrow, I might have to go out again.”

“I know.”

“And the day after that, I have a meeting.”

“All right.”

“And next week you’ll probably be busy with training.”

“Yes.”

She looked up.

“So you can’t keep me all to yourself.”

“I know.”

She touched his cheek.

“But you can ask me to stay when you miss me.”

His expression softened.

“I will.”

“And you can tell me when you want attention.”

He gave her an amused look.

“I think I’ve made that quite clear today.”

She laughed.

“Very clear.”

He kissed her hair.

Then, after a moment, he said, “Xiaoran?”

“Hm?”

“Stay a little longer.”

She smiled.

“Yichen, we’re going to sleep.”

“I know.”

“So I’ll be here tomorrow morning.”

He looked at her.

“Good.”

She settled against him again.

A few seconds passed.

Then she felt him press another kiss to her hair.

She smiled into his chest.

Usually, she was the one who wanted just five more minutes, one more hug, one more kiss before letting him go.

Yichen had always been affectionate in a way that made her feel wanted without ever making her feel held back.

But every so often, even someone as composed as him wanted to be selfish with the person he loved.

And today, he had decided that he was going to be.

She slipped her arms around him.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Tomorrow, I’ll be the clingy one again.”

He laughed.

“All right.”

“Don’t complain.”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t get used to being the one who gets chased.”

He lowered his head, his smile brushing against her forehead.

“Too late.”

She giggled.

Then he kissed her once more, and she finally closed her eyes.

chapters.desc: His birthday falls on an away game. She takes the train down with Ning, and the cake arrives as crumbs.
chapters.title: Birthday, Away
chapters.epigraph: “I wanted to be here today.”
chapters.content:
The cake arrived as crumbs.

Not metaphorically.

Not slightly damaged.

Crumbs.

Xiaoran stared at the open cake box on the back seat of the taxi. Ning stared too.

For several seconds, neither spoke.

Then Ning said, carefully, “I think we have a situation.”

Xiaoran slowly closed the box.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You were going to.”

Ning looked at the box again.

“It’s not a cake anymore.”

“It’s still a cake.”

“It’s a collection of cake-related materials.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

The original cake had been a small chocolate cake with a simple message written in white icing.

HAPPY BIRTHDAY, YICHEN.

Now the message was partially buried beneath a collapsed layer of cream, and one side of the cake had slid into the other.

They had ordered it from a bakery near the hotel where the Herons were staying for the away game, and collected it themselves, which had been the mistake, because the taxi driver took the roundabout at a speed the cake hadn’t agreed to.

The bakery had assured them it would arrive in perfect condition.

It hadn’t.

Ning looked at her.

“What do we do?”

Xiaoran took a breath.

“We fix it.”

“With what?”

She looked into the box, then at the small bag of candles, then at the plastic cake knife.

“...Optimism.”

Ning laughed.

Yichen’s birthday fell on the same weekend as an away fixture, his third with the first team.

It wasn’t ideal.

He had training the day before, the match on his birthday, and the team train home the next morning. His teammates had already planned a small celebration at the team hotel, but Xiaoran wanted to do something of her own. She and Ning had taken the train down after Ning’s last seminar, and booked a twin room in a cheaper hotel across the road from the team’s, where wives and girlfriends weren’t allowed past the lobby.

The plan was simple.

A small cake. A few candles.

A quiet celebration after the match.

She had even chosen a flavor he liked. Now she was sitting in a hotel room with a collapsed cake, a packet of spare napkins, and Ning trying to reshape the cream with a plastic spoon.

“Maybe we can turn it into a trifle,” Ning suggested.

Xiaoran looked at her.

“That’s not a birthday cake.”

“It’s dessert.”

“It’s supposed to say happy birthday.”

Ning looked at the broken icing.

“Technically, the words are still there.”

Xiaoran leaned closer.

The message now read:

HAPPY BIR... YICH...

She closed her eyes.

Ning began laughing.

“Stop laughing!”

“I’m sorry!”

“You’re not!”

“I’m trying!”

Xiaoran sighed.

Then she picked up the spoon.

“Give me that.”

It took forty minutes, a second trip to the bakery for a tube of icing, and most of Ning’s patience. Then they put the box on the desk, washed the cream off their hands, and took a taxi to the arena, driving round the roundabout so slowly that the driver asked if they were all right.

They sat in the away section, twelve rows up, among perhaps forty Herons fans who had made the trip and one loud drum. Nobody around them knew whose birthday it was. Xiaoran found this unbearable and lasted until halfway through the first quarter, when she told the woman beside her, who told her husband, who told the drum.

By the third quarter, the whole away section was singing happy birthday every time Yichen touched the ball. He heard it. She knew he heard it, because the second time, running back on defense, he looked straight up at row twelve with an expression of pure betrayal, and Ning laughed until she had to sit down.

He scored eleven. The drum played a special roll for each one. Ning filmed all of it, for evidence, and sent it to Meilin, who replied from four hundred kilometers away with nothing but a row of drums.

When Yichen returned from the match, he was tired but in a good mood.

His team had won.

He had played well, and his teammates had already wished him happy birthday several times throughout the day. He had forty minutes before curfew, and he crossed the road to her hotel expecting Xiaoran to be waiting with something small. Ning had tactfully gone to the lobby with her laptop.

He found her standing beside the desk, looking suspiciously proud of a covered cake box.

“Happy birthday.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Thank you.”

She walked over and kissed his cheek.

“How was the game?”

“Good.”

“Your ankle?”

“Fine.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

Something in his face eased.

“Yes, Xiaoran.”

She nodded.

“Good.”

He glanced at the box.

“What’s that?”

“Your birthday cake.”

He looked at her, then at the box.

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

He smiled.

“All right.”

She lifted the lid.

Yichen looked down.

There was a moment of silence.

The cake was no longer round. The cream had been pushed back into place, the chocolate decorations were scattered unevenly, and the icing message had been rewritten with a steady hand.

It now read:

HAPPY BIRTHDAY, YICHEN

The letters were slightly crooked.

One candle leaned to the left.

Another was buried in the cream.

Yichen looked at it, then at Xiaoran.

She folded her arms.

“Don’t.”

He looked back at the cake.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re thinking something.”

“I’m thinking it looks very good.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re lying.”

“A little.”

She gasped.

He laughed and pulled her closer.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

He kissed her cheek.

Then her cheek.

Then, because she was still looking a little disappointed, he kissed her properly.

When he pulled away, she was smiling again.

“Make a wish.”

He looked at the candle.

“All right.”

She lit it.

He closed his eyes, then blew it out.

Xiaoran clapped.

“Happy birthday.”

Yichen smiled.

“Thank you.”

They sat at the foot of the bed and ate the cake from the box.

It was delicious.

A little messy, but delicious.

Yichen took a bite and nodded.

“Good.”

Xiaoran watched him.

“Even though it looks like it survived a natural disaster?”

He smiled. “Because of that.”

She laughed.

He took another bite, then looked at her.

“You made this?”

“Not exactly. The bakery made it. Ning and I repaired it.”

“How long did that take?”

“Long enough.”

He glanced at the cake.

“I can tell.”

She hit his arm lightly.

“You’re supposed to be grateful.”

“I am.”

He put his fork down and turned toward her.

“Very grateful.”

His voice was quieter now.

Xiaoran looked at him.

He brushed a small spot of cream from the corner of her mouth.

“Thank you for coming all this way.”

That made her grin.

“Of course.”

“You could have celebrated with me when I got back.”

“I wanted to be here today.”

He met her eyes.

Then he leaned forward and kissed her hair.

“That’s enough for me.”

She leaned into his shoulder.

They ate the rest of the cake slowly, talking about the match, the journey back, and the ridiculous delivery.

At one point, Yichen looked down at the box.

“Did you take a picture before fixing it?”

Xiaoran went still.

Then she looked at him.

“...Yes.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Show me.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s embarrassing.”

“For whom?”

“For everyone.”

He held out his hand.

“Let me see.”

She hesitated, then handed him her phone.

He opened the photograph.

The cake was almost completely collapsed. The message was upside down, and one of the chocolate decorations had fallen onto the lid.

Yichen stared at it.

Then he laughed.

Not a polite laugh.

A proper one.

Xiaoran buried her face in her hands.

“I knew you would!”

He was still laughing when he handed the phone back.

“It’s wonderful.”

“It’s horrible.”

“It’s memorable.”

She met his eyes.

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“I’ll remember this birthday.”

She shook her head.

“Unfortunately.”

He kissed her temple.

“Fortunately.”

Later, with eleven minutes left before curfew and Xiaoran half asleep against his shoulder, Yichen took a photograph of the remaining cake.

The box was messy.

The icing was uneven.

There were crumbs on the table.

He sent it to the group chat.

Yichen: Thank you for the cake.

Meilin replied almost immediately.

Ning: You’re welcome. I did most of the repair work.

Xiaoran: LIES.

Ning: I was emotionally supportive.

Yichen: Very important contribution.

Ning: Thank you.

Xiaoran lifted her head.

“What are you doing?”

“Thanking everyone.”

She looked at the phone, then at him.

“Don’t encourage her.”

“She helped,” he said.

“She laughed at me.”

“Both can be true.”

Xiaoran gave him an offended look.

He kissed her, briefly.

“Happy birthday.”

She smiled.

“Happy birthday, Yichen.”

He put his phone away and drew her closer for the last eight minutes. Then he kissed her, and went back across the road, and was in his room at curfew to the second, with cream on his sleeve that Kou Ran, his roommate on away trips, pointed out at breakfast in front of the entire team.

chapters.desc: Seven days to their fifth anniversary, the lift still broken, and a pact of one surprise each that neither of them keeps very well.
chapters.title: The Week Before
chapters.epigraph: “I get one surprise. That’s fair.”
chapters.content:
There were seven days left until their fifth anniversary, and Lin Xiaoran wasn’t counting.

She happened to know it was seven days away because she had checked the calendar that morning, again at lunch, and once more on the fourth-floor landing outside her studio while getting her breath back. The lift was still broken. It had been broken for four years. She had come to think of the stairs as a kind of personal trainer who didn’t charge.

Five years since a boy with an umbrella had walked her home in the rain. She thought that deserved something special.

She had already decided on the general idea: a nice dinner, somewhere warm, with pretty lighting and food they both liked. Nothing extravagant. She didn’t want it to look as if she were trying to compete with the kind of places Yichen could afford without checking his balance. She wanted somewhere that felt like them.

And she had found it.

A small restaurant on a quiet lane off Wukang Road, eight tables, a wooden door with no sign, and a menu that changed every week depending on what the owner had found at the market. She had saved a photograph of its window three weeks ago, a picture of a table with two glasses and a candle in a jar, and then spent most of an evening reading every review on the internet.

There was one problem. The anniversary itself was on Sunday, the sixth of December, and the restaurant was closed on Sundays.

So it would be Saturday. The night before. She found she liked that even better: an anniversary eve, like a festival.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday evening she sat cross-legged on her bed with the reservation page open. Saturday at seven had two tables left. She took one, and in the box marked Special requests she typed, after some thought:

Anniversary dinner (five years) for my boyfriend, Zhou Yichen. Please don’t mention it if he calls you for anything. A small bouquet on the table, pale pink and white, nothing big.

She pressed confirm. Then she took a screenshot and sent it to Meilin, four hundred kilometers away, who was supposed to be writing her own thesis.

Xiaoran: I booked it.

Meilin: The secret restaurant?

Xiaoran: Yes!

Meilin: Does he know?

Xiaoran: No. It’s a surprise.

Meilin: Lin Xiaoran, you have never once surprised that man.

Xiaoran: This time is different.

Meilin: That’s what you said about his birthday.

She put her phone away, satisfied, and didn’t think about his birthday.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the road and up eleven floors, Yichen was looking at the same restaurant’s confirmation email.

Saturday. Seven o’clock. Two guests.

He had seen the photograph three weeks ago over her shoulder, a window with a candle in a jar, and had watched her save it, and say nothing about it, and look at it twice more that week when she thought he was reading. He had booked a table the same night. In the box marked Special requests he had typed:

Anniversary dinner (five years) for my girlfriend, Lin Xiaoran. Flowers on the table, small. A card, which I’ll bring.

He didn’t know she had done the same. Not yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday afternoon the restaurant called him.

“Mr. Zhou? This is Ms. Pei, from the restaurant on Saturday. I’m so sorry to bother you. We’re a very small place, and I read all the booking notes myself, and I have two tables at seven on Saturday that both say anniversary dinner, five years. One of them is for a Lin Xiaoran. The other one is from a Lin Xiaoran, and it’s for a Zhou Yichen.” The owner had a voice like someone trying not to laugh in church.

Yichen was in the university library. He put his pen down carefully.

“I see.”

“I didn’t want to seat you at two separate tables. It seemed sad,” Ms. Pei said.

He laughed then, into his hand, in the silent study area, and a girl at the next desk looked up and then away.

“Could you cancel mine, and put my requests on her table? The card is mine. The flowers too, if that doesn’t cause trouble,” he said.

“She’s also asked for flowers.”

“Then one bouquet. Whichever she asked for.”

“And I’m not to tell her?”

He thought about Xiaoran saving the photograph, and her face when she finally got to say surprise, and how rarely she ever got to say it to him.

“Please don’t,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Unfortunately, Ms. Pei was a honest woman, and on Thursday she sent Xiaoran a message asking whether Miss Lin would like her pale pink bouquet to include the white ranunculus Mr. Zhou mentioned, or keep it as it is.

Xiaoran read it in the library, sitting next to Luo Jiayi, who was supposed to be helping her with subtitles and was instead reading over her shoulder.

“Mr. Zhou mentioned?” Jiayi said.

Xiaoran read it again. Then she opened their chat.

Xiaoran: Yichen.

Yichen: Hm?

Xiaoran: Did you book a restaurant for Saturday?

The typing dots appeared, stopped, and appeared again.

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: Which one?

Yichen: The one you booked.

Xiaoran put her phone down on the desk and her forehead down beside it. Jiayi laughed until a librarian came over.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang her that evening. She was lying on her bed staring at the ceiling, and he sounded calm and unmistakably amused.

“So.”

“So. Meilin said I’d never surprised you once.” She turned on her side.

“You surprised me on Wednesday. The owner rang. I nearly fell off my chair.”

“You didn’t.”

“I put my pen down very carefully. I cancelled mine. You were first. It’s your dinner.”

“I wasn’t first. You saw me save the photograph.”

“I did.”

“That’s cheating.”

“It’s paying attention,” he said, and she couldn’t argue with that, so she complained instead about Ms. Pei’s honesty for a while, and he listened, and at the end he said, “Did you ask for a card?”

“No. Did you?”

“Yes.”

“What does it say?”

“It’s a surprise.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

“You get one surprise. I get one surprise. That’s fair,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday, Xiaoran changed her outfit twice. Jiayi, who had come over to supervise, rejected the first one before Xiaoran had finished putting it on, approved the second, and stood back with her arms folded like a tailor.

“Good. Now don’t fall down the stairs.”

Four flights later, Xiaoran came out of the building door slightly out of breath. Yichen was leaning against his car at the curb. He looked at her without saying anything, which she had learned was worse, or better, than anything he could say, and then he opened the passenger door.

“You look beautiful.”

“I took the stairs in these.”

“I know. I could hear you from here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant was warm and lit, and smelled of butter and something with ginger in it. Ms. Pei herself showed them to the table by the window, the one from the photograph, with a candle in a jar. There was one small bouquet, pale pink with a few white ranunculus, and beside it a little envelope.

Ms. Pei put the menus down and said, to nobody in particular, “Five years. Congratulations. I only had to cancel one table,” and went away.

Xiaoran picked up the envelope. Yichen watched her open it.

Five years. I’d still choose you, every time, even the rectangle.

She read it twice. The rectangle was the long way home, the second time he had walked her home, past the same peaches twice. She hadn’t known he remembered.

“You wrote this?”

“It’s very short.”

“Too short?”

She shook her head and put it in her bag, carefully, in the inside pocket.

Then she took out her own envelope and slid it across the table. Inside was a photograph from their first winter, the two of them outside the school gate in their winter uniforms, both looking at the camera with the expressions of people who hadn’t yet learned how to stand next to each other in a picture. On the back she had written:

Five years ago I didn’t know the boy beside me would become my favorite person. I suspected.

He looked at it.

“You kept this.”

“Meilin took it. I stole it from her phone.”

He turned it over and read the back again and didn’t say anything, and she let him not say anything, because she knew what it looked like when Zhou Yichen was moved and trying to hide it, and she had decided long ago to let him have that.

They ordered whatever Ms. Pei said was good, which was everything. They talked about their theses, and Meilin’s thesis, and the Herons, who still wanted an answer, and the small things that had happened that week, which were mostly about restaurants. At some point Xiaoran reached across the table and took his hand.

“Tomorrow, is the real one,” she said.

“I know.”

“What are we doing?”

“It’s a surprise.”

“You said one surprise each.”

“That was for Saturday. Sunday has its own rules,” he said.

She narrowed her eyes. He ran his thumb over her knuckles and didn’t explain, and she found, to her own surprise, that she didn’t want him to.

When they left, Ms. Pei was standing at the door with her coat on, and she said, “Next year, one booking,” in the voice of a woman who had been through something.

“Mine,” said Xiaoran.

“Mine,” said Yichen, at the same time.

Ms. Pei closed the door on both of them.

chapters.desc: Their fifth anniversary falls on a Sunday. He remembers what she blurted out behind the library at graduation, and brings a ring that is not a proposal.
chapters.title: Five Years, on a Sunday
chapters.epigraph: “I want to marry you one day.”
chapters.content:
Sunday mornings had always been Xiaoran’s favorite kind of morning.

There was no rush to get to campus, no lecture to catch, no presentation waiting to be delivered. No one needed her to make a decision before noon. She could wake up slowly, steal half of Yichen’s blanket, and pretend she hadn’t heard him asking whether she wanted breakfast.

Today, however, was the sixth of December, and she had a plan.

An important plan.

She had been thinking about their fifth anniversary for weeks, and she had decided that five years deserved something more memorable than their usual routine.

Not that she disliked their usual routine.

Their usual routine was excellent.

But five years was five years.

She was currently sitting cross-legged on Yichen’s bed, scrolling through the photos she had taken of them over the years, when he came out of the bathroom.

“You’re awake.”

She looked up. “I’ve been awake.”

“How long?”

“Long enough.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

“Why do you always need exact information?”

He walked over, wearing a loose T-shirt and sweatpants, his hair still slightly damp. He bent and kissed her hairline before looking at her phone.

“What are you looking at?”

“Nothing.”

He glanced at the screen.

It was a photo of them from their first year together. Xiaoran had been making a silly face at the camera while Yichen looked at her instead of the lens.

“Nothing?” he repeated.

“Private archival material.”

“Should I be concerned?”

“Very.”

He sat beside her, and she immediately leaned against his arm.

“Happy five years,” she said.

His expression softened.

“Happy five years.”

She smiled, then lifted her phone again.

“Look. We were so young.”

“That was four years ago.”

“Exactly. So young.”

“You say that as if we’re old now.”

“We’re practically historical.”

He laughed.

She swiped to another picture. Then another. There were photographs from high school, university orientation, their first campus date, Chengdu in the rain, New York in the snow, basketball games, birthdays, and countless ordinary moments that neither of them had thought important when they happened.

Yichen looked at them with her.

“You kept all of these?”

“Of course.”

“Why?”

“Because I like them.”

She stopped at one photograph.

It was taken during their graduation from high school. Xiaoran was holding a bouquet, smiling brightly at the camera. Yichen stood beside her in his graduation clothes, one arm around her shoulders.

She stared at it, then laughed.

“What?” he asked.

“Do you remember what I said that day?”

“Which part?”

She turned to him with an exaggeratedly innocent expression.

“I proposed to you.”

He met her eyes.

“By the fence behind the library. Then you said you meant someday. Maybe. In theory.”

“That was a very clear clarification.”

“It clarified nothing.”

“And then you told Yuhao!”

“He asked.”

She burst out laughing.

“And you said you’d probably say yes.”

“If you asked seriously later.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He smiled, looking entirely too pleased with himself.

She pushed his shoulder.

“Three and a half years, and I still haven’t had a real answer.”

“Have I not?”

“No.”

He looked at her for another second, then reached for her hand.

“Happy anniversary, Xiaoran.”

“You’re changing the subject.”

He kissed the back of her hand.

“Then I’ll answer you later.”

She blinked.

“Later?”

“Mm.”

She studied his face, but he had already stood up.

“Come on. Let’s get breakfast.”

She watched him walk toward the bedroom door.

Something about his expression made her suspicious.

But she decided not to investigate.

Not yet.

They spent the morning doing little.

Yichen made breakfast while Xiaoran sat on the kitchen counter, supposedly helping by keeping him company. She stole pieces of fruit from the chopping board, complained that he was taking too long, and asked whether he had considered opening a restaurant.

“I have a contract with the Herons,” he reminded her.

“You can have two careers.”

“That’s ambitious.”

“You’re good at basketball and cooking. It’s a waste not to explore your options.”

He set a plate in front of her.

“Eat.”

She looked down.

“That was quick.”

“Because I didn’t listen to your business proposal.”

She laughed and picked up her fork.

After breakfast, they went out.

Yichen had suggested taking her somewhere, but he refused to tell her where. Xiaoran had tried asking him three different ways, and all three attempts had failed.

“Is it a restaurant?”

“No.”

“A shopping mall?”

“No.”

“A basketball court?”

He turned to her.

“Why would I take you to a basketball court for our anniversary?”

“Because you’re a basketball player now. Maybe you’ve forgotten how normal people celebrate.”

“Is that what you think?”

“Yes.”

He smiled.

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re doing that thing again.”

“What thing?”

“Smiling without telling me anything.”

“Would you prefer I looked unhappy?”

“No. I prefer you to be transparent.”

“Noted.”

He took her hand as they walked.

The afternoon was cold but bright, the kind of winter day that made the city look clear. They wandered through a quieter part of Shanghai, stopping at a small bookstore and then a café where Xiaoran insisted they share a pastry.

Yichen let her choose.

He always let her choose when she was excited about something.

At one point, she stopped in front of a display of little decorative objects.

“Look.”

He followed her gaze.

There were small ceramic houses, miniature trees, and tiny figures arranged in a winter village.

“That’s cute,” she said.

“Do you want one?”

She considered it.

“No. We don’t need it.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes. I just like looking.”

He didn’t insist.

They continued walking.

A few minutes later, she slipped her hand into his coat pocket because hers were cold.

Yichen looked down.

“Cold?”

“Very.”

“You should have brought gloves.”

“I brought you.”

He turned his head.

She smiled proudly, as if she had delivered a clever answer.

“That’s convenient,” he said.

“Very. You’re warm.”

He squeezed her hand inside his pocket.

They returned to his apartment before dinner.

Xiaoran had spent the entire journey home trying to guess whether he had arranged something else. She suspected he had bought her a gift, but she couldn’t tell from his behavior.

He was acting normal.

Almost too normal.

He put their coats away, brought her a glass of water, and asked whether she wanted to rest before dinner.

She sat on the sofa, watching him move around the apartment.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Are you hiding something?”

He turned.

“What makes you think that?”

“You’re being suspiciously calm.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Would you like me to panic?”

“No, but—”

He walked over and sat beside her.

He opened his arms.

She moved closer, and he took her hand.

He didn’t say anything.

Then he looked at her.

“Do you remember what you said at graduation?”

She blinked.

“The proposal?”

“Mm.”

“Of course. You were very difficult.”

Something in his face eased.

“You said someday, maybe, in theory.”

“I said it more romantically than that.”

“You said it into your hands.”

“Well, my memory is more reliable.”

He gave a quiet laugh.

She looked at him more carefully.

“Why are you asking?”

Yichen released her hand and reached into the pocket of his trousers.

When he placed the small box in her palm, she stopped speaking.

It was a simple, dark-colored box.

She looked down at it, then at him.

“What’s this?”

“Open it.”

Her fingers moved slowly over the lid.

Inside was a ring.

A delicate band, understated and elegant, with a small stone set into it. It wasn’t extravagant. It wasn’t designed to attract attention from across a room.

It looked like something she could wear every day.

Something that belonged on her hand.

Xiaoran stared at it.

For several seconds, she didn’t move.

Yichen watched her.

He said, “I thought about getting something more elaborate. But I didn’t think you’d want something you had to be careful with every time you washed your hands or cooked.”

She looked up.

“You chose it?”

“Yes.”

“By yourself?”

“Yes.”

She looked back at the ring.

“It’s beautiful.”

“I’m glad.”

Her thumb brushed the edge of the box.

“Is this…?”

“A promise ring.”

She raised her eyes again.

He took a breath, though his voice remained steady.

“It’s not a proposal.”

She nodded slowly.

“I know.”

“I don’t want to ask you to marry me before we’re ready. I want us to finish our degrees, find our footing, and have jobs that we’ve chosen for ourselves. I don’t want you to feel that you have to make a decision about your future just because I have. But I remember what you said that day.”

Her eyes had begun to shine.

“You were joking, but I wasn’t sure I wanted to treat it as a joke,” he said.

She met his eyes.

“Yichen…”

“I want to marry you one day.”

The words were simple.

He didn’t dress them up. He didn’t make them sound like a grand declaration. He said them with the same calm certainty with which he told her he would pick her up after class.

And somehow, that made them even more overwhelming.

He said, “But I want to ask you properly. When we’ve both started working. When we’re ready to make that decision as adults who have built their own lives.”

He looked at the ring in her hand.

“Until then, I want this to be a promise. Not a deadline. Not an obligation. Just something that reminds us where we’re going.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

She was trying hard not to cry.

Yichen noticed.

His expression softened.

“Hey.”

She shook her head.

“I’m fine.”

“I know.”

“I’m just—”

She laughed, but her voice trembled.

“You can’t say things like that so casually.”

He reached up and brushed his thumb beneath her eye.

“I wasn’t being casual.”

She turned to him.

“I know.”

A tear slipped down her cheek anyway.

He wiped it away.

She looked down at the ring again.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Anything.”

“Why now?”

He considered the question.

“Because today is five years.”

She gave him a watery smile.

“That’s very obvious.”

“And because I wanted you to know that I remember.”

Her smile faltered slightly.

“Remember what?”

“That day. What you said. The way you looked at me when I didn’t give you a proper answer.”

She laughed.

“I was very offended.”

“I remember.”

“You said probably.”

“I was eighteen and Yuhao was screaming.”

“You were already annoying.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Probably.”

She looked at the ring again.

“And now?”

“Now I know.”

He reached for her hand.

“May I?”

She nodded.

He lifted the ring from its box and slipped it onto her finger.

It fit.

Xiaoran stared at her hand.

Then she turned it slightly, watching the small stone catch the light.

Yichen waited.

She finally looked up.

“So…”

“Mm?”

“Does this mean you’re accepting my proposal?”

He looked at her, then that slow, familiar smile appeared.

“The one you made behind the library?”

“Yes.”

“I thought I was supposed to ask properly.”

“You can still ask properly later.”

“Then I suppose I should be careful not to waste my opportunity.”

She laughed.

He leaned forward and pressed a kiss into her hair.

“Happy five years.”

She wrapped her arms around him.

He held her close, one hand resting against the back of her head.

For a while, she didn’t say anything.

Then, against his shoulder, she whispered, “I want to marry you too.”

His hand paused.

She pulled back.

“One day. When we’re ready.”

He held her gaze.

“All right.”

“And I want a proper proposal.”

“I know.”

“With flowers.”

“Of course.”

“And I want to wear a pretty dress.”

“Naturally.”

“And you have to look handsome.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“That’s a requirement?”

“A very important one.”

He laughed and kissed her.

“Then I’ll do my best.”

She leaned her forehead against his.

“You’re going to have to do better than your best.”

“How demanding.”

“You’re marrying me.”

“Not yet.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed, catching her before she could pull away.

“One day. I’m promising you one day,” he said, pressing a kiss to her cheek.

Dinner was later than planned.

Not because either of them had forgotten to eat, but because Xiaoran kept looking at her hand.

She looked at it while Yichen ordered food. She looked at it while they waited.

She looked at it again when he handed her a glass of water.

Eventually, he noticed.

“Do you like it?”

She looked up.

“What?”

“The ring.”

She held her hand up.

“Obviously.”

“You’ve been looking at it for twenty minutes.”

“It’s new.”

“I understand.”

“And it’s from you.”

“I understand that too.”

She smiled and reached across the table.

“Do you know what I was thinking?”

“What?”

“That behind the library, I really thought you’d laugh at me.”

He studied her.

“I wanted to say yes properly.”

“Then why didn’t you?”

He took a moment before answering.

“Because I knew you were joking, and I didn’t want to turn something playful into a promise neither of us understood yet.”

She looked at him.

He said, “I wanted to be able to give you an answer that I could stand behind.”

Her expression softened.

“That’s very you.”

“Is that good?”

“Very good.”

He reached for her hand.

“Besides, Yuhao was screaming.”

She laughed.

“He was so loud.”

“The birds left.”

He considered her.

Then he smiled.

“I think I got the better deal anyway.”

She immediately looked pleased.

“Correct.”

He rubbed his thumb over her ring.

“Though I should warn you.”

“What?”

“You’ll have to keep me for a long time.”

She stared at him.

Then her expression turned mischievous.

“Is that a threat?”

“A promise.”

She smiled, and he lifted her hand to kiss her knuckles.

That night, Xiaoran took a photograph of the ring.

She didn’t post a picture of the box or write a long caption. She took a photo of her hand resting on Yichen’s, their fingers intertwined, and added the date.

6 December 2026.

Then she showed him.

“Do you think it’s okay?”

He looked at the picture.

“Yes.”

“Should I post it?”

“If you want to.”

She thought about it, then uploaded it.

Her caption was short.

Five years. And he still hasn’t officially accepted my proposal.

Yichen read it over her shoulder.

He laughed.

“That’s what you’re going with?”

“Yes.”

“You’re making me look difficult.”

“You are difficult.”

He took out his phone.

A moment later, he posted a picture too.

It was the same photograph, but he added his own caption.

Five years with my favorite person. I haven’t forgotten what she asked me at graduation. I’ll ask her properly when the time comes.

Xiaoran read it.

Then she read it again.

Her smile grew.

“That’s so sweet.”

He put his phone down.

“Good.”

She leaned into him, resting her cheek against his chest.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“Do you think we’ll be different in another five years?”

He looked down at her.

“Probably.”

“How?”

“We’ll have jobs. Different schedules. More responsibilities.”

“Maybe a home.”

“Maybe.”

“Maybe a kitchen where you cook and I supervise.”

“That part seems likely.”

She laughed.

“And maybe we’ll have a proper dining table.”

“You’re very invested in furniture.”

“Because your sofa is not a dining table.”

“You seem to enjoy eating on it.”

“That’s beside the point.”

He smiled and drew her closer.

She looked down at her ring once more.

“Do you think we’ll remember today?”

“Yes.”

She considered that.

Then she lifted her head.

“Promise?”

Yichen looked at her.

He had promised her many things over five years. Some were small: to pick her up, to call when he arrived, to bring her favorite dessert. Others had been more difficult: to keep choosing each other through university, distance, uncertainty, and all the changes that came with growing up.

This one pointed toward something they hadn’t reached yet.

He took her hand and kissed the ring.

“Promise.”

Xiaoran smiled.

Then she curled closer against him, her fingers resting between his.

Outside, the Sunday evening settled over the city. Xiaoran kept turning the ring with her thumb, and he let her.

chapters.desc: Mrs. Zhou has been making her mother’s braised beef wrong for twenty years. She would like Xiaoran’s help, as long as her son never finds out.
chapters.title: His Mother’s Kitchen, Without Him
chapters.epigraph: “I know you love her. I can see it.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Zhou Yichen’s mother told Xiaoran was that she wasn’t allowed to tell her son.

The second thing she told her was that the recipe was wrong.

“For twenty years. I’ve been making it wrong for twenty years,” she said, standing in front of the kitchen counter with a wooden spoon in her hand.

Xiaoran looked down at the handwritten recipe between them.

Then she looked at Auntie Zhou.

“Twenty years?”

“At least.”

“How did you find out?”

His mother sighed, almost dramatically.

“Your boyfriend.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Yichen?”

“Of course, Yichen. Who else would it be?”

It was a Saturday afternoon in the Zhou family home. Yichen had left earlier for Herons training, with a promise to be back before dinner. His mother had invited Xiaoran to spend the afternoon with her, saying she needed an extra pair of hands in the kitchen.

Xiaoran had assumed they were preparing a normal family meal.

She hadn’t expected a culinary investigation.

His mother pushed the recipe toward her.

“Read this.”

Xiaoran leaned closer.

The paper was old, its edges slightly yellowed. The handwriting was neat but faded in places, with several corrections written in the margins.

“Braised beef with preserved mustard greens?” Xiaoran read.

“His grandmother’s recipe.”

“That sounds delicious.”

“It is delicious. Or it used to be.”

Xiaoran looked up.

His mother lowered her voice.

“Yichen said it tastes different from what his grandmother used to make.”

“Has he?”

“Last month. He was eating dinner here and said something like, ‘This isn’t quite the same.’”

Xiaoran tried not to smile.

“That’s very specific of him.”

“He has always been particular about food.”

That sounded familiar.

His mother pointed at the recipe.

“I asked him what was different. He said he couldn’t explain it. Then he mentioned that when he was little, his grandmother used to make it differently.”

Xiaoran studied the page.

“Have you asked Grandma?”

“She’s away with Yichen’s uncle’s family this month. And I thought I’d try to figure it out before she comes back.”

She handed Xiaoran a small bowl.

“Here. Taste this.”

Xiaoran dipped the spoon into the sauce.

It was rich, savoury, slightly sweet.

She tasted it carefully.

“It’s good.”

His mother looked disappointed.

“That’s not helpful.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t apologize. I know it’s good. I’ve been making it for twenty years.”

“Maybe that’s the problem.”

His mother stared at her.

Xiaoran froze, then slowly smiled.

“Auntie, I was joking.”

His mother laughed, shaking her head.

“You’re just like him. Always saying something when I don’t expect it.”

She turned back to the stove.

“Come. Let’s start again.”

They spent the next forty minutes preparing the ingredients.

Xiaoran washed the preserved mustard greens while his mother cut the beef. They worked comfortably together, exchanging small bits of conversation between instructions.

His mother was easy to be around. She didn’t make Xiaoran feel like a guest who needed to be entertained. She gave her things to do, asked whether she wanted more tea, and occasionally reminded her to keep her hair away from the stove.

At one point, Xiaoran reached for the sugar.

His mother stopped her.

“Not so much.”

Xiaoran looked at the recipe.

“It says two spoons.”

“Yes, but I usually put in one and a half.”

“Why?”

His mother paused.

“Because Yichen doesn’t like it too sweet.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“Doesn’t he?”

“No. When he was young, he used to pick out anything too sweet. His grandmother would always tell him he was fussy.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“He’s still a little fussy.”

His mother laughed.

“Don’t tell him I said that.”

“I won’t.”

They added the seasonings.

Xiaoran glanced at the handwritten recipe again.

There was something odd about the ingredient list.

She leaned closer.

“Auntie?”

“Hm?”

“What’s this?”

His mother came over.

Xiaoran pointed to a line near the bottom.

“Is that vinegar?”

His mother squinted.

“That’s what I thought.”
