“How much do you usually add?”

“One spoon.”

Xiaoran tilted the paper toward the light.

“But the handwriting looks like it says two.”

“Two?”

“Maybe.”

His mother leaned over her shoulder.

They stared at the faded characters together.

Then Xiaoran noticed something else.

There was a small note beside the ingredient.

Last. A little.

“Add at the end. Only a little,” Xiaoran read.

His mother went quiet.

Then she turned toward the stove.

“Oh.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“What?”

“I’ve been adding it at the beginning.”

She stared at the pot.

“For twenty years.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

His mother looked at her.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’m trying not to.”

His mother sighed, then began laughing herself.

“Twenty years. His grandmother will never let me hear the end of this.”

Xiaoran finally laughed too.

“Maybe that’s why it tastes different.”

“Perhaps.”

His mother took the spoon and stirred the pot.

Then she tasted the sauce again.

Her expression changed slightly.

She looked at the recipe, then at Xiaoran.

“Well.”

“Well?”

“That might be it.”

The kitchen became quieter after that.

The dish was simmering, and Xiaoran was wiping the counter when his mother spoke again.

“Xiaoran.”

“Yes, Auntie?”

“Can I ask you something?”

Xiaoran turned.

“Of course.”

His mother dried her hands on a towel.

“Have you and Yichen talked about what happens after graduation?”

The question was gentle.

But it landed differently from the ordinary things they’d been discussing.

Xiaoran looked at her.

“A little.”

“A little?”

“We’ve talked about jobs. Where we’d like to work. Things like that.”

His mother nodded.

“He’s staying in Shanghai, with the Herons.”

“I know.”

“And you?”

Xiaoran hesitated.

“I’ve been looking too. There are a few studios I’m interested in, and some graduate programs I’ve been considering.”

“Here?”

“Some here. Some elsewhere.”

His mother nodded again.

She didn’t immediately ask which places.

Instead, she pulled out a chair and sat down.

Xiaoran slowly joined her.

“I don’t want to make you uncomfortable. But I was wondering whether you two have discussed what happens if your plans don’t line up perfectly,” his mother said.

Xiaoran looked at her hands.

She understood what the question was really about.

Not whether she loved Yichen.

Not whether they were serious.

They had been together for years. His parents knew that. They had watched the relationship grow from the time they were teenagers into something much more settled.

The question was about the future.

The part neither of them could fully predict.

“We have. Not in every detail, but we’ve talked about it,” Xiaoran said eventually.

“And?”

That made her grin.

“We’re still figuring it out.”

His mother looked at her.

“Does that worry you?”

Xiaoran thought about it.

“A little.”

She hadn’t expected to say that so easily.

Perhaps because it was just the two of them in the kitchen. There was no Yichen beside her, no need to make the answer sound reassuring.

“Sometimes I think about what happens if I get an opportunity somewhere else. Or if he gets one. I don’t want either of us to feel like we have to give something up before we’ve even had a chance to try.”

His mother listened without interrupting.

Xiaoran continued, quieter now.

“I love him. But I also want to build my own life. I think he wants the same thing.”

“He does.”

His mother’s answer came immediately.

Xiaoran looked up.

“I know. He has never asked me to choose between him and my work,” she said.

His mother smiled.

“That sounds like my son. Although he can be quite stubborn.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Very.”

“And he sometimes thinks he can solve everything by being quiet and sensible.”

“Yes.”

“Does he do that with you?”

Xiaoran considered it.

“Sometimes. But I tell him when he’s being annoying.”

His mother laughed.

“Good.”

She reached across the table and lightly touched Xiaoran’s hand.

“I want you to know something. Whatever happens after graduation, I hope you won’t feel that you need to make yourself smaller to fit into his life.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Yichen has always known what he wants. Even when he was little, he could be very determined. But that doesn’t mean the people he loves should have to arrange their lives around him.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“And I don’t want you to think that because you’ve been with him for so long, everyone expects you to have everything decided already.”

Xiaoran lowered her eyes.

She didn’t know what to say.

Then she admitted, “I think I’m more afraid of disappointing myself than disappointing anyone else.”

His mother looked at her with a kind of understanding that made Xiaoran’s throat feel slightly tight.

“Then don’t disappoint yourself.”

She squeezed her hand.

“There’s plenty of time to work things out.”

They returned to the recipe after a few minutes.

The sauce had thickened, and the beef was beginning to soften.

His mother tasted it again.

Then she handed Xiaoran the spoon.

“Try.”

Xiaoran did.

She paused.

It was still rich, but the flavor was more balanced. The vinegar had brightened the sauce instead of blending into it, and the sweetness no longer lingered quite so heavily.

She looked up.

“Oh.”

His mother smiled.

“Different?”

“Very different.”

“Better?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Much better.”

His mother looked genuinely pleased.

“Then we’ll keep it this way.”

She picked up a pen and crossed out the old instruction.

Beside it, she wrote the correction.

Xiaoran watched her.

“Shouldn’t we tell Yichen?”

His mother considered it.

“Not yet.”

“Why?”

“Let him taste it first.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“You want to surprise him.”

“Of course.”

She wrote something else in the margin.

Corrected after twenty years.

Underneath, in smaller handwriting, she wrote:

With Xiaoran.

Xiaoran noticed.

“Auntie.”

His mother glanced at her.

“What?”

“You don’t have to write my name.”

“I know.”

She put the pen down.

“But I want to.”

Yichen returned just before dinner.

Xiaoran heard his voice from the hallway.

“Mom?”

“In the kitchen!”

He appeared a moment later, wearing a dark university sweatshirt, his hair slightly untidy from the wind.

His eyes found Xiaoran first.

“You’ve been here all afternoon?”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

He walked over and kissed her temple.

“Did you eat?”

“Not yet.”

“Why?”

“Because your mother was making something.”

He looked toward the stove.

“What?”

His mother turned around with a smile that was just a little too pleased.

“Something you’ve been complaining about.”

Yichen looked at the pot, then at the handwritten recipe beside it.

He stepped closer.

“What’s this?”

“Your grandmother’s recipe.”

He glanced at the page, then at the correction.

His expression changed.

“You changed it?”

“I corrected it.”

He looked at the note, then at his mother.

“You added the vinegar at the end?”

His mother lifted her chin.

“Yes.”

Yichen was quiet.

Then he tasted the sauce.

He didn’t say anything immediately.

Xiaoran watched him.

His mother watched him too.

He took another spoonful.

Then he nodded.

“This is closer.”

His mother looked triumphant.

“Closer?”

“Much closer.”

She crossed her arms.

“Well, thank you.”

Yichen looked at the recipe again.

“Grandma always added it at the end.”

“Apparently, I forgot.”

“Apparently.”

His mother gave him a look.

“Don’t sound so pleased.”

He smiled.

Xiaoran was trying not to laugh.

Yichen glanced at her.

“You helped?”

“Your mother was very patient with me.”

“She usually is.”

His mother made a noise of protest.

“Excuse me?”

Yichen smiled and moved aside as his mother handed him a bowl.

“Go wash your hands. Dinner is almost ready.”

He obeyed.

As he passed Xiaoran, he brushed his fingers against hers.

A small, familiar touch.

She smiled at him.

He looked at the recipe one more time before leaving the kitchen.

Dinner was warm and took a long time.

His father joined them, and the conversation moved from university to work, from a recent basketball match to an upcoming family gathering.

Yichen ate the braised beef without much comment.

His mother watched him from across the table.

Finally, she asked, “Well?”

He looked up.

“What?”

“Does it taste right?”

He chewed, swallowed, and nodded.

“Yes.”

His mother smiled.

“Good.”

Yichen looked at the dish again.

“Why did you suddenly change it?”

His mother lifted her teacup.

“Because I wanted to.”

He glanced at Xiaoran.

She was looking down at her rice, smiling to herself.

His eyes narrowed slightly.

“What did you two do this afternoon?”

“Nothing,” Xiaoran said.

His mother laughed.

“Your girlfriend helped me fix your grandmother’s recipe.”

Yichen looked at Xiaoran.

She finally raised her eyes.

“You’re welcome.”

“Thank you.”

Then his mother added, casually, “We also talked about graduation.”

Xiaoran nearly dropped her chopsticks.

Yichen turned toward his mother.

“Oh?”

His mother looked perfectly innocent.

“What? We were talking.”

He glanced at Xiaoran.

She gave him a small, helpless smile.

He understood immediately.

Not the details.

But enough.

He didn’t ask in front of his parents.

Instead, he reached beneath the table and found her hand.

Later, after dinner, Yichen walked Xiaoran to the front door.

His mother had gone upstairs, and his father was watching television in the living room.

Yichen helped Xiaoran put on her coat.

Then he looked at her.

“What did you and Mom talk about?”

She adjusted her scarf.

“Cooking.”

He waited.

“And?”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Your grandmother’s recipe.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Fine.”

She met his eyes.

“Graduation.”

His expression softened.

“What about it?”

“She asked whether we’d talked about our plans.”

He nodded.

“What did you tell her?”

“That we had. That we’re still figuring things out.”

“Good.”

She studied his face.

“You’re not upset?”

“Why would I be?”

“Because we haven’t decided everything.”

Yichen looked at her.

Then he reached up and tucked the end of her scarf neatly beneath her coat.

“We’re allowed not to have everything decided.”

She looked down.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

She nodded.

He smiled a little.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“I’ve been thinking about it too.”

She looked up again.

“About graduation?”

“About what comes after. I want to stay in Shanghai if the right opportunity comes. I know you have your own plans. I don’t want to assume you’ll choose the same place just because I do.”

She was quiet.

“I don’t want you to choose something smaller because it makes things easier for me. And I don’t want to choose something just because I’m afraid of being far away from you,” he said.

Xiaoran’s eyes softened.

“So what do we do?”

“We keep talking.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“That’s your solution?”

“For now.”

“Very practical.”

“I’m a Business student.”

She laughed.

He drew her closer, resting his hands lightly at her waist.

“I want a future with you. That part isn’t uncertain,” he said.

Her smile faded into something softer.

“But I don’t think we need to decide the entire shape of it before we’ve even graduated.”

She turned to him, then nodded.

“Okay.”

He kissed her temple.

“And when you get an opportunity, I want to hear about it before you start worrying about whether it fits into my plans.”

She smiled against his chest.

“You’re making it difficult to be dramatic.”

“Would you like me to disagree with you?”

“No.”

“Good.”

She wrapped her arms around him.

For a while, they stayed that way.

Then she lifted her head.

“Your mother wrote my name on the recipe.”

Yichen looked down.

“She did?”

“Yes. In the margin.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Then it’s official.”

“What is?”

“You’re part of the recipe now.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“That’s a terrible line.”

“I thought it was good.”

“It’s terrible.”

He kissed her cheek.

“All right.”

She leaned up and kissed him properly before stepping back.

“Good night.”

“Message me when you get home.”

“I will.”

He watched her walk toward the taxi he had called. Just before she opened the door, she turned around.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Your mother said the recipe was wrong for twenty years.”

He smiled.

“I know.”

“How did you know?”

“Grandma told me when I was younger.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“What?”

He looked entirely unbothered.

“She said Mom had been making it wrong for years.”

“Then why didn’t you tell her?”

He considered the question.

“Because she liked making it for us.”

Xiaoran blinked.

He said, “And it was still good.”

She looked at him.

Then she laughed. “You’re both terrible.”

Yichen smiled.

“Good night, Xiaoran.”

She got into the car, still smiling.

When Yichen returned to the kitchen, his mother was putting the leftover food away.

He picked up the handwritten recipe.

The correction was written neatly beside the old instruction.

Corrected after twenty years.

And underneath it:

With Xiaoran.

He looked at it.

“Mom.”

His mother turned.

“What?”

“You wrote her name.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She looked at him as if the answer were obvious.

“Because she helped me.”

He nodded.

Then he placed the recipe back on the counter.

His mother watched him.

“She’s a good girl.”

Yichen looked up.

“I know.”

“She has her own plans, you know.”

“Mm.”

His mother smiled.

“Good.”

She wiped her hands.

“Don’t make the mistake of thinking that loving someone means they should automatically fit into your plans.”

Yichen was quiet.

Then he smiled.

“I won’t.”

His mother reached over and lightly touched his arm.

“I know you love her. I can see it.”

He looked down at the recipe again.

His mother continued, “But when you graduate, there will be a lot of decisions. Let her make hers. And make sure you make yours honestly.”

He nodded.

“I will.”

She studied him.

Then, with a smile, asked, “And when are you going to bring her here again to help me cook?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Why?”

“Because she has better handwriting than you, and now I have someone who can correct my recipes.”

He laughed.

“That’s your reason?”

“Of course.”

He folded the corner of the recipe carefully, making sure not to cover Xiaoran’s name, and put it back in the drawer where it lived, between the rice cooker’s manual and a takeaway menu from 2009.

chapters.desc: A small studio in Shanghai and the Beijing company from her internship both want her. He tells her not to choose a smaller future to make their schedule easier.
chapters.title: Job Fair
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want my worry to become your limitation.”
chapters.content:
The spring job fair was in the second week of March, and Xiaoran had prepared for it as if she were going to war.

There were three copies of her résumé in a folder, a digital portfolio saved on her laptop and phone, a notebook containing questions she had researched the night before, and a carefully selected outfit that had taken her nearly forty minutes to decide on.

She had even practiced introducing herself in front of the mirror.

Twice.

The third attempt had been interrupted by Yichen walking into the bedroom and asking whether she was auditioning for a television program.

She had thrown a cushion at him.

Now, standing in front of the university’s employment fair, she was beginning to regret not bringing a fourth copy of her résumé.

“Relax,” Yichen said.

She turned to him.

“Don’t tell me to relax.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You just did.”

“I said relax.”

“Exactly.”

He looked at the folder in her hands.

“You’ve checked everything?”

“Yes.”

“Portfolio?”

“Yes.”

“Résumé?”

“Yes.”

“Phone charged?”

She paused.

He raised an eyebrow.

Xiaoran immediately took out her phone.

“Eighty-two percent.”

“Good.”

She put it away and looked at him suspiciously.

“Why are you so calm?”

“Because I’m not the one looking for a job.”

She blinked at him.

“That’s not supportive.”

He smiled and adjusted the strap of her handbag where it had slipped down her shoulder.

“You’re prepared. You know what you’ve done. Just talk to them.”

She met his eyes.

Then she nodded.

“Okay.”

He lowered his head slightly.

“And don’t forget to enjoy it.”

“Enjoy a job fair?”

“You’re meeting people who might want to work with you.”

She considered that.

Then her expression brightened a little.

“That’s actually a nice way to think about it.”

“I know.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“Don’t look so pleased.”

“Go on. I’ll be around.”

She turned toward the entrance, took three steps, then came back.

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

She held out her hand.

He glanced at it.

“What’s this?”

“Luck.”

He took her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Good luck.”

That made her grin.

Then, as she walked away, he called after her.

“Xiaoran.”

She turned.

“Yes?”

“Your folder.”

She looked down.

She had nearly left it on the bench.

He held it out.

Her face went blank.

Then she hurried back and took it.

“Don’t tell anyone.”

“I won’t.”

“Especially not Meilin.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

She gave him a warning look and disappeared into the crowd.

Yichen watched her go, smiling to himself.

The fair was busier than Xiaoran had expected.

There were companies from different industries, recruitment teams standing behind booths, students moving between them with résumés, and a steady stream of conversations that made the entire hall sound like one enormous interview.

She started with the companies she was less interested in.

It was a strategy.

She wanted to warm up before approaching the studios and media companies she had actually researched.

The first conversation went well. The second was a little awkward. By the third, she had found her rhythm.

She explained her eight weeks in Beijing the summer after second year, the campaign proposal her supervisor had sent back three times, and the noodle-shop campaign she had rewritten four times before anyone saw it.

When one recruiter asked about a challenge she had faced, she described the noodle shop: an owner who wanted students, and students who only wanted it cheap.

She explained what she had learned about audience research and how she would approach the campaign differently now.

The recruiter nodded, taking notes.

“That’s a thoughtful reflection. A lot of candidates focus only on what they achieved.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I think understanding what could have been done better is also important.”

“Absolutely.”

By the time she moved to the next section, she was feeling more confident.

Then she saw the booth.

Morrow Studio, Shanghai.

A creative production studio specialising in branded films, digital campaigns, and short-form storytelling.

She had researched them the previous evening.

Their work was visually distinctive, and several of their campaigns had caught her attention because they combined commercial objectives with strong narrative concepts.

She approached the booth.

A woman in her early thirties greeted her.

“Hello. Are you interested in our creative team?”

“Yes. I’m studying Media, and I’m particularly interested in content strategy and creative production.”

“Great. Do you have a portfolio?”

Xiaoran handed over her folder and opened the digital version on her laptop.

The recruiter, whose name tag read Lin Qian, began looking through it.

“Tell me about this project.”

Xiaoran leaned slightly closer.

“That’s Before the Morning Comes. I directed it with my partner, Chi Yuan, for the faculty showcase last May.”

Lin Qian spent a few moments reviewing the opening and reading the accompanying description.

“Interesting. What was your main responsibility?”

Xiaoran explained the development process, how she had worked through the initial concept, coordinated with her team, and made decisions about pacing and visual language.

She also discussed the difficulties of maintaining a consistent creative direction when different people had different interpretations of the story.

Lin Qian listened carefully.

“Did you enjoy directing?”

“Yes. Although I also enjoy the strategy behind a project. I like understanding why a particular story should be told, who we’re telling it to, and what we want the audience to take away.”

“So you don’t want to limit yourself to production?”

“Not necessarily. I would like to understand the entire process.”

Lin Qian smiled.

“That’s good. We’re looking for people who can think creatively but also understand the objectives behind the work.”

She asked Xiaoran a few more questions about her previous experience and the kind of projects she wanted to work on.

Then she closed the folder.

“I’d like our creative director to look at your portfolio. Would you be available for a formal interview next week?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Yes. Absolutely.”

Lin Qian handed her a card.

“Send me your updated portfolio and résumé. I’ll arrange something.”

Xiaoran accepted it with both hands.

“Thank you so much.”

“Thank you. I enjoyed speaking with you.”

She stepped away from the booth, looking down at the card.

Then she looked at it again.

A formal interview.

She hadn’t expected that to happen so quickly.

Her phone vibrated.

Yichen: How’s it going?

She took a photograph of the card and sent it.

Xiaoran: LOOK.

He replied almost immediately.

Yichen: Interview?

Xiaoran: Next week.

Yichen: Congratulations.

Xiaoran: I haven’t even interviewed yet.

Yichen: They wouldn’t invite you if they weren’t interested.

Her mouth tipped up.

Xiaoran: I’m going to pretend to be calm.

Yichen: How’s that going?

Xiaoran: Terribly.

He sent a laughing emoji.

She put her phone away and continued walking.

There was another booth she wanted to visit.

The booth from Beijing was larger, and she knew the logo before she could read the name: the company where she had spent eight weeks the summer after second year.

Their recruitment team was speaking with several students, and a digital display showed photographs of their office, production facilities, and recent campaigns.

Lanshan Media Group, Beijing.

At the end of the internship, one of the senior staff had asked whether she’d come back. She had laughed and said she had two more years of university. In January, her old supervisor had sent a two-line message: the graduate program was open, and she should apply.

She had. She hadn’t expected much. The program took few people.

She approached the booth.

A recruiter looked up.

“Hello. Are you here for our graduate program?”

“Yes.”

“Have you applied online?”

“Yes. I’m Lin Xiaoran.”

The recruiter checked her tablet.

Her expression changed slightly.

“Ah. Your supervisor from the summer program put a note on your file.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Really?”

“And your portfolio went straight to our content strategy team.”

She tried not to look too surprised.

“Thank you.”

The recruiter introduced herself as Zhang Wen and asked Xiaoran to sit down.

They spoke for nearly twenty minutes.

Unlike the conversation at Morrow Studio, which had focused heavily on creative production, this one explored Xiaoran’s ability to think across different business functions.

Zhang Wen asked about her campaign experience, her understanding of digital audiences, and how she would approach a project with limited resources.

Xiaoran spoke about the summer campaign in Beijing: a reading app that had to win over teenagers and the parents who paid for it.

She described the balance between something a fifteen-year-old would open and something a parent would trust.

Zhang Wen listened.

“What would you do differently if you had the opportunity to run that campaign again?”

“I would gather more insights from parents and students earlier in the planning stage. We had a good understanding of the platform’s objectives, but I think we could have made some creative decisions more effective if we had tested our assumptions earlier.”

Zhang Wen nodded.

“That’s sensible.”

She looked at Xiaoran’s portfolio again.

“And your showcase film is quite different from the campaign work.”

“Yes.”

“Do you prefer one?”

Xiaoran thought about it.

“I like different parts of both. With film, I enjoy developing an idea and translating it into something people can experience. With marketing, I enjoy understanding the audience and figuring out how to communicate something effectively.”

“So you’re interested in both creative development and strategy.”

“Yes. I don’t think they’re necessarily separate.”

Zhang Wen smiled.

“That’s a good answer.”

She closed the portfolio.

“Our Beijing office has a graduate position in the content and brand strategy team. It’s a structured program, and successful candidates will have the opportunity to work across several projects.”

Xiaoran listened carefully.

“We’d like to invite you to the next round of interviews. The team would be interested in meeting you.”

For a moment, Xiaoran didn’t respond.

Then she smiled.

“Thank you. I’d be very happy to.”

Zhang Wen handed her another card.

“One thing I should mention: the position is based in Beijing. The team expects successful candidates to relocate.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“I understand.”

“Would that be something you’d consider?”

She hesitated.

Not because she had never considered living in Beijing.

She had.

But it was different when someone asked her to make it a practical decision.

“Yes, I’d consider it,” she said.

Zhang Wen nodded.

“Good. We’ll be in touch about the next stage.”

Xiaoran thanked her and stepped away.

She walked several meters before stopping.

Then she looked down at the two cards in her hand.

One Shanghai.

One Beijing.

Two interviews.

Two different opportunities.

She stared at them.

Then she whispered to herself:

“Oh.”

Yichen found her near the café area.

She was sitting at a small table with her laptop open, two business cards placed neatly beside her notebook.

He approached from behind.

“Finished?”

“Yichen!”

He sat down opposite her.

“How was it?”

She didn’t answer immediately.

Instead, she pushed the two cards toward him.

He looked at them.

Then he looked at her.

“Both?”

She nodded.

“Both.”

He picked up the first card.

“Morrow Studio.”

“They want to interview me next week.”

He picked up the second.

“Lanshan.”

“They also want me for the next round.”

He set the cards down.

“That’s good.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“That’s all?”

“What else?”

“Can you be a little more excited?”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Congratulations.”

She waited.

He leaned forward.

“Look at you.”

Her expression softened.

“Thank you.”

He glanced at the cards again.

“How different are the positions?”

She immediately became more animated.

“Very different. Morrow is more creative production. They work on branded films, campaigns, short-form content. I think I would get to be involved in the development process and maybe eventually work with directors and production teams.”

He nodded.

“And Beijing?”

“More structured. It’s a graduate program in content and brand strategy. I’d get to work across different projects and teams.”

“Which one do you prefer?”

She looked down at the cards.

“I don’t know.”

He didn’t rush to fill the silence.

She said, “I like Morrow’s work. Their creative direction is really interesting. I can imagine myself learning a lot there.”

“And Lanshan?”

“I think the program would give me broader experience. More exposure to strategy and different parts of the business.”

She leaned back.

“They’re both good.”

“Then that’s a good problem to have.”

She turned to him.

“No.”

“Then yes.”

She laughed.

He reached for her hand.

“Don’t make yourself choose before you’ve even interviewed.”

“I know.”

“Talk to both teams. Find out what the actual work looks like. Ask about the people, the responsibilities, the opportunities to grow.”

She nodded.

“And think about where you want to be.”

She looked at the Beijing card.

“That’s the difficult part.”

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Because of the city?”

“Beijing is far.”

“Yes.”

“And you’re here.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him.

He was still holding her hand.

“Would you mind?”

He tilted his head slightly.

“Would I mind what?”

“If I moved to Beijing.”

He didn’t answer immediately.

Not because he didn’t know what he wanted, but because he wanted to answer the question she was actually asking.

“Would I miss you?” he said.

She nodded.

“Of course.”

He rubbed his thumb over her knuckles.

“Would it be difficult? Yes.”

She looked down.

“But would I want you to reject a good opportunity just because I’m in Shanghai?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Then you already know my answer.”

She looked up again.

Something in his face eased.

“I want you to have a career you’re excited about, Xiaoran. I don’t want you to choose a smaller future just because it makes our schedule easier.”

Her eyes softened.

“But I don’t want to be far away from you.”

“I know.”

“And I don’t want you to feel like you have to support me if I leave.”

“Xiaoran.”

She stopped.

He leaned closer.

“I’m not supporting you because I have to. I’m supporting you because I want to.”

She held his gaze.

Then she smiled.

“You’re being very reasonable.”

“Should I be less reasonable?”

“No.”

He smiled.

She picked up the two cards again.

“I think I’ll go to both interviews.”

“Good.”

“And then I’ll decide.”

“Good.”

She studied him.

“You’re not worried?”

“About what?”

“That I’ll go to Beijing.”

He met her eyes.

“I’d rather miss you than watch you turn down something you really want because you’re afraid of missing me.”

She was quiet.

Then she reached across the table and touched his cheek.

“You’re really good at saying things that make me like you more.”

He caught her hand and kissed her palm.

“That’s fortunate.”

She laughed.

The first interview was at Morrow Studio.

It took place the following Wednesday in a bright office with large windows and an open production area.

Xiaoran arrived fifteen minutes early.

She had prepared for the interview carefully. She knew the studio’s recent campaigns, had reviewed the job description, and had prepared questions about the role.

Lin Qian greeted her and introduced her to the creative director, a man named Gao Yan.

The interview was detailed.

They discussed her portfolio, her final film, and her previous marketing experience. Gao Yan asked how she handled creative disagreement and what she would do if a client rejected an idea she believed in.

Xiaoran answered thoughtfully.

She explained that she would first try to understand the client’s concern rather than immediately defend her idea. She believed creative work had to serve a purpose, and if the purpose wasn’t being communicated clearly, she needed to reconsider how she presented it.

Gao Yan seemed interested.

At the end, he closed her portfolio.

“I think you’d fit well with the team.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you.”

“We’re still speaking with other candidates, but I’d like to move you forward.”

She nodded.

“Of course.”

“One question. If we made you an offer, would you be comfortable starting in Shanghai?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

That got a smile out of him.

“I think we can give you quite a bit of room to grow here. You’ll be involved in real projects from the beginning, not just supporting work.”

Xiaoran listened carefully.

It sounded exciting.

It also sounded like the kind of environment where she would have to learn quickly.

She left the office feeling optimistic.

But she didn’t know yet whether it was the right place.

The Lanshan interview took place two days later, online.

The interviewers were from the Beijing office: one from recruitment and another from the content strategy team.

It was more structured than the Morrow interview.

They asked about her experience, her analytical approach, and how she would respond to a campaign that was performing below expectations.

Xiaoran described how she would review audience behavior, examine the campaign’s performance against its objectives, and identify whether the problem was with the content, targeting, distribution, or the underlying strategy.

The content strategy manager nodded.

“Good. And what would you do if the creative team disagreed with your recommendation?”

“I’d want to understand their reasoning. I wouldn’t assume that the data automatically tells us what creative decision to make. It helps us identify a problem, but we still need judgement to decide how to solve it.”

The manager smiled.

“That’s a balanced answer.”

They discussed the graduate program, the expected workload, and the possibility of moving between teams.

Then the recruiter asked:

“Are you comfortable relocating to Beijing?”

Xiaoran took a breath.

“Yes. I’d be open to it.”

“Do you have any concerns?”

She thought about the question.

“I’d want to understand the relocation support and the working arrangements. But professionally, I’m comfortable with the opportunity.”

“That’s reasonable.”

The interview ended on a positive note.

When she closed her laptop, she sat.

Two interviews. Two teams.

Two different possibilities.

She didn’t feel the same excitement she had felt at the job fair.

Instead, she felt the weight of a decision approaching.

That evening, she went to Yichen’s apartment.

He was reviewing footage from his latest game when she arrived. He looked up as she entered.

“How was it?”

She put her bag down.

“Good.”

“Good?”

“Very good, actually.”

He closed the laptop.

He reached for her.

She walked over, and he pulled her into a hug.

She rested her cheek against his shoulder.

“I think they liked me.”

“I know.”

She leaned back.

“How do you know?”

“Because they invited you to interview.”

“That’s not the same.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right. Tell me.”

She sat beside him and explained the interview. She told him about the creative director’s questions, the team structure, and how much responsibility the role might offer.

Then she told him about Lanshan.

When she finished, he asked, “Which one made you more excited?”

She thought about it.

“Morrow.”

He nodded.

“Which one made you think more?”

“Lanshan.”

“Why?”

“Because it feels like a bigger decision. It’s a graduate program. A structured path. I might learn more about strategy and business.”

“And Morrow?”

“I’d get to work on projects I genuinely like.”

He turned to her.

“Those aren’t mutually exclusive.”

“I know.”

She leaned back against the sofa.

“That’s why it’s difficult.”

Yichen reached for her hand.

“Have you thought about what you want your first job to give you?”

She considered it.

“Experience. Good people to learn from. The chance to work on projects that matter.”

“Anything else?”

She tilted her head.

“I want to feel like I’m becoming good at something.”

“Then ask them how they’ll help you do that.”

“You’re making this sound very simple.”

“It’s not simple. But you don’t have to decide based on the company name or how impressive the program sounds.”

She looked down at their hands.

“I think I’m afraid of choosing wrong.”

He was quiet.

Then he said, “You might.”

She looked up.

He said, “Not because you’re careless. Sometimes you make the best decision you can with what you know, and later you learn something you couldn’t have known at the time.”

She listened.

“That doesn’t mean you chose badly.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You’re making me feel better.”

“Good.”

She leaned against him.

“Do you ever feel like everyone else knows what they’re doing?”

“Yes.”

She turned her head.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

“But you always seem so sure.”

“That’s because I don’t usually announce every time I’m uncertain.”

She laughed.

He kissed her.

“You’re allowed to figure things out.”

She closed her eyes.

“Okay.”

The offers came the following week.

Morrow called first.

Lin Qian explained that the creative director had been impressed with Xiaoran’s portfolio and interview. They wanted to offer her a junior creative producer position, with opportunities to work across branded films and digital campaigns.

The offer included a starting salary, a clear reporting structure, and a six-month review.

Xiaoran thanked her and asked for the written offer.

She was still processing it when her phone rang again.

Lanshan.

Zhang Wen told her that the content strategy team wanted to move forward with her application.

They were offering her a place in the graduate program.

The program included rotations across content strategy, campaign planning, and brand development. The position was based in Beijing, with a planned start date after graduation.

Xiaoran thanked her and asked for the written details.

Then she sat at her desk.

Two offers.

Not just interviews anymore.

Two companies wanted her.

She stared at the emails.

A smile slowly appeared on her face.

Then she picked up her phone and called Yichen.

He answered while leaving the training facility.

“Hello?”

She didn’t say anything.

He paused.

“Xiaoran?”

“Yichen.”

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then?”

She took a breath.

“I got both.”

There was a short silence.

Then he smiled.

“Both offers?”

“Yes.”

“Congratulations.”

She laughed.

“I got both!”

“I heard you.”

“They both want me.”

“I know.”

She could hear the smile in his voice.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“I’m really happy.”

“I’m happy for you.”

She sat back in her chair.

“Morrow offered me the creative producer position. And Lanshan offered me the graduate program.”

“That’s excellent.”

“One in Shanghai. One in Beijing.”

“I remember.”

She laughed.

Then she became quiet.

“What do I do?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

“Have you read both offers?”

“Yes.”

“All the details?”

“Mostly.”

“Then let’s read them properly tonight.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Together?”

“Of course.”

She looked at the emails again.

“Okay.”

“And Xiaoran?”

“Mm?”

“Don’t forget that you earned both of them.”

Her smile softened.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

She laughed.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He opened the car door.

“I’ll come over after training tomorrow. We’ll look through everything.”

She nodded, then remembered he couldn’t see her.

“Okay.”

“Congratulations, filmmaker.”

She smiled.

“Thank you, basketball player.”

They spent the following evening at his apartment, comparing the offers.

Yichen had made tea.

Xiaoran had brought her laptop and a notebook.

They sat at the dining table, with the two offer letters open side by side.

She had created a comparison sheet.

Yichen looked at it.

“You made a table.”

“Yes.”

“Of course you did.”

She pointed at the screen.

“Don’t underestimate the power of a table.”

“I’m not.”

“Good.”

They went through the details one by one.

Morrow offered a more direct creative role. She would work closely with the production team and gain practical experience in content development and branded storytelling.

Lanshan offered a structured graduate program, broader exposure, and the opportunity to build a foundation in content and brand strategy.

The salaries were different. The benefits were different.

The working environments were different.

And the cities were different.

Xiaoran rested her chin on her hand.

“Which one would you choose?”

Yichen looked at her.

“I’m not you.”

“I know. I’m asking what you think.”

He considered the two documents.

“I think both are good opportunities. But I wouldn’t choose Lanshan just because the program sounds more prestigious, and I wouldn’t choose Morrow just because it’s in Shanghai.”

She nodded.

“That’s what I was thinking.”

“Which job would you want to wake up for?”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“That’s a difficult question.”

“Then think about it.”

She looked at the Morrow offer.

“I can imagine myself working there.”

Then she looked at Lanshan.

“I can also imagine myself there.”

Yichen leaned back.

“Then maybe you need more information.”

“Such as?”

“Ask to speak with someone who would work with you directly. Ask about the projects you’ll actually handle. Ask what success looks like after six months.”

She nodded slowly.

That made her grin.

“You sound like you’ve become very experienced.”

“I’ve learned a few things.”

“From basketball?”

“From working with people.”

She studied his face.

Then she closed her laptop.

“I think I want to sleep on it.”

“Good.”

She stood and walked around the table.

Yichen looked up as she came to stand beside him.

She leaned down and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you.”

He caught her hand.

“For what?”

“For not telling me to stay.”

He held her gaze.

“Would you have stayed?”

She thought about it.

“I don’t know.”

“Then I’m glad I didn’t.”

She rested her forehead against his.

“You’re not worried?”

“I am.”

She blinked.

“Really?”

“Of course. If you move to Beijing, I’ll miss you.”

Her expression softened.

“But?”

“But I don’t want my worry to become your limitation.”

She looked at him.

Then she kissed him, slowly, with both offer letters still open on the screen behind her.

He held her.

And for a while, neither of them said anything.

Later that night, Xiaoran sat at the edge of his bed, looking at the two offer letters on her laptop.

Yichen was in the bathroom.

She glanced at the ring on her finger.

Five years together.

A promise made in December.

A future they had begun to imagine, but not yet built.

She opened a blank document.

At the top, she typed:

What do I want from my first job?

Then she began writing.

She wrote about the work she wanted to do, the skills she wanted to develop, the kind of people she wanted to learn from, and the person she wanted to become.

When Yichen came out, he found her still typing.

“Still thinking?”

She nodded.

“Just organizing my thoughts.”

He came over and sat beside her.

“Anything interesting?”

She turned the laptop slightly.

He read the heading.

Then he looked at her.

“Good question.”

She smiled.

“I think I need to answer it before I choose.”

He nodded.

She closed the laptop.

“Not tonight, though.”

“Not tonight.”

She leaned against his shoulder.

“Can we just have a normal evening?”

He put his arm around her.

“Of course.”

She looked up.

“No job talk.”

“All right.”

“No contract talk.”

“All right.”

“No basketball. That’s becoming difficult.”

She laughed.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He smiled and kissed her temple.

“Fine.”

She settled against him.

After a few minutes, she spoke again.

“Actually, one thing.”

He looked down.

“What?”

“When I become successful, you have to be proud of me.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Only when?”

That made her grin.

“Well, I’m not successful yet.”

He took her hand and kissed the ring.

“I’m proud of you now.”

Her expression softened.

“Good.”

He studied her.

“And when you become successful, I’ll be proud of you then too.”

She smiled and rested her head against his chest.

Two offers sat in her inbox, and she fell asleep before she had chosen either.

chapters.desc: Beijing has made her an offer. Everyone wants to know why not, and she wants to be the one who answers.
chapters.title: Why Not Beijing
chapters.epigraph: “I understand that you want the job.”
chapters.content:
The disagreement began with a question about dinner.

It was a Sunday evening, and Xiaoran was sitting at the dining table with her laptop open, a half-finished bowl of soup beside her. Her father had just returned from the study, where he’d been reading something on his tablet. Her mother was cutting fruit in the kitchen.

Yichen was sitting beside Xiaoran.

They were both home for the weekend, and he had come over for dinner, as he did most weekends they were home now, and was helping her mother arrange the dishes. Nothing unusual.

Until Xiaoran’s father looked at her laptop.

“What’s that?”

She looked up.

“Oh. It’s an offer.”

Her father pulled out a chair.

“What offer?”

Xiaoran hesitated for half a second. Not because she intended to hide it, but because she knew the conversation wouldn’t be a short one.

“It’s from Lanshan. In Beijing. The company I interned at, the summer after second year.”

Her father looked at her.

“Beijing?”

She nodded.

“They were at the spring job fair. My old supervisor put a note on my file. I had an interview last week, and they sent me the details yesterday.”

“Is it an internship?”

“No. A graduate position.”

Her father glanced at the laptop.

“What kind of company?”

She turned the screen slightly toward him.

“You know what they do. Brands, digital campaigns, commercial content. The role is junior creative producer. I’d be involved in planning, coordinating shoots, working with creative teams, and eventually handling projects.”

Her father read the details.

He said nothing.

Then he asked, “Where is the office?”

Xiaoran showed him.

“Where would you live?”

“They have some accommodation recommendations. I’ve also been looking at apartments nearby.”

“How much is the salary?”

She answered.

“Is that enough to live in Beijing?”

“I’ve calculated the expenses. Rent, transport, food, everything. It’s manageable.”

Her father continued reading.

Then he closed the laptop halfway.

“No.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

She hadn’t expected agreement immediately.

But she hadn’t expected that, either.

“Dad, you haven’t even—”

“I’ve read enough.”

“Enough to know what?”

“That it’s in Beijing.”

Her mother came out of the kitchen with a plate of fruit. She glanced between them, sensing the change in atmosphere.

“What’s wrong?”

“Your daughter wants to go to Beijing.”

Her mother put the plate down.

“For work?”

Xiaoran nodded.

Her mother looked at the laptop.

“Is this the company you mentioned last week?”

“Yes.”

Her father leaned back.

“Why does it have to be Beijing?”

The question was quiet.

But it wasn’t really a question.

Xiaoran put down her spoon.

“Because the opportunity is there.”

“There are companies here.”

“I know.”

“Shanghai has plenty of creative studios.”

“I know, Dad.”

“Then why go so far away?”

She took a breath.

“Because I want to try.”

Her father looked at her.

“Try what?”

“Working somewhere new. Being responsible for myself. Learning how a bigger production team operates. This position is a good fit for what I’ve been studying, and it’s the kind of work I want to do.”

“You can find that here.”

“Maybe. But this is the offer I have now.”

Her father looked unconvinced.

“You’re graduating soon. You should think carefully about what kind of life you want. Don’t make a decision just because someone offered you a job in another city.”

“I’m not.”

“Then what are you basing it on?”

“The role. The experience. The work.”

“And the distance?”

Xiaoran’s fingers tightened slightly around her spoon.

“What about it?”

“You’re going to move to another city. You’ll be on your own. You don’t know anyone there.”

“I can make friends.”

“That’s not the point.”

“Then what is?”

Her father didn’t answer immediately.

Her mother sat down beside him.

“Let her explain.”

He glanced at his wife, then back at Xiaoran.

“I’m listening.”

But his expression said he had already decided.

Yichen had been quiet throughout the conversation.

Not absent.

Not distracted.

He had listened to every word, his attention moving between Xiaoran and her father. He knew about the position. He knew she’d been excited when she first told him about the interview, and how she’d spent several evenings researching the company and its previous projects.

He also knew she hadn’t accepted anything yet.

She had wanted to discuss it with her parents before making a decision.

Now she was sitting across from her father, trying to explain why she wanted something he didn’t want her to have.

Yichen didn’t interrupt.

He didn’t say Beijing was a good idea. He didn’t tell her father that Xiaoran was capable of living independently. He didn’t offer to visit her every weekend, or suggest that the distance wouldn’t matter.

He knew she hadn’t asked him to defend her.

And he knew her father hadn’t asked him for his opinion.

So he stayed quiet.

Her father eventually turned toward him.

“Yichen.”

“Yes, Uncle?”

“What do you think?”

Xiaoran looked at him too.

Yichen set down his glass.

“About the position?”

“About her going to Beijing.”

He took a moment.

“I think the position is worth considering.”

Her father frowned slightly.

“Why?”

“Because the work seems relevant to what she’s studied, and she’s interested in the role.”

“That’s all?”

Yichen nodded.

“That’s what I know about it.”

Her father studied him.

“Would you be comfortable with her going?”

Xiaoran’s eyes moved toward Yichen.

He didn’t look at her immediately.

“Yes.”

Her father leaned back.

“Just like that?”

Yichen met his gaze.

“Uncle, I don’t think my comfort should decide whether she takes a job.”

The table went quiet.

Xiaoran looked down at her bowl.

Her father didn’t seem pleased with the answer.

“You’re together. It’s not unreasonable to consider how a decision like this affects both of you.”

“I agree.”

“Then?”

Yichen spoke calmly.

“If Xiaoran wants to discuss how we’d manage the distance, I’ll discuss it with her. But I don’t think she should reject an opportunity simply because I’m in another city.”

Her father looked at him.

“And what if it affects your plans?”

Yichen didn’t answer too quickly.

“Then we’ll talk about our plans.”

“What if you don’t agree?”

“We’ll have to understand why.”

Her father seemed to wait for something more.

A promise, perhaps.

An assurance that Yichen would ask Xiaoran to stay.

Or that he would make a decision on her behalf.

But Yichen only picked up his glass.

He hadn’t come to dinner to negotiate Xiaoran’s future.

After dinner, Xiaoran went to her room for her charger. When she came back, she found her father and Yichen in the living room.

Her father was sitting on the sofa. Yichen was standing beside the bookshelf, looking at a photograph.

Neither seemed to be arguing.

But the atmosphere was still serious.

“Are you two talking about me?”

Her father looked up.

“Should we not?”

She walked over.

“You can talk about me when I’m here.”

Yichen turned toward her.

His expression was neutral, but his eyes softened.

“Your father was asking about my plans after graduation.”

Her father nodded.

“Since everyone is making plans.”

Xiaoran sat down.

“Then we should all make plans together.”

Her father looked at her.

“Xiaoran, I’m not saying you can’t work in another city.”

“You said no.”

“I said I don’t agree with the idea.”

“That’s the same thing to me.”

He sighed.

“You’re too quick to turn everything into an argument.”

She looked at him, frustrated.

“Because I feel like I have to defend every reason I give you.”

Her father was quiet.

She continued, more carefully this time.

“I’m not asking you to be happy that I’m moving away. I’m asking you to understand why I want to go.”

Her father looked at her.

Then he said, “I understand that you want the job.”

“But you don’t understand why I want Beijing.”

“Why not find something closer?”

“Because I don’t want to choose a city before I choose the work.”

Her father frowned.

She took a breath.

“I’ve spent four years studying Media. I’ve worked on projects, built my portfolio, taken every opportunity I could find. I know I’m still inexperienced, but I want to start somewhere that will challenge me.”

“Beijing isn’t the only place that can challenge you.”

“No. But this company is offering me a chance.”

“Other companies might too.”

“Maybe they will. But I can’t keep rejecting something real because something better might appear somewhere else.”

Her father looked away.

For a moment, Xiaoran thought he might finally understand.

Instead, he said, “You don’t know what it’s like to live alone in a city like that.”

She swallowed.

“Then I’ll learn.”

“You think it’s that simple?”

“No. I think it’ll be difficult. I think I’ll miss home. I’ll probably get lost. I’ll have days when I don’t know what I’m doing, and I’ll have to figure things out.”

She met his eyes.

“But that’s part of growing up, isn’t it?”

Her father didn’t answer.

Yichen remained quiet.

Xiaoran glanced at him.

He was listening, not waiting for an opportunity to speak.

She was grateful for that.

The conversation ended without an agreement.

Her father went to his study.

Her mother stayed in the living room with Xiaoran, who had started rearranging the fruit on the plate without noticing.

“Are you upset?” her mother asked.

“A little.”

“Your father is worried.”

“I know.”

“He doesn’t think you’re incapable.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“Then why does he keep talking as if I am?”

Her mother sighed.

“Because sometimes knowing someone is capable doesn’t make it easier to let them go.”

Xiaoran looked down.

Her mother reached over and touched her hand.

“That doesn’t mean he gets to decide everything.”

She smiled.

“You’re on my side?”

“I’m on your side. I’m also your father’s side.”

“That’s very convenient.”

Her mother laughed.

Then she looked toward Yichen.

“Yichen, you must be tired. You’ve been sitting through our family discussion.”

He smiled politely.

“It’s all right, Auntie.”

Her mother nodded.

“Thank you for coming.”

“Thank you for dinner.”

She went upstairs shortly afterward, leaving the two of them alone.

Xiaoran sat for a while.

Then she leaned toward Yichen.

“You didn’t say much.”

He met her eyes.

“You didn’t need me to.”

“I know.”

He took her hand.

“Do you want me to say something?”

She considered it, then shook her head.

“No. I just wanted you here.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“I’m here.”

She tucked herself against his shoulder.

After a moment, she murmured, “Did you think I was being unreasonable?”

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“No.”

She looked up.

“You’re not just agreeing with me?”

Yichen considered his answer.

“I think it’s a decision you need to make with all the information available. I think you should understand the job, the living arrangements, the financial side, and what you want your first few years of work to look like.”

She nodded.

“And?”

“And I think you’re allowed to want something that takes you away from home.”

Her expression softened.

He brushed a strand of hair behind her ear.

“But I won’t tell you that Beijing is automatically the right choice just because you want it. You still have to decide whether the opportunity is right.”

“That’s fair.”

He kissed her hair.

“You can be excited about it and still be careful.”

She closed her eyes.

For the first time that evening, her shoulders relaxed.

The next morning, her father found the printed offer on the dining table.

There were notes in the margins.

Questions about the probation period, housing allowance, working hours, insurance, and the company’s policy for new graduates.

He picked it up.

Xiaoran came out of her room shortly afterward.

She stopped when she saw him reading it.

“Morning.”

“Morning.”

She poured herself a glass of water.

“Those are the details I was telling you about.”

“I see.”

He turned a page.

“Have you checked the accommodation yourself?”

“Yes. I spoke with the housing coordinator. I also looked at other options.”

“What about the commute?”

“I checked that too.”

“Have you spoken to anyone currently working there?”

“Two people. One of them is a junior producer.”

He looked up.

Xiaoran continued.

“I asked about the workload, the team structure, and what the first six months are like.”

Her father looked back at the paper.

She didn’t ask whether he had changed his mind.

She didn’t want to spend another morning trying to convince him.

Instead, she sat down and began eating breakfast.

After a while, he asked, “When do they need your answer?”

“By Friday.”

He nodded.

“Don’t rush.”

“I’m not.”

He folded the paper and put it back on the table.

Then he said, “Send me the accommodation details.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“Okay.”

It wasn’t approval.

But it wasn’t the same no as the night before.

And for now, she could work with that.

That afternoon, Yichen received a message from her.

Xiaoran: My dad asked for the accommodation details.

Yichen: That’s good.

Xiaoran: He still doesn’t agree.

Yichen: He doesn’t have to agree today.

Xiaoran: You’re very calm.

Yichen: Would you prefer me to panic?

Xiaoran: A little. So I don’t feel like I’m the only one being dramatic.

He laughed under his breath.

Yichen: You’re doing enough for both of us.

She sent him an angry sticker, then another message.

Xiaoran: Do you really not mind?

He knew what she meant.

He typed, deleted, and tried again.

Yichen: I won’t pretend I wouldn’t miss you.

A few seconds passed.

Yichen: But missing you isn’t a reason to ask you to stay somewhere you don’t want to be.

She read it twice.

Then she called him.

He answered almost immediately.

“Hello.”

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You’re supposed to be my boyfriend.”

“I am.”

“You’re supposed to be selfish sometimes.”

He laughed.

“I can be selfish.”

“Then why aren’t you?”

He was silent.

“Because I love you.”

She went quiet.

He continued.

“And I want you to have a life you’re proud of. I want to be part of it, Xiaoran. I don’t want to be the reason you make it smaller.”

She pressed her lips together.

“You’re making me emotional.”

“Are you crying?”

“No.”

“All right.”

A pause.

Then he said, “Should I come over?”

That made her grin.

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll see you later.”

That evening, Xiaoran was sitting on the floor of her bedroom, sorting through printed documents when Yichen arrived.

He sat beside her.

She showed him the accommodation details, the job description, and the list of questions she still wanted to ask the company.

He read everything carefully.

He pointed out one clause she hadn’t noticed, asked whether the company had clarified the probation period, and suggested she ask about relocation support.

She wrote it down.

Then she looked at him.

“You know, you’re allowed to have an opinion.”

“I have several.”

“About Beijing.”

He considered the question.

“I think you could do well there.”

She smiled.

“Thank you.”

“I also think you might find the first few months difficult.”

Her smile faded slightly.

“That’s not very encouraging.”

“It’s not meant to be discouraging.”

He looked at her.

“You’ll be learning a new job, living somewhere unfamiliar, and managing everything yourself. Some days will be exhausting.”

“But I think you can handle it.”

She looked down at the documents.

Then she asked, “Would you visit?”

His mouth curved.

“Yes.”

“Even when you’re busy?”

“Yes.”

“Would you complain about the train tickets?”

“Probably.”

She laughed.

“Yichen!”

“I’m being honest.”

She leaned against him.

“Would you miss me?”

“Every day.”

That made her grin.

He kissed her hair.

“And I’d still want you to go if that’s what you decide.”

She closed her eyes.

For a while, they sat together on the floor, surrounded by papers and the uncertain shape of their future.

Neither of them knew exactly where they would be six months later. Xiaoran knew only that the decision would be hers.

She made it three weeks later, on her own, for reasons that turned out to have nothing to do with anyone’s comfort, including his.

chapters.desc: Mr. Zhou invites her to lunch at his office, alone, because there is something he would like to say before she decides.
chapters.title: Lunch at Zhou Logistics
chapters.epigraph: “He asked what I think of you.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came on a Wednesday morning.

Not to Yichen.

To Xiaoran.

She was sitting in the university library, halfway through reviewing her final-year project notes, when her phone lit up.

Uncle Zhou (Logistics): Xiaoran, are you free for lunch this Friday?

She read the message twice.

Yichen’s father occasionally sent her messages, usually to ask whether she was coming over for dinner or to remind her to bring something home. He had invited her somewhere alone exactly once before, to dinner at his hotel in her third year, the week the Herons had nearly not picked his son, and she still remembered every word of it.

She replied politely.

Xiaoran: Hello, Uncle! I should be free. Is there something happening on Friday?

His answer came a moment later.

Uncle Zhou (Logistics): Nothing special. I’d like to have lunch with you. I’ll send you the address.

Then he sent the location.

Zhou Logistics.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

She knew the company, of course. It was the family business Yichen’s father had built over twenty-five years, the one whose name was on the Herons’ sponsor boards, which was a sentence Yichen still didn’t like hearing. She had heard about it at dinners, but she had never been inside the office.

She looked at the message again.

Then she opened her chat with Yichen.

Xiaoran: Your father invited me to lunch.

Yichen: That’s nice.

Xiaoran: Alone.

A pause.

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: At Zhou Logistics.

Another pause.

Yichen: Have you accepted?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: Then enjoy lunch.

She stared at his reply.

Xiaoran: That’s all?

Yichen: Would you like me to come?

Xiaoran: NO. He invited me alone.

Yichen: Then I won’t interfere.

She frowned at the screen.

Xiaoran: You’re not curious?

Yichen: A little.

Xiaoran: A LITTLE?

Yichen: I trust my father.

She put her phone down.

That was the problem with Zhou Yichen.

He could make a perfectly reasonable response sound like he was deliberately withholding information.

On Friday, Xiaoran arrived at Zhou Logistics fifteen minutes early.

She had changed outfits twice that morning.

The first blouse had felt too casual. The second had seemed too formal. Eventually, she’d settled on a light blue blouse, dark trousers, and a small handbag.

She checked her reflection in the lobby glass, then checked the time, then checked the message again.

A receptionist approached.

“Miss Lin?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“Yes.”

“Mr. Zhou is expecting you. Please come with me.”

She followed her upstairs.

The office was larger than she’d imagined, but not in the intimidating way she’d expected. There was a reception area, several meeting rooms, and a busy open office beyond the glass partitions. People were moving between desks, carrying documents and speaking into phones.

She noticed the company logo on the wall.

It made her feel strangely aware that this was a place where Yichen’s father wasn’t someone’s father.

He was the person in charge.

The receptionist led her to a private dining room.

“Please wait here. Mr. Zhou will be with you shortly.”

“Thank you.”

Xiaoran sat down.

She placed her handbag beside her chair and looked around.

There were framed photographs on one wall: company milestones, warehouse openings, a few formal group photographs. One showed Yichen’s father standing with a group of employees in front of a logistics facility.

She was studying it when the door opened.

“Xiaoran.”

She stood immediately.

“Uncle.”

He smiled.

“Sorry to keep you waiting.”

“It’s all right. I arrived early.”

“I know. My assistant told me.”

He gestured toward the chair.

“Sit. Have you been waiting long?”

“Not at all.”

He sat opposite her.

She wondered whether she should ask why he’d invited her.

Then he looked at her and said, “You must be wondering why I asked you here.”

She smiled awkwardly.

“A little.”

He laughed.

“Good. At least you’re honest.”

Lunch began with ordinary conversation.

He asked about her final-year studies, whether her graduation project was progressing well, and how she was finding the process of applying for graduate positions.

Xiaoran answered honestly.

She told him about her portfolio, her interest in creative production, and the opportunities she’d been considering.

He listened carefully.

“Do you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

“What part?”

She thought.

“I like that there’s always something to solve. Sometimes it’s a creative problem, sometimes it’s a communication problem, sometimes it’s simply figuring out how to make an idea work with the resources you have.”

“That sounds familiar.”

“Probably because every job has its own problems.”

“That’s true.”

He took a sip of tea.

“Yichen tells me you’ve been working very hard.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“He does?”

“Occasionally.”

She laughed.

“He doesn’t tell me what he says about me.”

“That’s probably wise.”

She smiled.

Then his father continued, “He also mentioned you’re considering opportunities outside Shanghai.”

Her smile became a little more cautious.

“Yes.”

“Beijing?”

She nodded.

“Among others.”

“Have you made a decision?”

“Not yet. I’m still looking at the role, the company, and the practical arrangements.”

He nodded.

“Good. You shouldn’t make that decision lightly.”

She met his eyes.

“I don’t intend to.”

Something in his face eased.

“I know.”

There was something reassuring about the way he said it. Not as if he was testing her, but as if he believed she was capable of making a thoughtful decision.

Then he put down his chopsticks.

“Xiaoran, may I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“What do you think of Yichen?”

She blinked.

It was such a sudden change of subject that she almost forgot how to answer.

“Yichen?”

His father smiled.

“Yes. My son.”

She laughed.

“That’s a very broad question.”

“Then take your time.”

She looked down at her tea.

What did she think of Yichen?

She knew him in ways that were difficult to explain to anyone who hadn’t spent years beside him. She knew his habits, his expressions, his silences. She knew how he behaved when he was tired, how he looked when he was concentrating, and how his mouth curved when he was trying not to laugh at her.

But answering his father felt different.

“He’s very dependable,” she began.

His father nodded.

“Is he?”

“Yes. He doesn’t always say much, but he pays attention. He remembers things. And he takes his responsibilities seriously. Sometimes too seriously.”

His father laughed.

“That sounds like him.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“He can be stubborn, too.”

“That also sounds like him.”

“And he thinks he’s very good at hiding when he’s worried.”

His father looked at her with interest.

“Is he not?”

“Not from me.”

There was a brief silence.

Then his father smiled.

“That’s good.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

He said, “He’s always been a quiet child. Even when he was younger, he rarely told us everything that was on his mind. We usually had to work it out ourselves.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“He’s still like that.”

“I know.”

His father looked toward the window.

“He has always wanted to do things properly. Sometimes I wonder whether he gives himself enough room to make mistakes.”

Xiaoran listened.

“He’s still young,” she said.

“Yes. But he doesn’t always remember that.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Then you should remind him.”

His father laughed.

“I’ve tried.”

After the main course, his father asked whether she wanted dessert.

She agreed.

While they waited, he looked at her again.

“There’s something else I wanted to tell you.”

Xiaoran straightened slightly.

He noticed.

“Don’t look so nervous. This isn’t a job interview.”

She laughed, embarrassed.

“Sorry.”

He laughed under his breath.

“I wanted to thank you.”

“For what?”

“For being with Yichen.”

She looked down.

His father continued, his voice calm.

“I know you’ve been together a long time. I’ve watched the two of you grow up. You’re both approaching graduation now, and the next few years will probably be very different from what you’re used to.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yes.”

“He may have opportunities that take him away from home. You may have opportunities that take you somewhere else. There will be decisions that aren’t easy. I don’t want you to feel that you have to arrange your life around his.”

Xiaoran looked up.

It wasn’t what she’d expected him to say.

“Uncle...”

“Yichen has his own ambitions. You have yours. I hope you both take them seriously.”

She listened.

“Don’t give up something important simply because you think it will make things easier for him. And don’t expect him to give up something important just to make things easier for you. Talk to each other. Make decisions together when they affect both of you.”

“That’s all.”

Xiaoran looked down at her hands.

She thought of the conversations she’d had with Yichen about Beijing. Of how he had listened without trying to decide for her. Of how he had told her he wanted to be part of her future, not the reason she made it smaller.

She smiled.

“He’s said something similar.”

His father raised his eyebrows.

“Has he?”

“Yes.”

“Then perhaps I’ve taught him something.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Perhaps.”

He smiled too.

Then he said, “Although he was stubborn long before he met you.”

She laughed again.

When lunch was over, his father walked her back toward the lift.

“Thank you for coming,” he said.

“Thank you for inviting me. Lunch was lovely.”

He nodded.

“Come by again sometime.”

“I will.”

The lift arrived.

Before she stepped inside, he called her once more.

“Xiaoran.”

She turned.

“Yes?”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Don’t worry too much about what Yichen thinks of your decisions.”

She turned to him.

“He thinks the world of you.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I know.”

“Good.”

The doors closed.

And only when she was alone did Xiaoran finally let out the breath she’d been holding.

It was a Friday, so she went back to his flat. He was sitting on the sofa with a laptop open, but he looked up as soon as he heard the door.

“How was lunch?”

She put down her handbag.

“Your father is very nice.”

Yichen closed his laptop.

“I know.”

“He asked about my studies.”

“Sounds like him.”

“And my job applications.”

He nodded.

“Anything else?”

She looked at him.

Then she smiled.

“He asked what I think of you.”

Yichen paused.

A faint change crossed his face.

“What did you say?”

“That you’re dependable.”

He nodded.

“Accurate.”

“Stubborn.”

“Also accurate.”

“Quiet.”

“Yes.”

“And that you think you’re good at hiding when you’re worried.”

He met her eyes.

That made her grin.

“Not very accurate, apparently.”

He leaned back.

“What else?”

She walked over and sat beside him.

“That you take your responsibilities too seriously.”

He considered it.

“Did he agree?”

“Very much.”

Yichen sighed.

“Wonderful.”

She laughed.

Then she leaned against him.

“He also told me not to arrange my life around you.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Did he?”

“He said we should both take our ambitions seriously.”

Yichen was quiet.

Then he smiled.

“That’s good advice.”

She looked up.

“Did you know he was going to say that?”

“No.”

She studied his face.

Then she asked, “Why did he invite me alone?”

Yichen thought.

“Maybe he wanted to talk to you without me answering for him.”

She frowned.

“Would you have answered for him?”

“Probably.”

She laughed.

He reached over and tucked her hair behind her ear.

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She let her head drop onto his shoulder.

“Your father likes me.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“I know.”

She lifted her head.

“How?”

“He’s invited you to lunch alone.”

She smiled.

“You’re not surprised?”

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

Something in his face eased.

“Xiaoran, he likes you very much.”

She felt warmth spread through her chest.

Then she looked at him suspiciously.

“Did he tell you to say that?”

“No.”

“You’re sure?”

“Quite sure.”

She leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

Yichen smiled.

Then, just as she was settling back against him, he asked, “Did you tell him about the time I got lost in the shopping mall when we were younger?”

Xiaoran froze.

Slowly, she turned her head.

“...No.”

He turned to her.

“Good.”

She started laughing.

“Why? Are you embarrassed?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“Because he already knows.”

She stared.

“How?”

Yichen’s smile deepened. “You told my mother. At New Year. My mother tells him everything.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

chapters.desc: The first-round interview with a Shanghai studio is online, and from the waist up she looks entirely professional.
chapters.title: Interview Outfit
chapters.epigraph: “I think I represented myself well.”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had decided that online interviews were one of humanity’s greatest inventions.

She had also decided that whoever invented the concept of business casual had never considered the possibility of being interviewed from a bedroom.

At eighteen minutes to ten, she stood in front of the mirror in her studio, inspecting herself. It was the first round for Morrow Studio, the one in the city, the one she hadn’t told anyone she wanted more than Beijing.

White blouse. Navy blazer. Hair neatly tied back, with two loose strands framing her face. Light makeup. Small earrings.

Professional.

Presentable.

Like someone who knew exactly what she was doing.

She looked down.

Pink pajama shorts.

With tiny yellow ducks printed all over them.

Perfect.

Her laptop was positioned on her desk, angled slightly upward. Behind her was a carefully arranged bookshelf, a small plant, and a framed photograph she had moved twice because it looked too personal.

She checked her camera.

Then her microphone. Then her internet connection.

Then the time. Her interview was at ten.

She had prepared for this. She had researched the company, reviewed her portfolio, written down possible questions, and practiced her introduction until she could deliver it without sounding like she was reading from a script.

She was ready.

Her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Good luck today.

Xiaoran smiled.

Xiaoran: Thank you.

Yichen: Don’t forget to breathe.

Xiaoran: I know how to breathe.

Yichen: You forgot last time you presented.

She stared at the message.

Xiaoran: That was different.

Yichen: Of course.

She was about to reply when another message appeared.

Yichen: Send me the blazer. I want to see it before they do.

She took a picture from the waist up, carefully, and sent it.

Yichen: Very professional. Your interviewer will be lucky to meet you.

She put her phone down, feeling better.

At five to ten, she opened the interview link. She checked her camera again. She took a sip of water.

At one minute to ten, the doorbell rang.

Xiaoran froze.

She looked at the clock, then at the door, then back at the clock.

The doorbell rang again.

“Oh, no.”

She had ordered lunch for later. Not now, ten minutes before an interview.

She hurried to the door, trying to keep her blazer from catching on the handle.

“Hello?”

“Delivery!”

She opened the door just enough to look outside.

A delivery driver stood there holding a large paper bag.

“Miss Lin?”

“Yes.”

“Your order.”

Xiaoran glanced at the bag, then at the driver, then at her watch.

“Could you—could you just leave it outside? Thank you so much.”

The driver nodded.

“Okay.”

She was about to close the door when he looked at her again.

“Miss, are you going to a meeting?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Ah. Yes.”

“Good luck!”

She smiled back automatically.

“Thank you!”

And closed the door.

She stood there for a second, holding her breath.

Then she looked down.

The pajama shorts. The ducks.

The delivery driver had seen the ducks.

She pressed her lips together.

“Never mind.”

She hurried back to her desk.

The interview had already started.

A woman appeared on the screen, smiling politely.

“Good morning, Xiaoran. Can you hear us?”

“Good morning. Yes, I can hear you clearly.”

“Wonderful. Shall we begin?”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Of course.”

For the next twenty-five minutes, she was perfectly composed.

She spoke about her Media coursework, the film she had made with Chi Yuan, the noodle-shop campaign, and the freelance shoots she had been doing since her second year, the first of which had paid for a lens. She explained what she had learned from coordinating a student project and how she approached feedback when working with others. She answered questions thoughtfully. She asked questions of her own.

She even managed to make the interviewer laugh once.

Nothing about the conversation suggested that she was sitting in a bedroom wearing duck-print pajama shorts.

When the interview ended, she thanked the panel and closed the meeting.

Then she sat completely still.

For three seconds.

Four.

Five.

And then she exhaled.

“Oh, my God.”

She leaned back in her chair.

Her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Finished?

She called him immediately.

He answered while she was still trying to pull the blazer off.

“Hello?”

“Yichen.”

“How did it go?”

“I think it went well.”

“Good.”

“Really well, actually.”

“That’s even better.”

She smiled, then glanced down at her shorts.

“Except—”

He heard the change in her voice.

“Except?”

“The delivery driver saw me.”

There was a pause.

“What?”

She covered her face.

“He saw me.”

“Who?”

“The delivery driver!”

Yichen was quiet.

Then she heard it.

A low laugh.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re laughing.”

“I’m listening.”

“Yichen.”

He laughed properly this time.

Xiaoran groaned and dropped her head onto the desk.

“I was wearing a blazer. I looked so professional. And then he looked down and—”

“Did he say anything?”

“He asked if I was going to a meeting.”

“And?”

“I said yes.”

“Then?”

“He wished me good luck.”

Yichen laughed again.

She lifted her head.

“Why are you laughing? It’s embarrassing!”

“I think that’s quite sweet.”

“He saw my shorts.”

“Did he?”

“Yes!”

“Then perhaps he was wishing the ducks good luck too.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He was smiling so broadly that she could hear it in his voice.

She narrowed her eyes at her phone.

“I regret telling you.”

“No, you don’t.”

She was quiet.

Then, reluctantly, she smiled.

“Maybe not.”

“How about the interview? Forget the delivery driver. How do you feel?”

Xiaoran looked at the closed laptop.

“I think I represented myself well.”

“Then that’s what matters.”

She nodded, even though he couldn’t see her. “Yes.”

“Good,” he said, and her expression softened.

“You’re coming over later?”

“I have training this afternoon. I’ll come after.”

“Okay.”

“And Xiaoran?”

“Hm?”

“Next time, wear trousers.”

She gasped.

“You’re supposed to be on my side!”

“I’m on your side. I’m also on the side of trousers.”

She hung up.

He sent her a message thirty seconds later.

Yichen: Ducks and all. Well done.

She stared at it, then smiled, and went to rescue her lunch from the doorstep. It had gone cold. She ate it anyway, sitting on the floor in the blazer and the ducks.

At one, her mother messaged.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Did you have the interview?

Xiaoran: Yes. It went well.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Which company?

Xiaoran: A studio in Shanghai. First round.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Not the Beijing one.

Xiaoran: The Beijing one is later.

There was a pause, the kind her mother used to leave at the dinner table when a report card had come home.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Your father says good luck. He also says wear proper shoes next time.

Xiaoran: It was online.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): He knows. He says the shoes know.

Xiaoran looked down at her bare feet, and the ducks, and decided that her father had been a fortune-teller in a previous life and had never mentioned it.

When Yichen arrived that evening, Xiaoran was already waiting downstairs.

She had changed into a comfortable outfit, but the memory of the morning was still fresh enough that she glared at him as soon as he approached.

“Don’t.”

He raised his eyebrows.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face.”

“My face?”

“You’re smiling.”

He met her eyes.

Then, deliberately, he let his expression settle into something neutral.

“Better?”

She blinked at him.

“No.”

He reached for her hand.

“How did the rest of your day go?”

“Fine.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

They walked toward the building entrance.

“You didn’t look ridiculous. Your interview outfit was perfectly appropriate. From the waist up,” he said, before she could open her mouth. He paused for exactly as long as it took her to relax.

She stopped walking.

He laughed and pulled her gently toward him before she could turn away, and kissed her. “You did well.”

“Even with the ducks?”

“Ducks included.”

She finally laughed.

And, for the rest of the evening, he was sensible enough not to mention them again.

At least not until she was comfortably seated beside him, eating dinner.
