Then he asked, casually, “Do you think the delivery driver will recognize you next time?”

She threw a tissue at him. He caught it, folded it neatly into a square, and put it in his pocket, which she found more annoying than if he had thrown it back. It went home with him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The email came on Thursday, while she was in the library pretending to edit subtitles. Second round. In person. Tuesday, ten o’clock. Please bring your portfolio.

She sent him a screenshot.

Xiaoran: IN PERSON.

Yichen: Congratulations.

Xiaoran: I have to wear trousers.

Yichen: I’ll clear Saturday. We’ll practice.

Xiaoran: Practice what?

Yichen: Everything they could ask. Bring your notes. I’ll bring questions.

She looked at that, with the feeling, which she would come to know well over the next five days, of someone who has asked for help and is about to get far more of it than she bargained for.

chapters.desc: A weekend at her grandparents’ house, a promise ring, and by noon half the town believes she is engaged.
chapters.title: The Ring at Grandma’s
chapters.epigraph: “Does he treat you well?”
chapters.content:
By eleven in the morning, Xiaoran had accidentally become engaged. By noon, half the town knew.

By two, her grandmother had already started discussing wedding dates.

And all of it had begun with a ring.

The ring wasn’t new.

That was perhaps the most important detail, although Xiaoran would spend the entire afternoon wishing she’d remembered it sooner.

It was the promise ring Yichen had given her on their fifth anniversary, in December. A delicate band she wore on her right hand, simple enough that most people wouldn’t notice it unless they were looking closely.

She rarely took it off.

Yichen had never asked her to wear it every day, nor had he attached any conditions to it. It was something they had chosen together, a quiet reminder of a promise they had made long before graduation became something they could see approaching.

They hadn’t announced an engagement. They weren’t engaged.

They were still university students, still figuring out their next steps, still having conversations about where they might work and what kind of lives they wanted to build.

Yichen had told her that when the time came, he wanted to propose properly.

Flowers. A pretty dress. A moment she wouldn’t have to share with a dozen relatives asking whether she’d eaten enough.

Xiaoran had told him she expected all three.

He’d said he knew.

So, naturally, when she took the Friday-evening bus up to her grandparents’ house for the weekend, she had no reason to think the ring would cause trouble.

On Saturday morning she came downstairs just before breakfast was finished.

Her grandmother was in the kitchen, supervising a pot of soup while an aunt arranged fruit on the dining table. The house smelled of steamed buns, ginger, and something sweet simmering on the stove.

“Xiaoran!”

Grandma came out with a dish towel over her shoulder.

“You’re up. Why didn’t you get up earlier?”

“It’s half past seven.”

“Half past seven isn’t earlier.”

Xiaoran laughed and hugged her.

Grandma patted her back, then held her at arm’s length.

“You’re thinner.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I ate breakfast.”

“That doesn’t mean anything. Come inside.”

Xiaoran followed her into the kitchen, carrying the small bag of fruit she’d brought. She helped set the table, washed her hands, and sat down to peel an orange while her grandmother continued asking questions.

How were her classes? Was graduation coming soon? Had she found somewhere to work? Was she sleeping properly?

And, inevitably—

“Where’s Yichen?”

“In Shanghai. He has training, and a meeting with the club.”

“Still playing?”

“Of course.”

Grandma nodded.

“That boy is always busy.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“He’s in his final year too.”

“Then he should come visit. I haven’t seen him in a while.”

“I’ll tell him.”

Grandma looked at her.

“Does he still take care of you?”

Xiaoran peeled another strip of orange.

“Grandma.”

“What?”

“Why do you ask that every time?”

“Because I want to know.”

“He does.”

“Good.”

Grandma returned to the stove.

Xiaoran thought that was the end of it.

It wasn’t.

The first person to notice the ring was her grandmother’s neighbor, Auntie Fan.

She arrived shortly before eleven, carrying a container of homemade pickles and an enthusiasm for other people’s lives that Xiaoran had always found slightly alarming.

“Ah, Xiaoran! You’ve come back!”

“Hello, Auntie Fan.”

Auntie Fan took her hand.

“Look at you. You’re all grown up now.”

Xiaoran smiled politely, then the older woman noticed the ring.

Her fingers stopped.

“Oh?”

Xiaoran looked down.

“What?”

Auntie Fan lifted her hand slightly.

“This.”

Xiaoran glanced at the ring.

“Oh. This?”

Auntie Fan’s eyes widened.

“Is this...”

She didn’t finish the sentence.

She didn’t need to.

Xiaoran immediately understood.

“No, it’s not—”

“Grandma!”

Auntie Fan turned toward the kitchen before Xiaoran could finish.

“Your granddaughter is engaged!”

Xiaoran froze.

From the kitchen, her grandmother’s voice came back.

“What?”

“She’s engaged!”

“No, I’m not!” Xiaoran called.

But it was too late.

Grandma appeared in the doorway, wiping her hands on her apron.

“What did you say?”

Auntie Fan pointed at the ring.

“Look! She’s wearing a ring!”

Grandma stared.

Then she looked at Xiaoran, then at the ring again.

For a few seconds, she said nothing.

Finally, she asked, calmly, “When?”

Xiaoran nearly choked.

“Grandma, I’m not engaged!”

Auntie Fan looked confused.

“But the ring—”

“It’s a promise ring.”

There was silence.

Grandma blinked.

“A promise?”

“Yes.”

“From Yichen?”

Xiaoran nodded.

Grandma looked at the ring again.

Then her expression softened.

“Oh.”

Xiaoran relaxed slightly.

“Yes. So it’s not—”

“Then he’s promised to marry you?”

Xiaoran stared.

“Grandma!”

Auntie Fan covered her mouth.

Grandma, however, seemed to have found a perfectly reasonable conclusion.

“Well, that’s good.”

“It’s not an engagement!”

“Did I say it was?”

“You just asked when!”

“I was asking when he gave it to you.”

Xiaoran opened her mouth.

Closed it, then looked at Auntie Fan.

The older woman was already smiling.

Xiaoran had a terrible feeling.

By eleven thirty, her grandmother had called her aunt. By eleven forty, her aunt had called her uncle.

By eleven fifty, someone had mentioned it to the woman who ran the fruit shop.

And by noon, Xiaoran’s phone had started receiving messages.

Cousin Lele (Breaking News): Congratulations!!!

Xiaoran: For what?

Cousin Lele (Breaking News): Grandma said you’re getting married!

Xiaoran: I’M NOT.

Cousin Lele (Breaking News): She said Yichen gave you a ring.

Xiaoran: It’s a promise ring.

Cousin Lele (Breaking News): That’s what engagement is before the wedding.

Xiaoran put her phone away.

She looked across the dining table.

Her grandmother was speaking to Auntie Fan again.

She could hear the words Yichen, graduation, and young people these days.

Xiaoran slowly lowered her forehead onto the table.

Grandma glanced at her.

“Don’t put your head there. It’s not clean.”

“Grandma.”

“What?”

“Please stop telling people I’m engaged.”

“I’m not telling people that.”

“Then what are you telling them?”

“That Yichen gave you a ring.”

“That’s the same thing to everyone!”

Grandma considered this.

Then she said, “Well, you should have explained earlier.”

“I did!”

“You were too quick. I couldn’t hear properly.”

Xiaoran stared at her.

Grandma returned to her soup.

Yichen found out a little after noon. He was at the Herons training center, sitting on a bench while the physio wrapped an ice pack around his ankle.

His phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: I need you to know something.

He replied.

Yichen: What happened?

Three dots appeared.

Disappeared.

Appeared again.

Xiaoran: Apparently we’re engaged.

He looked at the message.

Then he smiled.

Yichen: Apparently?

Xiaoran: Don’t laugh.

His smile widened.

Yichen: I’m not laughing.

Xiaoran: You are. I can feel it.

The physio, who was watching him, said, “You look happy. Was it the ice?”

Yichen ignored him and continued typing.

Yichen: How did this happen?

Xiaoran: My ring.

Yichen: The one you wear every day?

Xiaoran: YES.

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: Auntie Fan saw it. Grandma thinks you promised to marry me. The whole town probably knows by now.

He leaned back against the wall.

Then he typed:

Yichen: Your grandmother isn’t wrong.

Xiaoran stared at her screen.

She read the message once, then again.

Xiaoran: YICHEN.

Yichen: What?

Xiaoran: You are supposed to help me.

Yichen: I am helping.

Xiaoran: HOW?

Yichen: By not denying that I intend to marry you.

She stared at the message.

Then her phone rang.

She answered immediately.

“Zhou Yichen.”

His voice came through, calm and amused.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“Don’t use that voice.”

“What voice?”

“That voice.”

He laughed.

“Are you embarrassed?”

“I’m being publicly married without my consent.”

“That’s a serious accusation.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little.”

She groaned.

He let her complain before asking, “Did your grandmother say anything else?”

“She asked when we’re getting married.”

“And what did you say?”

“I said we’re still in university.”

“Reasonable.”

“Then she said that doesn’t matter because people can plan early.”

Yichen smiled.

“Also reasonable.”

“You’re not helping!”

He laughed again.

Then his voice softened.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Did it upset you?”

She paused.

The question caught her off guard.

He wasn’t teasing now.

“No. Not really. It’s just embarrassing. Everyone keeps looking at my hand,” she admitted.

“Then take the ring off if you want.”

She looked down at it.

“No.”

“All right.”

“I like wearing it.”

“I know.”

She turned the ring slowly with her thumb.

Then she said, a little quieter, “I just don’t want everyone thinking we’re getting married tomorrow.”

Yichen was silent.

“We’re not getting married tomorrow.”

“I know.”

“And when I ask you properly, I won’t leave you to explain it to Auntie Fan.”

That made her grin.

“Good.”

“I’ll tell her myself.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Please don’t.”

“Why?”

“She’ll probably start planning the wedding before you’ve finished asking.”

Yichen laughed.

“Then I’ll have to be quick.”

She could picture his expression: the slight curve of his mouth, the calm eyes, the way he always seemed to know exactly when she was about to become flustered.

“You’re terrible,” she muttered.

“Happy to help.”

The next surprise came when Yichen arrived at her grandmother’s house that afternoon.

He hadn’t planned to come. But Xiaoran had mentioned that her grandmother wanted to see him, and his meeting finished at one, and the drive up was four hours if the expressway behaved. He arrived just before six, carrying a box of pastries.

Grandma opened the door.

“Yichen!”

He smiled and greeted her politely.

“Grandma.”

She took the pastry box from him.

“You came.”

“Xiaoran said you wanted to see me.”

“Of course. Come in.”

He stepped inside.

Xiaoran appeared from the living room.

The moment she saw him, she narrowed her eyes.

“You.”

He met her eyes.

“Me.”

“You’re here.”

“I am.”

She glanced at her grandmother, then back at him.

“Don’t say anything.”

Yichen’s mouth curved.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Good.”

Grandma looked between them.

“Why are you two standing at the door?”

Yichen took off his shoes.

“Sorry.”

Grandma ushered him inside, then immediately asked whether he had eaten.

He said yes.

She asked whether he wanted fruit.

He said he would.

She asked about his classes.

He answered.

And then, inevitably—

“Yichen.”

He turned toward her.

“Yes, Grandma?”

She looked at him with a smile.

“That ring you gave Xiaoran is very pretty.”

Xiaoran shut her eyes.

Yichen glanced at her hand, then back at Grandma.

“Thank you.”

Grandma nodded.

“She likes it very much.”

“I’m glad.”

“She wears it every day.”

“I’ve noticed.”

Xiaoran opened her eyes.

He looked perfectly composed.

Grandma smiled.

“Young people should have something to look forward to.”

Yichen nodded.

“Yes.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“Yichen.”

He turned to her.

“What?”

“You’re not supposed to agree with everything.”

He leaned slightly toward her and lowered his voice.

“Would you prefer I argue with your grandmother?”

She glared.

That got a smile out of him.

Grandma, who had clearly heard enough to understand the exchange, laughed.

Later, while Yichen helped her grandfather carry a few things from the storage room, Xiaoran sat with her grandmother in the living room.

Grandma was sorting old photographs.

She picked up one from several years ago.

It showed Xiaoran and Yichen at a family gathering, both younger, standing beside each other with awkward smiles.

Grandma looked at it for a while.

“You’ve been together a long time.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yes.”

“Since school.”

“Mm.”

Grandma put the photograph down.

“Does he treat you well?”

Xiaoran smiled.

“He does.”

“Do you treat him well?”

She laughed.

“I think so.”

Grandma nodded.

Then she reached for Xiaoran’s hand.

The ring caught the afternoon light.

“I know you’re not engaged,” she said.

Xiaoran looked up.

“You know?”

“Of course I know. You explained it to me five times.”

Xiaoran laughed.

Grandma rubbed her thumb gently over the back of her hand.

“I only thought it was nice.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

“What is?”

“That he gave you something you wanted to keep wearing.”

She looked down at the ring.

Grandma continued.

“You don’t have to rush. You’re still young. Finish your studies. Find your work. Build your own life.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“But it’s good to know someone is serious about you.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“He’s serious.”

“I can see that.”

Grandma leaned back.

“Just don’t let everyone else’s excitement make you feel you have to hurry.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

For all the teasing and the sudden rumors, her grandmother had understood something important.

She wasn’t asking Xiaoran to marry.

She was happy that her granddaughter had found someone who loved her.

“Okay,” Xiaoran said.

Grandma patted her hand.

“Now go and see whether your boyfriend needs help.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“He’s carrying boxes, Grandma. He’s fine.”

“Then go keep him company.”

When Yichen returned, Xiaoran was waiting by the courtyard.

He had rolled his sleeves up, and there was a little dust on one shoulder.

She walked over and brushed it away.

“Did you survive?”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Your grandfather is very efficient.”

“Meaning?”

“He gave me three more things to carry after I finished the first two.”

She laughed.

“That’s how he is.”

Yichen looked at her hand.

The ring was still there.

“Feeling better?”

She nodded.

“Grandma knows we’re not engaged.”

“Good.”

“She said we don’t have to hurry.”

He looked at her.

“She’s right.”

Xiaoran smiled.

Then she lifted her hand between them.

“Do you regret giving me this?”

His eyebrows lifted slightly.

“Why would I?”

“Because now the entire town thinks we’re getting married.”

He looked at the ring, then at her.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“No.”

He took her hand and turned it gently, his thumb brushing over the band.

“I gave it to you because I wanted you to have it. What other people think doesn’t change that.”

She met his eyes.

His expression was quiet, sincere.

Then he said, “Although I should probably prepare myself for your grandmother asking about wedding dates next time.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“She’ll ask you directly.”

“I’ll answer.”

“What will you say?”

He held her gaze.

“That I’ll ask when I’m ready to do it properly.”

Her smile softened.

“And when will that be?”

“Not today.”

She made a face.

He smiled.

“But I know what I want.”

She looked down, shy all at once.

He lifted her hand and kissed the ring.

“Come on. Your grandmother is waiting.”

She followed him inside, still smiling.

They stayed the night, Yichen in the guest room under the fishing rods, and when they left on Sunday morning Grandma had packed food for both of them, reminded Yichen to drive carefully, and told Xiaoran to bring him back next month.

The engagement rumor hadn’t been corrected.

Not completely.

But Xiaoran no longer minded quite so much.

After all, the ring was still on her finger.

And Yichen was still holding her hand.

chapters.desc: The second round is in person, so he clears his Saturday, puts on a dark shirt, and becomes the most difficult interviewer she has ever met.
chapters.title: Mock Interview
chapters.epigraph: “Why should we hire you?”
chapters.content:
“Good morning. Thank you for coming in today.”

Xiaoran looked up from her notes.

Yichen sat opposite her at the dining table, his laptop open, a glass of water beside him.

He wore a dark shirt, his hair neat, his expression so serious she almost laughed.

Almost.

She straightened in her chair.

“Good morning. Thank you for having me.”

He nodded once.

“Please introduce yourself.”

She took a breath.

“My name is Lin Xiaoran. I’m a final-year Media student, and I’m particularly interested in creative production, digital storytelling, and brand communication. During university, I’ve worked on several projects involving—”

“Stop.”

She blinked.

“What?”

“You’re reading.”

She looked down.

Her notes were on the table.

“I was referring to them.”

“You’ve been looking at them for the last twenty seconds.”

“Because they’re there.”

He leaned back.

“An interviewer won’t be sitting across from you to admire your notes.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“You’re supposed to be supportive.”

“I am.”

“You’re being mean.”

“I’m being accurate.”

She picked up her pen and pointed it at him.

“You’re enjoying this.”

His mouth twitched.

“Continue.”

She narrowed her eyes.

Then she took another breath.

This time, she looked directly at him.

“My name is Lin Xiaoran. I’m a final-year Media student with a strong interest in creative production and brand storytelling. Throughout university, I’ve developed experience in content planning, visual communication, and working with different teams to deliver projects within deadlines.”

Yichen nodded.

“Better.”

She relaxed slightly.

“Thank you.”

“Can you tell me about a project you’re particularly proud of?”

She answered more confidently.

She talked about a university project, how she had approached the concept, the research she had done, the challenges her team had faced, and the final result.

Yichen listened without interrupting.

When she finished, he glanced at his notes.

“What was your specific contribution?”

She explained.

“What would you do differently if you had another opportunity?”

She paused, then answered.

“Probably spend more time validating the initial concept before moving into production. We had a few assumptions that changed later, and that affected our timeline.”

“Why didn’t you validate them earlier?”

She blinked.

“Because we were working with limited time.”

“That’s a constraint. Not an explanation.”

She met his eyes.

He looked back.

Calm. Patient.

Absolutely relentless.

Xiaoran took a sip of water.

“I think we relied too heavily on our initial understanding of the audience. We could have tested the idea with a smaller group before committing to the full production.”

Yichen nodded.

“Good.”

She exhaled.

Then he asked, “What did you learn from that experience?”

She smiled.

“That being excited about an idea isn’t the same as knowing it will work.”

Yichen’s expression softened slightly.

“That’s a good answer.”

She smiled back.

Then he turned a page.

“Tell me about a time you had a disagreement with a teammate.”

Xiaoran’s smile disappeared.

“Oh, no.”

“What?”

“That question.”

“It’s a common question.”

“I know. I hate it.”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t want to sound like I’m blaming someone.”

“Then don’t blame someone.”

She looked at him.

He waited.

She eventually began answering.

She described a group project where one teammate had repeatedly missed deadlines, how she had tried to understand the reason, how she had communicated the impact on the rest of the team, and how they had eventually reorganized the work.

Yichen listened.

Then he asked, “What if the teammate still refused to cooperate?”

“I’d escalate it to the project lead.”

“After how long?”

“After trying to resolve it directly.”

“How many attempts?”

She frowned.

“Why are you asking for a number?”

“Because ‘after trying’ can mean anything.”

She looked at him for several seconds.

Then she laughed.

“You’re a terrible boyfriend.”

His mouth curved.

“Shall I go easier on you?”

“Don’t you dare.”

“Then answer the question.”

She shook her head, smiling despite herself.

They had planned the mock interview for the evening.

Xiaoran had her second-round interview at Morrow Studio on Tuesday, in person, in trousers. She had already researched the company, prepared her portfolio, and written down possible questions.

She knew she could do the work.

What worried her was the interview itself.

She sometimes spoke too quickly when nervous. Sometimes she overexplained. Sometimes she knew exactly what she wanted to say but couldn’t find the right opening sentence.

Yichen had offered to help.

She had accepted.

She hadn’t expected him to become so convincingly professional.

After another few questions, she finally put her pen down.

“Can we have a break?”

Yichen checked the time.

“Five minutes.”

“Ten.”

“Seven.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re negotiating my break?”

“Yes.”

“Fine.”

He closed the laptop halfway.

Then he reached across the table and pushed her glass of water closer.

“Drink.”

She did.

He watched her.

“You’re doing well.”

She turned to him.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“You’re not just saying that because I’m your girlfriend?”

“No.”

She tilted her head.

“Then what?”

“Because your answers are good. You understand what you’ve done, and you can explain why you made certain decisions. You just need to stop treating every question like there’s one perfect answer you’re supposed to guess.”

She looked down at her notes.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

She nodded.

He reached over and turned her notebook toward himself.

“You’ve written full paragraphs for every possible question.”

“Preparation.”

“These are speeches.”

“They help me.”

“Then keep them. But don’t memorise them.”

She sighed.

“I get nervous.”

“I know.”

He reached for her hand.

His thumb brushed over her knuckles.

“You don’t need to sound like someone else.”

“That’s easy for you to say.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re good at interviews.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Who told you that?”

“You.”

“I’ve never told you that.”

“You always sound calm.”

“That’s different from being good.”

She studied him.

Then she smiled.

“Are you nervous about your own future?”

He was quiet.

“Sometimes.”

She looked at him with interest.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“About the contract?”

“Among other things.”

She squeezed his hand.

“You’re allowed to be nervous too.”

That got a smile out of him.

“I know.”

She leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“Okay. Seven minutes are over.”

He looked at the clock.

“Not yet.”

She laughed.

The second half of the mock interview was worse.

For Xiaoran, at least.

Yichen had moved from general questions to situational ones.

“Imagine you’re given a brief with an unrealistic deadline. What would you do?”

“Clarify the scope.”

“Then?”

“Identify priorities.”

“Then?”

“Discuss the timeline with the team.”

“What if the client refuses to extend the deadline?”

“Then I’d look at what can realiztically be delivered within the existing timeframe.”

“What if the client insists that everything must be delivered?”

She frowned.

“I’d explain the trade-offs.”

“What if they don’t accept them?”

“Yichen.”

He looked up.

“Yes?”

“Do you want me to get the job or not?”

He smiled.

“Very much.”

“Then stop trying to make me fail.”

“I’m trying to prepare you for someone who won’t make the questions easier.”

She sat back.

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am. That’s why I’m asking.”

He said it so that she stopped. He wasn’t smiling now.

He genuinely wanted her to be prepared.

Xiaoran took a breath.

“Fine. Ask me again.”

He did.

This time, she answered more carefully.

She explained how she would clarify the client’s priorities, assess the available resources, communicate realiztic expectations, and propose alternatives rather than saying no.

Yichen listened.

Then he nodded.

“Good.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Thank you.”

“One more.”

She groaned.

“How many more?”

“Two.”

“You said one more.”

“I said one more. That was one.”

She stared at him.

He laughed under his breath.

“Next question.”

The final question was one Xiaoran hadn’t prepared for.

Yichen looked down at his notes.

Then he asked, “Why should we hire you?”

She opened her mouth.

Nothing came out.

He waited, then away.

“I think...”

She stopped.

He didn’t interrupt.

She tried again.

“I think I’m a good fit because...”

Her fingers moved against the edge of the notebook.

She knew what she wanted to say.

She had worked hard. She had a portfolio she was proud of. She had learned to work with people, manage deadlines, and adapt when things didn’t go according to plan.

But somehow, saying it out loud felt different.

Yichen waited.

She looked up.

“I think I’m a good fit because I care about the work I produce. I don’t just want to finish a brief. I want to understand what it’s trying to achieve and how the final result will connect with the people it’s meant for. I know I still have a lot to learn, but I’m curious, and I’m willing to put in the work. I also know how to take feedback without losing sight of the original objective.”

Her voice became steadier.

“I think I can contribute a fresh perspective, but I also know when to listen. And I want to be somewhere that challenges me to become better.”

She finished.

The room was quiet.

Yichen closed his notebook.

“Thank you.”

“How was it?”

He met her eyes.

“Good.”

She waited.

His mouth curved.

“Very good.”

She leaned back, exhaling.

Then she covered her face.

“Oh, thank goodness.”

Yichen laughed.

A few minutes later, she moved to sit beside him.

“Was I really okay?”

He turned toward her.

“Yes.”

“Which answer was best?”

“The last one.”

“Why?”

“Because you stopped trying to say what you thought they wanted to hear.”

She held his gaze.

“You think I should answer more naturally?”

“I think you should answer honestly and clearly. Preparation is useful, but you can’t prepare for every possible question.”

She nodded.

Then she leaned against his shoulder.

“Thank you.”

He kissed her hair.

“You’re welcome.”

She looked up.

“Would you hire me?”

He considered it.

“Yes.”

Her face brightened.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

Then he said, “Although I’d need to discuss your habit of negotiating every break.”

She hit his arm.

“You’re not funny.”

“I’m a very fair interviewer.”

“You’re a terrible interviewer.”

He smiled.

“Would you like to give me feedback?”

She sat up straight.

“Yes, actually.”

He raised his eyebrows.

She pointed at him.

“First, you were too serious.”

“Noted.”

“Second, you asked too many follow-up questions.”

“That’s the point.”

“Third, you didn’t smile enough.”

He looked at her.

“Would you like me to smile during the actual interview?”

“Yes. It would be less intimidating.”

He leaned closer, a slow smile appearing.

“Like this?”

Xiaoran went quiet.

She looked at his face.

Then she looked away.

Yichen waited.

“Is that better?”

She pressed her lips together.

“...No.”

His smile deepened.

“Why not?”

“Because that’s not a normal interview smile.”

“What kind of smile is it?”

She picked up her notebook and hid behind it.

“Stop.”

He laughed.

On Tuesday, Xiaoran had her real interview. She had slept at his flat on Monday, because it was twenty minutes closer to the studio, and because she had asked.

She wore a simple blouse, a blazer, and the earrings she’d chosen the night before.

Yichen was sitting at the dining table when she came out of the bedroom.

He looked up.

Then he smiled.

“You look good.”

She turned once.

“Is it too formal?”

“No.”

“Too plain?”

“No.”

“Should I wear the other earrings?”

He stood and walked over.

He adjusted the edge of her blazer, then tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“You’re ready.”

She took a breath.

He held her gaze.

“Remember what we practiced.”

“Don’t memorise speeches.”

“Good.”

“Answer honestly.”

“Good.”

“Don’t treat every question like there’s one perfect answer.”

“Exactly.”

She nodded.

Then she reached for his hand.

“And if I get nervous?”

He squeezed her fingers.

“Take a breath. You don’t have to rush.”

She smiled.

He pressed a kiss to her temple.

“Good luck.”

She left with her portfolio and a confidence that felt a little more solid than it had the night before.

When she returned, Yichen was still at the table.

He looked up immediately.

“How was it?”

She put her bag down.

Then she stood in front of him.

He waited.

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I think it went well.”

His expression softened.

She began telling him about the interview.

There had been a question she hadn’t anticipated, but she had managed to answer it. The interviewer had asked about her portfolio, and they had spent a long time discussing one particular project. She had even asked questions of her own.

Yichen listened without interrupting.

When she finished, he reached for her hand. “You went in and said what you meant.”

“Even if I don’t get it?”

“Even then. The result matters, but it isn’t the only thing that matters.”

She tilted her head.

Then she leaned down and hugged him.

He wrapped his arms around her waist.

After a moment, she murmured against his shoulder, “You know what?”

“Hm?”

“I think you should charge people for mock interviews.”

He laughed.

“Would you recommend me?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Too intimidating.”

He kissed her cheek.

“Unfair review.”

She pulled back, smiling.

“One star.”

“Out of five?”

“One.”

He shook his head, amused.

Then she kissed him.

And for once, Yichen didn’t have a follow-up question.

chapters.desc: The camera was supposed to be off. She comes back to find forty minutes of him talking to it.
chapters.title: The Footage She Didn’t Use
chapters.epigraph: “Come back soon. I miss you.”
chapters.content:
The camera was supposed to be off.

That was the first mistake.

The second was leaving Yichen alone with it.

Xiaoran had been working on a short documentary-style university project for her final-year portfolio. It was about the routines people built around things they loved: the quiet repetitions, the unremarkable moments, the small habits that made a life feel like theirs.

She had initially considered interviewing athletes, then she’d considered musicians.

Then she’d decided she didn’t want to spend another week arranging interviews with strangers who might cancel at the last minute.

Yichen had volunteered.

Not because he was interested in being filmed, but because he knew she needed someone reliable.

He’d given her his one free afternoon of the week at the university court, where the Herons let him shoot on his days off, so she could film a few parts of his routine.

The project itself was going well.

The problem was that Xiaoran had a habit of forgetting to stop recording.

And Yichen had a habit of noticing when she was distracted.

That afternoon, she had placed the camera on a tripod near the side of the court while she checked the framing. The red recording light was on, but she wasn’t looking at the monitor.

“Yichen, can you stand there for a moment?”

He moved into position.

“Here?”

“A little to the left.”

He moved.

“Your other left.”

He met her eyes.

She frowned at the camera.

“Sorry. Your right.”

He moved again.

“Good.”

She adjusted the lens.

“Can you look toward the court?”

He did.

“Not like you’re posing.”

He turned to her.

“I’m not posing.”

“You look like you’re posing.”

“What should I do?”

“Just stand.”

He stood.

She watched the screen.

“Perfect.”

Then she walked away to retrieve the microphone she’d left on the bench.

Yichen remained in position for a few seconds.

Then he looked toward the camera.

“Is this still recording?”

No answer.

He glanced toward the entrance.

Xiaoran was nowhere nearby.

He looked back at the lens.

“Xiaoran?”

Silence.

He waited.

Then he sat down on the bench beside the camera.

“You’re not here.”

His voice came through the small microphone.

He looked at the camera.

“Obviously. You’re probably looking for something.”

He leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees.

“Your water bottle, perhaps. You left it near the equipment bag. Or your phone. You were looking for that ten minutes ago.”

He glanced toward the court.

A few teammates were practicing at the far end.

Then he looked back at the camera.

“I think you put it in your tote bag.”

He paused again.

“Actually, you put it in the side pocket. The one you never use because you say things disappear in it.”

He shook his head, amused.

“You’re very organized for someone who loses everything.”

A ball bounced somewhere behind him.

He turned his head, then looked back.

“Do you know what I think?”

He waited, as if expecting an answer.

“You probably won’t use this footage.”

Something in his face eased.

“You’re very particular about your projects. You’ll watch it later, decide the lighting is wrong, and delete the entire thing.”

He leaned back.

“Or you’ll say I didn’t look natural.”

A small pause.

“Which is strange, because I think I’m being quite natural.”

He glanced at the camera.

“Are you still there?”

The recording continued.

By the time Xiaoran returned, Yichen had been talking for nearly ten minutes.

She appeared from the corridor carrying her water bottle, a notebook, and the missing microphone.

“Sorry! I couldn’t find the—”

She stopped.

Yichen was sitting on the bench, looking directly at the camera.

He turned toward her.

“Found it?”

“Yes. I thought I’d left it in the editing room.”

He glanced at the microphone in her hand.

“Good.”

She put the equipment down.

“Are you ready?”

“Whenever you are.”

She checked the camera screen.

The recording was still running.

She blinked.

“Oh.”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“Nothing. I forgot to stop it.”

He laughed under his breath.

“I noticed.”

She pressed the button.

The red light disappeared.

“Sorry.”

“Don’t worry.”

She picked up the camera and checked the footage.

The timeline was longer than expected.

“Forty minutes?”

Yichen looked at the screen.

“Is that how long?”

“Yes.”

“What did I do?”

“Apparently, you talked to my camera.”

He smiled.

“Did it answer?”

“No.”

“Rude.”

She laughed.

Then she began packing up.

She didn’t think much about the recording.

Not until she returned to her apartment that evening and opened the files.

The first few minutes were ordinary.

Yichen talking about training. Yichen adjusting his position.

Yichen waiting.

Then came the part where he noticed she was gone.

Xiaoran smiled.

She continued watching.

He talked about her water bottle.

Then her phone, then the way she misplaced things.

She laughed.

“You’re so annoying.”

She kept watching.

At around the fifteen-minute mark, he started talking about her project.

He described the way she had explained the concept to him the previous night, sitting cross-legged on her bed with her laptop balanced on her knees. He remembered the exact words she’d used.

He even remembered that she’d changed the title three times.

Xiaoran stopped smiling quite so broadly.

He wasn’t talking to an audience. He wasn’t giving an interview. He wasn’t trying to make himself sound interesting.

He was speaking to a camera she had forgotten was recording, in the same easy tone he used when she was beside him.

At twenty-three minutes, he started talking about the first time she’d brought him to the sports center during their first year.

He remembered her getting lost. He remembered her calling him from outside the wrong building.

He remembered walking across campus to find her, only to discover she was standing in front of the correct building but had entered through the opposite side.

Xiaoran covered her mouth.

She remembered that day.

She’d been so embarrassed.

He’d never mentioned it again.

Until now.

At twenty-eight minutes, he looked directly into the lens.

“She’s probably going to complain about this later.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“She doesn’t like being filmed when she’s not ready.”

Xiaoran’s fingers rested on the trackpad.

“She’ll say she looks strange, or that she wasn’t prepared, or that I should have told her. But I think she looks nice when she forgets the camera is there.”

Xiaoran stopped moving.

Yichen looked down, then back up.

“She does that thing where she talks to herself when she’s concentrating. Sometimes she reads things out loud. Sometimes she makes a face at her laptop.”

His smile widened.

“She thinks nobody notices.”

A quiet laugh escaped him.

“I notice.”

Xiaoran felt her cheeks warm.

She lowered the laptop screen slightly, as if someone might catch her watching.

Then she opened it again.

The last twelve minutes were different.

Yichen had moved from the bench to the floor, sitting with his back against the wall. His training session had ended, and the court behind him was empty.

He was looking at the camera without much expression.

Then he spoke.

“You’re taking a long time.”

A pause.

“Which probably means you’ve forgotten something again.”

Something in his face eased.

“I don’t mind waiting.”

He glanced toward the entrance.

“Actually, I do mind a little. I’m hungry.”

Xiaoran laughed.

Then he looked back at the camera.

“Do you remember what you said about this project?”

He was quiet.

“You said you wanted to film ordinary things because people always think the important moments are the big ones.”

He tilted his head.

“I think that’s true.”

He looked down at his hands.

“Most of the time, I don’t remember what I did on a particular day. I remember that you were there. Or that you sent me a photograph of something ridiculous. Or that you were annoyed because I finished your drink.”

Xiaoran smiled.

He continued.

“Sometimes I think you don’t realize how much of my day is made up of little things involving you.”

Her smile faded into something softer.

Yichen looked toward the court again, then back at the camera.

“I don’t know if that’s useful for your project. Probably not.”

He smiled.

“But I thought I’d tell you anyway.”

A few seconds passed. Then, almost casually, to the empty room: “Come back soon. I miss you.”

The recording continued for another minute.

He didn’t say anything else.

He sat there, waiting.

Xiaoran watched the footage twice.

The second time, she paused at the moment he said he missed her.

She stared at the screen.

Then she closed the laptop.

For several minutes, she sat.

It wasn’t that the footage was dramatic. There was no grand confession, no carefully prepared speech, no moment that would make a stranger understand everything about their relationship.

It was just Yichen.

Talking to a camera because he thought she might be somewhere nearby.

Remembering things she had forgotten.

Noticing things she didn’t realize anyone noticed.

Waiting.

She opened the project folder.

The documentary was already close to its final edit. She had enough footage of Yichen’s training routine, the sound of basketballs against the floor, the squeak of shoes, the quiet conversations between drills.

The forty minutes didn’t belong there.

It wasn’t part of the story she was trying to tell.

And she wasn’t going to put something so personal into a university submission because it was beautiful.

She created a separate folder.

Unused Footage.

Then she renamed the file.

Yichen — 40 minutes.

She hesitated.

Deleted the generic title.

And changed it again.

For Xiaoran.

Yichen came over the following afternoon, up the four flights, and found her sitting at her desk with her laptop open and two cups of tea beside her.

“Working?”

“Almost finished.”

He placed a small paper bag beside her.

“I brought you something.”

She looked inside.

A pastry from the bakery she liked.

Her face brightened.

“Thank you.”

He leaned down to kiss her forehead.

“How’s the project?”

“Good.”

“Finished editing?”

“Almost.”

He pulled out the chair beside her.

“Can I see?”

She hesitated.

“Not yet.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to show you when it’s finished.”

“All right.”

He took his tea.

Xiaoran watched him.

Then she turned the laptop slightly toward herself.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you remember the other day, when I left the camera recording?”

He held her gaze.

“Yes.”

“You talked to it.”

“I did.”

“For forty minutes.”

He blinked.

“Forty?”

“Yes.”

He took a sip of tea.

“That’s longer than I expected.”

She met his eyes.

“You knew it was recording?”

“At first, I wasn’t sure.”

“And then?”

“Then I realized.”

She stared.

“You knew?”

He nodded.

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you stop?”

He considered the question.

“You weren’t there.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

That got a smile out of him.

“I thought you might find it later.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

Then she asked, “What if I had deleted it?”

“Then you would have deleted it.”

“Just like that?”

“Yes.”

He looked at her.

“It’s your camera.”

She felt something warm settle in her chest.

“Did you mean everything you said?”

His expression changed slightly.

Not surprised.

Just softer.

“You watched it?”

She nodded.

He looked down at his tea, then smiled.

“That’s a lot of listening.”

She nudged his arm.

“Yichen.”

“Yes.”

“Did you mean it?”

He turned toward her.

“Which part?”

She looked at him, embarrassed.

“The part about noticing things.”

He reached over and tucked a strand of hair behind her ear.

“Yes.”

She lowered her eyes.

“And the part about missing me?”

His smile became quieter. “That part most.”

She turned to him.

Neither spoke.

Then she leaned forward and kissed him.

He returned it gently, one hand resting against her cheek.

When she pulled away, he brushed his thumb beneath her eye, though she wasn’t crying.

“Why?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

That made her grin.

“I just like you.”

He laughed.

“That’s fortunate.”

“Very.”

A week later, the final project was submitted.

Xiaoran received a good mark and a few encouraging comments from her lecturer about the natural quality of her footage and her attention to detail.

Yichen asked to see the finished version.

She showed him.

He watched the entire documentary without interrupting.

When it ended, he looked at her. “I liked the way you edited the sound.”

She brightened.

“Really?”

“And the sequence near the end.”

“Which one?”

“The empty court.”

She held his gaze.

He said, “It felt familiar.”

She smiled.

“That was my favorite part too.”

He closed the laptop.

“Where’s the footage you didn’t use?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“What footage?”

“The forty minutes.”

She tried to look innocent.

“Oh. That.”

“Yes.”

She hesitated, then opened the folder.

He read the filename.

For Xiaoran.

His expression softened.

“You kept it.”

“Of course.”

He studied her.

“Why?”

She shrugged, embarrassed.

“Because I liked it.”

He didn’t say anything.

She said, “It’s not for the project. It’s just... for me.”

Yichen looked back at the screen.

The video thumbnail showed him sitting on the sports center bench, looking slightly amused.

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Then keep it.”

“I will.”

She closed the folder.

He reached for her hand.

“Although, next time, you should tell me when you’re recording.”

“Why?”

“So I can prepare something more interesting.”

She laughed.

“You talked for forty minutes without knowing what to say.”

“I knew what to say.”

“About my water bottle?”

“An important subject.”

She shook her head.

He leaned closer.

“Would you like another forty minutes?”

“No.”

“Thirty?”

“Yichen.”

“Twenty?”

She laughed and pushed his shoulder.

He caught her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“All right.”

“But I meant what I said,” he said, more.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Which part?”

“That I don’t mind waiting.”

She leaned against his shoulder.

“I know.”

“And that I miss you when you’re gone.”

“I know.”

He pressed his mouth to her hair.

“Good.”

She stayed beside him, their hands linked on the desk. The forty minutes stayed in their folder, For Xiaoran, which she never submitted, never showed her lecturer, and backed up to three separate drives.

chapters.desc: Her portfolio documentary is due tomorrow afternoon, and the render has been stuck at 98% for forty minutes.
chapters.title: Render Queue
chapters.epigraph: “I like that it’s quiet.”
chapters.content:
At a quarter to midnight, Xiaoran sent Yichen a message.

Xiaoran: It’s stuck.

He was brushing his teeth when the message arrived.

He finished, rinsed his mouth, and replied.

Yichen: What’s stuck?

Xiaoran: The render.

Yichen: How long?

Xiaoran: It says 98%.

He looked at the time.

Yichen: For how long?

Xiaoran: Forty minutes.

He stared at the screen.

Then video-called her. She answered with the expression of someone who had been personally betrayed by technology.

“Hello.”

“Have you tried leaving it alone?”

“Yes.”

“Have you tried restarting it?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s at 98%.”

He closed his eyes.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“How long has it been at 98%?”

“Forty minutes.”

“Then it’s probably not going to finish by itself.”

She looked at her screen.

“Don’t say that.”

He laughed.

The project was Xiaoran’s final-year portfolio documentary.

She had spent weeks editing footage, correcting color, adjusting sound, and making small changes that nobody else would probably notice.

The deadline was the next afternoon.

She had already exported a test version, checked the subtitles, and sent a rough cut to her supervisor.

This was supposed to be the final render.

It had been going well.

Until it wasn’t.

Yichen arrived seven minutes later, from across the road and up four flights, with two drinks and a small bag of food from the all-night shop.

He found Xiaoran sitting cross-legged in front of her laptop, staring at the progress bar.

“You’re still watching it?”

She looked up.

“Look.”

He set the drinks down and crouched beside her.

The screen showed 98%.

He examined the export settings.

“What’s the file format?”

She told him.

“Resolution?”

She told him.

“Frame rate?”

She told him.

He nodded.

“All right.”

She watched him.

“Can you fix it?”

“Maybe.”

“That’s not reassuring.”

“I haven’t looked at it yet.”

He pulled the chair closer.

She moved aside, making room.

Yichen checked the export settings, then opened the task manager to see whether the editing software was still responding.

“It hasn’t crashed,” he said.

“Then why isn’t it moving?”

“Could be processing a particularly heavy section.”

“Which section?”

He checked the timeline.

“Do you have any effects near the end?”

“Color grading. Some overlays. A few transitions.”

“How many?”

She gave him a number.

He met her eyes.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“That’s quite a lot.”

“It’s a documentary.”

“I know.”

He looked at the timeline again.

“Have you saved a copy of the project?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He leaned back slightly.

“Let’s not touch the original. We’ll try a lower-resolution test export of the last section and see whether there’s a problem there.”

She nodded.

He guided her through the steps, letting her handle the software herself while he pointed out where to check the settings.

The test export began.

This time, it finished.

Xiaoran exhaled.

“Oh.”

Yichen looked at her.

“That tells us the timeline itself is probably fine.”

“Then why—”

“Could be a memory issue, or one of the effects. We’ll narrow it down.”

She met his eyes.

“You sound like you’re fixing a business problem.”

“Is that an insult?”

“It’s a description.”

He kissed her temple.

“Let’s get your project exported first.”

They spent the next hour working through the timeline.

Yichen didn’t take over.

He didn’t pretend to know the editing software better than she did. He asked questions, helped her identify the heavy sections, and suggested testing smaller portions rather than restarting the entire process blindly.

Xiaoran removed one unnecessary effect, adjusted a few settings, and tried again.

The render reached 24%.

While it crawled, he made her drink half of what he’d brought, and she made him watch the opening, which was her grandmother’s hands shelling peas in the courtyard in the town, filmed the summer before, and which nobody but her grandmother had seen. He watched it without saying anything, which was the right thing to say. She had known he would. The bar moved.

Then 51%.

Then 76%.

She sat still.

Yichen watched the progress bar.

At 89%, she grabbed his wrist.

He looked down at her hand.

“What’s wrong?”

“Don’t move.”

He glanced at the screen.

“Why?”

“You’re going to jinx it.”

He stared at her, then slowly sat back.

“All right.”

At 94%, she stopped breathing.

At 97%, she leaned closer.

At 99%, she whispered, “Please.”

The progress bar moved.

100%.

The export completed.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

Then she threw both arms around Yichen.

“It finished!”

He laughed, catching her.

“Congratulations.”

She squeezed him.

“We did it!”

That got a smile out of him.

“You did it.”

“No, you helped.”

“I mostly sat here.”

“You were emotionally supportive.”

“That’s an important contribution.”

She pulled back and looked at him.

“Don’t make fun of me.”

“I’m not.”

She kissed his cheek.

Then she turned back to the laptop and checked the file.

The video opened. The first few seconds played. The sound was there. The image was clear.

The subtitles were aligned.

She moved forward through the timeline.

Everything looked fine.

Then she reached the final sequence.

A quiet shot of the university basketball court after training.

Yichen appeared in the frame, walking away from the camera.

That made her grin.

“Look.”

He leaned closer.

“That’s good.”

“You like it?”

“Yes.”

She watched the sequence again.

Then she glanced at him.

“I almost removed this shot.”

“Why?”

“I thought it was too long.”

He looked at the screen.

“I like that it’s quiet.”

“Me too.”

At twenty past one, Xiaoran finally closed the editing software.

She stretched her arms over her head.

Yichen handed her a drink.

“Eat something.”

She looked at the bag he’d brought.

“What did you get?”

“Something you like.”

She opened it.

Inside were two small sandwiches and a packet of fruit.

She smiled.

“You remembered.”

“I know what you eat when you’re working late.”

She took a bite.

Yichen sat beside her, looking at the exported file on the screen.

“Have you backed it up?”

She stopped chewing, then looked at him.

“...Yes.”

“Where?”

“External drive.”

“And?”

“Cloud storage.”

He nodded.

“Good.”

She swallowed.

“You’re very thorough.”

“Someone has to be.”

She leaned into his shoulder.

“Thank you for coming.”

He kissed her hair.

“You sounded like you were about to fight your laptop.”

“I was.”

“I could tell.”

She laughed.

Then she looked at the screen again.

The finished project sat in its folder, finally rendered, safely backed up, and ready for submission.

“Do you think it’ll be good enough?”

Yichen turned toward her.

“You’ve spent weeks making it.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

He considered the question.

“I think it reflects the work you’ve put into it. And I think there are parts you’ll still want to improve when you watch it tomorrow.”

She groaned.

“Don’t tell me that.”

He smiled.

“But tonight, it’s finished.”

She looked at him, then nodded.

“Tonight, it’s finished.”

He kissed her cheek.

“Come on. Let’s get you to bed.”

She reached for his hand.

“Can we watch the last sequence once more?”

He glanced at the clock.

“Once.”

“Promise.”

He sat back down beside her.

They watched the empty court, the soft lighting, and the final shot of the basketball rolling slowly to a stop near the baseline.

When the screen faded to black, Xiaoran closed the laptop.

Yichen looked at her, and she nodded, and he stood and offered her his hand.

She took it.

She slept four and a half hours.

When she woke, the studio smelled of coffee, which was wrong, because she didn’t own anything that made coffee. On the desk, beside the closed laptop, there was a paper cup from the shop downstairs, still warm, and a note in his slanted handwriting.

Training at 9. Backed it up a fourth time, to your blue drive. Don’t watch it again before you submit. (You will.)

She watched it again before she submitted. Twice. The second time, she changed nothing at all, which she decided counted as personal growth.

At two minutes to two, she uploaded it. The submission portal thought about it for an alarming length of time, long enough for her to stand up, sit down, and consider a career in accounting, and then showed a green tick and a line of small gray text: Submission received.

She took a screenshot, because she wasn’t a fool, and then a second one, in case.

Xiaoran: Submitted.

Yichen: At what percent?

Xiaoran: Very funny. It said 100.

Yichen: Then it’s finished.

Xiaoran: You said that last night.

Yichen: It was true last night too.

At four, her supervisor answered the submission with a single line, which was more than he usually gave anyone: Received. The ending is good.

She read it six times. Then she sent Yichen a screenshot of that as well.

Yichen: I told you. I liked that it’s quiet.

Xiaoran: You did.

Yichen: Go to sleep. Properly. In a bed.

She went to bed at nine, in daylight, and slept for eleven hours, and for once there was nothing left in the queue.

chapters.desc: Their mothers have started a group chat about flowers. Their fathers have still exchanged nothing but a nod.
chapters.title: The Mothers’ Group Chat
chapters.epigraph: “Your father fishes. Mine golfs.”
chapters.content:
The first flower arrangement arrived on a Tuesday morning.

Xiaoran hadn’t thought much of it when her mother sent her a photograph.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Look what arrived.

The photograph showed a beautiful arrangement of pale pink tulips, white roses, and little sprigs of greenery. It sat on the dining table at home, wrapped in cream paper and tied with a soft pink ribbon.

Xiaoran smiled.

Xiaoran: Pretty! Who sent it?

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Yichen’s mother.

She paused, then another message arrived.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): She said she saw them and thought I’d like them.

Xiaoran looked at the photograph again.

It was a lovely arrangement. Not extravagant, not overly formal. Just thoughtful.

She typed a reply.

Xiaoran: That’s so sweet of her.

Her mother sent a heart.

Then, a few minutes later, another photograph.

This one showed a second arrangement.

Yellow freesias and white lisianthus.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): I sent these to her in return.

Xiaoran laughed.

Xiaoran: Already?

Mom (Accounts Dept.): I can’t be the only one receiving flowers.

She put her phone down, still smiling.

It was a small thing.

Until the next morning.

At 9:12 a.m., Yichen’s mother sent a message to Xiaoran.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Good morning, Xiaoran. Have you eaten?

Xiaoran smiled at the familiar question.

Xiaoran: Good morning, Auntie! Yes, I have. Have you?

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): I have. Your mother sent me some lovely flowers yesterday.

Xiaoran: I saw! They’re beautiful.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): She has very good taste.

Xiaoran laughed.

Xiaoran: I’ll tell her.

A few seconds later, the older woman sent another message.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): I hope you like the flowers I sent her.

Xiaoran: She loved them. She said they were very pretty.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Good. I wasn’t sure whether she preferred pink or white.

Xiaoran smiled at the screen.

Xiaoran: She likes both.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Then I’ll remember that.

She put her phone down, then picked it up again.

Something about the conversation felt oddly familiar.

As if she were watching two people become friends through flower arrangements.

By Thursday, the flowers had become a regular topic.

Her mother sent Xiaoran a photograph of the tulips opening.

Yichen’s mother sent a picture of a new arrangement she’d made herself.

Her mother replied with a photograph of the flowers in a different vase.

And then Xiaoran received a message from Yichen.

Yichen: Do you know why my mother is asking me whether your mother likes hydrangeas?

She couldn’t help smiling.

Xiaoran: Because they’re becoming friends.

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: What’s wrong?

Yichen: Nothing. My mother has asked me to find out whether your mother prefers blue or white hydrangeas.

Xiaoran laughed.

Xiaoran: Ask her.

Yichen: I did.

Xiaoran: And?

Yichen: She said both, depending on the season.

Xiaoran sent him a laughing sticker.

Yichen: I’m beginning to think I’m being used as a flower information service.

Xiaoran: You’re doing a very important job.

Yichen: I’ll add it to my résumé.

The real surprise came that weekend.

Xiaoran was home for the weekend when her mother called her into the living room.

“Look.”

She held out her phone.

A new group chat was open.

The Flower Corner

Members: three.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

“Who’s in this?”

“Me, Yichen’s mother, and you.”

“Why am I here?”

Her mother looked at her.

“Because she asked me to add you.”

Xiaoran scrolled up.

The conversation had already begun.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): I found a lovely florist near the market.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Oh, please send me the address.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): I’ll send it when I get home.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Thank you!

Then, below that:

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Xiaoran, do you think Yichen would like some flowers for his room?

Xiaoran blinked.

She looked at her mother, then back at the phone.

“Why is Yichen involved?”

Her mother shrugged.

“Perhaps she wants to decorate his room.”

“But he doesn’t care about flowers.”

“Then perhaps she’ll choose something he can’t kill.”

Xiaoran laughed.

She typed into the group.

Xiaoran: Auntie, he likes flowers as long as he doesn’t have to take care of them.

Auntie replied almost immediately.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Then I’ll choose something easy.

Her mother sent a flower emoji.

Xiaoran looked at the group name again.

“The Flower Corner.”

Her mother smiled.

“It’s cute, isn’t it?”

Xiaoran couldn’t disagree.

The fathers, meanwhile, had made no progress at all.

They hadn’t, strictly speaking, met. Lin Hongwei and Zhou Mingyuan had once shaken hands over the bonnet of a car, in the dark, at the end of a gaokao, and exchanged perhaps a dozen words, which neither of them had ever mentioned to their children. Since then, nothing. When the mothers’ messages began arriving at all hours, her father read them over her mother’s shoulder, said “Hm,” and went back to the news. Across the city, according to Yichen, his father did exactly the same thing in a different chair.

“They’re the same man,” Xiaoran said on the phone.

“They are not the same man. Your father fishes. Mine golfs,” Yichen said.

“Badly?”

“Very badly.”

“Then they’re the same man.”

That evening, Xiaoran received a photograph in the group chat.

It was a picture of two small bouquets arranged side by side.

One had soft pink flowers.

The other had white and pale yellow ones.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): I made these this afternoon. Which one do you think your mother would prefer?

Xiaoran sent the photograph to her mother.

Her mother replied almost immediately.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): The pink one. But the yellow is lovely too.

Xiaoran passed the answer along.

A few minutes later, her mother sent another message.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Tell her I found a lovely flower market. We should go together next Saturday.

Xiaoran typed it into the group.

Xiaoran: Mom says she found a lovely flower market. You should go together next Saturday!

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Wonderful. Let’s go.

Then:

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): The fathers can come too.

Xiaoran stared at the message.

She looked toward Yichen, who was sitting beside her on the sofa.

“Your mother has invited our fathers to the flower market.”

He looked at the phone, then at her.

“Interesting.”

She waited.

He laughed under his breath.

“I wonder how long they’ll last.”

She laughed.

Saturday came.

The mothers had never actually stood in the same place before. They had exchanged forty photographs of hydrangeas, a florist’s address, two recipes and a long voice message about a neighbor, but they had met in person exactly never, and Xiaoran, who heard about it afterward from both sides, gathered that the first five minutes at the market gate had been extremely polite.

Then Mrs. Zhou had said, “Your daughter told me you don’t like roses that are too open,” and her mother had said, “Your son told me you think lilies smell like a hospital,” and they had looked at each other, and laughed, and from then on it was fine.

They bought peonies for themselves. They bought a small bunch of white ranunculus, together, which they argued over for twenty minutes, for a graduation that was two months away and a girl who wasn’t supposed to know about it. They bought tea, and drank it standing up at a stall, and talked about their children in a way that would have mortified both of them.

The fathers came along to carry things.

At 10:16 a.m., Xiaoran received a photograph.

Her mother and Yichen’s mother were standing in front of a stall, each holding a bunch of flowers. They were smiling at the camera.

Behind them, at opposite ends of the same stall, stood their fathers.

One was holding a paper bag.

The other was looking at his phone.

Xiaoran zoomed in.

Neither of them appeared to be saying anything. Each was holding a paper bag. Each was looking, with great concentration, at a bucket of tulips.

She sent the photograph to Yichen.

Xiaoran: LOOK.

He replied:

Yichen: They’re not talking.

Xiaoran: Do you think they will?

Yichen: Not before the parking runs out.

She laughed, then another message arrived from her mother.

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Your father bought flowers for the house.

Xiaoran blinked.

She typed back.

Xiaoran: Dad bought flowers?

Mom (Accounts Dept.): Yes. He said since we came all this way, we should bring something home.

Xiaoran turned toward Yichen.

“Your father?”

He checked his phone.

A message from his mother had arrived.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Your father bought flowers too. He said they looked nice.

Yichen smiled.

“Progress.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Maybe they’re becoming friends.”

He looked at the photograph again.

“Maybe.”

Then, a moment later, his phone vibrated.

His father had sent him a message.

Dad (Logistics): Your girlfriend’s father nodded at me. I nodded back.

Yichen stared at it, then showed Xiaoran.

She read it.

Her face brightened.

“See?”

“Yes. They’re making progress.”

She leaned against his shoulder, pleased.

A few seconds later, another message arrived.

Dad (Logistics): Tell him hello next time. From me.

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

Yichen looked at the screen, then at her.

“Well.”

She wiped the corner of her eye.

“At least they’re consistent.”

He put his arm around her.

“Hello is a good start.”

Two months later, at graduation, in two black gowns, she would turn round and find the two men standing together behind her, talking about the practicalities of the coming months as if they had been doing it for years, and she would think that, as far as she knew, they had never exchanged more than a nod.

chapters.desc: A water town an hour and a half from Shanghai, a pale blue hanfu, and a boyfriend who rates the outfit before she can ask.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Fell in Love with Hanfu
chapters.epigraph: “You were winding up to it.”
chapters.content:
The idea had started with Xiaoran sending Yichen a photograph.

It was a picture of an old Chinese street, its traditional wooden buildings lining a narrow stone-paved road. Red lanterns hung beneath the eaves, delicate bridges crossed a small canal, and the afternoon sunlight fell across the rooftops in a warm golden haze.

Xiaoran: I want to go here.

Yichen had been in the middle of reviewing a training schedule when the message arrived.

He looked at the photograph, then at her message.

Yichen: When?

Xiaoran: This weekend?

Yichen: All right.

Xiaoran: Can we dress up? Hanfu!

He glanced at the photograph again.

Yichen: You want to wear hanfu?

Xiaoran: YES.

Yichen: Then we’ll go.

He hadn’t thought much more about it.

Until Saturday morning.

The water town was an hour and a half’s drive from Shanghai, an old canal district that had been carefully preserved and developed into a cultural destination. It wasn’t entirely untouched by modern tourism—there were souvenir shops, cafés, and plenty of visitors—but the old architecture, stone bridges, narrow waterways, and traditional courtyards gave it an atmosphere that made Xiaoran feel as if she’d stepped into another period of time.

They arrived shortly before ten.

Xiaoran was already excited before they even entered the main street.

“Yichen, look!”

“I see.”

“There’s a little bridge!”

“Yes.”

“And a boat!”

“I see that too.”

She turned to him.

“You’re not excited?”

“I am.”

“You don’t look excited.”

He met her eyes.

“Would you prefer me to jump up and down?”

She laughed.

“No. That would be strange.”

“Then I’m expressing my excitement appropriately.”

She nudged his arm.

They walked past several shops before reaching the hanfu rental studio Xiaoran had bookmarked. It occupied the second floor of an old building, with wooden windows overlooking the street below. Inside, there were rows of garments in different colors and styles, accessories displayed in glass cabinets, and several makeup stations arranged along the wall.

Xiaoran’s eyes practically sparkled.

“Oh, my God.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Found something?”

“Everything.”

She moved toward a rack of garments, carefully touching the fabric of a pale blue robe.

The shop assistant greeted them and explained the rental packages. Xiaoran listened carefully, asking about the different styles, hair arrangements, makeup options, and photography packages.

Yichen stood beside her, listening.

“Would you like to try a more elaborate hairstyle? We have several options depending on the style of hanfu,” the assistant asked.

Xiaoran nodded enthusiastically.

“Yes, please.”

She looked at Yichen.

“Which color do you think I should choose?”

He looked over the racks.

There were soft pinks, pale greens, cream, lavender, and several shades of blue.

“Which one do you like?”

“That’s not helpful.”

“It’s your outfit.”

“But I want your opinion.”

He considered her.

“Light blue.”

She looked at the pale blue garment she’d been admiring earlier.

“Why?”

“I think it’ll suit you.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Okay. I’ll try that one.”

The assistant then turned toward Yichen.

“And would your boyfriend like to rent one as well? We have matching couple sets.”

Xiaoran immediately turned around.

“Matching?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Would you like that?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll rent one.”

The assistant brought out a dark blue set with understated embroidery, paired with a black belt and a matching outer robe.

Xiaoran looked at it, then at him.

“You’re going to look like a young master.”

Yichen raised an eyebrow.

“Is that good?”

“Very good.”

“Then I suppose I’ll trust your judgement.”

The styling process took longer than Xiaoran expected.

She was seated in front of a mirror while the stylist arranged her hair, carefully dividing it into sections and pinning it into an elegant half-up style. Delicate ornaments were added, including a small floral hairpin and dangling pearls that framed the sides of her face.

Her makeup was soft and delicate.

The stylist applied a light base, added a gentle flush to her cheeks, and carefully defined her eyes. A little color was added to her lips, making them look naturally rosy.

Xiaoran watched the transformation in the mirror.

“Do I look strange?”

The stylist smiled.

“Not at all. You look lovely.”

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen through the mirror.

He was sitting on a sofa nearby, looking through his phone.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Come and see.”

He put his phone away and walked over. He stopped behind her.

He didn’t answer.

His gaze rested on her reflection.

The pale blue hanfu was layered delicately, with long flowing sleeves and subtle embroidery along the collar. Her hair was arranged beautifully, and the ornaments gave her an appearance that was softer and more refined than her usual everyday style.

But it was still unmistakably Xiaoran.

Her expressive eyes.

The little crease between her eyebrows when she was uncertain.

The way she was currently looking at him through the mirror, waiting for his opinion.

His mouth curved.

“You look beautiful.”

Her expression brightened.

She turned slightly in her chair.

“The pins aren’t too much?”

He lowered his head, adjusting a small ornament that had become slightly loose near her temple.

“Does it feel uncomfortable?”

“No.”

“Then don’t worry about it.”

He looked at her reflection again.

“I like it.”

She smiled.

The stylist watched them with an amused expression.

“Your boyfriend looks very pleased.”

Xiaoran immediately became shy.

Yichen, however, smiled.

“He has good taste,” he said.

She met his eyes.

“Who?”

He met her eyes in the mirror.

“Me.”

She laughed.

When Yichen went to change, Xiaoran was still having the finishing touches done.

She was given a small fan, delicate enough to fit comfortably in her hand, and a little fabric pouch to complete the outfit.

She practiced holding the fan in front of the mirror.

The stylist showed her how to position her hands, how to turn slightly, and how to let the long sleeves fall naturally.

Xiaoran tried, then tried again.

“Like this?”

“Very good.”

Her mouth tipped up.

She was beginning to feel like she was playing a character in a historical drama, then the assistant called her attention.

“Your boyfriend is ready.”

Xiaoran turned.

And stopped.

Yichen stood near the doorway.

His outfit was dark blue, with a structured inner robe and a flowing outer layer. The embroidery was subtle, the sleeves neat, and his hair had been styled with a traditional hairpiece that kept it away from his forehead.

He looked different.

Not dramatically different, but enough that Xiaoran needed a moment to process it.

He looked like someone who belonged in the courtyard of an old Chinese residence, perhaps a young scholar or the son of a distinguished family.

His usual composed expression somehow suited the outfit even more.

He noticed her staring.

“What?”

Xiaoran blinked, then smiled.

“Oh.”

He approached.

“Oh?”

“You look...”

She searched for a word.

“Very handsome.”

His lips curved.

“Only very?”

“Extremely handsome.”

“Better.”

She laughed.

Then she looked at him again.

“Wait. Stand there.”

He stopped.

She took out her phone.

“Don’t move.”

“All right.”

She took a photograph, then another.

Then she looked at the screen.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You look like the male lead.”

“Of what?”

“A historical drama.”

He looked at her.

“And what are you?”

She lifted her chin.

“The female lead, obviously.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Naturally.”

She approached him and adjusted the collar of his robe.

“Now we match.”

He looked down at her hands.

“Do we?”

“Yes.”

She stepped back to admire them together.

Then, said:

“We look like a couple who would have a very beautiful love story.”

Yichen looked at her.

Then he reached for her hand.

“I think we already do.”

The first photography session took place in the courtyard behind the studio.

The photographer had prepared several traditional props and suggested a series of poses.

At first, Xiaoran was a little awkward.

She knew how to pose for ordinary photographs, but traditional hanfu photography required a different kind of elegance.

“Could you turn slightly? Yes, like that. Hold the fan a little higher.” the photographer instructed.

Xiaoran followed.

Yichen stood a short distance away, watching.

“Very good. Now look toward the camera.”

Click.

“Beautiful.”

The photographer checked the screen, then asked Yichen to join her.

“Could you stand beside her? Perhaps hold her hand.”

Yichen moved closer.

Xiaoran instinctively looked up at him.

“Where?”

“Here.”

He took her hand.

The photographer smiled.

“Look at each other.”

They did.

Xiaoran tried to maintain a graceful expression.

Yichen looked at her calmly.

Then, just as the photographer was about to take the picture, he leaned slightly closer.

“You’re very serious.”

She whispered back, “I’m trying to look elegant.”

“You already do.”

“Don’t distract me.”

His mouth curved.

Click.

The photographer lowered the camera.

“That one was lovely.”

Xiaoran looked at the preview.

It was a beautiful photograph.

She stood in her pale blue hanfu, her fan held delicately in one hand. Yichen stood beside her in dark blue, his hand wrapped around hers. Their eyes were on each other rather than the camera.

She looked at the picture for a while.

“Can we keep that one?”

The photographer laughed.

“Of course. It’s one of my favorites.”

Yichen glanced at the screen.

“So is mine.”

They spent the next hour walking through the old district.

Xiaoran was having the time of her life.

She wanted photographs on every bridge, beside every wooden doorway, near every lantern, and in front of every pretty building.

Yichen accompanied her without complaint.

He carried her phone, held her little pouch, and occasionally helped arrange the long sleeves of her hanfu when they became tangled.

At one point, she stopped beside a stone bridge.

“Yichen, can you take a picture of me here?”

He took her phone.

“How?”

“Like this.”

She positioned herself near the railing, holding the fan beside her face.

He took a photograph, then another.

Then he looked at the screen.

He crooked a finger at her.

She walked over.

He showed her the pictures.

She examined them carefully.

“Hmm.”

“What?”

“I think my face looks a little strange.”

He turned to her.

“It doesn’t.”

“Look at this one.”

“I am looking.”

“Doesn’t it?”

“No.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You’re just being nice.”

He returned the phone.

“Would you prefer an honest opinion?”

She nodded.

He looked at the photograph again.

“Your sleeve is covering your hand.”

She stared.

“That’s not what I meant!”

He laughed.

She hit his arm lightly with her fan.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He caught the fan before it could hit him again.

“All right. Come here.”

He moved behind her, gently adjusting her sleeve and helping her hold the fan at a more flattering angle.

“Try again.”

She posed.

He took the picture.

This time, she liked it.

“That’s better!”

He looked at the photograph, then at her.

“Yes.”

“See? You’re a good photographer.”

“I’ve had a lot of practice.”

“With me?”

“Who else?”

She grinned.

At a small riverside pavilion, they decided to take a break.

Xiaoran sat on a wooden bench, carefully arranging the layers of her hanfu so they wouldn’t wrinkle.

Yichen sat beside her.

She was still looking through the photographs.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you think I should do this again?”

“Rent hanfu?”

She nodded.

“Definitely.”

“Then we can come again.”

She smiled.

“Maybe next time I want a different color.”

“All right.”

“Maybe pink.”

“All right.”

“Or green.”

“All right.”

She turned to him.

“You’re agreeing too easily.”

He smiled.

“Would you like me to argue?”

“No.”

“Then what’s the problem?”

She laughed.

After a moment, she turned toward him.

“Do you like seeing me dressed like this?”

He looked at her.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He thought about it.

“Because you’re happy.”

She blinked.

He continued, his voice quiet.

“You’ve been excited about this since you sent me that picture. You’ve spent the whole morning looking at everything, asking questions, choosing accessories, and making sure we get enough photographs.”

“And?”

“And I like seeing you enjoy something.”

She tucked herself against his shoulder.

“That’s a very good answer.”

“I thought so.”

She laughed.

Then she reached for his hand.

“You’re very handsome today, you know.”

“Thank you.”

“Especially today.”

“Only today?”

She giggled.

“No. Every day.”

He pressed a kiss to her hair.

“Good.”

The next photography location was a narrow street lined with old wooden buildings. The sunlight was beginning to soften, casting long shadows across the stone pavement. Red lanterns swayed gently overhead, and a few tourists were walking past with shopping bags.

The photographer had suggested one final set of couple photographs.

This time, the concept was more natural.

“Perhaps you could walk together. Don’t look at the camera. Just talk to each other,” she suggested.

Xiaoran nodded.

Yichen took her hand.

They began walking slowly.

“What should we talk about?” Xiaoran whispered.

“Anything.”

“That’s not helpful.”

“Tell me what you’re thinking.”

She considered it.

Then said, “I think I would have liked living in an old town.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Why?”

“Imagine waking up in a house with a little courtyard, drinking tea beside the window, and walking to the market every morning.”

“Sounds peaceful.”

“And wearing pretty clothes.”

He laughed under his breath.

“You’d probably spend all your time buying accessories.”

She gasped.

“I would not.”

He held her gaze.

She paused.

“...Maybe.”

He laughed.

She squeezed his hand.

“Would you live in an old house with me?”

“Would it have modern plumbing?”

She looked at him.

“Zhou Yichen!”

“I’m asking a practical question.”

“You’re ruining my romantic imagination.”

His mouth curved.

“Then yes. I’d live in an old house with you.”

“Even if I wanted a little courtyard?”

“We’d find one.”

“And a wooden window?”

“All right.”

“And a small garden?”

“Yes.”

That made her grin.

“Then I want a little table where we can drink tea together.”

Yichen looked at her.

“We can have that.”

She was about to say something else when the photographer called out.

“That was perfect! Keep walking!”

Neither of them noticed the camera clicking several times.

When the photographer finally lowered it, Yichen kissed her on the bridge under the lanterns, carefully, so the hairpins would survive.

By late afternoon, they returned to the rental studio.

Xiaoran reluctantly changed out of her hanfu, watching as the stylist carefully removed the hair ornaments.

She had taken so many photographs that her phone was almost full.

Yichen had already changed and was waiting near the reception desk.

When she came out in her ordinary clothes, her hair was still partly styled, with a few loose curls framing her face.

He looked up.

“Finished?”

She nodded.

“Unfortunately.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

She walked over and showed him her favorite photographs.

He looked through them slowly.

There was one of her standing beneath the red lanterns, another of her sitting beside the river, and several of them together.

Then he stopped at a particular picture.

It was taken when Xiaoran hadn’t realized the photographer was watching.

She was standing on the bridge, looking toward the water. Her fan was resting against her chest, and the sunlight caught the delicate ornaments in her hair. She wasn’t posing. She wasn’t smiling at the camera.

She looked peaceful.

Yichen stared at it.

“This one.”

Xiaoran leaned closer.

“You like this one?”

“Yes.”
