“But I’m not looking at the camera.”

“I know.”

“Isn’t that bad?”

“No.”

He studied her.

“I like seeing you when you don’t know you’re being photographed.”

“Why?”

“Because you look like yourself.”

She looked at him, then gently took his phone.

“Send it to me.”

He did.

She saved it immediately.

They had dinner at a small restaurant near the water.

Xiaoran ordered noodles, a few side dishes, and a dessert she had seen someone eating at another table.

Yichen watched her study the menu.

“Are you sure you can finish all that?”

She looked up.

“Yes.”

Something in his face eased.

“All right.”

She took a bite of the noodles, then looked at him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Today was really fun.”

He nodded.

“I’m glad.”

“Thank you for coming with me.”

He put down his chopsticks.

“Why are you thanking me?”

“Because you didn’t have to.”

“I wanted to.”

That made her grin.

“I know. But you could have spent the day resting.”

He considered her.

“Xiaoran, I spend enough time doing things that are part of my schedule. Training, recovery, games, meetings.”

He reached over and wiped a little sauce from the corner of her mouth.

“Spending a day with you isn’t something I need to recover from.”

She laughed.

“That’s a terrible joke.”

He laughed under his breath.

She picked up another piece of food and placed it in his bowl.

“Here. You can have this.”

“Thank you.”

He put down his chopsticks.

“Ten.”

She held his gaze.

“Ten what?”

“The outfit. Out of ten. You were about to ask.”

“I was not!”

“You were winding up to it.”

She laughed so that the couple at the next table looked over.

“And you looked better laughing on the bridge than in any of the posed ones.”

Her expression softened.

“Yichen...”

“What?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing.”

She picked up her chopsticks again, trying to hide her smile.

That evening, on the drive back, Xiaoran was busy choosing which photographs to post.

She had narrowed them down to six, then five, then seven again.

Yichen glanced at her phone when they stopped at a traffic light.

“Still choosing?”

“It’s difficult.”

“You have hundreds.”

“Not hundreds.”

He looked at her.

“All right.”

She eventually selected three photographs.

One of herself beneath the lanterns.

One of them standing together in their matching hanfu.

And one candid picture of Yichen looking at her.

She typed a caption.

Today, I got to be the female lead in my own little historical drama.

She showed it to him.

He read it.

“Female lead?”

“Yes.”

“And who was the male lead?”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You.”

“Good casting.”

She laughed and posted it.

A few minutes later, notifications started arriving.

Meilin commented first.

EXCUSE ME??? WHY DO YOU LOOK LIKE YOU WALKED OUT OF A HISTORICAL DRAMA?

Yuhao followed.

Zhou Yichen looks like he’s about to inherit a family estate.

Then Meilin again:

The two of you look disgustingly good together. I’m saving this.

Xiaoran laughed.

Yichen glanced over.

“What are they saying?”

“Meilin likes the pictures.”

“Good.”

“Yuhao says you look like a rich young master.”

Yichen smiled.

“He’s not entirely wrong.”

She laughed.

Then she opened the picture of the two of them together again.

For a while, she looked at it.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Can I ask you something?”

“Go ahead.”

“If we really lived in that time...”

He glanced at her.

“What?”

“Would you have pursued me?”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Would you have noticed?”

She turned toward him.

“Of course!”

“Would you?”

“Yes!”

He seemed unconvinced.

She narrowed her eyes.

“Why are you smiling?”

“Nothing.”

“Yichen.”

He reached over and took her hand.

“I think I’d have found a way.”

She tilted her head.

“Even if I lived in a different city?”

“Yes.”

“Even if our families didn’t know each other?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I was difficult to pursue?”

He looked at her, his smile growing.

“That part wouldn’t have changed.”

She gasped.

“Excuse me?”

He laughed.

She squeezed his hand.

“Then you’d better be persistent.”

“I’ve had some practice.”

She smiled.

He brought her hand to his lips and kissed her knuckles.

“And I think I’ve been rather successful.”

Xiaoran looked down at their joined hands, then back at the photograph.

She set the photograph against the lamp, where she would see it first thing in the morning, and didn’t let go of his hand.

chapters.desc: Her final film is due on Friday. He is in another city with the Herons. At two in the afternoon the university portal rejects the file.
chapters.title: Thesis Week
chapters.epigraph: “To check the settings.”
chapters.content:
By Wednesday night, Xiaoran had developed a personal hatred for the number 94.

It was the percentage displayed on her laptop’s export window.

It had been stuck there for eleven minutes.

She stared at it.

The laptop stared back.

“Move.”

Nothing happened.

“Please.”

Still nothing.

She leaned closer, as if her physical proximity might persuade the machine to cooperate.

“You’re a computer. You’re supposed to be good at this.”

From the other side of the editing room, Jiayi looked up.

“Are you talking to your laptop again?”

“No.”

“You are.”

“I’m negotiating.”

Ning, who was sitting on the floor surrounded by printed documents, glanced over. “How’s the negotiation going?”

“Poorly. The other party is being unreasonable.”

Jiayi laughed.

Xiaoran looked back at the screen. Ninety-four percent.

She had been working on her final film for months. It was the culmination of her university years, the project that would represent everything she had learned about storytelling, directing, editing, and working with people who sometimes had entirely different ideas about what a film should become. She knew every frame by heart.

She also knew she was becoming increasingly unpleasant to be around.

Her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Still at the editing room?

She picked it up.

Xiaoran: No. I’ve moved into the laptop.

Yichen: Comfortable?

Xiaoran: Terrible. The landlord is unreasonable.

Yichen: Have you eaten?

She looked at the clock.

9:46 p.m.

Then at the half-empty bottle of water beside her.

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: What?

She hesitated.

Xiaoran: Food.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

She sighed.

Xiaoran: I had a sandwich.

Yichen: When?

Xiaoran: Today.

Yichen: What time?

Xiaoran: Why are you interrogating me?

Yichen: Because you’re avoiding the question.

She smiled despite herself.

Yichen was in another city with the Herons. They had traveled for an away fixture, followed by a few days of training and recovery before returning to Shanghai. His schedule was packed, and hers was worse.

They had agreed that they would call when they could, but neither expected the other to be available all the time.

Still, he had a way of making her feel as if he were sitting beside her even when he was several hundred kilometers away.

Xiaoran: I’ll eat something now.

Yichen: Good.

Xiaoran: You’re not my mother.

Yichen: No. Your mother would probably have called already.

Xiaoran laughed out loud.

Ning looked up.

“What’s funny?”

“Nothing.”

“Boyfriend?”

Xiaoran glanced at her phone.

“Unfortunately.”

Jiayi threw a scrunched-up piece of paper at her.

“Tell him to send food.”

Xiaoran caught it.

“He can’t.”

“Then tell him to send money.”

“He’s not my food delivery service.”

Ning looked at her.

“You’re right. He’s worse. He’ll ask what you’ve eaten and then tell you to order something.”

Xiaoran looked down at the phone.

Another message had arrived.

Yichen: Order something warm. I’ll call after the team meeting.

She looked up at her friends.

“He’s worse.”

Thursday morning, Yichen called while Xiaoran was walking across campus.

She answered with her phone tucked between her shoulder and ear, one hand holding a folder and the other carrying a coffee.

“Hello.”

“Where are you?”

“On campus.”

“Walking?”

“Yes.”

“Then why do you sound like you’re talking into your collar?”

She adjusted it.

“Because I have three hands.”

He laughed.

“How’s the film?”

“Almost done.”

“That sounds promising.”

“It isn’t.”

“What happened?”

She sighed.

“The sound in the final sequence is wrong.”

“Wrong how?”

“I don’t know. It just doesn’t feel right.”

He was quiet.

“Have you asked your sound editor?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

“He thinks it’s fine.”

“Then?”

“I think he’s wrong.”

Yichen smiled.

“Have you listened to it with him?”

“Yes.”

“Without watching the picture?”

She slowed her steps.

“What?”

“Just the sound. Close your eyes and listen.”

She considered it.

“Why?”

“Because you keep saying the sound is wrong. Maybe you need to hear it without looking for the problem.”

She was quiet.

“That’s actually a good idea.”

“I’m glad.”

“Don’t sound so pleased with yourself.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He laughed.

She reached the building and pushed the door open.

“Are you busy?”

“About to go into training.”

“Okay. I’ll let you go.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“Don’t let one sequence convince you the whole film is bad.”

She stopped in the corridor.

He said, “You’ve been working on this for months. You’re allowed to be frustrated with one part without deciding everything else is wrong.”

She looked down at the folder in her hand.

“Okay.”

“Good luck today.”

“You too.”

“And eat lunch.”

She rolled her eyes.

“Goodbye, Zhou Yichen.”

“Goodbye.”

She ended the call with a smile.

Then she opened her editing room door.

“Jiayi.”

Jiayi looked up.

“What?”

“Can we listen to the final sequence without the picture?”

Jiayi stared at her.

“Why?”

“Because I think I’ve been looking at it too much.”

Ning raised her head.

“That’s actually a good idea.”

Xiaoran put her folder down.

“Thank you.”

Jiayi turned back to the computer.

“Fine. Let’s do it.”

That evening, the Herons played their away game.

Xiaoran had promised herself she would watch the livestream.

She had also promised herself she would finish the final sound review.

By the time the game began, she had completed the review and was waiting for a new audio file to export.

Her laptop was open on the desk. The game played on her phone, propped against a stack of notebooks.

She watched Yichen take the court.

Even through the small screen, she could recognize him immediately.

His posture, the way he moved into position, the brief adjustment of his wristband before the game began.

Her mouth tipped up.

“Go, Yichen.”

Ning glanced over.

“Is he playing?”

“Yes.”

“How’s he doing?”

“The game just started.”

“Then why are you nervous?”

“I’m not.”

Ning looked at her.

Xiaoran turned back to the screen.

A few minutes later, Yichen made a clean pass that led to a basket. She smiled and tapped the screen as if he could hear her.

Then her laptop made a sound.

The export had finished.

She turned immediately.

The new file was ready.

She opened it and began checking the sequence.

For the next several minutes, she watched the scene carefully, headphones on, while the game continued in the background.

When she finally looked at her phone again, the score had changed.

The Herons were ahead.

Yichen had been playing well.

She smiled and sent him a quick message.

Xiaoran: I saw that pass.

He wouldn’t see it until after the game, but she sent it anyway.

Then she returned to her work.

It was only after midnight that her phone rang.

Yichen.

She answered.

“Hello.”

“Still awake?”

She looked at the laptop.

“Unfortunately.”

“How was the final sequence?”

“Better.”

“Better?”

“Much better. We fixed the sound.”

“Good.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“How was your game?”

“Good.”

“Just good?”

“We won.”

“I know. I watched.”

“I saw your message.”

She sat up a little.

“You did?”

“After the game.”

“Did you see the pass?”

“Which one?”

“The one I messaged you about.”

He thought.

“The pass to the corner?”

“Yes!”

“That was a good read.”

She smiled proudly, even though she hadn’t done anything.

“I know.”

He laughed.

There was a faint sound of movement on his end.

“Are you back at the hotel?”

“Yes.”

“Did you do your recovery, or are you lying on the bed in your kit?”

He gave a quiet laugh.

“Ice bath. Then the bed.”

“Good.”

A pause followed.

Then she asked, “Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then sleep.”

“I wanted to hear your voice.”

Her expression softened.

“Oh.”

He was quiet.

“How much is left?”

“Final review tomorrow. Credits. Submission.”

“You’re close.”

“Very.”

“Then finish it.”

She smiled.

“That’s the plan.”

He shifted slightly.

“Xiaoran?”

“Mm?”

“You’ve been working toward this for a long time.”

“I know.”

“Don’t forget to enjoy finishing it.”

She looked at the screen.

The timeline was finally clean. The audio had settled into place. The ending, which had troubled her for days, now felt exactly as she had imagined it.

“I’ll try.”

“Good.”

She lowered her voice.

“I miss you.”

“I miss you too.”

“Come back soon.”

“Saturday.”

“That’s still far away.”

“Two days.”

“Far.”

Something in his face eased.

“Do you want me to come back earlier?”

She knew he was teasing.

“Yes.”

“All right. I’ll inform the club that my girlfriend has issued an order.”

She laughed.

“Don’t you dare.”

“Understood.”

She lay back in her chair, holding the phone against her ear.

“Good night.”

“Good night, Xiaoran. Sleep when you’re done.”

“I will.”

“And don’t keep changing things just because you’re nervous.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Okay.”

Friday was the day everything went wrong.

Not the film itself.

The film was fine.

It was the submission system.

Xiaoran and her team had completed the final review before noon. They had checked the export, verified the subtitles, confirmed the file format, and prepared the accompanying documents.

They were ready to submit, then the university portal rejected the file.

The file size was too large.

Xiaoran stared at the message.

“No.”

Jiayi leaned over.

“What?”

“No.”

Ning came closer.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran pointed at the screen.

“The file is too large.”

Jiayi blinked.

“How much too large?”

“Enough.”

Ning checked the requirement.

“Can we compress it?”

“We can, but we need to make sure the quality doesn’t drop.”

“How long?”

Xiaoran looked at the export settings.

“Twenty minutes. Maybe thirty.”

Jiayi checked the time.

“We have more than an hour.”

“I know.”

“Then it’s okay.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer.

She knew it was okay. She knew they had enough time.

She knew the film was safe.

But after months of work, after all the late nights and revisions, the possibility of something going wrong at the final step felt unbearable.

She stood up and walked to the corridor.

Her phone was already in her hand.

She called Yichen.

He answered after several rings.

“Xiaoran?”

His voice was slightly breathless.

“Are you busy?”

“I’m between sessions. What’s wrong?”

She swallowed.

“The submission portal rejected our film.”

There was a short silence.

“Why?”

“File size. We’re compressing it, but I don’t know if the quality will hold.”

“How much time do you have?”

“An hour.”

“All right.”

She closed her eyes.

He didn’t immediately tell her it would be fine.

He didn’t dismiss the problem.

He asked, “What are you doing now?”

“Waiting for the new export.”

“Have you checked the settings?”

“Yes.”

“Have you tested the file?”

“Not yet.”

“Then do that first.”

She nodded, even though he couldn’t see her.

“Okay.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“You’re not going to lose months of work because a portal rejected one file.”

She pressed her lips together.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

She laughed weakly.

“You’re asking me the same question again.”

“Because you keep needing to hear it.”

Her eyes stung.

“I just wanted it to be done.”

“I know.”

“I wanted to submit it and stop thinking about it.”

“I know.”

He lowered his voice.

“Listen. You’ve done the work. You have a solution. Now you just need to finish this last part.”

She took a breath.

“Okay.”

“Can you do that?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

A voice called his name in the background.

He glanced away.

“I have to go.”

“Okay.”

“I’ll call you when I’m done.”

“Don’t worry. Focus on training.”

He was quiet.

“I’m still worried about you.”

That made her grin.

“I’ll be fine.”

“I know you will.”

The call ended.

Xiaoran stood in the corridor for another few seconds.

Then she wiped the corner of her eye and returned to the editing room.

Jiayi looked up.

“Everything okay?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yes.”

“Did you call him?”

“Yes.”

“Did he tell you to calm down?”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“No.”

Ning raised an eyebrow.

“What did he tell you?”

“To check the settings.”

Jiayi laughed.

“That’s very romantic.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“It was.”

At 3:18 p.m., the compressed file finished exporting. At 3:26, they completed the quality check. At 3:31, the portal accepted the upload.

At 3:34, Xiaoran received the confirmation email.

She stared at it.

Then she looked at her teammates.

“It’s submitted.”

Jiayi let out a cheer.

Ning clapped.

Xiaoran laughed, covering her mouth with one hand.

“It’s submitted.”

Jiayi stood and hugged her.

“We’re done!”

Ning joined them.

The three of them stood in the middle of the editing room, laughing and holding each other.

Then Xiaoran pulled away and looked at the screen.

The confirmation email was still there.

She took a screenshot.

And sent it to Yichen.

Xiaoran: SUBMITTED.

He was in the middle of a team meeting when the message came through.

He glanced at his phone.

Then he read it again.

A smile spread across his face.

He typed a reply.

Yichen: You did it.

Xiaoran: I DID.

Yichen: Congratulations, filmmaker.

She stared at the message.

Then she called him.

He answered a few minutes later.

“Hello.”

“It’s done.”

“I know.”

“It’s actually submitted.”

“I saw.”

She laughed.

“I can’t believe it.”

“I’m very proud of you.”

She went quiet.

Then she said, “I wanted you here.”

His expression softened.

“I know.”

“I wanted to run out of the room and hug you.”

“I wish I could have been there.”

She looked down at her ring.

“Me too.”

He was silent.

Then he said, “Can I tell you something?”

“What?”

“I’ve been waiting for your message all afternoon.”

She blinked.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I knew how much today mattered to you.”

Her eyes softened.

He said, “I wanted to know when you were done.”

She smiled.

“Well, I’m done.”

“Good.”

“And now?”

“Now you rest.”

She laughed.

“No celebration?”

“Training tomorrow morning, then the flight. I’ll be back Saturday evening. We can celebrate then.”

She considered it.

“Can we have hotpot?”

“Yes.”

“With the spicy soup?”

“Yes.”

“And dessert?”

“Yes.”

That made her grin.

“You’re very generous.”

“It’s your graduation project. You can have dessert.”

She laughed.

Then she said, “I love you.”

“I love you too.”

Saturday evening, Yichen returned to Shanghai.

Xiaoran had spent most of the afternoon doing absolutely nothing.

She had slept late, eaten a proper lunch, and watched a drama without feeling guilty about it.

She had also checked the submission confirmation email three times.

Not because she doubted it.

She liked looking at it.

When Yichen arrived, she was waiting outside his apartment.

He stepped out of the lift with his travel bag.

Neither said anything for a second.

Then she walked forward.

He put his bag down just in time to catch her.

She wrapped her arms around his neck, and he lifted her slightly off the ground.

“You’re back.”

“I’m back.”

She buried her face against his shoulder.

He kissed her hair.

“How’s my filmmaker?”

“Retired.”

“Already?”

“Temporarily.”

He laughed.

She leaned back and looked at him.

“Did you miss me?”

He gave her a slow smile.

“Enough to take the first flight back.”

Her mouth tipped up.

Then she kissed him, properly, in the corridor, with his travel bag still at their feet.

“Welcome home.”

He picked up his bag and took her hand.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yichen.”

“What?”

“Can we have one day without asking whether I’ve eaten?”

He considered it.

“No.”

She laughed and followed him inside.

They went out for hotpot later that evening.

Xiaoran had chosen the restaurant, the soup base, and most of the side dishes. Yichen had been allowed to choose the vegetables, though she had rejected two of his suggestions.

While they waited for the food, she told him about the submission, the celebration, and the moment the portal finally accepted the file.

He listened with his chin resting lightly against his hand.

“And then Jiayi hugged me. And Ning hugged me. And I nearly cried,” she said.

“You’ve been wanting to finish this for months.”

“I know.”

“You deserve to celebrate.”

She smiled.

Then she looked at him.

“Did you watch the final version again?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I wanted to.”

She tilted her head.

“And?”

He met her eyes.

“I liked it even more the second time.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Which part?”

“The ending.”

She looked pleased.

“Because of the silence?”

“Because you trusted it.”

She smiled down at the table.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “Do you think I should keep making films?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Yes.”

She nodded slowly.

“I do.”

“Then keep going.”

She reached across the table and touched his hand.

“Thank you.”

“For what?”

“For being patient with me this week.”

He turned to her.

“You don’t have to thank me for that.”

“I know. But I want to.”

He turned his hand and held hers.

“You were doing something important.”

“And you were doing something important too.”

He nodded.

They sat.

Then Xiaoran glanced at the food arriving at their table.

“Okay. Enough emotional conversation.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“Because I’m hungry.”

He laughed.

“Finally.”

She pointed her chopsticks at him.

“Don’t start.”

He served her first.

And when she reached for her phone to take a picture of the food, he noticed the ring on her finger.

The small stone caught the warm restaurant light.

He reached across the table and turned her hand slightly.

“Still wearing it?”

“Of course.”

“Good.”

She smiled.

“Why?”

“Just checking.”

She squinted at him.

“You’re copying me.”

“Maybe.”

She laughed and held his hand a little longer.

Later, back at his apartment, Xiaoran sat on the sofa with her legs across his lap.

Her laptop was still in her bag. Her final film was submitted.

Her deadlines were finally behind her.

Yichen was scrolling through something on his phone when she spoke.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“I think this was the hardest week of my university life.”

He put his phone down.

He rubbed his thumb over her ankle.

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

“You finished.”

“Yes.”

He held her gaze.

“Then I’m proud of you.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

A moment passed.

Then she said, “Next time you have an away game, I’m coming.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“To the game?”

“Yes.”

“Even if you have a deadline?”

“Obviously not if I have a deadline.”

“Then?”

“Next time.”

He smiled.

“All right.”

“And you have to come to my next film screening.”

“I will.”

“Even if it’s in another city.”

“I’ll come.”

She studied him.

“With flowers?”

“You brought them to my signing. It’s only fair.”

She smiled and settled against him.

A few minutes later, she lifted her head again.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Did you actually like my film?”

He looked down at her.

“Enough that I’ve watched it twice.”

She considered this.

Then she smiled, satisfied.

“Good.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair.

“Now stop interviewing me.”

She laughed.

“Fine.”

She closed her eyes and rested against him.

Yichen returned to his phone, but his free hand stayed intertwined with hers.

They had spent the week in different cities, each carrying something important that demanded their attention. He had played his games. She had finished her film. Neither had been able to stand beside the other at every difficult moment.

He had watched a film after a long game because she’d been waiting for him to see it. She had told him about a portal error at three in the afternoon and been told to check the settings, and found that it helped.

Xiaoran shifted closer.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“Next week, I want to do something fun.”

That got a smile out of him.

“All right.”

“No laptops.”

“Agreed.”

“No basketball.”

He glanced down at her.

“That’s a little unreasonable.”

She opened one eye.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed and kissed her, briefly.

“All right. No basketball.”

She smiled and closed her eyes again.

chapters.desc: Graduation day, both families in one row, and two fathers who have never said more than hello suddenly have a great deal to talk about.
chapters.title: Two Gowns
chapters.epigraph: “Maybe they’ll start inviting each other to dinner.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Xiaoran did that morning was change her mind about the dress.

The second thing she did was blame Yichen.

It was, in her opinion, entirely his fault.

He had told her the blue gown looked beautiful. He had also said the ivory one suited her. When she asked which one she should wear for the photographs before the ceremony, he had looked at both and said, quite calmly, that she looked beautiful in either.

That wasn’t an answer.

Now, standing in front of the full-length mirror in her apartment, Xiaoran held the two dresses against herself.

“Which one?”

Yichen sat on the edge of her bed, already dressed in a dark suit. His graduation gown was folded neatly beside him. He glanced up from his phone.

“The blue one.”

“You said that yesterday.”

“Yes.”

“And the ivory one?”

“Also beautiful.”

She turned around.

“You’re not helping.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She gave him a look through the mirror.

He put his phone down and stood. Walking over, he looked at the two dresses with the seriousness of someone examining an important business proposal.

“The blue one,” he repeated.

“Why?”

“Because you said you wanted something that looked good in the photographs outside the faculty building. The ivory one is prettier indoors.”

She paused.

He said, “And you’re wearing the blue one for the ceremony. It will look better with the gown.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“You actually thought about it?”

“I was listening.”

She lowered the dresses.

“Then why didn’t you say that yesterday?”

“You asked which one was prettier. I answered that question.”

“That’s not the same question.”

“I know that now.”

She tried not to smile.

He reached for the blue dress and held it out to her.

“Here.”

She took it.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

She went to change, but before closing the bedroom door, she looked back.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“Are you nervous?”

He met her eyes.

“About graduation?”

“Yes.”

“No.”

She eyed him.

“Not even a little?”

He considered it.

“Maybe about whether you’ll be ready on time.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Go get dressed.”

By the time they arrived at the university, the campus was already full of graduates and families.

There were flowers everywhere. Parents were carrying bouquets almost as large as their children. Friends were taking photographs beneath the university signs, adjusting each other’s collars, fixing hair, and trying to keep their graduation caps from falling off.

The atmosphere was strangely familiar and unfamiliar at the same time.

Xiaoran had spent years walking through these buildings.

She knew which staircase was always crowded, which café had the best iced coffee, which corridor had the most reliable air conditioning, and which corner of the Media building received the prettiest afternoon light.

But today, everything seemed to have a different meaning.

She looked down at the gown in her hands.

“I can’t believe we’re graduating.”

Yichen stood beside her, holding his own gown over one arm.

“We are.”

“That’s all you have to say?”

“What would you like me to say?”

“Something emotional.”

He turned to her.

“We’re graduating.”

She hit his arm.

He laughed and took her hand.

“Come on. Your friends are waiting.”

Jiayi and Ning were already near the Media faculty entrance. The moment they saw Xiaoran, Ning waved both arms.

“Finally! We thought you’d disappeared!”

“I was choosing a dress.”

Jiayi looked her up and down.

“Good choice.”

Xiaoran brightened.

“Really?”

“Yes. You look lovely.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“I told you.”

Xiaoran turned to him.

“Don’t take credit.”

Ning laughed.

The girls immediately gathered for photographs. They took pictures in front of the faculty sign, beside the staircase, under a tree, and in front of a wall that had become an unofficial graduation photo spot.

Yichen was patient through all of it.

He held their bags, took photographs, and occasionally suggested that they move slightly because the sunlight was falling across Xiaoran’s face.

At one point, Ning looked at him through the camera.

“Yichen, you’re actually very good at this.”

“He has experience,” Xiaoran said.

“With what?”

“Taking pictures of me.”

Yichen handed the phone back.

“She makes me practice.”

“I do not.”

He looked at her.

“Do you want to see the number of photographs in my phone?”

“No.”

“Then I won’t.”

Jiayi burst out laughing.

The ceremony hall was enormous.

Graduates were directed toward their respective seating sections while families were guided to the audience.

Xiaoran found her seat with Ning and Jiayi. Yichen was seated with the Business graduates, a few sections away.

Before the ceremony began, she turned around to look for her parents.

Her mother was already waving.

Her father sat beside her, holding a bouquet and wearing the expression of a man who had been instructed not to lose anything important.

Xiaoran waved back.

Then she noticed someone sitting beside her father.

She blinked.

Yichen’s father.

She looked again.

Yes.

Mr. Zhou was sitting beside her father.

In the same row.

Her eyes widened.

She immediately turned toward Yichen’s section.

He was looking in her direction.

When he saw her expression, he raised his eyebrows.

She mouthed, What?

He mouthed back, What?

She pointed toward the audience.

He glanced over.

Then he smiled.

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

He knew.

Of course he knew.

She turned back and found her father speaking to Mr. Zhou.

Her mother was smiling at something Mr. Zhou had said.

The two men seemed perfectly comfortable, which was strange, because as far as she knew they had never exchanged more than a greeting.

Xiaoran slowly faced forward.

This wasn’t what she had expected.

She had imagined her parents and Yichen’s parents meeting at family dinners, perhaps exchanging greetings at birthdays. She hadn’t imagined them sitting together at graduation as if they had been assigned to the same family delegation.

Her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Don’t look so worried.

Xiaoran: WHY ARE THEY SITTING TOGETHER?

Yichen: There were seats available.

Xiaoran: You arranged this?

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Are you sure?

Yichen: Yes.

She looked toward the audience again.

Her father was now showing Mr. Zhou something on his phone.

She turned back to her phone.

Xiaoran: They’re getting along.

Yichen: That’s good.

Xiaoran: Too well.

Yichen: Should I tell them to stop?

She bit back a laugh.

Xiaoran: No.

Yichen: Then pay attention to the ceremony.

She put her phone away.

A moment later, she glanced back one more time.

Her mother gave her a thumbs-up.

Her father raised his bouquet.

Mr. Zhou smiled and nodded.

Xiaoran faced forward, cheeks warm.

She had a feeling the two men were going to become friends.

And somehow, she suspected she would be the last person to know what they discussed.

The ceremony began with the usual formalities.

Speeches. Applause. Faculty introductions.

Xiaoran tried to listen, but her attention kept wandering.

She thought about the first day she had entered the Media building. She remembered being overwhelmed by the crowds during orientation, trying to find the right lecture hall, and worrying that everyone else seemed to know where they were going. She remembered Jiayi and Ning becoming her friends.

She remembered long nights editing footage, the frustration of failed exports, the relief of successful submissions, and the strange satisfaction of seeing a project finally become what she had imagined. She remembered the annual faculty showcase.

The competition she had won. The final film.

The people who had helped her along the way.

And Yichen.

Not because he had done the work for her.

He hadn’t.

But because he had been there through so much of it.

He had listened to her complain about deadlines, watched rough cuts when she needed another opinion, brought her food when she forgot to eat, and stayed beside her when she was convinced that everything was going wrong.

He had never made her feel that her ambitions were inconvenient.

When her name was called, Xiaoran stood.

The applause seemed louder than she expected.

She walked across the stage, accepted her degree certificate, and shook hands with the faculty representative.

For a brief moment, she looked toward the audience.

Her mother was smiling with tears in her eyes.

Her father was clapping.

And beside him, Mr. Zhou was clapping too.

She looked toward the graduates’ section.

Yichen was standing among the Business students, waiting for his own name to be called.

Their eyes met.

He gave her a small nod.

That made her grin.

Then she walked off the stage.

Yichen’s graduation came later.

Xiaoran watched from her seat as the Business graduates were called one by one.

When his name was announced, he stood without fuss, straightened his gown, and walked across the stage.

He looked as composed as he always did.

Even on graduation day.

She almost laughed.

He accepted his certificate, shook hands, and turned toward the audience.

His eyes found her quickly.

She raised both hands and clapped enthusiastically.

He smiled.

Not the polite smile he had given the faculty representative.

The real one.

The one she knew.

She felt a small, ridiculous warmth in her chest.

Four years.

They had entered university with different schedules, different buildings, different friends, and different ambitions.

They had learned to make room for each other’s lives without asking the other to become smaller.

And now, they were graduating on the same day.

When the ceremony ended, the hall filled with noise.

Families stood, graduates searched for one another, and the carefully organized seating arrangement dissolved into a sea of flowers, gowns, and camera flashes.

Xiaoran found Yichen near the exit.

She walked straight toward him.

He opened his arms.

She hugged him tightly.

“Congratulations,” she said against his shoulder.

He held her close.

“Congratulations to you too.”

She leaned back.

“We did it.”

“We did.”

She looked at his certificate, then at hers, then back at him.

“Do you think we’re adults now?”

He considered it.

“Legally?”

She laughed.

“Yichen.”

“Then yes.”

She leaned closer.

“Do you feel different?”

He held her gaze.

“Not particularly.”

“Me neither.”

He brushed a loose strand of hair away from her cheek.

“Maybe it’ll feel different when we start working.”

“Maybe.”

Then she smiled.

“But today, we’re just graduates.”

“Just graduates.”

He kissed her.

The photographs took longer than the ceremony.

First, Xiaoran with her parents.

Then Yichen with his parents. Then Xiaoran with Yichen’s parents. Then Yichen with Xiaoran’s parents, then the two of them together.

And finally, the inevitable photograph with both families.

Xiaoran stood between Yichen and her mother, while the two fathers stood behind them.

Her father looked at the camera.

Mr. Zhou looked at the camera.

Both mothers were smiling.

The photographer adjusted the angle.

“Everyone, look here!”

Xiaoran smiled.

The camera clicked.

Then the photographer said, “One more. The couple in the middle, move a little closer.”

Yichen placed his hand lightly at Xiaoran’s waist.

She leaned toward him.

The camera clicked again.

“Beautiful. One more!”

Xiaoran turned her head slightly toward Yichen.

He looked down at her.

She smiled.

The camera caught it.

Later, when they reviewed the photographs, that was the one she liked most.

The lighting was ordinary and her hair had come loose, but she was looking at him, and he was already looking at her.

Lunch was held at a restaurant not far from campus.

The seating arrangement was, once again, suspiciously convenient.

Their parents sat together.

Xiaoran and Yichen sat beside each other.

Meilin and Yuhao had joined them after the ceremony, and Yuhao was already making himself comfortable.

“Four years of university. And somehow, you two still look like you’re on a date,” he said, lifting his glass.

Meilin rolled her eyes.

“That’s because they behave like they’re on a date everywhere.”

Xiaoran looked offended.

“What’s wrong with that?”

“Nothing. It’s just exhausting.”

Yichen smiled and poured Xiaoran some tea.

Yuhao pointed at him.

“See? That’s what I mean. He’s been doing that for years.”

Yichen put the teapot down.

“Would you like some?”

Yuhao immediately held out his cup.

“Actually, yes.”

Meilin shook her head.

“Honestly.”

The conversation moved between university memories, future plans, and the inevitable questions about work.

Xiaoran’s father asked her about the Shanghai studio.

“When do you start?”

“The fifth of July.”

“And the Beijing one?” her mother asked.

“I said no in April. Very politely.”

Her mother smiled.

“Junior creative producer. Branded films and digital campaigns,” Xiaoran said, because her father was already reaching for his phone to write it down.

“That’s what you wanted, isn’t it?” her father asked.

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yes. I think it’s a good place to start.”

Mr. Zhou looked toward her.

“Congratulations. It’s important to begin somewhere you’ll have room to learn.”

“Thank you, Uncle.”

Yichen glanced at her.

She had told him she wanted to make films. She had told him she wanted to work on stories and understand the strategy behind them.

Now she was going to do exactly that.

He felt pleased.

His father turned toward him.

“And you?”

Yichen put down his chopsticks.

“The Herons have offered two more seasons.”

His father nodded.

“And?”

“I’ll give them an answer this week.”

Xiaoran looked at him. He had talked it through with her for three nights, but hearing him say it in front of both families made it feel official.

His father looked at him, then nodded.

“Good.”

There was no argument. Just a quiet acknowledgement.

Xiaoran noticed.

So did Yichen.

Their fathers began discussing the practicalities of the coming months. Work, basketball, travel, and the difficulty of arranging schedules.

At some point, Xiaoran’s father asked Mr. Zhou about the Herons’ next season.

Mr. Zhou answered.

Soon, they were discussing sponsorship and sports development.

Xiaoran leaned toward Yichen.

“Look at them.”

He glanced over.

“What?”

“Our fathers.”

He looked at the two men.

Her father was listening attentively while his father explained something about the club.

Yichen smiled.

“They seem to have plenty to talk about.”

“Should we be worried?”

“Why?”

“They’re going to become friends.”

“Would that be a problem?”

She thought about it, then sighed.

“No. But they’ll probably discuss us.”

He studied her.

“Probably.”

She leaned closer.

“We should be careful.”

“About what?”

“Everything.”

He laughed.

After lunch, they returned to campus for one final round of photographs.

The sunlight had softened.

Graduates were beginning to leave, but the university still felt alive with celebration.

Xiaoran stood beneath the Media faculty sign, holding her certificate.

Yichen took several photographs of her.

Then she took his phone.

“Now you.”

He stood beside the sign.

She raised the phone.

“Smile.”

“Not that smile.”

He looked at her.

“What smile?”

“The polite one.”

He gave her a more natural smile.

She took the picture.

“Better.”

Then she moved closer.

“Together.”

He put an arm around her.

She lifted the phone.

“Wait.”

He looked down.

“What?”

She adjusted his collar.

“It was crooked.”

He watched her fix it.

Then he gently straightened the small fold in her gown.

“There.”

She looked up.

“Thank you.”

He took the phone from her hand and held it out.

“Come closer.”

She leaned into him.

He took the photograph.

They looked at it together.

Both of them were smiling.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

“Four years ago, we were still in high school.”

“Yes.”

“We thought university would be so different.”

“It was.”

She looked up.

“Was it what you expected?”

He thought about it.

“Some things were.”

“Such as?”

“Studying. Basketball. Meeting new people.”

“And?”

He considered her.

“Having you around.”

That made her grin.

“That’s not different.”

“No.”

He brushed his thumb against her cheek.

“That was the part I hoped wouldn’t change.”

Her smile softened.

She looked down at the photograph again.

Then she said, “I think I’ll keep this one.”

“Only this one?”

“No. All of them.”

“Good.”

She slipped her hand into his.

They walked slowly toward the university gate.

Behind them, their parents were still talking. Her mother was showing Mr. Zhou one of the photographs. Her father was laughing at something Yuhao had said.

Xiaoran glanced back.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Our fathers are still together.”

He looked over his shoulder.

“Yes.”

“Should we go rescue them?”

“Do they look like they need rescuing?”

She watched them.

Her father was now holding Mr. Zhou’s phone, apparently looking at another photograph.

She sighed.

“No.”

Yichen smiled.

“Then let’s leave them.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re not worried?”

“About what?”

“That they’ll become too close.”

He leaned down slightly.

“Maybe they’ll start inviting each other to dinner.”

Xiaoran stopped walking.

“That’s exactly what I’m afraid of.”

He laughed.

She gave his hand a small tug.

“Come on. Let’s go before they make plans.”

He followed her, still smiling.

That night, Xiaoran sat on the sofa in Yichen’s apartment, her graduation gown folded over the armrest.

Her certificate was on the coffee table.

His was beside it.

Two degrees. Two different faculties.

Two people who had spent years studying in the same university but building their own lives within it.

She looked at the certificates.

Then she turned toward him.

“Do you remember our first day?”

Yichen was sitting beside her, scrolling through the photographs from the day.

“Yes.”

“I was so nervous.”

“You couldn’t find the lecture hall.”

She turned sharply.

“I found it.”

“After asking three people.”

“That doesn’t count.”

That got a smile out of him.

She leaned against him.

“I thought university would be so difficult.”

“It was.”

“I thought we wouldn’t have enough time for each other.”

“We didn’t always.”

She nodded.

“But we made it work.”

He put his phone down.

“Yes.”

She looked at him.

“Do you think we’ll be okay now?”

He knew what she meant.

The next few months would be different.

She would begin working at Morrow Studio. He would continue with the Herons, balancing training, games, and the final decisions about his future. Their schedules would change. There would be travel, deadlines, and days when they might not see each other as often as they wanted.

But they had never promised that everything would be easy.

They had promised to keep choosing each other.

He took her hand.

“We’ll work it out.”

She looked down at their joined hands, then at the ring on her finger.

“Four years ago, I asked you a ridiculous question at graduation.”

“You did.”

“And you still haven’t officially accepted.”

“I remember.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Don’t forget.”

“I won’t.”

She smiled and let her head drop onto his shoulder.

He kissed her hair.

For a while, they sat.

Then Xiaoran lifted her head.

“Do you think our parents will start arranging family dinners?”

“Probably.”

“Together?”

“Probably.”

She sighed dramatically.

“We’re never going to have privacy again.”

Yichen laughed and pulled her closer.

“You’re worrying about the wrong thing.”

“What should I be worrying about?”

“Your first day at work.”

She groaned.

“Don’t remind me.”

“You’ll be fine.”

She turned to him.

“How do you know?”

“Because I’ve seen you work.”

Her mouth tipped up.

He said, “And because you don’t give up easily.”

She leaned forward and kissed him.

When she pulled away, he brushed his thumb along her cheek.

“Congratulations, graduate.”

She smiled.

“Congratulations, graduate.”

Then she settled against him again.

On the coffee table, the two certificates lay one on top of the other, and neither of them got up to straighten them.

chapters.desc: Two more seasons with the Herons, or a graduate place at his father’s company. Then his father moves the sponsorship to another club.
chapters.title: Basketball or Business
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want anyone to have an excuse to question it.”
chapters.content:
The offer had been sitting on Yichen’s desk for three days.

He knew what he wanted.

The difficulty was that knowing what he wanted and deciding what to do with the rest of his life were two different things.

The Herons had offered him a two-season commitment. The terms were clear: he would continue as a full-contract player, with the club expecting him to participate in the regular season, training camps, promotional obligations, and the team’s development program.

Two seasons.

Two seasons in which basketball came first, and then he would decide again.

On the other side of his desk sat another folder.

His father’s company: a graduate place in operations at Zhou Logistics, starting in September.

The business he had grown up hearing about, the business his father had spent decades building, and the business that would eventually need someone capable of understanding more than just its name.

Yichen had never disliked the idea of working there.

He didn’t want to enter it because everyone had already decided that was where he belonged.

He looked at the two folders again.

Then his phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: Are you still at home?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: Have you eaten?

Yichen: Not yet.

Xiaoran: I knew it.

Yichen: What?

Xiaoran: Nothing. I’m coming over.

He looked at the message.

A moment later, another arrived.

Xiaoran: Don’t say you don’t need me to bring anything. I’m bringing food.

He laughed under his breath.

Yichen: I wasn’t going to.

Xiaoran: Good. You’ve learned.

He put his phone down and glanced at the folders once more.

Perhaps he would have an answer by the time she arrived.

Xiaoran came in carrying a paper bag and wearing the expression of someone who had already decided that the person she was visiting wasn’t to be trusted with his own meals.

“Why is your dining table covered in documents?”

Yichen closed the door behind her.

“Work.”

“Your work or your father’s work?”

“Both.”

She put the food on the table and looked at the folders.

Then she noticed the Herons’ logo on one of them.

“Ah.”

He took the bag from her.

“You’re very observant.”

“I have eyes.”

She pulled out the food containers and arranged them on the table.

“Have you decided?”

“Almost.”

She met his eyes.

“That’s not a yes or a no.”

“I’m considering the details.”

“That’s what people say when they’re trying not to answer.”

He smiled and took the seat opposite her.

She opened a container and pushed it toward him.

“Eat first.”

“Yes, boss.”

“Don’t use that tone.”

“What tone?”

“The one that makes it sound like you’re humoring me.”

He picked up his chopsticks.

“I wouldn’t dare.”

She sat across from him, watching as he began eating.

For a while, they talked about ordinary things. Her first week at Morrow Studio, a colleague who had accidentally sent a draft to the wrong client, the difficulty of remembering everyone’s names, and how she had already been asked to revise a presentation twice.

Yichen listened, occasionally asking questions.

Only when they had finished eating did Xiaoran glance toward the folders again.

“Can I ask something?”

“Of course.”

“Are you worried that if you choose basketball now, it’ll be harder to go into the business later?”

He leaned back slightly.

“Not exactly.”

“Then what?”

He considered his answer.

“I don’t want to spend two seasons playing basketball and then realize I’ve been avoiding something I should have started earlier.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“And?”

“And I don’t want to enter the company now, knowing I’ll keep wondering what I could have done if I’d given basketball two more seasons.”

She turned to him.

That, she understood.

He had worked too hard to reach this point to treat the opportunity casually. The Herons weren’t a hobby he could return to whenever he felt like it. His career was at a stage where commitment mattered.

She rested her chin on her hand.

“So you want both.”

“I want the opportunity to do both properly.”

“Then why are you looking at them as if one of them is going to disappear?”

He glanced at her.

“Because time is limited.”

“That’s a very Business student answer.”

“It’s also true.”

“I know.”

She reached across the table and tapped the Herons’ folder.

“How long?”

“Two seasons.”

“And after that?”

“I’ll reassess. I’ve discussed it with the club. I don’t want to promise them something I can’t commit to, and I don’t want to make decisions about the company before I have a better understanding of its operations.”

“Meaning?”

“I’ll finish the basketball commitment. In the meantime, I’ll continue learning about the business, but not pretend I can manage both at full capacity. After the two seasons, I’ll take a more active role. Start with operational exposure, learn the different divisions, understand the people and how decisions are made.”

She listened.

“Not walk into your father’s office and become the boss?”

He gave her a look.

“Absolutely not.”

She laughed.

“Good. I would hate to have to call you Director Zhou.”

“Would you?”

“Very embarrassing.”

He reached across the table and caught her hand.

“You’re already calling me that in your head.”

“Maybe a little.”

His mouth curved.

She squeezed his fingers.

“Yichen, I think you already know what you want.”

He met her eyes.

“You think so?”

“Yes. You’re just trying to make sure the decision doesn’t close every other door.”

He was quiet.

Then he nodded.

“That’s probably true.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Then don’t make a decision for the sake of keeping everyone comfortable.”

He turned to her.

“You’re not worried about the schedule?”

“Of course I am.”

He raised an eyebrow.

She said, “You’re going to travel. I’ll have work. We won’t always be in the same city. There will be times when I want to see you and you can’t come back, and times when you want me there but I have a deadline.”

He watched her carefully.

“But I don’t want to make that the reason you stop playing.”

His thumb moved over the back of her hand.

“Thank you.”

She smiled.

“Just don’t become so busy that you forget to call me.”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t pretend you’re fine when you’re exhausted.”

“I won’t.”

“And eat properly.”

He looked at her.

“That one seems to come up a lot.”

“Because you keep forgetting.”

He laughed.

She leaned forward.

“Go play your two seasons, Zhou Yichen.”

He held her gaze.

“You’re sure?”

“Yes. But I expect priority access to your match schedule,” she said, seriously.

He smiled.

“That’s manageable.”

“And I want to come to your games.”

“Of course.”

“And if I can’t, you have to send me a video.”

“I’ll send you the full game.”

She blinked.

“That’s too long.”

“You said a video.”

“I meant highlights.”

He laughed.

“All right.”

She looked at him for another moment.

Then she said, “I want to see you do something because you chose it. Not because you were expected to.”

He looked at her hand in his.

That was exactly what he wanted too.

His father was in his office when Yichen arrived the following afternoon.

Mr. Zhou looked up from the document he was reviewing.

“You’re early.”

“I wanted to speak with you.”

His father set the document aside.

“Sit down.”

Yichen took the chair opposite him.

Neither spoke.

The office was familiar. He had spent much of his childhood here, sometimes waiting for his father to finish a meeting, sometimes doing homework at the side table, sometimes listening to conversations he hadn’t fully understood.

Now he was sitting across from him with a decision of his own.

“I’ve decided to accept the Herons’ two-season commitment,” Yichen said.

His father didn’t look surprised.

“Have you reviewed the terms?”

“Yes.”

“With your agent?”

“Yes.”

“And you’ve considered what it means for your schedule?”

“I have.”

Mr. Zhou nodded.

“Then why are you telling me as if you’re asking for permission?”

Yichen looked at him.

“I’m not.”

His father smiled.

“Good.”

Yichen relaxed slightly.

“I also want to discuss the business.”

“Go on.”

“I don’t intend to enter the company full-time during those two seasons. I want to honor my commitment to the Herons and keep learning about the business where I can. After that, I’ll reassess and take on a more active role.”

His father listened without interrupting.

“I don’t want to be handed a position just because I’m your son. If I’m going to work there, I want to understand how the company operates. I want to know the people, the problems, and the responsibilities before I take on anything substantial,” Yichen said.

Mr. Zhou leaned back.

“That sounds reasonable.”

“I know the timing isn’t ideal.”

“Timing is rarely ideal.”

Yichen looked at him.

His father continued, “But I want you to understand something. The company will still be here in two years. If it cannot function without you entering immediately, then we have a much bigger problem than your basketball career.”

Yichen smiled slightly.

“That’s what I thought.”

“Your mother thinks you should enjoy being young while you can.”

“She says that often.”

“She’s usually right.”

A comfortable silence settled between them.

Then his father opened a folder.

“There is another matter.”

Yichen glanced at it.

“The Herons’ sponsorship?”

Mr. Zhou nodded.

“The company’s sponsorship agreement is due for review. I’ve decided we’re moving the sponsorship to another club.”

Yichen’s expression changed slightly.

“Another club?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

His father looked at him.

“Because I don’t want the company’s sponsorship and your position at the Herons to be connected in people’s minds.”

Yichen was quiet.

Mr. Zhou continued, “The company has supported the Herons for a period of time. That arrangement was made for commercial reasons, not because you were playing there. But now that you’re a contracted player, the situation is different.”

“People might assume the sponsorship influenced the contract.”

“Some people already do.”

Yichen’s expression remained composed, but his jaw tightened slightly.

His father noticed.

“I know you earned your place.”

“Then why move it?”

“Because I know you earned your place. I don’t want anyone to have an excuse to question it.”

Yichen looked at the folder.

“Will the club be affected?”

“The sponsorship will be transferred at the next contractual transition. The company will honor its existing obligations. The Herons have time to secure another sponsor.”

His father paused.

“This is a business decision. The company has other commercial priorities, and I believe the new partnership is more suitable for its current direction. Your position at the Herons is not part of the negotiation.”

Yichen studied him.

“And if I had chosen the business?”

“I would still have reviewed the sponsorship.”

His father answered without hesitation.

“Your career decision and the company’s sponsorship decision should not be confused.”

Yichen nodded slowly.

It was a distinction he appreciated.

Still, he asked, “You don’t think I’m making a mistake?”

His father looked at him.

“Do you?”

“No.”

“Then why should I?”

Yichen smiled.

His father closed the folder.

“I will tell you one thing. If you play for two seasons, play properly. Don’t treat it as a final opportunity you have to squeeze every possible achievement out of. Don’t play to prove something to me, and don’t play because you think you’ll disappoint someone if you stop.”

“I won’t.”

“And when you enter the company, don’t treat those two years as wasted time.”

Yichen looked at him.

“Playing basketball isn’t wasted time.”

His father nodded.

“Good. Then we understand each other.”

The news reached the Herons a few days later.

The club’s management had already been informed that Zhou Logistics wouldn’t renew its sponsorship. The announcement was handled through the normal commercial channels, with the company confirming its intention to support another club in the coming season.

Yichen heard about it from his agent.

He was reviewing a training schedule when his agent called.

“The sponsorship announcement is out.”

“I saw.”

“People are already talking.”

“About what?”

“Some think the company is distancing itself because you’re staying with the Herons. Others think it’s a way to remove the appearance of preferential treatment.”

Yichen was silent.

His agent continued, “The club has issued a statement confirming your contract was negotiated independently.”

“Good.”

“You’re not concerned?”

“No.”

His agent laughed.

“You’re very calm.”

“It’s a sponsorship agreement. Not my contract.”

“Fair enough.”

After the call, Yichen put his phone down.

He knew people would talk.

Some would assume his father was unhappy with his decision. Others would assume the company had been supporting him all along. Some might even suggest the sponsorship had been the reason he had received his full contract.

None of those assumptions changed what had happened on the court.

He had been evaluated. He had played.

He had earned his place.

And now he would have to continue earning it without anyone confusing his family name with his performance.

He found that he didn’t mind.

Xiaoran learned about the sponsorship change from Yichen himself.

They were sitting in his car after dinner. She had just finished telling him about a difficult client meeting when he mentioned it.

“The company has moved its sponsorship.”

She turned toward him.

“Already?”

“The announcement came out today.”

“How do you feel?”

“Fine.”

She studied his face.

“Really?”

He studied her.

“Really.”

She considered him.

“Does it bother you that people might think your father is doing it because of you?”

“It was his decision. The company has its own reasons.”

“But people might still talk.”

“They can.”

She looked out the window.

Then she turned back.

“Do you think your father is disappointed that you’re choosing basketball?”

Yichen thought about their conversation.

“No.”

“You’re sure?”

“He didn’t try to change my mind.”

“That’s good.”

“He also told me the company would still be there in two years.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“That’s very practical.”

“He’s a practical person.”

She looked at him.

“Are you relieved?”

He thought about it.

“Yes.”

“Because you made your decision?”

“Because I don’t feel like I’m leaving something unfinished.”

She nodded.

Then she reached across the center console and took his hand.

“I think that’s important.”

He looked down at their joined hands.

She said, “You can still learn about the business. You can still have a future there. But you don’t have to start everything at once.”

Something in his face eased.

“That’s what I told myself.”

“Good. Because if you tried to play basketball, manage a company, and finish another degree at the same time, I’d have to report you for unreasonable behavior.”

He laughed.

“To whom?”

“Me.”

“That sounds serious.”

“It is.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Then I’ll behave.”

The formal announcement of Yichen’s two-season commitment came a week later.

The Herons released a statement confirming that he would continue with the club under the agreed terms.

There was a photograph of him in his team jersey, standing with the club’s management.

His expression was composed, his posture relaxed.

Xiaoran saw it while sitting at her desk during lunch.

She stared at the photograph.

Then she saved it.

Then she sent it to him.

Xiaoran: Look at my boyfriend.

Yichen: I see him.

Xiaoran: Very handsome.

Yichen: Thank you.

Xiaoran: Very professional.

Yichen: I try.

Xiaoran: Very expensive to maintain.

Yichen: That’s a new description.

Xiaoran: Training food, shoes, travel, recovery. I need to prepare my budget.

Yichen: You don’t need to pay for any of that.

Xiaoran: I know. I’m making a joke.

Yichen: I know.

A moment later, he sent another message.

Yichen: Are you free this weekend?

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: I want to take you somewhere.

Xiaoran: Is it related to basketball?

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Business?

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Then what?

Yichen: A date.

She smiled at her phone.

Xiaoran: Accepted.

The date was at a quiet restaurant overlooking the river.

Nothing extravagant. Yichen had chosen it because the terrace was peaceful, and because Xiaoran had once mentioned that she liked watching the lights reflect on the water.

They sat side by side rather than opposite each other.

She was wearing a simple dress, and the promise ring caught the light whenever she moved her hand.

Yichen noticed it.

He always did.

They ordered dinner, talked about work, and discussed the coming season.

At some point, Xiaoran put down her glass.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“After two seasons, what do you think you’ll want?”

He considered her.

“From basketball?”

“From everything.”

He considered the question.

“I don’t know yet.”

“That’s okay.”

“I know I want to learn the business properly. I know I want to understand how the company works beyond what I’ve seen growing up. But I don’t know what role I’ll want, or whether I’ll be suited to it immediately.”

“That’s fair.”

“And I don’t know whether I’ll want to continue playing after two seasons. That depends on how things go.”

That made her grin.

“So you’re not making a five-year plan?”

“I have a general direction.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No.”

She held his gaze.

“I like that.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“What?”

“That you’re not pretending you know everything.”

He laughed under his breath.

“I never said I did.”

“Sometimes you act like you do.”

“That’s because you ask questions as if there is a correct answer.”

She laughed.

Then she looked at him more seriously.

“I think I’m proud of you.”

He looked at her.

“Why?”

“Because you chose something you really wanted, even though it would’ve been easier to follow the path everyone expected.”

He reached for her hand.

“Thank you.”

“And I’m proud of your father too.”

He looked mildly surprised.

“Why?”

“Because he didn’t make you choose between him and basketball.”

Yichen was quiet.

Then he nodded.

“Yes.”

She squeezed his hand.

“That’s not something everyone gets.”

He knew that.

His father hadn’t always understood what he wanted. There had been years when they spoke more about expectations than feelings, and times when Yichen had mistaken silence for disapproval.

But their conversation had been different.

His father had listened.

He had asked what Yichen wanted.

And when Yichen answered, he had allowed him to choose.

It mattered more than he had expected.

Later, when they were walking beside the river, Xiaoran slipped her hand into his coat pocket to warm her fingers.

He glanced down.

“Cold?”

“A little.”

He took her hand out and held it between both of his.

“Your hands are freezing.”

“That’s because you chose a riverside date.”

“You said you liked it.”

“I do.”

He rubbed her fingers gently.

They walked a little further.

Then Xiaoran looked up at him.

“So, two seasons.”

“Two seasons.”

“Then business.”

“Then I’ll see.”

That made her grin.

“Then you’ll see.”

He glanced at her.

“What about you?”

“What about me?”

“Where do you see yourself in two seasons?”

She thought about it.

“Hopefully making things I’m proud of. Maybe directing something bigger. Maybe managing a campaign. Maybe discovering that I want to do something completely different.”

He smiled.

“That’s a very uncertain answer.”

“Look who’s talking.”

He laughed.

She leaned against his arm.

“But I know one thing.”

“What?”

“I want to be able to look back and feel that I tried.”

He met her eyes.

“Then we’re the same.”

“Maybe.”

He stopped walking and turned toward her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“Thank you for supporting me.”

She blinked.

“Why are you thanking me?”

“Because I know it won’t always be convenient.”

She looked at him.

Then she lifted their joined hands.

“Do you remember when you supported me choosing between Shanghai and Beijing?”

“Yes.”

“You told me not to choose a smaller future just because it made our schedule easier.”

He nodded.

“Yes.”

“Well, I’m telling you the same thing.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

She said, “I don’t want you to choose a smaller future either.”

He turned to her.

Then he kissed her, there by the railing, with the river lights moving underneath them.

“All right.”

She smiled.

“And besides, I have a professional athlete boyfriend now.”

“Is that a complaint?”

“No. It sounds impressive.”

“Does it?”

“Very. I might put it in my portfolio.”

He laughed.

“Please don’t.”

She giggled and wrapped her arms around his waist.

He held her close, his chin resting lightly against her hair.

For the first time in weeks, the decision felt settled. He had chosen the life he wanted to try, and the people who mattered had given him room to do it.

On Monday morning, Yichen returned to the training facility.

The schedule was already waiting.

Strength work. Court sessions. Tactical review. Recovery.

His phone vibrated while he was changing into his training clothes.

Xiaoran: Good luck with your first full week of the new commitment.

Something in his face eased.

Yichen: Thank you.

Xiaoran: Don’t overwork.

Yichen: I won’t.

Xiaoran: Eat properly.

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: Call me when you’re done.

Yichen: I will.

A few seconds later:

Xiaoran: I’m proud of you.

Yichen: Then we’re even. What do you want for dinner?

Xiaoran: You. And dumplings.

He was still smiling when he walked past the new schedule outside the training court, his name printed beside the coming season. Two more seasons. He took a picture of it and sent that too.

chapters.desc: Her first day at Morrow Studio, a supervisor called Gao Yan, and a boyfriend under instruction not to walk her to the door.
chapters.title: First Day, Fifth of July
chapters.epigraph: “But you can wait until I get inside.”
chapters.content:
The first day of Xiaoran’s graduate job began with Yichen being told to park around the corner.

Not because he had done anything wrong.

Not because the building had no parking.

But because Xiaoran, who had spent the previous evening carefully planning her first-day outfit, checking her documents, and setting three alarms, had decided that arriving at her new workplace in her boyfriend’s car would be deeply embarrassing.

Especially if he walked her to the entrance.

Especially if anyone saw him.

And absolutely especially if he kissed her goodbye.

“Just drop me off here,” she said.

Yichen glanced at the office building ahead.

The entrance was less than twenty meters away.

“Here?”

“Yes.”

He slowed the car.

“There’s a drop-off area directly in front.”

“I know.”

“There’s also a parking garage.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you asking me to stop here?”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Because I don’t want you to park in front.”

He pulled to the curb.

“All right.”

She unfastened her seat belt and reached for her bag.

Yichen watched her.

Then he asked, quite calmly, “Are you embarrassed to be seen with me?”

She turned so quickly that her hair brushed her cheek.

“What? No!”

“Then what’s the problem?”

“There’s no problem.”

“You’re asking me to park around the corner.”

“Because—”

She stopped.

He waited.

She looked at the building, then back at him.

“Because it’s my first day.”

“I know.”

“And I want to walk in by myself.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

She blinked.

That was it?

No teasing? No argument? No attempt to persuade her?

Yichen reached over and straightened the collar of her blouse.

“Good luck today.”

She met his eyes.

“That’s all?”

“What else?”

“I don’t know.”

He smiled.

“Do you want me to give you a speech?”

“No.”

“Carry you to the entrance?”

“Yichen!”

He laughed.

She tried to look annoyed, but the smile had already appeared.

He leaned over and kissed her, briefly.

“Go on. You’re going to be late.”

Xiaoran opened the door.

Then, before getting out, she turned back.

“Wait.”

He met her eyes.

She leaned across the center console and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you for driving me.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And don’t leave yet.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“Why?”

“Just don’t.”

He nodded.

“I’ll wait.”

She got out, adjusted her bag, and walked toward the building.

Yichen watched her until she disappeared through the glass doors.

Then he checked the time.

He had told her he would wait.

So he did.

At 8:43, Yichen received a message.

Xiaoran: I’m inside.

He glanced at the building.

Yichen: I noticed.

Xiaoran: How?

Yichen: I’ve been watching you walk around the lobby looking for the reception desk.

There was a pause.

Then:

Xiaoran: You’re still there???

Something in his face eased.

Yichen: You told me not to leave.

Xiaoran: I meant until I got inside!

Yichen: You didn’t specify.

She sent him an exasperated sticker.

Yichen put his phone down and finally drove away.

Xiaoran’s first morning was a blur of introductions, unfamiliar names, passwords, and information she was trying hard to remember.

Her supervisor, Gao Yan, a small, fast woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, showed her around the studio. There were several meeting rooms, a small editing suite, a production area, and an open-plan office where people seemed to be moving between conversations with the ease of those who already knew exactly where everything was.

Xiaoran tried to look like she belonged.

She smiled when introduced to people, remembered as many names as she could, and took notes whenever someone explained a process.

By eleven, she had written down the same password twice and forgotten where she’d put her notebook.

By noon, she was beginning to feel more settled.

At lunch, she finally checked her phone.

There were three messages from Yichen.

Yichen: How’s your first morning?

Yichen: Have you met everyone?

Yichen: Remember to eat.

She smiled.

Xiaoran: It’s good! Everyone is nice. I have so many things to learn.

Yichen: That’s expected.

Xiaoran: I already forgot one person’s name.

Yichen: That’s less expected.

She laughed at her screen.

Xiaoran: Don’t bully me.

Yichen: I’m not. I’m impressed you remembered mine.

She rolled her eyes, then another message arrived.

Yichen: Did you have lunch?

She looked at the sandwich in front of her.

Xiaoran: Currently eating.

Yichen: Good.

She took a photograph of her lunch and sent it to him.

A few seconds later, he replied.

Yichen: Looks good.

Xiaoran: It’s okay. The coffee is better.

Yichen: Then next time get two coffees.

Xiaoran: One is enough.

Yichen: I know.

She smiled and put her phone away.

She didn’t know why, but having him on the other side of the city made the unfamiliar office feel a little less unfamiliar.

At 3:16 p.m., Yichen received another message.

Xiaoran: Can I ask you something?

Yichen: Of course.

Xiaoran: Do you think I looked nervous this morning?

He read it in the physio room at the Herons training center, with an ice pack on his shoulder.

He considered his answer.

Yichen: A little.

Xiaoran: I KNEW IT.

Yichen: You checked your bag three times before getting out.

Xiaoran: I was checking my documents.

Yichen: Then you checked your bag again after I told you everything was inside.

She didn’t reply immediately.

He could almost picture her expression.

Xiaoran: You notice too much.

Yichen: Occupational hazard.

Xiaoran: You’re not a detective.

Yichen: No. I’m your boyfriend.

She sent a heart.

Then:

Xiaoran: I think I’m doing okay now.

He laughed under his breath.

Yichen: I know you are.

By the time Xiaoran finished her first day, her head was full.

She had learned the team’s workflow, received her first assignment, and been introduced to more people than she could confidently remember. Her supervisor had been kind, but there was a lot to absorb.

She stepped outside at 6:08 p.m.

And stopped.

A familiar car was parked around the corner.

She stared at it.

The driver’s window lowered.

Yichen looked at her.

“Finished?”

She walked toward him, trying not to smile too obviously.

“What are you doing here?”

“Picking you up.”

“I didn’t ask you to.”

“You didn’t have to.”

She opened the passenger door, then paused.

“Wait. You parked here again?”

He glanced at the empty road around them.

“You told me to park around the corner this morning.”

“That was this morning.”

“Has the instruction expired?”

She laughed and got in.

Yichen waited until she’d fastened her seat belt.

“How was it?”

She let out a long breath.

“Good.”

“Just good?”

“Really good. But I think my brain is full.”

He nodded.

“That’s normal.”

“I met so many people. I had to introduce myself, explain my portfolio, learn the file system, understand the project process... I think I spoke too much in one meeting.” She paused, looking down at her hands.

“Did anyone complain?”

“No.”

“Then perhaps you didn’t.”

She looked at him.

“You’re supposed to say I did well.”

“You did well.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Thank you.”

He pulled away from the curb.

For a few minutes, she told him about her day. About the supervisor who had been welcoming, the colleague who showed her where the best coffee was, and the project she’d been assigned to help with.

Yichen listened, occasionally asking questions.

He didn’t interrupt or turn her stories into advice. He let her talk until she had exhausted the excitement of the day.

Then, at a red light, he looked over.

“Are you happy?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She turned toward him.

“That’s all?”

“What else?”

“I don’t know. Maybe you’re supposed to ask whether I want to go back tomorrow.”

“Do you?”

That made her grin.

“Yes.”

“Then that’s good.”

She reached across the center console and took his hand.

They stopped for dinner on the way home.

Xiaoran was still talking when their food arrived.

“And then Gao Yan said I could sit in on the production meeting next week. I don’t have to contribute yet, but I can observe. Isn’t that nice?”

“Very.”

“And she said she liked the way I presented my portfolio.”

Yichen smiled.

“She has good taste.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re biased.”

“Probably.”

She took a bite, then looked at him.

“Do you know what the funniest thing is?”

“What?”

“I spent so much time worrying about how I would look walking into the building this morning. I didn’t even think about what I’d actually say when people introduced themselves.”

He smiled.

“You were more concerned about me being seen with you?”

She paused, then narrowed her eyes.

“Don’t phrase it like that.”

“How should I phrase it?”

“I wanted to arrive independently.”

“Of course.”

“And I didn’t want people to see me getting dropped off.”

“Naturally.”

“And I definitely didn’t want you walking me to the entrance.”

He nodded.

“Understood.”

She studied him.

“You’re doing that thing again.”

“What thing?”

“Agreeing with me in a way that makes me sound ridiculous.”

His smile grew.

“You don’t need my help with that.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed, reaching across the table to take her hand.

When they got back to his flat, where she had left a change of clothes on Sunday for exactly this reason, Xiaoran went straight to the bedroom to change.

Yichen was putting the leftovers away when she came back wearing an oversized T-shirt and comfortable shorts.

She walked over and wrapped her arms around his waist.

He looked down.

“What’s this?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

She nodded against his chest.

He put the container away and rested his hands on her back.

“Long day?”

“Very.”

He kissed her temple. “You’re done now.”

She stayed there for a while.

Then she murmured, “You know, I was a little sad when you drove away this morning.”

He looked down at her.

“You told me to.”

“I know.”

“So I followed instructions.”

She lifted her head.

“You’re very obedient.”

“Only when the instructions are clear.”

She smiled.

Then she reached up and touched his cheek.

“Thank you for waiting.”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“I said I would.”

“I know.”

“And I wanted to.”

She turned to him, then kissed him.

It was a small, lingering kiss, the kind that made the day feel finished.

When she pulled away, he rested his forehead against hers.

“Tomorrow, do you want me to drop you at the entrance?”

She considered it, then shook her head.

“No. Around the corner.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right.”

“But you can wait until I get inside.”

“I can do that.”

“And maybe...”

She hesitated.

He raised an eyebrow.

“Maybe?”

“Maybe you can walk me to the entrance on Friday.”

His expression softened.

“Why Friday?”

“Because by then I’ll be familiar with everyone.”

“That makes sense.”

“And I won’t feel so nervous.”

He nodded.

“Then Friday.”

That made her grin.

“And you can kiss me goodbye.”

He turned to her.

“Only on Friday?”

She laughed.

“Don’t push your luck.”

He kissed her.

“Welcome to your first week, Lin Xiaoran.”

She smiled against his chest.

At ten, he walked her across the road and up the four flights to her studio, and carried her bag, and waited on the landing until she had found her keys, which were in the side pocket she never used.

chapters.desc: Her first salary, checked seventeen times by lunch, and the first dinner she pays for.
chapters.title: First Pay Slip
chapters.epigraph: “Not because I owe you. Because I want to.”
chapters.content:
Her first salary arrived on the last Friday of July, and by lunchtime Xiaoran had checked her bank account seventeen times.

Yichen knew because he had counted.

The first time had been when she woke up. The second was while brushing her teeth.

The third was during breakfast.

By the time they met for lunch, she had checked it another six times.

And now, sitting across from him in a café near her office, she was looking at her banking app again.

Yichen lowered his cup.

“Did the number change?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“No.”

“Then why are you checking?”

She turned her phone toward him.

“Look.”

He glanced at the screen.

Her first salary had arrived that morning.

The amount was displayed beneath her account balance, accompanied by a small transaction description from her employer.

Yichen looked at it, then back at her.

“Congratulations.”

Her mouth tipped up.

It wasn’t a large smile at first. More like she was trying to contain something that had been building inside her since she saw the notification.

Then it grew.

“I got paid.”

“I can see that.”

“My first salary.”

“I know.”

“From my job.”

He nodded solemnly.

“Yes, Xiaoran. That’s generally how salaries work.”

She kicked his shoe beneath the table.

He laughed.

She looked down at her phone again.

“I can’t believe it.”

He watched her.

It was a small thing, really. A salary notification. A number appearing in an account.

But he knew what it meant to her.

She had spent months working toward this. Her first days at Morrow Studio had been filled with unfamiliar names, unfamiliar expectations, and the pressure of proving that she deserved to be there. She had come home tired, sometimes frustrated, sometimes excited enough to talk about a project for an hour.
