She had learned how to communicate with clients, defend creative decisions, manage production schedules, and work with people who had entirely different ideas about what a project should become.

And now, for the first time, she had been paid for work that she had done as a professional.

He reached across the table.

He held out his hand.

She put her phone down and gave him her hand.

He kissed her knuckles.

“I knew you could.”

“Thank you.”

Then she picked up her phone again.

Yichen looked at her.

“Again?”

“I’m just looking.”

“At the same number?”

“It’s a very nice number.”

He laughed.

The idea came to her that afternoon.

They were walking toward the car when Xiaoran stopped.

“Yichen.”

He turned.

“Mm?”

“I want to take you to dinner.”

He met her eyes.

“We’re having dinner tonight.”

“I know.”

“Where?”

She smiled.

“Somewhere nice.”

He waited.

“And I’m paying.”

He turned to her.

Then his expression softened.

“All right.”

She blinked.

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“You didn’t even pretend to argue.”

“Would you like me to?”

She thought about it.

“No.”

“Then I’ll save us both the trouble.”

She laughed and took his arm.

“I’ve been thinking about it since this morning.”

“About dinner?”

“Yes. I want to use my first salary to buy you a meal.”

He glanced at her.

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.”

She met his eyes.

“You’ve taken me to so many places. You’ve paid for so many dinners. You’ve bought me things, driven me around, planned trips, and made sure I never had to worry about anything when we’re together.”

“That’s not a list of things you owe me for.”

“Mm.”

She stopped walking and turned toward him.

“That’s why I want to do this. Not because I owe you. Because I want to.”

He held her gaze.

Then he nodded.

“All right.”

Her face brightened.

She immediately opened her phone.

“Let me choose the restaurant.”

He glanced at the screen.

“Take your time.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You’re not going to secretly book somewhere else?”

“No.”

“Or call the restaurant and tell them you’re paying?”

“No.”

“Or give them your card?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Do you think I would do that?”

She eyed him.

“Sometimes.”

He laughed.

“Then you’ll have to watch me carefully.”

Choosing the restaurant turned out to be harder than Xiaoran expected.

She had initially wanted somewhere elegant, but the prices made her hesitate.

Then she found a place with a beautiful interior, but the menu looked too small.

Another restaurant had excellent reviews, but she wasn’t sure whether Yichen would enjoy the food.

She spent nearly an hour comparing options.

Yichen, who had been sitting beside her on the sofa, eventually asked:

“Are you choosing a restaurant or negotiating a business acquisition?”

“Both require careful consideration.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Of course.”

She showed him her shortlist.

“Which one?”

He studied the options.

“Where do you want to go?”

“That’s not helpful.”

“It’s your dinner.”

She looked at the screen again.

Then she pointed to one.

“This one.”

“Then let’s go there.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Okay.”

“Are you sure?”

She nodded.

“I checked the menu. It’s within my budget.”

He didn’t comment on the budget.

He said, “Then it’s settled.”

She booked a table.

Then she put her phone down and leaned against him.

“Do you know what I want?”

“What?”

“I want to be able to do this more often.”

He looked down at her.

“Take me to dinner?”

“Yes. Pay for things. Buy you something without you noticing the price first.”

He laughed.

“That last part might be difficult.”

She lifted her head.

“Why?”

“Because I usually notice.”

She groaned.

“You’re the worst.”

He kissed her temple.

“I’ll try to be less observant.”

The restaurant was lovely.

It had warm lighting, dark wooden furniture, and large windows overlooking the evening traffic.

Xiaoran had arrived a little early and checked the reservation twice.

When Yichen walked in, she was already sitting at the table, looking at the menu.

He approached and pulled out the chair opposite her.

“Waiting long?”

“No.”

He sat down.

She immediately handed him the menu.

“I’ve already looked.”

“I assumed.”

“There’s a dish I think you’ll like.”

He glanced at the menu.

“Which one?”

She pointed.

“This.”

He read the description.

“Looks good.”

“I thought so.”

He studied her.

“You’ve researched the entire menu, haven’t you?”

She smiled proudly.

“Yes.”

“Of course.”

They ordered.

Xiaoran chose a dish she had been wanting to try, while Yichen ordered the one she had recommended. She also insisted on ordering dessert before they had even finished their main courses.

“Why are you ordering dessert now?” he asked.

“Because if we wait, I’ll forget.”

“You won’t.”

“I might.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right.”

She looked pleased.

Dinner was easy.

They talked about her first month at work, the people she had met, and the projects she was beginning to handle more independently.

She told him about a client who had changed their mind three times about the same visual concept.

Yichen listened with the patient attention he always gave her.

“Did you agree with the final direction?” he asked.

“Not entirely.”

“Then?”

“I explained why I thought the earlier version was stronger. But they had a different objective, so we adjusted it.”

“Good.”

She turned to him.

“You’re not going to tell me I should have fought harder?”

“Do you think you should have?”

She considered it.

“No. I think I explained my reasoning properly.”

“Then you did your job.”

That made her grin.

Sometimes, she liked that he didn’t automatically tell her she was right.

He took her work seriously enough to ask her to think about it.

After a while, the food arrived.

Xiaoran watched him take the first bite.

“Well?”

“Good.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She looked pleased.

“I chose well.”

“You did.”

She rested her chin on her hand.

“Do you know why I chose this restaurant?”

“Because you liked the menu?”

“Partly.”

He waited.

She smiled.

“Because I wanted somewhere that felt special, but not somewhere I would be uncomfortable paying.”

He considered her.

“That’s sensible.”

“I know.”

She picked up her glass.

“I wanted to take you somewhere nice with my first salary. I didn’t want to spend more than I could comfortably afford just to prove something.”

Yichen nodded.

“That’s a good way to think about it.”

That made her grin.

“I think I’m becoming a responsible adult.”

“Are you?”

She kicked his shoe again.

He laughed.

After dinner, they ordered dessert.

Xiaoran had chosen a small chocolate cake to share, but when it arrived, she immediately took the first bite.

Yichen watched her.

“How is it?”

She nodded enthusiastically.

“Very good.”

“Then I’m glad we ordered it.”

She pushed the plate toward him.

“Try.”

He took a bite.

She watched him.

“Well?”

“Good.”

“Only good?”

“Very good.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“That’s better.”

They finished the dessert slowly.

When the waiter brought the bill, Xiaoran reached for it before Yichen could move.

He noticed.

But he didn’t interfere.

She took the bill folder and opened it.

She looked at the total.

Then she took out her card.

Yichen watched her.

She handed the folder to the waiter.

“Thank you.”

When the waiter left, she sat back.

Her expression was strangely serious.

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing.”

He waited.

She looked down at the table.

“I paid.”

“Yes.”

“With my salary.”

“I know.”

She held his gaze.

“You’re not going to say anything?”

He leaned back slightly.

“What would you like me to say?”

She thought about it.

Then her smile slowly appeared.

“That I did well.”

He took her hand across the table.

“You did very well.”

Her eyes softened.

He said, “Not because you paid for dinner. Because you worked for that salary, and you wanted to use a part of it to make someone you love happy.”

She looked down.

Then she squeezed his hand.

“You’re making it sound very emotional.”

“Isn’t it?”

She laughed.

“A little.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her fingers.

“Thank you for dinner.”

She smiled.

“You’re welcome. Next time, I’ll buy you something too.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You’re already planning the next one?”

“Of course.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Very.”

He laughed.

They walked out of the restaurant together.

The night air was cool, and the street was quieter than it had been when they arrived.

Xiaoran slipped her hand into his.

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

Her mouth tipped up.

Then she looked down at her hand.

The promise ring caught the light.

She turned it slightly.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Do you think I’ll get used to receiving my salary?”

“Probably.”

“Will it always feel this exciting?”

He thought about it.

“Maybe not in the same way.”

“That’s sad.”

“Not necessarily. The first time is special because it’s the first. Later, it might feel normal. That’s not a bad thing.”

She nodded.

“I suppose.”

“But I hope you keep remembering what you worked for.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I will.”

He opened the passenger door for her.

Before getting in, she turned around.

“Wait.”

He glanced at her.

She stepped closer and wrapped her arms around his waist.

He returned the hug.

“Thank you for letting me pay.”

He smiled against her hair.

“You’re welcome.”

“And thank you for not making it awkward.”

“Was I supposed to?”

“No. But you sometimes try to pay before I can.”

He laughed.

“I’ll be more careful next time.”

She leaned back and looked at him.

“Good.”

Then she tugged him down and kissed him.

“Thank you for coming to dinner, Mr. Zhou.”

He met her eyes.

“Thank you for having me, Ms. Lin.”

She climbed into the car, smiling.

Later, back at his apartment, Xiaoran opened her banking app again.

Yichen was changing out of his shirt when he saw her sitting on the bed.

“Checking your salary again?”

“No.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I’m checking my remaining balance.”

“Ah.”

She turned the phone toward him.

“Look. I still have enough.”

“That’s good.”

“And I didn’t spend too much.”

“I know.”

She put the phone down and looked at him.

“Today was nice.”

He came over and sat beside her.

“It was.”

“I liked paying for you.”

“I liked being taken out.”

She smiled.

She leaned against him.

“Then I’ll do it again.”

He put an arm around her shoulders.

“I’ll look forward to it.”

She looked up.

She laughed.

Then she became quiet.

After a moment, she said, “I think I understand something now.”

“What?”

“Why you like paying for things sometimes.”

He looked down at her.

She said, “It’s not always about the money. Sometimes it’s just nice to be able to do something for someone you care about.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Yes.”

She rested her head against his chest.

“I used to think I had to wait until I could afford something expensive to give you something meaningful.”

He brushed her hair away from her face.

“You don’t.”

“I know that now.”

She lifted her hand and looked at the ring.

“Today was meaningful.”

He kissed her hair.

“It was.”

She smiled and settled against him.

Her first salary had been deposited that morning.

By evening, a part of it had become dinner, dessert, and a memory she would probably remember long after the exact amount had faded from her mind.

It was the first time she had looked across a restaurant table, handed over her own card, and felt that she was giving him something from a life she was beginning to build for herself.

And Yichen, who had spent years taking care of her in ways both large and small, understood exactly why she had wanted to do it.

He held her a little closer.

“Congratulations on your first salary, Xiaoran.”

She smiled against his chest.

“Thank you. Next month, I’m buying you breakfast too.”

He laughed.

“All right.”

She closed her eyes, satisfied.

chapters.desc: His first full preseason with the Herons, and a fridge full of labeled containers he didn’t ask for.
chapters.title: Preseason Meal Prep
chapters.epigraph: “Because I know you’ll want something comforting after a difficult day.”
chapters.content:
Yichen’s first mistake was saying he could manage his own meals.

His second mistake was saying it while Xiaoran was standing in the kitchen.

She looked up from her laptop.

“Sorry?”

He was taking a bottle of water from the refrigerator.

“What?”

“What did you just say?”

“I said I can manage my meals.”

She slowly closed her laptop.

“During preseason?”

“Yes.”

“With your training schedule?”

“Yes.”

“Three meals a day?”

He met her eyes.

“That’s generally how meals work.”

She squinted at him.

“Don’t be clever.”

He smiled and took a drink.

“I’m not.”

She stared at him for another moment.

Then she stood.

“Fine.”

Yichen watched her walk toward the kitchen.

“Fine?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

She opened the refrigerator and began taking things out.

He looked at the ingredients, then at her.

“What are you doing?”

“Helping you manage your meals.”

Something in his face eased.

“I didn’t ask you to.”

“I know.”

She placed vegetables on the counter.

“But I’m doing it anyway.”

The idea had started with his preseason schedule.

The Herons’ preseason had started: double sessions, strength work, conditioning, film. It was his first full season with the first team, and his schedule was tighter than it had ever been.

He wasn’t bad at taking care of himself.

He ate properly, understood what his body needed, and was disciplined about recovery.

But he was also the kind of person who would finish a late training session, return home tired, and decide that a simple meal was enough.

Xiaoran had noticed.

She didn’t want to monitor him or turn his food into another responsibility.

She wanted to make the busy days easier.

So she suggested preparing a few meals in advance.

Yichen had agreed to the idea.

He hadn’t expected her to approach it like a production project.

On Saturday morning, she arrived with a notebook.

Yichen looked at it.

“What’s that?”

“Our meal-prep plan.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Of course.”

She opened it on the kitchen counter.

“I asked what you usually eat, checked what you have in the refrigerator, and made a list.”

He looked down. There were columns for ingredients, preparation, storage, and estimated portions, ruled in pencil, the way her mother ruled the household accounts.

He turned to her.

“You made a spreadsheet?”

“No.”

He glanced at the notebook again.

“That looks suspiciously like a spreadsheet.”

“It’s handwritten.”

“That doesn’t make it less of a spreadsheet.”

She ignored him.

“We’re making chicken, rice, vegetables, and some beef. We can prepare different combinations so you don’t get bored.”

“Sounds good.”

“And I want you to tell me if anything doesn’t work with your training schedule.”

“All right.”

She looked pleased.

Then she handed him an apron.

He took it.

“What’s this?”

“You’re helping.”

“I assumed.”

The kitchen quickly became busy.

Xiaoran handled the vegetables while Yichen prepared the chicken.

She had tied her hair up and was concentrating on cutting carrots into even pieces.

Yichen glanced over.

“Those are very precise.”

“They’re supposed to cook evenly.”

He looked at the cutting board.

“You’re cutting them into identical pieces.”

“Then why are you watching?”

“Because you’re very serious.”

She lifted her knife slightly.

“Cooking is serious.”

He smiled and returned to the chicken.

They worked comfortably together.

She washed and chopped vegetables, he seasoned the meat, and they took turns checking the rice. Occasionally, one of them reached across the other for a utensil, or their shoulders brushed as they moved around the kitchen.

At one point, Yichen reached for a bowl.

Xiaoran moved it away.

“Not that one.”

He held her gaze.

“Why?”

“That’s for the vegetables.”

He glanced at the bowl in his hand.

“Then which one?”

She pointed.

He took the other bowl.

A minute later, he reached for another container.

“Not that one.”

He studied her.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Am I allowed to use anything in this kitchen?”

She laughed.

“Yes. Just follow the system.”

He looked at the counter.

“Your system has more rules than my training schedule.”

“Your training schedule doesn’t involve food containers.”

“Thankfully.”

By noon, the kitchen counter was covered with prepared ingredients.

They arranged everything into containers, separating meals according to the days Yichen would need them.

Xiaoran checked each one against her notebook.

Yichen stood beside her, reading the labels.

“Monday.”

She nodded.

“Tuesday.”

“Yes.”

“Wednesday.”

“Yes.”

He picked up one container.

“What’s this one?”

“Chicken with vegetables.”

“And this?”

“Beef.”

He looked at the label.

“Why does this one say ‘eat first’?”

“Because it won’t keep as long.”

He nodded.

Then he picked up another container.

It had a small handwritten note on the lid.

For the day training is terrible.

She was busy putting the remaining vegetables away.

“What’s this?”

She glanced over.

“Oh. That one’s for when you’re especially tired.”

“What’s inside?”

“Something you like.”

He opened the container slightly.

His favorite noodles.

He looked at her.

“You made this too?”

“Just one portion.”

“Why?”

“Because I know you’ll want something comforting after a difficult day.”

He was quiet.

Then he set the container down and reached for her hand.

“Thank you.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You’re welcome.”

He kissed her hair.

The real problem came when they tried to fit everything into the refrigerator.

There were too many containers.

Xiaoran opened the refrigerator door.

Yichen stood behind her.

She moved one shelf, then another, then removed a bottle of juice.

“Where did this come from?”

He looked at it.

“Your mother gave it to me.”

“How long ago?”

“Last week.”

She turned.

“Yichen.”

“What?”

She held up the bottle.

“Why is it still here?”

“I haven’t finished it.”

She blinked at him, then placed it on the counter.

“Drink it today.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Yes, ma’am.”

She gave him a look.

He laughed and helped rearrange the shelves.

Eventually, they managed to fit everything inside.

Xiaoran stepped back, satisfied.

“Done.”

Yichen looked at the refrigerator.

“Impressive.”

“Now you don’t have to think about what to eat after training.”

He considered her.

“I still have to think about taking it out.”

“That’s not difficult.”

“You’re right.”

She closed the refrigerator, then leaned against it, looking at him.

“What?”

He shook his head.

“Nothing.”

“Tell me.”

He reached over and brushed a small piece of vegetable from her sleeve.

“I like that you think about these things.”

Her expression softened.

“It’s not a big thing.”

“I know.”

He took her hand.

“But you do it anyway.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You’re my boyfriend. I’m allowed to take care of you.”

He glanced at her, then kissed her.

Three days later, Xiaoran received a photograph.

It was a picture of an empty food container.

Yichen: Finished.

She couldn’t help smiling.

Xiaoran: Good. Which one?

Yichen: The chicken.

Xiaoran: Did you like it?

Yichen: Yes.

A moment later, another photograph arrived.

This time, it showed the container labelled:

For the day training is terrible.

It was empty too.

Yichen: This one was especially good.

Xiaoran laughed.

Xiaoran: I knew you’d like it.

Yichen: Can I request another one?

She smiled at her phone.

Xiaoran: You can request. I can’t promise.

Yichen: Understood.

Then:

Yichen: Thank you, Xiaoran.

She looked at the message, then replied.

Xiaoran: You’re welcome. Don’t skip your meals.

Yichen: I won’t.

She put her phone down and returned to her work.

A few minutes later, it buzzed again.

Yichen: I miss you.

She smiled.

Xiaoran: I miss you too.

Then another message appeared.

Yichen: And the noodles.

She stared at the screen, then burst out laughing.

Xiaoran: ZHOU YICHEN.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: Both can be true.

She shook her head, still smiling.

That evening, when Yichen returned from training, he found Xiaoran sitting on the sofa with her laptop.

He went to the kitchen first.

Opened the refrigerator.

Looked at the remaining containers, then took one out.

She watched him from the living room.

“What’s that?”

“Dinner.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Good choice.”

He warmed it up and brought it to the table.

Then he came over and kissed her hair.

“Thank you for preparing everything.”

She looked up.

“You’re welcome.”

He glanced toward the kitchen.

“Although I think we need more containers.”

She laughed.

“Already?”

“Yes.”

She closed her laptop.

“Then we’ll buy some next time.”

He nodded.

Then, after a moment, he said, “But next time, I’m making the noodles.”

She looked suspicious.

“Why?”

“Because you made them this time.”

“So?”

“So I should make something for you.”

That made her grin.

“All right.”

He held out his hand.

“Come eat with me.”

She took it.

They sat together at the dining table, and he glanced at her.

She was telling him something about a client brief at the studio, using her hands as she spoke.

He reached across the table and touched her fingers.

She stopped.

She smiled.

“You’re looking at me.”

“I know.”

“Why?”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Just because.”

And she went right back to talking, as if he hadn’t just made her heart feel a little too full over an ordinary dinner.

chapters.desc: She is moving in with Yichen in November. Her mother approved in September. Her father was fishing.
chapters.title: Telling, Not Asking
chapters.epigraph: “I liked that your door only had one name on it.”
chapters.content:
The decision had been made for eleven days.

Xiaoran had worked it out the way she worked out everything: the rent he already paid and the half she would now pay, the twenty-minute walk to Morrow instead of the five minutes across the road, the date her studio lease ran out, the four flights of stairs she wouldn’t miss. She had made a spreadsheet. Her mother would have approved of the spreadsheet.

She had also spoken to Yichen.

More than once.

They had been talking about it since the summer. They had looked at three flats they both disliked, gone through the rent more than once, and in September, on his sofa, decided on his. He had given her a spare key on a plain ring that he had clearly been carrying in his pocket for a week. He knew which weekend in November the van was booked, and he had cleared two shelves and half a wardrobe without once asking whether that would be enough.

Her mother had been told on the phone, had asked one question about the rent and one about whose name was on the lease, and had approved of both answers.

That left one conversation.

Her father.

She had postponed it twice.

Not because she intended to change her mind. She had been waiting for the right moment, which was becoming ridiculous, because there was no right moment to tell a father his daughter was moving in with someone.

On the second afternoon of the National Day holiday, home on the train for three days, she found him in the small storage room beside the kitchen.

He was trying to fix the handle of an old cabinet.

“Dad.”

He looked over his shoulder.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you standing there like that?”

She leaned against the doorframe.

“Can I talk to you?”

He put down the screwdriver.

“Of course.”

She had prepared a speech. A fairly good one, actually. It included the lease, the rent, the walk to work, and the fact that she had already considered the financial implications.

But when he looked at her, she found herself abandoning the entire thing.

“I’m moving in with Yichen.”

Her father didn’t immediately respond.

He looked at her, then slowly straightened.

“When?”

“November. The second weekend.”

“Your mother knows?”

“Since September.”

He absorbed this. “So I’m last.”

“You were fishing.”

He nodded once.

Xiaoran clasped her hands together.

“I’m telling you because I want you to know. I’ve thought about it carefully. I’ve done the rent, the lease, the walk to work. I know you might think it’s soon, and I know you’ll worry, but I’ve made my decision.”

She took a breath.

“I’m not asking.”

Her father looked at her.

There was no immediate argument. No sharp question about why she hadn’t waited, no reminder that she was twenty-two.

Instead, he asked, “Is your name going on the lease?”

Xiaoran blinked. “Yes. They’re adding me in November.”

“Have you read it?”

“Twice.”

“Then read it a third time before you sign.” She stared at him.

“Okay.”

“And keep your own copy. Not on his computer. Yours.”

“I know.”

“Do you, though?”

“Yes, Dad.”

He looked at her for another second.

Then he picked up the screwdriver again.

“All right.”

Xiaoran didn’t move.

“All right?”

He glanced up.

“Do you need me to say it again?”

She let out a breath that was almost a laugh.

“I thought you might be angry.”

“I’m not happy that you’re going so far away.”

Her smile faded slightly.

He put the screwdriver down again.

“That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t go.”

She met his eyes.

Her father sighed and rubbed his palm against his trousers.

“I worried when you went to Shanghai on your own. I worried when you took a studio up four flights of stairs with a lift that never worked. I’m going to worry about this too. You’re my daughter. I’m going to worry whether you’re twenty-two or forty.”

“Dad...”

“But I also know you didn’t make this decision yesterday. You’ve worked for it. You’ve thought about it. And if I keep telling you to stay because I’m worried, what am I asking you to do? Give up something you want so I can feel comfortable?”

Xiaoran’s eyes began to sting.

He looked away first, pretending to inspect the cabinet.

“I don’t want that.”

She swallowed.

“I don’t want you to think this means I’ll come home less.”

“I know.”

“I’ll visit.”

“I know.”

“And I’ll call.”

“I know, Xiaoran.”

He finally looked at her again.

“You’re moving across a road. You’re not going to another planet.”

She laughed, though her voice wavered.

“That’s not what it feels like.”

“It will feel smaller once you’ve unpacked.”

She wiped beneath one eye.

Her father noticed but didn’t comment.

Instead, he turned toward the cabinet, opened the bottom drawer, and pulled out a metal toolbox.

It was old, with scratches along the edges and a faded label on the lid. He set it on the floor between them.

Xiaoran looked down.

“What’s that?”

“A toolbox.”

“I can see that.”

“Then why did you ask?”

She gave him a look.

He opened it.

Inside were screwdrivers, a measuring tape, pliers, a small hammer, a utility knife, a packet of screws, and several other things she couldn’t identify.

Her father began taking things out and checking them.

“A flat with two people in it comes loose twice as fast. Handles, shelves, things like that.”

“Dad, it’s his flat. He has tools.”

“Does he?”

She thought about it. “He has a screwdriver.”

“One screwdriver.”

“Yes.”

“Exactly.”

He tested the screwdriver.

“Some of these are old. I’ll replace them.”

“You’re giving me this?”

“Yes.”

“But this is yours.”

“I have another one.”

She looked at the toolbox again.

It was clearly well-used. The handle had been repaired with black tape, and the metal inside had worn smooth in places from years of use.

“Dad, you don’t have to.”

“I know.”

He continued sorting through the tools.

“Do you know how to use a screwdriver?”

“Of course.”

“Which direction do you turn it to tighten a screw?”

She frowned.

“Clockwise.”

“And to loosen it?”

“Counterclockwise.”

He nodded.

“Good. At least you won’t destroy the furniture.”

“Dad!”

He laughed.

Then he took out the measuring tape and showed her how to lock it in place.

“Don’t pull it too far. It can snap back.”

She watched him.

He demonstrated how to use the small hammer, how to hold the pliers, and how to distinguish between the different screwdriver heads.

It was such an ordinary thing to teach.

Almost absurdly ordinary, considering what they had just discussed.

“Dad,” she said.

“Hm?”

“Are you really okay with it?”

His hands paused.

He met her eyes.

“I liked that your door only had one name on it.”

She nodded. “It’ll have two now.”

“I know. I’m okay with it.”

He closed the toolbox.

Then, after a moment, he said, “You don’t need my permission to grow up.”

Xiaoran’s eyes filled properly this time.

Her father looked uncomfortable.

“Oh, don’t start crying.”

She laughed through it.

“I’m not.”

“Your eyes say otherwise.”

She stepped forward and hugged him.

He was still holding the toolbox when she wrapped her arms around him. He stood there for a second, then set it down and held her properly.

His hand rested against the back of her head.

“You can come home whenever you want,” he said.

“I know.”

“And if anything goes wrong, call me.”

“I will.”

“Even if it’s late.”

“I know.”

“Even if you think it’s something small.”

She nodded against his shoulder.

“Okay.”

He held her a little longer.

Then he stepped back and picked up the toolbox.

“Come on. Let’s see if everything fits.”

She laughed.

“Where?”

“In your suitcase?”

“Dad, it’s a toolbox.”

“Then we’ll find another bag.”

Yichen, home for exactly one night before the Herons left for twenty-six days on the road, came round that evening.

He found Xiaoran sitting on the living room floor beside an open toolbox, surrounded by small metal objects.

He stopped at the doorway.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“My father gave me a toolbox.”

Yichen glanced at the tools.

“I see.”

“He taught me how to use everything.”

“That’s good.”

“He asked if I knew which way to turn a screwdriver.”

Yichen looked at her with great interest, and said nothing at all.

“Don’t start.”

He smiled and came over, crouching beside her.

“What’s in there?”

“Everything.”

He picked up a screwdriver and examined it.

“That’s a good set.”

“Apparently, it’s been with him for years.”

Yichen nodded.

He understood immediately that this wasn’t a box of tools.

He looked at her.

“Did you tell him?”

She nodded. “The lease, the rent, the second weekend in November.”

“And?”

She picked up the measuring tape and ran her thumb over the worn plastic casing.

“He said I don’t need his permission to grow up.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

He put the screwdriver down.

“That’s a good answer.”

She nodded.

Then she leaned sideways until her shoulder rested against his.

“He gave me the toolbox.”

Yichen looked at it again.

“That sounds like your father.”

“He’s going to replace some of the old tools before November.”

“Of course he is.”

That made her grin.

“He also told me to keep my own copy of the lease. Not on your computer.”

“Also good advice.”

“You’re both very annoying.”

Yichen laughed.

He slipped an arm around her shoulders and drew her closer.

“Shall I clear a third shelf?”

She looked up. “For the toolbox.”

“For the toolbox.”

“And don’t put it under the sink where I’ll never find it.”

He met her eyes.

“I won’t.”

She studied him.

Then she leaned forward and kissed him.

It was brief, but Yichen followed her when she pulled away, brushing his nose against hers.

“What was that for?”

“For being sensible.”

“I’ll try not to make a habit of it.”

She laughed.

He kissed her, briefly.

The toolbox sat open between them, filled with things that had been used to fix a hundred little problems around her childhood home.

In November it would go across the road with her and eleven floors up, onto a third shelf, where Yichen would put his one screwdriver beside it, out of respect.

chapters.desc: Twenty-six days, four cities, a missed call and an argument about dinner. They nearly make themselves lonely being considerate.
chapters.title: Away Season
chapters.epigraph: “Send each other one ordinary thing every day.”
chapters.content:
The first time Yichen told Xiaoran he would be away for three weeks in October, she said it was fine. The second time he mentioned that the schedule might extend by another week, she said it was still fine.

The third time, when he explained that the Herons would be traveling between cities for a series of away games, she looked at him.

Then she asked, “How many cities?”

“Four.”

“How many days?”

“Probably twenty-six.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

Yichen watched her.

“That’s all?”

“What else should I say?”

“I don’t know.”

She smiled and reached for his hand.

“Go play basketball.”

He met her eyes.

She squeezed his fingers.

“I know it’s part of the season. I know you can’t just come back whenever you want. I’ll be busy too.”

“Your studio has a major project coming up.”

“Exactly. We’ll both be busy.”

He studied her expression.

She was smiling, but he knew her well enough to notice the little things: the way she was turning the ring on her finger, the way her thumb kept moving over the same spot on his hand.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“If it’s difficult, tell me.”

She looked up.

“I will.”

He nodded.

Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“Besides, I’ll get to watch my boyfriend play away games. That’s quite impressive.”

He smiled.

“You already do.”

“I know. I’m just reminding people.”

He laughed and pulled her closer.

Neither of them knew yet how long twenty-six days could feel.

The first week was easy.

Almost suspiciously easy.

Yichen left on a Monday morning. Xiaoran accompanied him to the station, carrying his small travel bag while he handled the larger luggage.

He was dressed casually, with a cap pulled low over his forehead.

She stood beside him, checking the departure time.

“Do you have everything?”

“Yes.”

“Charger?”

“Yes.”

“Training shoes?”

He turned to her.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I packed them.”

“Okay. I’m just checking.”

He smiled and took the bag from her.

The announcement for boarding came shortly afterward.

She looked at him.

“Call me when you arrive.”

“I will.”

“And when you reach the hotel.”

“All right.”

“And after training.”

“Yes.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“Don’t just say yes to everything.”

He laughed.

“What would you like me to say?”

“That you’ll miss me.”

He lowered his head and kissed her, briefly.

“I’ll miss you.”

“Good.”

Then she wrapped her arms around him.

He held her for a little longer than usual.

When they finally separated, he brushed her hair away from her face.

“Go home safely.”

“You too.”

He picked up his luggage.

She watched him walk toward the platform.

Before disappearing into the crowd, he turned around once.

She waved.

He laughed under his breath.

Then he was gone.

That evening, Xiaoran received a photograph of his hotel room.

It showed a large bed, a desk, a window overlooking the city, and his suitcase placed neatly beside the wardrobe.

Yichen: Arrived.

Xiaoran: The room looks nice.

Yichen: It is.

Xiaoran: Have you eaten?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: What?

He sent her a photograph of his dinner.

She zoomed in.

Xiaoran: That’s not enough vegetables.

Yichen: There are vegetables.

Xiaoran: Three pieces of broccoli.

Yichen: Four.

She laughed.

Xiaoran: I’m reporting you to your nutritionist.

Yichen: Please don’t.

They called later that night.

Xiaoran was already in bed, her laptop open beside her. Yichen was sitting against the hotel headboard, his hair still slightly damp from his shower.

“How was training?” she asked.

“Good. We had a light session after traveling.”

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then sleep early.”

He held her gaze.

“You’re still working?”

“Just reviewing something.”

“What time is your meeting tomorrow?”

“Nine.”

“Then you should sleep too.”

She closed her laptop halfway.

“Look at us. We’re both telling each other to sleep.”

“Someone has to.”

That made her grin.

For a while, they talked about their day.

Nothing important.

A colleague who had misunderstood her instructions. A teammate who had made an amusing mistake during practice. The restaurant near the hotel. The weather.

When they finally said goodnight, Xiaoran felt that the distance wasn’t too bad.

They had their routines. They had their calls.

They were fine.

By the second week, their schedules began to collide.

Yichen’s games were usually in the evening, but training and team meetings occupied much of the day. Travel between cities made his schedule unpredictable.

Xiaoran’s studio, meanwhile, had entered the final stages of a major campaign.

She was working on a branded short film, coordinating with the production team and helping prepare the final presentation for the client.

The project was important.

It was also becoming increasingly exhausting.

On Wednesday, she sent Yichen a photograph of her desk.

There were two empty coffee cups, a notebook, a half-eaten sandwich, and her laptop displaying a timeline.

Xiaoran: My office has become my second home.

Yichen: Have you eaten properly?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: That’s not an answer.

Xiaoran: I had a sandwich.

Yichen: When?

She looked at the time.

It had been four hours.

Xiaoran: Earlier.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Don’t start.

Yichen: I’m not starting. Order something.

She sighed and put her phone down.

A few minutes later, a delivery notification appeared.

Yichen had ordered dinner to her office.

She stared at the notification.

Then she called him.

He answered after the second ring.

“Hello?”

“Why did you order food?”

“Because you haven’t eaten.”

“I could have ordered something myself.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

He was quiet.

“Because I wanted to.”

She leaned back in her chair.

“You’re not here, so you can’t keep sending food every time I forget to eat.”

“I know.”

“Yichen.”

“Xiaoran.”

She sighed.

He continued, gently, “You don’t have to make it difficult for me to take care of you just because I’m away.”

Her expression softened.

“I know.”

“Good. Eat before it gets cold.”

She smiled.

“Okay.”

After the call, she opened the delivery bag.

There was a handwritten note attached to the container.

Eat properly. I’ll call after the game.

She took a photograph and sent it to him.

Xiaoran: You’re very annoying.

Yichen: I know.

Xiaoran: Thank you.

Yichen: You’re welcome.

The first missed call happened on a Friday.

Xiaoran had been waiting for him to finish training.

He had told her he would call around eight.

At eight fifteen, she sent a message.

Xiaoran: Done?

No reply.

At eight forty, she tried calling.

It rang until the call ended.

She assumed he was still occupied.

At nine, she received a message.

Yichen: Sorry. Team meeting ran late. Heading to dinner now.

She looked at it.

Then typed:

Xiaoran: It’s okay. Eat first.

He replied with a heart.

She put her phone down and returned to her work.

At ten thirty, he called.

She was in the middle of editing a presentation.

“Hello?”

“Still working?”

“Yes.”

“Can you take a break?”

“Just five minutes.”

He heard the clicking of her keyboard.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You’re not taking a break.”

That made her grin.

“You’re not here. You can’t see me.”

“I can hear you.”

She laughed.

He asked about her day, and she told him about the client meeting.

But after a few minutes, she realized she was answering him without really thinking.

Her eyes kept moving toward the screen.

Yichen noticed.

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then let’s talk tomorrow.”

She met his eyes.

“But you called.”

“And you’re working.”

She hesitated.

“I wanted to talk to you.”

“I know.”

He looked at her through the screen.

“Finish what you need to finish. I’ll be here tomorrow.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

They said goodnight.

After the call ended, she stared at the dark screen.

She had wanted to talk to him.

But she had also wanted to finish her work.

She hadn’t realized how difficult it could be to want two things at once.

The following week was worse.

The Herons had two away games in four days.

Yichen’s team won the first.

He sent her a photograph from the locker room, still wearing his jersey, his hair damp with sweat.

Yichen: Won.

Xiaoran smiled at the photograph.

Xiaoran: I watched the last quarter!

Yichen: I saw your messages.

Xiaoran: You played well.

Yichen: Thank you.

Xiaoran: Especially that assist near the end.

Yichen: You noticed?

Xiaoran: Obviously. I’m a very knowledgeable basketball girlfriend.

He laughed when he read it. He wanted to call her, but the team was heading to a post-game meeting.

He sent a voice message instead.

“Thank you for watching. I’ll call you when I get back.”

She listened to it twice.

Then she went back to work.

The second game ended differently.

The Herons lost by a narrow margin.

Yichen played well, but the team had struggled to maintain their lead in the final minutes.

He was disappointed.

Not visibly, perhaps. He answered the post-game questions, spoke to his teammates, and reviewed the game footage.

But by the time he returned to the hotel, he was exhausted.

He called Xiaoran.

She didn’t answer.

He tried again.

Nothing.

He sent a message.

Yichen: Finished the game. Are you still awake?

There was no reply.

He waited.

At midnight, he finally put his phone down.

The next morning, he received a message.

Xiaoran: Sorry. I fell asleep while waiting for a file to export.

He stared at it.

Yichen: It’s okay. How’s the project?

Xiaoran: Still alive.

Yichen: That’s reassuring.

Xiaoran: How was the game?

He hesitated.

Then replied:

Yichen: We lost.

She answered immediately.

Xiaoran: I’m sorry. Are you okay?

He looked at the screen.

He wanted to tell her that he was disappointed. That he had been thinking about one particular play all night. That he was tired of replaying it in his head.

Instead, he typed:

Yichen: I’m fine. We’ll review it and prepare for the next one.

She sent a heart.

He put the phone away.

It wasn’t that he didn’t want to tell her.

He didn’t want to make her carry another thing when she was already struggling with her own deadline.

He didn’t realize she was doing exactly the same thing.

The first real argument happened over a missed call.

It was a Tuesday night.

Xiaoran had just finished a long day at the studio. The client had requested a major revision, and the team needed to present a new version the following morning.

She was exhausted.

Yichen had finished training earlier than expected and called her.

She was in the middle of a meeting.

She declined the call and sent a message.

Xiaoran: In a meeting. I’ll call you after.

Yichen replied:

Yichen: Okay.

An hour passed, then another.

She finished the meeting, went back to her desk, and began revising the presentation.

At ten, Yichen called again.

She answered, but her attention was divided.

“Hello?”

“Are you still at the studio?”

“Yes.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What did you have?”

She closed her eyes.

“Yichen, can we not do this right now? Do what?”

“Ask me if I’ve eaten every time you call.”

He was quiet.

Then he said, “I was just asking.”

“I know. But I’m working.”

“I can hear that.”

She rubbed her forehead.

“Then why did you call?”

The question came out sharper than she intended.

There was a brief silence.

“I wanted to talk to you.”

Her expression changed.

She looked at the laptop, then at the clock.

“I know, but I can’t always stop everything.”

“I didn’t ask you to.”

“Then what do you want me to do?”

He leaned back in his hotel chair.

“Nothing.”

She exhaled.

“Yichen—”

“It’s fine. Finish your work.”

He ended the call gently.

But the silence afterward felt worse than an argument.

Xiaoran stared at her phone.

She wanted to call him back.

She also wanted to finish the presentation.

And she was angry that she couldn’t do both.

She put her phone down.

Across the city, Yichen sat on the edge of his hotel bed, looking at the screen.

He knew she was under pressure.

He knew the timing was bad.

But he also knew he had been waiting all day to hear her voice.

And now he felt foolish for wanting it.

They didn’t speak properly the next day.

There were messages.

Good morning.

Have you eaten?

Good luck with the presentation.

How was training?

Nothing was wrong with any of them.

But something was missing.

Xiaoran’s presentation went well.

The client approved the revised direction, and her manager congratulated the team.

She should have felt happy.

Instead, the first thing she wanted to do was tell Yichen.

She opened their chat.

Then she stopped.

He was probably training.

She didn’t want to interrupt.

A few minutes later, her phone vibrated.

Yichen: How was the presentation?

Her mouth tipped up.

Xiaoran: Approved.

Yichen: Congratulations.

Xiaoran: Thank you.

She waited.

He didn’t say anything else.

She stared at the screen.

Then she typed:

Xiaoran: Are you free tonight?

Yichen: We have a team dinner. I’ll be back late.

Xiaoran: Okay.

She put her phone down.

It was ridiculous.

They were both trying not to inconvenience each other.

And somehow, they were becoming strangers for it.

That evening, Yichen called from his hotel room.

Xiaoran answered immediately.

“Hello.”

“Hi.”

She was sitting on her sofa, still wearing her office clothes.

He looked tired.

She studied his face.

“Are you okay?”

“Yes.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s not an answer.”

“Where have I heard that before?”

She didn’t smile.

“Yichen.”

“Are you upset?”

She hesitated, then nodded.

“A little.”

“About yesterday?”

“Yes.”

He waited.

She looked down at her hands.

“I know you wanted to talk. I wanted to talk too. But I was so tired, and the presentation was due, and I couldn’t think about anything else.”

“I know.”

“And then when you called, I felt like I was failing at something.”

He frowned slightly.

“Failing?”

“At being your girlfriend.”

His expression changed.

“Xiaoran.”

She continued before he could interrupt.

“I know that sounds stupid. But I keep thinking that I should be more available. I should watch your games, answer your calls, ask about training, and still finish my work. And when I can’t, I feel bad.”

He was quiet.

Then he said, “I don’t expect you to do all that.”

“I know you don’t.”

“Then why are you putting that pressure on yourself?”

She turned to him.

“Because I miss you.”

The words came out smaller than she expected.

Yichen’s expression softened.

She said, “I miss being able to tell you something the moment it happens. I miss eating dinner with you. I miss complaining about my day while you’re sitting beside me. I miss being able to hug you without scheduling it.”

He studied her.

Then he said, “I miss you too.”

She nodded.

“I know.”

He leaned forward slightly.

“Can I tell you something?”

She looked up.

“Yes.”

“I’ve been doing the same thing.”

She blinked.

“What?”

“I keep telling myself not to bother you because you’re busy. I don’t call when I want to because I assume you’re working. When we do talk, I try not to mention the difficult parts of my day because I don’t want to add to yours.”

She blinked at him.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He gave her a smile.

“Because I thought I was being considerate.”

She let out a quiet laugh.

“That’s exactly what I thought I was doing.”

“Apparently, we’re both very considerate.”

“Very stupid.”

He laughed.

She smiled for the first time that evening.

Then her expression softened again.

“I don’t want us to become people who only exchange schedules.”

“Neither do I.”

She looked at him.

“How do we fix it?”

He thought.

“Maybe we stop treating every call like it has to fit into the perfect schedule.”

She listened.

“If you’re working, tell me. I’ll understand. If I’m at training, I’ll tell you. But we don’t have to wait until we’re both completely free to talk.”

She smiled.

“And if one of us misses the call?”

“We call back when we can.”

“And no pretending we’re fine when we’re not?”

He nodded.

“No pretending.”

She held his gaze.

“Promise?”

“Promise. Also, I want you to tell me when you miss me.”

She blinked.

“I do.”

“Sometimes you say you’re fine.”

She looked away.

He smiled gently.

“You don’t have to be fine all the time.”

She was quiet.

Then she said, “I miss you.”

His expression softened.

“I miss you too.”

She leaned closer to the screen, as if that would make the distance smaller.

“Very much.”

“Very much?”

“Don’t make me repeat it.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re smiling.”

“I like hearing it.”

She laughed.

He considered her.

Then said, “I wish I could hold you right now.”

Her smile faded into something softer.

“Me too.”

They changed their routine after that.

Not dramatically.

They didn’t create an elaborate schedule or promise to speak for hours every night.

They became more honest.

Sometimes Yichen sent a voice message from the bus after a game. Sometimes Xiaoran called him while walking home from the studio, telling him about something that had happened before she forgot the details. Sometimes they spoke for only three minutes.

Sometimes they stayed on the phone for an hour.

If one of them was busy, they said so.

If one of them was disappointed, they said that too.

And if they missed each other, they stopped pretending that they didn’t.

One night, Xiaoran was reviewing a rough cut at home when Yichen called.

She answered with her laptop still open.

“Hello.”

“Busy?”

“Very.”

Something in his face eased.

“Should I call later?”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“No. Talk to me while I work.”

“About what?”

“Anything.”

He settled back in his hotel chair.

“All right.”

She returned to the timeline.

For a while, neither said anything.

Then Yichen began telling her about a teammate who had accidentally worn two different shoes to the team meeting.

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

“How does that even happen?”

“He said he was tired.”

“That’s not an excuse.”

“He seemed to think it was.”

She shook her head, still laughing.

Then she went back to editing.

Yichen watched her through the screen.

“How’s the film?”

“Better. I’m adjusting the sound.”

“Is that the part you were worried about?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want me to watch?”

She looked up.

“Now?”

“If you want.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Okay. But don’t judge me if it’s unfinished.”

“I won’t.”

She shared her screen.

He watched as the footage played.

When it ended, he said, “The transition feels smoother now.”

She looked pleased.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“You’re not just saying that?”

“No.”

She smiled and returned to the timeline.

Yichen remained on the call.

He didn’t need to say anything.

Neither did she.

It was enough to hear each other there.

The final away game of the trip was in Chengdu.

The Herons won.

Yichen played well, and the team had a good performance overall.

After the game, he sent Xiaoran a photograph from the court.

Yichen: Last away game. Won.

She was still at the studio, waiting for a final export.

Xiaoran: I knew you would.

Yichen: You watched?

Xiaoran: The second half. I was eating dinner at the same time.

Yichen: What did you eat?

She couldn’t help smiling.

Xiaoran: Proper food. Vegetables included.

Yichen: Good.

Then he sent a voice message.

“Last game is done. I’ll be back tomorrow evening. Don’t stay up waiting for me. You have work.”

She listened to it, then replied with her own voice message.

“Okay. But I’m still going to miss you until tomorrow. Also, I have something to show you when you come back.”

He replied almost immediately.

“What?”

She smiled.

“Secret.”

Yichen returned on Saturday evening.

Xiaoran had finished work early and gone to his apartment.

She had bought groceries, tidied the living room, and put a small vase of flowers on the dining table.

Nothing extravagant.

Just a familiar space waiting for him.

When the door opened, she was sitting on the sofa with her laptop.

Yichen stepped inside, pulling his luggage behind him.

She looked up.

Neither moved.

Then she closed her laptop and stood.

He barely had time to put his bag down before she crossed the room and wrapped her arms around him.

He laughed, catching her around the waist.

“Hello.”

She pressed her face into his chest.

“Hello.”

“Missed me?”

She nodded.

“Very much.”

He pressed his mouth to her hair.

“I missed you too.”

She tightened her arms.

“You’re home.”

“I’m home.”

He held her for a while.

Then he leaned back to look at her.

“What’s the surprise?”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Come.”

She took his hand and led him toward the dining table.

There was a small envelope beside the vase.

He picked it up.

Inside was a printed photograph.

It showed the two of them at the university on graduation day, standing beneath the Media faculty sign. Xiaoran was looking at him, and he was looking back at her.

On the back, she had written:

For the days when we can’t be in the same city.

He looked at it, then at her.

“You printed this?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She shrugged.

“Because I wanted you to have something that wasn’t on your phone.”

He laughed under his breath.

She said, “You can put it in your suitcase. Or your room. Or wherever you want.”

He turned the photograph over again.

Then he placed it carefully back in the envelope.

“Thank you.”

That made her grin.

“Do you like it?”

“I love it.”

He set it down and pulled her close again.

Then he noticed the laptop on the sofa.

“How’s your deadline?”

Xiaoran made a face.

“Don’t ask.”

He laughed.

“That bad?”

“Almost finished. I just need to send the final version on Monday.”

He brushed her hair away from her face.

“Then let’s have dinner.”

“Together.”

“Together.”

Dinner was simple.

They cooked something easy, ate at the dining table, and talked about the trip.

Yichen told her about the away games, the different arenas, and the long bus rides.

Xiaoran told him about the campaign, the client presentation, and the final changes she had made to the film.

They interrupted each other sometimes. They laughed.

They asked questions.

And neither of them looked at the clock.

After dinner, they settled on the sofa.

Xiaoran curled against his side, her legs tucked beneath her.

Yichen rested his arm around her shoulders.

“Are you tired?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Want to sleep?”

“In a while.”

He kissed her cheek.

She looked up at him.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Next time you’re away, can we do something?”

“What?”

“Send each other one ordinary thing every day.”

He glanced at her.

“An ordinary thing?”

“Yes. Not just match results or work updates. Something small. What you ate. Something funny you saw. A photograph of the sky. Anything.”

He considered it.

“That sounds nice.”

“And no pressure to make it interesting.”

“All right.”

She smiled.

“Even if it’s just a picture of your breakfast.”

“I’ll try to make it presentable.”

She laughed.

Then she rested her head against him.

He looked down at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“I don’t want you to think you have to make yourself available every time I’m away.”

She looked up.

“And I don’t want you to think you have to hide things from me because I’m away.”

“Deal.”

She held out her little finger.

He looked at it.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

He hooked his finger around hers.

“Deal.”

She smiled, satisfied.

Then she leaned up and kissed him.

It was a soft kiss, followed by another, and then a longer one when he cupped her cheek and drew her closer.

When she finally pulled away, she rested her forehead against his.

“Welcome home.”

He smiled.

“I’m glad to be home.”

Later that night, Yichen placed the photograph in the drawer beside his bed.

Not because he didn’t want to display it.

He wanted to find a proper frame first.

Xiaoran was already asleep beside him, one hand resting near his.

The away season had been difficult in ways he hadn’t expected.

They were both building lives that wanted their time, and sometimes their absence.

He had wanted to protect her from the difficult parts of his days, and she had wanted to protect him from hers. They had nearly made themselves lonely being considerate.

His phone vibrated on the bedside table.

A message from the Herons’ team manager confirming the next training schedule.

He read it, replied, and put the phone away.

Then Xiaoran shifted closer in her sleep.

He smiled and drew the blanket over her shoulder.

Tomorrow there would be another deadline and another session. He set the photograph by the lamp, where he’d remember to pack it.

chapters.desc: Packing up the fourth-floor studio, her parents bring her every note her father ever left her.
chapters.title: Boxes
chapters.epigraph: “Did you know I kept all of them?”
chapters.content:
The first box was for books. The second was for clothes she wouldn’t need before spring. The third was supposed to be for miscellaneous things, but Xiaoran had already filled it with a camera strap, two notebooks, a small lamp, and three mugs she insisted she couldn’t leave behind.

The lease on the studio had ended on Wednesday. The landlord, who had never once fixed the lift, agreed she could keep the key until Saturday, which was the most generous thing he had done in four years. Her parents had come up to Shanghai on the Friday train, for the move, with a suitcase of their own and a second suitcase of things from home that her mother had decided Xiaoran ought to have in the new flat. By the time her mother had climbed the four flights to the studio and got her breath back, Xiaoran was sitting in the middle of the floor surrounded by cardboard.

“How many boxes do you need?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“I don’t know.”

“How many have you packed?”

“Four.”

Her mother looked around.

There were six.

Xiaoran followed her gaze.

“Well, four are properly packed.”

Her mother sighed.

“You’re going to make a mess of this room. It’s only one room.”

“I’m organizing.”

“You’re spreading things across the floor.”

“That’s part of organizing.”

Her mother sighed.

She picked up an empty box and began folding the flaps.

“Your father has gone to buy more tape.”

“He’s already bought three rolls.”

“He doesn’t trust the tape we have.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Of course he doesn’t.”

Her mother placed the box beside her.

“Have you decided what to do with these?”

She was holding a small stack of papers.

Xiaoran looked over.

They were old notes.

Folded pieces of paper, some yellowed at the edges, some written on the backs of envelopes, others torn from notebooks.

Her father’s handwriting.

Xiaoran blinked.

“Where did you find those?”

“In the drawer of your old desk at home. There were more in your schoolbooks. I brought them up.”

Her mother placed them on the floor.

“I thought you might want to keep them.”

Xiaoran reached for the stack.

The first note was written on a small piece of lined paper.

Dinner is in the rice cooker. Don’t forget to eat.

Her mouth tipped up.

The second was on the back of a receipt.

Your umbrella is by the door. It will rain today.

The third:

I left the spare key with Auntie Fan. Call me if you need it.

She turned it over.

There was a date in the corner.

She had been fourteen. She remembered that day. She’d forgotten her key and stayed outside the apartment building until her father came home.

She unfolded another.

You said your presentation was today. Good luck. Don’t rush when you speak.

Her smile softened.

She remembered that one too.

She had been nervous before a school presentation. Her father had left early for work, and she’d found the note beside her breakfast.

There were more.

Some were practical. Some were reminders. Some were so short that they were almost ridiculous.

Milk is finished.

The parcel is with the security guard.

Don’t leave your wet shoes in the cupboard.

One, written in a hurry:

I know you’re upset. We’ll talk when you’re ready.

Xiaoran stopped.

She remembered that one.

She had argued with her parents over something she couldn’t even recall properly now. She had shut herself in her room and refused to speak.

Her father hadn’t forced her to come out.

He’d left that note outside her door.

She turned it over, but there was nothing else.

Her mother sat down beside her.

“Your father used to leave notes everywhere.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I know.”

“Sometimes I thought he was talking to you more through paper than in person.”

“He was always busy.”

“He was.”

Her mother picked up another note.

“Do you remember this one?”

Xiaoran read it.

Your school project is on the dining table. I didn’t touch it. I only moved the fruit bowl.

She laughed.

“He was so afraid of touching my things.”

“He was afraid you’d accuse him of ruining your project.”

“I probably would have.”

Her mother smiled.

They continued sorting.

There were notes from middle school and high school, from the year after she had come back from her grandparents’ to live with them, and from every holiday home from university. Some were written during exam periods. Others were from ordinary weekdays when her father had left before she woke up.

The older she got, the less frequent they became.

But they never disappeared entirely.

She found one from the winter holiday of her first year of university.

There’s food in the fridge. Your mother says you’re studying late. Don’t come home hungry.

Another from the day she had received a disappointing grade:

One result doesn’t decide everything. Come home and eat first.

And one from the morning she had left for university orientation, with her camera:

Camera battery is charged. I put the spare one beside your bag.

Xiaoran stared at that one for a while.

She hadn’t known he’d noticed.

She hadn’t even known he’d touched her camera bag.

Her mother looked over.

“What is it?”

“Nothing.”

She folded the note carefully.

“Just... I didn’t know he remembered that.”

Her mother gave her a smile.

“Your father remembers more than he says.”

They found the last note inside an old university textbook.

It had been folded into a narrow rectangle and tucked between two pages.

Xiaoran opened it.

You don’t have to be good at everything immediately.

Underneath, in smaller writing:

And you don’t have to pretend you’re not tired.

She read it twice.

Then she looked at the date.

It was from the summer after her second year.

She remembered that summer. She had come home with too many assignments, a student project she had agreed to help with from three hundred kilometers away, and a boyfriend she called every night at nine.

She had told her parents she was fine.

Apparently, her father hadn’t believed her.

Her mother glanced at the note.

“He left that after you fell asleep at the dining table.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“You remember?”

“Of course. He carried your laptop into your room and left that beside your books.”

Xiaoran lowered her eyes.

She ran her thumb over the paper.

“Why didn’t he wake me?”

“You looked exhausted.”

She laughed.

“He could’ve just told me to sleep.”

“Your father knows you. You would have said you had to finish something.”

Xiaoran couldn’t argue with that.

She placed the note with the others.

Her father came back up the four flights an hour later, out of breath, with two more rolls of tape.

He found the two women sitting on the floor, surrounded by notes.

He stopped.

Then he looked at the papers.

“What’s all this?”

Xiaoran held up one of them.

“Your handwriting.”

He looked at it, then at her.

“Why are you reading those?”

“Because Mom found them.”

He put his keys down.

“Those are old.”

“Very old.”

“Then why keep them?”

She met his eyes.

“You kept them.”

He frowned.

“I didn’t keep them. You did.”

She glanced at her mother.

Her mother smiled innocently.

“Some were in your books. Some were in your drawers.”

Her father looked mildly betrayed.

Xiaoran laughed.

“How many notes did you leave me?”

“I don’t know.”

“Do you remember this one?”

She held up the note about the umbrella.

He looked at it.

“That was a rainy day.”

“I know.”

“You were always forgetting your umbrella.”

“I was thirteen.”

“Still.”

She laughed.

Then she held up another.

“Your school project. You said you only moved the fruit bowl.”

“I didn’t want to touch your work.”

“You were afraid I’d get angry.”

“You were very particular.”

“I was not.”

Her father looked at her.

She considered it.

“Maybe a little.”

He shook his head.

Then his eyes fell on the note she had placed separately.

The one about not pretending she wasn’t tired.

His expression changed slightly.

“That one was from university.”

She nodded.

“I remember.”

He sat down on the other side of the papers.

For a while, he didn’t say anything.

Then he picked up one of the notes and looked at it.

“I used to leave these because I left early. I thought it was easier than waking you.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“You also left notes when you were home.”

“Sometimes.”

“You left one telling me not to forget the parcel when you were sitting right beside me.”

Her mother laughed.

Her father looked at her.

“That was important.”

“It was a box of printer paper.”

“Your project needed it.”

Xiaoran laughed.

He put the note down.

Then she asked, more, “Did you know I kept all of them?”

He met her eyes.

“No.”

She glanced at the pile.

“I did.”

He looked down at the notes.

Something softened in his face.

“Well, you don’t need to take every piece of paper across the road,” he said, clearing his throat.

Xiaoran smiled.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Good.”

She began gathering them into one pile.

Then she stopped.

“Actually, I think I’ll take these.”

Her father looked at the stack.

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

“They’re just reminders.”

“I know.”

He nodded, as if he understood.

Then he reached for the box beside her.

“Put them in here. Don’t fold them any smaller.”

She smiled.

“Okay.”

He carefully cleared a space at the top of the box, away from the heavier books.

That night, after her parents had gone back to their hotel, Yichen came across the road to help with the remaining boxes.

He found Xiaoran sitting at her desk, placing the notes into a small envelope.

He looked at the envelope.

“What’s that?”

“Every note my father ever left me.”

Yichen paused.

Then he came closer.

“Every one?”

“Almost.”

She handed him a few.

He read them.

The first was about dinner in the rice cooker. The second was about her umbrella.

The third was the note about her presentation.

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Your father has a very practical writing style.”

“He’s a practical person.”

Yichen picked up another note.

He read it, then looked at her.

“One result doesn’t decide everything. Come home and eat first.”

“He wrote that after I got a bad grade.”

Yichen looked at the paper again.

“That’s a good note.”

“He didn’t ask what happened until after dinner.”

“That sounds like him.”

Her mouth tipped up.

Yichen put the note down.

Then he noticed the envelope.

It was already full.

“You’re taking them with you?”

“Yes.”

He nodded.

“Good.”

“You’re not going to tell me I’m being sentimental?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

He sat beside her.

“Because you are.”

She gave him a small, offended look.

He smiled and touched her cheek.

“There’s nothing wrong with keeping something that made you feel loved.”

She looked down at the notes.

She didn’t say anything.

Then she leaned into his shoulder.

“I think I’ll put them in the drawer on my side of the bed.”

“That sounds good.”

“So when I forget something, I can pretend my father is still leaving me reminders.”

Yichen laughed.

“He probably will.”

She looked up.

“What do you mean?”

“I wouldn’t be surprised if he starts sending you messages about your umbrella.”

She laughed.

“He’ll probably ask if I’ve eaten.”

“Definitely.”

“And whether I’ve checked the door lock.”

“Mostly that.”

She rested her head against him.

Yichen reached for the envelope and placed it carefully inside the box.

Then he folded the cardboard flaps without sealing them.

“Let’s leave this one for last,” he said.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Why?”

“So we don’t put anything heavy on it.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Okay.”

At seven the next morning, the day of the move, her father climbed the four flights again, carrying a small piece of paper.

He placed it on the desk.

Xiaoran looked up from her laptop.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

She picked it up.

It was a new note.

His handwriting, unmistakable.

When you arrive, call home.

Underneath, he’d added:

And don’t forget your umbrella.

She laughed.

“Dad, it’s across the road.”

He looked at her. “Call anyway.”

She stood and hugged him.

He patted her back, looking over her shoulder at the half-packed room.

“Put it somewhere you can find it.”

“I will.”

“And don’t lose it.”

“I won’t.”

He stepped back.

“Good.”

Xiaoran folded the note and slipped it into the envelope with the others.

Her father watched her do it.

He didn’t say anything.

But when he left the room, he took the empty box with him and returned a few minutes later with another roll of tape.

He set it beside her.

“Your boxes need to be sealed properly.”

“Yes, Dad.”

He looked at the envelope one more time.

Then he reached over and gently pressed the cardboard flaps together around it, making sure the paper was protected.

“All right. This one’s ready,” he said.

And for once, Xiaoran didn’t argue that she could do it herself. She stood beside him, holding the box steady while he taped it shut.

chapters.desc: She moves into his apartment. Both sets of parents come to help, and within fifteen minutes she has lost control of her own kitchen.
chapters.title: Moving Day, Again
chapters.epigraph: “Now yours can stop pretending it’s visiting.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Lin Xiaoran learned about moving in together was that Zhou Yichen owned too many things. The second thing she learned was that he had somehow managed to make all of them fit into his apartment without her noticing.

The third thing was that her own belongings, which she had always considered perfectly reasonable in quantity, looked less reasonable once they were placed beside his.

She stood in the middle of his living room, holding a cardboard box against her hip.

“Yichen.”

He was crouching beside another box, checking its contents.

“Mm?”

“How many jackets do you own?”

He met her eyes.

“Why?”

“Because I found another one.”

“Where?”

“In the wardrobe.”

“That’s where jackets usually are.”

She looked at him.

“Don’t be clever.”

He smiled and returned to the box.

It was Saturday morning. Their move had officially begun at eight, although Xiaoran had arrived at seven thirty because she had been too excited to sleep.

Her lease had ended the previous week. After months of discussing the practicalities—rent, expenses, commuting distances, work schedules, and the amount of closet space they would need—they had finally decided to move into Yichen’s apartment.

It wasn’t a spontaneous decision.

They had visited several places together. They had discussed whether to rent somewhere new or use his existing apartment. They had gone through the expenses more than once, and Xiaoran had insisted on contributing a fair share rather than letting him cover everything because he could.

In the end, they chose to stay in his apartment for now.

It was spacious enough for two people, close enough to both their workplaces, and, most importantly, they both liked it.

Still, knowing something was the right decision and actually watching your belongings enter another person’s home were two different experiences.

Xiaoran looked around.

Her books were stacked beside his. Her desk lamp was on the dining table. Two boxes of skincare products had somehow occupied an entire corner of the kitchen counter.

And her boyfriend was apparently still hiding jackets.

“How many?” she repeated.

Yichen stood up.

“Enough.”

“That’s not a number.”

“Do you want to count them?”

She considered it.

“Actually, yes.”

He laughed and took the box from her arms.

“Go check your own boxes first.”

“My boxes are perfectly organized.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you say that?”

“Because you put your hair dryer in a box labelled ‘miscellaneous’.”

She opened her mouth, then closed it.

“That’s because I didn’t know what else to call it.”

“Hair appliances?”

“That’s too specific.”

He looked at her for a second.

Then his mouth curved.

“Of course.”

She squinted at him.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little.”

She turned away, pretending to be offended.

He caught her hand before she could walk off and kissed her knuckles, his thumb brushing over the promise ring on her finger.

“Come on. Let’s finish before everyone arrives.”

“Everyone?”

He turned to her.

She looked back.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“You said our parents would come later.”

“They are coming.”

“All of them?”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Yes.”

She slowly put her hands on her hips.

“Why did you say that as if it’s a normal thing?”

“Because it is.”

“Four parents. In one apartment. On moving day.”

“Six, counting us.”

She stared at him.

He bent and kissed her hairline.

“Don’t worry. They’ll help.”

That, Xiaoran thought, was precisely what she was worried about.

By ten thirty, the apartment had become a small family operation.

Yichen’s parents arrived first.

His mother came carrying two bags of groceries and a container of homemade food. His father followed with a toolbox, a folded step ladder, and the expression of a man who had already decided there were several things in the apartment that needed fixing.

“Xiaoran!”

Yichen’s mother greeted her warmly.

“Have you eaten? I brought breakfast.”

Xiaoran looked at the bags.

“Auntie, you didn’t have to bring so much.”

“It’s moving day. Of course I had to.”

She turned toward Yichen.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes, Mom.”

“Properly?”

He paused.

Xiaoran immediately answered for him.

“Not really.”

Yichen looked at her.

His mother gave him a disapproving look.

“Then eat first.”

He glanced at Xiaoran again.

She smiled sweetly.

He understood, then, that he had been betrayed.

“You’re enjoying this,” he murmured as his mother carried the food toward the kitchen.

“A little.”

His father was already examining a bookshelf.

“This needs to be moved.”

Yichen looked over.

“Why?”

“It’s too close to the window.”

“It has been there for four years.”

“And now there are two people living here.”

Xiaoran blinked.

Mr. Zhou turned toward her.

“Do you think it should be moved?”

She looked at the bookshelf, then at the window.

“Maybe a little?”

His father nodded, satisfied.

“Good. We’ll move it.”

Yichen stared at both of them.

“All right.”

His mother laughed.

“Don’t look so unhappy. Your father is helping.”

“I know.”

“Then go help him.”

Xiaoran covered her mouth.

Yichen looked at her.

“You’re enjoying this considerably more than I expected.”

She whispered, “Your father asked for my opinion.”

“And?”

“I’m influential.”

He laughed under his breath and went to move the bookshelf.

Xiaoran’s parents arrived shortly before eleven.

Her mother came in carrying a large box, which she insisted was light despite Xiaoran immediately reaching out to take it.

“Mom, give it to me.”

“It’s fine.”

“You’re holding it with both hands.”

“Because it’s a box.”

Her father walked in behind her, carrying another two boxes.

He looked around the apartment, then at Yichen.

“Busy day?”

Yichen stepped forward to greet him.

“Uncle. I’ll take those.”

“No need. I can carry them.”

Yichen took them anyway.

Xiaoran’s mother looked toward the kitchen, where Yichen’s mother was arranging food.

The two women greeted each other warmly.

Within five minutes, they were standing together discussing the kitchen storage. Within ten minutes, they had decided that the current arrangement was inefficient.

Within fifteen minutes, Xiaoran had lost control of her own kitchen.

“Should we put the bowls here?” her mother asked.

Yichen’s mother considered it.

“Maybe the upper cabinet. The lower one is easier for plates.”

“That’s true. And the glasses?”

“Near the refrigerator.”

Xiaoran stood between them.

“Actually, I was thinking—”

“Xiaoran, where are your tea cups?” her mother asked.

“That box.”

“Good. We’ll unpack those.”

Yichen appeared beside her, carrying a box of books.

He looked at the three women, then at her.

“Need help?”

She turned to him with an expression of quiet desperation.

He lowered his voice.

“What’s wrong?”

“They’ve taken over.”

He glanced toward the kitchen, then back at her.

“Should I rescue you?”

“Please.”

He nodded solemnly.

“All right.”

He walked into the kitchen.

“Mom, Auntie, Dad needs help with the bookshelf.”

His father, who was standing nowhere near the bookshelf, looked up.

Yichen continued smoothly.

“He said he needs two people.”

Both women looked toward the living room.

“Again?”

“Yes.”

They exchanged a glance, then began walking out.

Xiaoran stared at Yichen.

He picked up a tea cup.

“You’re welcome.”

She whispered, “You’re very good at this.”

“I’ve had years of practice.”

She smiled and took the cup from him.

“Your father is going to know you made that up.”

“He already knows.”

From the living room, Mr. Zhou called, “Yichen, are you coming?”

Yichen sighed.

“See?”

Xiaoran laughed.

By early afternoon, most of the boxes had been unpacked.

The living room looked noticeably different.

There was a new rug beneath the coffee table, chosen by Xiaoran after three weeks of sending Yichen photographs and asking him to compare shades of beige.

Her books occupied two shelves.

His basketball trophies and framed photographs had been moved to the study, making room for her small collection of cameras and film equipment.

The dining table now had two chairs that didn’t match.

Xiaoran liked them that way.

Her father had assembled a new storage cabinet. Yichen’s father had fixed a loose hinge and adjusted the bookshelf. Their mothers had reorganized the kitchen twice, though they insisted the second arrangement was much better.

At one point, Xiaoran walked into the kitchen and found both mothers standing in front of the refrigerator.

“What are you doing?”

“Making space,” her mother answered.

“For what?”

“Your food.”

Yichen’s mother smiled.

“And his.”

Xiaoran looked at the refrigerator.

There were containers on the shelves, fresh fruit in the drawer, and a row of drinks arranged neatly in the door.

That made her grin.

“Thank you.”

Her mother turned toward her.

“Don’t just thank us. You two need to keep the kitchen organized.”

“We will.”

“And don’t rely on takeout every day.”

“We won’t.”

Yichen walked in at that moment.

His mother pointed at him.

“And you. Don’t let her do all the cooking.”

He nodded.

“I won’t.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Because your mother is talking about you.”

“Your mother is talking about you too.”

Something in his face eased.

“Then we’re both in trouble.”

Her mother laughed.

“Good. At least you know.”

The only real disagreement of the day happened over the bedroom.

It wasn’t a serious one.

But it was the first time they discovered that moving in together involved more than deciding where to put furniture.

Xiaoran had brought a small bedside table from her old apartment. It was light wood, with one drawer and a little open shelf underneath.

She wanted to put it beside her side of the bed.

Yichen thought it would look better beside the window.

“It’s too close to the wardrobe here,” he said, moving it slightly.

“But I want it here.”

“Then the drawer won’t open properly.”

“It will.”

He crouched and pulled the drawer.

It opened halfway before hitting the edge of the wardrobe.

Xiaoran looked at it, then at him.

“That’s because you moved it too far.”

He shifted it back.

The drawer opened, but the table now obstructed the walkway.

Neither spoke.

Finally, Yichen said, “We can put it on the other side.”

“But that’s your side.”

“I don’t mind.”

She looked at him.

Then she shook her head.

“No. I want it here.”

He considered the space.

“All right. Let’s move the wardrobe slightly.”
