“You’ll move the wardrobe?”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s heavy.”

“That’s manageable.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You’re very indulgent.”

He stood and brushed his hands together.

“Only about furniture?”

She laughed.

“Don’t push your luck.”

He leaned down and kissed her cheek.

“Never.”

From the doorway, her mother watched them.

She smiled and walked away without interrupting.

By five, everyone was tired.

The last box had been unpacked. The cardboard had been flattened and stacked near the door. The apartment looked less like a storage facility and more like a home.

Yichen’s mother prepared an early dinner.

Their fathers sat together at the dining table, talking about work and the logistics of the move.

Xiaoran was in the bedroom, arranging the things on her side of the wardrobe.

Yichen appeared at the door.

“Need help?”

She held up two hangers.

“Where should I put these?”

He looked at the wardrobe.

“There’s space on the left.”

She looked at the left side, then at the right.

“Why is my side smaller?”

He leaned against the doorframe.

“Because you have more clothes.”

She gasped.

“That’s not true.”

He raised an eyebrow.

She pointed at him.

“Don’t look at me like that.”

He smiled.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

He walked over and took the hangers from her.

“Move over.”

He shifted a few of his jackets, then made room for her clothes.

She watched him.

“You’re really giving me this much space?”

“Yes.”

“But what about yours?”

“I’ll manage.”

She looked at the neatly arranged rows of his shirts.

Then at the growing collection of her own clothes.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Are you sure?”

He turned toward her.

“Xiaoran, we’re sharing a home. You don’t have to ask permission for every little thing.”

She met his eyes.

He said, “We’ll figure out the space together.”

Her expression softened.

Then she stepped closer and wrapped her arms around his waist.

He smiled and rested his hand on her back.

“Nothing?”

She nodded against his chest.

“I just like hearing you say that.”

He kissed her hair.

“Then I’ll say it again when you need to hear it.”

Dinner was louder than either of them expected.

Their parents had been getting along since graduation, but there was something different about sitting around the same table to celebrate their children moving into one home.

Xiaoran’s father raised his glass.

“Well. Congratulations to both of you.”

Yichen’s father nodded.

“Congratulations.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you.”

Her mother looked around the apartment.

“It’s strange.”

“What is?” Xiaoran asked.

“Last time we helped you move, you were still a student.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“That wasn’t very long ago.”

“It feels like yesterday.”

Yichen’s mother smiled.

“And now look at you two.”

She looked between them.

“Both working. Both taking care of yourselves. And now sharing a home.”

Xiaoran felt her cheeks warm.

Yichen reached beneath the table and took her hand.

His thumb brushed once over her ring.

Her father noticed the gesture.

He smiled, but didn’t say anything.

The conversation moved on to practical things.

Who would be responsible for which household expenses. Whether they should hire someone for deep cleaning. How often they would visit both families.

Xiaoran answered some questions, while Yichen answered others.

They didn’t agree on everything immediately, but they were comfortable discussing it.

At one point, her father looked at Yichen.

“Take care of each other.”

Yichen nodded.

“We will. And she’ll take care of me too, Uncle.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“Obviously.”

Everyone laughed.

Her mother shook her head.

“Good. At least she knows.”

By seven, both sets of parents were preparing to leave.

Yichen walked Xiaoran’s parents downstairs while Xiaoran’s mother hugged her in the doorway.

“Call me if you need anything.”

“I will.”

“And don’t feel you have to do everything yourself.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I know, Mom.”

Her mother glanced toward the living room.

Yichen was returning with her father, carrying an empty box.

“He’s a good boy,” she said.

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

“Mom.”

“What? I didn’t say anything wrong.”

“You’re embarrassing me.”

Her mother smiled and kissed her cheek.

“Then I’ll stop. Actually, one more thing.”

Xiaoran sighed.

“What?”

“Be happy.”

The words were simple.

But they made her throat tighten unexpectedly.

She nodded.

“I will.”

When her parents finally left, Yichen’s mother hugged her too.

“Come visit us when you have time.”

“We will.”

“And you can come over for dinner whenever you want.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you, Auntie.”

Yichen’s father shook her hand gently, then turned to his son.

“Call if you need anything.”

“I will.”

His father looked around the apartment one last time, then nodded.

“Looks good.”

Yichen smiled.

“Thanks, Dad.”

After they left, the door closed.

The apartment became quiet.

For the first time that day, there were no parents, no boxes, no tools, and no one asking where the kitchen towels belonged.

Just the two of them.

Xiaoran stood in the hallway.

Yichen looked at her.

“What’s wrong?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing.”

He walked closer.

“Tired?”

“Very.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Me too.”

She looked around.

The living room. The dining table. The kitchen.

The bedroom.

Their things were everywhere.

Her things.

His things.

Things they had bought together.

She felt a little overwhelmed.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“Can we look around?”

He glanced at the apartment.

“Now?”

“Yes.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right.”

They started with the living room.

Xiaoran stood beside the sofa, looking at the new rug.

“Remember when we bought this?”

“You sent me twenty-three photographs.”

“Because there were so many shades.”

“They looked identical.”

“They did not.”

He held her gaze.

“Of course.”

She ignored him.

Then they walked to the dining area.

She touched the edge of the table.

“Your mother brought the flowers.”

“She likes having flowers in the house.”

“I know.”

She looked at the two chairs.

One was his old chair. The other was hers.

“They don’t match.”

“I noticed.”

“Do you mind?”

“No.”

“Really?”

He pulled her chair out slightly.

“I like them.”

She smiled.

They went to the study next.

Her cameras were arranged on the shelf. His basketball equipment occupied the other side.

She pointed at the empty space between them.

“We need something here.”

“What?”

“I don’t know yet.”

“Then we’ll leave it empty.”

She looked at him.

“You’re not going to suggest a basketball?”

“No.”

“A trophy?”

“No.”

“A framed photograph of you?”

He smiled.

“Would you like one?”

She laughed.

“Absolutely not.”

He took her hand and led her toward the bedroom.

The bedside table was finally in place.

Her lamp sat on top of it. A small book was tucked into the open shelf.

She looked at the space beside the bed, then at his side.

“Looks different.”

“It does.”

She walked toward the wardrobe and opened it.

Her clothes were beside his.

They were hanging there, out of the suitcase for good, with space left for more.

She touched the sleeve of one of her cardigans.

A strange feeling settled in her chest.

She had lived alone before.

She had been perfectly capable of taking care of herself.

But this was different.

She was no longer visiting his apartment after work, or leaving a few things behind because she would come over again the next day. She was going to wake up here. She would leave for work from here.

She would come home and find him here, or sometimes find that he was away with the team.

Her toothbrush would be here. Her books would be here.

Her ordinary life would be here.

She turned to him.

“We really live together now.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“Yes.”

“That’s strange.”

“Good strange?”

She nodded.

“Very good strange.”

He opened his arms.

She stepped into them.

He held her close, resting his cheek against her hair.

For a while, they stayed like that.

“Wait.”

Xiaoran pulled away.

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“We forgot something.”

“What did we forget?”

She took his hand and hurried toward the bathroom.

He followed, mildly amused.

“What is it?”

“Something important.”

She opened the bathroom cabinet.

Inside were her skincare products, his shaving supplies, a few towels, and two small baskets.

She looked at the counter, then opened the drawer, then looked at the cabinet again.

Yichen watched her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Wait.”

She took her toothbrush out of the glass on the windowsill, where it had lived as a visitor for two and a half years, and his out of the holder by the mirror.

Two toothbrushes.

One was hers, with a pale pink handle.

The other was his, dark blue.

She held them up.

Yichen looked at them, then at her.

“Those?”

“Yes.”

She opened the cabinet beneath the sink and found a ceramic cup she had brought from her old apartment.

It was simple, cream-colored, with a tiny blue flower painted near the rim.

She placed it beside the faucet, then put his toothbrush in, then hers.

She stepped back.

Looked at them.

And smiled.

Yichen stood behind her, his hands resting lightly on her waist.

“Is that it?”

“Yes.”

He looked at the cup.

Two toothbrushes.

Side by side.

It was such a small thing.

They had signed paperwork, discussed expenses, moved furniture, reorganized wardrobes, and spent an entire day surrounded by their families.

Yet somehow, this was the moment that made the decision feel real.

Xiaoran looked at him through the mirror.

“Now it’s official.”

His mouth curved.

“Wasn’t it official when we moved your things in?”

“No.”

“When we put your clothes in the wardrobe?”

“No.”

“When your mother rearranged the kitchen?”

She laughed.

“Definitely not.”

He lowered his head slightly.

“Then this is the official moment?”

“Yes.”

He looked at the two toothbrushes again, then kissed her cheek.

“All right.”

She turned around.

“You’re not going to say anything?”

“What would you like me to say?”

“Something meaningful.”

He considered it, then looked at her.

“Good. Now yours can stop pretending it’s visiting.”

She blinked at him, then burst out laughing.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed too, catching her when she playfully pushed his chest.

“That’s meaningful?”

“I think so.”

“You’re terrible.”

He leaned down and kissed her.

It was a gentle kiss, warm and familiar, but she held onto his shirt when he started to pull away.

He smiled against her lips.

“Another one?”

She nodded.

He kissed her again.

When they separated, she rested her forehead against his.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Thank you.”

“For what?”

“For making room for me.”

He studied her.

Then his expression softened.

“Xiaoran.”

She waited.

“I didn’t make room for you because you were moving in.”

He brushed a strand of hair behind her ear.

“I made room because I wanted you here.”

She looked at him.

He said, “This is your home too. You don’t have to feel like you’re borrowing space from me.”

Her eyes softened.

“I know.”

“Good.”

She wrapped her arms around his neck.

“Then I have one more request.”

“What?”

“I want to buy matching towels.”

He blinked.

“Matching?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because the toothbrushes look lonely.”

He laughed.

“All right.”

“And matching cups.”

“Didn’t we just buy cups?”

“Those are for drinking.”

“Then what do we need?”

She thought.

“Matching bowls.”

He considered her.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Are we furnishing a home or opening a hotel?”

She laughed until she had to hold on to him.

He smiled, watching her.

“All right. Matching bowls too.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She kissed his cheek.

“You’re the best.”

“I know.”

She pulled back.

“Don’t become arrogant.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Too late.”

Their first night in the apartment was quieter than the day.

They ordered dinner because neither of them wanted to cook after spending hours unpacking.

Xiaoran sat cross-legged on the sofa, eating from a takeaway container while Yichen sat beside her, one arm resting along the back of the sofa.

A film played on the television.

Neither was paying much attention.

She leaned against his shoulder.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Do you think we’ll get used to this?”

“To what?”

“Living together.”

He considered the question.

“Probably.”

“How long?”

“I don’t know. A few days?”

She looked up.

“Only a few days?”

“Maybe a week.”

“That’s not long.”

He smiled.

“Are you hoping it takes longer?”

“No. I just thought it would feel more...”

She searched for the word.

“Different?”

He glanced at her.

“It already feels different.”

“How?”

He glanced around the apartment.

“Your shoes are by the door.”

She looked down.

Her shoes were indeed beside his.

“Your books are on my shelf. Your lamp is beside my bed. There’s a cup in the bathroom with both our toothbrushes. And I know you’ll be here when I wake up tomorrow.”

She looked at him.

He smiled slightly.

“That’s different enough for me.”

Her expression softened.

She put her food down and climbed closer, resting her head against his chest.

“Do you think we’ll fight?”

“Probably.”

She lifted her head.

“You’re very confident.”

“Two people living together will disagree about things.”

“Like what?”

“Where to put furniture. How many towels to buy. Whether the air conditioner is too cold.”

She looked offended.

“The air conditioner is always too cold for you.”

“Exactly.”

She laughed.

“Anything else?”

He thought.

“How to organize the kitchen.”

“Your mother already solved that.”

“Your mother may disagree.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

Then she grew quiet.

Yichen noticed.

“What is it?”

She looked down at her hands.

“I don’t want us to become careless with each other.”

His expression softened.

“Careless?”

“Like... because we’re always together, we stop making an effort.”

He considered her words, then took her hand.

“I don’t think living together means we stop dating.”

She looked up.

He said, “We still have to make time for each other. We still have to ask how the other’s day was. We still have to go out, or watch films, or do nothing together.”

She smiled.

“And when you’re away?”

“I’ll call.”

“And when I’m busy?”

“I’ll let you work.”

“And when we disagree?”

“We talk.”

She held his gaze.

She couldn’t help smiling.

He brushed his thumb over her ring.

“We don’t have to get everything right on the first day.”

“Okay.”

Then she leaned forward and kissed him.

“Good.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Good?”

“Yes. I approve of our household rules.”

He laughed and pulled her back against him.

That night, Xiaoran went to bed first.

Yichen was still in the bathroom when she climbed beneath the blanket.

She looked toward the doorway, then toward the bedside table.

Her phone was charging beside his. Her book was on the shelf.

Her cardigan was hanging over the chair.

That made her grin.

A few minutes later, Yichen came out.

He switched off the main light, leaving the bedside lamp on.

“Still awake?”

“Yes.”

He climbed into bed beside her.

She immediately moved closer.

He lifted his arm, and she settled against him with a quiet sigh.

“Comfortable?” he asked.

“Very.”

He kissed her temple.

“Goodnight.”

She looked up.

“Wait.”

He looked down.

“What?”

“Say it again.”

“Goodnight?”

She nodded.

His mouth curved.

“Goodnight, Xiaoran.”

She smiled back.

“Goodnight, Yichen.”

He turned off the lamp.

The room went dark.

For a while, neither spoke.

Then Xiaoran’s voice came from beside him.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“Tomorrow, can we make breakfast?”

“Of course.”

“And maybe buy those matching towels.”

He laughed.

“Go to sleep.”

She giggled and tucked herself closer.

He kissed her temple.

A little later, he felt her hand find his beneath the blanket.

He held it.

On the bathroom counter, two toothbrushes stood inside a small cream-colored cup.

In the wardrobe, their clothes hung side by side.

At the entrance, their shoes waited together.

There were still things to arrange. Bills to divide. Routines to learn. Habits to negotiate. There would be days when one came home exhausted and the other was still working. There would be mornings when they disagreed over the temperature of the air conditioner.

Tomorrow, they would begin figuring those things out.

But tonight, the apartment was quiet.

And for the first time, neither of them had to leave when the evening ended.

Xiaoran was already half asleep when she murmured, “Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“I’m glad we did this.”

He tightened his arm around her.

“So am I.”

She smiled against his chest.

“Welcome home.”

He lowered his head and kissed her hair.

“Welcome home, Xiaoran.”

And this time, home meant both of them.

chapters.desc: The day after the move, the mothers return to the kitchen for a third arrangement, and the fathers talk about parking.
chapters.title: Housewarming
chapters.epigraph: “She knows you live here.”
chapters.content:
On Saturday, moving day, the two mothers had arranged the kitchen twice and agreed that the second arrangement was much better. On Saturday night, after everyone had gone back to their hotels, Xiaoran had put everything back.

On Sunday, before the parents’ afternoon trains, there was to be a proper housewarming lunch. The first thing Zhou Yichen’s mother did when she walked into the flat that had, since yesterday, belonged to both of them was move the rice cooker.

The second thing she did was move the cups.

The third thing was look at the kitchen shelves and say, with quiet certainty, “This won’t do.”

Xiaoran, who had spent an hour of Saturday night putting her things and his things exactly where she wanted them, turned around.

“What won’t do?”

His mother stood in the middle of the small kitchen, holding a stack of bowls.

“The placement.”

Xiaoran looked at the bowls, then at the shelves.

Then at the woman who had gone out at eight that morning, from the hotel, and come back with two bags.

She smiled politely.

“What’s wrong with the placement?”

“These are too high. You’ll have to reach every time you want one.”

“I can reach.”

“Not comfortably.”

Xiaoran demonstrated by reaching up and taking a bowl from the shelf.

His mother watched.

“You’re standing on your toes.”

“Only a little.”

“Exactly.”

And just like that, the kitchen was no longer Xiaoran’s kitchen.

It had become a project.

Yichen had known something was going to happen when his mother announced on the phone at seven that she was picking up a few things on the way.

He had assumed she meant towels, a spare kettle, perhaps some kitchen utensils.

He hadn’t expected two large bags, a box of containers, a set of spice jars, and a small rack that she insisted would be useful.

His father, who had carried the bags up from the taxi, had been equally surprised.

“You’re taking all that?”

His mother had looked at him.

“She’ll need things.”

“She has things.”

“Not everything.”

And that had been the end of the discussion.

Now, in the kitchen doorway, Yichen stood at the kitchen entrance holding a carton of bottled water while watching his mother inspect the cupboards.

Xiaoran was beside the counter, holding a roll of kitchen labels.

“Yichen.”

He met her eyes.

“Yes?”

“Your mother has moved my rice cooker.”

He glanced at the counter.

“Has she?”

“She moved it from here to there.”

He followed her finger.

The rice cooker was now occupying the space where Xiaoran had planned to prepare food.

He nodded thoughtfully.

“That does seem inconvenient.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I haven’t taken a side.”

“You’re standing on her side.”

He looked down at his feet, then back at her.

“That’s because she’s standing in the kitchen.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

Yichen smiled and carried the water into the living room.

He had no intention of getting involved.

Not yet.

The flat was eleven floors up and bright. It had one bedroom, a study where his trophies had moved over to make room for her cameras, a living room with a large window that looked across the road at the building where she had climbed four flights of stairs every day because the lift never worked, a compact kitchen, and, as of yesterday, a proper desk by the window in a corner he had cleared for it. Until yesterday the kitchen had held a rice cooker, a blender, a great deal of protein powder and little else.

It wasn’t luxurious. But now it was theirs.

There was something deeply satisfying about seeing her belongings inside it. Her books on the shelf, her camera equipment in the cabinet, her favorite mug beside the kettle. The curtains she’d chosen were already hanging, and a small potted plant sat on the windowsill.

Yichen had carried her desk across the road the previous afternoon, with his father holding the other end and giving instructions about the stairs.

Her father had delivered the toolbox to the third shelf.

Her mother had brought bedding, cleaning supplies, and enough food to feed a small family for a week.

And Yichen’s mother had arrived with the intention of making the kitchen more functional.

Which, apparently, meant changing everything.

“Xiaoran, where do you keep the bowls?”

She pointed.

“Top shelf.”

His mother looked at her.

“Not anymore.”

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

Yichen, who had returned from the living room, leaned against the doorframe.

“What’s happening?”

“Your mother is relocating my kitchen.”

His mother turned.

“Not relocating. Improving.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Do you hear that?”

“I do.”

“Are you going to help?”

He looked at the kitchen, then at his mother, then at Xiaoran.

“I think you two are doing very well.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed.

His mother shook her head.

“Don’t just stand there. Bring me the small rack.”

He immediately went to get it.

Xiaoran watched him.

Traitor.

By half past ten, the kitchen had undergone a complete transformation.

The rice cooker was now on the far end of the counter. The bowls were on the middle shelf. The plates were stacked in a cabinet near the dining table. The utensils had been divided into separate containers.

The spice jars were lined up by height.

There was even a designated drawer for plastic bags.

Xiaoran stood in the doorway, looking at it all.

His mother wiped her hands.

“Much better.”

Xiaoran nodded slowly.

“Very organized.”

“Now you won’t have to search for anything.”

“That’s true.”

His mother smiled.

Then she asked, “Where did you put the mugs?”

Xiaoran pointed to the cabinet.

His mother opened it.

She looked inside, then looked at Xiaoran.

“Why are the mugs here?”

“Because I use them every day.”

“But they’re behind the glasses.”

“Yes.”

“You’ll have to move the glasses to get them.”

Xiaoran stared.

She had deliberately placed the mugs there because the cabinet door opened more easily from that side.

She took a breath.

“Actually, I like them there.”

His mother looked at the cabinet again.

“All right.”

Xiaoran smiled.

A small victory.

Then his mother added, “But I think we should move the glasses to the other shelf.”

Xiaoran’s smile disappeared.

The doorbell rang just after eleven.

Yichen opened it.

Xiaoran’s mother stood outside with two bags of groceries, a box of fruit, and, as it turned out, a perfectly clear memory of the second arrangement.

“Hello.”

“Hello, Auntie.”

She looked past him.

“Where’s Xiaoran?”

“In the kitchen.”

“Good. Help me with these.”

He took the bags.

Her mother stepped inside, removed her shoes, and walked toward the kitchen.

She stopped at the entrance.

Her eyes moved across the counter, then the shelves, then the drawers.

She turned her head.

“Xiaoran.”

Xiaoran appeared immediately.

“Mom!”

Her mother pointed at the kitchen.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran’s expression changed into one of quiet relief.

“Exactly.”

Yichen, standing behind them with the groceries, looked toward the ceiling.

He knew this was going to become a longer afternoon.

His mother emerged from the kitchen.

“Hello.”

“Hello,” Xiaoran’s mother replied warmly.

They greeted each other like the friends they had become over seven months and several hundred photographs of flowers, and asked about each other’s trains.

Then Xiaoran’s mother looked at the spice jars.

“Who arranged these?”

His mother smiled.

“I did. It’s easier to find everything this way.”

Xiaoran’s mother nodded.

She opened the drawer beneath the counter, then another, then the cupboard beside the refrigerator.

She looked thoughtful.

“Where do you usually cook, Xiaoran?”

“Here.”

“Where do you prepare vegetables?”

“On that counter.”

“And where do you put the things you’ve just washed?”

Xiaoran pointed.

Her mother considered the arrangement.

Then she gently moved a container.

“Actually, if we put this here, you won’t have to walk around the counter.”

His mother looked at the new placement.

“Hm.”

Xiaoran watched.

Her mother moved another container, then the knife holder, then the chopping board.

Yichen looked at the two women.

His mother folded her arms.

“That’s not a bad idea.”

Xiaoran blinked.

Her mother smiled.

“See? You can make it more convenient.”

She moved the chopping board closer to the sink, then turned to the spice jars.

“These should be here.”

His mother looked at them.

“But they’re already arranged.”

“Yes, but she uses salt and pepper more often than the others.”

A pause.

His mother looked at Xiaoran.

“Do you?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Every day.”

Her mother moved the salt and pepper to the front.

His mother watched, then nodded.

“That makes sense.”

Yichen looked at Xiaoran.

Xiaoran looked back.

Neither said anything.

But her expression was unmistakable.

Your mother started it.

He pressed his lips together to stop himself from smiling.

For the next forty minutes, the kitchen became a negotiation.

Not an argument.

Neither woman was rude, and neither seemed bothered by the other’s suggestions. They had different ideas about how the space should work.

Yichen’s mother believed in keeping things orderly and grouped by category.

Xiaoran’s mother believed in arranging things according to how often they were used.

His mother wanted the cooking utensils together.

Hers wanted the spatulas and ladles beside the stove.

His mother preferred the plates stacked neatly.

Hers wanted the everyday plates on the lowest shelf.

His mother had brought a small rack for cups.

Hers decided the rack took up too much counter space.

At one point, both women reached for the same container.

They stopped.

Looked at each other, then laughed.

“Perhaps we should ask Xiaoran,” Yichen’s mother said.

Xiaoran, who had been standing near the refrigerator, looked up.

“Me?”

“It’s your kitchen.”

Her mother nodded.

“Yes. You should decide.”

Xiaoran looked between them.

It was a trap.

A polite, well-intentioned trap.

She walked over and considered the shelves.

“I think...”

Both women waited.

She pointed.

“Let’s keep the plates here, the bowls there, and the mugs on this shelf. I can reach them easily, and I don’t have to move anything to get them.”

His mother looked at the arrangement.

Her mother considered it.

Then they both nodded.

“All right.”

Xiaoran exhaled.

Yichen, from the dining table applauded.

She turned.

“Don’t.”

He lowered his hands.

By noon, the kitchen was finally finished.

Or, at least, everyone agreed to stop touching it.

The two mothers sat in the living room with tea and fruit. They were already discussing the curtains, which were his, and whether they needed another blanket, which they didn’t.

Yichen was assembling the last dining chair.

Xiaoran stood in the kitchen, looking at the shelves.

She opened the cupboard.

The mugs were where she wanted them. The plates were accessible. The rice cooker was back on the counter.

The chopping board was beside the sink.

She couldn’t help smiling.

Then she noticed something.

The small rack her mother had rejected was still there.

It had been moved to the far end of the counter, where it didn’t take up much space.

She looked toward the living room.

“Uncle, do you want tea?”

Yichen’s father, who had arrived with his wife earlier but had wisely stayed out of the kitchen, looked up.

“That would be nice.”

She made tea for everyone.

When she brought the cups out, Yichen’s mother looked at the one she had been given.

“This is the cup I brought.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Yes. I put it on the shelf.”

Her mother looked at the cup.

“Good. At least you kept that one.”

His mother laughed.

“It’s a nice cup.”

Xiaoran sat down beside Yichen.

He handed her a small plate of fruit.

“How’s the kitchen?”

“Mine again.”

He turned to her.

“Congratulations.”

That made her grin.

“Your mother was very helpful.”

“I know.”

“My mother was also very helpful.”

“I know.”

She leaned closer.

“Your mother moved my rice cooker.”

“I heard.”

“And my mother moved it back.”

“I saw.”

She studied his face.

“You liked watching that.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He glanced toward the kitchen.

“Because you look happy.”

She paused.

Then she looked down at the fruit plate, hiding her smile.

The housewarming lunch was simple.

They had ordered a few dishes from a nearby restaurant, and Xiaoran had prepared rice and a small vegetable dish herself.

Her father arrived last, from a walk round the block to look at the parking, and went straight to check the toolbox he had brought.

“Where did you put it?”

“Third shelf,” Yichen said.

He went and looked. “Good.”

Yichen’s father watched this. “You gave them tools?”

“They might need them.”

“He has tools. I brought my box yesterday.” Yichen’s father said, loyally.

“And took it home again. He has one screwdriver,” said Xiaoran’s father. Yichen’s father, after a moment, conceded the point.

Xiaoran’s mother brought out the dishes.

Yichen’s mother helped set the table.

The fathers, who had discovered at a graduation in June that they could talk for an hour about parking, talked about the parking.

Occasionally, they glanced toward the kitchen, where their wives were once again discussing the placement of the dish towels.

Yichen’s father leaned toward Xiaoran’s father.

“How long do you think they’ll take?”

Xiaoran’s father looked toward the kitchen.

“Depends.”

“On what?”

“Whether they discover another shelf.”

Yichen laughed.

His father smiled.

“Should we help?”

Both men considered it.

Then, almost simultaneously, they looked away.

“No,” Xiaoran’s father said.

“Probably not,” Yichen’s father agreed.

After lunch, the two mothers began clearing the table.

Xiaoran stood to help, but Yichen’s mother stopped her.

“Sit. You’ve been working all day.”

“I can help.”

“I know. But sit for a while.”

Her mother nodded.

“Let us do it.”

Xiaoran sat back down.

Yichen reached for her hand beneath the table.

He was smiling.

She squeezed his fingers.

“You didn’t do anything today.”

“I assembled the chair.”

“One chair.”

“It was a difficult chair.”

She laughed.

He looked toward the kitchen.

“Also, I prevented a conflict.”

She gave him a disbelieving look.

“You did nothing.”

“Exactly.”

She laughed again.

Then she tucked herself against his shoulder.

The flat was noisy in a way it had never been when it was only his.

Her mother was asking where to put the leftover food. His mother was explaining which containers were better for refrigeration. Her father was telling Yichen’s father about the toolbox he’d given her.

Everyone had brought something.

Food, furniture, utensils, advice, old habits.

And it was beginning to feel less like his flat with her things in it and more like a place where people had gathered enough times to leave a little of themselves behind.

When it was time for the trains, Yichen’s parents were the last to leave.

His mother stood near the door, putting on her shoes.

“Xiaoran, call me if you need anything.”

“I will. Thank you for today, Auntie.”

His mother smiled and adjusted the collar of Xiaoran’s blouse.

“Don’t forget to eat properly. And if something in the kitchen isn’t convenient, you can move it.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“I will.”

Then she said, “Even if it’s something you arranged?”

His mother looked at her, then laughed.

“That most of all.”

Yichen stood behind them, smiling.

His mother turned to him.

“Take care of yourself.”

“I will.”

“And don’t make Xiaoran do everything.”

“I won’t.”

“Good.”

She patted his arm.

Then she left with his father.

Xiaoran closed the door.

The flat went quiet.

She leaned back against it and looked at Yichen.

“Your mother likes me.”

“Very much.”

“Even though I moved everything she arranged.”

“She knows you live here.”

Xiaoran laughed.

He came closer, taking her hand.

“Come on. Let’s check the kitchen.”

“Why?”

“To make sure everything is where you want it.”

She let him lead her.

They stood together in the small kitchen.

Yichen opened a cupboard.

“Plates.”

“Yes.”

Another.

“Bowls.”

“Yes.”

He opened the drawer.

“Utensils.”

“Yes.”

Then he looked at the counter.

“Rice cooker.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Back where it belongs.”

He turned toward her.

“Anything else?”

She looked around, then smiled.

“No.”

Yichen reached out and drew her toward him.

“Good.”

She rested her hands against his chest.

“Do you think our mothers will rearrange it again next time?”

“Probably.”

“Should I put a lock on the cupboards?”

He laughed.

“That might be excessive.”

“Then what do you suggest?”

He looked around the kitchen, considering.

“Perhaps we should invite them both to dinner more often.”

She stared at him.

“Why would that help?”

“They’ll get used to the arrangement.”

“Or they’ll keep changing it.”

“Then we’ll have to keep changing it back.”

She laughed and leaned into him.

He kissed her temple.

Then he looked at the kitchen once more.

“Your kitchen,” he said.

She smiled. “Our kitchen.”

He looked down at her. “Say that again.”

“Don’t get ahead of yourself, Zhou Yichen.”

His smile turned slow and knowing.

“Wouldn’t dream of it.”

She immediately recognized that expression.

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re thinking something.”

“I am.”

“What?”

He leaned closer.

“That you look very pleased with our kitchen.”

She blinked, then laughed, pushing lightly at his chest.

“That’s what you’re thinking?”

“Among other things.”

She shook her head, but her arms slipped around his waist.

Yichen held her there, looking past her at the small flat: her camera bag on his hook by the door, her mugs where his mugs had been, the rack his mother had brought sitting at the far end of the counter where nobody had won and nobody had lost.

Across the road, on the fourth floor, the window of her old studio was dark, and would stay that way until somebody else moved in and complained about the lift.

chapters.desc: Their first free Sunday in the new apartment, a video on her phone, and a challenge he takes far more seriously than she meant it.
chapters.title: A Kiss in Every Room
chapters.epigraph: “Then perhaps you should make a better rule next time.”
chapters.content:
It started because Xiaoran was bored, on their first free Sunday in the new apartment.

Or not bored, exactly. She had been perfectly content sitting cross-legged on the living room sofa, scrolling through her phone while Yichen worked on his laptop beside her.

But then she saw a video.

A couple had made a little challenge out of kissing in every room of their house. The video was edited with cheerful music, quick transitions, and captions that made Xiaoran smile.

She watched it twice.

Then she turned toward Yichen.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Let’s do something.”

He didn’t look away from his laptop. “What?”

She scooted closer, holding her phone out for him to see.

He glanced at the screen.

A couple kissing in a kitchen, then another clip in a bedroom, then one in a hallway.

He watched until the video ended, his expression unreadable.

Xiaoran waited.

“Well?” she asked.

Yichen looked at her. “You want to do that?”

“Yes.”

“What exactly?”

She lifted her chin serious about the proposal.

“A kiss in every room of our apartment.”

There was a pause.

Then Yichen closed his laptop.

“All right.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Really?”

“Why not?”

She hadn’t expected him to agree so quickly. She had prepared several arguments, including the fact that it was cute, harmless, and a good way to make ordinary days more interesting.

She hadn’t prepared for him to accept.

“You’re not going to make fun of me?”

“Should I?”

“No.”

“Then no.”

He put his laptop aside and stood up.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Where are you going?”

“To the kitchen.”

“Why?”

He held out his hand.

“Isn’t that where we start?”

Her smile appeared immediately.

“Oh! Right.”

She took his hand and followed him.

She was still giggling when they reached the kitchen.

“Okay. First room.”

Yichen turned to face her, his hand settling around her waist.

“What’s the rule?”

Xiaoran thought about it.

“Just one kiss in every room.”

“One?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

He leaned down and kissed her.

It was a simple kiss, and he tasted of tea. His hand rested at her waist while hers found his shoulder. When he pulled away, she was smiling.

“Done!”

Yichen looked at her.

“Done.”

She reached for his hand again, ready to move on.

But he didn’t immediately follow.

Instead, he glanced around the kitchen.

“Does the dining area count separately?”

Xiaoran turned.

“What?”

“The dining area. It’s technically part of the same open space, but there’s a different function.”

She looked at him.

Then she laughed.

“You’re taking this too seriously.”

“You suggested a challenge.”

“I thought it would be cute!”

“It is.”

He said it so calmly that she couldn’t tell whether he was teasing her.

She gave his hand a tug.

“Come on, professor. Next room.”

The bathroom was next.

Xiaoran stood in front of the mirror, inspecting the two of them in the reflection. Yichen was behind her, one hand loosely holding hers, the other resting at her waist.

“Wait. We should take a picture,” she said.

“Before or after?”

“Before.”

She lifted her phone, adjusted the angle, and took a picture of their reflection.

Yichen leaned down and kissed her cheek just as the camera clicked.

She looked at the photo.

“Hey! That wasn’t the kiss.”

“It was a kiss.”

“But I haven’t started counting.”

“Then you can count this one.”

Xiaoran turned around.

“You’re cheating.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted.

“Why not?”

“Because then you’ll finish before we even get anywhere.”

He met her eyes.

Then his mouth curved into that slow, knowing smile.

“Is that something you’re worried about?”

Xiaoran’s expression changed.

“No.”

“All right.”

He bent down and kissed her.

This time, he didn’t rush. His lips lingered against hers, his hand gently cupping her cheek. Xiaoran’s fingers curled into the front of his shirt before she remembered they were supposed to be completing a silly little challenge.

When he finally drew back, he brushed his thumb across her cheek.

“Bathroom. Done.”

She stared at him in the mirror.

“...You’re really enjoying this.”

“Very much.”

They moved to the bedroom.

Xiaoran went in first, already thinking about how she would explain the challenge to him later. Perhaps she should have made a rule about not taking too long in each room.

She turned around.

Yichen was standing by the doorway, looking at her.

“Why are you standing there?”

“Waiting.”

“For what?”

He held out his hand again.

Xiaoran smiled and walked toward him.

“You’re very demanding today.”

“You started it.”

“I know.”

She stopped in front of him and caught his face in both hands, intending to give him a quick kiss.

But Yichen’s hand settled at the back of her waist, keeping her close.

He kissed her once, then again, softer the second time, his forehead resting against hers when he pulled away.

Xiaoran’s eyes remained half-closed.

“That’s two.”

“Two what?”

“Kisses.”

“I thought the rule was one per room.”

“It is.”

“Then why are you counting?”

She opened her eyes.

“Because you kissed me twice.”

Yichen looked entirely untroubled.

“Good.”

She pressed her lips together, trying to look stern.

It didn’t work.

He kissed her hair.

“Bedroom. Done.”

“That wasn’t part of the challenge!”

“You’re right. I’ll remember that.”

He stepped back, leaving her to stare at him.

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

She was beginning to suspect she had made a mistake.

The study was next.

Since the move, the study held his books, a wide desk, his trophies and the framed photographs that used to be in the living room. Xiaoran walked straight toward the desk.

“This is where you spend too much time working.”

“Not too much.”

“Sometimes.”

He turned to her.

She leaned against the edge of the desk and pointed at him.

“One kiss. That’s it. No extra.”

Yichen approached.

“Understood.”

He placed one hand beside her on the desk and leaned down. Xiaoran expected another gentle kiss, but just before their lips met, he paused.

His eyes flicked to hers.

“May I?”

The question made her smile.

“Yes.”

He kissed her, his hand moving to her cheek. It was a little more deliberate than the previous ones, as if he were making sure she understood that even a small challenge from her could become something he wanted to savour.

When he pulled away, Xiaoran was still holding his sleeve.

“Done,” she whispered.

Yichen brushed a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“Done.”

She looked around the study.

“Do you think your desk is jealous?”

He glanced at it.

“Of what?”

“That you spend more time looking at me than at your laptop.”

Yichen laughed.

“That would be a serious problem for the desk.”

She giggled and pushed lightly at his chest.

“Next.”

They went to the balcony.

It was late afternoon, and the city was beginning to turn golden. A breeze moved the curtains behind them. Xiaoran stepped outside, her hair shifting gently around her shoulders.

She turned to face him.

“Here.”

Yichen came closer.

She expected him to kiss her immediately, but he looked at her first.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“You’re doing that again. Looking at me like that.”

His expression softened.

“Can’t I?”

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

She reached for his hand and placed it around her waist.

“You can. But you still have to kiss me.”

“Of course.”

He leaned down.

The kiss was gentle, accompanied by the faint warmth of the setting sun against her face. Xiaoran’s hands rested on his shoulders. When they separated, she stayed close, her nose brushing his.

“Balcony. Done.”

Yichen nodded.

“One more room?”

“Yes.”

They returned inside.

Xiaoran counted on her fingers.

“Kitchen, bathroom, bedroom, study, balcony...”

“Living room.”

She looked at him.

“That’s where we started.”

“We haven’t kissed there yet.”

“We have.”

“Not for the challenge.”

She stared at him.

Then she laughed.

“You’re unbelievable.”

Yichen took her hand and led her back to the living room.

The television was still on, paused at the opening menu of the film they’d been watching earlier. The popcorn bowl remained on the coffee table, and the blanket was still folded over the sofa.

Xiaoran looked around.

“All right. Last one.”

Yichen stood in front of her.

She lifted her chin, looking pleased with herself.

“One kiss. Then we’re done.”

“All right.”

She waited.

He didn’t move.

Instead, he looked at her with a quiet expression that made her feel as if she had forgotten something.

“What?” she asked.

He opened his arms.

She stepped closer.

Yichen placed both hands at her waist.

“Do you know something?”

“What?”

“You’ve spent the entire afternoon telling me where I can kiss you.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Yes?”

“And you’ve been counting every one.”

“Of course. It’s a challenge.”

He smiled.

“I’ve been trying very hard to follow the rules.”

She laughed. “You have not.”

“I have.”

“You kissed my cheek before I started counting.”

“An oversight.”

“And you kissed my forehead in the bedroom.”

“Another oversight.”

“You’re terrible at following rules.”

Yichen lowered his head slightly.

“Then perhaps you should make a better rule next time.”

Xiaoran looked at him, amused.

“What rule?”

He brushed his thumb over her waist.

“One kiss whenever I want, wherever I want.”

Her expression changed.

The smile on his face was subtle, but she knew that look.

It was the same expression he wore when he had already thought of something and was waiting for her to catch up.

“That’s not fair,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because then you’ll win.”

“Is that what this is about?”

“Yes.”

He laughed.

Then he leaned down and kissed her.

It was supposed to be the last kiss of the challenge, but Xiaoran’s arms slipped around his neck, and when he drew back, she followed him without thinking.

Yichen smiled against her lips.

“Another?”

She hesitated, then nodded.

He kissed her again, slower this time, his hand moving to the small of her back. Xiaoran forgot about counting, about the rooms, and even about the original video that had started all of this.

When they finally separated, she rested her forehead against his chest.

“Okay.”

Yichen stroked her hair.

“Okay?”

“The challenge is over.”

He glanced toward the sofa.

“Then shall we watch our movie?”

Xiaoran nodded.

He started to move, but she caught his hand.

“Wait.”

He looked back.

“What is it?”

She lifted her face.

“You forgot something.”

His eyebrows rose.

“What?”

She pointed toward the sofa.

“One kiss there.”

Yichen looked at the sofa, then back at her.

A slow smile spread across his face.

“That’s not a room.”

“It counts.”

“Does it?”

“Yes.”

He stepped closer.

“Then I suppose we should be thorough.”

Xiaoran laughed as he drew her into his arms.

And when he kissed her again, she decided that perhaps the challenge had been a good idea after all.

Later that night, when they were finally settled on the sofa, Xiaoran opened her phone and checked the original video again.

Yichen glanced over.

“Planning another challenge?”

“Maybe.”

“What kind?”

She smiled innocently.

“Nothing.”

He held her gaze.

Then he reached over, took her phone from her hand, and placed it on the coffee table.

“Let’s not give you any more ideas tonight.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

“You’re the one who took it seriously!”

“I was only following instructions.”

“You were enjoying yourself!”

“And that.”

She tucked herself against his side, still smiling.

Yichen kissed her hair.

After a moment, she murmured, “I think we missed the hallway.”

He closed his eyes.

Then he laughed.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Tomorrow.”

chapters.desc: Two sponges, one drying rack, and the first time he says, quite calmly, that he lives here too.
chapters.title: Our First Fight in Our Own Kitchen
chapters.epigraph: “Because I live here too.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Zhou Yichen learned about living with Lin Xiaoran was that she had a particular way of washing up. The second thing he learned was that she considered his way incorrect.

The third thing was that neither of them was willing to admit defeat.

It started on a Thursday evening.

Yichen had returned from training earlier than usual. His team had a lighter session that day, and he had managed to get home before seven.

Xiaoran was already in the kitchen, wearing an oversized T-shirt and a pair of shorts, her hair clipped away from her face. A pot was simmering on the stove, and the cutting board beside her was covered with chopped vegetables.

He stopped at the kitchen entrance.

“You’re cooking?”

She turned, looking pleased with herself.

“Yes.”

“What’s the occasion?”

She frowned.

“Why does there need to be an occasion?”

“There doesn’t.”

“Then don’t ask as if it’s unusual.”

He smiled and came closer, placing a hand against her waist before kissing her temple.

“What are we having?”

“Tomato and egg noodles.”

“Sounds good.”

“I know.”

He looked at the ingredients.

“Need help?”

“Can you wash those?”

She pointed at a small bowl of mushrooms.

“Of course.”

Yichen rolled up his sleeves and stood beside her at the sink.

For a while, the kitchen was filled with ordinary sounds: running water, the knife tapping against the cutting board, the bubbling pot, and Xiaoran humming along to the song playing from her phone.

It was nice.

Yichen liked coming home to this.

He liked seeing her belongings mixed with his, her favorite mug on the counter, her little kitchen towel hanging beside his. He liked that she had started buying groceries with both of them in mind.

He also liked that she was beginning to feel comfortable enough to take over the kitchen.

Perhaps a little too comfortable.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“Where’s the other sponge?”

She pointed toward the left side of the sink.

“Underneath.”

He looked.

There were two sponges.

One yellow, one blue.

“Which one?”

“The yellow one.”

He picked it up.

She glanced over.

“Wait. Not that one.”

He stopped.

“Didn’t you say yellow?”

“That’s for the counters.”

He looked at the two sponges again.

“Then the blue one?”

“Yes.”

He put the yellow one down and picked up the blue.

She returned to chopping.

A few minutes later, he reached for the dish soap.

“Not that one,” she said.

He paused.

“What’s wrong with this one?”

“That’s the one for washing vegetables.”

He looked at the bottle in his hand, then at the other bottle beside it.

They were both dishwashing liquid.

One was labelled for produce, the other for dishes.

He put the first bottle down.

“All right.”

Xiaoran glanced at him.

He used the correct soap.

They continued, then came the plates.

Yichen washed them, rinsed them, and placed them in the drying rack.

Xiaoran looked over.

“Not there.”

He turned.

“Where?”

“That side.”

He shifted the plate.

“No, the other side.”

He moved it again.

She watched him.

“Yichen, you’re putting them upside down.”

He looked at the plate, then at her.

“How else would I put them?”

“Like this.”

She took the plate from him and demonstrated.

He watched.

“All right.”

He reached for the next one.

She stopped him again.

“Wait, that one goes on the bottom.”

He looked at the plate.

It was the same size as the previous one.

“Why?”

“Because it’s heavier.”

He stared at her.

She stared back.

Then, perhaps sensing the danger of the conversation, she smiled.

“Just do it like that, okay?”

Yichen placed the plate where she wanted it.

“Okay.”

He didn’t sound upset.

But he was beginning to feel as if he had somehow become a guest in a kitchen he had lived in for four years.

The disagreement should have ended there.

It didn’t.

After dinner, Xiaoran carried the bowls to the sink while Yichen wiped the dining table.

He finished first and came over to help.

“Leave those. I’ll wash them.”

She shook her head.

“It’s okay. I’ll do it.”

“I can help.”

“I know, but you don’t have to.”

He reached for a bowl.

She moved it slightly.

“Careful. That’s the one I haven’t rinsed yet.”

He stopped.

“All right.”

She rinsed it and handed it to him.

He washed it.

Then she took it from his hands and placed it in the drying rack.

He met her eyes.

“Was there something wrong with how I washed it?”

“No.”

“Then why did you take it?”

“Because I wanted to put it there.”

He nodded slowly.

“Okay.”

He picked up another bowl.

She glanced over.

“There’s still some oil on that.”

He turned it under the light.

“I’ll wash it again.”

“It’s fine. I’ll do it.”

He put the bowl down.

The kitchen was quiet.

Then he said, “Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“Do you want me to help, or would you rather do it yourself?”

She met his eyes.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, every time I do something, you tell me to move it, change it, or do it again.”

Her expression changed.

“I was just telling you how I like things done.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

He dried his hands with the towel.

“I’m trying to help.”

“I know you’re trying.”

“But?”

She frowned.

“Why are you making it sound like I’m doing something wrong?”

“I’m not.”

“You’re clearly annoyed.”

“I’m a little annoyed, yes.”

She blinked.

It was the first time that evening he had said it plainly.

He continued, his voice still calm.

“I don’t mind helping. I don’t even mind doing it differently. But if you’re going to correct every small thing I do, then I don’t know what you actually want me to do.”

Xiaoran looked down at the sink.

She hadn’t thought about it that way.

To her, she had been explaining where things belonged. She had spent the afternoon arranging the kitchen, and she knew which sponge was for what, which bottles went where, and how she preferred the dishes to dry.

She hadn’t meant to make him feel unwelcome.

But she also didn’t like the feeling of being questioned.

“I wasn’t correcting you because I think you can’t do it,” she said.

Yichen nodded.

“All right.”

“I just wanted things to stay organized.”

“I understand.”

“Then why are you upset?”

He turned to her.

“Because I live here too.”

The words were simple.

They landed more heavily than either expected.

Xiaoran’s lips parted slightly.

He said, “I know you’ve just moved in. I know you’re still figuring out where everything goes. I want you to make this place yours. But I don’t want to feel like I’m doing everything wrong in my own kitchen.”

She turned to him.

She had no answer.

Then she folded the dish towel in her hands.

“I didn’t realize you felt that way.”

“I know.”

He didn’t sound angry anymore.

Just honest.

And somehow that made her feel worse.

Yichen finished drying the last few dishes and put the towel aside.

“I’m going to shower.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Okay.”

He pressed a kiss to her temple before leaving the kitchen.

It was a familiar gesture.

He hadn’t withheld affection or walked away dramatically.

But Xiaoran stood there for a while after he left, staring at the drying rack.

The plates were arranged exactly how she liked them. The bowls were stacked neatly.

The counter was clean.

Everything was in its place.

Except the atmosphere.

She looked toward the bathroom, then at the kitchen.

She had imagined their first disagreement would be about something more serious.

Maybe money. Maybe schedules. Maybe the amount of time he spent training.

She had never imagined it would be about where to put a bowl.

She let out a small breath.

Then she picked up the yellow sponge.

She looked at it.

“Ridiculous,” she muttered.

She put it back.

Then she took the blue one and placed it beside the sink.

After a moment, she moved the yellow one beside it.

Both sponges could fit there.

There was no reason they couldn’t.

When Yichen came out of the shower, Xiaoran was sitting on the sofa.

She had changed into her pajamas, and her laptop was open on the coffee table, though she wasn’t looking at it.

He glanced at her.

“Not working?”

She shook her head.

“Not yet.”

He sat beside her.

Neither spoke.

Then Xiaoran turned toward him.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“I’m sorry.”

He held her gaze.

She continued before she could lose her courage.

“I didn’t realize I was making you feel like you weren’t allowed to do things your own way.”

He was quiet.

She said, “I think I got too focused on arranging everything. I wanted the kitchen to be organized, and I kept telling you where things went. I didn’t think about how it sounded.”

Yichen looked at her face.

She was trying hard not to make excuses.

He reached for her hand.

“Thank you for telling me.”

She looked down at their joined hands.

“But I also want you to know something.”

He waited.

“I like having things organized. I don’t want to pretend I don’t care about where things go.”

He smiled slightly.

“I know.”

“And sometimes I might still tell you that something belongs somewhere else.”

“That’s fine.”

“But I don’t want you to feel like you can’t help me.”

He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“I don’t.”

She looked up.

“Really?”

“Not anymore.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re forgiving me too quickly.”

He laughed.

“Would you prefer a longer argument?”

“No.”

“Then?”

She leaned closer.

“Just making sure.”

He smiled and pressed a kiss into her hair.

Then she leaned into his shoulder.

After a moment, he said, “Can I tell you something too?”

She nodded.

“I don’t need you to change how you organize things. I just need you to let me learn.”

She held his gaze.

He said, “I won’t remember everything immediately. I might use the wrong sponge. I might put a plate in the wrong place. If I do, tell me. But let me do it first.”

She smiled a little.

She laughed.

“That’s very brave of you.”

“I’m willing to take the risk.”

She turned toward him.

“Then I’ll try not to supervise you.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Try?”

“Don’t be greedy.”

He laughed and pulled her closer.

She tucked her face against his neck.

“I’m sorry, Yichen.”

He kissed her hair.

“I know.”

A quiet moment passed.

Then she murmured, “But you did put the plates upside down.”

He looked down at her.

She immediately started laughing.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You’re doing it again.”

She burst into laughter, hiding her face against his shoulder.

He shook his head, smiling, and kissed her temple.

The next morning, Yichen woke up before her.

He made coffee, prepared breakfast, and went into the kitchen to clean the pan he had used.

He picked up the yellow sponge.

Stopped.

Looked at the blue sponge, then at the yellow one.

He considered the situation with the seriousness of a man facing a difficult tactical decision.

Finally, he chose the blue sponge.

He washed the pan and placed it on the drying rack.

Then he wiped the counter.

A few minutes later, Xiaoran wandered into the kitchen, still sleepy.

She stopped at the doorway.

Yichen was standing by the counter, pouring coffee into two mugs.

The kitchen was clean. The pan was washed.

The drying rack was arranged neatly.

She looked at the sink.

Both sponges were beside each other.

She smiled.

“Good morning.”

He turned.

“Good morning.”

She walked over and wrapped her arms around his waist.

“You’re awake early.”

“Training.”

She looked at the counter.

“You washed the pan?”

“Yes.”

“With the blue sponge?”

He glanced at her.

“Yes.”

She nodded approvingly.

“Good.”

He gave her a look.

She immediately laughed.

“Sorry.”

He handed her a mug.

She took it and leaned against the counter.

After a moment, she said, “I thought about something.”

“What?”

“We should make a list.”

He studied her.

“A list?”

“Of things we both need to know about the apartment. Like where things go.”

He considered it.

“That sounds reasonable.”

“And we can both add things.”

“All right.”

That made her grin.

“Then it won’t just be my rules.”

He considered her.

“Good.”

She took a sip of coffee.

Then added, “But the yellow sponge is still for the counters.”

He laughed.

“I know.”

“And the blue one is for dishes.”

“I know.”

“Just checking.”

He put his mug down and stepped closer.

“Xiaoran.”

“Yes?”

“Do you remember what we agreed last night?”

She looked up innocently.

“About what?”

“Letting me learn.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Yes.”

“Then let me.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

He kissed her.

“Good.”

She waited until he turned away before moving the dish towel he had placed slightly crooked.

He noticed.

Of course he noticed.

He looked over his shoulder.

She froze.

He smiled slowly.

“Really?”

She pressed her lips together.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You moved it.”

“It was crooked.”

He walked back toward her, looking far too amused.

She tried to step away, but he caught her around the waist.

“Unbelievable.”

She laughed.

“And you’re very handsome.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Changing the subject?”

“Yes.”

He smiled and kissed her.

She kissed him back, one hand resting against his chest.

When he pulled away, she was smiling.

“Have a good training session.”

“I will.”

“And don’t forget your water bottle.”

“I won’t.”

She watched him pick up his bag.

At the doorway, he turned.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“Leave the towel where it is.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed as he walked out.

That evening, Xiaoran came home later than expected.

She had been held up at the studio, and by the time she arrived, Yichen had already finished training and returned.

He was in the kitchen, preparing dinner.

She put her bag down and walked toward him.

“What’s that?”

“Stir-fried beef.”

She looked at the cutting board.

The vegetables were chopped, the sauce was prepared, and the rice cooker was running.

“You’re cooking?”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“Do you need help?”

“Can you wash the vegetables?”

She saluted.

“Yes, chef.”

She washed them, then placed them on the cutting board.

Yichen continued cooking.

They worked side by side, exchanging small comments about their days.

At one point, she noticed he had put the dish soap bottle in the wrong place.

She opened her mouth.

Stopped.

Looked at him, then picked up the bottle and moved it.

Yichen saw her.

He didn’t say anything.

Something in his face eased.

A few minutes later, he reached for a plate.

He placed it in the drying rack.

Upside down.

Xiaoran looked at it, then at him.

He looked back.

She inhaled.

He waited.

Finally, she said, carefully, “Would you like me to show you another way?”

He laughed.

“Please.”

She demonstrated.

He nodded as if receiving an important lesson.

“Understood.”

“Thank you.”

He leaned over and kissed her cheek.

“You’re welcome.”

They finished dinner together.

Afterward, Yichen washed the dishes while Xiaoran dried them.

She placed each one in the cabinet.

He handed her the last bowl.

She took it.

Their hands brushed.

It was ordinary.

Comfortable.

And perhaps that was what she liked most about it.

They weren’t going to become perfectly compatible overnight.

There would be more small disagreements. More discoveries about habits neither had noticed before. More moments when one of them would have to say, “That’s not how I do it. Then show me.” and the other would have to answer.

But they could learn.

They could make room.

And they could laugh about a sponge.

When the kitchen was clean, Xiaoran leaned against the counter and watched Yichen put away the last bottle.

“Yichen?”

He turned.

“Mm?”

“Do you think we’re doing okay?”

He glanced at her.

Then walked over and stood in front of her.

“I think we’re doing well.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

She tilted her head.

“Why?”

“Because now I know you take dishwashing very seriously.”

She laughed.

He brushed his thumb along her cheek.

“And you know I don’t mind learning how you do things. I just want you to let me.”

Her expression softened.

“Okay.”

He kissed her temple.

Then her cheek.

Then, when she reached for him, her lips.

She smiled against his mouth.

“Goodnight, Yichen.”

“It’s not even ten.”

“I know.”

“You’re going to sleep?”

“No. I just wanted to say it.”

He laughed and wrapped his arms around her.

She rested her cheek against his chest.

The kitchen lights were still on.

The counters were clean. The dishes were put away. Two sponges sat side by side beside the sink.

And in a home that had only recently become theirs, they had made their first small mistake together.

Loving each other had always been easy. Living together, it turned out, came with sponges.

Yichen pressed his mouth to her hair.

“Come on. Let’s turn off the lights.”

Xiaoran nodded.

Then she looked toward the sink.

“Wait. The sponge—”

He gently took her hand.

“Tomorrow, Xiaoran.”

She tilted her head, then laughed.

“Fine. Tomorrow.”

chapters.desc: A Herons team dinner, Fang Ze at full volume, and a question from across the table: is she his manager?
chapters.title: The Girlfriend Seat
chapters.epigraph: “She’s the person whose instructions I actually follow.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Xiaoran learned about being the girlfriend of a professional basketball player was that team gatherings were louder than she expected.

The second was that basketball players apparently ate as if someone might take their food away if they didn’t finish quickly enough.

She was beginning to understand why Yichen had developed such a particular habit of checking whether she had eaten.

Because apparently, he was just as bad.

“Zhou Yichen.”

Yichen looked up from his plate.

Xiaoran pointed at the vegetables beside his rice.

“Eat those.”

He glanced at them, then at her.

“I’ve eaten vegetables.”

“Two pieces of broccoli.”

“Three.”

“One of them was very small.”

Across the table, Fang Ze, who had signed with the Herons that summer and still hadn’t stopped calling him Captain, choked on his drink.

Yichen calmly picked up his chopsticks.

“All right.”

He took another piece.

Xiaoran nodded in satisfaction and returned to her own food.

Fang Ze stared at them.

Then he turned toward the teammate sitting beside him.

“Did you see that?”

His teammate shrugged. “See what?”

“Nothing. Just witnessed something extraordinary.”

Yichen didn’t look up.

“Eat your food, Fang Ze.”

“Yes, captain.”

“I’m not the captain.”

“You’re right. You’re someone’s captain at home.”

Xiaoran nearly laughed with her mouth full.

Yichen gave Fang Ze a brief look.

Fang Ze grinned and wisely returned to his dinner.

It was a team gathering after a demanding stretch of games. The Herons had booked a private dining room at a restaurant, inviting players, coaching staff, and a few partners and guests. Xiaoran had come straight from work, meeting Yichen at the venue after he finished training.

She had initially worried that she might feel out of place.

The team, however, had been welcoming. A few players already knew her from previous gatherings, and the others had been introduced properly tonight.

She had also discovered that professional basketball players weren’t nearly as intimidating off the court as they looked during games.

Some were surprisingly quiet. Some were loud. Fang Ze was apparently incapable of leaving anyone alone.

And Yichen?

Yichen was Yichen.

He had pulled out her chair, placed her bag beside him, and asked whether she wanted tea before he’d even taken his own seat.

He had also moved the spicy dishes farther away from her after noticing she had reached for them twice and then regretted it.

She was beginning to suspect that his teammates were watching them. They weren’t affectionate in public, but Yichen had a specific way of taking care of her, even when he was occupied with everyone else.

“Xiaoran, do you want some?”

She turned toward the voice.

It was one of the players’ partners, a cheerful woman named Ke Qiao, who was sitting across from her. She held up a plate of fried shrimp.

“Yes, please. Thank you!”

“You’re welcome. Take more. The boys eat like they’re training for another game tomorrow.”

“That’s true,” Xiaoran said, glancing at Yichen’s plate.

He noticed.

His eyes narrowed slightly.

She smiled sweetly and took a shrimp.

A few seats away, Fang Ze was telling a story about a training mishap. The table erupted in laughter, and Xiaoran turned to listen.

Yichen was speaking with one of the coaches, but his hand rested casually on the back of her chair.

It was an unremarkable gesture.

Except that when someone passed behind her chair, his hand shifted to her shoulder, making sure she wasn’t bumped.

Xiaoran didn’t even notice.

Ke Qiao did.

She watched the two of them before smiling.

“Can I ask you something?”

Xiaoran turned.

“Of course.”

“Are you his manager?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“My what?”

Ke Qiao laughed and pointed toward Yichen.

“His manager. You keep reminding him to eat, checking his food, and making sure he doesn’t forget anything. I thought perhaps the team had hired someone to supervise him.”

The people nearby heard.

Fang Ze immediately turned around.

“Oh, that’s a good question.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Why are you so interested?”

“Because I’ve been trying to get him to listen to me for years.”

One of the other players laughed.

“Good luck.”

Fang Ze leaned forward.

“Seriously. I told him to rest once, and he looked at me like I’d suggested he retire.”

Yichen, who had apparently heard the entire conversation, put down his glass.

He didn’t seem bothered.

In fact, there was a faint smile at the corner of his mouth.

Xiaoran was already laughing.

“I’m not his manager.”

Ke Qiao tilted her head.

“Then what are you?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth, but before she could answer, Yichen spoke.

“She’s the person whose instructions I actually follow.”

The table went quiet for approximately half a second.

Then Fang Ze made a sound of exaggerated disbelief.

“Excuse me?”

Yichen picked up his glass again.

“What?”

“Say that again. I want to record it.”

“Don’t.”

“Zhou Yichen, the man who ignores his teammates, coaches, and occasionally his own doctor—”

“I don’t ignore the doctor.”

“—has admitted that he follows his girlfriend’s instructions.”

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

“Yichen!”

He turned toward her.

“What?”

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

She lowered her voice.

“You’re making it sound like I’m very bossy.”

Yichen looked at her.

Then his smile deepened.

“Are you not?”

She blinked at him.

Fang Ze slapped the table.

“That’s it. She’s definitely the manager.”

Everyone laughed.

Xiaoran picked up a piece of broccoli from Yichen’s plate and placed it onto his rice.

“Fine. Since I’m apparently the manager, eat this too.”

Yichen looked at the broccoli.

Then he ate it.

Fang Ze leaned back in his chair.

“This is unbelievable.”

Ke Qiao laughed.

“At least someone can manage him.”

Yichen didn’t respond. He poured Xiaoran more tea when he noticed her cup was nearly empty.

And that, somehow, made the table laugh again.

Later, when dinner was nearly over, the conversation shifted toward the upcoming away games.

The players were discussing travel arrangements, training schedules, and the possibility of having a few days off after the next stretch.

Xiaoran was listening while scrolling through a few photographs she’d taken earlier.

One of them was a picture of Yichen sitting beside her, looking down at his food with his hair slightly messy from training.

She had taken it without telling him.

He looked handsome.

She was considering whether to keep it or send it to him when she felt a light touch against her knee.

Yichen.

He was still listening to the conversation, but his hand had found hers beneath the table.

He looked forward.

She smiled and threaded her fingers through his.

A few minutes later, Ke Qiao leaned toward her again.

“Does he always listen to you like that?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“Like what?”

“Well, you tell him to eat, and he eats. You ask him to drink water, and he drinks. I don’t think I’ve seen him argue once.”

Xiaoran considered it.

“He does argue sometimes.”

“Really?”

“Yes. Especially when I tell him to sleep earlier.”

Yichen heard that.

“I don’t argue.”

She turned toward him.

“You do.”

“I explain.”

“That’s arguing with extra steps.”

He laughed under his breath.

Ke Qiao laughed.

“See? You’re definitely his manager.”

Xiaoran sighed dramatically.

“Maybe I should start charging him.”

Yichen looked at her.

“How much?”

She hadn’t expected him to take the question seriously.

“Um...”

“Name your price.”

She squinted at him.

“Are you trying to buy your way out of following instructions?”

“No. I’m asking about your management fee.”

Fang Ze, who had been listening from the other side, immediately joined in.

“Careful, Yichen. If you pay her, she’ll start issuing official training orders.”

Xiaoran straightened.

“Actually, I have a few.”

Yichen turned to her.

“Let’s hear them.”

“First, you need to stop skipping meals when you’re busy.”

“All right.”

“Second, you need to stop pretending you’re not tired. That’s more difficult.”

“Yichen.”

“I’ll try.”

“Third, you need to tell me when your shoulder hurts instead of waiting until I notice.”

His expression softened slightly.

“All right.”

The table had gone quiet again, at the way he answered her: no irritation, no embarrassment, as if every word deserved his full attention.

Fang Ze looked between them.

Then he shook his head.

“Honestly, I don’t know what to say.”

Yichen glanced at him.

“Then don’t.”

“You’re really hopeless.”

Xiaoran laughed, and didn’t notice that Yichen was looking at her now.

When the gathering finally ended, Yichen helped Xiaoran into her coat.

She was saying goodbye to Ke Qiao when Fang Ze appeared beside them.

“Xiaoran.”

She turned.

“Yes?”

“I have a proposal.”

Yichen looked at him.

“No.”

Fang Ze ignored him.

“Would you consider becoming the official team manager?”

Xiaoran laughed.

“What would I have to do?”

“Make sure Zhou Yichen eats properly. If possible, convince him to take rest days. And perhaps teach the rest of us how to follow instructions.”

“That’s a lot of work.”

“We’ll pay you.”

Yichen put a hand at Xiaoran’s waist.

“She’s not available.”

Fang Ze grinned.

“Possessive.”

“Practical.”

“Then can we borrow her?”

“No.”

Xiaoran had to hold on to Yichen’s arm.

“You’re both ridiculous.”

Fang Ze pointed at Yichen.

“See? That’s why we need her. She can make him smile, too.”

Yichen gave him a look.

“Goodnight, Fang Ze.”

“Goodnight, Manager Xiaoran!”

Xiaoran waved as Yichen guided her toward the exit.

The drive home was quiet at first.

Xiaoran had taken off her earrings and was holding them in her palm, looking out at the city lights.

Yichen glanced at her.

“Sleepy?”

“A little.”

“Did you enjoy tonight?”

“Yes. Your teammates are funny.”

“Unfortunately.”

She laughed.

“Fang Ze is especially funny.”

“Don’t encourage him.”

“Why? He’s nice.”

“He’s troublesome.”

“He’s your friend.”

“That doesn’t make him less troublesome.”

She smiled and turned toward him.

He reached over and squeezed her hand.

“It’s yours, by the way. The instructions I follow. I wasn’t joking at dinner.”

She looked pleased.

“What about when I tell you to sleep?”

“I try.”

“When I tell you not to train too hard?”

“That one requires negotiation.”

She laughed.

“See? You don’t follow everything.”

“I didn’t say I was an easy employee.”

“You’re a terrible employee.”

“Then you should consider keeping me anyway.”

Xiaoran turned toward the window, smiling to herself.

A moment later, she spoke again.

“Actually, I liked what you said tonight.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Which part?”

“That I’m the person whose instructions you follow.”

He was quiet.

“Why?”

She shrugged, looking down at the earrings in her hand.

“I don’t know. It made me feel... Special, I guess.” She searched for the right word.

Yichen’s expression softened.

He waited until the car stopped at a red light before turning toward her.

“Xiaoran.”

She met his eyes.

“I don’t follow you because you tell me what to do.”

She blinked.

“I follow you because I know you care about me. And because I like letting you take care of me.”

She turned to him.

“Besides, you’re usually right,” he said.

She immediately smiled.

“Usually?”

“Don’t push your luck.”

She laughed, leaning over to kiss his cheek.

“Thank you.”

He turned his face slightly, catching her lips with his.

It was a brief kiss, warm and familiar.

When he pulled back, the light had turned green.

Xiaoran settled into her seat again, looking pleased with herself.

At home, Yichen went to the kitchen to get water while Xiaoran changed into her pajamas.

When she came out, she found him standing at the counter, drinking from a glass.

She walked over and looked at him.

“Have you eaten enough today?”

He lowered the glass.

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

“Yes.”

“Not just protein and rice?”

He smiled.

“Would you like to inspect my dinner?”

She considered it.

“Maybe.”

He set the glass down and opened the refrigerator, showing her the remaining food.

She looked inside, satisfied.

“Good.”

Yichen closed the refrigerator.

Then he turned toward her, placing both hands at her waist.

“Is the manager satisfied?”

She tried to maintain a serious expression.

“Not entirely.”

“What else?”

“You haven’t had enough water.”

He glanced at the glass on the counter.

“I just drank.”

“More.”

He smiled, reached for the glass, and finished it.

Xiaoran nodded.

“Excellent.”

He looked at her.

Then he leaned down, kissing her forehead.

“Anything else, Manager Lin?”

She slipped her arms around his waist.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Your girlfriend wants a hug.”

His expression softened immediately.

“That’s an order?”

She nodded.

“An important one.”

Yichen drew her into his arms.

“Then I should follow it.”

She rested her cheek against his chest, smiling.

A moment later, he kissed her temple.

“By the way,” he murmured.

“Hm?”

“You know you don’t have to remind me about everything, right?”

She looked up.

“I know.”

“I can take care of myself.”

“Mm.”

He brushed his thumb along her cheek.

“But you like doing it.”

“Yes.”

“Then I don’t mind.”

She looked at him before reaching up to kiss him.

“Good. Because I like taking care of you.”

Yichen smiled against her lips.

“I know.”

chapters.desc: He picked the film. She picked the far end of the sofa. He holds out a hand and waits.
chapters.title: Come Sit Here
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to wait for me to hold out my hand.”
chapters.content:
The movie had been Yichen’s choice.

This was important, Xiaoran thought, because she had already endured twenty minutes of him explaining why the film was worth watching. Something about the director’s previous work, the cinematography, and how the reviews had misunderstood the ending.

She had listened patiently.

She had even nodded at the appropriate moments.

But now, as the opening credits rolled across the television, she had one important objection.

The sofa was too big.

More specifically, the sofa was big enough for two people to sit comfortably at opposite ends, and Xiaoran had decided that this was precisely what she wanted.

She tucked her legs beneath a soft blanket, placed a bowl of popcorn beside her, and settled into the far corner.

Yichen stood by the coffee table, holding the remote, then at the empty space beside him.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Come sit here.”

She looked at the sofa. Then at him.

“I’m already sitting.”

“Not there.”

She followed his gaze to the other end of the sofa, where he had been sitting a moment ago.

“Oh. I’m comfortable here.” She adjusted the blanket over her knees.

Yichen regarded her for a second.

Then he sat down.

“All right.”

That was it.

No argument. No questioning why. No attempt to persuade her further.

He settled into his seat, picked up the remote, and pressed play.

Xiaoran blinked.

She had expected at least a little protest.

Perhaps a raised eyebrow. Perhaps that quiet, mildly amused look he gave her whenever he knew she was deliberately being difficult.

Instead, he appeared perfectly content.

How boring.

She turned her attention to the movie.

For about the length of the opening scene.

Then she glanced at him.

Yichen was watching the screen, one arm resting along the back of the sofa. His expression was relaxed, the television light moving across his face.

He looked comfortable.

Almost suspiciously comfortable.

Xiaoran looked away.

A few seconds later, she glanced again.

Still watching.

She shifted under the blanket.

Then she reached for the popcorn.

“Do you want some?” she asked.

Yichen looked over.

“Thank you.”

He leaned forward, took a handful, and returned to his seat.

No attempt to move closer.

Xiaoran frowned.

She wasn’t sure what she wanted him to do, but she was beginning to dislike how well he was behaving.

On the screen, the protagonist was having a dramatic conversation with his love interest. Xiaoran watched for a while, then looked toward Yichen again.

He was focused on the movie.

She eyed him.

Was he genuinely not going to ask again?

A few minutes passed.

Then, without turning his head, Yichen extended one hand toward her.

Palm facing upward.

Xiaoran looked at it, then at him.

“What?”

He didn’t answer immediately. His eyes remained on the television, his hand still held out between them.

“Over here.”
