His voice was quiet, almost casual.

Xiaoran looked at his hand for another moment.

“Why?”

“Because I want you here.”

She pressed her lips together, trying not to smile.

“You’re watching a movie.”

“I am.”

“Then watch your movie.”

“I can do both.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re not even looking at me.”

Yichen finally turned his head.

His eyes met hers, calm and patient.

“Do you need me to?”

His expression shifted, not quite a smile, but the beginning of one.

Xiaoran immediately looked away.

“No.”

“All right.”

He made no further comment.

His hand remained where it was.

Xiaoran stared at it.

It was ridiculous, really. He wasn’t even doing anything. He was holding out his hand, waiting for her to decide.

And somehow that was more difficult to resist than if he had pulled her over himself.

She put the popcorn bowl down.

Then she lifted the blanket.

Then she looked at him again.

“You’re not going to move?”

Yichen’s eyebrows rose slightly.

“Would you like me to?”

“No.”

“Then I won’t.”

She huffed.

A moment later, she reached across the sofa and placed her hand in his.

His fingers closed around hers immediately.

He gave her hand a gentle tug.

Not enough to pull her off her seat, just enough to invite her closer.

Xiaoran stood, carrying the blanket with her, and walked around the coffee table.

Yichen watched her approach with an expression that was becoming increasingly difficult for her to ignore.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Then perhaps I’m happy.”

She stopped beside him.

He looked up at her, still holding her hand.

“Come sit here.”

Xiaoran glanced at the space beside him.

It was perfectly reasonable.

There was plenty of room.

She could sit beside him, put her legs under the blanket, and watch the movie like a normal person.

Instead, she stood there for another second.

Then she turned sideways and lowered herself onto his lap.

Yichen’s hand moved instinctively to her waist, steadying her as she settled against him.

She looked back.

Neither said anything.

Then his mouth curved.

“Good.”

She adjusted the blanket around both of them, then leaned back against his chest as if this had been her intention all along.

Yichen’s arm rested around her waist.

His other hand reached for the remote.

Xiaoran looked at the television.

“Did I miss anything?”

“Not much.”

“What happened?”

“The main character confessed.”

Her eyes widened.

“Already?”

“Yes.”

“That was fast.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Some people don’t need two hours.”

She turned her head.

“Are you making fun of the movie?”

“No.”

“Then what are you talking about?”

He gave her a small, knowing smile.

Xiaoran stared at him.

Oh.

She understood.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Don’t use the movie to make fun of me.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He lowered his head slightly, his cheek almost brushing her hair.

“I’ve been asking you to come sit beside me for the last twenty minutes. I think I’ve been rather patient.”

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

“Twenty minutes?”

“Approximately.”

“You were counting?”

“No.”

“Then how do you know?”

“I have a general sense of time.”

She turned around as much as she could in his arms, looking at him with disbelief.

“You’re the worst.”

Yichen’s smile deepened.

“And yet you’re sitting on me.”

She opened her mouth.

Closed it.

Then she pulled the blanket up to her chin.

“Because the sofa is cold.”

“Of course.”

“And your side is warmer.”

“Naturally.”

“And I don’t want to sit all the way over there anymore.”

“I see.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Stop agreeing with everything I say.”

He gave a quiet laugh, then pressed a kiss to her temple.

“All right.”

For a while, they watched the movie.

Or rather, Yichen watched the movie.

Xiaoran watched the movie, then his face, then the movie again. Every now and then she reached for popcorn, and every time she did, his arm loosened just enough to let her move comfortably before settling around her again.

At one point, she leaned forward to retrieve her drink from the coffee table.

Yichen’s hand remained at her waist.

“Careful.”

“I can reach it.”

“I know.”

She picked up the glass and took a sip.

When she settled back, she found him looking at her.

“You keep looking at me.”

“You keep moving.”

“Because I’m getting things.”

“Of course.”

She gave him a suspicious look, then put her glass down.

A few minutes later, she shifted again, this time turning sideways so she could tuck her face into the space between his neck and shoulder.

Yichen glanced down.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Uncomfortable?”

“No.”

“Then?”

She pressed her cheek against him.

“Just want to sit like this.”

His expression softened.

He moved his hand from her waist to her back, rubbing it once in a slow, absent-minded gesture.

“All right.”

She smiled against his shirt.

The movie continued.

Somewhere in the middle, Xiaoran began commenting on the characters.

“Why would he say that?”

Yichen glanced at the screen.

“Because he’s upset.”

“Then he should say he’s upset instead of making her guess.”

“That’s reasonable.”

“Right? People make everything so complicated.”

He looked down at her.

“Do you?”

She lifted her head.

“Do I what?”

“Make me guess?”

Xiaoran thought about it.

Then she smiled.

“Sometimes.”

“Sometimes?”

“Maybe a little.”

Yichen’s fingers brushed lightly along her side.

“At least you’re honest.”

She giggled and hid her face against his chest again.

A little later, he reached for the popcorn bowl.

It was empty.

He looked inside, then at her.

“You finished it.”

Xiaoran looked at the bowl.

“Oh.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

“Good.”

She lifted her head, expecting him to complain.

He only put the bowl aside.

“Want more?”

She shook her head, then looked at the television.

“Actually, I think I want to watch another movie.”

Yichen glanced at the time.

“It’s getting late.”

“Just one more.”

“You said that about the previous one.”

“This one is shorter.”

“How much shorter?”

She hesitated.

“...I haven’t checked.”

He laughed.

Xiaoran reached up and touched his cheek.

“Please?”

Yichen looked at her hand, then at her face.

There was something deeply unfair about the way she asked. She could be stubborn for twenty minutes, refuse to sit beside him, and then look at him like that when she wanted something.

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“Choose one.”

Her face brightened immediately.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“You’re the best.”

“Is that why you came over here?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

She considered the question, then smiled.

“Because you held out your hand.”

Yichen’s gaze rested on her.

His expression softened into something quieter than his teasing smile.

“That’s all it took?”

“Mm-hm.”

He tilted his head and kissed her temple.

“Then I’ll remember that.”

Xiaoran settled back against him, reaching for the remote.

But just as she was about to choose another film, Yichen spoke again.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Next time, you can just come here.”

She looked over her shoulder.

“I know.”

“You don’t have to wait for me to hold out my hand.”

She smiled, a little sheepishly.

“Yes, I know.”

“Good.”

He kissed the corner of her mouth.

“Because I always want you beside me.”

For once, Xiaoran didn’t have a quick answer.

She looked at him, her fingers still resting on the remote, and felt that familiar warmth spread through her chest.

Then she leaned forward and kissed him properly.

It was supposed to be a small kiss.

A thank-you, perhaps.

But Yichen’s hand settled more securely at her waist, and when she drew back, his eyes were still on her lips.

“That wasn’t in the movie,” she whispered.

“No.”

“Then why did you do that?”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Because you’re here.”

Xiaoran’s cheeks turned pink.

She quickly turned back to the television and pressed play on the next movie.

Yichen said nothing.

He drew the blanket over her legs, rested his chin lightly against her head, and kept his arm around her waist.

This time, she didn’t move to the other end of the sofa.

In fact, when he shifted slightly to reach for the remote, she caught his wrist.

“Where are you going?”

He looked down at her hand.

“Nowhere.”

“Good.”

His smile returned.

“You’re quite clingy tonight.”

Xiaoran snuggled closer, entirely unashamed.

“You asked me to sit here.”

“I did.”

“So now you have to deal with it.”

Yichen lowered his head and kissed her hair.

“Gladly.”

chapters.desc: A missing spoon, new yogurt packaging and a miniature-cake crisis. By ten at night the cure is a convenience store and a duck called Professor Quack.
chapters.title: The Day Lin Xiaoran Lost Her Mind
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to become a miniature cake business owner tonight.”
chapters.content:
It started with a spoon.

More specifically, a spoon that had somehow disappeared from the kitchen drawer despite Xiaoran being absolutely certain she had put it there the previous night.

Yichen was in the kitchen making breakfast when he heard a loud, frustrated sigh behind him, then another, then a third.

He turned.

Xiaoran stood in front of the open drawer, wearing one of his oversized T-shirts, her hair tied into a messy bun, and an expression that suggested she was about to interrogate the entire household.

“What’s wrong?”

She didn’t look at him.

“Where is it?”

“Where’s what?”

“My spoon.”

Yichen glanced at the drawer.

There were several spoons inside.

“Which one?”

“My favorite one.”

He looked again.

“Isn’t that it?”

“No.”

He approached and examined the drawer.

There were four teaspoons, two tablespoons, and a small dessert spoon.

Xiaoran pointed at the empty space between them.

“That one.”

Yichen stared at the space, then at her.

“You’re looking for a spoon that isn’t there.”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

He opened the dishwasher.

“Maybe it’s here.”

“No. I washed it last night.”

He checked the drying rack.

“No.”

“Exactly.”

Yichen nodded thoughtfully.

“Then we’ll find it.”

Xiaoran turned to him.

Her eyes narrowed.

“You’re taking this too lightly. I’m sorry.”

“You don’t understand.”

“I can see that.”

“It was the perfect spoon. The handle was the perfect thickness. The bowl wasn’t too deep. It was the right size for yogurt, cereal, ice cream—everything.”

Yichen listened.

Seriously.

Then he asked, “Would you like me to file a missing-person report?”

She looked at him.

Something in his face eased.

“Too soon?”

“Zhou Yichen.”

“All right. I’ll look.”

And that was how his Saturday morning began.

By ten o’clock, Yichen had discovered that Xiaoran was having one of those days.

The spoon had eventually been found inside the container of cutlery they had taken out for dinner the previous evening.

Xiaoran had celebrated for approximately six seconds.

Then she discovered that the delivery app had changed the packaging of her favorite yogurt.

“This is not the same.”

Yichen looked at the container.

“It’s the same brand.”

“It’s not the same packaging.”

“Does the yogurt taste different?”

“I don’t know. I haven’t opened it.”

“Then how do you know?”

“Look at it.”

He looked.

It was, admittedly, a different shade of blue.

He nodded.

“I see.”

She turned the container around.

“Look at the font.”

He looked again.

“Yes.”

“They changed the font.”

“Terrible.”

“Don’t mock me.”

“I’m not.”

She sighed and put the yogurt back in the refrigerator.

Yichen watched her walk away.

Then he took a photograph of the packaging.

He had a feeling he might need evidence later.

At noon, Xiaoran decided to clean the apartment.

This wasn’t unusual.

What was unusual was that she had decided to clean everything at once, despite having no particular reason to do so.

She started with the living room.

Then the bedroom. Then the kitchen.

Then she returned to the living room because she had noticed a tiny mark on the coffee table.

Yichen had just returned from the gym.

He found her crouching in front of the table, rubbing the same spot with a cloth.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“What are you doing?”

“Cleaning.”

“I can see that.”

She rubbed harder.

He put his gym bag down.

“That mark isn’t coming off.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you still rubbing it?”

“Because it’s there.”

He crouched beside her.

“Let me see.”

She moved aside.

He examined the table.

It was barely visible.

“That’s probably from the mug.”

“I know.”

“We can use a proper wood cleaner.”

“I know.”

“Then—”

“Yichen.”

He stopped.

She met his eyes.

“Do you ever feel like everything is slightly wrong?”

He blinked.

“Everything?”

“Yes.”

She gestured vaguely at the room.

“The cushions. The lighting. The way the curtains fall. The fact that the dining chair is slightly crooked. The kitchen towel is hanging at an angle.”

Yichen looked around, then back at her.

“Not particularly.”

She closed her eyes.

“Of course you don’t.”

He almost laughed.

But then he noticed her expression.

There was something underneath the frustration. Something restless.

He touched her shoulder.

“Closer.”

“I’m cleaning.”

“Five minutes.”

“I haven’t finished.”

“The table will survive.”

She looked at him, clearly considering whether she should argue.

Then she allowed him to pull her up.

He wrapped his arms around her.

She stood stiffly.

Then she sighed against his chest.

“You’re annoying.”

“I’ve heard.”

“You’re too calm.”

“Someone has to be.”

She pinched his waist.

He laughed.

By three o’clock, the situation had escalated.

Xiaoran had changed outfits three times.

Not because they were going anywhere.

She had decided that none of her clothes looked right.

The first outfit was too casual. The second was too formal.

The third made her feel like she was dressing for a job interview she hadn’t applied for.

Yichen was sitting on the bed, folding laundry.

He watched her emerge from the wardrobe.

She stood in front of the mirror.

Turned sideways.

Looked at herself, then turned back.

“Do I look strange?”

“No.”

“You’re answering too quickly.”

He set down a T-shirt.

He reached for her.

She walked toward him.

He looked her over.

“You’re wearing a white top and jeans.”

“I know.”

“Do I look boring?”

“No.”

“Do I look too young?”

He tilted his head.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You’re wearing jeans.”

She stared at him, then burst out laughing.

It came out so that she had to sit down.

Yichen smiled and went back to folding, as if that settled it.

She covered her face.

“I don’t know what’s wrong with me today.”

He moved closer.

“Nothing’s wrong with you.”

“I’m being ridiculous.”

“A little.”

She lowered her hands.

He brushed her hair away from her face.

“But you’re allowed to have a ridiculous day.”

She turned to him.

Then, with absolute seriousness, she said, “I think I need to buy new clothes.”

Yichen closed his eyes.

“Of course you do.”

The real disaster happened at dinner.

Yichen had suggested ordering food because Xiaoran had spent the afternoon cleaning, changing clothes, and investigating why the new yogurt packaging looked different.

She agreed.

Then she opened the delivery app.

And became silent.

Yichen was reading a message from his coach when he noticed.

“What do you want to eat?”

She didn’t answer.

“Xiaoran?”

She turned the phone toward him.

“Choose.”

He looked at the screen.

There were dozens of restaurants.

“Anything?”

“Yes.”

He selected a familiar place.

“How about this?”

“No.”

He tried another.

“No.”

“Then what do you want?”

“I don’t know.”

He put his phone down.

“Do you want noodles?”

“No.”

“Rice?”

“No.”

“Hotpot?”

She considered it, then shook her head.

“Too much.”

“Something light?”

“Not that light.”

“Then what?”

She stared at the screen.

“I want something delicious.”

Yichen waited.

She continued.

“But not too oily. And not too bland. And I don’t want anything that gets soggy during delivery. Also, I don’t want to eat something I’ve eaten recently.”

“Understood.”

“Why are you smiling?”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He reached for his phone again.

“Let me solve this.”

Five minutes later, he had found three options.

Xiaoran rejected all of them.

Ten minutes later, she was lying face-down on the sofa.

“I hate food.”

Yichen looked at her.

“That’s a serious statement.”

“I hate choosing food.”

“That’s more understandable.”

“I want someone to decide everything for me.”

He put his phone down.

“All right. I’ll decide.”

She lifted her head.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“What if I don’t like it?”

“Then I’ll eat it.”

“What if you don’t like it?”

“Then we’ll both suffer.”

She blinked at him, then laughed.

Yichen ordered two dishes from a restaurant they both liked.

When the food arrived, Xiaoran ate almost half of his portion.

He said nothing.

He moved the container closer to her.

At nine, Yichen thought the day was finally over.

He was wrong.

He had just finished showering when he found Xiaoran standing in the bedroom, holding her phone.

She looked deeply troubled.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you think I’m wasting my life?”

He stopped drying his hair.

“What?”

She showed him her phone.

It was a video of a woman making elaborate miniature cakes.

“Look at her.”

He watched.

The woman was decorating a tiny cake with remarkable precision.

“She’s very talented.”

“She’s my age.”

“All right.”

“She has a successful business.”

“Good for her.”

“She travels.”

“That’s nice.”

“She makes beautiful things.”

He looked at Xiaoran.

She looked back.

Then she said, “What am I doing?”

Yichen put down his towel.

“You’re working.”

“That’s it?”

“You’re building your career.”

“But she has a business.”

“Then perhaps you can start one if you want.”

“She makes miniature cakes.”

“Do you want to make miniature cakes?”

Xiaoran thought about it.

“No.”

He nodded.

“Then I don’t see the problem.”

She looked at the video again.

“Maybe I should learn.”

“Do you like baking?”

“I like eating.”

“That’s different.”

She looked at him, then slowly put her phone down.

“I think my brain is broken.”

Yichen walked over and cupped her face.

“Your brain is tired.”

She held his gaze.

He said, “You’ve been working all week. You haven’t had a proper break, and you’ve spent today trying to fix things that weren’t broken.”

She opened her mouth, then closed it.

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“You don’t have to become a miniature cake business owner tonight.”

She burst out laughing.

“Why would you say that?”

“Because I think it’s important to establish that.”

She buried her face in his chest.

He wrapped his arms around her.

After a moment, she mombled, “I want to do something.”

“What?”

“Something fun.”

“All right.”

“Something stupid.”

“That can be arranged.”

She looked up.

Yichen smiled.

“What would you like to do?”

She thought.

Then her eyes brightened.

“Let’s go to the convenience store.”

He glanced at the clock.

It was nearly ten.

“For what?”

“Snacks.”

“We have snacks.”

“Different snacks.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

At ten thirty, they were standing in the convenience store.

Xiaoran had become a completely different person.

She was holding two packets of crisps, comparing them with the seriousness of someone choosing a university.

“This one has a new flavour.”

Yichen looked.

“Seaweed.”

“And this one is spicy.”

“You don’t like spicy.”

“I might like this one.”

“You said that last time.”

“Last time was different.”

He put both packets into the basket.

She tilted her head.

“You’re spoiling me.”

“You’re buying snacks.”

“Exactly.”

They wandered through the aisles.

She picked up a small pudding.

Then a chocolate bar. Then a drink she had never tried.

Then she found a ridiculous little keychain shaped like a duck.

She held it up.

Yichen looked at it.

“Do you need that?”

“No.”

“Then why are you buying it?”

“Look at its face.”

He examined the duck.

It had two tiny black eyes and an expression of profound confusion.

He nodded.

“Understandable.”

She put it in the basket.

At the cashier, Yichen paid.

Xiaoran looked at the bag, then at him.

“Do you think I’m childish?”

He took the bag in one hand and reached for hers with the other.

“Sometimes.”

She gasped.

He smiled.

“But I like you.”

“That’s a very convenient answer.”

“It’s a very honest one.”

They walked home slowly.

Xiaoran swung their joined hands.

The night air was cool, and the streets were quiet.

For the first time that day, she looked completely relaxed. At the crossing she tugged him down by the collar and kissed him, the snack bag bumping against her knees.

Back at the apartment, they spread their snacks across the coffee table.

Xiaoran opened the new crisps.

Took one bite.

Paused, then looked at Yichen.

“These are terrible.”

He laughed.

“You chose them.”

“I know.”

She took another bite, then another.

He watched her.

“Still terrible?”

“Yes.”

She passed him the packet.

He tried one.

“Not bad.”

“You’re just saying that.”

He ate another.

“Maybe.”

She leaned against him, holding the little duck keychain in her palm.

After a while, she said, “Today was weird.”

“Very.”

“I think I was going crazy.”

Yichen turned his head.

“You were a little dramatic.”

“A little?”

“All right. Considerably.”

She hit his chest.

He caught her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“But you were also tired.”

She looked down.

“Maybe.”

He rested his cheek against her hair.

“Next time you feel like the whole world is slightly wrong, tell me.”

“What will you do?”

“Probably make you eat something.”

She laughed.

“And?”

“Take you outside.”

“And?”

“Let you complain.”

She tilted her head back to look at him.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

Then she sat up.

Yichen looked at her.

“What now?”

She held up the duck keychain.

“I think we should name him.”

Yichen stared at it, then at her.

“All right.”

“What should we call him?”

He considered the duck’s expression.

“Director Zhou.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

“No!”

“Why not?”

“He’s not your employee!”

“Then what about Manager Lin?”

She laughed harder.

“That’s worse!”

Yichen took the duck and placed it on the coffee table.

“Fine. You name him.”

She thought.

Then announced, “His name is Professor Quack.”

Yichen nodded.

“Excellent.”

She leaned into him again, satisfied.

A few minutes later, she was asleep against his shoulder.

Yichen looked down at her.

The missing spoon, the yogurt packaging, the furniture, the outfits, the food, the miniature cakes, and the duck.

He smiled to himself.

Then he carefully lifted her into his arms and carried her to bed.

As he tucked the blanket around her, she stirred.

“Yichen?”

“I’m here.”

“Tomorrow…”

“Hm?”

“Can we buy the yogurt with the old packaging?”

He looked at her sleepy face and smiled.

“I’ll see what I can do.”

She nodded, satisfied, and closed her eyes.

Yichen kissed her, briefly.

“Good night, Professor Quack’s owner.”

Even half asleep, Xiaoran managed to frown.

“Don’t bully my son.”

He laughed.

chapters.desc: A Saturday at the mall turns out to mean the necklace she showed him for four seconds a week ago. The earrings, she pays for herself.
chapters.title: Everything Pretty, Everything Yours
chapters.epigraph: “I’m buying the one you actually want.”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had made one mistake.

She had agreed to go shopping with Zhou Yichen without asking what kind of shopping he had in mind.

It was supposed to be a casual Saturday afternoon at the mall, the first since her December pay had come in. They had finished lunch, and Yichen had suggested walking around before going home. Xiaoran had agreed happily, assuming they would browse a few stores, perhaps buy some snacks, and go to the supermarket downstairs.

Then he stopped in front of a jewelry boutique.

She looked at the store, then at him.

“Why are we here?”

“Shopping.”

“I know that. But why are we here?”

That got a smile out of him.

“Didn’t you say you wanted to look at jewelry last week?”

Xiaoran blinked.

She had said that. Briefly. While scrolling through her phone, she’d shown him a delicate gold necklace with a tiny pendant. She had mentioned liking it, then continued watching her video.

She hadn’t expected him to remember.

“You remember that?”

“Yes.”

She looked through the glass display.

“Yichen, I was just looking.”

“I know.”

“That doesn’t mean I need it.”

“Mm.”

He opened the door for her.

“Come on. Let’s have a look.”

She followed him inside, still a little suspicious.

She should have been more suspicious.

The boutique was quiet and elegant, with warm lighting and glass displays arranged neatly around the room.

A sales assistant greeted them.

“Good afternoon. Are you looking for anything in particular?”

Yichen glanced at Xiaoran.

“She’s looking.”

Xiaoran turned to him.

“Why are you making it sound like I’m on a mission?”

“Because you are.”

She laughed and approached the nearest display.

There were delicate necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and rings. Some were simple enough for everyday wear; others were more elaborate, with gemstones and intricate settings.

Xiaoran immediately gravitated toward a small collection of fine necklaces.

“Look at this one.”

Yichen stood beside her.

It was the necklace from her phone: a thin gold chain with a tiny pearl pendant.

“Pretty,” he said.

“Right? It’s very delicate.”

She examined it from different angles.

Then she noticed the price.

Her expression changed.

“Oh.”

Yichen noticed.

“What?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing.”

“Do you like it?”

“Yes, but it’s expensive.”

He looked at the necklace again.

“Would you wear it?”

“Of course. It’s beautiful.”

“Then try it.”

She hesitated.

“Yichen...”

“Just try it.”

The assistant brought it out and helped her put it on.

Xiaoran looked at herself in the mirror.

The pearl sat just above her collarbone, subtle and elegant. It suited her so naturally that she found herself smiling.

Yichen watched her reflection.

“Do you like it?”

She nodded.

“Very much.”

“Then we’ll take it.”

She immediately turned around.

“Wait!”

He met her eyes.

“What?”

“You can’t just say that.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Why not?”

“Because I haven’t even decided!”

He smiled.

“You’ve been looking at it for ten minutes.”

“That’s because it’s pretty!”

“And you like it.”

She pressed her lips together.

He looked at the assistant.

“We’ll take this one.”

“Yichen!”

He turned back to her, amused.

“What’s wrong?”

She lowered her voice.

“You can’t buy everything I look at.”

He gently touched the pendant.

“I’m not buying everything you look at. I’m buying the one you actually want.”

That made it harder for her to argue.

She looked at herself in the mirror again.

Then said, “Thank you.”

He kissed her temple.

“You’re welcome.”

The next store was a cosmetics boutique.

Xiaoran hadn’t planned on buying makeup, but she had been curious about a new collection she’d seen online.

She stopped in front of the display.

“Oh, this one.”

Yichen looked at the products.

“What is it?”

“New lip colors.”

She picked up a lipstick and examined the shade.

“It’s pretty.”

“Do you want it?”

She shook her head.

“I’m just looking.”

He gave her a knowing look.

“That’s what you said about the necklace.”

She laughed.

“Because I was looking!”

He took a step closer.

“Then look.”

She tried several shades on the back of her hand. One was a soft rose, another a warm peach, and another a muted berry.

She eventually chose two.

Then she looked at the price tags.

Her eyebrows rose.

“These are not cheap either.”

Yichen glanced at the shades.

“Which ones do you like?”

“These two.”

“Then take them.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re very generous with other people’s money.”

“Is it other people’s money?”

“Technically, yes. It’s yours.”

“Then I’m comfortable with the decision.”

She laughed, but she still put one of the lipsticks back.

Yichen noticed.

“Why?”

“Because I don’t need both.”

“Do you prefer one?”

She looked between them.

“I like both, but I probably won’t use them equally.”

“Then get the one you’ll use more.”

She considered it, then chose the rose shade.

Yichen nodded.

“Good choice.”

“You didn’t even help me.”

“I did. I prevented you from buying something you weren’t sure about.”

She laughed.

“How considerate.”

He took the lipstick and added it to the basket.

Things became more complicated when they reached the skincare section.

Xiaoran had a habit of being particular about skincare. Her skin could be sensitive, and she didn’t like buying products just because they were popular.

She examined a serum, read the ingredients, and put it down.

Yichen stood beside her, holding the shopping basket.

“Not suitable?”

“Not sure. I’d rather not experiment.”

He nodded.

“Then don’t.”

She turned to him.

“You don’t mind?”

“Why would I?”

“Because we’ve been shopping for a while.”

He glanced at the basket.

“We’re not in a hurry.”

That made her grin.

Then she noticed a small makeup pouch on a nearby shelf.

It was cream-colored, with a little embroidered flower.

She picked it up.

“That’s cute.”

Yichen looked at it.

“Do you need a pouch?”

“Not really.”

“Do you like it?”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

“Then?”

She turned it over in her hands.

“It’s just that I already have several.”

“Are they all full?”

She thought about it.

“...Yes.”

He nodded.

“Then perhaps you don’t need another one.”

“You’re supposed to spoil me.”

“I am. I’m also trying to make sure you can close your drawers.”

She burst out laughing.

“That’s not romantic!”

That got a smile out of him.

“It’s practical.”

She put the pouch back, still smiling.

A few steps later, he picked it up and placed it in the basket.

Xiaoran noticed.

“Yichen!”

He looked at her innocently.

“What?”

“You said I didn’t need it!”

“I said you probably didn’t need another one.”

“Then why did you buy it?”

He glanced at the little embroidered flower.

“Because you kept looking at it after putting it back.”

She went quiet.

Then she looked down at the basket.

“You’re really going to spoil me today, aren’t you?”

He smiled.

“That was the idea.”

By the time they reached the jewelry floor again, Xiaoran had begun to feel a little overwhelmed.

It wasn’t unpleasant.

She was happy. Happy.

But there were too many beautiful things, too many choices, and too many moments when Yichen casually offered to buy something she’d only glanced at.

She was starting to feel like she should be more careful.

She didn’t want to become someone who expected him to buy everything.

And she certainly didn’t want him to think that she measured his affection through expensive things.

So when he stopped in front of another boutique, she gently tugged his sleeve.

“Yichen.”

He turned.

“Hm?”

“Can we sit for a bit?”

He looked at her face.

“Of course.”

They found a quiet seating area overlooking the mall atrium. Yichen put the shopping bags beside his feet and handed her a bottle of water.

She drank a little.

He waited.

After a moment, he asked, “Tired?”

“A little.”

“Too much shopping?”

She shook her head.

“Not exactly.”

He turned to her.

“Then what?”

She held the bottle with both hands.

“I’m happy. I really am.”

“I know.”

“But I think I’m getting a little overwhelmed.”

He nodded.

“Because there are too many things?”

“Yes. And because you’re buying so much.”

He looked at the bags.

There were three, and one of them was small.

“Too much?”

“A little. I don’t want to turn into someone who expects you to buy everything she points at.”

Yichen reached for her hand.

“You put the second lipstick back, and the pouch, and you nearly walked past the necklace. I’m not worried.”

She looked down at their hands.

“I buy them because I like the face you make when you open the box. That’s all.”

She was quiet.

Then she leaned against his shoulder.

“You’re making it difficult to argue with you.”

“Good.”

She laughed.

He kissed her hair.

“Let’s take a break. We don’t need to buy anything else.”

“Okay.”

A few seconds passed.

Then she lifted her head.

“Can we still look at earrings later?”

Yichen smiled.

“Of course.”

The earring boutique was Xiaoran’s downfall.

She had intended to look at only one display.

But then she found a pair of tiny gold earrings shaped like flowers.

They were delicate, with a small pearl in the center.

“Yichen.”

He was looking at his phone.

“Hm?”

“Look.”

He approached.

She held the earrings up.

“These are pretty, aren’t they?”

He looked at them.

“Very.”

She placed them against her earlobe.

“Do you think they’d suit me?”

“Yes.”

That made her grin.

Then she noticed another pair beside them.

Small pearl drops.

She held those up too.

“What about these?”

He looked at both pairs.

“Both suit you.”

She sighed.

“That’s not helpful.”

He laughed.

“Which do you like more?”

She looked back and forth, then held up the flower earrings again.

“These.”

“Then those.”

Her mouth tipped up.

The assistant brought them out for her to try.

Yichen watched her in the mirror.

The tiny flowers framed her face beautifully. Xiaoran turned her head from side to side, examining the result.

“Do you like them?” she asked.

He nodded.

“Very much.”

She smiled.

“Okay. These, then.”

Yichen looked at the assistant.

“We’ll take them.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Wait, let me pay for these.”

He turned.

“Why?”

“Because you’ve already bought so much.”

He studied her expression, then nodded.

“All right.”

She looked relieved.

He handed her the box, and she paid for it herself.

When they walked out, she held the little shopping bag close to her chest.

“These are mine.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Yes.”

“I bought them.”

“I saw.”

She smiled proudly.

“With my own money.”

He laughed.

“Congratulations.”

She nudged him.

“Don’t laugh. I’m being independent.”

“I know.”

He reached for her hand.

“And I like that.”

They eventually stopped at a café.

Xiaoran sat down and immediately began taking everything out of the shopping bags.

The pearl necklace. The lipstick. The little embroidered pouch.

The earrings she’d bought herself.

She arranged them neatly on the table.

Yichen watched her.

“What are you doing?”

“Admiring.”

He laughed under his breath.

She picked up the necklace.

“I really love this one.”

“I know.”

She held it up against her neck.

“Can you help me put it on?”

He took it from her.

She turned around, moving her hair aside.

Yichen fastened the clasp carefully. His fingers brushed the back of her neck, and he adjusted the pendant so it sat neatly against her collarbone.

She looked down at it, then smiled.

“Pretty.”

He looked at her reflection in the café window.

“Yes.”

She turned around.

“You’re supposed to say the necklace is pretty.”

“I was.”

She laughed.

Then she picked up the lipstick.

“Should I try this?”

“Go ahead.”

She applied a little, pressed her lips together, then looked at him.

He studied her.

“That’s the one.”

She smiled, then leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

A faint lipstick mark appeared.

Yichen glanced at her.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked at the mark, then giggled.

“Oops.”

He took a napkin.

She caught his wrist.

“Don’t wipe it yet.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to take a picture.”

His mouth curved.

She took out her phone and snapped a photograph of the two of them, the lipstick mark visible on his cheek.

Then she looked at the picture.

“Perfect.”

Yichen leaned over to see.

“You’re pleased with yourself.”

“Very.”

He took the phone from her and looked at the picture again.

Then he returned it.

“Send that to me.”

She blinked.

“You want it?”

“Yes.”

Her mouth tipped up.

On the way home, Xiaoran was unusually quiet.

Not because she was tired of him, but because she was still thinking about the afternoon.

Yichen noticed her looking through the shopping bags again.

“Regretting anything?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Good.”

She turned toward him.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Thank you for today.”

He held her gaze.

“For what?”

“For remembering. You have training and games and everything, and you still remember a necklace I showed you for four seconds.”

He smiled.

He reached over and squeezed her hand.

“I remember because they’re about you.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

Then she looked down at their joined hands.

“Next time, I want to buy you something.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know. I want to.”

He studied her.

“All right.”

When they arrived home, Xiaoran carefully unpacked everything.

She placed the necklace in her jewelry box, arranged the lipstick in her makeup drawer, and put the little pouch beside her everyday bag.

Then she came out of the bedroom wearing the new earrings.

Yichen was sitting on the sofa.

He looked up.

She turned her head slightly.

“How do they look?”

He put his phone down.

“Beautiful.”

He held out a hand.

He crooked a finger at her.

She walked over and stood between his knees.

He touched one of the little flower earrings, admiring the way it sat against her ear.

“They suit you.”

She smiled.

Then she leaned down and kissed his forehead.

“Thank you for spoiling me.”

He looked up at her.

“You’re welcome.”

She kissed his cheek.

Then his other cheek.

Then she wrapped her arms around his neck.

Yichen laughed.

“What’s this?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

She nodded.

“I’m just happy.”

He placed his hands around her waist.

“Then I’m happy too.”

She rested her chin on his shoulder.

After a while, she lifted her head.

“Next time, I’m buying you something very expensive.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Yes.”

He laughed and pulled her closer, and the earrings caught the light when she kissed him.

chapters.desc: She keeps migrating to his side of the bed. Then one night she wakes up and finds he has moved over to hers.
chapters.title: His Side of the Bed
chapters.epigraph: “There’s enough room for both of us.”
chapters.content:
The first time Xiaoran stole Yichen’s side of the bed, it was an accident.

At least, that’s what she claimed.

Yichen had gone to bed earlier than usual after a long day of training. When Xiaoran finally finished her work and came into the bedroom, she found him already asleep on his usual side, facing away from her.

There was plenty of space on her side.

There was also a perfectly good pillow waiting for her.

But Yichen was warm.

And his side of the bed smelled of his shampoo and the clean laundry detergent they used.

So she climbed in, carefully lifted the blanket, and settled beside him.

Then, without much thought, she moved closer.

A little closer.

Until her cheek rested against his shoulder and one hand found the front of his shirt.

Yichen stirred.

“Xiaoran?”

She froze.

“You’re awake?”

“Apparently.”

She looked up at him in the darkness.

“Sorry. Did I wake you?”

“A little.”

She immediately began to move away.

His hand found her waist.

“Where are you going?”

“Back to my side.”

He pulled her gently toward him.

“You’re already here.”

She smiled against his shoulder.

“Your side is warmer.”

He pressed his mouth to her hair.

“Then stay.”

She did.

And by the time Yichen fell asleep again, she had somehow occupied nearly half his pillow.

He didn’t complain.

Not that night.

The second incident happened three days later.

Yichen came out of the bathroom after brushing his teeth and found Xiaoran lying diagonally across the bed.

Her head was on his pillow.

One leg was stretched across the middle.

His blanket had been pulled almost entirely to her side.

He stopped at the foot of the bed.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up from her phone.

“Hm?”

“Where am I supposed to sleep?”

She glanced at the mattress, then at him.

“Here.”

He looked at the narrow strip of space beside her.

“Here?”

“Yes.”

“That’s not a lot of space.”

“You can have more.”

She moved her leg.

He waited.

She moved it another few centimeters.

“There.”

Yichen looked at the space again.

“Generous.”

She grinned.

“You’re welcome.”

He climbed into bed, carefully reclaiming a small portion of his side.

Xiaoran immediately rolled toward him.

“You’re cold.”

“You’re taking my blanket.”

“That’s because it’s warm.”

“That’s my blanket.”

She looked at him as if he’d said something unreasonable.

“Are you saying I can’t use your blanket?”

He turned toward her.

“That’s not what I said.”

“Then what’s the problem?”

Yichen looked at her.

Then he reached over and pulled the blanket back up over her shoulder.

“No problem.”

She smiled and settled down.

A few seconds later, her hand found his arm.

Then her head moved closer.

Then her knee brushed his leg.

Yichen closed his eyes.

He had a feeling this was becoming a habit.

By the end of the week, it was no longer an accident.

Xiaoran had developed a consistent sleeping arrangement.

She would start on her own side.

Then, at some point during the night, she would migrate.

Sometimes it happened before Yichen fell asleep. Sometimes he would wake up in the middle of the night and find her curled against him, one hand tucked under his arm.

Occasionally, she would take his pillow too.

Yichen had begun to notice the pattern.

He also began to comment on it.

“Your side is over there.”

One night, he pointed toward the left side of the mattress.

Xiaoran was already lying on his side, comfortably arranged against his pillow.

She looked where he pointed, then back at him.

“I know.”

“Then why are you here?”

“Because I want to be.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Very convincing.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Do you want me to move?”

Yichen looked at the space she had left him, then at her face.

“No.”

She grinned.

“Thought so.”

He reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“You’re getting very comfortable.”

“I live here.”

“So do I.”

“Exactly. We should share.”

He laughed.

“That’s an interesting interpretation of sharing.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek.

“Goodnight.”

Yichen watched her settle back against his pillow.

“Goodnight, little thief.”

She giggled.

One evening, Yichen decided to test something.

He came into the bedroom first, changed, and lay down on his side of the bed.

He placed his phone on the bedside table and began reading an article.

Xiaoran came in a few minutes later, wearing one of his oversized shirts.

She stopped when she saw him.

“You’re already in bed?”

“Mm.”

She climbed onto the mattress, intending to settle on her own side.

Yichen watched from the corner of his eye.

She placed her phone beside her pillow.

Pulled the blanket over herself, then looked toward him.

He continued reading.

A few seconds passed.

She shifted slightly, then again.

Yichen turned a page on his tablet.

Finally, she gave up.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Are you busy?”

“Not particularly.”

She met his eyes.

“Can I come over?”

He lowered his tablet.

“Come over where?”

She pointed at him.

“Your side.”

He looked at the empty space beside him.

“You’re already on it.”

That made her grin.

“Then can I come closer?”

Yichen put his tablet away.

He opened his arm.

He held out his hand.

She immediately moved across the bed and tucked herself against him.

He kissed her.

He looked down at her.

“Why do you always want my side?”

She thought about it.

“It’s comfortable.”

“Your side isn’t?”

“It is.”

“Then?”

She played with the fabric of his shirt.

“You’re there. And you’re warm. And your pillow is nice. And I like being close to you.”

Yichen went quiet.

Something in his face eased.

“That’s quite a list.”

She looked up.

“Is it a problem?”

“No.”

He kissed her hair again.

“Not even slightly.”

The real discovery happened on a Wednesday night.

It was past two in the morning when Xiaoran woke up.

She wasn’t sure why.

Perhaps she had been dreaming. Perhaps she had heard something outside. Or perhaps she had shifted into a lighter sleep.

She blinked at the darkness.

The bedroom was quiet.

The air conditioner hummed.

Yichen was beside her, sleeping on his back.

She turned toward him.

Then she realized something.

She was no longer on his side of the bed.

He was.

More specifically, he had moved toward her.

A lot.

His pillow was now almost entirely on her side, his arm stretched across the space between them, and his body angled toward her.

Xiaoran stared.

She looked at the remaining space on his original side.

There was plenty.

He had deliberately moved.

She blinked again.

Then she looked at his face.

He was asleep.

His expression was relaxed, his breathing even. One hand rested near her waist, close enough that his fingers occasionally brushed her shirt whenever he shifted.

Xiaoran’s lips slowly curved.

Oh.

So that was interesting.

She carefully lifted her hand and touched his cheek.

Yichen stirred.

His eyes opened slightly.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

He blinked, still half asleep.

“Why are you awake?”

“You’re on my side.”

He met her eyes, then at the space between them.

He was quiet.

Then he closed his eyes again.

“Go back to sleep.”

Xiaoran tried not to laugh.

She moved a little closer.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Why did you move?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

His hand found her waist, drawing her nearer.

“You’re always coming over here.”

That made her grin.

“That’s not an answer.”

He opened one eye.

“Do you want me to move back?”

She shook her head quickly.

“No.”

“Then sleep.”

She giggled.

He looked at her properly now, a faint smile appearing despite his sleepiness.

“Xiaoran.”

She rested her forehead against his.

“You’re cute.”

He gave her a sleepy look.

He laughed.

Then he kissed her hair.

“Go to sleep.”

She settled against his chest, but she was still smiling.

A moment later, she whispered, “You like it when I steal your side.”

Yichen’s hand moved slowly along her back.

“I like it when you’re close.”

She lifted her head.

“Then why do you keep complaining?”

“Because you look pleased with yourself when you get caught.”

She laughed.

“That’s not true.”

He looked at her.

Her mouth tipped up.

“Maybe a little.”

He drew her closer, until there was almost no space left between them.

“Then I suppose I’ll have to make sure you don’t have to steal it anymore.”

Her expression softened.

“Really?”

“Mm.”

He kissed her hair.

“There’s enough room for both of us.”

She smiled and tucked her face into his neck.

“Goodnight.”

“Goodnight.”

The following morning, Xiaoran woke up later than usual.

Sunlight slipped through the curtains, and the bedroom was warm.

She stretched, then realized that Yichen was already awake.

He was lying beside her, scrolling through his phone, then at the bed.

She was practically in the middle.

He had almost no space left on his original side.

She grinned.

“Good morning.”

Yichen glanced down.

“Morning.”

She studied him.

“Did you sleep well?”

“Very well.”

“Even though I took your side?”

He put his phone down.

“You’re asking as though you didn’t already know.”

She giggled.

Then she moved closer and rested her chin on his chest.

“I noticed something last night.”

“What?”

“You moved toward me.”

He turned to her.

“Yes.”

“You didn’t even pretend to complain.”

“I was asleep.”

“Before that.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Maybe I was tired of reaching across the bed.”

“Reaching?”

He brushed her hair away from her face.

“Every night, I wake up with you somewhere near the edge of my side, and I have to pull you closer.”

Xiaoran stared.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because you were comfortable.”

She smiled slowly.

“So you were secretly making room for me?”

“Something like that.”

She leaned down and kissed his cheek, then the other.

Then his forehead.

Yichen laughed.

“What’s all this?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re being affectionate.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“You are.”

She kissed him again, this time on the lips.

When she pulled away, she looked satisfied.

“Then from now on, we can share your side.”

“Our side.”

She paused, then smiled.

“Our side.”

Yichen nodded.

“That’s better.”

A few nights later, Xiaoran came into the bedroom and found Yichen already lying down.

She climbed onto the mattress, intending to settle on her own side for once.

But before she could get comfortable, Yichen lifted the blanket.

He held her gaze.

He opened his arms.

She blinked.

“Where?”

He opened his arm.

“Here.”

She smiled and moved toward him.

He pulled her close, kissed her, briefly, and settled his hand at her waist.

Xiaoran looked up at him.

“You’re inviting me?”

“Yes.”

“To your side?”

“Our side.”

She grinned.

Then she snuggled against him, completely satisfied.

A few moments later, she whispered, “Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I think I’ve trained you.”

He opened his eyes.

“Have you?”

“Yes. You used to complain when I took your side.”

“And now?”

“Now you invite me.”

He looked at her, then a slow, knowing smile appeared.

“You’re mistaken.”

She frowned.

“About what?”

“I wasn’t trained.”

“Then why?”

He lowered his head and kissed her.

“Because I like sleeping with you close.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

She wrapped both arms around him.

“That’s a much better answer.”

He smiled and turned off the bedside lamp.

And that night, for the first time, he didn’t leave any space between them.

chapters.desc: Their sixth anniversary falls on a Monday. At dinner, she takes a photograph of him in the black shirt.
chapters.title: Six, on a Monday
chapters.epigraph: “I think you’ve made that easier.”
chapters.content:
The sixth anniversary of Zhou Yichen and Lin Xiaoran’s relationship fell on a Monday.

Xiaoran thought this was deeply unfair.

“Six years. And we get a Monday,” she said, staring at the calendar on her laptop.

Yichen, sitting at the other end of the sofa, looked up from his reading.

“Would you prefer Saturday?”

“Obviously.”

“Should I speak to the calendar?”

She turned toward him.

“Don’t be sarcastic. This is a serious matter.”

He closed his book.

“All right. What would you like to do about it?”

She considered the question.

Yichen had training all afternoon. She had a client shoot in Pudong in the morning and an edit due to Gao Yan by five. Neither of them could disappear for the day. The only thing they had managed to book was dinner, at eight, at the small place on the corner where the owner already knew their order.

They had agreed not to make a big production out of it.

Which, in Xiaoran’s opinion, was a unfortunate agreement.

“I think we should celebrate properly on the weekend. But Monday should still count,” she decided.

“It does count.”

“And you can’t just say happy anniversary in the morning and go to training.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

“Good.”

His mouth curved.

“Anything else?”

She squinted at him.

“You’re being suspiciously agreeable.”

“Would you like me to disagree?”

“No.”

“Then I’ll continue.”

She threw a cushion at him.

He caught it without much effort.

Six years.

It sounded like a long time when she said it aloud. Long enough that she sometimes forgot there had been a version of her life in which Yichen wasn’t the person she automatically looked for when something happened.

He had been there through the gaokao, university, two moves and a graduation, their first arguments that lasted longer than an afternoon, the first time they traveled together, and the countless ordinary days that had slowly become the most important parts of their relationship.

Six years, and he still looked at her with that same quiet attention.

Sometimes she wondered whether he knew how much she noticed it.

Judging by his expression, he probably did.

At 7:16 on Monday morning, Xiaoran woke up to find Yichen already awake.

He was sitting on the side of the bed, checking something on his phone.

She blinked at him.

“Why are you awake?”

“Good morning.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

“Training schedule.”

She made a small noise and pulled the duvet up to her chin.

Then she remembered.

Her eyes opened properly.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

He put his phone down.

“Happy anniversary.”

He met her eyes.

He said nothing.

Then his expression softened.

“Happy sixth anniversary.”

She smiled.

“Six.”

“Six.”

“That’s a lot.”

“It is.”

She reached out from beneath the duvet.

He took her hand.

“Do you remember our first anniversary?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“What did you give me?”

“A letter.”

“And?”

“Two bottles of water. Three yuan each.”

She laughed into the pillow. “From the shop by the gate.”

“You were thirsty.”

“I was not thirsty. You were nervous and you needed something to carry.”

He didn’t deny it. “You gave me nothing.”

“I’d spent everything on your birthday. You’d had a rabbit with a silver bracelet round its neck less than a month before.”

“I still wear it.” He turned his wrist to show her, which was unnecessary, because she hadn’t seen him without it in five years.

She was quiet. Then she pulled his hand closer and kissed his knuckles.

“Happy anniversary.”

He brushed his thumb over her fingers. “Happy anniversary, Xiaoran.”

At 12:18, a message arrived from four hundred kilometers away.

Meilin: Six years. SIX. Tell him I said he’s acceptable.

Xiaoran: He knows.

Meilin: Tell him again. And send me a photo tonight or I’ll assume you broke up.

The shoot in Pudong ran forty minutes over, because the client wanted the sky to look “more Shanghai” and the sky had its own opinions. Lin Qian, holding the reflector, asked twice whether Xiaoran was all right, since she kept smiling at a car park for no reason.

At 2:30, between the shoot and the edit, Xiaoran sent another.

Xiaoran: Wear the black shirt tonight.

Yichen: I own four black shirts.

Xiaoran: The one I like. With the collar.

Yichen: You like all of them. On yourself.

Xiaoran: Don’t argue on our anniversary.

Yichen: Noted.

The black-shirt photo happened at 8:21.

Nobody planned it. That was important.

He had come straight from training, hair still damp from the showers, in the black shirt with the collar, sleeves rolled twice on the way over, one higher than the other. He sat down opposite her while she was reading the menu she didn’t need to read, and when she looked up, he was looking at her.

Not at the menu, or at the owner, who was already writing their order down. At her, with the expression he had worn at the corner shop five years ago, holding two bottles of water as if they were evidence.

She lifted her phone before he noticed.

The lamp over the table caught the side of his face. One sleeve was uneven. He wasn’t posing. He looked, if anything, impatient, as if he was about to ask why she was taking so long to choose something she had chosen every time.

She took it.

“Did you just take a picture?”

“Yes.”

“Let me see.”

She turned the screen. He looked at it.

“My hair is wet.”

“Yes.”

“My sleeve is uneven.”

“Yes.”

“You’re not supposed to agree.”

“Would you prefer me to lie?”

He handed the phone back. “Delete it.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because you’re looking at me in it. I’m keeping it. Happy anniversary.” She locked the phone.

Under the table, she sent it to Meilin. The reply came in four seconds.

Meilin: oh. OH. okay, you’re not broken up.

They ate slowly. The owner brought them a plate of something they hadn’t ordered, said it was for six years, and refused to explain how he knew. It was braised beef with chestnuts, which neither of them had ever ordered, and which they finished. Xiaoran suspected Yichen. Yichen suspected Meilin, who had once rung the owner from four hundred kilometers away to order a birthday cake and had evidently kept the number.

When he had gone, Xiaoran reached into her bag and put two bottles of water on the table between them.

Yichen looked at them.

“Three yuan each. From the shop downstairs from Morrow. I had to argue, because they’re three-fifty now,” she said.

“You argued over fifty fen.”

“It had to be three. Otherwise it doesn’t count.”

He picked one up and turned it in his hand, the way he had turned the first one, and didn’t open it. She knew, without asking, that it was going on the shelf in the study next to the rabbit, unopened, until one of them knocked it over and it had to be drunk.

“This is my present. Five years late,” she said.

“It’s very good.”

“I know.”

They talked about the day.

She told him about the client and the sky, Meilin’s verdict on the photograph, and the note Gao Yan had sent back on her edit at five past five, which said only Good, and which from Gao Yan was practically a parade. Xiaoran intended to frame it.

He told her about training, Kou Ran’s poor attempt at a new shooting drill, and the coach’s schedule for the week, which had a back-to-back in it that neither of them mentioned again.

At one point, Xiaoran put down her chopsticks.

“Do you think we’ve changed a lot?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Since when?”

“Since we first got together.”

He considered the question.

“Yes.”

“How?”

“You’re more confident.”

She looked surprised.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She thought about it.

“What else?”

“You used to pretend you weren’t nervous before presentations.”

“I still do.”

“I know.”

She laughed.

He said, “You’re also better at saying what you want.”

That made her grin.

“That’s because you used to make me guess.”

“I still make you guess sometimes.”

“Exactly.”

He looked amused.

“What about me?”

She studied him.

“You’re more patient.”

“Was I impatient?”

“Sometimes.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You’ve never mentioned that.”

“Because I was young and forgiving.”

He laughed.

She reached across the table and touched his hand.

“But you’re also more comfortable telling me things.”

He looked at her, and didn’t argue.

“You used to think you had to work everything out by yourself.”

He didn’t immediately respond.

Then he turned his hand and held hers.

“I think you’ve made that easier.”

Her mouth tipped up.

They stayed like that.

Then she said, “I think we’ve become better at being together.”

He nodded.

“I agree.”

“Even when we’re busy.”

“Mostly when we’re busy.”

She met his eyes.

He squeezed her hand once.

“Six years doesn’t mean every day has been easy.”

“I know.”

“But I like the life we’ve built around each other.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“So do I.”

They returned home just before ten.

Xiaoran changed into one of his T-shirts and found Yichen in the living room, looking through his phone.

She walked over.

“What are you doing?”

“Looking for something.”

“What?”

He turned the screen toward her.

It was an old photograph.

Their first anniversary.

Or the winter of it: they were seventeen, in school uniforms and too many scarves, outside the school gate. Xiaoran was smiling at the camera, and Yichen was looking at her instead.

She laughed.

“Oh my God.”

“What?”

“Your hair.”

He looked at the picture.

“What’s wrong with it?”

“It was so short.”

“It was normal.”

“It was not.”

That got a smile out of him.

She took his phone and swiped.

There were more.

A photograph from their first university basketball match.

One from a summer trip.

One of them sitting on the floor surrounded by takeaway containers.

A blurry picture of Xiaoran sleeping against his shoulder on a train.

Then one from a rainy afternoon, when they had both been squeezed beneath a single umbrella.

She kept scrolling.

“Where did you get all these?”

“My phone.”

“I know that. I mean, when did you save them?”

“Over the years.”

She looked at him.

He seemed completely unbothered by the fact that he had kept a collection of photographs she had mostly forgotten existed.

She stopped at one.

It was a picture of them in their second year of university. Xiaoran was holding a drink, and Yichen was standing beside her with one arm around her shoulders.

She looked happy.

He looked happy too, though his expression was much more restrained.

“Do you remember this day?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“What happened?”

“You were angry because I beat you at bowling.”

She gasped.

“I was not angry.”

“You said you would never play with me again.”

“I was joking.”

“You refused to speak to me for twenty minutes.”

“Because you were laughing!”

He smiled.

She continued scrolling.

Then she found the black-shirt photograph.

It was already saved in his collection.

She looked at him. “I didn’t send you that.”

“Meilin did. Four minutes after you sent it to her. With a note.”

“What note?”

He scrolled and showed her.

Meilin: She’s keeping this one. So are you.

She smiled.

He took the phone back and placed it on the table.

Then he held out his hand.

He reached for her.

She went to him.

He drew her onto the sofa, and she settled beside him, her legs tucked beneath her.

For a while, they looked through the photographs together.

Six years, recorded in small pieces.

Not every important moment had been photographed. Some were too ordinary, some too private, and some had passed without either of them thinking to take out a phone.

But the collection was still there.

A quiet record of two people who had kept choosing to be beside each other.

Later, Xiaoran was brushing her teeth when Yichen came into the bathroom.

She looked at him through the mirror.

“What?”

He stood beside her, washing his hands.

“Nothing.”

She finished brushing and rinsed her mouth.

Then she looked at him.

“Happy anniversary.”

He laughed under his breath.

“You’ve said that already.”

“I can say it again.”

“Of course.”

She leaned against the counter.

“Do you think we’ll still be doing this in another six years?”

He dried his hands.

“Taking photographs?”

“Celebrating anniversaries.”

“Yes.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You’re very sure.”

He looked at her through the mirror.

“Would you like me to be uncertain?”

“No.”

He stepped closer.

“I intend to.”

She turned to him.

“Even if I’m still borrowing your shirts?”

“I’d worry if you stopped.”

She laughed.

He touched her cheek.

“And even if you keep complaining about Mondays.”

“I have a valid complaint.”

“I know.”

He kissed her cheek.

Then, after a moment, he said, “I hope there are many more Mondays.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

She wrapped her arms around his waist and rested her cheek against his chest.

“Me too.”

Before going to bed, Xiaoran opened her laptop at the dining table and made the photograph into a frame: a thin white border, nothing cropped, not the uneven sleeve or the damp hair or the corner of the menu. Underneath, small, she typed a caption.

Six, on a Monday.

He read it over her shoulder. “Can I have a copy?”

She laughed. “It’s a photo of you.”

“You edited it.”

He was completely serious. She sent it to him, and set the original as the background on her phone, and closed the laptop.

In bed, he turned off the lamp. On the bedside table, her phone lit once with a message she would read in the morning, and for a few seconds the screen showed the photograph: a Monday night, a black shirt, one sleeve higher than the other, and the expression he wore when he was looking at the person who had taken the picture.

chapters.desc: A free afternoon, his white shirt, a phone tripod and a boyfriend whose self-control lasts until five o’clock.
chapters.title: Xiaoran, Stop Being So Attractive
chapters.epigraph: “You’re already the person I want to look at.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had a specific problem.

His girlfriend was being unreasonable.

She hadn’t stolen his food, lost her phone, or called an unnecessary purchase an investment.

Today, Lin Xiaoran was being unreasonable by existing.

And Zhou Yichen was running out of patience with himself.

It had started that morning.

They had a rare free afternoon together. Yichen had finished training earlier than expected, while Xiaoran had managed to leave the studio without bringing work home. They decided to spend the day at home, which, in theory, was supposed to be relaxing.

Yichen was in the kitchen preparing lunch when Xiaoran appeared behind him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Look at me.”

He turned.

She was wearing one of his shirts.

Not just any shirt. A white one he’d left on the back of their bedroom chair the previous night. It was slightly oversized on her, the sleeves folded twice, the hem falling over her shorts. Her hair was loosely tied up, with a few strands framing her face.

She had also put on lip gloss.

He noticed.

He wished he hadn’t.

“What?” she asked.

Yichen looked at her for another second.

“Nothing.”

She tilted her head.

“Why are you looking at me like that?”

“You’re wearing my shirt.”

“Yes.”

“Is there a reason?”

She looked down at herself.

“Because it’s comfortable.”

“All right.”

She smiled, apparently satisfied with his response, then walked closer and leaned against the kitchen counter.

“What’s for lunch?”

“Whatever you want.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

“Then come and choose.”

She stepped beside him, peering into the pan. Her shoulder brushed his arm.

“Can we have noodles?”

“We had noodles yesterday.”

“Then rice?”

“There’s rice.”

“With what?”

He met her eyes.

“You’re asking me to decide, aren’t you?”

She smiled innocently.

“You’re very smart.”

Yichen looked at her, then returned to cooking.

He was going to survive the afternoon.

He was sure of it.

The first incident happened when Xiaoran decided to help him.

She stood beside him, reaching for the small bowl of chopped vegetables on the counter.

Yichen moved it closer.

“Careful.”

“I can reach.”

“I know.”

She gave him a look.

“Then why are you moving everything for me?”

“Because I can.”

She laughed and reached up to put the bowl away after he’d finished using it.

The shirt shifted slightly as she stretched.

Yichen stopped stirring.

His eyes moved away almost immediately.

He took a slow breath.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Could you pass me the soy sauce?”

She looked around.

“It’s behind you.”

“I know.”

She handed it to him.

Their fingers brushed.

She smiled.

“You’re acting strange.”

“I’m cooking.”

“You’re always cooking.”

“Then perhaps I’m acting normally.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

But before she could question him further, he turned back to the stove.

Xiaoran shrugged.

She was too busy thinking about lunch to notice that her boyfriend had just mentally asked for strength.

The second incident happened in the living room.

After lunch, Xiaoran decided to take a few photographs.

She had recently bought a small phone tripod and wanted to test it. She placed it on the coffee table, adjusted the angle, then stood in front of the sofa.

Yichen was sitting nearby, reviewing something on his tablet.

“Yichen.”

He looked up.

“Yes?”

“Is the angle okay?”

She posed.

It was nothing elaborate. She tilted her head, rested one hand on her waist, and smiled at the camera.

He looked at the screen, then at her.

“Looks good.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She moved closer to the tripod to check the result.

Then she took another picture.

This time, she turned slightly sideways.

“How about this?”

Yichen put his tablet down.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Are you taking pictures for something?”

“No. Just for myself.”

“Then they’re fine.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re not even looking properly.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I am.”

“You’re looking at your tablet.”

He set it aside.

“All right. Show me.”

She handed him the phone.

He looked through the pictures.

They were perfectly ordinary photographs of his girlfriend in his shirt, looking pretty and entirely unaware of how much effort he was putting into behaving like a normal person.

He returned the phone.

“Good.”

She stared.

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“You’re supposed to tell me if the light’s wrong.”

He looked at her.

“You’re beautiful.”

She blinked, then smiled.

“Oh.”

Yichen leaned back against the sofa.

“Was that sufficient feedback?”

She laughed.

“Maybe.”

She returned to her tripod.

He picked up his tablet again.

He was beginning to suspect that the afternoon wasn’t going to improve.

The third incident was worse.

Xiaoran decided she wanted to lie down.

There was nothing unusual about that. Their sofa was comfortable, the afternoon was quiet, and she often liked resting beside him while he worked.

She settled at one end of the sofa, then looked at him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

She patted the space beside her.

He put his tablet aside and moved closer.

She patted the cushion beside her.

“Sit.”

He sat.

She immediately leaned against him, resting her head on his shoulder.

For a few minutes, everything was peaceful.

Then she shifted.

Her legs moved across his lap, and she turned slightly so she could face him.

“Are you busy?”

“Not particularly.”

“Can I disturb you?”

He looked down at her.

“You already are.”

She gasped.

“That’s so mean.”

He smiled and brushed her hair away from her cheek.

“I didn’t say I minded.”

She smiled, satisfied.

Then she lifted her hand and began playing with the collar of his shirt.

Yichen watched her.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you looking at me?”

She shrugged.

“Because you’re handsome.”

“Thank you.”

She traced the edge of his collar with her fingertip.

“Very handsome.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“You’re doing that deliberately.”

She looked up at him, eyes wide with innocence.

“Doing what?”

He held her gaze.

She smiled, and it was the smile that told him she knew exactly what she was doing.

He exhaled through his nose.

“You’re enjoying yourself.”

“A little.”

He gently caught her hand.

“Behave.”

She laughed.

“Why?”

“Because I still have things to do.”

She looked at the abandoned tablet on the coffee table.

“Your work?”

“Yes.”

“You haven’t touched it for ten minutes.”

“Because someone keeps distracting me.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Who?”

He turned to her.

She laughed and buried her face against his chest.

Yichen closed his eyes.

He was beginning to understand that the afternoon had been designed specifically to test him.

The final incident happened around five.

Xiaoran had changed into a different outfit.

She’d put on a fitted top and a soft skirt because she wanted to go downstairs to buy something from the convenience store.

Yichen was by the entrance, putting on his shoes.

She came out of the bedroom, adjusting her hair.

“Ready?”

He looked up.

And stopped.

It wasn’t that the outfit was revealing. It wasn’t. It suited her. The fitted top, the skirt, the way her hair fell over her shoulders, and the little effort she’d made with her appearance.

She looked pretty.

Pretty.

And she was smiling at him as if she hadn’t just caused him to forget what he was doing.

“What?” she asked.

He held her gaze, then stood.

“Nothing.”

She approached.

“You’re doing it again. Looking at me and then pretending you weren’t.”

He took her bag from the console.

“Let’s go.”

She followed him, laughing.

But just before they reached the door, she stopped.

“Wait.”

He turned.

She walked toward him, reached up, and straightened the collar of his shirt.

“There.”

He looked down at her.

“Thank you.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

Then, instead of moving away, she rose slightly onto her toes and kissed his cheek.

A small, casual kiss.

The kind she gave him dozens of times.

Except today, for reasons he couldn’t explain, it was the last straw.

Yichen caught her waist before she could step back.

Xiaoran blinked.

“Yichen?”

He looked at her.

His expression had changed.

It had gone quiet in a way that made her aware of how close they were standing.

“What?” she whispered.

He looked at her lips, then back at her eyes.

“You’re doing this all day.”

“Doing what?”

He gave her a look.

She tried to smile.

“Being your girlfriend?”

His mouth twitched.

“Yes. And that.”

She laughed.

But he didn’t release her waist.

Instead, he drew her a little closer.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Do you know how difficult you’ve made it to concentrate today?”

Her smile widened.

“Really?”

“Very.”

She looked pleased.

“Why?”

“Because you’re being unfairly attractive,” he said, calmly.

She burst out laughing.

“Unfairly?”

“Yes.”

“That’s not my fault!”

“I know.”

“Then what do you want me to do?”

He studied her.

“Stop looking at me like that.”

She immediately widened her eyes.

“Like what?”

He closed his eyes.

“Exactly like that.”

She laughed harder.

“Yichen!”

He finally smiled, but there was something helpless about it.

He leaned down and kissed her.

At first, it was a brief kiss.

Then she reached up and held his face, smiling against his lips, and he kissed her again.

This time, he didn’t pull away immediately.

His hand settled more securely at her waist, while his other hand moved to the back of her head. He kissed her with a tenderness that gradually became harder to disguise, as if all the restraint he’d been practicing since morning had finally run out.

When he eventually drew back, Xiaoran was smiling.

Her cheeks were pink.

“That was...”

She paused.

Yichen brushed his thumb against her cheek.

“What?”

She turned to him.

“Not very disciplined.”

He laughed.

“No.”

She giggled.

Then, because she had apparently learned nothing, she leaned forward and kissed him again.

Yichen let out a soft laugh against her lips.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You’re making it worse.”

She smiled.

“Then don’t resist.”

He looked at her.

She thought he might say something teasing.

Instead, he lowered his head and kissed her again.

And this time, when she wrapped her arms around his neck, he stopped pretending he was in a hurry to leave.

They never made it to the convenience store.

At some point, Yichen abandoned the idea entirely, took her hand, and led her back toward the living room.

Xiaoran followed, looking far too pleased with herself.

He stopped beside the sofa and turned toward her.

He crooked a finger at her.

She stepped closer.

He tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Maybe.”

“Very much, apparently.”

She tilted her head.

“Are you complaining?”

He considered her.

Then he smiled that slow, knowing smile that always made her feel a little less clever than she thought she was.

“No.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair.

Then her cheek, then the corner of her mouth.

Xiaoran’s hands rested against his chest.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You’re very affectionate today.”

He laughed.

“You’re one to talk.”

She grinned.

He drew her into his arms, and she settled against him naturally.

For a while, neither of them said anything.

Then Xiaoran lifted her head.

“Can I ask something?”

“Of course.”

“Were you really holding back all day?”

He glanced at her.

“Yes.”

Her eyes widened.

She seemed to consider this.

Then her expression turned mischievous.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Would that have helped?”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“No.”

He laughed.

“Exactly.”

She wrapped her arms around him again, hiding her smile against his shoulder.

After a moment, she whispered:

“Well, I like that you find me attractive.”

He cupped her cheek.

“You don’t need to dress up, pose for pictures, or try to be anything. You’re already the person I want to look at.”

Her expression softened.

For once, she didn’t have a teasing reply ready.

She leaned forward and kissed him.

Yichen smiled against her lips.

When she pulled away, she whispered, “I love you.”

“I love you too.”

Then she glanced toward the door.

“Should we still go downstairs?”

He looked at her.

“Do you still want to?”

She considered it, then smiled.

“Actually, no.”

“Good.”

He drew her back into his arms.

And Xiaoran, who had spent the entire afternoon unknowingly testing the limits of her boyfriend’s self-control, finally settled down.

For approximately three minutes.

Then she looked up at him again.

“Yichen?”

He sighed, already smiling.

“What now?”

“I’m keeping your white shirt.”

He looked at her, then laughed.

“Then next time I have work to finish, I’m working outside.”

She grinned and kissed his jaw, and he didn’t open the tablet again that night.

chapters.desc: Five shades, one dinner reservation, and a man who cannot review a lipstick without looking at her mouth.
chapters.title: The Lipstick Problem
chapters.epigraph: “How many times do you want to kiss me?”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had been getting ready for nearly forty minutes.

Yichen knew this because he had checked the time twice.

Not that he minded.

He was sitting at the foot of their bed, already dressed in a charcoal shirt and black trousers, one ankle resting over the other. His watch was fastened, his phone was beside him, and he had been ready to leave for the past fifteen minutes.

Xiaoran, meanwhile, was standing in front of the dressing table with five lipsticks arranged in a neat row, the rose one from the mall among them.

She picked up the first one.

Applied it.

Pressed her lips together.

Looked at herself, then turned around.

“Yichen.”

He looked up immediately.

“Hm?”

“Which one?”

She walked toward him, holding her phone with the front camera open.

He glanced at her lips, then at the phone.

“Which one what?”

She blinked at him.

“Don’t tell me you forgot. I’m choosing a lipstick.”

“I remember.”

“Then look properly.”

He did.

The first shade was a muted pink, soft and natural. It suited her, although he was beginning to suspect that every shade would suit her because she was the one wearing it.

“That one is nice,” he said.

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“Nice?”

“Yes.”

“That’s not a very useful answer.”

“What would be useful?”

“Tell me whether it looks too pale, too dark, too orange, too red, or whether it makes my face look dull.”

Yichen considered this list.

“That’s quite a lot of requirements.”

“Because lipstick is complicated.”

He nodded solemnly.

“I see.”

She turned back toward the mirror.

“Wait. I’ll try another one.”

The second shade was a warm rose.

She applied it carefully, using the small mirror attached to the lipstick case. When she finished, she turned toward him again.

“What about this?”

Yichen looked.

It was slightly deeper than the first, giving her lips a more noticeable color.

“I like it.”

“More than the first?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He met her eyes.

“Would you like a detailed explanation?”

“Yes. It suits you.”

Xiaoran waited.

“And?”

“And I like looking at you.”

She blinked.

Then she rolled her eyes.

“You’re not reviewing the lipstick. You’re reviewing me.”

“Is there a difference?”

“Of course!”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

Xiaoran returned to the dressing table.

“You’re not taking this seriously.”

“I’ve been very serious.”

“You haven’t even looked at the colors properly.”

“I have.”

“Then tell me the difference between the first and second.”

Yichen looked at her.

“The second is warmer.”

She paused, then slowly turned around.

“...Oh.”

His expression remained calm.

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You’re actually paying attention?”

“Of course.”

Xiaoran smiled, pleased.

“All right. Next.”

The third shade was a soft coral.

She applied it, checked the result under the bedroom light, then walked toward him again.

“This one?”

Yichen looked at her.

She tilted her face slightly to the left, then to the right.

“Well?”

He was quiet for a second.

“Come closer.”

She stepped forward.

He lifted his eyes to hers.

“Closer.”

She moved another step.

“Why?”

“I can’t see properly.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Do you need glasses?”

“No.”

“Then why can’t you see?”

Yichen’s mouth curved.

“Perhaps you’re too far away.”

She laughed and stepped between his knees, holding her phone up.

“Here. Look.”

He did.

But his gaze kept returning to her mouth.

The coral shade was pretty. It brought a little warmth to her face, and the way she pursed her lips while waiting for his opinion was making it increasingly difficult for him to concentrate on the actual color.

“Well?” she prompted.

“Pretty.”

She sighed.

“Yichen.”

“What?”

“You’re doing it again. Looking at my lips.”

He didn’t deny it.

Instead, he looked at her eyes.

“Would you prefer I look somewhere else?”

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

“You’re supposed to look at the lipstick.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

He rested his hands lightly on her hips.

“I’m trying.”

She looked at him, then laughed.

“You’re hopeless.”
