“Apparently.”

She turned away, but not before noticing the small smile on his face.

The fourth shade was a deeper rose-brown.

This time, she took longer to apply it.

She carefully traced the edges, blotted once with a tissue, and stepped back to inspect herself.

Yichen watched from the bed.

She looked beautiful.

He had known that before she started. He had known it when she came out of the bathroom with damp hair, when she had stood in front of the wardrobe debating between two dresses, and when she had finally chosen the one she was wearing now.

But there was something about watching her take such care over a small detail that he found endearing.

She wasn’t doing it for anyone else.

She enjoyed looking pretty.

And he liked watching her enjoy herself.

“Yichen?”

He looked up.

“Yes?”

She held out her hand.

He stood and approached the dressing table.

Xiaoran turned toward him, holding up the lipstick.

“This one is more mature, right?”

He examined her face.

“Yes.”

“Too mature?”

“No.”

“Does it make me look older?”

Something in his face eased.

“How old would you like to look?”

“Don’t change the subject.”

“I’m not.”

She frowned at him through the mirror.

“You’re being difficult.”

He reached for her hand, gently lowering the lipstick.

“Look at me.”

She did.

Yichen’s gaze settled on her face.

“That color looks good on you.”

She waited.

“But?”

“No but.”

“Then why do you look like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re thinking something.”

He considered whether to tell her.

Then he decided he might as well.

“Because I keep thinking about kissing you.”

Xiaoran froze.

Her eyes widened slightly.

“...What?”

Yichen looked entirely composed.

“You heard me.”

She glanced at the mirror, then at him, then down at the lipstick in her hand.

“Yichen!”

“What?”

“I’m trying to get ready!”

“I know.”

“And you’re distracting me!”

He smiled.

“I thought I was the one being distracted.”

She turned around fully.

“You’ve been looking at my lips this entire time!”

“Yes.”

Her face grew warmer.

She tried to look annoyed, but the smile tugging at her lips betrayed her.

“Why didn’t you just say so?”

Yichen tilted his head.

“You were asking me to choose a lipstick.”

“Because I wanted your opinion!”

“You have it.”

“Which one?”

He looked at the row of lipsticks on the dressing table, then back at her.

“The second one.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“The warm rose?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“It brings out the color of your lips without making them look too dark. It suits the dress, too. And I think it’s the one I’d most like to kiss.”

Silence.

Xiaoran’s mouth opened slightly.

Then she looked away.

“You’re so...”

She couldn’t find the word.

Yichen smiled.

“Helpful?”

“No!”

He laughed.

She placed the lipstick on the dressing table, then turned back toward him.

“Fine. If you want to kiss me so much, why don’t you?”

Yichen’s expression changed.

Not dramatically.

Just enough for her to notice the faint shift in his eyes.

“Are you sure?”

She nodded, trying to maintain her confidence.

“Yes.”

He lifted his hand to her cheek.

Then he leaned down and kissed her.

It was gentle at first, his lips meeting hers with a warmth that made her fingers instinctively curl around his wrist.

When he pulled away, Xiaoran was still looking at him.

He glanced at her lips, then back at her eyes.

“The color is good.”

She let out a small laugh.

“You’re ridiculous.”

“That’s not the only reason.”

“What else?”

“It suits you.”

That made her grin.

Then, after a brief pause, she leaned forward and kissed him again.

This time, she was the one who pulled away first.

Yichen looked at her lips.

She noticed.

“Stop looking.”

“I’m looking at the lipstick.”

“No, you’re not.”

“Would you like me to prove it?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“How?”

He brushed his thumb lightly against her cheek.

“Put on the other shades.”

Xiaoran stared at him, then burst out laughing.

“Absolutely not!”

That got a smile out of him.

“Why?”

“Because then you’ll ask me to try every single one.”

“That’s one possibility.”

“And we’ll never leave!”

“That’s another.”

She shook her head, laughing as she turned back toward the dressing table.

Yichen returned to the bed, watching her pick up the warm rose lipstick again.

She applied one final layer, checked the result in the mirror, and pressed her lips together.

“All right. This one.”

“Good choice.”

She turned around.

She walked over to him, holding out her hand.

“Then let’s go.”

Yichen took her hand but didn’t stand immediately.

He looked at her once more.

Xiaoran sighed.

“What now?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking again.”

“Yes.”

She placed her free hand on her hip.

“Zhou Yichen, we have a reservation.”

“I remember.”

“Then stand up.”

He did, but before she could walk away, he gently caught her waist and drew her closer.

One last kiss.

When he pulled back, she looked at him with narrowed eyes.

“You’re going to ruin the lipstick.”

Yichen glanced at her mouth.

“Sorry.”

He didn’t sound sorry.

Xiaoran picked up her handbag.

“Next time, I’m choosing my lipstick without asking you.”

“All right.”

“And you aren’t allowed to distract me.”

“Understood.”

She walked toward the bedroom door.

Yichen followed.

Just before they left, he reached for her hand.

“Xiaoran.”

She turned.

“Hm?”

“The warm rose.”

“What about it?”

“Keep that one.”

She smiled.

“Because it’s your favorite?”

He squeezed her hand.

“Because I like the way you look when you wear it.”

She smiled more brightly.

Then she lifted their joined hands and gave his fingers a little swing.

“Fine. But I’m still buying the coral one.”

“I didn’t say you couldn’t.”

“And the rose-brown.”

“All right.”

“And maybe another shade.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“How many lipsticks do you need?”

She looked at him innocently.

“How many times do you want to kiss me?”

He stopped walking for half a second.

Then he laughed, shaking his head.

“That’s a very difficult question.”

Xiaoran beamed, pulled him out of the apartment, and they were seven minutes late for the reservation.

chapters.desc: The skirt has waited in the wardrobe since her birthday. Tonight she wears it, and he takes the pictures.
chapters.title: The Skirt Meilin Bought Her
chapters.epigraph: “Because you weren’t posing.”
chapters.content:
The skirt had been hanging in Xiaoran’s half of the wardrobe since her birthday.

Not because she didn’t like it.

Quite the opposite.

She liked it so much that she had been waiting for the right occasion to wear it.

It was a black mini skirt, slightly tailored, with a flattering high waist and a subtle pleated detail. It wasn’t extravagant, but it had a certain style to it. Meilin had picked it out for Xiaoran’s birthday, insisting that she needed something a little different from her usual collection of comfortable skirts and jeans.

At the time, Xiaoran had been delighted.

She had tried it on immediately, sent Meilin several pictures, and received a voice message that consisted mostly of Meilin saying, “Finally. Something that makes you look like you know you’re pretty.”

Xiaoran had laughed and promised to wear it soon.

Months later, it was still hanging there.

Until Friday evening.

She stood in front of the open wardrobe, holding the skirt against herself.

Then she looked at the mirror, then at the skirt again.

“Okay.”

She nodded.

“Today.”

From the bathroom, Yichen’s voice came.

“What’s today?”

Xiaoran turned around.

“Nothing!”

A pause.

“All right.”

She heard the shower running again.

She looked at the skirt, then smiled.

Tonight, she was finally going to wear it.

Yichen noticed something unusual when he came out of the bathroom.

Xiaoran was standing in front of the mirror, carefully adjusting the hem of her skirt.

She was wearing a simple fitted top, the black mini skirt, and a pair of shoes that made her legs look lovely. Her hair was down, with a slight curl at the ends, and she had put on a little more effort with her makeup than usual.

Yichen stopped by the bedroom door.

He didn’t say anything immediately.

Xiaoran noticed his reflection in the mirror and turned.

He walked over and stood behind her, his hands settling lightly at her waist, and looked at the two of them in the glass for a while before he said anything.

“You look beautiful.”

Xiaoran’s smile arrived before she could stop it.

He kissed her cheek.

“New?”

“Meilin gave it to me for my birthday.”

Yichen glanced at the skirt again.

“Ah.”

“I’ve wanted to wear it for a while, but somehow I never found the right occasion.”

“And tonight is the occasion?”

She nodded.

“We’re going out, aren’t we?”

“Yes.”

“Then I thought I should finally wear it.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Good decision.”

She looked at herself in the mirror again.

“I don’t usually wear skirts this short.”

“I know. You’ve been holding it up against yourself in front of this mirror since your birthday.”

She gasped.

“You saw that?”

“Every time.”

Yichen reached for his watch.

“Ready?”

“Almost!”

She hurried back to the mirror to check her hair.

Yichen watched her amused.

He had a feeling Meilin would be receiving a thank-you message tonight.

They were going to a restaurant for dinner, followed by a walk around the shopping district.

Nothing elaborate.

Yichen had made the reservation earlier that afternoon, and Xiaoran had been looking forward to it since he told her.

When they reached the elevator, she stopped.

Yichen turned.

“What happened?”

She looked down.

“My skirt.”

He met her eyes.

“What about it?”

“Do I need to keep pulling it down?”

He looked at the hem.

“No.”

“But when I walk, it moves.”

“That’s what skirts do.”

She gave him an unimpressed look.

“You’re not helping.”

He smiled and stepped closer, lowering his voice.

“You’re comfortable?”

“Then don’t worry about it.”

He offered his hand.

“And if you need to adjust it, just do so. There’s no need to spend the entire evening worrying about your clothes.”

She took his hand.

“Okay.”

The elevator doors opened.

As they walked toward the parking area, Yichen noticed her glancing down occasionally.

He didn’t comment.

Instead, he adjusted his pace to match hers.

The restaurant was busy, but their table was in a quieter corner.

Xiaoran was in a good mood.

She had been telling Yichen about something that happened at work when the waiter came to serve their drinks.

She thanked him, took a sip, and then noticed Yichen looking at her.

“You’re looking at me.”

“Am I not allowed?”

That made her grin.

“You’re allowed.”

He leaned back slightly.

“Enjoying your birthday present?”

She immediately understood.

“Yes!”

She looked down at her skirt.

“I should have worn it earlier.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“I don’t know. I kept saving it.”

“For what?”

She thought about it.

“Maybe I thought I needed a special occasion.”

Yichen nodded.

“And now?”

“Now I think I should just wear things I like.”

“Good.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Meilin would be very happy if she knew.”

“Tell her.”

“I will.”

She took another sip of her drink, then looked at him.

“Do you think she chose it because she knew I’d like it?”

“Probably.”

“She usually buys me things that are a little different from what I normally choose.”

“Maybe she wants you to try new things.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“She said I always buy the same type of clothes.”

Yichen smiled.

“She’s not entirely wrong.”

She gasped.

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am.”

“Then defend me.”

He considered this.

“Your wardrobe has a very consistent theme.”

“What theme?”

“Comfortable.”

She stared at him, then laughed.

“That’s because I have good taste.”

“Of course.”

She reached across the table and stole a piece of food from his plate.

Yichen watched her.

“Is that also good taste?”

“Yes.”

He pushed the plate closer to her.

After dinner, they walked around the shopping district.

The evening was cool, and the streets were illuminated by shop windows and decorative lights. Xiaoran walked beside Yichen, occasionally stopping to look at something.

At one point, she found a display of hair accessories.

She leaned closer to the window.

“Look.”

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Pretty?”

“Very.”

She pointed at a small black ribbon.

“That would look nice with this skirt.”

He looked at her hair.

“It would.”

She turned toward him.

“Should I buy it?”

“If you like it.”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“Maybe next time.”

They continued walking.

A little further ahead, they passed a shop window with a full-length mirror.

Xiaoran stopped.

Yichen noticed and stopped beside her.

She looked at their reflection.

He was wearing dark trousers and a neat shirt, his jacket draped over one arm. She stood beside him in her skirt, holding his hand.

She smiled.

“Wait.”

She took out her phone.

“Let’s take a picture.”

Yichen moved closer.

She held the phone up, adjusted the angle, and took a few pictures.

Then she examined them.

“Look!”

He looked.

“Good.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She zoomed in.

“Your expression is too serious.”

“I’m standing.”

“You can smile.”

He turned to her, then smiled.

She took another picture.

“Much better.”

She was about to put her phone away when Yichen reached for it.

“Let me.”

He took a photograph of her standing beside the window.

Xiaoran blinked.

“Why?”

“Because I like this outfit.”

She looked at him.

He took another picture.

This time, she wasn’t looking at the camera. She was laughing at something he had said, her head slightly turned toward him.

He checked the result.

“Good.”

She leaned closer to see.

“Oh.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Send that to me.”

“I will.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re going to keep it?”

“Of course.”

Her expression softened.

Then she slipped her hand back into his.

On the way home, Xiaoran was busy sending Meilin the photographs.

Xiaoran: Finally wore your birthday present!

Meilin: FINALLY???

Meilin: Show me.

Xiaoran sent the picture Yichen had taken.

A few seconds later, Meilin called.

Xiaoran answered.

“Hello?”

“YOU WORE IT!”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Yes!”

“How does it feel? Isn’t it cute?”

“It’s really cute. I love it.”

“Why did you take so long?”

“I was waiting for the right occasion.”

“Xiaoran, it’s a skirt, not a wedding dress.”

Yichen glanced at her from the driver’s seat, clearly hearing the conversation.

Xiaoran covered the microphone.

“She’s being mean.”

He smiled.

“Sounds familiar.”

She gave him a look before returning to the call.

“Anyway, thank you. I really like it.”

Meilin’s voice softened.

“You’re welcome. You look pretty.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Really?”

“Obviously. Also, your boyfriend better appreciate my excellent taste.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

He raised an eyebrow.

She turned back to the phone.

“He does.”

“Good. Tell him I expect a commission.”

Xiaoran laughed.

After they hung up, she placed her phone in her lap.

Yichen glanced at her.

“Good.”

She turned toward him.

“Meilin said you better appreciate her taste.”

“I do.”

“She expects a commission.”

He laughed.

“Tell her I’ll consider it.”

Xiaoran grinned.

When they arrived home, Xiaoran went straight to the bedroom to change.

Yichen followed a few minutes later and found her carefully hanging the skirt back in the wardrobe.

He leaned against the doorframe.

“Putting it away already?”

She turned to him.

“Of course. I don’t want it to get wrinkled.”

He watched her smooth the fabric.

“Are you going to wear it again?”

“Definitely.”

“Good.”

She closed the wardrobe and turned around.

Then she looked at him with a slightly mischievous expression.

“What?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

His mouth curved.

“You’re very pleased with yourself tonight.”

“Because I finally wore my skirt.”

“That must be it.”

She walked toward him and wrapped her arms around his waist.

“I’m keeping the pictures, by the way,” he said.

She grinned.

“Already?”

“Already saved.”

“Where?”

“On my phone.”

She looked delighted.

Then, after a moment, she tilted her head.

“Which one is your favorite?”

“The one where you’re laughing.”

She blinked.

“Why?”

“Because you weren’t posing.”

He brushed a strand of hair behind her ear.

“You looked happy.”

Her smile softened.

Then she kissed him before he could say anything else.

“Thank you for taking me out.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And thank you for liking my skirt.”

He laughed.

“You’re welcome.”

She started to pull away, but he caught her hand and drew her back.

“Although...”

She looked up.

“What?”

“I have one request.”

Her eyes narrowed playfully.

“What request?”

“Don’t leave it in the wardrobe until your next birthday.”

She burst out laughing.

“I won’t!”

“Good.”

He kissed her temple.

“Because I think Meilin chose well.”

Xiaoran smiled against his chest.

Later that night she sent Meilin one final message.

Xiaoran: He took pictures of me in it.

Meilin: I know. I have excellent taste.

Xiaoran laughed so loudly that Yichen looked up from his book.

“What?”

“Meilin.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Of course.”

She put her phone down, climbed onto the bed beside him, and tucked herself against his shoulder.

The skirt hung on the outside of the wardrobe door now, where she could see it.

chapters.desc: She is on the 3:40 train. He is supposed to be on the team train at 6:15, and isn’t.
chapters.title: The Train Back
chapters.epigraph: “I just want to stay with you.”
chapters.content:
The plan had been simple.

Xiaoran would return on Sunday afternoon.

Yichen would return on Sunday evening.

Xiaoran had spent the weekend at her parents’, for her mother’s birthday. Yichen had been in Hangzhou with the Herons for an away game on Saturday night, and the team train came back on Sunday at the same time as always, which was too late for dinner and too early for anything else.

They had exchanged their train schedules on Friday night.

Xiaoran: Mine arrives at 3:40 p.m.

Yichen: Mine is 6:15.

Xiaoran: You’ll be back late.

Yichen: Not too late.

Xiaoran: I’ll probably be home before you.

Yichen: Save me some dinner.

Xiaoran: Depends on whether you’re nice to me.

Yichen: I’ll try.

That had been the end of it.

Neither had mentioned that they were looking forward to seeing each other.

They didn’t need to.

Xiaoran’s train arrived at 3:40 exactly. She was home in the flat by a quarter past four, with her suitcase open on the floor and a bag of her mother’s pastries on the counter, and the flat was quiet in the way it only was when one of them was away.

Yichen: Home?

Xiaoran: Yes. You?

Yichen: Still on the team train. Two more hours.

She looked at the clock, and then at the empty sofa, and sent him a crying cat.

Yichen’s train arrived at 4:12 p.m.

It wasn’t the team train. The team train left Hangzhou at 4:40 and would get in at 6:15, as it always did, with twelve tall men asleep on each other’s shoulders and Fang Ze eating everyone’s crisps. Yichen had gone to Coach at breakfast and asked to travel back on his own, for a personal reason. Coach had looked at him over his coffee and then said, “Is the personal reason about one meter sixty?” and Yichen had said nothing, and Coach had said, “Go.”

He didn’t text her from the platform. He took a taxi from the station, and he was smiling at the back of the driver’s headrest for most of it.

Xiaoran was in the middle of unpacking when she heard the front door.

She froze.

There was a brief rustling sound, followed by the familiar click of the lock.

Then Yichen’s voice.

“Xiaoran?”

She looked toward the hallway. She stood there. She had been home for barely half an hour. Her suitcase was open on the floor, a cardigan was draped over the sofa, and she was wearing an old university T-shirt with her hair tied messily at the back of her head.

She hadn’t expected him yet.

“Yichen?”

He appeared at the doorway.

Their eyes met.

He was still carrying his backpack, his suitcase beside him. His hair was slightly untidy from the journey, and he looked a little tired.

But he was smiling.

Xiaoran stared.

Then she looked at the clock, then back at him.

“You’re early.”

“The train was early.”

“Trains aren’t two hours early.”

“This one was,” he said, with a perfectly straight face.

She took two quick steps toward him.

He barely had time to put his bag down before she wrapped her arms around his waist.

Yichen smiled and caught her, one arm settling around her back while the other came up to cradle the back of her head.

“Hello.”

She pressed her cheek against his chest.

“Hello.”

He kissed her hair.

“Missed me?”

She nodded against him.

“Very much.”

His smile softened.

“Me too.”

She drew back to look at him.

“How did you get here so quickly?”

“Taxi.”

“From the station?”

“Yes.”

“Did you even eat?”

“I had something on the train.”

“What?”

“Sandwich.”

She frowned.

“That’s not a proper meal.”

He looked amused.

“I was traveling.”

“Still.”

He moved her hair off her cheek.

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Rice.”

“With what?”

She met his eyes, then smiled.

“You’re copying my mother.”

“She’s usually right.”

Xiaoran laughed and hugged him again.

He held her, his cheek resting against her hair.

They had been apart for only a couple of days.

It wasn’t a long separation.

But there was something deeply satisfying about being back in the same room, with no train to catch, no messages to send, and no need to calculate the hours until they could see each other.

Yichen finally glanced toward the open suitcase.

“Have you unpacked?”

“Not yet.”

“Why?”

“I was going to.”

He looked at the cardigan on the sofa, then at the suitcase, then at her.

“Of course.”

“Don’t judge me.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face did.”

He smiled and kissed her temple.

“Go on. I’ll put my things away.”

They unpacked together.

Or, more accurately, Xiaoran unpacked while Yichen occasionally folded something and placed it in the correct drawer.

She was telling him about her weekend when she pulled out a small paper bag.

“I brought something.”

He looked over.

“What is it?”

“Guess.”

“Food?”

“Why do you always guess food?”

“Because you usually bring food.”

She gasped.

“That’s not true.”

He met her eyes.

She paused.

“...Not always.”

He laughed.

She opened the bag and showed him a small packet of pastries.

“These are from the shop near my house. You liked them last time.”

He looked at them, then at her.

“You remembered.”

“Of course.”

He leaned over and kissed her cheek.

“Thank you.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“You’re welcome.”

He took one out and broke it in half, offering her the larger piece.

She accepted it.

“How was the game?”

“We won by four.”

“Only four?”

He looked at her.

“You’re supposed to tell me you won by thirty.”

“Would you like me to lie?”

“Just a little.”

He shook his head.

She perched on the end of the bed, eating her pastry while he finished unpacking.

Then she asked, “Did you miss me?”

He looked over.

“Yes.”

“How much?”

He considered the question.

“Enough to be happy the train arrived early.”

“That’s a good answer.”

He closed the drawer and came over.

He stood in front of her, looking down at her with that familiar, teasing expression.

“Then I suppose I should be grateful.”

She tilted her head.

“For what?”

“That our trains were both early.”

She reached for his hand and tugged him closer.

“Very grateful.”

He leaned down and kissed her.

It was a slow kiss, the kind that came naturally when there was nowhere else either of them needed to be.

When he pulled away, she kept her arms around his waist.

“Can we stay home today?”

“We can.”

“No going out?”

“Not unless you want to.”

“No meeting friends?”

“I haven’t made any plans.”

She looked pleased.

“Good.”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“What’s the occasion?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

She nodded.

“I just want to stay with you.”

His expression softened.

“All right.”

At 6:30 p.m., they were sitting on the sofa.

Xiaoran had her legs stretched across his lap, and Yichen was scrolling through his phone with one hand while the other rested on her ankle.

Yichen’s phone buzzed on the coffee table. It was a message from Fang Ze, and it lit up the screen where they could both see it.

Fang Ze: Coach says next time you have a “personal reason,” bring the personal reason to the station so he can see she exists.

Xiaoran read it. Then she read it again. Then she turned and looked at him.

“Personal reason?”

He looked at the ceiling.

“The train wasn’t early,” she said.

“No.”

“You changed your ticket.”

“At breakfast.”

“You left the team?”

“I asked Coach. He said yes. He also said something about your height.” He put the phone away, too late.

“Why?”

He looked at her, and she saw him decide not to make a joke.

He said, “Because you were going to get home at four, and I wasn’t going to get home until six, and I didn’t want you to be in this flat on your own for two hours on a Sunday.”

“That’s ridiculous. It’s two hours.”

“I know.”

“I’ve been on my own for longer.”

“I know. That’s why.” He brushed his thumb over her ankle.

She didn’t have an answer to that, so she leaned over and kissed his jaw instead, and then, because she was who she was, she picked up his phone and replied to Fang Ze herself.

Yichen: She exists. This is her. Tell Coach thank you.

Fang Ze: HAHAHAHA. Hello, personal reason.

Later, they ordered dinner.

They ate on the sofa, watched half an episode of a show neither of them was invested in, and argued over whether the male lead was being unreasonable.

At some point, Xiaoran fell asleep against Yichen’s shoulder.

He noticed when her replies became increasingly delayed.

“Xiaoran?”

No answer.

He looked down.

Her eyes were closed, her hand resting loosely over his.

His mouth curved.

The television continued playing.

He lowered the volume, carefully moved the empty food containers to the coffee table, and reached for the blanket.

She stirred when he adjusted her position.

“Mm...”

“Go to sleep.”

She opened her eyes halfway.

“You’re still here?”

He turned to her.

“Where else would I be?”

She smiled sleepily.

“Good.”

He pulled the blanket over her.

She reached for his hand again before closing her eyes.

Yichen looked down at their joined fingers.

A few hours earlier, they had been on separate trains from opposite directions, one of them on the wrong train on purpose.

Now she was asleep beside him, her suitcase still half-unpacked and her pastries on the kitchen counter.

He bent and kissed her hairline.

“Welcome home,” he whispered.

Xiaoran, barely awake, murmured something.

He paused.

“What?”

She didn’t open her eyes.

“Welcome home too.”

His smile lingered.

He settled back against the sofa, keeping her hand in his.

Outside, at a quarter past six, the team train pulled into the station without him.

chapters.desc: One fan comments on every post he makes. Xiaoran is not jealous; she is conducting research. The next evening, he posts a photo of his own.
chapters.title: A Jealous Girlfriend’s Investigation
chapters.epigraph: “You’re very cute when you’re investigating.”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had a perfectly reasonable explanation for what she was doing.

She wasn’t stalking anyone.

She was conducting research.

There was a difference.

An important difference.

At least, that was what she had been telling herself for the past twenty minutes.

It started innocently enough.

Yichen had posted a photograph on his social media account that afternoon. Nothing unusual: a picture from training, taken by one of the team photographers. He was standing near the court in his Herons jersey, one hand holding a basketball, his expression relaxed, hair slightly damp from practice.

The caption was brief.

Back to work.

Within an hour, the post had collected thousands of likes and hundreds of comments.

Xiaoran had liked it, naturally. She had even saved the photograph because she thought he looked handsome.

Then she noticed a comment.

@momo_w: You look especially good today. Hope to see you at the next game! ❤️

Nothing strange.

Except the same account had commented on his previous three posts.

And the three before those.

And apparently, she had also replied to several of his team’s official posts.

Xiaoran scrolled upward.

One comment.

Two.

Three.

She stopped.

“Interesting.”

She tapped the profile.

The account belonged to a young woman. Her profile picture showed her smiling in front of a café window. There were photographs of flowers, restaurants, concerts, and several basketball-related posts.

Xiaoran looked at the screen, then at Yichen.

He was sitting on the other side of the living room sofa, watching a game replay on his tablet.

She looked back at the phone.

Hope you recover quickly, Yichen.

Your performance was amazing today!

No. 11 is my favorite.

Xiaoran’s lips pressed together.

She scrolled farther.

There was a photograph of the woman holding a Herons ticket, then another from the arena.

Then a picture of Yichen on the court, taken from the stands.

Xiaoran stared at it.

The photograph was actually quite good.

She enlarged it.

Then immediately felt annoyed with herself for thinking that.

“What’s wrong?”

Yichen’s voice came from beside her.

She almost dropped her phone.

“Nothing.”

He met her eyes.

“You’re making a face.”

“I’m not.”

“All right.”

He returned to his tablet.

Xiaoran glanced at him, then back at the profile.

She wasn’t jealous.

She was curious about the frequency of this particular person’s engagement.

That was all.

Ten minutes later, Yichen noticed something.

Xiaoran had stopped watching the drama playing on the television.

She was holding her phone at an unusual angle, her eyebrows drawn together, occasionally tapping the screen with a seriousness usually reserved for her work assignments, then at the television.

Then back at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“What are you looking at?”

“Nothing.”

He smiled.

“Nothing seems interesting.”

She glanced up.

“Are you watching me?”

“You’re sitting beside me.”

“That doesn’t mean you have to watch me.”

“I wasn’t aware I needed permission.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re distracting.”

Yichen put his tablet down.

“Then I should probably stop.”

He shifted closer.

Xiaoran immediately moved her phone away.

That was when he became interested.

His eyes followed the movement.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re hiding something.”

“I’m not.”

He held out his hand.

She looked at it, then at him.

“What?”

“Let me see.”

“No.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“Now I’m curious.”

“You don’t need to be.”

Yichen smiled.

It was a particular smile.

The kind that suggested he had already worked something out but was waiting to see how long she intended to maintain her story.

Xiaoran knew that smile.

She disliked that smile.

Mostly because she found it ridiculously attractive, which was deeply inconvenient when she was trying to be annoyed with him.

“You’re investigating someone,” he said.

She froze.

Yichen’s smile grew.

“Am I right?”

“No.”

“Then show me.”

“Why?”

“To prove me wrong.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

Then, after a moment, she turned her phone toward him.

“Fine.”

Yichen glanced at the screen.

A woman’s profile.

Several comments beneath his photographs.

He looked at the screen for a few seconds.

Then he looked at Xiaoran.

Understanding settled over his expression.

“Ah.”

Xiaoran immediately became defensive.

“Don’t say ‘ah’ like that.”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“You’re looking at my fan’s account.”

“I’m not looking at your fan’s account.”

He glanced at the phone again.

“Whose account is this?”

She hesitated.

“...A person.”

Yichen laughed.

Xiaoran frowned.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not laughing at you.”

“You are.”

He took her phone gently and returned it to her.

“You’re jealous.”

“I’m not.”

“All right.”

She met his eyes.

“Why do you always do that?”

“Do what?”

“Agree with me when you clearly don’t believe me.”

“Would you prefer I disagree?”

“Yes.”

He considered it.

“You’re jealous.”

She grabbed a cushion and hugged it against her chest.

“You’re unbearable.”

Yichen smiled and rested his arm along the back of the sofa.

“What’s bothering you?”

“Nothing is bothering me.”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked away.

He waited.

That was one of the things about Yichen. He rarely pushed when he knew she was still deciding whether she wanted to say something.

Eventually, she sighed.

“She’s commented on almost every post you’ve made recently.”

He nodded.

“Okay.”

“And she always says something about how handsome you are.”

“Does she?”

“Yes.”

He seemed to consider that.

Then he said, quite calmly, “I haven’t noticed.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“You don’t read your comments?”

“Sometimes. Not all of them.”

She looked down at her phone.

“She also goes to your games.”

“Many people do.”

“I know.”

Yichen watched her expression.

She wasn’t angry, exactly.

She looked a little troubled, a little embarrassed, and annoyed that he had caught her investigating.

He reached over and touched her chin lightly.

He held out his hand.

She leaned closer, though she tried to maintain a displeased expression.

“Do you want me to stop posting photographs?”

Her eyes widened.

“No!”

“Do you want me to stop playing basketball?”

“Yichen!”

He laughed.

“I’m asking.”

“Obviously not.”

“Then what would you like me to do?”

She looked at him.

She seemed genuinely unsure.

“I don’t know.”

He brushed his thumb along her cheek.

“Then you don’t have to decide right now.”

She lowered her gaze.

“I know you’re not doing anything wrong.”

“I know.”

“And I know fans will comment. That’s normal.”

“Yes.”

She was quiet.

Then she muttered, “But she comments a lot.”

Yichen’s mouth curved.

“That’s what you found after twenty minutes of research?”

Xiaoran immediately looked up.

“How did you know it was twenty minutes?”

He laughed.

“Because I’ve been watching you.”

She blinked at him.

Then she pushed his shoulder.

“Stop watching me!”

He caught her hand.

“You’re very cute when you’re investigating.”

“I’m not cute.”

“You’re right. Very intimidating.”

She tried to pull her hand away.

He didn’t let go.

“Especially when you enlarge the photographs.”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened.

“You saw that?”

“I saw you zooming in.”

“That was because I wanted to see the picture properly!”

“Of course.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed again and pulled her closer, kissing her forehead.

“All right. I’ll stop.”

She remained suspicious.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little.”

The next morning, Xiaoran woke up before Yichen.

She was still half-asleep when she reached for her phone.

A notification appeared.

Yichen had posted a story.

It was a photograph of his breakfast: eggs, toast, fruit, and a glass of milk.

The caption read:

Breakfast before training.

Xiaoran smiled.

Then she noticed another notification.

The same woman had replied to his story.

@momo_w: You always eat so well. Good luck today! ❤️

Xiaoran stared.

She blinked.

Then she slowly turned her head toward Yichen.

He was still asleep.

She looked at the phone again, then back at him.

She considered waking him. She considered not waking him.

She considered whether it was reasonable to send him a screenshot.

Finally, she placed her phone down.

She wasn’t going to investigate again. She had dignity. She was a mature adult. She was a working professional. She had a campaign presentation later that morning.

She wouldn’t spend her time looking at another woman’s social media account.

Five minutes passed.

She picked up her phone.

She opened the account.

“Just checking,” she whispered.

Yichen woke up to find his girlfriend sitting against the headboard, wearing an expression of intense concentration.

He blinked.

“Good morning.”

“Morning.”

He glanced at her phone, then at her face.

“Back to work?”

She froze.

“What?”

“Your investigation.”

Xiaoran immediately locked her screen.

“There’s no investigation.”

He smiled sleepily.

“Of course.”

She squinted at him.

“Go back to sleep.”

He reached for her waist and pulled her closer.

“Come here first.”

She allowed herself to be drawn into his arms, her phone still in her hand.

Yichen kissed her temple.

“Did you find anything?”

“No.”

“Nothing at all?”

She hesitated.

Then mombled, “She replied to your breakfast story.”

He laughed.

“Did she?”

“Yes.”

“Should I be worried?”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Don’t make fun of me.”

His smile softened.

“I’m not.”

She studied his face.

He was still sleepy, his hair messy, one arm wrapped around her waist.

He looked so comfortable that her annoyance began to dissolve.

“I know it’s silly,” she said.

“It’s not.”

She looked up.

“Really?”

He brushed her hair back.

“You’re allowed to be jealous.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

“But I don’t want to become the kind of girlfriend who checks every woman who comments on your posts.”

“Then don’t.”

She blinked.

Yichen smiled.

“If something bothers you, tell me. It’s faster than twenty minutes of research.”

She nodded slowly.

“Okay.”

He kissed her hair.

“And for the record, I don’t know that woman.”

“Have you ever met her?”

“Not that I remember.”

She looked relieved.

Yichen noticed.

Then his expression turned amused.

“Although I have to say, she’s received a lot of attention from you.”

Xiaoran groaned.

“Please forget this happened.”

“I don’t think I can.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed and kissed her cheek.

That evening, after training, Yichen came home earlier than expected.

Xiaoran was in the kitchen preparing dinner. She had tied her hair up and was wearing one of his old shirts.

He walked up behind her, placed his hands at her waist, and kissed her cheek.

“Smells good.”

“You’re early.”

“Training ended sooner.”

“Did you eat anything afterward?”

“Not yet.”

She pointed at the counter.

“There’s fruit. Eat some while you wait.”

He obediently reached for a piece of apple.

Xiaoran glanced at him, then smiled.

“Good.”

He turned to her.

“Am I being evaluated?”

“Yes.”

“How am I doing?”

“Acceptable.”

He laughed.

She returned to stirring the food.

A moment later, Yichen spoke.

“By the way.”

“Hm?”

“I posted something.”

She turned.

“What?”

“Check your phone.”

Xiaoran looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

“Just look.”

She wiped her hands and picked up her phone.

He had posted a photograph on his social media.

It was a picture taken that morning.

Not of his breakfast.

Of Xiaoran.

She was sitting at the kitchen counter in his shirt, hair tied up, looking down at a bowl of fruit. The photograph was slightly candid, with sunlight falling across her face.

She hadn’t known he had taken it.

The caption was simple.

Someone makes sure I eat properly.

Xiaoran stared at the screen, then at him.

“Yichen.”

He looked perfectly innocent.

“What?”

“You posted me?”

“Yes.”

“Without telling me?”

“You look nice.”

She looked back at the photograph.

It was actually a good picture.

Then she noticed the comments.

Fang Ze had already replied.

@fangze: Manager Lin reporting for duty.

Another teammate commented:

@herons_17: Finally, the person in charge has been officially introduced.

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

She turned toward Yichen.

“You did this on purpose!”

“Did what?”

“You know exactly what!”

He stepped closer, his hands returning to her waist.

“I thought people should know who’s responsible for my breakfast.”

She laughed and pushed his chest.

“I’m not responsible for your breakfast!”

“Then who is?”

“You’re an adult!”

“An adult who needs to eat.”

She looked at him.

Then, slowly, her expression became suspicious again.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Did you post this because of yesterday?”

Yichen looked at her.

A faint smile appeared.

“Perhaps.”

“You’re teasing me.”

“A little.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re enjoying this too much.”

He leaned closer.

“Would you prefer I post the investigation instead?”

Her mouth fell open.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed, catching her before she could push him away.

Then he kissed her.

Once on the cheek.

Then her forehead.

And finally, when she tilted her face up, on her lips.

She forgot what she had been about to complain about.

For a moment.

Then she pulled back.

“You’re still not allowed to laugh at me.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise?”

He nodded.

“Promise.”

She studied him.

“Even if I investigate again?”

His smile returned.

“That depends on how thorough your investigation is.”

She groaned and buried her face against his chest.

Yichen laughed, wrapping both arms around her.

After a while, she murmured, “I really wasn’t that jealous.”

“Of course not.”

“I was just curious.”

“Naturally.”

“And I only checked because she kept commenting.”

“I understand.”

She lifted her head.

“You’re not listening.”

“I am.”

“What did I just say?”

“You’re curious, not jealous.”

She smiled triumphantly.

“Exactly.”

Yichen looked at her.

Then he gently tucked her hair behind her ear.

“All right, my curious girl.”

She smiled.

And when he kissed her again, she didn’t object.

Later that night, Xiaoran checked his post one last time.

The woman had commented again.

@momo_w: She’s so pretty! You two look happy together. ❤️

Xiaoran stared at it.

Then she looked at Yichen, who was sitting beside her on the sofa.

He glanced at her phone.

“Everything all right?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

A pause.

Then she leaned against his shoulder.

“Actually, she has good taste.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Does she?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

Xiaoran smiled, slipped her hand into his, and gave it a little squeeze.

“Because she thinks you’re handsome.”

He laughed.

“And?”

She turned to him.

“And she thinks we’re happy together.”

His expression softened.

He raised her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“She’s right about that.”

Xiaoran smiled, satisfied.

Then she put her phone away.

Investigation concluded.

At least for tonight.

chapters.desc: Their first Spring Festival living together: a drive up from Shanghai, lunch at one house, dinner at the other, and a trunk full of food.
chapters.title: Spring Festival, Two Houses
chapters.epigraph: “Do you know what I liked most today?”
chapters.content:
The first Spring Festival after they began living together was supposed to be simple.

At least, that was what Xiaoran had told herself.

Two family meals. Two houses, twenty minutes apart across the same city, and three and a half hours of motorway between that city and Shanghai.

One lunch at the Zhou family home, one dinner at her parents’ house. They would spend the afternoon with Yichen’s family, cross town to hers for dinner, and drive back to Shanghai that night, because the Herons had given him exactly one day off.

It sounded perfectly manageable.

Until she realized that this was the first time she would be arriving at both houses as someone who no longer technically lived at either.

She was still Zhou Yichen’s girlfriend. Still Lin Xiaoran, the daughter who had a room at home and parents who would always ask whether she’d eaten.

But now she lived eleven floors up in Shanghai with Zhou Yichen, and her name was on the lease beside his.

They had their own refrigerator, their own laundry, their own routines. She knew which side of the bed he preferred, and he knew she always left her phone charging on the wrong side of the sofa.

They had become a little household.

And somehow, that made going home for Spring Festival feel different.

“You’re bringing too many things.”

Yichen stood beside the open suitcase, watching Xiaoran add another gift bag.

She met his eyes.

“This is for your parents.”

“There are already two bags for my parents.”

“This one is different.”

He glanced at the label.

“Tea?”

“Your father likes it.”

“He does.”

“And this is for your mother.”

He looked at the next bag.

“Skincare?”

“She mentioned wanting to try it.”

Yichen nodded.

Then he looked at the suitcase.

“And what’s that?”

“Snacks.”

“For whom?”

“Everyone.”

He met her eyes.

“Xiaoran, we’re going for one day.”

“Exactly. One very long day.”

He smiled.

She continued packing.

He watched her place another packet of snacks into the suitcase.

“Do you want me to carry that?”

“Yes.”

He lifted the suitcase.

It was heavier than expected.

He glanced at her.

“What did you put in here?”

“Clothes.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“And snacks.”

“Some snacks.”

He turned to her.

She smiled innocently.

He laughed and zipped it shut.

They left Shanghai at eight, in the dark, and arrived at the Zhou family home just before noon.

His mother was already waiting near the entrance.

“You’re here!”

Xiaoran stepped out of the car and greeted her warmly.

“Happy Spring Festival, Auntie!”

His mother hugged her.

“Happy Spring Festival, darling. Come in. It’s cold outside.”

Yichen took the bags from the trunk.

His father appeared behind his mother, looking toward the car.

“Yichen.”

“Dad.”

“You’re late.”

“We’re ten minutes early.”

His father checked his watch.

“Your mother has been waiting since eleven.”

His mother turned.

“I was not waiting. I was preparing lunch.”

His father nodded.

“She was preparing lunch beside the window.”

Xiaoran laughed.

Yichen carried the bags inside.

His mother took one of them and looked at the contents.

“You brought so much.”

“Just a few things.”

His mother looked at her.

“You’re always bringing things.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Because I can’t come empty-handed.”

“You can. You’re family.”

The words were spoken casually, almost as an afterthought.

But Xiaoran felt them settle somewhere warm in her chest.

She glanced toward Yichen.

He was setting the suitcase down near the stairs. He caught her looking and gave her a smile.

She smiled back.

Lunch at the Zhou family home was lively.

His mother had prepared several dishes, and his father had brought out a bottle of tea he had been saving for the holiday.

Xiaoran sat beside Yichen, listening to his parents discuss their plans for the coming year.

His father asked about Morrow, and whether Gao Yan had let her lead a shoot yet.

“Twice. Once badly,” she answered.

“Only once? Good.” He nodded, as if this were an excellent ratio.

His mother smiled.

“And the kitchen? Is it still the way we left it?”

Xiaoran immediately looked at Yichen.

He was already smiling.

“Yes. Although there were some disagreements,” she said.

His mother laughed.

“Your mother and I have different opinions.”

“Very different.”

“Did you put the rice cooker where I suggested?”

Xiaoran hesitated.

Yichen lowered his head, hiding a smile.

“Actually...”

His mother laughed.

“She moved it back.”

“It works better there,” Xiaoran defended herself.

“Of course. It’s your kitchen.”

Yichen finally looked up.

“She’s very protective of it.”

Xiaoran nudged his leg beneath the table.

His father smiled.

“Good. She should be.”

His mother nodded.

“Yes. A home should be arranged for the people who live in it.”

Xiaoran looked down at her bowl.

She didn’t know why that sentence made her feel so touched.

Perhaps because she was still getting used to the idea that the flat was theirs.

That she had a place to return to that wasn’t her childhood bedroom.

That she and Yichen had begun building a life that didn’t depend on either family’s household.

He was placing a piece of fish into her bowl.

She couldn’t help smiling.

After lunch, his mother insisted they stay for tea.

Yichen helped his father bring out the fruit while Xiaoran sat with his mother in the living room.

They talked about the holiday, the Herons’ schedule, and the studio.

Then his mother asked, “Will you two come home often?”

“As much as we can. His season makes it hard.”

His mother smiled.

“I know. But you should both have your own plans. Don’t make every decision around the other person’s schedule.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Uncle said something similar when he invited me to lunch.”

His mother laughed.

“That sounds like him.”

She looked toward the dining room, where Yichen was speaking to his father.

“He’s always been very independent. Sometimes too independent. But he’s also very attached to the people he loves.”

Xiaoran followed her gaze.

Yichen was listening to his father, his expression calm.

“I know.”

His mother looked at her.

“And you?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“What about me?”

“Are you happy living together?”

The question was gentle.

Xiaoran thought about it.

She thought about their mornings, the shared refrigerator, the laundry, the occasional arguments over what to order for dinner. She thought about coming home after a long day and finding Yichen already there, or waking up to his hand resting loosely over hers.

That made her grin.

“Yes.”

His mother nodded.

“Good.”

His mother touched her hand.

“Just keep talking to each other. And don’t be afraid to ask for help.”

Xiaoran nodded.

She was beginning to understand that the older women in both families had their own ways of giving advice.

Some gave it through questions.

Some through food.

And some through rearranging kitchen cupboards.

At four o’clock, Yichen checked the time.

“We should leave soon.”

His mother looked disappointed.

“Already?”

“We have another dinner.”

“I know.”

She stood and began packing food into containers.

Xiaoran immediately got up.

“Auntie, you don’t have to prepare so much.”

“Take it with you.”

“But we’re having dinner at my parents’ house.”

“Then you can eat it tomorrow.”

His father laughed.

“Your mother has been preparing enough food for three households.”

His mother ignored him.

She handed Xiaoran two containers.

“These are for you.”

“Thank you.”

Then she gave Yichen another bag.

“And this.”

He looked inside.

“More food?”

“Of course.”

He accepted it without complaint.

His mother adjusted Xiaoran’s scarf.

“Drive carefully. Call when you arrive.”

“We will.”

“And don’t let him drive too fast.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I’ll watch him.”

Yichen looked at her.

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

She gave him a sweet smile.

“Happy Spring Festival.”

His mother laughed.

The drive to Xiaoran’s parents’ took twenty minutes, across a city hung with red lanterns, with fireworks already going off over the river although it was barely five.

Xiaoran sat in the passenger seat, holding a container of food on her lap because the trunk was full. It was still warm through the lid.

For a while, they drove without talking.

Then Xiaoran looked at him.

“Are you nervous?”Then she looked at him.

“Are you nervous?”

“About what?”

“Going to my parents’ house.”

He held her gaze.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“Why would I be?”

She considered that, then smiled.

“Because this is the first Spring Festival we’re arriving together after living together.”

“I know.”

She looked down at the container in her lap.

“Does it feel different to you?”

Yichen thought.

“A little.”

“How?”

“Before, we visited our families and went back to wherever we were staying.”

“And now?”

“Now we’re going back to our place.”

She smiled.

Their place.

Two words that still made her feel unexpectedly happy.

Yichen reached over and touched her hand.

“Is that a problem?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Good.”

She turned her face toward the window, smiling.

Her parents were waiting when they arrived.

Her mother opened the door before they had even finished unloading the car.

“You’re here!”

Xiaoran stepped forward.

“Mom!”

Her mother hugged her, then immediately turned toward Yichen.

“Yichen. Happy Spring Festival.”

“Happy Spring Festival, Auntie.”

Her father appeared behind her.

“Come in. It’s cold.”

Yichen greeted him and carried the bags inside.

Xiaoran’s mother looked at the containers.

“What’s all this?”

“Food from Auntie.”

Her mother laughed.

“She sent food again?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Put it in the kitchen.”

Her father looked at Yichen.

“How was the drive up this morning?”

“Good. Three and a half hours.”

“Did you stop?”

“Once.”

Her father nodded.

“Good.”

Then he looked at the bags.

“You brought too much.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“That’s what I told them.”

Her father laughed.

Dinner was noisier than lunch.

Her mother had prepared several dishes, including Xiaoran’s childhood favorites. Her father had brought out the good tea, and there were already sweets and fruit arranged on the table.

Yichen sat beside Xiaoran.

Her mother kept adding food to his bowl.

“Eat more.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Have some of this too.”

“All right.”

Xiaoran watched the exchange.

“You don’t have to keep feeding him.”

Her mother looked at her.

“Why not?”

“Because he’s already eaten lunch.”

Her father looked over.

“Did you eat properly at the Zhou family home?”

Yichen nodded.

“Yes, Uncle.”

“Good. Then you can eat properly here too.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Dad.”

Her father smiled.

“What?”

“You’re both doing it.”

Her mother laughed.

“He’s our guest.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

He was eating, clearly enjoying himself.

Traitor.

After dinner, her father brought out a box of old photographs.

Xiaoran immediately recognized it.

“Oh no.”

Her mother laughed.

“What?”

“Why are you bringing that out?”

“Because it’s Spring Festival.”

“That’s not a reason.”

Her father opened the box.

There were photographs from her childhood, school events, family holidays, and university days.

Yichen leaned closer.

Xiaoran gave him a warning look.

“Don’t.”

Something in his face eased.

“What?”

“Don’t look too interested.”

“I am interested.”

She sighed.

Her mother picked up a photograph.

“Look at this one.”

It had been taken at her grandparents’ house, on her eighth birthday, the weekend her parents had driven down for it. Xiaoran stood beside a small table with a cake. Her hair was tied into two uneven ponytails, and she was making a face at the camera.

Yichen smiled.

“That’s cute.”

Xiaoran covered her face.

“Please.”

Her father picked up another.

“Here. Her first day of middle school. The September she came back to live with us.”

Yichen looked at it.

Xiaoran, twelve, was wearing an oversized backpack, standing with a serious expression and holding her mother’s hand tightly.

“She cried that morning,” her mother said.

“I did not.”

“You did.”

“Only a little.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Really?”

She glared.

He laughed under his breath.

“That’s adorable.”

“Don’t.”

Her father laughed.

Then he found a photograph from her first year of university.

She was standing beside Yichen at a campus event, holding a drink and looking toward the camera.

Yichen was looking at her.

Her father placed it on the table.

“This one is nice.”

Xiaoran looked at it.

She remembered the day.

She had been nervous about introducing Yichen properly to some of her university friends, although they had already been together for years.

Her father looked at the photograph.

“You two look happy.”

Yichen nodded.

“We were.”

Her father smiled.

“Good.”

He put the photograph back in the box.

Then he looked at Yichen.

“Take care of each other.”

Yichen met his eyes.

“We will.”

Xiaoran looked down at the table.

She didn’t need to say anything.

Her father already knew.

It was almost eight when they finally prepared to leave.

Her mother packed another bag of food.

Xiaoran protested.

“Mom, we have food from the Zhou family already.”

“Then you’ll have food for tomorrow.”

“We can’t eat all of this.”

“You can freeze some.”

Her father stood beside the door, holding a box.

“Take this too.”

Xiaoran looked at it.

“What is it?”

“New Year snacks.”

She laughed.

“Dad.”

“What?”

“You’re both sending us home with food.”

Her mother looked at her.

“You’re going home.”

The words made Xiaoran pause.

Her mother seemed to notice.

She smiled and corrected herself.

“Well. You’re going back to your flat.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Yes.”

Her father handed Yichen the box.

“Drive carefully.”

“I will, Uncle.”

“And call when you arrive.”

“Of course.”

Her mother hugged Xiaoran.

“Don’t work too hard.”

“I won’t.”

“Call us.”

“I will.”

Then her mother turned to Yichen.

“Make sure you both eat properly.”

Yichen nodded.

“I will.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“You’re taking responsibility for both of us now?”

He smiled.

“Apparently.”

Her mother laughed.

They were finally alone again at 8:26.

The car was full of food.

The back seat held two bags from the Zhou family, one box from Xiaoran’s parents, and a smaller bag of fruit that her mother had insisted they take.

Xiaoran leaned back.

“That was a lot.”

Yichen started the engine.

“Yes.”

“Your mother gave us food.”

“Yes.”

“My mother gave us food.”

“Yes.”

“And now we have enough food for the next week.”

He glanced at her.

“Probably.”

She looked at the containers.

Then she laughed.

“We’re going to have to reorganise the refrigerator.”

Yichen smiled.

“Again?”

“Yes.”

He reached over and took her hand.

She turned to him.

“What?”

“Happy Spring Festival.”

That made her grin.

“Happy Spring Festival.”

He drove for a while before she spoke again.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you think they see us differently now?”

He studied her.

“Who?”

“Our parents.”

He considered it.

“Perhaps.”

“Because we’re living together?”

“Probably.”

She looked out the window.

“I think I felt it today.”

“How?”

She thought about the way his mother had told her she was family. About her own mother saying she was going back to her flat. About both fathers asking Yichen to take care of them, and the way they had handed him food to bring home.

“They weren’t just treating us as two people who were dating anymore.”

Yichen listened.

“They were sending us home together.”

He looked at her.

Then he nodded.

“I noticed.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Does it feel strange?”

“No.”

“Not at all?”

He squeezed her hand.

“It feels right.”

She turned toward him.

He kept his eyes on the road, but his thumb moved slowly over the back of her hand.

After a while, she leaned her head against the window.

“Next year, we should invite them both to our place.”

Yichen smiled.

“All four of them?”

“Yes.”

“That’s going to be interesting.”

“Why?”

He considered her.

“Your mother and mine in our kitchen again.”

Xiaoran considered it.

Then she burst out laughing.

“Oh, no.”

“Exactly.”

“They’ll rearrange everything. Again.”

“Probably.”

“And our fathers will sit in the living room pretending not to notice.”

“Definitely.”

She laughed harder.

Yichen smiled and returned his attention to the road.

When they arrived home, it was almost midnight.

The flat was quiet.

They carried the food inside and placed everything on the kitchen counter.

Xiaoran took off her coat and looked around.

The small living room was still exactly as they’d left it. Her books were on the shelf, Yichen’s shoes were beside hers, and the two mugs they’d used that morning were still beside the sink.

She walked to the refrigerator.

“There’s no space.”

Yichen came up behind her.

“Move the drinks to the door.”

She opened it.

“Already full.”

He looked inside, then at the food on the counter.

“We can leave some for tomorrow.”

She nodded.

They worked together, finding places for the containers, putting fruit in the bowl, and stacking the snacks in the cupboard.

When everything was finally put away, Xiaoran leaned against the counter.

Yichen stood beside her.

She looked at the clock.

12:08.

“Happy Spring Festival,” she said again.

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Happy Spring Festival.”

She reached for his hand.

“Six years together, and our first Spring Festival living together.”

“Not bad.”

“Not bad?”

“Quite good.”

She laughed.

Then she stepped closer and wrapped her arms around him.

Yichen held her, his cheek resting lightly against her hair.

Xiaoran tilted her head back.

“Do you know what I liked most today?”

“What?”

“Both our mothers kept telling us to take care of each other.”

Something in his face eased.

“They’re not wrong.”

“No. But I think they still see us as children.”

“To them, we probably always will be.”

She smiled.

Then she rested her cheek against his chest.

He leaned down and kissed her.

Then he picked up the last empty food container from the counter.

“Come on. Let’s go to bed.”

She followed him, switching off the kitchen light.

The flat went dark behind them.

On the kitchen counter, beside the stacked containers, sat a red envelope from each family, which neither of them had seen anyone put in a bag.

chapters.desc: Looking for batteries, he finds her emergency snack drawer, and quietly starts restocking it.
chapters.title: The Secret Snack Drawer
chapters.epigraph: “It’s not just snacks.”
chapters.content:
Yichen discovered the secret snack drawer on a Thursday evening.

He wasn’t looking for anything interesting.

He was looking for batteries.

The television remote had stopped working, and Xiaoran had casually mentioned that she thought there might be spare batteries somewhere in the living room. Yichen opened the first drawer of the cabinet, found a few instruction manuals, two charging cables, and a collection of things neither of them remembered buying. The second drawer contained stationery.

The third drawer was unexpectedly difficult to open.

He pulled it once.

Nothing.

He pulled it again.

Something shifted inside.

Yichen frowned slightly and tried a different angle. The drawer slid open.

He looked down, then paused.

Inside was an assortment of snacks.

Not a small assortment.

There were chocolate bars, individually wrapped biscuits, gummy candies, crackers, dried fruit, little packets of potato chips, and several bags of snacks he recognized from the convenience store near their apartment.

Everything was arranged in neat little sections.

Some packages were stacked horizontally. Others were placed upright in small organizers. There was even a tiny basket containing sweets.

Yichen stared at it.

Then he picked up a small chocolate bar.

There was a handwritten label on the basket.

Emergency.

He looked at it for another moment.

Then he smiled.

“Interesting.”

Xiaoran was in the bathroom when he discovered her secret.

When she came out, she found Yichen sitting on the sofa with a chocolate bar in his hand.

She stopped walking.

Her eyes moved to the chocolate, then to him.

Then, slowly, toward the living room cabinet.

Yichen noticed the direction of her gaze.

“Good evening.”

“Why are you holding that?”

He looked at the chocolate.

“Is it yours?”

She didn’t answer.

His mouth curved.

“Ah.”

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“Where did you get that?”

He glanced toward the cabinet.

“From a drawer.”

Her expression changed.

He watched her face.

Then he laughed.

“Is that your secret?”

Xiaoran walked over immediately.

“Don’t touch it.”

He raised his eyebrows.

“Why?”

“Because that’s mine.”

“I gathered.”

She reached for the chocolate.

He held it just out of reach.

“What’s all this, then?”

“Nothing.”

He looked toward the cabinet.

“An entire drawer of nothing?”

She folded her arms.

“It’s an emergency supply.”

Yichen looked at the chocolate in his hand.

“Emergency?”

“Yes.”

“What kind of emergency requires seventeen varieties of snacks?”

“Different emergencies require different solutions.”

He laughed.

She looked at him with complete seriousness.

“Don’t laugh. It’s important.”

“All right. Explain.”

Xiaoran sat beside him, apparently deciding that if her secret had been discovered, she might as well defend it properly.

“Sometimes I get hungry at night.”

“Mm.”

“Sometimes I’m working and suddenly want something sweet.”

“Mm.”

“Sometimes I want something salty, but I don’t want to go downstairs.”

“Reasonable.”

“And sometimes I’m watching a drama and I need snacks.”

Yichen nodded slowly.

“That sounds like a very demanding emergency schedule.”

“It is.”

His mouth curved.

“Understood.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You’re not allowed to eat everything.”

“I haven’t.”

“You already took chocolate.”

“I found it.”

“That’s still taking it.”

He glanced at the wrapper.

“May I have this one?”

She considered it, then sighed.

“Fine. But only one.”

Yichen smiled and unwrapped it.

“Thank you, Manager Lin.”

She immediately reached for the cushion beside her and hit his arm with it.

After that evening, the drawer became a recurring subject of conversation.

Mostly because Yichen found it increasingly amusing.

The next morning, Xiaoran was looking for a particular packet of crackers when she discovered that someone had rearranged the drawer.

Not dramatically.

Just enough to make her suspicious.

The chocolate bars were stacked more neatly. The biscuit packets had been grouped by type. The gummy candies were no longer scattered across the bottom.

She stood in front of the open drawer, then called out.

“Yichen?”

He was in the kitchen.

“Yes?”

“Did you touch my drawer?”

He looked over his shoulder.

“Which drawer?”

She gave him a look.

He smiled.

“What happened?”

“You reorganized it.”

“Was it a problem?”

She examined the arrangement.

“No.”

“Then?”

She picked up a packet of chocolate biscuits.

“Why did you put these here?”

“So they’re easier to reach.”

She met his eyes, then at the drawer, then back at him.

“...Thank you.”

He nodded.

“You’re welcome.”

She closed the drawer.

A few seconds later, she opened it again.

Yichen watched from the kitchen.

She was smiling.

The real surprise came on Saturday.

Yichen had a morning training session, while Xiaoran had decided to spend the day working on a presentation from home.

By late afternoon, she was sitting at the dining table, staring at her laptop with an expression of deep dissatisfaction.

She had been working for almost three hours.

Her shoulders were tense, and she had rewritten the same paragraph several times.

Eventually, she pushed her chair back.

“I need a break.”

Yichen, who had returned from training and was sitting on the sofa reviewing footage, looked up.

“Good idea.”

She walked toward the living room cabinet.

Opened the drawer.

And stopped.

There were new snacks.

Several of them.

A packet of her favorite seaweed crackers.

Two chocolate bars.

A small box of strawberry-flavoured biscuits she hadn’t bought recently.

And a bag of the particular gummy candies she always searched for at the convenience store but frequently found sold out.

She blinked, then reached into the drawer.

There was a small handwritten note tucked underneath the basket.

For emergencies.

Xiaoran stared at it, then turned around.

Yichen was still on the sofa, apparently concentrating on his tablet.

She held up the note.

“Yichen.”

He glanced over.

“Hm?”

“What’s this?”

He looked at the drawer.

“Your emergency supply.”

She looked at the snacks again.

“Did you buy these?”

“Some of them.”

“Some?”

He put his tablet down.

“All right. Most of them.”

She looked at the drawer, then at him.

“Why?”

He shrugged.

“You were running low.”

She stared.

“How did you know?”

“I saw the drawer.”

“When?”

“A few days ago.”

She looked down at the snacks again.

He had remembered which ones she liked.

Not just the general categories, either.

He had bought the exact flavours.

She picked up the seaweed crackers.

“These were sold out last time.”

“I know.”

Her eyes lifted.

“You went to the convenience store?”

“On my way back from training.”

She looked at him for another moment, then a smile slowly appeared.

“You replenished my emergency supply.”

“Yes.”

“Without telling me.”

“That was the idea.”

She laughed.

Then she walked over to him, holding the packet of crackers against her chest.

“Why are you so nice?”

Yichen looked up.

“Because you’re easy to bribe.”

She laughed.

“With snacks?”

“Apparently.”

She leaned down and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you.”

He caught her hand before she could walk away.

“You’re welcome.”

Then he looked at the packet in her other hand.

“Are you going to share?”

She immediately pulled it closer to her chest.

“That’s an emergency supply.”

Yichen laughed.

“Of course.”

The drawer gradually became a shared project.

Not officially.

There was no announcement, no agreement, and certainly no formal division of responsibilities.

But Yichen began adding things whenever he noticed something was running low.

Sometimes he brought home a few packets from the supermarket.

Sometimes he added a new flavour he thought she might like.

Once, he bought a snack Xiaoran had mentioned wanting to try after seeing it in a short video.

She discovered it the following morning and sent him a message while he was at training.

Xiaoran: Did you buy this?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: Thought you might like it.

Xiaoran: You remembered?

Yichen: You mentioned it twice.

Xiaoran: I did not.

Yichen: Three times, actually.

Xiaoran: You’re exaggerating.

Yichen: Enjoy your snack.

She sent him a heart, then another.

Then a photograph of the empty packet an hour later.

Xiaoran: Very good. Approved.

Yichen replied with a single smiling emoji.

One evening, Yichen came home to find Xiaoran sitting on the living room floor.

The cabinet was open.

The snack drawer was completely emptied onto the floor.

He stopped.

“What’s happening?”

“Inventory.”

He glanced at the collection.

“Inventory?”

“Yes.”

She held up a small notebook.

“I think we need a system.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Do we?”

“Of course. We’re running low on chocolate.”

He glanced at the chocolate section.

There were still six bars.

“How many do you need?”

“At least ten.”

“Why ten?”

“For emergencies.”

He crouched beside her.

“What kind of emergency?”

She turned to him.

“Yichen, please don’t question the system.”

Something in his face eased.

“All right.”

She continued writing.

“Also, we’re almost out of strawberry biscuits.”

“I bought those yesterday.”

“Yes, but they’re very good.”

“Should I buy more?”

She nodded immediately.

“Please.”

He laughed.

She wrote something else, then looked at him.

“Do you want to add anything?”

He thought about it.

“Maybe some nuts.”

She frowned.

“That’s not a snack.”

“It is.”

“Not an emergency snack.”

“Why not?”

“Because emergency snacks need to be exciting.”

Yichen stared at her.

Then he laughed until she started laughing too.

“Fine. No nuts,” he said.

She nodded, satisfied.

A few weeks later, Yichen discovered something else.

The emergency supply had expanded.

There were now two drawers.

The original one contained Xiaoran’s favorite snacks.

The second contained things she had apparently decided were suitable for shared consumption: nuts, dried fruit, protein bars, and a few snacks Yichen liked.

He stood in front of the cabinet, then called out.

“Xiaoran?”

She came out of the bedroom.

“What?”

He pointed at the drawers.

“What’s this?”

She looked, then smiled proudly.

“Expansion.”

“Expansion?”

“Yes. The original drawer was becoming crowded.”

He opened the second drawer.

“What’s the difference?”

She pointed.

“That’s yours.”

He looked at the contents, then at her.

“You made me a snack drawer?”

“Well, technically, it’s a shared drawer.”

“How generous.”

She nodded.

“I know.”

He picked up a protein bar.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

He looked at the first drawer again.

“And this one?”

She immediately stepped forward.

“Mine.”

Yichen laughed.

“Understood.”

He closed both drawers.

Then he reached for her waist and pulled her closer.

“One question.”

“What?”

“If I eat something from your drawer, is it still an emergency?”

She considered it.

“Depends.”

“On what?”

“Whether you replace it.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Of course.”

She looked pleased with the arrangement.

Then he kissed her temple.

That night, Xiaoran was sitting beside him on the sofa, eating strawberry biscuits while Yichen watched a basketball game replay.

She held one toward him.

“Want one?”

He looked at it.

“From your emergency supply?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He took it.

“Thank you.”

She ate another, then leaned against his shoulder.

After a while, she glanced toward the cabinet.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I think the drawer is one of my favorite things in this apartment.”

He looked at her.

“Really?”

“It’s silly, isn’t it?”

“No.”

“It’s just snacks.”

He brushed his thumb over her shoulder.

“It’s not just snacks.”

She turned toward him.

He smiled.

“It’s you making room for little things you enjoy. And me making sure you have them.”

She held his gaze.

Then her expression softened.

“You’re making it sound very romantic.”

“Is it not?”

She laughed.

“Maybe.”

He kissed her.

She let her head drop onto his shoulder again.

A few minutes passed before she spoke.

“By the way.”

“Hm?”

“I think we should add another category.”

Yichen looked down.

“What category?”

“Bad-day snacks.”

He nodded seriously.

“All right.”

“Different from emergency snacks.”

“What’s the difference?”

“Emergency snacks are for when I’m hungry. Bad-day snacks are for when I’m sad.”

Yichen considered that.

“Understood.”

“And they should be chocolate.”

“Only chocolate?”

“Mostly.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Anything else?”

She thought.

“Maybe those strawberry biscuits.”

“I’ll remember.”

She tilted her head.

“Really?”

He kissed her temple.

“Of course.”

And the following morning, when Xiaoran opened the drawer, she found a small new basket tucked neatly beside the chocolate.

Inside were her favorite strawberry biscuits and two chocolate bars.

There was another handwritten note.

For bad days. Hopefully, you won’t need them often.

Xiaoran stood in front of the cabinet without moving.

Then she took a photograph and sent it to Yichen, who was already at training.

Xiaoran: You’re spoiling my emergency system.

Yichen: Is that a complaint?

Xiaoran: No.

Yichen: Good.

Xiaoran: I love you.

His reply came a few seconds later.

Yichen: Love you too. Don’t forget to eat lunch.

She smiled at her phone.

Then opened the drawer, took one strawberry biscuit, and closed it again.

The emergency supply was fully stocked.

chapters.desc: In the kitchen, at the mirror, in a crowded aisle: she notices where his hand always goes, and then she starts putting it back.
chapters.title: A Hand at Her Waist
chapters.epigraph: “Because whenever I move my hand away, you find a reason to stand closer.”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had recently discovered that Zhou Yichen had a habit.

A unfair habit, actually.

He liked holding her waist.

And he did it so naturally that she sometimes didn’t notice until she was already standing closer to him than she’d intended.

It happened in the kitchen first.

Xiaoran was standing in front of the refrigerator, deciding what she wanted to eat. She had opened the door several times, taken out a bottle of milk, put it back, and finally stood there staring at the shelves as if the answer might reveal itself.

Behind her, Yichen walked in.

“Still deciding?”

“There’s nothing to eat.”

He glanced at the refrigerator.

“There’s quite a lot.”

“Nothing I want.”

“Then what do you want?”

She turned her head.

“I don’t know.”

Something in his face eased.

“Very helpful.”

She was about to close the refrigerator when he stepped behind her. His hand settled at her waist, gently guiding her a little to the side so he could reach past her for a container.

“Excuse me.”

Xiaoran looked down.

His hand was still there.

She met his eyes.

“Why are you holding me?”

Yichen retrieved the container.

“Because you’re standing in front of what I need.”

“You could have asked me to move.”

“I could have.”

“But you didn’t.”

He looked at her, his expression perfectly composed.

“Would you prefer that?”

She considered it, then shook her head.

“No.”

“Then we’re fine.”

He kissed her cheek before walking away.

Xiaoran remained in front of the refrigerator for another moment.

She had forgotten what she wanted to eat.

The second time happened while they were getting ready to leave.

Xiaoran was standing in front of the bedroom mirror, fastening an earring. She had already put on her shoes, but she was still pushing at her hair.

Yichen was adjusting his watch. He looked at her through the mirror, then came up behind her.

His hands settled at her waist.

Xiaoran stopped moving.

He looked at her reflection, then gently adjusted a strand of hair that had fallen against her cheek.

“Your hair is fine.”

She smiled at the mirror.

“Okay.”

He didn’t move away.

Instead, he remained behind her, his hands resting comfortably at her waist, his chin almost touching her hair.

Xiaoran looked at their reflection.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Are we going somewhere or not?”

“In a moment.”

“Why?”

He met her eyes in the mirror.

“Because you’re standing here.”

She blinked.

“That’s not an answer.”

“You’re pretty.”

Her expression softened immediately.

Then she turned around in his arms.

“You could have said that earlier.”

“I’m saying it now.”

He laughed and leaned down to kiss her.

When he pulled away, his hands were still at her waist.

She looked down at them, then back at him.

“You’re doing it again. Nothing.”

That got a smile out of him.

“All right.”

By the afternoon, Xiaoran had started noticing.

They were at a department store, browsing through a homeware section. She had become interested in a set of mugs with a blue floral pattern.

Yichen stood beside her.

“Do you like them?”

“They’re cute.”

“Do you want them?”

She turned one over.

“Maybe. We already have mugs.”

“Not ones that match.”

She turned to him.

“That’s actually a good point.”

“I know.”

She laughed and placed it in the shopping basket.

Then she moved toward another display.

Yichen followed.

There was a narrow aisle between two shelves. Xiaoran was looking at a set of glasses when someone passed behind her with a trolley.

Yichen’s hand found her waist.

He gently drew her closer to him, making room for the trolley to pass.

It was quick, almost absent-minded.

But Xiaoran noticed.

The trolley passed.

He let his hand fall.

He looked back.

“What?”

That made her grin.

“Nothing.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You’re smiling.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“You’re allowed.”

She moved closer to him.

Then, deliberately, took his hand and placed it back at her waist.

Yichen looked down, then at her.

Xiaoran smiled sweetly.

“There.”

His expression changed.

Only slightly.

But she saw it.

“What’s this?” he asked.

She tilted her head.

“You seemed to like it.”

He stared at her before a slow smile appeared.

“You’re learning.”

She laughed.

That evening, they went out for dinner.

The restaurant was busy, and the host led them through a narrow passage toward their table.

Yichen walked behind Xiaoran, his hand resting lightly at her waist as they moved through the crowd.

When they reached the table, he pulled out her chair.

She sat down, looking at him with a smile.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re very gentlemanly today.”

“Today?”

She giggled.

He took his seat opposite her.

For a while, they discussed ordinary things: her upcoming project, his training schedule, a funny message Meilin had sent, and whether they should go somewhere on their next day off.

Then Xiaoran reached across the table to take his hand.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Why do you always hold my waist?”

He met her eyes.

“Always?”

“Recently, yes.”

He considered the question.

“Do you dislike it?”

She shook her head quickly.

“No.”

“Then what’s the problem?”

“There’s no problem. I’m curious.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Because I like holding you.”

She waited.

“That’s it?”

“Would you like a more complicated explanation?”

She laughed.

“Maybe.”

He leaned back slightly.

“It’s comfortable. You’re close to me. And I like knowing you’re there.”

She held his gaze.

Then her expression became a little softer.

“Oh.”

Yichen squeezed her hand.

“Does that answer your question?”

She nodded, and after a moment she said, “I like it too.”

His smile deepened.

“I know.”

She frowned.

“How?”
