Or perhaps it was because he knew exactly how much Xiaoran meant to him, and he understood that loving someone’s daughter wasn’t quite the same as being welcomed into a household.

That Saturday, he arrived at Xiaoran’s house shortly before lunch.

Her mother opened the door.

“Yichen! Come in. Have you eaten?”

“Not yet, Auntie.”

“Good. I made enough.”

From somewhere inside the house, Xiaoran called, “Mom, you said that yesterday too!”

Her mother turned toward the hallway.

“Because you didn’t eat enough yesterday!”

Yichen smiled and stepped inside.

Xiaoran appeared a moment later, wearing a loose T-shirt and shorts, her hair clipped away from her face.

“You’re early.”

“You told me to come before lunch.”

“I didn’t say this early.”

He glanced at his watch.

“Eleven thirty.”

“Exactly. Early.”

He pressed a kiss to her hair.

“Hi.”

She smiled, taking the small bag from his hand.

“What did you bring?”

“Fruit.”

“Good. Mom likes fruit.”

“I know.”

She looked inside, then looked up at him.

“Did you buy the expensive ones?”

“Would you prefer the cheap ones?”

“No, but—”

“Then we’re fine.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

He smiled and followed her into the house.

Lunch was noisy in the comfortable way family lunches usually were.

Her mother had prepared several dishes, and her father was sitting at the head of the table, reading something on his phone between bites.

Yichen sat beside Xiaoran.

Her father asked about his basketball training, then about the Herons’ game the week before, which he had watched on his phone with the sound off so as not to wake her mother. Yichen answered naturally, explaining that their team had been working on defensive coordination and that their next match would be more difficult.

“You’re still training every day?” her father asked.

“Most days, depending on the match schedule.”

“Don’t overdo it.”

“I won’t, Uncle.”

Xiaoran looked up from her food.

“He says that, but sometimes he comes back so tired he falls asleep before dinner.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“That happened once.”

“Twice.”

“Once and a half.”

She frowned.

“How do you fall asleep half a time?”

Her father laughed.

“Let him rest. He’s playing for the Herons. It’s not easy.”

Yichen smiled politely.

“Thank you, Uncle.”

The conversation moved on.

After lunch, Xiaoran’s mother asked her to help bring some things upstairs. Xiaoran protested that she had only just finished eating, but eventually went.

Her father remained in the living room with Yichen.

“Can you help me with something?”

“Of course, Uncle.”

“The rice cooker. I think the cord has been getting loose. Could you take a look?”

Yichen followed him into the kitchen.

It was a simple problem. The plug wasn’t sitting properly in the socket, and the cord had been pushed behind the cabinet. Yichen adjusted it, checked that the cooker was working, and put everything back.

“There. It should be fine now.”

Her father nodded.

“Good. Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

Yichen was about to return to the living room when he noticed a small folded piece of paper beneath the rice cooker.

It had been tucked under one of its rubber feet.

He picked it up.

“Uncle, is this yours?”

Her father looked over.

Then, casually, he said, “Ah. That’s for you.”

Yichen paused.

“For me?”

Her father nodded.

“Yes.”

Yichen looked at the paper.

His name was written on the front.

For Yichen.

He looked up again.

Her father was already washing his hands at the sink.

“Read it when you have time.”

Yichen glanced at the note once more.

“All right, Uncle.”

He didn’t open it. He carefully folded it back along its existing crease and slipped it into his pocket.

He had no idea what to expect.

Xiaoran found him sitting in the living room twenty minutes later.

She had finished helping her mother and was now holding a bowl of cut fruit.

“Why are you sitting here by yourself?”

“Your father asked me to check the rice cooker.”

“And?”

“It’s working.”

She placed the bowl on the coffee table and sat beside him.

“Did he ask you to fix anything else?”

“No.”

She met his eyes.

“Then why do you look so serious?”

Yichen glanced at her.

He smiled slightly.

“Maybe I’m tired.”

She eyed him.

“You’ve been here for less than an hour.”

“An exhausting hour.”

She laughed and leaned against his shoulder.

For a few minutes, they ate fruit and talked about her upcoming assignments.

Then Xiaoran noticed something.

A small corner of white paper was visible from the pocket of his trousers.

She pointed.

“What’s that?”

Yichen looked down.

“Something your father gave me.”

She immediately sat up.

“What?”

“A note.”

Her eyes widened.

“A note?”

“Yes.”

She looked at his pocket, then at his face.

“What does it say?”

“I haven’t read it.”

“Why?”

“He told me to read it when I have time.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

“You’re telling me my father gave you a mysterious note and you haven’t opened it?”

“That’s correct.”

“Why are you so calm?”

“Should I be worried?”

She leaned closer.

“Maybe.”

Yichen looked amused.

“Do you know what it is?”

“No!”

“Then how would you know whether I should be worried?”

“Because it’s from my father.”

He laughed.

She reached toward his pocket.

He caught her hand before she could take the paper.

“Don’t.”

“Let me see.”

“It’s addressed to me.”

“He’s my father.”

“And?”

“And I live here!”

“That doesn’t make it your letter.”

She looked at him in disbelief.

“You’re choosing a piece of paper over me?”

“At the moment, yes.”

Xiaoran gasped.

He kissed her hair before she could protest.

For the rest of the afternoon, Xiaoran became increasingly curious.

She tried asking indirectly.

“Did Dad say anything else when he gave you the note?”

“No.”

“Did he look serious?”

“A little.”

“Did he smile?”

“Yes.”

“Was it a normal smile or a suspicious smile?”

Yichen looked at her.

“How many kinds of smiles does your father have?”

“Several.”

He considered it.

“Then perhaps a suspicious one.”

Xiaoran sat upright.

“What?”

He laughed under his breath.

“Just teasing.”

She hit his arm.

“Yichen!”

He caught her hand, laughing.

“Relax.”

“How am I supposed to relax? My father has apparently written you a secret letter!”

“Perhaps it’s a shopping list.”

“Then why is my name not on it?”

“Maybe he doesn’t want you to know what vegetables he needs.”

She stared at him, then narrowed her eyes.

“You’re not taking this seriously.”

“I am.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Also true.”

She crossed her arms.

“Fine. Don’t tell me.”

He met her eyes, then reached over and gently pulled her closer.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“If your father wanted you to read it, he would have given it to you.”

She looked at him.

“I know.”

“Then let him have his conversation with me.”

She was quiet.

It was a reasonable answer.

She didn’t like it, but it was reasonable.

She let her head drop onto his shoulder.

“All right.”

Yichen kissed her hair.

“Thank you.”

A few seconds passed.

Then she whispered, “But you have to tell me if it’s something bad.”

His mouth curved.

“I’ll let you know.”

It was nearly five when Yichen finally opened the note.

Xiaoran was in her old bedroom, looking for a cardigan. Her mother had gone out to buy groceries, and her father was on the balcony watering his chili plants.

Yichen sat at the dining table, took the folded paper from his pocket, and opened it.

The handwriting was familiar.

A little uneven, but neat.

He read it once, then again.

It wasn’t long.

There were only a few lines.

Yichen,

Thank you for always treating Xiaoran well.

She’s a little stubborn. She doesn’t always tell people when she’s tired, and sometimes she acts as if everything is fine even when it isn’t.

I know she can take care of herself. We’ve raised her to be independent.

But I hope you will continue to look after each other.

You don’t need to be perfect. Just be honest with each other, and don’t let small things become big ones because neither of you wants to speak first.

And when things get difficult, remember that you can always come here.

You are welcome in this house.

Yichen remained still.

He read the final sentence again.

Then he folded the note carefully.

He didn’t know why those few lines affected him as much as they did.

Perhaps because Xiaoran’s father hadn’t written about money, or expectations, or what kind of future Yichen should provide.

He hadn’t asked him to promise anything impossible.

He had acknowledged that his daughter was someone who could stand on her own feet, while asking him to stand beside her.

And then there was that last line.

You are welcome in this house.

Yichen looked toward the kitchen.

The rice cooker sat on the counter.

He smiled a little.

Then he slipped the note back into his pocket.

Xiaoran came out of her old bedroom wearing a cardigan from her final year of high school, slightly too small for her now.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Are you ready to go?”

“In a minute.”

She came over and stood behind his chair, resting her chin on his shoulder.

“Did you read it?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

He turned to her.

“And what?”

“What does it say?”

He smiled.

“Nothing.”

She straightened.

“Nothing?”

“Nothing important.”

She blinked at him.

“Then why did he write your name on it?”

“Maybe he wanted to make sure I didn’t mistake it for someone else’s.”

“Yichen.”

He laughed.

She moved around the chair and stood in front of him.

“Tell me.”

He held her gaze.

She was wearing the expression she always wore when she wanted something and had decided that being cute would be more effective than arguing.

It usually was.

He reached out and took her hand.

“It’s something between your father and me.”

Her expression softened slightly.

“Is it about me?”

“Yes.”

She blinked.

“What did he say?”

Yichen stood.

Then he gently brushed her hair away from her cheek.

“He said you’re stubborn.”

Xiaoran’s mouth fell open.

“That’s it?”

“Among other things.”

“What other things?”

“That you don’t always tell people when you’re tired.”

She looked away.

He continued.

“And that you sometimes pretend everything is fine.”

She looked back at him.

“That’s not true.”

He raised an eyebrow.

She paused.

“...Not always.”

Something in his face eased.

“And he said I should look after you.”

Xiaoran’s expression changed.

She didn’t say anything.

Then she asked, “He said that?”

Yichen nodded.

“Yes.”

She looked down at their joined hands.

“What else?”

He considered telling her.

Then he decided against it.

“That’s all I’m telling you.”

She looked up sharply.

“Why?”

“Because he gave the note to me.”

“You’re a vault.”

“Apparently.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“Did he say something embarrassing?”

Yichen smiled.

“Perhaps.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed.

She tugged at his sleeve.

“Tell me!”

He kissed her hair.

“Your father likes me.”

She stopped, then looked at him.

“That’s what it says?”

“That’s what I understood.”

She studied his face.

He was smiling, but there was something quieter beneath it.

Something she couldn’t quite read.

She didn’t push.

Instead, she slipped her arms around his waist.

“Of course he likes you.”

Yichen rested his chin lightly against her head.

“Good.”

“He’s been liking you for ages.”

“I know.”

“He’s probably more comfortable with you than with me.”

“That would be concerning.”

She laughed against his chest.

When it was time to leave, Xiaoran’s father came out to see them off.

“Going already?”

“Yes, Uncle. Thank you for lunch.”

“Come again.”

“I will.”

Her father nodded, then looked at him.

“Did you read the note?”

Yichen met his eyes.

“Yes, Uncle.”

A small pause.

“All right.”

Yichen hesitated before adding enough that Xiaoran, who was busy putting on her shoes, wouldn’t hear.

“Thank you.”

Her father looked at him, then nodded once.

“Take care of each other.”

“We will.”

Xiaoran appeared beside them.

“What are you two whispering about?”

“Nothing,” her father said.

Yichen smiled.

“Nothing important.”

She looked between them.

Suspicious.

Suspicious.

Her father patted her shoulder.

“Go on. Don’t keep him waiting.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“You’re both acting strange.”

Yichen opened the door.

“Shall we?”

She gave her father one last look before stepping outside.

“Bye, Dad.”

“Bye. Message me when you get home.”

“I will.”

Yichen bowed his head slightly.

“Goodbye, Uncle.”

“Goodbye, Yichen.”

They walked toward the station together.

Xiaoran was quiet for a while.

Then she slipped her hand into his.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Are you going to keep the note?”

He looked down at her.

“Yes.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Why?”

He considered his answer.

“Because it’s important.”

She turned to him.

“Even though you won’t tell me what’s written?”

He smiled. “Because I won’t tell you.”

She groaned.

“You’re so annoying.”

He squeezed her hand.

“Your father is a good man.”

She held his gaze.

“I know.”

“He trusts you to make your own decisions.”

She nodded.

“And he trusts me to be beside you.”

Xiaoran slowed down.

Yichen stopped with her.

Then her expression softened.

“Did he really say that?”

Yichen brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“Something like that.”

She smiled, then leaned against his arm as they continued walking.

A few steps later, she spoke again.

“Do you know what I think?”

“What?”

“I think he wrote something embarrassing.”

Yichen laughed.

“Why?”

“Because you keep smiling whenever I ask.”

He glanced at her.

“Perhaps I just like you.”

She rolled her eyes.

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the one you’re getting.”

She laughed and squeezed his hand.

That night, back in Shanghai, while Xiaoran was in the shower, Yichen took the folded note out of his wallet.

He had placed it there carefully, away from the other receipts and papers.

He read it once more.

Then he folded it along the original creases and slipped it back.

Later, when he was reading in the living room and she had gone to bed, his phone vibrated. She was texting him from the bedroom, nine meters away, because she had decided this was a conversation better had in writing.

Xiaoran: I still think Dad wrote something embarrassing.

He laughed under his breath.

Yichen: You think too much.

Xiaoran: You know what? I think you’re hiding something.

Yichen: Perhaps.

Xiaoran: I’m going to ask him tomorrow.

Yichen laughed.

Yichen: You can try.

Xiaoran: Good night, traitor.

Yichen: Good night.

He put his phone down.

Then he went into the bedroom, where she was already asleep on his side of the bed again, and opened the drawer on that side, and put the note in, under the stubs from his father and the Herons contract, where he kept the papers that had changed something.

He didn’t tell her what it said for another year.

chapters.desc: He meant to watch game footage. She has ceramic cats, a duck in a knitted hat and twenty minutes of things to show him.
chapters.title: A Little Too Close
chapters.epigraph: “Because someone kept showing me ceramic cats.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had been sitting on the sofa for nearly forty minutes.

He had finished training earlier than usual, showered, changed into a dark T-shirt and comfortable trousers, and settled down with his tablet to review some footage from the previous Herons game.

It was supposed to be a quiet evening.

Then Xiaoran came home.

She greeted him with a kiss on the cheek, complained about a colleague who had sent her a file in the wrong format, stole two pieces of fruit from the kitchen, and disappeared into the bedroom to change.

When she returned, she had her phone in one hand and a sudden abundance of things to show him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Look at this.”

He paused the footage.

Xiaoran stood beside the sofa, holding her phone out. It was a picture of a little ceramic cat she’d found online.

“Isn’t this cute?”

He glanced at the screen.

“Very cute.”

“Look at its expression.”

He looked again.

“It looks unhappy.”

“Exactly! It’s so funny. I think it looks like you when you’re concentrating.”

Yichen raised his eyes.

“Does it?”

“Yes. Look. The little eyes. The mouth. Everything.” She zoomed in on the cat’s face.

He studied the picture.

“Do I really look like that?”

“Sometimes.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

She laughed.

Then, instead of sitting down beside him, she leaned over the back of the sofa, bringing her face close to his so she could show him another picture.

“And look at this one. It’s the same artist.”

Yichen tilted his head to see the screen.

A second ceramic cat appeared.

“That one’s better,” he said.

“Why?”

“It looks less angry.”

“You’re saying I’m wrong about you?”

“I’m saying the first one is more handsome.”

Xiaoran burst into laughter.

She was still leaning over him when she began scrolling through the artist’s other works. Her hair fell forward, brushing his shoulder. One hand rested on the back of the sofa, and her phone was held just beside his face.

Yichen returned his attention to the screen.

Or tried to.

“Wait, wait. This one!”

She moved the phone closer.

He looked.

A little ceramic duck wearing a knitted hat.

“Do you think we should buy it?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Where would you put it?”

“On the shelf.”

“The shelf is full.”

“We can make space.”

“You said that about the other duck.”

“That duck is different.”

“How?”

She paused.

Then she looked at him with great seriousness.

“That one has a different personality.”

Yichen looked at her.

A faint smile appeared at the corner of his mouth.

“Of course.”

Xiaoran grinned and continued scrolling.

She was apparently not finished.

For the next ten minutes, she showed him a series of things she had saved: a funny video, a café with beautiful desserts, a dress she liked, a cat that looked like it had committed tax fraud, and a short clip of a couple trying to assemble furniture.

Yichen listened to every explanation.

He answered her questions.

He even watched the entire furniture video when she insisted the man’s expression at the end was worth seeing.

But somewhere between the third ceramic animal and the fourth video, he noticed something.

Xiaoran hadn’t once considered sitting down.

She kept leaning over him, her upper body resting increasingly close against his shoulder, sometimes bracing a hand on the sofa, sometimes placing it on his chest without thinking.

Every time she wanted him to see something, she moved closer.

And every time she moved closer, he became a little less interested in whatever was on her phone.

He had been trying to be patient.

He really had.

But when she leaned across him again, bringing her face almost level with his, Yichen finally reached out.

His hand caught her waist.

Xiaoran stopped mid-sentence.

“Eh?”

He gently drew her toward him.

Not enough to startle her, just enough to make her straighten up and look at him.

Yichen’s hand remained at her waist.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Do you realize how distracting you are?”

She blinked.

Then she glanced at the tablet.

“Am I blocking the screen?”

He met her eyes.

“No.”

“Then what?”

His eyes moved over her face before returning to hers.

“You’re standing very close.”

She looked down.

Indeed, she was close.

Her hip was almost against his knee, his hand was still around her waist, and their faces were only a short distance apart.

But she didn’t see the problem.

“We live together.”

“I know.”

“And?”

“And you’ve been leaning over me for the last twenty minutes.”

She thought about it.

Then she smiled.

“Did you notice?”

Yichen gave her a look.

“How could I not?”

Her smile grew.

“Oh.”

He waited.

She looked at him for another second, then asked with exaggerated innocence, “Was I disturbing your work?”

“Not exactly.”

“Then?”

He leaned back against the sofa, his hand still resting at her waist.

“Here.”

Xiaoran’s eyes brightened.

“Why?”

“Because I want to see whether you can stay still for five minutes.”

She laughed.

“That’s easy.”

She put her phone on the coffee table and moved around the sofa, intending to sit beside him.

But Yichen caught her hand.

“Where are you going?”

“To sit.”

“Here.”

He gave her waist a gentle tug, and she ended up settling sideways on his lap.

Xiaoran looked at him, then at the sofa beside them.

“There’s a perfectly good seat.”

“I know.”

“Then why am I here?”

“Because you keep coming close enough to distract me. I thought I’d save you the trouble.”

She laughed, placing her hands on his shoulders.

“You’re blaming me?”

“Am I wrong?”

“Yes.”

Yichen raised an eyebrow.

“Then explain.”

She considered her answer.

“I was showing you things.”

“For twenty minutes.”

“Because there were many things.”

“Clearly.”

“And you were supposed to look at them.”

“I did.”

“Then why are you complaining?”

He turned to her.

Then he smiled.

Slowly.

Xiaoran’s expression faltered.

It was that particular smile again: the one that began at the corners of his mouth, his eyes remaining steady on hers, as if he had already thought of something amusing and was waiting for her to realize it.

She knew that smile.

She also knew she was usually the one who lost her composure first.

“You’re doing that on purpose,” she murmured.

“Doing what?”

“That face.”

“What face?”

She pressed her lips together.

Yichen’s thumb moved lightly against her waist.

“You were very talkative a moment ago.”

“I’m still talkative.”

“Then keep going.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“About what?”

“Whatever you wanted to show me.”

Xiaoran glanced at her phone on the table, then back at him.

She had completely forgotten what she had been showing him.

Yichen noticed.

His smile deepened.

“Forgot?”

“No.”

“What was it?”

She looked toward the table again.

“...The duck.”

“Which duck?”

“The one with the hat.”

“Ah.”

He nodded, pretending to consider it.

“Very important.”

“It is!”

“Tell me more.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“You’re making fun of me.”

“A little.”

She tried to look offended, but his hand was warm at her waist, and he was looking at her with such quiet amusement that it was difficult to maintain the expression.

Instead, she reached up and touched his cheek.

“You’re not very interested in my things today.”

“I’ve been listening to you all evening.”

“Not properly.”

“Not properly?”

She nodded.

Yichen tilted his head slightly.

“Then what should I do?”

She leaned closer, as if sharing a secret.

“Pay more attention.”

His eyes softened.

“All right.”

He lifted one hand to her cheek and kissed her.

It was a gentle kiss, but he didn’t immediately pull away. Xiaoran’s fingers slipped into his hair, and she returned it with a smile.

When they separated, she remained close.

Yichen brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“Is that better?”

“Much.”

“Good.”

She was quiet.

Then she looked at him again.

“Actually...”

“Hm?”

“I have another video.”

He closed his eyes.

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

“Wait! This one is really funny.”

“I believe you.”

“It’s only fifteen seconds.”

“That’s what you said about the furniture video.”

“That one was different.”

“How?”

“It was twenty seconds.”

He looked at her.

She grinned.

Then, instead of reaching for her phone, she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“Please?”

Yichen gave a quiet laugh.

“Show me.”

She reached across the coffee table to retrieve her phone, but before she could move too far, his arm tightened gently around her waist.

“Careful.”

“I can reach.”

“I know.”

She retrieved the phone and settled back against him.

This time, she didn’t lean over his shoulder.

She sat on his lap, her back against his chest, holding the phone between them.

Yichen rested his chin lightly against her shoulder.

“Is this the video?”

“Yes.”

She pressed play.

A tiny dog appeared on the screen, attempting to climb onto a sofa and failing spectacularly.

Xiaoran snorted into his shoulder.

Yichen watched the video.

Then he watched her laughing.

When it ended, she turned her head.

“Funny, right?”

“Very.”

“You didn’t laugh.”

“I was watching.”

“Watching what?”

He kissed her cheek.

“You.”

Her smile softened.

Then she turned back to her phone, trying to hide how pleased she was.

“You’re distracting me now.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted.

“Should I stop?”

She pretended to think.

Then she leaned back more comfortably against him.

“No.”

His arm settled around her waist again.

“All right.”

A few minutes later, Xiaoran put her phone down and began telling him about something that had happened at work. Yichen listened, occasionally asking questions, his fingers tracing small, absent-minded patterns against her side.

She was halfway through explaining a colleague’s strange presentation when she stopped.

“Wait.”

“What?”

She turned around in his arms.

“Did you finish watching your basketball footage?”

“No.”

“Why?”

He glanced at the tablet on the sofa.

“Because someone kept showing me ceramic cats.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re never going to let me forget that, are you?”

“Probably not.”

She leaned forward and kissed him once, then again, on the other cheek.

“Sorry.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Are you?”

She nodded solemnly.

“Very.”

He gave her a knowing smile.

“Then you can make it up to me.”

“How?”

“Stay here.”

She looked down at his arms around her waist, then back at him.

“That’s it?”

“For now.”

Xiaoran smiled and settled against his chest.

“Okay.”

Yichen picked up his tablet with one hand, keeping the other around her.

He returned to the footage.

Xiaoran remained quiet for almost a minute.

Then she lifted her head.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you think the duck with the hat would look better on the shelf or the coffee table?”

He stared at the screen.

A small smile appeared.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Show me the duck again.”

She beamed.

And Yichen, who had planned a peaceful evening of game footage, spent the next fifteen minutes comparing the decorative merits of two ceramic ducks while Professor Quack watched from her key ring on the table.

chapters.desc: At her studio’s networking evening, a brand representative keeps finding reasons to stand next to her. Yichen stays calm all night, and doesn’t let go of her waist at home.
chapters.title: A Little Too Friendly
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t think you can be stolen.”
chapters.content:
Yichen noticed him before Xiaoran did.

It wasn’t difficult.

The man had been standing beside Xiaoran for the better part of fifteen minutes, holding a glass of wine he barely seemed to drink. He was one of the brand partnership representatives invited to Morrow Studio’s annual networking event. Yichen had heard his name earlier during introductions, though he couldn’t remember it now.

What he did remember was how often the man laughed at Xiaoran’s jokes.

And how he kept finding reasons to stand closer.

Yichen stood a few meters away, speaking with one of the event organizers. He wasn’t deliberately watching them. At least, that was what he told himself.

He happened to notice when the man leaned closer to hear Xiaoran over the music.

Then again when he touched her elbow while making a point, then when he complimented her dress.

Xiaoran was wearing a simple black dress to her studio’s event, elegant without being flashy. Her hair was pinned loosely behind her ears, revealing the little flower earrings she often wore. She had spent nearly half an hour deciding whether to wear this dress or another one, eventually asking Yichen which looked better.

He had chosen this one.

He was beginning to think he had made an excellent decision for entirely inconvenient reasons.

“Mr. Zhou?”

Yichen turned his attention back to the person speaking to him.

“Yes?”

The conversation continued.

He remained polite, attentive, and perfectly engaged. He didn’t interrupt Xiaoran’s conversation or approach them because another man seemed interested in her.

He knew his girlfriend.

Xiaoran was friendly. She was expressive, enjoyed talking to people, and could become animated when discussing something she cared about. She was also perfectly capable of handling herself.

He trusted her.

That didn’t mean he had to enjoy watching someone else discover how charming she was.

Across the room, Xiaoran laughed at something the man said.

Yichen took a sip of his drink.

The organizer beside him continued talking about next quarter’s partnership opportunities.

Yichen listened.

Mostly.

A little later, Xiaoran finally excused herself and walked toward the refreshment table. She spotted Yichen almost immediately.

Her face brightened.

“Yichen!”

He turned.

“Finished networking?”

“Almost. My feet are tired.” She reached for a glass of water.

He glanced down at her shoes.

“Those?”

“I thought they were comfortable.”

“They were comfortable when I tried them at home.”

His mouth curved.

“That’s different from wearing them for three hours.”

“Exactly. I need to file a complaint with the shoe company.”

Yichen took her empty glass and placed it on the table.

“Want to sit?”

“Not yet. I should probably talk to a few more people.”

He nodded.

She studied his face.

“Are you tired?”

“No.”

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m listening.”

“To what?”

He met her eyes.

“To you.”

She smiled, then reached up to straighten the edge of his collar.

“You’re very handsome tonight.”

“Thank you.”

“Very serious, too.”

Yichen laughed.

“I don’t.”

“I know. But you look like you could.”

She gave his chest a light pat before turning toward a colleague who had called her name.

“I’ll come back later!”

“All right.”

He watched her leave.

Then he finished his drink.

He wasn’t angry.

That was the important distinction.

There was nothing Xiaoran had done that warranted an argument, and he wasn’t going to turn an ordinary professional event into something uncomfortable for her.

Still, when the evening finally ended, he found himself looking forward to having her to himself.

And judging by the way she slipped her hand into his as they walked toward the car, she was ready to leave too.

“Finally,” she sighed as he opened the passenger door.

Yichen smiled.

“That bad?”

“No. It was actually quite fun. But I think I’ve talked enough for one evening.” She settled into the seat and began removing one of her earrings.

He leaned over to help her with the seat belt.

“Did you have a good time?”

“Yes. I met a few people from other agencies, and one of the brand managers was interested in our next campaign.”

“That’s good.”

She met his eyes.

“How about you?”

“Productive.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Enough.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s not a very enthusiastic answer.”

He smiled and closed her door.

During the drive home, Xiaoran told him about the event.

She talked about a potential collaboration, a colleague who had accidentally spilled sparkling water on his own trousers, and the dessert table that had been disappointingly small.

Yichen listened, occasionally asking questions.

He didn’t mention the man.

Not yet.

When they arrived home, Xiaoran kicked off her shoes near the entrance and sighed with relief.

“Freedom.”

Yichen placed their keys in the bowl.

“Your feet?”

“Never making that mistake again.”

He looked at her.

“Want me to get you something comfortable?”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Can you get my slippers?”

He brought them over.

She slipped them on, then immediately walked toward him and wrapped her arms around his waist.

“Thank you.”

Yichen’s hands settled at her back.

“You’re welcome.”

She leaned against him before pulling away.

“I need to remove my makeup.”

“Go ahead.”

She took a few steps toward the bedroom, then turned back.

“Are you coming?”

“In a minute.”

“Okay.”

She disappeared into the bathroom.

Yichen remained in the living room, loosening his watch.

He was still thinking about the evening when she returned, now wearing a comfortable top and shorts, her face clean and her hair tied loosely.

She looked much more like the Xiaoran who belonged to their home.

“Better,” she announced, stretching her arms.

Yichen looked at her.

“Much better.”

She walked toward the sofa and sat down, patting the space beside her.

She patted the space beside her.

He joined her.

She immediately leaned against his shoulder, reaching for his hand.

For a while, they sat.

Then Yichen’s arm moved around her waist.

He drew her closer, his palm resting against her side.

It was a familiar gesture.

Except tonight, his hand stayed there.

A little longer than usual.

His thumb moved slowly against her waist, occasionally brushing the fabric of her shirt. Xiaoran noticed after a while.

She looked down, then up at him.

She tilted her head.

“You’re holding me.”

“Yes.”

“You usually do.”

“Yes.”

She studied him.

“You’re holding me differently.”

Yichen glanced at her.

He didn’t answer immediately.

Instead, he adjusted his arm, drawing her closer until her shoulder rested more comfortably against his chest.

Xiaoran looked at him again, then a smile appeared.

“Are you jealous?”

Yichen’s eyes shifted toward her.

There was a brief pause.

“Would that surprise you?”

Her smile widened.

“A little.”

“Why?”

“Because you looked so calm the entire evening.”

“I was calm.”

“Then?”

He turned to her.

“Being calm doesn’t mean I didn’t notice.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Notice what?”

Yichen’s expression remained composed.

“The man who spent most of the evening finding reasons to talk to you.”

She blinked at him.

Then her mouth slowly curved.

“Oh.”

He held her gaze.

“Something amusing?”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

She giggled.

“Nothing! I just didn’t realize you noticed.”

“Was it difficult to notice?”

She thought about it, then laughed again.

“Maybe not.”

Yichen’s hand moved slightly higher along her waist.

“He seemed particularly interested in what you had to say.”

“He works with one of the brands we’re trying to collaborate with. He was asking about our campaign.”

“I see.”

“And he was quite friendly.”

“Very.”

She turned toward him.

“So you are jealous.”

“I don’t like making assumptions about people’s intentions.”

“That’s a very diplomatic answer.”

“I’m trying to be fair.”

She smiled, then rested her chin against his chest.

“Well, he was friendly, but I wasn’t particularly interested in talking to him for that long.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted slightly.

“Why?”

“Because he kept asking questions that weren’t about work.”

He waited.

Xiaoran continued, counting on her fingers.

“He asked whether I lived nearby. Then whether I came to these events often. Then whether I usually came alone.”

Yichen’s expression didn’t change, but his hand became still against her waist.

“And what did you say?”

“I told him I lived on the other side of the river, that I came when work required it, and that I usually came with my boyfriend.”

Yichen looked at her.

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Actually, I think I mentioned you twice.”

“Twice?”

“Maybe three times.”

His mouth curved.

“Very thorough.”

“I was being polite.”

“I know.”

She watched his expression.

Then she asked, “Did you want to come over?”

Yichen considered the question.

“At one point.”

“Why didn’t you?”

He brushed his thumb over her side.

“Because you were having a conversation. I didn’t see a reason to interrupt.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

“You could have.”

“I could have.”

“I wouldn’t mind.”

“I know.”

She played with the cuff of his sleeve.

“Next time, you can just come stand beside me.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Would you like that?”

“Of course. I like introducing you to people.”

That got a smile out of him.

“All right.”

She leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

Then, with a little mischievousness, she asked, “Were you worried he’d steal me?”

Yichen laughed.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

He turned slightly, his hand settling more securely around her waist.

“I don’t think you can be stolen. You make your own decisions, and I trust you.”

Her teasing expression softened.

Yichen looked at her for another moment.

“But I can still dislike someone being overly familiar with my girlfriend.”

“Your girlfriend?”

“Yes.”

“Very possessive.”

“Is that a complaint?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

He leaned closer, his forehead almost touching hers.

“Good.”

Xiaoran smiled.

Then she seemed to remember something.

“Oh, wait.”

“What?”

“That man asked whether I had a boyfriend.”

Yichen’s eyes narrowed just slightly.

“And?”

“I told him yes.”

“Good.”

“Then he asked what you did.”

Yichen waited.

“I said you’re a professional basketball player.”

He nodded.

“And then?”

She grinned.

“I showed him a picture of you.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Which picture?”

“The one from our anniversary dinner.”

“The one in the black shirt?”

“Yes!”

He gave a small nod.

“All right.”

Xiaoran’s smile became wider.

“He said you were handsome.”

Yichen looked at her.

“And what did you say?”

She raised her chin.

“I said I knew.”

He laughed.

“Very modest.”

“I’m just telling the truth.”

His hand moved to the small of her back.

“And did you tell him anything else?”

She pretended to think.

“Maybe that you’re very busy, that you train a lot, and that you don’t like people disturbing you.”

“That’s an interesting description.”

“And that you’re very affectionate at home.”

Yichen’s eyebrows rose.

Xiaoran giggled.

“You look amused.”

“I’m wondering how much of our private life you shared.”

“Not much!”

“How much is not much?”

She leaned closer and whispered, “I told him you always hold my waist.”

Yichen looked at her.

Then at his own hand, which was currently doing exactly that.

A quiet smile appeared.

“Did you?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Then I suppose I should be consistent.”

Before she could ask what he meant, he drew her closer and kissed her.

He tasted of the event’s terrible sparkling wine, and his hand was steady at her back. Xiaoran’s arms slipped around his neck, and she smiled when he kissed her again, just a little longer this time.

When they parted, she stayed close.

“You’re still jealous.”

Yichen brushed her hair back.

“Perhaps.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I think it’s cute.”

“Do you?”

“Mm-hm.”

He gave her a quiet look.

“Don’t encourage me.”

“Why?”

“Because I might start asking you to come stand beside me at every event.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You can. I like standing beside you.”

His expression softened.

He kissed her cheek.

“Then I will.”

She settled against him again, and his arm remained around her waist.

After a few minutes, Xiaoran reached for the television remote.

“Should we watch something?”

“Sure.”

She turned on the television and began browsing.

Yichen stayed close, his hand still resting at her waist.

Eventually, she glanced down at it.

“You’re still holding me.”

“Yes.”

“Your hand hasn’t moved.”

“Do you want me to move it?”

She considered that.

Then she placed her own hand over his.

“No.”

Yichen smiled, and his hand didn’t move for the rest of the episode.

chapters.desc: He promised to teach her to swim. She spends most of the lesson studying something other than technique.
chapters.title: A Very Serious Swimming Lesson
chapters.epigraph: “Because you’re mine.”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had agreed to go swimming for one simple reason.

Yichen had promised to teach her how to swim properly.

That was it.

She hadn’t agreed because he mentioned the private swimming pool at a hotel he occasionally visited. She hadn’t agreed because he said the water was heated and the facilities were excellent. And she certainly hadn’t agreed because he casually mentioned that he usually swam a few laps after training.

No.

She was going because she wanted to improve her swimming.

At least, that was what she told herself when she packed her swimsuit the night before.

“Have you brought everything?”

Yichen stood beside the open wardrobe, watching her check her swimming bag for the third time.

“Yes.”

“Towel?”

“Yes.”

“Change of clothes?”

“Yes.”

“Swimming cap?”

She paused, then looked at him.

“Do I need one?”

“Not necessarily.”

“Then why are you asking?”

He smiled. “Just checking.”

She zipped the bag.

“You’re treating me like I’m going on a school trip.”

“You’re the one who packed three different snacks.”

“Swimming makes people hungry.”

“Before swimming?”

“Preparation.”

Yichen laughed and took the bag from her.

“Come on, then.”

The swimming facility was quieter than Xiaoran expected.

It was a private indoor pool with floor-to-ceiling windows, soft natural lighting, and a few people swimming in separate lanes. The water was a beautiful shade of blue, and the entire place smelled of chlorine.

She had zipped her promise ring into the inside pocket of her bag, because chlorine and small stones didn’t mix, and checked the zip twice.

Yichen had already changed when Xiaoran came out of the changing room.

He was standing near the pool, checking something on his phone.

He wore simple black swimming trunks.

His upper body was bare.

Xiaoran stopped.

Yichen looked up.

And saw her.

He didn’t say anything immediately.

His eyes moved over her face, then his lips curved.

“What?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Nothing.”

He put his phone down.

“Why are you standing there?”

“I’m looking.”

“At what?”

She met his eyes, then at the pool, then back at him.

“The facilities.”

Yichen glanced around.

“Good facilities?”

“Very good.”

He smiled.

He reached for her.

She walked toward him, trying hard to behave normally.

It wasn’t easy.

Because, although Xiaoran knew her boyfriend was athletic, she wasn’t accustomed to seeing him like this outside the context of a basketball game.

His shoulders were broad, his arms defined from years of training, and his abdomen—

She looked away, then looked again.

Unfortunately, Yichen noticed.

Of course he did.

He had been dating her for more than six years.

He knew exactly what her face looked like when she was trying to pretend she hadn’t noticed something.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Are you ready?”

“Yes.”

“Then let’s get in.”

She nodded.

But before following him, she glanced down once more.

Yichen’s smile deepened.

“Something interesting?”

She immediately looked up.

“No.”

“All right.”

He picked up her towel.

“Let’s go, researcher.”

The first fifteen minutes were dedicated to warming up.

Yichen was surprisingly patient.

He stood in the shallow end, showing her how to move her arms, how to control her breathing, and how to relax her legs instead of kicking frantically.

Xiaoran listened attentively.

Mostly.

“Don’t hold your breath.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“How do you know?”

“Your cheeks are puffed up.”

She exhaled.

Yichen laughed.

“Again.”

She tried once more.

This time, she managed to float with his support.

“See? You’re doing well.”

Xiaoran smiled.

She was pleased.

Then she looked at him.

“Can you let go?”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He slowly loosened his hold.

Xiaoran managed to stay afloat for a few seconds before immediately grabbing his arm.

“Wait!”

He caught her.

“Got you.”

She clung to his shoulders, laughing.

“That was scary.”

“You were doing fine.”

“I know, but you let go!”

“That’s usually how learning to swim works.”

She frowned.

“You’re supposed to be supportive.”

“I am.”

He adjusted his hand beneath her arm.

“Try again. I’ll stay beside you.”

She nodded.

This time, she lasted longer.

When she finally reached the edge, she looked extremely proud of herself.

Yichen rested his arms on the poolside beside her.

“Good job.”

She grinned.

“Did you see?”

“I was right here.”

“I did it!”

He leaned over and kissed her wet forehead.

“Yes, you did.”

She smiled so brightly that he couldn’t help smiling back.

For a while, swimming was going very well.

Then Yichen decided to demonstrate something.

“Watch.”

He moved away from the shallow end and positioned himself at the beginning of a lane.

Xiaoran held onto the pool edge.

“What are you doing?”

“Swimming.”

“I can see that.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Then watch.”

He pushed off.

His movements changed completely once he started swimming.

There was no hesitation, no unnecessary movement. His strokes were smooth and controlled, his breathing steady. He moved through the water with the kind of ease that came from years of physical conditioning.

Xiaoran watched him reach the other end, then turn, then swim back.

When he reached her, he surfaced and pushed his wet hair away from his forehead.

“How was that?”

She stared.

Yichen blinked.

He rested his forearms on the edge.

“You’re very quiet.”

“I’m observing.”

“Observing what?”

“Your swimming technique.”

His mouth curved.

“Of course.”

She nodded solemnly.

“Very professional.”

He laughed.

Then he noticed her eyes drifting down again.

This time, he didn’t bother pretending not to notice.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“Yes?”

“Would you like to ask me something?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He tilted his head.

“Then why are you staring?”

She was quiet for two seconds.

Then said, seriously:

“Do you have to be so muscular?”

Yichen stopped.

Then he laughed.

A genuine, low laugh that made Xiaoran’s cheeks turn pink.

“What?”

She looked defensive.

“I’m asking a question.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re swimming.”

He glanced down at himself, then back at her.

“I should probably stop, then.”

“No!”

He raised an eyebrow.

She immediately realized what she’d said.

“...I mean, you can continue. It’s good exercise.”

Yichen’s smile became more amused.

“Understood.”

The next few minutes were difficult for Xiaoran.

Not because the swimming was difficult.

Because Yichen had become aware of her attention.

And he was enjoying it.

He continued demonstrating different strokes, occasionally swimming a length before returning to her. Every time he surfaced, he pushed his hair back and looked at her with an expression that was becoming increasingly suspicious.

Xiaoran eventually decided she needed to regain control of the situation.

She moved closer.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

She held out her hand.

He approached.

She reached out and placed both hands on his shoulders.

He looked down at her.

“What is it?”

She studied him.

Then, with the utmost seriousness, asked:

“How many people have seen you like this?”

Yichen blinked.

“Like what?”

“Like this.”

He looked around the pool.

“People at the swimming facility?”

“Yes.”

“Quite a few, probably.”

She frowned.

“How many?”

“I haven’t counted.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“Do they look at you?”

Yichen stared at her.

Then his lips slowly curved.

“Sometimes.”

Xiaoran’s expression changed.

“Sometimes?”

He was clearly trying not to laugh.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Are you jealous?”

“No.”

“All right.”

He nodded.

She continued holding his shoulders.

“I’m just asking.”

“Of course.”

“Because you’re very noticeable.”

He smiled.

“That’s unfortunate.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

“Because I only came here to swim with you.”

She paused.

Then her expression softened.

Yichen lowered his head slightly.

“Does that help?”

She tried to maintain her serious expression.

“A little.”

He laughed.

“But you should probably stay near me.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“Should I?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She looked him directly in the eyes.

“Because you’re mine.”

Yichen went still for half a second.

Then he smiled.

Not his usual teasing smile.

Something warmer.

“Am I?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He leaned closer.

“Then I suppose I’d better stay where I belong.”

He kissed her, briefly.

Xiaoran smiled, pleased with herself.

Unfortunately, he wasn’t finished.

“And should I wear a sign?”

She blinked.

“What?”

“Something that says, ‘Reserved for Lin Xiaoran’?”

She looked at him, then splashed water at his chest.

“Don’t be ridiculous!”

He laughed and caught her hand.

A little later, Yichen suggested they swim together.

He showed her how to coordinate her breathing and movements, staying beside her as she attempted a short distance.

She was getting better.

Not fast, but better.

When she reached the end, she held onto the edge and looked at him proudly.

“How was that?”

“Good.”

That made her grin.

“Am I talented?”

“Very.”

“Are you just saying that?”

“You’re making progress.”

She nodded, satisfied.

Then Yichen pushed himself up slightly, resting his arms on the pool edge.

Xiaoran looked at him.

Water ran down his shoulders and chest. His hair was wet and falling slightly over his forehead.

She stared.

Then said, “I think I have another problem.”

He turned his head.

“What problem?”

She looked down at the water.

“I can’t concentrate.”

Yichen smiled.

“Why?”

She pointed vaguely at him.

“You.”

He laughed.

“Me?”

“Yes.”

“What am I doing?”

“Existing.”

His smile widened.

“That’s difficult to avoid.”

She sighed dramatically.

“I came here to learn swimming.”

“And you are learning.”

“But you’re distracting.”

“Would you like me to put a shirt on?”

She turned to him, then looked away.

“No.”

Yichen laughed and had to lower his head.

She immediately splashed him again.

After swimming, they sat beside the pool for a while.

Xiaoran was wrapped in a large towel, her hair damp and slightly messy. Yichen sat beside her, drinking water.

She had been unusually quiet.

He glanced at her.

“Tired?”

“A little.”

“Want to rest before showering?”

She nodded.

He placed his bottle down and reached for her hand.

She leaned against his shoulder.

They watched the water.

Then Xiaoran spoke.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Can I tell you something?”

“Of course.”

“I think I understand why you like swimming.”

He met her eyes.

“Why?”

“It’s peaceful.”

He nodded.

“And?”

“And you look very good doing it.”

He laughed.

“I see.”

She tilted her head to look at him.

“Don’t you agree?”

“About what?”

“That you look good.”

He pretended to consider.

“I haven’t really examined myself.”

She gave him an incredulous look.

“You’re ridiculous.”

He smiled and kissed her temple.

“Thank you.”

She returned her attention to the pool.

Then, after a moment, she said:

“Next time, can we come again?”

“Of course.”

“And maybe you can teach me more.”

“Certainly.”

She nodded.

Then added, “But I have one condition.”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

She reached over and took his hand.

“You have to stay close to me.”

Something in his face eased.

“I thought that was already the plan.”

“Good.”

She looked satisfied.

Then she glanced down at his abdomen again.

Yichen noticed.

He leaned closer.

“Anything else?”

She looked up innocently.

“No.”

“Nothing?”

“No.”

He smiled slowly.

“You’re staring again.”

Xiaoran’s cheeks turned pink.

“You’re imagining things.”

He leaned back, looking entirely too pleased with himself.

“All right, sweetheart.”

“Stop smiling like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you know something.”

He took another sip of water.

“I do know something.”

“What?”

He turned to her.

“You like my abs.”

Xiaoran froze, then immediately pulled the towel higher around herself.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed.

She turned away, pretending to be offended.

But he could see the little smile she was trying to hide.

In the car park he took the ring out of her bag before she could ask and slid it back onto her finger.

On the way home, Xiaoran was scrolling through the pictures they had taken.

There were several photographs of the pool, a few selfies, and one picture of Yichen standing beside the water.

She stopped at that one, then zoomed in.

Yichen glanced over from the driver’s seat.

“What are you looking at?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at the screen.

“That’s a good picture.”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

A moment passed.

Then she opened her messaging app.

Yichen recognized Meilin’s name.

He raised an eyebrow.

“Who are you sending it to?”

“Meilin.”

“Why?”

“She asked what I was doing today.”

He laughed under his breath.

“All right.”

Xiaoran typed something, then sent the picture.

A few seconds later, Meilin replied.

Meilin: HELLO????

Meilin: IS THAT YICHEN???

Xiaoran grinned.

Xiaoran: Yes.

Meilin: WHY DOES HE LOOK LIKE THAT?

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen.

Then typed:

Xiaoran: I know. Very distracting.

Meilin sent a string of laughing emojis.

Meilin: KEEP YOUR MAN.

Xiaoran laughed out loud.

Yichen glanced at her.

“What?”

She turned the phone toward him.

He read the messages, then looked at her.

“Keep my man?”

“Yes.”

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

“Good.”

He reached over at a red light and squeezed her hand.

“Because I’m not planning on going anywhere.”

That made her grin.

Then, after a moment, she said:

“Actually, Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Next time, I want to learn how to swim properly.”

“We’ll practice.”

“And I want to get stronger.”

“That’s a good goal.”

She nodded.

Then looked at him with a small, mischievous smile.

“But I also want to come swimming with you because...”

She paused.

He glanced at her.

“Because?”

She leaned closer.

“You’re very nice to look at.”

Yichen laughed.

“Is that the real reason?”

“One of the reasons.”

He shook his head, smiling.

“At least you’re honest.”

She settled back into her seat, pleased with herself.

And when they arrived home, she made one final declaration while unpacking her swimming bag.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“I think we should swim every week.”

He held her gaze.

“Every week?”

“Yes.”

“That’s quite a commitment.”

She nodded seriously.

“For my health.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Of course.”

She put her towel away, then turned around.

“And for your abs.”

Yichen burst out laughing.

Xiaoran grinned, completely unashamed.

chapters.desc: A night market, a row of game stalls, and a professional basketball player who misses three shots in a row.
chapters.title: The Plush Toy He Couldn’t Win for Her
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll teach you.”
chapters.content:
The night market had been Xiaoran’s idea.

Naturally.

Yichen had suggested a quiet dinner after his afternoon training, perhaps somewhere near the river. Xiaoran had agreed enthusiastically, only to send him a message twenty minutes later.

Xiaoran: Change of plan.

Yichen: What happened?

Xiaoran: There’s a night market nearby.

Yichen: All right.

Xiaoran: And there are games.

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: And prizes.

Yichen: Understood.

Xiaoran: I think we should go.

Yichen had looked at the messages, smiled, and replied.

Yichen: I’ll pick you up at seven.

Forty minutes later, he was standing beside her beneath a row of glowing red lanterns, holding two drinks while Xiaoran examined a stall filled with stuffed animals.

The night market was lively. Food stalls lined both sides of the street, filling the air with the smell of grilled meat, fried dumplings, sweet pancakes, and freshly made milk tea. Music played from a small stage farther down the road, while groups of friends and families wandered between stalls.

Xiaoran was delighted.

She had already bought grilled squid, a little paper bag of candied fruit, and a cup of strawberry milk tea.

Yichen had bought her everything she pointed at.

He was beginning to suspect that the evening would be expensive, although not in any way that concerned him.

“Yichen.”

He looked down.

“Hm?”

She pointed toward a game stall.

“Look.”

The stall had a row of colorful balloons attached to a board. Players were given darts and had to pop a certain number of balloons to win a prize.

Yichen glanced at the display.

“Do you want to play?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

She looked at the prizes.

There were several small plush toys, keychains, and one large white rabbit sitting on the top shelf.

Xiaoran pointed at it.

“That one.”

Yichen followed her finger.

“The rabbit?”

“It’s cute.”

“Do you want it?”

“Yes.”

He took out his wallet.

“Let’s try.”

She immediately caught his wrist.

“Wait.”

He met her eyes.

“We should compete.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Compete?”

“Yes. Whoever wins gets to choose what we do next.”

He considered this.

“And the loser?”

She smiled mischievously.

“Has to buy the winner a snack.”

Yichen laughed.

“All right.”

She held out her hand.

“Deal.”

He shook it.

“Deal.”

Xiaoran looked at him with great confidence.

She had absolutely no idea what she was getting herself into.

The first game was balloon darts.

Xiaoran went first.

She stood behind the line, holding three darts.

The stall owner explained the rules.

“Pop at least five balloons to win the medium prize. Seven for the large one.”

Xiaoran nodded seriously.

“Understood.”

She raised her first dart.

Threw.

Missed.

She blinked, then tried again.

Missed.

Yichen stood beside her, holding her drink and watching.

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“Don’t look at me.”

Something in his face eased.

“I’m not doing anything.”

“Your presence is distracting.”

He laughed.

She took her final dart.

Focused.

Threw.

The dart hit the board, bounced off, and landed on the ground.

Silence.

Xiaoran stared.

The stall owner gave her an encouraging smile.

“Would you like another round?”

She looked at Yichen.

He was pressing his lips together.

“Don’t.”

He raised his free hand.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

He laughed.

“Would you like me to try?”

She handed him the darts.

“Fine. Show me.”

Yichen stepped behind the line.

He examined the board, adjusted his grip, and threw.

Pop.

The first balloon burst.

Xiaoran blinked.

He threw again.

Pop, then another.

Pop.

His fourth dart hit.

His fifth dart hit.

By the seventh throw, he had won the large prize.

The stall owner smiled and handed him a small plush bear.

Yichen accepted it, then looked at Xiaoran.

She stared at him.

“...What?”

He held out the bear.

“Your prize.”

She looked at the toy, then at him.

“How did you do that?”

He shrugged.

“Just aim.”

She took the bear.

“That’s not an explanation.”

He smiled.

“Would you like me to teach you?”

“No.”

“All right.”

She hugged the bear against her chest, then looked toward the large white rabbit.

“That one is still cuter.”

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Then let’s try again.”

The second game was ring toss.

Xiaoran was determined to win this one herself.

She stood in front of the counter, studying the bottles.

The rings were small, and the bottles were arranged at different distances.

Yichen stood beside her.

“Which one do you want?”

She pointed to a little pink cat.

“That one.”

“All right.”

She took the rings.

The first landed on the counter. The second bounced off a bottle.

The third rolled away.

Xiaoran looked at the rings, then at the bottles, then at Yichen.

“These rings are defective.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Are they?”

“Yes.”

She handed them back to the stall owner.

“Can I try again?”

The owner laughed and gave her another set.

Yichen watched her take a deep breath.

She threw.

Missed.

She threw again.

Missed.

Her final ring landed around the neck of a bottle, wobbled, and slipped off.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Yichen looked at the bottle, then at her.

“Almost.”

She turned toward him.

“Don’t say almost.”

He laughed.

“All right.”

He took the rings.

Xiaoran folded her arms.

“Let’s see.”

Yichen tried once.

The ring landed perfectly around the bottle.

The stall owner looked impressed.

“Very good!”

Yichen tried again.

Another ring landed.

He won the little pink cat.

Xiaoran stared at him in disbelief.

“Again?”

He turned toward her.

“What?”

“You’re good at everything!”

He laughed.

“Not everything.”

“Name one thing.”

He considered it.

“Winning you a pink cat, apparently.”

She took the toy from him.

“That’s not what I meant.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Then you’ll have to be more specific.”

She looked at the pink cat in her hands, then at him.

A smile slowly appeared.

“Actually, you’re quite useful.”

“Thank you.”

She tucked the toy under her arm beside the bear.

Yichen looked at the growing collection.

“Are we starting a zoo?”

“Maybe.”

By the third game, Xiaoran had become suspicious.

The game involved throwing small beanbags into holes on a wooden board. Each hole had a different score, and the highest score won the largest prize.

She studied the board, then turned to Yichen.

“You’re not allowed to play.”

He looked amused.

“Why?”

“Because you’re too good.”

He laughed.

“You haven’t even tried.”

“I’ve seen enough.”

She paid for her turn.

Yichen stepped aside, still holding their drinks.

Xiaoran threw the first beanbag.

It landed in a low-scoring hole.

She threw the second.

It missed.

The third bounced off the board.

She stared at the result, then took a breath.

“Fine.”

She threw the fourth.

It landed in the highest-scoring hole.

Her face brightened.

“YES!”

Yichen smiled.

“Good shot.”

She turned toward him, delighted.

“Did you see?”

“I did.”

“I got it!”

“Very impressive.”

She threw the fifth.

Missed.

The sixth.

Missed.

Her final throw landed in a middle-scoring hole.

She didn’t win the top prize, but the stall owner gave her a small yellow duck.

Xiaoran accepted it proudly.

“Thank you.”

She turned to Yichen.

“See? I can win.”

He nodded solemnly.

“Of course.”

She held up the duck.

“Look at him.”

Yichen examined it.

“He’s cute.”

“His name is Dean.”

“Dean?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because he outranks Professor Quack.”

Yichen looked at the duck’s slightly crooked eyes, then at Xiaoran.

“Very intelligent.”

She smiled and tucked it into her bag.

They continued walking.

Yichen bought grilled corn while Xiaoran inspected a stall selling handmade hair accessories.

She tried on a small white flower-shaped clip and turned toward him.

“Pretty,” he said.

Her mouth tipped up.

“Then I’ll buy it.”

He reached for his wallet.

She stopped him.

“I can pay for this one.”

He turned to her.

“All right.”

She paid, then carefully placed the clip in her bag.

They walked a little farther until they reached another game stall.

This one had a row of basketball hoops.

Xiaoran stopped.

Yichen glanced at the display, then at her.

“No.”

She turned.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You were looking at the basketballs.”

She smiled.

“You’re a basketball player.”

“Yes.”

“So you should win something.”

He laughed.

“That’s not how it works.”

She pointed at a large plush shark hanging above the counter.

“That one.”

Yichen looked at it, then at her.

“Do you want it?”

“Very much.”

He paid for a round.

The stall owner handed him three basketballs.

Xiaoran stood beside the counter, looking extremely confident.

“Easy.”

Yichen glanced at her.

He smiled.

He took the first ball.

Shot.

It bounced off the rim.

Xiaoran blinked.

Yichen looked at the hoop, then at the ball.

He picked up the second.

Shot.

It hit the backboard and rolled out.

Xiaoran’s mouth slowly opened.

Yichen took the third.

Shot.

The ball hit the rim and bounced away.

There was a brief silence.

Then Xiaoran burst out laughing.

She bent forward, holding her stomach.

Yichen looked at her.

“Enjoying yourself?”

She could barely speak.

“You’re... you’re a professional basketball player!”

He laughed.

“I noticed.”

“How did you miss all three?”

“The hoop is smaller than it looks.”

She laughed harder.

Yichen took the balls back to the stall owner.

“Another round.”

Xiaoran immediately straightened.

“Wait. You’re trying again?”

“Don’t you want the shark?”

She looked at the plush toy, then at him.

“...Yes.”

He paid again.

This time, he adjusted his stance.

He took the first ball.

Shot.

The ball went cleanly through the hoop.

Xiaoran clapped.

“Yes!”

The second shot landed too. The third bounced off the rim, but he managed to win a medium prize.

The stall owner handed him a small blue shark.

Xiaoran took it.

She looked at the shark, then at Yichen.

“Not the big one.”

He nodded.

“Not the big one.”

She hugged the shark.

Then looked up at him with a determined expression.

“We’re coming back.”

He laughed.

“Of course.”

The night market grew busier as the evening progressed.

They stopped for food, sharing a plate of dumplings and a bowl of noodles. Xiaoran had begun arranging her prizes on the table.

The bear sat beside her drink.

The pink cat was next to it.

Dean the duck occupied the center.

The blue shark leaned against her bag.

Yichen looked at the collection.

“You’re carrying quite a lot.”

“Yes.”

“Happy?”

She looked at the toys, then at him.

“Very.”

“Good.”

She picked up Dean.

“Although...”

He held her gaze.

“What?”

She turned the duck around.

“Dean is lonely.”

Yichen raised an eyebrow.

“Is he?”

“He needs a friend.”

Yichen glanced at the collection.

“Doesn’t he have four?”

“Those are acquaintances.”

He laughed.

“Of course.”

She put the duck down and looked toward the game stalls again.

Her gaze stopped at the large white rabbit.

It was still sitting on the top shelf.

Its ears were long, its fur looked incredibly soft, and it wore a tiny blue ribbon around its neck.

Xiaoran stared at it.

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Still that one?”

She nodded.

He looked at the rabbit.

“Let’s go.”

She turned toward him.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She smiled and immediately stood up.

The final game was a claw machine.

It stood at the edge of the market, beneath a row of colorful lights.

Inside were several plush toys, including the white rabbit.

Xiaoran approached the machine as if she had found her life’s purpose.

Yichen stood beside her.

“Is this the one?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He examined the machine.

“Have you played before?”

“Of course.”

“Are you good?”

She met his eyes.

“Don’t ask unnecessary questions.”

He laughed.

She inserted a coin.

The claw moved.

She adjusted the joystick.

“Left... a little more... no, too much.”

Yichen watched her concentrate.

She pressed the button.

The claw descended.

It grabbed the rabbit by one ear.

Xiaoran held her breath.

The claw lifted.

The rabbit slipped.

It fell.

She stared at the machine.

“No.”

Yichen smiled.

“Unlucky.”

She inserted another coin.

This time, the claw caught the rabbit around its middle.

It lifted.

Moved toward the opening, then dropped it.

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

“Why?”

Yichen looked at the machine.

“Perhaps the claw strength is low.”

She turned toward him.

“Don’t defend it.”

He laughed.

She tried again.

And again.

And again.

The rabbit seemed to have developed a personal grudge against her.

Every time she almost won, it slipped away.

Yichen watched her expression become increasingly serious.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Maybe we should—”

“No.”

He stopped.

She inserted another coin.

That got a smile out of him.

“All right.”

Twenty minutes later, Yichen had bought them two more drinks.

Xiaoran was still at the machine.

Her brows were drawn together.

Her lips were pressed into a thin line.

The white rabbit had moved slightly closer to the opening, but not enough.

Yichen stood behind her, looking at the machine.

“How many attempts?”

She didn’t answer.

“Xiaoran?”

“Don’t count.”

He laughed.

She pressed the button.

The claw descended.

It caught the rabbit.

Lifted it.

Moved.

Dropped it.

Xiaoran stared, then slowly turned toward him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I think this machine is cheating.”

He nodded.

“Possibly.”

“Do you think I should report it?”

He laughed.

“To whom?”

“Someone.”

He looked at her, then gently touched her shoulder.

“Do you really want that rabbit?”

“Yes.”

“Then let me try.”

She hesitated.

“Are you good at claw machines?”

“No.”

“Then—”

“Trust me.”

She turned to him.

He took the joystick. He didn’t rush.

He studied the position of the rabbit, the shape of the claw, and the opening at the bottom.

Xiaoran stood beside him, watching with intense concentration.

“More to the left.”

He adjusted it.

“Not too much.”

He adjusted it again.

“Yichen, I think—”

“One moment.”

He pressed the button.

The claw descended.

Caught the rabbit around its body.

Lifted it.

Xiaoran held her breath.

The rabbit swayed slightly.

The claw moved toward the opening, then dropped it.

The plush toy landed inside.

Neither moved.

Then Xiaoran let out a loud gasp.

“OH!”

She grabbed Yichen’s arm.

“YICHEN!”

He laughed as she rushed toward the prize opening.

She reached inside and pulled out the rabbit.

The white rabbit was even softer than she had expected.

She hugged it tightly, then turned around.

Her eyes were shining.

“YOU GOT IT!”

Yichen laughed.

“I did.”

She ran toward him and threw her arms around his waist.

He caught her naturally, laughing as she hugged him.

“You got it! You got it!”

He wrapped his arms around her.

“Yes, I know.”

She leaned back to see him.

“You’re amazing!”

He laughed under his breath.

“Thank you.”

She held up the rabbit between them.

“Look!”

He examined it.

“Very cute.”

She nodded enthusiastically.

“Very!”

Then she looked at him again.

“How did you do that?”

He shrugged.

“Positioning.”

She stared.

“That’s your answer?”

“Yes.”

She squinted at him.

“You’re not allowed to be good at everything.”

He laughed.

They eventually left the night market with more prizes than they had planned to carry.

Yichen carried the food bags.

Xiaoran carried the plush toys.

Or at least, she tried.

The rabbit was quite large, and the other toys kept slipping from her arms.

Yichen watched her struggle, then held out his hand.

“Give me some.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I can carry them.”

His mouth curved.

“You’re going to drop Dean.”

She looked down.

Dean was indeed slipping.

She immediately handed him the duck.

“Okay. Just Dean.”

Yichen took it.

A few steps later, she handed him the pink cat, then the blue shark, then the bear.

Eventually, she was carrying only the large white rabbit.

Yichen looked at the collection in his arms.

“Interesting.”

She smiled innocently.

“You’re stronger.”

He laughed.

“Convenient.”

She slipped her arm through his free one.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

They walked toward the car, the night market lights glowing behind them.

After a while, Xiaoran looked up.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Which prize is your favorite?”

He looked at the toys.

“Probably the rabbit.”

She brightened.

“Really?”

“Because you wanted it so badly.”

Her mouth tipped up, then hugged the rabbit closer.

“I like it too.”

He studied her.

“What’s its name?”

She thought about it.

“Maybe...”

She looked at the rabbit’s blue ribbon.

“Little Master.”

Yichen laughed.

“Little Master?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because he looks like he comes from a rich family.”

He looked at the rabbit, then at her.

“Interesting.”

“And Dean is his advisor.”

Yichen laughed again.

“What about the others?”

“The pink cat is his younger sister. The shark is his bodyguard. The bear is... His friend.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Quite a complicated family.”

“Very.”

When they reached home, Xiaoran arranged the toys on the sofa.

Little Master sat in the middle.

Dean was placed beside him.

The pink cat and bear were arranged on either side, while the blue shark was positioned slightly behind them.

Yichen stood in the doorway, watching her work.

She stepped back.

Examined the arrangement, then moved Dean a little to the left.

“Better.”

Yichen smiled.

“Are they settled?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He walked toward her and slipped his arms around her waist.

“Did you have fun?”

She leaned back against him.

“Very much.”

“Even though you lost most of the games?”

She turned her head.

“I did not lose most of the games.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You didn’t?”

“I won Dean.”

“Yes.”

“And I nearly beat the ring toss.”

“Yes.”

“And I got the rabbit.”

“With my help.”

She turned around in his arms.

“That still counts.”

“Of course.”

She looked at him, then reached up and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you for tonight.”

He brushed his thumb against her waist.

“You’re welcome.”

She glanced at the toys.

“Actually, I think we should go to another night market next time.”

Yichen laughed.

“Another one?”

“Yes.”

“More games?”

“Yes.”

“More prizes?”

She nodded.

Something in his face eased.

“All right.”

She looked pleased.

“Next time, I want to win something myself,” she said, completely serious.

He lowered his head slightly.

“Then I’ll teach you.”

She considered that.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I take a long time?”

He laughed under his breath.

“We have time.”

Her expression softened.

Then she reached up and kissed him properly.

When she pulled away, he was smiling.

“Is that my reward?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“For helping you win the rabbit?”

“For being my teammate.”

He considered her.

Then glanced at the little collection on the sofa.

“Then I suppose we make a good team.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“The best.”

Yichen kissed her.

And just before they went to bed, Xiaoran returned to the living room to adjust Little Master’s blue ribbon.

Yichen watched her from the hallway.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“He’s already wearing it correctly.”

She frowned.

“I know. I just wanted to make sure.”

Yichen smiled.

“Goodnight, Manager Lin.”

She grinned.

“Goodnight.”

He turned toward the bedroom, then heard her voice again.

“Yichen?”

He looked back.

“Yes?”

“Do you think Little Master needs a girlfriend?”

Yichen stared at her, then laughed.

“Let’s discuss that tomorrow.”

chapters.desc: She has been stealing his shirts since December. Tonight it is the new dark blue one, and he reads the same paragraph four times.
chapters.title: His Shirt, Again
chapters.epigraph: “You look like you’re at home.”
chapters.content:
The first time Xiaoran wore one of Yichen’s shirts around the apartment, he hadn’t thought much of it.

Well, that wasn’t entirely true.

He had noticed.

It was his white shirt, off the back of the bedroom chair, on the December afternoon they never made it to the convenience store. She had kept it.

Then she had discovered that his other shirts were comfortable too, and three months later she took them whenever she pleased.

Tonight was no different.

Yichen was in the living room, reviewing a document on his tablet after dinner. He heard the bedroom door open, followed by the familiar sound of Xiaoran walking across the wooden floor.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you know where my hair clip is?”

He looked up.

And stopped.

She was wearing his dark blue shirt.

This wasn’t the white one, or any of the older shirts he had already given up to her unofficial wardrobe. It was a relatively new shirt, one he had worn only twice. The sleeves were too long for her, so she had folded them twice. The collar sat loosely around her neck, and the first few buttons were undone because she had apparently decided that fastening them properly was unnecessary.

Her hair was still slightly damp, falling over one shoulder.

She was looking at him expectantly.

Yichen didn’t answer immediately.

Xiaoran glanced down at herself.

“What?”

He blinked once.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He set his tablet down.

“You’re wearing my shirt.”

She looked down again, as if this were new information.

“Oh. This one?”

“Yes.”

“It’s comfortable.”

“I see.”

She walked closer, still searching through the little basket of hair accessories she had brought from the bedroom.

“Have you seen my hair clip?”

“What color?”

“White. The little flower one.”

He watched her search through the basket.

“On the dressing table.”

“I already looked there.”

“Then beside the mirror.”

She turned.

Found it.

“Oh!”

She picked it up triumphantly, then turned back toward him.

“Thank you!”

Yichen nodded.

She clipped her hair back, seemingly satisfied, and wandered toward the kitchen.

He watched her go.

Then he looked down at his tablet.

He read the same sentence three times.

It was becoming a problem.

Not because he disliked seeing her in his clothes. Quite the opposite. He liked it far more than he had any intention of admitting.

There was something about seeing Xiaoran in an ordinary piece of his wardrobe that affected him in a way he found difficult to explain. The shirt looked good on her, but it was the casualness of it that got him. The fact that she wore it without thinking, as if his things had naturally become hers to borrow.

She wasn’t dressing up for him. She wasn’t trying to get his attention.

She was wandering around their home, wearing his shirt, looking for her hair clip.

And somehow that was worse.

A few minutes later, she returned with a glass of water.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Can you help me with something?”

He looked up.

“What is it?”

She held out her phone.

“Look at this dress. Do you think I should buy it?”

He took the phone.

The dress was pale yellow, with a delicate neckline and a slightly fitted waist.

“It’s pretty.”

“Right? But I’m not sure about the color.”

“I think it would suit you.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She leaned over his shoulder to look at the picture again.

“Maybe I should get it in blue instead.”

Yichen glanced at the screen, then at her.

She was standing close enough that her shoulder brushed his. The loose collar of his shirt shifted slightly as she leaned forward, and a few strands of damp hair slipped against his arm.

He looked back at the dress.

“Either color.”

Xiaoran frowned.

“That’s not helpful.”

She took her phone back and scrolled through the other colors.

“What about this one?”

He looked.

“Pretty.”

“And this?”

“Also pretty.”

She lowered her phone.

“You’re not paying attention.”

Yichen looked at her.

“I am.”

“Then tell me which one you like best.”

He held her gaze.

Then he said, calmly, “The one you’re wearing.”

Xiaoran blinked.

She looked down at her shirt, then back at him.

“This?”

“Yes.”

“It’s not even mine.”

“I know.”

She smiled, amused.

“You’re so strange.”

He reached for her hand.

He crooked a finger at her.

She stepped closer.

Yichen drew her gently between his knees, where he was sitting on the sofa. His hands settled at her waist, and he looked up at her.

Xiaoran’s smile became curious.

“You’re doing that again. Looking at me like you have something to say.”

He considered her.

Then he asked, “Do you know why I keep looking at you?”

She smiled.

“Because I stole your shirt?”

“That’s one reason.”

Her eyebrows lifted.

“One?”

“Would you like the full explanation?”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Yes. Please enlighten me.”

Yichen’s thumbs moved lightly against her waist.

“First, that’s my shirt.”

“I know.”

“You’ve rolled the sleeves unevenly.”

She looked at her arms.

“They’re fine.”

“The left one is higher.”

“Nobody cares.”

“I do.”

She laughed and tried to pull her arm away, but he kept her close.

“Second, you’ve left three buttons undone,” he said.

Xiaoran glanced down.

“Because it’s more comfortable.”

“I know.”

“And?”

“And I find it distracting.”

Her laughter softened.

Yichen’s expression was calm, but there was something unmistakably different in his eyes now. He wasn’t making an exaggerated effort to tease her. He was telling her something he had apparently been keeping to himself.

She tilted her head.

“How distracting?”

He looked at her for a second.

“Enough that I’ve read the same paragraph four times.”

Xiaoran’s lips parted, then a smile slowly spread across her face.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She looked toward his tablet.

“Because of me?”

“Who else?”

She giggled.

“You’re exaggerating.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re a professional basketball player. You can concentrate under pressure.”

“On a basketball court.”

“So?”

“So this is a different situation.”

She laughed harder.

Yichen watched her, his expression softening.

He liked that laugh. He liked how quickly her amusement appeared, how her eyes narrowed slightly when she was trying not to laugh too much, and how she sometimes looked at him as if she couldn’t believe he had said something so straightforward.

He lifted one hand and tucked her hair behind her ear.

“Third,” he said.

Xiaoran immediately looked at him.

“There’s a third?”

“Yes.”

“What is it?”

He paused.

Then his gaze moved over her face, lingering before returning to her eyes.

“You look comfortable.”

She blinked.

Yichen’s voice was quieter now.
