“You wear my clothes like you’ve always belonged in them. You walk around the apartment, make yourself a drink, complain about work, ask me where your things are. You don’t even think about it.”

Xiaoran’s smile gradually faded into something gentler.

He brushed his thumb along her side.

“I like seeing you like that.”

She didn’t say anything.

Then she looked down at the shirt again.

“I didn’t know you liked it so much.”

“I thought that was obvious.”

“No, it wasn’t.”

“I’ve been looking at you all evening.”

“Maybe I thought you were looking at my hair.”

“Your hair?”

She nodded.

“Because it’s wet.”

Yichen stared at her.

Then he laughed.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“How did you arrive at that conclusion?”

She giggled embarrassed.

“I don’t know!”

He gently pulled her closer.

“Over here.”

“I’m already here.”

“Closer.”

She leaned forward, placing her hands on his shoulders.

Yichen looked up at her, and the corner of his mouth lifted.

“Do you know what else?”

She shook her head.

“I think you should stop borrowing my shirts.”

Her eyes widened.

“What?”

“They’re becoming difficult to keep in the wardrobe,” he said, once he’d let her react.

Xiaoran’s expression immediately changed.

She looked offended.

“Why?”

“Because you keep taking them.”

“That’s not a reason!”

“I have fewer shirts than I used to.”

“You have so many!”

“Apparently not enough.”

She folded her arms.

“Fine. I’ll stop.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted.

“Will you?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

He released her waist.

Xiaoran stared at him.

He picked up his tablet again.

She waited.

He returned to his document.

Her eyes narrowed.

That wasn’t how this was supposed to go.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You really want me to stop?”

He looked up.

A faint smile appeared.

“Do you want me to say no?”

She pressed her lips together.

He put the tablet aside again.

“Xiaoran, you can wear whatever you like. My shirts included.”

“Then why did you say that?”

“Because I thought you might want to know what happens when you wear them.”

She blinked at him.

“What happens?”

He reached out, catching her hand and drawing her closer again.

“I lose a considerable amount of concentration.”

She laughed, her cheeks turning pink.

“That’s your problem.”

“Apparently.”

“You should learn to control yourself.”

“I’ve been trying.”

His answer was so immediate that she stopped laughing.

Yichen looked at her.

Then his smile turned a little more pronounced.

“Would you like me to demonstrate?”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened.

“Demonstrate what?”

“How much concentration I have left.”

She gave a small, suspicious laugh.

“You’re not going to do anything.”

“Am I?”

He gently drew her down until she was standing close against him, her hands resting on his shoulders.

Then he kissed her.

It began, his hand resting at her waist while hers slipped into his hair. Xiaoran had expected a quick kiss, perhaps followed by another teasing remark, but Yichen lingered. He kissed her again when she smiled against his lips, and she found herself forgetting the dress on her phone and the hair clip she had spent several minutes searching for.

When he finally pulled back, she was still leaning toward him.

He brushed his thumb against her cheek.

“Still think I’m exaggerating?”

Xiaoran looked at him.

Her cheeks were warm.

“...Maybe a little.”

Yichen smiled.

“All right.”

She remained between his knees, looking down at him.

Then she grinned.

“Actually, I think I understand now.”

“Understand what?”

“Why you like me wearing your shirts.”

He waited.

She leaned down and whispered, “Because I look like your girlfriend.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“That’s not quite it.”

She blinked.

“Then what?”

He looked at her before answering.

“You look like you’re at home.”

Her smile became smaller.

More genuine.

Yichen reached up and pressed a kiss into her hair.

“And I like that.”

Xiaoran stood there for another moment, then bent down to wrap her arms around his neck.

He held her, his cheek resting against her shoulder.

After a while, she murmured, “Can I keep this one?”

He glanced at the dark blue shirt she was wearing.

“You’ve already claimed it.”

“So that’s a yes?”

“Yes.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Good. I like this one.”

“I noticed.”

She pulled back slightly.

“Should I wear another one tomorrow?”

Yichen looked at her.

He could have said no.

He could have reminded her that he had work to do, training footage to review, and a perfectly reasonable intention to spend the evening concentrating.

Instead, he brushed his fingers along the loose collar of the shirt.

“That’s up to you.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“You’re hoping I will.”

He gave her that slow, unmistakably amused smile.

“I wouldn’t complain.”

She laughed, then kissed his cheek.

“Then I’ll borrow another one.”

“Of course.”

“And maybe the white one.”

“All right.”

“The gray one too.”

He met her eyes.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“At this rate, I’ll have to start borrowing your clothes.”

She burst into laughter.

“You’re too big for my clothes!”

“Then I suppose I’ll have to buy more.”

She kissed him again, delighted.

Yichen let her, his hand settling at her waist.

A few minutes later, she finally wandered toward the bedroom to put her phone away.

Yichen picked up his tablet.

He looked at the document, then at the bedroom doorway.

He could still hear her humming as she moved around, completely unaware that she had just ruined his plans for a productive evening.

He smiled to himself and added two shirts to the basket on his phone, both in his size.

chapters.desc: A weekend in Suzhou, an umbrella he holds too far toward her, and every puddle in the old town.
chapters.title: A Rainy Night in Suzhou
chapters.epigraph: “Then we’ll come again when it rains.”
chapters.content:
The rain began just as they reached the old town, on the first evening of their weekend in Suzhou.

Xiaoran stood beneath the entrance of a small riverside street, looking at the sudden curtain of water falling from the sky.

A moment ago, the weather had been perfectly pleasant. The sky was cloudy, but nothing concerning. They had even debated whether to bring an umbrella when leaving the hotel.

Yichen had brought one.

Xiaoran had said it was unnecessary.

Now, she was looking at the rain with the expression of someone who had just been personally betrayed by the weather.

“Well.”

Yichen opened the umbrella.

“Well?”

She turned toward him.

“I think the weather forecast lied.”

He glanced at the rain.

“It said there would be showers.”

“Yes, but I thought it meant small showers. Like a little drizzle. Something romantic.”

He looked at the heavy rain hitting the stone pavement.

“Very romantic.”

“Don’t be sarcastic.”

He smiled and held the umbrella over her.

“Come on.”

They stepped onto the narrow stone walkway.

Suzhou looked different in the rain.

The white walls and dark tiled roofs seemed softer beneath the gray sky. Water streamed from the curved edges of traditional rooftops, while red lanterns glowed warmly along the narrow streets. The canals reflected the lights of restaurants and old buildings, their surfaces constantly disturbed by raindrops.

There were fewer people outside now.

The occasional passerby hurried beneath umbrellas, and the smell of rain mixed with the fragrance of freshly cooked food drifting from nearby restaurants.

Xiaoran loved it.

She walked slowly, looking at everything.

“Yichen, look.”

He followed her gaze.

A small wooden boat was moving along the canal.

“Pretty.”

“Very pretty.”

She looked at the reflections in the water, then at the old bridge ahead.

“Can we go there?”

“Of course.”

She took his hand.

And then, without warning, stepped directly into a puddle.

Splash.

Yichen looked down.

Xiaoran looked down too.

Neither spoke.

Then she lifted her foot.

“...Oh.”

He glanced at her shoes.

“Careful.”

“I didn’t see it.”

“Apparently.”

She met his eyes.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

His expression suggested otherwise.

She continued walking.

Three minutes later, she stepped into another puddle.

This time, Yichen stopped before she could take the next step.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Look down.”

She looked.

There was a puddle directly in front of her.

She stepped around it.

“See? I can do it.”

“Excellent.”

She gave him a satisfied smile.

Then she stepped into a third puddle.

Yichen closed his eyes.

Xiaoran burst out laughing.

The umbrella wasn’t small.

It wasn’t designed to accommodate Xiaoran’s habit of walking wherever she wanted while Yichen tried to keep both of them dry.

She wandered toward the edge of the walkway to look at a shop window.

Then she stopped to admire a lantern.

Then she moved closer to the canal to watch the boats.

Every time she moved, Yichen adjusted the umbrella.

At first, he managed.

Eventually, the rain began reaching his shoulder.

Xiaoran noticed when they passed beneath a row of old buildings.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Your shoulder is wet.”

He glanced down.

“A little.”

She frowned.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“You were looking at the shops.”

She looked at the umbrella, then at him.

“You’re holding it too far toward me.”

He raised an eyebrow.

She reached up and tried to adjust his hand.

The umbrella shifted.

A few drops landed on her hair.

She gasped.

Yichen laughed.

“Careful.”

“You’re making it worse!”

He took her hand away from the umbrella handle.

“Let me.”

She looked at his shoulder again.

“You’re going to get wet.”

“I’m fine.”

“That’s not fair.”

He looked down at her.

“What’s not fair?”

“You always do this.”

“Do what?”

“Give me all the dry space.”

He smiled.

“You’re smaller.”

“That doesn’t mean I don’t get wet.”

He glanced at her damp hair.

“You’re already getting wet.”

She looked offended.

“That’s because of the rain.”

“I see.”

She folded her arms.

He laughed, then moved the umbrella closer to the middle.

“There. Better?”

“Yes.”

He held out his free hand.

He held out his hand.

She stepped closer.

He placed his arm around her shoulders, drawing her against his side.

The umbrella seemed much more effective.

Xiaoran looked up at him.

“Oh.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Comfortable?”

“Very.”

They stopped at a small shop selling traditional Suzhou pastries.

Xiaoran immediately became interested.

The shop was warm and brightly lit, with glass displays filled with delicate pastries, small cakes, and local sweets.

She stood in front of the counter, examining everything.

“What’s that one?”

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Which?”

“That little white one.”

He looked at the display.

“Do you want to try it?”

“And that one.”

“All right.”

“And maybe the green one.”

He met her eyes.

“Are you hungry?”

She considered the question.

“Not particularly.”

Something in his face eased.

“Then why are we buying three?”

“Because we’re in Suzhou.”

“Reasonable.”

She turned toward him with a pleased expression.

He ordered several pastries, and they found a small table near the window.

Outside, the rain continued.

Xiaoran took a bite of one pastry and immediately looked delighted.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“This is good.”

He took a bite from the piece she offered.

“Not bad.”

She looked at him.

“Not bad?”

“Very good.”

“Better.”

She broke off another small piece and held it toward him.

He leaned forward and took it.

Then she noticed a little bit of pastry filling near the corner of his mouth.

“Wait.”

He paused.

She reached over and brushed it away with her thumb.

“You’re messy.”

He turned to her.

She wiped her thumb with a napkin.

Yichen watched her.

Then he leaned closer and kissed her cheek.

She blinked.

“What was that for?”

“Thank you.”

“For cleaning your face?”

“Yes.”

She laughed.

“You’re welcome.”

By the time they left the pastry shop, the rain had become heavier.

The street lamps had come on, and the old town was glowing against the darkening sky.

They walked along the canal, sharing the umbrella.

Xiaoran had become unusually quiet.

Yichen glanced down.

“Tired?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Cold?”

“A little.”

He tightened his arm around her shoulders.

“Better?”

She nodded.

They walked past a small bridge where several red lanterns hung above the canal.

Xiaoran stopped.

“Can we take a picture?”

Yichen looked at the bridge.

“Here?”

She nodded.

He passed the umbrella to her and took out his phone.

“Stand there.”

She moved beneath the lanterns.

The rain was falling behind her, the warm lights reflecting in the water. Her hair had become slightly damp, and she was holding the umbrella with both hands.

Yichen raised his phone.

“Look here.”

That made her grin.

He took a photograph, then another.

“One more.”

She tilted her head.

“Like this?”

“Yes.”

He took another.

She immediately walked toward him.

“Let me see.”

He showed her the photographs.

Her eyes brightened.

“Oh, I love this one!”

She pointed at the second picture.

Yichen looked at it.

She was smiling naturally, with the lanterns behind her and the canal reflected in the background.

“Good.”

“Can you send it to me?”

“I’ll send all of them.”

She turned to him.

“You’re so useful.”

He laughed.

“Thank you.”

She took his phone and held it up.

“Now one of you.”

He stood beside her.

She adjusted the angle, making sure the lanterns were visible.

“Come closer.”

He moved closer.

“Closer.”

He put his arm around her waist.

She smiled.

“Good.”

Just before she took the photograph, Yichen turned his face toward her.

She looked at him instead of the camera.

The picture captured both of them smiling at each other beneath the umbrella.

Xiaoran looked at it.

Then her expression softened.

“I like this one more.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re looking at me.”

He glanced at the picture, then at her.

“Then keep it.”

They continued walking until they reached a quieter stretch of the canal.

The shops were beginning to close, and the sound of rain had become more noticeable.

Xiaoran was still looking around when Yichen felt her hand slip slightly in his.

He looked down.

She was walking with her attention fixed on a small wooden boat passing beneath the bridge.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Watch your step.”

She looked down.

There was another puddle.

She stepped around it carefully.

Yichen smiled.

“Progress.”

She gave him a proud look.

“I’ve learned.”

Then she turned to look at a shop on the opposite side of the street and stepped directly into the edge of a much larger puddle.

Splash.

She stopped.

Yichen looked at her shoes, then at her face.

She slowly turned toward him.

“...Don’t.”

He pressed his lips together.

She narrowed her eyes.

“Don’t you dare.”

His shoulders moved.

He was laughing.

“Yichen!”

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not sorry!”

He laughed harder.

She turned away dramatically.

“Fine. I’ll walk by myself.”

He caught her hand before she could take another step.

He opened his arms.

She looked back.

He lifted his arm slightly, opening the space beside him.

“Under here.”

She hesitated for half a second, then moved closer.

He wrapped his arm around her shoulders, pulling her snugly against his side.

“Now stay here.”

She looked up at him.

“Why?”

“Because apparently, you can’t walk without finding every puddle in Suzhou.”

She laughed.

“I don’t do it on purpose!”

“I know.”

He adjusted the umbrella above them.

“And because it’s raining.”

She slipped her arm around his waist.

“Then you should hold me tighter.”

He looked down.

“Like this?”

He drew her closer until her cheek rested against his shoulder.

That made her grin.

“Yes.”

They continued along the canal like that.

The umbrella was now almost unnecessary between them. His arm sheltered her from the rain, while she stayed tucked against his side, occasionally looking up at the old buildings and lanterns.

After a while, she spoke.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you like Suzhou?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He looked ahead.

“It’s peaceful.”

“Me too.”

A few steps later, she said, “I think I like rainy Suzhou more.”

He glanced down at her.

She laughed.

“Interesting.”

She lifted her face.

“Because I get to walk like this.”

He held her gaze.

Then his expression softened.

He bent his head and kissed her hair.

“Then we’ll come again when it rains.”

Her mouth tipped up.

When they finally returned to the hotel, Xiaoran’s shoes were damp, the ends of her hair were slightly wet, and Yichen’s right shoulder was noticeably darker from the rain.

She noticed immediately.

“Look at your shirt.”

He glanced down.

“It’s fine.”

“No, it’s wet.”

“A little.”

She looked guilty.

“Because of me.”

He took the umbrella from her and closed it.

“Because of the rain.”

“But—”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

He reached over and gently tucked a damp strand of hair behind her ear.

“I had a good evening.”

“Really?”

“Very good.”

She smiled.

Then she looked down at their shoes.

“Although I think I should stop stepping into puddles.”

Yichen laughed.

“That would be a good start.”

She hit his arm lightly.

He caught her hand and brought it to his lips.

“Come on. Let’s get you warm.”

Later, after showering and changing into comfortable clothes, they sat together near the hotel window.

The rain was still falling outside.

Xiaoran was wearing Yichen’s shirt, her legs tucked beneath a blanket. Yichen sat beside her with one arm along the back of the sofa.

She was scrolling through the photographs from the evening.

“Look at this one.”

He leaned closer.

It was the photograph beneath the lanterns.

She enlarged it.

“Look at your shoulder. It’s completely wet.”

He glanced at the photograph.

“Yes.”

“And my hair.”

“A little.”

She held his gaze.

“You should have told me earlier.”

He smiled.

“You would have worried.”

“Of course I would.”

“I know.”

She leaned into his shoulder.

After a moment, she showed him the photograph of them looking at each other.

“This is my favorite.”

He looked at it.

“Mine too.”

Her mouth tipped up.

Then she opened the camera and took a photograph of their hands resting together beneath the blanket.

She posted it with a simple caption.

Rainy evening in Suzhou. Slightly wet shoes, too many puddles, and the best company.

Yichen read it over her shoulder.

“Too many puddles?”

“Many.”

He smiled and kissed her temple.

“Next time, I’ll bring a bigger umbrella.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“No.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“No?”

She nestled closer against him.

“This one is fine.”

He looked down at her.

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I like having to stand close.”

“Is that so?”

She nodded.

He leaned down, his voice quiet.

“Then perhaps I should keep bringing the small one.”

Xiaoran immediately blushed.

“You’re doing that on purpose again. Being smug.”

He laughed and pulled her closer, and outside the rain kept falling on the lake.

chapters.desc: The morning after the rain, she wakes before him and has breakfast set out on the balcony over the lake.
chapters.title: The Hotel Breakfast Date
chapters.epigraph: “I wanted to have breakfast with you without needing to go anywhere afterward.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Xiaoran noticed when she woke up was that the bed was too comfortable.

The second thing was that Yichen’s arm was heavy across her waist.

She opened her eyes slowly.

The hotel room was still dim, curtains drawn almost completely, with only a thin line of morning light slipping through the gap. The city outside was beginning to wake, but the room remained quiet, cool, and wonderfully peaceful.

Yichen was sleeping beside her.

He was lying on his back, one arm resting above his head, the other draped over her. His hair was slightly messy, and the blanket had slipped down to his waist.

Xiaoran watched him.

He looked different when he was asleep. Not dramatically different, but softer. The usual alertness in his eyes was gone, his expression relaxed, his breathing slow and even.

She smiled.

Then she remembered something.

Breakfast.

Her eyes moved toward the bedside clock. It wasn’t even seven.

She had specifically asked the hotel concierge the previous evening about private in-room breakfast arrangements. She had even spent fifteen minutes looking through the breakfast menu, comparing dishes and deciding what Yichen might like.

She had wanted to surprise him.

Carefully, she lifted his arm from her waist.

He stirred.

“Where are you going?”

Xiaoran froze.

His eyes were still closed.

“Nowhere.”

His hand found her waist again.

“Mm.”

She waited.

A few seconds later, his breathing settled.

She gently removed his arm once more.

This time, she succeeded.

She slipped out of bed, collected her phone and the hotel room-service menu, and tiptoed toward the balcony.

Before closing the bedroom door, she looked back.

Yichen hadn’t moved.

She smiled to herself.

Operation breakfast was officially underway.

Their room was a corner suite above the lake on the modern side of Suzhou.

The bedroom opened into a spacious living area, and beyond that was a private balcony with a small dining table. From there, the skyline stretched across the horizon, with the lake reflecting the pale morning light.

Xiaoran had noticed it immediately when they checked in the afternoon before, while the sky was still dry.

She had even told Yichen that the balcony was her favorite part of the room.

He had replied that he thought the view was nice too.

She suspected he hadn’t understood how much she liked it.

Now, she was determined to make use of it.

She called room service.

“Good morning. I’d like to order breakfast for two, please.”

The staff member greeted her warmly and asked what she would like.

Xiaoran opened the menu.

“Could I have the eggs Benedict, a fruit platter, and the French toast? And the smoked salmon platter. Actually, could I have the pancakes too?”

The staff member confirmed.

“And coffee?”

“One black coffee, please. And one iced latte.”

She glanced toward the bedroom.

“Could you make the latte less sweet?”

After confirming the order, she added one final request.

“Would it be possible to arrange everything on the balcony? The weather looks nice this morning.”

The staff member assured her they could.

Xiaoran thanked them and ended the call.

Then she looked at the order summary.

It was quite a lot of food.

She considered it, then decided it was fine.

They were on holiday.

There was no reason to be sensible about breakfast.

When Yichen finally woke up, the first thing he noticed was the empty space beside him.

He opened his eyes.

It was past seven.

He sat up, ran a hand through his hair, and looked toward the bathroom.

Empty.

Then he noticed the bedroom door was slightly open.

He could hear a faint sound from the living area.

A voice.

His girlfriend was talking to someone.

He got out of bed, pulled on the hotel robe, and walked toward the sound.

When he reached the living area, he stopped.

Xiaoran was standing near the balcony, arranging something on the table.

She had changed into a soft cream-colored dress, her hair loosely tied back. There were two glasses on the table, a small vase of flowers, and a few plates already being arranged by the hotel staff.

She was speaking to one of the staff members.

“Thank you so much. It looks lovely.”

The staff member smiled and left.

Xiaoran turned around.

And saw him.

Her face brightened.

“You’re awake!”

Yichen leaned against the doorway.

“Apparently.”

She looked him up and down.

“Why are you wearing the robe?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I was sleeping.”

“Right.”

He glanced at the balcony, then at the table, then back at her.

“What’s all this?”

She clasped her hands behind her back.

“Breakfast.”

“I can see that.”

“Surprise.”

He looked at the arrangement again.

The table was set for two, with breakfast dishes, fresh juice, coffee, and a little vase of flowers in the middle. The balcony doors were open, letting in the cool morning air.

Beyond it, the city was bathed in soft golden light.

Yichen’s expression softened.

“You arranged all this?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“When?”

“Earlier.”

“What time?”

“Not important.”

He looked at the clock.

“Xiaoran.”

“Six something.”

“You woke up at six?”

“Six thirty.”

He gave her a look.

“Why?”

She shrugged.

“I wanted to.”

He walked toward her.

He reached for her.

She stepped closer.

He placed one hand at her waist and kissed her, briefly.

“Good morning.”

That made her grin.

“Good morning.”

Then he kissed her cheek.

“Thank you.”

She looked pleased.

“Do you like it?”

He glanced at the table, then at the view, then back at her.

“I do.”

“Really?”

“Very much.”

She grinned.

“Good. Because I ordered too much food.”

He laughed.

They sat down to breakfast.

Xiaoran had chosen the seat facing the city, while Yichen sat opposite her.

For a while, neither spoke much.

The morning was beautiful.

The city was still relatively quiet, the sunlight gradually brightening the buildings in the distance. A few boats moved across the lake, and the breeze carried the faint sounds of traffic from far below.

Xiaoran poured coffee into his cup.

“Here.”

“Thank you.”

She passed him the eggs Benedict.

He looked at the spread.

“How many people are we feeding?”

“Two.”

“Are you sure?”

She nodded.

“We can finish it.”

He looked at the French toast, pancakes, fruit, salmon, and eggs.

“Very confident.”

She picked up a strawberry.

“We’re on holiday.”

“That’s your justification?”

“Yes.”

He smiled and took a sip of coffee.

It was exactly how he liked it.

Black, no sugar.

He met her eyes.

“You remembered.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Of course.”

He didn’t say anything more, but his eyes stayed on her.

She noticed.

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Can’t I?”

She smiled.

“You can.”

He reached across the table and brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“Thank you for arranging this.”

She tilted her head.

“It’s just breakfast.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you thanking me so seriously?”

“Because you woke up early to do it.”

She smiled a little shy.

“I wanted to surprise you.”

“You did.”

She looked satisfied.

Then she pointed at his plate.

“Eat your eggs before they get cold.”

He laughed.

“Yes, Manager Lin.”

After breakfast, Xiaoran decided that they should take photographs.

Naturally.

She took several pictures of the table, the flowers, the view, and her coffee.

Then she took a photograph of Yichen.

He was leaning back in his chair, one hand around his coffee cup, looking toward the skyline.

The morning light fell across his face.

She took the picture, then another.

Yichen turned his head.

“How many are you taking?”

“Not many.”

He looked at her phone.

“That’s at least six.”

“You’re handsome.”

He laughed.

“Is that the reason?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the photographs, then smiled.

“I like this one.”

He held out his hand.

“Let me see.”

She passed him the phone.

He looked at the picture.

It was a candid photograph. He hadn’t been looking at the camera, and his expression was relaxed.

He turned to her.

“Not bad.”

“Not bad?”

“Good.”

She eyed him.

“You’re supposed to say it’s beautiful.”

He looked at the photograph again, then back at her.

“It’s beautiful.”

That made her grin.

“Better.”

He handed her the phone.

“Take one with me.”

She stood up immediately.

“Okay!”

Yichen pulled out the chair beside him.

“Sit here.”

She walked around the table and sat beside him.

He slipped an arm around her waist, drawing her closer.

She raised the phone.

“Look at the camera.”

He did.

Her mouth tipped up.

“Again.”

“Why?”

“This one isn’t good.”

He glanced at the screen.

“You look fine.”

“I want another.”

He leaned closer, pressing his cheek against hers.

“Like this?”

“Yes.”

She took the photograph.

Then, just as she lowered the phone, Yichen turned and kissed her cheek.

She laughed.

“Wait!”

He kissed the other cheek.

“Yichen!”

“What?”

“I’m trying to take pictures!”

“Then take another.”

She looked at him.

He was smiling.

That particular slow, amused smile that always made her forget what she had been trying to say.

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re doing it on purpose. That face.”

He leaned closer.

“Which face?”

She looked away.

“Never mind.”

His smile deepened.

“All right.”

She immediately turned back.

“Don’t smile like that!”

He laughed and kissed her temple.

They didn’t leave the balcony immediately.

Instead, they moved their chairs closer together.

Xiaoran tucked herself against his shoulder, holding a glass of juice while Yichen looked through the photographs on her phone.

He paused at one particular picture.

It was a photograph of her.

She was sitting across the table, looking toward the city, with one hand resting beside her coffee cup. She hadn’t noticed him taking it.

He looked at it for a while.

“What’s this?”

She glanced at the screen.

“Oh.”

He tilted the phone slightly.

“When did you take it?”

“When you were looking at the view.”

He looked at the photograph again.

“You look happy.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“I was.”

“Good.”

She watched him.

Then asked, “Do you want to know why I planned this?”

He put the phone down.

“Tell me.”

She played with the edge of her glass.

“Because we always have breakfast together, but usually it’s just before work. Sometimes we’re rushing. Sometimes you’re checking your training schedule, and I’m checking my emails.”

Yichen listened.

“And even when we’re having breakfast at home, one of us usually has something to do afterward.”

She looked toward the skyline.

“I wanted to have breakfast with you without needing to go anywhere afterward.”

He was quiet.

Then his hand found hers.

“That’s a good reason.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I thought so.”

He brought her hand to his lips and kissed her knuckles.

“Then let’s stay here a little longer.”

She turned toward him.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“But don’t you want to go sightseeing?”

“We can go later.”

“Or shopping?”

“Later.”

“Or explore the hotel?”

That got a smile out of him.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I’m sitting with you. I’m not in a hurry.”

She met his eyes.

Then her smile softened.

“Okay.”

Eventually, the breakfast dishes were cleared.

The flowers remained on the table.

Xiaoran was reluctant to leave the balcony, so Yichen suggested they take a walk around the hotel grounds before going out.

She agreed, but only after insisting that they take one more photograph.

This time, she stood in front of the balcony doors while Yichen held the phone.

She was still adjusting her dress when he took the first one.

She walked toward him.

“Give me the phone.”

He raised it slightly.

He crooked a finger at her.

She stopped in front of him.

He took one last photograph.

Then he lowered the phone.

“Beautiful.”

She smiled.

“Thank you.”

He put the phone down and drew her closer by the waist.

“Although I think I prefer this.”

“Which?”

He kissed her.

She smiled against his lips.

When he pulled away, she looked at him with a little surprise.

“What was that for?”

“For breakfast.”

She laughed.

“That’s a very generous tip.”

“I thought so.”

Later that afternoon, Xiaoran posted three photographs.

The first was the breakfast spread overlooking the city. The second was Yichen holding a coffee cup, looking out at the skyline.

The third was a photograph of them together, her cheek pressed against his.

Her caption was simple.

An early morning, a slow breakfast, and my favorite view.

Yichen saw the post while they were waiting for the elevator.

He looked at her phone.

“Your favorite view?”

“Yes.”

He looked toward the elevator doors, then back at her.

“Which one?”

She gave him an innocent look.

“The city, obviously.”

He smiled.

“Obviously.”

The elevator doors opened.

She walked inside, still smiling.

Just before the doors closed, Yichen caught her hand and pulled her gently toward him.

“Although. I think I know which view you meant,” he said, lowering his voice.

Xiaoran looked up.

His expression was calm, but the corner of his mouth had lifted.

She immediately blushed.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed and kissed her temple.

“What?”

“You’re getting too confident.”

He slipped his hand into hers.

“Come on. Let’s go.”

Xiaoran was already planning the next breakfast before the elevator reached the lobby.

chapters.desc: The rain has gone. On their second day in Suzhou the gardens open early, and she has her camera.
chapters.title: Suzhou, the Second Day
chapters.epigraph: “But I like seeing what you remember.”
chapters.content:
The rain had gone by the time they came down from breakfast.

Overnight it had rinsed the whole of Suzhou and left, and what it had left behind was proper spring sunshine: wide and warm, lying across the hotel lobby in golden patches and turning the wet pavement outside into glass.

Xiaoran stopped at the revolving door.

“Is it really sunny?”

Yichen, who had checked the weather at six while she slept, and again over coffee while she photographed the coffee, held the door for her. “Look.”

Upstairs, over the last of breakfast, she had announced that she intended to spend the rest of the morning in bed. He had said that was fine, and turned toward the window, and mentioned, to nobody in particular, that the gardens opened at half past seven and would be quiet until ten.

That was unfair.

She liked gardens. She liked old buildings, little bridges, flowers, and places where she could take photographs without having to hurry. She had been looking forward to this part of their trip since they booked it.

“You knew,” she said, on the steps.

“I knew.”

He was still carrying the umbrella from last night, out of habit. She looked at it, and then at the sky, and laughed, and he folded it under his arm without comment and held out his other hand.

By the time they arrived at the gardens, the morning had settled into something almost impossibly pretty.

The paths were still quiet, the trees were fresh with spring growth, and sunlight filtered through the branches in shifting patterns across the stone walkways.

Xiaoran stopped just beyond the entrance.

Yichen stopped beside her.

Neither said anything.

Then she took out her camera.

“Oh, this is lovely.”

He looked around.

“It is.”

She raised the camera and began taking photographs.

The garden was full of small details: the curved roof of a pavilion, the reflection of white walls in the pond, a stone bridge arching over clear water, and flowers growing beside a narrow path.

She photographed all of it.

Yichen stood a little behind her, letting her take her time.

After a while, she turned around.

She opened her arms.

He walked over.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. Stand there.”

She pointed toward a section of the path where sunlight fell across the stone.

He looked at the spot.

“Here?”

“Yes.”

He stood where she indicated.

She lifted her camera.

“Look this way.”

He did.

“Not at me. Look over there.”

He turned his head.

She took a photograph, then another.

“Good.”

He waited.

She lowered the camera and studied him.

“You’re looking at me.”

“Because you’re taking pictures.”

She smiled.

“You’re very obedient today.”

He raised an eyebrow.

She took another photograph.

This time, he was looking at the garden rather than the camera. His hands were in his coat pockets, his posture relaxed, sunlight catching the side of his face.

She checked the screen.

It was beautiful.

She met his eyes.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Don’t move.”

He stayed still.

She took one more photograph.

Then she lowered the camera.

“Okay.”

He walked back to her.

“Was that enough?”

“For now.”

He glanced at the screen.

“Can I see?”

She showed him.

He looked at the photographs.

“Not bad.”

“Not bad?”

“Very good.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Better.”

He handed the camera back.

“You’re enjoying yourself.”

“Obviously.”

He met her eyes.

Then he reached for her hand.

“Come on.”

They wandered through the gardens without following a strict route.

Xiaoran liked that.

There was no need to rush from one attraction to another or keep checking the time. They could stop whenever something caught her attention, walk slowly along the water, or sit on a bench because the sunlight felt nice.

At one point, she stopped beside a pond.

There were fish moving beneath the surface, their shadows passing over the pale stones.

She crouched down.

“Look.”

Yichen stood beside her.

“What?”

“That one is huge.”

He followed her finger.

“Not particularly.”

“Look at it.”

“I am.”

“Compared to the others.”

He studied the fish.

“All right. It’s bigger.”

She looked satisfied.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

She took a photograph, then another.

A few seconds later, she noticed his reflection in the water.

She turned her camera slightly.

Yichen was standing behind her, one hand resting loosely in his coat pocket, watching her with a quiet expression.

She took a picture.

He noticed the shutter.

“Was that me?”

“No.”

He turned to her.

That made her grin.

“Maybe.”

He bent slightly to look at the screen.

She pulled it away.

“Don’t.”

“Why?”

“It’s a candid.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t look.”

He laughed.

She stood and tucked her camera away.

“You’re ruining my artistic process.”

“Sorry.”

He offered her his hand.

She took it, and they continued along the path.

The garden was busier by midday.

More visitors had arrived, and the sunlight had grown warmer. Xiaoran had taken so many photographs that she had already started thinking about which ones she would keep.

They stopped at a small pavilion overlooking the water.

Xiaoran sat down on the wooden bench.

Yichen went to buy drinks from a nearby stall.

When he returned, he found her looking through her camera.

“How many have you taken?”

She accepted the drink.

“Don’t ask.”

“That many?”

“There’s no such thing as too many photographs.”

He sat beside her.

“How many are you actually going to keep?”

“Most of them.”

“Most?”

“Some are blurry.”

He looked at the screen.

She showed him a photograph of a flower, then another of the pond, then a picture of a little bridge.

He listened as she explained which ones she liked and why.

He didn’t pretend to know anything about photography. He asked questions, occasionally pointing out something she hadn’t noticed.

At one point, she showed him a photograph of a tree.

He studied it.

“Why this one?”

She looked at the screen.

“Because the sunlight is pretty.”

“That’s all?”

“That’s enough.”

He looked at her, then at the photograph again.

“You’re right.”

She smiled and leaned against his shoulder.

They sat there for a while, drinking and watching people walk along the path.

A young couple passed them, stopping to take a photograph together.

Xiaoran watched them.

Then she looked at Yichen.

“Should we take one?”

He turned toward her.

“Together?”

“Yes.”

He put his drink down.

“Give me your phone.”

She handed it over.

He stood and held the phone out, adjusting the angle.

Xiaoran moved closer, one arm slipping around his waist.

“Wait.”

He looked down.

“What?”

She fixed the collar of his coat.

“Your collar is folded.”

He waited patiently.

She straightened it, then looked at the screen.

“Okay.”

He took the photograph.

She immediately asked to see it.

It was a simple picture. The garden behind them, sunlight on their faces, her cheek close to his shoulder. Yichen’s expression was relaxed, and Xiaoran was smiling at the camera.

She studied it.

“I like this.”

“Good.”

“Take another.”

He did, then another.

By the fourth, she was laughing because he had started deliberately making his expression more serious.

“Stop.”

He held her gaze.

“What?”

“You’re doing that on purpose. That’s your passport face.”

He smiled.

“Should I smile?”

“Yes.”

He leaned down slightly.

“Like this?”

She looked at him.

The smile was small, warm, and familiar.

She forgot to answer.

Then she nodded.

“Yes.”

He took the photograph.

They found a quieter path after lunch.

The trees grew closer together there, and the sunlight came through in scattered patches. The air smelled of damp stone and flowers.

Xiaoran walked a little ahead, stopping every few steps to take another photograph.

Yichen followed at an easy pace.

She had been unusually quiet for the last few minutes.

He noticed.

“What are you thinking about?”

She turned.

“Nothing.”

He gave her a look.

She smiled.

“Really.”

He waited.

She walked back toward him.

“I was thinking that I like traveling with you.”

He studied her.

“Why?”

“Because you don’t rush me.”

He glanced at the camera hanging from her neck.

“You’re taking your time.”

“Exactly.”

She looked around the garden.

“Some people would get impatient. They’d want to see everything, take the main photographs, go to the next place.”

“And I don’t?”

“No.”

“Why?”

She considered it.

“Because you let me look at things.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“I like watching you look at things.”

“That’s strange.”

“Why?”

“Because I’m not doing anything.”

“You’re doing plenty.”

She looked at him, waiting.

He reached for her hand.

“You get excited over small things. You stop walking when you see a flower you like. You take three photographs of the same bridge because you can’t decide which angle is better. You tell me about things I would have walked past without noticing.”

That made her grin.

He said, “I don’t mind waiting.”

She looked down at their joined hands.

“You’re very patient.”

“With you.”

She looked up.

He was smiling.

“That sounded very romantic,” she said.

“It was meant to.”

She laughed and moved closer, slipping her arm through his.

They continued walking.

The afternoon became warmer.

They found a small tea shop near the garden and decided to rest before heading back.

Xiaoran sat by the window, her camera placed carefully beside her.

Yichen ordered tea and something sweet for them to share.

When he returned, she was looking at the photographs again.

He placed the tray down.

“Still reviewing?”

“Just choosing my favorites.”

“How many?”

“Twenty-three.”

He sat opposite her.

“That’s quite a few favorites.”

“Don’t judge me.”

“I’m not.”

She turned the camera toward him.

“Look at this one.”

It was a photograph of him walking across the stone bridge.

He hadn’t known she was taking it. His head was slightly turned, and the sunlight had caught the edge of his hair.

He studied it.

“That’s nice.”

“I know.”

She showed him another.

This one was of his hand holding hers as they walked, then another of their reflections in the pond.

He looked at the pictures.

“You’re keeping these?”

“Of course.”

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

Something in his face eased.

“Then I’ll have to remember this trip properly.”

She tilted her head.

“Why?”

“So I can recognize everything when you show me the photographs later.”

She laughed.

“You were here.”

“I know.”

“You’re supposed to remember it yourself.”

“I will.”

He reached across the table and turned her hand palm-up, brushing his thumb over her fingers.

“But I like seeing what you remember.”

Her expression softened.

She turned her hand and held his.

The tea shop seemed quiet around them.

Then she picked up a piece of pastry and held it toward him.

“Eat.”

He leaned forward and took a bite.

Her mouth tipped up.

“Good?”

“Yes.”

She took a bite herself.

They left the gardens when the afternoon sun began to soften.

On the way back, Xiaoran became quiet again, this time because she was tired.

Yichen noticed her steps slowing.

“Do you want to sit?”

She shook her head.

“Not yet.”

“Your feet hurt?”

“A little.”

He looked at her shoes.

“Why did you wear those?”

“They’re comfortable.”

“They clearly aren’t.”

“They were comfortable this morning.”

He smiled.

“That’s not the same thing.”

She gave him a small, tired look.

He stopped beside a low stone wall.

He held out his hand.

She walked over.

He crouched slightly and checked the strap of her shoe, which had loosened.

“That’s probably rubbing.”

He fixed it, then stood.

“Better?”

She nodded.

He offered his hand.

She took it.

They walked more slowly after that.

When they reached the entrance, Xiaoran turned back for one last look.

The gardens were still bright, though the shadows had grown longer. A few visitors were taking photographs beneath the trees. Somewhere nearby, someone was laughing.

She lifted her camera and took one final picture.

Yichen stood beside her.

She lowered the camera and looked at him.

“Can you take one of me?”

He accepted it.

She walked a few steps away, standing where the sunlight fell across the path.

He raised the camera.

“Ready?”

She nodded.

He took the photograph.

Then he took another.

And another.

“That’s enough,” she called.

He lowered the camera.

She walked back to him.

“Let me see.”

He showed her.

The first was a little too posed. The second caught her looking toward the trees. The third showed her laughing at something outside the frame.

She liked the third best.

“That’s my favorite.”

Yichen looked at it.

“Mine too.”

She smiled.

Then she took his hand.

Back at the hotel, Xiaoran transferred the photographs to her laptop.

Yichen was sitting on the sofa, reading.

Every so often, she would turn the screen toward him.

“Look.”

He would look.

“Nice.”

“Look at this one.”

“Very nice.”

“And this?”

“Also nice.”

She turned around.

“You’re not paying attention.”

He closed his book.

He opened his arms.

She got up and walked over.

He moved his legs to make room, and she settled beside him with the laptop.

He looked through the photographs more carefully this time.

There were pictures of the garden, the flowers, the bridges, the pond, the tea shop, and the two of them.

He paused at one particular photograph.

It was taken without his knowledge.

Xiaoran was standing near the water, looking down at the camera in her hands. The sunlight touched her cheek and the loose strands of hair beside her face.

She looked completely absorbed in whatever she had been photographing.

Yichen studied it.

“Keep this one.”

She looked at the screen.

“You like it?”

“Yes.”

“But I’m not looking at the camera.”

“I know.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You’re always choosing the ones where I’m not looking.”

He considered her.

“You’re usually more interesting when you forget I’m watching.”

She gave him a look.

“That’s a very strange compliment.”

“It’s still a compliment.”

She leaned into his shoulder.

He wrapped an arm around her and looked back at the screen.

After a while, she said, “I think this was my favorite day.”

“Today?”

“Yes.”

“More than yesterday?”

She nodded.

“Yesterday was nice, but today was sunny.”

That got a smile out of him.

“So sunshine makes the difference?”

“Of course.”

He looked at the photographs again.

Then he said, “I liked today too.”

She lifted her head.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Even though I stopped every five minutes?”

“Yes.”

“And took too many photographs?”

“Yes.”

“And made you stand in the same place three times?”

He looked at her.

“That part was difficult.”

She gasped.

“Yichen!”

He laughed and pulled her closer.

“I’m joking.”

“You’re on very thin ice.”

“I know.”

She settled back against him.

The laptop screen remained open, displaying the photograph of the garden in sunshine.

Outside, the evening light was fading over Suzhou.

Xiaoran reached for the trackpad and saved the picture into a folder.

She named it Suzhou — Day Two.

Then, after a moment, she created another folder beneath it.

Us.

Yichen noticed.

He didn’t say anything.

He pressed his mouth to her hair and returned to his book, while she continued sorting through the photographs.

chapters.desc: She borrows his phone to check a menu and finds herself on his lock screen, in a picture she never knew he took.
chapters.title: A Photo He Keeps to Himself
chapters.epigraph: “Because I can’t take the same photograph twice.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had taken hundreds of photographs of Xiaoran.

Some were intentional.

Birthday pictures, holiday photographs, pictures of her standing beneath pretty lanterns during their trip to the water town, and the occasional selfie she insisted they take together because she thought they hadn’t taken enough lately.

Others were accidental.

Her sleeping against the car window. Her hand reaching across the dining table to steal food from his plate. Her reflection in a café window, unaware that he had lifted his phone to capture it.

He had a habit of photographing her when she wasn’t looking.

Xiaoran knew this.

She occasionally complained about it, when he showed her a picture in which she was chewing, blinking, or making an expression she considered unsuitable for public viewing.

Yichen usually kept those pictures anyway.

But there was one photograph he had never shown her.

It had been taken on a Sunday afternoon, several weeks earlier.

They had gone out for lunch and spent the rest of the day wandering around an old shopping district. Nothing special. Xiaoran had wanted to look at a stationery shop, then a small bookstore, and finally a dessert café she’d saved on her phone.

It was a warm afternoon, with sunlight filtering through the trees along the street.

She had been standing outside the café, waiting for him to finish paying.

Yichen had stepped out a moment later and found her looking through the glass window at the desserts inside.

She was wearing a cream-colored dress, a light cardigan over her shoulders, and the little flower-shaped earrings she had bought herself during their shopping trip.

The sunlight had caught the side of her face.

Her hair moved slightly in the breeze, and she was smiling at something she had seen inside the café.

It was a small, unguarded smile, the kind she never made for a camera.

She looked happy.

And, to him, unbearably beautiful.

He had taken out his phone and captured the moment.

Xiaoran hadn’t noticed.

When she finally turned around, she immediately asked whether he was ready.

He had put his phone away.

“Ready?”

“Yes. Let’s go.”

She had taken his hand and continued walking.

He hadn’t thought much about the photograph afterward, except that he had looked at it several times that evening.

Then he had set it as his phone wallpaper.

He didn’t tell her.

And, for several weeks, she didn’t notice.

Until one ordinary evening.

They were at home, preparing to order dinner.

Xiaoran was sitting on the living room sofa with her legs tucked beneath her, scrolling through a delivery app. Yichen had just finished showering and was sitting beside her, his phone in one hand.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you want noodles or rice?”

“Either.”

She met his eyes.

“That’s not an answer.”

“Then noodles.”

“Which noodles?”

He glanced at her screen.

“The one you want.”

Xiaoran sighed.

“You’re not helping.”

She continued scrolling, then remembered something.

“Oh, I need your phone.”

Yichen looked up.

“For what?”

“I want to check the restaurant’s menu. Mine isn’t loading properly.”

He handed it to her without hesitation.

Xiaoran unlocked the phone.

And stopped.

She stared at the screen.

Then she blinked.

Then she looked again.

It was a photograph of her.

She had never seen it before.

She was standing outside the dessert café, her head slightly turned toward the window, sunlight falling across her cheek.

Her expression was soft and happy.

The photograph was beautiful because she looked so naturally herself.

She tilted the phone slightly.

Then she looked at Yichen.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“What’s this?”

He glanced at the screen.

His eyes landed on the photograph.

For a brief moment, he said nothing.

Then he looked back at her.

“My wallpaper.”

“I can see that.”

She looked down again.

“Since when?”

“A while.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“You didn’t ask.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“How can I ask when I don’t even know you changed it?”

His mouth curved.

“That’s true.”

She looked at the photograph again.

“Where was this taken?”

“Outside the dessert café.”

She frowned.

“When?”

“That Sunday we went to the old shopping district.”

Her eyes widened.

“Wait. You took this?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“While you were looking inside the café.”

She looked at him.

“I didn’t even notice.”

“I know.”

“Why didn’t you show me?”

Yichen looked at her.

Then he answered.

“Because I liked it.”

She blinked.

“Isn’t that why you show me pictures?”

“Usually.”

“Then why not this one?”

He reached for his glass of water on the coffee table, took a sip, and put it down.

“I wanted to keep this one.”

Xiaoran went quiet.

She looked at the picture again.

There was something unexpectedly intimate about it.

She had seen plenty of photographs of herself. She knew what she looked like when she smiled at a camera, when she posed for a picture, when she tried to look pretty.

But this one was different.

She hadn’t known he was looking. She hadn’t been trying to look beautiful.

She had been enjoying her afternoon.

And Yichen had thought to keep that moment.

“Do you really like it that much?” she asked.

He turned his head toward her.

“Yes.”

“More than the pictures from our trip?”

“Different.”

“More than our anniversary photos?”

“Different.”

“More than the one where I’m wearing hanfu?”

That got a smile out of him.

“That one is very beautiful.”

“But?”

“But this one is my favorite.”

She turned to him.

“Why?”

Yichen was quiet.

Then he shifted slightly toward her.

She lowered the phone.

“Because you didn’t know I was taking it. You weren’t looking at me. You weren’t waiting for me to take a picture. You weren’t asking whether your hair looked right or whether the lighting was good.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I do that?”

“Quite often.”

“That’s because you take terrible pictures sometimes.”

“I’ve been told.”

She laughed.

Yichen reached over and gently tucked her hair behind her ear.

“You were just standing there, looking at something you liked. You looked happy.”

His thumb brushed her cheek.

“I liked seeing you like that.”

Xiaoran looked down at the phone again.

The photograph seemed even more precious.

She hadn’t realized that he had noticed such a small moment.

She hadn’t realized that he had kept it.

“Can you send it to me?” she asked.

Yichen looked at her.

“Of course.”

“Without the wallpaper crop. I want the original.”

“All right.”

“And don’t delete it.”

“I won’t.”

She looked at him with a playful expression.

“Actually, I think you should put a picture of us together as your wallpaper. Then everyone will know you’re taken.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Does my current wallpaper suggest otherwise?”

She looked at the screen, then back at him.

“...No.”

“Good.”

“But it’s only me.”

“Is that a problem?”

She shook her head, smiling.

“No.”

Yichen held out his hand.

“Give it back.”

She placed the phone in his palm, but before he could take it, she leaned closer.

“Wait.”

“Hm?”

“Can I see it again?”

He unlocked the screen and showed her.

She looked at the photograph for a few seconds.

Then she glanced at him.

“You really look at me like that?”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“Like what?”

“Like I’m something worth keeping.”

He didn’t answer immediately.

Instead, he put his phone down and reached for her hand.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“I have six years of photographs of you.”

She laughed.

“That’s a lot.”

“And I still take more.”

“I know. You take pictures of me eating.”

“Those are important records.”

“Yichen!”

He smiled, then brought her hand to his lips.

“But this one... I like having it where I can see it.” He paused, his gaze returning to hers.

She felt her cheeks warm.

“Why?”

“Sometimes I look at it before training. Sometimes when I’m traveling. Sometimes when I have a few minutes between things.”

His voice was as calm as ever.

“It reminds me of home.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

She hadn’t expected that.

She had thought he liked the photograph because she looked pretty in it. That alone would have made her happy.

But knowing he kept it for those moments when they weren’t together made something warm settle in her chest.

She moved closer and wrapped her arms around his waist.

Yichen’s arm came around her immediately.

“You’re making me emotional,” she murmured against his shoulder.

“Sorry.”

“Don’t apologize.”

He kissed her temple.

For a while, they stayed like that.

Then Xiaoran pulled back.

“Actually...”

Yichen looked down at her.

“What?”

“Can I take a picture of you?”

He blinked.

“Now?”

“Yes.”

She reached for her own phone.

Yichen glanced down at his casual clothes, then at her.

“Why?”

“Because I want a wallpaper too.”

She moved a little farther away, holding her phone up.

“Don’t pose.”

He gave her a faint smile.

“All right.”

“Don’t smile too much either.”

“Understood.”

“Just look at me.”

He did.

Xiaoran lifted her phone.

But before she could take the picture, Yichen’s expression changed slightly.

His eyes softened, and the smile that came was quieter than the teasing one, and meant for her.

She pressed the shutter.

Then she looked at the result.

“Oh.”

Yichen glanced at her screen.

“Good?”

“Very.”

She sat beside him again and showed him the picture.

He studied it.

“Not bad.”

“Not bad?”

“Very good.”

She smiled proudly.

Then she opened her wallpaper settings.

Yichen watched her select the photograph, adjust the crop, and save it.

A moment later, she turned the screen toward him.

His face filled her wallpaper.

That made her grin.

“Now we’re even.”

He looked at her phone, then at her.

“Are we?”

“Yes.”

“Then I suppose I should take another picture of you.”

She laughed.

“You already have hundreds!”

“Not enough.”

He reached for his phone again, and Xiaoran immediately leaned toward him.

“Wait. Are you going to change your wallpaper?”

“No.”

She blinked.

“Why not?”

He looked at her.

“I like this one.”

She smiled.

Then she reached up and kissed his cheek.

“Okay. Keep it.”

Yichen turned his head slightly.

“Thank you.”

She kissed his other cheek.

“You’re welcome.”

He caught her hand before she could pull away and pressed a kiss to her palm.

“Besides, I don’t think you’ll be able to replace it easily,” he said.

Xiaoran tilted her head.

“Why?”

He met her eyes.

“Because I can’t take the same photograph twice.”

She considered that.

Then she smiled.

“Then you should keep taking new ones.”

Yichen’s eyes softened.

“I intend to.”

Then he lifted his phone, and she was laughing too hard to stop him.

chapters.desc: One evening the promise ring is gone from her finger. They search the whole apartment before he finds it behind the soap dispenser.
chapters.title: The Ring on the Sink
chapters.epigraph: “The promise isn’t inside the ring, Xiaoran.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that something was wrong was that Lin Xiaoran stopped talking.

Zhou Yichen noticed it immediately.

He was sitting at the dining table with his laptop open, reviewing footage from the Herons’ previous game. The television was off, the apartment was quiet except for the soft sound of the kitchen exhaust fan.

Usually, when Xiaoran cooked, she narrated everything.

She talked about the recipe, complained about the vegetables, asked him whether he preferred more sauce, and occasionally announced that she was doing something dangerous with a knife even though she was only cutting a tomato.

Tonight, she had been unusually quiet for almost ten minutes.

Yichen looked toward the kitchen.

She was standing at the counter, concentrating on something in the pan.

He watched her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“Everything okay?”

“Yes.”

He returned his attention to the laptop.

A few seconds later, she said, “Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Can you come here?”

He closed his laptop.

“What’s wrong?”

She didn’t answer immediately.

Instead, she looked at the stove, then at the counter, then at her left hand.

Yichen walked over.

“What happened?”

“I think...”

She stopped.

He waited.

“I think I lost something.”

His expression changed.

“What?”

She lifted her left hand.

The ring finger was bare.

Yichen looked at it, then at her face.

Neither spoke.

“Your ring?” he asked.

She nodded.

The promise ring had been on her finger for well over a year.

It was delicate, understated, and easy to wear every day. A thin band with a small, subtle stone that caught the light when she moved her hand.

It wasn’t an engagement ring.

They had both been clear about that.

It was Yichen’s promise that when they were ready, when they had established their own lives and careers, he would ask her properly.

With flowers, a pretty dress, and everything she had once jokingly demanded.

She had tried hard not to cry when he first gave it to her, and failed.

Since then, she had rarely taken it off.

Now her finger was empty.

Yichen looked at her carefully.

“When did you last see it?”

“This afternoon.”

“Are you sure?”

She nodded.

“I remember washing my hands before cooking. It was still there.”

“All right.”

She looked increasingly distressed.

“I was washing the vegetables, then I prepared the meat, and I washed my hands again. I didn’t notice anything.”

“Did you take it off?”

“No.”

“Then let’s look.”

She turned toward the sink.

“I already checked.”

“Where?”

“Here. The counter, the sink, the floor.”

He nodded.

“Okay. We’ll check again.”

She swallowed.

“I don’t understand. It doesn’t just fall off.”

Yichen glanced at her finger.

“Has it felt loose recently?”

She hesitated.

“A little.”

He met her eyes.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I didn’t think it was that loose.”

He didn’t scold her.

He nodded.

“All right. Let’s find it first.”

They began with the kitchen.

Yichen switched off the stove and moved the pan to a safe spot. Xiaoran stood beside him, watching as he carefully checked the counter.

He moved the chopping board, lifted the kitchen towel, and looked beneath the small appliances.

Nothing.

“Maybe it fell into the sink,” Xiaoran said.

Yichen looked at the drain.

“Don’t turn the water on.”

“I haven’t.”

He checked the sink basin first, then the drain strainer.

Nothing.

Xiaoran’s breathing became a little uneven.

“What if it went down?”

“Let’s not assume that yet.”

“But the drain—”

“I’ll check.”

He crouched and examined the area beneath the sink.

There was no obvious sign of it.

He opened the cabinet, looked around the pipes, then checked the floor again.

Still nothing.

Xiaoran rubbed her bare ring finger.

“I should have taken it off.”

Yichen stood.

“Maybe.”

She met his eyes.

He continued gently, “But we don’t know where it is yet. Don’t start blaming yourself.”

She nodded, but her eyes were already turning glossy.

He noticed.

He reached for her hand.

He reached for her.

She stepped closer.

He held her hand between both of his.

“We’ll look properly. Don’t panic.”

She tried to smile.

“I’m not panicking.”

He looked at her.

She exhaled.

“Okay. Maybe a little.”

He kissed her hair.

“That’s allowed.”

They searched the kitchen again.

This time, Yichen checked the area around the stove while Xiaoran looked through the rubbish bin.

She carefully separated the paper towels and packaging from the vegetable scraps.

“Nothing,” she said.

“Check the food waste container too.”

She opened it.

A few vegetable peels, a piece of onion skin, and the remains of the ingredients she had prepared.

She stared at them.

“I don’t want to throw anything away.”

“Then don’t. I’ll check.”

He put on a pair of disposable gloves and carefully searched through the contents.

No ring.

He washed his hands and returned to the counter.

“Let’s check the living room.”

She followed him.

They looked beneath the sofa, around the dining table, and between the cushions.

Yichen checked the pockets of the cardigan she had worn earlier.

Nothing.

Xiaoran was becoming quieter.

At one point, she sat down on the sofa and stared at her hand.

Yichen returned from the bedroom.

“Not there either.”

She nodded.

He sat beside her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Do you remember the last time you took it off?”

She thought.

“Not recently. Maybe when we went swimming?”

“When was that?”

“Last month.”

“Did you put it back on?”

“Yes. I remember because you helped me.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

She looked down again.

“It’s stupid.”

“What is?”

“I’m so upset over a ring.”

Yichen turned toward her.

“It’s not stupid.”

She pressed her lips together.

“It’s not even an engagement ring.”

“I know.”

“And I know what it means. You don’t have to give me a ring to know you love me.”

He listened.

“But I liked wearing it. It reminded me of that day. And what you said,” she whispered.

Her eyes finally filled.

“I don’t want to lose it.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

He took her hand and kissed the bare finger.

“I know.”

She turned to him.

“We’ll keep looking.”

It was nearly ten when they returned to the kitchen.

Yichen had checked the bedroom, the bathroom, and even the laundry basket.

Xiaoran had retraced her movements from the afternoon.

Nothing.

She stood beside the sink, looking at the counter.

“I washed the vegetables here.”

She pointed toward the basin.

“Then I put the meat here. I remember because I moved the cutting board.”

Yichen followed her movements with his eyes.

“All right.”

“And then I washed my hands again.”

She turned on the tap slightly, demonstrating where she had stood.

Yichen watched her left hand.

“Wait.”

She stopped.

“What?”

“Do that again.”

She blinked.

“What?”

“Show me how you washed your hands.”

She looked confused but did as he asked.

She turned toward the sink, reached for the soap, and rubbed her palms together.

Then she moved her hands beneath the tap.

Yichen’s gaze shifted toward the sink.

“Did you use the soap dispenser?”

“Yes.”

“Which hand?”

“My right.”

He looked at the counter.

“Can you move?”

She stepped aside.

Yichen examined the narrow space between the soap dispenser and the faucet.

There was a small gap.

He reached behind the dispenser, then felt along the edge of the sink.

His fingers stopped.

He didn’t move.

Then he leaned closer.

“Xiaoran.”

Her heart seemed to stop.

“What?”

He crooked a finger at her.

She rushed toward him.

He was looking at the narrow space between the sink and the wall.

Something small was caught there, partially hidden beneath the edge of the soap dispenser.

A thin metallic glint.

Yichen carefully reached for it.

Then he lifted his hand.

The ring rested between his fingers.

For a second, Xiaoran didn’t move.

She stared.

Then she let out a breath that sounded almost like a laugh.

“Oh my god.”

Yichen smiled.

“Found it.”

She covered her mouth.

“That’s my ring.”

“I know.”

“That’s really my ring.”

He laughed.

“Yes, Xiaoran.”

She reached for it, but stopped before touching it, as if she needed to confirm it was real.

Yichen brought it closer.

The small stone caught the kitchen light.

There was a faint trace of water on the band.

“It must have slipped off when you washed your hands. It got caught behind the dispenser,” he said.

She stared at it, then looked at him, then back at the ring.

And she started crying.

Not loudly.

Just a few tears slipping down her cheeks as the tension finally left her.

Yichen’s smile softened.

“Hey.”

She laughed through the tears.

“I thought I lost it.”

“I know.”

“I looked everywhere.”

“I saw.”

She reached for him instead of the ring and kissed him, wet hands and all.

He wrapped an arm around her and held her close.

For a while, she stood against his chest.

Then she pulled back.

“Can I have it?”

He smiled.

“Of course.”

He placed it in her palm.

She held it carefully, turning it between her fingers.

Then she looked at him.

“Can you put it back on?”

His expression changed.

“Your finger?”

She nodded.

He took the ring from her hand.

But before putting it on, he examined the band.

“It’s loose.”

She looked away.

“I know.”

“How long?”

“A little while.”

He turned to her.

She made a small face.

“Don’t lecture me.”

“I’m not.”

“You have that expression.”

“What expression?”

“The one where you’re about to say something sensible.”

He laughed.

“Then I’ll save it for tomorrow.”

That made her grin.

He took her left hand and slipped the ring onto her finger.

It settled there, slightly looser than it should have.

He turned her hand gently, checking that it sat comfortably.

“There.”

She looked at it, then at him.

“Thank you.”

He kissed her knuckles.

“You’re welcome.”

They didn’t go back to cooking immediately.

Yichen made tea while Xiaoran sat at the dining table, turning the ring on her finger.

She looked at it several times.

He noticed.

“Still checking?”

“Just making sure.”

He placed a cup in front of her.

“It’s not going anywhere.”

She looked at him.

“Don’t say that. It might.”

He smiled and sat opposite her.

“Then we’ll get it resized.”

She looked down.

“Can we?”

“Of course.”

“Will it look different?”

“Not if we have it done properly.”

She considered this.

Then asked, “Do you remember why you chose this one?”

Yichen leaned back slightly.

“Yes.”

“Tell me.”

He held her gaze.

“You want me to tell you again?”

She nodded.

He laughed under his breath.

“I wanted something you could wear every day. Something that wouldn’t get in the way of your work, or feel too formal.”

She listened.

“And I didn’t want you to feel like you had to keep it safe in a box. I wanted it to be part of your life.”

She looked at the ring.

He said, “I knew you would probably wear it all the time.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Because I like it.”

“I know.”

“And now I have to take it off to cook.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I didn’t plan for the soap dispenser.”

She smiled.

He reached across the table and touched her hand.

“Do you remember what I told you when I gave it to you?”

“You said it wasn’t a proposal.”

“Correct.”

“And that you’d ask me properly when we’re ready.”

“Yes.”

She held his gaze.

“And you said you weren’t going to rush me.”

“I meant it.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“I know.”

She turned the ring once more.

Then said, “I think I was scared because it felt like losing that promise.”

Yichen looked at her.

She said, “I know a ring is just an object. But this one is something we chose together. It reminds me that we’re building toward something.”

He reached for her hand.

“The promise isn’t inside the ring, Xiaoran.”

“It’s between us.”

She was quiet.

He rubbed his thumb over her knuckles.

“The ring is something you can wear. Something that reminds you of it. But if you lose it, the promise doesn’t disappear.”

Her eyes softened.

“I know.”

“Good. Although I’d prefer you not to test that theory again.”

She laughed.

“Okay.”

The next morning, Yichen took her to have the ring checked.

They found a jeweller who could adjust the size without changing the design.

Xiaoran watched carefully as the jeweller examined it.

“Can you make it a little smaller?”

The jeweller nodded.

“Of course. It should fit more securely after adjustment.”

Yichen stood beside her.

“Could you also check the setting?”

“Certainly.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“You don’t have to worry so much.”

He glanced at her.

“I’m not worried.”

She raised an eyebrow.

He smiled.

“All right. A little.”

She laughed.

When the jeweller finished checking the ring, they were told it would be ready later that afternoon.

Xiaoran left the shop with an empty ring finger.

She kept looking at it.

Yichen noticed.

“Do you want to hold it until it’s ready?”

She shook her head.

“No. It’s safer here.”

He studied her.

“You’re learning.”

She laughed.

“Don’t tease me.”

He took her hand.

“Come on.”

That evening, they returned home.

The ring was back on her finger.

It fit properly now.

Xiaoran held her hand beneath the kitchen light, admiring how it sat against her skin.

Yichen was unpacking the groceries.

She tilted her head.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“If, one day, I actually lose it...”

He turned toward her.

She said, “Would you be upset?”

He considered the question.

“Would you be upset?”

She thought.

“Yes.”

“Then I’d probably be upset too.”

She frowned.

“That’s not comforting.”

He smiled and came closer.

“But I’d help you look for it.”

“And if we couldn’t find it?”

“Then we’d figure out what to do.”

She stared at him.

He touched the ring lightly.

“We could replace it. Or keep the memory of the original. Or choose something else together.”

“Even if it wasn’t the same?”

“Even then.”

He bent and kissed her hairline.

“Xiaoran, I didn’t give you this ring because I wanted you to spend the rest of your life worrying about losing it.”

She looked at him.

“I gave it to you because I wanted you to enjoy wearing it.”

Her smile softened.

“Okay.”

He kissed her cheek.

“Now, can you help me with dinner?”

“Yes.”

He returned to the groceries.

She watched him, then glanced at the sink.

The soap dispenser had been moved slightly away from the wall.

She smiled.

“Yichen?”

He looked over.

“Yes?”

“Do you think we should put the ring somewhere safe when I cook?”

He considered it.

“That might be a good idea.”

“Maybe a little dish.”

“All right.”

“Beside the sink?”

He considered her.

She immediately corrected herself.

“No. Not beside the sink. Somewhere farther away.”

He laughed.

“Good decision.”

She smiled proudly, then walked over and kissed his cheek.

A few days later, Yichen came home from training and found a small ceramic dish on the bedroom dresser.

It was cream-colored, with a tiny blue flower painted in the middle, the same as the cup their toothbrushes lived in.

Beside it was a handwritten note.

For my ring, when I need to take it off.

He picked it up and smiled.

Xiaoran appeared from the bathroom, drying her hands.

“Do you like it?”

He looked at the dish.

“Yes.”

“I thought it would be safer here.”

“Much safer.”

She walked over and looked at it with him.

Then she lifted her left hand.

The ring was still there.

Yichen glanced at her.

“You’re wearing it.”

“Yes.”

“Then what is the dish for?”

“For when I need to take it off.”

He nodded.

“Very practical.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Thank you.”

He put the dish back on the dresser.

Then he took her hand and kissed the ring.

She watched him.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“Do you think when you propose properly, I’ll still wear this?”

He glanced at her.

“You can wear whatever you want.”

She tilted her head.

“What if I wear both?”

Something in his face eased.

“Then I’ll have to find a ring that sits beside it.”

She laughed.

“You’re already planning?”

“I’ve had a little time to think about it.”

Her expression softened.

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“But not yet.”

“I know.”

“After we’ve built the life we want.”

She nodded.

“After we’re ready.”

He kissed her hair.

“Exactly.”

She leaned into him, smiling.

The promise ring caught the light between them. Tomorrow it would go in the ceramic dish before she cooked, and he would check anyway.

chapters.desc: She books a professional couple shoot. He poses as if he were at a board meeting, until the photographer asks them to forget the camera.
chapters.title: The Way He Looks at Her
chapters.epigraph: “Who else would I look at like that?”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had booked the photoshoot three weeks in advance.

She had researched photographers, compared portfolios, saved references, and created an entire album on her phone titled Couple Photoshoot Ideas.

There were photographs taken in studios, gardens, old streets, and beautiful apartments. Some were elegant and romantic. Others were playful, with couples laughing, running, or stealing kisses when the photographer wasn’t looking.

She had shown Yichen the album one evening.

He had scrolled through it carefully.

“How many photographs do you want?”

Xiaoran had looked at him.

“That’s your first question?”

“I’m trying to understand the scale of the operation.”

She had laughed.

“I just want some nice photographs of us.”

“We have plenty.”

“Those are mostly selfies.”

“What’s wrong with selfies?”

“Nothing. But I want professional ones. The kind we can frame.”

He had looked at her, then nodded.

“All right. Let’s do it.”

And that was how Zhou Yichen found himself standing in a photography studio on a Saturday morning, wearing a carefully selected dark charcoal suit while his girlfriend stood in front of a mirror, adjusting the collar of her cream-colored dress for the fourth time.

He had to admit, she looked beautiful.

Her hair fell in soft waves over her shoulders, and the dress suited her perfectly. She had chosen delicate earrings and a pair of heels, and her promise ring caught the light whenever she moved her hand.

He watched her adjust one loose strand of hair.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“You’re ready.”

She turned around.

“You look beautiful,” he said.

Her expression brightened, and she walked toward him, smoothing the front of his suit.

“You’re handsome too.”

“Thank you.”

She looked at him for another moment.

“Although you look a little too serious.”

He raised an eyebrow.

He laughed under his breath.

“I’ll try to remember.”

She laughed and took his hand.

The photographer, a woman named Anqi, greeted them warmly.

She was experienced, friendly, and immediately seemed to understand that Xiaoran was the enthusiastic half of the couple.

“You’re Lin Xiaoran, right? We spoke about the mood board.”

“Yes! Thank you for accommodating the references.”

“Of course. I loved your ideas. And Zhou Yichen?”

He shook her hand.

“Hello.”

Anqi glanced between them.

“Lovely. You two look great together.”

Xiaoran smiled.

Yichen gave a polite nod.

The first setup was a simple studio backdrop in warm beige, with soft natural lighting and a few pieces of furniture.

Anqi explained the process.

“We’ll start with some classic portraits. Nothing too complicated. Just stand together, look at the camera, and we’ll adjust as we go.”

Xiaoran nodded enthusiastically.

Yichen listened attentively.

The first few photographs went smoothly.

Yichen stood beside Xiaoran with one hand resting at her waist. His posture was straight, his expression composed. Xiaoran smiled at the camera, occasionally turning her face toward him.

Anqi checked the monitor.

“Beautiful. Let’s try one with you looking at each other.”

Xiaoran turned toward Yichen.

That made her grin.

He smiled back, although subtly.

The shutter clicked.

Anqi checked the image.

“Very nice. Maybe a little closer?”

Yichen moved closer.

“Good. Zhou Yichen, could you relax your shoulders a little?”

He did.

“Perfect. And Lin Xiaoran, perhaps place your hand on his chest.”

She did so immediately.

Anqi raised her camera.

“Lovely. Now look at each other.”

They did.

“Good. A little smile, please.”

Xiaoran smiled.

Yichen’s expression softened slightly.

Click.

Anqi looked at the monitor.

Then she smiled.

“You’re both very photogenic. But I have a feeling we’re going to get something even better once you stop thinking about the camera.”

Xiaoran looked curious.

“What do you mean?”

“Let’s take a short break from posing. Just talk to each other. Forget I’m here.”

Yichen nodded.

“All right.”

Anqi lowered her camera.

“Tell him something you like about him.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Right now?”

“Yes.”

She turned toward Yichen.

He looked at her expectantly.

For some reason, she became shy.

“Um...”

Yichen’s mouth curved.

“Go on.”

She glanced at the photographer, then back at him.

“I like that you’re patient.”

He tilted his head.

“Only that?”

She laughed.

“No. I like that you’re thoughtful. And that you always remember little things.”

His expression softened.

She continued, more comfortably now.

“And I like that you’re very handsome.”

He laughed.

Anqi raised her camera.

Click.

Xiaoran didn’t notice.

Yichen did.

He looked toward the photographer for a second before returning his attention to Xiaoran.

“Anything else?”
