“I like that you always let me have the last piece of dessert.”

“Not always.”

“Most of the time.”

“That’s because you take it before I can.”

She laughed.

Anqi took another photograph.

The next setup was outdoors.

The studio had a small garden with a stone pathway, flowering plants, and a wooden bench beneath a tree. The afternoon light was soft, filtering through the leaves.

Xiaoran loved it immediately.

“It’s so pretty.”

Yichen stood beside her.

“Do you like this one?”

“Very much.”

Anqi suggested they begin with a few photographs sitting together on the bench.

Xiaoran sat first.

Yichen sat beside her, leaving a small space between them.

Anqi looked through the camera.

“Could you move a little closer?”

Yichen shifted.

“Closer still.”

He moved again.

Xiaoran glanced at him.

“You’re being very cooperative.”

He met her eyes.

“Am I not usually?”

“You are. But you’re behaving like a very well-trained model.”

He smiled.

“Would you prefer otherwise?”

She thought about it.

“Maybe.”

Anqi lowered her camera.

“Actually, let’s try something different. Zhou Yichen, could you put your arm around her and let her lean against you?”

He did.

Xiaoran settled against his side.

“Good. Now, Lin Xiaoran, look at him.”

She turned.

Yichen was already looking at her.

“Lovely. And Zhou Yichen, perhaps kiss her forehead,” Anqi said.

He lowered his head and pressed a kiss to her temple.

Click.

Xiaoran smiled.

Anqi checked the photograph.

“Beautiful.”

Then she looked at them again.

“Could you stay like that for a moment?”

Yichen didn’t move.

His arm remained around Xiaoran, his fingers resting gently against her upper arm.

Xiaoran looked up.

“What?”

He brushed his thumb over her skin.

“Nothing.”

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Because you’re here.”

That made her grin.

“That’s a very strange answer.”

“Is it?”

She shook her head, laughing.

Anqi took another photograph, then another.

The camera captured the small smile on Xiaoran’s face and the way Yichen’s attention never seemed to leave her.

By the third setup, Xiaoran had become increasingly comfortable.

She was beginning to enjoy the process.

Yichen, meanwhile, had become noticeably less concerned about the camera.

It happened when Anqi suggested a playful series.

“I’d like you two to walk toward me. Hold hands, talk to each other, and don’t worry about posing.”

Xiaoran immediately stood.

“Can we walk together?”

Yichen looked at her.

“We’re supposed to.”

She laughed.

They began walking along the garden path.

Xiaoran held his hand, swinging their joined hands slightly.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you think the photographs will turn out well?”

“Yes.”

“How do you know?”

“Because you’re in them.”

She looked up, then narrowed her eyes.

“You’re trying to make me happy.”

“Is it working?”

“Maybe.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

She continued walking.

“Actually, I want one where I’m looking at you and you’re looking at the camera.”

“Why?”

“Because I want people to see how handsome you are.”

He turned to her.

“Then why would you be looking at me?”

“Because I’m admiring you.”

He laughed.

Anqi was already taking photographs.

“That’s wonderful! Keep talking!”

Xiaoran became more animated.

“And I want one where you carry me.”

Yichen looked down.

“Carry you?”

“Yes.”

“Here?”

“Yes.”

He glanced at the photographer.

Anqi smiled.

“If you’re comfortable, let’s try.”

Yichen looked at Xiaoran again.

“Are you sure?”

She nodded.

He stopped walking, placed one arm behind her back and the other beneath her knees, then lifted her effortlessly.

Xiaoran let out a surprised laugh.

“Yichen!”

“What?”

“You actually did it!”

“You asked.”

She instinctively wrapped her arms around his shoulders.

Anqi began taking photographs.

“Perfect! Stay like that!”

Xiaoran was laughing now, her face turned toward him.

Yichen looked down at her.

His expression had changed completely.

He wasn’t thinking about his posture or where to place his hands. He was looking at the girl in his arms, smiling at her as if the photographer and the camera had disappeared.

Click. Click.

Click.

Anqi lowered the camera slightly.

“That was wonderful.”

Yichen carefully put Xiaoran down.

She was still smiling.

“That was fun.”

He brushed a loose strand of hair away from her face.

“Did I hurt you?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Good.”

Then, almost absentmindedly, he kissed her.

Anqi captured it.

During the next break, Xiaoran went to look at the photographs on the monitor.

She stood beside Anqi, looking through the previews.

“Oh!”

She pointed at one.

“This one!”

It was the photograph of Yichen carrying her.

She looked delighted.

“Look at his expression!”

Anqi smiled.

“He’s very affectionate.”

Xiaoran glanced toward him.

Yichen was standing a little distance away, speaking with one of the assistants.

“He’s usually quite composed,” Xiaoran said.

“Not when he’s looking at you, apparently.”

Xiaoran smiled.

Then she looked at another photograph.

It showed Yichen kissing her forehead while she closed her eyes.

She stared at it for a little longer.

“I like this one too.”

Anqi nodded.

“It’s one of my favorites. You look very comfortable with him.”

Xiaoran’s smile softened.

“I am.”

The final setup was in a quiet indoor room with a large window.

The afternoon light came through the sheer curtains, creating a soft glow across the room. There was a cream-colored sofa, a small table, and a few books arranged on a shelf.

Anqi suggested a more relaxed concept.

“Let’s make this one feel like an ordinary afternoon at home.”

Xiaoran immediately liked the idea.

“Can we sit together?”

“Of course.”

Yichen sat on the sofa first.

Xiaoran sat beside him, then shifted closer until her shoulder touched his.

Anqi watched them.

“Actually, I have a suggestion.”

She looked at Yichen.

“Could you forget the camera completely? Just interact with her the way you normally would.”

Yichen nodded.

“All right.”

“And Lin Xiaoran, you don’t need to look at the camera either. Just do whatever you would usually do when you’re together.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Okay.”

Anqi lifted her camera.

“Let’s begin.”

For the first few seconds, Xiaoran wasn’t sure what to do.

Then she noticed Yichen’s watch.

She reached for his wrist.

“Your watch.”

He looked down.

“What about it?”

“Let me see.”

He held out his hand.

She examined it, turning his wrist slightly.

“Is this the one you wore last week?”

“Yes.”

“I like this one.”

Something in his face eased.

“You said that yesterday.”

“Because I still like it.”

She released his wrist, then leaned against him.

Yichen slipped his arm around her.

“Comfortable?”

“Mm.”

She adjusted herself, placing her head against his shoulder.

Anqi continued taking photographs.

Yichen lowered his head.

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Want to rest?”

She shook her head.

“No. I’m enjoying this.”

“Good.”

She lifted her face.

“Do you think we should get one of these photographs framed?”

“Which one?”

“The one where you’re carrying me.”

“Why that one?”

“Because I look happy.”

He looked at her.

“You look happy in all of them.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Then maybe the one where you’re kissing my forehead.”

“All right.”

She considered it.

“Actually, I want several.”

He laughed.

“How many?”

“At least five.”

“Very reasonable.”

She rested her chin against his chest.

“You’re not complaining?”

“Why would I?”

“Because you said we already have plenty of photographs.”

He held her gaze.

“Those are mostly selfies.”

She stared, then burst out laughing.

“You remembered!”

That got a smile out of him.

“Of course.”

She lifted herself slightly and kissed his cheek.

“You’re so cute.”

Yichen turned his face toward her.

“Am I?”

“Sometimes.”

He gave her a slow, amused smile.

It was the smile that always made her forget what she had been saying.

Yichen noticed.

“What?”

She looked away.

“Nothing.”

He leaned closer.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You’re staring.”

She pressed her lips together.

“I’m not.”

“All right.”

Then he gently caught her chin and kissed her.

It was supposed to be a quick kiss.

But when she smiled against his lips, he kissed her again.

His hand moved to the back of her head, fingers slipping into her hair. Xiaoran leaned closer, one hand resting against his chest.

Anqi continued shooting.

Neither of them noticed.

When they finally separated, Xiaoran was smiling, her cheeks slightly pink.

Yichen brushed his thumb along her cheek.

“What’s that expression?”

She laughed.

“You know.”

He smiled.

“Maybe.”

From behind the camera, Anqi spoke.

“That was perfect.”

They both turned toward her.

She lowered the camera, looking thoroughly pleased.

“I think we have it.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Really?”

“Yes. The last few photographs are exactly what I wanted.”

Yichen glanced at the camera.

“What did you capture?”

Anqi smiled.

“You two.”

The photoshoot ended a little after four.

Xiaoran was still excited as they collected their belongings.

She thanked Anqi several times and promised to leave a review once the photographs were delivered.

Yichen stood beside her, holding her bag.

When they finally stepped outside, she immediately reached for his hand.

“That was so much fun.”

He studied her.

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

“Good.”

She swung their hands.

“You were good.”

“Thank you.”

“Especially toward the end.”

His mouth curved.

“What happened toward the end?”

She looked up at him.

“You became very affectionate.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You were so serious at the beginning.”

“I was listening to the photographer.”

“You looked like you were attending a meeting.”

He laughed.

“Was I that bad?”

“Not bad. Just... very professional.”

He nodded thoughtfully.

“Understood.”

She squeezed his hand.

“But I liked the last part best.”

“Why?”

“Because you forgot about the camera.”

He looked down at her.

She smiled.

“You weren’t trying to look handsome. You weren’t trying to pose. You were just being yourself.”

He was quiet.

Then he lifted their joined hands and kissed the back of hers.

“That’s because I was looking at you.”

She looked up.

He continued walking, his expression perfectly calm.

Xiaoran stared at him.

Then her cheeks slowly turned pink.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You’re very good at saying things like that.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Like what?”

“Things that make me embarrassed.”

He considered her.

“Should I stop?”

She thought, then shook her head.

“No.”

He laughed.

The photographs arrived a week later.

Xiaoran opened the gallery while they were sitting together on the sofa.

Yichen was reviewing something on his tablet when she made a small sound.

“Oh!”

He looked over.

“What?”

“They’re here.”

She immediately moved closer.

“Look!”

She opened the gallery.

The first few were the formal portraits.

They were beautiful.

Yichen looked composed and handsome, while Xiaoran looked elegant and radiant. They stood close together, hands at each other’s waists, smiling gently toward the camera, then came the photographs from the garden.

The walking shots. The one where he carried her.

The one where she was laughing.

And finally, the indoor photographs.

Xiaoran stopped scrolling.

She stared at one.

It showed her sitting against Yichen’s chest, her head tilted up toward him. He was looking down at her with an expression so gentle and unguarded that she almost didn’t recognize it as something he would allow a camera to capture.

His hand was resting against her cheek.

She was smiling.

Not at the camera.

At him.

Yichen looked at the screen.

“That’s nice.”

Xiaoran nodded.

She moved to the next photograph.

It was the moment after their kiss.

Her eyes were slightly lowered, her cheeks pink. Yichen was smiling at her, his thumb still resting against her cheek.

She stared at it.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Look at your face.”

He leaned closer.

“What about it?”

“You look so...”

She paused, searching for the word.

He waited.

“Fond.”

He looked at the photograph again, then smiled.

“Do I?”

“Very.”

He took the phone from her and scrolled back to the photograph.

He studied it.

Then he said, “I suppose I was.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“You were?”

He looked at her as if the answer should have been obvious.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Who else would I look at like that?”

She went quiet.

Her fingers curled slightly around his sleeve.

Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“Me, I hope.”

Yichen smiled.

“Always.”

She let her head drop onto his shoulder.

After a moment, she looked at the gallery again.

“I want to frame this one.”

“Which?”

“The one where you’re looking at me.”

He nodded.

“Let’s frame it.”

“And the one where you’re carrying me.”

“All right.”

“And the one where we’re kissing.”

He glanced at her.

“Three frames?”

She considered it.

“Maybe four.”

He laughed.

“Of course.”

She smiled and opened the gallery again.

Yichen slipped his arm around her waist, pulling her closer as she began selecting photographs.

A few minutes later, she paused at the first formal portrait.

“Actually, this one should go in the living room.”

“Why?”

“Because it looks elegant.”

He nodded.

“And the others?”

“Our bedroom.”

He smiled.

“Then we should choose carefully.”

Xiaoran leaned against him, scrolling through the photographs one by one, then looked up from the phone.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Can we do this again next year?”

He looked down at her.

“Another photoshoot?”

“Yes. Maybe every year.”

He laughed under his breath.

“All right.”

She grinned.

“Then we’ll have photographs from every year.”

“Sounds good.”

She looked at the photograph on the screen one last time.

Then she turned and wrapped both arms around him.

Yichen laughed, his hand settling at her back.

“What is this for?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

She shook her head against his chest.

“I just want to hug you.”

He kissed her hair.

“Then hug me.”

And when Xiaoran eventually uploaded one photograph to her social media, she chose the one where she was looking at him and he was looking at her.

Her caption was short.

Somehow, my favorite photographs are always the ones where he forgets the camera exists.

Yichen saw it later.

He liked the post, then left a comment.

Hard to remember there’s a camera when you’re standing in front of me.

Xiaoran read it while sitting beside him.

She turned her head slowly.

He was looking at his phone, perfectly composed.

She stared, then covered her face with both hands.

Yichen glanced at her.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

His mouth curved.

“All right.”

She peeked at him between her fingers.

“You’re doing it again. Making me fall in love with you all over again.”

His expression softened.

He put his phone down, pulled her into his arms, and kissed her temple.

“Good, I was hoping you would,” he murmured.

chapters.desc: At her parents’ table on May Day, her grandfather asks Yichen when he plans to marry his granddaughter.
chapters.title: Her Grandfather’s Question
chapters.epigraph: “I intend to marry you, Lin Xiaoran.”
chapters.content:
The question came on the second night of the May Day holiday, at her parents’ table, between the second serving of fish and the arrival of dessert.

Which, Xiaoran would later decide, was a unfair time to ask it.

Her grandparents had come up from the small town for the holiday, four hours on the bus, with a box of eggs on her grandmother’s lap the whole way. Xiaoran had been happily eating. Her grandfather, who had raised her until she was twelve and considered this his qualification for opinions about her life, had been telling Yichen a story about an old neighbor who once tried to raise chickens on his balcony. Her mother was laughing, her father was pretending not to, and Yichen was listening with the polite attention he always gave older people.

Everything was perfectly ordinary.

Until her grandfather put down his chopsticks, looked at Yichen, and asked:

“So, when are you planning to marry my granddaughter?”

Xiaoran stopped chewing.

Her mother looked up.

Her father slowly put down his teacup.

Yichen, who had just reached for the teapot, paused.

It was a remarkably quiet three seconds.

Then he placed the teapot down.

“Grandpa,” Xiaoran said.

Her grandfather looked at her.

“What?”

“You’re asking that very suddenly.”

“I’ve been thinking about it for a while.”

“That’s worse.”

Her grandfather ignored her and looked at Yichen again.

“I’m asking him.”

Yichen nodded slightly.

“I understand.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

She knew that expression.

He wasn’t startled anymore. His face had settled into that composed, attentive look he wore whenever he was considering something seriously.

Which was precisely what made her nervous.

Her grandfather leaned back.

“You’ve been together for years. You’ve graduated now. You’re living together. You’ve met both families. I don’t think it’s an unreasonable question.”

“No. It’s not,” Yichen agreed.

Xiaoran looked at him again.

He continued calmly.

“I do intend to marry her.”

Her grandfather nodded, as if he had expected that answer.

“Then what’s stopping you?”

This time, Yichen didn’t answer immediately.

He glanced at Xiaoran.

She was looking at him, her expression caught somewhere between embarrassment and curiosity.

He turned back to her grandfather.

“Nothing is stopping me from wanting to. But I don’t want to treat it as something we should do simply because we’ve reached a certain age or because we’ve been together for a long time.”

Her grandfather studied him.

“Then how do you see it?”

“I want us both to be ready for it. Not just happy to say yes, but ready for what comes after.”

Xiaoran lowered her eyes to her bowl.

She could feel her cheeks warming.

Her grandfather nodded slowly.

“That’s a reasonable answer.”

Then he said, “But don’t take another ten years to decide.”

Xiaoran nearly choked.

“Grandpa!”

Her grandfather laughed.

Yichen smiled.

“I’ll keep that in mind.”

The conversation moved on, eventually.

Her mother asked whether anyone wanted more soup. Her father brought out another dish. Her grandfather began telling a story about his own wedding, which included an unusually long account of how difficult it had been to find a suitable car decades ago.

Xiaoran listened, but her attention kept drifting.

Every now and then, she glanced at Yichen.

He was perfectly normal.

He ate, listened, answered questions, and even laughed at one of her grandfather’s jokes.

How could he be so calm?

He had just told her family he intended to marry her.

Not that she didn’t know.

She knew about the promise ring. She knew he had told her before that he would propose properly, when the time was right. She knew he wasn’t someone who said things casually.

But hearing him say it in front of her grandfather made the possibility feel much closer.

It was no longer a vague someday. It had entered the dining room.

It had been served alongside the fish.

And now her grandfather was asking when.

When the meal ended, Xiaoran helped her mother clear the table.

Her mother watched her place the plates in the sink.

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m not.”

“You’ve been quiet since Grandpa asked Yichen that question.”

Xiaoran rinsed a plate.

“Because he asked it in front of everyone.”

Her mother smiled.

“Would you rather he asked you privately?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because now everyone knows I have to think about it.”

Her mother laughed.

“Darling, you’ve been thinking about it for years.”

Xiaoran nearly dropped the plate.

“Mom.”

“What?”

“Don’t.”

Her mother dried her hands.

“There’s nothing wrong with the question. And there’s nothing wrong if the answer isn’t immediate.”

Xiaoran looked down at the water running over the plate.

Her mother continued, more gently, “Just remember that getting married isn’t a finish line. You don’t have to reach it because everyone else thinks it’s time.”

“I know.”

“And you should be able to tell him what you want, too. Not just wait for him to decide.”

Xiaoran nodded.

Her mother touched her shoulder.

“Besides, I think your grandfather likes him enough to ask.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Grandpa likes everyone who listens to his stories.”

“That’s not true.”

“He likes Yichen because Yichen doesn’t interrupt.”

Her mother laughed.

“That’s also a very good quality.”

Yichen was in the living room with her grandfather.

They were looking at an old photograph album.

Xiaoran came out of the kitchen just in time to hear her grandfather say, “She’s always been stubborn.”

Yichen looked at the photograph.

“I know.”

“She doesn’t admit when she’s tired.”

“I know.”

“And when she wants something, she’ll pretend she doesn’t care until someone notices.”

Yichen smiled.

“I know.”

Xiaoran stopped at the doorway.

Excuse her?

Her grandfather turned a page.

“She’s a good child.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“She is.”

“Don’t let her work too hard.”

“I’ll remind her to rest.”

“And don’t spoil her too much.”

Yichen looked up.

“That might be difficult.”

Her grandfather laughed.

Xiaoran walked into the room.

“What are you two talking about?”

“Nothing,” her grandfather said.

Yichen looked at her.

“Your childhood.”

She immediately approached the sofa.

“Grandpa, don’t show him the embarrassing ones.”

Her grandfather smiled.

“He’s already seen them.”

“Which ones?”

Yichen looked at the album.

“The one where you refused to take off your rain boots indoors.”

“You remember that?”

“Your mother told me.”

Her grandfather laughed.

Xiaoran sat beside Yichen and tried to close the album.

“Enough.”

Yichen caught the edge before she could.

“Wait. I haven’t seen the next page.”

“You’re not supposed to.”

Her grandfather laughed.

“Good. You two can look through the rest together.”

He stood, leaving the album on the coffee table.

As he passed Yichen, he rested a hand on his shoulder.

“Think about what I asked.”

Yichen nodded.

“I will.”

Xiaoran looked between them.

Her grandfather gave her a knowing smile.

Then he walked away.

She waited until he was out of earshot.

Then she turned to Yichen.

“You’re both very suspicious.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Why?”

“Because you’re having private conversations about me.”

“We were discussing your rain boots.”

“That was not the only thing.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“No.”

“What else did he say?”

Yichen closed the album.

“That you’re stubborn.”

“Everyone knows that.”

“That you don’t admit when you’re tired.”

“That’s not true.”

He met her eyes.

She looked back.

Then she sighed.

“Fine.”

He smiled.

“And that you’re a good child.”

Her expression softened.

“Oh.”

Yichen watched her.

“He thinks you hung the moon.”

She looked down at her hands.

“I know.”

They left after tea, for the long drive back to Shanghai. He had training on the fourth.

Her father walked them to the car, carrying the small bag of food her mother had insisted they take.

“Drive carefully,” he said.

“We will,” Yichen answered.

Her father looked at Xiaoran.

“Call when you get home.”

“I will.”

Then he turned back to Yichen.

“About what Grandpa asked.”

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

Not again.

Her father smiled slightly.

“Don’t mind him too much. He likes to ask questions before people are ready to answer.”

Yichen nodded.

“I understand.”

Her father hesitated.

Then he said, “But it’s good that you’re thinking about it.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Dad.”

“What?”

“Can we leave?”

Her father laughed and stepped back.

Yichen opened the passenger door for her.

Before she got in, her father added, “And Xiaoran?”

She turned.

“Yes?”

“Don’t let him do all the thinking. It’s your life too.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I know.”

Her father nodded.

“Good.”

They drove for almost fifteen minutes before either of them spoke.

The evening traffic was manageable. Xiaoran sat with her hands folded over her bag, looking out at the passing shops.

Yichen drove.

Finally, she said, “You were very calm.”

He glanced at her. “Should I have looked frightened?”

“Maybe a little.”

His mouth curved.

“Would that have made you feel better?”

“Possibly.”

He laughed.

She turned toward him.

“Did you know Grandpa was going to ask?”

“No.”

She studied his face.

“Then why didn’t you look surprised?”

“I was surprised.”

“You didn’t look surprised.”

“I don’t think I reacted very much.”

“That’s the problem with you.”

He turned to her.

“What problem?”

“You always look like you’ve already thought about everything.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Not everything.”

She looked down at her left hand.

The promise ring was there, as it always was.

She turned it slightly with her thumb.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“When you said you intend to marry me...”

He waited.

“Did you mean soon?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

Not because he was avoiding the question, but because he seemed to be choosing his words carefully.

“I mean that I don’t see it as some distant possibility anymore.”

She looked at him.

He said, “We’ve graduated. We’ve started building our lives. We know what living together is like. We’ve seen each other when things are easy and when they’re not.”

She smiled.

“Mostly when they’re not.”

“Those count double.”

She looked out of the window again.

“So you have thought about it.”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

He laughed.

“Quite a lot.”

She turned back.

“Really?”

“Xiaoran, I gave you a promise ring.”

She looked at her left hand.

“I know.”

“I didn’t give it to you because I wanted to make a romantic gesture and leave the meaning unclear.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I know. Still.”

He reached over, resting his hand over hers at the center console.

“I want to marry you. That’s not the uncertain part.”

She met his eyes.

“Then what is?”

“The timing. How we want to do it. What we want our lives to look like when we do.”

She was quiet.

He said, “I don’t want you to feel that you have to fit your career around a wedding. And I don’t want us to rush through the things we’re still building just because we know we want to be together.”

She nodded slowly.

That was exactly like him.

He had never treated their relationship as a reason to put their individual lives on hold. When Lanshan had offered her Beijing, the spring before graduation, he had never once asked her to turn it down. He had only asked what she wanted, and waited until she knew.

She knew he would never ask her to give something up to make marriage easier.

But hearing him say it again made her chest feel warm.

“Would you want to get married while we’re still young?” she asked.

He smiled.

“How young?”

She gave him a look.

“Don’t be annoying.”

“I’m asking.”

“Before we’re thirty.”

He considered it.

“Yes.”

She blinked.

“That’s quite specific.”

“You asked.”

She looked down, smiling.

Then she asked, quieter, “Do you ever worry?”

“About what?”

“Getting married. Whether we’ll be good at it.”

He held her gaze.

“Of course.”

“You do?”

“I’m not worried about loving you.”

He said it without hesitation.

“I’m more concerned about whether we’ll keep doing the work properly. Whether we’ll communicate when we’re tired, whether we’ll make room for each other’s changing plans, whether we’ll remember that we’re on the same side when we disagree.”

Xiaoran listened.

He gave her hand another gentle squeeze.

“I think marriage deserves more than being certain that we love each other. It deserves us being willing to keep choosing each other when life becomes inconvenient.”

She was quiet.

Then she smiled.

“That’s a very Yichen answer.”

He laughed.

“Is that good?”

“Yes.”

She rested her hand over his.

“I worry about those things too.”

“I know.”

“But I don’t worry about whether I want to be with you.”

He looked at her.

She met his eyes.

“That’s not the uncertain part for me either.”

His expression softened.

Neither spoke.

Then she asked, “Have you thought about how you’d propose?”

He laughed under his breath.

“Yes.”

Her eyes widened.

“You have?”

“Some things.”

“What things?”

“I’m not telling you.”

She immediately sat up.

“Why?”

“Because then it wouldn’t be a surprise.”

“That’s unfair.”

He laughed.

“You just asked me whether I had thought about it. I answered.”

“That’s not enough information.”

“It’s all you’re getting.”

She stared at him.

Then she leaned back, folding her arms.

“Fine.”

His mouth curved.

A few seconds later, she said, “I still want flowers.”

“I remember.”

“And a pretty dress.”

“I remember that too.”

“And I don’t want you to ask me while I’m wearing an old T-shirt.”

He studied her.

“Noted.”

“Or when I’m eating.”

“That’s a very specific restriction.”

“Because you know me.”

He laughed.

“Anything else?”

She pretended to think.

“Don’t make me wait too long.”

His smile softened.

“I won’t.”

At home, Xiaoran changed into comfortable clothes while Yichen put away the food.

She was in the bedroom when he came in.

He found her sitting on the bed, looking at her ring.

He leaned against the doorframe.

“Thinking?”

“Yes.”

“About Grandpa?”

“About everything.”

He came over and sat beside her.

She held out her left hand.

“Do you remember when you gave me this?”

“Of course.”

“You were so calm.”

“I was nervous.”

She turned to him. “You were not.”

“I checked my pocket every ten minutes for a whole day.”

She looked delighted.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because you were already nervous enough.”

She laughed.

Then she looked at the ring again.

“I remember thinking that it was a promise, but I didn’t know exactly what you were promising.”

He watched her.

“And now?”

“Now I think I understand.”

She turned the ring once.

“It wasn’t a promise that everything would happen immediately. It was a promise that you knew where you wanted us to go.”

He was quiet.

Then he took her hand.

“That’s right.”

That made her grin.

“I think I like that.”

He brought her hand to his lips and kissed the ring.

“I meant it.”

“I know.”

She leaned against him.

They sat together for a while, the bedroom quiet around them.

Then Xiaoran lifted her head.

“Can I tell you something?”

“Anything.”

“I don’t want to get married just because our families are asking.”

“I know.”

“And I don’t want to wait just because we’re supposed to be young and enjoy our lives first.”

He considered her.

She said, “I want to marry you when we’re ready. But I don’t want us to pretend that we don’t know what we want.”

Yichen smiled.

“We don’t have to pretend.”

She looked at him.

“Then we’re agreed?”

“On what?”

“That we’re going to get married someday.”

He gave her a look.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I thought we’d established that.”

She smiled.

“I want to hear it again.”

He took her hand and turned it over, his thumb brushing across her palm.

“I intend to marry you, Lin Xiaoran.”

She felt her cheeks warm.

He continued, his voice quieter.

“Not because your grandfather asked. Not because we’ve been together for six years. And not because it’s the next thing people expect us to do.”

She turned to him.

“Because I want to build a life with you. The ordinary parts, the difficult parts, all of it.”

Her smile became smaller.

More sincere.

“Okay.”

He tilted his head, waiting.

“I want that too.”

He leaned in and kissed her.

It was a slow, familiar kiss, without any urgency. When he pulled away, she stayed close, her forehead resting against his.

Then she whispered, “But I’m still expecting flowers.”

He laughed against her cheek.

“I know.”

“And a pretty dress.”

“I know.”

“And I want you to look nervous.”

He drew back slightly.

“Why?”

“Because I want to know you’re nervous.”

He smiled.

“That’s a difficult request.”

“Try.”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“I’ll do my best.”

Two days later, Xiaoran received a message from her grandfather.

Grandpa (Chief Egg Officer): Did you talk to Yichen?

She smiled at her phone.

Xiaoran: Yes.

Grandpa (Chief Egg Officer): And?

She looked across the flat.

Yichen was at the dining table, reviewing something on his laptop. He glanced up when he noticed her smiling.

She typed.

Xiaoran: We talked.

Grandpa (Chief Egg Officer): Good.

A moment later, another message appeared.

Grandpa (Chief Egg Officer): Don’t rush. But don’t be afraid to be happy either.

Xiaoran read it twice.

Then she put her phone down and walked over to Yichen.

He looked up.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

She stood beside his chair and held out her hand.

He took it.

She looked at the ring on her left hand, then at him.

“Grandpa says we shouldn’t rush.”

Yichen smiled.

“He’s right.”

“He also says we shouldn’t be afraid to be happy.”

He glanced at her.

“He’s right about that too.”

She leaned down and kissed his cheek.

Then she rested her chin on his shoulder, watching the screen of his laptop without really reading anything.

Yichen moved his free hand to her waist.

“Are you going to stand there?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

She stayed where she was.

chapters.desc: Four hours beside a fishing pond, two fathers, no fish, and a great deal of conversation.
chapters.title: The Fathers Have Dinner
chapters.epigraph: “I think they have grown up.”
chapters.content:
The fishing pond, outside the city, had been recommended by Xiaoran’s father, on the Saturday of the Dragon Boat Festival weekend, when both families were home and both mothers had decided their husbands needed to be got out of the house.

It was quiet, apparently peaceful, and supposedly full of fish.

Yichen’s father had agreed to go because he had never fished in his life and had recently been beaten at golf by two clients and a nephew.

Neither man had anticipated spending four hours beside a pond without catching a single fish.

Nor had either expected to talk quite so much.

“Are you sure this is the place?”

Yichen’s father stood beside the car, looking at the entrance.

Xiaoran’s father checked the address on his phone.

“Yes. I’ve been here before.”

“When?”

“A few years ago.”

Yichen’s father glanced at him.

“Recently?”

“Not particularly.”

There was a pause.

Then Yichen’s father laughed.

“All right. Let’s see whether your memory is better than your fishing.”

Xiaoran’s father smiled.

“Don’t worry. I know where the good spots are.”

That confidence lasted approximately seven minutes.

They had rented two fishing rods, bought bait, and found a shaded spot beside the water. Xiaoran’s father arranged the equipment with the familiarity of someone who had done this many times before.

Yichen’s father watched him.

“Do you fish often?”

“Not as much as I used to. Work, family, things like that. You golf.”

“Badly, I’m told.”

“Your son told my daughter, who told her mother, who told me.”

Yichen’s father sighed. “Then it’s true.”

They settled into their chairs.

The rods were cast.

The lines disappeared into the water.

For a while, neither spoke.

Then Xiaoran’s father said, “So, how is Yichen doing?”

Yichen’s father turned slightly.

“He’s well. Busy.”

“Work?”

“Work, training. He’s always had too many things going on.”

Xiaoran’s father nodded.

“He’s like that.”

A small ripple appeared on the water.

Both men looked at it.

Nothing happened.

Yichen’s father picked up his tea.

“He’s always been quite focused.”

“Yes.”

“Even when he was young. If he decided he wanted something, he’d keep going until he got it.”

Xiaoran’s father smiled.

“Sounds familiar.”

They both looked at the pond.

Then Xiaoran’s father said, “Our children are quite similar in that way.”

Yichen’s father laughed.

“That’s true.”

The first hour was mostly about fishing.

The second was mostly about work.

By the beginning of the third, they had discussed their children, their marriages, the changing city, property prices, and the difficulties of finding a good mechanic.

Not a single fish had been caught.

Xiaoran’s father inspected his line.

“Nothing.”

Yichen’s father leaned forward.

“Maybe the bait isn’t right.”

“I used this last time.”

“Perhaps the fish have changed their preferences.”

Xiaoran’s father looked at him.

“Fish don’t change their preferences.”

“People do.”

“Fish aren’t people.”

Yichen’s father laughed.

“Fair enough.”

They adjusted the bait.

Cast again.

Waited.

The pond remained indifferent.

At some point, the conversation turned to the children.

It happened naturally.

Yichen’s father was telling a story about Yichen’s first university basketball season when Xiaoran’s father mentioned the time Xiaoran had called home from Shanghai, in her first month in the fourth-floor studio, because she couldn’t fix a loose cabinet hinge.

“She called you?”

“She called her mother first. Her mother called me.”

Yichen’s father laughed.

“What happened?”

“I told her the boy across the road probably had a screwdriver.”

“Did he?”

“One.”

“Did she fix it?”

“Eventually.”

He smiled to himself.

“She sent me a photograph afterward. The hinge was fixed, but she’d somehow managed to scratch the cabinet.”

Yichen’s father laughed.

“She’s always been independent.”

“Yes. Sometimes too independent.”

He looked at the water.

“She doesn’t like asking for help.”

Yichen’s father nodded.

“Yichen is similar.”

Xiaoran’s father glanced at him.

“Really?”

“Yes. He’ll solve something himself even when someone could easily help him.”

The two men exchanged a look, then both laughed.

“Those two,” Xiaoran’s father said.

Yichen’s father nodded.

“Exactly.”

They fell quiet again.

After a while, Yichen’s father said, “I’m glad they have each other.”

Xiaoran’s father looked at him.

“So am I.”

It was a simple statement.

But neither man treated it lightly.

Around the third hour, Yichen’s father finally caught something.

He sat up immediately.

“Wait.”

Xiaoran’s father looked over.

“What?”

“Something’s pulling.”

He reached for the rod.

The line tightened.

He pulled carefully, then a little harder.

For several seconds, both men watched, then the line went slack.

Yichen’s father stared at the water.

Xiaoran’s father looked at him.

“Did you get it?”

He slowly lowered the rod.

“No.”

“Was it a fish?”

“I think so.”

“Think so?”

Yichen’s father looked at the empty hook.

“It was definitely something.”

Xiaoran’s father laughed.

“Maybe a leaf.”

“It wasn’t a leaf.”

“Then a very small fish.”

Yichen’s father shook his head.

“You can laugh. Let’s see what you catch.”

Xiaoran’s father raised his eyebrows.

“All right.”

He adjusted his bait with exaggerated confidence.

Cast.

Waited.

Nothing.

Yichen’s father smiled into his tea.

“Perhaps the fish have changed their preferences.”

Xiaoran’s father gave him a look.

“Don’t start.”

By the fourth hour, the sun had moved.

Their tea had been refilled twice. The snacks were nearly gone. Both men had become comfortable enough to lean back in their chairs and talk without looking at their rods every few minutes.

Yichen’s father was telling Xiaoran’s father about a business trip from years ago.

Xiaoran’s father interrupted to ask about a particular hotel.

They discovered they had both stayed there, though several years apart.

That led to a discussion about travel, which somehow became a discussion about their wives.

“Your wife still likes arranging flowers?” Yichen’s father asked.

“Very much. Sometimes I think she buys flowers because she wants to rearrange the house.”

Yichen’s father laughed.

“My wife does the same. She’ll come home with something and tell me it’s for the living room.”

“Then three days later, it’s somewhere else.”

“Exactly.”

They laughed.

Xiaoran’s father picked up his cup.

“Women have their own ways of making a home.”

Yichen’s father nodded.

“That’s true.”

Then he looked at him.

“Speaking of homes, how are they finding it? Living together?”

“Well. She calls on Sundays. She says he’s tidier than she expected.”

“He isn’t. He copies her.”

“Then it’s working.”

Yichen’s father looked toward the pond.

“I think they understand something important. They don’t expect the other person to stop building their own life just because they’re together.”

Xiaoran’s father was quiet.

Then he nodded.

“That was something I worried about.”

“Really?”

“Last spring, when she was offered Beijing. I worried she’d go and be too far away. Then I worried she’d stay for the wrong reason.”

Yichen’s father listened.

“But I didn’t want to make her feel that loving someone meant she had to give up an opportunity.”

Yichen’s father nodded slowly.

“I understand. Yichen was very clear about that too. He didn’t want her to make a smaller life for herself just to keep things convenient.”

Xiaoran’s father looked at him.

“Yes. He said something similar to me.”

They sat.

Then Xiaoran’s father smiled.

“I think they have grown up.”

Yichen’s father smiled back.

“They have.”

It was almost time to leave when Xiaoran’s father finally asked the question.

He was looking at his fishing rod, checking the line.

“Have you thought about them getting married?”

Yichen’s father turned.

“Of course.”

“Do you think they’re ready?”

Yichen’s father considered the question.

“I think they know they want to. Whether they’re ready to do it now is something they should decide together.”

Xiaoran’s father nodded.

“That’s what I think too.”

He put the rod down.

“I don’t want to pressure them.”

“Neither do I.”

“But I suppose as fathers, we think about these things.”

Yichen’s father smiled.

“We do.”

Xiaoran’s father looked toward the water.

“She’s my only daughter. I know she’s grown up. I know she has her own home and her own work now. But sometimes I still think about whether she’s eating properly, whether she’s sleeping enough, whether she’s remembered to take an umbrella.”

Yichen’s father laughed.

“That’s familiar. I think about Yichen in much the same way. He’s capable, but that doesn’t mean he doesn’t need someone to look after him.”

Xiaoran’s father nodded.

“Do you think he will?”

Yichen’s father looked at him.

“Look after her?”

“Yes.”

He answered without hesitation.

“I do.”

Xiaoran’s father looked down at his hands.

“He’s always been good to her.”

“I’m glad.”

“And she seems happy.”

Yichen’s father smiled.

“She makes him happy too.”

The two men looked at each other.

There was a comfortable understanding between them now, one that had taken a nod at a flower market, a graduation and four hours beside a pond to develop.

They weren’t discussing their children’s relationship.

They were discussing the people their children had become.

After a moment, Yichen’s father said, “I think we should let them find their own timing.”

Xiaoran’s father nodded.

“Agreed.”

Then he looked at the pond.

“Although I wouldn’t mind if they hurried up a little. Her grandfather asked him at dinner on May Day. In front of everyone.”

Yichen’s father burst out laughing. “He told us. He said he answered properly.”

“He did,” said Xiaoran’s father, and looked almost proud, as if he had answered it himself.

When they finally packed up, the results were disappointing.

Two fishing rods.

One small container of unused bait.

Several empty tea cups.

No fish.

Xiaoran’s father inspected the water one last time.

“Next time, we should come earlier.”

Yichen’s father nodded.

“Perhaps.”

“Or try another pond.”

“That might be better.”

They returned the equipment and walked toward the car park.

At the entrance, Xiaoran’s father checked his phone.

There were two messages from Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Are you still fishing?

Xiaoran: Did you catch anything?

He showed the screen to Yichen’s father.

They looked at each other.

Then Xiaoran’s father typed.

Dad (Water Bureau): No fish.

A moment later, Xiaoran replied.

Xiaoran: FOUR HOURS???

Her father smiled.

Dad (Water Bureau): We had a good conversation.

Yichen’s father glanced at the message.

“She’s going to laugh at us.”

“Probably.”

Then another message arrived.

Xiaoran: What did you even talk about for four hours?

Xiaoran’s father looked at Yichen’s father.

He considered the question.

Then typed:

Dad (Water Bureau): Many things.

That evening, the two families had dinner together.

It had been arranged casually, with both mothers deciding that since their husbands were already spending the afternoon together, everyone might as well meet for dinner.

Xiaoran arrived with Yichen.

She greeted both fathers before sitting down.

“How was fishing?”

Yichen’s father smiled.

“Very good.”

She met his eyes.

“Did you catch anything?”

“No.”

She turned to her father.

“Dad?”

“No.”

She stared.

Yichen sat beside her, trying not to smile.

Xiaoran looked between the two men.

“Then what did you do for four hours?”

Her father picked up his teacup.

“We talked.”

“About what?”

“Work.”

“Then?”

“Family.”

“Then?”

“Life.”

She stared.

“That’s not a conversation. That’s four years of conversation.”

Yichen laughed.

His father smiled.

“Your father and I have a lot in common.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

He was already looking at her, amused.

She leaned toward him.

“Do you think they actually talked about fishing?”

“Probably not much.”

“Do you think they talked about us?”

Something in his face eased.

“Probably.”

She squinted at him.

“What do you think they said?”

“That you’re stubborn.”

She gasped.

“How do you know?”

“Because it’s true.”

She nudged his leg beneath the table.

Across from them, the two fathers had started talking again.

This time, they were discussing whether the pond was worth visiting another day.

Xiaoran watched them.

Her father was smiling. Yichen’s father was listening, occasionally adding something of his own. They looked entirely comfortable together.

She leaned closer to Yichen.

“I think they like each other.”

He glanced at them.

“Yes.”

“More than I expected.”

“They’ve had four hours to get used to each other.”

That made her grin.

Then her grandfather’s question from May Day came back to her.

Marriage. Timing. Families.

She looked at the two fathers again.

Perhaps this was another part of building a life together that she hadn’t thought about before.

Not just two people choosing each other.

Two families gradually becoming familiar.

Her father caught her looking.

“What?”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Nothing.”

He looked at Yichen.

“Take her fishing next time.”

Yichen nodded.

“All right.”

Xiaoran turned.

“Why?”

Her father smiled.

“Because apparently, someone needs to catch a fish.”

Yichen laughed.

“I’ll try.”

She turned to him.

“You’re going to take me fishing?”

“If you want.”

She thought about it, then smiled.

“Only if you promise we’ll actually catch something.”

He looked at her with a small, knowing smile.

“I’ll make no promises.”

She laughed.

Across the table, both fathers continued talking.

And when dinner ended, Yichen’s father asked Xiaoran’s father whether he wanted to go fishing again next weekend.

Xiaoran heard it.

She looked at Yichen.

He looked back.

Neither said anything.

They both knew what the answer would be.

Later that night, in the guest room at his parents’ house, where it was his mother’s turn to have them, Xiaoran received a message from her father.

Dad (Water Bureau): Yichen’s father is a good man.

She smiled at the screen, then another message arrived.

Dad (Water Bureau): We should go fishing again.

She typed back.

Xiaoran: Did you catch anything in the end?

Dad (Water Bureau): No.

Xiaoran: Then why?

His reply came a few seconds later.

Dad (Water Bureau): We still have things to talk about.

Xiaoran looked across the room.

Yichen was sitting on the bed, reading something on his phone.

She walked over and sat beside him.

He looked up.

“What’s wrong?”

She showed him the messages.

He read them, then smiled.

“Sounds like they’re becoming friends.”

She tucked herself against his shoulder.

“Four hours and not one fish.”

“At least they had a good time.”

She nodded.

Then, after a moment, she said, “I think our fathers are going to be difficult.”

He looked down at her.

“Why?”

“Because now they have each other.”

Yichen laughed.

She smiled and tucked herself closer to him.

Downstairs, through the floor, they could hear his father on the phone, saying the word pond.

chapters.desc: They put their photographs on the wall, and argue about whether the first one is straight.
chapters.title: The Frames Go Up
chapters.epigraph: “Yes. It feels like you.”
chapters.content:
The first photograph went up crooked.

Xiaoran noticed it immediately.

Yichen, who was standing on the other side of the living room with her father’s toolbox in his hand, hadn’t noticed anything at all.

“Done,” he said.

She stepped back from the wall.

Then she tilted her head.

“Wait.”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“Something’s wrong.”

He glanced at the frame.

“It’s straight.”

“No, it isn’t.”

He looked again.

It was, by all reasonable measurements, straight.

He checked the level resting on the shelf, then looked at the frame once more.

“Xiaoran.”

“Yichen.”

“It’s straight.”

She walked closer and pointed at the right side.

“That corner is higher.”

He came over, stood beside her, and examined it.

After a moment, he reached for the frame and adjusted it by a fraction.

“Now?”

She stepped back, then moved two steps to the left, then one step to the right.

“Hm.”

He waited.

She met his eyes.

“Better.”

“Good.”

He put the screwdriver back into the toolbox.

Then she said, “But maybe a little lower.”

Yichen closed his eyes.

She smiled.

“Just a little.”

The idea had started three days earlier.

They had been sitting on the floor of their living room, surrounded by photographs Xiaoran had printed from their recent trips and university years.

She wanted to put some of them up.

Not too many. She didn’t want the flat to look like a photography exhibition, and she didn’t want every available wall covered in pictures of them.

Just a few.

The kind of photographs that made a place feel lived in.

Yichen had agreed, and they had spent an evening choosing which ones to print.

There was the photograph from Suzhou: Xiaoran standing beneath the trees in the sunshine, looking away from the camera. There was the one from their sixth anniversary: him in the black shirt, one sleeve higher than the other, taken across a restaurant table on a Monday night.

There was a photograph from university, taken outside the sports center. Yichen was holding a basketball, while Xiaoran stood beside him with an expression that suggested she hadn’t quite understood why she had ended up in the team photograph.

And there were smaller pictures: a night market, a quiet café, a blurry photograph of their hands, and one of them laughing so hard that neither was looking at the camera.

They had chosen frames in different sizes, mostly simple wood and black.

Xiaoran had made a rough arrangement on the floor.

Now, two hours later, they were still arranging the photographs.

“That one should go here.”

Xiaoran stood in the middle of the living room, holding a frame against the wall.

Yichen looked up from the toolbox.

“Which one?”

“The Suzhou photograph.”

He came over.

She held it against a space beside the bookshelf.

“Here?”

He studied the wall.

“Maybe slightly to the left.”

She moved it.

“Here?”

“Yes.”

She looked at it, then at the other frames on the floor.

“Wait. What if we put the anniversary one beside it?”

Yichen glanced at the photograph.

“The black shirt?”

“Yes.”

“That one’s just me.”

She considered it.

“Is that bad?”

“No.”

“Then?”

He laughed under his breath.

“Nothing.”

“You’re making fun of me.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He took the frame from her and held it against the wall.

“Like this?”

She stepped back.

The two photographs sat beside each other, one slightly larger than the other.

She looked at them.

Then she smiled.

“Yes.”

Yichen nodded.

“All right.”

He marked the position.

She smiled and handed him the next frame.

The university photograph was the one that took the longest.

It was a little faded, and the colors weren’t quite as sharp as the newer prints.

Yichen was wearing his university basketball jersey. His hair was shorter, his expression younger, and he had one arm loosely around Xiaoran’s shoulders.

She was smiling at the camera.

Neither of them looked posed.

It had been taken by Jiayi after a match, when everyone was still sweaty and tired and the team had been making their way out of the sports center.

Xiaoran held the frame for a while.

“Do you remember this?”

Yichen looked at it.

“Yes.”

“You were annoyed.”

“We lost by two points.”

“Exactly.”

He smiled.

“You were trying to cheer me up.”

“I was.”

“You told me it was fine because the team had played well.”

“That’s true.”

“Then you bought me noodles.”

She turned to him.

“Because you were hungry.”

“I was.”

She smiled at the photograph.

“I liked that day.”

Yichen took the frame from her and examined it.

“So did I.”

He placed it against the wall, beside the newer photographs.

Xiaoran looked at the arrangement.

It was strange, seeing their university years displayed beside the life they had now.

The younger versions of themselves seemed to belong to another period, even though it hadn’t been that long ago.

They had been students then.

They had met between classes, shared drinks at the vending machine, spent long afternoons at the library, and arranged their days around lectures and basketball training.

Now there were work schedules, grocery lists, rent payments, and a shared calendar on the refrigerator.

They still had the same photographs.

But the life around them had changed.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you think we should put one of our first photographs up?”

He looked at her.

“Which one?”

“The really old one.”

He understood immediately.

Their first proper photograph together.

It had been taken the winter of their first anniversary, outside the school gate, both of them in uniform and too many scarves. Xiaoran had been smiling too brightly, and Yichen had been looking at her rather than the camera.

The print was small and slightly blurry.

He glanced at the empty space near the hallway.

“That one?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He considered it.

“Then it should go somewhere we can see it when we leave.”

“Why?”

“So we don’t forget where we started.”

She held his gaze.

He said it, already reaching for the next frame.

But she stayed still longer.

The drilling was interrupted by a phone call.

Yichen answered while Xiaoran sorted the remaining photographs.

It was Fang Ze.

“Are you home?”

“Yes.”

“Good. I need to ask you something.”

“What?”

“Do you still have my charger?”

Yichen looked toward the dining table.

“I think so.”

“Can I come over?”

“Later.”

“Why later?”

“We’re doing something.”

Fang Ze paused.

“What?”

Yichen glanced at the wall.

“Putting up photographs.”

There was a beat of silence.

Then Fang Ze said, “Photographs?”

“Yes.”

“Of you and Xiaoran?”

“Some.”

Another pause.

“How many?”

Yichen looked at the frames on the floor.

“Quite a few.”

Fang Ze laughed.

“You’re making a shrine.”

Yichen ended the call.

Xiaoran looked up.

“Who was that?”

“Fang Ze.”

“What did he want?”

“His charger.”

“Is he coming?”

“Later.”

She smiled.

“Good. We can ask him whether the frames are straight.”

Yichen looked at her.

“No.”

She laughed.

By late afternoon, the wall was almost finished.

The frames were arranged in a loose collection, not perfectly symmetrical but balanced enough to look intentional.

Xiaoran stood in front of it with her hands on her hips.

Yichen came to stand beside her.

“Finished?”

She looked at the wall, then at the remaining photograph on the table.

“One more.”

He followed her gaze.

It was a small photograph from their recent trip. They were sitting at a café, sharing a dessert. Xiaoran was laughing, and Yichen was looking at her with a smile that was almost impossible to miss.

She picked it up.

“Where should this go?”

Yichen examined the wall.

“There.”

He pointed to a small space near the center.

She held it up.

“Here?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the arrangement, then shook her head.

“No.”

He lowered his hand.

“Why?”

“It should go near the Suzhou one.”

“All right.”

She moved it, then stepped back.

“Maybe here.”

He waited.

She tilted her head, then moved it slightly.

He picked up the final frame.

“Where do you want this one?”

She pointed to the space beside the bookshelf.

“Here.”

He held it up.

She stepped back and examined it.

“Little higher.”

He adjusted it.

“Now?”

“Perfect.”

Fang Ze arrived twenty minutes later.

He walked into the living room carrying a bag of snacks and stopped immediately.

“Oh.”

Yichen looked over.

“What?”

Fang Ze surveyed the wall.

Then he looked at the two of them.

“You really did it.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Do you like it?”

Fang Ze walked closer.

There were photographs of gardens, trips, university days, and the two of them at different ages.

He stopped at the university basketball photograph.

“Is this the one after we lost to East Campus?”

Yichen nodded.

Fang Ze laughed.

“You look miserable.”

“I wasn’t.”

“You were.”

Xiaoran pointed at the photograph.

“That’s what I said.”

Fang Ze moved to the next frame, then another.

He looked at the anniversary photograph.

“Ah. The black shirt.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“You remember?”

“Of course. Xiaoran showed it to every partner at the Herons’ Christmas dinner.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“She showed everyone.”

Xiaoran shrugged.

“It was a good photograph.”

Fang Ze nodded.

“It is.”

He looked at the small first photograph near the hallway.

Then he turned toward them.

“That’s the oldest one, right?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yes.”

Fang Ze studied it.

“You both look so young.”

“We were young,” Yichen said.

Fang Ze smiled.

Then he stepped back and looked at the entire wall.

“Actually, this is nice.”

Xiaoran brightened.

“Really?”

“Yes. It feels like you.”

Yichen looked at him.

“What does that mean?”

Fang Ze shrugged.

“Not too organized. But everything has a place.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“That’s a compliment.”

“It is.”

Fang Ze walked toward the dining table.

“Where’s my charger?”

Yichen pointed to the counter.

Fang Ze picked it up.

Then he looked back at the wall.

“By the way, that one is crooked.”

Xiaoran immediately turned.

“Which one?”

Fang Ze pointed.

Yichen looked at it.

It was the first photograph they had put up.

The one Xiaoran had already made him adjust twice.

She squinted at him.

“Don’t.”

Fang Ze laughed.

After Fang Ze left, Xiaoran stood in front of the wall again.

The afternoon light was beginning to fade.

She looked at each photograph slowly.

The old one. The university one.

The anniversary picture.

Suzhou.

The night market.

The little moments that might have seemed insignificant to anyone else.

She was quiet for so long that Yichen eventually came to stand behind her.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

He rested his hands lightly at her waist.

“You’re thinking again.”

She leaned back against him.

“I like it.”

“The wall?”

“Yes.”

He looked at it over her shoulder.

“Good.”

She pointed toward the first photograph.

“That’s where we started.”

Then toward the university picture.

“That’s when we were figuring things out.”

Her finger moved to the anniversary photograph.

“That’s when we knew each other so well that we didn’t need to explain everything.”

Then she pointed to the Suzhou photograph.

“And that’s now.”

Yichen looked at the wall.

She turned her head slightly.

“Do you think we’ll keep adding to it?”

“Probably.”

“What do you think we’ll put up next?”

He considered the question.

“Whatever you take a photograph of.”

That made her grin.

“That’s not very imaginative.”

“I’m sure you’ll have ideas.”

She laughed.

Then she looked at the empty space at the end of the arrangement.

“There’s still room.”

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Yes.”

“For future photographs.”

“Yes.”

She turned around in his arms.

“Maybe one from our wedding.”

His expression changed slightly.

Not surprise, exactly.

More like the quiet recognition of something they had already discussed, now appearing in a more tangible form.

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“That would be nice.”

“And maybe one from a trip after that.”

“All right.”

“And one when we’re old.”

He met her eyes.

“Old?”

“Very old.”

“How old?”

“Old enough that we complain about our backs.”

He laughed.

“That sounds likely.”

She smiled.

“And maybe we’ll have so many photographs that we’ll need another wall.”

Yichen looked around the living room.

“Then we’ll find another wall.”

She seemed satisfied with that answer.

He brushed a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“Anything else?”

She shook her head.

Then, after a moment, she said, “I think we should take a photograph of this wall.”

Something in his face eased.

“Now?”

“Yes.”

She reached for her phone.

Yichen stepped beside her, and she took a picture of the frames.

Then she looked at the screen.

“Wait. You’re not in it.”

She turned the camera around.

He moved closer.

She leaned against him, lifting the phone.

The photograph captured the two of them in front of the wall, surrounded by the moments they had chosen to keep.

Xiaoran looked at it.

Then she smiled.

“Perfect.”

Yichen glanced at the screen and, for once, didn’t ask her to delete it.

She saved it.

A moment later, she took his hand and walked toward the kitchen.

chapters.desc: The first lease renewal with her name on it, and the first time she asks him not to choose for her.
chapters.title: The Renewal, Again
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll ask first. Then I’ll tell you what I think is best.”
chapters.content:
The reminder appeared on Xiaoran’s phone at 9:17 on a Tuesday morning.

Lease renewal — decision required within 14 days.

She read it once while brushing her teeth, dismissed it, and went back to making breakfast.

She read it again over coffee.

Then she opened the rental agreement.

And finally, she looked across the kitchen at Yichen.

“Yichen.”

He was standing by the counter, buttoning the cuff of his shirt.

“Hm?”

“Our lease is expiring.”

He looked up.

“I know.”

“You know?”

“The renewal notice came last week.”

“And you didn’t tell me?”

“I thought we’d discuss it this weekend.”

She looked at the agreement on her phone.

“Well, we should probably discuss it now.”

He finished fastening his cuff.

“All right.”

She turned the screen toward him.

“The landlord is offering another year. The rent has increased by four percent.”

“I saw.”

“Four percent.”

“Yes.”

“That’s quite a lot.”

He came over and looked at the screen.

“We can negotiate.”

“Maybe.”

He read through the terms, then handed the phone back.

“I’ll speak to the landlord.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Why? About the rent.”

“I can speak to him.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you going to?”

Yichen looked at her, a little puzzled.

“Because I was going to ask whether he’d consider keeping the current rate.”

She nodded slowly.

“Okay.”

He picked up his coffee.

“I’ll call him later.”

Xiaoran didn’t say anything.

But something about the conversation stayed with her.

Not the rent.

Not the landlord.

It was the way he’d said it so naturally, as if the decision to handle the renewal had already become his responsibility.

It would be the first renewal with her name on it.

He had renewed that lease every autumn since their first year of university, three times on his own, the way he did everything administrative: quickly, correctly, alone. Last November, when she moved in, he had handled it again. He had added her name, spoken to the landlord, checked the clauses and arranged the transfer, and Xiaoran had been happy to let him. She had been carrying boxes. She had been four months into a new job.

It hadn’t been an argument. She hadn’t felt bothered.

He was efficient. He was responsible. And he never made her feel as if she couldn’t do something herself.

But somewhere along the way, the arrangement had become automatic.

Yichen handled the flat’s administrative matters.

Xiaoran handled the interior, the household purchases, and most of the things that made the place feel like theirs.

They had never explicitly divided those responsibilities.

They had fallen into them.

And now, as she sat at the dining table reading the renewal agreement, she realized she didn’t want to fall into the same pattern again.

Not because she didn’t trust him.

Because she wanted to be part of the decision before it was made.

That evening, Yichen returned home to find Xiaoran sitting on the sofa with her laptop open.

A spreadsheet was on the screen.

He put his keys down.

“What’s this?”

“The flat.”

He came closer.

She had made a comparison between their current rent and several nearby listings. There were columns for floor area, location, commute time, deposit, maintenance fees, and lease terms.

Yichen looked at it.

“You’ve been busy.”

“I looked at a few places during lunch.”

He pulled out the chair beside her.

“Are you thinking of moving?”

“I’m thinking about whether we should renew.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

She turned her laptop slightly toward him.

“I found three flats that are worth considering. One is cheaper, but farther from the station. Another is more expensive, but the landlord includes maintenance. The third is similar to ours, but has a better study area.”

He read through the comparison.

“You’ve checked the commute?”

“Yes.”

“And the deposits?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She watched him.

He looked genuinely interested, asking questions about the listings and pointing out a few things she hadn’t considered.

It was the kind of discussion she had wanted.

But then he said, “I’ll arrange viewings for the two that look promising.”

Xiaoran’s fingers stopped moving on the keyboard.

“Yichen.”

“What?”

She took a breath.

“Don’t choose for me.”

The words came out more firmly than she had intended.

He went still.

The only sound was the faint hum of the air conditioner.

Then he closed the laptop slightly.

“All right.”

She met his eyes.

He didn’t look angry. He didn’t even look defensive.

But his expression had changed.

“What did I do?” he asked.

She rubbed her thumb against the edge of the laptop.

“You keep saying you’ll arrange things. You’ll speak to the landlord. You’ll decide which places are worth viewing. You’ll handle the paperwork.”

“I was trying to help.”

“I know.”

“Then—”

“I know you’re trying to help, Yichen.”

She looked at him properly.

“That’s why it’s difficult to explain. You’re not doing anything wrong. You’re not forcing me to agree with you. But sometimes you move so quickly from noticing a problem to solving it that I don’t get the chance to decide what I want.”

He was quiet.

She continued, more carefully this time.

“I don’t want you to stop helping me. I don’t want us to suddenly divide everything down the middle just to prove that we’re independent. But this is our home. I want to be involved in deciding what happens to it.”

Yichen listened without interrupting.

She looked down at the spreadsheet.

“And I don’t want to be the person who gets presented with two options after you’ve already decided which one is better.”

He nodded slowly.

“That’s fair.”

She turned to him.

He leaned back slightly, considering what she’d said.

“I think I’ve been treating the renewal as an administrative task.”

“It is an administrative task.”

“But not only that.”

She shook her head.

“It’s also where we live. It’s our money, our routines, our commute, our plans. And if we decide to move, I want it to be because we both want to.”

He looked at her.

Then he said, “I’m sorry.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

“You don’t have to apologize for wanting to help.”

“I should apologize for assuming I knew how you wanted me to help.”

She didn’t answer immediately.

He reached for her hand.

“I don’t want you to feel like a guest in a home we share.”

She squeezed his fingers.

“I don’t.”

“Good.”

He looked at the laptop.

“But I can see how I might have made you feel that way without realizing it.”

She leaned back against the sofa.

“I think I’m still getting used to living together.”

He smiled.

“A year next week.”

“I know. But sometimes I realize there are things we’ve never actually discussed. We just do them because one of us started doing them first.”

“That’s true.”

“And then it becomes a habit.”

He nodded.

“Like me handling the lease.”

“Exactly.”

He met her eyes.

“Would you rather we look at the options together first, then decide whether to renew?”

“Yes.”

“Then that’s what we’ll do.”

She smiled a little.

“And we’ll both speak to the landlord.”

“All right.”

“Not just you.”

“All right.”

She studied him.

“You’re agreeing very quickly.”

“I’m learning.”

She laughed.

He brought her hand to his lips and kissed her knuckles.

“Thank you for telling me.”

They spent the next two evenings looking at flats.

Not because they had decided to move, but because they wanted to know what their options were.

They visited the first one on Thursday.

It had a beautiful living room and a kitchen that Xiaoran immediately liked, but the bedroom was smaller than the photographs suggested.

Yichen noticed her measuring the space with her eyes.

“Too small?”

“Maybe.”

He looked around.

“We could fit the wardrobe here.”

“But then the bed would have to go closer to the window.”

“Would that bother you?”

She considered it.

“A little.”

They moved to the second flat.

The study area was excellent, but the building was older and the lift was unreliable.

Xiaoran looked at the narrow staircase.

Yichen glanced at her.

“Remember the water bottles?”

She laughed.

“Don’t remind me.”

That got a smile out of him.

They didn’t choose either.

On Saturday, they visited the third place.

It was a little more expensive than their flat, but the layout was sensible. The kitchen had enough counter space, the living room received good afternoon light, and the study was twice the size of theirs, big enough for two desks.

Xiaoran stood in the doorway of the study.

“This is nice.”

Yichen came up beside her.

“It is.”

She walked inside and looked at the window.

“I could put my desk here.”

“And I could use the other side.”

She turned toward him.

“You never work in our study. You work at the dining table.”

“Our study has my trophies in it. They watch me.”

She turned back to the window.

She imagined their desks facing each other, two different work schedules, coffee cups, books, cables, and the occasional disagreement about whose documents were taking up too much space.

It felt possible.

But she wasn’t ready to decide.

“Let’s think about it,” she said.

Yichen nodded.

“Let’s.”

He didn’t ask her to choose that afternoon.

On Sunday morning, they sat at the dining table with their laptops.

They had made a list of what mattered most.

Location. Cost. Space. Commute. Lease flexibility.

Yichen had added one more item.

“Future plans.”

Xiaoran looked at it.

“What does that mean?”

“Whether we expect our work arrangements to change in the next year.”

She nodded.

“That’s important.”

He turned his laptop toward her.

“I’ve been thinking about it. My work may require more travel next season. Your schedule could change too.”

“And mine, if Gao Yan gives me the Hangzhou account.”

“Exactly.”

She looked at the comparison again.

Their current flat was still the most practical option.

It was familiar, close to both their regular routes, and they had already made it feel like home. The rent increase was irritating, but not unreasonable compared with the alternatives.

Xiaoran leaned back.

“I think I want to renew.”

Yichen looked at her.

“You’re sure?”

“Yes. At least for another year.”

He nodded.

“I agree.”

That made her grin.

“But I want to negotiate the rent.”

“Of course.”

“And I want to ask for the air-conditioning maintenance to be included.”

“Good point.”

“And the water heater has been making that noise.”

“I’ll add that.”

She held his gaze.

He corrected himself.

“We’ll add that.”

“Better.”

He closed his laptop.

“Do you want to contact the landlord?”

She thought about it.

“Let’s do it together.”

He nodded.

The call took twenty minutes, most of them spent on the water heater.

Xiaoran led the conversation.

She introduced herself, confirmed the renewal terms, and explained that they were interested in staying but wanted to discuss the rent increase and maintenance arrangements.

Yichen sat beside her, listening.

When the landlord asked about the water heater, Yichen leaned closer and reminded her of the issue they’d noticed last month.

She repeated it.

The landlord agreed to arrange an inspection before the new lease began and offered a smaller rent increase than the original proposal.

It wasn’t everything they had asked for.

But it was reasonable.

When the call ended, Xiaoran closed her laptop.

“Well.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Well?”

“We’re staying.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Looks like it.”

She leaned back in her chair, looking around the flat.

The photographs on the wall caught her attention.

Their university years. Suzhou. The anniversary photograph. The small, slightly blurry picture from when they were teenagers.

She looked at the familiar sofa, the dining table, the mugs they had bought together, and the small collection of things that had accumulated over time.

“I like this place,” she said.

Yichen followed her gaze.

“So do I.”

She turned toward him.

“Next year, we should discuss the renewal earlier.”

“Agreed.”

“And maybe we should make a list of household things we each handle.”

He considered it.

“Would that make things easier?”

“Maybe. But I don’t want it to become a scorecard.”

“It won’t.”

“And if one of us is busy, the other can help.”

“Of course.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He found her hand on the table.

“Anything else?”

She pretended to think.

“Don’t choose for me.”

“I’ll remember.”

She tilted her head.

“Even when you think you know what’s best?”

He considered this honestly. “I’ll ask first. Then I’ll tell you what I think is best.”

She laughed.

That evening, Xiaoran was putting away the renewal documents when she noticed something.

Yichen had placed the signed agreement in their shared folder, but he had also added a small note to the household calendar.

Lease renewed — both agreed.

She stared at it.

Then she turned toward him.

“Yichen?”

He was on the sofa, reading.

“Hm?”

“Why did you write ‘both agreed’?”

He looked up.

“So that next November I remember.”

Her mouth tipped up.

He put his book down.

“Is something wrong?”

“No.”

She walked over and sat beside him, tucking her feet beneath her.

“I just like that.”

He looked at the calendar on the coffee table, then at her.

“Good.”

She let her head drop onto his shoulder.

After a moment, he said, “For what it’s worth, I never wanted you to feel like I was making decisions for both of us.”

“I know.”

“I tend to handle things quickly. Sometimes I forget that deciding something together takes longer.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Sometimes.”

He glanced down at her.

“I’ll try to ask before I start arranging everything.”

“That would be nice.”

“And you can tell me when I forget.”

She lifted her head.

“I just did.”

He laughed.

“Yes. You did.”

She leaned forward and kissed him.

Then she settled against him again.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lin Xiaoran is loud, dramatic, cries easily, and can get lost walking somewhere she’s been twenty times. Zhou Yichen is calm, patient, and very hard not to notice. He fell for her almost right away, and he has been spoiling her ever since.

From their last years of high school to university in Shanghai, The Softest Kind of Love follows the two of them through first dates and bad fights, exams and families, and the slow work of growing up without growing apart.

Main chapters tell the story in order. Side stories are small moments you can read whenever you like.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
This is a gentle romance, but a few chapters include:

• A crude, sexualized remark made about Xiaoran by a classmate (The One Time Zhou Yichen Lost His Temper)

• A physical fight between students (Xiaoran, Don’t Fight)

• A sports injury with some blood and a hospital visit (Don’t Scare Me Like That Again, Don’t Limp. I’ll Cry Again.)

• Hurtful rumors and a brief break-up scare (Should We Break Up?)

• Dieting and skipped meals after hurtful online comments (The Day Zhou Yichen Found Out Lin Xiaoran Was Dieting)

• Mild language and lots of crying

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
I wanted to write the kind of love story I like to read before bed: no cheating, no misunderstanding that drags on for twenty chapters, nobody secretly dying. Just two people who like each other a lot and keep choosing each other, even on the days one of them is being impossible.

Xiaoran is a bit of everyone who has cried over a math test or sulked because their boyfriend was too popular. Yichen is the person a lot of us wish we had, or wish we were—someone who notices when you’ve gone quiet.

Some chapters are silly. Some are soft. A couple of them made me cry a little while writing. Thank you for reading any of them at all.

— 甜慕
